## The Complete Course of Patrology, or Universal Library

The complete, integral, uniform, convenient, economical universal library of all the holy Fathers, Doctors, and ecclesiastical writers who flourished from the apostolic age to the time of Innocent III; a chronological reissue of all the monuments of Catholic tradition that have survived through the first twelve centuries of the Church, based on the most accurate editions, carefully collated with one another and with several manuscript codices, and corrected with the utmost diligence; continuously illustrated with dissertations, commentaries, and variant readings; enlarged with all works discovered after the extensive editions produced during the last three centuries; furnished with particular analytical indexes following each volume and each author of any importance; adorned with chapters properly arranged within the text itself, as well as with titles distinguishing the upper margin of each page and indicating its subject matter; expanded with works both doubtful and apocryphal, and with works possessing some authority in relation to ecclesiastical tradition; enriched with two general indexes: one of subjects, by consulting which whatever each Father has written on any theme may be seen at a glance; the other of Sacred Scripture, from which it may readily be learned which Fathers commented on the individual texts of the individual books of Scripture and in which passages of their works. An edition of the greatest accuracy, easily preferable to all others if one considers the clarity of the type, the quality of the paper, the integrity of the text, the perfection of the correction, the variety and number of the works reprinted, the extremely convenient format of the volumes and its consistent similarity throughout the entire work, the low price, and above all this collection, unique, methodical, and chronological, of six hundred fragments and minor works previously scattered here and there but now gathered for the first time in our library from works relating to every age, place, language, and form.

## Second Series

In which appear the Fathers, Doctors, and ecclesiastical writers of the Latin Church from Gregory the Great to Innocent III. Edited by J.-P. Migne, publisher of the Universal Library of the Clergy, or of the Complete Courses in the several branches of ecclesiastical learning.

Patrology was printed in two editions, one Latin and the other Greek-Latin. The Latin edition is sold for 1,200 francs; the Greek-Latin edition for 1,300. The purely Latin edition embraces all authors, both Western and Eastern; the latter, however, are supplied in it only in Latin translation.

# In the Year of the Lord 1099. Blessed Urban II, Pope

## Life of Blessed Urban II, by Dom Theodoric Ruinart

*(Posthumous works of Dom Jean Mabillon and Dom Thierri Ruinart, vol. III, beginning.)*

[Col. 0009]

## Notice

As early as the year 1706 these Acts of Pope Urban II had been prepared for the press—surely worthy to be brought to light, had the premature death of their author not deprived scholars of so exquisite a work. I confess that it was painful to see the precious remains of that great man struggling in the dust of a museum with cockroaches and moths, especially since, from many letters written both to Mabillon and to the author himself, I knew that this work had often been desired, long awaited, and earnestly requested. At last I now satisfy the wishes of so many scholars, and I do not doubt that this laborious collection will seem to match the other works of the same author and to deserve the same applause. Here, certainly, the reader will find the whole of Ruinart. The same labor, the same zeal in investigating ancient monuments, the same acumen in judging them, the same industry in explaining and at the same time arranging them: even if he had not prefixed his name to the codex, the character of the work itself would have disclosed its author.

Even without his own statement, it is not difficult to conjecture what causes induced him to collect the acts of Urban rather than those of some other Roman pontiff. One of them seems to have been that this supreme pontiff, endowed with outstanding gifts of intellect and character, not only adorned the See of Blessed Peter above many others both by the number of his achievements and by the holiness of his life, but was also, like the author, professedly Benedictine. By a natural inclination we are drawn toward those who, having followed the same way of life, have deserved well of it and added glory and honor to it. The other reason was undoubtedly that Urban had been born in the territory of the Church of Reims, perhaps even in the city of Reims itself; while the author, himself a native of Reims, whom would he have preferred to honor over a fellow citizen, especially one established in the supreme dignity of the Church?

He had divided this work into three parts. The first described Urban’s life, or acts; the second contained letters, diplomas, privileges, canons, and other documents of this kind; the third included various monuments drawn from published books or recovered from chartularies, most of them collated with ancient codices or even with originals, which were to serve as evidence.

Here we give the first part in full, and from the third everything that the author cites in the *Acts* and promises to provide. We have left the second part for Dom Simon Mopinot, successor to Dom Pierre Coustant, to publish someday, lest the same materials, published a second time, should both cause weariness and burden learned readers with excessive expense.

[Col. 0009]

# Life of Blessed Urban II, Pope

## I. Urban’s Name, Homeland, and Parents

[Col. 0009A]

No one doubts that Pope Urban, the second of that name, was called Odo before his pontificate—or, as others commonly write, Oddo, Otto, or Otho—and that he came from a noble family in Gaul and was educated in the Church of Reims. It is not, however, equally well established among authors where he was born. Some wish him to have been born at Reims or in some village of the district of Reims, around the year 1042; others at Châtillon, a sufficiently famous town above the Marne, which, although not far from the city of Reims and formerly—and especially at the time when Urban came into the world—belonging to the dominion of the Church of Reims, was nevertheless situated in the [Col. 0010A] diocese of Soissons.

Cardinal Pandulf, who wrote the lives of the popes under Gelasius II, expressly asserts that he was a Gaul born in the town of Châtillon, which lies above the River Marne in the archbishopric of Reims. Alberic agrees in his Chronicle, and this is the more common opinion among authors, especially recent ones. Hence, since all agree that Urban came from a noble family, some have considered it entirely certain and established that this pontiff descended from the noble family of the lords of Châtillon in French Champagne. Aubertus Miraeus, in chapter 115 of *The Ecclesiastical Notices of Belgium*, and Andreas Chesnius, in his *Particular History of the House of Châtillon*, regarded this as so certain [Col. 0011A] that they assigned Urban a place in the genealogical tree of the Châtillon family, where he is said to have been the son of Milo and the brother of Guido Manasses and another Milo.

Alberic, however, opposes this opinion. Although he, like the others, wrote that Urban was born in the town of Châtillon above the Marne, he nevertheless asserts, on the authority of Hugh and Guido, whom he cites, that Urban was the son of the lord of Lagery. He then adds concerning the same family relationship:

“He—the same Urban—had another brother, Ralph, the father of Gerard; Gerard’s son, another Gerard, begot Odo, the father of Giles of Lagery, a monk of Reims. Giles’s sister Hersendis was the mother of Baldulseus; or, as the manuscript codex reads, of Baldwin (*Balduinus*), monk of Igny.”

Certainly, in the obituary book of the monastery of Molesme in Champagne, on the Nones of June, Eucherius and his wife Isabel are commemorated as the father and mother of Pope Urban; according to the same record, we are to celebrate their anniversary solemnly. In that same obituary book, on the third day before the Kalends of August, Urban is said to have belonged to the congregation of that place—that is, to have shared in its prayers and other pious works.

But whether that Eucherius was the lord of Lagery, a village in the diocese of Reims, or Milo, lord of Châtillon, was Urban’s father, it must be acknowledged that Urban was a foster-son of the province of Reims. Indeed, since Lagery, whose lords—as we shall say below—perhaps arose from the lords of Châtillon, lies not far from the city of Reims, and since the fortress of Châtillon itself, although situated outside the diocese, nevertheless belonged to the Church of Reims, and its clients and vicars were the lords of Châtillon, both families generally resided at Reims, chiefly because they were soldiers of the Church of Reims; consequently Urban could have been born in the city of Reims from either family.

This is certainly suggested by Orderic Vitalis in Book VIII of his *Ecclesiastical History*, where he expressly calls him a citizen of Reims. “Odo,” he says, “a Gaul by birth, distinguished by nobility and gentleness, a citizen of Reims,” and so forth.

Nor should anyone think that Orderic said this rashly. For, besides the fact that Orderic is more accurate and careful than other writers, he could have learned this very point from his teacher John, who was born at Reims and well informed about these matters. John had been a scholastic of the Church of Reims, where he had undoubtedly been educated together with Odo, and later became a monk of Saint-Evroul, governing that monastery’s schools in Orderic’s time.

Guibert, abbot of Nogent, an accurate author himself and close in time and place, does not depart far from this opinion. He writes that Urban, descended from a distinguished stock in France, came from the territory and clergy of Reims and, after passing through many stages, finally reached the summit of the supreme pontificate.

From this it is clear how broadly the words of Abbot Guido are to be understood. In volume I of Labbe’s *Library*, chapter 8 of his history of the abbots of Saint-Germain of Auxerre, Guido wrote that Urban had been born and educated in the territory of the city of Auxerre. His authority in this matter should not, indeed, be very great, since he lived at the end of the thirteenth century. But another recent author from the same region, G. Viole, departed still further from the truth in his *Life of Saint Germanus of Auxerre*. On the basis of certain unknown false or misunderstood monuments, he wrote that Urban’s ancestors had founded the monastery of Régniac in the diocese of Auxerre. This claim must be rejected on the sole ground that the monastery of Régniac, of the Cistercian order, was built long after Urban’s death.

Finally, there is no need to linger over refuting those who said that Odo, Urban’s successor in the bishopric of Ostia, was his nephew, since they prove this by no argument apart from the similarity of their names. Certainly Baldricus does not say so. In the poems printed in volume IV of Chesnius’s *French History*, he praises this Odo because he shared with Urban the name Odo, had professed the same monastic life, held the same see, and was destined finally to possess the same dignity—he was predicting that the latter would become pope. Baldricus would not have omitted their kinship had any existed between them. Nor does Guibert say so in Book II of *The Sacred Expedition*, where he mentions this other Odo.

Urban’s parents, whoever they may ultimately have been, were lords of the village of Bainson, situated at the foot of the mountain on which the town of Châtillon stands. Hence it may perhaps reasonably be suspected that, although they were lords of the village of Lagery, they nevertheless descended from the line of the lords of Châtillon, as I said above: for not only Bainson but also Lagery lies not far from the town of Châtillon, and Urban is commonly called a man of Châtillon by the consensus of both ancient and recent authors.

That Bainson belonged to Urban’s parents is attested by Urban himself in a diploma concerning the priory of that place, which he states had been endowed from the property of his parents. For this place, which Theobald, bishop of Soissons, had first assigned to his Church, and which later, through the agency of another Theobald, count palatine of Troyes, had—as Chesnius reports—been subjected to the monastery of Coincy under an annual rent of twenty solidi payable to the canons of the Church of Soissons, was confirmed by the pontiff to the Cluniacs, not only by the apostolic authority with which he was endowed, but also because this rent had been established with the consent of his father, and because that place came to him by right of his parents.

The priory of Bainson still exists today. In the general catalogue of the benefices of the Cluniac order it is called Saint Peter of Buissono, in the diocese of Soissons, in Brie—or rather in Champagne—near Châtillon above the Marne.

## II. Urban Educated at Reims under Saint Bruno

[Col. 0012D]

Everyone unanimously acknowledges that Odo was educated in the Church of Reims, which was then a nursery of great men in Gaul, and indeed under the master Bruno, whose fame was celebrated throughout Europe in those days and was later to become much more illustrious when he became the first founder and father of the Carthusian order.

The commonly circulated authors everywhere transmit the tradition that Odo was Bruno’s pupil, and no one can rightly deny it, since it is equally certain, with no dissent, both that Bruno presided over the schools of the Church of Reims at that time and that Urban had been nurtured from childhood in that same Church.

An ancient author expressly affirms both points in the little work *On the Institutions of the Carthusians*, edited by Labbe in volume I of the *New Library* from an old Reims codex. He also adds that Bruno went to Rome at Urban’s insistence, since he had once been Urban’s teacher. This little work is found in a manuscript codex of the Charterhouse of Portes, written approximately forty years after Bruno’s death.

Someone may perhaps set against this the opinion of those who say that Bruno died at the age of fifty in the year 1101. For if this is admitted, then, since Urban died in the twelfth year of his pontificate, and indeed before Bruno, Urban must be said to have been older than Bruno, or at least his equal in age, and therefore unable to have been educated under Bruno’s direction. I shall easily demonstrate by clear arguments that this is false.

Before determining anything about Bruno’s age, however, two points must be established. First, almost all writers, both ancient and recent, unanimously called Bruno Urban’s teacher. Second, several other disciples of Bruno were raised to the episcopate while Urban was still alive, and the same could therefore have happened to Urban as to them.

It is certainly established in the case of Odo, brother of the duke of Burgundy and a prince of royal Frankish stock. Although, as he himself testified, he had studied letters under Bruno at Reims, nevertheless in 1085, at the urging of Vigerius, he became bishop of Langres, and thus three years before Urban ascended the apostolic throne.

Similarly, Lambert of Pultaria and Peter, abbots of Saint John of the Vines at Soissons, who likewise grew up under Bruno’s instruction, as they themselves state in the rolls sent after the holy man’s death, obtained these dignities while Urban was still alive.

Since these facts are entirely certain concerning them, I do not see why they should be denied concerning Urban, whom the testimony of ancient authors shows to have been made pontiff when he was of middle age and to have died while his vigor still flourished.

[Col. 0013D]

If we now inquire into Bruno’s age, it can scarcely be doubted that he lived beyond fifty years. To establish this, we must first determine when he ceased teaching at Reims.

Certainly, from the letters of Gregory VII and from Guibert, abbot of Nogent, it seems possible to infer that Bruno resigned the direction of the school of Reims on the occasion of the disturbances that Archbishop Manasses had caused in that Church, and therefore around the year 1076 or the following year.

At the beginning of 1078, Godefridus the chancellor, Bruno’s successor both in governing the schools and in the office of chancellor, signed the Council of Soissons in the case of the Church of Saint-Quentin.

But if Bruno had died in 1101 at the age of fifty, as his opponents wish, then in 1076 or the following year, when he relinquished responsibility for the schools, he would scarcely have reached his twenty-fifth year, or certainly his twenty-sixth. It is certain that he governed the schools of Reims for many years; this period could not have extended for only fifteen or twelve years. He would therefore have assumed the direction of these extremely famous schools at about the age of twelve, or at most fifteen—something no sane person, as it seems to me, would assert.

Among others who praised Bruno, the regular canons of the monastery of Noyon expressly affirm in the rolls sent to various places after his death that, when they saw the document announcing the death of Bruno, “the incomparable philosopher,” they lamented the loss of so great a man, “who had long been the supreme teacher of the Church of the see of Reims … and had long stood as the pillar of the entire metropolis.”

The other congregations of Churches and monasteries agree with the canons of Noyon in similar rolls, where they adorn him with various titles of honor. The canons of Saint Mary of Blois call him “this jewel of wisdom”; the monks of Saint-Lucien of Beauvais, “the light of the Churches”; those of Saint-Maximin at Micy, “the most illustrious sophist”; the canons of Bernay, “the teacher of teachers”; the canons of Saint Mary Major at Paris, “the glory of masters, the oar of the Reims crowd”; the canons of Saint-Gervais at Valois say that he “gave the nations and clergy a stream of learning”; those of Saint Timothy at Reims, that he “surpassed all teachers throughout the world”; those of Saint Mary of Spalding, that “as many became wise through his teaching as the mind cannot comprehend”; and the monks of Saint Nicholas at Angers, that “his teaching shone throughout the whole world,” so that the canons of the cathedral Church of Sainte-Croix at Orléans wish to be his followers.

It would be excessive to list the remaining eulogies. Yet one cannot omit the testimony of the canons of the cathedral Church of Saint Maurice at Angers, who assert that Bruno was the teacher not of children or minor clerics, but of serious men who were already learned and who studied the divine science—that is, theology—under him. This plainly indicates that he was already mature in age when he taught at Reims before his withdrawal.

Here are some of their verses:

His exceptional wisdom is celebrated everywhere,

More than Maro’s, Bruno’s eloquence is praised,

The glory of Plato grows pale before Bruno’s praise.

Here he surpassed the teachers; here he made

Supreme doctors, not by educating lesser men:

Here he was the teacher of teachers, not of little clerics.

For neither the dignity of his words nor their gravity

Did Bruno possess unless he were a man of great reason.

He proclaims excellent wisdom by teaching divine things.

Thus, in the Chronicle of Maillezais, Bruno is called by Adhemar “the perfect philosopher.” Among others, it was not Berengar—as some wrongly understand—but Fulbert of Chartres, who died in 1028, who had left Bruno as the heir of his philosophy.

Who, then, would say that such a man—whom nearly all the Churches of Gaul, England, and Italy eagerly commended as the most celebrated teacher of the sciences—earned these praises when he was only twenty years old, or a little more or less? Who, I ask, would persuade himself that Bruno, at that age, governed schools so famous for so long, and with such a reputation for learning and doctrine, that twenty years after his withdrawal his death was mourned by most of the more distinguished Churches of the Christian world as the death of the master of all teachers?

Finally, if it is permissible to introduce visions in support of our case, Bruno was an old man—and therefore forty-five or perhaps even fifty years of age—when he was staying in Calabria. For Count Roger, as he himself relates in the well-known charter concerning this matter, was besieging Capua when he was warned by an old man of venerable appearance, whom he believed to be the Venerable Father Bruno, to beware of the ambushes of a certain traitor named Sergius.

From all this it is easily inferred that nothing at all prevents us from accepting that Bruno was Urban’s teacher while Urban was studying letters at the school of Reims, and that this occurred around the sixtieth year of the eleventh century.

The sequence of events can therefore be arranged as follows. In 1055 Gervasius obtained the see of Reims. Shortly afterward he summoned Bruno to Reims, who had already been, as Manasses asserted in his apology, a canon of the Church of Saint Cunibert at Cologne, and entrusted him, together with the dignity of chancellor, with the direction of his Church’s schools.

At that time our Odo was being educated there among other noble clerics of his age. If we accept that in 1060 he had reached approximately his eighteenth year—a conclusion that seems almost certain—nothing at all prevents us from believing that he was educated under Bruno’s discipline at that time, later passed through various dignities, and finally obtained the Roman pontificate in 1088 at about the age of forty-six, an age still moderate, and died at last in 1099 at the age of fifty-seven, still vigorous and in the flower of his strength.

This discussion may perhaps have been treated at greater length than necessary; but the case of Bruno as well as that of Odo, or Urban, required it, since it is honorable for Bruno to have had so great a disciple, and for Odo to have been educated under the discipline of so holy a man.

How greatly Odo advanced under that famous teacher in literary studies and exercises of virtue is sufficiently and abundantly demonstrated by the few writings of his that survive, together with the distinguished deeds of his remaining life, which we shall set forth in their proper places.

## III. Whether Urban Was a Canon and Archdeacon of Reims; His Love for the Church of Reims

[Col. 0015D]

Various authors commonly state that Urban was not only brought up in the bosom of the Church of Reims but also held a place in the distinguished college of that Church’s canons.

Since that Church at the time surpassed the others not only in dignity but also in holiness of conduct and observance of the common life, some called its canons regular. From this arose the opinion of certain later authors, who wrote that Urban had once been a regular canon, and indeed of the Lateran congregation, as others added. So readily does error arise from preconceived opinions. But there is no time to linger over this.

[Col. 0016A]

What Alberic wrote in his Chronicle is more plausible: that Urban was archdeacon of the Church of Reims. If the catalogue of the archdeacons of Reims published by Marlot in volume I of *The Metropolis of Reims* is reliable, this is the same Odo who held that dignity in 1070.

Take care, however, not to confuse him with another archdeacon of Reims of the same name, who is recorded as having subscribed, among others, to various charters under the archbishops Wido and Gervasius. Since this latter Odo held the dignity in 1052, as is clear from a charter of Archbishop Wido reported by Marlot in volume II, he must necessarily have been someone other than our Odo, who was appointed pontiff in 1088 while he was still of moderate age, as Orderic Vitalis puts it.

Certainly the name Odo was more common at that time, so that no one can deny that there could have been two archdeacons named Odo in the Church of Reims during that century. If anyone should deny this, we shall offer as evidence the ancient obituary book of that Church, in which the death of Odo the archdeacon is recorded on the fifth day of February—clearly a different man from our Odo, who died as Roman pontiff at the end of July.

Urban continued to honor and foster the Church of Reims even after obtaining the pontificate, as will be clear from various letters that we shall present in their order. In a distinguished diploma he asserted the prerogatives of that Church and of its archbishops; in another he confirmed the privileges of the canons of the same Church, while defending the monks of Saint-Remi against Ingelram, bishop of Laon—not to mention the monks of Saint-Basle, whom he freed from the yoke of a secular advocate.

It is remarkable how greatly the pious pontiff labored to restore the episcopal see of Arras, which for nearly three hundred years had lacked its own bishop. He repeatedly testifies that he did this in order to restore the metropolitan Church of Reims to its ancient dignity.

Urban, as Hermann relates in his *History of the Restoration of Saint Martin of Tournai*, in volume XII of Acher’s *Spicilegium*, “because he had been educated in the Church of Reims, loved it greatly above the others; and so that he might restore to it its ancient dignity of twelve bishops, he labored with no little effort.”

Indeed, besides Arras, he had also attempted to free the Church of Tournai from the subjection of the bishop of Noyon. What he himself could not accomplish because of the difficulties that arose was achieved several years later by Eugenius III through the efforts of Saint Bernard.

The ancient prerogative of the province of Reims in Gaul was that, possessing twelve episcopal sees, it could settle canonical judgments within its own jurisdiction, without the assistance of other provinces.

When Bishop Ivo of Chartres wished to come to the aid of the endangered Church of Reims after the death of Archbishop Raynald, he sought Urban’s help in Letter 116. In that letter he commended the Church not only because it bore the crown of the kingdom and served as an example to nearly all the Churches of Gaul, whether of ruin or resurrection, but also because it had once been Urban’s mother:

“We ask that the metropolitan Church of Reims, once your mother, and so forth, be refreshed by your consolations.”

Ivo’s appeal was not in vain, as is clear from various letters that the pontiff composed on that occasion. In them he expressed in the tenderest words his sincere affection for this Church and confirmed it by his actions.

Among other passages, one in a letter to the clergy, religious order, knights, and people residing at Reims is especially notable. He addresses them as follows:

“The depths of our affection, most beloved children in Christ, have been constricted, because we know that you are deprived of the solicitude of a shepherd … But amid this tribulation, through the grace of almighty God, the inmost chambers of our charity are enlarged, because we rejoice with you, and so forth, with greater devotion.”

## IV–V. Urban Considers Withdrawal from the World; He Becomes a Monk at Cluny; Gregory VII Calls Him to Rome; The Occasion of His Summons

The Church of Reims therefore had good reason to take pride in so great a son. But Urban, aspiring to greater gifts, longed for a more perfect life, and there is no doubt that in this he was greatly assisted and strengthened by Bruno’s counsels and exhortations.

For Bruno, as is clear from a letter that he wrote much later from Calabria to Prior Ralph, used often to converse with other leading men of the Church of Reims—among whom Odo certainly belonged, as archdeacon—about contempt for the world and the joys of the life to come. By these conversations they encouraged one another to flee from the world.

Odo seems to have preceded the others. Several years before Bruno laid the foundations of the Carthusian order, Odo himself, having abandoned worldly pomp and cares, withdrew to the monastery of Cluny. There the most holy Abbot Hugh clothed him in the monastic habit. For this reason Odo calls himself Hugh’s son and foster-child in a letter that he wrote to him shortly after his elevation to the pontificate.

In what year this occurred is uncertain. But if Odo was that archdeacon of Reims whom we cited above from Marlot’s catalogue—as is probable—he was still living at Reims in 1070, since in that year he subscribed to a donation made to the Church of Rumi­gny, as may be seen in Marlot himself.

His conversion nevertheless cannot have been delayed for long afterward, if it is true that the Cluniac Chartulary seems to show that around 1076 he was already prior of Cluny. In that very year there were two other archdeacons, but never more, in the Church of Reims—namely Guido and Garinus—who are recorded as having subscribed, together with Bruno the chancellor, to a donation made by Archbishop Manasses to the monastery of Saint-Basle.

Once established at Cluny, Odo had as his instructor in the monastic life Peter, who later became abbot of Cava in Italy and bishop of Policastro, if we believe the ancient author who wrote the history of the dedication of the Church of Cava.

That author repeatedly calls Urban Peter’s disciple and praises him chiefly because, even after becoming pontiff, Urban always revered this same Peter as his teacher. Other ancient monuments of the monastery of Cava, especially its own records, preserved by Ughelli, agree with this.

The anonymous abbot of Venosa, however, who wrote the lives of Peter and the other first abbots of that place shortly afterward, says nothing about this matter. There is nevertheless another Life of Peter, which we possess from the same Roman manuscript; in it Urban is said once to have been Peter’s fellow student and to have accompanied him on his journey when Peter returned from Gaul to Cava.

Certainly no one can reasonably deny that the two lived together at Cluny, and the abbot of Venosa himself testifies that Peter, while staying at Cluny, exercised various offices there at the same time.

In any event, Urban himself not only called himself the son and foster-child of Blessed Hugh, as we have already observed from his letter, but also expressly professed that he had been trained by Hugh himself in monastic discipline.

Here are his words from a privilege that he granted to Hugh and to the monastery of Cluny in the first year of his pontificate:

“Moreover, there is this further reason why we are no less indebted to you and to your monastery: through you I received the rudiments of monastic religion, and in your monastery I was reborn through the second grace of the Holy Spirit.”

Yet Saint Hugh was more clear-sighted than to allow so great a light to remain hidden under a bushel for long. Therefore he appointed him prior of Cluny (around the year 1076). [Col. 0018C] Urban himself openly declared that he had once held this dignity in a sermon that he delivered at the dedication of the principal altar of that place, as we shall see below. Guibert, in Book II of his *History of Jerusalem*, testifies that this occurred not long after Urban’s conversion, in these words:

> Having become a monk at Cluny from being a cleric . . . not long afterward he held the office of prior, so that he might be of assistance to his abbot Hugh, who was occupied with various affairs.

What he accomplished after being appointed to this dignity is unknown to us, except that he is found subscribing several charters. He was present at Avalon when Hugh, duke of the Burgundians, subjected the church of Saint Mary in that fortress to Cluny. There Odo himself, prior [Col. 0018D] of Cluny, admitted this same Hugh, together with his brothers Odo and Robert, then a cleric, as well as Count Guy of Mâcon and other nobles of Burgundy who had assembled there, into the fellowship of the Cluniac brothers, so that from that time onward they might share in their prayers and alms, and also in the other benefactions of the aforesaid place. This assembly was held on 19 February 1078. Besides our copy, this is proved by the indiction I appended there, although the same donation is assigned to the preceding year in Volume VI of Acher’s *Spicilegium*. In the presence of the same Odo, the prior, a certain Bernard renounced in the chapter house the property that he had seized from the possessions which his brother Tosceran had donated upon entering the religious life, as is related in charters 146 and 605 [Col. 0019A] among those issued under Saint Hugh; the same Odo, prior, is also mentioned in charter 321.

From this we can infer how great his merit was. When Gregory VII, who at that time governed the Roman Church amid the most difficult circumstances, had asked Abbot Hugh for several monks distinguished in learning and virtue, whom he could employ as assistants in the Church’s most pressing affairs, Odo was the first chosen among them, according to Hermannus, so that he might be at the pontiff’s service in those straits (1078). Hermannus writes as follows in the already-mentioned *History of the Restoration of Saint Martin of Tournai*:

> During the time of Lord Hugh, abbot of Cluny, it happened that a canon of the Church of Reims, a man of great probity named Odo, abandoned the secular life [Col. 0019B] and became a monk in that same Cluniac Church. After he had lived there for several years with the greatest religious devotion, and Lord Pope Gregory VII had instructed the same Lord Hugh, the abbot, to send him some wise men from among his monks whom he could suitably ordain as bishops, Lord Hugh sent him, among others, the aforesaid Odo, whom the pope consecrated bishop of Ostia.

Guibert likewise reports that, as Odo’s merit advanced, he was sent to the city of Ostia at the command of Pope Gregory VII. Agreeing with these authorities, Orderic Vitalis, in Book IV of his *Ecclesiastical History*, adds that other Cluniac monks were also given to Odo as companions, that the pontiff welcomed them with grateful enthusiasm, and that Odo was chosen above the others as his counselor:

> When Pope Gregory requested him, Hugh, abbot of Cluny, sent to Rome Odo, the prior of the aforesaid Cluniac monastery, who had been a monk of the Church of Reims, together with other suitable monks. The pope joyfully received them as assistants sent to him by God. He chose Odo, in particular, as his counselor and appointed him bishop of the Church of Ostia.

Orderic assigns this to the year 1078, where, on the occasion of Gregory VII’s election to the papacy, he has brought together many events that occurred at different times during Gregory’s pontificate. That Odo did not visit Rome before 1078 is more than probable from the donation of Hugh, duke of Burgundy, mentioned above, which, as we have said, was made in that very year, when Odo was still prior of the monastery of Cluny. Unless, perhaps, one should say that Odo was summoned to Rome by Gregory before that time [Col. 0019D], then returned to Gaul, and afterward, in 1078, went back to Italy in order to accept the bishopric of Ostia.

Certainly Peter of Cava, who is said to have entered Italy with Odo, had not yet been recalled by Hildebrand, who was not yet pope, if we trust the other author of Peter’s *Life*. Yet there seems to be no necessity for admitting this double journey. The occasion for Odo and his companions to be summoned to Italy appears instead to have been the death of Gerard, bishop of Ostia. After Gerard died in 1077, as Berthold writes, Henry Augustus had installed in his place a certain factious man named John. Gregory feared that, if schismatics invaded more Churches in this manner, the affairs of the Catholics would deteriorate further. Therefore the most vigilant pontiff considered it worthwhile to have several men with him distinguished by holiness of life and a reputation for wisdom, whom, when circumstances required, he could place over widowed Churches, as Hermannus says. Among others chosen for this purpose were our Odo and Peter, who several years earlier had migrated from the monastery of Cava, near Salvinum, to Cluny—a man so energetic that at Cluny he held seven offices simultaneously, or even more, according to some accounts.

### VI. Whether Urban stayed at Cava

It can scarcely be doubted that, after arriving in Italy and paying their respects to the pontiff, these men turned aside to Cava, since an ancient author of the *History of the Dedication* of that place expressly states that they lived there together for some time [Col. 0020B]. Nor, in my view, could Urban otherwise have been included among the illustrious men of that monastery, as is commonly done. I admit that the Venusian abbot, who writes in the *Life of Saint Peter* that Peter returned from Gaul to Cava with Hugh’s permission, says absolutely nothing about Odo or about Peter’s companions whom Gregory had requested. But that silence is outweighed by the authority of the cited author of the *History of the Dedication of Cava*, by the other writer of the *Life of Saint Peter*, and by other Cavense records.

Moreover, since it is certain that both men, whether together or separately, migrated from Gaul to Italy at this time, it is plausible that, if neither was immediately raised to the pontifical dignity upon arrival, both spent some interval in a monastery—more likely at Cava than anywhere else, since Cava was attached to the Cluniac order, and since Peter, whose friend Odo at least was, had professed monastic life there as his companion at Cluny [Col. 0020C].

Some writers, deceived—I do not know by what authors—tell the story that Urban first embraced the canonical life at the Lateran monastery in Rome, then withdrew to Cava in pursuit of a stricter way of life; that from there he migrated to Cluny and lived there under Odilo or Hugh together with Hildebrand, who at that time was himself also a monk of Cluny; and that Hildebrand later summoned him to Rome as soon as he had been made Roman pontiff, and adorned him with the dignity of cardinal and with the bishopric of Ostia [Col. 0020D]. But all these things are mere nonsense, and I am reluctant to spend time refuting them.

### VII. Urban becomes bishop of Ostia

Odo and Peter were not permitted to remain long in the solitude of Cava. For in that same year, 1078, in which they had arrived in Italy, Gregory, after expelling the schismatic John—as Ughellus testifies in his *Sacred Italy*—created Odo bishop of Ostia. Peter, not long afterward, upon his return from Cluny, was ordained bishop of Policastro, as the second author of his *Life* relates.

Nor should we be deterred by the authority of the two authors of Saint Peter’s *Life*, where Peter is said to have been requested as bishop of the city of Policastro not only by the clergy and people, but also by Gisulf, prince of Salerno. Gisulf had already been deprived of the principality of Salerno by Robert Guiscard in 1075, as the anonymous Cassinese author writes in his *Chronicle*, and in that very year had fled to Gregory in Rome. What, then, could that dispossessed prince have contributed to Peter’s election if it took place in 1078? Unless perhaps he intervened with Gregory so that Peter, whom he knew well as a good and holy man, might be placed on the see of Policastro.

In this way the two authors of Peter’s *Life* can easily be reconciled with the other historians. For even though Gisulf had been expelled from his homeland, it was very much in his interest that someone known to him should obtain this dignity. Certainly Peter became bishop of Policastro not long after his return from Cluny, according to the author of the second *Life*. After spending little time in that office, he returned to the monastery of Cava and was immediately substituted for Abbot Leo shortly before Leo’s death, as is clear from both authors of his *Life*.

Leo, however, as seems certain from the Cavense Calendar and the short *Chronicle* arranged according to the Easter cycles, died in July 1079. All these events could easily have occurred within the space of one year and several months, and thus they agree perfectly with our chronology. The bull that Urban issued in favor of the people of Cava does not agree entirely with this account. But in that bull several events that occurred at different times have been compressed into a single narrative. Moreover, it has been disfigured by many interpolations, as is evident to the reader; nor is it consistent with itself in its various copies, so that many things appear in one copy that are absent from another.

[Col. 0021C] If, however, anyone regards it as certain that Peter was made bishop before Gisulf’s flight, as both authors of his *Life* certainly suggest, it will have to be said that Peter returned to Italy long before Odo, and that Odo followed him only several years later and met him at Cava; and that the second author of the *Life* was mistaken in believing that the journey which these holy men had undertaken separately was made by them together.

### VIII. He becomes the pope’s counselor

What Odo did during the first years after becoming bishop of Ostia is nowhere recorded by the ancient authors. Yet there is no doubt that at that time he was always at Gregory’s side, while Gregory was almost overwhelmed by great affairs [Col. 0021D]. The passage from Orderic already cited above can certainly be applied here, in which Gregory is said to have chosen Odo as his principal counselor.

In fact, throughout the first four years of his episcopate Odo remained constantly at the pontiff’s side, assisting him with his advice and service. This is suggested by Benno the pseudocardinal, the most bitter enemy of Gregory and of the Roman Church, who habitually calls Odo Gregory’s lackey. The same author relates in his *Life of Gregory VII* that, during the controversy over the Eucharist against Berengar at the Roman council of 1079, Gregory sent our Odo and Cunon to Saint Anastasia. There they were to devote themselves, together with Suppo, archpriest of that church, to fasting and prayer for three days, reciting three psalters and celebrating Masses, so that they might deserve to hear from God—as had once happened to Saint Gregory on a similar occasion—what ought to be believed concerning the Eucharist [Col. 0022A].

### IX. Concerning Wibert the antipope

The times were certainly exceedingly difficult, because of the grave conflicts that then raged most fiercely between the priesthood and the empire (1080). Henry, king of Germany, had made these conflicts almost incurable by choosing Guibert, a criminal man who had already been expelled from the see of Ravenna for three years, and having him proclaimed a false pontiff in that year, so that he might oppose this mask to Gregory, the legitimate pontiff.

This took place at Brixina, a city of Noricum, in a gathering of thirty schismatic bishops, in the year 1080, on 25 June, as may be seen in the commonly published authors [Col. 0022B].

### X. Urban writes Simon’s epitaph

In 1082 Odo was still staying in Rome, if it is true that he wrote the epitaph of Simon, formerly count of Crispeia and at that time a monk of the Jura, who died in that year, as Alberic notes. Nor is it surprising that this honor was granted to Simon, who was given a place among the apostolic tombs in the Vatican basilica—not only because of the exceptional nobility of his lineage, but chiefly because of his immense services to the Roman Church, for whose defense Gregory had summoned him to Italy, as is related in his *Life*, in Century V, Part II of the *Acts of the Saints of the Benedictine Order*.

### XI. After Wibert is enthroned in the Vatican basilica, a council is summoned. Odo is captured by Henry

[Col. 0022C]

Henry Augustus increased the calamities of the Church by a new crime in 1083. After having unsuccessfully attempted to seize the city of Rome in earlier years, he gained possession of one part of it in this year and, after capturing the Leonine City, arranged for his Guibert to be proclaimed pontiff in Saint Peter’s basilica under the false name of Clement III. He was enthroned not by the bishops of Ostia and Albano—or of Porto—to whom, according to the privilege granted to those sees by the Holy Fathers, this duty belonged, as Berthold says, but by the bishops of Modena and Rimini, who had been deposed and anathematized for many years. Other writers say that the enthronement was performed by other bishops [Col. 0022D].

Berthold’s authority should be preferred, since he was alive at the time and carefully arranged each event year by year, if only he were consistent with himself. Yet in the year 1084 he himself names the bishop of Arezzo instead of the bishop of Rimini, as do other authors. Gebehard, archbishop of Salzburg, writes in his letter to Hermann, bishop of Metz, that the bishops of Modena and Arezzo imposed upon Wibert not a blessing but the condemnation that they themselves bore. There is no doubt that both the bishop of Rimini and the bishop of Arezzo were present at this ceremony. For Berthold observes, under the year 1084, that besides those whom he names, other excommunicated bishops also took part in Wibert’s ordination, which Albert of Stade and other authors assign to the following year.

[Col. 0023A] Amid such great confusion, the leading men of the Church considered it worthwhile to assemble a synod whose statutes, Berthold says, concerning the kingdom’s affairs, neither Henry nor the Romans—indeed no one at all—would be permitted to violate. Gregory summoned it for November and sent letters about it to all the bishops and abbots.

Henry, however, having returned to Lombardy, swore an oath and promised complete security to all who either intended to go to the synod or, after it was finished, intended to return home. But, forgetting his promises and breaking faith shortly afterward, he ordered that many of those who were hastening to the council be seized on the way, including Odo himself, bishop of Ostia, whom Gregory had sent to him as legate. He had them detained in captivity and cruelly tortured with many torments [Col. 0023B].

Berthold should be heard on this matter; he explains it in these words:

> The envoys of the German princes were supposed to go to the council, but they were captured and disgraced by Henry on the road near Forum Cassii around the feast of Saint Martin, although he had promised by oath security to everyone seeking that synod. . . . They were highly devout monks and clerics, whom he had tortured in captivity; among them was the venerable Otto, bishop of Ostia, who had been captured—namely, the man sent to him by the Apostolic See.

So much for Berthold. But neither this treatment nor any harsher violence could ever move Odo away from obedience to Gregory, the legitimate pontiff. On the contrary, together with his colleagues, the bishops of Albano and Porto, he preferred, as Berthold states under the following year, to endure every extreme rather than become involved in Wibert’s sacrilegious ordination, which was the height of arrogant presumption. They proved their good intention by their actions, since, joined to the apostolic lord Gregory, they canonically condemned that same ordination by synodal judgment.

### XII. Peace is discussed; Odo is released

(Year 1084.) Religious men throughout the world endured with difficulty the Church’s many and grievous calamities. Some of them, who were suspected by neither party, undertook efforts to reconcile peace between the pontiff and the king. We learn this from Pandulf in his *Deeds of the Pontiffs*, where he specifically mentions Hugh, abbot of Cluny, among others. Together with other upright men, Hugh warned Henry not to make light of the anathemas imposed by so many pontiffs [Col. 0023D].

Henry obeyed—or at least, as that author suggests, pretended to obey. After releasing Odo and the other captives and granting them the freedom to return to their homes, he promised Gregory that he would make peace with him if Gregory would place the imperial crown upon his head. But when Gregory replied that he would do so only under certain conditions, which Henry refused, the matter remained unresolved. Henry, persisting in schism, solemnly received the crown from his Guibert; after this, it was no longer possible to remove that atrocious scandal from the Church.

I gladly quote Pandulf’s entire passage:

> In the third year also the king returned to besiege Rome. But when he learned that he himself was certainly regarded as excommunicated by the abbot of Cluny and by other religious men who feared God, he resorted to crafty arguments so that he might better deceive their simplicity. After the capture of the bishop of Ostia and many others, he received them and released them. He gave firm security to all who wished to visit Rome, and publicly confirmed it by oath. And, in order to pursue popular favor and goodwill completely, he declared in public that he wished to receive from Lord Pope Gregory the dignity of the imperial crown. . . . But Gregory replied: “I have frequently experienced the king’s cunning and deceit. If, however, he wishes to make satisfaction to God and the Church for the things in which he has manifestly sinned, I will gladly absolve him and place the imperial crown upon him with a blessing.” . . . But when the king, stung by his conscience, utterly refused to do this . . . the pontiff, distrusting him, withdrew into the fortress of Crescentius, etc.

### XIII. Henry is crowned by Guibert and excommunicated

Henry, who had invaded the Lateran basilica, received from his Guibert on the very day of the Lord’s Resurrection a crown in the Church—not a crown of glory, as Berthold says, but of shame—and besieged Gregory, the legitimate pontiff, in another part of the city. His efforts were nevertheless useless. For shortly afterward the pontiff was freed through the intervention of Robert Guiscard, the Norman ruler in Italy, and held a synod in the city itself, at which the schismatics were again excommunicated.

Concerning this synod, Berthold writes under this year:

> The Lord pope, having assembled a synod, again pronounced the sentence of anathema against Guibert the heresiarch, Henry, and all their supporters; he had already done so in Rome some time before, on the preceding feast of Saint John the Baptist, while Henry was still staying there.

He then adds that this sentence was proclaimed everywhere by the apostolic legates: namely, by Peter, bishop of Albano, in France, and by Odo, bishop of Ostia, in the German lands. This is the first mention of the apostolic legation that our Odo carried out in Germany.

### XIV. Odo as legate in Germany. He ordains Gebehard bishop of Constance

One of his chief concerns in that legation was to provide churches deprived of their bishops with prelates distinguished by strength of spirit and integrity of life, such as the necessity of those unjust times required [Col. 0024D]. Among these was Henry, count of Aslo, whom Schatenus records in the *Annals of the Church of Paderborn* as having been appointed bishop of Paderborn with the consent of King Hermann, the clergy, and the people, and by the authority of Odo, the apostolic legate.

The election of Reinward as bishop of Minden must also be referred to this period, if it is true—as the same author relates—that he was substituted for the deceased Egilbert by Otto, bishop of Ostia and apostolic legate of Pope Gregory throughout Saxony, amid the acclamation of the clergy and people.

But none of these men was more renowned than Gebehard, son of Duke Bartold, whom the legate, distinguished by holiness of life and the splendor of his birth, made bishop of Constance after he had been a monk of Hirsau; he would later become a legate of the Apostolic See and a most vigorous defender of the Catholic Church in Germany [Col. 0025A].

Berthold observes that Odo consecrated him this year, on 22 December, although he was unwilling—indeed, he protested and lamented bitterly—while the clergy and laity requested and praised him. The day before, that is, on the feast of Saint Thomas the Presbyter, he had been ordained together with Berthold himself, the author of the *Chronicle*, and other clerics.

Paul of Bernried also testifies in his *Life of Gregory VII* that Gebehard was consecrated by our Odo. Against so many witnesses, one should not follow the later author Bruschius, who writes that the consecration was performed by Peter of Albano.

The anonymous author of the apology for Henry IV blames this ordination on Otto—for the German writers like to call our Odo by that name—as though by this act he had violated the canons, daring to perform it without the permission of the archbishop of Mainz, although he was not the metropolitan of the province [Col. 0025B].

Everyone agrees, however, that Gebehard was a holy man and by no means unworthy of episcopal dignity. As Trithemius reports in the *Hirsaugiensis Chronicle*, after becoming a bishop he did not cease the fervor of regular life that he had customarily maintained innocently while living in the monastery.

Moreover, that Odo remained for some time at Constance and arranged many matters there for the good of the Church can be inferred from the canons of the council of Quedlinburg held in the following year.

### XV. Odo attends the conference in Saxony

At the beginning of the following year (1085), Odo met Hermann, whom the Saxons had elected king in place of Rudolf against Henry, and attended the conference held between the Saxons and Henry’s supporters on the fifteenth day after the feast of the Epiphany.

Nothing, however, was decided there, because after many disputes both parties left the conference applauding themselves as though they had won the victory. The authors do not agree on the location of the meeting. The abbot of Ursperg and Trithemius in the *Hirsaugiensis Chronicle* want it to have been held at Berberes, a town in Thuringia; others say that it took place at Gestrunga or Goslar, in the same province.

There Gebehard, archbishop of Salzburg, defended the Catholic party in an extended speech. When Werilo, archbishop of Mainz, replied in Henry’s favor, matters came to the point that the two sides fought fiercely not only with words but also with weapons [Col. 0025D].

At the same time Odo, the apostolic legate, placed under ecclesiastical interdict Udo, bishop of Hildesheim, who had abandoned the Saxons and gone over to the schismatic party.

Nothing, however, stirred the minds of the Catholics so deeply as the new assertion of Archbishop Wicelon, who did not hesitate to affirm in the full assembly that no person could remain subject to the divine laws for as long as he had been deprived of his possessions. Thereafter the Catholics did not hesitate to call this opinion a heresy and Wicelon himself a heresiarch.

### XVI. He summons the council of Quedlinburg

With Germany thrown into turmoil by these quarrels, those who adhered to Gregory decided to summon a synod in order to defend themselves and their supporters against the efforts of their adversaries [Col. 0026A]. It was held during the very week of Easter at Quedlinburg—or, as German authors of that period write, Quintilineburg—a city of Upper Saxony, while Odo the legate, King Hermann, and other nobles were celebrating the Easter festivities there.

Two archbishops, Gebehard of Salzburg and Hartwig of Magdeburg, came there with the legate, together with many other bishops. At this synod they enacted numerous and indeed distinguished measures, which Berthold assigns to this year.

At the same synod the so-called Wezilian heresy, of which we spoke above, was condemned. By synodal judgment, according to Berthold, the ordination of Lord Gebehard, bishop of Constance, which Odo had performed the preceding year, was praised and confirmed [Col. 0026B]. Indeed, as that author continues, everything that the aforesaid legate of the Apostolic See had arranged while he was at Constance was confirmed.

Anathema was then pronounced against the schismatic bishops, their leader Wibert, the invader of the Apostolic See, and his pseudo-cardinals: Hugh the White, John of Porto, Peter the chancellor, and others. So that no solemnity might be lacking, all the Fathers publicly proclaimed the sentence while holding lighted candles in their hands.

It is remarkable that in the subscriptions to this council, which are reported in the Appendix to Volume X of Labbe’s councils, Odo is listed only under the titles “monk of Cluny” and “legate of Pope Gregory,” with no mention of his pontifical dignity [Col. 0026C], although it is certain that he was then bishop of Ostia.

The bishops of Henry’s party, who assembled at Mainz in the third week after this synod had ended, likewise excommunicated the defender of Gregory and expelled the Catholic bishops from the cities under their authority, installing others in their place who adhered to them.

I pass over the names of the bishops of that assembly; they can be seen in the same Appendix to Labbe’s councils. The fourteen Catholic bishops of the council of Quedlinburg whom those men excommunicated were these: Gebehard of Salzburg; Hartwig of Magdeburg; Adalbero of Würzburg; Altmann of Passau; Bernard—or Wernher, or Werner—of Merseburg; Gunther of Zeitz; Benno of Meissen; Albert of Worms; Burkhard of Halberstadt; Hermann of Metz; Reginard of Minden; Wigold of Augsburg; Gebehard of Constance; and Henry of Bamberg.

### XVII. Gregory VII dies

Meanwhile Gregory, who had left Rome and first withdrawn to the monastery of Monte Cassino, died at Salerno on 25 May (1085), where he was honorably buried in the church of Saint Matthew, which he himself had consecrated.

As he was nearing death, he is said, when asked what he thought about his future successor, to have designated several men suited to that office: Hugh, archbishop of Lyon; Anselm of Lucca [Col. 0027A]; Odo of Ostia; or certainly Desiderius, abbot of Monte Cassino. So say most of the ancient authors.

Peter of Cassino, however, says that Gregory urged the bishops and cardinals to elect Desiderius, or, if that could not be done, one of the other three men mentioned. Paul of Bernried omits Anselm in his *Life of Gregory*, but, after listing the other three whom the pontiff had indicated, he adds:

> But because Otto had not yet returned from the regions of Germany and Gaul, where he had carried out an apostolic legation . . . and had prudently arranged several other matters for the strengthening of the Church; and because Hugh too was far away, inspecting the territories under his governance, he meanwhile advised that the nearby Desiderius be elected, although he would live only a very short time, etc.

Yet Desiderius could scarcely ever be persuaded to assume the pontificate, which everyone offered him immediately after Gregory’s death, and the matter was drawn out for a long time [Col. 0027B].

### XVIII. Odo passes through Cluny. He raises the body of Saint Maximus at Nantua. — Saint Hugh’s miracle

Having returned to Italy from his German legation in this year, Odo visited his fellow monks at Cluny on the way and there consecrated the church of the sick, as we learn from the history of the translation of Saint Maximus.

This translation was performed with solemn ceremony at the monastery of Nantua by our Odo in that same year. We shall reproduce the entire history, written by an anonymous contemporary author, from a manuscript of that place in the Appendix to this volume. For the moment, however, a few details should be drawn from it.

Nantua—today commonly called Nantua—is a celebrated monastery in the diocese of Lyon [Col. 0027C], among the Sebusians. Formerly it had been granted the title of abbey, but later it was subjected to the monastery of Cluny. The relics of Saint Maximus, whom they believed to have been bishop of Riez, were kept there without any cult, because they had not hitherto been uncovered from the earth and publicly displayed for the veneration of the faithful.

When Odo arrived, Hugh, abbot of Cluny and at that time also prior of the monastery of Nantua, judged that an opportunity had been offered to him to raise those sacred relics from the earth. Therefore, after taking counsel with Odo and the others who happened to be present there, and after first observing fasts and prayers, they transferred the bones of the holy bishop from an ancient tomb into a prepared reliquary on 27 August and displayed them for the public veneration of the people.

We infer that this occurred in that year from the very words of the cited history, where Hugh is said to have summoned the chapter on Sunday, 24 August. For between the year 1078, when Odo became bishop of Ostia, and the year 1088, when he ascended the Apostolic throne, Sunday fell on 24 August only once, namely in 1085. This solemn elevation of Saint Maximus’s body must therefore be assigned to that year.

It is certain, moreover, that in this very year Odo returned from Germany to Italy, and on that journey he could easily have visited Cluny and Nantua. The old calendar of Nantua contains a commemoration of the translation of Saint Maximus, and so forth, but places it on 25 August, which appears to be an error in our copy. For the history says that it was decided [Col. 0028A] that thereafter his feast should be celebrated on 26 August.

To this period must also be referred the remarkable event that is said to have occurred to Saint Hugh at Nantua while our Odo was staying there. When Hugh was informed that Willencus, then prior of La Charité, had departed this life, the holy man immediately went to the altar to offer a living sacrifice to God the Father for the deceased.

But the author of truth did not permit so great a man to be deceived. It was revealed to Hugh that it was not Willencus but Orius who had died. After completing the sacrifice, the holy abbot openly declared this to those standing by.

> There was present, says Hugh the monk, the contemporary author of the *Life of Saint Hugh*, Odo, who had been prior of Cluny, afterward bishop of Ostia, and then supreme pontiff of the Apostolic See, Urban II. After completing his legation, he discovered, in accordance with the man of God’s word, that it was not Willencus but Orius who had died.

After this Odo returned to Italy, where he neglected nothing, together with the other faithful of the Roman Church, to ensure that a worthy successor to Gregory would be given.

### XIX. Desiderius refuses the pontificate. Odo is nominated, but without effect

(Year 1086.) Nearly a full year had now elapsed since Gregory’s death without a pontiff, because Desiderius, abbot of Cassino, could in no way be persuaded to assume the governance of the Church. Berthold also attributed these delays to the schismatics, who, together with Guibert, were disturbing the Catholics through their factions.

Finally, however, as Peter the Deacon relates in the continuation of Leo of Ostia, Book III, Chapter 66 of the *Cassinese Chronicle*, all the faithful men of the Church and of blessed Peter who were in Rome—whether from the clergy, the nobility, or the people—assembled in the diaconia of Saint Lucy. There they began, with many prayers and tears, to press Desiderius, as they had already done openly and privately once, twice, and repeatedly, not to permit the Roman Church, which had elected him to the pontificate, to remain deprived of a shepherd any longer amid so great a crisis.

But they pleaded in vain. Therefore they asked him at least to judge who appeared suitable to him for undertaking so great a burden. Desiderius willingly accepted this condition and, after consulting Cencius, consul of the Romans, immediately nominated Odo, bishop of Ostia, as pontiff.

Everyone’s votes were going to Odo when, suddenly, as that author says, one of the cardinals—whose name he does not report—shouted that this election was contrary to the canons and declared that he would by no means consent, while the others opposed him and argued that, given the circumstances and the necessity, this course ought to be tolerated.

But they accomplished nothing, for the others could not bend him to their opinion. Peter does not state what contrary to the sacred canons was found in Odo’s election. Yet, if I judge correctly, that anonymous cardinal could have objected to nothing other than the fact that, since Odo was already bishop of Ostia, he could not be transferred to the governance of the Roman Church without some violation of the canons, which commonly prohibited the translation of bishops from one church to another.

What the Church forbids in order to restrain the excessive ambition of avaricious bishops, or their immoderate desire to rule the clergy, it sometimes permits, and indeed occasionally requires, when necessity presses—as it certainly did then, amid such great confusion [Col. 0029A].

Nevertheless, the stubborn persistence of that one man in his own opinion prevailed. All the others were forced to yield to him, and once again, by unanimous decision, they agreed upon the election of Desiderius. Immediately, whether he wished it or not, they proclaimed him pontiff under the name of Victor III, clothing him in a red cloak on Pentecost Day of the year 1086. But since he had not yet fully consented to his election, his consecration was postponed until the following year.

### XX. Odo consecrates Victor III
[Col. 0029B] In the following year (1087), after a council had been held at Capua, to which our Odo of Ostia had invited Hugh of Lyons, Victor, overcome by the prayers and tears of the bishops and princes who were with him, accepted the pontifical insignia which, immediately after his election, he had laid aside on returning to Cassino. On 21 March, Palm Sunday, clothed in purple and preceded by the cross, he solemnly proceeded in public. After celebrating the Paschal festivities on Monte Cassino, he went to Rome, where, after Guibert had been expelled from the Vatican basilica, he was consecrated there by our Odo of Ostia, Peter of Albano, and the bishops of Porto and Tusculum, along with other Roman bishops, and with cardinals, bishops, and abbots assisting. According to the authority of the same Peter, this took place on the Sunday after the Ascension, 9 May. Bertoldus, however, says that he was consecrated at the end of May, but this is perhaps a copyist’s error, and “at the beginning of May” should be read.

### XXI. Odo’s defense against Hugh of Lyons

Hugh of Lyons accuses Odo of bad faith, alleging that he had ordained Victor contrary to his own judgment and to the promises made to Hugh and others, after yielding to human weakness. He discusses the matter at greater length in two letters to Countess Matilda, whom he attempts to win over and draw to his side. In those letters he recounts what he had plotted against Victor. “When,” he says, “the bishop of Ostia had proceeded with us in complete agreement, once he saw that the abbot”—for so he was accustomed to call Victor—“was intending, through the power of Prince Jordan, to go to Rome to be consecrated, fearing perhaps that he would be deprived of his dignity if the consecration were performed by others first, he turned on the day of battle; forgetting his purpose and the pledge he had made to us—something of which I am ashamed to speak—he made peace with the abbot and showed him every mark of reverence as though he were pope.”

Yet what Hugh censures in Odo on the occasion of this ordination seems deserving of praise. For even if there was perhaps something blameworthy in Victor—something I would not dare to assert—it nevertheless could not have been of such importance that an election already completed and approved by everyone, indeed even by Hugh himself and his followers (as Hugh himself admits, and as Victor reproached him with at the Council of Benevento), ought to have been invalidated; especially since, had Odo attempted this, there was a danger that the Church, already shaken by so many storms, would on that account be afflicted by a new schism. Therefore the prudent man rightly judged it preferable to assent to Victor’s election, made and confirmed by the unanimous consent of all Catholics, rather than, under the appearance of greater zeal for discipline, stir up new disturbances.

For this reason Hugh himself and Cardinal Richard, abbot of Marseilles and formerly an apostolic legate—the only men who seem to have opposed Victor’s ordination—were rightly deprived of communion at the Council of Benevento by Victor, while the other Fathers approved this judgment by their decision and authority, as Peter reports in the *Chronicle of Cassino*, because they had separated themselves from the unanimity of the other Catholics. Indeed, Matilda, whom Hugh had solicited in two letters, could not be withdrawn from obedience to Victor.

The conduct of Hugh himself in this matter, as also of Richard, sufficiently and more than sufficiently shows that they had yielded to human weakness in the very matter for which they reproached Odo. For, as Victor himself explained before the Fathers at the Council of Benevento, before Victor had consented to his election, Hugh and Richard had hypocritically urged him to accept the pontificate and had then promised him complete submission. They hoped that he would persevere in his refusal and that, in this way, one or the other of them would attain the pontificate, which Victor stubbornly declined. But when Victor finally gave his consent, leaving them no hope of attaining this dignity unless Victor himself were expelled, the fire of ambition that had been kindled, as the pontiff said at the council just mentioned, burst forth like a furnace disgorging its flames. Frustrated in their expectation, they nearly broke into open schism and dared to criticize Odo and load him with abuse because he had ordained Victor.

But since they later washed away this blemish by returning to the unity of the Church, and since Hugh himself, in his second letter to Matilda, asserted that he had never withdrawn from communion with the other Catholics, I shall spare them a longer discussion of this fault, lest I seem to have wished to inflict pain upon their ashes and bones. I merely note that one of Hugh’s two letters to Matilda was inserted by Hugh of Flavigny in the *Chronicle of Verdun*, while the other was published from a manuscript of the monastery of Cluny in volume II of Acher’s *Spicilegium*. Finally, the acts of the Council of Benevento may be read in Peter the Deacon, book III of the *Chronicle of Cassino*. As for the letters of Urban which Hugh said had been shown to him by Hugh of Cluny—letters in which the pontiff warned the Cluniacs to withdraw from communion with Hugh himself and with Richard, abbot of Marseilles—we have nowhere seen them.

### XXII. The death of Victor III. Odo is designated as vicar and successor

Victor did not long retain the dignity which he had accepted with such reluctance. For when he fell ill at Benevento, where he was holding a council, and sensed that the day of his death was approaching, he immediately returned to Cassino. There, having appointed Oderisius in his place to govern the monastery, he summoned the bishops [Col. 0031A] and cardinals who were in his company and warned and instructed them, as Peter relates in book III, chapter 73, of the *Chronicle of Cassino, to elect Odo, bishop of Ostia, as Roman pontiff after his own death, which he did not doubt would soon occur, in accordance with the wish of the dying Gregory:

“Because he was present, he took him by the hand and handed him over to the other bishops, saying: ‘Receive him and place him upon the Roman see; and regard him as taking my place in all things, until you are able to do so.’”

Shortly afterward, in September, Victor died. But the election of his successor was postponed until the following year because of the difficulties of the times.

### XXIII. The election of Urban III. He writes letters about it, several of which survive

[Col. 0031B] About six months after Victor’s death, the matter of his successor was finally taken up. A meeting was held for this purpose at Terracina, a city of Roman Campania, in March 1088. There, with the unanimous agreement and acclamation of all the Catholics, Odo, bishop of Ostia, was proclaimed Roman pontiff under the name Urban II.

Everyone praised the fact that Odo’s nobility of birth, gentleness of spirit, graciousness of character, innocence of life, prudence and skill in handling affairs, unconquerable steadfastness in adversity, and the other virtues appropriate to a great pontiff were known to all. Ordericus Vitalis, in book VIII, writes that in those dark times he had been appointed by the God of Israel as a great leader against the foreigners, to whom the Lord entrusted the tower of David with its fortifications against Damascus. He represents him as follows:

“He was a Gaul by nation, distinguished by nobility and gentleness, a citizen of Reims, a Cluniac monk, of moderate age, large in body, discerning in modesty, pre-eminent in religion, and outstanding in wisdom and eloquence.”

Domnizo also praises Urban’s election in book II, chapter 7, where he calls him a rhetorician on account of his eloquence: “He spoke,” he says, “as Solomon did, and sat as a just lion.” Platina asserts that he was worthy, by his learning and holiness of life, of any high office.

Bertoldus deserves pardon, however, because, being situated in Germany, he wrote against the testimony of other authors and against Urban’s own letters that this election had taken place at Rome; nevertheless, he does not differ from the others in praising this pontiff. “At Rome,” he says, “the cardinals and bishops, together with the rest of the Catholic clergy and people, ordained Otto, bishop of Ostia, a man renowned for religion and learning, as pope CLXI; and they gave him the name Urban II, on 12 March.” The election of Urban is recorded on this same day in the brief chronicle of Cava under the Paschal cycles, and indeed also in Urban’s own letters written concerning the matter.

Bertoldus further testifies that the new pontiff immediately after his election sent encyclical letters throughout the Christian world. “On the following day,” he says, “having sent letters to all Catholics, he both announced his ordination to everyone and declared that in all things he would observe the footsteps of his predecessor, Pope Gregory of blessed memory.” Domnizo, book II, chapter 3, bears witness that Urban wrote to Countess Matilda at that time, or certainly shortly afterward, exhorting her to persevere in defending the cause of the apostolic see against the schismatics.

Ordericus, in the work cited above, further relates that Urban sent not only letters but also legates to various regions, in order to confirm the Christian princes in faith and unity. “Trusting in the Lord of heaven,” says this author, “who does not leave the rod of sinners upon the lot of the righteous, he sent legates and letters of Roman authority to the Franks, Greeks, and other peoples established throughout the world, so that they might remain unshakably firm in the Catholic faith and carefully guard against every division from the law of God and from the body of Christ, which is the Church.”

Several of those letters, written by Urban immediately after his election, survive. One is addressed to the metropolitan of Salzburg and to the other Catholic bishops of Germany, whom he urges, in brief but highly effective words, to persevere in obedience to the Catholic Church. He wrote another to the bishops of Vienne in the province of Gaul. After informing them of his election, he warns them to assist their metropolitan church, which was suffering serious losses because of the prolonged vacancy of its see.

On the same occasion and at the same time, the pontiff wrote to Hugh, abbot of Cluny, formerly his teacher in monastic discipline. In words of the greatest tenderness, he urged him to come to Rome as soon as it was lawful for him to do so, in order to bring him assistance in bearing so great a burden. Marlotus conjectures, from a charter issued at the beginning of the following year, that Raynaldus, bishop of Reims, received a similar letter from Urban, although the letter itself has perished. In that charter Raynaldus testifies that, at Urban’s invitation, he was going to Rome.

It is uncertain whether the new pontiff also wrote to the bishops of the English, whose chief see was then held by the blessed Lanfranc, archbishop of Canterbury. From the *Deeds of Saint Anselm*, however, it may be inferred that before the election of that saint Urban was neither accepted nor rejected in England.

### XXIV. Everyone loves Urban

[Col. 0032D] Such was the esteem in which Urban was held by everyone that no one failed to love him, and no one willingly failed to acknowledge him as the true and excellent pontiff, except the Emperor Henry and his followers. Yet through his prudence and gentleness he so won them over that most of them were ashamed to oppose so lovable and holy a man.

Thus, toward the end of his life, scarcely anyone remained who adhered to Pope Guibert. “Only,” says Ordericus, “Henry, prince of the Germans, and his attendants adhered to Guibert; but the Gauls, the English, and nearly all the other peoples throughout the world piously obeyed Urban.” Indeed, according to Bertoldus, the Pisans, Genoese, and many others from Italy, after defeating one of the African kings, made him tributary to the apostolic see. The *Pisan Chronicle* mentions this expedition, recording the capture of two strongly fortified cities on the feast of Saint Sixtus.

### XXV. A detailed account of his election from the *Chronicle of Cassino*

Until now we have praised various authors who, as occasion arose, wrote brief accounts of Urban’s election. It is now appropriate to present an excellent description of it, which Peter the Deacon inserted in book IV, chapter 2, of the *Chronicle of Cassino*. There he explains the entire sequence, with each circumstance, at length and in detail.

> “After Victor’s death, great sorrow and despair seized all of us who belonged to our party; and they scarcely knew what they should do or how they should concern themselves with the Church. Since the bishops were scattered in every direction, frequent messengers and repeated legates, sent both by the Romans [Col. 0033B] and by those from beyond the Alps and by Countess Matilda to those same bishops, urged and entreated them all to come together and strive to provide a head for Christianity [lacuna] the members would not fail the head with God’s help.
>
> “At last, therefore, having once again gathered together, they, along with our abbot Oderisius, sent letters to the Roman clergy and laity, the faithful of Saint Peter, asking that as many of them as could do so should come to Terracina during the first week of Lent; those who could not come were to convey their assent by their own letters, in the person whom they themselves should elect by unanimous vote.
>
