> “They likewise sent letters to all the bishops and abbots living throughout Campania, the Principate, and Apulia, asking that whoever could do so should come in person to the aforesaid place and at the appointed time, without a canonical excuse; those who could not come were to make every effort to transmit their consent either through suitable persons or by letter.
>
> “This was done. On the fourth day of the first week of Lent, namely 8 March, there gathered at Terracina, a city of Campania, together with the Roman bishops and cardinals named above and with our abbot Oderisius, forty archbishops, bishops, and abbots from different regions. From the city of Rome, John, bishop of Porto, brought the legation of all the cardinals and clergy who favored only the Catholic party; Benedict the prefect brought, by letter, the legation and unanimous consent of all the faithful laity.
>
> “Some of the legates from beyond the Alps and of Countess Matilda were also present, earnestly asking that, with the help and grace of the Holy Spirit, they should devote themselves to the matter for which they had assembled, so that they might carry joyful news back to those by whom they had been sent.
>
> “On the following day, therefore, everyone assembled together at the episcopal residence of the aforesaid city, in the church of the blessed prince of the apostles and holy levite of Christ, Caesarius. When they had taken their seats, the bishop of Tusculum rose in their midst and related in due order everything that Pope Gregory had previously established concerning the ordering of the Church and what Pope Victor had afterward established, together with the reason why all of them had then assembled in that place.
>
> “Then the bishop of Porto and the prefect Benedict rose and likewise reported the legation and consent of the faithful clergy and laity from Rome concerning this matter: namely, that whomever they should then promote to this office by unanimous vote, they would all receive and establish upon the apostolic see with equal and similar consent.
>
> “When the abbot of this monastery, the archbishop of Capua, and finally the others who had assembled had praised what had been rightly done and said . . . they finally determined by common agreement that during those three days—that is, Thursday, Friday, and Saturday—they would observe a three-day fast specifically for this purpose, in abstinence, prayer, and almsgiving, seeking through continuous prayers that the person worthy of so great a dignity might be divinely shown to them.
>
> “On Sunday, therefore, very early in the morning, they all assembled again in the same church. After they had discussed among themselves certain matters concerning this affair, three cardinal bishops who were the heads of that council—namely, the bishops of Porto, Tusculum, and Albano—rose and ascended the ambo. When silence had been made, they declared with one voice that it pleased them to elect Bishop Odo as Roman pontiff.
>
> “When, as custom requires, they asked whether this also pleased everyone, suddenly, with wondrous and complete unanimity, all loudly proclaimed that it pleased them and that they all judged him worthy to be pope of the apostolic see.
>
> “Then, when the bishop of Albano declared that it pleased them that he be called Urban, everyone immediately rose, removed his woolen cape, clothed him in a purple one, and, with acclamation and invocation of the Holy Spirit, led him to the altar of the blessed apostle Peter and placed him upon the pontifical throne on 12 March. After the same pontiff had solemnly celebrated Mass, they all returned joyfully to their own places, giving thanks to God.”

Thus Peter the Deacon; these words should be joined with what Urban himself says in the letters cited above.

### XXVI. The pontiff is healed by a miracle at Cassino; from there he promotes John the deacon

The same Peter relates in book IV, chapter 5, that after his election Urban visited the holy mountain of Cassino and that there, through the merits of Saint Benedict, he was freed from the severe pain in his side by which he was often afflicted and from which he was then suffering intensely. Peter adds that this miracle was performed by Saint Benedict as testimony to the presence of his own body at Cassino; “for,” he says, “the pontiff seemed to doubt this matter” (*Bullar. Casin.*, vol. I, p. 12).

Indeed, commonly circulated authors praise a bull of Urban issued on that occasion. But Baronius, under the year 1088, and other learned men reject it as spurious. Others may judge its authenticity; it cannot, however, be concealed that, because of its lack of chronological indicators, the implausibility of the matters contained in it, and even its very style, it has not without reason aroused suspicion of forgery among sensible and learned people.

Although we do not wish to deny that Urban recovered his health on the holy mountain through the merits of Saint Benedict, we do not accept what that author relates: that the holy Father appeared to the pontiff in order to assure him of the presence of his own body at Cassino, a presence which Urban had previously not believed. For it is clear from many other passages that Peter frequently inserted such little stories into his narratives on the occasion of miracles genuinely performed by Saint Benedict, although they cannot be reconciled with the truth of historical events.

If we believe the same author, Urban visited the monastery of Cassino again shortly before the synod of Troia. “At that time,” he says in chapter 7, “the aforesaid Pope Urban, coming again to these parts, ordained John Cajetan, a monk of this place—that is, of Cassino—as a deacon in the Lateran patriarchate.”

But John’s promotion, as Angelo de Nuce observes in this passage, must be referred to Urban’s first visit. This is established by several certain and indisputable documents, which are commonly found subscribed by John in this very year, 1088, the first year of Urban’s pontificate. Certainly Urban’s letters concerning the primacy of the Church of Toledo in Spain, the Cluniac privilege, and other documents bear this designation under John’s name until 1089, when he obtained the dignity of chancellor.

### XXVII. He dedicates the monastery of Bantinum and grants it a privilege; after its violation, the privilege is reaffirmed

Urban was still staying at the monastery of Cassino when Roger, duke, and his brother Bohemond, the sons of Robert Guiscard, together with Ursio, abbot of the monastery of Bantinum, situated near Acerenza in Apulia, invited him to consecrate the church of that place in honor of the blessed Mary. After the pontiff had done so, he granted the same monastery very extensive privileges through the intervention of those princes and of their counts and barons. These are explained more fully in the charter issued concerning the matter.

That privilege occupies the first place among Urban’s letters in the Labbean edition of the councils, but under this false title: “Concerning the church of Saint Mary of the monastery of Cassino, consecrated and endowed with privileges by him.” The letters of Paschal II confirming this very privilege of Urban are found in Ughellus, volume VII of *Italia sacra*, where he discusses the archbishops of Acerenza.

Moreover, when certain Apulian nobles—undoubtedly Roger and Bohemund being occupied elsewhere—harassed the monks of that place and even plundered the monastery’s property and documents, Urban wrote about the matter to Roger and his brother, asking them by their authority to restrain those rash men. He further threatened to subject such sacrilegious men to anathema unless they quickly came to their senses.

The pious princes obeyed the pope’s warnings and protected the monastery with a new privilege, subscribed by them and by other counts and noblemen, so that the sacred place might suffer no loss from the destruction of the charters and documents that had perished.

In that new instrument Roger and his brother Bohemund, among other things, congratulate themselves that through their efforts the supreme pontiff himself had consecrated the church of this monastery with his own hands. They then praise the privilege granted by that same pontiff, which, they testify, had been confirmed in the presence of thirty-two Catholic Fathers, each leaning upon a pastoral staff, and of an innumerable crowd of counts and barons.

And, so that nothing might be lacking to the security of the place, they explain under what conditions it had been granted by the pontiff:

> “The lord pope absolutely refused to consecrate the monastery until we had received it and all its possessions under the special and complete care and protection of ourselves and our heirs, and until the neighboring counts and barons who were present, bound by evangelical oaths at apostolic command, promised that they would everywhere preserve perpetual peace, protection, and general liberty for the same monastery and all its possessions.”

They then list various donations made by themselves and confirm and increase the monastery’s immunities.

Since the original privilege granted by Urban had been carried off together with the other charters and could no longer be found, the prudent princes arranged for another authentic copy to be made, which would possess the place and authority of the first. Their words deserve to be inserted here:

> “We,” they say, “moved inwardly by grief and outwardly covered with shame, because the precious apostolic instrument established at our entreaty, the product of our proper vigilance, and stolen in our time, has until now been impossible to find, have ordered this present similar instrument of release to be written by the hand of our notary, Master Theodosius, faithfully according to the copy we found made from it, with our counts and barons jointly bearing witness to the same memory; and we have confirmed it with a leaden seal impressed with our customary device, etc.”

These matters are found in Baronius under the year 1090, where this instrument, issued at Canusium in July, in the thirteenth indiction, is given in full, together with the subscriptions of Roger, Bohemund, and the other nobles.

### XXVIII. Concerning the false instrument of the dedication of Cava

From these facts it is easy to understand how far Ughellus departed from the truth in volume VII of *Italia sacra*, where, in his catalogue of the bishops of Acerenza, he attempts to assign the dedication of the monastery of Bantinum to the year 1093 on the basis of an old document, as he believes.

For although we do not deny that Urban may have visited Cassino in 1093 or at other times, as Peter the Deacon suggests in the continuation of the *Chronicle of Cassino*, and may even have met the aforementioned princes in Apulia on several occasions, nevertheless, if the documents praised in the preceding section are certain—and there can scarcely be any doubt that they are—the celebration of this dedication can hardly be postponed beyond the year 1088.

For in 1090, when Roger and Bohemund’s second instrument was issued, a considerable and indeed quite lengthy period must already have elapsed since the celebrated dedication. This would have given the nobles of Apulia time not only to forget their promises and plunder the property and charters of the monastery of Bantinum, but also to give Urban time, at the urging of Abbot Ursio, to admonish the aforesaid princes to suppress such a great scandal by their authority. In fact, according to their charter, they had already done so in July of that same year, 1090, after assembling the noblemen of the entire province.

It may now be useful to state what we think of this document of Ughellus. It seems to us to have nothing to do with the monastery of Bantinum, but either to have been fabricated by some rogue or certainly to refer to the monastery of Cava.

Indeed, no one knows the monastery of Saint Mary of Pauso, commonly called Doventuum, which is mentioned in that charter. Ughellus, followed by Lubinus in the *Catalogue of the Abbeys of Italy* and perhaps by certain other recent writers, could only conjecture that it was the monastery of Bantinum.

But if this document, whatever its character, is compared with the privileges of the monastery of Cava and with the history of its dedication, anyone can easily see that it was patched together from them. This is proved by the mention of the Most Holy Trinity, the identical indulgences granted in both places, the fact that both dedications took place in September, the same favors granted to both places and to the Church of Compostela, the fact that in both cases a bull in favor of the new dedication was issued at Salerno in October, and other matters which there is no opportunity to enumerate here. We shall discuss the dedication of Cava below, under the year 1092.

### XXIX. Urban’s journey to Sicily

That Urban crossed over to Sicily in the same year is testified not only by more recent authors but also by Geoffrey Malaterra, a Benedictine monk and a careful historian of those times, who, at Roger’s urging, wrote the history of Count Roger’s deeds in four books.

In book IV, chapter 13, he relates that Roger, count of Sicily, the brother of Robert Guiscard and therefore uncle of the other Roger, duke of Apulia, and of Bohemund, besieged Bucera, a city of Sicily, at the beginning of April 1088. There he received Urban’s legates with sealed letters in which the pontiff invited him to come as quickly as possible to Troia, where Urban himself was hastening, since he wished to confer with him about important matters.

The count appeared on the appointed day and, when the conversation had ended, dismissed the pontiff with many gifts. Geoffrey does not explicitly state what business was discussed between them, unless it was perhaps the matter he subsequently relates concerning the emperor of Constantinople, Alexius Comnenus. A few days earlier—that is, immediately after his election to the pontificate—Urban had sent the abbot of Crypta Ferrata, Nicholas, and the deacon Roger as legates to admonish the emperor with a fatherly rebuke because, in the provinces subject to him, he compelled Latin priests to celebrate with leavened bread after abandoning unleavened bread.

The same author adds that the emperor humbly accepted the pontiff’s rebuke and, through the same legates, who had already returned from their journey, invited Urban by letters written on tablets in golden letters to come to Greece within a year and a half, so that the matter might be discussed in a council to be held at Constantinople and a firm peace might thus be established in the Church by the common agreement of both peoples.

Roger advised Urban to do this, according to the same author. But the pontiff, fearing that in his absence the Guibertines, who were powerful at Rome, would completely prevail, did not dare undertake the journey. Instead, he again sent the same or other legates in his place to the emperor, and they reached some sort of peace with him in the following year.

We infer that some extremely urgent and unforeseen matter of great importance occasioned this journey to Sicily from the fact that the pontiff, who had been at Cassino only a few days earlier and had even gone to Apulia with Roger and Bohemund, the nephews of Count Roger through his brother, to dedicate the church at Bantinum, without thinking of anything else, returned to Terracina and suddenly, dismissing everyone, crossed to Sicily on a long and exhausting journey, as Geoffrey relates, in order to confer with Roger. That count, having captured Syracuse that year, according to Lupus Protospata, was then, in April, besieging Bucera, as we have said from Geoffrey.

Authors commonly cited by Rocchus Pirrus in *Sicilia sacra* say that Urban on this occasion celebrated Mass in a certain underground chapel of the cathedral church of Troia, and that an inscription was placed there in memory of the event, forbidding women thereafter to enter the place.

### XXX. He sends the pallium to Anselm, archbishop of Milan, and so forth

At that time the Church of Milan was enjoying relief under the pontificate of Anselm, a Catholic man. A few years earlier he had been appointed in place of the schismatic Tedaldus and had received the staff from the king. For this reason—or, as Ripamontius says, for some other uncertain cause—he had incurred the displeasure of Pope Gregory. Later, however, Urban pardoned his repentant guilt and, after restoring and confirming him in the see which he had voluntarily relinquished, sent him the pallium through Cardinal Herimannus, together with a letter whose only surviving fragment is found in the *Life of Urban* and will be included among Urban’s letters.

Urban acted almost similarly toward Henry, bishop of Suessiones. After accepting the investiture of his bishopric from King Philip, Henry came to Rome and voluntarily renounced his dignity before the pontiff. Although Henry resisted and was unwilling, Urban ordered him to return to his see, after receiving an oath that he would never communicate with those who had been excommunicated by the apostolic see, nor attend the consecrations of those who had occupied bishoprics or abbeys unlawfully.

Pandulfus relates that the same thing was done with the bishop of Beauvais, and Platina also testifies to it. But I return to Anselm of Milan.

Urban wrote to him concerning the reconciliation of those who had fallen away. From this letter Ivo, part IV, chapter 407, excerpted a decretal letter, which has been published in various places but greatly expanded from the commonly circulated version of Anselm of Lucca. It will be given among Urban’s letters, together with two other canons attributed in the Council of Beauvais of 1114 likewise to our pontiff. The first of these is addressed to the clergy, the second to the people of Milan.

Although some believe that both canons should be attributed to Alexander II, it did not seem appropriate to deny them to Urban, since perhaps both pontiffs applied exactly the same remedy to the same evil. Nor should it seem surprising that one and the same canon was promulgated by two pontiffs.

For the canon concerning the sons of priests, distinction 56, chapter 1, is largely repeated in chapter 11, beginning “Nisi aut,” which is assigned to Urban in both places and in fact occurs among the decrees of the Council of Melfi and of Urban’s other councils. Nevertheless, in the Council of Beauvais mentioned above it is said to be Gregory VI’s and Urban II’s; and in Ivo, part VI, chapter 410, Gregory VII’s and Urban II’s.

I once thought that the same judgment could be made concerning the canon *Clerico jaciente*, distinction 50, chapter 37, which was said to have been excerpted from Urban’s letter to Guernerius of Narbonne, who had died before Urban became pontiff. But afterward I learned from learned men that an error had entered the title and that it should read “to Guernerius of Merseburg,” who is in fact recorded as having lived in the time of Urban II. We shall therefore include that canon in the appendix under its genuine title.

In what year this letter to Guernerius was written is unclear. Bucelinus observes that Guernerius supported Gregory VII; nevertheless, among the Catholic bishops who subscribed to the Council of Quedlinburg in 1085, Bernard of Merseburg is listed. Whether this was the same man who was called Wernarius or Guernerius is uncertain, since Bucelinus does not list Bernard.

### XXXI. The Church of Cremona is endowed

[Col. 0039C]

In this same year Urban endowed the collegiate church of Saint Agatha at Cremona, which Gregory VII had enlarged, assigning to it the revenues of the churches of Saint Valerius and Saint Christopher, situated near the same city, as Joseph Bresceanus reports in the manuscript *Chronicle of Cremona* which we have before us.

The same pontiff is said by Merula to have changed the secular clergy of this basilica into regular canons around the year 1090; later, however, they returned to the secular state.

In this same year Urban also granted another privilege to the monastery of Santa Croce at Sassovivo, in the territory of Foligno. In the chronicle of that place, it is said to have been addressed to Mainardus, its founder and first abbot. We were not able to obtain a copy of it, nor of another privilege said to have been granted in this same year to Peter, abbot of Carrofium among the Pictones in Gaul, although, if I am not mistaken, the latter is none other than the privilege granted to the same monastery in 1096, which we shall discuss in its proper place.

### XXXII. Spanish affairs. Disturbances in the Church of Iria. The date of the Council of Husillos. The primacy of the Church of Toledo restored

As for Spanish affairs, the Catholic faith there was daily strengthened by new advances through the courage of the Christian princes, who, after expelling the Moors, recovered notable cities and sometimes entire provinces.

The author of the *Brief Account of Aragonese Affairs*, published by Pistorio in volume III of *Hispania illustrata*, states that Urban granted Alfonso, king of Aragon, his successors, and the nobles of the kingdom permission to receive the tithes in the territories they recovered from the Moors, except in episcopal sees and dignities.

While Urban was seated [on the papal throne], it was not Alfonso but Sancho and Peter who held Aragon; therefore, if I am not mistaken, this must be understood of Peter, to whom Urban granted this authority. Even if it is said to have been granted also to King Alfonso, this must refer to Aldefonsus or Alfonso, king of León and Castile, who at that time stood foremost among the Spanish kings. Having recovered Toledo from the barbarians several years earlier, he had assumed the title of emperor of Spain and arranged that Bernard, a Cluniac monk who then presided over the monastery of Sahagún, should be appointed archbishop of that city. This was the occasion for renewing the ancient splendor of that Church, which the prolonged domination of the barbarians had obscured.

For several years King Sancho had placed over the Church of Iria, to which the city of Compostela was then subject, a man of no little distinction named Diego. But, as the author of the *History of Compostela* says, he was so entangled in external affairs that he did not attend sufficiently to those within. Alfonso, moved—I do not know by what circumstance—cast him into prison. This caused great commotion and immense disturbances in that Church. Since everything was therefore falling into ruin, and upright men could not calmly endure the disaster of that most celebrated Church, which already then gloried in possessing the relics of blessed James, Alfonso, in order to remove from himself this injury, attempted to intrude another bishop in Diego’s place.

As he thought, the synod held at Saint Mary of Fusellis offered a suitable opportunity for carrying out this plan. It had been convened at that time by Richard, abbot of Saint-Victor, who had been appointed legate of the Apostolic See in Spain by Gregory VII. Accordingly, having sent in agents to prepare the way, Diego was craftily persuaded that, if he wished to be released from his chains, he should confess himself guilty before the council; his humility would undoubtedly soften the king’s heart, and no other path to liberty remained open to him. He consented, but the matter turned out otherwise than he had expected.

For when Alfonso had come to the council, and Diego had been brought in at his command, and, exactly as he had been instructed, had handed over his staff and ring to the legate and proclaimed before all the people that he was unworthy of the episcopal dignity, the legate immediately declared that he had fallen from that dignity and granted permission for another to be substituted in his place. Without delay, Peter, abbot of Candidiniensis, who had deliberately been waiting there, was designated bishop by the king and immediately appointed and consecrated.

He governed the Church of Iria for two years—that is, until 1091—when he was deposed at the Council of León by Rainerius, legate of the Apostolic See. By then Richard, after the matter had been referred to Urban, had been deprived of his apostolic legation. We learn all this from the old *History of the Church of Compostela*, written at the beginning of the twelfth century, at the command of a second Diego, the first archbishop of Compostela, by Gerard, a member of his household.

We shall quote in the Appendix the passages relevant to our subject from this history, excerpted in 1703 from the same manuscript belonging to the most learned Ferrera, rector of a parish church in Madrid, by the distinguished John Le Grand, who was then secretary to the illustrious Abbot Estreao, while the latter was serving in that city as ambassador of the Most Christian King to Philip V, king of Spain.

Among the other matters that we learn from the same history, one is especially worthy of notice: it can readily be inferred from it when the Council of Fusellis was held, though Spanish authors have assigned it to various dates. It should not be brought down to the year 1135, as Sandoval thought, nor to the pontificate of Paschal II, as Cardinal Aguirre, of blessed memory and an ornament of the Benedictine order, believed, who confused it with the Palentian council at which, as is read in the *Life of Blessed Gerald*, the privilege of the Church of Braga was recited. Rather, it must be said to have been held at the end of 1088 or the beginning of the following year.

For Peter, the abbot who occupied the Church of Iria at the time of that council, or at least immediately after it had ended, was deposed after two years of rule by Rainerius, legate of the Apostolic See, at the Council of León, which by universal agreement must be assigned to the year 1091. With the help of this same ancient monument, several of Urban’s letters are greatly illuminated. In them the pontiff vehemently complains to King Alfonso about the captivity of the bishop of Saint James and his unlawful deposition, attempted by Richard contrary to the rules.

From this we also learn why, after removing Richard’s legation, Urban entrusted his own authority in Spain to Bernard, bishop of Toledo. The remaining matters will be explained in their proper places.

While these disturbances were agitating the Church of Galicia, Bernard—already consecrated bishop of Toledo, as most believe, and this is the more probable view, or at least designated for that see, if what others maintain is true, namely, that he was consecrated by Urban, something Bernard himself never said—came to Rome against Richard, according to Roderick of Toledo, to lodge a complaint; or, as others prefer, to visit the thresholds of the Apostles and offer his services to the new pontiff, whether that pontiff was Victor, as some say, or his successor Urban, as seems more consistent with the ancient records.

He also intended on this occasion to obtain the restoration of the ancient privileges of the Church of Toledo. This can be inferred, and indeed is explicitly stated, in Urban’s letters. Certainly the same pontiff himself testifies, in a letter to King Alfonso, that Bernard, who had arrived with letters of recommendation from the king, was kindly received by Urban. In another letter to Hugh of Cluny, Urban says that Bernard was received by him with reverence both because of the king’s recommendation and because of Bernard himself and the See of Toledo, which he governed.

Urban immediately conferred upon him primacy over the other Churches of Spain. He issued a bull at Anagni on the Ides of October of this year, in which he declares that he grants Bernard the privilege of the pallium and primacy in Spain, prompted to do so by the petitions of King Ildefonsus and by the ancient prerogatives of the Church of Toledo. Concerning this he informed not only the king and Abbot Hugh but also all the archbishops of Spain.

Although the letters that the pontiff wrote on this matter lack chronological indications, everyone can see that they belong to this year. The privilege granted above to the Church of Toledo will have its place in the Appendix, as will Gregory IX’s rescript on the same matter to Roderick, archbishop of Toledo, who had asked that pontiff for authentic copies of his Church’s privileges. We leave the publication of the letters themselves to the industrious and learned collector of papal epistles, lest repeated editions of the same matters become burdensome to learned purchasers of books.

### XXXIII. Artald of Elne Is Consecrated by Urban

At about this time a serious controversy arose in the province of Narbonne between Artald, the elect bishop of Elne, and Dalmatius, his metropolitan, who refused to consecrate him because of suspicion of simony. After suffering this rejection, Artald went to Rome, where, having been cleared by an oath of purgation, he was himself consecrated by Urban.

This was, as may be conjectured, described at greater length in Urban’s *Deeds*, from which Gratian introduced a canon concerning Artald into his *Decree*, 8, q. 3, c. 2. There he is erroneously called bishop of Arles, as we shall explain. Since this canon concerns our Urban, it is worthwhile to investigate the error somewhat more carefully.

Francis Bosquet rightly censured the editors of Gratian for thinking that *Electensis* should be read instead of *Arelatensis*. He says that it is certain that the Church of Elne, although subject from the beginning to the province of Narbonne, was not adorned with an episcopal title before the time of John XXII. Yet the learned man was no more successful in defending the common reading, which he insisted should be retained in order to prove that the bishops of Arles were once subject to the metropolitan of Narbonne.

For neither did the Church of Arles ever belong to the province or primacy of Narbonne, nor is Artald ever mentioned among the bishops of Arles. Another way must therefore be found to resolve this difficulty. The distinguished Stephen Baluze seems to have discovered it in his additions to Book V, chapter 41, of *On the Harmony of the Priesthood and the Empire*. There he advises that the canon should read: “Artald, bishop of Elne,” for the Church of Elne was at that time subject to the metropolitan of Narbonne.

Indeed, Artald was then living, and held the see of Elne toward the end of that century, as is confirmed by these words from Book IV of *Marca Hispanica*: “Mention is made of Artald, the elect bishop of Elne, on the sixth day before the Ides of May, in the twenty-seventh year of King Philip.” If this year of Philip is reckoned from the death of his father, it must be assigned to 1088. We believe that Artald was elected in that year and consecrated at Rome toward its end, after Urban, following various journeys, had already returned there.

Baluze also cites two old manuscripts: one Putean manuscript, now in the Royal Library, and another kept by himself. In these Artald is called “bishop of Alanensis.” Although this reading is corrupt, it nevertheless confirms the authentic reading that we defend. Add to these Urban’s letter, written the following year to Rainerius, legate of the Apostolic See, in which the pontiff entrusts him with the investigation of this very case, without doubt, which concerned the bishop of Elne and the metropolitan of Narbonne.

Here the entire passage from Gratian’s *Decree* should be presented, since Urban’s *Deeds*, from which this canon is said to have been taken, are no longer available.

**After the election, an oath may be given for the protection of the Church, even by the person elected (8, q. 3, c. 2).**

> “Artald, bishop of Arles [read: of Elne], suffragan of the Church of Narbonne, came to Rome to be consecrated by the lord Pope Urban. For his own archbishop was unwilling to consecrate him because, after his election, he had sworn to the canons for the preservation of the Church’s property. He was therefore consecrated by the lord Pope Urban, after first being cleared with respect to this oath.
>
> “Concerning the oath that I made to the canons of our Church after my election, I made no agreement beforehand, before I was elected. The archbishop of Narbonne omitted my consecration for no other reason than this, as far as I know, nor am I conscious of any offense on account of which he should exclude me from the sacred anointing [manuscripts: from the priesthood].”

We learn from the letter to Rainerius just mentioned that the archbishop of Narbonne protested against this ordination. Yet it is clear that he lost the case, both from this canon and from the fact that Artald afterward governed the Church of Elne peacefully for a long time and attended various councils, especially the Council of Nîmes, where the pontiff himself was present among the other Catholic bishops, as Baluze proves in the places cited.

Moreover, the episcopal see of Elne—or Helenensis—after the various vicissitudes described by Baluze in his notes on Gratian, was transferred to Perpignan and finally, several years ago, withdrawn from the jurisdiction of the archbishop of Tarragona and restored to its ancient metropolitan, Narbonne.

### XXXIV. The Cluniac Privilege

Urban, who was at Anagni on the Ides of October, as is evident from the privilege of the Church of Toledo, returned to Rome shortly afterward. There, on the first day of the Kalends of November, he granted a very extensive privilege to Saint Hugh and his monastery of Cluny.

Among other matters worthy of notice, the pontiff acknowledges that he is indebted to the holy abbot and his monastery because through him he received the rudiments of monastic religion and, in that place, was reborn through a second grace of the Holy Spirit. By these words he clearly calls the monastic profession another baptism.

### XXXV. The Bishop of Maguelone Subject by Special Right to the Roman Pontiff

In the following month the pontiff confirmed to Bishop Gotofred the Church of Maguelone together with the county of Substantion, in a letter issued at Rome on the nineteenth day before the Kalends of January of this year.

Why Gotofred then needed confirmation of the Church of Maguelone, although he had obtained that see long before Urban became pontiff, we learn from Anthony de Verdala, bishop of the same Church, in his little work *On the Succession of the Bishops of Maguelone*, in Labbe’s first volume of the *New Bibliotheca*. That author reports that Peter, count of Melgueil, on the Kalends of May in 1085, gave Pope Gregory VII every right that he possessed in the bishopric of Maguelone, together with the county of Substantion, into the hands of Peter, bishop of Albano and legate of the Apostolic See, and of Gotofred, who was already bishop of that Church.

The pontiff, however, having accepted the donation, returned the county to Peter and his successors as a fief, under an oath of loyalty and an annual payment of one ounce of the finest gold. But every right that the Apostolic See had acquired by this donation he transferred to Gotofred. From that time Gotofred exercised the pontiff’s authority in this matter, and his Church was placed under the special protection of the Roman See.

Thus the counts of Substantion became feudal dependents of the bishops of Maguelone, while the bishops themselves became specially attached to the Roman pontiffs. All this provided the basis for the confirmation bull under discussion.

Later Gotofred bestowed many churches and possessions of his Church upon the canons, in order to encourage them to embrace the common life and the rule of Saint Augustine. The same author shows that in this matter he was assisted by Urban’s authority. He observes that on this occasion Urban granted Gotofred and his successors the power to persist in the effort that Gotofred’s predecessor had attempted in vain: namely, to convert the clergy to a canonical and religious life by argument, exhortation, and rebuke.

### XXXVI. He Commends Guido to the People of Vienne

In this same year, as we learn from the *Chronicle of the Bishops of Vienne*, published by Burno, archbishop of that city, the people of Vienne, after a prolonged delay of several years—the delay of which Urban complains in his letter to the bishops of that province—elected Guido as archbishop. He belonged to the family of the princes of Burgundy.

Guido immediately approached Urban, was kindly received by him, and was retained for some time in the Roman curia. When he later returned to Vienne, the pontiff commended him in letters addressed to all the orders of that city. The sequence of events suggests that these letters should be assigned to the end of this year.

### XXXVII. He Grants Privileges to Benedict, Bishop of Nantes

At about the same time, as appears likely, Urban replied to Benedict, bishop of Nantes, who, as we conjecture, had congratulated Urban upon his recent election. He confirmed the privileges of Benedict’s Church and of the monastery of Kemperlé, over which Benedict also presided as abbot.

But he postponed to another time the canonization of Saint Garloesius, which the same bishop had urgently requested, because the matter had to be considered in a plenary synod.

### XXXVIII. He Spends the Winter at Rome Amid Great Hardships

The pontiff spent the whole winter of this year at Rome, but in such great difficulties that scarcely were his necessities supplied. Guibert, together with the men of his faction, harassed the papal party so severely that they could not even breathe safely.

Gerohus, in Tegnagel, reports that Urban was held captive in a certain tower and later freed from it by Robert Guiscard. But this author carelessly attributes to Urban what happened to Gregory VII. More certain is the testimony of Domnizo, which we shall include in our Appendix from Book II, chapter 3. He says that a certain Odo of Tullières had been placed by Guibert in command of his own forces so that he might continually attack Urban by war.

No one, however, wrote better on this matter than Pandulf in his *Life of Gelasius II*. Gelasius was John Caetani, whom Urban created cardinal deacon and chancellor. Pandulf praises his steadfastness highly, especially because he never abandoned the pontiff, though he was almost overwhelmed by so many and such great calamities. It is worthwhile to quote the author’s words here:

> “In those days, therefore—not, as I believe, without an oracle of the consoling Spirit—Brother John Caetani, already a young man and a monk of Monte Cassino, was summoned by the entire Catholic Roman Church and by Pope Urban, who presided over it, to aid and advise amid such great disturbances and to share in the burden of care, and so forth.
>
> “Lord Urban . . . summoned him when the Alemannic persecution was impending, being so constrained by Guibert into the depths of misery that, among other things, he was scarcely sustained against the plots of his enemies by a certain most famous and illustrious man, Peter Leo, at Rome on the island of Lycaonia, between the two notable bridges of the Tiber; he was supported by the alms of Roman matrons and sometimes of poor women.”

If I am not mistaken, or at least, as we have already said, to the beginning of his pontificate may be assigned Domnizo’s verses from Book II, chapter 3. In them Urban, attacked by the Guibertines, is said to have written to Matilda, asking her, mindful of Gregory’s instructions, not to abandon the cause of the Church. The same author explains in what manly spirit that most courageous woman acted, and we shall discuss this in its proper place.

### XXXIX. Affairs in Germany and Henry’s Situation. Translation of Saint Stanislaus

However serious the disturbances in Rome and Italy—disturbances that the Henricians and the supporters of the pseudo-pope Wibert had stirred up at this time—the turmoil in Germany was no less severe. Cities and provinces were divided among various factions, and Henry himself repeatedly fell into danger of his life and empire.

Welf, duke of Bavaria, who opposed him, had occupied Augsburg at the beginning of this year, as Trithemius reports, having captured Sigefrid, the usurper of that city’s bishopric. At the same time, another schismatic who had previously invaded the see of Worms, repenting of his action, abandoned the bishopric, withdrew to Hirsau, and became a monk there.

Meanwhile Count Hugh of Egentheim recovered Alsace. When the people of Metz heard that Urban had been substituted in Victor’s place, and that this had been proclaimed in Germany, they expelled Bruno, the pseudo-bishop who, after the second invader—now repentant—had attempted to occupy that see. They openly declared that they would never receive any other bishop except Hermann, their true and legitimate pastor, who for that reason was being held captive by the Henricians in Tuscany.

Bruno consequently became so despised by everyone, as Bertold reports, that the following year he was compelled to return to the Catholic party.

In this year, or certainly the following one, as miracles at the tomb of blessed Stanislaus, bishop of Kraków, became more frequent, his sacred body was solemnly transferred on September 27 from the church of Saint Michael to the cathedral church. Innocent IV later decreed him the honors of the saints, and from then onward he has been celebrated among the martyrs. This is recounted at greater length by Longinus, the author of his Life.

Those prosperous events, however, were disturbed by the deaths of several holy men. Among them was Burchard, bishop of Halberstadt, whom the schismatics murdered with monstrous sacrilege on the eighth day before the Ides of April. He was soon followed in death by Wigold, bishop of Augsburg; Bernhard, formerly master of the schools of the Church of Constance; the distinguished teacher Bertold; and, most notably, Gebehard, archbishop and indefatigable champion of the Catholic Church of Salzburg. Urban had written his first letter after becoming pontiff to Gebehard and his colleagues concerning his election.

Gebehard died on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of July, as is recorded in his Life, published at Augsburg. He wrote a book against the schismatics, which Tegnagel presents in full in his collection.

Besides this, after the Saxons had been reconciled with Henry, Hermann, who had been elected king against him, was forced to withdraw into Lorraine. He died there shortly afterward and was buried at Metz. Later, however, circumstances changed, and the Saxons again rebelled against Henry. Stripped of his royal insignia, he was shamefully defeated and driven into flight.

Bertold reports this at the end of the year, writing that after a two-day siege Henry was forced to acknowledge that he was under anathema and to seek reconciliation. This reconciliation was neither long-lasting nor sincere. Shortly afterward, having forgotten his promises, he returned again to his vomit.

Although Dodochin, abbot of Saint Disibod, records this in the following year in the Appendix to Marianus Scotus, followed by Trithemius, preference must be given to the authority of Bertold, who was then still alive. He mentions the disaster inflicted upon Henry twice: at the end of this year and at the beginning of the following year, which, according to his custom, he reckons from the feast of Christ’s Nativity.

Bertold further asserts that the victory which Margrave Ekkehard on this occasion won over Henry was so great that the emperor, having lost his royal insignia and barely escaping from the hands of his pursuers, was forced to flee from Thuringia—where he was besieging the fortress of Gleichen—as far as Bamberg. There he celebrated the feast of Christ’s Nativity without any ceremony and in inglorious fashion.

### XL. A Decretal Letter to Pibo

At about this time Urban, questioned by Pibo, bishop of Toul, about various matters, replied to him with a decretal letter, with the consent of a synodal council. We infer that it was written in the first years of Urban’s pontificate because in chapter 4 the pontiff suggests that he is responding to Pibo before he had celebrated any general council.

But in 1089, as Bertold reports, Urban assembled a general synod of 115 bishops. Perhaps Pibo, after his journey to Jerusalem and after taking the monastic habit at the monastery of Saint-Bénigne in Dijon, was ordered shortly afterward to return to his own Church and then presented these difficulties to Urban. He had undertaken that journey in 1083 and had already returned to Toul by 1088; he died in 1107.

### XL bis. Urban Remains at Rome

Urban spent the first months of this year, 1089, at Rome on the island situated between the two bridges, as Bertold reports. He was in the same difficulties that we mentioned above from Pandulf, yet he withheld nothing useful that might enable him to benefit in every way the flock entrusted to him.

He dealt with major affairs while also attending to matters that did not seem particularly important. He was so devoted to what concerned the universal government of the Church that he did not neglect the private affairs referred to him. The sequence of his deeds will prove the truth of all this.

At the beginning of this year he granted a privilege, to be presented in its proper place, to the regular canons of Saint John in the Vineyards near Soissons. He wished, by placing them under the protection of the Apostolic See, to exhort them to observe ever more closely the stricter practice of their rule, which they had recently undertaken. Above all, therefore, he decreed that their canonical constitutions should be observed inviolably in their Church for all time.

Urban is said to have seen and approved these constitutions in an old chronicle of that place. Its author proves this from their title, which in his time was found in their authentic copy, and perhaps in the original itself. These are his words concerning Urban:

> “He was the first distributor of apostolic blessings and benefactions toward our canonical house—for this is how the ancient monasteries of regular canons were accustomed to be called—who approved and strengthened the constitutions proper and particular to us, as the title prefixed to them indicates:
>
> “‘Here begin the canonical institutions of the Church of Saint John in the Vineyards, issued according to the rule of Saint Augustine and confirmed by the good-memory man, Pope Urban II, which we must observe inviolably. They are completed in forty-two readings,’ etc.”

Certainly Urban’s special affection for the regular canons of Saint Augustine, who had recently been established and were flourishing in the Church, is proved by the various surviving documents of his, which will be presented in their proper places.

Among these, Gerosius, provost of Reichersberg, quotes a notable passage in his exposition of Psalm 64, or in the book *On the Corrupt State of the Church*, addressed to Pope Eugene III and published in volume V of Baluze’s *Miscellanea*. It did not seem necessary to publish it separately, since precisely the same words occur in most privileges of the regular canons.

Labbe also published another privilege of Saint John of Soissons from Sirmond’s papers, which we likewise possess in a manuscript of the Queen of Sweden, now in the Ottobonian Library at Rome. We would readily believe it to be an excerpt from the earlier privilege, except that, besides a few other differences, it bears a different chronological note.

It is not altogether unusual for the same pontiff to grant nearly the same rights to one place in two documents issued at different times. But in what year this one was issued we have been unable to discover, even by conjecture, especially since in the manuscript it has the form of a decretal.

### XLI. The Privilege of Saint-Victor of Marseille

The privilege that Urban granted to the monastery of Saint-Victor of Marseille in the first year of his pontificate must also be assigned to the beginning of this year—not, as the common copies give it, indiction XI, but indiction XII, which agrees with this year.

In the preceding year, on the tenth day before the Kalends of March—for it is said to have been issued in that month—Urban had not yet ascended the Apostolic See. Richard, the abbot to whom it is addressed, was still at that time staying in Spain, where he was carrying out the duties of the apostolic legation that he had received from Gregory VII, although he had first defected from Victor and perhaps afterward been reconciled to him.

But in this year Richard, having been deprived by Urban of that dignity because, as Roderick says, he had exercised the office of legate with insufficient caution, and perhaps for other reasons unknown to us, had returned to his monastery and was able to obtain this privilege from the pontiff.

It should not seem surprising that Urban then wished to gratify him. It was necessary to win over so important a man, whose spirit might have been embittered by the removal of his legation. In fact, Richard, like Hugh of Lyon, who had likewise withdrawn from obedience to Victor, afterward remained especially devoted to Urban.

The privilege of Marseille should therefore not be removed from this year. It will be presented elsewhere from the manuscript of Toulouse, belonging to Saint Mary of the Gilded.

### XLII. Affairs in Germany

Nothing was more deeply concerning to Urban than aiding Germany, which he knew was being greatly disturbed by the schismatics at that time. Besides Hermann of Metz, who had recovered his see a few days earlier, and a few others, only four Catholic bishops remained altogether in that region. “By their encouragement,” Bertold says, “the other Catholics in the German lands resisted the schismatics from the beginning.”

They were Adalbero of Naumburg, Altmann of Passau, Adelbert of Worms, and Gebehard of Constance. The last had been consecrated bishop by Urban when Urban was the representative of the Apostolic See in Germany and was well known to him. Once he became pontiff, Urban therefore appointed Gebehard legate of the Apostolic See throughout Germany, Bavaria, Saxony, and the neighboring regions, by letters issued at Rome on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of May—apparently in this year, as Bertold informs us.

The authority of these letters seemed so great that Ivo and Gratian deservedly praised them in their decrees as thoroughly certain and approved rules of law.

Bertold calls it a decretal letter; Cardinal Baronius calls it a synodal letter, because he thought it had been written from a synod. “This is evident,” he says, “from the fragment of it quoted by Ivo.” But its complete text, which we now possess, makes the matter entirely certain. The pontiff himself testifies that he wrote it after consulting his brothers and after the question of excommunication—the principal subject of the letter—had long been discussed. Indeed, in subsequent councils nothing was decreed on this matter except what was prescribed in that letter.

Among the many other matters that Urban particularly commends to his new legate, he lays down excellent rules concerning the manner in which excommunicated persons are to be received into penance. In those bitter times great caution was necessary, lest the Church’s discipline be weakened by too readily receiving the fallen, or, conversely, lest the spirits of those who had incurred excommunication through something like necessity or certainly through fickleness of mind rather than malice be embittered by excessive severity.

For, as Bertold observes, Guibert and his accomplices did not cease ordaining their followers in various places by right and wrong, often even after receiving payment. Thus the evil of excommunication spread so far that even Catholics could scarcely preserve themselves unharmed from its contagion.

The prudent and pious pontiff therefore distinguished several degrees among the excommunicated, so that the recklessness of the proud and obstinate might be resisted while assistance was also given to the weakness of the simple and infirm.

Urban’s statement in that letter that, in assigning these degrees of penance, he followed in the footsteps of Gregory VII is confirmed by a fragment of the letter that Hugh of Flavigny reports in his Chronicle. In it Gregory, said to be near death, is said to have absolved and blessed everyone except Henry and Guibert, together with the principal persons who had supported their wickedness and impiety by counsel or aid.

If it is asked in what synod the grave question concerning the excommunicated, about which Urban wrote to Gebehard, was discussed, the answer will not be easy—unless perhaps it is said to have occurred at the general synod of 115 bishops that Urban is said by many, following Bertold, to have assembled in Rome in this year. At that synod, the same author says, “he confirmed the ecclesiastical statutes of his predecessors by apostolic authority.”

There is, however, a difficulty in this view: Urban says that he wrote the letter to Gebehard after consulting his brothers, but a little later he openly admits that this had not been done in a general synod.

Whatever the case may be, it is certain that at the synod held at Rome—or wherever else the council mentioned by Bertold took place—Urban acted more mildly, as he decrees in his letter, toward those who had defected to the schismatics only through opportunity, fear, or force and had afterward returned to the Church.

Accordingly, as the same author reports, the Romans became so enraged against Guibert that he was shamefully expelled by them and forced by oath to promise that he would no longer dare to invade the Apostolic See. As a result, after the prolonged discord in the kingdom between Catholics and schismatics had begun somewhat to subside, they came to judge it more reasonable to establish peace with one another rather than continue the war.

Indeed, matters had progressed so far that, after a conference between Henry and those who stood with Urban, some hope appeared that peace might be restored in the Church and the empire. They promised Henry that they would always provide him with aid and counsel if, after dismissing Guibert, he wished to return to ecclesiastical communion through a Catholic pastor. Henry was not entirely opposed to this condition.

But the bishops of his own faction resisted, fearing that once peace had been made with Guibert they too would be deposed. Therefore, on this occasion, they thoroughly dissuaded him from being reconciled to the holy Church.

### XLIII. The Fury of the Schismatics. The Death of Bishop Bonizo

On that occasion, it seems, the schismatics’ hatred of the Catholics grew so great that they dared to kill several Catholic bishops as well.

The spirit recoils from recounting the cruel death of Bonizo of Sutri. After the people of Piacenza had received him as their bishop when he had been expelled from his own city, the schismatics savagely murdered him, as Bertold reports, gouging out his eyes and cutting off nearly all his limbs. From his epitaph, published by Ughelli in volume II of *Sacred Italy*, we learn that this occurred on July 14.

The schismatics inflicted nearly the same punishment on Liprand, a Milanese priest, whose nose and ears they cut off as an insult.

Lambecius lists several short works by Bonizo in volume II of the *Imperial Library*: an Augustinian paradise composed entirely from the teachings and words of blessed Augustine, which he dedicated to Saint John Gualbert; a *Decretal Book*; and an *Epitome of the History of the Roman Pontiffs*, which Martin of Troppau praised.

He also wrote a book *On the Sacraments* to Walter, abbot of the monastery of León, which Mabillon found in a manuscript of the Ambrosian Library. More relevant to our subject is his book *On the Deeds of Urban*, mentioned in the same place. Bonizo himself praises it near the end of the *Epitome* in these words, quoted by Lambecius in Book II, chapter 8:

> “But if anyone wishes to know the acts of Pope Urban and about his victory, let him read the book that he wrote against Hugh, namely the schismatic cardinal surnamed ‘the White’; there he will find fully clarified whatever he wishes to know.”

But that work either perished or certainly lies hidden somewhere unknown; likewise the dialogue of Gualfredus, bishop of Siena, on the two apostolic claimants, in which he presented Urban and Guibert as interlocutors, as may be seen in Ughellus, volume III of *Italia sacra*. But let us return to the schismatics, who were raging no less in Germany than in Italy. There, Count Hugo of Egensheim, a vigorous defender of the Catholics, while staying without suspicion at Strasbourg with the bishop, was treacherously killed by the bishop’s servants on the day before the Nones of September, as Bertold relates. In this same year, as the same author reports, Bishop Peter of Albano, surnamed Ignitus, renowned above all for persecuting the Simoniacs, died; the commonly used Martyrologies commemorate him on the sixth day before the Ides of January. In the same year, on the fourth day before the Nones of May, as Abbot Hugh of Flavigny records in the *Chronicle of Verdun*, in volume II of Labbe’s *Bibliotheca nova*, Theodoricus, bishop of Verdun, died, reconciled to the Roman Church by Gerard, formerly archdeacon and then a monk of Saint-Vanne, to whom the pontiff had granted the power of absolving excommunicated persons, as Laurence of Liège relates somewhat more fully in his *History of the Bishops of Verdun*, in volume XII of Acheri’s *Spicilegium*.

### XLIV. Mathilda marries Welf.

Meanwhile Urban, wishing to strengthen the Catholic cause with renewed force, wanted Countess Mathilda, the widow of Duke Godfrey, to be given in marriage to Welf, the son of the other Welf, duke of Bavaria. Bertold reports that this was in fact done in this year—not so much on account of incontinence, for they never used marriage, as the same author asserts a little farther on, as on account of obedience to the Roman pontiff, so that Mathilda might be able to assist the holy Roman Church more vigorously against the schismatics.

Some maintain that on the occasion of this marriage Urban hastened as far as Siena in Tuscany, where he is said to have met Mathilda; Bertold, however, passed over this point in silence. He does testify that the enemies of the Catholics left nothing undone to harass Welf, whom nevertheless they attempted to attack in vain. Therefore, since, as the same author continues, they could not resist him, they implored a truce from him until Easter through the intervention of his wife. Henry could do no more. Distressed by the aforesaid marriage, he prepared an expedition into Saxony, from which shortly afterward, his forces broken, he was compelled to return without honor.

### XLV. The zeal of Bishop Gebhard.

Meanwhile Gebhard was making energetic use of the authority of the apostolic legation with which he had been endowed at the beginning of this year, as we have said. He deserves particular praise under this title because, as Trithemius reports, amid his episcopal duties he never ceased cultivating the fervor of regular life which he had imbibed under Abbot Wittelmo of Hirsau. He consecrated, with Urban’s authority, the monastery of Hirsau, recently rebuilt by that same holy abbot, and the cell of Reichenbach. But his magnanimity in defending the causes of the Church shone forth above all on the occasion of a certain Otto, a count in Alemannia, whom he excommunicated for the public adultery he had committed with the wife of Count Louis, whom Otto had taken to himself while her husband was still alive.

It was not enough for this new John the Baptist to denounce the living adulterer; he also pursued him after death, which Otto had endured unrepentant. For when Louis’s soldiers, unable to tolerate such disgrace to their lord, had cut off Otto’s head, and his body had been buried in a monastery he himself had founded, Gebhard ordered it to be thrown out and given, as Bertold reports in the words of Scripture (Jeremiah 22:19), “the burial of an ass”—that is, to be left without burial. This was indeed done, and his possessions were plundered by the soldiers, so that, as the same author says, the Prophet’s curses against Judas the traitor might be fulfilled in him: “And strangers shall plunder his labors” (Psalm 108:11).

### XLVI. The exemption of Fécamp is confirmed.

With no less courage Urban himself vindicated the majesty of the apostolic see in Normandy. When William, archbishop of Rouen, had placed all Normandy under interdict because Count Robert of Gisors had taken away a town belonging to his Church, and the monks of Fécamp, because they were subject solely to the Roman pontiff, had refused to suspend the divine office, they were excommunicated by the archbishop.

But when the matter was referred to Urban, he himself prohibited the archbishop from using the pallium. He restored it to him only after many prayers and embassies had been sent to Rome by both the archbishop himself and the count. To prevent anything similar from happening to the Church of Fécamp in the future, he confirmed its privileges by a new charter. I have not been able to find Urban’s letter itself, but information about the matter survives in an old document written at that time, which will be presented in full in the collection of pontifical letters. Whether Eadmer, book IV of the *New History*, should be understood as referring to this interdict when he writes that it was lifted through the intervention of Saint Anselm, others may determine.

### XLVII. He protects the monks of Bec at Pontoise.

About the same time Urban wrote to that same William, archbishop of Rouen, on behalf of the monks of Bec who lived in the church of Saint Peter at Pontoise. The inhabitants of the town of Pontoise, associated with the canons of Saint-Mellon, were trying to prevent them from ringing the bells for the divine office. The pontiff declares this irreligious and inhuman, and wishes them henceforth to be free to do so. The letter was issued across the Tiber on the third day before the Kalends of August; we therefore conjecture that it should be assigned to this year.

### XLVIII. The privilege of Saint-Pons-de-Thomières.

Shortly before that time, namely on the Kalends of July themselves, Urban granted an important privilege to Frotard, abbot of Saint-Pons-de-Thomières in Narbonese Gaul. By it he exempted that place from the jurisdiction of every bishop and adorned it with several other prerogatives. We owe this document to the kindness of the most illustrious Stephen Baluze; and, unless I am mistaken, it is the last bull in which John used the title “pre-signator of the lord pope.”

### XLIX. Urban writes about restoring the city of Tarragona.

On the same day the pontiff also wrote to the nobles of Catalonia, exhorting them to repair the city of Tarragona so that it might be a firm defense against the Saracens and so that the episcopal see might be restored there.

For many years by then, the care of the Church of Tarragona had been entrusted to the bishop of Ausona, since the metropolitan dignity in that province had been extinguished and transferred to the archbishop of Narbonne by decree of the comprovincial bishops and with the consent of the peoples. Berengar, bishop of Ausona, was pressing especially hard for this restoration, hoping that by this means he would undoubtedly attain metropolitan dignity. Indeed, as the pontiff himself testifies in a certain letter, he remained in Rome for a long time for this very reason, having come there at the beginning of this year, or at the end of the preceding one, to visit the thresholds of the apostles and render his service to the new pontiff.

These letters were issued at Rome on the Kalends of July in this year. The Church of Tarragona, however, did not recover its dignity until two years later, as we shall say.

### L. John the deacon becomes chancellor.

The letters which Urban wrote on that occasion are said to have been issued through the hands of John, cardinal deacon and chancellor of the holy Roman Church. Previously, as we have said, John had always used the title “pre-signator of the lord Urban.” It may therefore be conjectured that he then first obtained the dignity of chancellor of the Roman Church.

Certainly Pandulf, in his *Life of Gelasius II*—who was this same John—observes that he was appointed chancellor by Urban, who at that time was staying at Rome, between the two bridges, in great difficulties. He therefore did not receive this office at the monastery of Cassino, when he was first admitted into the pontiff’s entourage, nor during the rest of the period spent on the various journeys in which he accompanied the pontiff.

These are Pandulf’s words, following his account of the calamities which the pontiff had endured at Rome toward the end of the preceding year and at the beginning of this one:

> Then Pope Urban, most learned and eloquent, recognizing in Brother John a truly wise and prudent man, ordained him, brought him into his service, and, after profound deliberation, appointed him his chancellor, so that through the eloquence given him by the Lord, and under the dictation of the Holy Spirit, John might restore at the apostolic see the style of ancient wit and elegance, now almost entirely lost, and bring back the Leonine rhythm with radiant speed.

Indeed, nearly all Urban’s bulls were issued through the hands of John, the cardinal deacon, and so forth.

It is therefore surprising that Peter the Deacon, in book 31 of *On Illustrious Men of the Monastery of Cassino*, praised a certain Cardinal Leo who wrote a great many letters in the name of Pope Urban and made his register. In this passage Marus, after censuring Baronius, Possevinus, and other authors who confused this Leo with Leo Marsicanus, commonly called the Ostian, the author of the *Chronicle of Cassino*, whom Peter had discussed in the preceding chapter, adds that this Leo wrote several letters, of which, he says, twenty were published under Urban’s name in volume VII of Binius’s *Councils*.

Yet I have nowhere been able to find any bull or letter of Urban said to have been written by Leo. Rather, as we have said, most, indeed almost all, were written by John. It is surprising that Peter omitted this even when he was writing about that John under the name of Gelasius II.

### LI. Archbishop Rainald’s journey to Rome.

Around the middle of this year Rainald, bishop of Reims, arrived in Rome at Urban’s invitation. It may be inferred that he began this journey before the end of May from his charter issued that year, 1089, in the twelfth indiction and the thirtieth year of Philip, king of the Franks, and therefore before the twenty-third day of May. On that very day Philip began the thirtieth year of his reign; he had been consecrated at Reims before the death of his father, on the holy day of Pentecost in 1059.

In that charter, published by Marlot in volume II of *The Metropolis of Reims*, book II, chapter 4, Rainald says that, at the request of Lord Pope Urban, as he was preparing to visit the thresholds of the apostles and the Roman Church, he first prayed before the body of his most blessed and glorious patron Remigius, then went to the chapter to speak about his journey, and there granted an altar from the village of Saint-Remigius to Abbot Henry and the entire congregation of the great monastery of Remigius.

Since, as Bertold reports, Urban received this year letters from Philip, king of the Franks, promising him due submission, it is likely that Rainald brought them. For, as the pontiff himself testifies in a certain letter, Rainald was especially acceptable to Philip. Perhaps he spent the remainder of this year in Rome, since, as we shall say below, he received a very substantial privilege from Urban toward the end of this year.

### LII. Peace made with the Greeks.

It may also be inferred from Bertold that some agreement between the Greeks and Latins was reached at this time. He reports that Urban absolved the emperor of Constantinople from excommunication through his legates. This was Alexius Comnenus, who, as we saw from Geoffrey Malaterra, §29, had invited Urban to Constantinople in the preceding year so that, after a council had been convened, a disputation might take place between Greeks and Latins, saying that he would gladly consent to a Catholic discussion.

It is therefore likely that, although Urban was unable to do this in person because of the difficulties of the times, he nevertheless sent his legates to Greece, and that they arranged this peace, such as it was, between the Latin and Greek Church, perhaps by allowing each people to retain its own rite. For the principal matter under discussion was the use of leavened bread in the Eucharist, until something more firmly established should be decreed in a general council.

### LIII. A settlement of the peace between the sons of Robert Guiscard arranged by Urban’s legate.

This year, as Rocco Pirro relates in volume III of *Sicilia sacra*, in Notice VI, which concerns the Church of Mazara, Urban is said to have arranged through his legate a peace between Roger and Bohemond, the sons of Robert Guiscard, who were quarreling over their paternal inheritance. The author produces a fragment of the thirtieth book of Leo Marsicanus’s histories of Gregory VII and Urban II, in which the history of this dispute is recorded.

But Leo’s work is unknown, unless—as I believe to be true—it is the *History of the Pilgrims*, which Peter the Deacon attributes to the same Leo in book III, chapter 30, of *On Illustrious Men of the Monastery of Cassino*. For that work deals with the peace concluded between Robert’s sons. These pilgrims do not appear to have been other than those who departed for the East after the Council of Clermont to undertake the sacred expeditions. Among them was Henry, a monk of the Benedictine order, who was sent by Urban as legate to establish harmony between the brothers. Later, having set out with Bohemond for the holy war, he became the first Latin patriarch of Antioch. In the praised fragment Leo, who had been Henry’s tutor, chiefly recounts his deeds on that expedition.

After prefacing a lengthy account of Henry’s parents, he continues as follows:

> When Henry was already a young man, in the year 1089 he was sent by Pope Urban II to make peace between the brothers Roger and Bohemond, who were disputing the kingdom of Calabria and Apulia after the death of their father Robert Guiscard. Appointed their arbiter and judge, he divided the kingdom between them with an equal balance. From there he returned to Urban to give an account of his successful legation.

Geoffrey Malaterra also mentions, in book IV, chapter 10, a certain disagreement that arose between Roger and Bohemond after the death of their father Robert and lasted for as long as two years. But since the same author, in the following chapter, seems to suggest that the dispute of which he speaks, arising in 1086, was settled through the counsel of the faithful of both princes, some may perhaps think that Geoffrey wrote about events occurring before Urban’s pontificate, while Leo wrote about another quarrel between the brothers, settled by Urban’s legate.

Yet it can easily be demonstrated that both authors were speaking of one and the same war, which broke out between those princes during Urban’s pontificate. For, apart from the fact that no one would say that two years intervened between Robert’s death, which occurred in July 1085, and the year 1086, Geoffrey himself removes all doubt when he says that Bari was ceded to Bohemond as the price of this peace. It is certain from John the archdeacon of Bari, who lived in those regions at that time, that the city of Bari was transferred from Roger’s power into the dominion of his brother Bohemond shortly before the synod of Melfi, which Urban presided over in 1089.

This author, in his *History of the Discovery of Saint Sabinus*, while discussing the consecration of Archbishop Elias, says that Elias was elected archbishop of Bari with the will and consent of Duke Roger, and therefore of the lord of that place. He then adds that Pope Urban, who at that time was celebrating a synod at Melfi, came to that same city at the invitation of Bohemond, who already held Bari under his own dominion, and there consecrated Elias.

From this passage it is clear that Bari belonged to Roger shortly before the synod of Melfi, since Elias’s election was made with his consent, and that shortly afterward it passed to Bohemond, since at the end of the council it is said already to have been under his dominion. Since Geoffrey wrote that this occurred as a condition of the peace that had been made, it must be concluded that the peace he mentions was concluded either shortly before the Council of Melfi or certainly during it, and therefore in the year 1089, which Leo also assigned in the cited fragment.

Our opinion is confirmed by the local authors Lupus Protospata and Robert of Salerno, who write that war broke out between Roger and Bohemond, the sons of Robert, in 1088. Nevertheless, I cannot agree with Peregrinius, who in his corrections to Lupus suspected that the agreement was made at the Council of Melfi itself. For, as is clear from Leo’s fragment, it was made through the intervention of Urban’s legate, who was absent; it therefore was not made at the Council of Melfi, at which Urban himself was present and presiding.

I would not, however, claim that the peace was made long before the council. Indeed, I would rather readily affirm that it was confirmed there by the authority of the pontiff and the Fathers, unless Leo had been silent about this matter in the cited fragment.

### LIV. The Council of Melfi, its canons, and other statutes—At this council Roger becomes the liegeman of the Holy See, and the mitre is given to Abbot Peter.

At the beginning of autumn in the present year Urban held that council at Melfi, a city of Apulia. Seventy bishops and twelve abbots are said to have attended it. According to Lupus Protospata in his *Chronicle*, all the bishops of Apulia, Calabria, and Bruttium came together there, along with Duke Roger and all the counts of Apulia, Calabria, and the other provinces.

This is perhaps the council which Bertold calls, under this year, a general synod of 115 bishops, in which Urban confirmed by apostolic authority the statutes of his predecessors. Some others, however—and it must be admitted, not without some probable foundation—maintain that the synod praised by Bertold was held at Rome, as we said above, no. 43.

Sixteen canons were enacted at this Council of Melfi. They contain excellent statutes, especially against simony and clerical incontinence. They also determine what age those promoted to sacred orders must have attained and who must be excluded from them. Clerics are forbidden indecent and secular clothing, and several other regulations are established concerning the property of monasteries. Finally, the bishops are warned to guard against false penances.

Moreover, John, cardinal deacon and chancellor of the Roman Church, in a letter to the abbot of Molesme appended to the canons of this council in Labbe’s edition, says several things about the council that at first sight seem to be missing from the published canons. Namely, whatever had been given to monasteries by princes up to that council was to remain secure and intact for them, while abbots were henceforth to abstain from such acquisitions. By this arrangement, he continues, the abbots refrained from invading churches, and the bishops did not wish entirely to strip the monasteries.

But by these words John intended nothing other than what had been established in canons five and six of the council against abbots who did not hesitate to receive church property given to them without the consent of the bishops.

Lupus Protospata also reports another statute of this council, one not found in the published canons: namely, that the “holy truce” was to be maintained by all subjects. Peregrinius insists that these words signify the agreement concluded between the brothers Roger and Bohemond, of which we spoke above. I would not oppose that opinion if Lupus’s words are understood as referring to the confirmation and maintenance of that pact, previously concluded.

At the same synod, Duke Roger, as Archbishop Romuald of Salerno testifies, became Urban’s liegeman. He promised under oath that he would preserve his fidelity to the Roman Church and to the pope and his canonically succeeding successors, and he received from him by means of a banner the land together with the honor of the duchy.

Ptolemy of Lucca agrees in his book *On Genealogies*, published by Zurita, where he writes that Roger made this oath at the Council of Melfi and confessed himself a liegeman of the Church for the lands of Apulia. The same author gathers there much information about Roger’s successors, who, after taking a similar oath, acknowledged themselves to be feudatories of the Church, and whom the pontiffs customarily invested by presenting a banner.

That Urban and Roger were very closely allied is evident from the fact that, at the command of both, William of Apulia described in verse the distinguished deeds of the Normans in Italy, as he himself testifies at the beginning of his work.

Most writers also maintain that the event commonly reported by published authors concerning Abbot Peter of Cava occurred at this synod: namely, that Urban sent him a mitre, which he was thereafter to wear, while Peter was sitting bareheaded among the other Fathers of the council.

Although it is not entirely clear on what occasion or in what place this happened, the event itself nevertheless appears certain, since it is reported by the anonymous abbot of Venosa in his *Life of the same blessed man*, which he composed shortly after Peter’s death. It may be useful to quote his words here:

> At the synod, while he was sitting bareheaded in accordance with his custom, Pope Urban of holy memory sent him a pontifical headdress. The man of God received it reverently, as was fitting, out of respect for the supreme pontiff, and greeted him with the utmost courtesy; nevertheless, even when requested by the pope, he scorned to use the priestly mitre.

Urban also ordered this holy man to drink a little wine, since, as the same author relates, he had almost lost his voice because his stomach was entirely weakened. The old anonymous poet reported after him by Ughellus in volume VII of *Italia sacra* relates the same. Such was our pontiff’s charity and concern for holy men.

We learn from Urban himself that Peter attended the Council of Melfi. In a decree issued at that time concerning the monastery of Cava, Urban testifies that Alfanus, archbishop of Salerno, and the bishop of Pertan had complained against Peter because he had invaded several monasteries belonging to them. When the pontiff examined this case during the council in his chamber, with several bishops assisting him, he pronounced judgment in favor of the monks of Cava, as he himself testifies in the cited decree, which will be presented from a copy made from the archives of Cava.

The Council of Melfi was assigned to the year 1089 by all the oldest authors, and a brief preface attached to its canons in a manuscript agrees with them.
