There would be no difficulty about this matter were it not that Baronius and most recent writers attempted to move it to the following year, undoubtedly misled by the authority of Romuald of Salerno, who, as they understand him, assigned the synod to the year 1090.

But unless this was a scribal error, as Peregrinius suspects, I fear that those authors were mistaken because of the method of reckoning used by most writers of that period in those regions of southern Italy. They began the year with the Roman indiction in the month of September, and thus anticipated the ordinary calculation by four months in designating the years.

The anonymous writer of Bari, edited by Peregrinius, and many other published writers from those regions regularly begin their years in this way. If Romuald followed them here, as is quite probable, he must be said to differ from the other authors in assigning the date of this synod, since it was held at the end of September, in the thirteenth indiction.

But whatever may be the case concerning Romuald’s opinion, it is certain that this synod was held in the year 1089. Other contemporary authors, together with Lupus Protospata, state this explicitly. Nothing clearer can be found on the matter than the testimony of John the deacon and chancellor, who attended this council, in the letter quoted above to the abbot of Molesme. He writes:

> In the second year of his pontificate, our lord Pope Urban held a council at Melfi, a city of Apulia.

And shortly afterward:

> This Council of Melfi was certainly held in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1089; and you should know that what we write we both heard and saw while present.

The same is proved by John the archdeacon of Bari, who, like the other authors, explicitly places the consecration of Archbishop Elias—which, according to Urban’s own testimony, took place in October 1089—immediately after the Council of Melfi.

He speaks as follows in the *History of the Discovery of Saint Sabinus*, under the year 1091 in Baronius and in volume VII of *Italia sacra*:

> After the death of Ursio, Elias succeeded him as archbishop of Bari. He had previously been the first abbot and held the body of Saint Nicholas in his care without ordination. After he had been elected archbishop by the will and consent of Duke Roger, son of the duke called Robert, we went to Melfi to Pope Urban, who was celebrating a synod there in the month of September. We asked him to descend as far as Bari and consecrate the aforesaid Elias to the dignity of the archbishopric. Lord Bohemond, who at that time already held Bari under his dominion, joined us in beseeching the same pope.

Urban’s own bull to Peter, abbot of Cava, issued this year on the eleventh day before the Kalends of October, agrees with this. Besides many other matters, the pontiff confirms to the monastery of Cava those possessions concerning which, he says, “recently”—that is, at the Council of Melfi, as is clear from the decree cited in the preceding section—a dispute had arisen.

### LV. Urban transfers the bones of Saint Nicholas to Bari and consecrates Elias as bishop.

Invited by Bohemond, Urban therefore crossed to Venosa after the Council of Melfi had ended, where he granted the bull just mentioned for the benefit of the monks of Cava. He then visited the Church of Bari, at that time extremely famous because of the frequent miracles said to occur at the body of Saint Nicholas, which had been brought there in this year, 1087.

There the pontiff placed the bones of the most blessed bishop with his own hands in the prepared place of access. Although, as he himself says, this was contrary to the custom of the Roman and apostolic Church, he consecrated Elias in his own see, Elias having been elected archbishop of Bari and Canosa—the two churches having already been united—out of devotion to Saint Nicholas and because the people earnestly requested it.

Urban himself explains all these matters more fully in the privilege, no. 26, which he granted on that occasion to Elias and his Church of Bari, issued on October 9.

We learn the precise day of Elias’s consecration from the anonymous writer of Bari, under the year 1095, who, following his customary practice, begins that year in the preceding September together with the indiction. He writes:

> In 1080, indiction XIII, in the month of September—that is, in the year 1089 according to the ordinary method of reckoning—Pope Urban entered the city of Bari on the day before the Kalends of October; and on the Kalends of October he built the confession of Saint Nicholas.

Lupus Protospata says almost the same under the year 1089:

> Urban came to the city of Bari and there consecrated the confession of Saint Nicholas and Elias as archbishop.

Elias, formerly a monk of Cava, had become abbot of Saint Benedict near the port of Bari. He was the first of all to receive into his church the body of Saint Nicholas, brought from Lycia in 1087. He was afterward placed in charge of the church newly built for that saint in the city of Bari itself, as Orderic Vitalis relates from John the archdeacon of Bari in book VII.

When Elias was finally elevated to the archbishopric, Eustace, founder of the monastery of All Saints near the same city, succeeded him in the administration of the abbey. Eustace was the second and last abbot of Saint Nicholas. When he too was elected archbishop, the Church of Saint Nicholas was transferred to secular canons, as Ughellus and, after him, Lubinus and others relate.

In 1106 Paschal II granted an important privilege to Eustace, abbot of Saint Nicholas. In it the pontiff testifies that, during the time of Victor III, the body of Saint Nicholas had been brought from overseas into the city of Bari and, by Urban II, buried in the lower crypt with the greatest veneration, in the place where, as he says, it is now honorably revered, with an altar consecrated above it in honor of the Lord.

### LVI. Whether a council was then held at Troia.

Baronius, Binius, Chesnius in their *Lives of the Pontiffs*, and the other followers of those authors maintain that another council was held at Troia in Apulia toward the end of this year. They call it the first Trojan council under Urban II, saying that it is mentioned by Peter the Deacon, Ivo of Chartres, Gratian, the Master of the Sentences, and many other celebrated authors.

Other learned men rightly oppose them, admitting only one Council of Troia under Urban II, held in 1093, as is clear from Bertold. They therefore insist that the first council, which Baronius and the other cited authors assign to 1089, must be eliminated. No author before them, whether from our age or from the age of our fathers, ever mentioned two councils held at Troia under Urban. Moreover, as Labbe observed, the statements that Ivo, Gratian, or other earlier authors derived from the Trojan council contain no chronological indication from which it could be inferred that they were enacted in one year rather than the other.

Finally, Peter himself, whose testimony Baronius seems chiefly to rely upon, nowhere acknowledged two synods at Troia. Indeed, in book IV, chapter 7, of the *Chronicle of Cassino*, he did not even assign a definite time to the Trojan synod, although his opponents derive their argument from that passage. He begins the chapter simply as follows:

> At a later time Pope Urban again came into these regions, to Monte Cassino, and so forth. At that time, while he was celebrating a synod at Troia …

But, you will say, in the passage just cited Peter reports that John Cajetan was ordained deacon by Urban at the time when the same pontiff was celebrating a synod at Troia. Since it is certain, as was proved above from many charters, that John was ordained deacon in the first year of Urban’s pontificate, it may be inferred that the Trojan synod mentioned here by Peter must be assigned to the beginning of Urban’s pontificate. Since it is equally certain that the same pontiff held a synod in that city in 1093, two Trojan councils would necessarily have to be admitted.

Yet nothing certain can be inferred from Peter’s testimony. As Angelus de Nuce observed in his notes on this passage, Peter did not preserve an exact chronology here, as often happened elsewhere. Moreover, John was ordained deacon by Urban when Urban first came to the monastery of Cassino. But Peter is explicitly speaking here not of that visit but of the pontiff’s second approach to the holy mountain. Therefore he must be understood as referring not to John’s first ordination but to his second promotion, namely, his promotion to the diaconate of the Lateran patriarchal church. That promotion can indeed be assigned to the year 1093, when the Council of Troia was held. Thus, even on Peter’s testimony, no necessity remains for admitting two Trojan synods. But we must return to the sequence of events.

### LVII. Urban consecrates the church of Brindisi.

After consecrating Elias as archbishop at Bari, Urban proceeded to Brindisi in the province of Hydruntum. Lupus Protospata, a contemporary author, records that in the present year he dedicated the church there. After the matters related above concerning the consecration of the archbishop of Bari, he adds:

> And the aforesaid Pope Urban consecrated the church of Brindisi.

Ughellus must be corrected on the basis of this testimony of Lupus, for in volume IX of *Italia sacra* he assigned this dedication to the preceding year.

Urban ordered the episcopal dignity of that church to be restored. Because of the calamity inflicted on Brindisi by the Saracens, it had been transferred to Oria. He wrote about this to Godinus, the bishop, who, finding residence at Oria more agreeable to him, had abandoned the title of Brindisi and was content with the name of bishop of Oria. Brindisi did not recover its dignity until after Urban’s death, as is clear from a letter of his successor Paschal, preserved by Ughellus in volume IX.

Ughellus remarks in the cited passage that Urban’s letter on this matter, of which he presents a fragment, is preserved in full in the *History of Brindisi*. But I have not been able to find this history, or at least the complete letter.

### LVIII. He visits Reggio.

Urban must be said to have penetrated as far as the extreme end of Calabria if it is true that in this year he visited Reggio, the metropolis of Further Calabria, and was received as a guest by Archbishop Arnulf, as is reported by Ughellus.

Although I do not wish to deny that Urban went to Calabria, this journey cannot have been undertaken by him after the Trojan synod. For in 1093, the year in which the Council of Troia was held—and, as we have proved, the only one under Urban—Arnulf had long since died. Ughellus, undoubtedly prejudiced by the opinion of recent writers who admit two Trojan synods, fell into this error and thereby transferred to another year what had occurred in this year, 1089.

### LIX. Urban ordains the bishop of Malta.

If conjecture is permissible, the ordination of Walter, the first bishop of Malta after Count Roger had recovered the island from the Saracens, must be assigned to this same journey. Rocco Pirro, in volume III of *Sicilia sacra*, testifies that Walter was ordained by Urban II in this year.

Certainly Walter, toward the end of this year—for the thirteenth indiction was already running—subscribed a certain instrument of Sicelgaita, the wife of Duke Robert. The same author reports it in volume II, in the notice concerning the Church of Palermo. That document cannot be placed later, since Sicelgaita died in the following year, on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of May, as we learn from the necrology of the monastery of Cassino.

### LX. Saint Bruno accompanies Urban.

The likelihood is more than strong that on this same occasion Bruno, founder of the Carthusians, traveled through Calabria with Urban. For he had been summoned by the pontiff, once his teacher—as we have said—when the holy man was teaching in the school of the Church of Reims; and this year he came to him. There can be no doubt that he also followed him into Apulia and Calabria, since Urban had summoned Bruno with the intention of using his counsel in the most difficult affairs, which were then frequently arising. Another indication of the same fact is that Bruno’s holiness was from that time so well known among the Calabrians that shortly afterward a place in that region was given to him for habitation, which in fact he inhabited the following year with some of his companions. This is established by a diploma of Count Roger, published by G. Surianus in his notes to the Life of Saint Bruno, and by Ughelli in volume IX, together with the confirmation of Theodore, bishop of Squillace.

### LXI. A Donation Made to the Monastery of Monte Cassino

Apparently on this same journey, while Urban was returning to Rome through the Hirpini, Baldwin, lord of the castle of Ponte Sant’Anastasio in the county of Telesia, visited him. With the consent and at the urging of the same pontiff, and with the agreement also of Roffridus, archbishop of Benevento, Baldwin gave the monastery of Monte Cassino the church of Saint Dionysius, situated near that castle; but not before he had repaired it from its foundations and enriched it with many gifts and possessions. Marius Vipera, in his chronology of the archbishops of Benevento, assigns this donation to the present year, on the basis of the register of Peter the Deacon and book IV of the Cassinese Chronicle. But what he adds from Falcon’s chronicle concerning a delegation of about 110 Beneventan nobles sent to Pope Urban is erroneous. That delegation must instead be assigned to Paschal II; Vipera could easily have noticed this, since he himself records it under the year 1102, that is, three years after Urban’s death.

### LXII. Whether Urban Was Present at the Election of the Abbot of Farfa

The election of Raynald as abbot of Farfa among the Sabines was also held this year. The author of the brief chronicle of that monastery—which chronicle, handwritten, is in our possession—asserts that Urban was present at it, although it is permissible to suspect that the name Urban entered that chronicle through a copyist’s error in place of Wibert. For Gregory, a monk of that place and an eyewitness, reports that Wibert, whom he calls Clement, possessed complete authority in this monastery, which was subject by special right to the emperor. Indeed, the same author, when relating the election in which Raynald was shortly afterward compelled to yield his place to Berard, says nothing about Urban or Guibert. Moreover, Diaconius and others list among Guibert’s cardinals Theodore, the abbot, and Maginulf, a monk of Farfa; and Theodore himself sought the pontificate under the name of Sylvester III.

### LXIII. The Council of Saintes

While these events were taking place in Italy, Amatus, bishop of Oloron and apostolic-vicar in Aquitaine, held a council at Saintes on 4 November. At that council, according to the Chronicle of Maillezais, he was transferred to the see of Bordeaux, which had remained vacant for nearly three years. Adhemar, bishop of Angoulême, testifies that this transfer was made despite the opposition of William, duke of Aquitaine—unless there is a copyist’s error, in which case “with William consenting” may perhaps be read—in a charter of donation that he made before that synod to the monastery of Saint-Maixent among the Poitevins; the charter is reported by the Sammarthani in volume I of *Gallia Christiana*.

At that same council, perhaps, the controversy between the monks of Vendôme and those of Saint-Aubin at Angers concerning the priory of Crédon was to be discussed, as is suggested by an old document published in volume II of Baluze’s *Miscellanea*. But the count of Anjou prevented this from happening, and no further information about that council could be obtained. The Sammarthani in *Gallia Christiana* and Lopezius in his *History of Bordeaux* incorrectly assign it to the preceding year, undoubtedly misled by the charter of Adhemar just mentioned, which is said to have been issued on the Nones of November 1088, in the twelfth indiction. It should instead read 1089. This is proved not only by the Chronicle of Maillezais just cited, but also by a charter of a certain William Ferran, reported by the Sammarthani themselves.

That William restored certain properties taken from the church of Saint-Seurin near Bordeaux in 1088, on the third day before the Nones of December, while Simon, bishop of Agen, was occupying the place of the archbishop of Bordeaux, who had already been dead for two years. This would certainly be false if Amatus had been made archbishop at the Council of Saintes in October of that same year. Indeed, after the death of Archbishop Gotcelin, which occurred in 1086, the see remained vacant for approximately three years, as the Sammarthani themselves observed, and therefore until 1089.

### LXIV. A Privilege for the Church of Reims and for the Monastery of Balma

As the year was drawing to a close, Urban returned to Rome and granted privileges to several churches and monasteries. The most notable was the privilege that he granted—or rather confirmed—to Raynald, archbishop of Reims, and to his church. It was issued at Rome on the eighth day before the Kalends of January; from this it may therefore be inferred that the pontiff celebrated the solemnity of Christ’s Nativity in the City that year. If you have leisure, read this privilege, copied from an old manuscript codex, in the Appendix. Three days later there followed another privilege granted to the noble monastery of Balma among the Sequani, which we received from the ascetics of that place, copied from the original document itself.

### LXV. The Journey to Rome of Dalmatius, Archbishop of Narbonne

The journey to Rome of Dalmatius, archbishop of Narbonne, can scarcely be postponed beyond the end of this year. Among other reasons, he undertook it because Urban’s widely circulated letter to the nobles of Catalonia concerning the restoration of the city of Tarragona had made him fear that, on this occasion—although the pontiff had declared that he desired this without prejudice to the rights of the Church of Narbonne—the province of Tarragona might be removed from his jurisdiction. The pontiff had sufficiently indicated that he would do this unless the bishop of Narbonne could prove, by the authority of a Roman privilege, that this ancient metropolitan church had been subject to him.

Dalmatius was well aware that he did not possess such a privilege. We infer that he undertook this journey at that time from the fact that, in March of the following year, he held a provincial council in his metropolitan city, having returned from his journey to Rome. This is evident because at that very synod the controversy between Dalmatius and the abbot of Crassus was brought to an end. Dalmatius had complained about it to the pontiff at Rome, and Urban had entrusted its settlement to his legate Raynerius.

For if those disputes had been settled before the Roman journey—as the acts of this synod plainly declare that they were settled there—Dalmatius would have brought them afterward before the pontifical tribunal at Rome in vain, and Urban likewise would have written to his legate in vain concerning their settlement. Furthermore, the fact that this synod was held at the beginning of the following year is evident from its acts, published by Baluze among the councils of the province of Narbonne and by Labbe in the appendix to volume X of the general councils. There it is expressly stated to have been held in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1090, on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of April.

### LXVI. Urban Entrusts Various Affairs to His Legate Raynerius

[Col. 0064C]

What Dalmatius achieved on that journey must be learned from the letters that Urban wrote on the occasion. First, the pontiff commended him to the clergy and people of Narbonne, and also to the count and viscount; he ordered them to show him obedience and honor as a father and vicar of Christ, threatening to strike with the sword of anathema those who retained the goods of the Church of Narbonne.

Next, he wrote two letters to Cardinal Raynerius, whom he had sent as legate to Spain. In them he especially charged him to investigate the injuries that Dalmatius complained he had suffered from Frotardus, abbot of Tomer. Perhaps that abbot was abusing the notable privilege that, as we have said, he had received from Urban in July of this year. For this reason the pontiff insists particularly in both letters to the legate that he examine this case most carefully, since he is said to have been sent especially for it.

Frotardus, who had come to Rome first, reported matters very differently, as Urban himself says in the first letter, from the account that Dalmatius had given to the pontiff in the presence of the legate before the latter’s departure for Spain. Dalmatius and the bishop of Barcelona appeared to have come to Rome chiefly to demand the justice of the Apostolic See against that abbot.

Finally, Urban wrote to Frotardus himself, ordering him to submit completely to the judgment of the legate and, if the reports concerning him were true, to make full and appropriate satisfaction to both bishops. Finally, the pontiff especially commends to him that he revere and love the bishop of Narbonne as his own spiritual father and shepherd . . . .

### LXVII. He Commends the Province of Tarragona to the Archbishop of Narbonne

As for the metropolitan right over the province of Tarragona, which Dalmatius feared he would shortly be deprived of, Urban, since the matter was difficult, instructed his legate that, while the city of Tarragona was being restored, he should introduce no innovation whatsoever in this regard. For the matter, as the distinguished Pierre de Marca says in book IV of the *Marca Hispanica*, was precarious and uncertain. Therefore Urban did not dare disregard Dalmatius’s complaints. As the pontiff himself puts it, Dalmatius declared that he had suffered prejudice through the removal of the bishops of Tarragona, whom the Church of Narbonne had possessed for four hundred years without any other church’s protest.

On the other hand, Urban was not unaware of the ancient dignity of the Church of Tarragona, which had miserably fallen through misfortune, not because of any wicked deed. When the metropolitan city itself had been occupied by barbarians, the remaining bishops of the province, together with their churches, had been assigned—without consulting the Roman pontiff—to the protection and care, rather than the jurisdiction, and still less the servitude, of the metropolitan of Narbonne, as the nearer metropolitan.

Accordingly, amid these complications, the prudent pontiff, wishing to injure no one even outwardly, judged that he should act cautiously and by a provisional decree established that, until the city of Tarragona was restored, the bishops of the province of Tarragona should be subject to the archbishop of Narbonne as their own metropolitan.

But because shortly before this he had conferred primacy over all Spain upon the archbishop of Toledo, without prejudice to the rights of the metropolitans, he wished those same bishops to obey the archbishop of Toledo as their primate, until the archbishop of Narbonne could demonstrate by reliable authority that he had been their primate.

Dalmatius had told Urban that his church possessed privileges concerning the primacy, and he had produced many documents to prove it. Therefore Urban prescribed to his legate that he investigate those privileges carefully—not in order to judge them, but so that this important matter might be referred to the pontiff himself.

Matters remained in this state until the year 1091. All this is explained at greater length in four letters of Urban. Here it is worth observing that, besides these letters of Urban published by Labbe in volume X of the councils, another letter concerning these controversies appears in the appendix to that volume. It is addressed to Cardinal-Priest L.; it concerns the controversy between the archbishop of Narbonne and the abbot of Comminges. But this letter is in fact the very letter addressed to the legate Raynerius, whose fragment Labbe himself had already included, under the same title, among Urban’s other letters.

He was misled by the copy that he used, in which a copyist’s error had introduced L. instead of R. into the heading, just as “Comminges” had been written instead of “Tomer.” I therefore wish to warn the reader lest anyone, on this account, introduce a monastery of Comminges otherwise unknown, or, as happened to Cardinal Aguirre, accept a legate of Urban named L., who never existed.

In these letters the most vigilant pontiff says many admirable things about the office of a legate. In particular, he warns Raynerius not to allow himself, through favoritism or excessive zeal, to be carried away against either party contrary to the rules of truth and justice.

In this same year Attilanus, bishop of Zamora, is said to have been canonized by Urban in the Roman Martyrology. Whether this is true, however, is not agreed among the authors, including the Spanish ones.

### LXVIII. The Privilege of the Monastery of Saint John of Pinna

Before we leave Spain, something must briefly be said about the celebrated monastery of Saint John the Baptist of Pinna. Sancius, king of Aragon, sent its abbot Aymericus to Rome to ask Urban to confirm the privileges of his monastery. The pontiff granted the request of the king and the abbot, apparently toward the end of this year or certainly at the beginning of the following year, as may be inferred from the king’s own diploma reporting the matter. It is dated in the Spanish era 1138, on the eighth day before the Ides of May, in the third year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Urban II, in the year from the Lord’s Incarnation 1090, in the thirteenth indiction, and so forth.

It is remarkable how many gifts and privileges the kings of Aragon bestowed upon this holy place, which had been designated for their burial. But Sancius surpassed the others above all: three or four times he sent the abbots of that monastery to Rome to assert the privileges and possessions that kings and prelates had conferred upon it.

It is useful to reproduce here what relates to Urban in one of his diplomas. He speaks as follows:

> “After Abbot Sancius had died and Lord Aymericus had been placed in his position as abbot, desiring to fortify and protect this monastery completely, under both apostolic and royal patronage, I sent Lord Aymericus, the abbot, to Rome, to the most blessed Pope Urban II. I earnestly begged his fatherhood to receive the aforesaid place under the protection and patronage of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul, and to grant that place such a privilege that it might be protected and defended by their patronage from the rapacity of wicked men, from the invasion of bishops, from the prejudice of cardinals and archbishops, and from the evil domination of succeeding kings; and that the abbot of that place, both he and his people, might freely appeal to the Roman See in all ecclesiastical or secular causes and judgments, as well as in the appointment of abbots.
>
> “That most blessed Father Urban, having heard the petition of my humility—moved, I believe, not by my merits but by the grace of Saint John—received this place under apostolic protection, and, granting it a privilege of liberty, fortified it with apostolic patronage.”

Such are the words of Sancius. I have thought it useful to report them somewhat more fully in order to make up for the deficiency of the privilege itself, which I was unable to find. Jerome Blanca presents the royal diploma in full in his commentaries on the affairs of Aragon.

### LXIX. Urban’s Decree Concerning Freedom in Marriage

[Col. 0067A]

On this or another occasion the same king consulted Urban about his own niece: whether she ought to be joined to a man against her will, to whom, under pressure of necessity, he had promised her as a bride. The pontiff replied that this should by no means be done. Ivo and Gratian adopted his response on this matter in their Decrees, and Hildebert reported it in book II, letter 26, elsewhere numbered 42.

I have assigned the matter here because it nowhere bears a date. Sancius, who had ruled the Aragonese from the year 1067, died on 4 June 1094 while besieging the city of Huesca. His response is found in Ivo, *Decretum*, page 8, chapter 24; in Gratian, 31, question 2, chapter 3; and in the *Cassinese Bullary*, F. 2, page 118.

### LXX. A Letter on Behalf of the Monastery of Polirone

[Col. 0067B]

There is another letter of the same pontiff, written to Countess Matilda toward the end of this year, or at least begun before the siege of Mantua at the beginning of the following year, on behalf of the monastery of Polirone against the bishop of Mantua. He unjustly retained the church of Saint Florian, which belonged to that monastery. Urban therefore wished Matilda to compel the bishop to restore it.

### LXXI. Thiemo Is Ordained Archbishop of Salzburg

At the beginning of the year 1090, when the Catholics were gaining strength in Bavaria, as Bertoldus relates, they elected Thiemo, formerly abbot of Saint Peter, as archbishop of Salzburg. Altmann, bishop of Passau and legate of the Apostolic See, immediately consecrated him in a solemn rite, assisted by the Catholic bishops Adalbero of Würzburg and Meginward of Freising.

Following in the footsteps of his most holy predecessor Gebhard, as is read in the Life of that same Gebhard, Thiemo labored greatly in the defense of Catholic truth and the propagation of divine religion. The author of the Salzburg Chronicle, in Canisius, volume VI, observes that this ordination was celebrated on the seventh day before the Ides of April, and adds that Thiemo was presented with the pallium by Urban II.

### LXXII. Various Privileges

At the same time—if no error has entered into the designation of the year and month—Urban received under the special protection of the Roman Church the provostship of Reitempurch, situated in the diocese of the Bavarian city of Freising, which had been taken from the Apostolic See by Welf, duke of the Bavarians, and his wife Judith. Hundius reports the bull concerning this matter in volume III of the *Metropolis Salisburgensis*.

But the chronological indications attached to it are not sufficiently consistent. It is said to have been issued at Anagni in February of this year, in the fifteenth indiction, whereas the indiction in that year was the thirteenth. Moreover, the sentence from Sacred Scripture customarily used on the seal suits Urban III rather than Urban II. Nevertheless, this bull cannot be attributed to Urban III. Whether Lanfranc, who drafted it while the chancellor John was absent or otherwise prevented, used a different biblical sentence is uncertain. All the remaining details in these notes agree perfectly with one another, and there seems to be no reason to doubt its authenticity. Perhaps these errors entered through the carelessness of copyists.

Urban nevertheless does not yet appear to have returned to Rome on 25 March of this year, when, on that very day, the bishops of the city—that is, the cardinals Ubaldus of Sabina and John of Tusculum—are said to have dedicated the church of Saint Mary ad Pineam during the time of Lord Pope Urban II, according to an old inscription reported by Martinellus in *Roma sacra* and by Mabillon. Shortly afterward, however, while residing at Rome, he issued various diplomas in different places.

Among these is a privilege for the monastery of regular canons of Saint Antoninus among the Ruthenians, issued at Rome on the fifth day before the Kalends of April. There, on the Kalends of April themselves, he granted another privilege to William, abbot of the monastery of Saint Theofredus among the Vellavi, in the diocese of Le Puy; it lists and confirms the possessions of that monastery.

Another privilege, published by Baluze in his *Miscellanea*, volume II, page 117, was granted in favor of Hugh, bishop of Grenoble, on this same day of this year, as it seems to us. Baluze, however, as in our copy—which we possess from the chartulary of the Church of Grenoble—gives the following year, but this is probably a copyist’s error. Not only do the other chronological indications attached to it designate the present year, but it is also said to have been written by the hand of Gregory, scriniarius and notary of the sacred palace, just as the preceding privilege, issued on this same day, and several others of the same period are said to have been. The diplomas of the following year do not contain this statement, nor, if I remember correctly, do any others from other years.

In this bull the pontiff forbids the alienation of ecclesiastical property and orders that the possessions of a deceased bishop or of a church not be seized by anyone. He wishes them to be preserved intact by the canons for the future successor of the bishop.

Another notable privilege, published by Tamburini, *De jure abbatum*, volume II, page 468, was granted by Urban to the Vallombrosan monks shortly after the preceding one, namely on 6 April. In it he confirmed not only the rights and possessions of the principal monastery of Vallombrosa, but also the entire congregation of many monasteries listed there, founded several years earlier by John Gualbert.

The pontiff then decreed that other monasteries subsequently added to this new congregation should enjoy the same privileges, and that the abbey of Vallombrosa itself should be the head of all of them. He therefore established that, in the election of its abbot, not only the monks of that place but also the superiors of all the other monasteries of the congregation should possess the right to vote. If one of those abbots were elected to the general government, he was to leave his own abbey and transfer to the principal monastery, by whose direction all the united monasteries were to be governed.

It was issued at Rome in the year 1090, in the thirteenth indiction, on the eighth day before the Ides of April, in the third year of Urban’s pontificate. All these indications agree perfectly. Yet it is strange that the privilege nowhere names the abbot who then presided over Vallombrosa. Perhaps, since it had been granted for the benefit of the entire congregation in order to establish its general government, the pontiff judged it better to address it universally to all its members than specifically to any one abbot. At that time Rusticus, the successor of Blessed John Gualbert after Rodulfus, presided over Vallombrosa.

### LXXIII. A Decree Addressed to Rusticus, Abbot of Vallombrosa, and Others; and Another Possibly Concerning the Limits of the Diocese of Bayonne

This is the same Rusticus who, together with Peter, bishop of Pistoia, consulted Urban about the ordination of Daimbert. Daimbert had been ordained deacon by Wecilo, archbishop of Mainz, who was both a schismatic and a simoniac; nevertheless, the pontiff himself had consecrated Daimbert bishop of Pisa.

Urban’s response was published by Labbe in volume X of the councils from a manuscript codex of Saint-Victor in Paris. Another response to the same men should be joined to it—or rather, as seems probable, another part of the same response, which is found in Gratian, I, question 7, chapter 24, concerning Daibertus.

In both responses Urban acknowledges that he was not unaware that Daimbert had received the diaconate from the schismatic Wecilo. Nevertheless, the pontiff replies that since Daimbert had not been ordained simoniacally, and had emerged from the heretics in body and spirit, he had constituted him a deacon anew, in full, when the need of the Church arose, because he had labored to the utmost of his ability for the benefit of the Church.

Neither response contains any chronological indication. Since it is certain that Daimbert’s ordination, on account of which those letters were written, must be assigned to the early years of Urban’s pontificate, they can scarcely be placed later than this year. I have therefore thought it appropriate to include them here.

I once also thought that Urban’s bull concerning the boundaries of the diocese of Bayonne in the province of Gascony could be assigned here. The bull is reported by the Sammarthani in volume II of *Gallia Christiana*, in the work cited by them on this matter. They say that it was issued on the fifth day before the Ides of April, in the thirteenth indiction, in the year 1106. Urban, however, had died by that year; I therefore conjectured that the copyist’s error should be corrected on the basis of the indiction, which corresponds to 1090.

But after examining the records of that Church, which the most illustrious bishop René-François de Beauveau ordered to be communicated to me, I discovered that the error belonged to the Sammarthani, who carelessly attributed a bull of Paschal II to Urban. In it, however, the indiction should be read as the fourteenth—or else it must be said that the pontiff, as on many other occasions, followed the Pisan reckoning, by which the year began at the end of the preceding March.

### LXXIV. The Privilege of the Major Monastery

In this same month a privilege was issued at Rome for the Major Monastery near the city of Tours, addressed to Bernard, its abbot. Urban received the monastery, as it had already been granted by Victor III, under the special protection of the Apostolic See. Among other provisions, he established that the elected abbot should receive consecration from the archbishop of Tours, but without any profession being exacted from him.

The pontiff inserted this clause because of the profession that bishops at that time wished to require from abbots when they were ordained. The abbots, by contrast, including those who were not exempt, refused to make it, because they found in it, I know not what, of a simoniacal character. Moreover, exempt abbots feared that by this arrangement they might appear to be subjected to the jurisdiction of bishops. This controversy is discussed at greater length in the preface to the first part of the *Acts of the Saints of the Order of Saint Benedict*, Eleventh Century, section 3.

The privilege of the Major Monastery was issued on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of May. It subsequently gave rise to major controversies. By ancient custom the archbishop and clergy of the city were accustomed to celebrate the Easter festival at the Major Monastery. On that occasion many unlawful acts were committed, wholly unfitting for so great a solemnity; these were abolished by the privilege. The clergy took this badly and attempted everything against the monks. They even obtained from Archbishop Rodulfus a sentence of excommunication against them in order to invalidate the privilege. Thereafter they raged against the monks as though in open war, going so far as to seize the grain that was being brought to the monastery.

After Archbishop Rodulfus died, another of the same name succeeded him in the see and in his hostility toward the monks. Although he could not obtain the pallium from Urban without first promising to obey the privilege of the Major Monastery, he soon forgot his pledge and, following the example of his predecessor, continued to harass the monks. This lasted until, after the matter had been discussed in various assemblies of bishops, an agreement was finally reached at the Council of Clermont, as we shall relate under the year 1095. Nevertheless, it can easily be inferred from Ivo’s letter 108 that these quarrels flared up again after Urban’s death.

At that time, or certainly, as seems likely, somewhat earlier, Urban had written to Bernard, abbot of the same place, when he was considering resigning the government of the monastery. Bernard feared that something defective had entered into his own ordination. But if there had been any fault, and however it had occurred, the pontiff forgave him on the condition that thereafter he continue to watch over the salvation of his brothers with greater vigilance and fervor.

From Ivo of Chartres’s letter 73 we understand—unless I am mistaken—that the very matter for which Bernard’s ordination was criticized was nothing other than the profession he had made to the archbishop when he was blessed. For Ivo says there that he is astonished that the brothers of the Major Monastery were reluctant to obey their abbot, on the grounds that, having been blessed by an excommunicated archbishop, he had promised subjection to that archbishop’s metropolitan see. This seemed frivolous to Ivo, who in this matter was by no means favorable to abbots and monks.

### LXXV. The Council of Toulouse

While Urban was conducting these affairs in Italy, his legates held a council at Toulouse in Gaul, around the feast of Pentecost. Bertoldus calls it a general synod and writes that bishops from various provinces gathered there, and that Urban, through his legates, corrected many matters in ecclesiastical affairs that required correction.

At that council, as the same author continues, the bishop of Toulouse was cleared of the charges brought against him, and a delegation was sent to restore Christianity in the city of Toledo, at the request of the king of Spain.

Some have assigned this council to the year 1089, and others even to the preceding year; they say that Bernard, archbishop of Toledo, attended it while returning from his Roman journey, as Rodrigo of Toledo maintains. But Bertoldus’s authority, since he was then living, deserves preference. He expressly asserts that it was held in 1090, around the feast of Pentecost.

We do not, however, deny that Bernard of Toledo attended it. This may be inferred from Urban’s letter to the faithful of Gothia, concerning the monastery of Saint Giles.

What that delegation to Spain was, sent at the insistence of King Alfonso to restore Christianity in Toledo, can scarcely be understood unless we say that these words refer to the acceptance of books of the divine office edited according to the rite of the Roman Church. Thus, after the Gothic books had been abolished, the Spanish Church would henceforth use the Roman books. Certainly, in the following year, through the agency of the apostolic legate Raynerius, who had also attended this council, this was provided for at the Council of León, as we shall relate there.

### LXXVI. The City of Tarragona Given to the Roman Pontiff

After the Council of Toulouse had been dissolved, Raynerius, Urban’s legate, proceeded to Spain through Catalonia. There Raymund, count of Barcelona, having assembled the leading men of the province, solemnly donated the city of Tarragona to the Apostolic See, on the condition that he and his successors should hold it and everything belonging to it from the hand and voice of Saint Peter and his vicar, the apostolic representative of the Roman See, paying him for five years a census of twenty-five pounds of the purest silver.

The donation was made through Lord Raynerius, cardinal of the Roman Church, “who,” Raymund says, “is now exercising the legation in our regions.” It was dated in the Spanish era 1128, in the year from the Lord’s Incarnation 1090.

This document of donation was published by Labbe, Aguirre, and other collectors of councils. Among the others who subscribed it was Berengarius—something truly surprising unless it is due to the copyist’s liberality—with the title of archbishop of Tarragona, although he did not obtain that dignity until the following year. Perhaps Berengarius, bishop of the Church of Ausona, to which the diocese of Tarragona was united, had already assumed the name of metropolitan, though he did not obtain its authority until the following year.

### LXXVII. Urban Protects the Monastery of Banzi

Meanwhile, Urso, abbot of the monastery of Banzi in Apulia, brought complaints before Urban against certain leading men of that province who had seized the monastery’s property and documents and had robbed the abbot himself, after subjecting him to insults, in the manner of bandits. The pontiff was indignant at this and immediately wrote letters to Roger and Bohemond, the princes of Apulia, warning them to provide an appropriate remedy for so serious a scandal.

They in fact did so, as we explained at greater length under the year 1088. Urban’s letter on this matter contains no chronological indication. But it can easily be inferred that it was written this year, and indeed before July, from the document of Roger and Bohemond that Baronius reported in full.

It was issued at Canosa in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1090, in the fifth year of the duchy, in July, in the thirteenth indiction. In that document the princes, stirred by Urban’s admonitions, summoned the leading men of the province at Canosa and confirmed the privileges and possessions of the monastery of Banzi, attempting in this way to repair, as best they could, the injuries inflicted upon so holy a place.

### LXXVIII. Concerning the Son of Jordan, Prince of Capua; the Count of Le Mans Is Excommunicated

Here I would also like to recall another example that demonstrates Urban’s zeal against those who violated the rights of justice. It is the judgment that the pontiff provisionally pronounced against Raynaldus Rinellus, who was accused of having betrothed to himself, more by abduction than with the hope of a lawful marriage and against her parents’ will, the young daughter of Jordan, prince of Capua.

That this Raynaldus was certainly a violent man is clear from book IV, chapter 9, of the Cassinese Chronicle, where it is said that he deceitfully seized the castle of Fractae from the inhabitants of Cassino and afterward attempted to retain it by force and arms.

We assign this judgment, reported by Ivo and Gratian, to the present year because Jordan’s death prevents it from being placed later. Camillus Peregrinius proves from ancient authors that Jordan died toward the end of this year.

Another example of Urban’s concern to correct abuses is supplied by Orderic Vitalis in book VIII, where he writes that Hugh, count of Maine, was placed under ecclesiastical interdict by the same pontiff this year because he had repudiated his lawful wife, the daughter of Robert Guiscard.

### LXXIX. The Schismatics Grow Insolent at the Death of the Catholics. Bishop Stephen of Halberstadt Replies to Them
When the truce had ended—which, as we said in the preceding year, was supposed to last until Easter—and when Hermann, bishop of Metz, and Bertold, duke of Alemannia, the most vigorous defenders of the Apostolic See, together with Bertold’s sister, the queen of the Hungarians, had died in May, as Bertold writes, and shortly afterward Eggebert, margrave of Saxony, had perished—murdered, as they say, by the intrigues of the abbess of Quedlinburg, who was the sister of Henry Augustus—the schismatics decided to return to arms. They did so with such elation of spirit, on account of what seemed to them their happy successes, that they openly proclaimed that the cause of the pontiffs was finished.

Such, certainly, was the opinion of Walbram, bishop of Magdeburg (Trithemius calls him bishop of Zeitz or Naumburg in his *Chronicon Hirsaugiense*). At that time he wrote a letter to Prince Louis, seeking to draw him over to Henry’s side by representing the affairs of the pontifical party as desperate, since its principal supporters had, as he boasted, miserably perished by the just judgment of God. [Col. 0073A]

But the Catholics were very far from sharing that opinion, as we learn from Louis’s reply, which was delivered in his name to Waltram by Stephen—also called Herrand—formerly abbot of Ilsenburg and then bishop of Halberstadt. Both letters were reported by Dodo, abbot of St. Disibod, in his *Appendix to Marianus Scotus*, where they may be consulted. Certainly, this Stephen deserves a place among Urban’s vigorous defenders, on account of many other writings in which, according to Trithemius in the passage cited, he is said to have defended the Church. It would have served our purpose to have the four letters to Pope Urban which that author mentions. But they have been lost.

## LXXX. Henry’s expedition into Italy. The military organization of the Bolognese and other cities of Lombardy. — Penance permitted to soldiers in a just war

[Col. 0073B]

Meanwhile Henry, having prepared his expedition, entered Italy. As he ravaged Lombardy, Welf, duke of Italy, encouraged by the exhortations of his wife Matilda, as Bertold writes, attempted to resist him. But Domnizo testifies that Matilda herself led her own armies; he describes the whole expedition admirably, though in rough verse, in his fourth chapter, which for that reason we reproduced almost in full in the Appendix.

Sigonius thinks that on this occasion the great battle of Sorbara was fought, in which Ebrard, bishop of Parma, and Gandulf, bishop of Reggio—who were supporting Guibert’s party—were captured by Matilda’s victorious troops. But this most learned man is mistaken: the victory at Sorbara occurred before Urban’s pontificate, as Domnizo himself testifies, although in chapter 3 that author mixed in several matters concerning Urban which he reported prematurely. Indeed, Bertold, a witness beyond all exception, records the deaths of both bishops in the year 1085.

Moreover, when Henry was besieging Mantua this year, Welf and Matilda exempted the city from every tribute and tax, so that they might keep it increasingly faithful to them; a charter to this effect was issued at Mantua in the year 1090, on the fifth day before the Kalends of July, and is reported by Sigonius. These acts of generosity, however, did not prevent the city’s surrender, which took place the following year.

This year, as Bertold reports, a great famine suddenly afflicted many regions, although no great barrenness of the soil had preceded it. There is therefore no doubt that it arose from those internal divisions stirred up by the schismatics. [Col. 0073D]

The historians of Bologna (Girardacci, *History of Bologna*, book II), and Sigonius as well, report that the citizens of their city rendered excellent assistance to the pontifical cause amid those disturbances of war. They also relate that on this occasion a military organization was established, divided into four cohorts corresponding to the four tribes into which the city had been divided, each cohort being assigned its own tribunes and standards. Hence, they say, the Bolognese came to be called standard-bearers. Sigonius adds that the other cities of Lombardy likewise adopted the same institution, following the example of the Bolognese. [Col. 0074A]

Since at that time the pontifical party was openly fighting the schismatics, a scruple arose in some minds: whether the faithful of Christ who had killed excommunicated persons in the battles then frequently occurring ought to be subjected to penance. Unless my conjecture deceives me, Urban’s rescript to the bishop of Lucca should be referred to this question; Ivo of Chartres and Gratian included it in their decretals.

When asked about this matter, the pontiff replied that although those who killed excommunicated persons in a just war—such as the war then being waged—should not be considered homicides, nevertheless, since something sinister might have entered into their intention, a suitable satisfaction was to be imposed upon them according to that intention.

Earlier, the Fathers of the council of the province of Reims, in the year 923, had likewise subjected to penance those who had taken part in the battle of Soissons, where Robert and Charles were fighting over the kingdom. For it is undoubtedly scarcely possible that in such civil wars anyone fights solely with peace or the public good in view. Indeed, on a similar occasion St. Ambrose praised Theodosius the Great because, after his victory over the tyrant Eugenius, he abstained for a time from the sacred rites. On this matter, see Isidore of Pelusium, book IV, letter 200.

## LXXXI. The Carthusian house is restored to Bruno’s disciples. He himself withdraws with others to Calabria. He refuses the archbishopric of Reggio. His influence with the pontiff

What Urban did amid these upheavals is not reported by the ancient historians. But Bruno, founder of the Carthusians, whom—as we said—the pontiff had summoned to himself from Gaul in the preceding year, was then with him, assisting him with his counsel. Bruno’s disciples were also with him. Unable to endure the absence of so great a father, they had followed him into Italy shortly after his departure, leaving the Carthusian house behind. Bruno therefore entrusted the site of the Carthusian house to Seguin, abbot of La Chaise-Dieu.

But whether because those good hermits could not devote themselves peacefully to their regular exercises amid so many disturbances, or because Bruno himself was distressed that his beloved Carthusian house should be left entirely empty, he finally persuaded them to return there and live under the governance of Landuin, whom the holy man had appointed prior of the Carthusian house in his place. [Col. 0074D] Urban’s letter was obtained for them, in which he asked Seguin to restore the Carthusian wilderness to them. This was done on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of October of this year.

From this it may be inferred that Bruno’s disciples left Italy around the month of July. Not long afterward Bruno himself withdrew to Calabria with Landuin and other companions. There, when they were found while hunting by Roger, count of Calabria and Sicily, as the commonly circulated accounts relate, they received from him a site suitable for founding a monastery.

Whatever the truth of that story, Roger himself wished everyone to know, in a charter issued this year for their benefit, that through God’s mercy men of holy religion—namely Bruno and Landuin with their companions—had come from Gaul to the region of Calabria. They had chosen to serve God alone, despising the vanity of worldly glory. I quote the pious prince’s words:

> “Recognizing their desire, and wishing to be assisted by their merits and prayers before God, I obtained from their charity, by many entreaties, that they should choose for themselves in my land a habitable place where they might prepare whatever dwellings they wished for the service of God.”

He then assigned them a solitary place between Arena and the town of Stilo, together with the entire surrounding forest, extending for a league in every direction.

The same Roger had the church of this hermitage consecrated in the year 1094. Another charter, published by Roccho Pirro in volume III of *Sicilia sacra*, states that this was done by the archbishop of Palermo, assisted by five other bishops. [Col. 0075B] The prince’s first donation was confirmed and enlarged by Theodorus, bishop of Squillace, in whose diocese the new Carthusian house was situated, as is clear from his charter, dated 16 December of this year. Urban confirmed it, together with Roger’s donation, two years later, and finally Paschal, his successor, confirmed it as well, as may be seen in Ughelli, volume IX of *Italia sacra*.

How highly Urban esteemed Bruno is evident from the fact that, when the Church of Reggio was then vacant—the principal metropolitan church of Calabria—he tried by every means to raise Bruno to it, but without success. The holy man preferred his Carthusian house to all the dignities of the world; indeed, he would have preferred it even to the pontiff’s own retinue, had he been permitted to do so. He declares this himself in a letter written to his Carthusians, in which he says:

> “As for me, brothers, know that after God I have one sole desire: to come to you; and whenever I can, I shall fulfill it in deed.”

There he says more about contempt for the world and the happiness of those who, freed from every worldly concern, can devote themselves to God alone in solitude. Similar statements, and still more extensive ones, are found in another letter of his to Ralph the Green, then provost and later archbishop of Reims, formerly his intimate associate when Bruno was living in that city.

We therefore assign to this year Bruno’s election to the archbishopric of Reggio, which the commonly circulated accounts usually place in 1095, because that see was vacant under Urban’s pontificate only in this year: namely, after the death of Archbishop Arnulf. When Bruno refused that dignity, Rangerius was appointed in his place toward the end of this year. He confirmed the privilege of Theodorus, bishop of Squillace, mentioned above, on 17 December 1090, as elected archbishop of Reggio; thereafter, until the year 1106, he is recorded as subscribing various councils and public instruments under the title of archbishop, as may be seen in Ughelli, volume IX of *Italia sacra*. [Col. 0075D]

Although Bruno therefore shone with no dignity, his influence with the pontiff was no less great. This is proved, among other things, by a letter of Paschal II to Landuin, Bruno’s successor in the governance of the Calabrian monastery. The pontiff addresses him as follows:

> “We have learned that you have succeeded the master Bruno, of holy memory. Let the spirit of that same man therefore be in you; let there be in you the same vigor of the eremitical life and the same constancy of conduct and gravity. For whatever authority and power the master’s prudent wisdom and religious devotion merited from the Apostolic See, with the Lord’s help, we personally grant to you, accompanied by that same spirit.”

Certainly Urban sometimes summoned not only Bruno but Landuin himself to his presence, as is clear from a brief letter of his.

## LXXXII. Urban visits Campania. — The privilege of St. Basolus

Around the middle of this year, since he could scarcely breathe freely in Rome, Urban decided to visit the provinces subject to Roger and Bohemond, so that he might attend somewhat more freely to ecclesiastical affairs there. It is certain that he was in Campania around the middle of August this year, from the privilege of St. Basolus, issued at Sinuessa on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of September and addressed to Burchard, abbot of that place.

## LXXXIII. He writes to St. Anselm on behalf of Fulco, bishop of Beauvais. — Anselm’s reply

A little earlier—namely, on the Kalends of August themselves, for the sequence of events makes clear that this occurred in the present year—the pontiff had written from Capua to blessed Anselm, then abbot of Bec in Normandy, commending to him Fulco, bishop of Beauvais, formerly a monk of Bec and one of Anselm’s disciples.

Because Fulco seemed unequal to bearing so great a burden if left alone, the pontiff instructed the blessed abbot that he himself—or, if prevented, at least one of his brothers—should always attend that bishop as his monitor, corrector, and adviser. He then informed Anselm that he had pardoned whatever defect might have entered into the ordination of that bishop. Finally, he entrusted various matters to Anselm, which are explained in his letter.

There, as also in many of Urban’s other letters, one may observe the pontiff’s solicitude and care in summoning learned and devout men to himself, so that they might assist him in bearing the burdens of the pontificate.

After some time Anselm replied to Urban’s letter, explaining to him the circumstances of Fulco’s election, through whom he had received that letter. He asserted that he had given his consent only because he had been compelled by the insistence of the king of the Franks and the clergy of Beauvais, with the agreement of the archbishop of Reims and without anyone’s resistance. “Thus,” said the holy man, “if I had not done this, I should fear offending God.”

He therefore asked the pontiff to send letters to the archbishop and the other bishops of the province of Reims, and even to the nobles of Beauvais, so that Fulco—who had already set out for Rome for the second time, against the malicious men by whom he was almost overwhelmed—might be fortified by Urban’s authority.

In this letter, which is letter 33 of book II, the holy man expressed his sympathy with the pontiff, who was placed amid such tribulations. He therefore promised him the prayers of himself and his brothers, so that God might lighten his evil days “until a pit is dug for the sinner.” Finally, he foretold that God would not leave “the rod of sinners over the lot of the righteous,” because he would not abandon his inheritance and “the gates of hell would not prevail against it.”

At the end he requested a privilege for his monastery of Bec, although it is uncertain whether he ever obtained it. What later happened to Fulco will be related in what follows.

## LXXXIV. He confirms the privileges of the Church of Ravello. Ordinations of bishops. Perhaps Berengar of Venosa. Was Guitmund bishop of Aversa?

Meanwhile, while Urban was at Salerno, he confirmed the privileges of the Church of Ravello, or Rebello, which his predecessor Victor III had raised to the status of an episcopal see. He issued the charter on the very day of the Nones of October.

[Col. 0077B]

Urban also created various bishops around this time. Among them, Peter, in book IV, chapter 7, of the *Chronicle of Monte Cassino*, praises two taken from the Cassinese monastery: Benedict, for the island of Sardinia, and Rainald, for Gaeta. This latter, according to the same author in the following chapter, consecrated the altar of St. Erasmus this year and, according to an anonymous chronicle, the church of St. Andrew on the Holy Mountain in the following year.

In this same year, as we have already said, Rangerius assumed the governance of the Church of Reggio. He had first been a monk at the Major Monastery near Tours; from there he was transferred to Cava and became known to Urban. According to Ughelli, volume IX of *Italia sacra*, Urban then made him cardinal and archbishop of Reggio.

The same author, in volume VI, writes that the friend of St. Vincent of Volturno was also created by Urban this year cardinal priest of Santa Croce in Jerusalem. He was later made bishop of Isernia and finally died at Monte Cassino during the pontificate of Calixtus II.

Berengar’s promotion to the bishopric of Venosa can also apparently be assigned to this year. He had been educated at the monastery of Saint-Evroul in Normandy under the blessed abbot Theodoric. He followed Robert, Theodoric’s successor, whom the usurper Osbern had forced to leave the monastery, into Apulia. After governing the monastery of the Holy Trinity at Venosa for many years, he was finally promoted by Pope Urban, as Orderic Vitalis reports in book VII, to the episcopate of that city on account of the merit of his life and his teaching in wisdom. Yet the same author, in book III, says that he received the bishopric of Venosa after being elected by the people. Both statements may indeed be true. It is surprising, however, that Ughelli did not include this Berengar in his catalogue of the bishops of Venosa in volume VII of *Italia sacra*.

The same Orderic Vitalis, in book IV, praises Guitmund, a monk of the monastery of the Holy Cross of Saint-Budern, or Saint-Leufred, in Normandy. After various vicissitudes, Gregory VII appointed him cardinal of the Holy Roman Church, and Pope Urban, already proven in many respects, solemnly ordained him metropolitan of the city of Aversa. A bull of Calixtus, in Ughelli, volume I of *Italia sacra*, agrees with this; but it is scarcely possible to understand how the statement can be reconciled with the testimony of other contemporary authors.

No one, of course, is unaware that Guitmund, or Witmund, a monk of Saint-Leufred celebrated for his writings against the errors of Berengar, was appointed bishop of Aversa. Besides Orderic, Bishop Ivo of Chartres, letter 78; William of Malmesbury; and other serious authors repeatedly affirm this.

Yet Ivo, in part IV of his *Decretum*, chapter 213, and Gratian, distinction 8, chapter 5, under the words “If custom,” together with others, produce a decretal from a letter of Gregory VII written to Witmund of Aversa. No one would say that an error had entered into that title if he consulted the manuscripts and printed editions cited in Baluze’s notes to Gratian.

What, then? If conjecture is permitted, either there were two bishops of Aversa named Guitmund, as Ughelli suspected, or Gregory certainly created our Guitmund the first bishop of Aversa, and Urban adorned the same man with the title and honor of archbishop by granting him the pallium—both to distinguish so great a man with some singular prerogative and to gratify the Norman princes who had founded and especially cherished that city.

Certainly Orderic suggests that on this occasion Urban granted Guitmund some special privilege for the sake of the Normans. He says:

> “This city was constructed in the time of Leo IX by the Normans, who had first inhabited Apulia; and it was called Aversa by the Romans because it was being built by factions hostile to them . . . Rich in the wealth of the Cisalpine peoples . . . by the choice of the Normans it obediently obeys the pope alone, from whom it received Guitmund, the sophist, as pontiff, splendidly adorned with the pallium of mystical distinction. As archbishop he governed it for a long time and rejoiced, freed from every exaction of mortals by apostolic privileges.”

These statements are offered as conjectures until someone discovers more certain evidence.

Urban replied to this Guitmund concerning the acceptance of alms from excommunicated persons, provided that they had repented. Ivo, and after him Gratian in his decretals, included this letter—or at least a notable portion of it—written around the month of July, though in an uncertain year.

## LXXXV. The death of Adalbero, bishop of Würzburg

At the time when Urban was providing shepherds for various churches in Italy, he lost in Germany an outstanding and unconquered defender of the Apostolic See: Adalbero, bishop of Würzburg. Although he had been exiled from his homeland and frequently driven from his see, he nevertheless did not cease dedicating churches, restoring monasteries, founding new ones, and performing the other duties of his order.

After countless dangers, as Bertold says, and various persecutions—the author of his Life agrees—he ended his days in a good confession on 6 October. He was buried in the monastery of Lambach, which had been founded by his parents and enriched by him with many benefactions, and which he had assigned to the Benedictine order.

We published his Life, written by a nearly contemporary monk of Lambach, among the *Acts of the Saints of the Order of St. Benedict*, part II, sixth century.

## LXXXVI. The institution of the Aroasian congregation of regular canons

[Col. 0079A]

This year was also marked by Urban’s institution of the congregation of regular canons of Aroasia. It was so called from the principal monastery of Aroasia in the diocese of Arras, which is said formerly to have had twenty abbeys subject to it.

Their first provost—for at that time abbots were not yet accustomed to preside over regular canons—was Hildemar. Together with two other hermits, he laid the foundations of this order. James of Vitry describes the austerity of their life admirably in chapter 23 of his *Historia occidentalis*; Locrius and other authors subsequently praised it in various places. But to pursue these matters in greater detail does not belong to our purpose.

## LXXXVII–VIII. The erection of the abbey of Talmont

[Col. 0079B]

Around the same time, the church of Saint Mary at the town of Talmont in Saintonge, which was made illustrious by the body of the martyr St. Hippolytus, was transferred from the clerical to the monastic order. Fulcher was appointed its first abbot, together with other monks from Angériac, under the protection of the monastery of Angériac, to which this new abbey was to remain subject.

This was done at the direction of Geoffrey, lord of Talmont and founder of the place. To obtain this very thing from Pope Urban, he had gone to Rome. According to an old document, the pope was greatly pleased by the matter. By the authority of the blessed Peter and Paul and by his own authority, he carefully approved everything that was being done with respect to the church, both by the donor—namely Geoffrey—and by the recipient, Odo, abbot of Angériac. In doing so he followed his predecessor Hildebrand, a man of great and admirable holiness, who, while still alive, is known to have granted this same concession to Geoffrey.

Thus, as the same charter states, by the authority of the Apostolic See and by privilege, Odo established monks in that place. One of them, named Fulcher, was blessed as abbot by Bishop Ramnulf. Power was granted to everyone who wished to contribute his property to the new abbey.

We have taken these details from the old document itself, preserved in the archive of Angériac and dated to the year 1090, indiction 13. Geoffrey, the founder of this abbey, is the same man against whom another Geoffrey, abbot of Vendôme, wrote to Ramnulf, bishop of Saintes, in book III, letter 32. He asks the bishop not to grant Geoffrey any delay until he had first satisfied him according to the decree of the lord pope. But he does not explain the matter at issue.

## LXXXIX. The Henricians prevail at Rome. They capture Mantua

At that time—that is, at the beginning of the year 1091, to use Bertold’s words—the lord pope was staying in the region of Campania and was treated with the reverence owed to him by all Catholics, namely by the emperor of Constantinople, Philip, king of the Franks, and other princes of various kingdoms, both ecclesiastical and secular. The exception was the kingdom of the Germans, where many Catholics, deceived by avarice, voluntarily transferred themselves to the party of the excommunicated.

Henry was then moving every stone to draw everyone to his side by force or fraud. He even induced Romans of his own faction to attempt to seize and destroy by trickery the tower of Crescentius—which was then called the Castle of St. Angelo—and which until that time had obeyed the lord pope.

On this occasion the gentleness deeply rooted in the soul of that excellent pontiff shone forth greatly. As Bertold continues, Urban could easily have entered Rome with an army and subdued the rebels’ insolence, but he preferred to conduct his cause with gentleness, patiently yielding to the adversity of the times rather than fighting with arms.

That deed nevertheless emboldened Henry, who was then encamped at Mantua. Indeed, after a prolonged siege of eleven months, Mantua itself was captured on Good Friday, 11 April. According to Domnizo, through the treachery of its citizens, several neighboring cities rejected the rule of Duke Welf—or of his wife Matilda—and embraced Henry’s party.

As a result, the rebels in Rome became more insolent and allowed Guibert, the heresiarch whom they had expelled long before, to enter Rome again and harass the holy Church with his own— not blessings, but curses.

## XC. Urban remains in Campania. William, abbot of Hirsau, as envoy. The privilege of the Church of Catania

Meanwhile Urban traveled through various regions of Campania, compelled by circumstances to move back and forth as necessity required. When Trithemius reports this, he exclaims:

> “O times, O customs! At Rome, in the chair of St. Peter, Wigbertus, an idol, was sitting, while the true vicar of Christ could find no safe place in which to remain!”

At that time William, abbot of Hirsau, a man distinguished for holiness of conduct and faithfulness to the Apostolic See, had sent Gebehard, the prior of his monastery, to Urban with letters of petition, asking that a small portion of the relics of blessed Peter be sent to him.

The pontiff received Gebehard kindly, but, because Guibert was in possession of Rome, he could not give him anything from the apostles’ relics. Nevertheless, so that the envoy might not return empty-handed to so holy a man, who had frequently suffered persecution for the sake of the Apostolic See, the pontiff handed him other relics of the saints, which he was accustomed to carry with him, to take to the blessed abbot at Hirsau.

We have certainly seen here and there several documents from those times, even documents written in Gaul, which were said to have been issued while Urban presided over the Holy Roman Church “under the persecution of the tyrant Henry,” or under similar formulas expressing the same thing in other words.

Yet even amid these difficulties the pontiff was not without honor. The more distinguished men of both orders in the regions he visited generally accompanied him.

Thus, toward the end of January this year, when Pope Urban was at Capua, as Peter the Deacon relates in book IV, chapter 9, of the *Chronicle of Monte Cassino*, Rainald Rivellus—who shortly before had violently invaded the castle of Fractae belonging to the Cassinese monks—publicly made satisfaction to Abbot Oderisius there, in the presence of many Capuan clergy and nobles, standing barefoot, and obtained absolution. [Col. 0081A]

I know that some have postponed this event until the year 1092, when the church of St. Andrew was consecrated, because they misunderstood Peter’s words. But Camillus Peregrinius rightly observed in his series of the abbots of Monte Cassino that this consecration took place on the same day, but not in the same year, as some have thought, in which Rainald invaded Fractae. There he proves, with many arguments—indeed, if I judge correctly, with decisive ones—that this public satisfaction must be assigned to the year 1111.

Whether the pontiff returned immediately afterward to Rome is uncertain. But it is certain from the privilege of the Church of Catania that he was at Anagni at the beginning of March. In that city, on the seventh day before the Ides of March, he granted the privilege to Ansgerius, bishop of Catania.

## XCI. The Council of Benevento. Its canons and date. The freedom of the Church of Monopoli asserted there. The Cassinese bull concerning the body of St. Benedict. The privilege of Holy Cross at Poitiers. The privilege of Crispinus

[Col. 0081B]

Shortly afterward, although the fury of the schismatics was raging, Urban convened at Benevento a general synod, as Bertold calls it. At it, by synodal judgment, he confirmed the sentence of anathema against Guibert the heresiarch and all his accomplices.

At that time the Church of Benevento was governed by Bishop Roffridus, who, according to Ughelli, honorably received the pontiff when he entered the city.

Four canons concerning ecclesiastical discipline are commonly circulated as having been enacted at that synod; they formerly stood among Urban’s letters. The fourth commands all men and women, both laypeople and clerics, to receive ashes upon their heads at the beginning of the Lenten fast.

This council was celebrated in the year 1091. Besides Bertold, this is expressly stated in an old Roman codex from which Labbe published its canons, and the date given is the fifth day before the Kalends of April, indiction 14. The Anianus codex does not disagree, although it gives the year 1090; from the chronological notes it supplies, however, it is readily apparent that it extends that year to the Paschal feast of the following year.

Both codices observe that so many bishops and abbots assembled for the council that their number could scarcely be recorded. Among them, if we believe Baronius, was the celebrated Peter, abbot of Cava, although other authors, as we have already said, hold a different view. Even though Peter resisted, the pontiff granted him the use of the mitre.

Whether this occurred at this council, or at the council of Melfi, or even at Clermont, as some prefer, or finally at Troia, as the local chronicle of Cava reports, makes no difference for proving Urban’s reverence toward holy men and Abbot Peter’s humility. Peter did this, if we trust the author of his Life, the abbot of Venosa, in order to condemn the arrogance of certain people by the example of humility—people who, while vainly exalting themselves, did not fear to usurp honors from the holy Church that were not due to them.

Labbe admits that he has no more information about this synod.

From a bull of Urban to Romuald, bishop of Monopoli, we nevertheless learn that the synod also dealt with the dispute between that bishop and the archbishop of Otranto, or Brindisi. The archbishop of Brindisi maintained that the Church of Monopoli ought to be subject to his metropolitan church. Romuald denied this, producing ancient documents in support of his case which proved that his church was subject only to the Roman pontiff.

After those privileges had been examined in full council, the archbishop of Brindisi lost his case, and the freedom of the Church of Monopoli was confirmed by the votes of all the Fathers. Urban himself testifies to this in a bull issued at Benevento this year on the Kalends of April, which may be consulted in Ughelli. [Col. 0082A]

From this it may be inferred that a bull issued in Urban’s name at Capua on that same day, “Concerning the presence of the body of St. Benedict at Monte Cassino,” can scarcely be assigned to this year, although it gives indiction 14 in its chronological notes, which in fact belongs to the present year—unless someone should wish to say that Urban granted the privilege concerning Monopoli at Benevento in the morning, then proceeded to Capua and there, on that very day, signed the bull of the Cassinese monks.

But this is not the only defect in that rescript, as we explained more fully under the year 1088. Nevertheless, it will be reported later in its proper place, lest we seem to begrudge our Cassinese brethren whatever value that document may have.

Of far greater—and indeed certain—authenticity is the privilege which Adèle, abbess of Holy Cross near Poitiers, obtained from Urban during the time of the same Beneventan council, on the fourth day before the Kalends of April. It will be given among Urban’s letters from a copy.

Finally, Urban was still staying at Benevento when Ravnerius, abbot of Crispinus in Belgium, came to him and obtained from him a document of protection for his monastery. This is reported by Surius and Bollandus under 7 April, in the Life of St. Aibert, who at that time was enclosed in the same monastery and accompanied his abbot on this journey. But nowhere have we been able to find a copy of that privilege.

## XCII. The churches of Sicily restored

At this time, as we learn from Geoffrey Malaterra and from various documents published in different places, Count Roger, after driving the Saracens from Sicily, directed his chief attention to restoring the churches that had been utterly destroyed by the barbarians.

For this reason he repaired monasteries everywhere and built some anew. He did all this on Urban’s advice, having received authority from him to erect new episcopal sees or restore old ones, even within monasteries, when circumstances required it.

Whenever difficulties subsequently arose concerning the arrangement of the churches of Sicily, the Roman pontiffs of that time judged that Urban’s constitutions ought to be consulted.
