Thus Paschal II, in a charter for the Church of Mazara, decrees that matters should remain in the condition in which, with God’s approval, the diocese of Mazara and the others had been arranged by Urban, of blessed memory, the Apostolic Pope.

Eugene III, in a bull to Robert, bishop of Messina, also confirmed the privileges of that Church, adhering to the disposition of Pope Urban.

No one, however, explained the matter better than Roger himself in the various documents prepared on this occasion. Among them we have selected one especially notable document, issued for the benefit of the Church of Catania and reproduced in full by Roccho Pirro.

In it Roger testifies that Urban, with his most holy lips—undoubtedly when he came to Sicily, as we related under the year 1088 from Malaterra—had commanded and asked him to undertake the care of the churches of Sicily. “Therefore,” Roger says, “throughout various suitable places in Sicily I built churches at the command of the supreme apostolic pontiff, and I installed bishops there . . . with his approval and permission, and he himself consecrating the bishops.”

The pious prince then grants the city of Catania to Bishop and Abbot Ansgerius.

In another charter, which the same Roccho Pirro presents, Roger, after listing many donations which he had made to the Church of Catania, adds that he had humbly entreated Urban to confirm his own constitution concerning the matter. Urban, he says, granted this request, uttering dire threats against those who might violate that church, so richly endowed, or remove anything from it, or ever disturb the monks serving God there.

This is the very bull mentioned above under no. 90. It was addressed to Ansgerius, bishop and abbot of Catania, because in the cathedral church of St. Agatha Benedictine monks were then regarded as canons, as in most of the other churches of Sicily, and the same man was both their abbot and their bishop. This custom still exists today in the metropolitan church of Monreale, and it continued to be observed in the Church of Catania until the end of the sixteenth century.

The Ansgerius mentioned here had been taken from the monastery of St. Euphemia. He later founded at Catania a celebrated monastery with a very large church, which, as Roccho Pirro reports, is the largest in all Sicily.

## XCIII. The bishoprics established by Roger. The see of Troina transferred to Messina
What those episcopal sees were that Count Roger established—or rather restored—in Sicily at that time, Robert, bishop of Troina or Messina, tells us in a charter for the monastery of Lipari, reported by Rocchus Pyrrhus in the account of the Church of Patti, volume III of *Sacred Sicily*. In it they are listed in these words:

“First Roger restored the Church of Troina to its former condition, and appointed the lord and venerable Robert as its first bishop; then the Church of Agrigento and that of Mazara; thereafter he established the Church of Catania, and finally that of Syracuse, etc.”

Geoffrey Malaterra gives more information in book IV, chapter 7, where he supplies the names of the bishops who first held these sees. “The count,” he says, “restores the churches throughout all Sicily. . . . In the city of Agrigento he raises a chair to pontifical dignity. . . . Having ordained and appointed over this Church a certain Gerland, a native of the Allobroges, a man, as they say, of great charity and learned in ecclesiastical disciplines. He did likewise at Mazara. . . . He ordained as bishop a certain Stephen of Rouen, a man of honorable life. [Col. 0084A] At Syracuse, moreover, he appointed Roger, dean of the Church of Troina. . . . , born in the province, and raised him to pontifical dignity. . . . At Saint Euphemia he arranged for a certain monk, a Briton by nationality, to be ordained for the Church of Catania.”

This is Ansgerius, of whom we were just speaking. The monastery of Saint Euphemia mentioned here was especially famous. In it Robert Guiscard had installed Robert, abbot of Ouche, who had been driven from his own monastery by an invader, together with other monks who had followed their abbot from Normandy. Hence it came about that in that place—as also at the Holy Trinity of Venosa and Saint Michael of Melito, the other two monasteries that the same prince entrusted to Robert’s governance—the customs of the monastery of Saint-Evroul of Ouche were in force, as Orderic Vitalis observed in book III of his *Ecclesiastical History*.

Now, if we are to believe Rocchus Pyrrhus, the episcopal see of Troina, then governed by Robert, was transferred to Messina at this time, or certainly in the preceding year, through the agency of the same Count Roger. This was done, moreover, on Urban’s advice, as Roger himself testifies in a document reported by the same author, in which the prince states that he had established the episcopal seat in the Church of Saint Nicholas, which he himself had built at Messina. Indeed, according to the same Rocchus Pyrrhus, most of the bishops whom we cited above from Malaterra are said to have been consecrated in this very year: Gerland at Agrigento, Stephen at Mazara, and Ansgerius at Catania; Roger was ordained at Syracuse in [Col. 0084C] 1093. We shall speak again of these prelates and their sees in their proper places when the opportunity arises.

### XCIV. Monasteries restored. Privilege of the monastery of Lipari. Saint Angelo of Militello. Roger’s general privilege.

Moreover, this religious prince labored no less diligently to repair and restore monasteries than to restore bishoprics, as his various documents preserved by Rocchus Pyrrhus prove. It is evident that Roger followed Urban’s direction in this matter from two of his own charters: one for the monastery of Saint Mary of Mili, and another for the monastery of Itala, or Gitala, near Messina. These charters are reported in part IV of *Sacred Sicily*, where the abbeys are discussed.

Among the other monasteries restored at that time was the celebrated Abbey of Saint Bartholomew, situated on the island of Lipari. In 1088 Roger placed over it Brother Ambrose, the very man whom Urban, while residing at Milazzo in Calabria, honored with a privilege in this year on 3 June. Around the same time the pontiff granted another privilege to the monastery of Saint Angelo of Militello, which Count Roger had built shortly before. The diploma itself gives no chronological indication, in the copy of it that we received from the most eminent Lord Cardinal Coloredo; but the correspondence of the circumstances and places led us to mention it here together with the other benefactions of Count Roger.

Roger also possessed from Urban a general privilege that whatever monasteries he endowed in his territories should be entirely free. He himself bears witness to this in a charter for the monastery of Boica in the diocese of Palermo, issued in 1098, in which he declares that the place was to be free from every burden, servitude, and molestation: “just as,” he says, “I received from the most holy lord Urban, Roman pope, the authority and protection to make my monasteries free from every person.” But we must now return to the sequence of Urban’s deeds.

### XCV. The churches of Corsica subjected to the Bishop of Pisa.

It is not entirely clear where Urban went after the conclusion of the Council of Benevento. If what Ughellus says in the preface to the catalogue of the bishops of Pisa, volume III of *Sacred Italy*, were true—namely, that Urban issued the bull in favor of the Church of Pisa on 3 June at Benevento—this would be certain for us. But since the same author later reproduced this very bull in full, dated 28 June, the matter remains uncertain.

The latter reading, however, is more than probably preferable. For, as is clear from another bull cited immediately afterward, Urban was at Mileto in Calabria on 3 June. It would scarcely have been possible for him to cover so great a distance in so short an interval, namely from Campania to farther Calabria. Furthermore, on the first day of July Urban was at Capua and therefore near Benevento. It is consequently plausible that, after the council had ended, he visited Calabria and, returning from there, issued at Benevento this important bull by which the churches of Corsica belonging to the Apostolic See were subjected to the Bishop of Pisa. [Col. 0085C] This favor had been earned by Dagbert, at that time bishop of Pisa, because of his own fidelity and that of the citizens of Pisa toward the Roman Church, to which they had always remained most devoted during those extremely difficult times.

### XCVI. The restoration of the metropolitan Church of Tarragona.

Shortly afterward—on the Kalends of July themselves—when, as we have just said, the same pontiff was at Capua, he completely restored the Church of Tarragona to its former dignity. Dalmatius, metropolitan of Narbonne, having had rejected by the pontiff the letters of Pope Stephen that he produced to establish his claim—letters found to be spurious or at least interpolated—lost his case, since he had been unable to prove by any credible document that the metropolitan Church of Tarragona had been subjected to his Church by any apostolic authority. Taking advantage of this opportunity, Urban immediately appointed Berengar, bishop of Ausona, whose predecessors in that Church had been entrusted with the care of the diocese of Tarragona, as archbishop of Tarragona, something he had long been contemplating; he also granted him the pallium and issued a diploma concerning the matter. As a result, the archbishops of Narbonne lost all the metropolitan jurisdiction that they had exercised over the province of Tarragona for so long.

### XCVII. The Council of León concerning the see of Iria and ecclesiastical offices.

Meanwhile, on the occasion of the funeral rites of King García, as Spanish writers relate, the apostolic legate Reynerius, Bernard, archbishop of Toledo, and other bishops and abbots had gathered at León, where they held a council. The case of Diego, bishop of Santiago, was discussed there—a case that Urban, as is clear from the letters cited above, had especially commended to Reynerius. Peter the abbot, whom, as we said, Richard had allowed to be appointed to this see in 1088, was indeed deposed at this synod.

Diego, however, did not regain his see, either because he was unworthy of it or—what is more probable—because the Fathers did not dare to do so, lest they should thereby aggravate the anger of King Alfonso, who disliked him. Accordingly, the care of his Church was again entrusted to Diego Gelmírez, until the pontiff should determine, as we may conjecture, what ought to be done. This certainly seems to be inferable from the *History of Compostela* cited above, a fragment of which, as we have already promised, we shall reproduce in the Appendix. From it, moreover, it is clear that the abbot Dalmatius, from the Cluniac family, was finally ordained bishop of Compostela, or Iria, after an interval of one year, with Diego and Peter passed over and by the authority of the holy Roman Church.

Furthermore, many regulations concerning ecclesiastical offices were enacted at this Council of León, as Roderic of Toledo in book VI, chapter 30, Luke of Tuy, and other authors have reported in various places. Some interpret this as referring to the change from the Mozarabic Office to the Roman Office, which had already been ordered at other councils in Spain, and believe that the following can be understood in this sense: that the ecclesiastical offices in Spain were to be governed according to the rule of Saint Isidore.

But the late Cardinal Aguirre points out that this passage has nothing to do with the Mozarabic Office. He maintains that the words designate nothing other than the letter of Saint Isidore written to Landefredus, bishop of Córdoba, in which each of the offices and their regulations is explained in detail. Since these matters had undoubtedly been neglected for a long time because of the invasions of the Moors, the Fathers of the synod judged that they should be restored to practice.

Finally, the council decreed that, abandoning the Gothic letters invented by Bishop Ulfilas, the Gallican characters should henceforth be used.

### XCVIII. Deaths of holy men in Germany. Disorders there.

Many distinguished men died in Germany at this time. Among them was the celebrated Count and Margrave Frederick, an outstanding defender of the Apostolic See. As Berthold says under the following year, where he gives a fuller account of him, Frederick “under secular dress, after the manner of Saint Sebastian, played the part of a most valiant soldier.” His death occurred on 29 June.

He was soon followed by the most holy William, abbot of Hirsau. In the midst of persecutions, as the author of his Life records in the *Acts of the Saints of the Benedictine Order*, he pursued the cause of the Catholic Church with unconquered spirit and dared everything for its defense. So great was his zeal that he often received and supported in his monastery an almost innumerable multitude of people of every condition who fled to him. He departed to heaven on 5 July. [Col. 0087A] One month later, on 6 August, he was followed by Saint Altmann, bishop of Passau. His Life, written by an anonymous monk of Göttweig and different from the one published by Tegnagel, was printed at Augsburg in 1619 together with the Life of Saint Gebhard of Salzburg and that of Saint Adalbero, bishop of Würzburg. All of these men became especially renowned in defense of the Catholic Church during those utterly ruinous times.

Shortly before William, two other abbots, also celebrated for the holiness of their lives and their fidelity to the Apostolic See, had died: Wulfelm, abbot of Brauweiler in the diocese of Cologne, on 21 April, and Benedict of Chiusa, in the Alpine passes, on 31 May.

In the following August, as Berthold relates, Welf, duke of Bavaria, met Henry in Lombardy, intending to make peace with him if Henry would agree to dismiss Wibert and restore the properties that had been unjustly taken from Welf. When Henry rejected these conditions, the duke returned to Alemannia, where the disturbances grew so great that shortly afterward the question of choosing a new king was discussed. “This would actually have been done,” says Berthold, “if the laziness or ill will of certain persons had not prevented it.” So much for him.

### XCIX. A new form of religious life in Germany.

It is remarkable that, in such disastrous times, a new way of life arose in Alemannia that imitated the apostolic manner. Although these men appeared by their dress to be neither clerics nor monks, as the same Berthold relates as an eyewitness, they were nevertheless by no means unlike those . . . [Col. 0087C] who, renouncing the world, devoted themselves and their possessions most earnestly to communities of both clerics and monks living according to a rule, so that they might deserve to live together under their obedience and serve them.

This was the “square religion” praised by Paul of Bernried in the *Life of Gregory VII*. When some people, driven I know not by what spite or envy, dared to criticize it, Urban undertook its defense. While serving among the Germans as apostolic legate, he had come to know well the holiness of this pious institution. Accordingly, in this year he solemnly approved and confirmed it by letters addressed to the superiors of the monasteries.

When, in the following year, as the same author relates, a certain layman who had professed this new way of life rashly abandoned it, Urban ordered him, by letters written to Gebhard, bishop of Constance and his legate, to be struck with anathema unless he immediately attempted, through suitable penance, to wash away the crime of his apostasy and so great a sacrilege.

As the fame of this new institution increased, not only did innumerable men and women who lived in the cities or near the monasteries embrace so holy a purpose—paying daily service to the clerics and monks under whose obedience they lived, like slaves—but the same form of life was also adopted in villages and rural places. There, as the same Berthold testifies, countless daughters of peasants did not cease to renounce marriage and the world, live under the obedience of some priest, and obey religious persons with the utmost devotion. [Col. 0088A] “Many villages too,” he says, “entirely gave themselves over to religion and unceasingly strove to outdo one another in holiness of conduct.”

“Thus,” Berthold exclaims, “God deigned wonderfully to console his holy Church in a time of danger, so that she might rejoice over the conversion of many, though she had long continued to grieve over the estrangement of the excommunicated.”

Unless I am mistaken, what Gerhoh reports in the *Syntagma on the State of the Church*, published by Tegnagel, chapter 16, should be referred to this movement: namely, that many clerics and monks, because of the persecution, embraced a harsher life in suburban fields and rural monasteries.

### C. Restoration of the monastery of Pavilly.

After the monastery of Saint Austreberta at Pavilly, which had been destroyed by the Northmen, had been restored in Gaul by Walter, abbot of the Holy Trinity of Mont, or Saint Catherine, near Rouen, Urban wrote to William, archbishop of Rouen, in whose diocese that place lay. He urged him to promote and complete this pious undertaking, and he granted to all who contributed anything to the same monastery a remission of a quarter of the penances imposed by a bishop or priest.

The papal letters were issued at Cessimi—others read Cossini, perhaps Cassini—on 12 October of this year. One of our associates copied them when they had been inscribed on a stone erected from the ruins of the church. On the same stone, appended to the papal diploma, was a donation of the site made to Abbot Walter by Thomas of Pacisy, a knight. William the archbishop and other noblemen were said to have subscribed that instrument.

### CI. Urban’s letters for Saint Cyprian of Poitiers.

This year, as we infer from the date of Ivo of Chartres’s ordination, Urban was at the town of Alatri in Latium at the beginning of November. There, on 2 November, he granted letters to Raynald, abbot of Saint Cyprian of Poitiers, by which he confirmed to him whatever right and canonical authority he possessed in the Church of the Holy Cross at Engla.

In this rescript the pontiff used the following precaution. He feared—at Ivo’s warning, since Ivo, then elected bishop of Chartres, was at Urban’s court and was shortly afterward to be consecrated by him—that, if the church were simply granted to Raynald, Raynald might expel the clerics living there and transfer it to monks.

We learn from Ivo himself, in letter 36 to Peter, bishop of Poitiers, that this nevertheless happened shortly afterward. In that letter he complains bitterly against the bishop because, after long requesting and obtaining a cleric to be placed over this Church of Engla, he later rejected him in order to install monks of Saint Cyprian there.

After citing Urban’s letters on the matter, Ivo argues that they ought not to support the monks’ cause. He declares that he learned this from the pontiff himself, in whose presence he had been when the letters were dictated—not, as Juretus thought he had corrected the text in his notes on this letter of Ivo, “at his side,” but “at Alatri,” as the ancient manuscripts read and as Urban’s letters themselves altogether prove.

### CII. Ivo of Chartres’s ordination: the year in which it occurred.

[Col. 0089A]

The pious pontiff also labored greatly this year on behalf of the Church of Chartres, which Bishop Geoffrey was undermining, being guilty of many crimes, as is clear from Ivo’s letter 8. Several years earlier, Geoffrey had been removed from office by Hugh of Die, legate of the Apostolic See in Gaul. But, claiming that he had been unjustly condemned, he went to Rome. When none of his accusers appeared, Gregory VII, after he had sworn an oath over the body of Saint Peter, restored him to his see, having in some measure cleared him of the stain of simony.

Later, however, accusations against him were renewed. Once his crimes had become fully known to Urban and he had been unable to prove himself innocent of them, he was again expelled from his see by papal authority, and the people of Chartres were given permission to substitute another bishop in his place. They immediately elected Ivo by unanimous consent—the man whom Urban had recommended to them.

Richerius, metropolitan of Sens, refused to consecrate Ivo. He maintained that Geoffrey’s deposition had been carried out contrary to the canons because the examination of his case ought first to have been conducted by himself and the bishops of his province before it was brought before the papal tribunal. Foreseeing that he would obtain nothing from Richerius, Ivo went to Urban. As the pontiff himself testifies in letters issued on this matter, Ivo was consecrated by him, without prejudice to the obedience owed to the Church of Sens. This occurred, according to the letters, toward the end of November, but without any year being specified.

Consequently, authors remained uncertain in which year Ivo’s consecration should be placed. Some wrote that it occurred in 1090, others in 1091, and others in the following year.

Labbe assigned it to 1091 because Ivo is said to have been consecrated by Urban on 13 November, which in that year fell on a Sunday. Moreover, if the same author correctly assigned the Council of Étampes to 1092, Ivo’s ordination, which took place at the end of November, must necessarily be referred to the preceding year. It is certain that Richerius, the metropolitan, summoned this council in order to annul Ivo’s ordination, which, as we have just said, he maintained had been performed contrary to the canons. [Col. 0089D]

This calculation is supported by a charter cited by Juretus, said to have been issued in the twenty-fifth year of Ivo’s episcopate. Ivo himself also mentions the same number of years of his episcopate in another charter reported by Juretus. But if the twenty-five years are subtracted from 1115 or the following year, when Ivo is said to have died—years that he must be acknowledged to have completed, or at least begun, in the episcopate—the year 1091 is obtained. His ordination should therefore be assigned to that year.

To these arguments must be added an ancient document reported by Aegidius Bri in his *History of Perche*. In it Robert of Bellême transferred the Church of Saint Leonard of Bellême to the monks of the Greater Monastery in 1092. Ivo, already a bishop, subscribed that charter and therefore must have been consecrated at least in the preceding year. [Col. 0090A] Since he was ordained by Urban in Italy toward the end of November, as is established, he could not have returned to his diocese before at least the beginning of the following year.

Even if all these arguments did not establish the matter completely, it nevertheless appears certain from Ivo’s own testimony. In letter 67 to Pope Urban, whom he had heard was somewhat displeased with him, Ivo asks that, now that seven years had passed since he had cultivated the vineyard entrusted to him to the best of his ability, he might at last be permitted to leave it in the eighth year.

But if we add seven complete years to 1092, the year in which most people wish Ivo to have been ordained, we arrive at the end of 1099, when Ivo would have begun the eighth year of his episcopate. For, as is certain, he was consecrated at Rome in November. Yet this cannot be said, since Urban was already dead by then, having been taken up to heaven in July of that same year. Indeed, since this letter was written after the feast of Christ’s Nativity, as Ivo himself indicates there, it would have to be assigned to 1111, long after Urban’s death—something no one could maintain.

Everything agrees perfectly with our calculation. We say that this letter was written by Ivo at the beginning of 1099, while Urban was still alive, when Ivo, if he had begun his episcopate in 1091, was entering its eighth year. The events related in the letter also fit the year 1099: namely, the coronation of King Philip by Rodulf, archbishop of Tours, celebrated on the preceding feast of Christ’s Nativity, and the election of a certain young John as bishop of Orléans on the feast of the Holy Innocents. Sausseius, from the *Monuments of the Church of Orléans*, in fact assigned the consecration of John and his rival, whose name was Sanction, to the year 1099—seven years, as he observed, after the ordination of Ivo of Chartres.

“But,” you will say, “Sigebert, a serious authority who lived in Ivo’s time, assigned his ordination to the year 1092 in his Chronicle.” Even if this passage appears in some copies of Sigebert, it is clear from other copies that the addition is secondary; in them these words do not appear. They are certainly absent from Miraeus’s edition, which is more accurate than the others.

Let us nevertheless grant that Sigebert wrote this. He, like any other author, could have written that Ivo entered upon the see of Chartres in 1092, since, although he had been consecrated by Urban at Capua in Italy toward the end of the preceding year, he could not actually have taken possession of his Church until 1092. This argument is directed against those who postpone Ivo’s ordination beyond 1091.

Others, however, such as Souchet in his notes on Ivo’s letters, raise a different difficulty. They maintain that Ivo’s ordination cannot be postponed beyond 1090, proving this from the fact that he died in 1115 after having completed at least twenty-five years in the episcopate. Furthermore, in letter 268, addressed to Walon of Beauvais and other bishops apparently gathered at the Council of Beauvais held in December 1114, Ivo expressly says that he had already spent twenty-five years in the episcopate. Finally, in a charter issued in that same year, 1114, the sixteenth year of Pope Paschal is coordinated with Ivo’s twenty-fifth year. These facts certainly prove that Ivo’s ordination must be assigned to 1090 at the latest.

But if Ivo’s death is assigned to 1116, as some calendars have it, there will be no difficulty concerning the years of his episcopate. Even if he was ordained in 1091, he can then be said to have completed twenty-five years in the episcopate before his death. Let us nevertheless grant that he died in 1115, as the calendars of Chartres prefer, since everyone agrees that his death occurred toward the end of December. Even according to that calculation, Ivo must be said to have reached the twenty-fifth year of his episcopate and could therefore have written shortly before his death that he had already spent twenty-five years in the episcopate, using the round number, as is customary.

The other difficulty is more serious, if no error has crept into the copy of the charter cited by Souchet. Yet the authority of this fragment does not seem so great that it can overturn the opinion received by all authors, including the ancient ones, who all place Ivo’s ordination after 1090. If anyone should prove this charter, or similar charters, to possess wholly unquestionable authority, I shall not strongly object, since Urban was in Campania, where he ordained Ivo, in 1090 as well as in the following year. The arguments we have brought forward establish above all that Ivo was consecrated by Urban before 1092, the year preferred by most writers.

After celebrating Ivo’s ordination, the pontiff addressed an exhortation to him, in which, according to the custom of earlier times, he gave him distinguished admonitions concerning the office entrusted to him. This will be included among Urban’s letters, followed by letters from the same pontiff addressed to the clergy and people of Chartres on 24 November, and by others issued on the following day to Richerius, metropolitan of Sens, at Capua, so that they might be informed of Geoffrey’s deposition and Ivo’s ordination.

Richerius did not stop there. In the following year, chiefly at the instigation of the bishop of Paris, he held the Council of Étampes with the intention of overturning Ivo’s ordination. Ivo’s letters on this matter should be consulted, especially letter 8, addressed to Richerius himself, and letter 12, addressed to Pope Urban.

The efforts of Ivo’s adversaries nevertheless failed. He governed the Church of Chartres until his death, though not without grave and almost continual anguish and anxiety, which he repeatedly mentions, especially in letters 3, 12, and 25 addressed to Urban himself. In these letters he boasts that he is the uterine and special son of the Apostolic See, precisely because he had been consecrated by the pontiff himself.

The Roman journey of Ivo should apparently also be connected with what he writes in letter 211 to Rodulf, archbishop of Reims, concerning the relationship of kinship between the son of the count of Flanders and the daughter of the count of Rodon. There he says that he was present at the Roman court when their genealogy was examined at the command of Pope Urban.

### CIII. The liberty of the clergy of Flanders vindicated.

The Church of Flanders was also disturbed this year—or, as others prefer, in the following year—by Count Robert, surnamed the Frisian. He attempted to revive a long-obsolete evil custom by decreeing that, once clerics had been deprived of the power to make wills, their inheritance should be assigned to the fisc.

The Flemish clergy suffered this injustice with great difficulty. When neither the prayers nor the admonitions of abbots and bishops had any effect on the count—and when even the authority of the metropolitan of Reims could not draw him back from his purpose—the matter was referred to Urban. He immediately wrote to Robert to deter him from such oppression. The letters were issued at Castrum Neti on 2 December, or, according to Locrius, at Saint Peter’s in 1091.

Urban had certainly returned to Rome by November of this year, if Ivo is speaking in letter 27 to Eudo of the Italian journey on which he was ordained by Urban. The passage reads:

“As for the pope himself, about whom you asked me . . . in November I entered Rome peacefully with him; in January I left him there. He is still there and, insofar as God grants him strength, struggles against the adversaries of the Roman Church.”

No one should be troubled by the fact that some writers placed Urban in Rome and others outside Rome at that time because of Guibert’s faction. By “Rome,” many people—especially foreigners—also understood places near the City, which Berthold commonly designates by the expression “the territory of Saint Peter.”

Robert did not obey Urban’s admonitions until the following year, when the case was brought before the Council of Reims. There the Fathers warned him that, unless he quickly obeyed the admonitions of the pope and the bishops and restored what had been taken away, he himself would be subjected to a terrible anathema and his entire land to ecclesiastical interdict. Fearing these threats, he fully satisfied the Fathers and the clergy, as we learn from the acts of that council, which Labbe inserted in volume X of the *Councils*, after Sirmond had copied them from the manuscript of Mont-Dieu.

### CIV. Gervinus confirmed in the see of Amiens.

[Col. 0092D]

We believe that the election of Gervinus—formerly a monk of Saint-Remi and abbot of Centula—to the bishopric of Amiens should also be assigned to this year. When some attempted to overturn it, he went to Rome with letters of recommendation from his metropolitan, intending to defend his case before the pontiff. After two months had passed without any accuser appearing against him, the pontiff approved his election and issued letters to the people and clergy of Amiens, ordering them to regard him as their true and legitimate pastor.

Later, when he was accused again, he was again cleared at Rome and, having obtained new letters from the pontiff, was confirmed in his see. [Col. 0093A] The first letters were issued in December, but they do not specify the year. Nevertheless, they do not appear capable of being assigned beyond this year.

For they were not issued at the end of 1093. In that very year Gervinus, already a bishop, subscribed a charter for the Church of Saint Acheolus; indeed, he took part in the Council of Reims held in March concerning the Church of Arras. This makes it impossible to assign them even to the end of 1092. It is not plausible that Gervinus, within so short an interval, having scarcely returned to his see with the papal letters, should have been harassed by his own people, attended the Council of Reims, been accused there of simony, and then gone to Rome again, where he was cleared for a second time. All these events would have had to occur within six months if Urban’s first letters were issued at the end of December and the second in the following July.

Therefore, if I judge correctly, it is more reasonable to assign Gervinus’s first Roman journey to the end of 1091 and the second to 1093, after the Council of Reims. On this reconstruction, this bishop, having received Urban’s letters at Rome on 20 December 1091, departed and returned to Amiens at the beginning of the following year. After he had spent some time there, he was again harassed—perhaps because, as Urban indicates in the second set of letters, he opposed the depravity of clerics living with concubines; or certainly because of his own vices, since he was not held in high esteem by most authors of his age.

In any event, at the Council of Reims at the beginning of 1093, which he is known to have attended, he was accused of simony. He therefore decided to go to Rome, where, having been cleared on this second occasion as well, he obtained letters from the pontiff issued on 18 July. They will be presented in their proper place.

These remarks are conjectural, pending the discovery of more certain evidence. It will not be difficult to assign these letters to other years as well.

### CV. Urban celebrates the feast of the Nativity of the Lord outside the City.

As this year was drawing to a close, Berthold writes, the pontiff returned to the territory of Saint Peter and celebrated the feast of the Nativity of the Lord outside the City, since Guibert, entrenched in a fortress near Saint Peter’s, could not have been expelled without bloodshed—something the pious pontiff detested above all.

Meanwhile Henry, no gentler in Lombardy, where he had already been staying for two years, was turning everything upside down and sparing neither places nor persons in his attempt to detach Welf and his wife Matilda from Urban’s allegiance. But in vain. As the war grew more and more intense, Welf the elder, duke of the Bavarians, prevented Henry from meeting the king of Hungary at the conference that they had arranged by common agreement.

### CVI. Matilda’s victory over the emperor.

At that time—that is, at the beginning of 1092—Conrad was in Lombardy with his father Henry. Both were intent on seizing the possessions of the deceased Countess Adelaide of Turin, which were owed to the son of Count Frederick.

Sigonius relates that this year the emperor occupied many places after crossing the Po, but lost one of his sons, who was killed in battle and buried at Verona. He does not give the son’s name, nor does Domnizo, from whom he borrowed this account.

Domnizo, however, in book II of the *Life of Matilda*, chapter 7, describes in greater detail the wars fought during these years between Henry and Matilda. He also praises at length a certain John, abbot or hermit, who obtained for the countess, through the prayers of himself and his monks, the victory he had foretold to her when she was fighting near Canossa in October. In that battle Matilda’s soldiers captured Henry’s standard and deposited it in the monastery of Saint Apollonius.

### CVII. Urban’s party prevails.

On 25 March Henry was staying at the castle of Montiglio, as is clear from one of his charters reported by Ughelli in volume V of *Italia sacra* [Col. 0094B]. In it he grants Berinzona to Peter, bishop of Como, on account of his fidelity and the purity of his service; for Henry omitted nothing that might secure bishops and other nobles for his party. This, however, did not deter the people of Como from choosing a Catholic bishop for themselves. Accordingly, when they substituted Guido for Peter—a man most devoted to Urban—they would not allow Landericus, whom the emperor was attempting to intrude, to obtain the throne of their Church.

Indeed, if those who were contaminated by the stain of simony or by the heresy of the Nicolaitans are excluded, one will find few who adhered to Henry. By contrast, from almost every part of the Christian world, bishops and archbishops—even of the principal sees—together with abbots and faithful Christians of every rank, [Col. 0094C] gathered to Urban as to their proper shepherd and the legitimate successor of Peter. At that time those in Alemannia who adhered to Urban unanimously appointed Berthold, the brother of Gebehard, bishop of Constance, previously called duke in name only, as duke of Swabia, “for the defense,” as Berthold says, “of holy mother Church against the schismatics.” Thiemo—or, as Berthold calls him, Dimo—metropolitan of Salzburg, together with the bishops of Constance and Worms, consecrated Ulrich bishop of Passau on Pentecost itself. This action, as the same author adds, greatly strengthened the Catholics of Bavaria in their obedience to the Apostolic See.

### CVIII. King Eric of the Danes implores Urban’s aid. The establishment of the metropolitan see of Lund.

[Col. 0094D]

At the same time—an event remarkable enough to have occurred amid so great a disturbance of the Roman Church—Eric, king of the Danes, driven to desperation by the archbishop of Hamburg, who followed Henry’s party, came to Urban so that, through apostolic protection, he might defend himself and his kingdom against that prelate’s efforts. Saxo Grammaticus relates the matter in book XII of his *Danish History* in these words:

> As it happened, the archbishop of Hamburg had decided that Eric should be punished with an anathema on account of empty and false suspicions. Fearing this, the king forestalled the sentence by an appeal and immediately set out for Rome. There, after his case had been examined with the greatest care, he powerfully refuted the pontiff’s accusation and returned superior to his accuser in every aspect of the defense. Nor was it enough for Eric to have defeated the archbishop in court; he also sought to free himself and the peoples under his rule from the archbishop’s jurisdiction, which he obtained later on another journey to Rome.

Perhaps he came there a second time because the archbishop of Hamburg had refused to obey the judgment of Urban, whom he did not recognize. After the city of Lund had been raised to a new metropolitan see, not only Denmark but also Sweden and Norway were henceforth subject to it, before archbishops were established at Uppsala and Nidaros by Eugenius III. Consequently, the authority of the archbishops of Hamburg was greatly diminished on this occasion. At that time, as we gather from the same Grammarian, Ascer was bishop of Lund; shortly before Eric’s first journey to Rome, he had succeeded Egino.

### CIX. The establishment of the metropolitan see of Pisa.

[Col. 0095B]

In this same year Urban also established a new metropolitan see in Italy, namely that of Pisa. He assigned to it as suffragans the bishops of the island of Corsica, who had previously been directly subject to the Roman pontiff; in the preceding year he had already entrusted the care of the island’s churches to Daibert, bishop of Pisa. The pope declares that he did this with the consent of his clergy and at the request of Countess Matilda, chiefly, among other reasons, because of the outstanding services rendered to the Apostolic See by the Pisans and by their bishop Daibert, to whom he granted the honor of the pallium. They had remained faithful to the Roman Church always and everywhere, even amid the storms of persecution and war.

The bull of establishment, preserved by Ughelli, was issued at Anagni [Col. 0095C] on 22 April of this year. The Genoese took the establishment of this metropolitan see badly, since they did not want the Corsican bishops to be subject to the bishop of Pisa. Although this arrangement of the suffragans was somewhat altered, the privilege of Pisa nevertheless remained firm and unshaken.

### CX. The privilege of Saint Sophia of Benevento. Another for the monks of Silvaniacum.

Urban had already been staying at Anagni since the beginning of the preceding month, as is clear from the privilege that he granted there on 14 March to Madelmus, abbot of the monastery of Saint Sophia near Benevento.

In April, in the same place, he granted another privilege to certain monks or hermits who, a few years earlier, had begun to build a monastery at a deserted place called Silvaniacum, in the territory of the Bituriges [Col. 0095D]. Two of them had approached the pontiff to obtain letters of protection from him, but the prudent pontiff granted them only subject to a condition, since he did not know either the place or those monks well.

We assign these letters to this year, although the copy places them in the preceding year, not only because the fifteenth indiction is noted there and because they were issued at Anagni on 11 April, where Urban was then staying, but also because an ancient document of the same place, in which precisely the same chronological indications occur, is said to have been written on a bissextile day before the Kalends of March. That indication can apply to this year, 1092, but not to the preceding one. It reads as follows:

> In the year 1091 from the Incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ, in the fifteenth indiction, while Urban was pope of the most holy Roman Church, under the persecution of the tyrant Henry, with Philip reigning in France, on the bissextile day before the Kalends of March, I, Raynandus the pagan, etc.

He grants certain possessions to Andrew, prior of the monks of Silvaniacum, beneath his forest called Corniliacum. This is the same Andrew who was a disciple of Saint John Gualbert, father of the Vallombrosan monks, and who, as they say, was brought to France by a certain count of Chalon, settled there first, and later became the first abbot and founder of the celebrated monastery of Casal Benedetto among the Bituriges. Orderic Vitalis mentions him near the end of book VIII.

After becoming abbot, he obtained another privilege from Urban in 1099, as we shall relate in its proper place [Col. 0096B]. Silvaniacum—or rather Corneliacum (Cornilly)—still depends under the title of a priory upon the abbey of Casal Benedetto, situated in the duchy of Saint-Aignan.

### CXI. The pontiff urges the restoration of Tarragona. The privilege of Saint Lawrence of Aversa.

On 1 May—or, as another edition has it, toward the end of April—Urban wrote to Berengar, archbishop of Tarragona, and reproved him because the restoration of the city of Tarragona was being neglected, although in the preceding year he had conferred upon him the honor of the pallium on the condition that both he and the other leading men of the province devote all their efforts to completing this work.

These letters are said by Odoricus Raynaldus to have been issued on 25 April; in the *Councils of Spain* of Cardinal Aguirre, volumes II and III, however, they are dated on the Kalends of the same month [Col. 0096C]. It matters little which reading is preferred. We infer that they were issued at Anagni because the pontiff was still in that city at the time: on the seventh day of the same month he granted there a notable privilege to the monastery of Saint Lawrence near Aversa, whose abbot and monks had splendidly assisted him when he was in the difficulties we have described. A copy of that privilege, which we obtained from the archives of the place through our friend, the Reverend Father Dom Erasmo of Gaeta, dean of Cassino, will be presented in its proper place.

### CXII. Fulco, abbot of Divas, takes refuge with Urban.

About this time Fulco—formerly a monk and prior of Utica, and for twenty years already abbot of Saint Mary above the Dives in Normandy—had governed the monastery entrusted to him strictly, according to Orderic Vitalis, book X, and had advanced the church in many ways. But, through the envy and instigation of Satan, he was unjustly accused and deposed, and took refuge with Urban. We gather from the same author that this occurred in the present year, for he records that Fulco died an old man on 30 March 1106, after seven years of exile and an equal number of years following his restoration.

John, a monk of the same place, had been given to him by Roger, abbot of Utica, as a companion for the journey. He was a man renowned for piety and learning, whom Orderic calls his own teacher and instructor in sacred letters. He was appointed Fulco’s traveling companion not only on account of his own outstanding qualities but also, if I judge correctly, because, having been born at Reims and having become a monk after being a Reims schoolmaster, he was undoubtedly known and agreeable to Urban. He could consequently incline the pontiff’s mind in Fulco’s favor, which we infer in fact happened. After spending several years in the monastery of Cassino, he recovered his position in 1099, as we shall relate there.

### CXIII. The council of Étampes concerning Ivo; the Parisian council for Saint Cornelius of Compiègne; the Reims council for the Flemish clergy; the Soissons council against Roscelin.

Meanwhile Ivo, having returned from Italy, where he had been ordained bishop of Chartres by Urban, suffered much at the hands of his rivals, especially from the bishops of his province, who met at Étampes with Richer, archbishop of Sens, in order to depose him by synodal judgment. But he appealed to the Apostolic See and, as we said in the preceding year, frustrated their efforts.

For this year Labbe also cites a council of Paris and the confirmation there of the privilege of Saint Cornelius of Compiègne. But the chronological indications found in King Philip’s charter—the only source from which we know of this synod—together with the subscriptions of the bishops appended there, fit the year 1072 better, as Marlot has already observed in volume II of the *Metropolis of Reims*. There is no doubt that this council was held in that year; therefore one must say that the error arose from a copyist’s carelessness [Col. 0097C].

The same Labbe, as well as Iperius in the *Chronicle of Saint Bertin*, also presents another council as having been held at Reims in this year concerning Robert, count of Flanders, who, as we said, was attempting to deprive the clergy of his dominion of the right to make wills. Although it is certain that this synod was actually convened at Reims, it is not entirely clear whether it should be assigned to this year or the following one.

More important was the council of Soissons, which Raynald, metropolitan of Reims, convened this year against Roscelin, a cleric of Compiègne who was then disseminating new errors concerning the persons of the most holy Trinity. Later authors called him the teacher of Peter Abelard, either because Abelard really was his disciple or at least because both defended similar errors.

What those false doctrines were is explained by Saint Anselm in book II, letter 41, to Fulco, bishop of Beauvais, and in his book *On the Incarnation*, which he dedicated to Pope Urban. In that work Anselm refutes Roscelin, who asserted that the three persons in God were three things in the same way as three angels; he also refutes the slanders that this deceitful heretic had rashly spread against Lanfranc and against Anselm himself. Roscelin had shamelessly lied that such great men had supported his cause.

He was compelled to abjure his heresy before the fathers of the synod. Nevertheless, if we believe Ivo, letter 7, he continued afterward to defend it in secret disputations, as people of his sort customarily do [Col. 0098A]. His efforts, however, were unsuccessful.

### CXIV. Urban condemns King Philip’s adulterous marriage. Ivo and others resist it. Who celebrated it?

Although Urban was gentle in disposition and exceptionally devoted to peace, and although, being then placed in great difficulties, he seemed to need the favor of princes in order to protect himself against the plots of the emperor Henry and his followers, he nevertheless never concealed their vices or complied with their wrongful desires in order to win their allegiance.

Accordingly, he never approved Philip, king of the Franks, who, having dismissed his own wife, was attempting to contract an adulterous marriage. On the contrary, he forbade every bishop ever to dare place a crown upon the woman whom the king was illicitly seeking to marry [Col. 0098B], and, according to Ivo, letter 28, threatened the prince that unless he abandoned his evil purpose he would place him under ecclesiastical interdict.

When the king could not be diverted from his decision by any warnings or prayers, he was deprived of communion by Hugh, the apostolic legate, because he had repudiated his own wife Berta and publicly taken another woman—Bertrada, the wife of Fulk, count of Anjou—with the complaisance of certain bishops.

The letters of that religious pontiff concerning this matter, and the surviving decrees of the councils, bear witness to how diligently Urban labored and how concerned he was to deter the king from so great a crime, whether by admonishing and imploring him personally or through others, and even by threatening him. Certainly Ivo of Chartres, a witness beyond all objection, testifies that Urban wrote serious letters about this affair to all the archbishops and bishops of the kingdom. As is certain from his letter 25 to Urban himself, Ivo had received them for distribution among the other bishops.

Orderic Vitalis likewise testifies to this in book VIII of his *Ecclesiastical History*. He writes that on this occasion the devout pontiff sent legates of the Apostolic See into Gaul and, through letters and the preaching of priests, rebuked, implored, and reproved the erring king, who had repudiated his lawful wife and joined an adulteress to himself against the law of God.

The most prudent pontiff did not handle the matter rashly. Weighing everything carefully, he omitted nothing that seemed conducive to an investigation of the case [Col. 0098D]. Thus, after receiving envoys from the count of Anjou, who sought the restoration of Bertrada, he had the degrees of consanguinity calculated and demonstrated in his presence, as Ivo reports in letter 211 to Raynald, archbishop of Reims, before pronouncing any decision. He did not wish anything to be done precipitately, so that Ivo—perhaps at times more impetuous than was proper and impatient of delay—seems to criticize his slowness in this matter in letter 30.

Ivo himself, when invited by the king to Paris for the marriage, refused to go unless the grounds for the divorce had first been approved by the bishops in a general council, as he himself declared in his letter 15 to the king. Indeed, he sent a copy of the letter he had written to the king to the other bishops who had also been summoned to the marriage [Col. 0099A], together with another letter in which he warned them not to become like mute dogs unable to bark. He also wrote on the same matter to Raynald, archbishop of Reims, to whom he promised that he would not attend the marriage unless Raynald himself celebrated it. Since, he said, the Church of Reims possessed the crown of the kingdom, nothing ought to be done without the consent of its bishop.

Philip indeed claimed that the case had been decided by Pope Urban and approved by Archbishop Raynald and his suffragans. Ivo did not believe these assertions. It is more than probable that Raynald never consented to Philip’s marriage.

It is certain that Raynald never celebrated this marriage, although by the privilege of his Church’s bishops that duty belonged to him. Urban, moreover, condemned it not obscurely or privately but openly and in explicit words on more than one occasion. This is clear from his letter to Raynald and the other bishops of the province of Reims, in which he gravely reproved them for failing to prevent so great a scandal by their authority [Col. 0099B].

Indeed, if Orderic may be believed, no bishop in Gaul consented to the king’s desire. The same author, after the words quoted above, praises the religious commitment of the Gallican prelates, because none of them, as he believed, deigned to perform this detestable consecration. They stood firm, he continues, in the rigor of ecclesiastical rectitude, seeking to please God rather than human beings; and all unanimously condemned the shameful union with an equal anathema.

He then adds that, if Philip happened to arrive at any town or city, all the ringing of bells and the general singing of the clergy ceased [Col. 0099C]. Hugh of Flavigny relates that this occurred at Sens for nearly fifteen days, but that author confuses together events that took place before and after Urban’s death. The event occurred when, after Urban’s death, Philip returned to his vomit and was placed under ecclesiastical interdict by the legates of Pope Paschal at the council of Poitiers. Nothing, however, prevents its having occurred under both pontiffs. William of Malmesbury, in book V of his *Deeds of King Henry*, says that when Philip had been excommunicated by the Apostolicus, wherever he went, no divine service was performed there.

Certainly, in the passage cited above, Orderic accuses Odo, bishop of Bayeux, of betrayal, because, after receiving the churches of the town of Mantes as compensation for his unfortunate service, he celebrated this detestable betrothal of King Philip and Bertrada, which the bishops of France refused to celebrate [Col. 0099D]. The Malmesbury author just cited reports that this was done by William, archbishop of Rouen, and writes that for this reason Urban placed him under ecclesiastical interdict, from which he was absolved only after many years through the intervention of blessed Anselm.

It is certain that this marriage was not celebrated by Raynald, archbishop of Reims, to whom, according to Ivo, that duty belonged by the ancient prerogative of his see. Urban nevertheless reproved Raynald because he had not prevented it from being performed by the bishop of Senlis [Col. 0100A], his suffragan.

Whether Odo of Bayeux or William were first present at the betrothal of Philip and Bertrada, whose marriage the bishop of Senlis later blessed, is uncertain. Hugh of Flavigny certainly also attacks other bishops for the same offense. He asserts that Philip found among the bishops of his kingdom men whom he could make his allies and ministers of so great a sacrilege: namely, Philip, bishop of Troyes, and Walter of Meaux, to whom he gave the bishopric so that, while the former performed the consecration, the latter might agree to it and serve as its minister.

Ivo, in letters 66 and following, is a witness that Philip and his concubine Bertrada made bishoprics and abbeys available for sale. Yet the same Ivo, an entirely trustworthy authority, testifies in letter 16 that Walter, bishop of Meaux, did not consent to this adulterous marriage, at least before it took place [Col. 0100B]. I therefore believe that Hugh did not write about these matters with sufficient accuracy, especially since Urban himself, in the letter already cited more than once to Raynald, archbishop of Reims, and his suffragans, explicitly affirms that the marriage was performed by the bishop of Senlis.

### CXV. The dedication of the church of Cava.

From the same letter of Urban, issued in October of this year, 1092, it is certainly established that Philip’s divorce from his wife Berta occurred in this very year. Other authors, following the writer of the *Chronicle of Tours*, have generally and mistakenly assigned it to the following year. Clarius, a contemporary author, agrees with this dating. In his *Chronicle of Saint Peter Vivo of Sens* he expressly states that in 1092 Philip dismissed his wife Berta and took Bertrada. Some report that Philip abducted her in the church of Saint John while the canons of Saint Martin were blessing the sacred fonts on the vigil of Pentecost. Besides the evidence already cited, other records also prove that this occurred in this year.

The dedication of the church of the monastery of Cava by Urban himself was celebrated in this year. Not far from Salerno there is an oratory where the pontiff is said to have stopped when he went to Cava. Since the history of the dedication contributes greatly to illustrating the deeds of this pontiff, I thought it appropriate to present it in full in the Appendix, from Ughelli, volume VII of *Italia sacra*, and from the Bollandist volume for March [Col. 0100D]. There it is reproduced from a manuscript of the same place, copied at the end of the *Life of Saint Peter*, who then governed that monastery.

Even today, in this very basilica, one can see an inscription carved in stone and placed in memory of so great a solemnity. In the *Annals* of Baronius and in Chesne’s *Lives of the Pontiffs* it is given as follows:

> The cross sculpted in this stone, which you see, the most holy Urban II, Roman pontiff, during the sacred dedication of this church, anointed with oil with his own hands as a sign of the sacred rite, in the year of salvation 1092, on the Nones of September, in the fifteenth indiction.

The memory of this dedication is celebrated not only by the brief chronicle of the monastery of Cava according to the Easter cycles [Col. 0101A], but also by the Benedictine calendars on 5 September, as well as by Ferrarius in his *General Catalogue of the Saints Who Are Not in the Roman Martyrology*.

In his annotations for the same day Ferrarius cites two charters of Urban granted to that Church on the occasion of its dedication, but he reports their chronological indications incorrectly. We have both documents before us.

The first is the very privilege that Urban is said to have granted to this place after completing the dedication and after returning to Salerno. It was subscribed by him and by the other bishops and cardinals who had accompanied him. It was issued in this year on 14 September, in the fifteenth indiction and the fifth year of his pontificate. In it the pontiff confirms the privileges previously granted to this monastery by Gregory [Col. 0101B] VII, together with all the properties that Duke Roger and other noblemen had bestowed upon the place.

The other charter of Urban, commonly circulated as having been granted on the same occasion, was published in volume I of the *Casinensis Bullarium*. It is, as it were, an abridgment of the former; or rather, the former is nothing other than this document expanded. But the chronological indications, which are sound in the first, are inconsistent in this one and do not fit the present year.

It is said to have been issued at Salerno in this year, 1092, on 24 January, in the fifteenth indiction and the fifth year of Urban’s pontificate. At that time—namely, in January or February of this year—the basilica of Cava had not yet been dedicated.

If, however, these indications are referred to the following year, counting the beginning of the year from the Easter solemnity, as is often done, provided that Urban could then have been at Salerno, nothing in these indications—or indeed in the entire document—would need correction except the indiction. In my judgment, the authenticity of the latter appears more probable than that of the former. Or, if both are accepted, the latter was a confirmation of the former privilege in nearly the same words, as has sometimes occurred elsewhere. Accordingly, the first was issued in this year, while the second was issued in 1093, when its other chronological indications fit.

Moreover, we recently received another copy of this second bull from the Cava archives. It contains no indication of place or time; from this it may be inferred that the indications found in the cited copies were added or corrupted by someone. Besides the two bulls mentioned here, we have already referred above [Col. 0101D] to one issued with Urban’s decree in favor of the people of Cava. These two documents appear to have much better—or rather, entirely certain—authenticity.

### CXVI. A rescript for the Carthusian house in Calabria.

Most published authors state that Bruno, founder of the Carthusian order, was summoned by Urban to Italy in 1092. It has already been demonstrated above that this occurred much earlier.

This year, when the pontiff was in Calabria, he confirmed and praised the donations made by Count Roger to Bruno, who at that time was residing in the monastery of Torre in the diocese of Squillace, and which had been approved by Bishop Theodore. He added several privileges recorded in his rescript on the matter, issued on 14 October [Col. 0102A].

It is therefore surprising that Urban, if one believes the rescript concerning this matter published by Ughelli, should toward the end of his life have rescinded, or at least restricted, these privileges of the monastery of Cava in favor of Alfano, archbishop of Salerno.

Nevertheless, when the matter concerned the granting of pontifical ornaments to our Cassinese abbots, the Cava privilege was cited and praised in the congregation of the cardinal interpreters of the Council of Trent, as Tamburini testifies in *On the Law of Abbots*, disputation 23, question 1. Indeed, whenever that same privilege has been challenged, it has always stood—and still stands—firm and inviolate, as is clear from various authentic documents preserved in the archive of that place together with papal charters and the decrees of congregations or commissioners [Col. 0102B].

Urban’s rescript, whatever its nature may ultimately be, will be given in its proper order, lest we appear to have concealed anything in favor of our own people.

### CXVII. Urban’s judgment concerning the Church of Crediton. He comes to Matera.

Several ancient documents prove that Urban was in Calabria during this month and the next. Among these must be counted his decree, issued after many disputes between the two parties, concerning the monks of Vendôme and the monks of Saint-Albans of Anjou, who had long been litigating over the church of Saint Clement of Crediton.

Amatus, archbishop of Bordeaux and Urban’s legate in Aquitaine, had already issued a judgment in Urban’s name. But since neither party was willing to abide by his decision, the case was referred to the pontiff himself, and envoys were sent from both sides. They met in the province of Calabria at the monastery of Saint Mary called Malina.

The case was vigorously argued before the pontiff on the first day, but it was not settled. The same occurred on the following day. On the third day, however, which was 20 November, after the matter had been investigated at length and in detail, the dispute was finally settled amicably. The pontiff was then seated in the city of Anglona in Apulia, with many bishops, cardinals, counts, and other ecclesiastical and secular persons present [Col. 0102C].

The agreement was that the church of Saint Clement of Crediton should remain with the monks of Vendôme, on the condition that they cede to the monks of Saint-Albans one of three churches in compensation [Col. 0102D]. In fact, the monks of Vendôme gave the opposing party the church of Saint John above the Loire, which the monks of Saint-Albans still possess today.

It is remarkable that Goffrid, who shortly afterward became abbot of Vendôme, protested against so solemn an agreement. That he did so is clear from his letter to Paschal II, the eighth letter of book I. There he says that Urban had been deceived by the monks of Saint-Albans in this affair. He adds that the judgment previously issued by the same pontiff had been revoked after he had seen the privileges of the monks of Vendôme.

Nevertheless, Urban’s original decree remained in force. His successor Paschal, after also considering Goffrid’s complaints, confirmed it by a new charter in 1115, as may be seen in Baluze, volume II of the *Miscellanea* [Col. 0103A], where that charter is published together with the other acts of the dispute. Goffrid’s letters on this matter should also be consulted, namely letters 8 of book I and 44 of book IV, together with Sirmond’s notes.

Besides these documents, we possess the judgment of Amatus, the apostolic legate, which was issued in Bordeaux in Urban’s name at the beginning of this year, before the pontiff had decided anything concerning the matter, as we have said.

Urban’s own decree, which is included among his letters, is said in some copies to have been issued at Taranto on 24 November in the year 1092; in others, in the following year. The reading makes no difference. It is certain from the year of Urban’s pontificate, which is given as the fifth in every copy, and from the sequence of events, that it must be assigned to 1092. Nevertheless, it could correctly be called 1093 in that document according to the custom of many authors of that age and region, who—as we have already observed more than once—began the year, together with the indiction, in September in those more distant regions of Italy [Col. 0103B].

Lupus Protospata used this reckoning, as is clear from other passages, when he wrote:

> In the year 1093, in the first indiction, Eugenia, abbess of the monastery of Saint Benedict of Matera, died in October; in the same month Pope Urban came to Matera and arrived at the monastery of Saint Eustasius with a great multitude of people.

Little remains concerning these monasteries, as may be seen in Ughelli, volume VII of *Italia sacra*, and in Lubin’s *Account of the Abbeys of Italy*. The dioceses of Matera and Acerenza, however, joined together, have a single archbishop [Col. 0103C].

### CXVIII. The Church of Arras is separated from that of Cambrai.

When Gerard, bishop of Cambrai, died on 11 August of this year, the people of Arras began to consider restoring to its former freedom their church, which, after Arras had been destroyed by the Vandals, had been entrusted to the care of the bishop of Cambrai, as the nearer prelate.

Although the undertaking appeared difficult, the opportunity for attempting it was then more favorable than ever. Urban had been born and educated in the province of Reims; he knew well the ancient dignity of the Church and city of Arras, and he was not unaware of how much the people of Arras had suffered from the people of Cambrai, who were attached to the emperor Henry, Urban’s own bitter enemy.

The pitiable condition of the Church of Cambrai favored the cause of Arras, for Cambrai was then divided into various factions over the election of a successor. Henry increased these disturbances, believing it greatly in his interest to place in that see someone whom he could safely trust.

The expectation of the people of Arras did not deceive them. Urban, having found an opportunity to restore the former dignity of the Church of Reims—as he often testified in his letters—received the envoys of Arras kindly and omitted nothing that might satisfy their desire. After many disputes on both sides and many labors and anxieties [Col. 0104A], they finally obtained a bishop of their own.

Many letters were written back and forth concerning this matter. Various assemblies were held on the occasion, both at Reims and at Arras; indeed, several councils were also celebrated, and embassies were sent to Rome. We shall report in their proper places whatever pertains to our purpose. Anyone who wishes to learn more about this matter than is reported by us, by our Locrius or Acherius, or at least by Labbe, should consult volume V of the *Baluze Miscellany*, where he will find a careful account of the entire affair together with various letters and other records, all copied by that learned man from an ancient manuscript of the Church of Arras.

Urban, therefore, having received the embassy of the people of Arras, immediately wrote to the clergy and people of that city [Col. 0104B], ordering them to cast off the yoke of Cambrai, choose a bishop of their own, and present the person elected to their metropolitan for consecration.

To prevent the metropolitan himself from being deterred by any difficulty from carrying out this ordination, the pontiff also wrote to him. At that time the metropolitan was Raynald, who had been placed in charge of the Church of Reims after the deposition of Manasses. Urban stated that he wished the metropolitan see of Reims to be restored to its ancient dignity when the Church of Arras had recovered its own bishop—that is, that, adorned with twelve episcopal sees, it would no longer need to appeal to foreign provinces when judgments had to be rendered according to the canons.

As we have already said, this was once a special prerogative belonging solely to the province of Reims in Gaul [Col. 0104C], as may be seen in the older records.

Urban wrote two letters on this matter. Although the year is not explicitly stated in them, it can easily be understood from the sequence of events. The letter addressed to Archbishop Raynald contains no indication of place or time. The other, addressed to the people of Arras, is said in some manuscripts to have been issued on 2 December, without any designation of place.

The old manuscript before us, however, identifies the place itself, namely Castranetum; other manuscripts and printed editions read “Rome.” Perhaps Castranetum was a place near Rome where the pontiff was then staying, since he was not yet able to enter the city because of the faction of Guibert.

For, as Berthold writes, Pope Urban celebrated Christmas this year outside Rome, in the territory of Saint Peter [Col. 0104D], because he was still unable to enter Rome without an armed force. The Guibertines and excommunicated persons still had great power there and would not easily permit themselves to be driven out without violence.

### CXIX. The people of Constance reject a false bishop.

Shortly before that feast, Ulrich—who had already received from the emperor Henry the bishopric of Aquileia together with the abbey of Saint Gall—also attempted to seize the bishopric of Constance by expelling Gebhard and installing one of his own monks, a man devoted to him named Arnold. Both efforts, however, failed.

The citizens of Constance, although that intruder had already received investiture from the emperor, disgracefully expelled him from the city, together with his associate, who had come there with him shortly before Christmas in order to take possession [Col. 0105A].

### CXX. The apostolic legation is restored to Hugh of Lyon.

At the close of the same year, or certainly at the beginning of the following one, through the intercession of Ivo of Chartres—as can be gathered from his Letter 12 to Urban and Letter 109 to his successor Paschal—the dignity of apostolic legate in Gaul, which Hugh, archbishop of Lyons, had long lacked, was restored to him. It had been taken from him in the time of Victor III because, after approving and praising that pontiff’s election together with the other Catholic bishops, he had nevertheless later joined Richard, abbot of Marseilles, and attempted to invalidate it, indeed withdrawing from obedience to him. Accordingly, both men were excommunicated and deprived of the apostolic legation at the Council of Benevento by that same Victor III. Yet, although their audacity had been so great—an audacity which Hugh had also attempted to justify in a letter addressed to Matilda, as we have already explained in its proper place—neither of them defected to the schismatics; rather, shortly afterward, when Urban was elected pope following Victor’s death, they adhered to him inviolably.

Ivo congratulates Hugh in Letter 24 addressed to him on the restoration of the legation by Urban. There he proves that the pope had to be obeyed by Hugh, who, because of the difficulties of the times, was somewhat reluctant to accept this dignity. The same Ivo indicates when this occurred by saying that at that time a second Ahab, namely Henry, had arisen in Italy, and a new Jezebel in Gaul, namely Bertrada, as Hugh of Flavigny also calls her. It is clear that this letter was written toward the end of the year, or at the beginning of the following one, because in it Ivo asks Hugh to inform him at what place he might conveniently meet him around the beginning of Lent.

### CXXI. Guibert in Lombardy. Whether Urban granted the privilege of Figeac at Rome. The privilege of Cava.

At this time, as Bertold relates, Guibert was staying in Lombardy with his emperor, Henry, and was plotting with him whatever he could against Welf and his wife Matilda, the daughter of Saint Peter; Domnizo gives a fuller account, and excerpts from him will be presented in the Appendix. Sigonius agrees in Book IX of *On the Kingdom of Italy*, where he described the events of this period from these authors.

[Col. 0105B]

Urban, however, was still at Rome in February of the year 1093, if the privilege of Figeac is genuine and no error has entered its chronological notices. It is said to have been issued at the Lateran in this year 1093, in the fifth year of Urban’s pontificate, on the fifth day before the Ides of February. But even if those chronological notices are sound, the place of issue is faulty, since Urban had not yet then gained possession of the Lateran palace. As we have just said from Bertold, he had been compelled to celebrate the feast of Christ’s Nativity outside the city, since he could not have entered it without bloodshed—something the pious pontiff had always abhorred. Indeed, Urban did not recover the Lateran until the following year, through the assistance of Goffrid, abbot of Vendôme, who, as we shall relate, contributed a large sum of money toward this purpose.

[Col. 0105C]

Certainly, this diploma appears altogether doubtful. Apart from the fact that its contents are scarcely consistent with the circumstances of that time, what is especially objectionable is that it is addressed to a Bishop Stephen of Cahors, otherwise entirely unknown. Cruceus reports more about him in his *History of the Bishops of Cahors*; the reader may consult it if he wishes.

The privilege of Cava, which we discussed under the preceding year, possesses somewhat greater authority. It is said to have been issued at Salerno on the nineteenth day before the Kalends of February, in Urban’s fifth year, in the fifth indiction, in the year 1092, although the notices of place and time are so inconsistent that they cannot be accepted. We leave both documents to the judgment and criticism of learned readers.

[Col. 0106A]

Moreover, although throughout the entire period during which the Lateran palace—the principal seat of the Roman pontiffs—was in the power of the Guibertists Urban was never able to enter within the walls of the city of Rome, he nevertheless frequently stayed in its suburbs, or, as Bertold commonly says, in the territory of Saint Peter. He was therefore considered to be present at Rome. It is consequently not surprising that some of his letters are found described as having been issued at Rome during this period, just as many authors of that age write that bishops and abbots had then gone to Rome to visit Urban or the thresholds of the Apostles.

### CXXII. Fulco, Bishop of Beauvais, Confirmed in His See

[Col. 0106B]

Such were Urban’s letters to Fulco, bishop of Beauvais, and others to the clergy and people of the same city, said to have been issued at Rome on the sixth or sixteenth day before the Kalends of March. In these letters the pontiff confirms the sentence previously issued by Gregory VII concerning the castellany of Beauvais. The sequence of events proves that they were written in this year.

For Fulco, whom we have already discussed above, had been accused before Urban of having badly administered the affairs of his bishopric and of having involved himself in the crimes of certain evildoers. He received those letters in February. He immediately went to Rome to prove his innocence before the pontiff, prepared to surrender his see whatever the outcome of the case. This indeed was the opinion of Saint Anselm, formerly his teacher and abbot at Bec, as can easily be understood from Letter 34 of Book II, written to Urban himself, although in the preceding letter Anselm had commended him to the pope.

[Col. 0106C]

Afterward, when Anselm had become archbishop of Canterbury, he again pleaded humbly before the pontiff on Fulco’s behalf, in Book III, Letter 37, asking him to assist Fulco as his prudence should judge. Nor was the commendation of so great a man in vain. For when Urban had examined Fulco’s innocence, and could not endure that a bishop should be unjustly oppressed, he confirmed him in the see of Beauvais, purged of the heresy of simony which some had imputed to him, and ordered him to remain there.

Indeed, when the same bishop, after returning to Gaul in the following year, was summoned before the bishops of his province for this matter, the pontiff rebuked them for daring to reopen a case judged by the Apostolic See. Urban’s letter on this subject to Raynald, archbishop, and his suffragans is extant. Since it was written at the beginning of May in the year 1094, as we shall demonstrate in its proper place, it proves conclusively that the two letters under discussion here, together with Fulco’s purgation, must be assigned to the present year, 1093.

[Col. 0106D]

### CXXIII. The Council of Troia. Its Canons

At the beginning of spring in this year, to quote Bertold’s exact words, Lord Pope Urban convened at Lent a general synod of nearly one hundred bishops from different provinces in Apulia, and took care to provide suitable assistance through synodal action for the various needs of the Churches.

[Col. 0107A]

Romuald, archbishop of Salerno, writes in his *Chronicle* that this synod was held at Troia, an episcopal city of Apulia, and nearly all authorities agree with him. Some more recent writers, however, have called it the second council, because they accepted that another had been convened by Urban in the same city in 1089. But, as we have already said, the ancient authors recognize only one council for the year 1089; it must therefore be established from Bertold’s testimony and from other certain and indisputable records that this council was celebrated in 1093.

Labbe presents its title, copied from manuscript codices, in Volume X of the *Councils*, in these words:

> In the year of the Incarnation of the Lord 1093, on the fifth day before the Ides of March, a council of nearly 75 bishops and 12 abbots convened at Troia in Apulia.

[Col. 0107B]

The same number of bishops and abbots is said to have been present in Ivo’s printed copies, although the text cited by Labbe gives eighty. Peter the Deacon also mentions the same synod in Book IV, Chapter 7 of the *Chronicle of Monte Cassino*, but nowhere gives the number of pontiffs or abbots who assembled there.

[Col. 0107C]

Two canons of this council survive, which the compiler of the papal letters will present after Urban’s letters.
