The first concerns the dissolution of marriages contracted within a specified degree of consanguinity; it is frequently cited and transmitted by Ivo of Chartres, Gratian, the Master of the Sentences, and other authorities. The second, enacted on the occasion of the Truce (*treuga*; printed as “Treviae”), decrees that those who violate it are to be punished by excommunication.

### CXXIV. Urban Grants a Privilege to the Church of Saint Paul of Narbonne

[Col. 0107D]

After the council was dissolved, Urban returned to Rome, as we infer from the privilege he granted there in this year to the Narbonnese Church of Saint Paul, in the sixth year of Urban’s pontificate, on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of April, in the first indiction. These chronological notices present no difficulty.

In this diploma the pontiff praises the canons of Saint Paul for the regular manner of life which they had recently embraced. He says that to revive this form of life is scarcely to be considered a lesser merit “than to preserve the flourishing religious observance of monks.” Similar praises frequently occur in other privileges granted by Urban to regular canons. He believed that in this way good men could be strengthened in persevering in their purpose, while others whose lives were not so strictly bound by the Rule could be encouraged to embrace the same institution.

[Col. 0108A]

### CXXV. Conrad Abandons the Cause of His Father, the Emperor

Meanwhile the affairs of Henry Augustus were going from bad to worse, with most people daily falling away from obedience to him and to the pseudo-pope Guibert. For at that time, according to Bertold, in Lombardy the most prudent soldiers of Saint Peter—the duke Welf and his wife Matilda—who had already been fighting courageously against the schismatics for three years, were finally, with God’s help, greatly strengthened against them.

But nothing aided the Catholic cause so much as the defection of Conrad, Henry’s own son, from his father to Duke Welf, to whom he thereafter adhered unwaveringly. Bertold gives no reason for this unexpected change; but from Dodechin we learn that it occurred because of Praxedis, whom that author calls Adelaide, the queen and wife of Henry. The emperor is said at that time to have hated her so deeply that he exposed her to be dishonored by his courtiers, and even by Conrad himself.

[Col. 0108B]

The pious prince, who, as the same author says, was conspicuous in every form of goodness and integrity, humble and modest, recoiled from so great a crime. But his enraged father, provoked by this refusal, became so incensed against him that he thereafter refused to regard him as his son, asserting that he was not his father.

Then Conrad, abandoning his father, fled to the pope’s party with those who were devoted to him. Indeed, many others, as Domnizo records, struck with horror at so monstrous a crime, first resolved to despise Henry and Guibert, and then entirely to abandon their cause. On this occasion the strength of the Catholics is said to have received a great increase.

Bertold bears witness that the more distinguished cities of Lombardy—Milan, Cremona, Lodi, and Piacenza—at that time conspired against Henry for twenty years. In this way the Catholics, having occupied the Alpine passes, prevented Henry’s supporters from Germany from reaching him in Lombardy. Accordingly, the people of Augsburg, encouraged by the example of the neighboring cities, rejected the pseudo-bishop whom Henry had placed over them and elected a Catholic pastor for themselves.

[Col. 0108C]

### CXXVI. The People of Lorraine Adhere to Urban

The peoples of the cities of Lorraine also honored Urban with no less zeal—namely, those of Metz, Toul, and Verdun. They altogether refused to render obedience to Egilbert, bishop of Trier and metropolitan of their province, because he maintained communion with the schismatics.

[Col. 0108D]

The people of Metz went further. Having rejected him—certainly Adalbero, for so Meurissius and others call him in the *History of the Bishops of Metz*, or Albert, as we shall say below, whom the emperor wished to place over them—they elected as their bishop Poppo, formerly archdeacon of Trier, a Catholic man and one most devoted to the Apostolic See. As Bertold records, they had him consecrated by Gebehard, bishop of Constance and legate of the Apostolic See, on the sixth day before the Kalends of April, in the middle of Lent.

### CXXVII–VIII. Conrad Becomes King of Lombardy

[Col. 0109A]

Yet one unexpected event nearly undermined so many successful developments: namely, the captivity of the prince Conrad, whom Henry had seized after entrapping him by treachery. But shortly afterward, as Bertold writes, Conrad was rescued through God’s mercy and turned that mourning into joy.

Soon afterward, with the consent of Duke Welf of Italy and his wife Matilda, he was raised to the kingship and solemnly crowned by the bishop of Milan, with a great gathering of the faithful of Saint Peter adding splendor to the ceremony.

Meanwhile Welf, duke of Bavaria, arrived in Lombardy. When he joined himself to Urban’s followers, that sudden reversal so depressed Henry’s spirit that, in Bertold’s words, he withdrew into a certain fortress, where he remained for a long time without royal dignity and, overcome by excessive grief, is said to have wished to surrender himself to death. But, forestalled by his own men, he was unable to carry this out.

[Col. 0109B]

From Udalscalc’s *Life of Egino*, in Canisius, Volume II of *Ancient Readings*, we learn that Henry spent some time then at Verona, but in such dire straits that, surrounded on every side, he was allowed neither to enter Lombardy, because Lady Matilda opposed him, nor to leave Italy, since the German princes had completely blocked his return to Germany. For the Catholic cause was prospering no less in those regions than in Italy.

### CXXIX. Welf the Elder Becomes a Knight. The Assembly at Ulm

Shortly afterward, when Welf the Elder had returned to Germany, Bishop Gebehard, as Bertold relates, received him into knighthood, just as he had long before done with his own brother Berthold, duke of Alemannia.

[Col. 0109C]

Then, at Ulm, in a large assembly of the princes of Alemannia, where the same bishop was present with his brother Berthold and with Welf, it was decreed by common consent that everyone should be bound to obey Bishop Gebehard in every respect according to the statutes of the canons, and Berthold the duke and the counts according to the law of the Alemanni.

Next, as the same author continues, the dukes and counts, the greater and the lesser, swore that they would observe firm peace from the seventh day before the Kalends of December until Easter, and from Easter for two years. To remove every fear of violating that agreement from the minds of the faithful, the princes who had attended the assembly returned to their own territories and compelled each person under their authority to swear individually to this peace.

[Col. 0109D]

### CXXX. Monasteries Founded in Alemannia

At this time several monasteries were also newly established in these regions and, as Bertold reports, were dedicated by Gebehard, legate of the Apostolic See.

The first was built from its foundations in the Black Forest by Duke Berthold, brother of the same bishop. Gebehard himself dedicated it this year, on the first day of August, after it had been endowed with abbatial dignity and placed under the special protection of the Apostolic See.

[Col. 0110A]

In the following month the same bishop consecrated another in honor of Saint Martin. Count Hartmann and his brother Odo had founded it on their own allodial property, precisely where the rivers Danube and Haris meet.

At the same time, a third monastery, not far from the preceding one, was consecrated by the same pontiff under the name of Saint George. In it, as in the preceding monastery, Otto, abbot of Saint Blaise, established regular discipline.

In addition, Sigefrid, abbot of Schaffhausen, fearing that the assaults of the schismatics might force him to abandon his monastery, obtained this year from Richard, abbot of Saint Victor of Marseilles, a cell called Nobiliacum. There he and his monks would have a place of refuge if the necessity of abandoning their monastery ever arose. For this reason he furnished the house with everything necessary for the observance of regular discipline.

### CXXXI. The Council of Rheims Concerning the Restoration of Arras

[Col. 0110B]

In Gaul, after receiving from Pope Urban—as we said under the preceding year—the right to elect their own bishop, the people of Arras wrote to Raynald, metropolitan of the province, asking him to send from his own side to Arras some prudent and noble cleric, or an abbot, who could act as his representative at the election.

He replied that he had assigned to the Cambrai people, who were attempting to obstruct this election, the Sunday called *Oculi mei semper*, that is, the third Sunday of Lent, which fell on March 20 that year, as the date on which they should present the reasons for their opposition at the council of the entire province that he had ordered to be held at Rheims at that time.

[Col. 0110C]

For this reason he also warned the people of Arras to be present on the appointed day, so that they might defend their case before the fathers of the council against the efforts of the Cambrai people.

The legates of both Churches therefore appeared on the appointed day. First, after praising the ancient records of the provinces of Gaul and producing many testimonies of the ancients—especially those drawn from the *Life and Testament of Saint Remigius*—the people of Arras asserted that their city, once one of the more distinguished cities of Belgica Secunda, had formerly possessed its own bishop. Consequently, according to the decrees of the pontiffs and councils, this right ought to be restored to it now that the city had been recalled to its former splendor, especially since Pope Urban himself had decreed in letters that this should be done.

When the Cambrai legates offered no reply and produced nothing in support of their case, the archbishop declared that the restoration of the bishopric of Arras had in fact been ordered by the pontiff. He immediately ordered Urban’s letters on this matter, both those addressed to himself and those addressed to the people of Arras, to be brought forward. Burchard, abbot of Saint-Basolus, and Dudo, chaplain, who had recently returned from the Roman court, openly testified that all this was so.

[Col. 0110D]

Then, after requesting the advice of the bishops and others who were present, the archbishop was prepared to assent to the wishes of the people of Arras, although those present were asking for a delay, when the people of Cambrai, despairing of their case, appealed to the Apostolic See.

The archbishop immediately admitted this appeal, with the consent of the entire council, and assigned both parties a day—the Sunday before the Ascension, or certainly the following week—on which they were to defend their case before the Roman pontiff, to whom he would write concerning the matter. The council was then dissolved.

### CXXXII. The Case Is Heard Before the Pontiff

[Col. 0111A]

A few days later John and Drogo, chosen by the people of Arras to conduct their case before the pontiff, set out for Rome. Urban received them kindly. After waiting in vain for the legates of Cambrai, and after the period fixed by the Council of Rheims had elapsed, he sent them back to Raynald, archbishop, with letters ordering him to consecrate the bishop elected by the people of Arras; or, if he did not wish to do so, to send the man to the Apostolic See, where Urban would consecrate him, without prejudice to the rights of the Church of Rheims.

These letters, like the others which the pontiff wrote to the people of Arras on the same occasion, contain no chronological notices. Yet from the course of events it can easily be gathered that both sets were issued one or two days after the Sunday within the octave of the Ascension—that is, on the last or penultimate day of May.

[Col. 0111B]

The legates therefore returned to Gaul and immediately went to Rheims to deliver the pontiff’s letters to the archbishop. After receiving them, he advised the legates to return to Arras without delay and press forward with the election. But he refused to write the letters which they were demanding from him to the clergy and people of Arras, doubtless fearing that by doing so he would turn the people of Cambrai against him. He gave as his reason that it was unnecessary and inappropriate for him to add his own letters to the pope’s letters, which had already commanded the election of a new bishop once and again—although the pontiff had in fact ordered him to do so.

### CXXXIII. Lambert Is Elected. The Archbishop of Rheims Delays the Consecration

[Col. 0111C]

Content, therefore, with Urban’s letters alone, the legates returned to Arras. The day for holding the election was immediately announced as the sixth day before the Ides of July, which was a Sunday.

On that day not only the clergy of Arras but also the clergy of several neighboring Churches were summoned. Among them were the canons of the collegiate Church of Lille, whether for greater solemnity, because of an ancient custom, or because of an association between the two groups.

[Col. 0111D]

On that day an almost innumerable multitude of clergy and laity assembled in the principal Church of Saint Mary. After the solemn celebration of Mass and the preliminary invocation of the Holy Spirit, Urban’s letters concerning the restoration of the dignity of the Church of Arras and the election of a bishop were publicly read from the pulpit.

When Lambert, cantor of the Church of Lille, had been designated bishop by the provost Gualbert, the dean Guibert, and all the other canons, in unanimous agreement in the chapter, he was immediately presented before the whole Church. Thus he was elected by the clergy, acclaimed and praised three times by the people, and, although unwilling, was chosen, seized, and enthroned in the episcopal seat.

When he protested, together with the other canons of Lille, who were distressed that so great a man was being taken from them, Urban’s sentence from his first letter was publicly read. It ran as follows:

[Col. 0112A]

> To the man who shall have been elected by the canonical consent of the clergy and people, we prohibit by apostolic authority from evading by any pretense the election imposed upon him under this new arrangement.

Thus everyone acquiesced in the election that had been made.

A letter was immediately sent to Raynald, the metropolitan, asking him to indicate the day on which the consecration of the new bishop was to take place. He replied without setting a date that he would discuss the matter with the other bishops of his province at a great assembly of bishops and clergy which he would hold at Rheims on the feast of Saint Mary, in the middle of August.

When the day had been announced and the legates of Arras appeared to ask about the matter, the archbishop again requested a delay, this time until the feast of All Saints.

[Col. 0112B]

Exhausted by so many delays, the people of Arras sent legates to Rome for the third time: Odo the cantor and John the deacon. They were to report the whole matter to the pontiff and once more implore his assistance against the archbishop, who seemed by such evasions to be attempting to elude the apostolic commands.

The letters which the people of Arras wrote to the pontiff on this occasion will be presented in their proper place, as will those which the pontiff himself, receiving the legates of Arras kindly, as was his custom, wrote to Raynald on this matter. In them he ordered Raynald, within thirty days after receiving Urban’s own letters, either to consecrate Lambert himself or to send him to Rome to be consecrated in the Roman court.

[Col. 0112C]

He repeats nearly the same command in another letter which he wrote on the same occasion to Lambert himself, the elected bishop. Since this letter is said to have been issued on the fifth day before the Ides of October, we infer that the preceding letter, which bears no date, was also written at the beginning of October.

Accordingly, after receiving Urban’s letters around the middle of November, the archbishop wrote to Lambert, the elected bishop of Arras, instructing him to send a legate to him within the octave of Saint Andrew. Through this representative, Lambert was to be informed of what the archbishop had decided concerning his consecration together with the other suffragans of his province.

The legates of Arras did indeed appear at the appointed time, but even then they were unable to obtain a definite answer from the archbishop. Therefore, impatient with so many delays, the people of Arras finally decided that the elected bishop himself should be sent to Rheims to the archbishop, so that the latter might either consecrate him at the time fixed by the pontiff—as they had repeatedly demanded—or, in accordance with the apostolic command, send him to Rome with letters of recommendation, where the pontiff himself would consecrate him.

[Col. 0112D]

Lambert accordingly went to Rheims. There, on a Sunday which was the fifteenth—or rather, the fifteenth day before the Kalends of December—and which was the final limit of the period fixed by the Roman pontiff for his consecration, he presented to the archbishop, in the name of the clergy and people of Arras, a letter asking him finally to bring this affair to an end in one way or the other, as the pontiff had ordered.

[Col. 0113A]

> We offer repeated thanks to your excellence and dignity, the people of Arras say in this humble petition, because until now you have willingly extended assistance to us as a pious father . . . . Yet we are greatly astonished that your fatherhood has grown so cold at the conclusion of our affair, since, within the term imposed by the Apostolic See upon your magnificence for the consecration of our elect, you have neither summoned our elect to consecration by a solemn letter from yourself, as we had supposed, nor designated a fixed day within that period. Now, since henceforth the consecration cannot take place within the three-year limit, we humbly ask, with all due respect, that you be willing to give us letters of your authority to be delivered to the Apostolic See, as he ordered, for the consecration of our elect.

Since no avenue of evasion remained, Raynald granted Lambert permission to go to Rome. He gave him letters for Urban, and, after receiving them, Lambert left Rheims on the very eve of Christ’s Nativity. After various dangers and the difficulties of the journey, he reached Rome at the beginning of the following year, as we shall relate there.

[Col. 0113B]

The letters which Raynald had written to Lambert, and those which the same archbishop and the Church of Arras finally wrote on this occasion to be delivered to Urban, will be included in the collection of papal letters, after those which Urban himself, as we have just said, had written shortly before to both parties.

From the letters which Raynald last wrote to Urban through the elected bishop of Arras, as well as from the pontiff’s reply, we understand the reason why that prelate had delayed the consecration of the new bishop for so long, and the cause of all his evasions: he feared that, if he readily consented to the restoration of the bishopric of Arras, the people of Cambrai, who obeyed the schismatic emperor Henry, would seize the opportunity to withdraw from obedience to him and to the Church of Rheims.

[Col. 0113C]

He therefore preferred that the ordination should be performed by the pontiff rather than by himself, so that the people of Cambrai would have no occasion for complaint against him or against his Church. Other special letters of his to the pontiff concerning the affairs of Cambrai bear on this matter; Urban replied to them, as we shall relate under number 145.

### CXXXIV. Gervin Confirmed in the Bishopric of Amiens

[Col. 0113D]

We have already discussed above, in §104, Gervin, bishop of Amiens, who was confirmed by Urban on the throne of Amiens despite the accusations of his rivals. Later, however, he was again harassed by his own people and was forced to visit the pontiff once more. On this occasion too he was kindly received and obtained a second letter, addressed, like the first, to the clergy and people of Amiens. In it Urban ordered them to regard Gervin, purged of simony, as their true and legitimate pastor.

It was issued on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of August in this year, if my conjecture is correct. For this reason the compiler of the papal letters will report it as received from the distinguished scholar Étienne Baluze.

### CXXXV. The Bishop of Dol Obtains the Pallium

Around the middle of the same year, it seems, Rolland, bishop of Dol in Brittany Minor, came to Urban to implore the pontiff’s assistance against the prince of Dol, who had invaded the property of his Church, and also to obtain from him the pallium, which some of his predecessors had already possessed.

[Col. 0114A]

Urban willingly granted the protection of the Apostolic See against the invaders of Church property, issuing letters on this subject to the prince and people of the city of Dol. But in granting the use of the pallium, which Rolland was especially demanding—since he called himself archbishop, like his predecessors for more than two hundred years—Urban showed himself more difficult.

The equitable pontiff feared that by doing so he might undermine the rights of the Church of Tours, which he knew to be the one true and ancient metropolitan Church of the province of Lyon III. Rolland could obtain nothing until, producing letters of Gregory VII, he had proved that the use of the pallium and the provision of archiepiscopal jurisdiction in Brittany Minor had been granted to his predecessor Irenaeus.

[Col. 0114B]

But since he produced only copies of these letters, Urban required him to swear under oath that the autograph letters of Gregory contained neither more nor less than what he himself asserted. Once this had been done, the pontiff, without prejudice to the rights of the metropolitan Church of Tours, granted him the honor of the pallium and archiepiscopal honors, just as Pope Gregory had done for Irenaeus.

He issued letters on this matter which, although they contain no chronological notice, must nevertheless certainly be assigned to this year on the basis of those issued in the following year concerning the same controversy.

### CXXXVI. Ralph, Archbishop of Tours, Proceeds against the People of Dol. He Obtains the Pallium

[Col. 0114C]

Rolland was still in the pontiff’s entourage when Ralph, archbishop of Tours, arrived at Benevento, where the pontiff was then staying, to oppose him.

Ralph brought many arguments against the people of Dol before the pontiff, seeking to establish the rights of his Church over Dol and the other Churches of Brittany. Rolland replied only that he had not come to engage in litigation, although he was prepared to answer together with the bishops of his province at a suitable time.

Urban therefore, with the agreement of both parties, fixed a time for them in the middle of the following Lent, when the matter was to be settled. The pontiff himself recounts these events at length in the sentence which he issued against the people of Dol in the following year, as we shall relate there.

[Col. 0114D]

During this journey Ralph experienced what is recorded about him in the *Deeds of the Bishops of Tours and the Abbots of Marmoutier*. The author of these *Deeds* relates that Ralph was never able to obtain from Urban the pallium which he earnestly requested until he had promised to cease harassing Marmoutier, to consent to the privilege of that place, and to obey the pontiff entirely.

After he had made this promise in the presence of several monks of the same monastery who were there, the pontiff granted him the honor of the pallium. Yet he did not keep his promises, nor did he cease persecuting the monks of Marmoutier, as we shall relate in its proper place.

### CXXXVII. The Dedication of the Monastery of Pauso

[Col. 0115A]

In Volume VII of *Sacred Italy*, in his catalogue of the archbishops of Acerenza, Ughellus presents under this year an ancient document, as he himself believes, concerning the dedication of the church of the monastery of Saint Mary of Pauso, commonly called Deventuum.

According to this document, the pontiff himself had consecrated the place shortly beforehand, if the document possesses any credibility, and had enriched it with extensive indulgences. All these acts are said to have been confirmed by a papal bull issued at Salerno on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of October in this year.

But these claims, as we already said under the year 1088, possess no authority. We mention them here only so that they may deceive no one.

### CXXXVIII. Urban Asks the Council of Bordeaux to Arrange Collections

[Col. 0115B]

Around this time, when some hope of recovering the city of Rome began to appear, the most gentle pontiff—who had never wished this to be achieved through bloodshed—convinced himself that it could be accomplished through money and gifts.

He therefore wrote letters to various provinces, inviting the bishops and abbots not to refuse, on that occasion, to provide some assistance to the Roman Church from their own resources.

We possess two letters on this matter. The first, issued on the fourth day before the Nones of November and certainly in this year, as the sequence of events proves, was addressed to the bishops and abbots established throughout Aquitaine, Gascony, and Lower Burgundy. The second was addressed to Raynald, abbot of Saint Cyprian near Poitiers, whom the pontiff had appointed, together with Gervasius, abbot of Saint-Savin, to collect such funds.

Perhaps the Council of Bordeaux was held on the occasion of this collection. It was convened by Amatus, archbishop of that city and legate of the Apostolic See. Concerning it, the following words are found in the *Chronicle of Maillezais*:

[Col. 0115C]

> In the year 1093 . . . there was a council at Bordeaux.

More information about this council is found in the *Chartulary of Saint Peter of La Réole*, which presents a document concerning the restoration of the monastery of Saint Caprasius of Ponton to the monastery of Fleury, on which La Réole depended. This restoration was carried out at the council by Bernard, bishop of Aire, acting through Osger, the prior.

From this charter we learn that several bishops and abbots attended the council. The following subscribed to it: Amatus, archbishop of Bordeaux and vicar of the Apostolic See; William Bernard of Auch; and the bishops Simon of Agen, Raynald of Périgueux, Adhemar of Angoulême, Odo of Bigorre, Berard of Comminges, Peter of Dax, Stephen of Bazas, and Bernard of Aire.

[Col. 0115D]

The authors do not report what Urban achieved through these collections, unless the matter is to be connected with his entry into Rome toward the end of this year, as we shall shortly relate. It may also be connected with the fact that Goffrid, appointed abbot of Vendôme in this very year, had been unable to approach the pontiff because he was still suffering from a four-day fever, as is clear from his Letter 1, Book I, addressed to Urban himself. Apparently prompted by these letters, he came to Rome toward the end of this year or at the beginning of the following one with a large sum of money and, as we shall relate under the following year, became a great assistance to the pontiff.

### CXXXIX. Privileges for the New Monastery of Poitiers, Saint-Quentin of Beauvais, Bourgueil, and the Church of Syracuse.

Some privileges Urban granted to various churches as this year was drawing to a close. One of these was for the New Monastery of Poitiers, by which the privilege granted to that place by Gregory VII was confirmed, together with the church of Saint Nicholas, which, after the badly behaving canons had been expelled from it, had been assigned to the same monastery at a provincial council. This bull, transcribed from the archive of that place, was issued on 17 October at Ceprano, a place in Latium, in the diocese of Veroli, on the river Liri. From Ceprano the pontiff came to Anagni, where we gather from various charters that he spent some time. The first of these was issued for the benefit of the regular canons of Saint-Quentin near Beauvais, on 11 November; the second, on the twentieth of the same month, for the monastery of Bourgueil in the diocese of Angers, which was then governed by the celebrated Baldric, later bishop of Dol; the third was addressed to Roger, bishop of the Church of Syracuse in Sicily, to whom Urban, having recently consecrated him, confirmed absolutely everything that Count Roger had bestowed upon the Church of Syracuse. An error has crept into Rocchus Pyrrhus’s *Sacred Sicily*, where this bull is said to have been issued in the fifteenth indiction; for all the other chronological notes agree perfectly with the present year, which it expressly and in fact indicates. Indeed, Roger at that time organized the episcopal churches during the conquest of Sicily, as he himself testifies in two charters of the same year, reported by that same Rocchus Pyrrhus: one was issued for the Church of Agrigento, the other for the Church of Mazara, in the month of October.

## CXL. The Christians prevail in Spain. Rescript for Saint Saturninus.

[Col. 0116C]

What Roger was doing in Sicily, various Christian princes were likewise doing in Spain for the advancement of the Catholic religion, intent namely on restoring in those regions, once the Moors had been expelled, Christ’s dominion together with the earthly kingdom. A reliable witness to this is Bertold for this year. He writes that Alfonso, king of Castile and León—whom that Cluniac author calls an obedientary of the abbot—after often overthrowing and putting the pagans to flight, repaired during this period many churches that had been destroyed by those barbarians. Sancho, king of the Aragonese, was acting against the Moors with no less courage; Urban calls him his dearest friend in a rescript to the abbot of Saint John of Peña. The time at which this rescript was issued is unclear; but since King Sancho, whom Urban greets in that document, died at the beginning of June of the following year during the siege of the city of Huesca, it can scarcely be assigned later than the present year. In it the pontiff rebukes the abbot of Peña for having seized the tithes of the church of Saint Saturninus of Toulouse that were owed to the canons.

## CXLI. Decretal letter to Dominic, patriarch of Grado. The Lérins privilege.

A decretal letter of Urban to Dominic of Grado, concerning the exclusion of subdeacons from the dignity of their orders if they are unwilling to remain continent, may likewise be assigned, by a similar argument, to this year. Gratian included a fragment of that letter in the *Decree*, distinction 32, chapter 2, “Let them be ashamed.” We infer that Dominic, to whom this letter is addressed, died toward the end of this year or at the beginning of the next from the fact that, according to Ughelli in *Sacred Italy*, John and Peter succeeded him one after the other in the Church of Grado in 1094.

Finally, to this year we assign the privilege of the monastery of Lérins, addressed to Abbot Aldebert. Although the commonly circulated copies bear no chronological note, Barrali, who had examined the monastery’s ancient documents, dates it to this year in the Lérins chronology. To the same year, if I judge correctly, should be assigned the bull for the Benedictine nunnery of Saint Mary in Campo Marzio at Rome, by which Urban appointed two Roman abbots and one from Rimini as custodians of that place’s possessions, as recorded in that institution’s chronicle apud Martinelli. It is said to have been issued at Saint Peter’s on 28 November, in the sixth year of Urban’s pontificate, which the author of the chronicle, Hyacinthus de Nobili, incorrectly interprets as the year 1094. There is, however, this difficulty: according to the bull for the Church of Syracuse cited above, Urban was still at Anagni on the Kalends of December themselves.

## CXLII. The death of Anselm, archbishop of Milan. Arnulf succeeds him.

Toward the end of this year Pope Urban lost Anselm, archbishop of Milan, a most vigorous champion of his party, by whom, as we have said, Conrad had been adorned with the crown of the kingdom of Lombardy several months earlier. Bertold indicates the year of his death, while we learn the day from an ancient catalogue of the archbishops of Milan, published by our Mabillon in volume I of the *Museum Italicum*. There Anselm is said to have occupied the see for seven years, five months, and four days, and to have died on 4 December, being buried in the basilica of the Apostles.

Arnulf, or Arnolf, was appointed in his place; Bertold calls him Arnold of the Silver Gate. Puricellus, Sigonius in his *History of the Italian Kingdom*, and Papebrochius in the catalogue of the bishops of Milan in volume VII of the Bollandists’ *May* provide more information about these men, but it is not relevant to our purpose.

Some may perhaps think that Arnulf was the very archbishop of Milan who, as is related in Urban’s *Life*, was ordained by only one Catholic bishop, while many others were indeed present and assenting but did not lay on hands because they were schismatics; and that he is the man said to have received his investiture from Henry and therefore, after being deprived of office by the apostolic legate, to have withdrawn into a monastery and remained there until Urban restored him to his church and bestowed the pallium upon him. But these details fit Anselm, his predecessor, better. For it is established that Anselm was imposed upon this see by Henry, although afterward, as we have said under the year 1088, he joined Urban’s party.

Indeed, as is clear from Bertold, a contemporary and careful author, Arnulf was consecrated not by one bishop—although this occurred only after a full year had elapsed from his election—but by three Catholic bishops, whose names the same author records, as we shall relate in its proper place. This has been mentioned on the occasion of Anselm’s death.

## CXLIII. Anselm becomes archbishop of Canterbury. He quarrels with the king.

The loss suffered by the Roman Church through the death of Anselm of Milan was splendidly repaired by the appointment of another Anselm as archbishop of Canterbury. This took place on that very day, namely 4 December, on which Anselm of Milan departed this life. Yet serious disagreements subsequently arose between this holy man and King Henry, and they afflicted the English Church for a long time.

After the death of Lanfranc, the Church of Canterbury had remained without a bishop for four full years. Then, on 6 March of this year, the first Sunday of Lent, Anselm—at that time abbot of Bec—was elected in his place, with the greatest acclamation of the whole kingdom and of the king himself. He had perhaps crossed into England on certain business of his monastery, without thinking of anything of the sort.

The holy man moved every stone to rid himself of so great a burden, considering in all sincerity that he was not suited to it. He thought he had found a suitable opportunity for declining this dignity in the schism that was then afflicting the Roman Church. Since, with the king’s approval, it had not yet been declared in England whom one ought to regard as the true pontiff, he publicly announced that, whatever turn affairs might take, he would always obey Urban, as he had done until then. He affirmed that this was truly his intention, partly because he hoped that, once he had made this declaration, the English would reject him.

But he accomplished absolutely nothing. They remained steadfast in their purpose. He himself testifies to this in letter 24 of book III, writing thus to Hugh of Lyon:

> Before I gave my assent, I openly said that I favored our lord Pope Urban and opposed Guibert. For six months I did and said everything I could without sin in order to be released.

A little later he offered a distinguished and public proof of his reverence and obedience toward Urban the pontiff, when he dedicated to him the book on faith, or on the Incarnation of the Word, which he had written against the heretic Roscelin, entrusting it to Urban’s judgment. It will not be out of place to set down here Anselm’s own words with which he presented this book to him:

> To the lord and Father of the whole Church sojourning on earth, the supreme pontiff Urban, brother Anselm, in life a sinner, in habit a monk, called by God’s command or permission to be bishop of the metropolitan church of Canterbury, offers due submission, humble service, and devoted prayers.

He then entrusts his book to the pontiff’s judgment in these words:

> Since divine providence, he says, has chosen your holiness to whom it would entrust the preservation of Christian life and faith and the governance of its Church, it is rightly referred to no one else if anything contrary to the Catholic faith arises in the Church, so that it may be corrected by your authority. I submit my work for your examination, so that if anything in it needs correction, it may be amended by your judgment, and whatever conforms to the rule of truth may be strengthened by your authority.

Since nothing, therefore, could deter the English from demanding Anselm as archbishop, and since he had the support of his own archbishop—that is, the archbishop of Rouen, in whose diocese Bec is situated—as well as the advice of all good men, he was finally consecrated at Canterbury on 4 December 1093. Shortly afterward he solemnly celebrated the feast of Christ’s Nativity together with the king.

It is indeed surprising that he was ordained by the English bishops, who were still uncertain whether they ought to obey Pope Urban or his rival Wibert, when Anselm himself openly protested that he would never withdraw from obedience to Urban, as we have just related. Yet no one, not even the pontiff himself, counted this as a fault either in Anselm or in the English bishops. Thus, when Walter later reproached Anselm for this very matter, Anselm defended himself chiefly with the argument that the pontiff, knowing of it, had not only failed to disapprove the action but had afterward granted him the pallium without any difficulty.

Such were the broad beginnings of Anselm’s pontificate; but how quickly they were turned into bitterness! When Anselm refused, as Eadmer reports, to give King William one thousand pounds of silver as thanks for his generosity, he incurred the king’s indignation. These were the first seeds of discord between King William and the holy bishop. Shortly afterward they grew greatly, when the holy prelate wished to offer the same king salutary counsels as he was preparing to depart on an overseas expedition. These events took place in 1093 and at the beginning of the following year. What followed after the king’s return to England we shall relate under the year 1095.

## CXLIV. Urban resides at Rome.

Having returned to Rome toward the end of this year, Urban solemnly celebrated the Nativity of the Lord there, while Guibert’s faction was daily weakening, as Bertold records at the beginning of the year 1094; for this author customarily begins his years with the Nativity of Christ.

At that time Guibert was staying at Verona together with the Emperor Henry, so dispirited that, according to the same Bertold, he pretended that he would willingly resign the papacy if peace could not otherwise be restored to the Church. Nevertheless, he still had many men at Rome devoted to his party, who, accommodating themselves to circumstances, secretly awaited an opportunity to stir up new disturbances.

Urban concealed the matter because they could not have been driven from the city without a military expedition. As we have often said with Bertold—and he repeats it almost every year—the most gentle pontiff abhorred nothing so much as armed conflict and the enlargement of his authority through the shedding of blood. Therefore, as the same author continues, since he could not easily expel his opponents without military force, he preferred to tolerate their injustice for a time rather than disturb the Roman citizens with an armed hand.

## CXLV. The plots of the Guibertines.

It is astonishing that such leniency on the pontiff’s part did not soften the minds of the Guibertines. On the contrary, while Urban was staying near Saint Mary the New in a very strong fortification, and they still occupied the Tower of Crescentius, or the Mausoleum of Hadrian—that is, the Castle of Saint Angelo—they blocked, like pirates, every approach across the bridge over the Tiber for travelers wishing to reach the pontiff. If anyone happened to fall into their hands, they held him captive and treated him in a manner more than barbarous.

This happened to the abbot of the cell of Saint Peter in Alemannia, whom Gebehard, bishop of Constance, and Duke Bertold, his brother, had sent as their legate to Urban. Hence Egino, who later became abbot of Saint Afra at Augsburg, is praised by Udalscalch, the author of his *Deeds*, because, having been sent by Gebehard more than once to Urban, he laid aside his monastic habit, put on secular clothing, and under this disguise evaded the vigilance of the Guibertines and reached the pontiff. In the same way Goffrid, abbot of Vendôme, says in book I, letter 8, that he made himself the servant of his servants so that he would not be recognized by Urban’s enemies.

## CXLVI. The division of the Churches of Arras and Cambrai is confirmed.

These events were taking place at Rome at the beginning of the year 1094. When Urban heard that Lambert, the elected bishop of Arras, was arriving in the city from Gaul to be consecrated there—something Raynald had feared, as we have already said, lest, if he himself laid hands upon Lambert, the people of Cambrai should withdraw from obedience to the Church of Reims—he wrote to the same archbishop, promising him apostolic protection against anyone who attempted to ordain a bishop at Cambrai apart from the metropolitan of Reims.

After this he instructed the same archbishop not to delay assigning to both the Church of Arras and the Church of Cambrai their own proper bishops, unless perhaps the people of Cambrai wished to come to Rome during the next Lent to plead their case in the presence of Lambert, the elected bishop of Arras.

Finally, he confirmed the election of Manasses, archdeacon of Reims, as bishop of Cambrai. Raynald had written to him that the Cambresians had made this election by the general consent of all, and Urban confirmed it on condition that the people of Cambrai would not disturb the restoration of the Church of Arras, although they had rashly bound themselves to do so by oath.

All these matters are contained in Urban’s letter to Raynald himself, who, as we have already said, had written to him separately concerning them. Although the pontiff’s reply bears no chronological note, the matters it contains sufficiently indicate that it should be assigned here. Indeed, in the following year, after Gualcher had been rejected, Manasses’s election was confirmed at the Council of Clermont, as we shall relate in its proper place.

## CXLVII. Lambert, elected bishop of Arras, arrives at Rome. Urban consecrates him and grants him a privilege. Various letters concerning the matter.

Meanwhile, after many dangers of travel and winter—described at length in his little book in Locrius and Baluze, volume V of the *Miscellanies*—Lambert arrived at Rome, at the portico of Saint Peter, on the Friday before the Sunday *Esto mihi in Deum protectorem*. The author of his *Deeds* says that this was 17 February, two days before Quinquagesima Sunday, which that year fell on the twenty-ninth of the same month.

Since access to the pontiff, who was then staying near Saint Mary the New, was difficult because of the Guibertines’ plots, Lambert left his companions at Saint Peter’s and approached Urban alone at first light the following day. “Prostrating himself before him with tears,” he asked to be released from the election, asserting that he was unequal to so unbearable a burden, both because of Henry’s hostility—for Cambrai belonged to Henry—and because of the hostility of the wealthy clergy and laity of Cambrai, and finally because of the poverty and extreme devastation of the Church of Arras.

“But the most blessed pope,” as that author continues, “after granting absolution and giving the blessing customary to the apostolic see, received him with the holy kiss. Making light of all these things, he said to him: ‘Brother, the sufferings of this present time are not worthy of the future glory that will be revealed in us,’ and other words of consolation which, he says, do not fully return to his memory.”

The pontiff then asked him where his companions were and commissioned Daibert, archbishop of Pisa, to arrange, together with Peter Leonis, that Lambert’s companions be brought from the portico of Saint Peter, where they had remained, to the prepared lodging. This was done immediately. From then on Lambert and the others who had arrived with him had free access to the pontiff.

For some time it was awaited whether the people of Cambrai might arrive to defend their case. But at last, when the appointed time for pleading the case had long since passed, Urban, having taken the advice of his bishops, cardinals, and the Romans, had the entire case of the Church of Arras read aloud and fixed a day on which Lambert was to be ordained bishop of Arras.

This was a Sunday of Lent. After the envoys of Cambrai had been awaited in vain for an entire month—as the pontiff himself declared in his bull—Lambert was consecrated bishop of Arras by Urban himself.

The circumstances of his ordination are related by the already mentioned author of Lambert’s *Deeds* in these words:

> He, Lambert, at last finding rest, was ordained at Rome near Saint Mary the New by the apostolic lord Urban, in the year of Christ 1093—he reckons the beginning of the year from Easter, and all the chronological markers he gives, as the course of events itself necessarily requires, designate the year 1094—on 19 March, then observed as the Sunday *Laetare Jerusalem*, that is, the fourth Sunday of Lent, in the presence of the venerable bishops John of Tusculum, Humbald of Sabina, John of Porto, Bruno of Segni, and also the lord Daibert, archbishop of Pisa, together with the cardinal priests and a very great multitude of Romans.

A few days later Urban granted Lambert an important privilege to establish the restoration of the Church of Arras. It was later read and confirmed at various synods and finally at the Council of Clermont; Paschal II and the subsequent pontiffs repeatedly praised and approved it.

It was issued on 23 March, in the second indiction, in the year 1093. As we have just said, in documents issued concerning this affair the beginning of the year was generally reckoned from Easter. Urban, however, did not follow this practice in other bulls issued at that time, as can be observed in the judgment concerning the Church of Tours against Dol and in other documents.

This privilege will be given among Urban’s letters, as will the four letters that, for the same reason, the pontiff wrote in the following days: one to the archdeacons of the Church of Arras; one to the abbots and abbesses of the same diocese; one to Raynald, archbishop, and the other bishops of the province of Reims; and finally, a few days later, one to Robert, count of Flanders.

From that time the see of Arras remained established. The author of Lambert’s *Deeds* says that the bull of its restoration, together with the letters of Paschal II in which he protested that he would never depart from the institution concerning this matter established by his predecessor Urban of holy memory, was preserved at Reims in the Church of Blessed Mary, in the sacristy, in a golden casket commonly called the *berceolum*. This may be seen in Baluze, volume V of the *Miscellanies*, p. 275, where that learned man, as we have already noted, published the *Deeds* in full together with the documents pertaining to them.

## CXLVIII. The bishop of Dol and the other bishops of Brittany are restored to Tours.

At the very time when Lambert was consecrated at Rome, Ralph, archbishop of Tours, was pursuing there his lawsuit against the bishop of Dol, who, as we said under the preceding year, was seeking the title and rights of metropolitan of Brittany Minor, following the example of several of his predecessors.

But when neither the bishop of Dol himself nor anyone else on his behalf appeared at the appointed time, while the archbishop of Tours produced against him various decrees of earlier pontiffs and even of councils, judgment was pronounced against Dol. The metropolitan Church of Tours was restored to its former right, and jurisdiction over Dol and the other churches of Brittany Minor was asserted for it.

Urban confirmed this decree by his bull, in which he recounted the entire course of the controversy. The bull was issued on 5 April of this year and will be presented in its proper place together with the same pontiff’s letter to all the bishops of Brittany Minor, in which he informs them that this dispute had finally been settled in favor of the archbishop of Tours. He therefore commands them to obey him as their true and proper metropolitan.

Urban’s decree gained such authority that in later times, whenever this controversy flared up again—which happened more than once—the pontiffs always judged that recourse should be had to it. Innocent III did so after others, and finally, by a solemn judgment, entirely removed the bishops of Dol from every hope of ever recovering metropolitan dignity.

Our Edmund Martène published the complete proceedings of this celebrated case, together with various letters and other ancient documents relating to the controversy, in his new collection of ancient writers, published at Rouen in 1090. Yet neither there nor anywhere else have we been able to find Urban’s letter which the people of Tours cite in their replies to the objections of Dol, on page 148. In it the pontiff testifies that the ferocity and stubbornness of the Bretons had been so great that they could not be recalled to obedience to the Church of Tours by any excommunication, and that they had even declared that they would abandon the Christian faith if they were compelled to do so by any means.

## CXLIX. Lambert is enthroned at Arras.

[Col. 0123B]

After these matters had been completed at Rome, Ralph of Tours and Lambert of Arras, both bishops, decided to return together to Gaul. They left Rome on the Friday of *Quasimodo geniti*, that is, 21 April, and entered the sea at Ostia. On the very day of Pentecost Lambert returned to Arras and, before the third hour, was enthroned in the episcopal seat with the greatest consent and acclamation of all the clergy and people.

## CL. Goffrid of Vendôme’s expenses on behalf of the Roman Church. Urban’s straits.

Before we leave Rome, however, we must discuss Goffrid, abbot of Vendôme, who was also staying in the city at that time. He had arrived some time earlier to bring assistance to the pontiff, who was placed in the greatest difficulties.

In the preceding year, on 21 August, as recorded in the Vendôme Chronicle, otherwise called the Angevin Chronicle and edited by Labbe, Goffrid was ordained abbot of Vendôme by Ivo, bishop of Chartres. When he heard that Urban was in severe distress, he resolved to come to his aid.

He therefore immediately set out for Rome. How much he benefited the pontiff there can be learned from his letter 8 of book I, written to Paschal, Urban’s successor. After stating that he was the pontiff’s own and special son, not an adopted one, and that his monastery, by the will of its founders, was the personal allod and patrimony of blessed Peter, he adds that he had spent thirteen thousand solidi, “of our currency,” in the service of the Roman Church, compelled by love alone and by no necessity whatsoever.

He later explains the whole matter more fully. It is therefore worthwhile to quote his very words, since they give an excellent picture of the condition of Urban and the Roman Church at that time:

> Among the other services that my humility rendered to the Roman Church in her time of need, there is one which, because it was especially noteworthy, I can neither must nor ought to pass over in silence . . .
>
> In the first year in which, by God’s will or permission, I assumed the name of abbot, I heard that the lord Pope Urban, of blessed memory, was hiding in the house of John Fricapan and was laboring courageously against the Guibertine heresy. Although our place was poor, I nevertheless came to Rome, wishing to share in his persecutions and labors and desiring, to the best of my ability, to supply his want—which, by God’s grace, I did.
>
> It would take too long to recount all the evils I suffered on the journey and in the city, becoming in every respect the servant of our servants so that I would not be recognized. Like another Nicodemus, I came by night to the lord pope in the house of the aforesaid John. There I found him almost stripped of all temporal goods and heavily burdened by another’s debt.
>
> I remained with him there throughout Lent. If it is permissible to declare the truth, I bore his burdens, insofar as I could, upon the shoulders of charity. Fifteen days before Easter, Ferruchius, whom Guibert had appointed guardian of the Lateran palace, spoke with the lord pope through intermediaries, asking him for money in exchange for returning to him that tower and house.
>
> The lord pope therefore spoke with the bishops and cardinals who were with him and asked them for money. But he was able to find very little among them, since they were oppressed simultaneously by persecution and poverty. When I saw him not merely sad but weeping because of his extreme distress, I too began to weep. Weeping, I approached him and told him to make an agreement with Ferruchius without fear.
>
> There I spent gold and silver, coins, mules, and horses. Thus we obtained and entered the Lateran palace, where I was the first to kiss the lord pope’s foot, in the apostolic see on which no Catholic pope had sat for a very long time.

In a subsequent letter written to the same Paschal, he congratulates himself that, after Pope Urban and the foremost son of the holy Roman Church, Peter Leonis had taken the Lateran palace from Guibert, at the cost of the immense sum of money that he had spent for this purpose.

Goffrid repeats the same point more briefly in various places, especially in letter 13 of the same book to Pope Calixtus. There, speaking again of the services he had rendered at his own expense to the Roman pontiff, he says that he had spent more than twelve thousand solidi, a sum which, according to his own testimony, was worth one hundred marks of silver.

## CLI. The Vendôme privilege.

Shortly before Urban recovered the Lateran with Goffrid’s assistance, namely on 14 March, he granted the monastery of Vendôme an important privilege by which its rights and possessions were asserted. This was later confirmed at the Council of Clermont, as we shall relate in its proper place. The privilege will be given in full from the archive of that monastery among Urban’s letters.

Two letters of the same pontiff, said to have been issued at Rome on 31 March, should also be assigned here. In the first, the pontiff wrote to William, count of Poitiers, urging him to restore to the monks of Vendôme the church of Saint George situated on the island of Oléron, which he had given to a certain Eblon, one of his soldiers. The second was addressed to Amatus, legate of the apostolic see, and two other bishops. In it the pontiff instructed them to regard William as excommunicated unless, within the time he had prescribed, he caused the property unjustly taken from the monks of Vendôme to be restored.

We infer that these two rescripts cannot be postponed beyond the present year from the fact that William testifies in a charter issued on this matter that he received these letters from Urban before Urban had come to Gaul to celebrate councils. This charter, which greatly contributes to the elucidation of Urban’s deeds and contains the entire course of this controversy—which frequently flared up again—can already be found in Besly’s proofs for the history of the counts of Poitiers. It will, however, be collated again with the ancient parchment documents of the monastery of Vendôme. Both pontifical rescripts will be produced from the archive of that place among Urban’s letters.

## CLII. Goffrid is made a priest by Urban. The church of Saint Prisca.

[Col. 0125B]

After Urban had obtained possession of the Lateran palace, he ordained Goffrid, who in the preceding year, when he was still only a deacon, had been blessed as abbot by Ivo, bishop of Chartres, as a priest this year. He also restored to him the church of Saint Prisca, from which the monks of Vendôme had been expelled by the Guibertines.

Goffrid himself repeatedly testifies to these matters in various letters of book I, especially letter 14 to Pope Honorius. Likewise, in letter 2 written to Calixtus II, he boasts that he had been loved by Urban as his only son.

As for the church of Saint Prisca, its title was that of a cardinal priest, which the abbots of Vendôme retained for a long time. Its site was inhabited by the monks of Vendôme, but this is not the place to discuss these matters at greater length. Sirmond gives more information about them in his notes on Goffrid’s letters.

Certainly, many years ago the monks of Vendôme lost possession of it, and today the abbots of Vendôme are called cardinals in name only. Sirmond observes that they were still honored with this dignity at the time of the Council of Constance.

## CLIII. The ordination of the bishop of Ravello.

Since Goffrid’s ordination shows that Urban was publicly conferring orders at the Lateran palace at that time, the consecration of Constantine, bishop of Ravello, may perhaps be assigned here. Ughelli says, in volume I of *Sacred Italy*, that Constantine succeeded Urso this year and was ordained by Urban because that church is directly subject to the Roman pontiff.

## CLIV. Urban’s party prevails in Germany.

Urban’s affairs were progressing no less favorably in Germany at that time than among the Italians. Bertold observes that this occurred because of the great harmony prevailing between Welf, duke of Bavaria, and Bertold, duke of Alemannia. As a result, peace was extended from Francia, Germany, and Alsatia through Bavaria and even as far as Hungary.

The same author observes that this peace was firm and lasting because the princes did not cease to administer justice in their respective territories. Among them, he writes, Duke Bertold stood out above the rest.

To prevent the commerce which many, according to their condition, could scarcely or scarcely at all avoid with excommunicated persons from disturbing this tranquillity, the prudent pontiff moderated the sentence of excommunication after the example of Gregory VII. According to the same Bertold, travelers, peasants, servants and maidservants, and the wives and children of excommunicated persons did not incur that stain by associating with them, unless perhaps the excommunicated persons themselves, through their own perverse will, bound themselves with the chains of excommunication.

## CLV. The Synod of Constance.

This public tranquillity provided Gebehard, bishop of Constance and vicar of the apostolic see, with an excellent opportunity to restore ecclesiastical discipline in these provinces. With this purpose, as Bertold relates—the only source from which we know of this assembly—he canonically celebrated a great synod at Constance during the Greater Week before Easter, with innumerable abbots and clerics, Duke Welf of Bavaria, Duke Bertold of Alemannia, and the other princes of Alemannia. There he corrected many things that needed correction.

At that synod the incontinence of priests and the violence of the Simoniacs were condemned. It was also decreed that the fast of March should be observed in the first week of Lent, according to the statutes of the holy Fathers, and that the fast of June should be observed during the very week of Pentecost.

Certainly, at that time different Churches had different customs concerning the observance of these fasts. On this subject Sigebert wrote a separate treatise, which, if a suitable opportunity should ever present itself, we shall publish from a manuscript copy. There is also a decree of the Council of Clermont on the same matter. More information is found in Sirmond’s notes on Goffrid of Vendôme, book III, letter 23, which is addressed to Hildebert of Le Mans.

At the same synod the peculiar custom of the diocese of Constance was also abolished: it had been accustomed to celebrate the entire week of Easter festively, but at Pentecost only a single day, contrary to the established practice of neighboring Churches and almost all the Churches of the Christian world. It was decreed that three full days should be observed both at Pentecost and at Easter.

Finally, the case of Queen Praxedes was discussed. At the beginning of this year, according to the same Bertold, she had secretly left the Emperor Henry, who was then staying at Verona, and fled to Matilda. She herself is said to have come to this synod. When she had set forth before everyone all that she had suffered from her husband, she easily moved them all to pity her.

Domnizo also described her flight in his verses, but says nothing about her journey to the Synod of Constance.

## CLVI. Disasters in Germany. Many are converted.

Bertold adds much about the disasters that afflicted almost the whole of Europe this year, but Germany above all. So great was the mortality at Regensburg, he relates, that within twelve weeks eight thousand five hundred people died in that city. In one village, whose name the same author withheld, eleven hundred people died within six weeks; [Col. 0127A] in another, forty people died in a single day. Yet this destruction of bodies brought salvation to souls. For those attacked by that disease, as though certain that they would soon die, prepared themselves for death in such a way that they then willingly performed what, says Bertold, could scarcely have been expected at another time even from holier men. Those who survived, however, were so terrified by fear of the threatening disease that they entirely abstained from vices and sins, and thus many were brought on that occasion to better conduct; indeed, most of them returned to themselves and abandoned the schismatics.

At that time Manegold of Lautenbach, founder of the community of regular canons at Murbach, was renowned in Alsace. By the authority granted him by Urban, he restored to ecclesiastical communion many who came to him in a body, including some of the province’s most distinguished men; after receiving a salutary penance, they thereafter detested the company of simoniacal and incontinent priests and remained faithful in obedience to the Holy See and the legitimate pope. Hence, as the same Bertold observes, ecclesiastical religion, long since extinguished in those regions, was wonderfully rekindled, with monasteries also restored or newly founded.

For besides Murbach, constructed by Manegold as we have just said, and the other monasteries mentioned above, the monastery of Saint Blaise in the Black Forest began this year to be built from its foundations, on 11 September, under Abbot Otto. On that same day the abbot sent Prior Hermann, with several companions, into the eastern kingdom, to the march bordering Hungary, [Col. 0127C] to establish a new abbey in the diocese of Passau, at a place called Cotheric. There, according to Bertold, regular clerics originally lived; but later they obtained from the Roman pontiff, and through him from their own bishop, permission to lay aside their clerical habit and profess the monastic life. That monastery, called Göttweig, is famous: according to the Life of Saint Altmann, bishop of Passau, it was founded by him and still survives today under the Benedictine Rule.

Also very renowned at that time in those regions, under Abbot Theoger—later bishop of Metz—was the monastery of Saint George in the Hercynian Forest, later transferred to Villingen. In letters issued this year, the pontiff received it under the special protection of the Apostolic See. [Col. 0127D] Certainly Urban considered Theoger, as his Life records, comparable to the apostles and to apostolic men.

## CLVII. Urban protects Fulco, bishop of Beauvais.

At the beginning of this year in Gaul, the bishops of the province of Reims dared to reopen the case of Fulco, bishop of Beauvais, which, as we said under the preceding year, had been judged by Urban. They were rebuked by the pontiff in letters concerning the matter, addressed to Raynold, the metropolitan, and his suffragans at the Lateran on 12 May, and therefore in this year—for in the preceding years the Lateran was not in Urban’s power. In the following year, however, when Fulco died, the same pontiff was staying far from Rome in Lombardy during the month of May. [Col. 0128A]

On this occasion Ivo, bishop of Chartres, who in Letter 30 had admonished Fulco himself to remember his office and strive to overcome worldly pride not with the weapons of worldly malice—which seems to have been the principal charge brought against him—but with the weapons of Christian warfare, could not bear, after hearing of his absolution by the pontiff, that his case should be reopened by the bishops of Belgica in a provincial assembly. We understand this from his Letter 3 in the new edition. After commending Fulco to Urban, to whom he was writing, he continues concerning him:

> It does not seem to me that it can reasonably be done that what deserved to reach its conclusion under the examination of your judgment should be reopened by an inferior person. [Col. 0128B]

Indeed, as Ivo had written shortly before—and Urban himself confirms this in the letters to Anselm cited in their proper place—Fulco, who was otherwise a man of remarkable simplicity and not altogether capable of governing so great a diocese, was nevertheless attacked by many, not so much out of zeal for justice as from rivalry toward his virtues. Once restored to his Church by papal authority, however, he governed it until the end of his life.

## CLVIII. Dispute between the archbishop of Vienne and the bishop of Grenoble.

At nearly the same time a serious controversy arose in Gaul between Guy, archbishop of Vienne, and Hugh, bishop of Grenoble, concerning the district of Salmoriacum, which each claimed belonged to his own [Col. 0128C] diocese. Hugh himself published a treatise on the matter, entitled *On the Injuries Inflicted by Guy, Archbishop of Vienne, upon the Church of Grenoble*, and so forth. In this book the holy man explains in detail the entire course of the controversy and reports the papal letters written on its account.

That little work contains not only what is necessary for understanding the controversy, but can also contribute greatly to illuminating other acts of Urban and assigning each of them to its proper time. Since it contains almost nothing irrelevant to our purpose, we thought it appropriate to reproduce it in full in the Appendix, from a manuscript collated with Jacques Petit’s edition, [Col. 0128D] while leaving to the editor the letters of Urban contained in it.

The whole substance of that famous dispute is as follows. The Church of Grenoble possessed the district, or archdeaconry, of Salmoriacum when Guy, archbishop of Vienne, claiming that it had anciently belonged to his own Church, brought a lawsuit on the matter against Hugh, bishop of Grenoble. When the matter could be settled neither at Vienne nor before the Romans, after various disputes, Guy invaded the district by force. The canons of Grenoble, angered by this, appealed to the Apostolic See. Urban received their complaints and immediately entrusted Hugh of Lyons, his legate, with judging the case. After hearing the parties at Baon, Hugh granted provisional relief to the people of Grenoble and promised that he would definitively settle the dispute at the next council he was to hold in Gaul. [Col. 0129A]

Guy, however, disregarding all this, retained the district and sent legates to Rome. Without any mention of the controversy, they asked the pontiff for a general confirmation of the privileges and possessions of his Church. Since Urban suspected no evil, Guy easily obtained it. This may perhaps be what Geoffrey, abbot of Vendôme, hints at in Book I, Letter 11, written to Guy himself after he had become pope under the name of Calixtus II, where he recalls how, when he was formerly at Rome, he had labored before Urban on behalf of Guy and his legates.

Certainly Guy’s legate soon obtained the privilege he desired. In it—perhaps the pontiff was entirely unaware of the controversy over the district of Salmoriacum, or perhaps what the legate had decided concerning it had been concealed from him—he arranged for “all authority in the archdeaconry of Salmoriacum” to be inserted among the other rights of the Church of Vienne. [Col. 0129B] Nor was this difficult for the Vienne legate, since Warmund, Guy’s predecessor, had already obtained an almost identical privilege from Gregory VII, though with a condition that is omitted in this one. Indeed, the same privilege was later confirmed more than once by subsequent pontiffs, especially by Guy himself when he became pope under the name of Calixtus II.

This is certainly remarkable, since Urban himself repeatedly declared in various letters that he had been deceived in this matter. For when the people of Grenoble discovered the fraud, they immediately sent legates to Urban at Rome to complain to him about this fraudulent surreptitious acquisition of the privilege and to report that Guy, despising the authority of the legate of the Apostolic See, had not obeyed his judgment. After hearing them, the pontiff immediately wrote one letter to Hugh of Lyons and another to Hugh, bishop of Grenoble, ordering them to settle the entire dispute over the district of Salmoriacum without taking any account of the privilege Guy had recently obtained. [Col. 0129C]

Hugh of Lyons, however, after receiving Urban’s letters, judged that the whole matter should be referred to the Council of Autun, which he was to celebrate several months later. [Col. 0129D] This was in fact done, as we shall see below.

## CLIX. Fulco, count of Anjou, absolved at the assembly at Saint-Florent. The privilege of Mont-Belle.

At that time the same Hugh, bishop of Lyons, received another commission from Urban: namely, that he should restore Fulco Rechin, count of Anjou, to communion if this could be done without compromising justice. Fulco had long been excommunicated because he had captured and imprisoned his brother Geoffrey.

Since Hugh judged the matter to be of no small importance, he invited several bishops and abbots to deliberate with him. They therefore assembled with him at the monastery of Saint-Florent: Aldebert, archbishop of Bourges; Ouveldus, or Ivellus, bishop of Le Mans; and the abbots William of Saint-Florent, Bernard of Marmoutier, another Bernard of Saints Sergius and Bacchus, Girard of Saint-Aubin, Nuald [perhaps Natalis] of Saint-Nicholas, Buldric of Bourgueil, and Geoffrey of Vendôme. All unanimously judged that Fulco should be absolved under certain conditions, one of which was that he should not take a wife without the legate’s counsel, since he was blamed for the number of wives he had.

That this took place in the year 1094, on the very day of the Nativity of Saint John the Baptist, is proved by an old document drawn up on the matter and subscribed by all the bishops and abbots named above. Sirmond published it in the materials prefixed to the works of Geoffrey, abbot of Vendôme.

Urban was still at Rome at that time. For on 29 June, [Col. 0130B] the day consecrated to the martyrdom of blessed Peter, he granted there a privilege to the monastery of Mont-Belle near Piacenza, as is clear from the *Ecclesiastical History* of that city, published by Pietro Maria Campi, a canon of Piacenza. This monastery, which formerly belonged to our Benedictine order, was finally united in 1484 by Innocent VIII to the congregation of the Hermits of Saint Jerome, as Lubin observed in his *Account of the Abbeys of Italy*.

## CLX. The adulterous marriage of King Philip. The Council of Reims. The profession of Lambert of Arras. The division of the Church of Arras from that of Cambrai confirmed.

Serious disturbances were then agitating Gaul because of King Philip. As we have already said, he had driven away his wife and persisted in retaining Bertrada, whom he had joined to himself in an adulterous union, despite the admonitions of the bishops and of the pontiff himself. Much material on this matter is found throughout the letters of Ivo, bishop of Chartres. There is no doubt that the Council of Reims, convened this year on 18 September, was held on this account.

Since Berta, Philip’s legitimate wife, died this year, as Clarius records in the *Chronicle of Saint Peter of Viviers*, Philip perhaps hoped that the bishops would moderate somewhat their severity toward Bertrada, whom he had taken in her place. He moved heaven and earth and promised everything so that, as Ivo writes in Letter 47 to Guy the steward, this woman might at least be left to him for some time. Yet nothing concerning Philip’s marriage is found in what survives from the Council of Reims—unless perhaps this is reflected in the fact that Ivo, invited to the synod, refused to go, as is clear from his Letter 35 to Richer of Sens and the other Fathers assembled there. He refused chiefly because he foresaw that it would not be permitted him to speak the truth at that synod.

Accordingly, he reproaches the other bishops for excessive indulgence, which was especially destructive to the king. If they had wished, following the practice of skilled physicians, to apply remedies and cauteries suited to his illness, they would have brought him to perfect health. [Col. 0130D]

That many bishops and princes assembled for the Council of Reims is attested by Raynold, archbishop of Reims, in a letter to the count of Flanders. Nor is this surprising, since the king himself attended and wished many bishops to be present there. From the already cited Clarius we learn that in this year, 1094, King Philip gathered the archbishops and bishops of his kingdom in the city of Reims. He also obtained from Richer, metropolitan of Sens, who was displeased that the council was being held outside his province, that Richer should come to Reims with the other bishops, since Raynold, confined by gout, could not travel from his see.

Three archbishops and seven bishops who attended the synod are listed in the manuscript before us. They were Raynold of Reims, Richer of Sens, and Ralph of Tours, the metropolitans; and the bishops Geoffrey of Paris, Walter of Meaux, Hugh of Soissons, Helinand of Laon, Rabodo of Noyon, Gervin of Amiens, and Hugh of Senlis. [Col. 0131B] What they decreed, however, is found neither in this manuscript nor in any other known record.

We can nevertheless say something about the same synod from the acts of Lambert, bishop of Arras, who is known to have attended it. It is therefore surprising that he is not listed among the others whom we have just enumerated from the manuscript.

After obtaining possession of his see on Pentecost, as we said, Lambert did not come to Reims to make, according to the canons, the customary profession of submission owed by the bishops of Belgica Secunda to the mother church and its archbishop. The metropolitan Raynold complained about this, as is clear both from Lambert’s letters of apology to Raynold and from others addressed to the clergy of the metropolitan church. In them Lambert declares that he had not yet been able to undertake the journey, which he promised to make with all his heart as soon as he was given the opportunity.

In fact, he came to Reims shortly afterward and made his profession on 21 September, the feast of the blessed apostle and evangelist Matthew, in the second indiction, in the year 1094—and indeed at the very council that had begun on 17 September, as is clear from Raynold’s letter to Robert, count of Flanders.

Lambert’s consecration, after he had made his ecclesiastical profession in the customary manner, was confirmed by Raynold the metropolitan and the other bishops of the province, in accordance with the commands of the lord pope Urban. [Col. 0131D] The same Raynold testifies to this in the letter just mentioned to the count of Flanders, and therefore it should be included among Urban’s letters.

We also learn from our already cited manuscript that the privilege of the Church of Arras was read out there. It records that this took place in the metropolitan basilica of the Blessed Mary Ever-Virgin, Our Lady, at a provincial and celebrated council attended by King Philip of the Franks. Raynold presided, with the two archbishops and seven bishops listed above seated in council, while the archdeacons and abbots of the province of Reims, together with an honorable clergy and people, were also present.

The old author wrote this shortly after the deaths of Raynold of Reims and Hugh, bishop of Soissons. He calls the former “illustrious and of venerable memory” and the latter “the lord of worthy memory”; he lists the others without any additional epithet, except that he calls Hugh, bishop of Senlis, “glorious.”

Lambert himself indicates in a letter to Odo, bishop of Cambrai, that the division between the two Churches—Cambrai and Arras—was confirmed at the same synod. Odo apparently wished to overturn, by imperial authority, the boundaries established between the two Churches.

In this letter Lambert testifies that the Church of Arras had been separated from that of Cambrai through the counsel and assistance of Robert, count of Flanders, in whose power Arras lay; through the permission and consent of Philip, king of the Franks, whose kingdom is known to include Arras; through the councils held at Reims under Archbishop Raynold; and through the authority of the Apostolic See and Urban II, Roman pontiff. [Col. 0132B] It is therefore clear that the restoration of this ancient episcopal see was not completed without legitimate conditions, as some more recent writers have thought.

We also learn from another manuscript of ours that something further occurred at the same synod. Manasses, elected to the Church of Cambrai, secretly encouraged by persons unknown, asked that Arras be restored to the Church of Cambrai. We should reproduce the words of our author:
