> “While therefore the venerable archbishop of Reims, Raynold, was urging Manasses, archdeacon of Reims and already designated bishop of the Church of Cambrai, to take care to receive sacred orders and episcopal consecration under the title of the Church of Cambrai, he said, at the urging of certain people: ‘Give Arras back to me.’ The prudent and wise archbishop replied almost by way of rebuke: ‘Lord Manasses, do you wish to be the first person excommunicated by the Apostolic See and to become a violator of its decrees and constitutions?’ Thus, for this presumptuous demand and contradiction at Arras, he acknowledged his guilt when rebuked by the archbishop, asked forgiveness, and, having made satisfaction, received absolution at the council.””

That author says nothing more about the synod except that, before Lambert left Reims, he was invited to the Council of Autun by Hugh, archbishop of Lyons, who had summoned it to be held on 15 October in accordance with Urban’s command. Manasses, however, was not ordained until a long time afterward because of the schism of Walcher, archdeacon of Cambrai, who, elected by the men of his faction, was attempting to seize the Church of Cambrai.

## CLXI. The Council of Ostia, or of the Aedui. King Philip is excommunicated. The privilege of Arras. The case of the archbishop of Tours against the monks of Marmoutier, and the dispute over the district of Salmoriacum.

Our first knowledge of the Council of Autun comes from Bertold, who writes that a general council was assembled this year on 25 October in a city of Gaul commonly called *Ostion*, by Hugh, archbishop of Lyons and legate of the Apostolic See, together with archbishops and abbots from various provinces. These words gave Baronius and his followers an opportunity to introduce a Council of Ostia, otherwise entirely unknown.

But it is absolutely certain that this was the Council of Autun, which contemporary authors establish as having been held this year. Bertold, a foreigner, called it “Ostion” from the vernacular name of the city of Autun—*Ostun*, or rather *Otun*, as it is pronounced—which later led those who fell into this error to fabricate a city called Ostia.

Hugh of Flavigny, an abbot in the very diocese of Autun and a serious and careful author of that period, mentions this Council of Autun, or of the Aedui, in the *Chronicle of Verdun*. He reports that thirty-two bishops, together with many abbots and religious men, assembled there, but says nothing about what the Fathers decreed. [Col. 0133B]

Bertold nevertheless reports some extracts from its decrees. He says that at this synod the excommunication of King Henry, Guibert, and their accomplices was renewed; that King Philip was also excommunicated because, while his own wife was still alive, he had taken another woman in her place; that the Simoniacal heresy and the incontinence of priests were condemned under threat of excommunication; and finally that monks were forbidden to usurp in parishes the parochial offices belonging to priests. All these things, the same author says, were established there and confirmed by the Apostolic Legation. [Col. 0133C]

Lambert, bishop of Arras, was invited to the same synod, as we have already said, and attended it, as we learn from our manuscript. It records that he was kindly received there by the lord Hugh and read out the privilege of the venerable archbishop of Reims—that is, the privilege he had obtained from that prelate to confirm the restoration of the see of Arras—in the presence of a large assembly of archbishops, bishops, and abbots, as well as a considerable multitude of clergy and people.

Accordingly, Hugh immediately wrote in Urban’s name to the count of Flanders, instructing him to regard Lambert as the true and legitimate bishop of Arras and exhorting him to assist Lambert in recovering the property of the Church of Arras. This letter, written in Urban’s name, will be presented among his letters after comparison with our manuscript.

The same synod also dealt with the serious controversy that had long been pending between Rodulf, archbishop of Tours, and the monks of Marmoutier, concerning the privilege granted to them by Urban, as we said under the year 1090.

This case had shortly before been argued at the Council of Brioude before the same legate Hugh, with two other archbishops seated beside him, namely those of Auch and Narbonne, together with many bishops and abbots from various provinces and persons of different ranks and dignities. But what could not be settled there would have reached a more favorable conclusion at this Council of Autun [Col. 0134A] if Archbishop Rodulf had been willing to stand by the agreement to which he appeared to have consented.

For after much debate on both sides—on one, Rodulf himself and Joellus, bishop of Le Mans; on the other, Bernard, prior of Marmoutier at Reims, Hilgod, bishop of Soissons and then a monk of that house, who had obtained the privilege at Rome, and Hilgod’s brother Andrew—peace was finally made between them. It was soon broken, however, as we gather from the conference at Dol.

There, in the presence of the same Hugh and Amatus, archbishops and legates of the Apostolic See, together with the bishops of Poitiers and Le Mans and many others, the same case was again argued with much contention. Abbot Bernard and his monks stood on one side, and Archbishop Rodulf with his clergy on the other. But nothing was accomplished there either, and the dispute remained undecided until the following year, when, as we shall say there, it was entirely settled at the Council of Clermont.

These matters are reported more fully in the booklet on the affairs of Marmoutier published by Bochellus at the end of the *History of Gregory of Tours*. Those who desire further information should consult that work. Ivo of Chartres also wrote to Rodulf of Tours about the matter in Letter 235. From it we learn that what displeased the archbishop most in this case was that Abbot Bernard refused to make a profession of submission to him.

Guy, archbishop of Vienne, and Hugh, bishop of Grenoble, also came to that Council of Autun. [Col. 0134C] Their dispute over the district of Salmoriacum was likewise argued before the Fathers of the synod, but was not settled. For when Guy was on the point of being condemned after producing false letters, he promised that he would make satisfaction to Hugh as soon as possible at Vienne. He did not, however, keep his promise, as can be seen in Hugh’s booklet, which is included in the Appendix to this volume.

## CLXII. Disturbances on account of King Philip.

There is no doubt that the excommunication pronounced against King Philip at the same Council of Autun caused disturbances in several parts of Gaul. Certainly the Fathers of the Council of Reims were more moderate, perhaps because they were more attached to Philip. Raynold, archbishop of Reims, who presided over that synod, enjoyed great influence with the king. Hence, when Urban wrote to Hugh of Lyons concerning the case of the district of Salmoriacum, he advised him, in order to preserve peace and conduct the matter more easily, to make use of the counsel of the archbishop of Reims, since the king’s case was handled more familiarly in his hands—because of the dignity of his see and perhaps because of his personal merits. For Urban himself and other distinguished men of his age praised this prelate highly.

In any event, if I judge correctly, the Council of Troyes was summoned on account of this excommunication. According to Ivo, in Letter 46 addressed to Urban, it was to be held on the first Sunday after the feast of All Saints, and the archbishops of Reims, Sens, and Tours had invited their suffragans to it.

Since, however, we find no council held at Troyes at that time, this may perhaps be the very council held at Reims in September of this year by those three archbishops, as we have seen. It was doubtless transferred to that city because, as we observed from Clarius, Raynold, archbishop of Reims, was confined by illness and could not travel outside his city.

On that interpretation, the council would not have been summoned because of an excommunication already issued—for it preceded the Council of Autun—but because Philip feared that the same thing would happen to him at the Council of Autun, as in fact it did.

Whatever the truth may be, from Ivo’s aforementioned letter we learn that Philip, angered by this sentence, sent legates to Urban to ask the pontiff for impunity for this offense, as Ivo puts it. They were also to threaten that, unless the crown—that is, the ceremony by which he was crowned in the Church on the principal feasts—were restored to the king after he had been released from the anathema, he would soon withdraw from Urban’s obedience. [Col. 0135B]

Meanwhile Ivo, who refused to attend this council because he feared that the assembly might undertake something against justice or against the Apostolic See, and who never ceased publicly and privately, in writing and speech, to oppose Philip’s adulterous marriage, was invited by the king to attend his court. He refused to go because of the prohibition that Urban had imposed upon the king, as he writes to Philip himself in Letter 28, concerning the bed of the adulterous woman whom Philip illegitimately kept in the place of a wife.

Because of this opposition, the same prelate was imprisoned and the property of his Church was seized, as is clear from several of his letters—not, indeed, by the king’s order, but by people whose actions the king concealed. Indeed, although the king had invited Ivo to the council, he not only refused to provide him with safe passage, as Ivo complains in Letter 35, but also forbade anyone to give him, as Ivo himself testifies in Letter 28, the oath of security that the pontiff had nevertheless ordered.

For this reason Ivo, wearied and disgusted by so many disturbances, wrote to Urban more than once asking that, after being released from episcopal responsibilities, he be permitted to live a private life.

## CLXIII. Urban deals moderately with the king.

After the Council of Autun, Urban received Philip’s delegation, which we mentioned above from Ivo’s Letter 46, and seems to have dealt with him more mildly. Perhaps he had already decided to examine this difficult and highly important matter more carefully with the other bishops at the Council of Piacenza.

As a result, however, some bishops who had previously been entirely opposed to the king began to waver somewhat. Ivo tried to confirm them in their original position. We have no doubt that his Letter 16 should be assigned to this context. In it he writes to Walter, bishop of Meaux:

> I advise you not to approve, either in word or deed and without due consideration, the king’s marriage, which before it was contracted you did not praise because reason opposed it.

The same must be said of his letter to Fulco of Beauvais, which will be cited below.

Furthermore, if we are to believe Hugh of Flavigny, the pontiff not only forgave Philip, bishop of Troyes, and the same Walter, bishop of Meaux, who had acted treacherously, as that author writes; he also compelled Hugh, his legate, by letters issued at Rome, to receive them back into communion and the kiss of peace. [Col. 0136A]

No one should therefore imagine that Urban ever consented to Philip’s marriage, or at least that, from human fear, he resisted the king’s desire less courageously than he should have. Hugh of Flavigny seems to suggest this. On the contrary, it is certain that Urban never departed from truth and righteousness in this matter, as is clear from his letter on the subject to Raynold, archbishop of Reims, and his suffragans.

Indeed, Ivo himself—no one would say that in this matter he spared Urban or anyone else—encourages Fulco, bishop of Beauvais, who may have been thinking such thoughts, to persevere in Letter 30. He also sends him a copy of the pontiff’s letter written after the king’s legates had departed, saying:

> “So that you may know that although the lord pope does not move ahead, he nevertheless does not retreat.”

Those who favored the king, however, spread this report among the people. It gave Hugh of Flavigny, and perhaps some others, an opportunity to speak somewhat more freely about Urban on this occasion, but entirely without justification.

There were also people who tried to draw Ivo over to the king’s side, or at least persuade him to conceal the matter. This is proved by two of his letters, Letters 23 and 47, to Guy, the king’s steward, who had invited him to reach an agreement with the king under this pretext, but in vain.

The fearless bishop remained firmly committed to what he had begun, fortified by Urban’s letters written on this matter to the archbishops and bishops of Gaul. Hence Ivo did not cease, as he had always done, to denounce those bishops whom he believed to be excessively indulgent toward the king’s wickedness.

## CLXIV. Urban’s letters to the count of Toulouse concerning Moissac and the cemetery of the Blessed Mary of the Golden.

Before bringing this year to a close, something must be said about several letters of Urban which, although lacking chronological indications, seem from their contents to belong to the present rather than to another year. Certainly some of them cannot be assigned to a date later than this year.

The first is addressed to William, count of Toulouse. In it the pontiff praises the prince for certain pious works and for the protection he had provided to the monasteries of Moissac and Lézat. He then grants him permission to be buried in the cemetery established at the Church of the Blessed Mary, together with all his descendants.

In this letter Urban mentions other letters he had issued on behalf of Asquilinus, abbot of Moissac, to the bishop of Cahors. We possess these letters from a manuscript in which they are addressed to William, bishop of that city. But since no bishop of that name presided over the Church of Cahors during Urban’s lifetime, I fear that an error entered the manuscript in reporting the name. Without doubt it should read Gerard, who governed that Church throughout Urban’s lifetime.

It may therefore be inferred that in the earliest copies of the letter only the first letter of his name, G, was written, and that scribes rashly expanded it as William instead of Gerard. Aymeric Peyrat, abbot of Moissac, certainly made many errors in his *Chronicle* when reporting these letters, as he says, from an original that could scarcely be read. This is clear from the authentic copy preserved in the Colbert Library.

We assign these letters to the present year because William appears to have relinquished the county of Toulouse either this year or, at any rate, the next. In the preceding year, the Church of Saint Mary had not yet been assigned for the burial of the counts, as is clear from an old document dated 1093 and reported by Catel.

After lengthy disputes between the Churches of Saint Stephen and Saint Saturninus over the right to the cemetery, it was established by agreement among the parties, under Isarn of Toulouse and the other bishops of the province, that bishops, counts, knights, their wives, and their sons and daughters should be buried at Saint Saturninus, while everyone else should be buried at Saint Stephen. No mention was made of the Blessed Mary.

Accordingly, only after that agreement had been reached can William—who was devoted to the holy Mother of God—be said to have obtained from Urban that both he and his descendants should be buried in her celebrated basilica. Urban’s grant was later confirmed by his successor, Paschal II.

Even today, in that church commonly called the Blessed Mary of the Golden (*La Daurade*), which belongs to our congregation of Saint Maur in the Benedictine order, there can be seen an epitaph inscribed on marble for one of the sons of Count Alfonso, who died in infancy in the following century. It praises Urban’s decree in these verses:

> The holy man Urban, Roman pope the second,  
> Commands this to be the cemetery of counts.  
> Moreover, as I have learned, he orders them buried here,  
> Having issued a sacred command to the citizens to that effect.

Around the same time the pontiff granted the monks of La Sauve-Majeure, who lived at Saint Anthony, permission to be buried in their own church, contrary to what had been established by Simon, the bishop. This is clear from a document of that Simon, subscribed by Saint Gerald, abbot of La Sauve-Majeure, who died in the year 1095.

## CLXV. The rashness of the canons of Bélin is restrained.

[Col. 0137D]

Toward the end of this same year may also be assigned the letter of that pontiff addressed to Durannus, bishop of Auvergne, who died the following year, against the canons of Billom. These canons had committed an atrocious sacrilege by plundering the church and all the sacred and ordinary furnishings of the priory of Saint-Loup, which depended upon the Celsinian monastery of the Cluniac order. This controversy, which Durannus had not settled, flared up again shortly after his death, when the matter was brought before the court of his successor, William. The men of Billom were completely defeated in their case, as is related more fully in an old document that we saw in the Celsinian cartulary.

## CLXVI. Urban prevails in Tuscany. Henry in Lombardy. The synod of Piacenza is announced.

[Col. 0138A]

Urban had long since departed from Rome, as Berthold writes, when, toward the end of this year, he celebrated the Nativity of the Lord with the greatest glory in Tuscany. There he had an indefatigable defender of his cause in Dagobert, or Daibert, bishop of Pisa, whom the same pontiff, as we have said, had already honored with the pallium and with the other archiepiscopal insignia and rights. At the beginning of October Urban was staying at Pisa, if we believe the letters—which, in this matter, why should we not believe?—that Humbald, bishop of Limoges, forged, as we shall say under the beginning of the year 1096.

Meanwhile Henry, that is, toward the end of this year and the beginning of the next, as Berthold continues, was staying in Lombardy [Col. 0138B] almost entirely deprived of royal dignity. His son Conrad, who at the beginning of the year 1093 had been proclaimed king of Italy, had joined forces with Countess Matilda and the other faithful supporters of Saint Peter, as they were called, and controlled the entire strength of his father’s army in Lombardy. Therefore the pontiff, whose affairs were then prospering so greatly, thinking that this favorable opportunity ought to be used well, summoned, says Berthold, a general synod in the middle of Lombardy, in the city of Piacenza, among the schismatics themselves and against them. By letters sent with canonical and apostolic authority he summoned to it the bishops of Italy, Burgundy, France, Alemannia, Bavaria, and the other provinces.

We learn from a letter written on that occasion by Raynold, archbishop of Reims, to Lambert, bishop of Arras, that these letters had been sent to all the metropolitans, so that [Col. 0138C] they might invite their suffragans, together with the abbots subject to them, to the council. This letter will be included among the letters of Urban, since the pontifical letters themselves no longer survive.

## CLXVII. Urban comes to Bologna.

Ghirardacci writes in his History of Bologna that the pontiff, having departed from Tuscany, went to Bologna. He says that the citizens received him there with great display and that, when he departed, he was escorted by three companies of Bolognese cavalry, which accompanied him as far as Clermont, doubtless both for protection and as a mark of honor.

## CLXVIII. Urban celebrates the synod of Guastalla. He is received at Canossa by Matilda.

[Col. 0138D]

Sigonius, in Book IX of *On the Kingdom of Italy*, relates that at that time Urban held a synod at Guardescallum, or, as it is commonly called, Guastalla, surrounded by a great company of cardinals, bishops, and Italian princes. Other authors report the same. Indeed, in the *Life of Urban*, among the other councils that Pandulfus records as having been celebrated by him, there is one called Ewardastallense in Lombardy. He writes that a preface concerning the blessed Mary was composed there, the one commonly attributed to Urban.

Yet since it is nowhere reported that anything was enacted there, it is likely that this synod was convened solely so that the matters necessary for the journey to Gaul and for the Council of Piacenza, which the pontiff was about to celebrate, might be properly arranged. Sigonius himself supports this conjecture: he assigns the same synod to the end of the year 1094 and then adds that Urban, having departed from there, was received at Canossa with magnificent display by Countess Matilda. Ripamontius also testifies that the pontiff visited Guastalla and Canossa, and other authors agree with him.

Domnizo says something about Urban’s arrival in Lombardy, but he does not specify the place where he was received by Matilda, nor does he mention any synod other than that of Piacenza. Ciaconius, however, places before the Council of Piacenza another synod at Villa Rastalla, on the bank of the Po, and writes that Matilda attended it.

## CLXIX. Urban at Cremona. He grants a privilege to Saint Giles and to the Parthenon of Cremona.

[Col. 0139B]

On his way to Piacenza Urban passed through Cremona. There he wrote a letter to all the faithful of Gothia on behalf of the monks of Saint Giles of Valle Flaviana, to whom Count Raymond had restored certain possessions that he himself and his predecessors had unjustly taken from that monastery.

In the pontifical letters concerning this matter, which were later read aloud and confirmed at the Council of Piacenza and were issued at Cremona on 18 February of this year, mention is made of Hervira, Raymond’s wife. We record her name here because it is reported in various forms by various ancient authors.

The same pontiff granted a privilege to Gissa, abbess of the monastery of Saint John the Evangelist near the city of Cremona. Since the manuscript from which we possess it gives no chronological indication, it seemed appropriate to assign it here. It is remarkable, however, that no mention of this monastery is found—not even in Lubin’s *Catalogue of the Abbeys of Italy*. From this charter we learn that its founders were Count Bernard and his wife Bertha, in the time of Gregory VII.

## CLXX. The Council of Piacenza.

Toward the end of February the pontiff arrived at Piacenza, intending shortly to celebrate the council, which everyone agrees was held in this year. If the author of the *Chronicle of Maillezais*, together with some other writers, assigned the Council of Piacenza to the year 1094, they followed in this matter the ancient Gallic method of reckoning, which began the year at Easter.

At that time, if we believe Ughelli, the Church of Piacenza was governed by Addo, or Aldus, counselor of Henry Augustus. After Bonizo of Sutri, that author places before him Vindicius, in 1091, and Watrius, a Gaul by nationality; perhaps Urban had opposed these men to this Henryan bishop in the same way that the citizens of Rome, most devoted to the Roman Church, had earlier adopted Bonizo.

Moreover, such a multitude of people from every nation under heaven gathered for the council that no church, no public or private building, and not even any street of the city could contain them. Therefore the pontiff held the synodal assembly outside the city, in a field, as Berthold himself testifies. He also writes a little further on that nearly four thousand clerics and more than thirty thousand laypeople attended it. Hence the Acts of the council, preserved by Holstenius and Labbe, testify that the council met in the field on the first and third days, because so great a crowd had assembled that no church could accommodate them.

## CLXXI. When the Council of Piacenza was held, and who attended it.

Berthold writes that this synod was celebrated around the middle of Lent—that is, on the Kalends of March themselves, according to an old manuscript cited by Labbe; Domnizo agrees in the verses that we shall report in the Appendix.

The Acts already cited state that it lasted seven days, in these words: “Finally, on the seventh day, after prolonged discussion, the chapters of the synod were brought forward and approved with the assent of the entire council.”

We may certainly infer that it did not continue beyond eight days from Urban’s letter to the people of Noyon, issued on 9 March after the synod had been concluded. Yet nowhere is it stated how many bishops attended or who they were, except that an old Saxon chronicle, which we possess in manuscript, says that Henry was deprived of ecclesiastical communion at this synod by nearly two hundred Fathers. Albert, abbot of Stade, likewise testifies to this in his *Chronicle*.

The Acts that we have just cited from Labbe state that this synod was held under the presidency of the lord Urban, with the bishops and abbots both of Gaul and of Lombardy and Tuscany. Berthold also affirms that several bishops from Alemannia, Bavaria, and other provinces came to it. Among them he names, on this occasion, Dimon, or Thiemon, archbishop of Salzburg, and Udalric, bishop of Passau, from Bavaria; Gebehard of Constance, from Alemannia; and Udalric, abbot of Reichenau. Certainly Udalric, as the same author writes, was consecrated abbot by the pontiff himself at that time.

We learn the names of several other prelates from other records. Thus Hoel, bishop of Le Mans, is said in the *Acts of the Bishops of that Church*, published in volume III of Mabillon’s *Analecta*, to have gone to Rome at that time and to have been kindly received by Urban; he attended with him the apostolic council at Piacenza.

We infer the same concerning Radbod, bishop of Noyon, from the letter cited shortly above, and concerning Hugh of Grenoble from the letters relating to the controversy over the district of Salmoray. There is no doubt that the archbishops of Narbonne and Arles attended the same synod, together with the bishops of Nîmes and Maguelonne, to whom Urban entrusted this year the examination of the case of the monks of Psalmodi against those of Saint Victor of Marseille, if the document drawn up on that matter is reliable. More probably, however, the year 1094 has slipped into the beginning of that document in place of 1096.

Other ancient records may perhaps provide us with the names of additional participants, but none lists more than the privilege of Saint Giles already mentioned. At this synod many cardinals and bishops, together with three abbots, confirmed it with Urban; their names are appended to the privilege.

Nearly all published authors have transmitted the tradition that Saint Bruno, founder of the Carthusians, was present at the same synod as the pontiff’s counselor [Col. 0141A]. I have no intention of challenging this opinion. But I cannot agree with those who assert that at that time the pontiff offered this holy man the archbishopric of Reggio in Calabria. For, as we have already said elsewhere, it follows that this must be assigned to another time, because the see of that Church was not then vacant.

Whatever the case may be, it is certain that Bruno, although he accompanied Urban as far as Piacenza, did not return with him to Gaul. Perhaps he would have found it burdensome to travel through so many cities and provinces. He therefore withdrew to Calabria, where he had already laid the foundations of his order and had been endowed with many possessions, as is clear from charters of Count Roger and others that are found throughout published books.

## CLXXII. What was discussed at the same council. Concerning the divorce of Empress Praxedis. King Philip is excommunicated. Holy expeditions.

[Col. 0141B]

Orderic Vitalis, at the beginning of Book IX, states that Pope Urban carefully dealt at the Council of Piacenza with peace and with other matters beneficial to the holy Church. What this author has presented in summary deserves to be examined somewhat more carefully, one matter at a time and insofar as is permissible, from other writers and especially from Berthold.

Praxedis Augusta had come to this synod. The Saxon chronicler already mentioned calls her Adheleidis, as does Dodechin. The Fathers approved her withdrawal from the Emperor Henry after hearing from her of various insults and unheard-of obscenities of fornication that she had suffered from her husband [Col. 0141C]. Accordingly, she was granted pardon for the offenses she seemed to have committed only unwillingly, and the penance that would have been imposed to expiate such great crimes was remitted, because she had not been ashamed to confess her sins openly.

After receiving absolution at the council, she is said to have returned to her homeland. There, shut away in a monastery and devoting herself to the exercises of the religious life, she died a holy death.

Philip, king of the Franks, who in the preceding year, as we have said, had been excommunicated by Hugh, legate of the Apostolic See, at the Council of Autun because of his adulterous marriage, sent a delegation to this synod and received from the pontiff a truce until Pentecost. Hugh himself, because neither he nor anyone sent by him had attended the synod to which Urban had summoned them [Col. 0141D], was suspended from the office of apostolic legate.

Envoys of Alexius, emperor of Constantinople, also came to the same synod to implore the aid of the pontiff and of the Christian princes against the infidels, who had conquered everything as far as the walls of Constantinople. When these matters had been presented at the council, many people already bound themselves to undertake an expedition to those regions. This was in a sense a prelude to that famous expedition which was later decreed at the Council of Clermont.

Indeed, Peter the Hermit, as the commonly circulated historians of the Jerusalem expeditions write, had returned from the East and met with the pontiff before he left Rome, already in the preceding year [Col. 0142A]. In the name of the patriarch of Jerusalem, he explained to him how necessary it was for the Christian princes, joining their forces together, to undertake a holy expedition to the East for the recovery of the sacred places and the protection of the Christians who lived in those regions and were oppressed under the yoke of the infidels.

Therefore, while Urban, after concluding the Council of Piacenza, was coming to Gaul to celebrate another council for the same reason, Peter himself traveled through various provinces with the purpose of preparing the minds of the people, and especially of the nobles, and persuading the princes to undertake these expeditions.

## CLXXIII. Heresies proscribed.

At the same synod the heresies that were then disturbing the Church were proscribed. The principal ones were those of the Simoniacs and of persons who had been ordained by them, that is, by men known to be such; likewise, that of the Nicolaitans, namely, incontinent priests and other higher clerics [Col. 0142B].

There also, as Berthold reports, the terrible anathemas against the Berengarian heresy, which had already been pronounced very frequently in ancient times, were renewed; and the judgment of the Catholic faith was confirmed against it: namely, that when the bread and wine are consecrated on the altar, they are converted not only figuratively but also truly and essentially into the body and blood of the Lord.

Finally, anathemas with burning candles against Guibert and his accomplices—something that had already been done more than once—were once again pronounced and renewed by the unanimous vote and consent of all the Fathers.

Domnizo relates that the deeds of Guibert and Henry were condemned by the Fathers. He reports that the crimes of Henry against Praxedis, once publicly disclosed [Col. 0142C], gave many people an occasion to abandon the emperor. This encouraged Urban to undertake his journey into Lombardy and to hold a synod there. See the verses of that author in the Appendix.

## CLXXIV. Reichenau is placed under the bishop of Constance.

Berthold testifies that at this synod Urban prohibited Udalric, abbot of Reichenau, whom he himself had consecrated at that time, from exercising any authority over the clergy and people of the island of Reichenau, and granted that authority to Gebehard, bishop of Constance, who was present at the council. Consequently, when Udalric shortly afterward interfered in its affairs, he was reprimanded in a letter from Urban. That letter, however, has perished.

## CLXXV. Canons. Concerning Church discipline.

At the same synod excellent regulations concerning morals and ecclesiastical discipline were also established and promulgated. Berthold lists some of their provisions.

“Among other things,” says that author, “it was decreed that those who refused to abandon concubines, hatred from the heart, or any mortal sin were not to be admitted to penance. No priest was to admit anyone to penance unless his own bishop had entrusted him with this care. Those who dwell bodily, but not in mind, among the excommunicated, if they come properly to confession, are not to be denied the Eucharist, provided that they have not shared in the sacraments of the excommunicated. The ordination of those ordained by excommunicated persons is not to be considered invalid, provided that they are able to prove that they did not know their ordainers were excommunicated” [Col. 0143A].

From this canon it is clear that the Fathers of that council did not consider ordinations performed by excommunicated persons to be invalid.

“It was also decreed that nothing whatsoever should ever be demanded for chrism, baptism, or burial; and finally, that the fasts of the Four Seasons should be observed in the fixed weeks designated there.”

Baronius writes that fifteen canons of this council are found in the collection of Anselm, bishop of Lucca. They do in fact occur frequently in manuscript codices of that author, but this must be understood of additions made to the collection, since Anselm had gone to heaven nine years before that synod.

Those Anselmian canons are precisely the ones that Labbe published from various manuscript codices in volume X of the *Councils*, for they entirely agree with the regulations that we cited from Berthold. They also occur frequently in the various decretals of Gratian and other compilers.

The first seven of them were enacted against the Simoniacs or against those who had received orders from them. The next five concern those who had been ordained by the antipope Guibert himself, by his accomplices, or by other schismatics.

The fifteenth, which is absent from some codices but is nevertheless cited by Gratian, forbids anyone to be ordained without a title, or anyone ordained in one church to transfer to another, and forbids anyone to hold a title in two churches.

Some codices add a canon frequently cited by various authors, directed against clerics who receive the investiture of ecclesiastical dignities from laymen.

## CLXXVI. The preface concerning the Blessed Mary.

[Col. 0143C]

The tradition has become established among the commonly published authors that Pope Urban added to the nine ancient prefaces a tenth, concerning the blessed Mary, at this council. This is expressly stated in an old manuscript codex of the archmonastery of Saint-Remi at Reims, written approximately five hundred years ago. After a decree concerning the nine prefaces, attributed to Pope Pelagius, has been reported, the following words are added in the same hand:

“The tenth was added at the Council of Piacenza celebrated under Pope Urban.”

They say that the matter occurred as follows. When the pontiff was celebrating the sacred rites at Saint Mary of Campania, a temple of the most ancient piety, so that God might bring the council’s undertaking to a favorable conclusion, he had begun to offer the preface. Suddenly, by divine inspiration, to the astonishment of the people, he burst forth into those most sweet words:

“And that we may praise, bless, and proclaim you in veneration of the blessed Virgin Mary, who conceived your Only-Begotten Son through the overshadowing of the Holy Spirit and, with the glory of virginity remaining, poured forth into this world the eternal light, Jesus Christ our Lord, through whom,” etc.

The universal Church subsequently approved this preface by adopting it, and still retains it today.

Some maintain that it was composed by Saint Bruno. Pandulfus, however, expressly states in his *Life* that it was composed by Urban himself—not at Piacenza, but at the synod of Ewardastallum, as we have already noted.

Peter Maria Campi has more to say about this preface in Book XII of his *History of Piacenza*, under the year 1095 [Col. 0144A]. Since his account is not sufficiently consistent with itself, it did not seem appropriate to reproduce it here.

## CLXXVII. The privilege of Saint Giles is confirmed. Likewise, that of Cluny. The dispute over the district of Salmoray.

At the Council of Piacenza certain private affairs of monasteries and other churches were also dealt with. We have certainly already observed above that Urban’s charter, in which certain possessions restored by Count Raymond to the monastery of Saint Giles were recorded, was read aloud and approved before the Fathers of this council.

The privileges of the monastery of Cluny were also confirmed there, as the pontiff himself testifies in a charter concerning the matter, issued a few days later and addressed to Saint Hugh.

We learn from Hugh’s own memorandum that the dispute over the district of Salmoray between Guido, archbishop of Vienne, and Hugh, bishop of Grenoble, which had already been debated at various assemblies, was also discussed at this synod. In it he reports a letter from the pontiff to Guido, issued at Piacenza on 12 March, to recall him to a better frame of mind.

But without success. On the preceding day the pontiff had written to Robert, count of Flanders, asking him to assist Lambert, bishop of Arras, in recovering the property of his own Church, which had been alienated because of its union with the Church of Cambrai.

On that same day, according to our manuscript codex, the same pontiff wrote another letter to Walter, elect of Cambrai, asking him not to attack what the Apostolic See had decreed concerning the division of the Churches of Cambrai and Arras. From these letters it may be inferred that the Council of Piacenza also dealt with the restoration of the Church of Arras, which had already been confirmed at many councils [Col. 0144C].

## CLXXVIII. After concluding the synod, Urban grants various privileges. Hirsau, and others. Letter to the people of Noyon. Two letters on behalf of the Church of Arras. One concerning the Salmoray dispute. The privilege of Maguelonne. The privilege of Cluny.

We have collected as much as was possible concerning the affairs dealt with at the synod itself. But it does not follow from this that the letters we have cited were written while the council was still in session, since it is certain from the letter addressed to the clergy and people of Noyon concerning Radbod, bishop of that city, that the synod had ended on 9 March.

In it Urban writes that he was sending Radbod back to his own city, since he had arrived at the council “which, by the Lord’s favor, we held at Piacenza.”

The pontiff therefore did not leave Piacenza immediately after the end of the council, whether because not everything necessary for his journey to Gaul had yet been arranged, or for any other reason—which it is of no interest to guess. During the time he spent there, he wrote letters concerning various matters, some of which, because they concerned the Council of Piacenza, we have mentioned above. The rest may be treated briefly here in chronological order.

First we encounter the notable privilege granted to the monastery of Hirsau, then governed by Gebehard, a disciple of Saint William, to whom the privilege is addressed. It was issued on 8 March, and therefore on the final day of the Council of Piacenza [Col. 0145A], or certainly, if the council was completed within seven days, on the day immediately following its celebration.

It is not surprising that Urban favored the monks of Hirsau so greatly, since it is certain that no one in Germany was more zealous than they in pursuing the schismatics by word and writing, as is evident from the apology of Henry Augustus published by Freher in his collection of authors of German history.

We also learn from the *Life* of Saint William, published in volume VI of the Benedictine *Acta Sanctorum*, that the monastery of Hirsau was always the safest refuge, during the time of Abbot William, for all who supported Gregory VII.

Trithemius and several others also published another privilege of the same place, but one of much less authority, if I judge correctly. Nevertheless, it did not seem right to omit it entirely, lest I appear rashly to reject what others have regarded as genuine. This is especially so because Trithemius testifies in the *Chronicle of that Place* that it was approved and accepted by Richard, metropolitan of Mainz.

On the following day, 9 March, Urban wrote the letter to the people of Noyon that we have already cited more than once, on behalf of their bishop Radbod, asking them to receive him as their pastor. Indeed, while he had been staying at the Roman court, no one had accused him of any crime.

Two days later, on 11 March, the same pontiff wrote one letter to Walter, elect of Cambrai, and another to Robert, count of Flanders, on behalf of the Church of Arras, as we said in the preceding section [Col. 0145C].

These were followed by the pontiff’s letter to Guido, archbishop of Vienne, concerning the district of Salmoray, also cited above. It was written on 12 March.

On 14 March Urban confirmed various possessions granted by Bishop Godfrey to the canons of Maguelonne, who had embraced the regular life according to the rule of Saint Augustine. He gave them his blessing and absolution from their sins.

Antonius de Verdala, bishop of that same Church, who wrote its history of bishops, published in volume I of Labbe’s *Library*, mentions this rescript. He does not state whether Godfrey himself, who perhaps was then at Piacenza, personally obtained it; this is nevertheless likely, since he is said to have labored greatly to restore the regular life of the canons of his Church.

This privilege was followed by another, exceptionally comprehensive, which the pontiff granted two days later, on 16 March, to Saint Hugh, abbot of Cluny. It lists the churches subject to that monastery in various provinces and confirms all the other privileges of earlier pontiffs.

Urban then prohibited—as he says, “just as Gregory had decreed in a Roman synod, and as we ourselves recently decreed at Piacenza”—any archbishop, bishop, or even apostolic legate from exercising any power to place the Cluniacs under interdict or excommunication, or to hear their cases [Col. 0146A]. He also extended to Hugh’s successors the authority to use the mitre and the other pontifical ornaments that had already been granted to Abbot Hugh for the eight principal feast days.

Urban was still at Piacenza at the beginning of April. On 4 April he granted a nearly identical privilege to the monastery of Saint Victor of Marseille, addressed to Cardinal Richard, its abbot, who had long served as legate of the Apostolic See in Spain.

In our copies it is said to have been issued in the year 1096. This is an error made by the scribes, which can easily be corrected from other chronological indications, unless, as may be observed in many other charters of this and the following year, the year in this privilege begins with the preceding month of March.

## CLXXIX. Richer, bishop of Verdun, obeys Urban.

[Col. 0146B]

While these events were taking place in Italy, Richer, who seven years earlier had been elected bishop of Verdun and had received the staff from Henry Augustus, went to Hugh, archbishop of Lyon. After renouncing the schism, he was consecrated by Hugh on the holy day of the Lord’s Resurrection. Shortly afterward, on the second Sunday after Easter, he was received at Verdun with immense applause from the citizens, through the efforts of Rodulf, abbot of Saint Victor, who was a most ardent defender of Urban’s cause.

We learn this from Lawrence of Liège in his *History of the Bishops of that City*, published in volume XII of Acher’s *Spicilegium*.

## CLXXX. Urban is received at Cremona by King Conrad.

[Col. 0146C]

At the beginning of April the pontiff left Piacenza and traveled through many cities, as Domnizo records. First, as the sequence of his journey, combined with the accounts of the ancient authors, seems to require, he went again to Cremona. There, on 10 April, according to Berthold, he met Conrad, the son of Henry and king of Italy.

Conrad performed for him the office of *strator* and swore fealty concerning his life, his limbs, and the Roman papacy. Urban received him as a son of the holy Roman Church and solemnly promised before the people to give him counsel and assistance in obtaining the kingdom and acquiring the imperial crown, subject, of course, to the rights of that Church and to the apostolic statutes [Col. 0146D], especially those concerning the prohibition against a layman usurping investiture in spiritual offices.

When Ivo, bishop of Chartres, received news of this, he wrote to the pontiff to congratulate him. I have no doubt that his Letter 43, addressed to Urban, belongs here. In it he says that his joy could not be expressed within the limits of words, “because he had heard that the Roman Church was prospering so greatly under Urban’s rule that, having almost reached the harbor, the kingdom of Italy, long rebellious, was now almost entirely silent in his presence, and the new king”—without doubt Conrad—“had wholly placed himself in his [Urban’s] hands, for the will of God and of Urban.”

Indeed, as Sigonius observed, after Emperor Henry had departed from Italy, everyone soon hastened to Conrad’s side. Already at the beginning of this year, as we said from Berthold, the same prince, having joined himself to Matilda, controlled the entire strength of his father’s army.

## CLXXXI. Welf rises against Matilda. Conrad marries the daughter of Count Roger.

At that time Matilda was nevertheless compelled to withstand a new enemy, namely Welf the father, duke of Bavaria. He was deeply distressed that his son Welf was living separated from the bed of his wife Matilda. Fearing that in this way he would be deprived of her possessions, he defected to Henry so that he might extort those possessions from her, by force if not voluntarily. But his efforts were fruitless.

Matilda, undaunted, eluded his stratagems and broke his power; and this is not surprising. For, as William of Malmesbury relates—although he was not usually favorable either to Urban or to Matilda—forgetful of her sex and no inferior to the ancient Amazons, a woman led armored ranks of men into battle.

Welf was no more successful in Alemannia, where, as Berthold testifies, he labored in vain with several other princes to secure Henry’s restoration to the kingdom.

Meanwhile Conrad, whose power was increasing daily, went to Pisa with royal pomp. There he took as his bride the daughter of Roger, count of Sicily and Calabria, with an unprecedented amount of money. Geoffrey the monk, in Book IV, testifies that this was done on the advice of Urban and Matilda; he mentions letters written by the pontiff to Roger on that occasion [Col. 0147C].

Those letters have perished, but their substance, according to that author, was as follows: Urban wrote to Roger that it would bring him great honor and advantage if his daughter were joined in marriage to the king’s son, her future husband; and that the young man, devoted to the faith of the holy Roman Church but insufficient in resources to fight against his father, who was unjustly attacking him, would, if his father supplied the means together with his daughter, be [manuscript variant: “defeated” / “strengthened”] in resources and thus prevail in overcoming the enemies of the holy Church of God.

Geoffrey adds that Roger fulfilled this request, sending for the purpose a great fleet together with many costly gifts.

## CLXXXII. Peter, king of Aragon, most devoted to the Apostolic See.

At this same time Urban received a letter from Peter, king of Aragon, in which Peter, in addition to the filial obedience owed to the pope, also bound himself to pay the census that his father Sancho had once established, in the time of Gregory VII, as payable to the Apostolic See.

The illustrious Peter of Marca cites this letter from John Briz Martineius, abbot of Pina, in his *History of Béarn*, and says that it was written in this year.

This year is also given by a notable bull of Urban, apparently issued on the occasion of this letter for the benefit of the same king. In it Urban congratulates the king on his reverence and goodwill toward the Church. He then complains that he was suffering opposition from certain prelates who ought to have favored him. Finally, he grants to him, to the princes of his lineage, and to other nobles of the kingdom many distinguished rights over churches that they had either liberated from the yoke of the Saracens or newly built [Col. 0148A].

This privilege will be included among Urban’s letters from the Hispanic historians. Its chronological indications are sufficiently consistent, but it has the disadvantage of being said to have been issued at Rome on 16 April of this year, at a time when Urban was certainly in Lombardy.

John is also called there the *praesignator* of Lord Urban, a title which, as we have observed, he had used only in Urban’s earliest years, when Peter was not yet king. These matters, however, may have resulted from the carelessness of copyists. This is all the more likely because the other details in this document agree very closely with the truth of events and the circumstances of the times.

## CLXXXIII. The regular canons of Saint Leo of Toul first obtain abbots.

[Col. 0148B]

At that time the pontiff was traveling through various cities of Lombardy, as Berthold testifies, in order to win them over to himself and strengthen them by his presence, so that they would not abandon him after his departure for Gaul.

He was certainly in those regions when Lutolf, dean of the Church of Toul, obtained from him a privilege for a monastery that he had recently founded near that city in honor of Saint Pope Leo IX, who had been bishop of Toul before attaining the papacy.

At that place Lutolf had established regular Augustinian canons under the rule of a provost. The bishop of Toul later solemnly consecrated this provost as abbot.

What the privilege of Urban contained is uncertain, since it has not been possible to recover a copy of it. On this occasion, however, Berthold noted something worthy of attention: namely, that a practice first became current in those regions whereby the heads of monasteries of clerics, which the Romans called canonical houses, previously called only provosts, came to be called abbots and consecrated under that title, with the sole exception that they did not carry staffs.

This custom later spread to other regions as well. Thereafter the provosts of regular canons not only abandoned the title of provost and called themselves abbots, but also, with the permission of the pontiffs, adopted the use of the mitre and the other insignia of abbots.

See Rupert, Book IV on the Rule of Saint Benedict, where he reports a letter written on this occasion by Frederick, archbishop of Cologne.

## CLXXXIV. Urban grants a privilege at Milan to the Church of Carcassonne. Letter concerning the Salmoray dispute. Humbald, bishop of Auxerre, is consecrated. Arnulf of Milan. The translation of Herlembald.

[Col. 0148D]

Urban spent much of the month of May at Milan. There, on the 21st, he confirmed the regular canons whom Peter, bishop of Carcassonne, had established in his cathedral and other churches, issuing a rescript to that effect. A few days later another document was added, addressed to the clergy and people of the archdeaconate of Salmoriacum, in which the pope ordered them to obey the bishop of Grenoble until the Apostolic See should decree otherwise.

Urban had already arrived at Milan at the beginning of this month, if the ancient records of the Church of Auxerre do not mislead us. They state that Humbald, bishop of that city, was ordained by the pope himself at Milan on 2 May; and indeed, according to the brief chronicle published by Labbe in volume I of the *Bibliotheca nova*, this occurred in the present year, as other ancient documents also confirm. Hugo, monk of Saint-Marien of the same city, must therefore be corrected, where his chronicle states that Humbald ruled the Church of Auxerre in 1096 after Robert—provided, that is, that these words are to be understood as referring to the beginning of his administration, or that the year did not begin in March. Most other Gallican authors followed this reckoning, especially when discussing Urban’s journey.

As for the statement in the *Deeds of the Abbots of Saint-Germain* that, in the first year of Humbald’s administration, Urban held the Council of Nîmes, it must be understood as referring to Humbald’s enthronement. Since he had been consecrated in Italy in May, he could not take possession of his see before July; and that author reckoned the years of his administration from that point. In any case, since it is certain that he had been consecrated at Milan before Urban’s journey into Gaul, his ordination cannot be postponed beyond May of this year.

The *History of the Bishops of Auxerre*, chapter 53, published by Labbe in the place cited, gives the following account:

> Humbald was elected bishop by the clergy and people of the city of Auxerre. After his election, he was presented at Milan, a city of Italy, by the clergy to Pope Urban, who had gone down into Lombardy on account of certain persons deviating from sound doctrine, to be consecrated; and there he was consecrated by the same pope and brought back to his own city, etc.

[Col. 0149C]

Among all that Urban accomplished at Milan, the restoration of Arnulf, archbishop of that city—or, more accurately, his initial installation in this see, to which he had been elected two years earlier—was especially noteworthy. Arnulf, as Bertold relates, had been appointed in 1093 in place of the deceased Anselm, but had been placed under interdict by the papal legate because he had received the ring and staff from the emperor. He bore this penalty patiently, withdrew to a monastery to expiate his offense, and lived there privately until, according to the same Bertold, with the permission of the Roman pontiff, he was consecrated by Thiemar, archbishop of Salzburg, Udalric, bishop of Passau, and Gebehard, bishop of Constance, who were on their way to the Council of Piacenza. Shortly afterward Urban bestowed the pallium upon him, and he obtained full possession of his Church.

[Col. 0149D]

In old manuscript catalogues of the bishops of that Church, as Puricello reports, it is stated that on the feast of Saint George Arnulf proceeded from the church of Saint Dionysius to his own see, seated on a certain white horse together with twelve Milanese standard-bearers.

The arrival of Arnulf and Urban in Milan shortly afterward so altered the state of affairs in that city that, as Sigonius says, its citizens, overcome by Urban’s authority—having previously fought among themselves—laid aside their ancient hostilities and returned to harmony with such a transformation of their spirits that nobles and commoners kissed one another in the squares and streets, their tears of joy flowing freely.

This is what that author reports. Yet he is mistaken, as we already observed under the year 1093, when he wrote that Arnulf had then been reordained by the Catholic bishops because, in his view, he had been consecrated with only one Catholic bishop laying hands upon him.

Moreover, if Ughellus, Ripamonti, and several other widely followed authors are to be believed, Arnulf accompanied Urban when he set out for Gaul and attended the Council of Clermont with him. Before they left that city, however, they transferred to the church of Saint Dionysius the body of Herlembald, or Herne­bald, a certain martyr and leader of the Catholics in that city, who had been killed by the schismatics in the time of Gregory VII. There it was placed beside the body of another martyr of that period, Ariald by name, a Milanese deacon.

[Col. 0150B]

It seemed worthwhile to reproduce here, from Ughellus, his epitaph, although it may seem strange that his memory is nowhere found in the martyrologies. It reads:

> Here lies Herne­bald, a revered soldier of Christ,  
> Slain, yet destined to possess heaven’s dwelling.  
> He rejects the incestuous and condemns simonies,  
> And the servants of Venus and wicked Simon put him to death.  
> Urban, supreme pontiff, also called the Second,  
> And our Arnulf, a pious and kindly shepherd,  
> Bury the bones of this blessed man.

## CLXXXV. Urban dedicates a church at Como and one at Asti. He confirms the privilege of the monastery of Fruttuaria, and likewise that of Pinerolo.

[Col. 0150C]

At the beginning of June Urban came to Como, where, with great ceremony, he dedicated the church of Saint Abundius, bishop and patron of that city, whom, as Sigonius says, the city venerates with exceptional devotion. According to the ancient tradition of that city—and the sequence of events agrees entirely with it—this took place on 3 June.

From there he proceeded to Vercelli, as we gather from Albert of Aachen’s *History of Jerusalem*. He then visited Asti, a city of Liguria, if the ancient local tradition is true, according to which the principal church of that city was consecrated by that pontiff.

Ughellus assigns this event to the following year, on Urban’s return from Gaul. Augustine of the Church’s opinion, however, is more plausible: he holds that the pontiff celebrated this dedication before his arrival in Gaul, although he records it at the beginning of the year 1096, perhaps following an inscription reported by Ughellus. That inscription gives the same year, undoubtedly according to the Pisan reckoning, by which the year begins in the preceding March and anticipates the ordinary year by nine months.

Indeed, the day of the Kalends of July, on which the dedication is said in that inscription to have taken place, cannot belong to the year 1096. It is certain that Urban was still in Gaul on that date in 1096. Here is the inscription itself, as Ughellus says he copied it from an old calendar, in volume IV of *Italia sacra*, in his catalogue of the bishops of Asti:

> On the Kalends of July, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1096, the church of Asti was dedicated by the lord Pope Urban, who relaxed and remitted one year and forty days of the penance imposed upon all truly penitent and confessed persons who should come to this church, and to venerate God and the blessed Virgin Mary, on the day of its dedication and throughout the octave; and the lord bishop of Asti remitted forty days.

Whether this inscription is wholly authentic and ancient I leave to others to judge.

Otto was then governing the Church of Asti, and according to Ughellus Urban is said to have dedicated this church at his invitation. Bruno, bishop of Signi, Urban’s constant companion and faithful friend, assisted him; Bruno had been born in Asti and had been a canon of that Church before becoming a bishop.

While the pontiff was still there, he confirmed and enlarged the privileges of the monastery of Fruttuaria, then governed by Abbot Ubertus or Guibertus, if we may believe Augustine of the Church, who makes this assertion in chapter 27 of his *Piedmontese Chronology*. He is mistaken, however, in assigning the event to the year 1089, although, since this privilege has been lost, it is extremely difficult to correct the error with certainty.

[Col. 0151B]

We also infer that Urban passed through Pinerolo from a bull granted in this year to Ubertus, abbot of the monastery of Saint Mary situated near that city. By it, all the possessions that had been bestowed upon him by Countess Adelaide and others are confirmed. The pontiff then forbids anyone ever to alienate any of them.

We were unable to obtain a copy of this charter, although we repeatedly arranged for friends to write to Pinerolo about it. The reason was doubtless that this monastery, now held by the Feuillants, was burned down in the wars of earlier times.

[Col. 0151C]

Whether the pontiff also visited the famous monastery of Saint Michael at Chiusa is uncertain. It is nevertheless clear from bulls of subsequent pontiffs that this place had been granted a privilege by Urban, though the document has been lost.

Such, insofar as we have been able, is what we have gathered from various documents concerning Urban’s deeds before he came into Gaul. What he accomplished during this journey we shall relate after first presenting some information about English affairs, which were greatly disturbed in this year on account of Saint Anselm.

## CLXXXVI. The disturbances in England on account of Saint Anselm. The assembly at Rockingham. Anselm consults Hugh, archbishop of Lyon. He receives the pallium. He writes to the pope.

[Col. 0151D]

Since nearly everyone had defected from Henry and his antipope Guibert, whom he called Clement III, only William, surnamed Rufus, king of England, remained. Although he did not obey Guibert, he had not yet been willing publicly to recognize Urban as the legitimate pontiff. Thus, as Eadmer says in book I of the *New History*, there were two men in England who were called Roman pontiffs, Urban and Clement. This matter occupied the Church of England so completely that for many years after the death of Gregory VII it was unwilling to submit or obey any pope in any place.

Nevertheless, when Anselm had been sought for the archbishopric in 1093, he had declared before the king himself and all the orders of the kingdom that he would obey no one but Urban. On that condition he had ascended the throne of Canterbury.

[Col. 0152A]

But the king, hostile to him, as we have already said, rejected his counsels as though they were insults. When Anselm, recently returned to England, proposed that he be granted permission to visit the pontiff in order to request the pallium, and when the king asked which pope he wished to visit and Anselm answered “Urban,” the king, as Eadmer and the other English writers report, growled at the name of Urban. He declared that he had not yet accepted Urban as apostolic pontiff, and that it was neither his own custom nor that of his father to allow anyone to name a pope in his kingdom without his election.

Anselm tried in vain to remind him that at Rochester, when he had been sought for the archbishopric, he had declared that he would never depart from obedience to Urban. The king, for his part, could not persuade Anselm that he owed the king complete faith and obedience even if he did not recognize Urban as pontiff. It therefore seemed best to refer the matter to a general assembly of all the bishops and nobles of the kingdom.

This assembly was held at Rockingham in the year 1095, on 11 March. Eadmer, who gives a fuller account, testifies that Anselm spoke with such firmness of spirit and episcopal vigor about his own election and about the obedience owed both to the Roman pontiff and to the king that, since the king’s purpose had failed, the assembly was dissolved after three days and a postponement was granted until Pentecost. In the meantime most of the bishops denied obedience to Anselm, because they saw that the king was hostile to him; the lay nobles did not do so.

[Col. 0152C]

Anselm, anxious about what he should do amid so grave a crisis, was considering resigning his see. No hope seemed to appear of bending the king’s mind or obtaining his permission to visit the legitimate pontiff, from whom he had not yet received the pallium.

He consulted Hugh, archbishop of Lyon, who at that time was acting as the pontiff’s representative in Gaul, by sending him a letter. This is letter 24 of book III, in which he gives him an excellent account of the condition of the English Church.

While he was turning these matters over in his mind, two clerics whom William had sent to Rome—having despaired of breaking Anselm’s constancy—in order to discover whether Urban or Guibert was more powerful there, returned to England with Walter, cardinal-bishop of Albano. Walter brought with him, in Urban’s name, the pallium destined for Anselm, archbishop of Canterbury.

[Col. 0152D]

This brought some hope of peace. The king immediately decreed that throughout England Urban alone should be regarded as the true and legitimate pontiff.

When the legate brought the pallium to the king instead of to Anselm, however, the king hoped to receive some money from the archbishop—at least the sum that the archbishop would have spent on the journey had he gone to Rome, or at least whatever the king himself had spent to obtain the pallium from Urban. But nothing could be extorted from Anselm.

Indeed, Anselm was asked, for the sake of the royal majesty’s magnificence, to allow the king at least to place the pallium upon him solemnly. The holy bishop firmly refused even this, declaring that he would never give any money for the pallium and would never allow any human being to place it upon him.

[Col. 0153A]

And so it happened. After various disputes on both sides, reported in different places by Eadmer, William of Malmesbury, and other authors, the parties finally agreed that the pallium should be placed upon the altar and that Anselm should then take it and arrange it upon himself. Thus Anselm received the pallium without any stain of simony, and Urban, without any loss to ecclesiastical liberty, began to be regarded by the king and the people as the true and legitimate pontiff in England.

William of Malmesbury writes that when Walter came to Canterbury carrying the pallium in a silver casket, Anselm went out to meet him barefoot amid the applause of the people, clothed in priestly garments. After the pallium had been placed upon the altar of the Savior, Anselm fitted it upon his own shoulders and then proceeded to celebrate the sacred rites.

Since William observes that this took place on Sunday, 10 June, it is clear that the event occurred in the year 1095, when that date fell on a Sunday.

After receiving the pallium, Anselm wrote a letter to Urban—letter 37 of book III—to thank him for so great a benefaction and to excuse himself for not having gone to Rome to receive it from him personally. Here one may admire the modesty and charity of the blessed man: among the other reasons he gives for his excuse, he says not a word about the very serious troubles he had endured on that account from the king and the bishops.

## CLXXXVII. England is pacified, and Herbert is restored to the see of Thetford. Privileges for the monasteries of Saint Ives and Battle.

After this, communication between Urban and the English became free, and Herbert, who had been driven from his see by the king’s ministers because he had recognized Urban as pontiff, recovered it.

He had been a monk of Fécamp and had become abbot of Ramsey before obtaining the bishopric of Thetford, not without suspicion of simony. When, for this reason, he went to Rome to submit himself to Urban’s judgment, he was rebuked by the king and deprived of the staff that the pontiff had returned to him as a penitent.

Once matters had been settled as we have described, however, he was left in possession of his see. In the following year he transferred it to Norwich, where he had built a new basilica, and he held it peacefully until his death.

About the same time William, prior of Saint Ives in the county of Huntingdon, which depended upon the abbey of Ramsey, received from Urban a privilege confirming all the possessions and immunities of that place. It is found in the *Monasticon Anglicanum*, where it bears no chronological indication.

The same pontiff, according to Eadmer, granted the monks residing in the abbey of Battle near Exeter permission to be buried in their own monastery. Paschal II cites the letters that Urban wrote on this matter to Osbern, bishop of Exeter, in letter 97; but the letters themselves have perished.

[Col. 0154A]

We certainly learn from Anselm himself, book III, letter 20 to the same Osbern, that the Exeter clerics were hostile to the monks of that place. Anselm urges Osbern to protect the monks of Battle residing in his city against the injuries of the clerics and to allow them to ring the bells for the divine office, as the monastic order requires, although Osbern had forbidden them to do so.

But we must now return to Urban’s journey into Gaul.

## CLXXXVIII. Urban crosses into Gaul.

Urban, as Guibert testifies at the beginning of book II of his *History of Jerusalem*, and as other authors commonly agree, was stirred by the appeals of Alexius, emperor of the Greeks, and still more by the danger threatening the Christian world, which was being wasted by the daily incursions of the barbarians. Above all, he was moved by the desire—urged by everyone—to recover the holy places.

After arranging affairs successfully in Lombardy, he began to turn toward Gaul, either by sea, as Bertold relates, or, as many other authors generally maintain, by crossing the Alps. It was apparently in the latter part of July, as may be gathered from Hugh of Flavigny.

In his chronicle Hugh reports that Hugh, archbishop of Lyon, had returned from Compostela on the third day before the octave of Saint John the Baptist and had received news of the pope, who was coming from Apulia and hastening toward Gaul.

The tradition of the people of Asti also supports this chronology. As we have said, they believe that the principal church of their city was consecrated by Urban on the Kalends of July of this year, while he was hurrying into Gaul. Those who claim that the pontiff arrived at Maguelonne on the vigil of the apostles Peter and Paul in this year must therefore be mistaken—for no ancient author says so. In its proper place we shall show that this event must be assigned to the following year.

## CLXXXIX. He celebrates the feast of the Assumption at Anicium. The dedication of the church at Valence.

It is certain from Bertold and other authors that Urban, who had come into Gaul to celebrate a council, celebrated the Assumption of the Mother of God at Anicium, a city of the Vellavi commonly called Le Puy.

Geoffrey, prior of Vigeois, agrees in his chronicle, in volume II of Labbe’s *Bibliotheca*, adding that Urban—whom he calls a man worthy of praise—came into Gaul through Burgundy and France. These words encompass the whole of the journey that he made before the Council of Clermont.

If the chronological note of the pontiff’s own letter to Lambert, bishop of Arras, is not misleading, Urban was already staying at Anicium around the middle of July. The letter is said to have been issued there on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of August.

[Col. 0154D]

But I would be mistaken unless the reading should be “the eighteenth day before the Kalends of September,” which is the very day of the Assumption of blessed Mary, as authors of that age mention, as we have said.

It must indeed be acknowledged that an error has entered Urban’s letter at this point. In the month of July, which has six Nones, no day occurs that is the eighteenth before the Kalends of August—unless the notary called the fifteenth day of August “the eighteenth day before the Kalends of August,” counting it as belonging to August, although the Kalends are commonly said to be named from the following month. Other examples of this practice might perhaps be produced.

This must be said if it is true that the principal basilica of the city of Valence was dedicated by Urban, while he was hastening to the Council of Clermont, on the Nones of August. There seem to be compelling arguments that this is indeed true.

First, the old chronicle of the bishops of Valence says the following concerning Bishop Guntard:

> During his episcopate, Urban II, pontiff of good memory and Roman pontiff, caring for the Churches of Christ, while going to the general council and passing through this city on his way to Clermont, etc.

Hugh, bishop of Grenoble, explicitly testifies to the same thing in the frequently cited little book that we shall reproduce in full in the Appendix.

That this church was dedicated on the Nones of August is proved by its annual solemnity, assigned to that very day in an ancient Missal; indeed, it is still celebrated each year at Valence on the same day.

All these considerations are supported by an old inscription, carved in uncial letters on stone and affixed to one of the doors of the same church. It survived the fury of the Calvinists, although somewhat damaged, when they destroyed the church in the sixteenth century. It reads:

> In the year from the Incarnation of the Lord one thousand ninety-… , on the Nones of August, Pope Urban II, together with twelve bishops, dedicated this church in honor of the blessed Virgin Mary and of the holy martyrs Cornelius and Cyprian.

It is impossible to determine who those twelve bishops were who attended the celebration with Urban. From Hugh’s little book, however, we learn that Guido, archbishop of Vienne, came to meet the pontiff when he arrived at Valence to dedicate the principal church of that city.

There the pontiff appointed a day at Romans on which he wished to settle definitively the dispute over the village of Salmoriacum, which had long been pending between Guido and Hugh, bishop of Grenoble.

Hugh attended on the appointed day, as he himself relates. Guido, however—undoubtedly because he distrusted his own case—occupied the fortress of Rotman and threatened to hold the pope there if he gave judgment against him. Therefore the pontiff, being most gentle, reserved judgment in this lawsuit for a future synod.

Whether he actually visited Romans at that time is not entirely certain. Hugh seems to suggest that he did, but he observes that on this occasion the pontiff was dispossessed of his lawful property, namely the abbey of Rotman, which belonged to the Roman Church.

## CXC. At Anicium he announces a council to be held at Clermont.

It is clear from this that, after dedicating the church at Valence at the beginning of August, Urban arrived at Anicium shortly before the middle of that month, whether by way of the town of Rotman or by some other route. There he had decided to celebrate the council that was later held at Clermont.

Contemporary authors explicitly attest this. “After crossing the Alps,” says Albert of Aachen in book I of his *History of Jerusalem*, “he decreed that an assembly of all western France and a council should be held at the city of Le Puy of Saint Mary.”

According to William of Tyre, he had first intended to convene this synod at Vézelay and then at Le Puy. But, as may be conjectured, since affairs had not yet been arranged, he finally announced, while he was at Anicium, that it would be held at Clermont, a city of Auvergne.

Certainly, the letter by which the pontiff invited Lambert, bishop of Arras, to this council was issued at Anicium, as we have just said. Bertold, speaking of Urban while he was at Le Puy, says that “by apostolic authority he appointed a synod at Clermont for the octave of Saint Martin, and by letters sent out he invited bishops from various provinces to it by canonical summons.”

[Col. 0156B]

We learn from a letter written on this occasion by Raynald, archbishop of Reims, to Lambert of Arras, that these letters were addressed to the metropolitans so that they might summon, in the pontiff’s name, not only their suffragan bishops or abbots, but also other heads of Churches and even secular princes.

It was especially worthwhile for princes to come to the council, since it was to be held chiefly for the purpose of decreeing a military expedition against the infidels, a matter that concerned them most directly.

Because Urban’s encyclical has perished, this letter of Raynald, the metropolitan, will be included among the letters of that pontiff. It will be followed by the other letter already mentioned above, which the pontiff wrote to Lambert, urging him to be ready to defend the case of his Church against the people of Cambrai at the council soon to be held.

## CXCI. Urban travels through various regions. He is received everywhere with celebration.

Since the pontiff found that affairs were not arranged so that the council could be celebrated within a few days, he decided to visit various cities and provinces. There he could dedicate churches or, by appearing in person, more easily settle matters that had long been raised but could not be brought to an end.

We learn that he did this from various ancient instruments and papal charters scattered throughout the records.

It is remarkable with what affection and reverence the pontiff was received everywhere. This was due to the sincere devotion naturally present in the minds of the Franks toward the Apostolic See and its bishops. That devotion was then all the greater because the pontiff himself had arisen from the nobility of the Frankish people, was renowned for holiness, virtue, and learning, and was richly endowed with distinguished qualities of soul and body.

Guibert adds another reason for such joy:

> As the pope enters the borders of our kingdom, he is received with such joy and such a gathering of cities, towns, and villages as had never been known in the memory of anyone then living, since it seemed that no bishop of the Apostolic See had ever before come into these regions.

No pontiff is remembered to have come into Gaul between the time of Leo IX and the time of Urban.

## CXCII. He dedicates the church of La Chaise-Dieu. He grants privileges. Likewise to the nunnery of Blasiliacum.

Urban, after leaving Anicium, seems first to have turned aside to the monastery of La Chaise-Dieu. There, at the request of Pontius, the abbot of that place, he solemnly dedicated the church begun by Saint Robert, the monastery’s first abbot and founder, and completed by Pontius himself, in honor of the martyrs Saints Vitalis and Agricola, on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of September.

[Col. 0157A]

The pontiff himself attests this in a bull that he granted shortly afterward to the same monastery at Saint-Gilles.

An ancient author of the history of that place speaks as follows:

> In the year 1095, Pope Urban, at the request of our abbot Pontius, dedicated with solemn rite, on 18 August, the basilica of La Chaise-Dieu, begun by blessed Robert and then completed and finished. Shortly afterward he made the monastery free and exempt from the jurisdiction of bishops, as is clear from the papal charter.

Geoffrey, prior of Vigeois, agrees.
