In his chronicle he says that in this year Urban consecrated the monastery of Saint Robert of La Chaise-Dieu in honor of Saints Agricola and Vitalis, whose relics Bishop Renco of Auvergne had once placed there, on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of September.

In an old notice appended to the papal bull mentioned shortly afterward, certain bishops who attended the pontiff at this solemnity are named. As it reads there:

> The solemnity of this dedication took place on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of September, in the presence of and with the cooperation of the lord Pope Urban and the reverend bishops Hugh of Lyon, Aldebert of Bourges, Amatus of Bordeaux, Durand of Auvergne, Hugh of Grenoble, Gerald of Cahors, John of Porto, Daibert of Pisa, and Bruno of Signi.

In memory of this benefaction, Urban’s name became famous not only in the principal monastery of La Chaise-Dieu but also in the cells subject to it, as is clear from the necrology of Saint Robert of Cornillon near Grenoble.

Besides the bull mentioned above, Urban granted another privilege to the same monastery, one recorded here, which may also have been issued on the occasion of this dedication. Our copy bears no chronological note, which is why it seemed appropriate to mention it here.

It lists the principal monasteries then subject to La Chaise-Dieu and confirms its possessions. The pontiff also forbids the abbot of that place to make a profession of subjection to anyone, while preserving the reverence owed to the bishop of Auvergne.

On the very day on which the church of La Chaise-Dieu was consecrated, Urban, at the request of Florentia, abbess of the nunnery of Blasiliacum, confirmed the privileges of that place and, following the example of his predecessors, received under the special protection of the Apostolic See the monastery itself, which had been offered by Countess Ermengarde, its founder, to Saint Peter.

[Col. 0157D]

The pontiff says nothing, however, about the complaints that the nuns and clerics of that place had brought before him against the monks of La Chaise-Dieu. They claimed that the monks had forcibly seized and retained the church of Saints Stephen and Leo, which belonged to the monastery of Blasiliacum.

The letter of the people of Blasiliacum written on this occasion will be included among Urban’s letters. It will be followed by the privilege itself, which Philip, archbishop of Bourges, translated into French and confirmed by his own testimony on the Thursday of Holy Week in the year 1243, after examining it and recognizing it as genuine.

## CXCIII. Whether Urban visited the abbey of Rotman.

It is uncertain where Urban first turned after the dedication of La Chaise-Dieu, as he proceeded toward the furthest borders of Occitania and Provence.

We do have before us a privilege granted on the tenth day before the Kalends of September of this year to the canons of the cathedral church of Cahors, who had recently adopted the regular life. But since the commonly circulated copy says that it was issued at Rome—which is entirely impossible—it can contribute almost no clarification, unless “at Rome” should be read as “at Romans,” a place in the Dauphiné, in the diocese of Vienne, where there was a distinguished abbey and where, as we have said, the pontiff had decided to settle the dispute over the village of Salmoriacum.

This restoration would be more attractive if the bull had been issued at the beginning of this month, when it is certain, as we have proved, that Urban visited Valence, from which city the monastery of Romans is not far distant.

Nevertheless, it seemed appropriate to assign that bull here. Like many others, it gives the year 1096, reckoning the beginning of that year from the preceding March. It is certain from other indications that it belongs to the present year and cannot belong to the following one.

## CXCIV. He passes through Nîmes. He stays at Saint-Gilles. The privilege of La Chaise-Dieu.

Toward the end of August the pontiff seems to have visited Nîmes. Although he dedicated the church of that city only in the following year, as we shall show there, the author of the Chronicle of Maillezais wrote that Urban then—that is, in the year 1096—returned to Nîmes. This sufficiently suggests that he had already visited the city.

It is certain that this year the pontiff celebrated the feast of Saint Giles, on the first day of September, in the monastery of that saint at Flaviana Valley, which belonged to the diocese of Nîmes.

[Col. 0158C]

The pontiff himself attests this in a privilege that he granted shortly afterward to Odilo, abbot of that place. He says that, burning with devotion toward blessed Giles, he restrained the bishop of Nîmes, who was hostile to the monks of that place.

He was still there on 7 September, when he granted La Chaise-Dieu a privilege. In it, as we have just said, he confirmed another privilege already granted to the same place, adding several prerogatives in favor of the basilica that he had recently consecrated.

## CXCV. He blesses the site of a monastery at Tarascon.

From there Urban passed through Tarascon, a town in Provence situated on the left bank of the Rhône, a little below Avignon. He sprinkled with holy water and blessed with his own hand a certain site that Countess Stephanie had given to the monastery of Saint Victor of Marseille for the construction of a church.

Three cardinals and the abbots of Saint Victor and Montmajour assisted him. On 11 September he erected a cross there and granted an indulgence to those who contributed anything toward the construction of the church, so that a monastery in honor of Saint Nicholas, with a cemetery, might be established there.

The priory of Saint Nicholas mentioned here still exists near Tarascon and remains subject to Saint Victor of Marseille.

## CXCVI. At Avignon he grants a privilege to Saint-Gilles.

On the following day, 12 September, Urban granted at Avignon the privilege mentioned above to the monastery of Saint-Gilles, where he had been staying.

[Col. 0159A]

By this charter the pontiff confirmed to Abbot Odilo and his monks the abbey of Saint Eusebius and their other possessions. He also wished them to be held under the special protection of the Apostolic See and guarded like the pupil of his eye.

## CXCVII. At Tricastin he grants privileges to the canons of Saint-Ruf.

On the 19th of the same month, at Tricastin, a city of Saint Paul in the Dauphiné, the pontiff issued a bull in favor of Albert—or rather Arbert—abbot of Saint-Ruf and of its canons.

Their monastery, the head of the congregation of that name, was then situated near the walls of Avignon. Later, because of the disasters inflicted by the Albigensians, it was transferred to the suburb of Valence and finally, in the sixteenth century, into that city itself.

In this charter Urban lists the churches subject to Saint-Ruf and confirms them, together with its other possessions, while preserving the canonical reverence owed to the bishop of Avignon.

[Col. 0159B]

We also possess, from a manuscript codex, another rescript of Urban addressed to Albert, likewise abbot of Saint-Ruf, but without any chronological note. It contains splendid praise of the canonical life, precisely the sort found throughout the other letters and bulls addressed to regular canons.

But in volume IV of *Gallia Christiana*, in the catalogue of the abbots of Saint-Ruf, the Sammarthani distinguish Arbert and Adelbert as though they had been two different abbots. They attribute to the former the privilege first mentioned by us and reproduce most of it. Concerning Adelbert they say nothing except that Urban II sent him a rescript which, they report, is preserved in the archives of the abbey.

I would be mistaken if the same man were not the recipient of both of Urban’s rescripts, although his name, as often happens, may have been written differently by different authors. In any event, it is of little importance to us.

Besides these documents, two canons of nearly the same subject occur in Ivo, Gratian, and other collectors of decretals. The first, at Gratian, cause 19, question 2, chapter 2, is inscribed, “There are two,” and is attributed to the chapter of Saint Rufus, or Rufinus, although it is not found in Urban’s letters. The other, in the same cause, question 3, chapter 3, begins, “We decree to the abbot of Saint Rufinus,” and is excerpted from the second of the privileges mentioned above. It is preceded by another canon on the same subject, but without any attribution.

## CXCVIII. The origin of the monastery and order of Saint Anthony.

Authors commonly report that Urban at that time provided the occasion for founding the celebrated monastery of Saint Anthony. For, as they say, while he was travelling through the province of Vienne [Col. 0159D] that year, he heard of a certain nobleman, called Guido by some and Guigo Desiderius by others, who was accustomed to carry with him, on journeys in various directions, the body of Saint Anthony, that great patriarch of the hermits. He had received it from his ancestors after it had been brought from Constantinople some years earlier. The pope is said to have taken this very badly and, under threat of anathema, forbidden that it should be done thereafter; he ordered that such venerable relics be deposited in some church chosen by Guido himself, under the custody of monks living properly.

Guigo obeyed Urban’s commands and, having summoned monks from Montmajour near Arles, deposited the sacred body in the village called Mota Desiderii [Col. 0160A] and entrusted it to them. Later, when the disease commonly called Saint Anthony’s Fire was raging, a hospice was added to the monastery, where the poor arriving from every direction could be received; several brothers were assigned to serve them. At first these men obeyed the monks for some time, but afterward, having become arrogant because of the immense alms being distributed, they refused to remain subject to them. Serious quarrels and dissensions arose between the two groups. As these increased day by day, matters reached the point that the hospital brothers, having grown more powerful and completely shaken off the monks’ yoke, began to act independently, and eventually developed into a distinguished order that still exists today. This, they say, was the origin of the abbey and order of Saint Anthony. But let us follow the sequence of the pope’s journey.

## CXCIX. Urban Grants Privileges at Mâcon

It is probable that Urban passed through Vienne and Lyons, although we cannot prove this by any documents. We infer, however, from an old notice of a privilege that he was at Mâcon on 17 October. On that very day—and, indeed, in the year 1096 rather than 1095, as most documents of that period customarily date it—he granted a privilege to the monastery of the regular canons of Saint Peter situated near that city, and immediately afterward departed for Cluny. I was unable to find a copy of this privilege; therefore I thought it appropriate to report in its place the notice of it found in the Appendix, taken from an old manuscript codex and transmitted by Severtius.

## CC. Urban Grants a Privilege to the Bishop of Mâcon at Cluny. He Dedicates an Altar

[Col. 0160C] The following day, 18 October, while the pontiff was at Cluny, Landric, bishop of Mâcon, who had doubtless followed him, requested the protection of the Apostolic See. Urban readily granted it by issuing a bull confirming to him and his successors all the possessions and privileges of the Church of Mâcon. The pontiff also forbade anyone to dare inflict any violence upon the clerics of that Church, its cloister, or its houses. The document was issued on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of November.

When Urban arrived at Cluny, Saint Hugh, the abbot of that place, had already been engaged for seven years in constructing a magnificent basilica, which he wished to have dedicated by the pontiff himself. Since the building was still far too incomplete, the holy abbot arranged matters so that at least the high altar would, upon the pope’s arrival, be in a condition to be consecrated by him. This was in fact done on 25 October. The author of the *Chronicle of Cluny* mentions this dedication under the year 1095, as does Orderic Vitalis at the beginning of Book IX, where he says that Urban dedicated many holy basilicas in Gaul, elevating them through privileges of the Apostolic See. He then expressly praises the consecration by Urban of the altar of Saint Peter at the monastery of Cluny.

What this author and others commonly praised on such occasions in a single word is described at greater length in an old document published under the title “The Liberty of the Place of Cluny” in the *Cluniac Library*. There it is said that not only the high altar but also the morning altar was consecrated by Urban, while three other altars were consecrated by three other bishops, namely Hugh of Lyons, Daibert of Pisa, and Bruno of Signia. A sufficiently lengthy speech is then reported, which the pontiff is said to have delivered during the solemnities of the Mass and consecration; in it he defined the boundaries of the monastery’s jurisdiction. [Col. 0160D]

In addition, we find in an ancient manuscript codex another notice of the same event. After listing the many benefits Urban had conferred upon the monastery of Cluny, it says that Saint Hugh decreed that, as long as the pontiff lived, a special commemoration of him should be made during the general Mass; and that after his death, besides the customary suffrages for each of the monks of that place, the anniversary of his deposition should be solemnly celebrated in perpetuity.

The boundaries of the Cluniac *ban* or jurisdiction established by Urban were subsequently confirmed by the pontiffs, especially Innocent II, who on this very day—the day on which Urban had consecrated the high altar—dedicated the basilica itself, as is evident from the diplomas of that pope and others published in the *Cluniac Library*. Hence the memory of both dedications is commemorated together in several ancient Martyrologies. This latter dedication took place in 1130, not in the following year, as the Cluniac chronicler mistakenly states. [Col. 0161A]

Urban also endeavored to assert not only the rights and prerogatives of the principal monastery at Cluny but also those of the other houses belonging to it, as is clear from many documents found here and there. In this connection his bull issued in the eighth year of his pontificate—that is, the present year—is commended; in it he confirms the rights and exemption of the monastery of La Charité of Blessed Mary above the Loire. But the bull itself has disappeared. We owe our knowledge of it to the *Acts of the Controversy* that arose in 1220, under Roland, abbot of Cluny, on the occasion of the election of the prior of La Charité. [Col. 0161C]

## CCI. Whether He Held a Council at Rheims. He Dedicates the Church of Dol

If we are to believe André Chesne, Urban held a council at Rheims in October of this year. There he confirmed the anathema previously pronounced against King Philip, decreed a holy expedition against the infidels, and established that henceforth everyone should observe a fast on the vigil of the Assumption of the Virgin Mary, Mother of God. Finally, he summoned another council to be held at Clermont in the following month. [Col. 0161D] This is what Chesne says in his published *History of the Roman Pontiffs of Gaul*.

But how far this truly learned man departed from the truth is shown not only by the silence of other ancient and modern authors, but also by the sequence of Urban’s journeys and by all the documents of his period that we have produced. These prove sufficiently that no synod was held at Rheims at that time. Indeed, Raynold, then metropolitan of Rheims, invited his suffragans to the council of Clermont at Urban’s command. He says in the letter already mentioned to Lambert that he had withdrawn the provincial council which he had summoned to be held at the beginning of November for this reason. The pontiff himself then warned Lambert by a special letter [Col. 0162A] to be prepared to defend at the council of Clermont the recent restoration of his Church, since men from Cambrai would be present to contest it.

Finally, in the *Deeds of Lambert*, where the events of this year are related in continuous sequence, and where the journey of the bishops of the province of Rheims to the synod of Clermont is described carefully and individually, there is no mention whatsoever of this synod. It must therefore rightly be believed to be fictitious.

Nor is what Souchet, in his notes to Ivo’s Letter 78, and Robert, following Amalric of Béziers in the old *Gallia Christiana*, say any more certain—namely, that Urban dedicated the church of the abbey of Dol near Bourges in this year. The sequence of the papal journey scarcely allows this; indeed, the dedication is said in the *Chronicle of Tours* to have been performed by Paschal II, Urban’s successor. [Col. 0162B]

## CCII. He Transfers the Body of Saint Majolus at Souvigny. He Grants a Privilege at Montluçon

Urban therefore left Cluny and came to Souvigny, near the Bourbon town of Moulins. There he transferred the body of Saint Majolus to a more suitable place and made Archimbald swear over the tomb of his father, Archimbald IV, that throughout his life he would preserve intact the possessions which his father and ancestors had bestowed upon the monastery.

The pontiff himself attests to this in a bull which he granted to the monks of that place at Montluçon on the Ides of November. In it he declares that, in the presence of Durand, bishop of Clermont, he had taken the monastery of Souvigny under the special protection of the Apostolic See and confirmed its possessions, which he lists individually. [Col. 0162C] Joellus, archbishop of Rheims, declared in a public document, sealed with his own seal, that in 1245, at the request of the monks of Souvigny, he had examined and compared this bull and found it complete and unaltered.

We learn from an old document in the Souvigny cartulary that the pontiff spent nearly eight days in that place. The document was composed on the occasion of the Bourbon prince Archimbald, mentioned above, who was attempting to renew the evil customs imposed by his father and relaxed by that same father when he was near death.

“I quote the words of the charter itself:

“‘At the same time, when the lord Pope Urban II had come into Gaul for certain purposes beneficial to the holy Church, and was staying at Souvigny for nearly eight days, he sat one day in the chapter-house. Then the whole community of the brothers sitting around him fell at his feet and began to implore his help concerning the evils which they had long endured.

“‘The lord pope most graciously received their petition. On the following day, when the aforesaid Archimbald asked him to absolve his father’s soul by apostolic authority, after completing the absolution, and before Archimbald himself departed from him—indeed, before he removed his feet from the tomb—the prince, admonished by the pope, abandoned all the aforementioned evil customs which he had unjustly sought to enforce. And, so that he might better remember his promise, he received from that same pope the kiss of peace.’”

But he soon forgot his promise and renewed those practices. Consequently, the matter was brought before the council of Clermont, as we shall relate below. [Col. 0162D]

## CCIII. Urban Arrives at Clermont

[Col. 0163A]

After travelling through these provinces, Urban arrived at Clermont on 14 November or the following day, while bishops from various regions of the Christian world were hastening there. Among them was Lambert of Arras, who had left his city on 28 October and passed through Provins in the Sénonais. After leaving that town on the eighth day before the Ides of November, he was captured by a certain knight, Guarnerius, from the castle of Pont.

When the pontiff was informed of this, he immediately rebuked Guarnerius by letter for so great an act of audacity. At the same time he wrote another letter to Richerius, archbishop of Sens, instructing him to warn the same knight and, if he did not repent, to place him under excommunication together with his lord in that place. [Col. 0163B] Before Guarnerius received these letters, however, he had already been reproved by his brother Philip, bishop of Troyes, and had made satisfaction to Lambert. Having been reconciled with Lambert, he honorably escorted him as far as Auxerre, where Lambert arrived on the fifth day before the Ides of the same month.

On account of this deed, Canon 32 of the council of Clermont seems to have been composed, as we shall say in its proper place. At Auxerre Lambert found, besides Richerius of Sens, his provincial and neighboring bishops Gervin of Amiens and Gerard of Thérouanne. With them he completed the remainder of his journey and arrived at Clermont on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of December, which was a Sunday. There the pontiff kindly received him with the holy kiss, and Lambert received the apostolic blessing.

## CCIV. Other Bishops and Others Assemble at Clermont

[Col. 0163C]

When everything had been arranged for the celebration of the council—for Urban had sent Henry the Sicilian ahead long before, the man who, after many changes of fortune, eventually became cardinal and patriarch of Antioch—archbishops, bishops, abbots, and illustrious men of nearly every order, almost beyond number, assembled with Pope Urban at Clermont on the appointed day from nearly all parts of Europe.

The author of the *Chronicle of Saint Vannes of Verdun*, in Volume I of Labbe’s *Library*, says that bishops from almost the entire world had gathered for that council, except the Lotharingians, Germans, and Hungarians. Robert, however, writes in Book I of his *History of Jerusalem* that it was a most celebrated assembly of French and German bishops and princes.

The Germans—some of whom were especially devoted to Urban—may not have assembled there because only a few months earlier, as we have seen, they had attended the council of Piacenza. Among the Lotharingians, if we are to believe Meurisse and the Sammarthani, there were present Poppo, bishop of Metz, and Pibo of Toul. Pibo, if we believe P. Benedict, a Capuchin and author of the new *History of Toul*, returned to his diocese from the council, which he had attended with Renard, count of Toul, and his brother Peter, and brought with him many nobles of that region to undertake the holy expedition.

Richerius, bishop of Verdun, who shortly before that time had renounced Henry’s party and been consecrated by Hugh of Lyons, sent gifts and envoys to Urban while the pope was at Clermont, as Laurence of Liège testifies in his *History of the Bishops of Verdun*. [Col. 0164A] No bishop from England is ever recorded as having come there. Nevertheless, the monk Boso, who later became abbot of Bec, was sent by Anselm, archbishop of Canterbury, and attended there in his name, as we learn from Boso’s Life.

## CCV. Their Number

Bertold reports that thirteen archbishops with their suffragans assembled for this synod, which he calls general, and that 205 pastoral staffs were recorded there. Orderic Vitalis says at the beginning of Book IX that Urban gathered all the bishops of Gaul and Spain at Clermont and held a great council there. He says that thirteen archbishops, 225 bishops, and a multitude of abbots and other persons attended, to whom the care of the holy Churches had been entrusted.

The author of the *Deeds of Bishop Lambert of Arras* agrees. He says that the same number of archbishops and bishops, together with the Roman cardinals, assembled for this general council, and that in addition there were more than ninety abbots, besides respectable and religious clerics and laymen from various regions and provinces. He repeats the same figure later, except that in some printed and manuscript copies he gives fourteen archbishops. One of our codices, and the older one at that, gives only thirteen.

In an old notice of the same council preserved by Labbe from a codex of Cencius Camerarius, twelve archbishops, eighty bishops, and countless abbots are said to have sat with Urban. More clearly, the *Chronicle of Saint Peter Vivus of Sens* says that 300 bishops and abbots were present at the council. The recent author of the *Deeds of God through the Franks* gives 310 bishops and abbots altogether.

Finally, Guibert says that the council was all the more celebrated because it was desirable to see the face and hear the words of a person so eminent and extraordinary—meaning Urban. He then adds:

“There, besides the ranks of bishops and abbots, whom some had counted at approximately four hundred by their prominent staffs, the learning of all France and of the adjoining counties flowed together.”

Nor is it surprising that the French hastened with such enthusiasm to so illustrious and extraordinary an assembly. [Col. 0164D] For, in addition to their natural ardor, King Philip, in order to comply with Urban’s wishes, had granted all the bishops and abbots of his kingdom permission to travel there in complete safety. The pontiff himself attested this in the letter to Guarnerius mentioned above.

Since no accurately written Acts of this council survive, it is not surprising that different authors sometimes assigned different numbers to the bishops who attended it. Those who assigned a smaller number than the others seem to have done so because, as all the prelates were not present at every session, they counted only those who attended a particular session. This happens frequently in documents composed especially for some particular matter.

Thus Urban himself, in the decree confirming the primacy of Lyons, says that besides Richerius, archbishop of Sens, twelve archbishops with eighty bishops and more than ninety abbots were present at that decision. More relevant still is the fact that the author of the *Deeds of the Bishops of Tours and the Abbots of Marmoutier* lists only a few prelates who subscribed the privilege of that monastery at the council, although he had previously observed that the council itself was held in the presence of nearly five hundred Fathers. [Col. 0165A]

## CCVI. The Sees and Names of Some Participants. The Pope’s Officials

These remarks concern the number of bishops who assembled at the synod of Clermont. But who they were and of what sees they were bishops, no one, I think, would wish to guess in the absence of reliable documents. Nevertheless, we thought it worthwhile to list some whom we have encountered here and there while examining the records of those times; others may perhaps be identified by others.

Some of them were cardinals from the pontiff’s entourage, that is, his officials: namely, John, bishop of Porto; Bruno of Signia; Walter, or Gualterus, of Alba, or rather of Albano, who shortly before had been papal legate in England; and Daimbert, archbishop of Pisa.

The book *On the Deeds of the Archbishops of Tours*, mentioned above, adds Rangerius, archbishop of Reggio; Richard, perhaps the man who was then abbot of Saint Victor and a cardinal, or perhaps the archdeacon of Metz whom we shall mention below from Meurisse; John Galtellus, or rather Gaetanus, the pontiff’s chancellor; Gregory of Pavia, a deacon; and Hugh of Verdun, a deacon and officials of the Roman Church. Gregory mentioned here is, unless I am mistaken, the cardinal of that name who, according to Robert in his *History of the Holy Expedition*, made a confession in the council on behalf of everyone after Urban’s speech and obtained absolution.

Elsewhere I find the cardinals Teuso and Ranchio, to whom we should add, among the pope’s officials, Milo, formerly a monk of Saint-Albin and later his legate, and Henry the Sicilian, already mentioned above. While Urban was still at Piacenza, he had sent Henry ahead into Gaul to make the necessary arrangements for the synod. [Col. 0165D]

Besides these men—if indeed he was not one of them—Meurisse, in his *History of the Bishops of Metz*, mentions Richard, archdeacon of Metz. He says that Richard, once expelled by Emperor Henry together with his bishop Herimann, and given the bishopric of Albano by Gregory VII, was made by Urban at this synod a cardinal and legate to Lotharingia and Germany.

Ughelli does indeed list Richard in the catalogue of the bishops of Albano, but says that Urban made him cardinal priest and Paschal II made him bishop; he confuses him with Richard, abbot of Marseille. Perhaps Ughelli, like Meurisse, has combined different persons and different periods. For at that time it was Walter, not Richard, who was bishop of Albano. [Col. 0166A]

Besides the archbishops of Pisa and Reggio mentioned above, the archbishops were Hugh of Lyons and Amatus of Bordeaux, both papal vicars in Gaul; Bernard of Toledo, himself Urban’s vicar in Spain; and the following others: Raynold of Rheims, Adebert of Bourges, Rodulf of Tours, Richerius of Sens, Dalmatius of Narbonne, Guido of Vienne, Berengar of Tarragona, and [Peter] of Aix, or perhaps of Aix-en-Provence.

Some, as we have already observed, add Anselm of Milan, though I would not dare assert that this is true. Roland of Dol, who was called an archbishop on account of the honor of the pallium, does not seem to have held a place among the metropolitans.

Among the bishops, from the province of Rheims, I find Lambert of Arras, Gerard of Thérouanne, Gervin of Amiens, Roger of Beauvais, Letald of Senlis, Gualcher of Cambrai, and the other suffragans of that metropolitan see, as the author of the *Deeds of Lambert* relates. The pontiff himself implies this in the letter to the people of Cambrai written on the day after the council was dissolved. Among them was certainly Hugh of Soissons, as Dormasius, the historian of Soissons, observes. [Col. 0166B]

We must also add Hilgodus, formerly bishop of that Church, who had then resigned his see and was living at Marmoutier. He was the very man whom some later claimed, after being elected abbot, ought to be blessed again; Ivo opposed this in Letter 88 to Paschal II, written on that subject.

From the province of Trier, as we have already observed, Poppo of Metz and Pibo of Toul are said to have attended, together with an envoy of Richerius, bishop of Verdun. From the province of Lyons came Agano of Autun and Landric of Mâcon. From Rouen came Odo of Bayeux, Gislebert of Évreux, and Serlo of Sées, in their own names and in those of other prelates of the same province whose envoys they were, as Orderic relates in Book IX.

From Tours, or the third province of Lyons, came Hoel of Le Mans, Geoffrey of Angers, Benedict of Nantes, and Roland of Dol, who sought a place among the metropolitans. From Sens, or the fourth province of Lyons, came Ivo of Chartres, John of Orléans, and the other suffragans of that province, according to Urban’s bull concerning the primacy of Lyons.

From Vienne came Hugh of Grenoble and Guntard of Valence. From Arles came Desiderius of Cavaillon, who died at the time of the council, and William of Orange, who was attached as a companion to Adhemar of Le Puy, leader of the holy expedition.

From Bourges came Durand of Clermont, to whom, after his death, William was appointed as successor—indeed, some say that Urban himself consecrated him—Humbald of Limoges, and Adhemar of Le Puy, or Anicium, who was appointed leader or standard-bearer of the crusaders.

From Bordeaux came the other Adhemar of Angoulême, Peter of Poitiers, Ramnulf of Saintes, Raynold of Périgueux, who is said to have died a martyr in the holy expedition, and Raymond of Rodez. From Narbonne came Geoffrey of Maguelonne, Bertrand of Nîmes, and, according to some, Bertrand of Lodève, who is said to have died in the holy expedition in 1099. [Col. 0167A]

From Spain came Dalmatius of Iria, or Compostela, and Peter of Pamplona. Papebrochius, in his *Propylaeum*, or *Essay toward a Catalogue of the Roman Pontiffs*, says of Urban II that Saint Olegarius of Barcelona was the only bishop from Spain to attend this council of Clermont and that he carried its Acts back to Barcelona. But the learned man is mistaken. He carelessly applied to Urban’s council what is said in the Life of that saint, under 3 March, about another council of Clermont held under Pope Innocent II. This is clear from the very passage of Olegarius’s Life that he cites, namely Chapter 4.

Among the abbots who attended the same council, we gather the following from various records: Richard of Saint Victor of Marseille, who was a cardinal of the Roman Church; Gervin, abbot of Centula and at the same time bishop of Amiens, who was compelled at the council to resign the abbey; Guibert of Saint-Germain of Auxerre, deprived either at this synod or certainly at that of Nîmes the following year; and Robert, abbot of the chief monastery of Saint-Remi at Rheims and the first author of the *History of Jerusalem*, who was himself later compelled to resign the government of his monastery.

Lambert, abbot of Saint-Bertin, was also present, according to the *History of the Morini*. So was Lanzo of Saint Vincent of Metz, to whom Urban granted a privilege the following year. Baldric, then abbot of Bourgueil and later bishop of Dol, was present as well; he wrote the *History of the Jerusalem Expedition* and other works. Hugh of Cluny was also there, famous in his own right, as is shown, among other things, by the bull of Paschal addressed to him concerning the subjection of Saint Cyprian of Poitiers, which Souchet includes in his notes to the Life of Bernard of Tours.

There were also Bernard of Marmoutier and Stephen of Noyers from the diocese of Tours; Geoffrey of Vendôme, famous for his deeds and writings; Jarento of Saint-Bénigne of Dijon; and Guntard of Jumièges, who died near the end of the council, as Orderic Vitalis relates in Book X. The same author says in Book IV that Guntard had gone to the council with his fellow pastors of Normandy. From this it may be inferred that several abbots from the same province attended the synod, although their names have been lost. [Col. 0167B]

To these must be added Natalis, abbot of Saint Nicholas near Angers; William of Saint-Florent from the same diocese; Gausmar of Saint Peter of the German Island, or of Celle, near Troyes; Raynold of Saint Cyprian; Gervasius of Saint-Savin; and Peter of Charroux among the Poitevins; Peter of Aniane in the diocese of Maguelonne; Adhemar of Saint-Martial near Limoges; and from the same diocese Gerard of Uzerche; and Ansculf of Saint-Jean-d’Angély in the diocese of Saintes.

From Auvergne, in addition to Peter of Saint-Alyre of Clermont, there were Peter of Aurillac and Prultus of La Chaise-Dieu; the anonymous abbot of Saint-Symphorian of Thiers; and the dean of Saint Peter of Mauriac. To these should be joined Alodus, abbot of Saint-Vaast, and Hamericus, abbot of Aquicinctus, who are said in Lambert’s *Deeds* to have travelled to the council with their bishop Lambert of Arras and other leading men of the same diocese. [Col. 0168A]

Ermengaud, abbot of the monastery of Saint Michael at Chiusa, from the province of Turin, was also present, as we learn from a letter of his that we possess in manuscript. In it he asks Ramnulf, bishop of Saintes, to settle the dispute concerning the Church of Vallis which he had with the abbot of Saint-Jean-d’Angély, as Ramnulf had promised him at the council of Clermont.

## CCVII. The Council Begins

After bishops from every quarter had assembled, Urban began the council on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of December, the very eighth day of the feast of Saint Martin, as Bertold observes. Clarius agrees with him in the *Chronicle of Saint Peter Vivus of Sens*, as does the notice of the council itself extracted from the already mentioned codex of Camerarius. [Col. 0168B]

Urban himself had certainly announced in his letter to Lambert of Arras that the synod would be held on the octave of Saint Martin. That this means the actual eighth day is clear from Raynold of Rheims’s letter of invitation, written in Urban’s name to the same Lambert. It explicitly says that the council was to be held on the octave of Saint Martin, namely on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of December. The *Chronicle of Maillezais*, therefore, must be corrected, since it says that the council was convened on the third day before the Ides of November.

## CCVIII. The Death and Funeral of Durand, Bishop of Clermont

This great solemnity was somewhat disturbed by the death of Durand, bishop of the Auvergne city itself, which occurred on the first day of the council. Formerly abbot of La Chaise-Dieu, he was governing the Church of Clermont when the pontiff came there to celebrate the council. He had exhausted himself in preparing what was necessary for fittingly receiving the pontiff and the other bishops. As a result, he contracted a severe illness, and when the pope arrived, his life was already almost despaired of.

Hugh of Flavigny, in his *Chronicle of Verdun*, says that Urban visited and absolved him while he was already drawing his final breath; on the following night—that is, the first day of the council—he surrendered his spirit to the Creator. [Col. 0168C]

The funeral arrangements were undertaken by Hugh, bishop of Grenoble; Jarento, abbot of Saint-Bénigne; and Pontius, abbot of La Chaise-Dieu. All three had lived a monastic life under him at La Chaise-Dieu. Never, it was said, had more distinguished funeral rites been seen. For, together with the Roman pontiff, so many bishops and illustrious men of every order from almost the entire Christian world appeared to have assembled for them.

Hugh of Flavigny described them briefly in the passage cited:

“‘He was washed and cared for with the greatest diligence by his sons—that is, by the abbot of Dijon, the abbot of La Chaise-Dieu, the bishop of Grenoble, and others. And thus, before the council began, while the whole world was hastening to his funeral, he was committed to the earth with glory by the pope himself and the bishops of the land; and William of Basia obtained his see, with the approval of the clergy and people and by command of the same apostolic lord.’”

Baldric, then abbot of Bourgueil, wrote two epitaphs for the same prelate. In them he testifies that his funeral was like a triumph and that he died thirteen days before December, in these verses: [Col. 0168D]

> God’s highest grace arranged his celebrated rite,  
> A funeral that took the likeness of a triumph.  
>   
> Urban, the pope, summoned the general synod,  
> And twice a hundred Fathers moved to do him honor.  
>   
> The third [day], which precedes the tenth light before December,  
> Took from him the light of this present life.

And in the other epitaph he writes, among other things:

> Say that his funeral resembled a triumph,  
> And that it displayed the signs of God’s providence;  
> Urban was present, surrounded by a hundred bishops,  
> While the number of abbots was even greater.

## CCIX. What Was Done at the Council of Clermont, and Why Its Canons Are Reported Differently by Different Authors

[Col. 0169B]

No one will deny that many matters, and matters of great importance, were handled at the council of Clermont. Yet it would be extremely difficult to examine them individually, since most of the records of that period have disappeared, while those that survive are scattered among various authors and do not always present events in the same way. Indeed, what is more remarkable, the canons of that council differ in different authors.

To prevent you from supposing that the surviving canons were fabricated by those authors, remember that one author reported certain canons and another different ones, omitting those which they did not consider relevant to themselves. Moreover, even the canons reproduced by all or most of them are not presented in the same order or in the same words, because those authors intended to report only their substance, not their actual wording. They should therefore be called abridgments or summaries of the canons rather than the canons of this council themselves.

Bertold presents three of the principal matters of the synod in a few words:

“In that synod,” he says, “the lord pope confirmed the same statutes that he had confirmed at the preceding synod of Piacenza. In addition, he excommunicated Philip, king of the Franks, because, having dismissed his own wife, he joined the wife of one of his soldiers to himself in marriage. There also he announced that another synod would be held at Tours in the third week of the following Lent.”

But Canon 5 from the manuscript codex of Cencius Camerarius expressly states that not only the decrees made at Piacenza, but also those established at the earlier synods of Melfi, Benevento, and Troia, were confirmed at Clermont. [Col. 0169D]

Lambert of Arras likewise implies, in a charter granting the priory of Ambrès to Walter, abbot of the Holy Trinity of Rouen, that some canons of earlier councils were read and confirmed at the same synod. In that charter he decreed that the monk placed in charge of that house, because he belonged to another diocese, should promise canonical obedience to him and his successors, “just as it is confirmed,” he says, “in the Council of Chalcedon, and renewed at Clermont by Urban II, of venerable and worthy memory.”

Some say that Fulk, count of Anjou, brought a lawsuit at that council against the king of the Franks over Bertrada, whom the king had taken from him; other authors are silent about this. But not only Bertold, but also Ivo of Chartres in Letter 211, William of Malmesbury, Sigebert, and many others repeatedly assert that King Philip was excommunicated there on account of that abduction. [Col. 0170A]

Some have therefore raised the question whether the kingdom of France was also placed under interdict at that time. They do so needlessly, since it is certain that excommunications of this kind never affected populations, and still less deprived them of anything due from their obedience or reverence toward kings. This is clear from the writings of Ivo and others of that period who attacked Philip’s adulterous marriage with particular fervor.

Urban did judge that, in order to remove so great a scandal from the Church, Philip should be deprived of communion and that he should be excluded from the solemnity of his coronation. At that time such a coronation was normally performed by the archbishop of Rheims, or, in his absence, by another bishop, on the principal feast days. Nor do Ivo and similar authors of that period mean anything else when they speak of deprivation or restoration of the crown.

## CCX. Collections of the Canons of the Council of Clermont

Among those who appear to have taken greater care than others in collecting the canons of Clermont, we must count the author of the codex of Lambert, bishop of Arras, who presents thirty-two canons of that council. Labbe added ten from an old parchment belonging to Pierre Pithou, nine from the codex of Cencius Camerarius, and thirteen from the Dionysian codex. These had been copied in French by Belleforest in Book IV of the *Annals of France* and translated into Latin by Serarius.

Twenty-five canons altogether are listed by Orderic Vitalis at the beginning of Book IX, and almost as many by William of Malmesbury and Matthew Paris, English authors. Besides all these, a number of others occur here and there in various authors cited on particular occasions. Since they concern the affairs of private churches or individuals, they are not included with the others. You will find all of them collected together among Urban’s letters.

## CCXI. What Was Established in Them. Benefices. Investitures. Truces
The pontiff was chiefly concerned, in drawing up the canons of this council, to devise suitable remedies against the vices that were then flourishing in the Church, especially in the Gallican Church—as Orderic Vitalis long ago observed in Book IX. Hence, in most of [Col. 0170D] those decrees, the abuses that were then commonly committed in obtaining or retaining ecclesiastical benefices are censured; accordingly, simoniacs, concubinarians, and illegitimate persons are excluded from them. Plurality of benefices and transfers from one to another are likewise forbidden. It is decreed that anyone wishing to attain some ecclesiastical dignity must have been advanced through the order appropriate to that rank; that no layman or cleric below the diaconate may be elevated to the episcopate; and that laymen must pay tithes and must not, after their death, seize as plunder the goods of churches or ecclesiastical persons. The times for fasts and ordinations are established.

Investitures are prohibited by the commonly circulated Canons 15 and 16, though with the qualification [Col. 0171A]—as Ivo interprets them, asserting that he heard it from Urban himself, in Letter 60 to Hugh, archbishop of Lyon—that the council excludes kings only from corporeal investiture, not from election, insofar as they are the head of the people, or from concession, and so forth. Since the kings of the Franks agreed with the pontiffs on this matter, no controversy over investitures disturbed the Gallican Church. But the following canon, directed against those who render liege fidelity to kings, never had any force in Gaul, as is clear from Ivo’s Letter 190 to Paschal II. Juretus, in his notes on that letter, and Peter de Marca, Book VIII of *On Concord*, chapter 21, discuss the matter.

Provision was also made at this council for public security, especially for those who, by their condition or nature, [Col. 0171B] were bound to abstain from all the tumult of arms. Hence, by the canon establishing certain days of truce, it was decreed that at all times monks, clerics, women, and those accompanying them should remain in peace. These truces later became famous, chiefly on the occasion of the holy expeditions, under the names of the Truce of God and the Peace of God. Among many other authors, the most illustrious Peter de Marca discusses them learnedly, as is his custom, in his notes on this canon. In other notes on this Council of Clermont he also has much to say about communion, confirmations, and so forth, as he does in the books *On Concord* and in the treatise *On Primacies*. It is not relevant to our purpose to discuss all these matters more fully here.

## CCXII. The canon concerning the redemption of altars. Disturbances arising from it. Abbot Goffridus of Vendôme vindicated.

[Col. 0171C]

It is remarkable that the canon concerning the redemption of altars, which is so frequently celebrated by authors, is absent from the commonly circulated collections of the canons of this synod. Yet, besides the copy of Cencius Camerarius preserved by Labbe in volume X of the *Councils*, and another from the monastery of Aniane preserved by Baluze in his notes on chapter 31 of Book VI of *On the Concord of the Priesthood and the Empire*, this canon is cited by Goffridus, abbot of Vendôme, in Book III, Letter 12 to Ulger, bishop of Angers, and by Pope Paschal II in letters to Ramnulfus, bishop of Saintes, and Ivo, bishop of Chartres, who had attended this council.

Perhaps the compilers of the canons omitted it because it is repeated in precisely the same words at the Council of Nîmes from this Council of Auvergne. Whatever the case, the learned Peter de Marca and Jacobus Sirmundus observe that the occasion for enacting this canon was the following. Since many pious men had previously bestowed upon monasteries churches founded by themselves, or churches in any way subject to their jurisdiction, the diocesan bishops had permitted this—for their consent was necessary for the transaction—on the condition that at fixed times, namely whenever the vicars, or, as they were called, the persons or priests who maintained the care of such parishes in the name of the abbot or monks, were changed, a definite sum of money should be paid to them. This payment was called the redemption of altars, and such altars were said to have been granted *under personal tenure*. Other altars [Col. 0172A], which owed no payment, were considered to be held impersonally.

But after some time pious and clear-sighted men observed that these payments could not be made without the stain of simony, as Ivo wrote in Letter 12 to Urban himself, the pontiff first at the Council of Auvergne, then at the Council of Nîmes, and finally other pontiffs after their example forbade that any money should thereafter be given to bishops for the redemption of altars. Yet, lest on this pretext bishops should attempt to take away and appropriate altars donated to monasteries—since they had given their consent only on the burden of receiving that payment—it was decreed at the council that monasteries which had possessed such altars or tithes for thirty years should be left in peaceful possession of them [Col. 0172B]. We learn that this was the intention of the council and of Urban himself from the pontiff’s letters on the matter to Ingelram, bishop of Laon, and also to the monks of Saint-Bertin.

But when the pontiff had declared that this decree was enacted without prejudice to the bishops’ annual census, which by ancient right they were accustomed to receive from the churches, or, as they called them, the altars, of their dioceses, certain bishops attempted on this pretext to add the sums they received at each change of the persons—as we have explained—for the redemption of altars to that old annual census which they were accustomed to receive under the name of synodals, visitation dues, procuration, or some other designation. In other words, they sought to increase the old obligation by adding a new payment [Col. 0172C]. But the abbots and monks protested.

There is no doubt that Goffridus of Vendôme’s Letter 12 of Book III to Ulger, bishop of Angers, and another letter of his to G., legate of the Apostolic See, Book I, Letter 27, belong to this dispute. Indeed, the pontiffs themselves undertook the monks’ protection in this matter, as is clear from one letter of Pope Paschal to Ivo, bishop of Chartres, and Ramnulfus, bishop of Saintes, and from another written on the same subject by Gaufridus, likewise bishop of Chartres and legate of the Apostolic See—drawn from Goffridus, Book I, Letter 27—to R., archdeacon, and Hu., dean of the Church of Angers. Baluze reproduced these letters in his notes on Book VIII, chapter 31, of *On the Concord of the Priesthood and the Empire*.

Therefore, so that nothing in this controversy may be confused, [Col. 0172D] one must carefully distinguish the exaction of a new census, or its addition to the old on the occasion of the redemption of altars, from the obligation of the old census. Everyone admitted, if I am not mistaken, that the old census of which we have just spoken was payable to the bishops. The dispute between certain bishops and abbots concerned whether, in place of the redemption of altars abolished by the synod, some new census ought or could be introduced, or the old one increased.

Certain prelates maintained this, while the abbots denied it—and rightly so, as is clear from the letters of Urban and Paschal cited above, in which the pontiffs took the monks’ side against the bishops. In fact, the only matter at issue between Goffridus, abbot of Vendôme, and Ulger, bishop of Angers, together with the other bishops, was the exaction of this new census [Col. 0173A]. Thus, although in the letter cited from Baluze’s edition Paschal admitted that some annual census was owed to the bishops, he nevertheless declared that the census which Ivo and Ramnulfus were attempting to extort—by attaching to the redemption of persons, under changed names, duplications incompatible with simplicity—was to be rejected everywhere.

Nor could this be foisted upon those bishops, since they themselves had attended the Council of Auvergne, as Paschal asserts there after Urban. Goffridus, moreover, nowhere undertook to attack the old census, nor did he ever maintain in any way that it had been prohibited at the Council of Auvergne. Rather, he rejected the census that Ulger was attempting to introduce anew.

Goffridus maintained, as he himself wrote in Book I, Letter 27 to Gaufridus, bishop of Chartres, that Urban’s decree at the Council of Auvergne against the simony of the redemption of altars—an abuse that had been called heretical depravity at that great council—would be annulled if what had previously been paid only once, through the vicars, were thereafter extorted by the bishops under the name of a newly instituted annual census. It made little difference for the creation of simony whether the money was paid less frequently, as had previously been the case, namely only when the persons changed, or more frequently, that is, every year, under another name.

Goffridus repeats much the same argument in Letter 12 of Book III, written to Ulger himself. Yet in these controversies the old census [Col. 0173C] owed to the bishops was never at issue. Hence the learned Baluze would seem unjustly to accuse Goffridus of rashness in his notes on Gratian, 1, question 3, *quaesitum*, as though that abbot had maliciously removed from the Council of Clermont’s canon a clause intended to preserve the bishops’ annual census, so that he might deny them every census whatsoever, whether the old synodal census—as Baluze himself calls it—or the new one.

For it is certain from both of Goffridus’s letters cited above—as, I believe, will also be evident to anyone who reads them attentively—that he spoke only of the new census which the bishops wished to introduce in place of the payment formerly made whenever the vicars changed. Thus the bishops against whom Goffridus was acting lost their case, and by the authority of the pontiffs that new census, which they had attempted to exact, was entirely abolished [Col. 0173D].

As for why the clause “without prejudice, of course, to the census,” and so forth, is absent from the Vendôme cartulary, it is useless to speculate, since there was never any dispute about it between Goffridus—or his successors—and the bishops. The people of Vendôme never claimed, on the authority of that canon, to be exempt from every census, but only from paying that new census which the bishops wished to introduce in place of the redemption of altars. In reality, their claim was correct.

Perhaps these words were not removed by the people of Vendôme, but were added by others in other manuscripts to make the canon easier to understand. Thus, in the manuscript of Saint-Aubin, someone added *synodal* after the word “census” [Col. 0174A], so that no shadow of difficulty would remain in the canon.

## CCXIII. Appendix to the canon concerning the redemption of altars

Canon 7 of the commonly circulated collections appears to be an appendix to the preceding canon concerning the redemption of altars. It decrees that altars which have been given to canons or monks through personal tenure should, after the death of the persons concerned, revert to the bishops, unless the bishops themselves confirm them to the monasteries by letters or privileges. The thirty-year possession prescribed in the canon concerning the redemption of altars, for securing the altars to the monasteries, is here invoked.

The provision that vicars instituted by monks in the parishes should receive the care of souls from the bishops, while the monks should render an account of temporal matters [Col. 0174B], presents no difficulty. If anyone wishes to know more about this matter, let him consult Baluze’s additions to chapter 31 of Book VI of *On the Concord of the Priesthood and the Empire* by the most illustrious Peter de Marca, as well as the other interpreters of canon law.

## CCXIV. Other decrees

Besides these canons, Goffridus, abbot of Vendôme, in Book II, Letters 29 and 30 to Gaufridus, bishop of Chartres, “praises the judgment delivered by Pope Urban at the Council of Auvergne, with all the bishops and abbots who were present praising it, that whoever had been dispossessed without summons and judgment should also be invested without summons and judgment, lest under cover of a summons and judgment there should be delay, and through the delay the dispossession should remain either prolonged [Col. 0174C] or perpetual.” Consult the notes on Ivo of Chartres’s Letter 172.

Ivo likewise praises another decree of the same council, by which it was enacted that anyone excommunicated by one bishop should also be excommunicated by the neighboring bishops. These observations concerning those canons seemed worth making. Those who desire more will find the published books *On the Decrees of the Councils* available to them. The most illustrious Peter de Marca, however, composed particular notes on the canons of Clermont in volume X of Labbe’s *Councils*; his book *On Primacies* is also relevant here.

## CCXV. Various cases treated at the Council of Clermont. The primacy of Lyon

Among the various cases discussed at the Council of Clermont, the celebrated one concerning the primacy of Lyon deserves attention. Gebuin, archbishop of Lyon, had obtained letters from Gregory VII confirming to him the primacy over the four provinces of Lyon—namely Lyon itself, Rouen, Tours, and Sens. The pope also sent other letters to the metropolitans of those provinces, ordering them to show the Church of Lyon the honor and reverence, as the pontiff put it, “established by our predecessors,” toward their churches.

Rodulfus of Tours immediately obeyed the papal letters, perhaps because he hoped that by this means, with the pope’s support, Dol and the other bishops of Brittany Minor, who had withdrawn themselves from obedience to his Church, might more easily be restored. Richerius of Sens, however, who himself claimed to possess the primacy by virtue of a privilege of John VIII, [Col. 0175A] utterly denied every form of subjection to the Church of Lyon.

The archbishop of Rouen followed his example; his province at that time was not subject to Frankish rule, and consequently Gregory’s decree was then of little benefit to Gebuin. But after Gebuin’s death Hugh was transferred from the see of Die to the Church of Lyon. Since he possessed the greatest authority by virtue of the vicariate of the Apostolic See entrusted to him, he left no stone unturned to assert the primacy of his see. Finding an excellent opportunity to accomplish this, he brought the case before the Council of Clermont, where it had already been debated in various lesser councils.

Richerius of Sens was summoned and was present. After various evasions, when he kept postponing his response from day to day, he lost the case on the sixth day. Two days later, while his suffragans were still promising obedience but he continued to refuse to do so, he was deprived of the use of the pallium and of jurisdiction over his suffragans until he obeyed the decree [Col. 0175B].

The same penalty was decreed against the archbishop of Rouen, who was not present at the council, unless within three months he promised in writing—if he could not do so orally—to submit to the primate of Lyon. In this way the primacy of Lyon prevailed over those churches. All these matters are explained more fully in Urban’s bull issued several days later on the subject.

## CCXVI. The dispute over the district of Salmoriacum

A controversy was then being pursued with no less contention, although it was not equally important, between Guido, metropolitan of Vienne, and Hugh, bishop of Grenoble, concerning the district of Salmoriacum, each claiming that it belonged to his own diocese. The case was decided in Hugh’s favor, as we have already said happened more than once; he was released from obedience to Guido, his metropolitan, until Guido obeyed the council’s decree, as the pontiff himself declared in a letter to Guigo, count, and to the clergy and people of Grenoble.

## CCXVII. Concerning the archbishopric of Dol

The case of the Church of Dol was also dealt with there. Its bishops were attempting to withdraw from subjection to the metropolitan Church of Tours. The matter had already been decided by Urban, as we have said. But because Rolland, bishop of Dol, had been given the pallium and was using the title and insignia of an archbishop, Rodulfus of Tours feared that his successors, too, might aspire to the same status.

He therefore arranged for Urban’s decree concerning the subjection of the Church of Dol to be confirmed at the council. Rolland was indeed compelled to obey Rodulfus, his metropolitan, as William, bishop of Poitiers, testifies; before becoming bishop, there is no doubt that William had attended that council in Rolland’s company. Martenius reproduced the document concerning this matter in his *New Collection of Ancient Writers*, p. 68.

## CCXVIII. Concerning the privileges of Marmoutier

The case, already debated in many assemblies, between the same Rodulfus and the monks of Marmoutier was also brought before this synod. Rodulfus wished them to be regarded as excommunicated. When the monks complained about this before the pontiff [Col. 0176A] and the other Fathers of the council, the archbishop denied that he had done so—if we trust the monk who wrote the *Book of the Deeds of the Archbishops and Abbots of Marmoutier*, edited by Bochelle—and replied that, if anything of the kind had ever escaped his lips, it had proceeded more from agitation and indignation of mind than from deliberation.

It therefore seemed appropriate, leaving aside the circumstances, to examine the case itself more carefully. After the matters concerning it that had been debated and decided in various councils and assemblies had been reviewed, the pontiff had the privilege he had granted to Marmoutier read aloud before the entire assembly. Then, after demonstrating in a few words that it contained nothing that could not have been granted by the Apostolic See, he confirmed and authorized it, in the name of God, blessed Peter the Apostle, all the apostles, and himself, with irrevocable force.

This decree was issued in the presence, on one side, of the archbishop and his clerics, and on the other of Bernard, abbot of Marmoutier, with his monks. Among the latter were Rangerius, cardinal and archbishop of Reggio; Gausmarus, abbot of Saint Peter of Troyes; Stephanus, abbot of Nogent; and Hilgodus, who had resigned the bishopric of Soissons.

From the Roman curia there were present the bishops of Porto, Pisa, and Segni; Richard, abbot of Saint-Victor of Marseille; and the cardinals Heron and Albert, together with others. Among the Gallican bishops were Hugh of Lyon, Amatus of Bordeaux, Rainoldus of Reims, Richerius of Sens, Rolland of Dol, and the archbishops of Narbonne and Aix. The bishops included Hoël of Le Mans and Gaufridus of Angers, both of whom, from the province of Tours, had labored greatly to settle this controversy, as Ivo reports in Letter 231.

From the other provinces there were Ivo of Chartres, John of Orléans, Roger of Beauvais, and the bishops of Nantes and Poitiers, together with other bishops, abbots, and nobles. They all acclaimed, “Fiat, fiat”—“Let it be done, let it be done”—in confirmation of the privilege.

## CCXIX. Other privileges affirmed. Vendôme. Arras

Other privileges of churches and monasteries were also approved at that council. Certainly, Goffridus, abbot of Vendôme, affirms this concerning the privilege of his monastery, as Urban himself does in various rescripts. In Book II, Letter 17 to Gaufridus, bishop of Chartres, Goffridus presents Urban’s decree on the matter, which will be published in its proper place among the letters of that pontiff [Col. 0176D].

At that time Eblo was also excommunicated, with the agreement of all the religious persons who were present, because he unjustly retained the Church of Oléron, which belonged to the people of Vendôme. We have William, duke of Aquitaine, as a witness to this, since he affirms it in his charter.

During the same synod Urban granted a notable privilege to the nunnery of Saint Mary of Saintes, which had been placed under the jurisdiction of the Roman Church by its very founders. The privilege, addressed to Arsende, the abbess [Col. 0177A], was dated 26 November in the year 1096, reckoned as 1095 according to the Pisan computation, as is the case with many other documents of that period.

The account given by the author of the *Deeds of Lambert* concerning the confirmation of the privilege, renewal, and restoration of the Church of Arras must be carefully noted. He reports that on 28 November, when the pontiff was just about to bring the council to an end, he ordered the document to be read before the entire council, in which fourteen archbishops, 225 bishops, and ninety or more abbots sat with the Roman cardinals, along with almost countless other persons.

It was read distinctly and clearly, and was attentively heard in profound silence by the entire assembly of the council, praised and confirmed [Col. 0177B] in the year of the Lord Christ 1095. It is therefore not surprising that from then onward the exemption of the Church of Arras from the Church of Cambrai always stood unshaken, since, after various provincial and Roman synods, it had finally been approved and confirmed by so many and such eminent prelates in a general council.

## CCXX. The schism in the Church of Cambrai suppressed

The cause of the people of Arras was aided by the schism that had arisen at this time in the Church of Cambrai, namely between Manasses, elected bishop after having been archdeacon of Reims, whom the archbishop of Reims, the metropolitan of the province, supported, and Gualcherius, who was said to have sought the see by simony.

Gualcherius had indeed come to the council, intending, as he claimed, to defend the rights of his Church against the people of Arras. But when his own case was examined, he was found unworthy of the episcopal rank. He therefore fled. After he had been summoned three times in vain to plead his case before the Fathers, and had failed to appear, he was deposed from every priestly and episcopal office, as is recorded in the *Deeds of Lambert*, while Manasses’s election was approved. He was threatened with excommunication if he should attempt thereafter to interfere in the governance of the Church of Cambrai, as Urban himself states in a letter on the matter to the people of Cambrai [Col. 0177C].

A certain unknown person had consecrated Gualcherius as bishop. But because he had obtained this election and the episcopal blessing of the Church of Cambrai by invasion, and through the hands of the excommunicated Emperor Henry, the holy council, having adjudicated the bishopric to Manasses, decreed that a bishop should be ordained for the Church of Cambrai after Gualcherius had been rejected [Col. 0177D].

Nevertheless, Manasses was not consecrated until near the end of the following year, because of the absence of the count of Flanders and the disturbances stirred up by Gualcherius himself. This is clear from a letter of Manasses, archbishop of Reims, to the people of Cambrai, although the day appointed for the consecration had been set for the octave of Pentecost, as we learn from another letter of the same metropolitan inviting Lambert, bishop of Arras, to attend.

Manasses was later succeeded by Odo, formerly abbot of Saint Martin of Tournai, who was also ordained by Manasses, the metropolitan, with Lambert of Arras and other bishops of the province assisting him. Meanwhile Gualcherius, aided by Emperor Henry and by the countess of Mons, who favored him against the legitimate bishops, continued to foster the schism in that Church. We learn this from the treatise *On the Restoration of Saint Martin of Tournai* in volume I of the *Spicilegium*, and from various letters reproduced in volume V of Baluze’s *Miscellanies*.

These disturbances gave the Sammarthani an opportunity to err in *Gallia Christiana*, where they admitted two Manasses and two Gualcherii at this time, on account of the various documents in which Manasses, then Gualcherius, then Manasses again, and again Gualcherius are mentioned.

## CCXXI. Gervinus, bishop of Amiens, deprived of the abbey of Centula

At that time Gervinus governed the Church of Amiens in the same province of Reims. He had become abbot of Centula after having been a monk at Saint-Remi in Reims, and had obtained this office not without suspicion of simony [Col. 0178B]. Nevertheless, once cleansed of that fault, as we said above in sections 114 and 134, he retained both the abbey and the bishopric, to the great detriment of the monastery, whose possessions he was wasting.

Since there was no hope of improvement, the brothers of Centula sought counsel from the Church of Reims. They were advised to disclose the desolation of the place to Pope Urban, who at that time was about to hold a council at Clermont, and to implore his merciful favor.

Their case indeed prospered. For while presiding at the council, the pontiff pronounced sentence against Gervinus and deprived him of the abbatial staff and of the monks’ governance. This was doubtless the reason for the enactment of Canon 4, reported by Orderic and other authors [Col. 0178C], which forbids anyone to be both bishop and abbot.

Hariulfus, a native author, reports the sentence pronounced by the pontiff against Gervinus in the *Centulian Chronicle* in volume IV of the *Spicilegium*. It reads as follows:

> “You have treated the abbey of Saint Richarius, once noble and wealthy, so disastrously that you stripped its church of its ornaments and exiled many monks who resisted your vices. You therefore deserved to lose entirely every grace of ecclesiastical dignity, as a slaughterer of Christ’s sheep and a destroyer of the holy Church. But, lest we seem to strike you with a double punishment, be content with the bishopric of Amiens, which you acquired with such harshness. Let the monks of Saint Richarius have the freedom to choose an abbot whom you must presume in no way to oppose. In the power of the Holy Spirit, we command you to observe this.”

Gervinus therefore returned to his own see, deprived of the abbey of Centula. A few years later he was also compelled to resign the bishopric and withdrew to Marmoutier, where he subsequently died. In his place, after the see had been vacant for nearly two years, the holy Godefridus was appointed at the Council of Troyes in 1095. He had previously been abbot of the monastery of Saint-Quentin near Péronne, as Guibert of Nogent reports in Book II, chapter 2, of his *Life*.

## CCXXII. The union of the monasteries of Figeac and Conques confirmed

At the same Council of Clermont the union of the monasteries of Conques and Figeac under a single [Col. 0179A] abbot was confirmed. Because the monks of Conques had elected an abbot of their own contrary to that arrangement, the Fathers of the council deprived him of his office.

But since this arrangement became a perpetual source of disputes, it was changed at the Council of Nîmes in the following year, as we shall relate there.

## CCXXIII. The presumption of the abbot of Aniane restrained

Bertrand, bishop of Maguelonne, complained before the Fathers of the synod, as Gariet reports in his *History of the Bishops of that Church*, against Peter, abbot of Aniane. He alleged that Peter, disregarding the diocesan bishop himself, invited foreign bishops to consecrate churches and perform other pontifical functions in his monastery. He even absolved excommunicated persons on his own authority and dared other things [Col. 0179B] against the rights of the Church of Maguelonne.

The pontiff restrained this presumption, while preserving the privileges of the monastery of Aniane, and confirmed the judgment that Alexander II had previously rendered in a similar case.

## CCXXIV. Various other cases of lesser importance

Many other controversies were brought before the Council of Clermont, but the ancient authors did not consider them important enough to report, or at least they are not matters that ought to be set out more fully here.

Among them was the complaint of the canons of Saint Stephen of Toulouse, who are said to have reclaimed from the Cluniacs the Church of Saint Mary, which they claimed belonged to their jurisdiction. There were also various disputes between Hugh, abbot of Cluny, and Pontius, abbot of La Chaise-Dieu. These were suppressed there by Urban’s authority and through the intervention of Hugh, archbishop of Lyon, and Aldebert, archbishop of Bourges, as is clear from a document drawn up on the matter on 28 November [Col. 0179C].

Perhaps what Paschal II says in the privilege granted to Saint Hugh in 1100, published in the appendix to the *Cluniac Bibliotheca*, should also be referred to this matter. There the pontiff confirms everything concerning which no question had been raised against Hugh at the Council of Clermont.

The same holy Hugh brought before the council the case of the monks of Silvanès against Archimbald, prince of Bourbon, who continued to harass them, as we have already said above, following the example of his father. His father, frequently admonished in vain by the blessed abbot and rebuked at the synod held at Charlieu on that account, had not repented until near death.

Archimbald, forgetful of his father’s promises—and indeed of the promises made by his own people, as stated above in section 202—to the pontiff, was still hostile to Silvanès. Therefore Hugh, as is reported in the document cited there, informed the pope’s ears of the matter at that great synod held in the city of Auvergne [Col. 0179D].

The same pope, always ready to comply in every respect with the wishes of the aforementioned father, summoned Archimbald to the council and compelled him to promise that, following the advice of the archbishop of Bourges, the bishop of Le Puy, William of Bafia—for this was the man who had succeeded Durannus, the deceased bishop of Clermont—and certain other noblemen, he would correct everything that he had wrongfully done against the lord abbot [Col. 0180A]. Shortly afterward he in fact did so before those same men at Silvanès, where they had assembled for a hearing convened on the matter, as the public document of that hearing establishes.

At the same synod Stephanus, prior of Saint-Flour in Auvergne, complained against Bernard and his sons. Urban excommunicated them because they had invaded the Church of Saint Martin of Calidæ Aquæ, as will be said below in section 232. Eblo suffered a similar punishment, as we have already said, because he was unjustly occupying the churches of the people of Vendôme on the island of Oléron.

Various possessions were also asserted at the same council to belong to the Cluniac monastery; it would be useless to list them individually. Nor is there room to say more about the association of prayers that certain abbots from various provinces, gathered at this council, entered into among themselves [Col. 0180B]. We learn of it from an old record of the matter preserved in a manuscript of the monastery of Saint-Illidius in that city.

It mentions, together with the abbot of Saint-Illidius, the abbots of Saint-Florent, Saint-Nicholas of Angers, Saint-Cyprian near Poitiers, Saint-Savin likewise in Poitou, and La Chaise-Dieu; as well as the monks of Port-Dieu and Saint Peter of Mauriac, and the abbot and monks of Saint Symphorian of Thiers.

## CCXXV. The holy expedition decreed there. The pontiff’s addresses. The bishop of Le Puy elected commander of the armies

Nothing brought greater renown to the Council of Clermont among later generations than that celebrated expedition to the Holy Land, which was first decreed and proclaimed there with the common consent and acclamation of all orders. On this occasion, widely circulated authors praise Urban’s eloquence [Col. 0180C]. In reality, Eugenius III writes to Louis, king of the Franks, that Urban thundered like a heavenly trumpet in order to inspire him to undertake a similar expedition.

Guibert, abbot of Nogent, should be heard on this subject. After praising the pontiff’s courage in proclaiming the expedition, he portrays him presiding over the council in these words:

> “It was there possible to observe with what serene gravity and weighty courtesy he presided; and, to use the words of Sidonius, with what peppered eloquence that most eloquent pope thundered against every matter brought before him. It was observed with what modesty the most illustrious man endured the loquacity of those who noisily thrust their cases upon him, and how little he valued anyone’s personal status except according to God.”

This was especially apparent, as that author continues [Col. 0180D], in the fact that he excommunicated King Philip with such authority that he scorned the intercessions of distinguished persons and the presentation of numerous gifts, and did not fear to remain within the boundaries of the king’s own realm.

When the various matters brought before the council had been completed, the pontiff, as Robert, abbot of Saint-Remi, who was present, reports, went out into a spacious square, since no building could contain the multitude. There he delivered an address, which the same author summarizes, to stir the hearts of those standing there to undertake the expedition.

He moved them so deeply that they all immediately cried out, “God wills it! God wills it!” These words were later adopted as the watchword of the pilgrims in the old French form *Deu lo wolt*. Soldiers and other pilgrims used them to encourage one another to act courageously during the more difficult parts of their journeys and roads, or in the midst of battles against the unbelievers [Col. 0181A].

The same author relates that Cardinal Gregory—later made pope and called Innocent II—immediately after Urban had finished his exhortation, made his confession on behalf of all those prostrate on the ground. In this way, by striking their breasts, they all obtained absolution for the wrongs they had committed. After absolution, and after the blessing that followed it, they received permission to return to their homes, so that they might provide themselves with what was necessary for so great a journey—thereafter called the Way of God—and exhort others who were absent to undertake the same expedition [Col. 0181B].

On the following day, as the same author continues, after summoning the bishops, Urban proposed that they should deliberate about choosing a leader for the sacred expedition. By the unanimous agreement of all, Adhemar, bishop of Le Puy, was elected, since he was exceedingly suitable for both human and divine affairs, most skilled in both kinds of knowledge, and exceptionally energetic in his actions. Although unwilling, he immediately accepted, like another Moses, the leadership and governance of the Lord’s people, with the blessing of the lord pope and the entire council. Guibert relates that, wherever they went, the pope entrusted his own authority over the Christian people to him; hence, he says, he laid hands upon him in the manner of the apostles, giving his blessing at the same time. How excellently Adhemar fulfilled the duties of this legation, that author says, is proved by the marvelous outcome of so great an undertaking. Indeed, the distinguished deeds of that prelate are frequently commemorated by the authors.
