Following his example, other bishops subsequently gave their names to the sacred expedition; William of Orange is said to have done so at the Council of Clermont itself. Bernard, archbishop of Toledo, had likewise bound himself by this vow, but the pope absolved him from it, because, in view of the troubled situation in Spain, it was preferable that he remain there. Paschal II mentions this absolution in his letter to the clergy and people of King Alfonso’s realm, at Tamaya on 3 April; there it is said that Urban changed Bernard’s vow into a commitment to promote the restoration of the city and Church of Tarragona. If we believe Bonfinius and other historians, Saint Ladislaus, king of Hungary, was elected leader of this expedition, and, as they say, had already undertaken that office; but domestic disturbances and even the death by which he died in that year prevented him from carrying it out.

[Col. 0181C]

The speeches which the pope delivered on that occasion were published by Baronius and in various editions of the councils, from ancient authors and old manuscripts. They were reproduced by William of Malmesbury, Orderic Vitalis, Robert, abbot of Saint-Remi, and Guibert, abbot of Nogent, as well as by William of Tyre and other ancient authors who deliberately wrote the history of this and the subsequent sacred expeditions; these works were published together in 1611 at Hanau by the Wechel press under the title *Gesta Dei per Francos* [Deeds of God through the Franks].

[Col. 0182A]

No one, however, should call their authenticity into question merely because they are reported differently by different authors. Most of those writers, as Baldric and Guibert themselves admit, did not reproduce the speeches in Urban’s exact words, but only according to their meaning and intention, as they had been able to retain them by listening. Moreover, since the pope had spoken on this subject more than once, who would deny that one author reported one of his speeches and another a different one? Those which we are able to find more genuine will be presented in an appendix.

**CCXXVI. Urban’s greatness of spirit in promulgating this expedition. The expedition instituted in place of penance. Prayers instituted on the same occasion.**

[Col. 0182B]

From these writers—whose works those devoted to sacred history will not regret examining—it can be seen how much Urban accomplished in promulgating and promoting this expedition. On this occasion Orderic Vitalis, in Book VIII, praises him as having been appointed by the God of Israel as the great leader against the Philistines, to whom He had entrusted the tower of David with its defenses facing Damascus. He has more to say in Book IX. Guibert says that on this occasion the same pope offered everyone a splendid proof of his greatness of spirit, since, when he himself first provided the incentive for this expedition, the whole world was astonished at how it could be accomplished.

Indeed, it is remarkable that a poor pope—as Urban then was—without the assistance of kings and without any levy or tax, gathered so great a multitude of princes, noblemen, and others from every order, status, and kingdom, who hastened voluntarily and eagerly to so difficult an expedition. Their only payment held out to them was the remission of sins, and their only reward the hope of eternal life.

They had, as we have already said, the words *Deu lo wolt* [God wills it] as their password, and the cross as their military sign; they impressed its image upon their garments above the right shoulder blade. Hence the names “cross-bearers” and “crusaders” came into use. Hermann records in his *History of Saint Martin of Tournai* that, at the Council of Clermont, Urban instructed the bishops that, when they had returned to their dioceses, they should enjoin upon their subjects, as a form of penance for the remission of sins, that they give their names to these expeditions.

[Col. 0182C]

Hence, in canon 2 of the commonly circulated edition, one reads that whoever set out to liberate the Church of God in Jerusalem should regard that journey as a substitute for all penance. Orderic agrees, and I shall not hesitate to quote his words here:

> “The prudent pope,” he says, “summoned all who were suitably able to bear arms to war against the enemies of God; and from the hour when they took up the Lord’s cross, by God’s authority he absolved all penitents from all their sins; and he piously relieved them from every burden imposed through fasts and other mortifications of the flesh,” and so forth.

Another canon was also established everywhere in favor of the crusaders: namely, that all their possessions should remain safe, always and everywhere, with every legal pretext set aside, until their return. Later popes confirmed these two privileges for those who gave their names to similar expeditions, following Urban’s example, as is expressly stated in the Lateran Council held under Calixtus II in 1122.

I saw, in the Bigot codex, now belonging to the Royal Library, a letter of Paschal II to the archbishops, bishops, and abbots of Gaul. In it, after the capture of Jerusalem, the pope orders that the possessions of the brothers returning after the divinely achieved victory should be restored to them, just as had been decreed by synodal decision under Urban of blessed memory.

[Col. 0183A]

To prevent soldiers who had taken the cross from turning back halfway through the journey and abandoning the army out of fickleness or under any pretext, Orderic says in Book X that Urban had established by general authority, and by apostolic command had caused to be inviolably observed throughout the Latin world, that all who had taken Christ’s cross and had not completed the journey to Jerusalem because of a failure of will should either set out again upon the road in the Lord’s name or, struck by anathema, suffer punishment outside the Church. Indeed, as everyone knows, when Count Stephen of Blois had deserted the army after being terrified by some sort of fear, he was later compelled to return to the expedition, during which he died in 1101.

It is also reported that, on this very occasion of the sacred expedition, the canonical hours of the blessed Mary—which had previously been instituted by Peter Damian in his monasteries—began to be frequently recited by the clergy and even by the laity, at Urban’s direction. In this way, those who were unable to undertake the expedition might at least assist the soldiers by these prayers, winning for them the patronage of so great a Virgin. Geoffrey, prior of Vigeois, adds in chapter 27 of his *Chronicle* that the office of the same blessed Virgin, which is still celebrated on Saturday, was instituted on this occasion.

Some even praise Saint Antoninus for reporting that the pope established at the council that, from the very day on which the army was to depart for the expedition, a signal should be given morning and evening in all cathedral churches and monasteries by the triple ringing of a bell, so that the people might be stirred to pour forth prayers for the expedition’s successful outcome. This institution may have provided the occasion for the custom of ringing the Angelus, which later became widespread everywhere.

[Col. 0183D]

Besides these measures, Robert of Torigni, in his additions to Sigebert—which our Acherius published after the works of Guibert—writes that a decree was made in the authentic and renowned Council of Auvergne: any city that could be wrested from the pagans by crossing the great sea should, without any opposition, be held perpetually under the dominion or rule of holy Jerusalem. He also testifies that this was shortly afterward confirmed by all at the Council of Antioch.

**CCXXVII. Urban’s defense of the promulgation of these expeditions.**

[Col. 0184A]

This would be the place to defend Urban against the abuse of certain people who unjustly reproached him, alleging either that he had proclaimed this expedition unjustly against peoples over whom, as they claim, he possessed no right, or at least rashly, thereby involving Christian princes and peoples in wars so arduous and dangerous.

It is easy, however, to remove both accusations from Urban, since it can readily be demonstrated that those wars were just and almost necessary for the Christian world. What could be imagined more equitable than that the common father of all the faithful should gather the strength of Christians into one force to blunt the assaults of a common and insolent enemy who was plotting everything against them? And what could be more necessary for the protection of the Christian commonwealth than to repel arms by arms when those enemies had already devastated many Christian provinces, were threatening others, and were hostile to all?

No one who wishes even briefly to survey the histories of those times will dare deny that this was then the condition of the Christian world. To say nothing of Spain, Sicily, and the regions of Italy, nearly the whole East—against which that expedition was directed above all—was occupied by Muslims. It was not only the holy city of Jerusalem, or Nicaea, Antioch, and other famous cities, together with the vast regions nearest to those cities, that groaned under their tyrannical yoke; many other provinces of the empire of Constantinople were also being harassed by those barbarians, and most of them had already been subjected to their rule.

[Col. 0184B]

They had devastated everything as far as the walls of the imperial city of Constantinople. “Urban,” says Count Fulk in the frequently praised fragment of his history, “admonished our people to go to Jerusalem, to conquer the pagan people who had occupied that city and the whole land of the Christians as far as Constantinople.”

What wonder, then, if the common father and shepherd of the Christians attempted to come to the aid of the Christian commonwealth in so great and urgent a danger, especially when the emperor himself, together with the Eastern Churches and peoples, had repeatedly implored assistance from him by letters and envoys? The truth of this is proved not only by the Acts of the Councils of Piacenza and Clermont, but is also repeatedly attested by contemporary authors themselves, Bertold, Guibert, and others.

It was always the opinion of everyone that Urban had deserved exceedingly well of the Church on this occasion. An old inscription carved near Saint Peter in the apostolic palace publicly testified to this in the following words:

> **URBAN II, AUTHOR OF THE EXPEDITION AGAINST THE INFIDELS.**

**CCXXVII bis. At Clermont, Urban grants privileges to churches, etc.: to Saint Dionysius of Nogent; to Molesme. Letter to the people of Grenoble. Proceedings against Aniane.**

The synod of Clermont was dissolved on the fourth day before the Kalends of December; as we observed above from Lambert’s codex, the privilege of the Church of Arras was then read and confirmed before everyone.

[Col. 0185A]

Urban granted several other privileges during the days that followed at Clermont, where he remained until the beginning of December. On the third day before the Kalends of December, he confirmed for the Cluniac monks the monastery of Saint Dionysius of Nogent, listing individually its possessions situated in various dioceses. On the same day he received the monastery of Molesme, then governed by Saint Robert, under the protection of the Apostolic See, while preserving the diocesan right of the bishop of Langres, at whose request the pope granted this privilege.

On that same day he also wrote a letter to Count Guigo, the clergy, and the people of Grenoble, in which, as we stated in section 216, he informed them that the archdeaconry of Salmoray had been vindicated for the Church of Grenoble.

[Col. 0185B]

On the same day as well, if we may trust Gariel, the author of the *History of the Bishops of Maguelonne*, the same pope ordered that the diploma of Alexander II, granted in favor of Bertrand, bishop of Maguelonne, against Peter, abbot of Aniane, be inserted into the Acts of the Council of Clermont, so that henceforth the abbots of Aniane would dare nothing beyond the limits of their authority. As we stated in its proper place, Bertrand had brought complaints about this matter before the synod.

**CCXXVIII. He writes to the people of Cambrai and to those of Angoulême.**

On the following day, that is, on the day before the Kalends of December, the pope wrote to the people of Cambrai, in accordance with what had been established at the synod, to admonish them concerning the sentence pronounced against Gualcher, the intruded bishop; we discussed this matter at length above, in section 210.

[Col. 0185C]

On the same day he sent another letter to the canons of Angoulême, in which the pope confirmed to them the provostship of Juilly, which Bishop Adhemar had granted to them while they were living in common.

**CCXXIX. Decree concerning the primacy of Lyons.**

On the Kalends of December Urban issued a celebrated bull. After recounting the various disputes concerning the primacy of Lyons that had taken place at the council, he asserted and confirmed the primacy of that Church over the four provinces of Lyons. He says that eight archbishops, eighty bishops, and ninety or more abbots had participated in this decision.

The distinguished Peter de Marca was the first to publish this bull. From Orderic Vitalis, Book IX, we further gather that synodal letters were written in the name of the council to absent bishops, at least to those who had sent letters of excuse. For when Odo and the other prelates of Normandy had attended the council with letters of excuse from their fellow provincials, they returned with the apostolic blessing and carried synodal letters to their fellow bishops.

**CCXXX. Urban dedicates the church of Celsinac.**

At last Urban left Clermont and traveled through various regions, as he had done before the council. In these places he consecrated churches and monasteries wherever he went, settled disputes, provided for the peace of sacred places, held councils, and finally bound everyone to himself through his kindness and blameless conduct.

On 3 December he first halted at Celsinac, a famous monastery of the Cluniac order, and solemnly dedicated its church, as he himself testifies in a bull issued several days later. Remembering so great a benefit, the monks of that place inserted Urban’s name, with an eulogy, in their obituary book, in these words:

> “The fourth day before the Kalends of August: office for the lord Urban, pope. This venerable and God-worthy apostolic man, among his other praiseworthy works, also dedicated this monastery with great authority and devotion on the third day before the Nones of December. On the day of that consecration, throughout succeeding generations, he granted the greatest and most desirable absolution to all who confessed their sins, came together for the feast of that day, and fulfilled their vows.”

**CCXXXI. He grants a privilege to Cluny at Brioude. Another at Compostela.**

[Col. 0186B]

From there the pope proceeded to Brioude, where there was a noble and ancient college of canons, commonly called counts. On 4 December, by a distinguished rescript, he confirmed to Saint Hugh the churches, altars, and tithes that had hitherto been granted to the Cluniac monks.

On that same day he granted a bull addressed to Dalmatius, bishop of Compostela, who had been present at the Council of Auvergne, and to his successors. By this document he transferred the episcopal see, which had hitherto remained at Iria, to Compostela, in honor of Saint James, whose body had long before been believed to be preserved there. He then adorned this church with a new privilege, decreeing that its bishop should recognize no metropolitan except the Roman pontiff.

[Col. 0186C]

The Church of Compostela did not, however, remain long in this position, for Calixtus II later increased its authority and dignity by making it a metropolitan see. Letters concerning this matter survive from the year 1124.

**CCXXXII. He dedicates the church of Saint-Flour and grants it a privilege. A privilege for Marcigny. Piperac becomes an abbey. The death of John, bishop of Porto, at Saint-Flour.**

Leaving Brioude, Urban went to the town of Saint-Flour, invited by Stephen, the prior of that place of the Cluniac order. There, as reported in an old account published by Mabillon in the appendix to volume VI of the *Annales Benedictini*, no. 25, he permanently granted to the monks of Saint-Flour the church of Saint Martin of Aigues-Caldes, which had been assigned to them at the Council of Clermont against certain invaders, and he confirmed that grant by the authority of his privilege.

This may perhaps be the privilege that Prior Peter and the monks of that place, almost entirely consumed by excessive age, presented to Urban IV for renewal, as the learned Étienne Baluze observed from their petition in his notes to the *Lives of the Avignon Popes*, p. 740. We were unable to obtain a copy of either privilege.

At that time, however, the pope, accompanied by the sacred college of cardinals, dedicated, as the old documents of the place report, the newly constructed basilica of Blessed Florus the confessor. His relics were placed behind the altar in an elevated position, in a reliquary closed with three locks. We infer that this took place on 7 December from the anniversary solemnity of its dedication, which is still celebrated on that very day in that church, raised to episcopal rank by John XXII.

[Col. 0187A]

On the same day the pope granted two privileges there in favor of the Cluniacs: one for the nuns of the convent of Marcigny, founded by Saint Hugh, and another for the monks of Celsinac, which we have already mentioned above.

On this occasion, as may reasonably be conjectured, Bernard, who governed the canons regular of Piperac under the title of provost, obtained the elevation of his church to the status of an abbey. It is reported that Urban did this around that time; and Piperac is not far from Saint-Flour. Moreover, as we observed from Bertold, Urban granted the title of abbot to provosts of canons regular, though without the use of a pastoral staff.

It is also likely that Urban remained for some time at Saint-Flour because of the illness of John, bishop of Porto, who died and was buried there. Even now his tomb can be seen in the right aisle of the cathedral church, between the first and second columns, but, as I was assured, without any inscription.

[Col. 0187B]

As stated in the aforementioned little book, the most holy Urban endowed the monastery of Saint-Flour with a privilege not only out of devotion to Saint Florus and reverence for the consecration of that place by him, but also because of his special affection for the true father, John, cardinal-bishop of Porto, who had been buried there.

**CCXXXIII. Urban passes through Aurillac. The fortunes of Maurice Burdin.**

[Col. 0187C]

We learn from an old chronicle of that place, published in volume II of Mabillon’s *Analecta*, that Urban later went to Aurillac. There we read the following concerning Peter of Solignac, then abbot of the same monastery, which eventually defected from the Benedictine order to secular canons:

> “After the Council of Clermont, which that same abbot had attended, he conveyed Pope Urban to Aurillac.”

From there the pope entered the region of Limoges and, at the invitation of Abbot Gerard, turned aside to Uzerche. He had decided to dedicate the monastery church there, in accordance with his promise to him; but Bishop Humbald of Limoges, for some reason unknown to me, diverted Urban from that plan. Perhaps he wished the pope to celebrate the solemnity of Christ’s Nativity at Limoges.

Urban, as we said shortly before, remained on the journey somewhat longer than he had expected because of the illness of John, bishop of Porto. Nevertheless, if we believe the local chronicler, Gerard, angered against the bishop, joined himself to Adhemar, abbot of Saint-Martial. The bishop was accused before the pope by these men and was shortly afterward, as we shall relate, deprived of his see. Gerard, however, died the following month, on the feast of Saint Maurus.

When Urban passed through Uzerche, Maurice Burdin, a monk of that place, was living there. Bernard, archbishop of Toledo, who at that time may still have been in the pope’s retinue, found him to be a capable man suited to conducting important affairs and persuaded him to cross with him into Spain.

[Col. 0187D]

Everyone knows what later happened to him. After obtaining the bishopric of Coimbra, he acquired the metropolitan see of Braga and was honored with an apostolic legation. Finally, by Emperor Henry, in opposition to Pope Gelasius, he was declared Roman pontiff, and, after a life marked by various fortunes, ended it miserably in prison.

But we must return to Urban. According to Geoffrey, prior of Vigeois, he lodged at Uzerche on the feast of Saint Thomas, that is, on the twenty-first day of this month. From there he departed and arrived at Limoges two days later. What he accomplished in that city may usefully be reported from Geoffrey of Vigeois’s *Chronicle*, part I, chapter 27, in volume II of Labbe’s *Bibliotheca*; it runs as follows:

**CCXXXIV. Urban’s acts at Limoges. The dedication of Saint-Martial.**

On the tenth day before the Kalends of January Urban arrived at Limoges. On the feast of Christ’s Nativity he sang the Mass of the cockcrow of the Lord’s Nativity in the church of the maidens of Saint Mary, called “at the Rule,” a noble monastery of the Benedictine order that still exists. He celebrated the Mass of the dawn in the royal basilica at Saint-Martial. From there, crowned in triumph, he returned to the apostolic episcopal see—that is, the cathedral church, as it is called—because the people of Limoges rejoice to number Saint Martial, the first bishop of that see, among the apostles. There he completed the remaining offices of the solemnity.

On the following day, which is after the feast of the Innocents, he dedicated the cathedral church in honor of the protomartyr Stephen and rested the next day. On the day before the Kalends of January he consecrated the royal basilica—that is, the monastery of Saint-Martial, as he had called it above—in honor of the Savior of the world, and strengthened its ancient liberty and noble prerogative with new privileges.

[Col. 0188C]

Urban’s bull concerning the privileges of Saint-Martial was issued several months later at Saintes. This monastery, however, passed from the Cluniac order to secular canons.

But let us continue Geoffrey’s narrative:

> “Many bishops attended this dedication of Saint-Martial, which took place in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1095; their names must not be passed over in silence. Hugh of Lyons, Audebert of Bourges, Amatus of Bordeaux, Robert, or rather Daibert, of Pisa, Rangerius of Reggio—all these were archbishops. Bruno of Segni was first among the bishops; then Peter of Poitiers, Arnulf, or rather Ramnulf, surnamed of Barbesieux, of Saintes; Rainald of Périgueux; Raymond of Rodez; Humbald of Limoges—all these were bishops.

> “After the Roman pontiff had blessed the water, they sprinkled the basilica around it according to ecclesiastical custom. The lord pope consecrated the venerable altar with his own hands and solemnly celebrated Mass upon it. Then he went out publicly to bless the people. Such a multitude was there that, around the city and for less than a mile, nothing but human heads could be seen. So great was the abundance of offerings that the chest of the apostolic tomb—that is, of Saint Martial—which was commonly called the *Gauteau*, overflowed with them in addition to being full of other gifts.”

[Col. 0189A]

This is Geoffrey’s account. Shortly before, however, if that passage may properly be attributed to him after being recovered from another manuscript, he had written that Urban dedicated the church of Saint Stephen and the monastery of Saint Martin. In place of Saint Martin, one must doubtless read Saint Martial, although there is also a monastery dedicated to Saint Martin at Limoges.

In neither place does he say anything about the dedication of Saint Mary of the Rule. Yet we read in two old manuscript chronicles of Saint-Martial that it was performed by Urban, who, according to Geoffrey himself, sang the midnight Mass there.

For the rest, almost all these events are narrated in the same words in an old account of the Church of Limoges written on this subject, which various authors published after Besly. In it we read that all the bishops listed above celebrated the solemnity of Christ’s Nativity together with Urban at Limoges; they accompanied him as he went to Saint-Martial and, after he had first delivered a sermon to the people, returned with him, crowned, to the greater church.

[Col. 0189B]

All these men, as the account says, came together again with Urban on the sixth day of the Nativity of the Lord, which fell on a Sunday, and went with him to Saint-Martial, where he spent eight days. On the following day, after they had sprinkled the basilica inside and out with water previously blessed by the pope himself, Urban washed the altar of the Lord and Savior with that same water, anointed it with chrism and holy oil, placed relics of the saints there, and finally, with an innumerable crowd of people present and Mass sung there, decreed that the day of this dedication, the second day before the Kalends of January, should thereafter be solemnly observed each year.

This basilica had once been built by Louis the Pious but, damaged by various disasters, had been restored to its former splendor by Adhemar, abbot of that place, shortly before the pope arrived at Limoges.

**CCXXXV. Urban did not go to Arles this year. The reconciliation of the bishop of Würzburg.**

From these sources, supported also by other authors, it is clear how far Bertold, otherwise an author beyond reproach, departed from the truth when he wrote in his *Chronicle* that Urban celebrated the day of the Lord’s Nativity at Arles that year, with the bishops of various provinces, in the greatest glory.

Although he was mistaken in this, we should not deny his credibility when he relates that the bishop of Würzburg, who was well known to him, around this time abandoned the party of the schismatics and approached Urban to seek absolution from him. He obtained it from him, Bertold says, but with the provision that the same mercy should be completed for him by the pope’s legates in the German lands.

**CCXXXVI. Urban issues various charters, places Bassac under the monastery of Angeriac, and provides for Saint-Eparchius. He protects Figeac. He arranges for the churches of Saint-Martial to be restored.**

[Col. 0190A]

These solemnities did not prevent Urban from attending to other matters as well, as is proved by various charters issued during these very days. One of them is addressed to Ansculf, abbot of Angeriac, to whom he subjected the monastery of Bassac. It was issued at Limoges on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of December.

On the same day and in the same place, the pope wrote to Adhemar, bishop of Angoulême, instructing him to restrain the presumption of the monks of Saint-Eparchius. They refused to obey the abbot of Angeriac, to whom their monastery was supposed to be subject, even after a sentence of excommunication had been pronounced against them.

[Col. 0190B]

To comply with the papal commands, Adhemar invested Ansculf, abbot of Angeriac, with the abbey of Saint-Eparchius in a full chapter, in the presence of his canons, handing him the pastoral staff. Ansculf then appointed Hugh, a monk of Angeriac, as abbot of Saint-Eparchius, as is related in the instrument drawn up concerning this matter.

On that same day, the second before the Kalends of January, on which the pope consecrated the basilica of Saint-Martial, he issued there a decree in favor of the monastery of Figeac, addressed to the bishop of Cahors and other neighboring bishops, against those who had unjustly invaded the possessions of that place.

At about the same time, as we learn from Geoffrey’s *Chronicle*, Pope Urban solemnly invested the church of Saint-Martial and its abbot Adhemar with the church of Saint Peter of Montandrieu and with the churches of Saliom, together with their appurtenances. There the body of Saint Martin the abbot lay in rest—that former prince of the region whose Life, the same author laments, was lost during the incursions of the Normans, to the great detriment of that monastery.

**CCXXXVI bis. The privilege of Tulle.**

In the following year, on 2 January, while Urban was still at Limoges, he granted a privilege to William, abbot of Tulle, by which he received the possessions of that monastery under the protection of the Apostolic See. In it the pope mentions certain soldiers living in that city who had been excommunicated for their evil deeds. On their account he forbids that the monastery itself be excommunicated, unless those excommunicated men should happen to be admitted there for the divine offices.

**CCXXXVII. Humbald, bishop of Limoges, is deposed.**

Humbald then presided over the Church of Limoges. After various disputes, he had been confirmed in that see by virtue of apostolic letters, though letters falsified by Humbald himself.

While the pope was staying at Saint-Martial, he happened at some point to rebuke Abbot Adhemar for having admitted this bishop without Urban’s approval, contrary to what had been decided concerning him at Rome. Astonished at this, the abbot showed the pope the apostolic letters that Humbald had returned to him. Recognizing the fraud, Urban immediately deposed Humbald publicly.

[Col. 0191A]

After some time William, prior of Saint-Martial, was appointed in his place. Geoffrey of Vigeois relates these events in his *Chronicle*, chapters 26 and 28, and the *Chronicle of Maillezais* agrees with him.

No one, however, had yet seen the letters falsified by Humbald. We shall publish them, together with an old account of the affair, in an appendix, from a manuscript codex of the Church of Limoges that had belonged to the distinguished Antoine Faure, provost of the Church of Reims, and that the learned Baluze communicated to us.

**CCXXXVIII. He consecrates the altar of Carrof.**

Since Urban went to the monastery of Saint-Martial on the day before the Kalends of January and, as we have already observed, spent eight days there, it is easy to infer that he celebrated the feast of the Epiphany there. Whether he returned to the city on the following day, however, we do not know.

It is certain that on the Thursday before the feast of Saint Hilary, which falls on 13 January, he consecrated with his own hands the altar of the basilica of the monastery of Carrof among the Poitevins, at the invitation of Peter, abbot of that place, with many bishops assisting him.

[Col. 0191B]

We learn this from an old account, which we shall publish in an appendix after recovering it from the archives of that monastery. The same fact appears in the manuscripts of Sirmond in volume II of Labbe’s *Bibliotheca nova*, p. 755; but there the word “before” has been omitted, and the consecration is mistakenly said to have taken place on the feast of Saint Hilary.

Urban himself, in the privilege of that monastery, by which he confirms the possessions and privileges granted to it by Leo IX and Alexander II, decrees that no one except the Roman pontiff may dare to pronounce a sentence of excommunication or interdict against that altar, which he himself had consecrated with his own hands.

**CCXXXIX. He celebrates the feast of Saint Hilary at Poitiers, etc. He blesses the new monastery.**

The author of the *Chronicle of Maillezais* bears witness that Urban celebrated the feast of Saint Hilary, which occurs on 13 January, in the city of Poitiers itself.

[Col. 0191C]

At that time Peter, bishop of the same city, settled a dispute that had arisen between the monks of Trizay and the canons of Sainte-Croix of Loudun, and the pope himself subscribed to his decision, together with Amatus, archbishop of Bordeaux, Hugh, archbishop of Lyons, Girard, bishop of Angoulême, and others, as is recorded in an old copy.

The pope himself held another hearing in the church of Saint Hilary, but this must be assigned to the month of March, when Urban visited Poitiers again.

The blessing of the new monastery in the same city must, however, be brought into this context. It was performed by the pope himself not on the sixth day before the Kalends of February, as the *Chronicle of Maillezais* states, but on the eleventh day before the Kalends of February, as is established by old documents from the place.

This is demonstrated by an old manuscript martyrology of that place, in which the church is said to have been consecrated on the feast of Saint Vincent, in these words:

> “The abbot, the lord Gerard II, during whose time our church was dedicated and consecrated on the feast of Saint Vincent by the hands of the supreme pontiff Urban II,” and so forth.

In another codex we read:

> “On the eleventh day before the Kalends of February, Urban II, together with three archbishops and an equal number of bishops, dedicated a church in honor of the holy Mother of God and of the blessed apostles John and Andrew. He then reverently consecrated this principal altar in honor of the holy martyrs Stephen the protomartyr, Lawrence, Vincent, Chrysanthus, and Daria, and placed their relics there.”

Urban himself testifies in his charter that this church had been consecrated by him and therefore ought to be under the special protection of the Apostolic See.

**CCXL. He is led to Angers by Milo. There he preaches the crusade.**
After this, as the author of the Chronicle of Malleais continues, the pontiff proceeded to Angers and blessed the monastery of Saint Nicholas, situated near that city. It is recorded in the Angevin Chronicle, in Labbe’s *Bibliotheca nova*, volume I, that Urban was brought there by Milo, his own legate, formerly a monk of Saint Albinus—and indeed so that he might consecrate the church of Saint Albinus. But the monks of that place, for I do not know what reason, refused to allow this, as another Chronicle records in an old manuscript belonging to Queen Christina of Sweden, now preserved in the Ottobonian Library at Rome. The matter is set out there as follows:

> “In the year 1096, Pope Urban came down to the city of Angers and consecrated the church of Saint Nicholas. For the monks of Saint Albinus refused to have their church consecrated, although this was the principal reason why the pope had come, brought by Milo, formerly a monk of blessed Albinus and at that time his legate.”

Hugh, abbot of Flavigny, mentions this Milo in his *Chronicle*, where he writes that Milo was made a bishop. But the name of his see is not given in Labbe’s edition because the manuscript is damaged at that point; this lacuna can easily be supplied from the domestic records of Saint Albinus, in which Milo is repeatedly called bishop of Palestrina. He is, in fact, the very man who, after Bernard’s death, was advanced to this see against Hugh Candidus, the notorious schismatic. In that capacity he took part in the election of Paschal II, by whom he was sent as legate to Gaul; finally, about the year 1101, as Ughelli writes, he died.

Count Fulk of Anjou gives another reason for Urban’s journey to Angers in a fragment of his *History*, published in volume X of Acheri’s *Spicilegium*: namely, that he might rouse the inhabitants of that province to undertake the holy expedition. The old Chronicle of Saint Albinus says the same. Nor is this surprising; for, says the author of the Chronicle of Malleais, wherever the pontiff went, “he ordered men to make crosses, to go to Jerusalem, and to free it from the Turks and other peoples.” An old author apud Chesnium, volume IV, p. 90, agrees, reporting that Urban commanded all the bishops to preach this expedition, each in his own diocese, and that they actually carried out his order.

As everyone knows, this was indeed the principal reason for the pontiff’s journey into Gaul. No other witness to the matter besides Urban himself need be sought: at that time he wrote letters to the princes and other faithful of Flanders in order to inform them of the expedition decreed at the Council of Clermont and of the indulgences granted to those who undertook it. He therefore warns them all that, if any wished to set out at that summons, they should be fully prepared by the approaching feast of the Assumption of the Mother of God. At that time Adhemar, bishop of Le Puy, appointed the pontiff’s vicar for the expedition, was to begin the journey with the other cross-bearers.

## CCXLI. He confirms Manasses, archbishop-elect of Reims. The dispute at Tournus is postponed.

Urban came to Angers as Lent was approaching, as Count Fulk testifies. There he learned of the death of Reginald, pontiff of Reims, who, as we learn from a letter of the clergy of Reims to Lambert of Arras and from the verses of Balderic of Bourgueil, where he calls him a patriarch, died on the twelfth day before the Kalends of February. It is therefore surprising that Labbe assigns his death to the preceding year, since it is certain—not to mention many ancient documents—that this prelate took part in the Council of Clermont in November.

Urban immediately approved with praise the election of Manasses, provost of that same church, who had been appointed in Reginald’s place. This is clear from three letters of Urban written at Angers on the eighth day before the Ides of February concerning this matter, in which he warmly expresses his affection for the Church, clergy, knights, and people of Reims.

Ivo of Chartres had also written to Urban on Manasses’ behalf, in Letter 48, saying that it was of the greatest importance that confirmation of his election not be delayed, on account of the distinguished prerogatives of the Church of Reims, which, he says, had once been Urban’s mother but was now his daughter. This see possessed the diadem of the kingdom and, by reason of its dignity, was accustomed to serve the other Gallican churches as an example either of ruin or of restoration.

At the same time, the monks of Tournus approached the pontiff to complain against the bishop and canons of Angers, because they were unjustly claiming for themselves the churches of the castle of Doué, which belonged to their monastery. But since the canons, on the contrary, maintained that these churches were theirs by right, and the pontiff saw that the dispute was of some importance, he referred it to the forthcoming Council of Tours, where, as we shall relate in its proper place, it was in fact argued.

## CCXLII. Urban dedicates the basilica of Saint Nicholas. He transfers the body of Count Geoffrey. He writes to the monks of Saint Viton.

On the fourth day before the Ides—that is, February 10—the basilica of Saint Nicholas, situated in the suburb of Angers, was dedicated by Urban. The same day, still celebrated in this monastery, is assigned not only by the old manuscript Chronicle of Saint Albinus but also by the charter of the foundation of Sainte-Marie de Rota near Credon. Accordingly, Orderic Vitalis must be corrected: in Book IX he wrote that the dedication of Saint Nicholas took place in mid-Lent.

Certainly Count Fulk of Anjou, who was present, expressly reports in a fragment of his *History of Anjou* that this basilica was dedicated on Septuagesima. Urban’s bull in which the dedication is mentioned was issued in February and therefore before the beginning of Lent—not to mention the Council of Tours, which was held under Urban’s presidency in mid-Lent, when he was no longer at Angers.

How solemn this dedication was may be inferred from the fact that various charters are repeatedly found among the Angevin records, dated by the year or day of its dedication. Indeed, Natalis, the abbot, is especially praised for this reason in the verses of Balderic of Bourgueil apud Chesnium, volume IV: he had secured the pontiff’s performance of the dedication.

To ensure that the memory of its solemnity would be transmitted to later generations, the same pontiff ordered in the aforementioned bull that those who wished to gather for its annual celebration should be protected from every enemy incursion, and he granted them many privileges. He also established—and, as Count Fulk testifies in the fragment of his *History* mentioned above, ordered by edict—that each year, at the same season in which he had performed the dedication, a public festival should be celebrated at Saint Nicholas, and that one-seventh of the penances should be remitted to the people who gathered for the celebration.

On the same occasion, at the request of Count Fulk, who was present, the pontiff transferred the body of Geoffrey Martel, who had died in the monastic habit and had been buried in the chapter-house of that monastery, into the church he had dedicated. Fulk himself relates this in the fragment just mentioned. At the pontiff’s prompting, Fulk also gave part of the forest of Gâtine to Saint Nicholas for the repose of Geoffrey’s soul.

This donation, however, later provided abundant material for a major dispute between the monks of that place and those of Saint Albinus, since the latter claimed that the entire forest belonged to them. The dispute was finally settled through the assistance of Geoffrey of Meaux, bishop of Angers, and William, abbot of Saint Florent. This can be seen in Pelleterius’ *History of Saint Nicholas*, where, among many other records, he publishes the instrument of this settlement.

Pelleterius, however, is not sufficiently consistent in identifying the place where Geoffrey’s tomb stood in his own time. Today, not far from the high altar, there is a tomb without any inscription which is thought to be Geoffrey’s. Yet an old document says, on p. 29, that his body was then transferred into the nave of the church and buried there. A little earlier, on p. 25, Pelleterius himself had written:

> “The evidence for this burial is supplied by a painting and by a stone raised about three feet above the ground, in front of the altar of Saint Andrew, which stands to the left of the high altar, bearing this epitaph: ‘While he flourished …’”

None of these things is visible today.

On this same day of the dedication of Saint Nicholas, that is, on the fourth day before the Ides of February, Urban wrote to Philip, bishop of Châlons, urging him to free the monks of Saint Vitonus of Verdun, who lived in the priory of Saint Nicholas in his diocese, from the harassment of some of his parishioners, and ordering that they should thereafter remain secure under his protection.

## CCXLIII. An eclipse. Confirmation of the monastery of Rota. Robert of Arbrissel, abbot of that place.

The next day, namely the third day before the Ides of February, as we read in the Angevin Chronicle published by Labbe, while the aforesaid pope was residing in the city of Angers, the moon, when it was thirteen days old, suffered a terrifying eclipse.

> “On that day the same pontiff, in the chamber of Geoffrey, bishop of that city, by the laying on of his hands confirmed the foundation of the monastery of regular canons of Sainte-Marie de Rota, situated near Credon. The foundation had been made the previous day by Reginald, son of Robert the Burgundian. The foundation charter was subscribed by Hugh, archbishop of Lyon, and Amatus, archbishop of Bordeaux; and by the bishops Ivo of Chartres, Hoel of Le Mans, and Walter of Albano. With Urban, Geoffrey of Angers and Bruno of Signi subscribed it; as did the cardinals Teuthio, Albert, and Rangerius; and the pope’s clerics Emorrand of Soissons and Milo, monk of Saint Albinus.”

All of these men had attended the dedication of the church of Saint Nicholas, to which a large part of the Roman senate is said to have gathered. The documents concerning this matter have been published by the Sammarthani in volume IV of *Gallia Christiana* and in volume II of Baluze’s *Miscellanea*.

The abbot of the monastery of Rota—and its first abbot—was Robert of Arbrissel, who shortly afterward was to become the founder of the monastery of Fontevraud and of the entire order, during the final years of Urban’s pontificate.

When Urban heard of Robert’s reputation, he summoned him to Angers and, at the solemn dedication of Saint Nicholas, “to which,” says Balderic, the author of Robert’s *Life*, “one might have thought the whole breadth of the world had gathered,” he ordered him to preach. As the same author continues, the words of Robert’s sermon greatly pleased the lord pope. Accordingly, having entrusted him with the office of preaching, he made him, after himself, a second preacher of the word of God. After carrying out this commission in various dioceses, Robert resigned the governance of his monastery in order to devote himself more freely to the ministry of the word.

## CCXLIV. Pope Urban visits Saint Maurus.

Leaving the city of Angers, the pontiff visited the formerly famous monastery of Glanfeuil, dedicated to Saint Maurus. At that time it had been subject to the monks of Fosses for nearly two hundred years. The monks of the place, together with the neighboring inhabitants and the leading men of the province, complained to Urban about this and implored him to free so distinguished a place from foreign domination.

But he judged that this cause, which appeared to be of some importance, should be brought before the Council of Tours, to be celebrated in the following month. The Fosses monks should thereby be given an opportunity to defend themselves, and the matter should be judged only after the arguments on both sides had been carefully weighed. This was in fact done, and the Fosses monks lost the case, as we shall relate below.

## CCXLV. Did he free Geoffrey the Bearded at Chinon?

From there the pontiff proceeded to Chinon, in the territory of Tours toward Poitiers—if it is true that he visited that town, as Orderic Vitalis suggests—in order to free Geoffrey the Bearded, formerly count of Anjou, who had been held captive there for many years on the order of Count Fulk the Rechin.

That author says in Book X that Urban, through exhortation and authority, freed him from his bonds. In Book IX he writes that the same Geoffrey was released in the presence and at the command of Pope Urban, having been confined in prison at the castle of Chinon for nearly thirty years.

This is what Orderic says. But if we follow other commonly cited authors, either Geoffrey was never freed from prison—as Hildebert expressly states in his *Life of Saint Hugh*, since he was living there at the time—or else his release occurred much later than Urban’s arrival in Gaul, as may be seen in Menagium, Book III of the *History of Sablé*, chapter 16. It is not our concern to pursue these difficulties at greater length.

## CCXLVI. At Sablé he issues a bull for Saint Nicholas.

On the sixteenth day before the Kalends of March—that is, February 14—Urban confirmed by a charter issued at Sablé, a town situated on the borders of Anjou and Maine, the privileges and possessions of the monastery of Saint Nicholas of Angers, whose basilica he had consecrated with his own hands a few days earlier.

In this bull he decrees many benefits, as we have said, in favor of those who should visit the same basilica on the anniversary of its dedication.

## CCXLVII. Pope Urban remains three days at Le Mans.

Count Fulk also testifies that Urban visited the city of Le Mans in the fragment already mentioned. There it is said that he spent three days at the expense of Bishop Hoel, as recorded in the *Acts of the Bishops of that City*, published in volume III of Mabillon’s *Analecta*. On this occasion that prelate is praised because, among all the titles of his predecessors, he alone had been honored with the sacred hospitality of the universal pope and prince of all priests.

Urban’s arrival at Le Mans became so celebrated among the peoples of that region that it was sometimes used as an era in public documents.

Apparently on this occasion—or certainly while he was at Angers—the same pontiff entrusted Hoel with the task of restoring Loconais to the monks of Saint Albinus. That place, formerly given to them by King Childebert, had been seized by certain noblemen.

## CCXLVIII. He remains eleven days at Vendôme. He annuls the profession made to the bishop. He consecrates the altar of the Crucified One.

From there the pontiff departed for Vendôme, where he remained for eleven days, as testified by Geoffrey, then abbot of that place. In Book I, Letter 18, Geoffrey writes the following to Conon, the legate of the Apostolic See:

> “Pope Urban, of blessed memory, and the lord who is now Pope Paschal, remained in our church for eleven days through the grace of their charity. They examined our privileges, read them aloud with their own mouths, and confirmed them by a decree of their authority.”

On this occasion, without doubt, Urban learned from the monks of that place that, when Geoffrey was blessed as abbot by Ivo of Chartres, he had made a profession to him as though to his diocesan bishop. The pontiff took this badly and severely rebuked the abbot, calling him “a deceived dove without a heart.” He therefore annulled what had been done unlawfully, and, after returning to Rome, enacted by a solemn decree that no abbot of Vendôme should thereafter make profession to any bishop. Paschal, Urban’s successor, later confirmed this again by his apostolic authority.

Geoffrey himself relates all these matters in Letters 7 and 11 of Book II, written to Ivo. He also gives the decree itself in Letter 27 to Geoffrey, Ivo’s successor. We shall publish it in its proper place.

The following passage concerning that monastery must also be included here. It is found in the Angevin Chronicle, apud Labbe, volume I of the *Bibliotheca nova*, under the year 1095 according to the old reckoning, by which the beginning of the new year was taken from Easter:

> “In the same year, on the fourth day before the Kalends of March, Pope Urban consecrated the Crucified One of the monastery of the Holy Trinity at Vendôme, and remitted one-seventh of their sins to all who each year celebrated there the anniversary of that consecration.”

The same account is found in an old manuscript of the monastery of Vendôme. By the name “Crucified One,” however, we should understand the altar of the Holy Cross, which still stands behind the high altar and is commonly called the Matutinal altar. This is established by an old manuscript Missal of the same monastery, in which the feast of this dedication is recorded under the title “Concerning the Matutinal altar,” and so forth. We shall publish the complete notice in the Appendix.

## CCXLIX. The Council of Rouen.

While the pontiff was visiting these regions, the prelates of Normandy, together with abbots and other clerics and the leading men of the province, were summoned by William, the metropolitan, to Rouen for a provincial council in February. There, as Orderic relates in Book IX, they unanimously reviewed the decrees of the synod held at Clermont; they also confirmed the apostolic decisions, adding eight canons, which the same author reports and which are found in Labbe.

## CCL. The apostolic mission of Abbot Jarenton to England.

To this same period belongs the apostolic mission of Jarenton, abbot of Dijon, to England, which Hugh of Flavigny describes in his Chronicle of Verdun.

King William of England had indeed obtained from Walter, bishop of Albano, who had brought the pallium for Saint Anselm in Urban’s name, an agreement that no legate would be sent from the Apostolic See to England without the king’s command. But Jarenton’s reputation was so great, and his steadfastness of mind in addressing the king was so free from flattery, that the king, afraid to oppose him openly, promised that he would comply with his counsels and wishes.

The cunning king, however, intended to deceive the unsuspecting simplicity of this pious man. He had already secretly sent messengers to Urban to ask him for a new postponement. After obtaining it in fact and informing Jarenton of it, Jarenton, having accomplished nothing, immediately departed from England.

Returning to Gaul, he stopped in Normandy, where he established peace between the same king and his brother, the duke of Normandy, who shortly afterward departed for the holy war.

But our narrative must return to Urban’s journey.

## CCLI. Pope Urban arrives at Tours. He writes on behalf of Manasses, archbishop-elect of Reims. He preaches publicly. He dedicates the basilica of the Major Monastery. Regulations for Saint Martin.

At the beginning of March Urban arrived at Tours, where he seems first to have lodged at the Major Monastery. For he came there on the third day of that month, as may be inferred from the account of the dedication of the basilica of that place, which took place on the sixth day before the Ides of March, the eighth day after his arrival at the monastery.

From this we can reconstruct the entire sequence of days that the pontiff spent on this journey. As we have seen, on February 14 he was at Sablé. The next day he departed and arrived at Le Mans, where he remained for three days—that is, on the sixteenth and the two following days. On the nineteenth he proceeded to Vendôme. Since, according to Geoffrey’s letters, he spent eleven days there, he could not have departed before March 2 or 3; and thus he must in fact have arrived at Tours on one of those two days.

On the fourth day of that month he wrote to the suffragan bishops of the Church of Reims, urging them not to delay any longer the ordination of Manasses, their elected metropolitan. They complied with these letters, for Manasses was consecrated in the basilica of the monastery of Saint Remigius on the tenth day before the Kalends of April by Hugh of Soissons, with five other bishops of the province present and laying hands upon him.

He had resolved to visit the pontiff immediately after his inauguration, as is clear from his letter to Lambert of Arras, published by Baluze in volume V of the *Miscellanea*. Whether he did so, however, is uncertain.

Meanwhile, Urban frequently visited the church of Saint Martin, at times staying in its castle, at times in the city itself, and at times in the nearby Major Monastery, for as long as he remained at Tours.

On the seventh day before the Ides—that is, March 9, which was a Sunday—after celebrating Masses at the Major Monastery, the pontiff went to a wooden platform that had been prepared above the bank of the Loire. There he delivered an address. An innumerable crowd of people of every condition and age attended, together with Count Fulk of Anjou, then lord of Tours, and other nobles.

It is more than probable that on this occasion the pontiff spoke about the holy expedition. This, unless I am mistaken, is where we should place the event recorded in the *History of Amboise*, volume X of the *Spicilegium*: Hugh of Chaumont and Hameric of Couronne are said to have sewn the banner of the holy cross in the church of Saint Martin of the Major Monastery, in the pope’s presence and with many others joining them.

The next day, the sixth day before the Ides of March, the pontiff, together with other bishops and cardinals, solemnly dedicated the greater basilica of that monastery; on the following day he blessed the cemetery.

An old author apud Bochellus has described these ceremonies excellently, listing the names of the bishops who were present. We have thought it appropriate to reproduce his account in full in the Appendix, together with an old notice concerning certain rights which Hugh of Chaumont, mentioned above, ceded to the monastery on that occasion.

The importance of this dedication is also attested by various documents from the same place, said to have been issued from the year in which it took place. It is reported that the pontiff then entered the monks’ chapter-house, sat with them, and, after giving an exhortation, granted them absolution according to the custom of those times.

Since Urban had therefore frequently visited the church of Saint Martin for seven days or more, on the second day before the Ides of March, while staying in its castle, he issued an order regulating the manner in which legates of the Apostolic See were to be received in that basilica.

And because certain privileges of that church had granted its canons the right to have their own bishop, Urban decreed that henceforth, in place of such a bishop, they should adhere specially to the Roman pontiff, and that their more serious causes should depend upon his judgment.

On this occasion it is useful to report what is found in an old manuscript concerning the iron chains which may still be seen joining the four principal columns of the choir of that basilica near the vault. It reads:

> “Pope Urban II, as a sign of the union of the proper bishop of this church with the Roman pontiff and the Roman Church, ordered the four chief columns of the choir of the same church to be encircled by four iron chains.”

The Chronicle of Tours says that the same pontiff visited the tomb of Saint Martin for seven days and more, as we have already stated, and that each day he was solemnly received at the treasurer’s gate by the clergy of that church.

## CCLII. The Council of Tours. Marbod ordained bishop of Rennes there. Restoration of the monastery of Saint Maurus at Glanfeuil. Cormaric restored to Saint Martin. Those who attended the council. The primacy of the bishop of Lyon confirmed. Whether King Philip was absolved there. Eblo excommunicated. The privilege of Bainson. The privilege of Tournus. The dispute between the monks of Tournus and the canons of Angers settled. The foundation of Rota confirmed. The privilege of Saint Vincent of Metz.

In the following week, which was the third week of Lent, the lord pope, as Bertold records, held a synod with bishops of various provinces in the city of Tours, where once again he strengthened the decrees of his previous councils by the assent of a general synod.

Orderic Vitalis says the same at the beginning of Book IX; the author of the Chronicle of Malleais asserts that the council was held in the monastery of Saint Martin.

Whether new canons were enacted there is uncertain, since none are found anywhere, and the council appears to have been held chiefly so that the pontiff might add authority to the preceding synods.

Nevertheless, we learn from ancient authors and documents that various matters were discussed there and various cases brought to a conclusion.

There, moreover, Marbod, as the Sammarthani report from the cartulary of Saint Albinus in *Gallia Christiana*, was elected bishop of Rennes from the office of archdeacon of Angers and, with God’s consent, was ordained pontiff by the reverend Pope Urban in the holy Council of Tours of the Church of the Apostolic See.

The monks of Saint Albinus testify to the same in an encyclical letter concerning his death. After resigning his bishopric, he had become a monk among them and died in 1123.

Among the other causes discussed there, the restoration of the monastery of Saint Maurus at Glanfeuil to its former liberty is especially notable. The abbots of Fosses had deprived it of that liberty for more than two hundred years.

The author of the Chronicle of Malleais mentions the matter. Peter the Deacon, in Book IV of the *Chronicle of Monte Cassino*, adds that on this occasion Glanfeuil was restored to the principal monastery of Monte Cassino, as it had always been before the invasion of the Fosses monks.

But no one explained the matter better than Urban himself in two bulls issued concerning it: the first addressed to Gerard, the new abbot; the second to Oderisius, abbot of Monte Cassino, to whom the restoration was made.

In these bulls, forty-four Fathers—that is, archbishops, bishops, and abbots—are said to have attended the Council of Tours. They considered it a matter of religious obligation not to pronounce on this affair without careful examination and mature deliberation.

Thus, when Ivo of Chartres later appealed to Pope Paschal against this judgment at the instigation of the Fosses monks, in Letter 159, he could obtain nothing. Thereafter the monks of Glanfeuil remained free from the yoke of Fosses.

The body of Saint Maurus, however, was retained at the monastery of Fosses. From this circumstance it gradually acquired the name of Saint Maurus, which it still bears today. It lies about two leagues from the city of Paris, and its monks have been converted into canons.

The Council of Tours also dealt with the monastery of Cormaric, which had been unjustly torn away from the jurisdiction of Saint Martin. It was therefore decreed that it should be restored to him and that, thereafter, whenever the abbot of Cormaric died, his staff should be placed upon the tomb of Saint Martin. The man who had been lawfully elected as his successor would then receive it by common command of the dean and chapter, before being blessed as abbot by the archbishop of Tours according to the common custom of the Church.

These matters are treated more fully in Urban’s bull issued at Poitiers several days later. From it, as well as from the old instrument of the dedication of the church of the Major Monastery mentioned above, we learn the names of several bishops who attended the council.

But neither there nor in any other ancient record have we been able to find the name of Bernard, archbishop of Toledo, although some more recent writers wish him to have come to this synod. He certainly took part in the following June in the dedication of the church of Saint Saturninus at Toulouse, and in July in the Council of Nîmes, as we shall relate in their proper places.

Since no acts of that council survive, it is not surprising that we are ignorant of the names of most of those who gathered there. Even those who are known are generally known by chance, as has happened in most cases.

Thus we learn that Benedict, bishop of Nantes, and Raynald, abbot of Saint Cyprian, were then at Tours only from a donation made by that bishop to Saint Cyprian at that time. We shall give the notice of this donation in the Appendix.

Likewise, from a bull of Urban issued in 1099 in favor of Hugh, bishop of Lyon, it is clear that this prelate again brought complaints before the council against Richer, metropolitan of Sens, who still refused to obey the decree concerning the primacy of Lyon over his church.

Those who say that King Philip was absolved from excommunication at this council are mistaken. For it is certain from Urban’s own letter, written shortly afterward to the bishops of France, that several Gallican bishops did indeed wish to attempt this at the time, but that the Fathers of the synod resisted them together with the pontiff.

The excommunication long before issued against Eblo, the invader of the church of Saint Gregory on the island of Oléron, which belonged to the monks of Vendôme, was also confirmed there. We cite William, count of Poitiers, as witness to this in the frequently mentioned document, which will be reproduced in its proper place.

On the thirteenth day before the Kalends of April—that is, March 20—the pontiff affirmed by an apostolic rescript the liberty of the monastery of Bainson, situated not far from the castle above the Marne, which he says belonged to him by inheritance from his parents.

On that same day he granted another privilege to Peter, abbot of Tournus. After confirming that place, its goods, and its possessions, the privilege asserts that, in accordance with the judgment rendered at the Council of Tours itself, the same monastery should possess the two churches situated at Loudun, which the monks of Saint Florent claimed as belonging to them by right.

Besides this bull, an old document on the matter survives among the proofs for the *History of Tournus*, published by Chifflet from an old copy. It preserves one decree of this synod that was previously unknown.

Calixtus II confirmed Urban’s judgment in a privilege granted in 1122 to Abbot Franco, also published there by Chifflet, p. 409.

We have stated that Urban brought before the Council of Tours the dispute between the same monastery and the bishop and canons of the cathedral church of Angers concerning certain churches of the castle of Doué.

The outcome of the dispute must be learned from a charter of Geoffrey, bishop of Angers, which may be found among the proofs for the *History of Tournus*. It says that the Fathers assembled at Tours before Hugh of Lyon, Ralph of Tours, Guy of Vienne, and Hildebert of Bourges, archbishops; Bruno of Signi, Hoel of Le Mans, and William-elect of Auvergne, bishops; and the cardinals Adalbert and Teuthio, together with other judges delegated by the pontiff.

After much had been presented on both sides, when the judges were about to pronounce sentence, the parties, through the intervention of the judges, agreed to the following arrangement: certain rights and revenues of the Church of Angers, specified in the charter, were to be reserved, while the churches of Doué were to remain with the monks. After the death of the canons who still remained there, the monks would be permitted to replace them.

On the twelfth day before the Kalends of April, the foundation of the monastery of Rota near Credon was confirmed in the same council. As we have said above, Urban had already approved it at Angers.

On that day, which was celebrated because of the feast of Saint Benedict, the apostolic man celebrated Mass with the greatest devotion, as an old document records apud the Sammarthani and in volume II of Baluze’s *Miscellanea*.

On that same day the pontiff also granted a privilege to Lantzo, abbot of Saint Vincent of Metz. After affirming its goods and possessions, he confirmed to the abbot and his successors that, in the absence of the bishop of Metz, the abbot of Saint Vincent could, on feast days, celebrate the solemnity of Mass in the cathedral church of the city wearing sandals and a dalmatic, as had already been established by his predecessors.

## CCLIII. The conclusion of the Council of Tours. Solemn procession.

I do not remember ever reading on what day the Council of Tours ended, although everyone agrees that it was held in the third week of Lent.

Yet, unless I am mistaken, it concluded with the famous procession described by Count Fulk of Anjou, who was present, in the fragment of his *History* already mentioned. He writes:

> “After decrees had been issued by the venerable council, the pontiff was crowned in mid-Lent and, in a solemn procession, was led from the church of Saint Maurice, which is the archbishop’s see, to the church of blessed Martin. There he gave me a golden flower which he was carrying in his hand. In memory and affection for him, I in turn established that it should always be carried by me and my successors in the Osanna—that is, as I infer, in the Palm Sunday procession.”

The Chronicle of Tours reports that the same pontiff, in mid-Lent, crowned himself in the church of Saint Martin with a palm crown according to Roman custom and there celebrated Mass at the Lord’s altar.

It is not entirely clear whether he did this on the Thursday of mid-Lent itself, or on the following day, when, as we have said, he celebrated Mass with the greatest devotion on the feast of Saint Benedict, or rather on the following Sunday, which that year was the first Sunday after mid-Lent, as is clear from the chronological tables. The last possibility, however, is more likely.

For the procession in which the pontiff customarily carries a golden rose was held on this very Sunday of mid-Lent, when *Laetare* is sung, and this was already customary in antiquity, as is clear from the old Roman ordines edited by Mabillon in volume II of the *Museum Italicum*, from Cangio’s *Glossary*, and from various other authors.

## CCLIV. The privilege of Corbie. The reconciliation of the bishop of Strasbourg. Letter to the bishops of France. The judgment of the Council of Arles.

On the following Tuesday, namely the eighth day before the Kalends of April, a day celebrated because of the feast of the Annunciation of the Lord, Urban, still residing at Tours, granted a privilege to Nicholas, abbot of Corbie, by which he confirmed the distinguished rights and prerogatives of that place.

Perhaps the pontiff was still there when, not long after the Council of Tours, as Bertold relates, he received the bishop of Strasbourg back into communion after the bishop had repented of his excommunication, subject to his purging himself of the charges brought against him.

To the same period may also be assigned Urban’s letter to Richer of Sens and the other bishops of France, who appeared to be continuing to uphold the excommunication decreed against King Philip on account of his adulterous marriage.

In this letter the pontiff summons those same prelates to a council which he had decided to hold at Arles toward the end of June. In fact, however, it was held at Nîmes.

## CCLV. At Poitiers the pope confirms the privilege of Saint Martin. A hearing concerning the dispute between the canons of Saint Hilary and the monks of the New Monastery. The privilege of Angles.

Toward the end of March the pontiff returned to Poitiers, as three charters issued there at that time for the canons of Saint Martin inform us. In the first, the pontiff declares that he had completely eradicated the stain of simony that had prevailed in obtaining prebends [Col. 0203B] in the Church of Saint Martin; he then praises and confirms the privileges of that distinguished basilica, and repeats what he had already established on another occasion: namely, that, once its own [office or jurisdiction] had been suppressed, he himself and his successors, the Roman pontiffs, would take its place. This bull was issued on the fourth day before the Kalends of April [29 March]; Pope Innocent, at Lyons, on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of May [14 April], in the fifth year of his pontificate, approved it and confirmed it with a new bull, having transcribed and collated it word for word from the original. In the second rescript, issued on the following day, that is, the third day before the Kalends of April [30 March], Urban exhorts all the archbishops and bishops of Gaul to protect the privileges and possessions of the Church of Saint Martin located in their respective dioceses. On that same day a third privilege was issued [Col. 0203C], by which, in accordance with what had been decreed at the Council of Tours, the monastery of Cormery is asserted to belong to the basilica of Saint Martin. Together with Pope Urban, the other archbishops and bishops listed there subscribe this charter.

There is no doubt that on this same occasion the blessed pontiff also visited again the tomb of Saint Hilary, whose feast he had already solemnly celebrated in January. For there, together with many bishops and nobles, he held a hearing in the chapter-house of Saint Hilary in order to settle the dispute that had arisen between the canons of that church and the monks of the New Monastery over the church of Saint Nicholas, which, as we have already said, had been assigned to those monks. The pontiff delivered judgment on this matter [Col. 0203D] with three archbishops, an equal number of bishops, two abbots, and very many other distinguished men of both orders sitting beside him, as he himself relates in a rescript issued several days later at Saintes concerning the matter. Moreover, if one may infer it from the proximity of the places, Urban’s privilege granted to the monastery of Angoulême among the Poitevins, for the regular canons, may also be assigned to this period. This privilege is praised by the Sammarthani from a bull of Innocent III in volume IV of *Gallia Christiana*; nor is it permissible to say more about it, since it has not been possible to recover it.

### CCLVI. At Saint-Maixent he grants a privilege to the monks of Glanfeuil.

On the day before the Kalends of April [31 March], at Saint-Maixent in the same province, Urban lodged in the noble Benedictine monastery that gave its name to the town [Col. 0204A]. There he granted Gerard, the new abbot of the monastery of Saint-Maur at Glanfeuil, a most extensive privilege, an exemplar of which, already praised above, will later be published among the pontifical letters, having been extracted from the archive of the monastery of Monte Cassino.

### CCLVII. Pope Urban passes through Saint-Jean-d’Angély and grants privileges.

From there the pontiff entered Saintes and turned aside to the town of Saint-Jean-d’Angély, to the monastery of Saint John, as he himself testifies in the rescript by which he confirmed to Abbot Ansculf and the other monks of that monastery the possessions of the place, especially the Church of Bury, situated in the diocese of Beauvais. We include here that rescript, which in the Angély cartulary [Col. 0204B] lacks chronological notes; but a privilege of the New Monastery of Poitiers informs us that he spent 7 April there, for it is said to have been issued at Angély on that very day. There too the excommunication pronounced against Eblo, the invader of the Church of Saint George on the island of Oléron, was renewed, as is recorded in the frequently cited document of William, duke of Aquitaine.

### CCLIX. At Saintes he celebrates Easter. The privilege of Saint Martial. The privilege of Saint Aubin. He confirms the customs of the Church of Reims. Eblo the invader is cursed. He consecrates the altar of Saint Eutropius.

From there the pontiff proceeded to Saintes, where he solemnly celebrated the festival of the sacred Resurrection of the Lord, as Count Fulk records in a fragment of the *History of Anjou* [Col. 0204C], and as various ancient documents repeatedly attest. The author of the Chronicle of Maillezais agrees, adding after the Council of Tours mentioned above: “From there he returned to the city of Saintes and celebrated Holy Easter there.” By these words that author seems to indicate that the pontiff visited the city of Saintes twice, something not found in the other writers. Sirmond wrote in his notes on Geoffrey of Vendôme that Urban was received there by Bishop Ramnulf on the Ides of April [13 April]. But one may infer from this alone that it occurred at least a day or two earlier, since it is unlikely that Urban would have set out on a journey on Easter Day itself. Certainly, as we have seen, he had arrived at Angers eight days earlier; and it is established that he was at least at Saintes on the eve of Easter [Col. 0204D], as we gather from his bull issued on that very day in favor of Adhemar, abbot of Saint Martial of Limoges.

That privilege is noteworthy. After confirming to the monastery various possessions and churches, which the pontiff lists individually, it “established that, in the absence of the bishop of Limoges, the abbot of Saint Martial, together with the principal canons of the church, should have particular responsibility for the diocese, and also that the episcopal election should be arranged chiefly at his discretion; and finally, that the principal affairs of that Church should be conducted with his advice even when the bishop was present.” Our Stephanotius had transcribed this bull from the Limoges original, and we also possess it from other manuscripts and printed editions [Col. 0205A]. The distinguished Étienne Baluze collated it, as he himself told me, against another original in the monastery of Cluny; but the copy found there lacks the lead seal, and several variant readings occur. In both originals the date is given as 1097 instead of 1096, a practice likewise observable in many other documents of wholly unquestionable authenticity—namely, those in which, according to the Pisan reckoning, the year from the Incarnation of the Lord begins in the preceding March. Pope Paschal II confirmed the same privilege in another bull, issued at Rome in 1103 and sealed with lead. The learned Baluze assured me that he had seen both originals at Cluny.

On Easter Monday, which fell on 14 April [Col. 0205B], the pontiff confirmed there all the possessions of the monastery of Saint Aubin of Angers by a bull. A charter issued on the same day and in the same city in favor of the New Monastery of Poitiers reports what the pontiff had established at the assembly held at Saint Hilary, mentioned above, on the occasion of the disputes that had arisen between the canons of Saint Hilary and the monks of the New Monastery residing at the priory of Saint Nicholas. Finally, on that same day the pontiff also confirmed the customs of the Church of Reims at the request of its canons, who had sent several of their number to Urban for this purpose; he received them graciously. William Marlot reproduces the papal letters and considers the customs mentioned in that rescript to be precisely those [Col. 0205C] published by him in volume II of the *Metropolis of Reims*.

In the same city the pontiff cursed Eblo, who had already been excommunicated so many times for his invasion of the Church of Saint George on the island of Oléron. This was confirmed by the judgment of the archbishops, bishops, abbots, and religious clerics, who had established that he had long unjustly held the land of the monks of Vendôme. Thus he departed cursed by the pope. A mandate was given to Amatus, archbishop of Bordeaux, to visit William, duke of Aquitaine, and exhort him to arrange the restoration of that land to the monks of Vendôme; and this was in fact done. All these matters are recorded in the charter of the same duke. Although Besly had already published it, we considered it worthwhile to reprint it from the Vendôme cartulary, since the entire course of this affair is clearly displayed there and it can contribute greatly to elucidating Urban’s acts [Col. 0205D].

At this time the Cluniac monks, who for several years had occupied the ancient monastery of Saint Eutropius at Saintes and had renovated the crypt containing the relics of the holy martyr, together with its two altars, took advantage of this distinguished opportunity. They approached the pontiff and asked him not to disdain consecrating at least one of these altars with his own hand. He granted their request, leaving the consecration of the other altar to Ramnulf, the diocesan bishop. It is recorded in an old notice written by a contemporary author [Col. 0206A] that this took place on Low Sunday. We shall reproduce the notice in the Appendix to this volume. From this it may be inferred that Urban spent approximately two weeks at Saintes.

### CCLX. Whether Urban visited Angoulême.

Whether he went from there to Angoulême is uncertain. But from chapter 33 of the *History of the Bishops and Counts of that City*, published in volume II of Labbe’s *Bibliotheca*, we learn that the restoration of a provostship of the Church of Saint Peter—that is, the cathedral church—was made at the urging of Bishop Adhemar and confirmed by that pontiff.

### CCLXI. At Bordeaux he dedicates the major church.

Whatever the truth of that matter, it is certain that Urban arrived at Bordeaux toward the end of April, where on the first day of May he solemnly dedicated the major church. We learn this from an old codex cited by Lopes [Col. 0206B].
