Although it erroneously states that this consecration took place in 1026, the sequence of events proves beyond doubt that it must be assigned to the present year. Certainly Urban himself testifies in a rescript to the canons of Bordeaux that he had consecrated the major church of that city; and those listed in the document were companions of his journey.

It will not be out of place to reproduce here the description of the ceremony from that old codex, as it is presented by Darval in the supplement to the Bordeaux chronicle and by Lopez in chapter 5 of his history of the same city:

“In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1016—read 1096—that is, on the Kalends of May [1 May], the Bordeaux Church, which is the house of the Lord, was dedicated in honor of the blessed apostles Andrew and Peter, and of the blessed John [Col. 0206C] the Baptist, Saint Stephen, Lawrence, and the martyr Vincent, and of the blessed confessor Macarius, and of the holy virgins Agatha and Eulalia. Their relics were placed in the major altar at the very consecration by the lord pope and by Amatus, legate of the Holy Roman Church and archbishop of Bordeaux. Five deans were present, as well as Simeon, bishop of Agen; Bruno, bishop of Signi; Albert [Walter], bishop of Albano; and other cardinals.”

It is remarkable that the anniversary of this dedication is celebrated on 21 April, perhaps because it coincides with the feast of the blessed James and Philip, or perhaps because of some other ancient consecration of that church.

### CCLXII. At Nérac he dedicates the church of the monastery of Saint Thomas.

[Col. 0206D] Passing through Nérac, a town of Gascony, the pontiff solemnly consecrated there a church in honor of Saint Thomas and Saint Nicholas. Arsinus of Albion, having granted the village of Locus on that condition, installed there monks summoned from the monastery of Saint Peter of Condom, at the request of his brother Raymond, who was then abbot of Condom. In the sixteenth century the monks of that place imitated the monks of the Church of Condom, which had been made a cathedral by John XXII; they exchanged their monastic habit for the secular dress of canons. We shall give in the Appendix a brief notice of this dedication from the Condom cartulary.

### CCLXIII. At Layrac he confirms the monastery of Montaut for Cluny.

On the Nones, or 7 May, the same pontiff visited Layrac [Col. 0207A], where there is a Cluniac priory. There, in a rescript addressed to Hugh, abbot of Cluny, he confirmed that William, later archbishop of Auch, had given the cell of Saint Michael of Montaut, with all its dependencies, to Cluny when he became a monk. That rescript will later be published among Urban’s letters, transcribed from an old copy, perhaps from the original.

### CCLXIV. At Toulouse he grants a privilege to Moissac. The privilege of Saint Orientius.

On the same day, unless the chronological notes in our copies are misleading—or at any rate, the place where the rescript was issued is genuine—the pontiff arrived at Toulouse. There he issued letter no. 192 to the neighboring bishops on behalf of the monks of Moissac, asking them to protect their possessions, each within his own [Col. 0207B] diocese.

Several days later the pontiff himself visited the monastery of Moissac. There, on the third day before the Ides of May [13 May], he wrote another letter to Saint Hugh on behalf of the Cluniac monks of Saint Orientius near Auch, by which he confirmed, as had already been decreed by Leo IX, their right to a cemetery. The same pontiff confirmed these letters in another rescript, as we shall relate below in its proper place. Urban also consecrated the altar of the Holy Savior in that monastery, if we may trust the chronicle written by Aymeric de Peyrac, abbot of the place. The same author reports that, while Urban was present there, one cardinal died and was buried in the monastery arch; at his tomb, he declares, he saw the cardinal’s hat hanging high above it, almost entirely consumed by excessive age [Col. 0207C].

### CCLXV. At Toulouse he grants a privilege to Belleloc. He dedicates the Church of Saint Saturninus. A dispute between the canons of Toulouse and the monks of Cluny.

After returning to Toulouse, the pontiff attached the monastery of Belleloc among the Limousins to the Cluniac order, since no regular discipline was being maintained there, issuing a letter to Saint Hugh on the 23rd of this month.

On the following day, that is, the ninth day before the Kalends of June [24 May], Urban solemnly dedicated the Church of Saint Saturninus in the same city, as various authors have noted and as the pontiff himself testified in a bull issued to the canons of that Church several months later. Certainly [Col. 0207D] Paschal II, in a letter to the king of Aragon, says that the Church of Saint Saturninus had been consecrated by Urban, his predecessor, together with seventeen archbishops and bishops, and furnished with apostolic privileges. Amelius, bishop of Toulouse, likewise confirmed the privileges granted by Gregory VII, Urban II, and Paschal II concerning the liberty of the Church of Saint Saturninus.

But the matter is set out more fully by the author of the ancient Chronicle cited by Catel, book II, chapter 3 of the *History of the Counts of Toulouse*, and in the Appendix from an old manuscript, where we read:

“In the year of the Lord 1096, indiction IV, on the ninth day before the Kalends of June [24 May], the lord Pope Urban, together with Bernard, archbishop of Toledo; Amatus, archbishop of Bordeaux; the archbishop of Pisa; Tisus [the archbishop of Albano]; Galterus, bishop of Albi; and Peter, bishop of Pamplona [Col. 0208A], with ten others, consecrated the Church of Saint Saturninus, martyr and bishop of Toulouse, and the altar in honor of that most glorious martyr and of Saint Assisclus the martyr. He placed there the greater part of the head of the most glorious Saturninus, the relics of Saint Assisclus the martyr and of other saints, and the relics of Saint Exuperius, bishop of Toulouse.”

The pontiff was still staying in that city when the canons of the cathedral Church of Saint Stephen brought complaints before him against the monks of Saint Michael of Clusa. The monks maintained that the Church of Saint Gavella, which had been granted to the Church of Toulouse, belonged to them by right. The pontiff appointed a hearing at Saint Mary of the Elect, where this dispute was to be settled; but when the monks refused to attend, the matter remained unresolved [Col. 0208B]. Its entire course—which is of no concern to us here—may be found in an old document published by Catel in book V of his *Commentaries on the History of Occitania*, p. 875. Certainly several monasteries in these regions were subject to the monastery of Clusa. Among them, a lost bull of Urban lists the monastery of Mansi Garnerius near Verdun on the Garonne, in the diocese of Toulouse, now attached to the Congregation of Saint Maur.

### CCLXVI. Pope Urban visits Carcassonne.

Leaving Toulouse, the pontiff proceeded to Carcassonne, as the geographical situation and the sequence of days seem to require. We learn from old compilations of the history of that city [Col. 0208C] that he arrived there on Wednesday, 11 June, and spent five days in the city. They read as follows:

“In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1096, indiction IV, on the seventy-fourth [perhaps the twenty-fourth] day of the moon, Wednesday, Pope Urban entered Carcassonne and celebrated Masses there. Blessing and absolving the living and the dead, he also blessed the stones of the Church of Blessed Nazarius, that is, the cathedral church; these stones, as Besly interprets it, had been prepared for completing that church, whose construction had been begun long before. On the following Friday he celebrated Masses upon the altar of the blessed Mary, ever-virgin, and of the Holy Savior; he preached a sermon to us; he absolved the cemetery with his own hands by sprinkling it with salt; and thus, after remaining with us for five days, he departed with praise and thanksgiving, having made the sign over the living and the dead.”

Besly, in his *History of the Bishops of Carcassonne* [Col. 0208D], and the Sammarthani, in their catalogue in volume II of *Gallia Christiana*, agree with this. The abbey of Saint Mary and the Holy Savior, whose altar is mentioned here, was situated in the suburb of Carcassonne and in the following century passed to secular canons. Later, after being destroyed during the military disturbances of the Albigensian wars, the site—or rather the place where it had stood—passed to the Capuchin Fathers, who have a convent there. As Besly observes, Pontius was abbot of the place in 1085; but whether he was still alive when Urban came there is unknown. Peter was then bishop of the Church of Carcassonne. In the diocese of that city there is also the distinguished monastery of Saint Mary of Crassus, to which Urban is said to have granted a privilege, now lost, in the bulls of later pontiffs [Col. 0209A].

### CCLXVII. He then visits Thomières. The privilege of Pamplona.

From there Urban departed and celebrated the Nativity of Saint John the Baptist at the town of Thomières, distinguished by the name and monastery of Saint Pontius, which was later erected as a cathedral church. On that very day he confirmed the privileges and other rights of the Church of Pamplona, specifying its diocesan boundaries individually. The papal bull on this matter is addressed to Peter of Roda, or Rota, bishop of that city, who had previously been a monk of Termes.

### CCLXVIII. Urban consecrates Maguelone.

It may easily be gathered from the letters of Ivo of Chartres that Urban then turned aside to Montpellier [Col. 0209B]. But it is not equally certain, according to many authorities, whether he consecrated the island of Maguelone at that time, although all agree that this was done by that pontiff either in this year or the preceding one. Certainly, if Urban dedicated the church of Asti on the Kalends of July [1 July] in 1095, as he hurried toward Gaul, then it cannot be said that he was at Maguelone at the end of June of that same year.

And indeed, if Arnaldus de Verdala, bishop of Maguelone, were consistent in his account of his predecessors, there would seem to be no difficulty. But he confuses events and dates. He assigns this blessing of the island to the year 1096, but immediately adds the celebration of the Council of Clermont, which no one can deny was held in 1095 [Col. 0209C]. If, however, we are willing to rely on the chronological notes that he provides—and he could much more easily have erred in assigning the year than in reporting the chronological notes, which he does not seem to have invented—it is much more probable that Urban performed this act in the present year, 1096, when he was returning to Italy.

This author says that the pontiff arrived at Maguelone on the eve of the feast of the Apostles and blessed the island on the second day after his arrival, which was a Sunday. These chronological indications do not at all fit the year 1095, but fit 1096 exactly. In that year 29 June, the day sacred to Saints Peter and Paul, fell on a Sunday. It is useful to quote Arnaldus’s entire passage, in which he represents in a few words all that Urban did at Maguelone [Col. 0209D]:

“In the year 1096, on the eve of the feast of the Apostles Peter and Paul, Pope Urban II, who had crossed the Alps to visit and confirm the churches of Gaul, entered Maguelone at the request of Bishop Gotofredus and stayed there for five days. On the second day after his arrival, namely Sunday, after almost the entire clergy and people of the bishopric of Maguelone had assembled, he preached a sermon. In the presence of the archbishops of Pisa and Tarragona, and of the bishops of Albano, Signi, Nîmes, and Maguelone; with Count of Substantion, William lord of Montpellier, and nobles from throughout the surrounding land in attendance, he solemnly consecrated the whole island of Maguelone. He granted to all who had been or would be buried there absolution from all their sins, and bestowed many other privileges upon that Church. He decreed that it should be honored in second place after the Roman Church, and earnestly admonished the faithful from every place to arrange to be buried there. Then Bishop Gotofredus established that, in commemoration and veneration of this procession, every year on that day a solemn procession should be made by the clergy and people around the said church, and that twelve poor persons should be fed.”

### CCLXIX. At Montpellier he deals with the election of the bishop of Paris.

At Montpellier, which today is the seat of the bishop of Maguelone, the pontiff, at the request of King Philip, investigated the election of William as bishop of Paris. Some regarded William as suspect in faith for this reason: the elected William was the brother of Bertrada, whom Philip had taken as his wife after repudiating his former wife. There was therefore reason to suspect that he had been requested by the Parisian clergy through some form of favor or human fear.

Urban entrusted the examination of the matter locally to Ivo, bishop of Chartres, an upright man strongly opposed to all flattery, who was then present at the Roman court. He arranged that, if the canons of Paris removed by oath every suspicion of simony, William could be ordained by Richer of Sens, his own metropolitan. On this sole occasion Richer was granted permission to use the pallium, which had been forbidden him at the Council of Clermont because he had refused obedience to Hugh, primate of Lyons.

When the Parisian clerics had cleared themselves by oath of having made the election on their own, William was ordained by Richer before the feast of Saint Remigius. Ivo relates this in letters 50 and 54. Even before that time he had written in William’s favor in letter 43, since William, having been brought up in the Church of Chartres, was well known to him. Here it is worth observing how carefully Urban guarded against anything improper entering episcopal ordinations. The vigilant pontiff adopted these precautions solely to remove even every appearance of evil from this election.

### CCLXX. Urban holds a council at Nîmes. He consecrates the cathedral church. A dispute between the bishop of Toulouse and the canons of Saint Saturninus. The privileges of Saint Saturninus confirmed. The dispute between Figeac and Conques. Raymond’s cession to Saint-Gilles. The rights of the monastery of Ripoll preserved. The primacy asserted for the bishop of Lyons. Guibert, abbot of Auxerre, deposed. The case of Anselm, the elected bishop of Beauvais, suspended. Was King Philip deposed there? The monks vindicated. The privilege of Saint-Martin-des-Champs.

[Col. 0210D]

At the beginning of July Urban held a council at Nîmes, a distinguished city of the province of Narbonne. We have already observed from the pontiff’s letter to Richer of Sens, cited above, that he had first summoned this council to Arles. At this council some matters established at earlier synods were confirmed, while others were newly enacted; together they are included in sixteen canons in the customary editions of the councils [Col. 0211A], but the acts of the council have perished.

Therefore, in order to present here something beyond the canons already mentioned, which will one day be published together with the other councils of Urban, it is worthwhile to record what we have been able to find in various ancient monuments concerning this synod. First, several prelates who attended the Council of Nîmes are listed in the charter of Count Raymond by which he confirmed the Flavian Valley to the monastery of Saint-Gilles. There were six metropolitans in all: Daimbert of Pisa, Hugh of Lyons, Amatus of Bordeaux, Bernard of Toledo—these three were legates of the Apostolic See—together with Hugh of Besançon and Guido, archbishop of Vienne. There were five bishops: namely, Galterus of Albano, Bruno of Signi, Gotofredus of Maguelone, Hugh [Humbaldus] of Auxerre, and Bertramnus of Nîmes [Col. 0211B]. There were also five non-episcopal cardinals, among them Richard, abbot of Marseille. The charter itself, which is more complete in Acher’s *Spicilegium* than in Labbe’s councils, is included in the Appendix.

Peter de Marca, in *Marca Hispanica*, col. 472, and Cardinal Aguirre, following him, in volume III of the *Councils of Spain*, write that three other Spanish bishops—Berengar of Tarragona, Bernard of Girona, and Artaldus of Elne—and an equal number of abbots—Peter of Cuxa, Benedict of Banyoles, and Bernard of Ripoll—also came to the same synod.

We have the names of more participants from Urban’s own charter issued in the case of the bishop of Toulouse and the canons of Saint Saturninus. For there, besides the seven metropolitans mentioned above, three other archbishops are named [Col. 0211C]: Radulfus of Tours, Gibelinus of Arles, and the archbishop of Embrun; the pontiff testifies that these, together with eighty-six bishops and abbots, were present at the same council. The names of others may be extracted from other monuments, some of which survive and will be cited below. Certainly, for example, no one, as it seems to me, will deny that Ivo of Chartres attended the same council, since, as he himself testifies in the letters cited above, he spoke with Urban at that time at Montpellier about William’s election as bishop of Paris.

No one, so far as I know, has expressly recorded on what day that synod began or was completed [Col. 0211D]. But from documents belonging to the cathedral Church of that city we learn that the pontiff was already at Nîmes on 6 July. These documents state that on that very day the church was consecrated by Urban in the presence of several archbishops and bishops, together with Count Raymond. Perhaps the synod began with this solemnity. Certainly, on the seventh day before the Ides [8 July], the dispute that had long been pending between the bishop of Toulouse and the canons of Saint Saturninus was considered there. As the pontiff himself testifies in the bull cited above, the matter was settled after various disputes on the fifth day before the Ides of that month [11 July].

It would be superfluous to set out the entire course of this controversy here, since it is contained in Urban’s aforementioned charter and in another of his bulls to the canons [Col. 0212A] of Saint Saturninus. Both will be presented in their proper places.

It is clear from an old document of the cathedral church of Toulouse concerning the same matter, published by Catel and subsequently by Labbe in volume X of the councils, that the canons were reluctant to accept Urban’s judgment. In that document they introduce Pope Callistus II, who had attended the Council of Nîmes as archbishop of Vienne, speaking as follows:

“I was present at the Council of Nîmes, at which the lord Pope Urban presided, together with many others, and there I heard the clerics of Saint Saturninus appeal to the lord pope, asking that he take away from Bishop Isarnus, who at that time held it in his possession, the fourth part of the offerings of the altar of blessed Saturninus and give it to them. The lord pope seemed to yield to their petitions, while Bishop Isarnus resisted them with great courage,” and so forth.

They then add that Guido himself, together with his brother, the archbishop of Briasson—read, of Besançon—strongly defended Isarnus’s side at the synod, so that Isarnus did not consent to Urban’s judgment until after the council had ended, when he was promised that he and his men would always have their livelihood from the Church of Saint Saturninus; and this he did enjoy as long as he lived.

The same canons nevertheless admit that, when the controversy was later reexamined in the presence of Callistus himself, the cathedral church, after many disputes had been conducted in various places concerning the matter, was unable to obtain anything. They insist, however, that this was attributable to the negligence of the bishop who then presided over the Church of Toulouse. But let us return to the council.

[Col. 0212C]

At the council all the privileges and rights that Urban and Count Raymond had granted to the Church of Saint Saturninus at its dedication were confirmed. This is evident not only from the papal bulls but also from other ancient documents. Catel presents two charters on this subject in his *History of the Counts of Toulouse*. In the first, Count Bertrand decrees as follows, on page 153:

“I establish the Church of Saint Saturninus as free from all [burdens], just as Pope Urban, with his bishops, and my father Count Raymond made it free in the consecration of that church and at the Council of Nîmes.”

William, count of Poitiers, and his wife Philippia say exactly the same thing on page 166 in another charter issued in 1098 [Col. 0212D].

On the seventh day before the Ides, that is, 9 July, the council dealt with the dispute between the monks of Figeac and Conques, which had arisen because the two monasteries had been joined under a single abbot; this union had become the source of many disagreements. What Urban decreed concerning the matter at the council will be explained below, where we shall discuss his rescript issued on this occasion at Flavian Valley.

On 12 July the aforementioned Count Raymond, in the presence of the pontiff and the entire council, relinquished the Flavian Valley, together with all the rights and customary dues that he had held, whether justly or unjustly, in the Villa Flaviana and its dependencies, to Abbot Odilo and the monastery of Saint-Gilles [Col. 0213A]. This is clear from the charter of the count himself and from Urban’s bull confirming it.

Berengar, bishop of Tarragona, likewise satisfied Bernard, abbot of Ripoll, who had brought complaints before the council against the bishop because, disregarding the privileges of the Apostolic See, he had placed under interdict the churches subject to the monastery of Ripoll. Berengar declared that this had been done without his knowledge. Perhaps the clerics of Ausona, in whose diocese—today that of Vic, then united to the Church of Tarragona—the monastery of Ripoll was situated, had done it without consulting him. It was therefore sufficient for the bishop to promise that in future he would faithfully observe the apostolic privileges.

This is related by the distinguished Peter de Marca in book IV of *Marca Hispanica*, and by Cardinal Aguirre [Col. 0213B] after him in volume III of the *Councils of Spain*. More information is found in an old history of the same place, published in the Appendix to *Marca Hispanica*, no. 44. For, as it says there, Berengar, so that nothing similar might be attempted in the future, praised and strengthened the privileges of the monastery and confirmed them with his own hand, a charter being drawn up to that effect. Shortly afterward the same Abbot Bernard is said to have followed Urban to the monastery of Saint-Gilles, where he obtained from him a distinguished privilege confirming all its rights and possessions.

Hugh, bishop of Lyons, also lodged a complaint at the Council of Nîmes against Richer, metropolitan of Sens, who had still not been persuaded to recognize, in accordance with the decrees of the Councils of Clermont and Tours [Col. 0213C], the primacy of the Church of Lyons. Hugh’s primacy was again confirmed at this synod, but Richer never submitted to him. For that reason he was placed under interdict and died shortly afterward, as may be gathered from Urban’s own rescript issued in 1099.

In the same council, Guibert, abbot of Saint-Germain at Auxerre, was summoned by Humbald, bishop of that city, on account of various crimes laid to his charge and was compelled to resign. Urban handed his staff to the bishop, on the condition that he appoint to this monastery a monk from La Chaise-Dieu, the Major Monastery, or Cluny, who would strive to restore regular discipline in so distinguished a place—and one deservedly so called. Guido, abbot of that same house, recounts this more fully in his *Deeds of His Predecessors*, volume I of Labbe’s *Bibliotheca*. This occasion provided the opportunity for introducing Cluniac monks into the monastery, as may be gathered from Urban’s rescript, which we shall discuss below.

We learn of another important matter treated in the same synod from a letter of Lambert, bishop of Arras, to Pope Paschal II. He states that Gerard, bishop of the Morini, was suspended from every episcopal office in the synod of Nîmes by Urban of blessed memory. Indeed, Manasses, archbishop of Reims, wrote to the same Lambert that he should entrust to him the care of the church of the Morini, which, as he says, had devolved upon him, since Gerard, its bishop, had not been granted the power to exercise his office.

For what reason this injury was inflicted upon Gerard is nowhere stated, either there or in the other letters published in volume V of the *Miscellanies of Baluze*. Malbrancus says, in book IX of *The Morini*, chapter 7, that Gerard was accused of simony and was also convicted because money had been given—without his knowledge—to secure this bishopric for him. The author of the *Life of Saint John*, who succeeded Gerard in that see, explains the matter more clearly. He says that Gerard had indeed been elected by the clergy and desired by the people, but that the king’s consent had been obtained, without Gerard’s knowledge, by a payment of money, which Gerard was afterward compelled to repay.

Gregory VII had doubtless been unaware of this. In book II, letter 1, he commended Gerard to Robert, count of Flanders, as canonically elected and as having entered the sheepfold of Christ through the door. Whatever the truth may be, the cited letters show that the case of this bishop was difficult to judge: they make clear that Gerard was suspended from every episcopal office, but was not deprived of his see. Hence Lambert of Arras did not hesitate, in the following year, to commend his case to the pontiff, as we shall see below.

The case of Anselm, the elected bishop of Beauvais, met with almost the same fate in that council. It was indeed discussed there, but not settled. Although many, including Hugo, bishop of Lyon, interceded on Anselm’s behalf, the pontiff nevertheless refused to approve his election; nor did he annul it, as may be gathered from Ivo’s letter 55. In that letter Ivo urges Urban to continue favoring Anselm and to assist the church of Beauvais, which was seeking him and had been thrown into great turmoil because his ordination was suspended—either by settling the matter himself or at least by allowing its judgment to be made by the metropolitan and the other bishops of the province. Urban also wrote to Hugo concerning this same Anselm, in letter 200.

If we trust the *Chronicle of Malleais*, Philip, king of the Franks, was reconciled to the Church by Urban at this council. Bertold does not disagree, although he does not specify the place where this occurred. He writes in his *Chronicle*:

> Philip, king of Gaul, who had long been excommunicated for adultery, at last, while the lord pope was still staying in Gaul, came quite humbly to make satisfaction; and, having renounced the adulterous woman, he was received back into favor, and showed himself very ready to serve the lord pope.

From these words some infer that Philip was present at the synod of Nîmes. Since the authors are silent on the matter, this is nevertheless improbable, especially since Ivo approached Urban in Philip’s name and spoke with him at Montpellier at that time. Indeed, Philip does not appear to have been fully reconciled to the Church before the beginning of the following year, as is clear from a letter of the pontiff himself to Manasses of Reims and the other bishops of France, written on that occasion and to be included in the Collection. Add to this canon 10 of this council, directed against adulterous marriages, which seems to concern Philip.

The canon of Tours tells fables in his *Chronicles* when he says that on this occasion Philip lost all the elections to the bishoprics of his kingdom and that the election of the bishop of Angers was then conferred upon Count Fulk.

The Fathers of the Council of Nîmes also vigorously defended the position of monks and the dignity and holiness of monastic life against their rivals, who, as they claimed on the precedent of earlier times, were attempting with rash audacity to exclude monks from clerical functions. This was accomplished chiefly through two canons.

This concludes the account of the Council of Nîmes.

The council appears to have been dissolved on the day before the Ides of July. On that day Urban claimed the monastery of Saint-Martin-des-Champs near Paris for the Cluniac order and confirmed its possessions, which he lists individually, by a privilege addressed to Hugo, abbot of Cluny.

### CCLXXI. Urban at Saint-Gilles. His precept concerning Figeac. The privilege of Ripoll. The privilege of Banyoles.

On this very day, or certainly the next, the pontiff left Nîmes and turned aside to Saint-Gilles in the Flavian Valley. There he confirmed by rescript what had been decreed at the Council of Nîmes concerning the dispute between the monks of Figeac and Conques. The rescript was issued at the monastery of Saint-Gilles on the Ides of July and was published from an old parchment by our Jean Mabillon in *The Benedictine Centuries*, century III, part II, p. 448.

It states that each place was to have its own abbot—or, as the pontiff calls him there, its own cardinal abbot—yet in such a way that Figeac, which the Cluniacs had claimed, would remain under the care and provision of the abbot of Cluny.

But in another copy, transcribed from the Figeac archives and communicated to us by the distinguished Étienne Baluze, the mention of the abbot of Cluny is omitted, and the council is said to have determined that each monastery should remain under the care of its own abbot. Which reading should be preferred others may decide. It is certain, however, that the monastery of Figeac remained under the Cluniac order until the sixteenth century, when its monks, laying aside their cowls, were changed into secular canons. That rescript, with its variants of reading, will be included among Urban’s letters.

On the seventeenth day before the Kalends of August, on the occasion of the acts committed against the churches of the monastery of Ripoll, as we mentioned shortly before, Urban confirmed the privileges of that monastery, also listing its possessions individually, in an impressive bull issued at the monastery of Saint-Gilles. On the following day, the same Urban fortified the monastery of Banyoles with an apostolic privilege, addressed to Abbot Benedict, issued there.

The distinguished Peter de Marca reported this privilege, as well as the preceding one, in book IV of his *Hispanic Marca* under the year 1097. But the other chronological notes, the sequence of events, and the place where they were issued prove conclusively that they must be assigned to the year 1096, even though they bear the year 1097 according to the Pisan computation, by which, as we have already observed more than once, the beginning of the year is reckoned from the preceding March.

On the fourteenth day before the Kalends of August, he granted an important privilege to Galburga, or Walburga, abbess of Saint Scholastica at Juvigny in the diocese of Trier. It was cited in a judicial proceeding in the year 1128 between Lanzon, abbot of Saint Michael on the Meuse, and Hardwig, abbess of Juvigny, published by Baluze in volume IV of the *Miscellanies*. From it we gather that Hardwig was elected in 1124, eighteen years after Walburga’s death; Walburga must therefore be said to have died in 1106.

On the following day Urban was still staying at the monastery of Saint-Gilles, as is indicated by his diploma for the church of Saint Saturninus. In it the pontiff gives a full account of the case between the canons of that church and Isarnus, bishop of Toulouse, which had been debated at the Council of Nîmes, as we said above.

### CCLXXII. Another privilege granted by Urban at Avignon. Another for Saint-Gilles. Another for the monastery of Saint Andrew. The church of Avignon given to regular canons.

He repeats almost the same matter in a bull issued two days later to the canons of that same church at the monastery of Mont Andaon, or Saint Andrew, situated in the suburb of Avignon, which is now called Villeneuve. On that same day, namely 22 July, he confirmed the gift of the Flavian Valley made by Count Raymond to the monastery of Saint-Gilles at the Council of Nîmes, as we explained in its proper place.

So that he might not appear ungrateful toward his hosts, on the following day he received the monastery of Saint Andrew, where he was then staying, under apostolic protection and fortified it with privileges. The bull issued for this purpose was addressed to Abbot Peter.

The Sammarthani say in volume I of *Gallia Christiana*, on the basis of the public registers of the Church of Avignon, that Urban II handed over the principal church of that city to regular canons and wished Alfonso, king of Aragon, who was then count of the province, to be numbered among them. We will not deny this, but they do not report on what occasion it occurred, and there is no opportunity to guess.

### CCLXXIII. Whether the pontiff visited Arles.

It is no clearer whether the same pontiff ever visited Arles, where he is nevertheless said to have been received with magnificent ceremony by Gibelin, archbishop of that city, who was then in the pontifical entourage when Urban returned from Gaul to Italy. Some, following Saxius and the Sammarthani, write this, but not on the basis of reliable monuments; certainly they cite no evidence at all in confirmation of the matter.

It is indeed established from the pontiff’s own letter, already cited several times, to Richer and the other Gallic bishops, that he had summoned a synod to that city. But it is no less clear that the synod was not held there. This can be confirmed from Ivo’s letter 56, in which he replies to King Philip, who was complaining against Hugo of Lyon because, after two councils had been held in Gaul by the pontiff himself that year—namely, the councils of Tours and Nîmes—Hugo had summoned a third after Urban’s departure.

Hence it is conjectured that the synod which Urban had summoned to Arles was the very one that the same pontiff celebrated at Nîmes. Nevertheless, we do not wish wholly to deny that Urban visited Arles, from which city he was then not far away.

### CCLXXIV. The privilege of Montmajour issued at Cavaillon.

Perhaps the pontiff was there at the time when William, abbot of Montmajour near that same city, presented him with a petition against the invaders of his church’s possessions. A few days later, on the third day before the Kalends of August, Urban confirmed at Cavaillon the privileges and possessions of that monastery at the request of Abbot William, issuing a bull that will be presented together with the cited petition.

In that bull, however, not all the monastery’s possessions are listed about which the abbot had complained in his petition. In my opinion, this was because the pontiff did not wish to pronounce, without hearing the opposing parties, on matters under dispute or on matters not expressly stated in the privileges of earlier pontiffs.

Here it is worth observing that in this bull of Urban, in accordance with his customary scriptural expression, we find simply the words “we read, we confirm.” We find the same words used in a similar manner in other bulls of his.

### CCLXXV. Urban consecrates the church of Saint Eusebius at Apt.

At the beginning of August the pontiff went to Apt Julia, where, according to Pope Anastasius IV, he consecrated the suburban church of the monastery of Saint Eusebius. For Anastasius writes in a bull granted to the same monastery in 1154:

> We strengthen by the text of this present privilege every liberty and exemption of the aforesaid monastery, granted by our predecessor Urban, who consecrated the church of Saint Eusebius.

We gather that this dedication took place in the present year from the local documents of that house. They say that, during the abbacy of Abbot Guilafred, Urban solemnly consecrated the basilica of Saint Eusebius, newly erected from its foundations, on the Nones of August.

It is certain that Urban was in that region during this year. The day of the Nones of August, which no one would say was carelessly specified here, indicates that the event should be assigned to this rather than to the preceding year. For on the very Nones of August of the preceding year Urban consecrated the cathedral church of Valencia, as we said in its proper place.

There is a common opinion in these parts that not only the church of Saint Eusebius but also another priory church in the neighboring village called Clarus Mons, where there was once a notable castle, was consecrated by the same pontiff. As evidence of this, they say that a right hand, as if blessing the people, was carved into the wall of each church. Although this figure was cut away at Saint Eusebius during the restoration of the basilica, it still remains above the main door of the church of Clermont. That it was actually placed there in memory of its dedication is suggested by the inscription nearby, written in ancient characters:

> 12 January: dedication of the church.

But this cannot be attributed to Urban unless perhaps it was placed some time later by someone who, with Bertold, believed that Urban had celebrated the feast of Christ’s Nativity at Arles.

### CCLXXVI. Whether he visited Marseille.

If we trust Guesnau and other more recent authors, Urban also visited Marseille when he returned from Gaul to Italy. There, they say, he was received with great ceremony by the monks of the famous monastery of Saint Victor. But among the ancient authorities there is profound silence on this matter. Indeed, it is not even clear by what route or on what day he left Gaul, although it is certain that he spent several weeks in those coastal regions.

### CCLXXVII. The departure of the crusaders.

The twenty-fifth day of August, as we learn from Urban’s letter to Robert, count of Flanders, cited above, had been appointed for the departure of the crusaders. Their undertaking may have begun while Urban was still present in Gaul.

Among others, Fulk, count of Anjou, speaks of it in this way in a fragment of his history. After recounting the various journeys made by the pontiff at the beginning of this year, he continues:

> In the following summer, at his command, not only the people but also the leaders of the peoples set out on the journey to Jerusalem. Their names have been recorded here for the clear knowledge of posterity: Hugh the Great, brother of Philip, king of the Franks; Robert, duke of the Normans; Robert, count of Flanders; Raymond, count of Saint-Gilles; Stephen, count of Blois, son of Theobald, count of Champagne; Godfrey of Lorraine; and his father Eustace, count of Boulogne. Adhemar, bishop of Le Puy, whom Urban had appointed leader of the expedition at the Council of Clermont, joined their company, as did many other nobles and bishops of great virtue . . . Many reached Constantinople through Pannonia in order to shorten the journey; many others reached the port of Saint Nicholas, that is, Bari in Apulia, and then Constantinople.

Other authors collected in the book *The Deeds of God through the Franks* agree with this. Fulcher reports that many departed in companies during each month from March through October, as opportunity conveniently presented itself. An anonymous contemporary author also recorded this; our Mabillon published him, previously unpublished, in volume I of the *Italian Museum*.

For the rest, the aforementioned Fulk accuses some of rashness because they crossed the sea without waiting for the others and, on that account, were routed and defeated by the infidels.

Urban had already left Gaul when the bishops whom he had appointed to settle the dispute between the monks of Psalmodi and those of Saint Victor at Marseille assembled at the castle of Caisso on 16 September and settled the matter, freeing the monks of Psalmodi from subjection to the monks of Saint Victor. We shall present in the Appendix the instrument of this decision, which is indeed a distinguished document.

### CCLXXVIII. Urban returns to Italy.

“Thus,” says Bertold, “the lord pope, having put affairs in Gaul in good order, after the reconciliation of the king of the Franks and after many councils, at last returned to Lombardy with great triumph and glory. He solemnly celebrated the Exaltation of the Holy Cross at Hortorium [perhaps Mortarium], a notable place between Ticinum and Novara in the duchy of Milan, near Pavia, and had many bishops and princes in his entourage.”

Shortly afterward, on the eighth day before the Kalends of October, according to an old catalogue published by Mabillon in volume I of the *Italian Museum*, Arnulf, bishop of Milan, died. Anselm of Buis was substituted for him and put on the archiepiscopal stole, or pallium, brought to him by the legate of the lord pope, as Laulph of Saint Paul relates in Puricellus and Ughellus, volume IV of *Sacred Italy*.

I fear, however, that this delivery of the pallium by a legate must be assigned to another Anselm, whom we discussed under the year 1093, as we observed there from Pandulf in the *Life of Urban*.

### CCLXXIX. He grants a privilege at Cremona to Saint Basolus.

We gather that the pontiff was staying at Cremona on the day before the Ides, or 14 October, from a bull granted there to the monastery of Saint Basolus in the region of Reims. Although the year 1098 is given in the old copy that we used, all the chronological notes appended there, in addition to the circumstances of place, persuade us that it must be referred to the present year.

In it, as in the present work, the following words are inserted between crosses in place of a scriptural expression: “we read, we confirm, holy Basolus.” The pontiff may perhaps have used them because of his particular affection for Saint Basolus, in whose monastery’s vicinity he had been born or at least brought up.

The secular advocates of that monastery were entirely abolished. If Urban belonged to the family of the lords of Castillon, these advocates were his own cousins.

### CCLXXX. Latin bishops substituted for the Greeks in Calabria.

At this time, after Theodore, bishop of Squillace, had died among the Calabrians, Count Roger resolved to establish in that church a Latin bishop, setting aside the Greeks, the last of whom had been Theodore, because many more Latins—namely, Normans—than Greeks were then living there.

He carried this out in fact, with the agreement of the other Latin bishops whom he had summoned from Sicily for this purpose, especially Saxon, or Sasson, bishop of Cassano, who was Urban’s vicar in Calabria. John was therefore immediately transferred from the deanery of Mileto and placed over this church, as is read in Roger’s charter, published by Ughellus in volume IX of *Sacred Italy*, p. 591.

All this was confirmed by Urban. On the same occasion he also placed this church directly under the Roman See, omitting every metropolitan, as we understand from Paschal’s bull reported on the same page, for Urban’s diploma on this matter has been lost.

### CCLXXXI. Crusaders visit Urban at Lucca.

When Urban had reached Lucca, a city of Tuscany, Robert, count of Normandy, and Stephen, count of Blois, who were hastening through Italy to the holy expedition, came to him there. Many others followed them, as Fulcher relates; he himself was among them. After receiving the pontiff’s blessing, they immediately proceeded to Rome.

But the Guibertines, whose insolence had not yet been fully suppressed, were plundering the offerings of pilgrims approaching the Vatican basilica. They even killed some whom they knew to be devoted to Urban. Those brigands, however, were soon driven out and scattered after the pontiff’s arrival in the city.

### CCLXXXII. Matilda meets Urban.

Domnizo testifies that Countess Matilda went to meet Urban when he returned from Gaul. He expressed his return to Italy and his arrival in Rome in barbarous verse. Sigonius says in book IX of *On the Kingdom of Italy* that Urban, honored with the highest distinctions by Matilda and the other leading figures in Lombardy, went to Rome.

Bertold compares his return to the city with a triumph. Following his custom, he begins the year 1097 with the Nativity of Christ and writes:

> At last the lord pope returned to the apostolic see with great glory and rejoicing and celebrated the Nativity of the Lord most gloriously at Rome with his cardinals; for almost the whole city of Rome had been subjected to him, except the tower of Crescentius, in which the Guibertines were still hiding.

Domnizo sings that Guibert himself had been driven out by the populace; see his verses on this matter in the Appendix.

That Matilda accompanied Urban all the way to Rome, although that author does not state it, can be inferred from a letter of the pontiff himself to Hugo of Lyon, written some time later. It contains these words:

> We came peacefully as far as Rome with Countess M.; we entered Rome most honorably with a very large escort preceding us.

Fulcher also testifies that, with the help of the same countess, the pontiff brought under control the city, which the Guibertines still held. Sigonius, in the passage already cited, says that it had been occupied by Guibert but was conquered by Urban II, while the false pontiff was driven into the citadel with the assistance of those whom the pontiff had encouraged to undertake the holy expedition.

Other authors agree with Fulcher, who observes that in that very year, in which the Franks passed through Rome on their way to Jerusalem, Urban obtained the whole of the apostolic authority. Robert, in book II of his *History of Jerusalem*, testifies that so great was the number of princes and soldiers who came to Rome that year that many of them, since the houses were insufficient, were compelled to pitch tents outside the city.

Certainly, Orderic Vitalis himself, in book X, testifies that Robert, duke of Normandy, and Odo, bishop of Bayeux, had a conference with Urban at Rome. After receiving his blessing, he writes, they wintered in Apulia.

Other authors likewise tell essentially the same things about these and other pilgrims. After visiting the holy places of Rome, they also visited the monastery of Monte Cassino, as Peter the Deacon writes in book IV, chapter 2, of the *Cassinese Chronicle*, so that they might commend themselves and their affairs to the holy Father Benedict and to the prayers of his monks.

### CCLXXXIII. Henry’s miserable condition.

Henry’s affairs in Italy were no more prosperous than those of his false pontiff. In Urban’s absence he had besieged Nocera, but without success, as Domnizo relates in his description of the siege.

Matilda, in Bertold’s words, had fought for almost seven years, virtually alone with her followers, against Henry, the heresiarch Guibert, and their accomplices. At last, in this year, she completely drove the emperor from Lombardy, he having undoubtedly been terrified by the arrival in Italy of so many great men who, at Urban’s urging, were hastening to the holy expeditions, and she having recovered her possessions.

Henry went to Regensburg with a few companions and spent the whole summer there. He then stayed for some time in considerable privacy near the castle of Nuremberg and finally moved to Nemetum, where he remained for a long time in similar seclusion.

### CCLXXXIV. Urban celebrates a council at the Lateran.

Since Urban was prevailing at Rome, where, as he himself wrote to Hugo of Lyon, he was living honorably, safely, and confidently, he decided, in order to secure the city more and more firmly for himself, to bind its citizens and all its districts by oaths to their duty.

Indeed, he already possessed the Lateran palace from the very beginning of the year 1097, as is clear from his bull to Hugo, abbot of Cluny, issued at the Lateran on the fifth day before the Ides of January, in the fifth indiction. In it he confirmed the privileges and possessions of the monastery of Cluny and of the places subject to it.

As a most vigilant pontiff, he referred the prosperity of his affairs to the advantage of the Church and immediately summoned a council, undoubtedly so that the measures established in the Gallic synods might also be extended into Italy. Sigonius calls it a general council in book IX of *On the Kingdom of Italy*, and Otto of Freising and other authors agree with him.

The pontiff himself testifies in the letter to Hugo of Lyon cited shortly above that this synod was solemnly celebrated at the Lateran. Although the letter bears no chronological notes, it can easily be gathered that it belongs to the beginning of this year because it mentions Daimbert, recently elected archbishop of Sens, who is known to have been substituted for Richer at the beginning of this year.

The same is proved by the case of the elected bishop of Limoges mentioned there, for William was ordained bishop shortly afterward. The letter is certainly an important one, since it deals with many serious affairs of various churches in Gaul and demonstrates Urban’s zeal in preserving the rules of the Church. It will be published later from a copy made from the Baluze manuscript.

Although it seems certain from what has been said that Urban celebrated this council at the Lateran not long after his return to the city, we must admit that scarcely anything survives from its acts or decrees. Perhaps nothing new was enacted there.

We think that only the following can be assigned to it—for Urban held no other synod at the Lateran: a fragment of a letter to Godfrey, bishop of Maguelonne, in which the pontiff determines, in accordance with what he had promulgated at the Lateran Council, how the alms of the dead who had wished to be buried in monasteries should be divided.

That statute, which appears in some copies after canon 12 of the *Questa*, and in Gratian at 13, q. 2, will be published among Urban’s other letters as number 210.

### CCLXXXV. The ordination of Daimbert, bishop of Sens, postponed.

After Richer, archbishop of Sens, died toward the end of the preceding December, as we have already observed, Daimbert was substituted in his place. But since he, following in the footsteps of his predecessor, refused to submit to the primacy of the church of Lyon, Archbishop Hugo intervened to prevent him from being ordained by the bishops of the province.

On this occasion Ivo of Chartres, who had been invited by Daimbert to consecrate him, consulted Urban about what ought to be done in letter 165. Ivo excuses himself to the pontiff because, after his departure from Urban’s entourage, he had not yet been able to return to him or at least greet him through messengers.

He then commends to him the bishop of Paris, who had gone to Rome. The abbot of Lagny was refusing obedience to this bishop under the pretext of a new privilege obtained from the pontiff.

We have that privilege of Lagny before us. Since the copy bears no chronological note, we think it can be assigned here on the basis of this letter of Ivo and should therefore be presented by us in the Appendix.

We gather that Ivo’s letter was written at the beginning of this year because, when he wrote it, he had not yet heard what had happened to Urban as he entered Rome. He himself testifies to this in these words:

> Concerning the peace of the holy Roman Church and your prosperity, may the Lord grant us to hear what we desire.

### CCLXXXVI. Gerard, bishop of the Morini, relinquishes his see.

Around the same time, while the church of the Morini was being disturbed by various tumults because Gerard, its bishop, had been suspended from office at the Council of Nîmes, as we said, Lambert, bishop of Arras, to whom Manasses, metropolitan of Reims, had entrusted the care of that church, wrote to Urban on Gerard’s behalf.

We do not know what the pontiff replied. But Gerard, perhaps weary of so many delays, and unable, as the author of the *Life of John*, his successor, says, to excuse himself completely, resigned the episcopate. That author, followed by Malbrancus, reports that Gerard withdrew to the monastery of Mont-Saint-Éloi near Arras. After John was appointed in his place shortly afterward, as we shall say below, Gerard spent the remainder of his life there in peace.

Since Urban’s response is lacking, we have thought it appropriate to present Lambert’s letter on this matter in the Appendix. Urban had previously written to Gerard against those who despised the canons, but only a fragment of that letter survives in Ivo.

### CCLXXXVII. The pontiff’s affection for the monks whom he raises to dignities.

At the beginning of this year, or certainly toward the end of the preceding one—for the manuscript *Chronicle of Cava* gives the year 1096—Pope Urban gave the church of Saint Paul to Peter, abbot of the Holy Trinity at Cava.

There is no doubt that he did this to strengthen regular discipline in so celebrated a place, or perhaps to restore it where it had grown somewhat lukewarm. The religious pontiff omitted nothing to ensure that observance of the rule, especially of the Benedictine order, would be carefully maintained in monasteries.

This is proved by his various bulls, in which he declares that he grants privileges to monasteries chiefly so that monks, freed from secular affairs and concerns, may aspire more fervently to heavenly things. He knew that such sacred places, when inhabited by good and devout monks, were like nurseries of great men who could assist the Church in her distress.

He paid particular attention to promoting to ecclesiastical dignities any monk of this kind whom he happened to find hidden somewhere. We have already praised some of them, but two in particular must be mentioned here.

The first was Albert, who, as Ughellus reports in volume VII of *Sacred Italy*, was this year made a cardinal priest and eventually archbishop of Siponto after having been a monk of Saint Savinus of Piacenza.

The other was Saint Bernard, a Florentine nobleman of the Uberti family. Urban admonished him once and again without success, but finally, after employing ecclesiastical censures, compelled him to come to him, as is recorded in his *Life*. In this very year Urban created him cardinal priest of the title of Saint Chrysogonus.

After holding many legations and becoming bishop of Parma, Bernard, renowned for miracles and holiness, departed this life during the pontificate of Paschal II.

Two others may be added to these: Milo, a monk of Saint-Aubin of Angers, whom we have already mentioned and whom Ughellus says was around this time substituted for Bernard, bishop of Palestrina, against Hugo the White, a pseudocardinal and notorious schismatic; and John Marticanus, whom Ughellus says Urban created bishop of Tusculum.

This may perhaps be the same John whom Hugo of Flavigny mentions in his *Chronicle*. If that author’s account is genuine, however, he became bishop somewhat later than this year. For Hugo says that Urban brought him with him when returning from Gaul to Rome and first gave him an abbacy and then a bishopric.

Here are Hugo’s own words:

> In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1181, John, bishop of Tusculum, was sent by the pope to England concerning the tribute of Saint Peter. He had been a regular canon of Saint Quentin of Beauvais, but, having violated his profession, laid aside his habit and returned to the world. Unable to endure the reproach, he became a monk of Bec. Although Roman by birth, he gained the familiarity of Pope Urban when the pope came to Gaul; he was brought back to Rome, and, after the bishop of Lavicanus had died, having already been endowed with a certain abbey, he was promoted from abbot to bishop.

If this is the same John as the abbot of Saint Saviour near the city of Telese, with whom Saint Anselm stayed, as we shall say in the following year from Eadmer’s book II of the *New Works*, it can scarcely be said that Urban made him a bishop. Eadmer, as may be inferred, ought not to have passed over that fact in silence.

Certain considerations seem to show that these men were the same, while others suggest that they were different men bearing the same name. Certainly both were Romans by birth, both monks of Bec, and both lived under Abbot Anselm at the same time.

But Hugo’s John had been a canon of Beauvais and was brought into Italy by Urban himself. The man praised by Eadmer, on the other hand, is said to have come to France for the sake of literary study and, moved by Anselm’s reputation, to have undertaken the monastic life at Bec. Some years later Urban summoned him to place him over the monastery at Telese.

Certainly, from all this it is clear that Urban omitted nothing in summoning religious men to himself from every quarter, so that he might employ their services in the most difficult affairs. On this subject, as we have already observed, he wrote to Anselm himself, then abbot of Bec, asking that if he had any such man in his congregation, he should either bring him along or, if he could not come himself, send him to Urban.

In letter 48 the same pontiff recalls a certain John, who had been made a monk of Bec after having been a Roman cleric. Finally, Eadmer, in the *Life of Saint Anselm*, praises another Peter, a Cluniac monk and a man of great authority, who had been chamberlain to Popes Urban and later Paschal.

Some, but without justification, suspect that this was the famous Peter who later became abbot of Cluny and was called the Venerable. That Peter had already been born in 1092, while Urban was sitting as pontiff.

### CCLXXXVIII. The Council of Saintes.

Between these events, Amatus, archbishop of Bordeaux and legate of the Apostolic See, celebrated a council at Saintes on 2 March. Labbe and others assign it to the preceding year, although the charter of Vendôme from which our information is derived gives the fourth indiction and the year 1096 (see *Anecdota Thesauri*, vol. IV, p. 123). However the indiction may be corrupt here; if no error has entered the year, it must be remembered that in this charter, as often happens, the year begins with the feast of Easter. Certainly, the instrument of La Sauve-Majeure explicitly assigns the year 1097 to the instrument made at this council for the restoration of the lands of Doeria and Tosco, which Achelmus, abbot of that place, obtained there.

The author of the *Chronicle of Maillezais* does not disagree. Although he refers this synod to the year 1096, he nevertheless places it only toward the end of that year, after recounting many other events that had occurred throughout its course. In a word, it is entirely certain that this synod was not held in March 1096. At that time Amatus, who is said to have presided over it, could not have been at Saintes, since he was then ill at Tours in the pope’s company, where Urban was holding a council, as is shown by the instrument of the dedication of the basilica of the Greater Monastery and is established by other incontrovertible documents.

Furthermore, Raymond, archbishop of Auch, who is said to have attended the synod of Saintes, had not yet been promoted to that church in March 1096; the pope bestowed the pallium on him in 1097. Moreover, Marbodus, one of the Fathers of Saintes, was consecrated by Urban at the Council of Tours itself. Hildebert, bishop of Le Mans, also attended that synod; he succeeded Johel, who died on 29 July 1098, as is recorded in the acts of that church (*Analecta* of Mabillon, vol. III, p. 302). Hence, unless a copyist’s error has intruded, this synod must be assigned to the year 1098. What proves conclusively that it was not held in 1096 is the charter of Vendôme itself, from which we derive its principal information. It records many things done at this synod which, nevertheless, it says occurred in May and the following months, right up to the end of 1096.

From it we learn that forty-three bishops and abbots alike assembled for this council at Saintes. Besides Amatus, eight bishops subscribed the instrument, together with three abbots: Geoffrey of Maillezais, Guarnerius of Saint-Maixent, and Geoffrey of Vendôme. Two other abbots are mentioned in the instrument of the agreement then concluded between the monasteries of Angériac and Charroux: namely, Peter of Charroux and Ansculf of Angériac.

At that synod, according to the *Chronicle of Maillezais*, it was ordered that everyone should fast on the vigils of the apostles. There the serious controversy between the monks of Nantoni and the canons of Saint-Émilion was also dealt with. We learn of it from a letter written by those same canons to Pope Urban, in which they attribute such grave crimes to the monks of Nantoni that it is scarcely credible that religious men could have committed them. Since Urban’s reply is lacking, we shall include these letters in the Appendix.

### CCLXXXIX. Glanfeuil confirmed as belonging to Monte Cassino

In the same month of March, at Terracina, Urban issued a bull in favor of the monastery of Monte Cassino, addressed to Oderisius, abbot and cardinal. By it he restored to him the monastery of Saint-Maur of Glanfeuil, freed—as had been determined at the Council of Tours—from the yoke of the monks of Fosses.

### CCXC. Urban visits Capua and elsewhere

On this journey, as may be conjectured, the pope visited Capua, whose bishop at that time was Sennes; Ughellus states that Urban spent eight days there during this year. Certainly it can scarcely be denied that Urban then went as far as Benevento. This is proved by his rescript to Peter, king of the Aragonese and Pamplonese, issued at Benevento on 4 March, which must necessarily be assigned to this year.

It was issued after 1094, in which year Sancius, the father of King Peter, was pierced by an arrow and died during the siege of Huesca in June. Nor can it be assigned to either of the following two years, which the pope spent in Tuscany and on his journey through Gaul; nor to 1098 or 1099, since in March of both those years Urban was in Rome. Only the present year therefore remains to which this rescript can be assigned. In it the pope warmly commends the Church of Pamplona to the king and to the other faithful of those regions.

### CCXCI. He preaches the expedition at Theate

Perhaps Urban undertook this journey in order to meet Roger, duke of Apulia. Or certainly he was visiting these regions in order to proclaim there, as in other places, the holy expedition. This seems to be suggested by Berardus in book III of the *Chronicle of Casauria* (*Spicilegium*, vol. V), where Urban is said, while preaching this expedition, to have visited Theate. He remained there for two days and, together with the bishops and barons, held a common conference concerning the road to Jerusalem.

On this occasion Raynulfus, then bishop of Theate, obtained from the pope confirmation of many possessions of his church that had recently been restored or granted to it; Urban’s rescript on this matter will be discussed below. At the same time Grimoardus, the elected abbot of the monastery of Pescara, or Casa Aurea, afflicted by various calamities inflicted by neighboring Normans and other powerful men, came to Urban. Since he could neither appeal to the emperor against them nor find refuge with anyone else, he approached the pope, who received him kindly. Having received the pastoral staff from Urban’s hand, he was blessed by him as abbot; until then the abbots of that place, instead of a pastoral staff, had used a royal scepter. Urban then blessed him as abbot. From that time, as Berardus reports, this abbey, which until then had obeyed the emperor alone, came under the protection of the Apostolic See.

On this occasion, in the authentic manuscript of his *Chronicle*, now preserved in the Royal Library, Urban is represented handing the pastoral staff to Abbot Grimoardus and addressing him in these two verses:

> In place of Caesar’s scepter I extend to you this right-hand staff,  
> That you may rely upon it securely: Peter gives you more than Caesar.

### CCXCII. Crusaders of every nation set sail for the East

Meanwhile, most of the soldiers of various nations who had set out for the holy expedition and taken the route through Italy were at that time in the maritime regions visited by Urban. Among them were Robert, count of Normandy, and Stephen, count of Blois, who shortly afterward—that is, on 5 April—set sail from the port of Brindisi with their soldiers and forces.

Ciaconius asserts that Urban wished to depart with them, but that he was detained by the Catholics, who did not wish the Roman Church, shaken by so many disturbances, to be left without a shepherd. At that time princes and peoples from all Europe were gathering for those expeditions, following the example of the Franks and stimulated by Urban’s exhortations—or at least by the fame of his undertaking.

On this occasion Peter the Deacon observes in the *Chronicle of Monte Cassino* what Robert had already written in book II of his *History of Jerusalem*, together with other local authors: Bohemond and others in Apulia, Calabria, and Sicily, having suspended their other wars or set aside their private affairs, joined the soldiers of the holy expedition who were passing through Italy.

Orderic Vitalis gives a fuller account. He writes that Englishmen, Bretons, Gascons, and even the Galicians of farthest Spain came there, as did from Italy the Venetians, Pisans, Genoese, and others who inhabited the shores of the Mediterranean or the Ocean. There was scarcely a city in Italy that did not boast of having supplied soldiers for the undertaking.

The same author asserts in book IX that four thousand Apulians served under the leadership of Tancred, and thirty thousand Lombards and Milanese likewise served under Bohemond. He has an especially fine account of this expedition and of those who joined it; the other writers of that period agree with him. On this subject one should read the verses of a certain poet of the period, Fulk, published in volume III of Chesne’s *Historians of the Franks*. In them, like many other authors, he also praises those who traveled by another route through Germany.

Berthold praises Count Harduin of Alemannia and Otto, bishop of Strasbourg, although a schismatic, because he undertook this route with the others. Unless I am mistaken, this is the same Otto whom, as we said above, Berthold reports as having been reconciled with Urban in the preceding year. Ulrich, bishop of Chur, is also celebrated for this undertaking. He left the care of his diocese to Gerold, a monk of Pfäfers, and set out with many others for the expedition.

### CCXCIII–IV. At Rome Urban writes to the emperor Alexius on behalf of the crusaders. He enlarges Monte Cassino’s privileges

[Col. 0227B]

After Urban had proclaimed these expeditions, chiefly at the urging of Alexius, emperor of Constantinople, he thought it appropriate to write to him concerning their successful outcome, in order specifically to commend the crusaders to him. But that deceitful emperor disappointed the hope of the Christians. Fearing that he might be overwhelmed by so great a multitude of foreigners, he prepared secret snares for them and, withdrawing everywhere the supplies necessary for their sustenance, caused many of them to perish.

Shortly afterward, however, he entered into some sort of alliance with them, after they had, as the anonymous author of Bari reports, given him security concerning his kingdom at Constantinople. At last he bestowed many gifts upon them and supplied vessels by which they could penetrate the lands of the infidels. These were the beginnings of those famous expeditions, which thereafter continued for so many years amid varying fortunes. It is not our purpose to discuss their events at greater length. One should read the authors whom, as we have already more than once observed, the volume entitled *The Deeds of God through the Franks* brings together.

Returning, as we have just said, to Rome, Urban there granted a notable bull to Oderisius, cardinal and abbot of Monte Cassino. In it he added new privileges to those already granted to the monastery of Monte Cassino and confirmed its possessions, which are for the most part listed individually. This bull, partly already published in the *Bullary of Monte Cassino* from the chartulary of Peter the Deacon preserved in the library of Prince Pamphili, will someday be produced in full among Urban’s letters.

It was issued this year on 27 March.

### CCXCV. Urban protects Cluny

In April of this same year the pope undertook the protection of the monks of Cluny, whom certain people were troubling. He issued a rescript to Abbot Hugh, determining that, even if neighboring places were under interdict, or even entire dioceses in which Cluniac monks lived, they would nevertheless be permitted to celebrate the divine offices with the doors closed.

At the same time a serious controversy arose between these same Cluniacs and Peter, abbot of Tournus, and his monks. The Cluniacs contended that the others had unjustly usurped the fishery in the Saône and the boraria of the Saille River. Hugh, cellarer of Cluny, had pursued this suit in the court of the count of Mâcon. But when the monks of Tournus refused to submit to any judgment, the matter was brought before Urban. He immediately wrote to Hugh, archbishop of Lyon, instructing him to prohibit Peter of Tournus from sitting in the abbatial chair until he had satisfied the Cluniacs.

Peter finally obeyed this command in 1097, in the fifth indiction and the forty-ninth year of Hugh’s ordination, as is recorded in the old instrument from which we have taken this account.

### CCXCVI. Privilege of the Church of Auvergne

On 18 April the same pontiff confirmed, in a notable bull, all the privileges and possessions of the Church of Auvergne. He also determined that its bishop should hold the first place in the ordination of the metropolitan of Bourges.

### CCXCVII. The possessions of the Church of Theate confirmed

On the following day the same pontiff wrote to the clergy and nobles of the county of Theate concerning the matters which he had determined while present among them at Theate in the preceding March. Ughellus gives the rescript—or rather a fragment of it—but it is completely mutilated. It can easily be supplemented from the bull of Paschal II, which the same author reports in volume VI, in his catalogue of the bishops of Theate. There he lists individually, from Urban’s document, various possessions restored or granted by Counts Robert and Tassio, his brother, which Urban had confirmed to Bishop Raynulfus and to his Church, together with other possessions acquired by him.

### CCXCVIII. King Philip absolved

[Col. 0228C]

At that time a messenger sent by Philip, king of the Franks, arrived in Rome to see Urban. Having taken an oath, he affirmed that the king had never returned to Bertrada, whom he had dismissed at the pope’s command. Urban therefore wrote to the bishops of Gaul, and especially to Manasses, archbishop of Reims, to whom the royal crown principally belonged, declaring that the king was absolved from every interdict and could therefore wear the crown, according to the custom of that age, on solemn occasions.

In the *Spicilegium* this letter lacked a chronological note; in our manuscript it is said to have been issued at the Lateran on 24 April.

### CCXCIX. He safeguards the rights of Saint Orientius

Shortly afterward, on 29 April, Urban wrote to Raymond, who had assumed the administration of the metropolitan church of Auch in this year, instructing him to restrain the boldness of the clergy of that Church, who, contrary to the decree of Pope Leo and also to Urban’s own decree, had violated the cemetery of Saint Orientius.

### CCC. The death of Ulrich

Toward the end of October, Count Ulrich, Urban’s most energetic partisan and defender in Germany, died. He was buried at Bregenz on 27 October. According to Berthold, he had established monks there by this year.

### CCCI. The rights of the Church of Narbonne confirmed

When the archbishop of Narbonne died during this year, Urban transferred Bertrand, whom he himself had previously consecrated bishop of Nîmes, to that metropolitan see, following the election of the bishops of the province and compelled by necessity. He testifies that he would not thereafter permit such a transfer to anyone else.

We learn this from his diploma, by which he confirmed to Bertrand the rights of the metropolitan Church of Narbonne and its primacy over the metropolitan Church of Aix. It is said to have been issued at the Lateran on 6 November and has already been published by the illustrious Pierre de Marca in the Appendix to his book *On Primacies*.

Two other rescripts from the same codices, relating to this metropolitan see, will be appended. Neither bears a chronological note. Both were issued against the archbishop of Aix, who refused to obey the primate of Narbonne: one was addressed to the archbishop of Aix himself, the other to Hugh of Lyon, vicar of the Apostolic See.

### CCCII. Privilege of the Church of Veroli

The privilege of Veroli must also be assigned to this period. According to the copy of Ughellus’s edition, if it is reliable, Urban granted it this year—indeed at the year’s end—to Albert, bishop of that Church. The sixth indiction appended there supports this dating.

Certainly, as with the privilege of Narbonne discussed in the preceding section, Lanfrancus, acting in place of the chancellor, subscribed this privilege. We therefore conjecture that both documents were drawn up at nearly the same time, around November, while Chancellor John was absent or ill.

### CCCIII. Robert, abbot of Saint-Remi, confirmed by Urban

[Col. 0229C]

In this same year, as is explicitly recorded in an old instrument which we possess from the manuscript of Mauriac and which the late and learned Cangius extracted from the archive of the great monastery of Saint-Remi at Reims and published in his *Latin Glossary*, Urban, having returned from Gaul to Rome, gave judgment in favor of Robert, abbot of that same monastery, against Bernard, abbot of the Greater Monastery.

Robert, a monk of the Greater Monastery, had been requested by the monks of Saint-Remi to become abbot in place of Henry some years earlier. Bernard had granted him on the condition that, if he should ever forget his profession and do anything contrary to the rule, he would submit to the correction of the abbot of the Greater Monastery.

This is what happened. Robert, after becoming abbot, attended the Council of Clermont with the others. Later—whether justly or unjustly I do not know—he acquired a bad reputation with Bernard, who said that he had learned that Robert was doing many disorderly and irregular things.

Bernard therefore first admonished Robert by letter. When he received no reply, he notified him through suitable persons of a day on which he was to come to the Greater Monastery and render an account of his life and conduct in chapter. When Robert paid no attention even to the admonitions of his own archbishop, Bernard excommunicated him. Manasses, the metropolitan, and the other bishops and abbots of the province of Belgica confirmed this sentence at a council held at Reims and judged that Robert ought to be returned to his abbot, since he was still subject to his discipline by virtue of his former profession.

Robert, however, appealed to the Apostolic See and went to Rome to defend his case. After hearing him, the pontiff annulled what both Bernard and the Fathers of the Council of Reims had done. He declared that as soon as a monk had become abbot of another monastery, he was emancipated and ought no longer to be subject to the abbot of his former monastery.

We learn all these things from the instrument just mentioned and from three letters written on the matter. Lambert, bishop of Arras, first wrote to Urban, giving him an account of the entire affair. The second is the pontiff’s own sentence invalidating the decision of the council. The third is Robert’s letter to Lambert, inviting him to undertake the defense of his case, which the pontiff had judged to be just. We have thought it appropriate to include all these letters in the Appendix.

Moreover, if I judge correctly, the verses of Baldricus, abbot of Bourgueil, to Odo, bishop and cardinal of Ostia, published in volume IV of Chesne’s *History of the Franks*, should also be referred to this controversy. In them he commends to Odo the case of the abbot of Saint-Remi, whom the archbishop of Reims had expelled from the monastery even though the pope had confirmed him.

Certainly Robert does not seem ever to have been restored to his dignity. Perhaps, wearied by these disturbances, he yielded his place to Burchardus and undertook the journey to Jerusalem. After returning to Gaul, he later composed, in the Saint-Remi cell called Senuc, a history of the Jerusalem journey and of the holy expedition.

Nevertheless, in 1111, at the Council of Poitiers, as Hugh of Flavigny records in his *Chronicle*, the matter of his unjust expulsion and Burchard’s unlawful substitution was again discussed. Although his promotion was found to be authentic and canonical, his entry legitimate, and his conduct holy, certain difficulties nevertheless arose because of apostolic letters that seemed to some to be of doubtful authenticity. The examination of those letters was referred to the Apostolic See, and the matter remained unresolved.

Burchard, however, was soon afterward compelled to relinquish his position, but Robert was not thereby restored. For in this same year Azenarius, from the noble family of the lords of Trimouille, became abbot of Saint-Remi, as Marlotus gathers from various charters in his *History of the Metropolitan Church of Reims*.

Robert was later deprived even of the administration of the cell of Senuc, which had been granted to him for the remainder of his life. The same author proves this from a rescript of Calixtus, issued at the Lateran on 15 May, and therefore after the year 1120, when Calixtus first came to Rome in June.

### CCCIV. Council of Girona

Toward the end of the current year—that is, on 13 December—Bernard, bishop of Toledo and Urban’s vicar in Spain, held a council at Girona, as is recorded in *Marca Hispanica* and in Cardinal Aguirre’s *Collection of Councils*, in order to strengthen the dignity of ecclesiastical liberty.

Besides Bernard, the metropolitan of Tarragona and the bishops of Roda, Barcelona, and Girona attended this synod, together perhaps with others whose names have been lost.

### CCCV. Baldric becomes bishop of Noyon and Tournai

In Gaul, the Church of Noyon, which throughout this year had been shaken by various disturbances, recovered peace. At the beginning of the year Baldric, formerly cantor of Thérouanne, had already been elected bishop of that Church in place of the deceased Rabbodi. The date of his consecration had been fixed for the eighth day after Pentecost by Manasses, metropolitan of Reims, as is clear from that archbishop’s letter to Lambert, bishop of Arras.
