But certain people intervened, asserting on the basis of some letters of Urban—though I do not know which letters—that on this occasion a proper bishop ought to be restored to the people of Tournai, just as one had been granted to the people of Arras. Baldric’s ordination was therefore postponed until the following year.

The difficulty was not without some foundation. Before its destruction, the city of Tournai had possessed its own bishop and seemed to have been entrusted only provisionally to the care of the bishop of Noyon. Moreover, the city was no less extensive or populous than Arras, to which, through Urban’s agency, its own bishop had been restored. Indeed, the pope himself seemed to have declared this to be his intention in a letter to the people of Noyon, where he had confirmed only those privileges of the bishops of Noyon that had been granted by legitimate pontiffs.

The archbishop of Reims therefore thought it appropriate to send Baldric, the elected bishop himself, to Rome, so that he might plead the cause of his Church before the pope. But Urban, for reasons I do not know—perhaps because he had grown weary of the serious labors which the restoration of the Church of Arras had forced him to endure—decided that nothing should be changed on that occasion. He issued a provisional rescript to Manasses, archbishop of Reims, instructing him to provide for the long-vacant Church on that occasion in the best way he could according to God’s will.

Manasses did not hesitate. He immediately fixed the Sunday following the feast of the Epiphany for Baldric’s consecration and issued letters to that effect. Baluzius published them, together with four other letters on the same subject, from the manuscript of Lambert, in volume V of his *Miscellanies*.

We infer that Urban’s letter must be assigned to the end of this year because Baldric’s epitaph states that he died on 31 May 1092, in the fifteenth year of his episcopate. He must therefore have begun his episcopate before May of that year. This agrees perfectly with our reckoning, according to which Baldric was consecrated by Manasses on the first Sunday after Epiphany, after receiving the papal rescript shortly before, toward the end of the present year, 1097.

This Baldric was the author of the *Chronicle of Cambrai and Arras*, in which he continued the history of events from Clovis I to the year 1030. The *Chronicle of Thérouanne* is also attributed to him. Vossius says in book II of *On Latin Historians* that it was preserved in manuscript in a monastery in the region of Le Mans, while Marlotus says that it was printed in his *Metropolitan Church of Reims*. But I am mistaken if this work is anything other than the *Chronicle of Cambrai*, which everyone knows.

### CCCVI. Urban remains in Rome while Guibert flees

According to Berthold, under the year 1098—which, following his usual practice, he begins with the Nativity of Christ—the Lord Pope celebrated Christmas at Rome and established the greatest possible peace within the city and its territory. There also he solemnized Easter with great glory.

The same author adds that Guibert, the false pope, was then in the region of Ravenna, to which he had withdrawn when Urban arrived in Rome, as Donizo sings. Guibert “lost a certain fortress above the Po, called Argentum, in which he had always placed the greatest hope, since from it he could easily harass those passing by.”

Sigonius, however, writes that Guibert secretly escaped from Rome and withdrew at that time to Alba in the Marsi, where he had a strong garrison. Wherever Guibert may have been, it is certain, as Eadmer relates in book II of the *New Works*—having himself experienced that danger—that after being driven from Rome he laid snares, through himself and his followers, by every means at his disposal for every religious person who attempted to travel to Rome.

Hence, the same author says, certain bishops, monks, and religious clerics were captured during that persecution, stripped of their possessions, subjected to many insults, and killed. As Eadmer continues, the men of the Alemannic king were chiefly responsible for this. It may therefore be inferred that the persecution raged no less in Germany than in these regions of Italy.

Berthold agrees, observing that Manegold, provost of Marbach and an outstanding defender of Urban, was then seized by Henry and held for a long time in captivity because he refused to adhere to the schismatics. In this same year Rulhandus, archbishop of Mainz, unwilling to support Emperor Henry, was forced to flee and withdraw to Thuringia, as Dodechin reports. That he was restored to the Catholic Church by Lord Urban is testified by Urban’s successor, Paschal himself, in a letter to Gebhard, bishop of Constance, transcribed by Serarius in book V of *The Affairs of Mainz* from a manuscript.

### CCCVII. Gebhard, formerly an abbot, becomes guardian of the Holy Sepulchre

At that time also, as Berthold relates, Gerhard—or rather Gebhard—abbot of Schaffhausen, with the approval of Pope Urban, relinquished the governance of his monastery and set out with the other crusaders for the holy expedition.

When the city of Jerusalem was captured by the Christian armies in the following year, he was appointed the first guardian of the Lord’s Sepulchre, as the same author records. This is the same Gebhard to whom the priest Bernard dedicated his book *On Avoiding the Excommunicated and Reconciling the Fallen, and on the Authority of Councils and Pontiffs*, published by Tegnagel.

Berthold, under the year 1091, praises another book by this same Bernard and says that he left many other monuments of his own learning. He criticizes him, however, for judging that those ordained by excommunicated persons ought to be ordained again.

### CCCVIII. Daimbert consecrated metropolitan of Sens

[Col. 0233A]

Meanwhile Daimbert, who had long since been elected metropolitan of Sens and who, after many evasions, had finally acknowledged the primacy of the Church of Lyon, was consecrated at Rome by the pope himself. He returned to Sens with the archiepiscopal pallium and was received there with solemn ceremony in his church on 18 April.

This, however, was not the end of the controversy over the primacy of Lyon. It soon flared up again, because the archbishops of Sens were reluctant to be subjected to another who himself gloried in the title of primate of Gaul and Germany.

### CCCIX. Rescript for the monks of Saint-André at Vienne

[Col. 0233B]

We think that Urban’s letter in favor of the monks of Saint-André at Vienne may also be assigned to the beginning of this year. Guido, archbishop of that city, harassed them and their servants so severely that he even detained some of them in prison.

This rescript was issued at the Lateran on 8 February, but the year is not stated. Since Urban could have spent February at the Lateran in 1097 and in the two following years, it is not entirely clear to which of these three years the papal letter should be assigned.

If conjecture is permissible, it does not seem to have happened at the beginning of 1097, when the monks of Vienne are said to have gone to Rome to bring their complaints against the archbishop before Urban, for the pope had only just reached Rome at that time. We choose the middle course and assign the rescript to 1098, while not wishing to oppose too strongly anyone who prefers another judgment.

### CCCX. The monastery of Saint-Vigor placed under Saint-Bénigne

The fact that the pontiff remained in Rome throughout March of this year is proved by the privileges granted there to various churches. The first was issued at the Lateran on 14 March. It confirms the donation of the monastery of Saint-Vigor of Bayeux, made by Odo, bishop of Bayeux, to Jarento, abbot of Saint-Bénigne of Dijon.

On the same day, and in the same year, if I judge correctly, the pontiff wrote to Ivo of Chartres and Ramulfus, bishop of Saintes, in favor of the monks of Vendôme, whom he declared exempt from all subjection to bishops. Geoffrey, abbot of that place, reports another letter of the same pontiff on this subject, addressed several days later to all the sons of the Church, in letter 27 to Geoffrey, Ivo’s successor.

### CCCXI. Letters for Saint-Michael on the Meuse

At that time Urban also granted the monks of Saint-Michael on the Meuse, in the diocese of Verdun, permission to abandon the custom of burying their brothers in the old monastery and henceforth to bury them lawfully near the new monastery.

The pope’s letter on this matter was issued at the Lateran on 26 March of this year and addressed to Abbot Ulrich, who had consulted him for that reason. From the letters of both men it is clear that this abbot was especially devoted to Urban, and that his monastery, during the time of the schism, was a common refuge of the Catholics.

### CCCXII. The beginnings of the Cistercian Order

Nothing seems to have given greater distinction to the present year than the origins of the monastery and order of Cîteaux, under the leadership of Saint Robert, abbot of Molesme. At the beginning of this year he relinquished the governance of his monastery and migrated into the Cistercian wilderness with twenty-two of his disciples. There, on 21 March, a day sacred to the holy father Benedict, he laid the first foundations of the celebrated order.

Waleric, the diocesan bishop of Chalon, gave his approval; Odo, duke of Burgundy, provided assistance; and Hugh, metropolitan of Lyon, confirmed everything by his own authority and that of Urban, whose vicar in Gaul and legate of the Apostolic See he was.

Hugh’s letter on this subject was published by Labbe in volume I of the *New Library*, and by Manriquez and others. What happened thereafter to Robert will be explained in its proper place.

### CCCXIII. Privilege of Urgell

As for affairs in Spain, the pope confirmed the possessions of the Church of Urgell in a diploma addressed to Odo, bishop of that Church, on 6 April, in the sixth indiction and the eleventh year of the pope’s pontificate. These chronological notes agree with the present year.

The copy published in *Marca Hispanica*, however, gives the year of the Incarnation as 1099. This is either a copyist’s error or, as often happened elsewhere, the year is reckoned there from the preceding March.

Shortly afterward, on 11 May, Urban wished to restore the city of Huesca—which King Sancho of Aragon had taken from the Moors in 1096—to its former dignity, by restoring to it the episcopal see that had been transferred to Jaca.

The late Cardinal Aguirre published a notable bull on this matter in volume III of his *Councils of Spain*. In it the pontiff confirms the donations made to that Church by various kings of Aragon and includes many other matters not unworthy of notice.

### CCCXIV. Anselm’s journey to Rome. He withdraws into solitude
Now indeed it is time to return to Anselm of Canterbury, who came to Rome at the beginning of spring of this year. Since, as Eadmer relates at length, [Col. 0234D] new difficulties were arising daily between him and William, king of England, Anselm had asked the king to grant him permission to go to Rome, which he finally obtained, after many quarrels, on the Ides of October of the preceding year. Without delay, having arranged the affairs of his church, he prepared for the journey and went to Dover, where, by order of the king, his baggage was searched. Then he crossed over to France, and there celebrated the feast of the Nativity of Christ with Saint Hugh, abbot of Cluny. Proceeding from there to Lyon, he was received with great pomp by another Hugh, archbishop of that city. There, fearing that perhaps this journey might displease the pope, he remained anxiously in doubt, not knowing whether he ought to go farther. Therefore he sent a messenger with letters to Urban, so that he might learn from Urban himself what ought to be done.

[Col. 0235A] This is the letter numbered 166 in the published editions of Book III, which Eadmer presents in full in Book II of the *New Works*, with this inscription:

> To the lord and Father, revered with love and loved with reverence, the supreme pontiff Urban, Brother Anselm, servant of the Church of Canterbury, offers due submission and the devotion of his prayers, etc.

In it, after setting forth to the pontiff the various tribulations by which he had been harassed and almost worn down from the beginning of his episcopate, the holy man asks him to grant permission for him to resign his see. But when the pontiff received the letters of so great a man, he rejoiced and gave him no other answer than that, putting aside every excuse, he should come immediately to Rome. The holy man obeyed him without delay and departed at once. After celebrating, near Susa, in the monastery of Saint [Col. 0235B] Justus of the Val di Susa, and then at Saint Michael of Chiusa, the solemnities of the Lord’s Passion and Resurrection, and after successfully avoiding the ambushes of the Guibertines that had been prepared for him, he finally arrived in Rome with only two companions.

On the following day he was presented to Urban in the Lateran palace, where, by the pope’s order, he had been lodged. He humbled himself, as was customary, at the feet of the supreme pontiff, but was immediately raised by him to receive his kiss and was ordered to sit in a chair. All the nobility of the city of Rome and of the curia had gathered there, eager to see so great a man. After the pontiff had heard from him the reasons for his journey and had publicly spoken at length in his praise, he promised him full assistance. He then ordered the holy man to remain with him for the time being in the Lateran palace, [Col. 0235C] where he was to await the result of that assistance.

Meanwhile Urban wrote a letter to the king of the English, and Anselm did likewise. But the king, after receiving both letters, did not even deign to touch the one that was Anselm’s. These and the other matters that we relate concerning Anselm are narrated more fully in the *Life* of that same saint and in the books of the *New Works* by Eadmer, his companion and inseparable fellow traveler and fellow laborer, who was present at the events. In those works he says much more about the exceptional veneration shown to Anselm by everyone in the city.

But Anselm was weary of being honored in this way. Therefore, after spending ten days in Rome, he went, at the invitation of John, once his disciple at Bec but then abbot of Saint Savior near the city of Telesia in Terra di Lavoro, [Col. 0235D] to stay with him. John led him to a village belonging to his monastery, called Sclavia, situated on a neighboring mountain. There Anselm spent some time living entirely free from the commotion of the curia, devoted chiefly to spiritual exercises and the study of sacred matters. Anselm made excellent use of this leisure and completely finished the distinguished work that he had begun long before in England, under the title *Why God Became Man* (*Cur Deus homo*).

Since there was a shortage of water there, he is said to have obtained a living spring from God by his prayers. When Peter of Diensis was once staying at Bec, he expressed this miracle, among other deeds of Anselm, in verses that I once read in a manuscript, with considerable elegance for the period.

### CCCXV. The Pontiff Visits Duke Roger

[Col. 0236A]

At this time Duke Roger of Apulia was besieging the city of Capua. Having heard of the holy man’s fame, he invited him to come to him, and went out to meet him when he arrived, accompanied by a great crowd of nobles. The holy man remained with him for several days, but far from the noise of the court, in a secluded place that the prince had ordered to be prepared for him as a mark of favor.

Meanwhile Urban, so that the affairs of Italy might not be disturbed by this war, also went to Roger’s camp to arrange peace. Since he could not then secure it, he decided to remain there—or at least in the vicinity, as Eadmer relates—with Saint Anselm until the city’s surrender, so that these disputes might more easily be settled.

Orderic, briefly repeating Anselm’s deeds in Book X, [Col. 0236B] writes that he found Urban in Apulia, attended the Council of Bari with him, and preached the Lord’s cross at Clermont. But this otherwise accurate and diligent author confuses the events and their dates. He rightly refers his readers to Eadmer, who in this matter deserves to be heard much more than Orderic should be believed concerning what he himself had related about it.

Geoffrey Malaterra, however, an author of that period who was himself present at the events, reports that when Urban accomplished nothing in Roger’s camp, he devoted himself to ecclesiastical rather than military affairs, turning his mind away from every disturbance. He gave his apostolic blessing to the princes—for both Rogers and Richard, prince of Capua, were there—and to the entire army, and withdrew to Benevento, where he remained [Col. 0236C] until the siege of Capua was lifted.

### CCCXVI. He Withdraws to Benevento

Perhaps during this siege, when no hope of arranging peace appeared, the pontiff went to Benevento, a city which, as the same author observes, was under apostolic jurisdiction, and afterward returned to Roger once Capua had been captured.

Certainly Urban himself implies that he visited Benevento at this time in a letter written in the following November to Anso, lord of that city, which we shall discuss below. On that occasion the pontiff confirmed Anso in the principality of the city of Benevento, from which he was deprived only three years later by Paschal II, as Peregrinius explains more fully at the beginning of his *Corrections to the Chronicle of Falcon*.

Urban himself also seems to recall this journey in a rescript issued toward the end of this year to the monks of Cassino against the abbess of Cingoli. He says there that he had left Rome for ecclesiastical business and, in the presence of both parties, had dealt with the lawsuit between that abbess and Oderisius, abbot of Cassino. This rescript, like the letter to Anso, appears in its proper order near the end of this year in our collection.

Moreover, the siege of Capua is mentioned by Lupus Protospata, the anonymous writer of Cassino, and other authors, but they assign it to different years because they used different systems of reckoning—unless this resulted from scribal error, as can be seen in Peregrinius’s *Corrections*.

### CCCXVII. Anselm Is Not Permitted to Resign His See

[Col. 0237A]

Eadmer writes that immediately after the lifting of the siege of Capua, Anselm went with Urban to Aversa. There the pontiff lodged in the city itself, while Anselm stayed in the nearby monastery of Saint Lawrence, belonging to our order.

When Anselm one day asked the pontiff there to permit him, after resigning his episcopate, to live privately in a monastery, Urban not only refused his consent but, rebuking him in sharper words, commanded him under obedience never to abandon the care of the flock entrusted to him.

It is worth reproducing the pontiff’s exact words:

> “The pope,” says that author, “hears what he requests and immediately, astonished, exclaims: ‘O bishop! O shepherd! You have not yet suffered slaughter or wounds, and you seek to evade the care of the Lord’s fold. Christ tests Peter’s love for him through the care of his sheep; and Anselm—Anselm, I say, that holy man, so great and distinguished a man—wanting only to rest, does not hesitate to expose Christ’s sheep, to be torn apart by the bites of wolves even before the battle. Ah, what shall I say? With what love does he hope to be joined to the Lord, who flees that by which the Lord himself, as his witness, is shown to be loved? Let such things be far from you, far from your religion, dearest brother Anselm; rather, do not trouble me further with these matters.
>
> “‘Know that I not only do not grant you what you ask; indeed, in the name of Almighty God and in the place of the most blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, I command you under holy obedience not to abandon the care of the English kingdom entrusted to you, so long as you are able to retain it, as you have done until now. But if, because of the tyranny of the prince who now rules there, you are not permitted to return to that land, nevertheless, by the right of your Christianity, remain always its archbishop. Throughout your life retain over it the power of binding and loosing, and use the pontifical insignia according to the custom of the supreme pontiff wherever you may be.’”

To this Anselm promised obedience and replied that he fled neither slaughter nor wounds, nor even death itself. He had wished to resign his see, he said, because it had seemed impossible for him to show complete obedience to blessed Peter while also maintaining the allegiance that the English claimed was owed to an earthly king.

The pontiff replied:

> “‘You are guided by reason,’ he said. ‘And so that I may not appear unconcerned about these and other wrongs unjustly inflicted upon you, or unwilling to avenge them with the sword of Saint Peter, I advise you to present yourself at the council that I have decided to celebrate at Bari, before the body of blessed Nicholas, on the Kalends of October. There you will hear and see what I have resolved to do, by an equitable judgment, concerning that English king and his followers and like-minded men, who have risen against the liberty of the Church of God.’”

After hearing this, the man of God, as Eadmer continues, returned to Sclavia, intending to remain there until the Council of Bari.

How greatly the holy man valued obedience can be learned from William of Malmesbury. In Book I of *The Deeds of the Bishops*, he relates that Anselm obtained from Urban the appointment of someone whose commands he would be bound to obey. Eadmer was appointed to this position, and Anselm obeyed him, so that he scarcely dared even to turn over in bed without his permission.

### CCCXVIII. Urban’s Meeting with Roger

Meanwhile, after Capua had been captured, the pontiff learned that both Rogers had gone to Salerno. He decided to go to them there before Count Roger returned to Sicily.

When Urban arrived with the archbishops and the rest of his retinue, a solemn procession went out to meet him. He spent several days there, refreshed by frequent conversation with Count Roger, for they were the closest of friends, as Geoffrey Malaterra relates in Book IV.

On that occasion, as the same author writes, Urban noticed that Roger was displeased because Robert, bishop of Troina, had been appointed apostolic legate in Sicily without consulting him. Urban therefore altered the arrangement of affairs and granted this dignity hereditarily to Roger himself, on account of his outstanding merits toward the Church. He promised that, during the lifetime of the count—or of any surviving heir who might act as an executor of paternal ecclesiastical zeal—he would never send another legate to Sicily against Roger’s will.

From this arose the famous apostolic constitution on the matter, issued in this year on the third day before the Nones of July. After Geoffrey, it will be published by various authors and compared with manuscript codices. Yet although its other chronological details may be genuine, the indiction in it has been corrupted.

Much has been written here and there on the occasion of this constitution, but it is not relevant for us to investigate the matter at greater length. If desired, one may consult Baronius, volume XI; Rocchus Pyrrhus, [Col. 0238C] volume II of *Sacred Sicily*, pages 452 and following; and other authors.

Whether this legation also extended into Calabria, where Sasso, bishop of Cassano, was then exercising an apostolic legation, is uncertain, though Geoffrey seems to suggest that it did.

### CCCXIX. The Primacy Is Granted to the Church of Salerno

Shortly afterward, specifically on 20 July, the pontiff, at the request of the other Roger—that is, the duke of Apulia—and of Archbishop Alfanus, granted an important privilege to the Church of Salerno, conferring upon it primacy over the two metropolitan sees of Conza and Acerenza, which had once been subject to it by metropolitan right.

The bull was issued on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of August in the year 1099, according to its copies; but this year must be understood as beginning in the preceding March, so that it can be assigned to the present year. The fourth indiction supplied there, however, cannot be excused unless the error is attributed to the copyists.

This would be the place to discuss another rescript of Urban’s by which, in favor of the same church, the privileges of the monastery of Cava were revoked, if it were not said to have been issued at Rome. The seventh indiction that it bears could suit this year. We shall discuss it below.

### CCCXX. Rescript for Saint Bruno

What Urban granted in September of this year to Saint Bruno, founder of the Carthusian order, who was then living in the wilderness of Squillace, is wholly genuine and entirely beyond doubt. It confirmed and established all the possessions that Count Roger and John, bishop of Squillace, had bestowed upon his monastery.

It was issued at Salerno in September of this year, in the sixth indiction. From this we infer that Urban remained in that city until the Council of Bari.

### CCCXXI. The Crusaders Capture Antioch

While these events were taking place in Italy, the crusaders, after various battles and after conquering many cities here and there during this and the preceding year, occupied Antioch in June of this year.

Shortly afterward, however, the barbarians, roused from various provinces by the report of so great a disaster among their people, gathered together as though they were going to fight for the common safety. They surrounded the Christians in that city so closely that no hope of escape now appeared to them.

But when human resources failed, help from above arrived. A sacred lance was discovered—apparently not without the suspicion of a miracle—which was believed to be the lance with which the side of Christ the Lord had been pierced. Our men’s courage was so greatly aroused that, presenting this as a sure sign of victory, the soldiers poured forth against the armies of the barbarians, inflicted a great defeat upon them, and utterly routed and overthrew them.

All these events, besides the authors of the history of the holy expeditions, are reported by the Christian leaders and princes themselves in a letter written to Urban at that time. After narrating the victory, they announce to him the death of Adhemar, bishop of Le Puy, who had been appointed legate of the apostolic see and leader of the expedition. After overcoming many hardships and once affairs had been entirely pacified, he had died at Antioch on the very Kalends of August.

They then ask the pontiff himself—who had been the principal author and promulgator of the holy expedition—to come to the East as their leader and prince. After having obtained the chair of Peter at Rome, where he had now been seated for several years, they wished him to enjoy a similar honor in the other chair of that same apostle, at Antioch.

This letter was written on 11 September, in the fourth indiction, as indicated by the edition of Baluze, Book I of the *Miscellanies*, page 419, where it is more complete than in Fulcher’s *Deeds of God through the Franks*. It did not seem worthwhile to reproduce it in full, since it can easily be found in those authors. Here, therefore, it is enough to give its title:

> To the holy and venerable lord Pope Urban, from Bohemond, Raymond, count of Saint-Gilles, Godfrey, duke of Lorraine, Robert, count of Normandy, Robert, count of the Flemings, and Eustace, count of Boulogne: greetings, faithful service, and, as sons to their spiritual father, true submission in Christ. We all wish and desire to make known to you how great was the mercy of God, and by how evident an aid of that same God Antioch was captured by us, etc.

What the pontiff replied to this letter is unknown to us. It is certain, however, that he never undertook any journey to the East.

There is no doubt that the mission of Daimbert to the crusaders must also be assigned here. Bertoldus mentions it in this year in these words:

> “The lord pope,” says that author, “sent his legation to that same multitude, namely the venerable Theobert, archbishop of the Church of Pisa, who would be present among them in all matters in the place of the apostolic see and would restore the churches in the places from which the pagans had been expelled.”

After Jerusalem had later been captured, when Arnulf yielded his place, Theobert was proclaimed patriarch of that city, as many other authors have observed.

The Genoese are said at that time to have brought home from Myra, a city of Lycia, the relics of Saint John the Baptist, which they still possess in their metropolitan church.

Among the Christian princes, only the emperor of Constantinople disturbed these Christian victories. So much so, Bertoldus says, that he did not hesitate to devastate by fire even cities that had been captured by the westerners and return them to the pagans. He also prohibited, as far as he could by his authority, every pilgrim from traveling to Jerusalem.

### CCCXXII. The Schismatics’ Assembly at Rome

Although in those times, when everyone everywhere seemed unanimously to agree to obey Urban, the schismatics’ cause ought to have been entirely hopeless, they nevertheless did not abstain from their assemblies, even though Guibert was absent. This is clear from their pseudosynodal letter, which was addressed—as they themselves falsely claim—to all who fear God and care for the welfare of the Roman state. Baronius reproduced it from Benno’s *Life of Hildebrand* under this year, and Labbeus included it in the appendix to volume X of the *Councils*.

From this letter we learn who the chief supporters of the Guibertine faction were then at Rome. Their names and dignities are listed in the following order:

Adalbert, bishop of Santa Rufina of Silva Candida; John, bishop of Ostia; Hugh, bishop of Palestrina; Albert, bishop of Nepi; Benno, cardinal priest of the city of Rome; Octavian, designated cardinal priest; Paul, primicerius of the Roman Church; Nicholas, elected abbot of Saint Sylvester in the city of Rome; N., abbot of Saint Pancras in the city of Rome; the clergy; and the illustrious princes Theobald of Chinebio and Udalric of Saint Eustace, together with the Roman people.

They say that they met three times in different churches of the city of Rome to destroy the heresies invented by Hildebrand—whom they still called Gregory VII. First, on the Nones of August, at Saint Blaise; then, on the eighth day before the Ides, at Saint Celsus; and on the following day at Saint Mary, called the Rotunda. Thus they still possessed these three churches in Rome. There they condemned those heresies.

They then promise safety to anyone wishing to attend the next synod, which they planned to celebrate around the Kalends of November.

This letter was issued at Rome against the schismatics, as they called them, in a sacred assembly, in the year 1098 from the Incarnation of the Lord, in the sixth indiction, on the seventh day before the Ides of August.

But when they foresaw with certainty that none of the Catholics would come to their assembly, they called heaven and earth as witnesses that they in no way consented to the Catholics’ perversity—for that is how they spoke of the Catholics. To prove this in deed as well, they immediately threw into the fire the books of those same Catholics that they had in their hands, because, despite the various councils convened and repeated over sixteen years, the Catholics had never been willing to heed their admonitions.

This is what concerns the schismatics, who, together with Benno the pseudo-cardinal, liked to call our pontiff “Turban,” because, as they falsely accused him, he continued to cause disturbances by following in Gregory’s footsteps. But the insults of such men are matched by the many praises of the true pontiff. Indeed, even the schismatics were compelled, however unwillingly, to admit that Urban loved peace and was the gentlest of all the people who at that time dwelt upon the earth—as Scripture says of Moses.

What that heresy was which the schismatics attributed to Gregory VII we learn from the same Benno in his *Life of Gregory*, where he says:

> “The glorious Hildebrand and his footman Turban, dissolving the decrees of the Council of Chalcedon by a new power, agreed not only in words but also in public writings to communicate and baptize outside the Church. Their own writings reveal how blind and heretical they were, etc. Both fell into the heresy of Liberius, who, after publicly communicating with excommunicated persons, split the unity by making two churches, etc.”

Thus the schismatics did not hesitate to call the Catholic leaders and lovers of unity schismatics.

### CCCXXIII. The Council of Bari Celebrated This Year

The Catholics, on the appointed day of the Kalends of October—or, as the anonymous writer of Bari states, on the third day of that month—assembled at Bari, the famous city of Apulia, for the council summoned by Urban.

[Col. 0241C] This synod seems to have been convened chiefly so that the Greeks and Latins might reach agreement concerning the faith, lest differences in belief should harm the holy expeditions.

Baronius and his followers, and even Labbeus in volume X of the *Councils*, assigned this synod to the preceding year. Others rightly disagree, following Lupus Protospata and the anonymous writer of Bari, contemporary and local authorities, who testify that it was celebrated at the beginning of October of the year 1099—which they begin, according to their custom, with the preceding September, in the year 1098.

We have another witness to the same matter, beyond all exception: Eadmer, who took part in that council. As we have already said, he reports in Book II of the *New Works* that Anselm extorted permission from William, king of the English, in October of the year 1097 to go to Rome, and then follows in detail the sequence of events in the life of the blessed bishop up to the Council of Bari. He therefore narrates that the council was convened in the following year, and consequently in 1098.

Next, according to the same author, after that synod Urban returned to Rome and granted King William a truce until the feast of Saint Michael of the following year. Neither the king nor the pontiff, however, reached that date. But if that truce had been granted immediately after the Council of Bari in 1097, both William and Urban would have lived until its expiration. It is certain that both reached the year 1099.

From these facts, which are entirely certain, one may also infer that the Roman synod assigned by some to the year 1098 is not different from the one celebrated in the following year, as contemporary authors report. Baronius and Labbeus, having moved the date of the Council of Bari back by one year because they placed it incorrectly, carelessly assigned it to 1098 together with its canons.

### CCCXXIV. The Acts of the Council of Bari

Although we owe our principal knowledge of what took place at the Council of Bari to the English historians who wrote about it in connection with Saint Anselm, it was not, as has already been noted, unknown to other serious authors who were close to it in place and time.

Certainly the anonymous writer of Bari says that many members of the clergy and noblemen assembled there, in these words:

> In the year 1099—which, like the indiction, he begins with the preceding September, as we have just said—in the seventh indiction, on the third day of the month of October, Pope Urban came with many archbishops, bishops, abbots, counts, and they entered Bari, and they were received with great reverence. A wondrous seat inside the church of the most blessed Nicholas, confessor of Christ, was prepared for Lord Elias, our archbishop. Here he uses *sextum* in place of the proper case, as will be clear below from Malmesbury. He held a synod there for one week. After completing eight days, he departed in peace, and in the month of July Urban himself died.

Lupus Protospata asserts that 180 bishops attended this synod, which Urban himself calls plenary in his rescript concerning the cell of Cingoli. But no one has recorded who they were.

From William of Malmesbury we learn where and in what manner the pontiff sat in the council:

> “Then,” he says, “they came to the council. The apostolic lord, seated before the body of Saint Nicholas on carpets and coverings, wearing the chasuble and pallium, ascended the tribunal; the others sat wearing capes.”

A little farther on he observes that the Roman archdeacon sat before the pope, as was customary.

At the Council of Reims in 1094, Pope Leo, wearing priestly vestments as though about to celebrate Mass, proceeded to the council with the cross and the book of the Gospel carried before him by ministers of the sacred order, etc.

In this council Anselm, archbishop of Canterbury, was ordered to sit beside Urban as a mark of honor, or perhaps so that he might be heard more easily when disputing against the Greeks. Previously, as the same author writes, the pontiff, when a disturbance arose, had forgotten to designate a special and honorable place for him.

Eadmer gives the same account of the chasuble and the pontiffs’ capes. He says, however, that Anselm initially sat first in rank among the other bishops, but that when the dispute grew heated he was told to come closer.

The same author says:

> “When the supreme pontiff had discussed many matters concerning the Catholic faith with eloquent reasoning and reasonable eloquence, the Greeks raised the question of the procession of the Holy Spirit. The pontiff attempted to establish it with many arguments, most of them drawn from Anselm’s letter that he had once entitled *On the Incarnation of the Word*.”

John of Salisbury gives the same account in his *Life of Anselm*.

But, Eadmer says, when the matter proceeded at greater length, [Col. 0243A] and Anselm was still seated among the other leading fathers of the council, according to the dignity of his see, the pontiff cried out:

> “Father and teacher Anselm, archbishop of the English, where are you?”

With the assistance of the bishops who were near him, he was immediately raised and brought to the apostolic seat, as William relates, and was ordered to sit beside the archdeacon.

The pontiff then addressed him, according to Eadmer, who was present:

> “What are you doing, I ask? Why do you remain silent among the others? Come, come, I beg you; ascend to us and help us, fighting for your mother and ours, whose integrity you see these Greeks attempting to take away, and to plunge us into the same wickedness if they are given the opportunity. Come to our aid, then, as one truly sent here by God for this purpose.”

The following day Anselm performed this task magnificently, the same author writes, with the Holy Spirit guiding his heart and tongue. He treated, discussed, and resolved the question so effectively that no one in the assembly remained who did not acknowledge that he had been satisfied by the discussion.

When the holy bishop had finished speaking, the pontiff looked at him and said:

> “Blessed be your heart and understanding, and blessed be your mouth and the word of your mouth.”

The holy man later treated these same arguments, which he had presented before the council fathers, more fully in a book *On the Procession of the Holy Spirit*, at the request of his friends, especially Hildebert, then bishop of Le Mans, as is clear from his Letter 22. William, a monk of Jumièges, also reports this in Book VI, chapter 9. Anselm did this so that Catholic teaching might spread throughout the entire Christian world.

Later, when he was questioned about these matters by Waleram, bishop of Neuburg, the bishop Anselm referred him to those treatises. On that occasion something remarkable occurred: Anselm refused even to greet this bishop in the customary manner, solely because he still believed him attached to the Henrician schism, as Anselm himself testifies. See his letters, or replies, to Waleram’s questions and complaints.

For now, however, let us continue with what took place at the synod.

The council then came to Anselm’s case against William, king of the English. When the pontiff had publicly set forth before the sacred assembly the injuries inflicted upon the blessed man, everyone cried out that King William ought to be struck with the sword of blessed Peter. Anselm alone opposed this.

When the holy man heard this, as Eadmer relates—and the other English writers agree—he immediately rose and, falling to his knees before the pope, who was already prepared to excommunicate the aforementioned king, scarcely succeeded in preventing him from doing to the king what the common judgment of all had proclaimed.

From Urban’s letter to Anso, lord of Benevento, we learn that the monks of Cassino came to the same council to assert their claim to the monastery of Saint Sophia at Benevento. But since the abbot of that place withdrew from the council, the dispute remained undecided.

A second dispute of the Cassinese monks, against the abbess of Cingoli, had the same outcome there. Since she did not appear, judgment in the case was postponed to another time, as the pontiff himself testifies in the letter addressed to the monks of Cassino, which we shall mention below.

### CCCXXV. Privilege of the Church of Agrigento

On the sixth day before the Ides of October, the pontiff was still at Bari when he confirmed the boundaries of the diocese of Agrigento as they had been established by Count Roger. He did so in a diploma that praises, with many commendations—and rightly so—the outstanding merits of Duke Robert and his brother, Count Roger, toward the Church.

You can find this bull in Rocchus Pyrrhus, though its chronological details require some correction. The eighth indiction recorded there does not suit this year; at most, it should be the seventh, reckoned from September or from the beginning of October.

This error may have arisen through the fault of the copyists. When they noticed that the privilege bore the end of the year 1099, they may have wished to adjust the indiction to the ordinary civil year. But by the end of that year Urban had already died.

Therefore, it must be said that in this bull the pontiff used the system of reckoning followed in the region of Bari, where he was then staying. According to that system, as we have already said, the year, like the indiction, began in October of the preceding civil year.

Others may perhaps say that the diploma begins the year from the Incarnation—that is, from March of the preceding year—as was often done elsewhere. But the result is the same, since by either reckoning it is clear that the year 1099 is correctly assigned here for the ordinary year 1098.

### CCCXXVI. The Council of Bordeaux

[Col. 0244C]

In Gaul, in the same month, specifically on the third day before the Nones of October, Amatus, legate of the apostolic see in Aquitaine and then archbishop of that city, held a council at Bordeaux. Roland of Dol, Peter of Agen, and other bishops from various provinces are said to have assembled there with him.

But what was established at that council, or on what occasion it was convened, is entirely unknown. Labbeus himself gives no further information in volume X of the *Councils*.

### CCCXXVII. Urban Passes through Benevento

After the Council of Bari, Urban, returning to Rome, passed through Benevento. There he had decided to settle the dispute between the monastery of Cingoli and the Cassinese monks, who wished to subject it to themselves. He wrote to the abbess of that monastery with the intention that she should no longer delay appearing before him to pursue her case.

Nevertheless, even then the matter remained unresolved, as the pontiff himself explains more fully in the diploma already mentioned, which will be presented in its proper place.

In the same place, at the monastery of Saint Sophia, where he perhaps had lodgings, he examined the case of the abbot of that monastery, who refused to obey the abbot of Cassino, but did not settle it.

Indeed, shortly afterward, on the third day before the Nones of the following November, while he was at Ceprano, he wrote to Anso, lord of Benevento, instructing him, after hearing both parties, to decide the dispute. If, however, the monks of Saint Sophia refused to answer him in this matter because he was a layman, he was to set a day on which they would come to Rome to receive judgment from the pontiff himself.

This is the rescript of Urban so often mentioned. That it must be assigned to 3 November of this year is established with certainty by its reference to the recently celebrated Council of Bari.

### CCCXXVIII. He Writes at Rome on Behalf of the Monks of Vendôme

After Urban returned to Rome, near the end of November he confirmed the privileges of the monastery of Vendôme in several diplomas, all of which are said to have been issued on the same day.

From this we infer that Goffridus, abbot of that place, who enjoyed great influence with Urban, was then staying in Rome at his titular church of Saint Prisca, where the monks of Vendôme lived. He could therefore easily have obtained all these privileges from the pontiff.

They were not included in a single diploma because they concerned different matters. Rather, they were mostly confirmations of earlier grants already contained in various rescripts than concessions of new privileges. Hence several documents of almost identical tenor appear, issued, as we have said, on one and the same day.

We recovered four such documents from the archives of Vendôme. Goffridus himself supplies a fifth in Letter 27 of Book II. All of them will be included in the collection of papal letters.

### CCCXXIX. At Rome Goffridus Speaks about the Bishop of Angers

I believe that Goffridus’s journey to Rome must also be assigned to this period. He himself reports it in Book I, Letter 28, addressed to Hugh of Lyon, where he admits that he was questioned by the pope about Geoffrey, bishop of Angers, and that he told the pope certain things about that bishop which could not be concealed from him.

We infer that these matters were of no small importance from the fact that shortly afterward that same Geoffrey, at Urban’s urging, resigned his bishopric and became a monk of Cluny. This is noted from the *Chronicle of Saint Aubin* by Sirmondus in his notes on Letter 1 of Book III of Goffridus, and by Juretus in his notes on the letters of Ivo of Chartres.

The same Goffridus at that time undertook the defense of Ivo, bishop of Chartres, whom certain persons had accused before Pope Urban. For I have no doubt that the matters which Goffridus himself wrote about that accusation in Book II, Letter 18, must be referred to this occasion, whatever Sirmond may say, since in his notes he argues that this letter belongs to the time of Paschal II. Certainly, if this letter of Goffridus is compared with Letter 67 of Ivo, written to Urban himself at the beginning of the following year, everyone will perceive—as I am indeed convinced—that both letters concern one and the same affair.

Goffridus writes in his letter that he found the pope at Rome, possessing that city and the Roman Church at that time in great peace and tranquillity. Such, indeed, was the state of affairs at Rome under Urban at that time, as Bertoldus and others explicitly relate; but Urban was ill-disposed toward Ivo, evidently because of the controversy over the primacy of Lyons, as can easily be inferred from what follows in the same letter. Ivo, however, says in the letter mentioned that he likewise learned that the pope had been stirred up against him on account of certain letters—also mentioned by Goffridus—concerning the primacy of Lyons, and all these details fit together perfectly. Since Ivo’s letter was written, as he himself testifies, shortly after the feast of Christ’s Nativity, at the beginning of the eighth year of his episcopate, it must necessarily be assigned, as we have said elsewhere, to the beginning of the year 1099, and consequently Goffridus’s letter must be assigned to that time as well.

### CCCXXX. King Philip again placed under interdict

From the same letter of Ivo we learn that Philip, king of France, did not long persevere in penance after his reconciliation, since once again that year he was placed under ecclesiastical interdict for having recalled Bertrada, by order of the papal legate. Nevertheless, Archbishop Rodulfus of Tours did not fear to place the crown upon him at the Nativity of the Lord, despite the interdict, as is clear both from the same letter of Ivo and from the following letter to Hugh of Lyons.

Hence I conclude that the statement found in a certain charter of Saint Julian of Tours—that Philip received the crown at Tours in the year 1091 from the hands of Archbishop Rodulfus—is either erroneous, or, more probably, must be understood of another coronation of the same king. For at that time kings were customarily crowned on great solemn occasions by the archbishop of Reims, if he was present; or, in his absence, by the diocesan metropolitan; or by any other person who, at the king’s command, acted in place of the archbishop of Reims.

Ivo indicates in Letter 84 to John, another legate and cardinal, written shortly after Urban’s death, that the interdict imposed upon the king by the legate had been confirmed by Urban. Yet it can be established with certainty from Urban’s rescript to Manasses of Reims, mentioned above under the year 1098, that the sentence of this second interdict could not have been issued before the end of the year 1097.

We learn that the king did not obey it both from the letter of Ivo mentioned above and from what was later done at the Council of Poitiers. Guibertus certainly indicated that King Philip had frequently fallen and relapsed, in Book I of *On Pledges*, section, chapter 1, where he observes that King Philip lost, through offences he had incurred, the privilege of curing scrofulous swellings about the neck—a privilege which his son Louis VI commonly exercised after making the sign of the cross.

### CCCXXXI. The Privilege of Saint Cucuphas

On the first day of December of this year Urban granted a notable privilege to the monastery of Octavium of Saint Cucuphas, near Barcelona, in which the individual possessions of that place are listed.

Several days later the pope issued another rescript, often cited by us already, in which, after separately recounting various disputes, he decreed that the monastery of Cingoli near Capua, together with the nuns residing there, ought to be subject to the abbot of Monte Cassino. It is said to have been written at Rome on 7 December by the hand of Peter the scrinarius, and to have been issued the following day through the hands of John, cardinal deacon—a formula that frequently occurs in subsequent charters.

### CCCXXXII. The King of England Obtains a Truce

Meanwhile Anselm, whom Eadmer records as having returned to Rome together with Urban after the Council of Bari, was awaiting the outcome of his case. But a messenger who then arrived in the city on behalf of King William frustrated all his hopes. After many arguments on both sides, he finally obtained from the pope, at the feast of the Nativity of the Lord, a truce for the king until the feast of Saint Michael the Archangel; but neither party reached that date.

Eadmer suggests that the truce was obtained by a minister of King William through distributing gifts and making promises to those whom he had observed to be receptive to them. William of Malmesbury does not hesitate to extend this charge even to Urban, although he is sometimes more hostile than is proper toward the Roman pontiffs.

For what reason, indeed, would the pope have stubbornly refused to grant King William a truce which he could scarcely have denied to any human being, however lowly and contemptible? The same amount of time was required to summon witnesses from England and to bring forward the documents that seemed necessary for the examination of the case.

Certainly Urban, who at his first meeting with the king’s messenger had fixed Easter as the time for hearing the case, could not fail to extend the truce for some period, since the king himself, through his messenger from the remotest parts of the world, and promising that he would give satisfaction even after the case had been examined, was pressing the request with particular insistence. I mean a king for whom the needs of the Church and the circumstances of the times required more lenient treatment; a king, finally, who not long before had approached obedience to the pope, rejecting the schismatics.

Certainly neither then nor afterward did Urban ever appear to comply with the evil wishes of King William, nor did he show Anselm less favor in the future than before. Indeed, as Eadmer himself relates, when the holy man wished to return to Lyons, the pope forbade him, because he had decided to hold a council at Rome during the third week after Easter.

### CCCXXXIII. Honors Conferred upon Anselm

The position in which the holy man was held and the honor bestowed upon him in the city throughout this entire interval are explained by the same author, both in Anselm’s *Life* and in the books of the *New Works*, in these words:

> “We therefore remained,” says that author, “for nearly half a year, constantly living near the pope and, as it were, sharing a common life with him; for there seemed to be not two courts, but one court belonging to both. Thus the pope himself frequently came to Anselm, dealing joyfully with him and holding court for him. He also gave him lodging in which we lived. . . . Anselm himself, in the gatherings of nobles, in processions, at stations, always and everywhere stood second only to the pope; he was honored above all and welcomed by all. The author adds in the *Life* something worthy of remembrance. In those times, Englishmen coming to Rome desired, by their offerings, to honor Anselm’s feet in the same manner as the feet of the Roman pontiff.”

Nor did Urban suffer any envy on this account, or ever take it ill. Rather, when he learned that Anselm had never wished to accept this devotion of the English, he admired in the man his humility and contempt for the world, and ordered him to hold back from doing so no one who wished to perform this act of piety; instead, he was to receive patiently all those who came for that purpose. Such was the humility of both holy men and their charity toward one another.

### CCCXXXIV. Anselm’s Conversations with the Pope

The conversations between Anselm and the pope which Eadmer praises undoubtedly correspond to several letters of that holy man, in which he responds to various questions according to what he had heard from Pope Urban.

Thus, in Letter 130 of Book III, he dissuades Peter, a monk of Saint-Martin of Sées, from going to Jerusalem, because such a journey would be contrary to the vow of stability and to the obedience owed to the apostolic authority. For, says Anselm, the pope “had commanded with great authority that monks should not undertake this journey without the obedience of their superior.” He adds: “I was present when the apostolic authority defended this judgment.”

The apostolic authority whose name Anselm does not state here was expressly identified as Urban by Goffridus, abbot of Vendôme, in Letter 21 of Book IV. In that letter he attempts, as Sirmond believes, to restrain Odo, abbot of the Great Monastery, from the same desire to make a pilgrimage:

> “Urban, who had ordered laymen to make a pilgrimage by going to Jerusalem, had forbidden the pilgrimage itself to monks; and he testifies that he heard this from the pope’s own mouth.”

On another occasion Anselm asked Urban that he might sometimes be permitted to moderate the strictness of the canons somewhat, since this seemed to him more conducive to the state of affairs in England. He easily obtained this both from that pontiff and from Paschal, as is clear from a letter of Paschal himself, Book III, no. 45 among the *Anselmian* letters.

At times questions concerning various matters of ecclesiastical discipline were also introduced into these familiar conversations. To this category, it seems, belongs the question which Anselm treats in Book III, Letter 159: whether an altar that had been moved from its proper place ought to be consecrated again.

There, as also Ivo does in Letters 72 and 80, together with other canonists of that age, he judges that on such an occasion not only the altar but the church itself ought to be consecrated anew. We learn that this was done at Lobbes from the *Deeds of the Abbots of that Place*, in Volume VI of the *Spicilegium*, p. 609. This rite, however, has now fallen into disuse.

According to Anselm’s testimony, this question was debated before Urban in the presence of several bishops, with everyone freely stating what seemed correct to him. It is therefore clear that people of several ranks, and indeed of different orders, were present at such conferences. Certainly, as we have just seen, both Anselm the archbishop and Goffridus the abbot were present when the question of the monks’ pilgrimage to Jerusalem was discussed in such an assembly of the pontiff.

Perhaps the archpriest of Angers had attended one of these conversations. According to the *Life* of Robert of Arbrissel, when Robert proposed that the widow Petronilla should become abbess, the archpriest openly testified that, when he was at Rome, he had heard from Urban II that a widow of four husbands could, if required by the needs of an abbey, be placed in charge of it.

### CCCXXXV. The Schismatics’ Reverence for Anselm

The great reputation for holiness and learning which Anselm enjoyed at Rome was not without benefit to the Church, since many schismatics, moved by it, joined Urban’s obedience, following the example of so eminent a man, while, as John of Salisbury observes in Anselm’s *Life*, the followers of Henry raged.

What Eadmer relates on this subject is remarkable:

> “What shall I say of certain citizens of the city, a great multitude of whom, because of their loyalty to the emperor, were hostile to the pope himself? At times they gathered together, wishing, because of their hatred of the pope, to seize Anselm and his companions as he went from the Lateran to Saint Peter’s. But as soon as they saw his face, they were terrified, threw down their weapons, fell prostrate on the ground, and asked to be distinguished by his blessing.”

This is mentioned merely as an example; much more may be found in Eadmer and in other English authors, whom one may consult.

### CCCXXXVI. Urban Announces a Synod at Rome

As the strength of the Henry-party at Rome diminished day by day, Urban prevailed more and more against his opponents, so that, as Bertoldus says, after celebrating the Nativity of the Lord at Rome in great peace, he then held the city entirely under his authority.

For, as that author continues, he kept the fortress of Sant’Angelo, together with other fortifications, in his power, and, with God’s help, dealt quite vigorously with all his rivals in the city, either pacifying them or subduing them by force.

Since the pontiff judged that it was in the interest of Christianity that a general council be summoned, he announced everywhere by letters that his synod would be held at Rome after Easter, during the third week.

From Eadmer and Bertoldus it can easily be inferred that he spent the remaining time until the celebration of the synod in the city, although we do not know what he did during that interval, except that he granted two privileges to two monasteries, both of which survive.

The first is for the monastery of Aniane in Occitania, addressed to Peter, abbot of that place, and issued at the Lateran on the 14th. The second, dated the 19th of the same month in the portico of Saint Peter, adorns with notable privileges and rights the monastery of Saint Saturninus in the diocese of Urgell, whose abbot Peter then was.

These two privileges are said to have been written by Peter the scrinarius and issued through the hands of John the deacon.

Another bull of Urban is cited, by which the monastery of Gellone of Saint William of the Desert, previously subject to Aniane, was freed from that subjection. But I have not been able to see it, nor is it preserved in the archive of either monastery.

### CCCXXXVII. The Roman Council

Meanwhile bishops from various provinces gathered at Rome for the council summoned by Urban. Hoveden calls it a great council; the codex of Lambertus calls it a general synod; and so do Bertoldus, the contemporary author of the *Life of John of Ternannay*, and others.

That same Bertoldus writes that 150 bishops and abbots, together with innumerable clerics, were present. The codex of Lambertus states that primates, archbishops, and bishops had been summoned, while Eadmer observes that those gathered from Italy and Gaul sat in the form of a circle.

Since Anselm, archbishop of Canterbury, had no assigned place, a seat was placed for him in the circle by order of the pontiff—that is, directly opposite the pope. As Eadmer continues, this position is customarily regarded as one of considerable honor in such an assembly.

Certainly, at the Council of Reims in 1099, the Fathers sat arranged in the form of a circle, so that Pope Leo IX, seated with his face turned toward the tomb of Saint Remigius, had before his eyes, directly opposite him, the archbishops of Reims and Trier, who occupied the chief seats.

In the ancient records of the province of Reims, the bishop of Cambrai appears to have held the place opposite the metropolitan, as did the bishop of Dol in the province of Tours. Although both these churches are distinguished among the others, neither is the *protothronus*, or primary see, of its province after the metropolitan see.

For in Belgica Secunda the church of Soissons, and in the third province of Lyons the church of Le Mans, have always possessed this dignity, as is clear from the older records of Gaul.

The council was held in the basilica of Saint Peter, as is expressly stated by the old codex of its canons called that of Lambertus of Arras. It was held during the third week after Easter, as Bertoldus and Hoveden state; and the codex of Lambertus is entirely explicit that it took place on the second Sunday after *Albas*, the Sunday on which the mercy of the Lord is commemorated.

When that codex adds that the decrees of the same synod were issued on the day before the Kalends of May, it implies that the synod continued throughout that entire week. Thus neither the *Chronicle of Malleac* was mistaken when it records that the synod was celebrated on the seventh day before the Kalends of May, nor were the codices cited by Binius, Sirmond, or Labbe, which prefer the 7th, the 6th, or even the second day before the Kalends of May.

Certainly, on the Sunday of the third week—which this year fell on 24 April, that is, the eighth day before the Kalends of May—several bishops gathered together at Rome subscribed a papal rescript in favor of Hugh of Lyons, who was contending with Daimbert of Sens over the primacy.

From this rescript we learn that Daimbert at that time acknowledged the primacy of Lyons, and we discover the names of several bishops who took part in that Roman council. They were, in addition to Daimbert of Sens and several cardinal priests of the Roman Church: Anselm of Canterbury, Leodegarius, metropolitan of Bourges, and Amatus, metropolitan of Bordeaux; and the bishops Walter of Albano, Odo of Ostia, Guntardus of Todi, Leutaldus of Meaux, and Ismeon of Die, who was also the legate of Hugh of Lyons.

Although only one bishop of the province of Reims, Letaldus, is mentioned here, several others from that province were present at the synod, as Manasses the metropolitan testifies in the letter concerning the bishop of Thérouanne which we shall cite below.

This is expressly stated in Lambertus’s codex, both in manuscript and in the edition published in Volume V of Baluze’s *Miscellanea*, where these words are found:

> “Lambertus, bishop of Arras, also took part in this council together with the other bishops of the province of Reims.”

There were also present, as will become clear from what we shall say shortly, Bisantius, archbishop of Trani; Reingerus of Lucca; Humbaldus of Auxerre; and Godefroy of Maguelonne. To these must be added Norgandus of Autun, whom Hugh, already abbot of Flavigny, met at Sézéloc after Norgandus had returned from Rome, as Hugh himself relates in his *Chronicle*.

Finally, Hugh, bishop of Grenoble, also seems to belong among their number. After Urban’s return to Italy, Hugh remained for two years in Apulia, detained there by illness, as he himself testifies in the booklet *On the Dispute Which He Had with Guido of Vienne Concerning the Archdeaconry of Salmorac*.

This synod is said in the codex of Lambertus to have been summoned because of the errors and heresies of the Greeks. The codex adds that its decrees also concerned them, in these words, reported by Baluze:

> “What decrees the aforesaid Pope Urban issued before the body of Saint Peter concerning the Latin and Greek Church, concerning the ministers of the altar, concerning those ordained by simoniacs, and concerning ecclesiastical benefices and offices acquired for money, the diligent reader will be able to discover by reading.”

It is therefore surprising that nothing specifically concerning the errors of the Greeks appears in the published canons of this council. This may have happened because the collectors of these canons, being Latins, included only those matters which concerned the Western Church, just as the matter enacted there on the occasion of Saint Anselm is mentioned only by English writers.

Likewise, Bertoldus and other authors generally record only that at this synod Urban confirmed the statutes of his predecessors, renewed the anathemas repeatedly pronounced and confirmed against Guibertus and his accomplices, and dealt with promoting the expedition to Jerusalem.

The seventeen canons of this council which are commonly circulated had for the most part already been promulgated at earlier councils, as will be clear to anyone who reads them.

But nowhere have I been able to find the report of the author of the *Chronicle of Malleac*: namely, that at this synod the pontiff decreed that every Christian should fast every Friday for his sins, especially for those of which he had forgotten and had not confessed.

With regard to English affairs, Eadmer, in Book II of the *New Works*, and Roger Hoveden after him, write that:

> “At the same synod Urban pronounced a sentence of excommunication against the enemies of the holy Church, and against all laymen who granted investitures, or clerics who accepted them, or those who consecrated such men to the office of the honor bestowed upon them. Finally, against those who become the servants of laymen for the sake of ecclesiastical honors—for this seems execrable, says the pontiff—that the hands of priests, which have risen to such eminence that they create, through their ministry, the God who creates all things, something granted to none of the angels, and offer that same God for the redemption and salvation of the whole world before the sight of God the Father Most High, should be degraded to such disgrace as to become servants of hands that are polluted day and night by obscene contagions,” and so forth.

After this sentence had been pronounced, everyone acclaimed: “Let it be done, let it be done!” and the council was concluded with these words.

Anselm himself testifies that he heard all this at the council from Pope Urban, of venerable memory, in Book III, Letter 73, to Paschal II.

Boso, later abbot of Bec, a friend and disciple of Saint Anselm, could never be induced to render homage to King Henry, who was also duke of Normandy, because he had promised the pope, as is stated in Anselm’s *Life*, that he would never do so.

Nor should we omit what Eadmer says that Reingerus, bishop of Lucca, did at this synod. Because of the powerful voice with which he was endowed, he had been appointed by the pontiff to read publicly what had been decreed at the synod. While carrying this out, he suddenly interrupted the sequence of the decrees, changed the expression of his face and the tone of his voice and the bearing of his whole body, struck the ground with his foot, and inserted many words in Anselm’s honor. He bitterly complained about what Anselm had suffered from the king of the English and about the fact that, after so long a stay in the city, his case had not been settled.

But, after the pope’s admonition, he continued the reading of the canons and finally approved, together with the others, the decrees which had been made on this matter, as we have just related.

Meanwhile the pontiff did not neglect the cases of those who appealed to him. Sometimes he dealt with them alone; or, if they were important enough to merit it, he referred them to the synod.

Thus, during the council, on 26 April, at the request of Abbot Andrew, he confirmed by a bull the property and possessions of the monastery of Casale Benedicti, which Andrew had built near Bourges according to the institutions of the Vallombrosans and under the Rule of Saint Benedict.

On the following day, at the request of Amatus, archbishop of Bordeaux, and of Fulco, abbot—who perhaps had come with that bishop to Rome for the council—he granted another privilege to the monastery of Sainte-Croix of Bordeaux.

More important matters, however, were being dealt with in the council.

Among them was the canonization of Saint Nicholas the Pilgrim. According to the discipline of that age, such cases had to be confirmed by the common assent of a plenary synod; Urban himself had already established this in a letter to Benedict of Nantes, as we stated in its proper place.

Accordingly, Bisantius, archbishop of Trani, who was promoting Nicholas’s canonization, recited before the entire council the miracles performed by him, at Urban’s command. After these had been read, the pontiff granted him permission to establish whatever seemed best in the matter for the glory of God. He issued letters concerning this to the clergy, nobles, and people of the city of Trani. From the matter itself anyone can easily understand that these letters belong to the present year, even without any chronological notes.

The schism of the Church of Thérouanne was also compressed—that is, brought to an end—at this synod, when John was confirmed as bishop of that city. The diocesan abbots had chosen him after rejecting the others, once Gerardus, who, as we have said, had been suspended from his offices by his own people at the Council of Nîmes, had withdrawn to the monastery of Mont-Saint-Éloi.

The principal author of this settlement was Lambertus, abbot of Saint-Bertin, a friend of Saint Anselm, who, as Malbrancus relates, delivered an address on the matter before the Fathers of the synod.

The pontiff wrote letters concerning this affair to Manasses, archbishop of Reims, then to the people of Thérouanne, and also to John himself, whom he forbade to dare oppose his election. Only the last of these letters survives; it will be presented below from the *Life* of John himself.

In place of the letters written to Manasses, we shall give in the Appendix a letter of that archbishop to the people of Thérouanne, exhorting them to receive John in accordance with the commands of the pontiff and the council. That they actually obeyed is clear from their own letter to Lambertus of Arras, reported by Baluze in Volume V of the *Miscellanea*.

There they say that they had received the pope’s letters concerning the confirmation of the election of Lord John, archdeacon of Arras, and they declare that they would obey them with heart and mind.

Shortly afterward, namely on 4 June of this year, John was ordained priest. Then, in the following month, on 17 July, he was consecrated bishop at Reims by Manasses the metropolitan. Finally, he was received at Thérouanne with the greatest rejoicing of the clergy, nobles, and people, and on the ninth day before the Kalends of that same month he was enthroned in the episcopal chair, as John, the contemporary author of his *Life*, relates in the account preserved by Bollandus under 27 January, the day on which his memory is celebrated in several martyrologies.

Abbot Lambertus, who is said to have pleaded for John’s election at the synod, had long been planning, attracted by the reputation of the Cluniacs, to introduce them into his monastery of Saint-Bertin, where regular discipline had grown lax.

Taking advantage of this Roman journey, he obtained the permission, with the intervention of Countess Clementia, who carried letters concerning the matter to the same pontiff.

Without delay the pope wrote to Hugh, abbot of Cluny, and instructed him to take the monastery of Sithiu-Saint-Bertin under his care. Count Robert of Flanders confirmed this arrangement in 1106, after returning from his pilgrimage to Jerusalem, as is clear from his charter reported in the *Bibliotheca Cluniacensis*, col. 538.

Lambertus himself, after shortly afterward relinquishing the administration of his monastery, withdrew to Cluny and by a new profession bound himself more strictly to the Rule. Later he was sent back to his own abbey, where he administered it until the end of his life.

The monks of Bertin, however, and Lambertus himself, were unable for long to endure the yoke of the abbot of Cluny after the death of Saint Hugh, as Iperius recounts at length in the *Chronicle* of that place and Malbrancus in Book IX of *On the Morini*.

Letters of Pope Honorius II concerning this matter are extant, written in favor of Peter of Cluny to the abbot of Saint-Bertin, who refused to obey him. But there is no time to pursue these matters at greater length.

The monastery of Saint-Germain near Auxerre experienced almost the same fate at this synod, although for different reasons. Its abbot had been deposed at the Council of Nîmes.

After his restoration had long been attempted, always without success, and the distinguished place was consequently deteriorating without a head, the Fathers of the council decided, after three years—as can be inferred from the *Deeds of the Abbots of that Place*—to entrust its administration to Hugh, abbot of Cluny, at the request of Count Stephen and his wife.

Urban’s letters concerning this matter survive. In them the pontiff orders that the arrangement be carried out, but in such a way that the place should not remain without its own abbot.

How much effort was later required to free this abbey from the yoke of the Cluniacs may be learned from Guido’s *Deeds of the Abbots of Saint-Germain*, in Volume I of Labbe’s *Bibliotheca*.

A dispute was subsequently heard before the Fathers of the same synod concerning the right to the cemetery in the city of Bordeaux. The canons of the cathedral church of Saint Andrew claimed that its possession belonged to them, while the clerics of Saint Severinus opposed them.

The latter, however, lost the case, as we learn from Urban’s rescript, which he issued several days later on the matter to the canons of Saint Andrew.

The monks of Molesme also came there to complain against their abbot Robert, who, after leaving them, had gone to the Cistercian wilderness, where he established a new abbey.

The Fathers of the council granted their request. The pontiff himself, moved by the tireless complaints of the monks of Molesme, as the *Chronicle of Arles* records, wrote to his legate in Gaul, Hugh, instructing him to attempt to persuade Robert to return to his monks at Molesme; or, if that could not be done, to settle the matter so that the brothers of both monasteries might thereafter remain peacefully in their respective places.

A decree was issued on the matter, providing that thereafter the monks of those monasteries should not continue to transfer from one place to another.

Urban’s letter will be given from various manuscript and printed sources, and his decree on the same matter will later be given from Orderic Vitalis.

After receiving Urban’s letters, Hugh discussed the matter with the other bishops and abbots of the province at a conference at Port-Ancilla. There it was decreed that Robert, after returning the pastoral staff of the Cistercian abbey to the bishop of Chalon and releasing the Cistercian monks from the promise of obedience they had made to him, should return to Molesme with those who wished to follow him. Henceforth, no one was to be permitted to transfer to another monastery except in accordance with what the Rule of Saint Benedict allowed.

Robert therefore returned to Molesme, appointing Alberic as abbot of Cîteaux in his place, and remained there until the end of his life.

These were the beginnings of the Cistercian order. Together with the birth of Saint Bernard, they brought distinction to the pontificate of Urban, having arisen in the year 1091.

For these matters one should consult Manriquez’s *Cistercian Annals*, Orderic Vitalis, and the anonymous author published by Labbe in Volume I of the *Bibliotheca*. These authors, like many other writers of ecclesiastical history, also provide ancient documents.

In the same year, and perhaps at the same synod, Fulco of Deauville, abbot of the monastery of Saint Mary in Normandy, was restored to his position. As we have already related from Book X of Orderic, he had been unjustly accused and deposed seven years earlier at Satan’s instigation. He spent those years at Monte Cassino, apparently on Urban’s advice, after fleeing to him for refuge.

We can determine the time of his deposition and restoration from the same author. Orderic writes that Fulco died at Guenta—that is, Winchester—in England on 3 April 1106, in the seventh year of his restoration, which had taken place after the additional seven years he had spent in exile at Cassino.

The same Orderic affirms that Fulco then returned to his abbey through letters of the pope, but those letters have perished.

### CCCXXXVIII. Anselm Leaves Rome

On the first day after the council had been dissolved, Anselm, having received permission to depart from the pontiff, left Rome, as Eadmer testifies. After overcoming the dangers along the roads occupied by the supporters of Henry and Guibertus, he reached Lyons safely, where he was received with the greatest honor by Archbishop Hugh.

It does not belong to our present purpose to pursue his deeds at greater length; they must be sought in Eadmer and in the other English authors.

### CCCXXXIX. The Privilege of Psalmodi

On that same day, namely the Kalends of May, the pontiff confirmed the possessions and privileges of the monastery of Psalmodi in Septimania, issuing a charter which will be given from the original document, now indeed torn and almost worn away, but nevertheless of unquestionable authenticity.

After various changes of fortune, this monastery was transferred to Aigues-Mortes and clothed in secular garb; finally, several years ago, it was united to the new bishopric of Alès, which had been detached from Nîmes.
