Two days later the pontiff issued the rescript in favor of the canons of Bordeaux which we have just mentioned. On the following day, 10 May, he granted a notable privilege to the monastery of Conques in the Rouergue, confirming its rights and possessions while abolishing an abuse that had become established in those regions: the practice of carrying the relics of saints, even against the wishes of the monks, to public assemblies.

Shortly afterward, on 14 May, the pontiff granted privileges to the canons of the mother church of Rodez, who had adopted the regular life, and secured various possessions for them so that they could maintain their common life, issuing a charter.

In the same month of May, with no day assigned, Urban’s rescript to Alfanus, bishop of Salerno, is recorded. In it, after revoking privileges which, as the document says, had been granted to the monastery of Cava through deception, he returned and confirmed that monastery and the other monasteries of the same diocese to the archbishop.

It is said to have been issued at Rome in the year 1098, in the seventh indiction, in the month of May; but these chronological notes are inconsistent with one another.

Indeed, in May of the year 1098 Urban had apparently already departed for Apulia. It therefore seemed preferable to assign the document to the present year, to which the seventh indiction belongs.

It is remarkable, however, if this rescript is genuine, that Urban should have said in it that he had until then been deceived in this matter and that, only after seeing at Rome the privileges of the Church of Salerno, previously unknown to him, he had corrected his judgment. For after the privileges and rights had been granted to the monastery of Cava, he had visited Salerno more than once and, while residing there the previous year, had confirmed those privileges and rights, without making any mention of this deception.

All these considerations make that rescript highly doubtful, not to say false.

Indeed, in the year 1089 the same pontiff, after seeing—as we have related—the documents and agreements produced by both sides at the Council of Melfi, had pronounced in favor of the monks of Cava.

More recently we received the observations of a learned man from that region concerning this privilege, which he had carefully examined. He says that he had inspected it in the archiepiscopal archive of Salerno, written on a complete and sound piece of parchment, but in a script unsuitable for this period, with chronological notes that were false, and without any sign, seal, or subscription.

In any case, from that time the abbey of Cava never lost its privileges. Pope Gregory XIV expressly confirmed them in a special rescript after many pontiffs of different periods.

The document of the Church of Salerno, whatever its character may be, will nevertheless be given from Ughelli. We leave the judgment concerning its authenticity to others.

### CCCXL. The Archdeaconry of Salmorac Is Secured for Hugh of Grenoble
At the beginning of June, Urban, having returned from the Vatican to the Lateran, replied to his own legate in Gaul, Hugh of Lyon, on the second day before the Nones of that month, in favor of the Church of Grenoble and against Guido, archbishop of Vienne, who had once again invaded the churches of the archdeaconate of Salmor. At the end of the letter the most religious pontiff admits that until then he had been too lenient in permitting the transfers of bishops in Gaul [Col. 0256C]; he then adds that henceforth, in accordance with the statutes of the Council of Nicaea, he would abstain from that abuse. This is the last rescript issued by Urban that survives with chronological notes. Another, addressed to Hugh of Grenoble himself, will be appended to it; in that document he entrusts to him and to the bishop of Maguelonne the adjudication of the case being disputed between the monks of Vigilius and Cluny, but it bears no chronological indication. Other letters of Calixtus to the same Hugh and to P., bishop of Die, concerning the same Church of Vigilius, are extant in the Chartulary of Calmels. In one manuscript we find them attributed to Urban, but wrongly, as is clear from two other copies, as well as from their date, the day before the Kalends of May, which cannot belong to Urban. Gratian, in 35.2 and 3, cites a fragment of another [Col. 0256D] rescript of Urban to the same Hugh concerning extraordinary pollution; it will be presented in its proper place among Urban’s decrees.

## CCCXLI. Rescript for Corbiniacum

We believe that Urban’s rescript in favor of the monks of Saint-Remigius at Reims, whom Ingelram, bishop of Laon, was harassing on account of the altar of Corbiniacum, must likewise be assigned to the final period of Urban’s pontificate. Since Ingelram is said to have taken possession of that see only in the year 1098, after the death of Elinand, who had taken part in the ordination of the metropolitan Manasses in 1096, a period of not less than approximately one year is required for that bishop to have caused trouble for the monks, and for them to have appealed to Urban and obtained that rescript.

## CCCXLII. Adalbert, Abbot of Schaffhausen

[Col. 0257A]

Meanwhile, on 24 June, the Nativity of Saint John the Baptist, Gebhard, Urban’s legate in Germany, solemnly blessed Adalbert as abbot of the monastery of Schaffhausen, in place of Gerhard, who, with the pontiff’s consent—as we have said from Berthold—had relinquished the administration of the monastery.

If Theobald, as the commonly circulated catalogues report, assumed the government of the monastery of Malleais only in this year, Urban’s decree must also be recorded here: he ordered that this abbot make satisfaction to Hugh of Cluny, whom he had evidently offended. What the matter was is not known. We report Urban’s decision from a manuscript letter of Paschal II, his successor, to Peter of Poitiers. After prefacing some remarks about the monastery [Col. 0257B] of Saint-Cyprian, it adds:

> “Concerning the abbot of Malleais also, we command that, in accordance with the precept of the lord Urban, he make satisfaction to the abbot of Cluny. Otherwise, see that you do not yourself incur the indignation of the Apostolic See on their behalf, and that they do not escape a sentence proportionate to their deserts.”

Perhaps that abbot, like the abbot of Cyprian’s monastery, refused to submit to Cluny.

## CCCXLIII. The Rights of the Church of Maguelonne Vindicated

About this same time, Count Raymond of Melgueil, excommunicated by Godefroy, bishop of Maguelonne, because he had invaded the rights of that Church, went to Rome, following Godefroy, who had departed somewhat earlier, undoubtedly in order to attend the council. When both had pleaded their case before the pontiff, the count was [Col. 0257C] convicted by the bishop of having violated his father’s testament. Accordingly, in the presence of the cardinals and other distinguished men, he surrendered into the hand of the lord pope the things he had invaded; after doing homage to him, he received the county back from the pope on the condition that he pay the Roman pontiff one ounce of gold each year. After returning to his homeland, the count confirmed all this in a public court on the Nativity of Saint Mary, and immediately departed for Saint James.

Arnaldus de Verdala, in volume I of Labbe’s *Bibliotheca nova*, Gariel, in his *History of the Bishops of Maguelonne*, and, in part, the Sammarthani brothers in volume II of *Gallia Christiana*, refer to an instrument concerning this matter drawn up in the year 1099.

## CCCXLIV. The Cemetery of Saint Vincent at Le Mans Secured

[Col. 0257D]

About the same time a serious dispute arose at Le Mans between the canons of the cathedral church and the monks of Saint Vincent concerning a deceased canon, whose body certain factious members of the canonical community had buried in unconsecrated ground. Yet by ancient custom, confirmed equally by law, the right belonged to the monks of Saint Vincent, so that bishops and canons were to be buried in their cemetery.

After many quarrels, when the dispute could not be settled by the bishop’s authority, the monks referred the matter to Urban, to whom the bishop wrote a letter on their behalf. We have thought it appropriate to present this letter in the Appendix from the Chartulary of Saint Vincent, both because it sets out the entire course of the matter, [Col. 0258A] and also because of the reputation of its author. The author was surely Hildebert, famous for many other writings: both the circumstances of the period and, if my conjecture does not deceive me, the correspondence of style leave scarcely any room for doubt.

Whether Urban decided anything concerning the matter is uncertain; perhaps death prevented him from doing so. In the chartulary of the same monastery, however, there is an agreement concluded between the canons and the monks of that place during the episcopate of Hildebert and the abbacy of Ranulf. It was agreed that the canons should indeed be buried in the Vincentian cemetery, but in a more honorable place, separated from the burials of laypeople. We do not doubt that this agreement was made on the occasion of the dispute.

## CCCXLV. Urban’s Death at Rome

[Col. 0258B]

Urban’s letter to Albert, bishop of Metz, may finally be assigned to this period. Gratian cites it in 1.5, canon 3; it concerns a certain man who had obtained the priesthood by offering money. This Albert is the same Adalbero or Albero who, after Hermann’s death, had been intruded by the emperor Henry into the see of Metz against Poppo. See the *Chronicle of Sithiu*, p. 600.

Certainly, from the *Life of Saint Theoger*, which we shall publish in the twelfth century in the *Acts of the Saints of the Order of Saint Benedict*, as well as from this letter of Urban, it can be gathered that this Albert, or Albero, was at some point regarded as a bishop. The author of the aforementioned *Life* discusses him at length and relates that his deposition was decreed at the Council of Reims in 1115, presided over by the legate Conon; Theoger himself was substituted for him.

[Col. 0258C] After this letter several others, together with a number of Urban’s decrees, will be appended. Since they bear no date, or at least no determinate date, they could not properly be assigned to any particular year.

After Urban had endured innumerable labors for the Church, when affairs had at last been entirely settled, when the fortifications in the city itself that the schismatics had occupied for so long had been recovered, when he had won over all the Romans, and when the universal Church had been restored to a more peaceful condition than it had experienced—or could reasonably have hoped for—for a long time, he finally, full of merits rather than of days, departed to heaven. As some authors observed, his death had been foretold by an eclipse and other celestial signs. It occurred at the very time when, in [Col. 0258D] the East, the holy city of Jerusalem was captured by the Christian army, toward whose expedition the pious pontiff had strongly urged them.

He fell ill at Rome, as Orderic Vitalis testifies at the beginning of book X, where he says that, about to receive his reward from God for the good endeavors in which he had especially excelled, he departed this life on the fourth day before the Kalends of August. It is certainly established from a letter written concerning the matter by Paschal, his successor, to Hugh, abbot of Cluny, which we shall include in our Appendix, that he died at Rome on that day in the year 1099.

He held the pontificate for eleven years, four months, and eighteen days. Berthold wrote, in round numbers, five months, and there is no disagreement about this among ancient or modern writers, although some, because of different methods of calculation, have expressed the year of his death differently. [Col. 0259A] In the *Chronicle of Kemperlegium*, in volume I of Baluze’s *Miscellanies*, he is nevertheless said to have ended his life on the third day before the Kalends of August, perhaps through a copyist’s error. Other chroniclers almost everywhere assign the fourth day, and the obituaries of monasteries and other churches agree with them, except that of Molesme, in which the congregation of that place records him on the third day.

Afterward his memory was celebrated in many places because of the benefits they had received from him—for example, in Cluny, in Casa Dei at Cornillon, in Flavigny of Saint-Gilles, in Limoges of Saint Martial, in the New Monastery at Poitiers, at Nantua, in Dijon of Saint Benignus, and in the obituaries of many other churches which he had consecrated or fortified with privileges.

[Col. 0259B]

His body was carried from the house of Peter Leo near Saint Nicholas in the Tullian Prison, where he had died, through the Trastevere district to the Vatican Basilica, in which it was honorably buried. In the *Deeds of Lambert, Bishop of Arras*, the religious pope Urban, worthy of memory, is said to have entered in the year 1099, on the fourth day before the Kalends of August, in the seventh indiction, upon “the way of all flesh,” and to have been buried in the Church of the blessed apostle Peter beside Saint Leo the pope and the author of the Council of Ephesus.

Manlius and others who have written about the Vatican Basilica report that Urban’s tomb was constructed in a sufficiently beautiful form and is still seen near the oratory of Adrian I. The faithful visit it because of the memory, as Baronius reports, of so great a pontiff, who deserved so well of the universal holy Church.

[Col. 0259C] His friend Peter Leo, who arranged the funeral and whom Godefroy, abbot of Vendôme, calls “the foremost son of the holy Roman Church” in book V, letter 9, testified that Urban’s funeral was celebrated with great solemnity. In his epitaph, which we shall present in the Appendix from Orderic Vitalis together with other poems and encomia, Peter Leo is the subject of the passage. We have thought it preferable to relegate Urban’s *Life* by Pandulf, the verses of Domnizo, and other excerpts to that place rather than present them here, so as not to interrupt the sequence of the narrative too much.

Paschal, his successor, asserts in the letter already mentioned that Urban’s funeral was celebrated with the mourning and sadness of the entire city of Rome, because so great a pontiff, so distinguished in learning and life, had been lost.

[Col. 0259D]

In another epitaph of his, which we shall likewise give at the end from Orderic and which is attributed to Philip, abbot of La Sauve-Majeure, Urban is said to have been taken from this life while still in the vigor of age. Indeed, the most strenuous labors that he endured throughout his pontificate, and the various journeys he completed during the final years of his life, sufficiently indicate that he had not then been broken by old age.

Orderic Vitalis, as we have already said, sets out the qualities of his body and soul in a few words in book VIII, where he writes that Urban was physically imposing, distinguished by moderation, supreme in religious devotion, outstanding in wisdom and eloquence. At the beginning of book X he says that Urban governed [Col. 0260A] the Apostolic See energetically and courageously and departed from this world to receive from God a reward for the good endeavors in which he had especially excelled:

> “How praiseworthy were his works is widely proclaimed throughout the world by the brilliance and fame of his greatness; even the lamentations of his enemies, when he died, bore witness to it.”

A little farther on he says:

> “While Pope Urban shone in the house of the Lord, driving darkness from the hearts of mortals by his preaching and example and banishing it by the dignity of his office, Guibert’s efforts were rendered fruitless.”

Finally, he asserts that Urban died rejoicing in holiness, so great was his confidence in God’s mercy.

Albert of Stade reports that, when near death and prompted by divine inspiration, Urban designated Cardinal Raynerius, abbot of Rome, as his successor; other writers have observed the same.

[Col. 0260B] Fulcher of Chartres, chaplain of Baldwin, king of Jerusalem, says in his book *On the Expedition to Jerusalem* that Urban was an outstanding man in life and morals, who always strove prudently and vigorously to advance above all else the condition of the holy Church. Comparing him afterward with Guibert, he says:

> “Urban, a prudent and venerable man, renewed peace and restored the rights of the Church to their former condition; and as he traveled through the regions, he reconciled to God many peoples who had strayed in some respects.”

And because, he says, Urban strove with all his strength to exalt everything belonging to God, almost everyone willingly submitted themselves to his fatherly authority under his obedience. He adds:

> “He had been rightly elected and consecrated by the cardinal bishops and was accepted by the greater and holier part of the people, although his opponents disparaged his works as invalid and null.”

Finally, he says that Urban was more successful [Col. 0260C] and more just, indeed stronger, since he had subjected his desires as though they were enemies. On the other hand, he portrays Guibert as:

> “Irritated by the spur of pride, stirring up the people to confusion with the support of the emperor. Although he exercised authority among those who agreed with him and abounded in power and riches, the better part of the people nevertheless never wished to follow him.”

The ancient author of the *Deeds of the Franks Who Conquered Jerusalem* agrees, saying that this same pontiff was an outstanding man, instructed in life, morals, prudence, and knowledge, and so forth.

While Urban was still alive, Deusdedit, then cardinal priest of Saint Peter at the Chains, of the title of Eudoxia, who published a second collection of canons during Urban’s pontificate, called him “a man preeminent in knowledge and religion.”

[Col. 0260D] Adelferius, a contemporary author, writes similarly in part II, chapter 1 of the *Acts of Saint Nicholas the Pilgrim*, in the Bollandists under 2 June:

> “When Urban, second in the Roman See, perhaps a saint, most glorious, powerful in deed and teaching and overflowing with the fountain of eloquence, following in the footsteps of the apostles and apostolic men and devoted to pastoral care, was successfully governing the administrations of the churches…”

Gerohus, in chapter 16 of his *Syntagma*, published by Tegnagel, sums everything up in fewer words:

> “Urban showed himself the legitimate successor of Gregory VII—and indeed of Peter himself—not only in dignity but also in virtue.”

Berardus, author of the *Chronicle of Casauria*, like many other writers, calls him a man of holy or blessed memory, in whom the Church possessed a good shepherd, a lover of Christendom, and a defender of the faith.

[Col. 0261A] Accordingly, John of Collemedio, author of the *Life of Blessed John of Thérouanne*, congratulates his own age that under the pontificate of Urban—whom shortly before he had called “the most powerful opponent of the simoniacal plague”—the Gallican Church had bishops outstanding in religion and learning:

> “O happy times, in which benefits granted from above are proved! Behold: while Urban presides, while Urban watches over the Lord’s flock with pastoral vigilance, and while he prudently arranges, one by one, the watchful guards of his sheepfold, he effectively prevents the bites of ravenous wolves from reaching the sheep whom you, Christ, redeemed.”

[Col. 0261B] Laurentius of Liège, in the *History of the Bishops of Verdun*, writes that this same most ardent defender of ecclesiastical privilege departed in a happy death. Paschal, his successor, testifies in the frequently mentioned letter that his death was precious in the sight of the Lord, in these words:

> “The ending itself proves how holy and pleasing to God Urban’s teaching and life were.”

He concludes that God should therefore be thanked for this.

Finally, after recounting many actions of the same pontiff in his *Chronicle*, Aymericus of Périgueux, abbot of Moissac, says that many matters should be concluded in a few words. He calls Urban happy in praise of his care for sacred things and places dedicated to God, for the eradication of the schism, and for the correction of the most powerful kings; but he calls him still happier because of his virtues and merits, which by God’s mercy obtained for him the enjoyment [Col. 0261C] of heavenly glory:

> “Therefore there is abundant cause for rejoicing that, through the prayers of this most holy man, after the deadly schism had been removed, the Church received the remedy for an ancient wound and, under the protection of one most powerful lord, true peace and restored unity.”

There is no point in listing the other encomia of him that occur throughout the authors, since those we have cited are more than sufficient to establish the reputation of his holiness.

The fact that Urban also shone after death through miracles is testified by Guibert, abbot of Nogent, a man by no means credulous and very far removed from the religiosity of women. [Col. 0261D] At the beginning of book II of his *History of Jerusalem* he writes:

> “The splendid end of his state of mind, marked by miracles, bears witness to it. For after he had died and been buried, as the bishop of Ostia who succeeded him relates, when many signs were already occurring, a certain young man stood at his tomb and invoked the loss of his limbs upon himself if any sign had ever been performed through Urban’s merits—Urban, who was called Odo—and if one were to occur. He had not yet moved his foot from the place when, having lost the use of speech and been struck by paralysis affecting one side of his body, he died the following day, himself bearing witness to Urban’s miracles.”

The author of an ancient chronicle, published by Chesne in the proofs to the *History of the House of Châtillon*, chapter 8, recounts the same miracle.

It is therefore not surprising if his tomb is said once to have been frequented by the faithful. Certainly not only ancient and modern writers, [Col. 0262A] but also Roman pontiffs, repeatedly call him a man and pontiff of holy or blessed memory in their letters and decrees. Paschal, his successor, declared on various occasions, and especially in the profession of faith that he made at the Lateran Council in 1112—which all the Fathers approved by their acclamations—that he would never depart from Urban’s path.

Godefroy of Vendôme, the author of the *Life of Saint Peter, Abbot of Cava*, and many others likewise honor him with the title of holy man. Peter the Deacon, in book IV of the *Chronicle of Monte Cassino*, calls Pope Urban a man of holy memory, plainly and truly apostolic. Domnizo has more in his verses, which are found at the end. Berardus, already mentioned, in the *Chronicle of Casauria*, and the very ancient author of the *History of Jerusalem*, published in volume I of Mabillon’s *Museum Italicum*, simply call him Saint Urban.

[Col. 0262B] Finally, Pandulf writes in his *Life* that Urban gave his soul back to God as a confessor and good athlete of Christ; in the life of Paschal, his successor, he calls him “the lord Pope Urban, magnanimous and of solemn memory.”

It should therefore not seem surprising if Urban’s name is found inscribed in many martyrologies or catalogues of saints on 29 July, the day on which he departed this life, although it must be admitted that his feast was never celebrated in the Church.

His memory is recorded in these words in the Benedictine *Martyrology* of Arnold Wion and Hugh Menard:

> “At Rome, the deposition of blessed Urban II, pope, formerly a Cluniac [Col. 0262C] monk, author of the Crusade for the recovery of the Holy Land and the most ardent defender of ecclesiastical liberty; after enduring many injuries inflicted by the emperor Henry IV, exile, severe hardships, and other things of that kind, he finally died a confessor distinguished by holiness.”

The same encomium of holiness is attributed to him in Dorgain’s *Calendar*, where he is additionally said to have instituted the Office of the Blessed Mary and to have invented the ringing of bells morning and evening for the Angelic Salutation.

He is also mentioned with the title “blessed” by Philip Ferrarius in his catalogue of saints who are not included in the Roman Martyrology. Bucelinus has more in his Benedictine *Menology*, as do Saussayus in the *Gallican Martyrology* and Arnold Wion in the *Lignum Vitae*. To these may be added Vincent of Beauvais, Saint Antoninus, Trithemius, [Col. 0262D] Platina, Michael Buchinger of Colmar, Onuphrius Panvinius, Ciaconius, and others who have written something about holy men or Roman pontiffs. It is neither possible nor worthwhile to list them individually.

In a word, scarcely any ancient or modern author of chronicles or ecclesiastical history can be found who, whether deliberately or when an occasion arose, did not pursue our Urban with praise. At least the principal ones we have praised in their proper places whenever a suitable opportunity for doing so presented itself.

Urban also deserved a place among ecclesiastical writers. Some have attributed to him not only various letters but also other short works, as may be seen in Platina, Wion, and similar authors. Charles of Saint-Jacob, in the *Pontifical Library* [Col. 0263A], reports that he wrote against the doctrines of heretics and, while serving as Gregory VII’s legate, about the injuries inflicted upon him by the emperor Henry, besides several speeches and various letters.

We possess the speeches that he is said to have delivered at the Council of Clermont, together with a few others, as well as a fairly large number of letters; but we do not know the remaining short works. Perhaps that author took this information from Platina, who says that Urban, the most holy pontiff, strengthened the Church against the doctrines of heretics not only by his works and example but also by his writings.

Bergomensis, in book XII, and Trithemius, in the *Chronicle of Hirsau*, under the year 1087, say much the same. Trithemius writes of Urban:

> “He was a man outstanding in learning and holiness, who by word and deed, as well as by his writings, courageously defended [Col. 0263B] the Church against the attacks of heretics, and wrote and decreed much for the common benefit.”

These statements suit Urban very well, even if he wrote no more than what has survived for us. Whatever the case may be concerning his writings, it is certain that he was a learned and educated man.

Domnizo repeatedly calls him a rhetorician. Pandulf, in the *Life of Gelasius II*, calls him highly learned and eloquent; Balderic, in his epitaph, which is included in the Appendix, calls him a teacher “at whose death the eloquent tongue of the world collapsed.”

In Urban’s own *Life*, which you will also find there, Pandulf says that he was an energetic man, learned in the divine Scriptures, imbued with ecclesiastical traditions, and steadfastly persevering in their observance.

I would be interminable if I wished to collect here everything that occurs throughout the authors concerning his learning and eloquence, which the writers of his age especially praised when they wrote about the sacred expeditions. It is enough to hear Guibert of Nogent, one witness standing for all. He writes [Col. 0263C]:

> “His eloquence was assisted by agility in literary learning. For he seemed to have no less freedom in speaking Latin than any advocate can have fluency in his native tongue. Nor did a multitude of disputants obstruct the ingenuity with which he composed; rather, although he was surrounded by the elegant expressions of grammarians worthy of praise, he was thought, by his literary brilliance, to surpass the overflowing abundance of orators and to ride above the witticisms of every kind of discourse.”

[Col. 0263D] Bergomensis praises his letters as full of substance. Baronius valued them so highly that he did not hesitate to assert that there were as many jewels as characters. He laments the loss of a large part of them, while giving as a sample several fragments from the letter addressed to Lucius, provost of Saint Juventius. In these fragments the pontiff truly displays profound learning in adducing testimonies from Sacred Scripture and the holy Fathers to establish the Catholic Church’s tradition concerning the validity of baptism and the other sacraments.

This letter, entirely intact, together with many others previously unknown, will be published in the collection of pontifical letters.

[Col. 0264A] This would be the place to discuss the illustrious men who flourished under Urban’s pontificate or the cardinals whom he promoted to that dignity. But we have dealt with the former in their proper places whenever they contributed something to the Church’s benefit, and we have mentioned the cardinals whom we found to have been created by Urban on at least probable evidence. It is therefore unnecessary to discuss either group at greater length here.

Ciaconius, Onuphrius, and others following them list thirty-seven cardinals promoted by Urban, apart from those whose identities are unknown. In most cases, however, they give only the names.

Among them were seven bishops, [Col. 0264B] five of whom took part in Paschal’s election: Odo of Ostia, Urban’s successor in that see, who consecrated Paschal; Gualterius of Albano, successor to Blessed Peter Igneus; Milo, a monk of Albano who became bishop of Palestrina; Maurice, who succeeded John of Porto after the latter died in Gaul; and Crescentius of Sabina, whose predecessor Ubaldus had also been promoted by Urban after Gregory’s death. The seventh of these bishops was John, bishop of Tusculum, about whom we have said much above.

There were sixteen priests: Oderisius, abbot of Monte Cassino, whom Urban ordained priest from the diaconate; Robert of the title of Saint Clement; Albert, later archbishop of Siponto; Raynerius, who succeeded Urban under the name Paschal, of the title of Saint Clement; Rangerius, a monk of Marmoutier whom the same pontiff ordained archbishop of Reggio; Alberic, of the title of Eudoxia at Saint Peter’s in Chains, and therefore [Col. 0264C] the successor of Deusdedit, the famous collector of canons; Peter, of the title of Equitius, or Saints Peter and Martin in the Mountains; Amicus, abbot of Saint-Sauveur, of the title of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem; Paul, of the title of Saint Sixtus; Boniface, of the title of Saint Mark; John, of the title of Saint Anastasia; Robert, a Frenchman from Paris, of the title of Saint Eusebius; Risus, of the title of Saints Lawrence and Damasus, who was archbishop of Bari; Bernard Ubertinus, of the Camaldolese order, of the title of Saint Chrysogonus, later bishop of Parma; Theoderic the German, of the title of Saints John and Paul, afterward famous for many legations in Germany; and Laudulfus, of the title of Saint Lawrence in Lucina.

Godefroy, abbot of Vendôme, must be added to these; under the name of cardinal he held the title of Saint Prisca, and Urban himself ordained him priest.

[Col. 0264D] Thirteen deacons are listed. They are: Bernard; Gregory, abbot of Subiaco, of the title of Saint Lucia at the Seven Gates; Damian; John; Azo; Leo of Marsica, a Cassinese monk, who is said to have written several letters in Urban’s name—we discussed him in § 51; Jonathas, of the title of Saints Cosmas and Damian; Theodinus, a Cassinese monk, of the title of Saint Mary in Portico; Theobald, of the title of Saint Mary Nova; Comes, of the title of Saint Mary in Aquiro; Gregory, of the title of Saint Angelo, who later became pope under the name Innocent II; John, of the title of Saint Adrian; and finally John Gaetan, of Saint Mary in Cosmedin, Urban’s chancellor and eventually the pontiff called Gelasius [Col. 0265A] II.

Those authors list these men. Other cardinals mentioned in the matters discussed above also appear among them, [Col. 0266A] but they may have been promoted by earlier pontiffs.

# APPENDIX TO THE LIFE OF POPE URBAN II

*(The diplomas of Urban contained in this Appendix are given a more appropriate place among the letters of the blessed pontiff.)*

[Col. 0265]

# HISTORY OF THE TRANSLATION OF THE RELICS OF SAINT MAXIMUS AT NANTUA

From a manuscript of Nantua.

[Col. 0265B]

After many radiant signs had made it evident that Maximus ought to be placed in a more honorable and exalted position, it happened that Hugh, the venerable Father of the monastery of Cluny and likewise rector of Nantua, was present. I mentioned him above, explaining that Maximus had judged that his revelation should be postponed and deferred until Hugh’s time.

When Hugh learned of these extraordinary events, and compared with them the great miracles he had heard about Maximus of Riez, he further said, on the testimony of one of the clerics who had lost it [variant: deferred it], that Maximus’s very body, which belonged to the people of Nantua, had been apportioned to the people of Vienne. He came to the chapter on Sunday, the ninth day before the Kalends of September, and there discussed with the brothers the matter at hand: namely, how it might be possible to exalt so holy a man, who lay buried in the earth, so that he who was exalted in heaven would not remain dishonored in the ground of his burial.

[Col. 0265C] Among the men who took part in the consultation was Odo, then bishop of Ostia, now Saint Pope Urban, a man of great prudence in learning and authority and grace in divine matters. He himself praised the proposal, and the others present agreed that Maximus should be exalted and displayed in an elevated place for all to admire and behold, since he had been found worthy of discovery by such signs and, once discovered, had been distinguished by so many miracles.

[Col. 0265D] But the excellent Father, deliberate and discerning in all the matters he undertook, judged that the matter should be postponed until he had carefully sought, through fasting and vows of prayer, the judgment of the heavenly will. He therefore ordered that the inquiry take place on the following day, so that, by fasting and conducting the litanies in procession, it might become known to the people what pleased God in this matter.

Meanwhile, while the community went to the chapter, he secretly withdrew from the others and approached the place of the tomb. He devoted himself to prayer all the more freely because he was alone, and there kindled such a flame of devotion and experienced such grace of compunction that he thought it impossible to doubt that the man lying there was truly great before the Lord. Dead, yet living among the living and alive among the dead, he possessed such divine power that he turned into embers those whom he had touched as coals, and infused ardor of spirit and warmth of piety in God [variant: so greatly; the transmitted reading is uncertain].

Thus the secret investigator returned to his companions and ordered that preparations be made for receiving or replacing the treasure of that venerable little body when it was transferred. When the following day had passed and the fast had been completed, as the third hour of daylight came, the venerable Father returned to the chapter and, with everyone’s agreement, decreed that what he had postponed should be done, so that it might be carried out with greater deliberation.

He ordered a certain brother named Richard, who knew the place where he had reburied the body with the aforementioned William when it had been carried back to the church, to open the grave carefully and prepare everything he thought necessary for such a task, so that, when the community was present, no delay would impede the work of the translation.

He also instructed the brothers to sing and devote themselves to psalmody, and ordered that no one approach except those who had been summoned. Yielding by right to Lord Odo, of episcopal rank, he assigned him the principal responsibility: to put his hand to the work, touch and remove the first bones with due reverence, and begin and complete the entire undertaking until the venerable body was placed in another little receptacle of its own. He nevertheless did not exempt himself, but swore that he too would apply his hands after the bishop’s.

[Col. 0266B]

After the chapter had thus ended, they all conducted a solemn procession. They admitted no one into the basilica from the very large crowd that had gathered for this purpose; instead, they themselves remained standing around and began to sing psalms, and they gave no room to those who wished—or, according to another reading, those who ought—to approach.

[Col. 0266C] Then the bishop of Ostia, outwardly and inwardly purified and girded with faith, approached, no less than his clothing testified by its whiteness. He took up the exorcism as a shield and, with episcopal authority, forbade it, if it belonged to the sinister side, to dare to appear or offer itself for removal. But if it recognized itself as belonging to the merits of him whom it was believed to be, whose flesh this had been, it was to have leave to appear and to offer itself for removal.

What more is there to say? Whatever had touched the heart of the lord abbot, touching the bishop’s mind as well, breathed upon it in such a way that he himself declared with certainty that something divine lay in that place. From it burst forth such a spiritual blessing that it revived the hearts of those who approached as though the author of sweetness himself were present.

Understanding, then, what he signified who was speaking through signs, the lord [abbot] approached humbly and, laying in his hand, reverently began the extraction of the bones; thereafter he made room for his father, so that the latter might become the second extractor, since he had not wished to be first. Thus, little by little, as the brothers took turns, and as those who were permitted to approach and perform this task did so, the work was carried out with due care, so that the precious pearl of that body might be lifted from the depths in which it had lain and, to be placed in a higher position, received into a vessel fashioned and fitted to its size; thus it was raised amid divine praises, to be venerated thereafter in a more fitting place.

When these things had been completed peacefully and without popular tumult, it would be superfluous to reiterate in words or commend in writing how the crowd that had rushed in beforehand had danced, shouted for joy, offered praise and thanksgiving, and made vows, since this may sufficiently be judged from the report of the miracles performed and heard of everywhere. For scarcely could silence be obtained so that the man himself might speak and be heard addressing the assembly, whether about Pope Gregory VII, whose cause was then being debated throughout almost the entire world, or about this Maximus, whose identity had been established by so many signs, whose recent translation was under discussion, whose initial feast was being celebrated and ordered to be celebrated thereafter, and who, although he was not usually perceived through the benefit he conferred, could not be seen in himself. When silence had nevertheless been granted, after many such matters as I have already mentioned had been made known, this too is reported to have been established and proclaimed: henceforth, on that day, the celebration of this translation should be attended by the people, on which—toward the end of August, namely the third day before the Kalends of September—the market has from ancient times customarily assembled at Nantoacum. The brothers, however, were not granted permission to hold it, except on the seventh day before the Kalends of September, when the day of the translation falls, as happened then, in the same year in which the church of the infirm was dedicated by that same venerable bishop Odo, then at the Cluniac monastery.

Here, then, Maximus first began to rise like Lucifer; thereafter, like the sun, he extended his rays as far as he could spread his midday radiance, once translated through the hands of such praiseworthy persons.

The manuscript codex contains several miracles that occurred after that translation. We omit them, however, since they have no bearing on Odo.

[Col. 0267]

## FROM THE HISTORY OF THE CHURCH OF SAINT JAMES OF COMPOSTELA

By authority of Diego, second bishop of the see of Compostela and its first archbishop; written by Gerald, a member of that prelate’s household.

[Col. 0267A] Moreover, Diego Peláez was raised by King Sancho to that same chair of Saint James. At this time, among the Spaniards, the Gothic law was obliterated and Roman law adopted. The aforementioned Diego flourished for a long time in nobility and distinction in this present life, but he became so entangled in external affairs that he did not preserve, as he ought, the inward intention required by the norm of ecclesiastical conduct. Therefore, as his merits demanded, he was seized by King Alfonso and remained in chains for fifteen years.

[Col. 0267]

## THE PROMOTION OF PETER, A MONK OF THE MONASTERY OF CARDENAS, TO THE BISHOPRIC OF COMPOSTELA

[Col. 0267B] Meanwhile, Lord King Alfonso, a Catholic man, discerning upon profound consideration that the Church of the most blessed apostle, placed in the danger of widowhood, could not remain without loss unless it were fortified by pastoral provision, endeavored to raise another man to the pontifical chair of the Church of Saint James. Accordingly, while Richard, cardinal and legate of the Holy Roman Church, was holding a council at Santa María de Fusellos, King Alfonso attended and ordered the aforementioned bishop, whom he had for a long time kept in chains, to come to the council as though released, but still under guard—that is, so that he might depose him from episcopal dignity.

Then the aforementioned bishop, under fear of the king and hope of liberation, suffered prejudice at the hands of the Roman cardinal; and, declaring before the entire council that he was unworthy of the episcopate, he returned his ring and pastoral staff to the cardinal. The cardinal, however, granted permission for another man, named Peter, the abbot of Cárdenas, to be enthroned in the pontifical chair of the Church of Saint James. [Col. 0267C] After this, although that bishop had suffered prejudice, he was nevertheless again handed over to the king’s custody. Consequently, when these matters were finally debated at Rome, the aforementioned Richard, cardinal and legate of the Holy Roman Church, was pierced by the dart of confusion and disgrace. For Pope Urban and the Holy Roman Church severely rebuked and humiliated him, since he had previously aggravated by prejudice and unjustly deposed the bishop of Compostela after handing him over to captivity. He too, therefore, was burdened by the legation through which he had presumed to undertake such acts.

King Alfonso, however, with the common counsel of the wise men of Hispania, placed before this apostolic Church a certain abbot of the monastery of Cárdenas, named Peter. He remained bishop for two years in the government of the flock entrusted to him, but because he had been raised to the summit of so great an honor without the consent of our mother, the Holy Roman Church, he was justly and canonically deposed at a council held at León by the lord cardinal Rainerius (1091), who later became pope in the city of Rome and took the name Paschal.

Obeying with willing and devoted spirit the commands of Lord Diego, second bishop of the see of Compostela, I have committed to these pages, as faithfully as I could, the deeds of his predecessors. Now, with divine grace going before me, I begin to describe and recall to the memory of posterity the successes that the reverend bishop attained in this dignity, the adversities that he manfully endured in it, and those things that, with the Lord’s cooperation, he prudently and wisely accomplished for the honor of God and the benefit of his Church. Our help is in the name of the Lord, who made heaven and earth. Amen.

[Col. 0267]

## ON THE ELEVATION OF DIEGO GELMÍREZ

[Col. 0267C] Since, therefore, Lord Raymond, a suitable and prudent man, grieving for the Church of Compostela because it had not been duly organized according to the institutions of the canons, as we explained above, and having consulted four bishops—namely Peter of Lugo, Gonzalo of Mondoñedo, Roderic of Tui, and Peter of Ourense—addressed certain elders and the people of this Church out of the affection of inward piety, saying:

“Go, and, taking counsel among yourselves, whoever you wish to request from me as protector and defender, by the mercy of the Lord you shall be able to have immediately.”

Hearing this, they took counsel apart and all the princes of Galicia came together in the presence of Lord Raymond. Standing before him, they unanimously and earnestly requested from him a certain cleric named Diego Gelmírez, an honorable man of great discretion. They remembered that his father Elias had governed for many years with remarkable prudence and the strictest administrative discipline the neighboring province, namely the territory between the two rivers Ulla and Tambre.

The venerable count yielded wholeheartedly to their request. He placed Lord Diego, a canon of the Church of Saint James, whom he honorably retained at court as his chancellor and secretary with the permission and authorization of all the canons, over all the land and dignity of the most reverend James. Supported by a steadfast purpose that could not be dislodged and aided by the prudent counsel of the noblest men, Diego began to restore what had been destroyed, preserve what had been restored, and bring what had been preserved, through much labor, almost to a condition of rectitude.

[Col. 0269]

## ON DALMACHIUS, A CLUNIAC MONK PROMOTED TO THE BISHOPRIC OF COMPOSTELA

[Col. 0269B] Furthermore, after the passage of one year, the venerable King Alfonso, his son-in-law Lord Raymond, and his most noble wife, Lady Urraca, with the counsel of the clergy and people of Saint James, made a certain monk of the Cluniac order, Dalmatius, a chaste and religious man, bishop of the Church of Compostela, with the authority of the Holy Roman Church and, with God’s help, the blessing and permission of his abbot.

Finding the see like an uncultivated vineyard, he devoted himself with the most ardent love to the welfare of the holy Church, according to the pattern of sacred doctrine that he knew. For when Lord Urban, the most provident bishop of the Holy Roman Church, was holding a council at Clermont, the same religious Dalmatius presented himself before the lord pope at that council together with certain bishops of his province, who, joined to his Holiness by genuine charity, had remained with him. There, greatly honored by all, he obtained from the lord pope, through his most earnest pleas, the privilege written below—something that none of his predecessors had been able to obtain—together with the following letters concerning the confraternity of this Church.

### The Freedom of the Church of Compostela

Urban, bishop, etc.

[Col. 0269]

## THE DEATH OF BISHOP DALMATIUS AND THE SECOND ELEVATION OF DIEGO GELMÍREZ

[Col. 0269C] Returning from there adorned with so great a gift, he adorned the Church of Compostela with the strength of freedom. But because that which death seeks to overthrow does not endure, what lasted eight days now burns us with grief. The clerics, therefore, who thought they had reached the harbor of rest after so many dangers and tribulations, were shaken here and there amid the storms of this world, just as a ship is customarily driven from the shore when a tempest arises in mid-sea.

But the mercy of almighty God, which, according to the ordering of his providence, extends the hand of perfect consolation to those shipwrecked in a broken vessel, divinely inspired our Catholic governor, King Lord Alfonso, and his most pious son-in-law, Count Lord Raymond, together with his wife Lady Urraca, so that they might mercifully draw them back from such continual assaults to the harbor of tranquility. That this was done is rightly described in order.

The clergy and people of the Church of Saint James, mindful of all the benefits that Lord Diego Gelmírez had first bestowed upon them, earnestly strove to knock at the door of mercy of the aforementioned princes with an insistent petition. Through their favor they obtained the same Lord Diego as governor and lord.

[Col. 0269]

## THE REMOVAL OF THE FIRST DIEGO FROM THE EPISCOPATE

[Col. 0269D] The aforementioned Lord Diego Peláez, now freed from the king’s custody, learned that the most holy Bishop Dalmatius had paid nature’s due and that this other man alone held the entire dignity—not with pontifical authority, but temporarily through delegated power. He hastened to Rome and there loudly complained that he had unjustly lost his pontifical dignity and had suffered violence.

Thus it came about that, after the death of Lord Dalmatius, this Church, placed amid various anxieties, left the matter unresolved for four years. During those four consecutive years, Lord Diego Gelmírez, as vicar, governed the entire dignity of this Church with the common counsel of the good and their consent. At length, inspired by divine mercy and persuaded by providence for the common good, the same excellent King Alfonso wished to determine the causes of the aforesaid matter, which had been debated through so prolonged a delay. He sent his messengers to Rome, together with clerics of this Church, to set forth and examine their arguments against the accusations which the same Diego Peláez was still unjustly bringing against it.

When they arrived at Rome with pious intent, they found Pope Urban, of blessed memory, to whom they had been sent, dead, and Paschal already substituted in his honor. Before attaining the papacy, this Paschal, then called Rainerius, had already been legate in Hispania and knew with complete certainty the whole of this dispute and the affliction of the Church of Saint James.

The most reverend bishop P. of the Holy Roman Church, listening with keen discernment to their arguments and objections with an open ear of the heart, and distinguishing through subtle consideration the full extent of so great an unrest, judged, as justice dictated, that Diego Peláez was unworthy of so high a dignity. Therefore, this Church, which for fifteen years had remained almost languishing amid the miseries mentioned above, was freed by the Lord’s mercy. The same pope sent the following letter to our venerable king and to the clergy and people of Saint James.

[Col. 0271A] That author continues the history of Diego’s election: he went to Rome and first obtained the pallium, and finally obtained from Calixtus II that the Church of Compostela should be elevated to a metropolitan church.

[Col. 0271]

## FROM DOMNIZO, ON THE LIFE OF THE DUCHESS MATILDA

*(Book II, chapter 4)*

[Col. 0271A]

When Henry became king, he grew a grave enemy  
Of the holy Church and of the beloved lady Matilda;  
Wherever he could take something for himself, everywhere  
He seized lands by every means wherever he held power,  
Especially the towns and strongholds that the countess  
Had possessed beyond the mountains from her mother.  
He took them all away, except the fortress of Brigerinum,  
Perhaps because it was great, rich, and lavishly supplied on every side.  
The king attacked it but could not set foot within it.

When twice five years had nearly passed since  
The king had departed from Italy, he armed  
Horsemen’s backs with men, swearing that for seven seasons  
He would remain upon Matilda’s land, neglecting peace.  
He summoned dense forces and descended into the Italian kingdoms.

The third month was flowering with leaves and grasses.  
A certain city dear to the aforementioned lady remained;  
It had long been called Mantua,  
Rich enough in many goods and commodities.  
The king, desiring it, pitched his tents around it.  
The noble and strong Matilda, the most eminent teacher (variant: leader), soon filled it with warriors at her own expense.  
Holding the mountains, she despised all her enemies.  
The king’s dark battle-phalanx often brought war against the city.  
The citizens and the countess’s champions rushed forth;  
They killed and shattered the German host and drove it away.  
The city was well protected, etc.

[Col. 0271]

## PRIVILEGE OF THE CHURCH OF MÂCON

[Col. 0271B] In the name of the incarnate Word. Let it be known to all the sons of the holy Church of God that, in the year 1096 from the Incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ, and on the seventeenth day of October, at Mâcon, Lord Urban, pope by the providence of God and the second of that name, of blessed memory, granted the monastery of Saint Peter near the city of Mâcon many commendable apostolic privileges and concessions. Among other things, by his own initiative, he eternally excommunicates and curses all persons, whatever their condition, [Col. 0272B] who rashly and unlawfully harass the aforesaid monastery, its canons, and all its members, and those who disorderly and unjustly retain its privileges, liberties, goods, possessions, tithes, offerings, instruments, immunities, statutes, revenues, estates, and exemptions.

But upon all who preserve the goods and rights of that monastery, may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ and of the apostles Peter and Paul. Amen.

[Col. 0271]

## PRAYERS DELIVERED BY URBAN AT THE COUNCIL OF CLERMONT

*(Published separately below.)*

[Col. 0271]

## NOTICE OF THE CONSECRATION OF THE HIGH ALTAR OF THE MONASTERY OF CARROUF BY POPE URBAN II IN 1096

[Col. 0271C] Since from ancient times the ecclesiastical custom has wisely prevailed of committing to writing, for the memory of posterity, whatever it has judged useful to the interests of the Christian religion, we have decided that it would be fitting to transmit in writing to our successors, as though alive and recent, how the high altar at Carrouf was consecrated by Lord Pope Urban II in the time of Lord Peter, after Abbot Fulcrad.

When the aforementioned pope was celebrating a council at Clermont, the prudence of the aforesaid abbot humbly approached the majesty of that apostolic man and asked that his special kindness deign to visit and console the monastery of Carrouf, and that he solemnly consecrate its principal altar.

For long before this, the most holy Pope Leo, a contemporary of Charles the Great, had blessed another altar in the same monastery by apostolic authority; above it, however, the people of Carrouf had built another altar. For the consecration of this altar and the reconciliation of the entire monastery, therefore, the abbot sought the apostolic right hand.

Since the pope was always pious, after taking counsel with great men, he inclined his pastoral ears to the abbot’s prayers and, with that holy company of his, at last reached Carrouf under divine guidance. At his arrival, the magnitude and character of the joy displayed by nobles and peoples in honor of so venerable a place and in due reverence for the Roman pontiff can more readily be weighed by a discerning observer.

This place, dedicated especially to the honor of the King of kings from ancient times, had until then been held in the highest honor not only by neighboring peoples but also by those from far away. Everyone, moreover, rejoiced exceedingly, giving thanks to divine mercy that they had seen so great a shepherd in our region, since it can be shown that such a thing had happened to very few of his predecessors. Thus, in view of so great a novelty, peoples flocked from every side with joyful hearts; for the eye could scarcely be satisfied with seeing, or the ear with hearing.

They believed that they would obtain a great indulgence of their sins if they could in any way gather, as was fitting, for the service of so glorious a consecration; and, by the Lord’s accomplishing it, their devout desire served to bring this about.

At last, the religious apostolic man, about to consecrate the altar of the supreme Savior through the power of the Holy Spirit, climbed the steps of the altar and stood before it. Worthy persons surrounded him and cooperated with humble devotion in so great a mystery; their names will be written individually below. How beautiful and salutary it was to behold those episcopal and archiepiscopal hands, and even the papal hands—how reverently, skillfully, lovingly, and eagerly they performed their office in turn!

The shepherd Urban himself, beginning everything courteously and graciously, as the head and teacher of all, abundantly sprinkled the altar with consecrated water, infused it with oil and chrism, and anointed it with his own hands. With a modest expression he instructed his sons in the Lord to do the same, and labored with all the strength of mind and body until he had completed everything, as apostolic custom requires in so sublime an office.

After the consecration had been completed according to ecclesiastical custom, the same Roman pontiff celebrated solemn Mass upon the altar. Present at this work were Lord Amatus, archbishop of Bordeaux and legate of the Holy Roman See; Hugh, archbishop of Lyon and likewise legate; Daimbert, archbishop of Pisa; Rainger, archbishop of Reggio; Peter, bishop of Poitiers; Bruno, bishop of Signi; and John, cardinal deacon.

These things were done on the fourth day before the Ides of January, namely on Thursday, which at that time fell before the feast of Saint Hilary, in the year 1096 from the Incarnation of the Lord, in the eighth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Urban II.

[Col. 0274A]

### Concerning the Morning Altar

This consecration is to be celebrated by the faithful in honor of the holy and undivided Trinity on the fourth day before the Kalends of March. It was performed by Lord Pope Urban in honor of the most victorious cross and of Saint Eutropius, martyr and bishop of Xaintes, who rests in the present church.

There Lord Pope Urban promulgated a general decree and established a perpetual memorial, so that in future generations peoples might always assemble for the anniversary of the consecration and honor the house of their God for the remission of their sins. The pope, often to be remembered, granted all Christians who came to this consecration a seventh part of their penances, so that, however great their vow, the very difficulty of coming together might benefit those who performed penance in this manner.

The Mass for this solemnity follows; it was said on that day.

[Col. 0274B] In the chartulary of the same monastery there is found an old document of a donation made, as may be conjectured, at the advice of the same pontiff. It begins as follows:

“When at a certain time the apostolic lord Urban, perhaps by the disposition of God, was traveling through and visiting our region, he was honorably received into the monastery of the Holy Trinity, which is situated there, by the abbot and the monks serving God in that place. While he was staying there, a certain knight, Hubert, son of a man named Manuus, came to him. Hubert’s son had died some time earlier, having been overtaken by certain misfortunes. After, in great grief over him, he had spoken at length with the apostolic lord concerning the absolution of that soul—indeed, of his own, his father’s, and his mother’s—he offered to God, that is, to the Holy Trinity, half of the chapel, etc.”

[Col. 0273]

## TEXT CONCERNING THE DEDICATION OF THE CHURCH OF OUR HOLY GREATER MONASTERY

[Col. 0273C] In the year 1095 from the Incarnation of the Lord, on the sixth day before the Ides of March, with the moon at eleven, the epact at twenty-three, and the concurrent at two—the thirty-seventh year of Philip, king of the Franks, and the thirteenth year from the ordination of Bernard, our abbot—Urban II, the glorious pope, in no respect unworthy of apostolic dignity, came from the city of Rome and visited Gaul solely out of charity.

At the Council of Clermont, in the presence of nearly five hundred fathers—archbishops, bishops, and abbots—while all of them, together with Ralph, archbishop of Tours, acclaimed and authorized the privileges of liberty and immunity that the pope himself had sent to us and to our monastery from the city of Rome through the hands of our reverend brothers Lord Bernard of Reims, surnamed Pontius, then our prior, and Lord Rangerius, who later became a cardinal priest of the Holy Roman Church and thereafter archbishop of Reggio, and who sat in the aforesaid council as archbishop and cardinal—the pope authorized those privileges in the eighth year of his apostolate, that is, on the octave of the winter feast of Saint Martin.

Finally, for the sake of peace and concord between us and the canons of Saint Maurice of Tours, who at that time had not ceased persecuting us for ten years (on the occasion of the removal of the Easter station, about which we spoke under the year 1090), after he had visited our monastery, had been received by our poverty in the manner fitting and adequate for the time, and had rested, or refreshed himself, among us for seven days at no small expense, on the eighth day after his arrival—namely, the sixth day before the Ides of March, the date noted at the beginning of the page—he dedicated to God, in honor of the holy cross, the most blessed Mother of God and perpetual virgin Mary, and the holy apostles Peter and Paul, as well as blessed Martin, the principal basilica of this Greater Monastery of ours, in which the brothers devote themselves day and night to divine service.

On the preceding day, which had been Sunday, after celebrating the Masses according to custom, he went to the wooden platform prepared for him, as customary, on the bank of the Loire, in order to address the people. Standing upon it with the archbishops, bishops, and cardinals, he solemnly delivered for a very long time a word of exhortation to the innumerable people who had eagerly gathered from every direction for this very purpose. He passionately praised and extolled the order and religious life of our monastery, while no less severely cursing the conduct of our adversaries, namely the canons, and especially denouncing the tyranny that they had exercised against us for ten years.

The pope explained and established our innocence in the hearing both of the illustrious Count of Anjou, Fulk the Younger, and his nobles, who were present at the address, and of all who had flocked there from every direction. He declared that he had adopted us as special sons of the Holy Roman Church, whom thereafter no archbishop or bishop could excommunicate for any reason whatsoever without his permission or that of his successors. Finally, after commending our monastery and us to the aforesaid count, his nobles, and the rest of the people, he blessed us according to the tenor of the aforesaid privileges and absolved all who faithfully guarded, defended, and honored us and all that belonged to us.

But he cursed all who disturbed, harassed, afflicted, or dishonored us or anything belonging to us, and until they made satisfaction to God and to us and repented, he bound them with the chain of perpetual anathema.

Returning from there after the address had ended, he took his meal that same day in our refectory with two archbishops and one bishop [al., four bishops] and his cardinals. Then, as has been said, on the following day he solemnly dedicated our church.

The archbishop of Tours, Ralph of Orléans, attended that dedication. At the pope’s command, he placed beneath the high altar relics of the saints whose names are listed below. Together with the archbishop of Lyon and Primate Hugh, he carried on his own shoulders into the principal basilica the relics of the saints that had spent the preceding night in the chapel of the infirm, which had been dedicated the day before by Bruno, bishop of Signi, at the pope’s command.

Together with the aforementioned Lord Rangerius, he made the Latin alphabet, while Rangerius made the Greek one, and, at the pope’s command, placed the sign of the cross in oil upon the walls of the basilica. He then immediately consecrated the altar of the Crucified One at the pope’s command.

In the high altar, therefore, the ineffable sacrament of Christ’s body was placed together with these relics of the saints: a particle of the most victorious cross of Christ; material from the garments of the glorious Mother of God; hairs from the head and beard of the apostle Peter; material from the clothing of John the Evangelist; and relics of the holy martyrs Stephen, Maurice, Cyprian, Hermes, Saturninus, Ferreolus, Nereus, Achilleus, and Pancratius; of the confessors Maurice, Avitus, Sulpitius, Gundulphus, and Desiderius; and of the virgins Amatalia and Praxedes.

After the relics of the saints had been placed according to custom and the high altar consecrated, Count Fulk, Robert of Rupes, and Hugh of Calvomonte endowed it, at the pope’s command. The other nobles also, of whom there was a great number present, contributed an endowment highly acceptable to us: namely, their assistance, protection, and counsel.

[Note: [Col. 0275C] In the *History of the Bishops of Tours and of the Abbots of the Greater Monastery*: Hugh of Amboise, Rainald of Ferlé of the castle, and Raguellan of Maillezais. Jed., etc. Hugh of Calvomonte and Hugh of Amboise are the same person. See the following instrument.]

[Col. 0275C] The names of the pontiffs who attended this dedication are as follows: Hugh I, archbishop of Lyon and legate; Ralph of Orléans, archbishop of Tours; the aforementioned Rangerius; and Bruno, bishop of Signi.

Lord Amatus, archbishop of Bordeaux, was ill among us, in an outer chamber, but the dedication itself was nevertheless carried out with his assistance and counsel. These cardinals were present: Albert, priest; Thesto, priest; Gregory, deacon of Ticinum; and John Garcellus, deacon and primicerius. All of them had been present at the Council of Clermont. Our lord abbot Bernard and Otho, abbot of Puy, were also present.

On that same day the cemetery beyond the wall of our cemetery, extending as far as the road that led to the mills, was consecrated by Lord Rangerius and the bishop of Signi in the pope’s presence. On the following day the pope himself consecrated the cemetery of Saint Nicholas by sprinkling blessed water. At his command, Lord Hugh the primate and Lord Rangerius consecrated the cemetery by sprinkling blessed water all along the bank of the Loire as far as the wooden cross above our mills; from there they proceeded along the road toward the church of Saint John, as far as the boundary of the cemetery consecrated the day before; then westward, between our garden and vineyard, as far as the road leading from Saint Nicholas to the gate of our monastery.

They then continued through the vineyard, namely as far as Morevum of the town, sprinkling water through the pasture and vineyard outside the town almost to the church of Saint Gorgonius. From there they went in a straight line as far as the Loire itself, and then returned again to the place where they had begun sprinkling the water, consecrating the cemetery in a circuit, as has been said.

[Col. 0276B] Hugh of Calvomonte, son of Sulpicius of Amboise, while still a boy, and his mother, who was the niece of Geoffrey of Calvomonte, consented to the sale made to the monks of the Greater Monastery of two quarters of land in the cultivation of Rathon. Later, when he had become a young man and had succeeded his father in his dignity, and when he possessed Calvomonte together with Amboise in place of his uncle Geoffrey, he wished to reclaim those same quarters.

Meanwhile, by God’s will, Pope Urban, a glorious man, graciously visited our humility. A few days later he came to the Greater Monastery and solemnly dedicated our basilica; Hugh himself attended the dedication. After the altar had been consecrated and anointed according to custom, the pope, seated, summoned Fulk—namely, the count of Anjou, who had recently taken Tours from Theobald of Blois—and the crowd of nobles standing around. He admonished them to provide the newly dedicated church and altar with an endowment according to customary practice.

Having been prompted by us, he summoned the aforementioned Hugh to him and urged him to leave those quarters to us. Hugh did so gladly. A multitude was present for this matter, since it had gathered from every direction for so great a celebration.

Among the others, the following are named: from the clergy, Hugh the primate and archbishop of Lyon; Ralph, archbishop of Tours; Cardinal Rangerius, formerly archbishop of Reggio; Bruno, bishop of Signi; Albert, cardinal priest; Tezo, cardinal priest; Gregory, cardinal deacon of Pavia; and then our lord abbot Bernard of Saint-Venant, etc.

From the laity: Fulk, count of Anjou; Sigebrannus, his constable; Robert of Rupes; and Gausbert, provost of Calvomonte. Finally, Hugh’s sisters, Adenordis and Ermendis, likewise consented.

[Col. 0275]

## SYNOD HELD IN 1096

In it the monastery of Psalmodi was freed from the dominion and government of the abbots of Saint Victor of Marseille.

[Col. 0275C] Account of the settlement made between Richard, abbot of Marseille, and his monks, and Fulco, abbot of the monastery of Psalmodi, and the monks of that monastery.

In the year 1094 from the Incarnation of the Lord, the monks of Psalmodi came before the presence of Pope Urban and lodged a complaint with him against the abbot of Marseille [Col. 0276C] and his monks, alleging that they had subjected the monastery of Psalmodi to themselves contrary to apostolic authority.

When the venerable pope heard this, he summoned the abbot of Marseille, namely Richard, who had then been his legate in those regions, and ordered him to hear and settle this complaint in accordance with the judgment of Bertramnus, metropolitan of Narbonne [Note: [Col. 0276C] At that time Dalmatius was archbishop of Narbonne; Bertramnus succeeded him, and Raymond was substituted for Bertramnus in the see of Nîmes in the year 1096. Hence the names of those bishops must be corrected here; nevertheless, these were the men who held those sees when the case was concluded. If, however, the beginning of this document reads 1096 rather than 1094, everything will agree.] and Gibelinus, archbishop of Arles, and of the bishops Raymond of Nîmes and Geoffrey of Maguelonne, who were then present before him.

This affair provoked the monks of Marseille, and Richard himself, to such anger that they not only retained Psalmodi by force, but also expelled from their monastery the monks who had brought the aforesaid complaint before the lord pope.

Consequently, driven by extreme necessity, the monks of Psalmodi went to Rome to appeal and expelled the people of Marseille from their midst, from the least to the greatest. They swore upon the four Gospels that henceforth they would have no participation with the people of Marseille in the aforesaid monastery.

Accordingly, the aforementioned Richard approached the archbishops and bishops named above and requested that justice be done for him on the authority of the lord pope. After taking counsel, they assembled together and first restored Psalmodi to the people of Marseille. Once all the Psalmodians had left the monastery on account of their oath, they then appointed a day and place on which so great a dispute should be heard and settled.

Finally, on the appointed day, the people of Marseille and the Psalmodians came with the judges mentioned above, before whom the lord pope had placed the settlement of the aforesaid complaint. When everyone from both sides was standing around, Gibelinus, archbishop of Arles, spoke as follows:

“The first party approves the proceedings: let the Psalmodians state the grounds on which they complain against the people of Marseille.”

Stephen Calcatellus then rose, to whom the others had entrusted the response on behalf of himself and the others, and said:

“Our brothers, the Psalmodians, complain to God and Saint Peter, and to you, archbishops and bishops, who, by order of the lord pope, must decide our complaint against the Massilians: they have seized the monastery of Psalmodium by violence, by the hand of a layman, by bloodshed, by the expulsion of the monks, and finally by the concession of money, and have taken it away from us, although Psalmodium, according to the apostolic privileges—namely, those of John and Stephen—and according to the royal decrees, that is, those of Charles, Louis, and the other kings, whose authorities we possess here, has always been free and ought to be subject to no one except the Roman Church.

“Our brothers the Psalmodians also complain against the Massilians because, after they had submitted the aforesaid complaint to the lord pope, and while, by his command, the matter ought to have been brought to an end, this lord Richard, who is present here, expelled from their own monastery the Psalmodian monks who had made the aforesaid complaint, and caused them to go away and die in foreign lands. This is the complaint over which our brothers the Psalmodians complain against the Massilians, apart from the other evils that they have inflicted upon Psalmodium.”

To this Richard, abbot of Massilia and legate of the Apostolic See, replied with his Massilians:

“No one doubts, my brothers, that the monks of Psalmodium lived in a worldly manner and outside the Rule until the time of our predecessor Bernard, abbot of Massilia. Wishing to correct their faults, and at the request of Count Raymond, with the advice of his nobles, he obtained the aforesaid monastery, made it regular from being irregular, and held it in that condition until the day of his death. From then onward, I, who succeeded him, have held it to the present day under regular discipline, with the monks of that place receiving abbots and priors from our monastery through legitimate successions. This is the response we make to their complaint.”

While the Massilians and Psalmodians were discussing these and many other matters among themselves, the judges said to the primate, the apostolic legate, that if the Massilians possessed any other authority against the Psalmodians, they should produce it. They also ordered that the privileges and royal decrees should be presented to them, by which it was said that Psalmodium ought to be subject to no other Church except the Roman Church.

Having thus considered the arguments and supporting grounds of both parties, and examined the authorities concerning Psalmodium, the archbishops Bertrand and Gibelin and the bishops Gotofred and Raymond, with the aforesaid Richard present among them because he was the legate, pronounced judgment on the aforesaid complaint as follows:

“Although, lord Richard, you hold the place of the lord pope in our region, nevertheless, by his authority and with your consent, it has been granted to us to establish perpetual peace by settling the entire dispute between the Psalmodians and the Massilians.

“The judgment is this: According to the privileges of the apostles John and Stephen, and the royal decrees of Charles, Louis, and the other kings, the most ancient right over Psalmodium belongs solely to the Roman Church, and it ought to be subject to no one except the lord pope alone. For this reason the Psalmodians, so that their case might be decided more quickly, firmly swore that they would never again have fellowship with the Massilians in the aforesaid Psalmodium; and therefore, after Psalmodium had been restored to the Massilians by investiture, they all left their monastery seeking justice.

“It is therefore not fitting for you, lord Richard, who are the vicar of blessed Peter the apostle, to diminish the rights of blessed Peter, nor to defend or retain what was wrongly entrusted or acquired by your predecessors; rather, it is fitting to correct and amend such things canonically. And because the Massilians do not possess authorities by which they can justly hold Psalmodium, we decree that their monastery be freely and absolutely restored to the Psalmodians, and that the Massilians have no further lordship there.

“We also command, if it pleases you, that this judgment be written and presented to the lord pope; and if he approves it, it shall remain in force and be preserved at Psalmodium, so that thereafter no disturbance may arise between them on this matter.”

Richard, having taken counsel with the Massilians, replied:

“We approve and accept your judgment, and in perpetuity we release Psalmodium, with everything belonging to it, to God, Saint Peter, the lord pope, and the monks thereof, with charter and without charter.”

This was done publicly at the castle of Caislarum, in the place called Toirozella, while Philip was reigning as king of the Franks, in the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1096, on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of October, the feast day of Saints Lucius and Geminianus, in indiction IX [IV], concurrent IV, epact XV, calendar key XI, in the presence of the aforesaid judges and of Ebrard, abbot of Saint-Tiberius; Fulco, abbot of the same monastery of Psalmodium; Stephen Calcatellus; Raymond Stephen; William Archimibert; William Bonasus; William of Albanis; Raymond Itherius; William Bernard; Stephen Bernard; Pontius of Nocetum; and Peter Bernard; of the monks Julian Gondricus and Gunther, priest; and of the laymen Raymond of Cavi, [Col. 0278D] his brother Raynerius, Pontius Gaucelin, his brother Gaucelin, Pontius Bremund of Sommedrio, his brother Bremund, Pontius Peter of Saint-Just, Raymond of Saint-Julian, Bremund of Lestrancheriis, his brother Bertrand, Raymond Gaultier, Raymond Eldric, Raymond Rainon, and William Itherius.

I, Richard, abbot of Massilia, on the eighth day after the aforesaid decision, the eighth day before the Kalends of October, at Montpellier, approve this decision, together with this charter, to the monks of Psalmodium in perpetuity.

Sign: I, Pontius Stephen, confirm.  
Sign: I, Bernard Petiti, confirm.  
Sign: I, William, confirm.  
Sign: I, Armannus, confirm.  
Sign: I, Arnaldus, confirm.  
Sign: I, Pontius, confirm.  
Sign: I, Ebrard, confirm.

All these men were Massilian monks.

[Col. 0279]

This act of approval was made by order of the aforementioned Richard, in the presence of Bertrand, archbishop; Gotofred, bishop of Maguelonne; Angerius, archdeacon; Gaucelin of Lunel; Raymond Rainon; and many others. Pontius wrote it at the dictation of Gotofred the bishop.

[Col. 0280]

This decision was sent to Pope Urban II, who confirmed it with his bull, issued at Rome at Saint Peter’s, by the hand of John, cardinal deacon, on the Kalends of May, in indiction XII, in the year 1099, the twelfth year of his pontificate. We possess it.

[Col. 0279]
