## EXCERPT FROM THE BOOK OF FULCO, COUNT OF ANJOU

In which he describes the origin of his lineage and the deeds of his ancestors and of himself.

(In Acherius, *Spicilegium*, vol. X, p. 393.)

At the end of this year, 1096, as Lent was approaching, Pope Urban of Rome came to Angers and admonished our people to go to Jerusalem to conquer the pagan people who had occupied that city and the entire land of the Christians as far as Constantinople. Then, during Septuagesima, the church of Saint Nicholas was consecrated by the pope himself.

The same apostolic man also established and ordered by edict that, at the same season in which he had carried out the consecration, a public festival should be celebrated each year at Saint Nicholas, and that one-seventh of the penances should be remitted to the people who gathered for that celebration.

Departing from there, he came to Le Mans, and from there to Tours. There, after issuing decrees to the venerable council, he was crowned in mid-Lent and, in solemn procession, was led from the church of Saint Maurice to the church of Saint Martin, where he gave me the golden flower that he was carrying in his hand. In memory and out of love for him, I in turn decreed that it should always be carried at the Hosanna by me and my successors.

[Col. 0281]

## DIPLOMATIC NOTICE CONCERNING THE LETTERS OF BLESSED POPE URBAN II

(Jaffé, *Regesta pontificum Romanorum*, 448.)

In the bulls of Urban II, the years of the Incarnation are sometimes reckoned according to the customary system, whose beginning was Christ’s nativity; sometimes according to the Florentine years, as in 1094, which began three months after the nativity; and sometimes according to the Pisan years, especially in 1095 and 1096, which began nine months before it. Nor is the reckoning of the indictions everywhere consistent. For the indiction that earlier pontiffs had used seems to have been entirely abandoned, namely, the Constantinopolitan indiction; the notaries sometimes adopted the Constantinian or Caesarean indiction, which began on 25 September, and sometimes the Pontifical or Roman indiction, which began on 1 January.

The following sentence is added:

“BLESSED BE THE GOD AND FATHER OF OUR LORD JESUS CHRIST” (5, 9, 63, 83, 93, 106, 113, 126, 167, 179, 218, 219, 236, 289);

in place of which it is sometimes written between two circles:

“WE READ, WE CONFIRM” (211).

Gregory, cardinal deacon (127, 186); Hugh (127); Herimannus (127). Roger, cardinal deacon (127, 177). Cardinal Rainerius (241); John (241).

# LETTERS AND PRIVILEGES OF BLESSED URBAN II, ROMAN PONTIFF

## [GENUINE]

### I. Letter of Pope Urban II to the archbishop of Salzburg and other bishops

He informs them of his election as supreme pontiff and urges them to fight courageously for the Church. (Year 1088.)

[Dom Martène, *Amplissima Collectio*, I, 520, from a manuscript of Saint-Germain-des-Prés.]

[Col. 0283A]

Urban, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the venerable archbishop of Salzburg and the other most reverend bishops—the bishops of Passau, Würzburg, Worms, Augsburg, and Constance—and to the venerable abbots, the most glorious Welf B. and B., and all the greater and lesser faithful of blessed Peter: greeting and apostolic blessing.

[Col. 0283B]

We wish your blessedness to know what has recently taken place concerning us. Our most reverend brothers, the bishops and cardinals—namely, those of Savona, Tusculum, Albano, Segni, and Porto—bearing the legation, consent, and petition of all the lay faithful favorable to our party and of the clergy electing at Rome; together with the most religious abbot of Cassino, representing all the deacons; and Cardinal R., of the title of Saint Clement, representing all the cardinals; and B., the prefect, representing all the lay faithful, assembled at Terracina with twenty-one bishops and four abbots.

After a three-day fast had been observed jointly with many prayers, on the Sunday, finally, the fourth day before the Ides of March, they entrusted to me, the most unworthy of all, against every vote and desire of mine—God knows how greatly I resisted—the government of the Apostolic See. Electing me with the consent of all the aforesaid faithful, both present and absent, and asserting that they possessed in this matter the authority and command of my predecessors of holy memory, Gregory and Victor, they imposed upon my strength a burden far beyond my capacity.

But since, to speak before God, I was compelled to undertake so great a burden in such a dangerous time, not through any ambition for honor or presumption whatsoever, but solely because the obedience of so many and such religious men—which could not be disregarded without danger—required it, and because I placed my confidence in the mercy of almighty God, we ask and entreat you in the Lord Jesus to remain firmly in the fidelity, devotion, and goodwill that you began and have always shown to the lord and our predecessor of blessed memory, Gregory, and to assist the holy Roman Church, your mother, with every aid and counsel within your power.

As for me, trust and believe in me in all things as you did in our most blessed father, Pope Gregory. Desiring to follow his footsteps entirely, I reject everything he rejected, condemn what he condemned, wholly embrace what he loved, and confirm and approve whatever he judged sound and catholic. Finally, in every matter, I think and agree in every respect as he thought, whether on one side or the other.

Now, therefore, I beg and embrace your brotherhood: act courageously and steadfastly, and be strengthened in the power of God’s might, advancing against the enemy and setting yourselves as a wall before the house of Israel, so that you may stand in battle as the Lord’s most valiant warriors on his day.

You who are spiritual must instruct by word and example those who are not instructed, and exhort them as you know how and as the necessity of this dangerous time requires. For when I was among you, I found you all to be such that I could cry out in the words of the Lord himself: “Truly I say to you, I have not found such faith in Israel”; and: “The one who perseveres to the end will be saved.”

Moreover, pour out continual prayers before the mercy of almighty God, so that he may graciously restore his holy Church to its former state. May the God of peace himself swiftly crush Satan beneath your feet. May the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you all, beloved in Christ.

[Col. 0284C]

Issued at Terracina, on the third day before the Ides of March.

[Note: [Col. 0283D] Urban II was made supreme pontiff on the fourth day before the Ides of March, in the year 1088. On the following day, that is, on the third day before the Ides of March, Bertold says under this year that, having sent letters to all Catholics, he announced his ordination to everyone and declared that he would observe in all things the footsteps of his predecessor, Pope Gregory of pious memory. We publish these letters, which Baronius desired, all the more willingly because they contain more about Urban II’s election—material either found nowhere else or reported quite differently.]

### II. Letter of Pope Urban II to Hugh, abbot of Cluny

He announces that the pontificate has been conferred upon him and asks Hugh to come to him. (Year 1088.)

[Mabillon, *Annales Benedictini*, V, 251.]

Urban, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Hugh, most reverend abbot of Cluny, and to all his holy community: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Because we know that your holiness is greatly eager for the exaltation of the Roman Church, we wish briefly to inform you of what has taken place concerning us.

We therefore make known to your affection that at Terracina, a city of Campania, the bishops and cardinals of the holy Roman Church—namely, those of Porto, Sabina, Tusculum, Albano, and Segni—together with sixteen other bishops, four abbots, and a great many other religious men, assembled.

The bishop of Porto declared himself the legate of all the Roman clergy who favored the catholic party; the abbot of Cassino, a cardinal deacon, declared himself the legate of the other deacons; P., cardinal of the title of Saint Clement, declared himself the legate of all the cardinals; and the prefect of the City asserted that he represented all the laity.

After they had persisted earnestly for three days in fasting, supplications, and great prayers to God, they finally elected me pope on the fourth day before the Ides of March, although I was entirely unworthy of this.

I call God as my witness that I did not consent because of ambition or desire for any dignity. Rather, I feared disobeying so many and such great men, and feared offending God if, in such a time, when the Church was imperiled so far as it depended upon me, I did not come to its aid—especially since they asserted that my predecessors, men deserving every veneration, namely Gregory and Victor, had divinely commanded this to them.

I therefore ask you, most desired of men, and earnestly implore you: if you possess any affection of piety, if you remember your son and pupil, deign to console me, who greatly desire this, by your presence, and, if it is ever possible, visit your holy mother, the Roman Church, by the arrival we so greatly desire.

But if this cannot be done, do not hesitate to send to us such men from among your sons and my fellow brothers that I may see you in them and receive you, and, placed amid immense troubles, hear words of your consolation; men who may represent to me your charity and affection, and tell me how you and the whole assembly of our brothers are faring.

I also ask you to urge the entire congregation of the holy brothers to pour out prayers before the mercy of almighty God, so that he may graciously restore both us and his holy Church, which appears to be subject to such great dangers, to its former state. For you should know that this matter rests upon you more particularly than upon anyone else. Farewell.

Issued at Terracina on the third day before the Ides of May.

[Note: [Col. 0285D] This letter appears to have been written on the day after his election, and therefore perhaps “the third day before the Ides of March” should be read, unless he returned to Terracina after the dedication of the monastery of Bantin, from where he sent it to Sicily. Yet it is hardly probable that Urban informed his most affectionate father of his election so late.]

### III. Letter of Pope Urban II to the bishops, clergy, and people of the province of Vienne

Concerning the election of the archbishop of Vienne, since this metropolis had long been without a pastor. (Year 1088.)

[D. Bouquet, *Recueil*, vol. XIV, p. 689, from the Floriac Library, part III, p. 74.]

[Col. 0285D]

Urban, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the venerable bishops and brothers in office: Gontard of Valence, Guido of Geneva, Conrad of Maurienne, Hugh of Grenoble, Ismion of Die, and John of Viviers; and to all the clergy and people of the Church of Vienne: greeting and apostolic blessing.

We do not wish your brotherhood to remain unaware that solely by the grace of God, without any preceding merits of our own, we have been elected by the unanimous and universal consent of the Catholics to the Roman Church and the summit of the Roman pontificate.

Therefore, since Scripture testifies that “a brother helping a brother is a fortified and strong city” (Prov. XXIII, 19), we ask and entreat you in the Lord Jesus Christ to pray unceasingly to the Lord both for us and for your holy mother, the Roman Church, so that, after overcoming every obstacle raised by enemies, we may bring to worthy and pleasing results what we have been able to begin by his will.

You should know with certainty that we greatly love your Church and, among the other Churches entrusted to our care, desire to honor it with an intense devotion of love.

Since, therefore, your metropolis has long been known to be without a pastor, we command you by apostolic instruction to make every effort to elect for that Church a suitable and capable pastor as soon as you can. Such delay usually brings great loss and great destruction upon souls.

You also know that it has been provided by canonical authority that a Church should not remain vacant of its bishop for more than three months; how much less, therefore, through the course of so many years!

And because, while a Church is vacant, certain irreligious persons commonly seize its property and revenues, we command that this be prohibited in every way by apostolic authority. We also specifically command that the Church of Romans and the Church of Saint Peter of Campania, which are known to have belonged from ancient times to the right and jurisdiction of the Church of Vienne, remain peacefully with that Church.

We decree, under the apostolic authority of its pontiff, that no person, great or small, molest or diminish either those Churches themselves or their goods, but that they remain peacefully and unimpaired for the Church of Vienne. May almighty God bless you as you obey our commands.

### IV. Letter of Pope Urban II to Lanfranc, archbishop of Canterbury

Concerning the Church’s distress and the pontificate he has undertaken. (Year 1088.)

[Edited by Theiner, *Disquisitiones criticae*, p. 207.]

[Col. 0286D]

Urban, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Lanfranc, most reverend archbishop of the holy Church of the English: greeting and apostolic blessing.

We believe that your prudence, dearest father, is not unaware of how many storms and tempests have for a long time tossed the ship of Peter, bringing it almost to shipwreck, whether because he was negligent or, rather, asleep.

Nor do we doubt that your religious devotion has heard that, at the request and under the compulsion of the entire Catholic Church alone, with the unavoidable command of our two lords and predecessors, Gregory and Victor, preceding it, and with the extreme necessity of the times pressing us, we have been advanced—entirely unworthy and wholly unequal to so great an office, I know not by what judgment—to the supreme priesthood of the Roman See.

How and in what manner this occurred, if perhaps you have not learned it fully, our beloved son Roger, cardinal subdeacon of our Church, will be able to relate in complete order.

Now, therefore, because we know that in this period you alone among the foremost are a noble and true son of the holy Roman Church, your mother, by this letter we invite your brotherhood to her service, her defense, and finally the obedience owed to her. We earnestly beseech you to extend to her, amid such great needs and dangers, the right hand of your counsel and assistance.

Your religious prudence and outstanding faith are, by God’s grace, renowned and celebrated throughout the world. Nor is it unknown that the Church over which you preside ought to be especially obedient and devoted to the Roman Church, through which it received the beginnings of the catholic faith and was freed from demonic slavery.

Let your prudence therefore strive and labor, as far as it knows and can, to assist the Roman Church in every way. Let it strive to join our Churches, separated by the diversity of their regions, through unity of catholic conduct. If you find anything in those parts opposed to the Apostolic See, or anything that perhaps resists its authority, rebuke it according to the wisdom divinely given to you, restrain it firmly, and take care to correct it shrewdly.

Let your authoritative brotherhood also approach, exhort, and admonish the king himself, our dearest son, so that he too, according to his rank and office, may strive to aid and honor his mother, the Roman Church, which is laboring under many dangers and the greatest necessities, by his counsel and comfort.

Since, as Scripture says, “a friend is proved in adversity,” and likewise, “a friend is not known in prosperity, nor is an enemy concealed in misfortune,” let him not consider this time of necessity something to be disregarded. If he owes any fidelity or friendship to the Roman Church, let him now, when the opportunity is especially great, show himself generous and devoted.

As for the money that blessed Peter customarily used to receive from that kingdom, let him send it through our aforesaid son Roger, or through another faithful legate of his, together with him or as far as Cluny, as soon as he can, so that he may obtain the favor of blessed Peter and find us always ready and willing to promote and exalt his kingdom.

Moreover, commending ourselves most devoutly to your prayers, we strongly commend to you the bearer of this letter, Roger. We ask you to grant him assistance in every matter in which he may need it in the service of blessed Peter.

Issued at Terracina on the fourth day before the Ides of April.

### V. The primacy of the Church of Toledo in Spain is restored

(Year 1088.)

[Mabillon and Ruinart, *Ouvrages posthumes*, III, 344.]

Urban, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Bernard, most reverend brother and archbishop of Toledo, and to his successors forever.

It is clear to all who know the decretal institutions of the saints how great the dignity of the Church of Toledo was in ancient times, how great its authority was in the regions of Spain and Gaul [Note: [Col. 0287] This should be understood of that part of Gaul which was subject to the Visigoths, namely, the province of Narbonne.], and how great were the benefits that proceeded through it in ecclesiastical affairs.

But because the people deserved it by their sin, that city was captured by the Saracens, and the freedom of the Christian religion there was reduced to nothing, so that for nearly three hundred and seventy years no dignity of a Christian pontificate flourished there.

In our own times, however, with divine mercy looking upon its people, through the zeal of the most glorious king Ildefonsus, through the efforts of the Christian people, and with the Saracens expelled by the strength [variant: rights] of the Christians, the city of Toledo has been restored.

Therefore, by the will and unanimous consent of the peoples, bishops, and princes of the province, and of the distinguished king Ildefonsus, it pleased the majesty of God that you, dearest brother Bernard, should be elected the first bishop of that city after so long a time.

And so, responding to heavenly grace’s mercy, because you have humbly sought the authority of the Roman Church through so many dangers by land and sea, we do not refuse to restore the Christian authority of the Church of Toledo.

We rejoice also with the greatest joy of heart and, as is fitting, give great thanks to God, because he has deigned in our time to grant the Christian people so great a victory. With his help, we desire to stabilize and increase the condition of that city, according to our resources—both because of the Roman Church’s customary goodwill and the reverence due to the Church of Toledo, and because we have been moved by the petitions of our dearest son, the most excellent King Ildefonsus.

We therefore confer upon you, venerable brother Bernard, the pallium, by the blessing of the apostles Peter and Paul, that is, the fullness of every priestly dignity. And, according to the established fact that the bishops of that city existed in ancient times, by the sanction of our privilege we appoint you primate throughout all the kingdoms of Spain.

Let all the bishops of Spain regard you as primate, and if anything worthy of inquiry arises among them, let them refer it to you, while preserving the authority of the Roman Church and the privileges of each metropolitan.

Therefore, by the terms of this privilege, we confirm the Church of Toledo in perpetuity to you and, if divine grace permits, to your canonical successors, and so forth.

Issued at Anagni by the hand of John, cardinal deacon and pro-signator of the Holy Roman Church and of the lord Pope Urban II, on the Ides of October, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1088, in indiction XI, in the first year of the pontificate of Pope Urban.

### VI. Letter of Urban II to Ildefonsus, king of Galicia

He congratulates him on the recovery of the Church of Toledo from the Saracens. He commends Bernard, archbishop of Toledo, whom he has presented with the pallium and appointed primate throughout all the kingdoms of Spain. (Year 1088.)

[Mabillon and Ruinart, *Ouvrages posthumes*, III, 346.]

Urban, etc., to Ildefonsus, king of Galicia.

There are two principal powers by which this world is governed, King Ildefonso [Note: [Col. 0289D] Also called Aldefonsus or Alfonsus, styled emperor of Spain. Son of Ferdinand and brother of Sancho, king of Castile, who succeeded in 1072 and reigned until 1109.]: priestly dignity and royal power [Col. 0289B]. Yet priestly dignity, dearest son, so far surpasses royal power that we shall have to render an account concerning those very kings to the King of all. Therefore pastoral care compels us to provide, as far as we can, not only for the salvation of the lesser but also of the greater; and in order that we may restore unharmed to the Shepherd the sheep entrusted to us, we must take particular care for your salvation, since Christ has made you a defender of the Christian faith and of the Church.

Remember, remember, my most beloved son, how great a glory of divine majesty grace has bestowed upon you; and just as He Himself has ennobled your kingdom above others, so strive to serve Him more devotedly and familiarly than others. For the Lord Himself says through the prophet: “Those who honor me I will honor; [Col. 0289C] but those who despise me shall be dishonored” (1 Samuel 2:30).

Therefore we give thanks to the Lord and to your labors because the Church of Toledo has been liberated from the power of the Saracens. At the prompting of your exhortations, we received with due honor and reverence our venerable brother Bernard, bishop of that city; and, granting him the pallium, we also bestowed upon the Church of Toledo a privilege corresponding to its ancient dignity. We have established him as primate throughout all the kingdoms of Spain, and whatever the Church of Toledo is known to have possessed in ancient times, we have decreed that it shall likewise possess in the future through the generosity of the apostolic see.

Receive him as a most dear father, and take care to obey whatever he announces to you from the Lord; and do not cease to exalt his Church through temporal assistance and benefactions.

Among the other proclamations of your praises, news has reached our ears of something that we could not hear without profound sorrow: namely, that you captured the bishop of Saint James and, while he was in captivity, deprived him of episcopal dignity [Col. 0290A]. You should know that this is wholly contrary to the canons and intolerable to Catholic ears. It has grieved us all the more because we embrace you with all the greater affection.

Now, most glorious King Ildefonso, in the name of God and the apostles we command you, entreating you to restore this same bishop, through the archbishop of Toledo, to his full dignity. Do not excuse this action by attributing it to Cardinal Richard, for it is wholly contrary to the canons, and Richard was not then exercising a legation of the apostolic see.

Whatever he then did—we judge it null and void, since Pope Victor, of holy memory, had deprived him of his legation [Note: [Col. 0289D] Richard, abbot of Saint-Victor of Marseille, had been sent as legate to Spain by Gregory VII after Bernard, his brother. At the Council of Benevento in 1087 he was excommunicated, together with Hugh of Lyon, because, after approving Victor’s election, they subsequently withdrew from obedience to him, as we have related in the Deeds of Urban, from the Chronicle of Cassino, Book III, chapter 72.].

Once the bishop has been restored to his dignity, for the remission of sins and in obedience to the apostolic see [Col. 0290B] [Note: [Col. 0289D] We discuss this matter concerning the bishop of Compostela in the Deeds of Urban; see above the excerpts from the History of Compostela.], let him come with your legates to our presence, to be judged canonically. Otherwise you would compel us to act against your affection unwillingly, something we too would prefer not to do.

Remember the religious ruler Constantine, who did not even wish to hear the judgments of priests, considering it unworthy that those called gods [Note: [Col. 0290D] Labbé, Aguirre, and others print *deos*; perhaps *dictos deos* should be read; see Rufinus and others.] should be judged by human beings.

Therefore hear the Lord and His apostles speaking through us, if you wish to be heard by them and by us in the matters you have requested. May the Lord, King of kings, enlighten your heart with the radiance of His grace, grant you victories, exalt your kingdom, and allow you always to live in such a way that you may happily enjoy your temporal kingdom and rejoice eternally in the everlasting one. Amen.

## VII. Urban II admonishes the archbishops of Spain concerning the restoration of the primacy of Toledo. (1088)

[Mabillon and Ruinart, *Posthumous Works*, III, 349.]

[Col. 0290C]

**Urban, etc., to the archbishop of Tarragona [Note: [Col. 0290D] I fear that “of Tarragona” has intruded here. For when Bernard, bishop of Toledo, received the primacy in 1088, the Church of Tarragona had not yet been restored as a metropolitan see. Nor does this letter seem capable of being assigned to a later year, since it is addressed not to the archbishop of Tarragona alone but to all the archbishops of Spain, in order to admonish them concerning the restoration of the primacy of Toledo, which took place in this year. Callistus II, in Letter 34, writes that Urban granted the Churches of Oviedo and León to the archbishop of Toledo.] and to the other archbishops of Spain.**

Whoever wishes others to be subject to him ought not to disdain being subject also to others. For this order of governance and precedence is observed not only in the earthly Church but also in the heavenly Church, with the King of all arranging that, under the universal Prince, some should rule over others.

Accordingly, by the authority of our privilege, we have decreed that the archbishop of Toledo shall be primate throughout all the kingdoms of Spain, without prejudice to the authority of the apostolic see and to the privileges of each of the metropolitans. Therefore, if anything serious should occur among you, since you are far from the apostolic see, you shall have recourse to him as your primate over all; and by his judgment you shall settle whatever difficulties arise for you.

If, however, something should perhaps be incapable of being settled even by his judgment, it shall properly be referred to the apostolic see, as the prince of all sees. Those among you who lack their own metropolitans shall meanwhile be subject to him as to their proper metropolitan. Farewell.

## VIII. Letter of Urban II to Hugh, abbot of Cluny, concerning the primacy conferred upon the Church of Toledo. (1088)

[Mabillon and Ruinart, *Posthumous Works*, III, 350.]

[Col. 0291A]

**Urban, etc., to Hugh, abbot of Cluny, etc.**

We received with reverence our venerable brother Bernard, bishop of the Church of Toledo, both at the request of your affection and out of respect for his religious character and for the honor of the Church of Toledo. To him, as he devoutly and simply approached the majesty of the apostolic see and the Roman Church as the mother of all, we granted, as was fitting, the ancient safeguards of his Church, as you requested; and we willingly bestowed a document of our privilege, filled with its former dignity.

We have made him primate of all the bishops who are in Spain, and, together with the grant of the pallium, we have given him whatever your affection asked of us concerning this matter.

It is therefore fitting that you respond to our love with corresponding devotion and faithfully serve us and the Roman Church with our assistance. For we love you and your brothers with particular affection, and we take all the properties of your monastery, wherever it is free to do so, under the special protection of our hands [Col. 0291C], so that neither any bishop nor any legate—unless we have specially entrusted this to him—may presume to judge your affairs against your will, without prejudice, however, to the rights of the bishops which they are known to have possessed over them until now.

Therefore always remember us in all your prayers to the Lord. Just as we specially cherish you and what belongs to you, so take care to commend us spiritually to the Lord; and assist us and the Roman Church wherever it is necessary and wherever opportunity permits. May almighty God cherish, preserve, and protect us by His grace. Amen.

## IX. Urban II confirms the possessions and privileges of the monastery of Cluny and grants Abbot Hugh the use of the mitre, dalmatic, gloves, and sandals. (1088)

[*Bibliotheca Cluniacensis*, p. 514.]

[Col. 0291D]

**Urban, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Hugh, most holy abbot of Cluny, and to his successors forever.**

Although by the authority and goodwill of the apostolic see we are debtors to all the sons of the holy Church, we ought nevertheless to devote ourselves with a more attentive charity to venerable persons and places, especially those that have always adhered more closely and more devoutly to the apostolic see and that shine with the greater glory of religion.

Therefore, most holy, most reverend, and most beloved brother, a singular prerogative of affection is owed by us to you, both because of your ancient familiarity with the apostolic see [Col. 0292A] and because of the most noble religious character of yourself and your monastery.

There is also this reason that makes us no less indebted to you and to your monastery: through you I received the beginnings of monastic religion. In your monastery I was reborn through the second grace of the Holy Spirit, and the Roman Church is known to have bestowed upon it, until now, the care of its affection and protection with especially abundant grace.

Whatever liberty, immunity, or authority is known to have been granted to you, to your successors, and to your monastery through the privileges of our predecessors, we too grant, deliver, and confirm by the text of this decree.

We add that the monastery of Saint Mary of Charity; the monastery of Saint Martin of the Fields near Paris; the monastery of Saint Denis near Nogent; Saint Mary of Nazareth; Saint Gervais of Exis; Saint Mary of Arles; Saint Peter of Campo Rotundo; Saint Genesius in the bishopric of Elne; Saint Paul in the Valley of Oil; Saint Mary of Cubaria; Saint Mary of Salella; Saint Mary of Toulouse; and the monastery of the Holy Trinity at Marcignac, which you built on your own allod, shall never be withdrawn from the governance and administration of you or your successors.

All the other privileges that our predecessors granted to your monastery we likewise grant and confirm. The monastery of Moissac, in the liberty in which it now exists, shall remain so in the future, unless perhaps the bishop has committed something for which he ought to be deprived of his authority.

Whoever, moved by a desire for a better life, wishes to come to your monastery shall be freely received by you and your successors, according to the rule of our holy father Benedict.

Furthermore, we decree and establish that no one thereafter acting in your region as a legate in the place of the Roman bishop may, without his permission or command, dare to speak against you or your monasteries, unless he has been specially sent for that purpose. Nor may the bishops in whose dioceses your properties lie judge your monks or monasteries at all, without prejudice to the canonical right which they have hitherto possessed over them. If they have any case against them, let them summon you or your successors. If the dispute cannot be settled by you, let it be referred to the apostolic see, to be decided solely by its judgment or that of its legate.

We grant you, with particular devotion, the privilege of using the episcopal mitre during solemn processions and Masses. On the principal festivals—that is, on the five which you regard as principal—as well as on Epiphany, the Ascension, and the dedication of your Church, you may wear the dalmatic, gloves, and sandals.

This is granted both as a visible sign of your religious dignity and as an expression of our special affection, which, because of the merits demanded by the apostolic see, you have earned to a greater degree.

It is fitting that your holiness, just as you are honored in a special way by the Roman Church, should likewise labor with singular devotion for the service and advantage of that same Church, so that what has hitherto been granted to you by it may remain secure and stable [Col. 0293A], and so that your monastery may in the future more worthily attain the rewards of greater glory.

Given at Rome through the hands of John, deacon of the holy Roman Church and prosignator of the lord Pope Urban II, on the Kalends of November, indiction XI, in the year of the Incarnation of the Lord 1088, in the first year of the pontificate of the same lord Pope Urban.

## X. Letter of Pope Urban II to Geoffrey, bishop of Maguelonne. He receives from him the investiture of the county of Substantion and the bishopric of Maguelonne. Accordingly, he places that Church and county under the special protection of the Roman Church and entrusts to him the collection of an annual census of one ounce of gold from the aforesaid county. (Around 1088)

[D. Bouquet, *Collection*, vol. XIV, p. 690.]

[Col. 0293B]

**Urban, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Geoffrey, bishop of Maguelonne, and to his successors forever.**

The entire body of the holy Church, through the merciful God and the blood of His only-begotten Son, our Redeemer, is known to have been endowed with its own perpetual liberty. Yet through the cunning of wicked men and the negligence of shepherds, certain Churches throughout the world have been subjected to the authority of secular powers.

For this reason, through the regard of heavenly mercy, we have been promoted to the universal governance of the apostolic see, so that we ought in every way to provide for what concerns their salvation and glory, in order that, freed from every bond of servitude [Col. 0293C], they may always enjoy their liberty.

For this purpose almighty God established the Roman Church as the mother and principal Church of all Churches, so that, under its direction, what is evil may be corrected and what is right may be confirmed.

Therefore, brother Geoffrey, bishop of Maguelonne, we confirm in perpetuity by right that the Church of Maguelonne shall remain, together with your canonical successors, under the special liberty of the Roman Church. Through the culpable negligence of the shepherds who had been in those regions, the counts of Substantion had for many years drawn that Church under the yoke of their servitude by an impious custom.

But Count Peter [of Melgueil], of blessed memory, moved by the fear of God, restored the entire bishopric to Blessed Peter and his vicars, and renounced it by a written instrument [Col. 0293D]. He likewise left the county, which belonged to his jurisdiction, under the authority of Blessed Peter and his vicars by a testamentary document, on the condition that his heirs should become soldiers of the Roman pontiff and hold the county from his hand.

If the succession of heirs should fail, the county was to be held under the administration of the Roman pontiff and the care of the bishop of Maguelonne. He further established that, for the sake of his heirs, an annual census of one ounce of gold should be paid to the Lateran palace.

Accordingly, receiving the investiture of the bishopric of Maguelonne and the county of Substantion from the hand of your fraternity, in the place of the aforesaid count, and religiously confirming the provisions of the county’s donation, we receive that Church and county for special protection under Blessed Peter and the Roman Church, without prejudice to the authority and reverence of the metropolitan of Narbonne, provided that he has been legitimately ordained.

We confirm in perpetuity that the Church itself is to be governed by you and by your canonically appointed successors. Whatever is known to have justly belonged until now to the bishopric of Maguelonne or to the common property of the brothers living there, whether through the generosity of kings or counts or through the offerings of any of the faithful, and whatever it may justly acquire in the future [Col. 0294A] in cities and towns, churches, tithes, and other revenues, we grant, deliver, and confirm by this document of our decree.

We establish and decree that no priest or cleric of any order whatsoever, no emperor, king, or count, may diminish, remove, appropriate for his own rights, or divert under the pretext of any cause or occasion for other supposedly pious purposes, out of avarice or as an excuse for it, anything that has been given or may in the future be given to the Church of Maguelonne by anyone.

Since it often happens that, against the will of clergy and people, secular powers wickedly strive to enthrone persons, we decree and establish that, when you who are bishop die, or when any of your successors dies, no secular power may claim for itself any right or honor in the appointment of the bishop. Instead, according to the statutes of the canons, one shall be appointed whom the clergy and people freely elect by common counsel and without corruption.

Furthermore, to your fraternity and your successors, so long as they are such as to deserve the communion and grace of the apostolic see, we entrust the care of the aforesaid county of Substantion, so that you may collect its annual census. As a demonstration of the special liberty received from the Roman Church, you and your successors shall pay one ounce of gold each year from the bishopric to the Lateran palace.

Given at Rome on the nineteenth day before the Kalends of January, through the hand of John, deacon of the holy Roman Church and prosignator of the lord Urban II, in the year of the Lord 1088, in the first year of the pontificate of the same lord Urban [Col. 0294D].

## XI. Letter of Urban II to Pistorio and Rusticus, abbots of Vallombrosa. Concerning Wezelon [Note: [Col. 0293D] That Guezelon was a heretic. The present letter of Pope Urban II, together with many others transcribed above, was sent for printing from a manuscript of the library of Saint-Victor in Paris by the reverend lord Jean Picard, regular canon of that same church of Saint-Victor. Since it had hitherto been printed nowhere and contains a decretal constitution concerning simony, I judged it worthy of publication. This Guezecelo, as the said lord Picard rightly noted, is the same person whom the abbot of Ursperg commonly calls Wicelo, successor of the deceased Siegfried, archbishop of Mainz—or rather, the invader of the Church of Mainz, imposed by King Henry—as is clear from what was said above at the Council of Quedlinburg under Gregory VII. It is no objection that Ursperg calls him Wecilo, whereas Pope Urban here calls him Guezelon. For it is customary among the French and other peoples that all proper names written by the Germans initially with a double W should be written by them with the first letter changed from V to G; thus *Wezelon* would have been written *Guezelo*. —Sev. Bin.] after he had been deposed as archbishop of Mainz for simony. (Around 1088)

[Mansi, *Councils*, XX, 664.]

**Pope Urban II to Pistorio and Rusticus, abbots of Vallombrosa.**

[Col. 0295A]

You have written to us that a great scandal has arisen among you because we consecrated the bishop of Pisa, who had been ordained a deacon by the heretic Guezelon.

We certainly know that Guezelon was a heretic and that he had invaded the bishopric of Mainz through the crime of simony. For that reason—or in order to acquire another position—he had long served a king placed under anathema, and for the position he had acquired he continued to serve him throughout his life.

We ourselves also excommunicated him in a synodal council for the same reason, since he had been consecrated by excommunicated persons; we condemned him and deposed him from every ecclesiastical office, without any hope of restoration.

## XII. Privilege of Pope Urban II for the abbey of Saint John of the Vines. (1089)

[De Louen, *History of the Royal Abbey of Saint-Jean-des-Vignes*, Proofs, p. 281.]

[Col. 0295B]

**Urban, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his dearest brother Roger, abbot of the canonry of Saint John, called “of the Vines,” near Soissons, and to the brothers established and to be established there under the rule of blessed Augustine: greeting and apostolic blessing.**

It is fitting that we grant assent to just desires and lend an ear to just petitions, since, although unworthy, we have been appointed by divine dispensation as heralds and guardians of justice on the lofty watchtower of the apostles Peter and Paul.

Therefore, since, inspired by the Lord [Col. 0295C], you have chosen the said canonry according to the rule of blessed Augustine, we rejoice with due devotion in your good and praiseworthy resolve. So that praiseworthy beginnings may be followed by even more praiseworthy growth, we receive you with paternal affection, as our dearest sons, together with all your dependencies, under the protection of the apostolic see, and we fortify you by the privilege of our document.

First, we establish that the canonical institutions of your order shall be observed inviolably in your church for all time, according to God and the rule of blessed Augustine.

Furthermore, whatever possessions and goods you may acquire in the future, whether through the generosity of kings and bishops or through the offerings of the faithful [Col. 0295D]—without prejudice to the due reverence owed to the diocesan bishops—shall remain whole and inviolate for you and for your possessors.

We further add and forbid that any secular priest be appointed in your parish churches unless he has been presented by your abbot, with the consent of your chapter, to the diocesan bishop. You may ordain canons of your cloister for service in your parish churches.

By the present decree we also establish that no person of ecclesiastical rank may exact anything from you or from the churches belonging to your jurisdiction, apart from synodal dues; and no one may establish a new church or churchyard within the boundaries of your parishes without your consent and that of your bishop.

We also establish that no one may bury parishioners of your churches without the consent of the parish priests, or receive your serfs into the brotherhood without your consent. Nor may anyone receive control of the boundaries of your parishes from a lay or ecclesiastical hand without your consent.

If any land from which a tithe is customarily paid to you should happen to be transferred to another owner, the tithe shall nevertheless be paid to you from it. No one shall presume to exact tithes from your newly cultivated lands, which you work with your own hands or at your own expense [Col. 0296A].

We therefore decree that no one whatsoever may take away your property or harass it with any exactions.

If anyone should presume, by reckless boldness, to violate this privilege of our sanction, we separate him from Christ and from the body of the Church by apostolic authority. But may peace and mercy from the Lord be preserved for those who uphold it. Amen, amen, amen.

Given at Rome through the hands of John, cardinal deacon of the holy Roman Church and prosignator, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1089, indiction XII, on the third day before the Ides of January, in the first year of the pontificate of the lord Urban.

## XIII. Urban II grants a bull to the monastery of Saint-Victor of Marseille. (1089)

[See Mabillon and Ruinart, *Posthumous Works*, III, 51.]

[Col. 0296C]

## XIV. Letter of Urban II to Geoffrey, bishop of Constance. He orders a fugitive from the monastery of Schaffhausen to be recalled for the third time and delivers him, for refusing obedience, to anathema. (1089)

[Mansi, *Councils*, XX, 707.]

**Urban, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved brother and fellow bishop Geoffrey of Constance: greeting and apostolic blessing.**

Our beloved son N. has complained to us [Col. 0296D] that a certain man named N., after offering himself and all that he possessed upon the altar of the Lord Savior and of all the saints at Schaffhausen, presumed, by apostatizing at the instigation of the devil, to separate himself and his possessions from that same monastery.

We therefore wish and enjoin upon your charity that, according to evangelical authority, you admonish this man canonically for the second and third time to return. If, however, which God forbid, he persists in his wickedness, since you have at hand the sword with which to punish every disobedience as your office requires, do not delay unsheathing the sword of excommunication against him [Col. 0297A], so that, if he remains incorrigible, the others may be afraid.

We commend to you, as a faithful son, the labors and hardships of the universal mother, the Roman Church. Given at Rome on 10 April.

## XV. Letter of Urban II, written from the Roman synod, to Gebhard, bishop of Constance, constituting and confirming him as apostolic legate and overseer of the Churches in Saxony and Alemannia. (1089)

[Mansi, *Councils*, XX, 715.—Taken from Vatican Codex 382 by Schannat, from which Harthzeim, *German Councils*, III, p. 210.]

[Col. 0297B]

**Urban, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Gebhard, bishop of Constance: greeting and apostolic blessing.**

Because we recognize that, after the Lord, you are a particular work of our hands, and because we know that a special grace of religion is in you, we strive, with the Lord’s assent, to assist you and to provide particular help for your needs. You should know that the questions which you have reported in your letters as being debated in your regions are also frequently raised among us.

Therefore, after consulting the brethren and having long considered the question of excommunication, we confirmed the judgment of our holy predecessor Gregory and, with the Lord’s inspiration, determined it as follows.

First, we judge that the arch-heretic of Ravenna, the invader of the Roman Church, together with King Henry, the head of that same perversity, is alienated from and excommunicated by all the members of the Catholic Church.

Second, those who provide assistance to their wickedness by arms, money, counsel, or obedience—especially by accepting ecclesiastical orders or honors from them or their supporters: these we bind principally with the bond of anathema.

Third, we have not ourselves excommunicated those who communicate with them; but because they defile themselves by that communion, we do not receive them into our fellowship without the penalty of penance and absolution. For it is established by the holy canons that whoever communicates with excommunicated persons is to be excommunicated.

We have nevertheless distinguished the forms of their penance and absolution with such moderation that whoever, through ignorance, fear, or the necessity of some especially important business, has defiled himself by their company, greeting, prayer, or kiss may share in our fellowship through the remedy of a lesser penance and absolution.

But those who have fallen into this voluntarily or negligently we wish to receive under such disciplinary restraint as will instill fear in the others. The administration of this discipline, insofar as it belongs to your care, we entrust to your judgment, to be observed according to circumstances and the suitability of the persons, as you deem appropriate.

Fourth. Concerning clerics ordained by excommunicated bishops, we have not yet fixed a judgment, because the contagion of a general evil must be burned away by the cautery of a general synod.

For the present, however, we respond to your fatherly concern as follows: those ordained by bishops who were then excommunicated but had formerly been Catholic may remain in the orders they received, provided that they did not receive those orders simoniacally and that it is established that the bishops themselves were not simoniacal; and provided also that their more religious life and distinguished learning appear to merit it.

After imposing whatever penance you judge appropriate, we do not permit them to ascend to higher orders unless the greatest necessity and utility demand it, and their holy conduct recommends it. Even then, this should be granted only rarely [Col. 0298B] and with the greatest caution.

Fifth. Concerning priests, deacons, and subdeacons who, after receiving their order, have fallen into some crime, whether openly or secretly: it is indeed established by the judgment of the canons that they are to be barred from ecclesiastical offices.

Nevertheless, we entrust to your discretion and prudence whether some who have not been marked by the stigma of infamy should, when the necessity of the Church requires it and their holy conduct merits it, be restored to their former ranks.

I say this by way of indulgence, not command, so that your authority in your regions may be greater against the heretics, while the authority of the canons and the decretal regulations of the holy Fathers remains intact.

If anyone, God forbid, whether after receiving office or before receiving it [Col. 0298C], should be found guilty of a capital crime, whether secretly or openly, we remove such persons—especially those who still live according to the world—from every ministry at the altar.

Sixth. It is certainly established that the island of Reichenau is specially included under the jurisdiction of Blessed Peter and the Roman Church. But since we do not sufficiently remember the privilege which they hold from the Roman Church, we cannot easily determine the matter.

Nevertheless, without prejudice to the authority of that privilege, we grant you alone all episcopal governing power over the clergy and people living there, except the monks. We command your obedience also to ensure that you regularly appoint a Catholic abbot there in our place.

Not only there, but also in the monastery of Saint Gall [Col. 0298D], and in any others that may be without their own abbots, rely on our authority and, with the counsel of those whom you know to be concerned, take care to elect abbots and consecrate those elected.

We likewise enjoin upon you to attend to the bishoprics of Augsburg and Chur, and also to the others to which the bishop of Passau cannot be summoned or cannot be present.

Seventh. We have also entrusted to him, as to you, oversight in our place of Saxony, Alemannia, and the other neighboring regions, so that you may reject ordinations that ought to be rejected, strengthen those that ought to be strengthened, and, after consulting religious men, arrange whatever ecclesiastical business must be arranged, until, with the Lord’s consent, you are able to receive a legate of the apostolic see [Col. 0299A].

You who burn with zeal for God and excel in knowledge and learning must devote yourselves with every care and diligence to ecclesiastical interests, knowing that we too will gladly assent to those interests of yours. Do not in any way be slow to share the labors of the Roman Church and to relieve them through the aid of your assistance.

May almighty God pour over you the abundance of His blessings, preserve you unharmed, and bring you to eternal life.

Given at Rome on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of May, in the year of the Incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ 1089.

## XVI. Letter of Pope Urban II to the bishops of Germany. He indicates whom they are to regard as excommunicated. (1089)

[Mansi, *Councils*, XX, 719.]

[Col. 0299B]

**Urban, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the bishops of Germany established in the unity of the Church: greeting and apostolic blessing.**

After consulting the brethren and having long considered the question of excommunication, we confirmed the judgment of our holy predecessor Gregory and, with the Lord’s inspiration, determined it as follows.

First, we judge that the arch-heretic of Ravenna, the invader of the Roman Church, together with the head of that same perversity, is alienated from and excommunicated by all the members of the Catholic Church.

Second, those who provide assistance to their wickedness by arms, money, counsel, or obedience—especially by accepting ecclesiastical orders or honors from them or their supporters [Col. 0299C]: these we bind principally with the bonds of anathema.

Third, we do not ourselves excommunicate those who communicate with them; but because they defile themselves by that communion, we do not receive them into our fellowship without the penalty of penance and absolution. For it is established by the holy canons that whoever communicates with excommunicated persons is to be excommunicated.

Nevertheless, we have distinguished the forms of their penance and absolution with such moderation that whoever, through ignorance, fear, or the necessity of some very important and especially necessary business, has defiled himself by their company, greeting, prayer, or kiss may share in our fellowship through the remedy of a lesser penance and absolution [Col. 0299D].

But those who have fallen into this voluntarily or negligently we do not wish to receive except under such disciplinary restraint as will instill fear in the others.

## XVII. Bull of Pope Urban II for the Augustinian canons regular established by Bishop Berengar in the monastery of Saint John of Ripoll. (1089)

[Flórez, *Sacred Spain*, vol. XXVIII, p. 292, from the cartulary of Saint John of Ripoll.]

**Urban, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his dearest brother Berengar, bishop of Ausona, and to the future superiors after him in the abbey of Saint John of Ripoll, forever.**
[Col. 0300A] It is fitting that we heed just petitions and grant assent to just requests, since, by the Lord’s authority, although unworthy, we have been set as heralds upon the lofty watchtower of the chief apostles, Peter and Paul. Therefore, dearest brother, because, with God inspiring you, you rescued the abbey of Saint John beside the river Ter and the river of Rivipoll from secular domination and established canons there according to the Rule of Saint Augustine, we, taking thought for the growth of their religious profession, willingly assent to your petition and have received that same church under the special protection and guardianship of the Apostolic See. Count Bernard of Besalú, having been stripped of his power through the security he had offered and having also bestowed that church through his own generosity, surrendered it to the Lord into your hands, [Col. 0300B] while you, for the aforesaid canons, assigned it to the practice of holy life and enriched it by the grant of your own estates. Therefore, so long as they and their successors preserve the path of religion according to apostolic discipline, we confirm the aforesaid church to them in honor of the Apostolic See and exclude from it all secular domination, decreeing by the power of the Holy Spirit and the authority of the apostles Peter and Paul that everything which today it possesses through your grant, or through the donation of the aforesaid count, or through the offering of other faithful persons, and whatever it may justly be able to acquire in the future, with the Lord’s generosity, shall remain entire and inviolate for them.

But those who knowingly retain goods belonging to that place, after learning the contents of this present privilege, if, after being warned a second or third time, they do not restore them within forty days or make suitable satisfaction by agreement, we restrain from the thresholds of the churches. You, therefore, venerable brother B., who … have been recognized as having enriched that same church through your diligence … and also through your gifts, shall, in our place, provide them with patronage and lordship throughout your lifetime. After your death, no one shall be appointed abbot over them except one whom they themselves, by common consent—or the more distinguished part of them—shall have chosen, in honor of the Apostolic See and with the consent of Bernard, count of Besalú, according to the fear of God; yet the canonical reverence due to the bishops of Ausona shall remain, so long as they treat the aforesaid abbey benevolently.

Therefore, dearest sons, you ought fervently to pursue the path of the regular order, so that, the freer you are from secular disturbances, the more diligently you may devote yourselves to divine service. As a sign of the liberty received from the Roman Church, it is fitting that you pay three mancuses of Valencian coin each year to the Lateran palace and observe more carefully the decrees of the Roman pontiffs.

But if, in the future, any archbishop, bishop, king, prince, duke, marquis, count, viscount, or any person whatsoever, great or small, powerful or powerless, knowingly presumes to infringe or rashly violate this privilege of our decree, and attempts to overturn the order established for the aforesaid abbey, or to invade, harass, or wickedly apply its goods to his own uses, then, after being warned a second or third time, if he does not correct the matter by suitable satisfaction, we separate him from the body of Christ and the Church by apostolic authority. May peace from God and reward be preserved for those who preserve this privilege, both in the present and in future ages. Amen. Amen. Amen.

Given at Rome through the hands of John, cardinal deacon and pro-signatory of the Lord Pope Urban II, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1089, indiction XII, on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of June, in the pontificate of the same Lord Urban II.

The following is read at the end.

At the council held at Toulouse, attended by twenty bishops and numerous abbots, Rainerius, cardinal and legate of the Holy Roman Church, and Amatus, archbishop and legate of Pope Urban, together with the other [Col. 0301B] bishops, adjudicated the matter and complaints which the clerics of Saint John had brought before them concerning Richard, the abbot, and his Marseilles monks: namely, that Richard and his monks should restore to blessed John and to those clerics all the estates, possessions, ornaments, and other movable goods which they had taken, given away, or caused to be given away while they held the church of Saint John, and which they had consigned to robbers.

And further:

Rainerius, cardinal of the Holy Roman Church and its legate, to the venerable bishops B. of Girona, B. of Ausona, B. of Urgell, A. of Elne, and B. of Barcelona, greetings. We wish it to be known to your dignity that the clerics of blessed John of Rivipoll have lodged a complaint [Col. 0301C] at the Council of Toulouse concerning your parishioners, who, setting aside all reverence, take away churches and certain ecclesiastical estates from blessed John. Therefore we admonish you, and by apostolic authority command you, to warn them to desist from this robbery and to compel them by preaching and excommunication to restore to blessed John what belongs to his right. If they are unwilling, let them know that they are excommunicated and expelled from all Christian communion by the authority of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul, of the most reverend Pope Urban, and of the entire assembly of the Council of Toulouse, until they repent and abandon what they have seized. We likewise command you, by the authority of the Holy Roman Church, to excommunicate them until they render worthy satisfaction.

### XVIII. Privilege of Pope Urban II for the monastery of Jesus Nazarene. (Year 1089.)

[AYNSAY, *Foundation, excellences, grandeur, and memorable matters of Huesca*. Huesca, 1619, folio 1, p. 454.]

[Col. 0301D]

Urban, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his dearest sons in Christ, the regular brothers of the church called Jesus Nazarene, and to their successors who shall live according to the rule, forever.

A just petition of the faithful ought to be completed with the fulfillment it seeks, so that the holy devotion of those who labor in the Church may shine forth and ecclesiastical usefulness may continually advance, with the Lord always granting increase. Therefore, because our dearest son in Christ, the holy king of Aragon, or of Pamplona, requested that your church, built by him in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ Nazarene, be specially received under the protection of the Roman Church, etc.

And the said bull continues; among the favorable clauses it contains for this house are the following:

“For we establish and by apostolic authority decree that you shall remain free from the yoke of absolutely every human being, whatever his order, and subject only to the holy and apostolic Roman Church, so that you may serve Almighty God tranquilly and peacefully,” etc.

“We confirm,” etc., “everything which that king, or any of the faithful, has granted to you from his possessions, or which any of the bishops have granted from their own right, and whatever in the future, with the Lord’s assent, you may justly and lawfully acquire,” etc.

“Moreover, let no bishop be permitted to excommunicate the brothers of that church, whom we have specially chosen as sons of the Roman Church, or to place them under an interdict from divine worship. Rather, under the sole protection and judgment of the Apostolic See, let them remain free and secure, with the Lord’s assent,” etc.

This bull concludes with these words:

“Therefore, if any archbishop, bishop, emperor, king, prince, duke, marquis, count, viscount, judge, castald (steward), or any person whatsoever, great or small, powerful or powerless, should knowingly presume in the future to act rashly against the sanction of this privilege of ours, and should attempt to invade, harass, or apply to his own uses the goods of that church, then, after being warned a second or third time, if he does not correct the matter by suitable satisfaction, we separate him from the body of Christ and the Church by the power of apostolic authority, and decree that he shall be subject to the penalty of forfeiting his honor. But may peace from God and mercy be preserved for those who preserve it, both in the present and in future ages. Amen, amen, amen.”

Given at Rome on the Kalends of July through the hands of John, cardinal deacon of the Holy Roman Church and pro-signatory of Lord Pope Urban II; in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1089, indiction XII, in the second year of the pontificate of the same Lord Pope Urban.

### XIX. Urban II grants a privilege to Frotard, abbot of Saint-Pons-de-Thomières, by which he exempts the place from the jurisdiction of every bishop and adorns it with several other prerogatives. (Year 1089.)

[RUINART, *Life of Urban*, in MABILLON and RUINART, *Posthumous Works*, III, 57.]

[Col. 0302D]

### XX. Letter of Pope Urban II to the nobles of the province of Tarragona concerning the restoration of the church of Tarragona. (Year 1089.)

[MANSI, *Councils*, XX, 701, from the chartulary of the church of Tarragona.]

Urban, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his dearest sons, Bernard, count and marquis of Barcelona; Ermengald, count of Urgell; Bernard, count of Besalú; and to all the bishops, viscounts, [Col. 0303A] and other nobles and powerful persons of the provinces of Tarragona and Barcelona, whether clerics or laymen, greetings and apostolic blessing.

Our dearest and most reverend brother, Berengar, bishop of Ausona, came to the threshold of the apostles with great devotion and labor and remained with us for a long time. Delighted, as was fitting, by his wisdom and good character, we carefully examined the privileges by which his church—namely, the church of Tarragona—has been granted to the Roman Church. For our part, both out of reverence for the saints and out of affection for the aforesaid brother, we desire to honor and exalt that church as justice requires.

Therefore, since it is fitting that bodily things serve spiritual things, temporal things eternal things, and earthly things heavenly things, we exhort and beseech your prudence in the Lord to strive with all your strength to restore the condition of the city of Tarragona to such an extent that an episcopal see may be maintained there. We therefore command you, for the penance and remission of your sins, to labor with the utmost devotion and zeal, using your power and wealth for the restoration of that church.

To those who are about to go to Jerusalem or to other regions in a spirit of penance or devotion, we recommend that they devote all the labor and expense of that journey to the restoration of the church of Tarragona, so that, with the Lord’s help, an episcopal see may safely be established there and that same city, set against the peoples of the Saracens, may be celebrated as a wall and bulwark of the Christian people. To them we promise, through God’s mercy, the same indulgence they would deserve if they completed the long journey they had undertaken.

If we learn of the fulfillment of your good will and of the concern of your fervent zeal, we shall most willingly grant to our aforesaid brother and to the church of Tarragona whatever pertains to its ancient dignity, and shall follow your bodily offerings with spiritual honors, without prejudice, however, to the rights of the church of Narbonne. For if the bishop of Narbonne is unable canonically to vindicate the province of Tarragona by the authority of his privilege, we shall not fail, free from every complaint, to restore its right to the church of Tarragona and to confer the dignity of the pallium upon our brother Berengar, insofar as we see that your efforts deserve it.

Again and again, dearest sons, we admonish you to assist our brother Berengar in restoring the church of Tarragona, so that you may receive glory in the present and eternal life in the future. Moreover, if our legate reaches you, with the Lord’s assent, take care to show him the obedience due for the sake of the Apostolic See.

Given at Rome on the Kalends of July through the hands of John, cardinal deacon and chancellor of the Holy Roman Church, in the second year of Lord Pope Urban II; indiction XII.

### XXI. Urban II grants a bull to the monastery of Saints Anianus and Laurence. (Year 1089.)

[In the Vatican registers. V. PERTZ, *Archive* VII, 21.]

### XXII. Privilege of Urban II for the clerics and laymen of Velletri. (Year 1089.)

[BORGIA, *History of the Church and City of Velletri*, Nocera, 1723, quarto, p. 204.]

[Col. 0304A]

Urban, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to all the clerics and laymen of Velletri faithful to blessed Peter, greetings and apostolic blessing.

We know, dearest brothers, that it is not unknown to you with what savage cruelty Guilbert the heresiarch, invader of the Apostolic See and ancient enemy, in our times, through the apostates and tyrants of the holy Church—Hugh the White and John of Porto, antipope bishops, and Peter, once chancellor, Uvezelo, and the tyrant Otto, limbs of the devil—has led astray the sons of God, thinking that by flatteries and brutality he could subject them to his feet. But trusting in him who does not despise his own, we shall steadfastly restrain their assault through you and our other sons.

Therefore, at present, we send to you our beloved Rainerius the priest, our steward Formosus, and our messenger Fornix, with these written instructions. From them, as from us, you will hear what battles our faithful are bravely waging and how we have resolved to hasten beyond the mountains for the benefit of Christ’s bride.

Since, therefore, for the Church you have endured mockeries, blows, chains, prisons … [the parchment is here torn and damaged], and various deaths, we, by apostolic authority and with the confirmation of the bishops and Roman nobles, having completely removed from you all things that can in any way prove an impediment, [Col. 0304C] confirm to you forever all your usages and the longstanding customs introduced among you by anyone.

Let it be permitted to you to make an agreement with your bishops and, without an obligation of words, to render to your bishops or to those ordained by them, on behalf of the Apostolic See: namely, a third part of wills; a third part of bread offerings alone; wax from three Masses; and a fourth part of tithes. If your church lacks its own bishop, let the right of the bishop belong to the church and accrue to the clerics.

We grant you the city’s viaticum and alms specially assigned to you. Provided that you clerics, together with the bishop, as you are accustomed and as you have arranged with me, pay to our court the modest expense of one meal, while you laymen collectively provide us with the expense of another meal, and military service and parliament: military service by the maritime route and through Campania.

Moreover, we confirm that, without any contradiction, you may possess cultivated and uncultivated lands, forests, mountains, hills, plains, marshes, and everything contained in the ancient privileges of your city known to us. May you remain forever in quiet, peace, and possession of your right.

But whoever, God forbid, should become a violator of this edict of ours, or should attempt to impose upon it any condition of any kind, shall be bound by the bond of anathema. Whoever, however, guards and observes it shall obtain the grace of blessing and, when Peter the key-bearer, whose vicars we are, opens the way, shall ascend to the height of heaven.

[Col. 0305A] Written by the hand of Girard, scrivener of the Holy Roman Church, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1089, indiction XII.

+ I, Peter, by the grace of God bishop of Albano, was present and subscribed.

+ I, Minutus, by the grace of God bishop of Lavicanum.

+ I, Bruno, bishop of Segni, have given assent through this triangle.

[Col. 0305B] Given at Rome on the eighth day before the Ides of July through the hands of John, cardinal and chancellor of the Holy Roman Church.

### XXIII. Letter of Urban II to Anselm, abbot of Bec.—That he should assist a bishop inexperienced in ecclesiastical affairs; that he should not delay visiting the Apostolic See; and that he should send to it what Hubert, his subdeacon and legate, had collected from the census of blessed Peter. (Year 1089.)

[*Works of Saint Anselm*, p. 353.]

Urban, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Anselm, venerable and dearest abbot, greetings and apostolic blessing.

Knowing the distinction of your religious commitment and learning, we have made allowances for what seemed unjust in the ordination of the bishop of Beauvais, and, trusting in the zeal of your diligence, we imposed upon him the care of the bishopric against his will and resistance. Now, therefore, we commend him to you especially, so that in all things you may assist him, admonish him, correct him, and advise him as your son; and, whenever you yourself cannot be present, you shall order one of your brothers—one who is solicitous for him with spiritual zeal—to be present with him, so that whatever appears less canonical in his beginnings may, through good progress thereafter, be brought to useful effect.

If we command anything to you, whether through that bishop of Beauvais or through our son Roger, concerning the service of the Holy Roman Church, you shall execute it, as befits such a man, promptly and with the greatest readiness.

We wished to retain with us your monk John, a son of our Church. A complaint by the Roman Church against you remains concerning this matter, because you presumed to make one of its clerics a monk and to advance him to higher orders. Nevertheless, yielding to the prayers of the bishop of Beauvais, we send him back to you under this condition: before a year has elapsed from the present Lent, you must either send him back to us or come yourself and bring him with you, together with any other member of your congregation whom you know to be useful to us.

Moreover, do not delay visiting the Apostolic See as soon as you can, so that we may enjoy the presence of our mutual affection with the devotion that is due.

If any possessions of our subdeacon Hubert, who is said to have died among you, have been left with you, send them to us as soon as possible. For when he received a legation from our predecessor of holy memory, Gregory, in the kingdom of the English, he is said to have collected much from the census of blessed Peter. If these things are with you, we wish them to be sent to us promptly, so that they may benefit the needs of the Holy Church.

Given at Capua on the Kalends of August.

### XXIV. Letter of Urban II to Pibo, bishop of Toul. (Year 1089.)

[MANSI, *Councils*, XX, 676.]

Urban, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved brother Pibo, bishop of Toul, greetings and apostolic blessing.

Concerning the questions which Adalbero, a son of your Church, brought to us, these chapters have been confirmed by us, with the synodal assent of the council, through the grace of God.

[Col. 0306B]

**Chapter I.** The bishop shall distribute all the offices of his bishopric—namely, archdeaconries, archpriesthoods, deaneries, and any canonical provostships of his church—freely and without any sale. Whoever gives them for a price shall be subject to deposition.

**Chapter II.** We remove from every sacred order those who, from the subdiaconate onward, have devoted themselves to wives, and we decree that they shall lack both ecclesiastical office and benefice. If bishops have consented to their misconduct, they shall know that they are forbidden to exercise their own offices.

**Chapter III.** *(D. LVI, “Of priests.”)* We decree that the sons of priests are to be removed from the ministries of the sacred altar, unless they have been religiously approved through life in monasteries or among canons. Without prejudice, however, to these chapters, we permit those who either purchased prebends before this prohibition of the Apostolic See, or unknowingly possess prebends that had been purchased, to retain them, if in your judgment their persons appear worthy of them.

But to those who, invalidating the security of their possession, have presumed, after receiving the subdiaconate, to devote themselves to wives, we entirely forbid both office and marriage. Since by apostatizing they have destroyed themselves and preferred bodily pleasure to the Lord, we decree that penance be imposed upon them throughout their entire lives, either in monasteries or among regular canons.

The sons of priests who, in accordance with the condition of our command, have been religiously approved through life either in monasteries or among canons, because they have renounced their fathers’ sins together with their worldly possessions [or: “the possessions of the world”], we judge, in view of the distinction of their religion and learning, that they may be tolerated by apostolic moderation and permitted to advance to sacred orders and ecclesiastical honors.

**Chapter IV.** Concerning clerics ordained by excommunicated bishops, we have not yet fixed a judgment, because the contagion of a general evil must be burned away by the cautery of a general synod. For the present, however, we answer your fraternity as follows: those ordained by bishops who were once Catholic but excommunicated—provided that they did not receive those orders through simony, that it has been established that those bishops were not simoniacs, and, further, that their more religious life and distinction of teaching appear to make them worthy—may, after the penance you judge suitable has been imposed, remain in the orders they received. We do not permit them to ascend to higher orders unless the greatest necessity or usefulness of the Church demands it. Even this, however, must be granted more rarely and with the greatest caution.

**Chapter V.** We decree that bishops and clerics who are known to be simoniacs must be entirely removed from sacred offices and benefices. Churches polluted by such simoniacs are to be prayed in only as though they were ordinary places, until, after the altars have been overturned, they are consecrated by the blessing and anointing of a Catholic bishop.

[Col. 0307B]

**Chapter VI.** Concerning those ordained without titles: although such ordination is judged contrary to the sanction of the holy canons, we leave it to your discretion, in view of the present need of the Church, whether some of them may be permitted to remain in the orders they have received, provided that it is otherwise established that they were ordained without misconduct.

**Chapter VII.** In accordance with the common custom of the Church, we separate bigamists and husbands of widows from the sacred orders by the authority of our office. Your religious zeal shall preserve all these matters, as apostolic precepts consonant with the judgments of the holy councils, in the Church entrusted to it, with God’s help, and shall make them known to others for preservation.

Nor should the multitude of barking dogs frighten your old age. For greater is he who is in us than he who is in them. Indeed, while strengthening his disciples, he said: “Do not be afraid, little flock, because it has pleased your Father to give you the kingdom.” May he himself, in his mercy, strengthen and protect us and lead us to the heavenly kingdoms. Amen.

### XXV. Urban II confirms the possessions of the monastery of Cava. (Year 1089.)

[DOM RUINART, *Life of Urban II*. MABILLON and RUINART, *Posthumous Works*, III, 65.]

### XXVI. Letter of Urban II to Elias, bishop of Bari.—Concerning the translation of the relics of Saint Nicholas and the dignity and rights of the church of Bari. (Year 1089.)

[MANSI, *Councils*, XX, 645.]

[Col. 0307D]

Urban, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his dearest brother Elias, archbishop, greetings and apostolic blessing.

Because in our times Almighty God has deigned to visit the church of Bari—which, by God’s authority, you govern, dearest brother, and which is also called Canosa—with the body of his blessed confessor Nicholas, we, by God’s authority, as vicars of the apostles Peter and Paul, descending into the province of Apulia to carry out ecclesiastical business, were invited by the prayers of our dearest sons of the Roman Church, Duke Roger and his brother Bohemond, and by your prayers. Out of our special devotion to blessed Nicholas, we visited your city.

With a great multitude of people gathered from every direction and rejoicing as we brought the relics of blessed Nicholas into the place prepared as a shrine, we consecrated you, dearest brother, in your own see, contrary to the custom of our Roman and Apostolic Church, overcome by reverence for blessed Nicholas and affection for your people.
