Embracing you as a special son of the Roman Church in the arms of our deepest love, and desiring, with the Lord’s generosity and justice’s favor, to exalt your church of Bari—which is also regarded as the church of Canosa—and to glorify your people both temporally and eternally, we confirm to you by the authority of this document the entire archbishopric of Bari, which is also that of Canosa, so that you and your successors may govern, administer, and possess it by episcopal right, without prejudice to the authority of the Roman Church, which, by the Lord’s institution, is the prince of all churches and to which, as to a mother, the highest reverence must be offered by all.

Therefore, without prejudice to the justice of any churches, following the tenor contained in the privileges of our predecessors, we grant to you and your successors, to possess and govern forever, the possessions or dioceses of the church of Bari or Canosa. These are: Canosa, Bitetto, Bitonto, Modugno, Giovinazzo, Molfetta, Ruvo, Trani, Canne, Minervino, Acquaviva, Montemilone, Lavello, Rapolla, Melfi, Bitalbis, Salpicupersanum, Palimarum, and likewise [Col. 0308C] the other places known to lie within the coastal region.

We also confirm to you these and other municipalities, whether cities adjacent to the aforesaid cities or situated far away but belonging to them, and all estates and farmsteads together with houses and vineyards, male and female servants, farms and farmsteads, mills, ports, mountains and meadows, together with parishes or churches and all their titular churches or chapels, and likewise monasteries of men or women, Greek or Latin, with all ecclesiastical orders; and whatever honor, possession, or dignity it had held through lawful donation and according to ancient grant; and whatever does not contradict justice and is shown to have been added from ancient times; and whatever in the future the church of Bari and Canosa may justly acquire.

Granting such privileges by the present decree of our authority, we establish that no king or emperor, bishop, person endowed with any dignity, or anyone else shall dare to diminish, alienate, or apply to his own uses anything that has already been donated to that church by any people from their own right, or that may henceforth, with the Lord’s favor, happen to be donated.

Moreover, we grant your fraternity the use of the pallium according to custom, so that you may use it during the solemn celebration of Mass only on these feasts: the Nativity of the Lord, Saint Stephen, the Epiphany, the Lord’s Supper, the Resurrection, the Ascension, Pentecost, the Nativity of Saint John the Baptist, the feasts of the apostles, [Col. 0309A] the three feasts of Saint Mary, the feasts of Saints Nicholas and Sabinus, the feast of All Saints, the anniversary of the day of your ordination, the ordination of bishops or other clerics, the consecration of churches, and also the translation of the Lord’s confessor Nicholas.

We therefore exhort your fraternity that the honor of so great a dignity, which is the adornment of the entire priestly order, should correspond to your character. Let it provide beauty and grace not only to your outward person but also strengthen your inner person with manifold virtue. For these are the obligations of the pallium, these the obligations of such a garment: that you love God with your whole heart, your whole soul, and all your strength, and your neighbor as yourself.

Although the adornment of all virtues is necessary for the use of the pallium, charity, which surpasses all things, ought nevertheless to accompany inseparably the person endowed with this dignity. Therefore, let your life and knowledge, as examples of all good things, be a model and rule for your subjects, so that, if anything blameworthy is found in them through human weakness, it may be corrected toward uprightness by consideration of your conduct and your sincerity.

Strive to regulate the rights of your administration in such a way that you burn with zeal for rectitude in correcting vices, yet do not exceed the measure of moderation. And, to express much in few words, whatever you read repeatedly in the sayings of the holy Fathers, judge it useful for the edification of yourself and of those subject to you, so that, instructed by your teaching and following the footsteps of the good shepherd, they may reach with you the kingdom of the supreme Shepherd and, with God’s assent, receive the happiness of eternal life. Amen.

The seal is immediately appended to this.

Given at Bari through the hands of John the deacon, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1089, in the second year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Urban II, indiction XIII, on the ninth of October.

### XXVII. Letter of Urban II to Rainald, archbishop of Reims.—He grants him the pallium and asserts the primacy of the whole province of Second Belgica and the right to consecrate the kings of the Franks. (Year 1089.)

[MABILLON and RUINART, *Posthumous Works*, III, 352.]

Urban, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Rainald, his dearest brother, archbishop of Reims, [Col. 0309D] and to his legitimate successors forever.

The Church acknowledges that the power of binding and loosing in heaven and on earth was principally entrusted by God to blessed Peter and his successors in the words with which the Lord addressed Peter: “Whatever you bind on earth will be bound in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth will be loosed in heaven” (Matthew 18:18). By the authority of the same God, his own steadfastness and the confirmation of another’s faith are likewise granted to him, when it is said: “I have prayed for you that your faith may not fail, Peter; and you, once converted, strengthen your brethren” (Luke 22:32). Therefore we, who, although unworthy, sit in Peter’s place, ought to correct what is wrong, strengthen what is right, and in the whole Church so arrange what must be arranged according to the judgment of the internal Judge, that our judgment may proceed from his countenance and our eyes may see equity.

Therefore, assenting to the just petitions of your Fraternity, and in accordance with the ancient custom of the Church of Reims, we confirm by the authority and benevolence of the Apostolic See, through the page of this decree, the pallium granted to you; and we judge that you are to be primate of the whole province of Second Belgica, according to the dignity of your predecessors. We further decree that you owe subjection and obedience to no one except the Roman pontiff, and that judgment in every case concerning you is to be determined solely by the decision of the Roman pontiff.

Moreover, we confer upon you and your successors the first and principal authority to consecrate the kings of the Franks: just as blessed Remigius is known to have established the first Christian king in that kingdom when he converted Chlodovech to the faith, so you and your successors, who by the Lord’s disposition exercise in the Church of Reims the office of that same Saint Remigius, shall exercise the primary authority to anoint and ordain the king or queen.

[Note: Philippus of Bec, exhausted by old age, mentions this prerogative of consecrating queens in his letters of apology to Henry the Great, saying that, at eighty-six years of age, he could not attend the coronation of his wife, the queen.]

We further decree and confirm by the authority of this present document that, just as the kings of the Franks first receive the insignia of the diadem through the imposition of your hand, so also, [f. add.: “it is necessary”] in the solemn processions in which those same kings are to be crowned, no other archbishop or bishop shall crown them when you, or any of your Catholic successors, are present.

[Note: Saint Bernard defended this prerogative of the archbishops of Reims when writing to Eugene III, Letter 247. See the fuller notes on this letter, and Marlot, *On the Inaugurations of Kings*.]

Therefore we exhort your affection to repay the favor of the Apostolic See with the subjection that is due, and to observe its decrees inviolably; and we urge you to use every effort to require that they be observed by the peoples of France subject to you. Since we desire, with special devotion, to preserve the whole ancient dignity of your Church, we decree that the entire honor, dignity, and excellence that our predecessor is said to have conferred upon blessed Remigius shall remain with you and your legitimate successors.

[Note: Namely, the vicariate of the Apostolic See, by which, in addition to the primacy, the archbishops of Reims were once, and even now are, called primates throughout Gaul under the title of born legate; for this reason two crosses were formerly carried before them, as is recorded in the ancient Ritual. Urban attributes this grant to Hormisdas, following Hincmar, although it should rather be said to have been conferred by Anastasius. Moreover, lest the kings of the Franks appear less generous toward the see of Remigius than the pontiffs were, they made the archbishop of Reims the first duke and peer of France.]

Accordingly, let your affection, dearest brother Raynold, know that, following the custom of your predecessors, you are to use the pallium only for the celebration of Mass, and only on the appointed days: namely, the Nativity of the Lord, the Circumcision, and the Epiphany; Holy Saturday; the Resurrection and the following Monday; the Ascension; Pentecost; the solemnities of holy Mary, Mother of God and Virgin; the birthdays of John the Baptist and of all the apostles; and the feasts of Saints Nicasius, Remigius, and Martin. You may also use it at the commemoration of All Saints; at the consecration of the chrism, of churches, and of bishops and other clerics; at the blessing of the king and queen; on the anniversary of your consecration; and on the dedication day of the churches of Saint Mary and Saint Remigius.

Since the honor of this garment must be preserved by a modest vitality of conduct, we exhort you to make the adornments of your character correspond to it, so that, by God’s authority, you may rightly be distinguished in both respects. Therefore, dearest brother, whose office binds you to pastoral care, love your brethren; let even adversaries, because of the Lord’s commandment, be joined to you in affection; pursue peace with all; devote yourself to works of piety and holiness, without which no one will see God; abound in virtues; let the breastplate of judgment shine within you, joined with the action of the shoulder-piece.

Proceed thus in the sight of God, and offer an example to the whole flock entrusted to you, so that they may see your good works and glorify our Father who is in heaven. Let speech be on your tongue and the fervor of zeal in your heart. Cultivate the Lord’s field entrusted to you while it is permitted; sow in fear while there is time; do good without growing weary, so that in due season you may reap without failing. Therefore, vigilantly abandoning earthly affairs, yearn for heavenly things; forgetting what lies behind, stretch yourself with greater effort toward what lies ahead. Let your mind not dissolve in worldly vanity, but run and converge toward that one end which David regarded with marvelous sweetness when he said: “One thing I have asked of the Lord; this I will seek: that I may dwell in the house of the Lord all the days of my life” (Psalm 26:4). May the Holy Trinity surround your Fraternity with the protection of its grace and grant you to reach the end that has no end.

Given at Rome by the hand of John, cardinal deacon of the holy Roman Church, in the year of the Incarnation of the Lord 1089, in the thirteenth indiction, on the eighth day before the Kalends of January, in the second year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Urban II.

### XXVIII. Urban II confirms the possessions of the monastery of Balma in the Sequani region, at the request of Hugh, archbishop of Besançon. (Year 1089.)

[Mabillon and Ruinart, *Posthumous Works*, III, 355.]

URBAN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his dearest son Hugh, abbot of Balma, and to his legitimate successors forever.

The Church acknowledges that the power of binding and loosing in heaven and on earth was principally entrusted by God to blessed Peter and his successors in the words with which the Lord addressed him: “Whatever you bind on earth will be bound in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth will be loosed in heaven” (Matthew 18:18). By the authority of the same God, his own steadfastness and the confirmation of another’s faith are likewise granted to him, when it is said: “I have prayed for you that your faith may not fail, Peter; and you, once converted, strengthen your brethren” (Luke 22:32). Therefore we, who, although unworthy, sit in Peter’s place, ought to correct what is wrong, strengthen what is right, and in the whole Church so arrange what must be arranged according to the judgment of the internal Judge, that our judgment may proceed from his countenance and his eyes may see equity.

Therefore, assenting to the pious petitions of you, dearest son Hugh, and of Hugh, archbishop of Besançon, we confirm by the page of this decree the monastery of Balma for you and your legitimate successors to govern and administer, together with all the properties belonging to that monastery, both monasteries and churches.

[Note: This is the celebrated monastery that was later made subject to its daughter Cluny, on account of Saint Berno, abbot of that place, who migrated thence and became the first abbot of Cluny and the teacher of Saint Odo. It still survives in the county of Burgundy; see the *Bibliotheca Cluniacensis*.]

Namely: the monastery of Saint Mary of Grand-Fontaine with all its dependencies; the monastery of Saint Peter of Gaude with all its dependencies; the monastery of Saint Mary within the city of Besançon, called Jusanum, with its dependencies;

[Note: Saint Donatus, bishop of Besançon, at the beginning of the seventh century gave the monastery of Jussanum a rule drawn almost wholly from the Benedictine Rule. This place has now passed to the Minims.]

the monastery of Saint Eugendus of Ética with all its dependencies; the monastery of Saint Lautenus with all its dependencies; the church of Saint John of Balma with the chapel of Francet; the church of Saint Gervasius of Victor with its dependencies; the church of Saint Nicholas of Carnet; the church of Laviniacum; Mont Huin, Caveriacum, Cavaniacum, Brariacum with their dependencies; the churches of Saint Desideratus, Laedo, Sisintiacum, Laracnum, and Desna with their dependencies; the church of Dumbles with its dependencies; the churches of Guars, Mont-Tolosa, Asna, Mont-Alacer, and Nebla Castle with their dependencies; the churches of Sarmacia, Sabonaria, Olaefracta, Costumna, Mulnet, Ver, Biviliacum, Saint Maurice and Saint Germanus of Grava, Baia, Bellimont, Mont Roolenus, Esicon, Rancinacum, Gelerengis, and Beneventum with all their dependencies; the churches of Bella-Vavra and Ciensisville with the chapel of the Castle, Saint Renebert, Saint Stephen of the Bridge, Don-Peter of Arlico, and Wistruciacum, with their dependencies; the church of Poloniacum, with the chapels of Castle Mariacum, Platana, and Saint Sabinus, and with all its dependencies; and the churches of Aquae, Solciacum, and Spincta with their dependencies.

Furthermore, by the page of this present privilege, we decree by apostolic authority that whatever the same monastery now possesses, or may hereafter legitimately acquire through the generosity of princes, the grant of pontiffs, or the offerings of the faithful, shall remain secure and inviolate for you and your successors. Therefore we decree that no person at all may rashly disturb the monastery, remove or diminish the possessions subject to it, or burden them with reckless harassment; rather, everything shall be preserved intact, for the benefit of those whose support they were granted to provide, without prejudice to the canonical reverence owed to the archbishop of Besançon.

If, in the future, any archbishop or bishop, emperor or king, prince or duke, count or judge, or any person whatsoever, great or small, powerful or powerless, knowingly attempts to act against this page of our privilege, and, after being warned a second or third time, does not make amends by suitable satisfaction, we separate him from the body of Christ and the Church by the authority of apostolic power. But may peace from God and mercy be preserved in the present and future ages for those who maintain it.

I, Urban, bishop of the Catholic Church.

Given at Rome on the fifth day before the Kalends of January, by the hand of John, cardinal deacon of the Holy Roman Church, in the year of the Incarnation of the Lord 1088, in the second year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Urban II.

### XXIX. Letter of Urban II to Rainerius, cardinal priest. — He gives many instructions concerning Spanish affairs. (Year 1089.)

[Mansi, *Councils*, XIX, 698.]

You yourself, dearest brother, recognize how much confidence we placed in your religion, and with what faith and charity we sent you back to those regions. Act, therefore, in accordance with the hope we have in your prudence, and, with the Lord’s help, strive to define canonically every matter you can, especially those concerning which you were sent—namely, the disputes reported between the archbishop of Narbonne and the abbot of Comminges.

For our most reverend brother, the archbishop of Narbonne, whom we have long known to be distinguished in life and religion, came to us with our venerable brother, the bishop of Barcelona, and complained at length against the abbot of Comminges: specifically, that, supported by secular powers, he invades the churches of the archbishop’s diocese; that he receives those excommunicated by the archbishop without any absolution from him; that he caused a bishop to be consecrated in the see of Jaca without the archbishop’s permission; and—horrible to hear—that one who had died under anathema was exhumed by his monks and buried within the monastery.

Among other matters, he humbly reported that he had suffered prejudice through the removal of the bishops of Tarragona by the Roman Church, since [the text reads: “when it had possessed them and thereafter”] the metropolitan church of Narbonne had previously presided over them for four hundred years without anyone’s objection. Therefore, exercising our office in those regions, command the bishops of Tarragona by our authority that meanwhile they obey the archbishop of Narbonne as their own metropolitan, until, with the Lord’s help, the Church of Tarragona is restored. But let them show reverence to the archbishop of Toledo as primate, until the archbishop of Narbonne can demonstrate with certain authority that he was their primate. For your Fraternity knows that we established the archbishop of Toledo as primate in such a way that the privileges of the other metropolitans remain intact.

Also admonish the abbot, as a man of holy reputation, commanding him henceforth not to accept anything belonging to episcopal jurisdiction without the bishop’s permission, and to make appropriate amends for the injuries inflicted upon the archbishop of Narbonne; moreover, let him honor him as his proper and holy consecrated bishop, and strive to preserve peace with him inviolably in fraternal charity.

In everything, show yourself mindful of Roman authority, so that no suspicion concerning you may remain. Since the archbishop of Narbonne recalled that his church possessed privileges concerning the primacy, which, having been transferred by his predecessor, he nevertheless hopes to recover with the Lord’s help, investigate the matter carefully and endeavor to report your findings to us. If the authority of the privileges cannot be found, work with the princes of the land for the restoration of the Church of Tarragona. Meanwhile, command the bishops of Tarragona to obey him as their own metropolitan.

Investigate carefully the case of the bishop of Elne, and determine everything by just judgment between the bishop of Narbonne and him. We likewise command you to exercise the same judgment concerning the monastery of Crassus, between the archbishop of Narbonne and the monks of that monastery.

### XXX. Letter of Urban II to Raynerius, priest and legate of the Holy Roman Church. — He appoints him judge between the bishop of Barcelona [Bertrand] and the abbot of Saint-Pons of Thomières [Frotard]. (Year 1089.)

[Mansi, *Councils*, XX, 679.]

URBAN, servant of the servants of God, to his dearest and sweetest brother Raynerius, priest and legate of the holy Roman Church: greeting and apostolic blessing.

After you had departed from us, our dearest brothers, the bishops of Narbonne and Barcelona, came to us demanding the justice of the Apostolic See concerning their complaints against the abbot of Saint Pontius. The bishop of Barcelona complained, saying that, after undertaking the office of bishop, he had peacefully possessed the monastery of Saint Cucufas for an entire year under his own authority, as a special benefice of his Church, and that the abbot whom he had himself elected, with the consent and approval of Richard, legate of the Roman Church, had been installed there according to the rule; but that afterward the abbot of Thomières, together with his monks, forcibly expelled him from the monastery against the bishop’s opposition.

Your Fraternity recognizes how differently the abbot of Saint Pontius reported these matters while you were still with us. It will therefore be your responsibility—you to whom we have entrusted the examination and determination of such affairs in those regions—to investigate this case carefully and, with the Lord’s help, act so that justice does not lose its place, and so that you are not swayed to one side by anyone’s favor or zeal.

Remember the counsel we gave you when you departed, and, having consulted religious men, arrange what must be arranged so that Roman equity is exposed to no reproach, and so that in everything your judgment, carrying out the truth, does not abandon the path of apostolic discernment. Indeed, know that you are suspected because you dwell in the house of the adversary. Offices often change the dispositions of minds from rigor.

Therefore we command your affection not to omit, for the sake of the abbot or any other person, the complete determination of this case by an irrevocable sentence; nor are you to permit any of them to appeal further to the Apostolic See concerning it. Also determine with a wholly just and irrevocable judgment the case of the Church of Saint Sylvester, which the monks of Psalmodi are said to have taken away from Saint Rufus. The remaining matters seem to be missing.

### XXXI. Letter of Urban II to Frotard, abbot of Thomières. — He urges him to make satisfaction for the injuries inflicted upon the archbishop of Narbonne. (Year 1089.)

[Mansi, *Councils*, XX, 678.]

URBAN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his dearest and most reverend brother Frotard, abbot of Thomières: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Recently our most reverend brothers Dalmatius and Bertrand, bishops of Narbonne and Barcelona, came to us and complained at length against your Fraternity. The bishop of Narbonne asserted that you had invaded his churches, received persons excommunicated by him, and, without his permission, consecrated a bishop in the see of Jaca. He also said that your monks had exhumed a dead man under anathema and buried him within the monastery. This appears horrible even to hear.

If these things are true, we earnestly ask and command your religiousness, by the judgment of our legate, to make appropriate satisfaction to him for all these matters, henceforth to abstain from invading what belongs to episcopal jurisdiction, and to maintain firm peace with him, as is fitting for you.

Moreover, the bishop of Barcelona complained that the monastery of Saint Cucufas, which belongs to his jurisdiction, had been taken from the monks by your invasion and their forcible expulsion; he likewise asserted that the same had been done with the monastery of Saint Lawrence. Since he is a man of such moral dignity and pontifical grace that we cannot disbelieve him, and since you formerly reported the matter to us differently, we have entrusted the judgment of this case to our legate, to be concluded by an irrevocable sentence; and we wish you to obey his judgment, so that neither you nor he may hereafter be permitted to appeal to the Apostolic See concerning it.

Furthermore, we earnestly ask you—as we have confidence in your special and familiar religious devotion—to honor and love the bishop of Narbonne as your own spiritual father, in view of the one whose office he exercises.

### XXXII. Letter of Urban II to Count Raymond, Viscount Aymeric, and the clergy and people of Narbonne. (Year 1089.)

[Mansi, *Councils*, XX, 678.]

URBAN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the clergy and people of Narbonne, namely to Raymond, count, and Aymeric, viscount, his dearest sons: greeting and apostolic blessing.

We received our most reverend brother Dalmatius, your archbishop, when he came to us, with the reverence due to him; and, having long recognized his integrity and religious devotion, we commended him to your affection through letters of the Apostolic See.

Therefore, beloved sons, obey him as your beloved and Catholic Father; show him reverence and due subjection in all things as the vicar of the Lord; render in full to each church the tithes belonging to it; and preserve intact for him whatever belongs to episcopal justice. Listen devoutly and willingly to whatever he says to you from the Lord, and obey it.

For he exercises among you an embassy on behalf of Christ, entreating you on Christ’s behalf to be reconciled to God. Therefore, hearing and honoring him as Christ, correct your conduct, abstain from vices, and take care to please God in all things. For if you strive to please God, you will certainly have a shepherd pleasing to God; and when he intercedes for you before the supreme Judge, he will be heard more abundantly, unless your sins hinder him.

But to those who unjustly retain and violently seize the goods of the Church of Narbonne, we declare in the name of the Lord Jesus and command by apostolic authority that they either return them to the archbishop or make with him such an agreement as ought to satisfy him, lest, by unjustly retaining and seizing earthly goods, they incur danger to their souls and be deprived of eternal goods. If they despise our commands, when a renewed complaint reaches us, we shall wield the vengeance of the canons and the sword of the Spirit. But may divine mercy guard those who obey our admonitions.

### XXXIII. Letter of Pope Urban II to the clergy and people of Vienne. — He commends the archbishop of Vienne and commands that what the provost Ataldus had squandered from the goods of the Church of Vienne be restored. (Year 1089.)

[D. Bouquet, *Collection*, vol. XIV, p. 691, from *Bibliotheca Floriacensis*, part III, p. 76.]

URBAN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons, the clergy and monastic order, as well as the nobles and people residing at Vienne: greeting and apostolic blessing.

We received your venerable and dearest archbishop, a son of blessed Peter and our brother, when he came to us, with appropriate reverence and the due sweetness of charity. Since previously he had been unknown to us by face, we wished to test the honesty of his conduct and the outstanding diligence of his character, and therefore decided to keep him with us for some time with especially devoted affection.

Thanks be to God, for in him we found both the savor of knowledge and the good fragrance of honesty. Greatly pleased by the maturity of his conduct, the integrity of his diligence, and the prudence of his mind, we have made him dearer from being dear, and more familiar from being familiar, so that henceforth we regard him in the Roman Curia not as a Gaul but as a Roman.

Accordingly, as he returns to you, we accompany him with our letters and commend him more earnestly to your affection, so that he who until now has been dear and venerable to you in himself may henceforth, through us, be held still dearer and more venerable. For, both in fulfillment of the obligation of general equity and because of our special affection for him, whatever honor and dignity our predecessors conferred upon the Church of Vienne, we shall, by the Lord’s gift, preserve firm and perpetual.

Concerning the goods of your Church which the provost Ataldus squandered, we command absolutely that they be restored into the hands of the same archbishop. If anyone should presumptuously retain those goods in defiance, they will certainly experience the vengeance of apostolic justice. For we intend, with justice as our guide, not to diminish the Church of Vienne in its ancient goods, but by God’s grace to preserve and increase them. May almighty God guard you inwardly and outwardly with the right hand of his power.

### XXXIV. Letter of Pope Urban II to the suffragans of the Church of Arles. — He informs them that the oaths extorted from Bishop Guibalin have been declared invalid by him; he declares those who captured him infamous. (Around the year 1089.)

[Mansi, *Councils*, XX, 700.]

URBAN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the suffragans of the Church of Arles: greeting and apostolic blessing.

All those oaths which your confrater, Archbishop Guibalin, is known to have sworn unwillingly and under every kind of coercion, against the justice and religious order of the Church, we judge by the authority of our decree to be entirely invalid, since, as we have stated, they oppose God and the constitutions of the Church; and, with the Lord’s approval, we decree that they shall remain permanently invalid for the Church of Arles.

But those who, after capturing that man, dared to entangle him in wicked oaths by terrifying him with swords and mutilations of his limbs, we decree to be infamous forever; and unless they perform suitable penance, we exclude them from the body and blood of Christ and from entry into the churches.

### XXXV. Bull of Urban II for the canons of Pistoia. (Year 1090.)

[Zacharia, *Anecdota of the Middle Ages*, 222.]

URBAN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his dearest sons, the canons of the Church of Pistoia, and to their successors forever.

It is fitting that we, who, although unworthy, are established by the Lord’s disposition as cultivators and proclaimers of justice in the lofty watchtower of the chief apostles Peter and Paul, should assent to just vows and lend our ears to just petitions. Since, therefore, moved by due charity toward pilgrims, you have built, with the Lord’s help and at your own expense, a hospice beside the gate of your city of Pistoia called Saint Peter, we rightly commend your devotion; and by the authority of this present document we decree that one tenth of the tithes given to you by the people, and one tenth of your labors, as you have unanimously established, shall henceforth and forever be given to that hospice.

Moreover, by apostolic authority we decree that whatever the same hospice now justly possesses, or may hereafter justly and canonically acquire through the grant of pontiffs, the generosity of princes, or the offerings of the faithful, shall remain secure and inviolate for it.

Therefore we decree that no one at all may rashly disturb that house, capture anyone within it, or remove, diminish, or burden with reckless harassment the possessions subject to it. Rather, everything shall be preserved intact for the uses of those for whose preservation they were granted, and for the benefit and salvation of those who offered them.

We grant a privilege of the same tenor to the other hospices situated throughout your episcopate: namely, the one built beside Villa Quarrata; the one beside the town of Caparia; the one in the meadow called the Bishop’s; the one beside the place called Brandellian Cross; and the one built at Bliscet through your devotion and expense. By the authority of this present document we confirm that these are to remain forever subject to your hospice beside the gate of Saint Peter, as it presently exists.

As for the hospices situated outside the city, by the decree of this privilege we establish that no one may presume, within one stadium of them, to capture anyone, plunder, or disturb them in a hostile manner. We entrust all their ordinances and arrangements to you and your successors, to be determined by the common will of those among you who are more spiritual and religious, after consultation with the brothers of Valle Imbrose and with the consent of your bishop, provided that he is Catholic and religious.

We appoint as rectors over these houses men who will take care of them according to God and diligently minister to the poor and to those who come to them.

If, in the future, any bishop, archbishop, emperor, judge, prince, duke, count, viscount, or any other person, small or great, powerful or powerless, knowingly attempts rashly to act against this page of our privilege, and, after being warned a second or third time, does not make suitable satisfaction, we separate him from the body of Christ and the Church by the authority of apostolic power.

But may those who, for love of God and neighbor and in obedience to the institution of the Apostolic See, strive to enrich and exalt the aforesaid houses with their goods be enriched or endowed with the blessing of God and his apostles and with the remission of sins. May they, assisted by these, reach eternal life. Amen.

Written by the hand of Gregory, scrivener and notary of the sacred palace.

B. V.

Given at Rome by the hand of John, cardinal deacon of the Holy Roman Church, in the year of the Incarnation of the Lord 1089, in the thirteenth [twelfth] indiction, on the fourth day before the Ides of January, and in the second year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Urban II.

### XXXVI. * Urban II takes under his protection the monastery of Raitenbuch, founded by Welf, duke of Bavaria, and his wife Jutta. (Year 1090.)

[Lang, *Regesta*, I, 104.]

### XXXVII. Privilege of Pope Urban II for the canons of Saint Antoninus, in the diocese of Rodez. (Year 1090.)

[D. Martène, *Thesaurus Anecdotorum*, I, 248.]

URBAN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his dearest son Peter, provost of the canonry of Saint Antoninus the martyr, situated in the territory of Condac, and to his successors to be canonically appointed, forever.

Although, by the authority and benevolence of the Apostolic See, we are debtors to all the sons of the holy Church, it is nevertheless fitting that we show more devoted charity toward those places and persons that adhere more specially and familiarly to the Roman Church and that are distinguished by the grace of more abundant religious devotion. [lacuna]

Since, therefore, as our venerable brother Bishop Amatus reported to us, we have learned that the aforesaid canonry was founded at the command of Pope Gregory VII of blessed memory, through the mediation both of Bishop Amatus and of our most reverend brother Hugh, archbishop of Lyon, when it was deprived of every monastic and canonical religious observance, it is fitting for us to extend the hand of benevolence to such good beginnings and to provide for the peace of religious life.

For this reason, assenting to your just petitions, dearest son Peter, and moved by the letters of our aforesaid brother Bishop Amatus, we receive the aforesaid canonry of Saint Antoninus into the right, guardianship, and protection of the holy Roman Church. By this present decree we confirm all its privileges, together with everything that it now justly possesses or may hereafter, by the Lord’s generosity, justly acquire; and by apostolic authority we decree that it shall remain free from the power of all persons whatsoever under the protection of the holy Apostolic See, without prejudice to canonical episcopal justice, so long as the canons who now serve our Lord God there, or those who will serve there in future, strive to live according to the rule, to live communally, to possess nothing individually, and to observe both the apostolic statutes and those of blessed Jerome and Augustine concerning clerics living in common.

Therefore we decree and establish that no one at all may rashly disturb that canonry, remove or diminish the possessions subject to it, or burden them with reckless harassment; rather, everything shall be preserved intact for the uses of those whose support they were granted to provide.

Therefore, dearest sons in Christ, you ought to labor with greater diligence and devotion at the formation of regular discipline, so that, in proportion as you are free from secular tumult, you may more earnestly aspire with every virtue of mind and soul to please God. Above all, strive to observe the venerable decrees of the Roman Church, by whose patronage, with the Lord’s approval, you have been fortified against the yoke of all living persons.

As a sign of the liberty received from the Roman Church, you shall pay five solidi of the currency of that land each year to the Lateran palace.

If, in the future, any archbishop or bishop, emperor or king, prince or duke, count or viscount, judge, or any person whatsoever, great or small, powerful or powerless, knowingly attempts rashly to act against this page of our privilege, and, after being warned a second or third time, does not make suitable satisfaction, we separate him from the body of Christ and the Church by the authority of apostolic power.

But may peace from God and mercy be preserved in the present and future ages for those who maintain these provisions. Amen, amen, amen.

Written by the hand of Gregory, scrivener and notary of the sacred palace.

Given at Rome by the hand of Hotesculf, priest acting as chancellor, on the fifth day before the Kalends of April, in the year of the Lord 1090, in the thirteenth indiction, in the third year of Lord Pope Urban II.

### XXXVIII. Privilege of Pope Urban II for the Church of Grenoble. (Year 1090.)

[Baluz., *Miscellanea*, Lucca edition, III, 8.]

URBAN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his dearest brother Hugh, bishop of Grenoble, and to his legitimate successors forever.

The Church acknowledges that the power of binding and loosing in heaven and on earth was principally entrusted by God to blessed Peter and his successors in the words with which the Lord addressed Peter: “Whatever you bind on earth shall be bound also in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth shall be loosed also in heaven.” By the same Lord’s authority, confirmation both of his own firmness and of the faith of others was likewise granted to him, when it was said: “I have prayed for you, Peter, that your faith may not fail. And you, once converted, strengthen your brothers.”

It is therefore incumbent upon us, who, although unworthy, occupy Peter’s place, to correct what is wrong, confirm what is right, and in every Church so arrange what must be arranged according to the judgment of the interior Judge, that our judgment may proceed from his countenance and our eyes may see equity.

Accordingly, dearest brother in Christ, Hugo, bishop of Grenoble, assenting to your just petitions, by the authority of this present decree we confirm to you and your legitimate successors the right to govern, administer, and possess in perpetuity the bishopric of Grenoble, with the authority of the Roman Church preserved in all respects.

We therefore decree that no one at all, by any deceitful trickery, may invade, diminish, or take away the possessions of your bishopric, or seize or retain its tithes without your permission, or hold churches belonging to your jurisdiction through lay hands. Rather, everything which your Church has hitherto justly possessed, or which in the future, with the Lord’s assistance, it may justly and canonically acquire, shall always remain whole and undiminished in your hands and those of your successors.

Moreover, we confirm to you and your successors, by the authority of this privilege, the Church of Saint Donatus, situated in the archbishopric of Vienne, which, with the Lord’s help and episcopal authority, you wrested from tyrannical power, to be governed, administered, and possessed in perpetuity. We decree that none of your successors may grant that same church, freely or for a price, to any person or church; rather, it shall always remain immutably under the authority and possession of the bishop of Grenoble, together with everything belonging to it.

Since, moreover, the perverse presumption of certain people has grown to the point that ecclesiastical property is seized when bishops have died, we prohibit by apostolic authority that, when the end of your life or that of any of your successors arrives, anyone should presume to plunder the property and possessions of your Church. Rather, everything shall remain free and undisturbed in the power of the canons, to be preserved intact by the one who is canonically ordained bishop over them.

Furthermore, desiring the decrees of the holy canons to be preserved inviolably everywhere, we establish and decree that no one presume to receive into communion or consign to burial those whom you have placed under interdict or excommunicated.

It shall indeed be your intention, dearest brother, to devote vigilant care to the flock entrusted to you and to observe inviolably the decrees of the Roman Church, so that, as the fruit of your labors increases, you may be able to attain eternal life.

If, hereafter, any archbishop or bishop, emperor or king, prince or duke, count or viscount, judge, or any person whatsoever, great or small, powerful or powerless, knowingly attempts rashly to act against this page of our privilege, and, after being warned a second or third time, does not correct the matter by suitable satisfaction, we exclude him from the Church of Christ by the authority of apostolic power.

May peace from God and mercy be preserved for those who maintain these provisions, in the present and future ages. Amen, amen, amen.

Written by the hand of Gregory, scrinarius and notary of the sacred palace.

Given at Rome through the hand of John, cardinal deacon of the holy Roman Church, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1091, indiction XIII, in the third year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Urban II, on the Kalends of April.

### XXXIX. Urban II confirms the possessions of the monastery of Saint Theotfred of Calmiliacum. (Year 1090)

[Mabillon, *Acts of the Saints of the Benedictine Order*, V, 274.]

[Col. 0322A]

### XL. Privilege of Urban II for the Vallumbrosans. (Year 1090)

[Zacharia, *Anecdota of the Middle Ages*, 223, from the archive of Saint Michael of Furculis.]

Urban, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his dearest sons, the entire congregation of Vallombrosa: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Since, by the authority and benevolence of the apostolic see, we are debtors to all the sons of the holy Church, we ought to devote a more earnest attention of charity especially to those places and persons which adhere more particularly and familiarly to the Roman Church and which excel through a greater grace of religion.

Therefore, since, by the divine mercy going before and following after, the simplicity of your religious life displays the fragrance of a good reputation both near and far, and since, with the Lord’s approval, we desire to add advancement to your progress, we receive your monastery, dedicated to the honor of the blessed ever-virgin Mary, into the ownership, protection, and safeguarding of the Roman Church and the apostolic see. Fortifying it with the privilege of apostolic authority, we decree that it shall remain free from the yoke of all princes.

Therefore, by this page of our privilege, we establish by apostolic authority that whatever your monastery justly possesses today, or may hereafter justly and canonically acquire through the grant of pontiffs, the generosity of princes, or the offering of the faithful, shall remain secure and undiminished for you and your successors. By “successors” I mean those who strive to preserve the same religious observance and constancy of faith, and energetically to serve almighty God in the same purpose.

May you receive chrism, holy oil, the consecration of altars and basilicas, and the ordination of clerics from any Catholic bishop whom you wish who possesses the favor and communion of the Roman Church. Supported by our authority, let him grant what you request.

Furthermore, we establish and decree that no one at all may purchase or disturb the same monastery, take away possessions subject to it, diminish them, or harass them with rash vexations. Rather, everything shall be preserved intact, so that it may benefit the uses for which it was granted, namely, their support and administration.

Nor shall any bishop have the power to repeat excommunication or interdict against you, so that you, who are special sons of the apostolic see, may not be rashly exposed to the judgment of anyone else.

Since, moreover, several holy monasteries—namely, the congregation called Saint Salvii near Florence; Saint Fidelis of Strumii; Saint Saviour of Sophena; Saint Mary of Nerana; Saint Coxianus of Monte Schalario; Saint Angelus of Passiniano; Saint Lawrence of Cultuboni; Saint Saviour of Ficiclo; Saint Angelus near Pistoia; Saint Saviour of Vadeno; Saint Peter of Mischeto; Saint Paul of Rasolo; Saint Reparata of Marradio in the diocese of Faenza; the congregation of Rivis Caesaris; the congregation of Fontana Taonis; and the congregation of Monte Armato in the diocese of Bologna—have, by the Lord’s inspiration, agreed with you upon the same form of religious life, we grant by apostolic authority to them also, and to all who hereafter wish to join themselves completely to the same religious observance, the freedom of this privilege, for as long as they strive to persist in the same unity of religion and custom.

We establish, moreover, that your monastery, situated in the Valley of Vallombrosa, shall be regarded as the head of them all.

When, by divine arrangement, the end of your pastor’s life arrives, whoever is to be substituted in his place—for he must preside over both you and all the others—shall be chosen with the consent and judgment of all those who preside over the other monasteries. If, by the Lord’s arrangement, one of those abbots should happen to be elected to this general administration, he shall move principally to your principal monastery, and then, by his judgment, all the other monasteries united to you shall be administered, just as it is known to have been done in the days of John, your first abbot, of venerable memory.

Therefore, dearest sons in Christ, do not neglect the grace that is in you, which was given to you through the unity of holy observance and religion. Meditate on these things; devote yourselves to them, so that your progress may be manifest to all (1 Tim. 4:15). For you have become participants in Christ, provided that you retain firm to the end the beginning of his substance [or “confidence”] (Heb. 3:14). Remember what the Lord says: “Whoever perseveres to the end will be saved” (Matt. 24:13). Thus let your light shine before men, so that they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven (Matt. 5:16).

As a sign of the freedom received from the Roman Church, you shall pay every year to the Lateran palace twelve arm-lengths of haircloth.

If, hereafter, any archbishop or bishop, emperor or king, prince or duke, count or judge, or any person whatsoever, great or small, powerful or powerless, knowingly attempts rashly to act against this page of our privilege, and, after being warned a second or third time, does not correct the matter by suitable satisfaction, we exclude him from the body of Christ and the Church by the authority of apostolic power.

May peace from God and mercy be preserved for those who maintain these provisions, in the present and future ages. Amen, amen, amen.

Written by the hand of Gregory, scrinarius and notary of the sacred palace.

Given at Rome through the hand of John, cardinal deacon of the holy Roman Church, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1090, indiction XIII, on the eighth day before the Ides of April, in the third year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Urban II.

Bartholomeus, formerly an ordinary judge and notary by imperial authority, saw and read the written privilege, the apostolic letters, and all the writings from which this copy was made. As I found them there, I transcribed them here, faithfully copied them, and, for greater assurance, affixed the sign of my hand by authority granted to me by the venerable Father, Lord Thomas, by the grace of God bishop of Pistoia, in the bishopric of Pistoia, in the presence of Lord Ticcius, plebanus of the parish of Laiatico, and the priest Junctus, chaplain of the aforesaid parish, and Armaleone, formerly of the Infrangipani, and Curso Doni, witnesses summoned and called for this purpose, in the year of the Nativity of the Lord 1288, indiction II, on the twentieth day of September.

### XLI. Urban II takes the monastery of Marmoutier under his protection and confirms its possessions. (Year 1090)

[Mabillon, *Benedictine Annals*, V, 272.]

[Col. 0324B]

In this same year Bernard, abbot of Marmoutier, obtained from Urban II a most extensive privilege. In it the pontiff states at the outset that, although he is a debtor to all churches, he ought nevertheless to care with a more earnest charity for those places and persons which excel through a greater grace of religion, and especially for the monastery of Saint Martin, both because of devotion and reverence for the blessed confessor and because of the distinction of religious life by which the monks of that holy place excelled.

For this reason he says that he confirms all its possessions and receives the same place under his protection. He forbids public Masses to be celebrated there by bishops, and forbids the monks to be compelled to attend external stations or funerals against the will of their abbot, or to be excommunicated by anyone. Rather, he orders that all their more serious cases depend upon the judgment of the apostolic see.

The abbot’s election is to be free. If he possesses communion with the apostolic see, he is to receive consecration gratuitously from the archbishop of Tours, without any demand for a profession. Otherwise, he is either to approach the Roman pontiff to be consecrated or offer himself for consecration by any bishop.

The pontiff establishes the same provisions concerning the sacred chrism, the consecration of altars or basilicas, and sacred ordinations.

Then, addressing the monks, he adds: “Therefore, dearest sons in Christ, you ought to apply yourselves more carefully and devotedly to the formation of regular discipline, so that, the freer you are from secular disturbances, the more fully you may breathe after God in peace and devote yourselves more earnestly to the virtues of mind and soul.”

Finally, for this freedom he orders that one ounce of gold be paid each year.

Written by the hand of Gregory, scrinarius and notary of the sacred palace.

Given at Rome through the hand of John, cardinal deacon of the holy Roman Church, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1090, indiction XIII, in the third year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Urban II, on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of May.

### XLII. Urban II grants a bull to Burchard, abbot of Saint Basolus. (Year 1090)

[Mabillon and Ruinart, *Posthumous Works*, III, 87.]

### XLIII. Urban II confirms the freedom and possessions of the Church of Ravello at the request of Bishop Ursus. (Year 1090)

[Ughelli, *Sacred Italy*, I, 1183.]

[Col. 0325A]

Urban, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved brother in Christ, Ursus, bishop of Ravello, and to his successors to be canonically appointed, forever.

The dignity of the holy Roman and universal apostolic Church requires that it reward and exalt those who faithfully adhere to it. Since, therefore, you earnestly sought the fidelity and freedom of the Roman Church and anticipated it with your services, your city has, by the Lord’s provision, reached the point that in the time of our predecessor, Victor III, of revered memory, it deserved to obtain a bishop.

We therefore, rejoicing no less in your exaltation, both confirm the enactments of our predecessor and add to you this freedom: henceforth the Church of Ravello shall be free from subjection to every power and shall remain under the right and dominion of the Roman pontiff alone.

It is fitting indeed that you, who have grown greatly in bodily matters, should also, by the Lord’s generosity, grow through the reception of spiritual gifts.

Therefore, cherishing your Church especially in the bosom of the apostolic see, we legitimately confirm to you, fellow bishop Ursus, and to your legitimate successors, the entire extent of the diocese of Ravello by the authority of this present page, granting you the power within it, without anyone’s opposition, to prepare chrism.

[Col. 0325C] [Many things are missing from the privilege because it was cut apart and sewn together with thread, as it presently survives.]

You shall observe the statutes of the Church inviolably, with the Lord’s help, and always strive with all your strength for its honor.

If, hereafter, any archbishop or bishop, emperor or king, prince or duke, patrician, count or viscount, judge, or any person whatsoever, great or small, powerful or powerless, knowingly attempts to take away the freedom granted to you, and, after being warned a second or third time, does not correct the matter by suitable satisfaction, he shall be separated from the body of Christ and the Church and shall be liable to the danger of losing his honor and office.

May peace from the Lord and mercy be preserved for those who maintain these provisions, in the present and future ages. [Col. 0325D] Amen, amen, amen.

Given at Salerno through the hand of John, cardinal deacon of the holy Roman Church, on the Nones of October, indiction XIII, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1090, in the third year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Urban II.

### XLIV. Letter of Urban II to the clergy and people of Chartres—Concerning the deposition of Bishop Geoffrey and the substitution of Ivo, consecrated in his place. (Year 1090)

[Mansi, *Councils*, XX, 650.]

Urban, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons in Christ, the clergy and people of Chartres: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Both out of devotion and reverence for the blessed ever-virgin Mary and in fulfillment of the duty of our office, we have devoted particular love, protection, and care to your Church. Considering with a more favorable spirit the long-lasting troubles that it suffered under Geoffrey, formerly its bishop, and having examined the truth of the matter at greater length and with greater diligence, by the Lord’s generosity we have satisfied justice.

Anticipating and following your good intention, we consecrated without delay the venerable priest Ivo, whom you canonically and lawfully elected according to our instructions after Geoffrey had been deposed by us, so that your Church might suffer no further loss in this matter.

Now, sending him back to you as one consecrated by the hands of blessed Peter, we ask and entreat you in the place of blessed Peter to receive him kindly and honor him with the obedience owed to a true pastor; observe with due care what he announces to you; and strive with all your efforts to please God, so that he himself may be able to please God and, by worthy intercession, appease him for your transgressions.

For if you resolve to please God, you will undoubtedly have a pastor pleasing to God, and you will find us ready to hear you in your necessities.

As for Geoffrey, who returned the bishopric unconditionally into our hands, openly acknowledging himself unworthy, we have ordered and do order that no one presume in any way to give him support for invading or disturbing the bishopric again. Otherwise, we decree that both he and his supporters shall be subject to excommunication.

May divine grace preserve you in obedience to our instructions.

Given at Capua on the eighth day before the Kalends of December.

### XLV. Letter of Pope Urban II to Richer, archbishop of Sens—He commends to him Ivo, bishop of Chartres, and declares Geoffrey anathematized if he attempts to invade the bishopric. (Year 1090)

[Mansi, *Councils*, XX, 651.]

Your diligence recognizes how many troubles the Church of Chartres endured on behalf of Geoffrey, formerly its bishop, and how many complaints were brought to the apostolic see. At last, after the truth of the matter had been investigated more carefully, by the Lord’s generosity we satisfied justice, and he renounced the bishopric into our hands without any condition whatsoever.

We then sent letters to your fraternity, indicating the order of what had happened and asking that you contribute your assistance to the people of Chartres in choosing and consecrating a bishop.

Supported by our permission, the people of Chartres canonically elected the venerable priest Ivo as bishop. When they had requested from you, according to the custom of the Church, the grace of consecration, your fraternity refused to lay hands upon him.

When they therefore came to us and requested his consecration, we, who had long known the man’s religious character and had granted permission for his election, could not fail to respond to their just petition.

Sending him back consecrated, with his obedience to your Church preserved, we ask for the sweetness of your affection: once every source of contention has been quieted, embrace him with due kindness and grant him your assistance in governing the Church.

We have decreed, moreover, that Geoffrey, if he attempts to invade the bishopric or disturb the Church, shall himself and his supporters be subject to anathema.

Given at Capua on the seventh day before the Kalends of December.

### XLVI. Letter of Urban II to Altmann, bishop of Passau. (Fragment—Year 1090)

[*Life of Altmann*, in Bolland, II, August, p. 174.]

[Col. 0327B]

Urban, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his dearest brother Altmann, bishop of Passau: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Hearing of your diligence in the affairs of God and in the labors of the Church, we rejoice in the Lord. For this reason we have heard your requests concerning matters which seem contrary to the custom of our Church, etc.

### XLVII. Letter of Urban II to the abbots Lanzo and Rudolf and to Adalbero, primicerius—He confirms the election of the bishop of Metz made by them. (Year 1091)

[Mansi, *Councils*, XX, 705.]

Urban, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons in Christ, Lanzo and Rudolf, abbots; Adalbero, primicerius; the archdeacons; and all the Catholic clergy and people of the Church of Metz: greeting and apostolic blessing.

We rejoice, dearest sons in Christ, because you rejoice in the Lord; because the lamp of the Catholic faith, which remained in Herimann, bishop of holy memory, has not yet been extinguished; and because you have provided a worthy successor for a good predecessor.

Therefore, granting the support of apostolic authority to your good desires, by these present letters we approve your election. We also grant assent to your petitions, so that it may be within your discretion from which Catholic bishops he should most appropriately receive consecration.

The following must certainly be investigated in every way: whether he was ordained deacon simoniacally by the hand of that man called the archbishop of Trier. Whatever he received from him in an extraordinary and unworthy manner, we judge by the authority of the Holy Spirit to be invalid; therefore, by the present authority, we order that he receive the same orders from some Catholic bishop. For such an ordainer, since he possessed nothing, could give nothing.

Therefore, dearest sons in Christ, persevere in what you learned from our most reverend fellow bishop Herimann, now a fellow citizen of the angels. Do what you are doing, because the Lord will grant an eternal crown to those who trample upon the serpent’s head. May he grant you to fight faithfully by his grace and deem you worthy of the reward of the eternal prize.

Given at Benevento on the Kalends of February.

### CHAPTER XLVIII. Urban II confirms the possessions of the nunnery of Saint Cross at Poitiers. (Year 1091)

[Mabillon, *Annals of the Order of Saint Benedict*, V, 282.]

[Col. 0328A]

Adelais presided over the most noble nunnery of Saint Cross at Poitiers after Abbess Petronilla. From Urban II she obtained protection by the apostolic see and confirmation of its possessions, by a diploma given at Benevento through the hand of John, cardinal deacon of the holy Roman Church, on the fourth day before the Kalends of April, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1091, in the fourth year of Urban’s pontificate.

At the end of the diploma he admonishes the abbess and sisters to respond to the kindness of the apostolic see through holy acts, to devote themselves more diligently to the formation of regular discipline, and to strive with all their strength toward eternal glory.

In the same diploma the pontiff establishes that the collegiate church of Saint Radegund shall remain subject, as before, in perpetuity to the administration of Saint Cross. This had earlier been determined at the Council of Saintes by Amatus, bishop of Oloron, and Hugo, bishop of Die, legates of the apostolic see; Gregory VII had likewise confirmed it by his letters, addressed to Hugo and the other clergy of that same church.

### CHAPTER XLIX. Letter of Urban II to Romuald, bishop of the Church of Monopoli—He declares, on the judgment of the Council of Benevento, that the bishopric of Monopoli is subject not to the Church of Brindisi but to the Roman see. (Year 1091)

[Mansi, *Councils*, XX, 739.]

[Col. 0328C]

Urban, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved brother Romuald, bishop of the Church of Monopoli, and to his successors to be canonically appointed, forever.

The authority of the sacred canons and pontifical decrees demands that the more important cases of the Churches be settled by the judgment of the apostolic see. Although unworthy, we preside over it by divine arrangement, and we extend the same care to all the Churches throughout the world, insofar as the divine goodness of his apostolic majesty grants us knowledge and ability.

When, therefore, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1091, a synodal council had been gathered in the Church of Benevento in our presence, and the bishop of Brindisi, or Oria, had lodged a complaint against your fraternity, the documents of both your Church and his were examined.

After these had been investigated before us by the entire council with more careful inquiry, our venerable bishops and cardinal priests adjudged that the Church of Monopoli, supported by the greater authority of pontifical documents, did not owe subjection and obedience to the Church of Brindisi.

Approving their judgment, we confirmed it with the strength of our authority. By the page of this present privilege, we decree that you and your successors shall remain forever free from subjection to the Church of Oria or Brindisi, under the obedience of the apostolic see alone.

We establish that whatever the Church of Monopoli has hitherto justly possessed or now possesses, or may hereafter justly and canonically acquire—in castles, villages, woods, churches, and monasteries—shall remain secure and undiminished for you and your successors, to be governed, administered, and possessed by episcopal right, with reverence for the Roman and apostolic Church preserved in all respects.

When you die, or any of your successors dies, the clergy and people of Monopoli shall have the freedom, with all wrongdoing excluded, to elect a bishop canonically; the man elected shall be consecrated by the Roman pontiff.

If, hereafter, any archbishop or bishop, emperor or king, prince or duke, count or viscount, judge, or any person whatsoever, great or small, powerful or powerless, knowingly attempts rashly to act against this page of our privilege and, after being warned a second or third time, does not correct the matter by suitable satisfaction, we decree that he shall be liable to the danger of losing his honor and office, and we exclude him from the body of Christ and the Church by the authority of apostolic power.

May peace from God be preserved for those who maintain these provisions—deservedly—in the present and future ages. Amen, amen, amen.

Written by the hand of Lanfranc, notary of the sacred palace.

Given at Benevento through the hand of John, cardinal deacon of the holy Roman Church, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1091, indiction XIV, on the fourth day before the Kalends of April, in the fourth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Urban II.

### L. Urban II takes the monastery of Saint Bartholomew on the island of Lipara under his protection and confirms its possessions. (Year 1091)

[Ughelli, *Sacred Italy*, I, 775.]

[Col. 0329C]

Urban, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved brother Ambrosius, abbot of Lipara, and to his successors regularly appointed, forever.

Since all islands, according to the provisions of royal law, are held to belong to the public jurisdiction, it is certainly established that, by the privilege of the religious emperor Constantine, all the western islands were granted as their own property to blessed Peter and his successors, especially those situated around the coast of Italy. Many of them, however, because of the sins of their inhabitants, were captured by the Saracens and lost the glory of the Christian name.

Among these, Lipara, once distinguished by the body of the apostle Saint Bartholomew, is known to have been reduced to the condition of a desert. After many years had passed and the power of the Saracens had been restrained by the power of divine mercy, religious brothers entered the island out of devotion to divine service, took care to build monasteries as dwellings there, and by their industry established many settlers on the same island.

We, therefore, to whom, by divine will and through the height of the apostolic see, the care of all the Churches has been entrusted, although we acknowledge from the records of the sacred Gregorian document that a bishopric once existed on that island, nevertheless establish by the authority of this present page that, since the smallness of the place and the scarcity of its inhabitants no longer merit the dignity of a bishop, it shall have a monastery and possess the whole extent of the island.

We also receive under the special protection of the holy Roman and apostolic see the monastery itself, over which your fraternity presides, with the Lord as its author, consecrated in honor and under the name of Saint Bartholomew.

Therefore, by this page of our privilege, we establish by apostolic authority that whatever the same monastery justly possesses today, or may in the future justly and canonically acquire through the grant of pontiffs, the generosity of princes, or the offering of the faithful, shall remain secure and undiminished for you and your successors.

We decree that no one at all may rashly disturb the same monastery, take away possessions subject to it, retain what has been taken away, diminish them, or harass them with rash vexations. Rather, everything shall be preserved intact, so that it may benefit the uses for which it was granted, namely, their support and administration.

When you, the abbot of that place, die, or any of your successors dies, no one shall be placed over it by any deceitful trickery or violence unless he has been chosen by the common favor of the brothers or by the sounder part of the brothers’ council. The man elected shall then approach the Roman pontiff to be consecrated.

Therefore, beloved sons in Christ, you ought to devote yourselves fervently to the formation of regular discipline and to observe the precepts of divine law with greater diligence, so that, the freer you are from secular disturbances, the more diligently you may strive with all the powers of mind and soul to please God.

[Col. 0330C] As a sign of the freedom received from the Roman Church, you shall pay one ounce of gold each year to the Lateran palace.

If, hereafter, any archbishop, bishop, emperor or king, prince or duke, count or viscount, judge, or any person whatsoever, great or small, powerful or powerless, knowingly attempts rashly to act against this page of our privilege and, after being warned a second or third time, does not correct the matter by suitable satisfaction, we decree that he shall be liable to the danger of losing his honor and office, and we exclude him from the body of Christ and the Church by apostolic authority.

May peace from God and mercy be preserved for those who maintain these provisions, in the present and future ages. [Col. 0330D] Amen, amen, amen.

Given at Milazzo through the hand of John, cardinal deacon of the holy Roman Church, on the third day before the Nones of June, indiction XVIII, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1091, in the fourth year of the pontificate of Lord Urban II.

### LI. Urban II entrusts the island of Corsica, restored under Gregory VII to its former jurisdiction of the Roman Church, to Daimbert, bishop of Pisa, and his successors. (Year 1091)

[Ughelli, *Sacred Italy*, III, 369.]

Urban, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved brother Daimbert, bishop of Pisa, and to his successors canonically appointed, forever.

Since all islands, according to legal statutes, are held to belong to the public jurisdiction, it is also established that, through the generosity and privilege of the religious emperor Constantine, they were granted as their own property to blessed Peter and his vicars.

When, however, many calamities occurred by the judgment of divine providence, the Roman Church suffered the loss of this property in some places. Nevertheless, according to both canonical and legal institutions, the property of the Roman dignity is excluded neither by the passage of time nor by the division of kingdoms nor by any duration of possession.

Although, therefore, the Roman Church was deprived of possession of Corsica for many years, Corsica is nevertheless known, with the Lord’s help, to have returned to the Roman Church’s jurisdiction under our predecessor Gregory VII.

We, therefore, yielding to the petitions of our dearest brother Daimbert, bishop of Pisa, of the noble citizens, and of our dearest daughter in blessed Peter, Countess Matilda, entrust and grant the aforesaid island, in our place, to the Church of Pisa, with the counsel of the cardinal clerics and our other faithful.

This is to be understood as follows: for as long as the city of Pisa receives a bishop not by tyrannical invasion but by the canonical election of the clergy and people through the hands of the Roman pontiff—as it is known to have received Landulf, Gerard, and you, dearest brother Daimbert—and for as long as it persists in the fidelity toward the Roman Church that it displays today, it shall enjoy the benefit of this grant or lease.

The condition is added that each year, without any excuse, it shall pay fifty pounds of Lucanian coin to the Lateran palace.

We establish by our apostolic authority that the terms of this grant shall remain entirely undisturbed for as long as they preserve, with due devotion, the terms of the fidelity and payment prescribed above.

Therefore, we ask our successors, both out of reverence for the blessed ever-virgin Mary and out of love and familiarity with the most noble city of Pisa, always to show the same honor to the Church of Pisa.

We also ask Daimbert’s successors as bishop and all the citizens of the city of Pisa who will follow after the present times always to display the same fidelity and devotion toward the Roman Church, so that, with the Lord’s favor, firm faith, kindness, and friendship may remain between both parties.

Given at Benevento on the fourth day before the Kalends of July through the hand of John, cardinal deacon of the holy Roman Church, indiction XIV, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1091, in the fourth year of the pontificate of Pope Urban II.

### LII. Letter of Urban II to Berengar, bishop of Ausona—He appoints him archbishop of Tarragona. (Year 1091)

[Mansi, *Councils*, XX, 648.]

[Col. 0332A]

Urban, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved brother Berengar, bishop of Ausona, transferred to the metropolitan see of Tarragona, and to his successors canonically appointed, forever.

Among the foremost cities of Spain, Tarragona was illustrious and pagan; this is also demonstrated by the judgments of Christian writings. But the Lord is just in his ways and holy in all his works; although he is held to be incomprehensible in many judgments, he can never be deemed blameworthy in any. He himself transfers kingdoms and changes times. It seemed good to him once to exalt the glory of the city of Tarragona in that same place; it seemed good to him to visit the sins of his people in that same city. For when a Christian people dwelt there, he visited their iniquities with the rod and their sins with scourges.

But behold: now that three hundred and ninety years have passed since the people of the Hagarenes made the aforementioned city almost deserted, he has deigned to inspire the hearts of its rulers so that, according to the command of the apostolic see—which, although unworthy, we preside over by God’s authority [or: with God as author]—they should undertake the restoration of that city. Indeed, Berengarius, count of Barcelona, prompted by the persuasion of our authority, for the salvation of his soul, together with the nobles under his power, not only undertook the restoration of the aforesaid city, but also transferred the city itself and all the land under his authority to Blessed Peter and his vicars by a lawful agreement, and established that a census of five pounds of silver should be paid annually to the Lateran palace [addition: each year].

Therefore, with God’s assistance, we desire to become cooperators in this restoration. We praise the institution of the aforesaid count, together with the liberties and customs which he is known to have promulgated for the new settlers of the city of Tarragona, and by our authority we decree that they remain ratified. Since we receive under the special protection of the apostolic see the whole land of that count which he offered to Blessed Peter, as well as the city of Tarragona and the people gathered there with the Lord’s favor, we likewise confirm, insofar as it extends, the liberty granted to it by Count Berengarius’s written document [or: writing], so that they shall pay nothing further to anyone unless of their own free will they make themselves debtors to the Roman Church.

Therefore, so that all these things may remain unshaken with God as their author, following the privileges of our predecessors who once established the Church of Ausona as the vicar of Tarragona, we grant to you, dearest son Berengarius—for it is chiefly through your efforts that this restoration has been undertaken—the pallium, that is, the fullness of all priestly dignity, through the grace of the Roman Church’s liberality.

Moreover, to you and to your legitimate successors, who shall be duly appointed and who shall labor with equal zeal for the restoration of the city and church of Tarragona, we confirm by this charter of privilege the right to possess the aforesaid church of Tarragona as your own property, together with all the churches which it is known to have possessed by its own right from ancient times. Concerning those presently subject to the power of the Saracens, we command that, when it pleases God to restore them to the power of the Christian people [the text is lacking here: “to restore …”], they be returned to the due obedience of your church, while the authority of the Roman Church remains secure in all respects.

Furthermore, we grant the Church of Ausona to you and your successors to possess for as long as it takes, with God as author, for the Church of Tarragona to be restored through your efforts to the fullness of its former status. You must use the pallium, therefore, only within the church during the solemn celebration of Mass, and only on the principal feasts: namely, the Nativity of the Lord, Epiphany, Hypapante, the Lord’s Supper, Holy Saturday, the first and second days of the Resurrection, the Ascension of the Lord, Pentecost, the three feasts of Saint Mary, and also of Saint Michael and Saint John the Baptist; on the feasts of all the apostles and of those martyrs whose relics are contained in your church; likewise at the commemoration of all the saints; at the consecrations of churches, bishops, and clerics; on the annual day of your consecration; and also at the solemnities of the holy virgin Thecla and of the holy martyr Fructuosus and his companions.

Therefore, most reverend brother, we exhort you with intimate affection always to show yourself worthy of the pontificate of so great an honor, taking care to live without offense to Christians and Saracens, and striving, with God’s gift, to seek out unbelievers for the faith through words and examples. Thus may you excel outwardly in the eyes of men through the dignity of the pallium, so that inwardly you may possess excellence in virtue before the eyes of the majesty above.

Certainly, by the charter of this privilege and by the authority of our office, we decree that whoever recognizes that he has hitherto unjustly held goods belonging to the Church of Tarragona should henceforth strive to restore them to that same church, out of fear of divine judgment and reverence for the apostolic see. But if in the future any archbishop or bishop, emperor or king, prince or duke, count or viscount, judge or any magistrate, ecclesiastical or secular person, knowingly and rashly attempts to act against this charter of privilege, and, after being warned a second or third time, does not correct the matter by suitable satisfaction, we decree that he shall be subject to the peril of his honor and office, and we separate him from Christ and from the body of the Church. But for those who preserve these provisions, may peace and mercy from God be preserved throughout the present and future ages. Amen, amen.

Given at Capua on the Kalends of July, by the hand of John, cardinal deacon of the holy Roman Church, in the fourth indiction, in the year 1091 of the Lord’s incarnation, in the fourth year of the pontificate of the lord Pope Urban II.

### LIII. Letter of Pope Urban II to the priors of Vallombrosa and Camaldoli, instructing them not to withdraw from communion with the bishop of Pisa. (1091)

[MITTARELLI, *Camaldolese Annals* III, appendix, 92.]

URBAN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, sends greetings and apostolic blessing to the venerable sons in Christ R. . . ., prior of Vallombrosa, and M. . ., prior of Camaldoli, and to the congregations entrusted to their governance.
