We rightly praise the zeal of your religious devotion and give thanks, because you burn with immense fervor against the depravity of simony and compel others also to burn. But we marvel at this in you, and we censure it: that, contrary to the constitutions of the holy Fathers, before the matter has been proved and before the case has been decided, you suspend your holiness from communion with our brother, the bishop of Pisa.

For it is not fitting that you, who are constantly devoted to divine services, should act otherwise than you are instructed by divine disciplines. God himself, who knows hidden things, did not wish to judge the evil of the Sodomites merely on hearing of it, before he had clearly investigated what was being said: “I will go down,” he says, “and see whether they have fully acted according to the cry that has come to me.” Hence the blessed martyr and pontiff Evaristus says: “Heard-of evils should move no one, nor should anyone ever believe reports made indiscriminately without certain proof; rather, let him carefully inquire into what he has heard, lest by acting precipitately he do something wrong.”

For if God, who knew everything, did not wish either to believe or to judge all the evil of the Sodomites—whose cry had reached heaven—until he himself, carefully investigating it with faithful witnesses, truly learned from their deeds what he had heard, then how much more must we, who are human and sinful and to whom the hidden judgments of God are unknown, take precautions and judge or condemn no one before true and just proof, as the Apostle plainly says: “Who are you to judge another’s servant? He stands or falls before his own master.”

Blessed Augustine, expounding this passage of the Apostle, says: “For he did not wish a human being to be judged by another human being according to the arbitrary judgment of suspicion, or even by an extraordinary judgment usurped outside the proper order, but rather according to the law of God and the order of the Church, whether the person has confessed voluntarily or has been accused and convicted. Otherwise, why did he say, ‘If anyone is named a brother who is a fornicator or an idolater,’ and so forth, unless he wished that naming to be understood as that which occurs when a sentence is pronounced against someone according to judicial order and with integrity? For if mere naming is sufficient, many innocent people must be condemned, since someone is often falsely named in connection with a crime.”

It was therefore fitting that, meditating day and night on the law of the Lord, you should have observed these and many similar principles, and that before a legitimate inquiry you should neither have withdrawn yourselves from communion with the bishop of Pisa nor marked him with so great an infamy. Nevertheless, because we venerate your voice on account of the merit of your religious devotion, and believe that you acted out of love of justice, we pardon your simplicity in this matter through apostolic kindness—especially since in your letters you have identified others as the authors of this accusation and have removed yourselves from its purpose.

But we ask you, and as sons of obedience we command you, to take care to identify those persons to us by name, so that, with God as author, once the accusers are known, this disgrace may either be canonically proved or removed. Moreover, we wish you to know that they were summoned by us some time ago through letters from the people of Pisa. Therefore, if they have not yet begun to come, admonish them in our place to come to us, in obedience to the apostolic see. And lest they perhaps complain that they cannot appear by the earlier deadline, we extend the postponement until the coming Nativity of Blessed Mary.

But if even then they disdain to come, let them know that they will be punished by canonical retribution. If they do come, however, we emphatically wish you to send two or three of your number together with them before our presence, so that they may examine and settle this matter.

Meanwhile, cease defaming our brother and refuse his communion in no way. Whoever among you is residing in the diocese of the Church of Pisa should likewise not refuse to render him the obedience that is due. For the rest, we beseech you to commend us in your prayers to almighty God.

Given at Troia on the twelfth day before the Ides of July.

### LIV. Urban II urges William, archbishop of Rouen, to restore the monastery of Saint Austreberta at Pavilly, “and grants to all who contribute anything to the same monastery a remission of one quarter of the penances imposed by a bishop or priest.” (1091)

[RUINART, *Life of Urban*, in MABILLON and RUINART, *Posthumous Works* III, 103.]

### LV. Letter of Urban II to the clergy and people of Amiens. — He states that he has confirmed Bishop Gervinus. (1091)

[MABILLON, *Benedictine Annals* V, 280.]

URBAN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, sends greetings and apostolic blessing to the clergy and people of Amiens.

Our most reverend brother Gervinus, your bishop, came to the apostolic see and reported his case to us, supported by letters from our most reverend brother Rainoldus, archbishop of Reims, and from his legates. We approved his canonical election and rejected the man who had intruded himself unlawfully. We also kept Gervinus with us for a long time, waiting to see whether anyone wished to oppose him. After no one had brought any charge against him during the two months he spent with us, tempering the rigor of justice with merciful condescension, we send him back to you confirmed in his place and office.

Therefore, by apostolic authority, we admonish your fraternity to show him every obedience as a suitable shepherd, and to devote every care, through counsel and assistance, to retaining and governing the bishopric, so that with him you may rejoice both in his teaching and in your obedience. If, after this admonition, anyone should presume to oppose him concerning the bishopric or refuse to submit to him as his bishop, we confirm by apostolic authority the sentence with which he has punished that person for disobedience.

Given on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of January.

### LVI. Letter of Urban II to the superiors of laymen living a common life. (1091)

[BERNOLD, *Chronicle*, under the year 1091.]

We have learned that some people disparage the custom of your monasteries, by which you receive laymen who renounce the world and transfer themselves and their possessions to a common life, accepting them to be governed in obedience. But we, having examined this manner of life and custom with our own eyes, judge it praiseworthy and all the more worthy of perpetual preservation because it has been impressed with the form of the primitive Church. We approve it, call it holy and catholic, and confirm it by these letters with apostolic authority.

### LVII. Letter of Urban II to G[ebhard], bishop of Constance, Welf and B[erthold], dukes, and Count B. — He urges them to protect the abbot of the monastery of Saint Saviour at Schaffhausen against Tuto, who is attempting to take away an estate donated to the monastery. (1092)

[MANSI, *Councils* XX, 708.]

URBAN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, sends greetings and apostolic blessing to the bishop of Constance N. and to Counts N. and N.

Letters from the abbot of the monastery of Saint Saviour have come to us, complaining before God and Saint Peter that a certain man named N. came to the aforesaid monastery, renounced the world, made a promise of stability according to the custom of the monastery, and handed over and confirmed his property to that church according to the law of the Suebi, before many witnesses. The abbot, as a devoted, prudent, and faithful steward, built a monastery beautifully on that estate, appointed brothers, and established the other things belonging to the monastic rule.

But after the aforesaid N. saw that everything had been organized and completed through the abbot’s labor and zeal, and after the monastery had possessed the same estate for seven years and more without any opposition, he, instigated by the devil, now denies that he ever made the transfer. If he has suffered any inconvenience because of it, he threatens not only to take the estate away but also to destroy the monastery itself.

Therefore, most excellent sons, we earnestly beseech you, out of devotion to and reverence for the Lord Saviour and Blessed Peter, and for love of us, to take care to prevent this man from such great apostasy and to assist the abbot and the monastery. Innocentius says: “An error that is not resisted is approved.” And the Apostle says: “Not only those who do such things are worthy of death, but also those who consent to those who do them.”

We wish you, son, to admonish this pestilent man canonically a second and a third time—if this has not already been done—so that he may repent. If he refuses, then, so that the others may be afraid, draw the sword of anathema against him, so that, handed over to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, he may learn not to blaspheme and may be saved on the day of the Lord.

May divine grace preserve you unharmed and obedient to our admonitions, and defend you from every evil.

### LVIII. Confirmation of the canonical foundation of Saint Mary at Rettenbach, which is received under the protection of the apostolic see; confirmation of all its possessions, together with the grant of certain privileges. (1092)

[COCQUELINES, *Bullar. privileg. summ. pont. ampl. Collect.* II, 67.]

URBAN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his dearest son Uldaric, provost of the chapter situated at the place called Raïtenpuech in honor of Saint Mary, God’s holy mother and virgin, and to his canonically appointed successors, forever.

The Church acknowledges the power of binding and loosing in heaven and on earth, principally entrusted by God to Blessed Peter and his successors, in those words with which the Lord addressed Peter: “Whatever you bind on earth will be bound also in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth will be loosed also in heaven” (Matthew 16:19). To him also, by that same God as author, firmness in himself and confirmation of the faith of others are granted, when the Lord says to him: “I have prayed for you, Peter, that your faith may not fail; and you, once converted, strengthen your brothers” (Luke 22:32).

It is therefore necessary for us, who, although unworthy, occupy Peter’s place, to correct what is perverse, strengthen what is right, and arrange in the whole Church those things that must be arranged according to the will of the eternal Judge, so that judgment may proceed from his presence and our eyes may see equity (Psalm 16:2).

Since, therefore, the most faithful sons of the Roman Church, Duke Welf of Bavaria and his wife Judith, established, for the salvation of their souls, a canonical community of brothers living according to the rule of Blessed Augustine at the place called Rettenbach, and offered that same house to Blessed Peter with devotion, we receive the aforesaid canonical community—which, by God’s providence, you are known to preside over—under the perpetual protection and special guardianship of the apostolic see, both out of reverence and devotion for Blessed Mary, God’s mother and ever-virgin, whose name has been given to the place, and out of love for our aforesaid sons, as well as out of regard for your religious fraternity.

Therefore, by this present page of our decree, we confirm that it is to be governed and administered by you and your legitimate successors, together with everything already granted to it from the resources of the aforesaid dukes or through the offerings of other faithful people.

Accordingly, by this present charter of our privilege, we establish by apostolic authority that whatever the same community legally possesses today, or may hereafter lawfully and canonically acquire through the grant of pontiffs, the generosity of rulers, or the offerings of the faithful, shall remain secure and unimpaired for you and your successors.

We decree that no one at all shall be permitted rashly to disturb this canonical community, or violently to take away, diminish, or harass with presumptuous vexations the possessions subject to it. Rather, everything shall be preserved intact and shall contribute in every way to the needs of those for whose support and governance it was granted.

When the provost of this place dies, or any of your successors, no one shall be placed over it through any form of subterfuge except one whom the brothers unanimously, or the sounder part of the brothers’ council, has chosen. You shall receive the consecrations of altars and basilicas, the ordinations of clerics, chrism, holy oil, and the other matters belonging to episcopal office from the bishop of Freising . . ., in whose diocese you are—provided that he is a Catholic, possesses the grace and communion of the apostolic see, and is willing to provide these things freely and without corruption.

Otherwise, you shall be permitted to approach any Catholic bishop you wish and receive from him the sacraments of consecration, or to have recourse to the apostolic see, which, supported by apostolic authority, shall without hesitation grant what is requested.

Moreover, we appoint as your advocate or protector Duke Gulfo, a man of distinguished valor, and after him his sons, if by God’s favor he should have such sons, so that they may be useful to your church and executors of their father’s institution. If this does not occur, it shall be for you to choose whichever suitable protector of your Church you prefer, one who will energetically and reverently perform this service of divine worship without exacting secular profit.

But we give thanks to the almighty Lord, whose mercy is better than sacrifices, because you are renewing the commendable life of the holy Fathers and reviving, at the prompting of the Holy Spirit, the institutions of apostolic discipline that arose in the beginnings of the holy Church but have now, as the Church has grown, almost entirely disappeared.

For from the beginnings of the holy Church two forms of life were established for her children: one by which the weakness of the infirm is sustained, and another by which the blessed life of the stronger is perfected; one remaining in little Segor, and the other ascending toward the higher places of the mountain; one redeeming daily sins through tears and almsgiving, and the other seeking eternal merits through daily perseverance; those who hold to the former make use of earthly goods, while those who follow the latter despise and abandon earthly goods.

This latter life, which by divine favor turns away from earthly things, is divided into two portions under almost one and the same superior: namely, that of canons and that of monks. By God’s mercy, the second has now become widespread and shines throughout the whole world; the first, however, has almost completely ebbed away as the fervor of the faithful has grown cold.

The martyr and pontiff Urban established this life; Augustine organized it in his rules; Jerome instructed it in his letters; Gregory commanded Augustine, archbishop of the English, to institute it. It should therefore not be considered a lesser merit to sustain this primitive life of the Church, with the Lord’s spirit inspiring and advancing it, than to preserve the flourishing religious life of monks through the perseverance of that same spirit.

We therefore confirm your undertaking by the authority of our office, exhorting you to remain steadfast in it, and, as though God were exhorting you through us, beseeching you to do so. Accordingly, to all who profess canonical life in your community according to the rule of this order and, with the Lord’s assistance, persevere in it, we, although unworthy vicars of the apostles, grant their blessing and the remission of sins, by the authority granted to them and to us by the Lord. We establish that no one shall be permitted at all to alter this form of your order, from which we confidently expect much fruit in the Lord.

We also establish that no member of your profession, after placing a person over his head in God’s stead [that is, after submitting to a superior], may, prompted by frivolity or under the pretext of a stricter religious life, dare to leave the same cloister without the permission of the provost and the entire congregation. No abbot, bishop, or monk shall receive one who leaves unless he has a letter of security issued jointly by the community.

We also decree that the tithes of the newly cultivated lands of the same canonical community belong to it, without prejudice to the rights of neighboring churches.

You, therefore, dearest sons in Christ, must labor with even greater care and devotion in the discipline of the rule, so that, the freer you are from secular disturbances, the more earnestly you may strive with all the strength of mind and body to please God. Above all, take care to observe the venerable decrees of the Roman Church, under whose protection, by the Lord’s gift, you have been fortified against every yoke imposed by the living.

As a sign of this liberty from the Roman Church, each year you shall pay to the Lateran palace, for the daily use of us and our successors, one white linen cloth and a stole.

If in the future any archbishop, bishop, emperor, prince or duke, count or viscount, judge, or any person whatsoever, powerful or powerless, knowingly and rashly attempts to act against this charter of our privilege and to invalidate anything that has been granted or established, then, after being warned a second or third time, if he does not correct the matter by suitable satisfaction, we decree that he shall be subject to the peril of his honor and office, and by the authority of apostolic power we separate him from the body of Christ and the Church. But for those who preserve these provisions, may peace and mercy from God be preserved throughout the present and future ages. Amen.

Given at Anagni on the Kalends of February, in the year 1090 of the Lord’s incarnation, in the fifteenth indiction, in the pontificate of the lord Pope Urban II.

Written by the hand of Lanfranc, acting in place of the chancellor of the sacred palace, with his sign.

### LIX. Bull of Pope Urban II for the monastery of Catania. [Note: The chronological notices are defective.] (1092)

[*Acta sanctorum* of the Bollandists, February, vol. I, 655.]

URBAN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved brother Ansgarius, bishop of Catania and abbot, and to his canonically appointed successors, forever.

As we are taught by the truthful writings of the most blessed Father and most elegant teacher Gregory I, it is established that Catania—where Blessed Agatha was born and suffered—once shone with the glory of episcopal dignity. But after the island of Sicily was captured by the peoples of the Saracens, both there and throughout the other cities of the province, the glory of the episcopate declined and the dignity of the Christian faith perished.

After nearly four hundred years, however, when divine clemency looked upon its people, the same island was restored to Christian rule through the most vigorous Count Roger. Moreover, that distinguished count, a most devoted son of the Roman Church, desiring everywhere, as circumstances allowed, to restore the former glory of the cities, determined that the mother church of Blessed Agatha, situated at Catania, should become a monastery, so that brothers serving God there might implore the mercy of almighty God for his salvation, for the soul of his deceased wife, and for the souls of the soldiers who had restored that land to Christian rule through their blood.

We therefore approve the devotion of so great a man, as is fitting, and by the authority of this present charter decree that the monastery shall remain there perpetually. But because, as we said above, the city of Catania is known to have once been distinguished by the prerogative of an episcopal see, we add and establish by this decree that in our time it shall return to that same prerogative. Whoever is elected by the monks as abbot in the aforesaid church shall also preside over the people as bishop.

Moreover, the entire city and whatever lies around it—cities, villages, or fortified settlements—which the aforesaid count has offered or will offer to the same monastery and to Blessed Peter, together with whatever may be found to have belonged by ancient right to the Church of Catania, whether in the diocese or in possessions, shall always remain wholly within the jurisdiction of the abbot and bishop. With the Lord’s assistance, the same abbot and bishop shall regularly and canonically govern both the clergy and the entire people.

Therefore, granting you, as the first bishop of the city of Catania after so many years, as though consecrated by the hands of Blessed Peter, by the authority of this present privilege, we decree that this decision shall remain permanently ratified for your successors also, so that they may always be consecrated by the Roman pontiff and may always preside as abbots over the monks and as bishops over the people.

Finally, so that these provisions may remain perpetually firm, whole, and unimpaired, we grant to our beloved son Count Roger, champion of the Christian faith, and to his wife, sons, and soldiers—for whose redemption he offered the city of Catania with its entire diocese, restored through his labor to Blessed Peter, prince of the apostles—the grace of God and of his apostles, blessing, remission of sins, and benevolence, through the authority of the apostolic office which we bear unworthily. Thus may their triumphs in the present, their magnificent deeds, gifts, and offerings flourish, and may they find the rewards of eternal blessedness in the future.

But if anyone—which may it not happen—should obstinately attempt to oppose these apostolic constitutions of ours, and, after being warned a second or third time, does not correct the matter by suitable satisfaction, let him know that he will be severely punished by the indignation of almighty God and the holy apostles, and pierced by the anathema of the apostolic see which he has despised. But for those who preserve these provisions, may peace and mercy from God be preserved throughout the present and future ages. Amen, amen.

Given at Anagni on the seventh day before the Ides of March, in the fourteenth indiction, by the hand of John, cardinal deacon of the holy Roman Church, in the year 1091 of the Lord’s incarnation, in the fourth year of the pontificate of the lord Pope Urban II.

### LX. Urban II undertakes to protect the monastery of Saint Sophia at Benevento and confirms its possessions and rights. (1092)

[MANSI, *Councils* XX, 699.]

URBAN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son in Christ Madelmo, abbot of the venerable monastery of Saint Sophia within Benevento, and to his successors regularly appointed in his place, forever.

The Church acknowledges the power of binding and loosing in heaven and on earth, principally entrusted by the Lord to the holy apostle Peter and his successors, in those words with which the Lord addressed him: “Whatever you bind on earth will be bound also in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth will be loosed also in heaven” (Matthew 16). To him also, by that same Lord as author, firmness in himself and the confirmation of complete faith are granted, when it is said to him: “I have prayed for you that your faith may not fail; and you, once converted, strengthen your brothers” (Luke 12).

It is therefore necessary for us, who, although unworthy, appear to occupy Peter’s place, to correct what is perverse, strengthen what is right, and arrange in the whole Church those things that must be arranged according to the will of the eternal Judge, so that our judgment may proceed from his presence and our eyes may see equity.

Therefore, assenting to your just petitions, we decree by the authority of this present charter that the monastery of Blessed Sophia, over which you are known to preside with the Lord as author, shall remain perpetually under the protection and jurisdiction of the apostolic see, as it has remained until now. It shall be regarded as subject only to the Roman Church and free from the yoke of all other churches or persons.

We also confer upon you and your successors, who are to be regularly advanced, everything that has been granted by the privileges of our predecessors to your predecessors or to you for the immunity or possession of the same monastery.

Moreover, we confirm for perpetual possession the cells, churches, or villages which the aforesaid monastery appears to have acquired justly and reasonably through its own industry, namely, the church, and so forth.

(The possessions of the monastery are enumerated.)

Therefore, by this present charter of our privilege, we establish by apostolic authority that whatever the same monastery justly possesses today, and whatever it may lawfully and canonically acquire in the future through the grant of pontiffs, the generosity of rulers, or the offerings of the faithful, shall remain secure and unimpaired for you and your successors.

We decree that no one at all shall be permitted rashly to disturb the same monastery, or to take away, retain after taking away, diminish, harass with presumptuous vexations, or otherwise trouble its possessions. Rather, everything shall be preserved intact and shall in every way contribute to the needs of those to whom it was granted for their sustenance and governance.

When the abbot now dies, or any of his successors, no one shall be placed over the monastery through any form of subterfuge or violence except one whom the brothers unanimously, or the sounder part of the brothers’ council, has elected. The person elected shall be consecrated by the Roman pontiff.

You shall receive chrism, holy oil, the consecrations of altars and basilicas, and the ordination of monks who are now to be advanced to sacred orders from the bishops in whose dioceses you are situated, provided that they possess the grace and communion of the apostolic see and provide these things freely and without corruption. If any of these conditions should obstruct the matter, you shall be permitted to receive the aforesaid sacraments from any Catholic bishop whom you wish.

But to you, whom we embrace with especially devoted charity, we personally grant this privilege through the particular benevolence of the apostolic see: five times each year—namely, on the day of the holy Resurrection, Pentecost, the Nativity of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ, the solemnity of the twelve holy brothers, and also the feast of the holy martyr Mercury—you may use gloves and campagi, but only at the solemn celebration of Mass.

If in the future any archbishop or bishop, emperor or duke, king, prince, count or viscount, judge, or any person whatsoever, great or small, powerful or powerless, knowingly and rashly attempts to act against this charter of our privilege or, with deliberate intent, to violate it, then, after being warned and admonished a second or third time, if he does not correct the matter by suitable satisfaction, we decree that he shall be subject to the peril of his honor and office and shall also be removed; by the authority of apostolic power we separate him from the body of Christ and the Church. But for those who preserve these provisions, may peace and mercy from the Lord be preserved throughout the present and future ages. Farewell.

Given at Anagni by the hand of John, deacon of the Holy Roman See, on the day before the Ides of March, in the fifteenth indiction, in the fifth year of the pontificate of the lord Pope Urban II, and in the year 1092 of the incarnation of our Lord and eternal Father Jesus Christ.

### LXI. Privilege of Pope Urban II for the monastery of Reinhardsborn. (1092)

[*Sacred Thuringia*, Frankfurt, 1737, folio, p. 61.]

Urban, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Gisilbert, beloved brother in Christ, abbot of the venerable monastery of the holy Mother of God and Virgin Mary and of Saint John the Evangelist, situated in the place called Reginherisbrunn, and to his successors regularly appointed, forever.

It is fitting for us to assent to just vows and to lend our ears to just petitions: although unworthy, we appear, by the disposition of the Lord, to be guardians and heralds of justice, placed upon the lofty watchtower of the chief apostles Peter and Paul. Therefore, beloved and venerable son in Christ, assenting to your just petitions, we have undertaken to cherish and protect, under the special guardianship of the Apostolic See, the monastery of Reginherisbrunn, over which, by God’s authority, you preside, in honor of the holy Mother of God and Virgin Mary and of Saint John the Evangelist, to whose name it is dedicated.

This monastery, as is known, Count Louis built at his own expense within the forest called Luiba [Col. 0343B] and enriched by the contribution of his possessions; for the salvation of his soul and of the souls of his parents, he offered it to the blessed apostles Peter and Paul and assigned it perpetually to the protection of the Roman pontiff. Therefore, confirming his vow by the favor of our assertion, we establish by apostolic authority in this document of our privilege that whatever the same religious count contributed to the aforesaid monastery—servile persons, fields, forests, meadows, waters and watercourses, mills, and holdings around the aforementioned forest of Luiba—and whatever it justly possesses today, or may thereafter justly and canonically acquire through the grant of pontiffs, the generosity of princes, or the offerings of the faithful, shall remain secure and inviolate for you and your successors.

[Col. 0343C] We decree, therefore, that absolutely no one shall be permitted rashly to disturb the same monastery, to remove or retain its possessions, to diminish them, or to harass them by presumptuous vexations. Rather, everything shall be preserved intact and shall in every way serve the uses of those for whose support and administration it was granted, without prejudice to the canonical right of bishops.

We further establish that the aforesaid count shall remain advocate of your monastery, as he was chosen by you, for as long as he lives; and, if they are suitable, his descendants shall succeed him. Henceforth we decree that no one may presume to be advocate of your monastery except one whom the brothers, by common consent, have chosen. As a token of the liberty received from the Roman Church, according to the constitution of the aforesaid count, you shall pay each year two solidi of your coinage to the Lateran palace.

If, however, in the future any archbishop or bishop, emperor or king, prince or duke, count or viscount, judge, or any other person, powerful or powerless, knowingly attempts to act against this privilege, then, after being warned a second or third time, if he does not make amends by suitable satisfaction, we decree that he shall be subject to the danger of losing his honor and office, and we separate him from the body of Christ and of the Church by the authority of apostolic power. But for those who preserve it, may peace from God and mercy be preserved in the present and future ages. Amen.

Given at Anagni through the hands of John, cardinal deacon of the Holy Roman Church, on the tenth day before the Kalends of April [March 23], in the fifteenth indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1092.

### LXII. Urban II confirms the possessions of the monks of Silvanès, “although,” he says, “your congregation and the place are still unknown to us.” (Year 1092.)

[Mabillon, *Annales Benedictini* V, 297.]

[Col. 0344A]

To the beloved sons gathered at the place called Silvanès for the service of almighty God and the warfare of monastic discipline: greetings and apostolic blessing.

Two of your brothers came to us and humbly sought the support of the Apostolic See, so that they might obtain for your place the privilege of apostolic protection. Although your congregation and the place are still unknown to us, nevertheless, because they reached us after great labors, we did not wish, in accordance with the customary mercy of the Apostolic See, to be altogether lacking either to their petition or to yours.

Therefore, by this document of the present decree, we grant and confirm whatever has been justly and reasonably granted to you and to your place up to this hour, and whatever shall in the future be granted justly and legally. Moreover, so that, with the Lord’s approval, the vigor of monastic religion that has already taken root there for three years may be strengthened and grow, we exhort both those nearby and those far away to honor, enrich, and exalt that place for the salvation of their souls by contributions of their goods, etc.

Given through the hands of John, cardinal deacon, on the third day before the Ides of April [April 11], in the fifteenth indiction, at Anagni.

### LXIII. Urban II subjects the Corsican bishoprics to the Church of Pisa, on account of the citizens’ merits toward the Roman Church, at the request of Countess Matilda. (Year 1092.)

[Ughelli, *Italia sacra* III, 369.]

[Col. 0344C]

Urban, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved brother in Christ Daibert, bishop of Pisa, and to his successors canonically appointed, forever.

Although, by the authority of the Apostolic See, we acknowledge ourselves debtors to all the sons of the holy Church because of our benevolence, nevertheless we ought to devote ourselves with more attentive charity to those places and persons that cling more specially and familiarly to the Roman Church and that merit its greater favor through more devoted obedience, more frequent services, and greater assistance.

For the Lord himself says through the prophet, “Those who honor me I will honor”; and, promising his disciples a reward for the hardships they had endured for him, he said: “You are those who have remained with me in my temptations, and I dispose for you, just as my Father disposed for me, a kingdom.”

Since, therefore, during such a great and long-lasting storm of schism, the glorious city of Pisa has for a long time made the holy Roman and apostolic Church its debtor through many labors and services, and since your fraternity, inflamed by the divine fire of charity for the liberty of that same Holy Roman Church, has not only expended its resources but is also prepared to expend itself, and has cooperated in our labors and become a participant in our tribulations in many ways, we take care, with the Lord’s cooperation, to answer such merits with benefits. Thus, just as we remember the past, so may they, endowed with the favor of such great grace, prove in future times more faithful and devoted to the Holy Roman Church, and may they continually respond to their kindly mother by assisting, helping, and serving her.

Indeed, the disposition of the divine majesty has deigned in our times both to make the glory of the city of Pisa illustrious through triumphs over the Saracens and to advance it through increase in temporal affairs, so as to exalt it above the neighboring cities. Therefore we, as followers and cooperators of divine mercy, have resolved also to glorify it in spiritual matters, as the testimony of ecclesiastical writings confirms that our predecessors once did for many cities.

Accordingly, with the counsel of our brother bishops, cardinal priests and deacons, and with the assent of our other faithful, indeed moved by their prayers, and also yielding to the earnest petitions of our most beloved daughter in Christ, Countess Matilda, who has exposed herself to every extremity for the cause of the Apostolic See, we commit and subject, by the authority of this present decree, the bishoprics of the island of Corsica to be governed and administered, in honor of our most holy Lady Mary, Mother of God, and of the holy apostles Peter and Paul, to the holy Church of Pisa, over which you, dearest brother Daibert, preside by God’s authority. We promote you, venerable brother, to be archbishop of that same island, granting perpetually the same jurisdiction and the same honor to your successors who shall enter by the legitimate election of clergy and people and through the hands of the Roman pontiff, just as Landulf, Gerard, and you yourself are known to have been ordained.

For the island of Corsica, through the length of its distances and the negligence of its shepherds, through the arrogance of its lords and the disuse of our legates, with many obstacles intervening, has grown lukewarm in obedience and devotion to the Apostolic See. Abandoned to dissolution and disorder, it has almost entirely neglected the discipline of ecclesiastical order. We desire and command, with the Lord’s approval, that this discipline be restored to the rule of justice and the vigor of Christianity through the vigilance of you and your successors, since you are nearer to them and more familiar with the Apostolic See.

Therefore, dearest brother in Christ, we commit to your jurisdiction, administration, and care the goods of those churches, to be governed and defended according to God, and whatever you find badly destroyed or unlawfully usurped is to be restored to ecclesiastical use, so that, by God’s authority, the discipline of ecclesiastical religion may flourish there once more.

[Col. 0345D] We therefore grant to your fraternity the pallium, that is, the fullness of pontifical office, through the generosity of the Apostolic See. By ecclesiastical law, you and your successors may use it only in celebrating the solemnities of Mass on the following solemn days: the Nativity of the Lord, Epiphany, the Hypapante [Presentation of the Lord], the Lord’s Supper, Easter, the Ascension, Pentecost, the three solemnities of the holy Mother of God and Virgin Mary, the feast days of Saint John the Baptist and of the holy apostles, the Commemoration of All Saints, the consecration of a basilica, the consecration of suffragan bishops, the ordination of clerics, your annual birthday, and also the solemnity of the blessed martyr and pontiff Sixtus, whose honor is to be maintained through the vigorous practice of effective deeds.

We wish you to vindicate the spirit of this garment in every respect. For the honor of this garment is humility and justice. Therefore let your fraternity hasten to show itself humble in prosperity and, in adversity, should it occur, upright with justice; friendly toward the good and opposed to the wicked; never suppressing anyone who speaks the truth openly; devoted to works of mercy according to the strength of your substance, yet desiring also to devote yourself beyond your ability; compassionate toward the weak; rejoicing with those who are benevolent; exulting in the joys of others as though they were your own; fierce in correcting vices; soothing the minds of your hearers in the enjoyment of virtues; and, in anger of spirit, terrifying without anger.

This, dearest brother, is the dignity of the pallium you have received. If you carefully preserve it, you will possess inwardly what you have shown yourself to receive outwardly.

Given at Anagni through the hands of John, cardinal deacon of the Holy Roman Church, on the tenth day before the Kalends of May [April 22], in the fifteenth indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1092, and in the fifth year of the pontificate of Lord Urban II.

### LXIV. Letter of Urban II to B[erengar], archbishop of Tarragona. He warns him not to act negligently in restoring the Church of Tarragona and to obey the primate, the archbishop of Toledo, now appointed his vicar throughout Spain and in the province of Narbonne. (Year 1092.)

[Mansi, *Concilia* XX, 682.]

[Col. 0346C]

Your Belovedness knows, venerable brother in Christ, in what manner and under what condition we granted you the pallium and privilege: namely, how you, in your own faith, and the primates of the neighboring provinces promised us in writing that you would establish the restoration of the Church of Tarragona by every means. Now, however, we frequently hear that your former diligence and zeal have already ceased and that the restoration of Tarragona is almost failing.

Therefore, by this letter, we admonish you to be a diligent worker toward the completion of this good work. Remember, nevertheless, that you were appointed archbishop in such a way that both you and all the bishops of the province of Tarragona must be subject to the archbishop of Toledo as primate. For this was established by you in the privilege of the Church of Toledo, and we wish it to remain wholly ratified. Now, all the more, because we have entrusted to him the exercise of the responsibilities of our solicitude throughout Spain and in the province of Narbonne.

Given on the seventh day before the Kalends of May [April 25].

### LXV. Urban II grants Guarino, abbot of the monastery of Saint Lawrence of Aversa, the use of the mitre and ring. (Year 1092.)

[Mabillon, *Annales Benedictini* V, 292.]

At Anagni, on the Nones of May [May 7], of this year, Pope Urban was present. At that time he granted the grace of apostolic protection to Guarino, abbot of the monastery of Saint Lawrence the Martyr, situated near the city of Aversa and said to belong to the jurisdiction of blessed Peter; at that time it was also said to have grown from a small foundation into a great one.

The pontiff says that he was moved to grant this privilege because the brothers of that monastery had faithfully shared in the tribulations and hardships of the Roman Church. Among the other prerogatives of that place, he grants to Abbot Guarino and his successors the use of the mitre everywhere in celebrations of divine worship, but the use of the ring only at Masses on the principal feast days and in assemblies of councils.

Given at Anagni through the hands of John, cardinal deacon of the Holy Roman Church, in the fifteenth indiction, on the Nones of May [May 7], in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1092, in the fifth year of the pontificate.

### LXVI. Letter of Urban II to Peter, abbot of Cava. Concerning the privileges granted to the same monastery. (Year 1092.)

[Mansi, *Concilia* XX, 652.]

[Col. 0347B]

Urban, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the most reverend brother Peter, abbot of the monastery of Cava, and to his successors to be canonically promoted: perpetual greetings and apostolic blessing.

Although, by reason of the authority and benevolence of the Apostolic See, we acknowledge ourselves debtors to all parts of the holy Church, those places and persons that have clung more specially and familiarly to the Roman Church, and that are known to excel through greater religious devotion, nevertheless induce us to devote ourselves to them with more attentive charity.

Therefore, adhering firmly to the institutions of our predecessor of apostolic memory, Gregory VII, we fortify by this document of our privilege the monastery of Cava, in which the highest religious observance flourishes, which he himself especially loved and fortified by the privilege of his institution; and we decree that it shall be entirely free from every yoke, both secular and ecclesiastical.

For that apostolic pontiff, while he was still exercising the office of archdeacon in the holy Roman Church, requested the aforesaid place from Gisulf, then prince of Salerno, in whose hands it had been. He also acquired from that prince and granted to the same holy place, absolutely and with all its inhabitants and future inhabitants, many cells that the prince himself had until then held in his own hands, both on Mount Cilento and in its dependencies and in the places called Pasciano and Metelliano, the castle of Saint Adjutus, and the dependencies of those places, together with their rights, forced labor services, auxiliary services, and payments, whether on account of lands or for each hearth in those places, as we ourselves have seen set out more fully in the register of that prince.

This donation we confirm by apostolic authority with certain knowledge. Moreover, when he sent to that famous place of Cluny, he summoned you from there to place you as abbot over the aforesaid monastery. Thereafter he loved, fostered, and protected you together with all the places and persons subject to you. Once he became pontiff, he confirmed their liberty by a document of his decree; thus, by God’s favor, it has remained free from the yoke of all living persons down to our own times.

In our days, however, Alphanus, archbishop of the Church of Salerno and our brother, began by every means to strive for the subjection of that place. When we were preparing to dedicate the basilica of that place, he complained that the rights of his Church were being diminished. We offered him abundant satisfaction concerning his right; but when he had reached the appointed and accepted time for action, he refused to undertake the action.

Thus, in the presence of our most reverend brothers, the bishops Ubaldo of Sabina, Oddo of Albano, Berard of Palestrina, John of Tusculum, Bruno of Segni, Rangerius of Rieti, Gerard of Troia, John of Riopoli, and the cardinals of our Church: Hermann, priest of the title of the Four Crowned Saints; Gregory, priest of the title of Saint Vitalis; Benedict, priest of Saint Susanna; Gregory, of the deaconry of Saint Mary in Via Lata; John, of the deaconry of Saint Mary in the Greek School; Peter, of the deaconry of Saint Hadrian; James, of the deaconry of Saint Eustace; and Tencrone, of the deaconry of Saint George at the Golden Veil; with our most beloved son Duke Roger also present, together with an innumerable crowd of clergy and laity, and with the assistance of our Lord Jesus Christ, whose place on earth we, although unworthy, occupy, we dedicated with our own hands the basilica at the place commonly called Metelliana Cava, on the Nones of September [September 5].

We granted the same monastery, in consideration of a certain special prerogative of charity that we had experienced in that monastery—or rather, because of its perfect observance of religion—an indulgence while we were still constituted in the lesser orders.

Whoever, by the Lord’s help, is placed in a state of penance, and comes to the aforesaid place and remains there for one day before the consecration of the basilica and throughout the following day, as well as on Holy Thursday and throughout the following day of Good Friday, shall obtain from the Lord, for all sins of which he has been truly contrite and has confessed, that indulgence and pardon which he would deserve by going to and returning from Saint James of Compostela.

At all other times and on all other days, those who come there out of devotion shall, by the special grace of the Apostolic See, obtain an indulgence of four years and the same number of forty-day periods for their sins.

Whoever comes to your chapel situated in the same monastery and consecrated on the same day by our venerable brother Bruno, the aforesaid bishop of Segni, on the days and feasts mentioned above, shall obtain from the Lord seven years and the same number of forty-day periods of indulgence for his confessed sins.

Likewise, those who come, on the aforementioned feast days and on all the feasts of the glorious Virgin, to the church built in the estate adjacent to and rising above the same monastery, dedicated on that day by our aforementioned venerable brother Rangerius, bishop of Rieti, shall merit from the Lord seven years and the same number of forty-day periods of indulgence. That church was built under the title of the Virgin.

We grant and confirm by perpetual edict that you and your successors may freely build churches throughout the lands belonging and to belong to your monastery, mark them with the cross, and exercise other pontifical and spiritual functions. The power of conferring sacred orders, consecrating basilicas and altars, and preparing chrism is, however, entirely withheld from you and your successors.

We decree that both the head of the monastery itself and the churches that it now possesses, whether parish or rural, situated only within the city and diocese of Salerno, shall be exempt, by the fullness of our power and special grace, from every episcopal right and jurisdiction. Thus neither you nor your successors, nor the brothers of that monastery nor the secular clergy, shall in any way be constrained in the aforesaid city and diocese by the Salernitan prelate and chapter through any legal right or contentious court. Rather, the churches, together with all their rights and dependencies, shall be fully subject to the monastery itself.

If you choose to promote any of your monks or secular clergy residing in the churches of the aforesaid city and diocese to sacred orders, it shall be lawful for you and your successors to summon whichever bishop you prefer, provided that he is Catholic; in other dioceses, however, the diocesan bishop must first be consulted. In the churches situated in the aforesaid city and diocese, the diocesan bishop shall presume to demand nothing. Rather, both the monks, if clergy are lacking, and the clergy themselves shall exercise, without anyone’s opposition, the entire priestly office required and demanded by the care of souls.

Concerning whatever is donated or bequeathed to the same monastery by Catholic Christians, whether among the living or in a last will, by anyone and anywhere, none of the diocesan bishops shall be permitted, under pretext of any custom, to demand a fourth or third part of those bequests or donations, whether immovable or movable.

If, as time goes on, anything is attempted by anyone against the terms of this concession, we now decree that such an act is void in law, and that no prescription based on the passage of time shall run in this matter.

If anyone chooses burial for himself at the same place or in its churches, it shall be lawful for you, your successors, and the brothers residing in the churches of that monastery to bury him in its cemetery without anyone’s opposition, provided that he is regarded as a Christian and Catholic.

We further establish, to remain perpetually valid, that whenever a dispute arises among the vassals of the same monastery, even if the monastery itself is involved, it shall be lawful for you, your successors, and the parties [perhaps “the fathers”] of that monastery to decide such complaints with justice, notwithstanding any common law enacted on this matter.

Moreover, when the aforesaid most excellent duke witnessed the solemnity of this dedication, he was, as we believe, moved by the divine Spirit and earnestly petitioned us and our apostolate to confirm by apostolic authority the donation and confirmation that he intended to make to the same monastery out of reverence for the holy and undivided Trinity and for the remedy of his sins, and to order that it be carefully inserted into our privilege.

Therefore, yielding to his most just petitions in this matter, and in favor of that place, which we pursue with special love and devotion alike, we caused those concessions and donations to be inserted into our present privilege for greater security.

### Privilege of Duke Roger for the monastery of Cava

The aforesaid duke granted to the same monastery in perpetuity that the fathers of that monastery, without any opposition from his heirs or successors, might exact and receive the entire tenth part of the fish caught in the sea from the ravine called Gallocauda [Gallocauta] as far as the river of Caetra [Caetera], which belongs to the territory of that monastery for five miles out into the sea.

The aforesaid monastery shall freely sell its merchandise without any payment, fee, or exit duty, not only on its own shores or in its own ports but throughout his entire duchy. He forever declared both the monastery itself and those who buy its merchandise free from every levy [or “preparation,” *praeparatio*].

He also granted that all the people whom the monastery has or shall have in the aforesaid places—Metelliano, Pasciano, the neighboring village, the castle of Saint Adjutus on Mount Cilento, and the dependencies of those places—both clergy and laity, shall always be free from every exaction of money or of any other goods that he, his heirs, or his successors might at any time decide to demand from his people for any need or cause.

He further granted that you should have free jurisdiction over those people and all their offenses, without any bailiff or minister of his, and that they should come to justice in the court of the monastery through its summons [the text has *summosam*, uncertain] and should reasonably be judged by judges whom you appoint. He also granted you the free power to appoint public notaries, both in civil cases and in all criminal cases except those in which the convicted ought lawfully to die. In all other criminal cases, in which they ought to undergo a punishment other than death, you may do whatever you wish. The same applies to duels, if they arise from such cases.

If appeals should be useful to your people, they shall appeal to your court, since the duke granted you perpetual power to raise, establish, and order whatever he and his successors might have been able to raise, establish, and order concerning the aforesaid people of those places and the tenement in which they live.

He also granted you in perpetuity that, wherever in his duchy you or your successors might personally be present, if one or more people there had been sentenced to death or to any punishment, you might free them as you wished. Wherever you traveled through his duchy and encountered condemned persons being taken to hanging or beheading, you might, if you wished, have them released.

If the vassal people of the monastery sell, offer, donate, or otherwise alienate the lands that they hold from the same monastery, and claim that their custom permits them to do so, the aforesaid duke enacted and firmly prohibited that, if it clearly appears that all lands held by those people from the same monastery belong to the monastery and have been alienated without its request, you may seize them and restore them to the lord of the monastery, notwithstanding any custom—unless perhaps they can defend themselves by lawful prescription or other just grounds showing that they have held those lands legitimately.

The aforesaid duke also granted that if any of his counts, barons, knights, or other Catholic persons throughout his duchy wish to offer and alienate, in whole or in part, to the said monastery anything that they hold from him in fief, they shall have the power to do so as they wish. The monastery may receive the goods thus transferred to it without any opposition from him, his heirs, or his successors, retain them in its dominion, and thereafter the fief, or part of it, shall be free from every service or levy.

If anyone, whether among the monastery’s vassals or others, who holds immovable or movable goods of his own dies without a legitimate or natural heir, or commits an offense by which those goods could legally fall into the hands of the state, it shall be lawful for you to recall those goods to your dominion, without any opposition from his heirs, his successors, or his officials; no power over those goods shall be reserved to him or to the state.

He also granted that you may summon those who hold the monastery’s goods to your court, to show how they hold those goods. If they cannot reasonably show that the goods belong to them, or cannot demonstrate that they are protected by lawful prescription, namely one hundred years, you may, by virtue of this concession, take possession of those goods and restore them to the dominion of the same monastery, the common law concerning this article being entirely revoked.

He further granted you in perpetuity that, if no manifest fault of you, your successors, or the fathers of that monastery should intervene against the same duke, his heirs, or successors, and if the aforesaid matters concerning his community should in future, for any other reason, be wholly or partly consigned to oblivion or omitted, he established by his oath then sworn in our presence and by this his sanction that the prescription itself should be held entirely void. [The transmitted wording is syntactically uncertain.]

Whenever you should thereafter bring his heir and successors before us concerning this matter, he gave and left firm instructions under the protection of our divine and apostolic blessing that all of them should confirm all those concessions and exceptions for you by their privileges, without any payment or tedious delay. None of them may presume to violate or alter them; rather, they must preserve and maintain them unharmed until you have remained in sincere faith toward him and his heirs and successors.

We ratify, approve, and confirm with certain knowledge, by apostolic authority and the fullness of our power, these concessions, confirmations, exceptions, and indulgences granted to the same monastery by that most beloved son, Duke Roger.

We decree and strengthen by perpetual edict that whoever harms or disturbs the said monastery in its rights, possessions, or liberties may be excommunicated by you, your successors, and the fathers of that monastery, whatever their preeminence or status may be, by the authority of this present privilege and after canonical warning has first been given; and they may be declared excommunicated and unable to be absolved unless they make worthy satisfaction.

This shall be so notwithstanding any privilege granted or to be granted to them that they may not be excommunicated or placed under interdict, unless that privilege makes full and explicit mention of this concession.

If anyone attempts to act against the authority of this decree, without prejudice to the reverence and dignity of the Apostolic See and its legates, let him know that he will lose the grace of the blessed apostle Peter and suffer the blow of apostolic indignation.

But may those who obey and preserve the writings of this privilege receive worthy recompense from God and obtain the apostolic blessing.

### Subscriptions

I, Urban, bishop of the Catholic Church, have subscribed.  
I, Ubaldo, bishop of Sabina, have subscribed.  
I, Berard, bishop of Palestrina, have subscribed.  
I, Oddo, bishop of Albano, have subscribed.  
I, John, bishop of Ascoli, have subscribed.  
I, Bruno, bishop of Segni, have subscribed.  
I, John, bishop of Riopoli, have subscribed.  
I, Rangerius, bishop of Rieti, have subscribed.  
I, Gerard, bishop of Troia, have subscribed.  
I, Hermann, cardinal priest, have subscribed.  
I, Gregory, cardinal priest, have subscribed.  
I, Benedict, cardinal priest, have subscribed.

Given at Salerno through the hands of John, cardinal deacon of the Holy Roman Church, on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of October [September 14], in the fifteenth indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1092, in the fifth year of the pontificate of Lord Urban II.

### LXVII. Urban II affirms to Saint Bruno, founder of the Carthusians, and to Laninus that the place was granted by Count Roger and confirmed by Theodore, bishop of Squillace. (Year 1092.)

[*Acta sanctorum* of the Bollandists, October, vol. III, day 6, p. 643.]

[Col. 0353A]

Urban, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons in Christ Bruno and Laninus: greetings and apostolic blessing.

The affection of a pious will ought to be brought to completion through diligent effort. Since, therefore, it is part of our office to provide, insofar as the Lord grants us power, for the quiet of the servants of God, we graciously assent to your petitions, most beloved and most reverend sons in Christ.

By this document of apostolic privilege, therefore, we establish by apostolic authority that the place which, by the Lord’s disposition, you have chosen for your habitation shall remain entirely free from the yoke, power, injury, and annoyance of all persons, together with the whole forest and mountain, land and water, for a space of one league [another reading: *leucae*] on every adjoining side, entirely under your administration and that of your successors, just as it was granted to you by our beloved son Count Roger and confirmed by our brother Theodore, bishop of Squillace.

Within the aforesaid space no one shall be permitted, on account of pasture, agriculture, fishing, timber, or any other cause, to inflict injury or annoyance upon you or your successors. Rather, you shall possess, administer, order, and distribute the whole according to your will.

If you should require anything further belonging to episcopal office, we grant you free permission by this decree to have recourse to whichever of the neighboring bishops you prefer.

We also decree that the use of the tithes from the labor of you or of your servants shall belong to you. If any offense of your servants should occur, all correction of them shall remain solely in your hands.

No one shall interfere in any matter belonging to you on any pretext without your consent, so that you may devote yourselves with free minds to the contemplation of almighty God and, by his favor, may attain the sweetness of his face.

If, however, in the future any archbishop or bishop, emperor or king, prince or duke, count [Col. 0353D] or viscount, judge, or any other person, powerful or powerless, knowingly attempts to act against this document of our privilege, then, after being warned a second or third time, if he does not make amends by suitable satisfaction, we decree that he shall be subject to the danger of losing his honor and office, and we separate him from the body of Christ and of the Church by the authority of apostolic power.

But for those who preserve it, may peace from God and mercy be preserved in the present and future ages. Amen, amen, amen.

Given through the hands of John, cardinal deacon of the Holy Roman Church, on the day before the Ides of October [October 14], in the first indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1092, and in the fifth year of the pontificate of Lord Urban II.

### LXVIII. Letter of Urban II to Rainald, archbishop of Reims, and his suffragans.—He rebukes them for having allowed the king to dismiss his wife and take another. (Year 1092.)

[MANSI, *Councils*, XX, 686.]

[Col. 0354A]

Urban, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable fellow brothers and fellow bishops, Rainald of Reims and his suffragans, greeting and apostolic blessing.

If you weighed with due consideration the office that you hold as priests, the disgrace of so great a crime would at least not have reached our ears unpunished. For since, as watchmen of the Lord’s Israel, appointed by God, you ought to proclaim their wickedness to the wicked and set yourselves as a wall before the house of Israel, we are astonished that you could in any way tolerate the king of so illustrious a realm—forgetful of human modesty, mindful of no fear of God—both abandoning his wife in an illicit manner and wickedly joining himself in love to the wife of his kinsman, against right, against law, against the sanctions of laws and canons, and against the customs of the whole Catholic Church.

This deed plainly portends both the confusion of the entire kingdom and the dissolution of your churches, and its disgrace rebounds upon your soul. For when one can oppose a sinner but does not do so, one consents. But you, dearest fellow brother Rainald, are especially struck by this guilt because the bishop of Silvanectum, subject to you, as we have heard, confirmed this crime of public adultery by his assent when he laid upon those adulterers the hand of priestly blessing. Even if they were marrying lawfully, the canons would nevertheless not permit such a blessing to be bestowed upon bigamists.

Therefore, having seen this letter, we command you by apostolic authority to take care to meet with the king promptly—a course your prudence ought already to have taken without our command—and, on behalf of God, of us, and likewise of yourselves, earnestly to admonish, reprove, entreat, and rebuke him, and compel him to desist from so great and horrible a crime. If he should despise this, necessity will press upon both us and you to gird ourselves, according to the duty of our office, to avenge the injuries done to divine law, and to pierce the adulterous Midianites with the sword of Phinehas.

[Col. 0354D]

Apply the same urgency to the recovery of our fellow brother, the bishop of Chartres. If the man who seized him should refuse to obey your warnings, subject both yourselves and him to excommunication; place under interdict the castles in which he holds him, and his territory as well, so that similar presumption may not henceforth be attempted against men of this order. As you love your order, so strive by every means to hasten this. Farewell.

Given on the sixth day before the Kalends of November, namely in the year of God’s Christ 1092.

### LXIX. Letter of Urban II to Goffrid, abbot of Saint-Albínus of Angers, and Bernon, abbot of the Holy Trinity of Vendôme.—He urges them to observe his judgment concerning their dispute. (Year 1092.)

[MANSI, *Councils*, XX, 684.]

[Col. 0355A]

Urban, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons in Christ, Goffrid, abbot of Saint-Albinus of Angers, and Bernon, abbot of the Holy Trinity of Vendôme, greeting and apostolic blessing.

In the year of the incarnation of the Lord 1092, in the fifth year of our pontificate and the first indiction, when I was in the province of Calabria at the monastery of Saint Mary called Matina, the monks of Saint-Albinus—Girard the prior, Milo, and Stephen—lodged a complaint against the monks of the Holy Trinity of Vendôme, namely Frotmund the prior and Ingebald the doorkeeper, who were present. They alleged that the brothers of Vendôme were unjustly and violently retaining the church of Saint Clement of Créon, which had been justly acquired by the monks of Saint-Albinus according to the custom of those times and possessed peacefully and without interruption for thirty years.

As each side endeavored to defend its case with its documents and arguments, the matter was debated at length and in detail on the first day of the complaint, but could not be brought to any conclusion. On the second day, likewise thoroughly discussed, it still reached no conclusion. On the third day, namely the twelfth day before the Kalends of December, while we were seated in the city of Anglone in Apulia, with religious and venerable bishops and cardinals, or deacons, of the holy Roman Church presiding, and with the most glorious Roman nobles and counts of Apulia, Bohemond and William, also standing by, the matter was again examined for a long time and in detail. At last, by God’s inspiration, it became clearer toward which side justice inclined.

Since each party confronted us with its own arguments—on one side the abbots’ agreement, the confirmation of pontiffs, and that of legates of the Roman Church; on the other, lawful entry and canonical possession for thirty years—we, who ought to weigh the causes of all the faithful in an even balance, took thought for the interests of both sides and preferred to settle the dispute by the fairness of a suitable agreement.

All who were present with us therefore commended this judgment. With the brothers of both monasteries consenting and confirming their good faith by pledging it into our hands, concord and peace were established between them in this manner: the monks of Vendôme were to give forever to the monastery of Saint-Albinus one of these three churches—either the church of Manitilium, or Saint Saturninus, or Saint John above the Loire—whichever the entire community of the Holy Trinity should choose, together with everything presently belonging to that church, movable and immovable, inside and outside it, within thirty days after they had returned home.

The brothers of Saint-Albinus therefore renounced into our hands and those of the brothers of Vendôme every dispute and every claim arising from this matter. The brothers of Vendôme, for their part, returned one of the aforementioned churches into our hands, and through us invested the same monks in it.

[Col. 0356A]

By the authority of this present document, therefore, we admonish and command your fraternity to keep and observe forever hereafter, as ratified and unshaken, this agreement arranged and established by us for the sake of peace and quiet. Whichever party does not accept the judgment of our decision or presumes to violate it shall be subject both to the severity of the canons and to the penalty of the lawful settlement, namely one hundred pounds of gold, and shall entirely lose the case.

Given at Taranto, on the eighth day before the Kalends of December.

### LXX. Letter of Urban II to Robert, count of Flanders.—That he should refrain from harassing clerics. (Year 1092.)

[MANSI, *Councils*, XX, 745.]

[Col. 0356B]

Urban, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son Robert, a vigorous soldier of all Flanders, greeting and apostolic blessing.

Remember, dearest son, how much you owe almighty God, who, contrary to the will of your parents, made you great from little, rich from poor, and a glorious prince from humble beginnings; and, what is greatest and rare among the princes of this world, endowed you with the gift of letters, knowledge, and religion. Remember him, therefore, who made you such, and strive in every way not to be found ungrateful for such great benefits.

[Col. 0356C]

Honor him, therefore, in his churches, and henceforth do not presume on any pretext to harass them, whatever their condition may be; nor, after their departure, convert their estates to your own use. Do not violently seize the money or anything else that they leave from their patrimony. Rather, let them be free both to serve God and to distribute their patrimonial possessions to whomever they wish.

If you claim that this has arisen from ancient custom in your land, you should know that your Creator said: “I am the truth,” not “custom” or “usage.” Therefore, dearest son, what we have said we both wish you to observe and command you through the keys of the blessed chief of the apostles; and, by honoring Christ, honor yourself in the matter of the liberty of clerics. He himself will honor the one who honors him, bearing witness to his own honor.

Farewell.

[Col. 0356D]

Given at Castranetum, on the fourth day before the Nones of December.

### LXXI. Letter of Urban II to the clergy and people of Arras.—That, having shaken off the yoke of the bishop of Cambrai, they should choose a bishop to be consecrated by the metropolitan. (Year 1092.)

[MANSI, *Councils*, XX, 671.]

Urban, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the clergy and people of Arras, greeting and apostolic blessing.

The Church of Arras, one of the nobler provincial churches of the metropolitan church of Reims, rich in the solemn records of the canons, was formerly the principal seat of a bishopric and had its own pontiff. It obtained its own diocese and the other episcopal rights through documents grounded in the firm reasoning of antiquity.

[Col. 0357A]

We therefore wish and command by apostolic authority that, once the yoke of subjection to Cambrai has been shaken off your Church and the dignity formerly possessed in the earliest times with reasonable firmness has been recovered, you diligently elect for yourselves and your Church a cardinal bishop useful to you, have the elected man consecrated by the hand of your metropolitan, and incorporate him into your Church.

By apostolic authority we forbid the man who has been elected by the canonical consent of clergy and people to evade, through any dissimulation, the election imposed upon him under this new arrangement. For it commonly happens that, during a time of persecution, Churches deprived of their orders, their peoples, and even temporal resources are temporarily entrusted to other Churches; but after they begin, by God’s gift, to abound once more in what had been diminished, they recover their former dignity.

At Castranetum, on the fourth day before the Nones of December.

### LXXII. Letter of Urban II to Rainald, archbishop of Reims.—He commands him to consecrate as bishop the man whom the clergy and people of Arras shall elect. (Year 1092.)

[MANSI, *Councils*, XX, 670.]

Urban, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved fellow brother Rainald, archbishop of Reims, greeting and apostolic blessing.

Let your fraternity know that the Church of Arras was one of the noble churches of the metropolitan church of Reims, had most religious men as its bishops, and possessed the other episcopal rights through documents grounded in firm arguments.

[Col. 0357C]

We therefore command and order you not to delay consecrating and incorporating into that Church the man whom that Church, by the canonical consent of clergy and people, shall elect for itself as bishop. For it commonly happens that, during a time of persecution, Churches deprived of their orders, their peoples, and even temporal resources are temporarily entrusted to other Churches; but after they begin, by God’s providence, to abound once more in what had been diminished, they recover their former dignity.

For it belongs solely to the apostolic episcopate to join episcopates, to separate those joined, or even to establish new ones. Relying, therefore, on our authority, do not fear to carry this out. It is indeed our will, with God’s cooperation, to restore to its former rank the dignity of the twelve episcopates of the Church of Reims [or: “of the churches of Reims”; the printed text is corrupt: *Remensi et mos, episcopatuum. HARD.*].

[Col. 0357D]

### LXXIII. Letter of Urban II to Guimund, bishop of Aversa.—He approves what he did concerning Richard, son of Borrell. (Years 1088–1093.)

[GRATIAN, *Decretum*, cause XXIV, question 2, chapter 3.]

We certainly commend what your fraternity is reported to have done concerning Richard, son of Borrell, out of zeal for God and love of souls. But you must not fear him so greatly, nor must you abstain so completely from his alms. Among the fathers of our faith, blessed Pope Leo, an outstanding teacher, says: “Those with whom we did not communicate while they were alive, we ought not to communicate with when they are dead.”

It is therefore clear that with those with whom we communicated while they were alive—speaking by way of contrast—we may also communicate after their death. We, placed plainly between two opposing groups, namely the impious and the schismatics, can in no way, and are not permitted to, communicate with schismatics. But we have communicated prudently with sinners and plunderers because they have supported the Church up to the present and promise that they will remain faithful in the future. Otherwise, we would have to leave the regions of this world.

It was also under such a pledge that we recently granted him absolution at the feast of the Nativity of blessed Peter. Since, therefore, the aforesaid man did not depart either as one expressly excommunicated or as one who had expressly communicated with excommunicates, but remained in the faith and service of his lord, it is permitted for us prudently—that is, for as long as we tolerate them—to share in his alms and to aid the soul of the deceased in every way consistent with Christian religion.

### LXXIV. Letter of Urban II to Anselm, archbishop of Milan.—Concerning the reconciliation of those who have fallen. (Years 1088–1093.)

[MANSI, *Councils*, XX, 645.]

It seems appropriate to our discretion that, in accordance with the tenor of our command, when according to the custom of your Church you begin to bless the sacred orders to be given to any others, you should cause those whom your prudence has judged worthy of reconciliation to be present during the blessing and the laying on of hands. You shall complete for them all the other rites of consecration except the anointing, and thus reconcile them to the sacred ministries.

### LXXV. Guerner of Merseburg is granted permission for a cleric who killed a boy by throwing a stone to remain in his order after undertaking perpetual penance. (Fragment.—Years 1088–1093.)

[GRATIAN, *Decretum*, cause I, distinction 50, chapter 37.]

A boy is said to have been killed by a cleric throwing a stone. For love of you, we permit him to remain in his order, provided that he always remains in penitence and fear.

### LXXVI. Letter of Urban II to Albert, bishop of Metz.—That he should treat with gentleness a certain priest who had obtained his dignity by simony. (Years 1091–1093.)

[GRATIAN, *Decretum*, cause I, question 5, chapter 3.]

[Col. 0358D]

You have stated that the bearer of this letter obtained the dignity of the priesthood unwillingly because of the carelessness of his parents, who gave money not to the bishop but to a certain one of his princes. Although the holy canons declare that he ought to be deposed, nevertheless, because he committed this offense unknowingly and under compulsion, and because he voluntarily pleaded that he be deposed from that same order, we advise your fraternity—out of consideration for discretion, which is the mother of all virtues, rather than from the rigor of the canons—to extend to him the bowels of mercy and allow him to remain in the same order.

This is to be understood as follows: if + that Church, which he served, does not suffer a shortage of priests +, let him remain suspended from priestly office. But if the usefulness of the Church should perhaps require him to assume the care of its governance, let him, by concession of his bishop and through the obedience of the brothers, exercise the priestly office.

[Col. 0359A]

### LXXVII. Letter of Pope Urban II to all the bishops of Britain.—He grants the pallium to the bishop of Dol, without prejudice to the rights of the Church of Tours. (Year 1093.)

[MARTÈNE, *Thesaurus anecdotorum*, III, 878.]

Our fellow brother R. [Rolland], bishop of Dol, presenting himself before our presence in order to request the pallium, produced letters of our holy predecessor Gregory VII, which that same apostolic pontiff had sent to your fraternity concerning Evenus, bishop of Dol.

The tenor of those letters stated that the aforesaid pontiff had granted Evenus the use of the pallium out of love for you and for the whole province, on the condition that at a suitable time he should in no way refuse to appear for an examination of the complaint that the archbishop of Tours had previously brought before his own tribunal and that of his predecessors concerning the subjection of that see and its denied obedience.

After this, the same letters continue:

> “But if, when reason and justice have shown the matter, it should appear that it ought to be subject to him, we wish and decree by apostolic authority that the right of the holy Church of Tours be preserved and that due subjection be exhibited by the Church of Dol. Nevertheless, we grant and confirm the use of the pallium no less to him and to his successors, so long as their accession and their life are worthy of approval.
