If, however, it should be established by lawful defense that it is free from the yoke of this subjection, whatever privileges of dignity may henceforth appear to belong to it, apostolic authority will not deny them; meanwhile, we decree by the present authority that you exhibit to it the subjection and obedience due to an archbishop.”

The aforesaid fellow brother and fellow bishop Rolland then swore before our brothers upon the holy Gospels that Pope Gregory VII had sent the sense of these letters to the bishops of Britain, and that the copy contained neither less nor more than the letters he himself had sent.

[Col. 0359D]

Thus, assured of the truth of the apostolic letters, we granted our aforesaid fellow brother the gift of the pallium, under the same condition, through the generosity of the apostolic see. We therefore send him back to you with the Lord’s help and commend him to your love by this letter, so that, receiving him with all honor and reverence, you may assist him by fraternal affection and service in restoring the condition of the Church he has received.

### LXXVIII. Letter of Pope Urban II to the princes and people of the Church of Dol.—That they should restore the property taken from the Church of Dol. (Year 1093.)

[MARTÈNE, cited above, col. 879.]

We have heard that the property of the Church of Dol is being usurped through your violence to such an extent that our fellow brother R. [Rolland], archbishop of Dol, is unable to obtain any justice concerning the possessions of that Church.

We therefore command your love not to presume henceforth to retain the property of that Church against the will of its bishop. Otherwise, you will encounter the indignation of the apostolic see, and whatever sentence our fellow brother may pronounce against you by canonical authority, we shall confirm by apostolic authority.

### LXXIX. Urban II confirms the purpose of the canons of Saint Paul of Narbonne to profess the regular life. (Year 1093.)

[*Gallia Christiana*, vol. VI, Instruments, p. 26, from the archive of the archbishop of Saint-Paul of Narbonne.]

[Col. 0360B]

Urban, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons in Christ, William the abbot and his brothers in the church of blessed Paul situated beside the walls of Narbonne, who have professed the regular life, and to their successors who shall remain in the observance of the regular life, forever.

The inclination of a pious will ought to be fostered with eager diligence, so that ecclesiastical usefulness may receive strength and increase through the favor of the apostolic see. We have given thanks to almighty God, whose mercy is better than life, because you have undertaken to renew the approved life of the holy Fathers and have devoted yourselves, at the prompting of the Holy Spirit, to revive the institutions of apostolic teaching that were unfamiliar at the beginnings of the holy Church but, as the age advanced, had almost entirely been erased.

For from the beginnings of the holy Church two ways of life were established for her children: one by which the weakness of the infirm is sustained, and another by which the blessed strength of the stronger is perfected. One remains little in Segor; the other ascends to the higher places of the mountain. Those who hold to the lower way use earthly goods; those who follow the higher way despise and abandon earthly goods.

This latter way, which by divine favor turns away from earthly things, is divided almost into two portions of the same purpose, namely canons and monks. The second has now become sufficiently widespread throughout the whole world through divine mercy and shines brightly; the first, however, as the fervor of the faithful has declined, has almost entirely ebbed away. This was instituted by the martyr and pontiff Urban; Augustine ordered it by his rules; Jerome shaped it through his letters.

[Col. 0360D]

It should therefore scarcely be judged a lesser merit to revive this primitive life of the Church with the Lord’s Spirit breathing upon and pursuing it than to preserve the flourishing religious life of monks through the perseverance of that same Spirit.

We therefore confirm your vow and your purpose by the authority of our office, exhort you to remain firm in it, and, as though God were exhorting through us, entreat you to do so. As long, therefore, as you and your successors remain in the observance of this religious life, we receive your Church under the protection of the apostolic see, while preserving the privileges and the canonical right of the bishop of Narbonne.

Because some among you still have not devoted themselves to this purpose, we establish and decree that, once they have either converted to the regular life or departed from this world, all the property of your Church now held in their power, and whatever shall henceforth be given to your Church, shall pass into the use of those living regularly. No canon shall be made or ordained there unless he has professed that he will live canonically.

By apostolic authority we forbid any other abbot—also called the provost—to be placed over them except one whom the common election of the brothers living regularly, from their own college or, if necessary, from another, with the counsel of the archbishop and according to God, shall determine ought to be elected, and this for edification, not destruction.

Therefore, dearest sons in Christ, responding always with ever greater zeal to the efforts of our love, strive vigorously to fulfill what you have promised to God. Let your light shine before human beings, so that they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven (Matthew 5:16). To ensure that these things remain firm, we sanction them by the power of that Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit.

Given at Troyes by the hand of John, cardinal deacon of the holy Roman Church, on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of April, in the first indiction, in the year of the incarnation of the Lord 1093, in the sixth year of the pontificate of Urban II.

### LXXX. Letter of Urban II to Rainald, archbishop of Reims.—He again commands him to arrange for a bishop to be placed over the Church of Arras. (Year 1093.)

[MANSI, *Councils*, XX, 670.]

[Col. 0361C]

Urban, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved fellow brother and fellow bishop Rainald of Reims, greeting and apostolic blessing.

The clerics of Arras have returned into our presence with letters from your fraternity, humbly petitioning for the restoration of their Church. They awaited the arrival of the clerics of Cambrai until the time that had been fixed for both parties in the provincial council. But no one from Cambrai came before us.

We therefore communicate the same matter to your fraternity in repeated letters and give the same command. For we most earnestly wish the metropolitan church of Reims, with the Lord’s assent, to be restored to the integrity of its ancient dignity.

[Col. 0361D]

For that reason we absolutely command that a bishop be ordained in the Church of Arras, unless the Church of Cambrai should be able to vindicate possession of that city by a privilege of Roman authority. Justice requires this, the welfare of souls demands it, and the honor of the Church implores it.

If you fear the envy of rivals, or dread, because of the dignity of your religious character, the barking of those who obey, let whomever the clergy and people, with your approval, shall elect according to God in the aforesaid Church be sent to us with a common decree and letters expressing your concern. With the help of divine grace, and without prejudice to the right of your Church, we shall consecrate him as though by the hands of blessed Peter.

### LXXXI. Letter of Urban II to the clergy and people of Arras.—He writes to them what he wrote in the preceding letter to Archbishop Rainald. (Year 1093.)

[MANSI, *Councils*, XX, 671.]

[Col. 0362A]

Urban, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons, the clergy and people of Arras, greeting and apostolic blessing.

Two clerics of your Church, bearing letters from our most reverend fellow brother, the archbishop of Reims, have returned into our presence, humbly petitioning for the restoration of your Church. They awaited the arrival of the clerics of Cambrai until the time that had been fixed for both parties in the provincial council. But no one from Cambrai came before us.

We therefore communicate the same matter in repeated letters and give the same command. For we most earnestly wish the metropolitan church of Reims, with the Lord’s assent, to be restored to the integrity of its ancient dignity.

[Col. 0362B]

For that reason we absolutely command that a bishop be ordained in your Church, unless the Church of Cambrai should be able to vindicate possession of your city by a privilege of Roman authority.

If your archbishop should, through prudent dissimulation, withdraw from carrying out this command of ours, you shall arrange to send to us whomever you, with his consent, elect as your pastor according to God, together with a common decree and letters from that same archbishop. With the help of divine grace, and without prejudice to the right of the Church of Reims, we shall consecrate him.

### LXXXII. Letter of Urban II to the clergy and people of Amiens.—He orders them to obey Bishop Gerewinus, after his purification from simony. (Year 1093.)

[BALUZE, *Miscellanea*, Lucerne edition, II, 176.]

Urban, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the clergy and people of Amiens, greeting and apostolic blessing.

We judged that the accusation of simoniacal depravity brought against our venerable fellow brother Gerewinus, your bishop, before the metropolitan and the bishops of the province had no force, because we do not judge anyone to be condemned merely at the word of one person, especially one who is infamous or unsuitable. Therefore, since no one had brought a canonical accusation against him before us, we did not deem it necessary to require any purification from him.

[Col. 0362D]

Nevertheless, taking thought for the future reputation of his religious character, he voluntarily purified himself by touching the most holy Gospels, declaring that he had neither given nor promised money for the abbey of Saint-Riquier or for the bishopric of Amiens, and that no one else had done so for him with his knowledge.

Accordingly, considering him free from the injury of the present accusation, we send him back to you with the fullness of our favor. By the authority of our office, therefore, we command you to revere him as your own pastor with due obedience and to obey his instructions, so that, correcting your past errors, you may turn to observing the Lord’s commandments.

[Col. 0363A]

Concerning the clerics whom we have learned to be joined to women contrary to the discipline of the holy canons and in contempt of the practice of the Catholic Church, we command by apostolic authority that they entirely desist from such and other offenses in which they are entangled, and that, according to the judgment of their bishop, they devote themselves to divine service.

But if, which God forbid, disregarding our command, you should further presume stubbornly to resist your bishop, to your own detriment and ruin, whatever sentence he pronounces against you as justice dictates, we confirm by the weight of our authority.

Given on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of August.

### LXXXIII. Letter of Pope Urban II to all the faithful.—Concerning the church of Saint Mary of the monastery at Cassino, consecrated by him and fortified with a privilege. (Year 1093.)

[MANSI, *Councils*, XX, 643.]

[Col. 0363B]

Urban, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the whole body of Christ’s faithful, for perpetual remembrance.

In view of the mercy of God, by whose gift, although unworthy, we preside over the Catholic Church and the powers of all the faithful are sustained, it is fitting that the pious concern of the apostolic see and the dutiful generosity of princes should provide proper care for churches and labor mercifully with every diligence for their peace and quiet. Thus, by the working of divine clemency, those who possess their rights with even-handed moderation—prelates and subjects alike—may attain together the eternal joys promised to the faithful.

We therefore, wearied by the urgent prayers of our sons Roger, duke, and his brother Bohemond, and of Urso the abbot, came with a multitude of our fellow bishops to Mount Cassino to consecrate the monastery of Bantino, built in honor of the Mother of God. With her help, after we had duly completed its consecration with our devoted hands, and through the pious intervention of those illustrious men and of their counts and barons, we excluded by apostolic authority, through a general perpetual constitution, from the monastery itself, its churches, and all its possessions and places, present and future, all episcopal rights and all public exactions, for the sake of its complete liberty, security, and peace.

[Col. 0363D]

From the church of Saint Anastasia of Acherontia alone, built within the walls of the city, we permit the archbishop of Acherontia to receive one ounce of gold each year.

Meanwhile, establishing these matters irrevocably, we decree that the brothers of the monastery of Bantino shall receive chrism, holy oil, consecrations of altars or basilicas, ordinations of their clerics, and the other spiritual sacraments from diocesan bishops or from any Catholics who, supported by the command and authority of the apostolic see, are willing to favor them and, when the brothers request them, exhibit these same sacraments freely and without any corruption.

Furthermore, by the authority of blessed Peter, chief of the apostles, we sanction that no contradiction by anyone shall prevent people of any condition, clerics or laymen, who during life or at death wish to go to the aforesaid monastery, its churches, and its places with their possessions, or who, while remaining in their own homes, wish to confer any of their temporal goods by way of alms. The brothers shall possess quietly, generally, freely, and forever, under the protection of the apostolic see, whatever they have been given.

[Col. 0364A]

We also decree that no human being at all may rashly disturb the aforesaid monastery, take away or diminish its possessions, retain what has been taken away, or harass it with any kind of vexation [perhaps: “dare to do so” is missing], and that every title of opposition concerning this matter shall always be excluded.

We grant them all these things through the fatherly piety of the apostolic see, moved by the prudent counsel of our fellow brothers, the vigorous intervention of the aforementioned noblemen, and the fact that, after the entry of the Northmen, the monastery itself suffered countless grievous losses and unworthy injuries: the stripping of its interior possessions, the pitiable devastation of its lands, and the sacrilegious usurpations of bishops. These matters are briefly recorded in the privilege of Count Amicus.

Moved, therefore, by such evident reasons, the compassionate heart of the apostolic see withdraws and defends this monastery, together with all its possessions, present and future, as the possession of blessed Peter—whose right and property it is—from every right and service owed to any human being of whatever dignity or order, by the sword of anathema.

As a sign of the liberty received from the Roman Church, the abbots of that monastery shall pay one ounce of gold each year to us and to our successors.

[Col. 0364C]

If, therefore, in the future any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowingly attempting to act rashly against this page of our constitution, should, after being warned a second or third time, fail to correct his offense by worthy satisfaction, let him lose the dignity of his power and honor, recognize that he has made himself liable to divine judgment for the iniquity committed, and be separated from the most sacred body and blood of God and our Lord and Redeemer Jesus Christ; and at the final judgment let him be subject to divine vengeance.

But let there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ for all who preserve its rights for that monastery, so that here they may receive the fruit of good action and, before the stern Judge, find the rewards of eternal peace. Amen, amen.

The following subscriptions and seals were appended. Moreover, the pontifical sign, in which the names of the apostles and, on the reverse, images are cast in lead, bears this inscription in the outermost circle:

**BLESSED BE GOD AND THE FATHER OF OUR LORD JESUS CHRIST.**

### LXXXIV. Urban II decrees that those who visit the monastery of Saint Mary on appointed days shall enjoy absolution from sins. (Year 1093.)

[UGHELLI, *Italia sacra*, VII, 27.]

[Col. 0365A]

Urban, bishop, servant of the servants of God, for the perpetual remembrance of the matter, in honor of the supreme, indivisible, and most holy Trinity.

Perpetually enduring are the stations and indulgences granted by Pope Urban II to the religious and venerable monastery of Saint Mary of Pauso, commonly called Deventuum, whose church that same supreme pontiff consecrated with his own hands on the ninth day before the Kalends of September, in consideration of a certain prerogative of spiritual holiness which he experienced in that monastery—or rather because of his perfect observance of religious discipline when he was constituted in the minor orders in that same monastery. Namely, all the faithful who visit the said monastery out of devotion on the aforesaid ninth day before the Kalends of September, and throughout the following day, as well as on Holy Thursday and throughout Good Friday, during the octave, on the feasts following the Resurrection, and on all the feasts of the blessed Virgin Mary, shall obtain a plenary indulgence for all sins of which they have confessed—or at least repented, with the intention of confessing—and shall enjoy all the perpetual plenary indulgences, temporal graces, and remissions enjoyed personally by the city and church of Saint James of Compostela. At other times and on feast days, those who come there out of devotion shall obtain, by the special grace of the Apostolic See, four years and an equal number of forty-day periods of true indulgence. Those who visit the monastery’s greater chapel, consecrated on that same day by our venerable brother Bruno, bishop of Segni, on feast days and on every Sunday of the year, shall obtain seven years and an equal number of forty-day periods of true indulgence. Those also who visit the church built on the estate of that monastery, consecrated by our venerable brother Roger, bishop of [lacuna], on that very day, the ninth day before the Kalends of September, and on all Sundays and feast days, as well as on the feast days of the blessed Virgin Mary, in whose honor it was built and by whose name it is called, shall obtain the aforesaid indulgence of seven years and an equal number of forty-day periods.

All this appears from a leaden bull.

Given at Salerno through the hands of John, cardinal deacon of the holy Roman Church, on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of October, in the first indiction, in the year of the Lord 1093, in the sixth year of the pontificate of Pope Urban II.

### LXXXV. Letter of Urban II to Raynald, archbishop of Reims.—He reproaches him for not yet having consecrated the elect of Arras. (Year 1093.)

[Mansi, *Councils*, XX, 671.]

**URBAN**, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his most reverend brother and fellow bishop **Raynald** of Reims, greetings and apostolic blessing.

What we determined concerning the Church of Arras, both for the manifold salvation of souls, for the restoration of your metropolitan church, and also for the administration of justice, we have brought to completion. For although, in the course of time, a brother may be entrusted to a brother, or a sister to a sister, whether younger in years or weaker in bodily condition, nevertheless, when he or she has reached emancipation, the person will not on that account remain subject to the guardianship or care of the other under the sanctions of law. We are therefore distressed that you have resisted this constitution of ours and the restoration of your metropolitan church for so long and with such obstinacy, and that to this day you have delayed consecrating the elect of the Church of Arras. By the authority of these present letters, therefore, we command your reverence, once you have seen this letter, to arrange to consecrate that same elect within thirty days, putting aside every crookedness and setting aside every pretext for delay. But if, perhaps because of some more secret plan, you are unwilling to fulfill this, send him to us with the attestation of your letter. If you disregard this also, we command him to come to us, where he will receive the grace of consecration.

### LXXXVI. Letter of Urban II to Lambert, bishop-elect of Arras.—He congratulates him and informs him of the preceding letter to Raynald. (Year 1093.)

[Mansi, *Councils*, cited above, p. 672.]

**URBAN**, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved brother and fellow priest **Lambert**, elect of the Church of Arras, greetings and apostolic blessing.

We rejoice over you in the Lord, dearest brother, because, by his ordering, you have now at last been elected pastor of the Church of Arras, which for so long lacked the consolation of its own shepherd, in accordance with our command. For we hope that, through the knowledge and religious devotion divinely given to you, which has been reported to us by some of your countrymen, the greatest advantage, both in bodily and spiritual matters, will come to that Church. We wish you to know that we have written to the archbishop concerning your consecration. Therefore, arrange to present yourself before him. But if he is unwilling to consecrate you within thirty days after receiving our letter, we command you to come to us as quickly as you can. Meanwhile, guard the goods of the Church entrusted to you, both within and without.

Given on the fifth day before the Ides of October.

### LXXXVII. Letter of Pope Urban II to Gerald, abbot of the New Monastery of Poitiers.—He confirms to the New Monastery of that city the church of Saint Nicholas beside the walls of Poitiers, adjudicated to the canons at the Council of Saintes. (Year 1093.)

[Dom Bouquet, *Collection*, vol. XIV, p. 706.]

**URBAN**, bishop, servant of the servants of God, in perpetuity to his son in Christ **Gerald**, abbot of the New Monastery situated in the suburb of Poitiers, and to his successors regularly appointed.

We are known to have been raised to the Apostolic See, with Almighty God and blessed Peter cooperating, so that, in accordance with the ability divinely granted to us, we may strive to suppress injustice, raise up justice, and increase religion. Accordingly, we earnestly endeavor to provide for the peace of the servants of God, so that, freed from worldly disturbances, they may be able to cleave more ardently to divine contemplation. Therefore, assenting to your pious desires, dearest son Gerald, abbot, and to the just petitions of our most reverend brother, formerly my father, Hugh, abbot of Cluny, we too, by the authority of this present decree, grant to your New Monastery every liberty or immunity attributed to it after the privilege of our predecessor of apostolic memory, Gregory VII. Moreover, we grant to you and your successors in perpetuity the church of Saint Nicholas, built beside the walls of Poitiers by Countess Agnes, just as we know it was determined by our legate Amatus, bishop of Bordeaux, and by our most reverend brother Peter, bishop of Poitiers, in the presence of bishops and abbots, with the support of our son Count William, at a council [Note: Perhaps at the Council of Saintes, which was held by Amatus in 1081, or at the council said by the chronicler of Maillezais to have been held there in 1089], and just as our venerable son Rainald, abbot of the monastery of Saint Cyprian, publicly testified before us by a truthful declaration that it had been established.

Because the canons, having received the privilege from the Roman Church, refused to live according to its canonical provisions, and, when admonished by the bishop of that city or by our legates, stubbornly refused to strive toward the purpose of their rule, the kingdom of God was not undeservedly taken away from them, according to the evangelical judgment, and given to those producing its fruits. It is therefore your responsibility, dearest sons in Christ, to respond by worthy actions to the liberality [ed., liberty] and grace of the Apostolic See, and to labor diligently in the order of regular discipline, so that, the freer you are from worldly disturbances, the more ardently you may strive to please God with every virtue of mind and soul. But if any religious, priestly, judicial, or secular person, recognizing this page of my constitution, should act against it, etc.

Given [lacuna], through the hands of John, cardinal deacon of the holy Roman Church, on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of November, in the first indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1093, and in the sixth year of the pontificate of Pope Urban II.

### LXXXVIII. Letter of Pope Urban II to Raynald, abbot of Saint Cyprian of Poitiers.—Whatever right and canonical authority he had acquired over the church of Holy Cross at Engla, he grants to him and confirms by apostolic authority. (Year 1093.)

[D. Bouquet, *Collection*, vol. XIV, p. 696.]

**URBAN**, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son in Christ **R. [Raynald]**, abbot of Saint Cyprian, greetings and apostolic blessing.

Our duty reminds us to provide for the peace of the servants of God, so that, separated from worldly disturbances, they may be able to labor more freely in the service of Almighty God. Therefore we have assented to your prayers, dearest son in Christ Raynald. Whatever right or canonical authority over the church of Holy Cross at Engla was granted to your monastery, whether by the concession of those to whom it previously belonged [Note: This same church had also been given to regular clerics; but by force of this letter the clerics were later expelled and monks of Saint Cyprian were installed. Concerning this matter Ivo of Chartres brought a serious complaint to Peter, bishop of Poitiers, in Letter 36. After quoting Pope Urban’s letter, he argues that it ought not to support the monks’ case. He says: “Nor do the letters of the lord pope, at whose dictation we were present at his side [read: at Alatri], sufficiently protect your fraternity; they confirm to the abbot of Saint Cyprian that right over the aforesaid church which he said he possessed by the lawful concession of certain monks who—as we heard—approved the peaceful possession of the clerics but wholly disapproved the intrusion of the monks of Saint Cyprian. For the aforesaid abbot was striving by every means to have the priory of the aforesaid church granted to him by the lord pope. The lord pope refused to do this, despite our protests and our defense, as far as we could, of the liberty of the clerics, taking care—as he himself said—that on this pretext the aforesaid abbot might try to exclude the clerics and introduce his monks. You inflict a public injury upon the order of clerics, raising the order of monks to such ruinous arrogance that you strive to subject clerics to them; yet their excellence ought to be so great that, according to blessed Augustine, scarcely even a good monk makes a good cleric,” etc.], or by episcopal grant, we too grant it and confirm it by the authority of these present letters.

Given at the town of Alatri, on the fourth day before the Nones of November.

### LXXXIX. Letter of Pope Urban II to the bishops and abbots of Aquitaine, Gascony, and Lower Burgundy.—He orders them to have financial aid collected for procuring the liberty of the Apostolic See and sent to him through Rainald, abbot of Saint Cyprian of Poitiers. (Year 1093.)

[D. Bouquet, *Collection*, vol. XIV, p. 697.]

**URBAN**, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his dearest brothers, the bishops and abbots established throughout Aquitaine, Gascony, and Lower Burgundy, greetings and apostolic blessing.

Our most beloved and familiar son **R. [Rainald]**, abbot of the monastery of Saint Cyprian, having stayed with us for some time, has carefully observed both the oppression suffered by the Roman Church and the consolation which it hopes soon to receive [variant: in Christ]. [Note: That is, some hope was dawning of recovering Rome and the Lateran palace, where Guibert’s forces had established their defenses; for this purpose Urban spent a great deal of money.] Through him, therefore, we admonish you concerning your charitable solicitude, and in the place of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul we entreat you to burn with due vigor on behalf of your holy Roman Church, the mother of you all. We trust in the mercies of Almighty God, through the merits and prayers of the holy apostles, that soon the liberty of the Apostolic See will be restored and, through it, the long-desired tranquility of the other Churches throughout the world. Let each of you therefore strive, according to the ability divinely given to him, to assist its present labors, and let him not delay sending through the faithful bearer of this letter whatever, with God’s inspiration, he has decided upon with a cheerful heart [Col. 0369B]. Let each person’s contribution, however, be presented to our knowledge with an inscription bearing his name. But if perhaps you have neglected, with the devotion owed, to pour out the entrails of your charity toward the Apostolic See, at least do not in any way refuse to give the bearer of this letter and send through him to us whatever you recognize yourselves as owing from the annual census to the Lateran palace. If any of the abbots should refuse, for any reason, to restore to blessed Peter what is his due, let the bishops know that this has been enjoined upon them by our authority, and let them compel those abbots to render what must be rendered. May divine mercy protect those who obey our admonitions.

Given on the fourth day before the Nones of September.

### XC. Letter of Pope Urban II to Rainald, abbot of Saint Cyprian of Poitiers.—He entrusts him with the task of collecting money in aid of the Roman Church. (Year 1093.)

[Dom Bouquet, *Collection*, vol. XIV, p. 697.]

**URBAN**, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his dearest son **Rainald**, abbot of Saint Cyprian [Note: Rainald is the man of whom Geoffrey Grossus says in the *Life of Blessed Bernard, abbot of Tiron*: “Not far from this city [Poitiers] there is the monastery of Saint Cyprian, which at that time was governed by an abbot named Raynaud, a man highly learned in letters and endowed with such wisdom that he was a most eloquent advocate in public councils. For this reason he was also well known and esteemed in the Roman curia, and was regarded as the most famous man in Aquitaine.”], greetings and apostolic blessing.

Trusting in your religious devotion and prudence, we impose upon your affection the obedience enjoined by the apostle Paul: just as Paul admonished the Gentiles whom, with God’s help, he had converted concerning the ministry that was being performed for the saints who lived in Jerusalem, so you too must faithfully and devotedly urge the bishops, nobles, and other Catholics of your land to remember the poor of the Roman Church and not neglect to supply their need from their abundance. To carry this out, we have appointed our dearest son **G. [Gervasius]** [Note: “Gervasius, who at that time was living in the monastery of Saint Cyprian, a man of the greatest abstinence and distinguished by the adornment of every virtue,” says Geoffrey in the same work. Amatus, however, legate of the Apostolic See, sharply rebuked him], abbot of Saint Sabinus, as your companion in this labor, so that you may be able to relieve the straits of our afflictions more promptly. Let each person therefore cheerfully offer to the blessed apostles Peter and Paul what he has determined in his heart, and let them deposit their contributions with you under their recorded names, so that through you their charity may become known to the Roman Church, and so that the Roman Church may be bound to hear them in their needs as pious and honorable men. Strive in small matters, so that it may become evident what we ought soon to hope from you even in the greatest matters. Moreover, we command you to collect diligently the census from the monasteries that belong to our jurisdiction [Note: Most monasteries that belonged to the Apostolic See, or that enjoyed the privilege of exemption, were bound to pay the Roman Church annually a census of one ounce of gold, or even five solidi].

### XCI. Urban II grants a bull to the regular canons of Saint-Quentin of Beauvais. (Year 1093.)

[Ruinart in the *Life of Urban*; Mabillon and Ruinart, *Posthumous Works*, III, 139–140.]

### XCII. Likewise, to the monastery of Bourgueil. (Year 1093.)

[Ruinart, cited above, p. 140.]

### XCIII. The Church of Syracuse, after Count Roger expelled the Agarenes, is confirmed, with a penalty of excommunication imposed against anyone who disturbs it in any way. (Year 1093.)

[Cocquelines, *Collection of Bulls*, II, 77.]

**URBAN**, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved brother **Roger**, bishop of the city of Syracuse, and to his successors canonically promoted to the episcopate.

We believe that it is known to nearly all the Christian peoples throughout the world that the island of Sicily, once illustrious with many noble Churches, rich in resources and populous, had shone through the religious devotion of many men and had been renowned for the martyrdom of certain most holy martyrs and virgins. But, because of the demands of sin, so great a splendor of affairs and such excellence of morals were suddenly reduced to nothing. For the savage race of the Saracens entered the aforesaid island and, of all the worshipers of the Christian faith whom it found there, killed some by the sword, condemned others to exile, and oppressed many more with pitiable servitude. Thus for nearly three hundred years the Christian religion ceased to worship its God there.

But the God who rules all things, whose wisdom and strength transfer kingdoms and change times whenever he wills, brought from the western regions the soldier Roger, a man excellent in counsel and most vigorous in war. Through great labor, frequent battles, and the repeated slaughter and shedding of the blood of his soldiers, with the Lord’s help he liberated that region from the servitude of the pagans. Therefore, when he was recently restoring the Church of Syracuse, he chose our venerable son Roger, dean of the Church of Troina, as bishop of the Church of Syracuse, with the counsel of the bishops of that province, and presented him to our hands for consecration.

Following, therefore, with priestly zeal the affection of his pious devotion and assenting to his just petitions, by the authority of this present privilege we grant and confirm to you and your successors the Church of Syracuse, over which, by God’s agency, you preside as Roger’s venerable brother in Christ, to govern, order, and, with the Lord’s favor, extend. Whatever was granted to that Church by our aforesaid son Count Roger, lying within these boundaries: from the castle of Limpiados to the river Salsus, where it flows into the sea, as shown above within the boundaries of the castle of John Anaor; from there, proceeding toward Mauraneum, it ascends to the river of Cathaelfar and then goes to the Iron Bridge, proceeding toward Heutbachayn, which flows into the river of Paternione Natenius; and thus this river runs to Visam, falling into the sea; from there along the seacoast to Syracuse; from Syracuse to the castle of Limpiados, which is Caltha, where this boundary began. Within these boundaries are Syracuse with all its dependencies—Lentina, Nota, Pantegra, Cassibula, Bizinias, Essina, Calthaelfar, Lespera, Isbarbia, Modica, Sclicla, Anaor, Ragusa, and Butera with all their dependencies—and the other castles and estates that have been or will be built within the aforesaid boundaries. Whatever thereafter is lawfully granted to that Church by anyone, we decree by the page of this present decree that it shall remain secure and inviolate for you and your successors, and we enact and sanction that from all those Churches you shall perpetually possess the tithes, ecclesiastical customary payments, and episcopal rights.

We decree that absolutely no person may rashly disturb the aforesaid Church or harass it with presumptuous vexations, but that everything, as designated above, shall be preserved forever unmoved and intact. You, dearest brother in Christ, attend to the office entrusted to you with due diligence. Take care that what you are called may shine in the sight of God; let your light shine, so that unbelievers may be converted to the Lord by your good examples and continual exhortations, and that believers may glorify God the Father who is in heaven. But if any priest, king, prince, duke, count, judge, or any secular person, knowingly recognizing this page of our confirmation, should rashly attempt to act against it, and, after being warned a second or third time, should not correct the matter by suitable satisfaction, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and honor, become separated from the most sacred body and blood of God and our Lord and Redeemer Jesus Christ, and at the final judgment be subject to strict punishment. But let the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with all who preserve the just rights of this Church, so that both here they may receive the fruit of good action and, before the strict Judge, find the reward of eternal peace. Amen, amen, amen.

Given at Anagni through the hands of John, cardinal deacon of the holy Roman Church, on the Kalends of December, in the first indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1093, and in the sixth year of the pontificate of the lord Pope Urban II.

### XCIV. Urban II writes to the congregation of the monastery of Vendôme that it has been reported to him that the bishop of Chartres (Ivo) “extorted a profession” from Geoffrey, their abbot, “at his consecration.” He rescinds this profession and orders “that henceforth the abbot of their monastery make no profession to the bishop.” (Year 1093.)

[Works of Geoffrey of Vendôme, edited by Sirmond, octavo edition, p. 87.]

**URBAN**, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the venerable congregation of the monastery of Vendôme, greetings and apostolic blessing.

It has been reported to us that the bishop of Chartres extorted a profession from your dearest son Geoffrey, your abbot, at the consecration which he received from him. Because we recognize that this was done against the authority of the Roman Church, know that we have mercifully forgiven the abbot this offense. We nevertheless annul the profession itself in such a way that it possesses no force whatsoever. Moreover, we have established by the privilege of our authority, and by these present letters we prohibit, that henceforth the abbot of your monastery make a profession to the bishop. If anyone in the future attempts to act against these provisions, let him be kept from the thresholds of the holy Church and remain excommunicated until he repents and satisfies the Roman Church.

Given at Rome on the eighth day before the Kalends of December.

### XCV. Letter of Urban II to Rainald, archbishop of Reims.—He warns him not to listen to the people of Cambrai, who are claiming the Church of Arras for themselves. (Year 1093.)

[Mansi, *Councils*, XX, 672.]

**URBAN**, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved brother and fellow bishop **Rainald** of Reims, greetings and apostolic blessing.

Your prudence ought to have labored more diligently to restore the dignity of the Church entrusted to you. We are therefore astonished that even now you incline your ears to the unjust outcries of the people of Cambrai, so that the Church of Arras might be subjected to them, when it is clear that they are unwilling to accept even the cleric of their own Church whom, according to the tenor of your letters, they unanimously elected, except through the hand of an excommunicated heretic. For this alone they deserve to suffer the loss of their due dignity. Do not in any way fear that on this pretext the metropolitan Church of Reims will lose its right over the Church of Cambrai. Whoever there presumes to be ordained except through the archbishop of Reims will be struck, together with his ordainer, by the sword of apostolic severity.

Therefore it is necessary for your vigilance to insist watchfully that neither Church be left without a bishop of cardinal rank, unless perhaps the people of Cambrai produce a privilege of Roman authority subjecting the Church of Arras to them. Accordingly, brother, let your excellence take care to warn them, so that when the people of Arras come to us in the coming Lent for confirmation of their elect, they too may present themselves before our hearing with the authoritative documents of their Church. Furthermore, we praise and confirm the election which you have reported that they generally made of our common son Manasses, unless any circumstances arise that ought to be restrained by the holy canons. To bring this about, we are prepared to absolve the people of Cambrai from that rash oath, provided that they too are prepared to receive their elect and, according to your counsel, to offer repentance for that rashness. Otherwise, we confirm the sentence of interdict imposed upon them and communicated to your fraternity.

### XCVI. Pope Urban issues a canonical ruling concerning the king of Aragon, who had firmly promised under oath that he would give his niece to a certain knight. (Between 1088 and 1094.)

[Mansi, *Councils*, XX, 713.]

Concerning the marriage of your niece, whom, with necessity pressing, you firmly promised under oath to give to a certain man, we decide, as equity dictates, that if she entirely refuses that man, as is said, and persists in the same determination of her will, so that she absolutely denies that she will marry him, you must by no means compel her, unwilling and resisting, to be joined in marriage to that man. Since those who are one body ought also to be of one mind, she might otherwise, if joined against her will to another man, incur either the guilt of discord or the crime of fornication, contrary to the command of the Lord and the Apostle. It is clear that the evil of this sin would fall upon the person who joined her to him against her will.

### XCVII. Letter of Urban II to the abbot of Saint John of Pinna.—He orders him not to take certain tithes from the canons of the church of Saint Saturninus of Toulouse. (Between 1088 and 1094.)

[Baluz., *Miscellany*, Lucchese edition, II, 180.]

**URBAN**, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the abbot of Saint John of Pinna, greetings and apostolic blessing.

The complaint of the canons of Saint Saturninus concerning the injury they suffer from you has now reached us, delayed neither by the length of the journey nor by the hardship of the undertaking. The bishop of Pamplona, a venerable and religious man, gave them in his diocese a certain church, from which you are taking the greater part of the tithes, against right, against the will of the aforesaid bishop, and, as they say, against the will and decision of Abbot Favel Pons. For Hugh of Conques, our cleric, much beloved in the Roman Church, asserts that the aforesaid abbot, after hearing the case of both sides, established peace between you and Hugh, and judged and approved that the canons of Blessed Saturninus should possess that portion of the tithes over which there had been a dispute between you. By retaining their tithes, you have broken that peace. You did not obey the letters of your abbot admonishing you to make amends. Therefore we admonish you and command you under obedience henceforth not to take the aforesaid tithes from the canons of Blessed Saturninus, and to satisfy them, in accordance with the judgment of the bishop of Pamplona, concerning those which you have retained. If within thirty days after seeing this letter you have not made amends, we admonish our brother the bishop of Pamplona, acting in our place, to constrain you and your monks in such a way that he will not allow you to incur the bond of anathema confirmed in the privileges of Blessed Saturninus, and so that no further complaint may reach our ears. Greet on our behalf our dearest friend King Sancho, and his sister the countess.

### XCVIII. Letter of Pope Urban II to William, archbishop of Rouen, and to the canons of Saint Mellon at the Bridge of the Oise and the inhabitants of that castle.—He orders them “not to forbid the monks of Bec to ring their bells at the hours according to their custom.” (Year 1094.)

[Mansi, *Councils*, XX, 701.]

**URBAN**, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved brother **William**, archbishop of Rouen, and to the canons of Saint Mellon at the Bridge of the Oise and the inhabitants of that castle, greetings and apostolic blessing.

It has been reported to us that you forbid the monks of Bec who are in the church of Saint Peter at the Bridge of the Oise to ring their bells at the hours according to their custom. Were we not sparing you, we would expose how irreligious and inhuman this is, and from what root it proceeds. Therefore, by paternal admonition and by our present authority, we command you no longer to issue or permit this prohibition. Rather, allow them, without any impediment, to ring the bells according to monastic custom and to observe their entire order in all things.

Given across the Tiber on the third day before the Kalends of August.

### XCIX. Bull of Pope Urban II by which he confirms the donation made by Countess Matilda to the monastery of Saint Blaise. (Year 1094.)

[Gerbert, *Diplomatic Code of the Black Forest*, vol. III, p. 33, from the archive of Saint Blaise.]

**URBAN**, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to all the faithful throughout Swabia, greetings and apostolic blessing.

Just as assent ought to be denied to those asking for unreasonable things, so we ought to join with benevolent agreement the requests of those seeking what is just. Therefore we have deemed it right to assent to the devotion of our dearest daughter **Countess Matilda** [Note: This Matilda is none other than the famous countess of Tuscany, still living at that time, who retained some possessions in that region from her maternal inheritance or from her first marriage to the duke of Lorraine]. For in the district of Speyer she offered to the monastery of Blessed Blaise, situated in Swabia, a possession of her own called Titensheim [Note: This place in the district of Speyer is called Didinesheim in Paulinus’s *Districts of Germany*, and today Deydesheim], for the salvation of her soul, together with certain other things which she asks to have confirmed by our authority.

Therefore, by the authority of this present decree, we enact that both the aforesaid estate and all the other things which that same countess offered to Blessed Blaise shall always remain intact and inviolate, entirely useful to the servants of God for whose support and governance they were granted. No person whatsoever may take them away from the aforesaid monastery, diminish them, or apply them to his own uses under the pretext of pious reasons. But if anyone, which God forbid, should attempt to act against this decree of ours, which shall remain perpetual, let him be struck with anathema and suffer the loss of his honor and office, unless he corrects his presumption by worthy satisfaction. But let peace and mercy from the Lord be perpetually preserved for those who observe these provisions. Amen.

Given at Rome on the eighth day before the Ides of February, in the third indiction, through the hand of John, cardinal deacon of the holy Roman Church, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1093, and in the sixth year of the pontificate of the lord Pope Urban II.

### C. Letter of Urban II to the Catholic Saxons.—He announces that he has consecrated the elect of Halberstadt, bypassing the metropolitan of Mainz because of the schism. (Year 1094.)

[Mansi, *Councils*, XX, 710.]

**URBAN**, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved brothers N., archbishop of Magdeburg, and N., bishop of Verdun, and to the other bishops and abbots of Saxony who persevere in the Catholic faith, greetings and apostolic blessing.

We do not believe that it is unknown to your prudence how our venerable brother **H. [Hervaudus]**, whom we named Stephen, was long ago elected in the Church of Halberstadt; nor how he was driven from that Church by deceit and flattery, threats and terrors. Yet the supreme mercy looked upon his people when it brought that same elect to the threshold of the holy apostles and into our presence. Since he could not be ordained in the metropolitan see of the Church of Mainz amid such a storm of schismatics, it allowed him to be consecrated in that very seat of the Roman Church, the mother of all Catholics.

When he came to us—unworthy though we are, yet charged, in the place and office of the prince of the apostles, with the care and ordering of all the Churches throughout the world—we recognized that his election was just and canonical, and, considering the necessity of the present time, with the counsel of our brother bishops and cardinals and the Roman nobles, and with the Lord’s consent, we consecrated him. It was indeed necessary for us, in accordance with the duty of the service entrusted to us, to attend to the long desolation of that Church and, with the Lord’s favor, to provide for the salvation of so many souls.

We therefore send him back as a companion in our labor, commended by this letter, beseeching and commanding you for Christ’s sake to labor with common counsel and assistance to uproot the thorns from the Lord’s field. Let no dissimulation hold you back and no sluggishness impede you from aiding him manfully in recovering the seat of his Church, and from using your power to restrain both clerics and laypeople who resist him. The man who, after the canonical election of this person, presumptuously and irreverently intruded himself into the Church of Halberstadt—we remove him from his unlawful usurpation by the page of this present decree, both because of his unfitness and because of the needs of that Church; and all who are bound to him by oath we release, insofar as episcopal honor is concerned, from the bond of that allegiance.

In those regions there are, in truth, no Catholic bishops in the dioceses. Therefore, if he should determine anything by the abundance of apostolic grace and the fullness of our authority, hold it ratified and employ him as a counselor in both divine and secular affairs. Act against him in everything in such a way that we may owe you thanks on his behalf and that the light of Catholic truth may shine against every opponent. May heavenly mercy preserve your fraternity unharmed for many years.

Given at Rome on the eighth day before the Ides of February.

### CI. Urban II informs all the sons of the Catholic Church throughout Saxony that he has consecrated Herrand as bishop of Halberstadt. He commands them to obey him and absolves everyone from allegiance to the usurper. (1094)

The following words are to be referred to Herrand’s consecration: “Done at Rome, in the church of Saint Mary called the New, on the fourth day before the Kalends of February [Sunday, 29 January], in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1093, in the sixth year of the pontificate.”

[Wedekind, *Notes on Some Historians of the German Middle Ages*—Hamburg, 1823, octavo, III, 293, according to Jaffé, *Regesta Pontificum Romanorum*, p. 459.]

### CII. Letter of Urban II to the clergy and people of Halberstadt (1094)

He praises them for having elected another in place of the bishop who had fallen into schism, and approves their election.

> **Note [Col. 0375D–0376D]:** After Burchard II, bishop of Halberstadt, had been handed over to Neci for his defense of the Catholic party, the Catholic party elected Thietmar the deacon in 1088. But when he was killed not long afterward by a draught of poison administered by the schismatics, Hervaudus—also Stephen, abbot of Ilsenburg—was installed in the same see. I believe that Urban refers to him in this letter. I have taken this from Eckard’s *Saxon Annalist*.

[Mansi, *Councils*, XX, 708.]

**Urban, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons, the clergy and people of Halberstadt: greeting and apostolic blessing.**

It is judged no small loss to your salvation that your Church has for so long been deprived of the comfort of a shepherd. For our venerable brother, whom you had elected as bishop by common consent according to the prescriptions of the holy canons, was driven from your Church by the force of the schismatics, partly through deceit and flatteries, partly through threats and intimidation, contrary to the canonical sanctions and ecclesiastical customs. Nor was it permitted to abandon what had once been rightly and canonically undertaken with the permission or authorization of the Apostolic See.

Nevertheless, the favor of heavenly mercy looked upon you when it permitted him to come to the threshold of the holy apostles and into our presence. We, therefore, to whom—although unworthy—the care and administration of all the churches throughout the world are seen to belong in the place and stead of the prince of the apostles, recognizing that his election was just and canonical, and considering the necessity of the present time, since in such a storm of schismatics he could not receive consecration from the see of Mainz, consecrated him, with the Lord’s assent, in the first see of the chief of the apostles. Having consecrated him, we send him back to you with the commendation of these letters.

Therefore, remembering your ancient faith and obedience, receive him there with all the greater devotion, the more fully you recognize that you are debtors to your salvation and faith and to the Apostolic Church. For our predecessor in the Apostolic See, Gregory II, of holy memory, when he gave the pallium to the blessed Boniface, the first archbishop of your nation, and strengthened him with the authority of his office, instructed your churches in religion.

We, therefore, considering the prolonged desolation of your Church as a duty of our office, send this man to you as an instructor in your salvation. You ought to receive him with that much greater reverence and heed him with that much greater obedience, the more clearly you see that he has been sent from the very source of your faith and salvation.

Whoever treats him as his shepherd with the honor and affection due to him, we bestow upon him the blessing of almighty God and his apostles. But those who attempt to oppose this constitution of ours, we remove from the office of the clergy if they are clerics; and to laymen we deny participation in apostolic grace.

That man, moreover, who presumptuously and irreverently intruded himself into your Church after the election of this Catholic shepherd, we, both because of his personal unfitness and because of the necessity of your Church, remove in every way from his unjust usurpation by the terms of this present decree. All who are bound to him by oath, insofar as concerns the honor of the episcopate, we release from allegiance to him.

Therefore, beloved sons in Christ, receive this man as an angel of the Lord and a legate of the Catholic faith, and obey him in counsels concerning both divine and secular affairs. Since there are very few Catholic bishops in your regions, if he makes any provision in other dioceses from the greater abundance of apostolic grace and the fullness of our authority, let it remain ratified and unshaken.

May almighty God, through the merits of his apostles, absolve you from sins and make you sharers in eternal life.

### CIII. Letter of Urban II to Fulk, bishop of Beauvais

He lists many serious charges of which Fulk was accused and orders him to come, for the purpose of clearing himself, either to Rainald, archbishop of Reims, or to Urban himself. (1094)

[Dom Bouquet, *Collection*, XIV, 706.]

**Urban, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved brother FULK, bishop of Beauvais: greeting.**

Many serious charges against your fraternity have reached us, so that we cannot sufficiently express our astonishment and grieve deeply. For, both because of your remarkable character and because of your discipline in the monastic order, we had placed no small confidence in you, thinking that the rule of your former training restrained your simplicity from the corruptions of secular affairs.

Now, however, contrary to our opinion, we have heard certain things quite contrary to the purity of the priestly order. You are said—forbid it, O Lord!—to be involved in murders and betrayals of men.

> **Note [Col. 0377D]:** Ursio was then bishop of Senlis.

For the clerics of the Church entrusted to you complain that you cast Hubert, the brother of the bishop of Senlis, into chains during the Lord’s truce because of the seizure of money, broke open his houses and plundered his property, and finally handed him over to royal captivity.

For this reason the Church of Beauvais, long deprived of its services, laments because, as they loudly proclaim, you have entangled yourself in various wicked excommunications; because you make light of the anathema decreed by the bishops of your kingdom for the sake of common peace; because you receive into communion a man excommunicated by the Church of Paris; and because, rashly, you violated the settlement concerning the property of Odo the castellan, which had been confirmed in the presence of your predecessor Guido by our predecessor Gregory, of apostolic memory.

For Odo complains that you have inflicted many injuries upon him concerning that same castellany. At your instigation, his own serfs and dependents attacked him before his own house; and when they were unable to carry out murder and treachery, they found protection for their crime with you.

Your brother—Lancelin, count of Dammartin [Col. 0377D]—and the knights also attempted to ambush him while he was going to fetch his wife. Their hope was frustrated because he returned by another road, but they had you as the protector and patron of such wickedness.

Moreover, six days before the Nativity of the Lord, you had the doors of his house surrounded. Since he could not then be captured and killed there, you ordered the city gates to be watched until midday of the following day, so that he could not leave, and you took away the keys of the gates, which he himself had customarily kept.

You violently compelled Ancelbert, his servant; Isabella, the servant’s wife and his maidservant; and Helinand, Isabella’s brother—who had attempted to betray him—to be freed from him and placed beyond his power, together with their heirs. You support his chaplain, who had been plotting his betrayal, with your resources, and protect him under your safeguard as though he were innocent.

Therefore, by the authority of these present letters, we order you, once you have seen them, within fifteen days to restore his servants to his own power. For both royal and canonical institutions have provided that no one may be made free against the will of his masters.

If, however, the abbot of Saint Peter of Jumièges, to whom you cunningly handed them over, wishes to act against him on behalf of those servants, let them act before the archbishop of Reims, so that he may remain invested there after having previously lost possession here.

The wine and whatever you plundered from his house, and all the other things which he proves were unjustly taken from him, we judge must be restored within the prescribed period, either in kind or in something of equal value. The door of the church must also be opened again, since you blocked it with iron bars and stones out of hatred for him.

The matter concerning the aforesaid chaplain is to be dealt with before the archbishop of Reims at a suitable time. Meanwhile, you ought to be concerned that, by evading judgment, he does not withdraw elsewhere and join those to whom he is free as an enemy.

After restoring his property, take care to present yourself without fail within fifteen days to our brother, the archbishop of Reims. You are to make satisfaction, according to his judgment, for the complaints of the clergy and for these injuries—unless he should be so seriously ill that he could not determine such a case.

If that should happen, we invite you to our hearing within the period of three months. But if you neglect both requirements, and recognize that your conscience is stained by such crimes, you ought to abstain from the priestly office.

Moreover, it is useful for you carefully to remember what you promised into our hands when we restored you to the fullness of episcopal office: namely, that whenever we should command you, you would cease from episcopal office.

Therefore correct what is past and guard against what is to come, lest you be compelled, even unwillingly—forbid it, O Lord!—to fulfill what you freely promised.

Given on the sixth day before the Kalends of March.

### CIV. Letter of Pope Urban II to the clergy and people of Beauvais

He announces that he has vindicated the castellany for the knight Odo. (1094)

[Bouquet, *Collection*, II, 707.]

**Urban, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons, the clergy and people of Beauvais: greeting and apostolic blessing.**

From the letters of our predecessor Gregory, of apostolic memory, we have learned that a certain disagreement and dispute concerning the castellany had arisen between Guido, bishop of your city, and Odo the castellan, and that this dispute was concluded in the presence of that same apostolic predecessor.

For Bishop Guido restored to the hand of that knight everything that had become the subject of dispute. The lord apostolic confirmed this by his authority, establishing that, if anyone disturbed that settlement and seized the property of Odo the castellan by force, both he and his supporters were to be regarded as excommunicated; and that, while they were in the city or castle, no divine office was to be celebrated there until they returned to make satisfaction.

We too, under the same excommunication, confirm the same castellany to the aforesaid knight and his heirs, unless he should commit some offense for which he is judged, in the presence of the bishop of Reims or the Roman pontiff, to have forfeited the castellany.

Given at Rome, etc.

### CV. Urban II confirms the rights and possessions of the monastery of Vendôme. (1094)

[Ruinart, in *The Life of Urban*; Mabillon and Ruinart, *Posthumous Works*, III, 151.]

### CVI. Letter of Urban II to Lambert, bishop of Arras, or privilege of the Church of Arras. (1094)

[Mansi, *Councils*, XX, 668.]

**Urban, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved brother in Christ LAMBERT, bishop of Arras, consecrated by our hands, and to his canonically appointed successors forever.**

It is clear from the institutions of the holy canons that a province which consists of twelve bishoprics ought to remain intact and to possess its own metropolitan. The Second Belgic province is known to have possessed the integrity of a province, having once had twelve bishops, and the Church of Reims is rightly regarded as metropolitan, since it has customarily presided over so many suffragans.

But, because of the sins of the inhabitants, when the barbarians invaded and certain cities were laid waste, that number of twelve was diminished. Among these was the once noble and populous city of Arras, which had obtained Bishop Vedast through Saint Remigius. After the deaths of several bishops, it lost the dignity of an episcopal see and for some time was subject and obedient to the bishop of Cambrai.

In our own times, however, through the regard of heavenly mercy, the aforesaid city has been restored to such a condition that, both in the multitude of its people and in the abundance of its wealth, it surpasses the city of Cambrai.

It therefore seemed worthy to the Holy Spirit and to apostolic authority that a cardinal bishop should be restored to the Church of Arras. For the holy Council of Sardica decreed that a bishop should not be ordained indiscriminately, except either in cities which had had bishops or in those so populous that they deserved to have a bishop.

The Second Council of Africa likewise decreed that a diocese which had once had a bishop should have its own. And if, as time passed and faith in God increased, the people multiplied and desired to have their own ruler, then, with the consent of the person in whose authority the diocese was constituted, it should have its own bishop.

The blessed Gregory also ordered that a bishop be reordained at the town of Phausiana in Sardinia according to the former custom. We, therefore, mindful of the restoration of the Church of Arras and of the renewal of the metropolitan Church of Reims as required by our office, appoint you, dearest brother Lambert, unanimously elected by the consent of clergy and people, as successor to the blessed Vedast and to the holy bishops who once presided in that city.

By the terms of this present privilege, therefore, we establish as legitimate and perpetual that henceforth the Church of Arras shall always possess a cardinal bishop.

Whatever the blessed Remigius bestowed upon the aforesaid Church, and whatever it is established that it possessed in ancient times while it enjoyed episcopal dignity, we decree, subject to the lawful institutions and privileges of the Roman Church, shall remain ratified for you and your successors.

Among these possessions, we specifically confirm to the aforesaid Church two archdeaconries, one called Arras and the other called Obstrevand. We also order that the boundaries between the Churches of Arras and Cambrai be precisely those which can be proved to have existed in ancient times by written records, by the division of territories, or by any other reliable indications, so that, with God’s assent, the peace of the Churches may not be disturbed on any occasion and the provisions established for the salvation of the faithful may remain permanently secure and unshaken.

If, in the future, any archbishop, bishop, emperor or king, prince or duke, count or viscount, judge, or any person, great or small, knowingly attempts rashly to act against this privilege of ours, then, after being warned a second or third time, if he does not correct his offense with suitable satisfaction, let him lose the dignity of his power and honor, recognize that he stands guilty before the divine judgment for the iniquity committed, be separated from the most sacred body and blood of God and our Lord Jesus Christ the Redeemer, and be subjected to strict punishment at the final judgment.

May there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ for all who preserve these provisions for this place, so that here they may receive the fruit of good action and, before the strict Judge, find the eternal rewards of peace.

Blessed be God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ.

Saint Peter. Saint Paul. Urban, Pope II.

Written by the hand of Bonihominus, notary of the Sacred Palace. Given at Rome by the hand of John, cardinal deacon of the Holy Roman Church, on the tenth day before the Kalends of April, in the second indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1093 [Note: The date is falsely recorded—Hardouin], and in the seventh year of the pontificate of Urban II.

This privilege was read aloud at the Council of Clermont by order of Lord Urban II, who presided over it, together with the Roman cardinals, thirteen archbishops, 125 bishops, and ninety abbots and more, besides the honorable and religious clerics and laymen of various regions and provinces.

It was heard attentively and with great silence, and was praised and confirmed by the entire assembly of the council on the fourth day before the Kalends of December, in the fourth indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1095, and in the pontificate of Lord Urban II.

### CVII. Letter of Urban II to Alard of Arras, Bernard archdeacon of Obstrevand, and others

He urges them henceforth to obey Lambert, bishop of Arras. (1094)

[Mansi, *Councils*, XX, 674.]

**Urban, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons ALARD of Arras, BERNARD of Obstrevand, archdeacons, and to all the provosts and deans, together with all the clerics who are in the aforesaid archdeaconries: greeting and apostolic blessing.**

The authority of the Apostolic See compels it to provide for all the churches throughout the world and to come to the aid of those seeking their rights with paternal compassion.

Since, therefore, the Church of Arras, deprived of its proper dignity for many years, had endured the yoke of the Church of Cambrai, we judged it entirely fitting that, with the Lord’s favor, its lost dignity should be restored to it through the dignity of the Apostolic See.

For no document of Roman authority vindicates the subjection of the Church of Arras to the men of Cambrai, and the population of the city of Arras far surpasses that of the city to which it had hitherto been subject.

Relying, therefore, both on the decrees of the canons and on the examples of our predecessors, with the Lord’s assent we have now finally granted effect to the just wishes and urgent petitions of the people of Arras. We have consecrated as bishop the venerable man Lambert, whom they had brought to us, elected by common agreement and accompanied by a common decree.

By the authority of this privilege, we confirm that whatever is known to have belonged to the parish of Arras in ancient times is to be governed perpetually by him and his successors and possessed by episcopal right—specifically, the two archdeaconries, one called Arras and the other Obstrevand.

Therefore, by these present letters we admonish and command your devotion to take care henceforth to submit and obey him as a cardinal bishop, as one consecrated by the hands of Saint Peter.

Accordingly, we release both you and all the clerics who are in the aforesaid archdeaconries from your profession of obedience to the Church of Cambrai.

If any among you, having understood the tenor of this constitution of ours, should refuse to obey our aforesaid brother, the bishop of Arras, whatever sentence he imposes upon them with episcopal moderation shall remain firm by the force of our authority.

Given at Rome on the ninth day before the Kalends of April.

### CVIII. Letter of Urban II to Alold of Saint-Vaast, Richard of Marchiennes, Albert of Hasnon, Hameric of Anchin, abbots, and the abbesses of Saint Ragenfredis and Strum

He orders them to obey Lambert, bishop of Arras. (1094)

[Baluz., *Miscellanies*, Lucerne edition, II, 133.]

**Urban, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons ALOLD, abbot of Saint-Vaast; Richard, abbot of Marchiennes; Albert, abbot of Hasnon; Hameric, abbot of Anchin; and likewise to the abbess of Saint Ragenfredis and the abbess of Strum: greeting and apostolic blessing.**

“The authority of the Apostolic See,” etc., as above, up to: “we judged it fitting that we should incline the assent of our benevolence toward the sons of that same Church, who sought to recover their lost dignity.”

“And no document,” etc., as above, up to: “we confirmed it as to be possessed by episcopal right, specifically,” etc., as above, up to: “shall remain firm.”

Given as above.

### CIX. Letter of Urban II to Rainald, archbishop of Reims, and his suffragans

He commends Lambert, bishop of Arras, to them. (1094)

[Mansi, *Councils*, XX, 673.]

**Urban, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved brothers and fellow bishops, RAINALD of Reims and his suffragans: greeting and apostolic blessing.**

When the clerics of Arras had presented their elected bishop to our presence with a common decree, we kept them with us for a full month, awaiting the arrival of the men of Cambrai, in case they might bring some evidence by which Arras could be shown to be subject to the Church of Cambrai.

They did not come then, any more than they had come on previous occasions, nor did they send the reasons why they had not come.

We, therefore, considering the entirely just cause of the people of Arras and looking with apostolic gentleness upon their long labors for the restoration of their Church, fortified by the decrees of the holy canons and the authority of the Apostolic See, finally, with the Lord’s favor, appointed as successor to the blessed Vedast and to the other holy bishops who once presided in the Church of Arras the religious and wise man Lambert, whom they had brought to us.

In all things preserving the reverence due to the metropolitan Church of Reims—which, diminished for many past years, almighty God has now deigned, through our humility, to restore in part—we send him back to you with these present letters and commend him especially to your charity. We ask and command you to assist him diligently, as a brother and fellow bishop, in restoring the condition of the Church entrusted to him.

With God as author, we have established as a legitimate and perpetual rule that henceforth the Church of Arras shall possess a cardinal bishop. We firmly believe that, with God’s assent, this will greatly benefit both the growth of religion, the salvation of souls, and the temporal relief of that Church.

Now it is your responsibility, dearest brother Rainald, who are known to preside with metropolitan authority over both the Church of Arras and the Church of Cambrai, to invite by your letters all those who, according to the terms of our privilege, appear to belong to the parish of Arras to obey the bishop of Arras, and to support our sentence with your assistance, so that all clerics in the two archdeaconries—namely, Arras and Obstrevand—may be released from their profession of obedience to the Church of Cambrai.

If any should refuse to obey, whatever sentence you impose upon them with episcopal moderation shall remain firm.

Given at Rome on the eighth day before the Kalends of April.

### CX. Letter of Urban II to William, count of Poitiers

He urges him to return what he had taken from the monastery of Vendôme. (1094)

[The Works of Geoffrey of Vendôme, edited by Sirmond, duodecimo, notes, p. 91.]

**Urban, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son WILLIAM, count of Poitiers: greeting and apostolic blessing.**

We have often admonished your character to imitate the devotion and prudence of your excellent princely father. He honored the churches of his principality with the greatest devotion, enriched many of them from his own resources, and even built new ones from their foundations.

But we are astonished at you. Although you are powerful as a knight in other good pursuits, you are said in this respect to have degenerated from your father’s virtue: you disturb the rights of churches and despoil those which he founded.

It has reached us that you took from the monastery of Vendôme the church of Saint George, situated on the island of Oléron, together with a certain valuable estate.

Therefore, dearest son, by these present letters we admonish you that, if you love the favor of the holy apostles and of us, you are to restore entirely to their power that church and the other things you have taken from the monks of Vendôme.

For their property consists of alms given by your parents and of the patrimony of the Apostolic See. If, within thirty days after seeing these letters, you refuse to fulfill what we command, recognize without doubt that you have incurred our indignation and have been struck with the anathema of the Apostolic See.

The monastery of Vendôme and the property belonging to it are known to have been strengthened by apostolic authority in such a way that, if anything belonging to it has been taken away or alienated by anyone, you should not doubt that our predecessors excommunicated him. We cannot and ought not to absolve one whom those blessed men excommunicated; rather, by the same authority we confirm what they did.

Given at Rome on the second day before the Kalends of April.

### CXI. Urban II orders Amatus, legate of the Apostolic See, and two other bishops to regard William, count of Poitiers, as excommunicated unless he causes the property taken from the monks of Vendôme to be restored within the period he has prescribed. (1094)

[Ruinart, in *The Life of Urban*; Mabillon and Ruinart, *Posthumous Works*, III, 151.]

### CXII. Letter of Urban II to Robert, count of Flanders

He commends the Church and bishop of Arras to him. (1094)

[Mansi, *Councils*, XX, 674.]

**Urban, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son ROBERT, count of Flanders: greeting and apostolic blessing.**

You ought to rejoice greatly that, in your time, the churches situated under your rule are receiving back the dignity they had lost.

For behold, the city of Arras, which is the principal city in your county, has received a cardinal bishop through the dignity of the Apostolic See.

By these present letters we commend both him and the Church entrusted to him to your nobility, and, for the remission of your sins, we command you to venerate him with due obedience, protect and assist him, and extend the arm of your aid in every way toward restoring the property of that Church.

Given at Rome on the second day before the Kalends of April.

### CXIII. Judgment of Pope Urban II concerning the subjection of the Church of Dol to the Church of Tours. (1094)

[Marten., *Thesaurus of Anecdotes*, III, 879.]

**Urban, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved brother RADULF, archbishop of Tours, and to his canonically appointed successors forever.**

The authority of the holy canons decrees that the greater cases of the churches are to be decided by the judgment of the Apostolic See. We therefore wish both the manner in which the complaint of the Church of Tours against the bishop of Dol was handled in our time to be made known to the present, and its memory not to escape the future.

For Roland, bishop of Dol, came into our presence in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1093 and requested the pallium as archbishop of the Bretons. Although we had rejected his petitions for a long time, he produced letters of Gregory VII, of apostolic memory, by which it was shown that the same apostolic pope had granted the pallium to a certain Ivano, bishop of Dol, and to his successors, while preserving the complaint of the Church of Tours: namely, that if the Church of Tours could at any time prove by a legitimate action that Dol and the other bishops of Lower Brittany ought to be subject to the metropolitan Church of Tours, they would indeed be subjected to it, while the bishop of Dol would nevertheless retain the use of the pallium.
