After our brother, the bishop of Dol, had sworn that these letters of Pope Gregory contained neither less nor more than the pope had ordered, we granted him the pallium under the same condition.

After this, when we were at Benevento, your energetic self, dearest brother Radulf, archbishop of Tours, came to us and presented to our assembly letters of that same Pope Gregory. They stated that this case had been reconsidered at Rome in a council, where, after lengthy discussion, it had been decided that a council should be convened in the province by legates of the Apostolic See, so that the case might be examined more carefully.

If the bishop of Dol could not support himself by the authentic authority of any Catholic and legitimate pope, then both he and the other bishops of the Bretons were henceforth to obey the Church of Tours as their proper metropolitan, and his successors in the bishopric were never again to obtain the pallium.

The decision reached by the legates who had held the council in the province was also produced. Since the bishop of Dol had been unable to defend his case by any authentic authority, they established, by the judgment of Pope Gregory—[lacuna]—with writings and subscriptions in every respect, that both the bishop of Dol and the other Breton bishops were always to be subject to the Church of Tours.

When the bishop of Dol, who was still present, replied that he had not come to bring a case, but was nevertheless prepared to respond at a suitable time together with the bishops of the province, we agreed with both parties that they should appear before us in the middle of Lent of the following year. Whoever then withdrew or failed to appear without a canonical impediment was to lose his case.

When the appointed time came, while we were staying in the City, the bishop of Dol did not come at all, whereas your fraternity was present. The sentence of Pope Gregory VII was sought in the register and was found exactly as we had heard.

The records of Popes Nicholas and John were also produced, supporting the same position; as was the decree of Leo IX, confirming the same case with the addition of an anathema.

The excuses of our brother, the bishop of Dol, delivered through a messenger, were heard; at that time they did not appear legitimate.

After everything had been examined, it seemed, by the common counsel of our brothers John, bishop of Porto; Ubald, bishop of Sabina; John, bishop of Tusculum; Bruno, bishop of Segni; Daibert, bishop of Pisa; Lambert, bishop of Arras; certain other clerics of our Church; the Roman judges; and other men of consular rank, that the full definition of matters confirmed by so many apostolic pontiffs should not be delayed, nor should the man who had withdrawn by artful cunning profit from his absence.

We, therefore, confirming the statutes of the holy predecessors whom we have mentioned, decree by this present judgment that, just as they decreed, both the bishop of Dol and all the other bishops of the Bretons shall henceforth recognize the Church of Tours as their metropolitan and shall always show it the reverence due to it.

Nor shall any bishop of Dol, after Roland’s death, aspire to the use of the pallium at any time in the future.

We therefore exhort your diligence, dearest brother in Christ, to show yourself always worthy of the grace of so great a dignity. The higher you stand above others, the more brightly you should shine in the light of good works.

Pursue peace and holiness with everyone. In prosperity be humble; and in adversity, should it ever arise, be found upright with justice: a friend to the good, opposed to the wicked, never accepting anyone’s face against the truth, and never suppressing anyone who speaks in favor of the truth.

Apply yourself to works of mercy according to the measure of your resources, while nevertheless desiring to strive beyond the measure of your strength; sympathize with the weak; rejoice with those who wish well; exult over the joys of others as though they were your own; rage piously when correcting vices; delight the minds of your hearers when fostering virtues; in anger, preserve judgment without anger; and in tranquility, do not abandon the discipline of just severity.

Thus may you fulfill inwardly, before the eyes of the divine majesty, the office which you administer outwardly.

May heavenly favor preserve your fraternity unharmed for many years.

Written by the hand of Peter, notary of the Sacred Palace.

Saint Peter. Saint Paul.

Urban, Pope II.

Place of the monogram.

**Blessed be God and the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ.**

Given at Rome by the hand of John, cardinal deacon of the Holy Roman Church, on the Nones of April, in the second indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1094, and in the seventh year of the pontificate of Lord Urban II.

### CXIV. Letter of Pope Urban II to all the bishops established throughout Brittany

He confirms the judgments of the other supreme pontiffs and commands them to obey the archbishop of Tours as their metropolitan. (1094)

[Marten., *Thesaurus of Anecdotes*, III, 881.]

We do not believe that your fraternity is unaware that frequent complaints have reached the Apostolic See concerning the obedience denied to the Church of Tours by our brother, the bishop of Dol, and by certain others among you, and that many investigations of this same matter have been undertaken.

For we know that our predecessor, Pope Gregory, sent you two letters concerning this matter. We also believe that many of you were present at the Council of Saintes, where the same case was examined through a careful investigation by legates of that apostolic pope. Since the bishop of Dol had been unable to defend his case by any authentic authority, it was there established entirely according to the judgment of the aforesaid pope that both the bishop of Dol and all the other bishops of the Bretons should always be subject to the Church of Tours.

You were informed by our letters at that time how, in the preceding year, we granted the pallium to the bishop of Dol.

We then appointed both to him and to the archbishop of Tours a date on which each was to appear before us, together with the documents of his Church, for the resolution of this dispute. When the bishop of Dol did not come, the archbishop of Tours was present at the appointed time.

Then, in the hearing of both the clergy and the laypeople of the Roman Church, the matters conducted concerning this dispute in our time and in the time of Pope Gregory were reconsidered. The writings of the Roman pontiffs Nicholas, John, and Leo were also read aloud; in them it had been decreed that all the bishops of the Bretons must be subject to the metropolitan Church of Tours.

After all these matters had been examined with due care, it was adjudged by the common counsel of our brother bishops, of certain Roman clerics of our Church, and of the judges and other men of consular rank, that the full definition of matters confirmed by so many apostolic pontiffs ought not to be delayed.

Therefore, confirming their statutes, we too command you by the authority of these present letters that, as they decreed, you henceforth take care to show the archbishop of Tours the obedience proper to a metropolitan.

Given at Rome on the third day before the Ides of April.

### CXV. Letter of Urban II to Rainold, archbishop of Reims  
*He complains that Bishop Fulk of Beauvais, having been cleared of the charge before him, was required to undergo purgation again. (Year 1094.)*

*[Mansi, Councils, vol. XX, p. 711.]*

Urban, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his dearest brothers R., archbishop of Reims, and his suffragans: greetings and apostolic blessing.

We believe it is very well known to your Fraternity how, in the previous year, when Bishop Fulk of Beauvais came to the threshold of the apostles, he voluntarily renounced the episcopate entirely into our hands. But we, providing by apostolic dispensation for the need of the Church, imposed the care of the bishopric upon that brother, although he was unwilling and resisting, while nevertheless retaining the fullness of his pontifical office, because a rumor had arisen that his father had offered money for his election. After some time, however, both his father and Odo, a venerable canon of the Church of Beauvais, came into our presence and, having touched the most holy Gospels, declared him free from every suspicion of simoniacal depravity. Thus, since the brothers of our Church judged that justice had been satisfied, we restored to him the fullness of his pontifical office.

Since no one is ever permitted to reopen the judgment of the apostolic see; since no one’s confession concerning himself ought to be believed; and since no one can lawfully be condemned on the accusation of a single person, we are astonished by what presumption, after a sentence had been given by the vicar of Peter, you inflicted prejudice; by what spirit you condemned the aforesaid brother and our fellow bishop on the accusation of one man; and with what rashness you gave such credence to that one man, accusing himself of simony against another, that you nevertheless, to the injury of the man whom the Roman Church had absolved after a canonical examination of the same case, subjected him again to canonical purgation by judgment.

Since, therefore, you have stretched out your arm against your mother, the Roman Church, you deserve severe punishment, especially because you have trampled upon the authority of the holy canons. You in particular, dearest and most reverend brother R., archbishop of Reims, with the illustrious reverence due to our affection preserved, we consider deserving of correction in this matter, because in your presence you allowed so great an injury to be inflicted upon the prince of the apostles.

Accordingly, we judge that that accusation, and that sentence pronounced contrary to the ordinances of the holy canons, are altogether null, and we confirm that the bishop of Beauvais, a man of religious and simple life, has been restored to his place and office. Let any among you who have pronounced against him not a judgment but a prejudice know that, by the authority of Peter, they too will undergo judgment until they have made suitable satisfaction, and will pay, according to a lawful assessment, the loss which that brother has suffered.

We judge him to be so fully absolved that, if any question should subsequently arise against him, it is to be settled solely by the judgment of the Roman see. For the rest, we ask you, most reverend brother, archbishop of Reims, to assist the bishop of Beauvais, who possesses the fullness of our favor, in his needs, both spiritual and material.

[Col. 0389B] Given at the Lateran, 3 Idus of May.

---

### CXVI. Letter of Urban II to Hugh, archbishop of Lyon  
*(Year 1094.)*

*[D. Ruinart, Life of Urban; Mabillon and Ruinart, Posthumous Works, vol. III, p. 359.]*

Urban, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved brother and bishop Hugh of Lyon, legate of the holy Roman Church: greetings and apostolic blessing.

We have entrusted to your diligence, plainly and simply, the responsibilities of our solicitude and the foresight required for matters to be undertaken. But, for the preservation of peace and the easier conduct of the business, we have judged it more useful to seek the counsel of our brother, the archbishop of Reims, because the king’s case is handled more familiarly in his hands. It will be your responsibility, whether with his counsel or without it, according as you see the Lord provide you the opportunity, to exercise the office of the legation entrusted to you and to cut off, with the sickle of the divine word, the branches of vice that are springing up.

Your sagacity can investigate much better within the province what is the state of affairs concerning Guido, archbishop of Vienne, and Hugh, bishop of Grenoble, than we can, being so far away across such great distances of land. Therefore, whatever your Fraternity decides concerning this matter, we, secure in the integrity of your justice, confirm by our own assertion.

If the archbishop of Vienne should produce any letters of our authority, we wish you to know that we have granted to him or to the Church of Vienne nothing except what he is known to have possessed lawfully until now, even if something may perhaps appear to have been extorted by subreption—which God forbid. For we wish each person’s rights to be preserved.

With the Lord’s help, therefore, make every effort to settle their disagreement as quickly as you can. In this and in other matters belonging to God, be ready to show yourself as God’s minister with the most fervent spirit. May divine grace preserve your holiness, who pray for us.

[Col. 0389D] Given at Rome, 17 Kalends of June.

[Note: He was Rainold, who, because of the dignity of his see and his own merits, possessed great influence with the king.]

---

### CXVII. Letter of Urban II to Hugh, bishop of Grenoble  
*He informs him of what was stated above in the letters to Hugh of Lyon. (Year 1094.)*

*[Ruinart, Life of Urban, as above, p. 360.]*

[Col. 0390A]

Urban, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved brother Hugh, bishop of Grenoble: greetings and apostolic blessing.

Concerning your case, we have written to our brother Hugh, archbishop of Lyon, that whatever he decides in our place, we confirm by our own assertion. If the archbishop of Vienne should produce any letters of our authority, do not think that they harm your case. For we have granted to him or to the Church of Vienne nothing except what he is known to have possessed lawfully until now. For we wish each person’s rights to be preserved.

May divine mercy preserve your Fraternity, who pray for us.

[Col. 0390B] Given at Rome, 17 Kalends of June.

---

### CXVIII. Privilege of Urban II for the canons of Pistoia  
*(Year 1094.)*

*[Zacharia, Anecdota of the Middle Ages, p. 224.]*

Urban, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons in Christ, Ugo, provost, and the other brothers of the canonical community of Pistoia, and to their successors who shall persevere in the observance of regular life, forever.

The affection of a pious will ought, with devoted effort, to be brought to completion, so that ecclesiastical usefulness may receive strength and increase through the favor of the apostolic see. Therefore we accept your religious vows and willingly grant assent to your equitable petitions, so that we may fortify, by the privilege of our authority, the order of canonical life which you have professed.

By this present decree, therefore, we establish that no living person may separate you or your successors from the fellowship of canonical life, nor may any of you, after profession, be free to depart from the congregation and pursue the precipices of a broader way. For this reason, we decree that, if anyone among you should stray from his purpose, no person may obstruct you, or your successors, or the others who preside, from correcting him and restraining him according to the discipline of the rule.

When you, or the other rectors of your canonical community, die, no one shall be placed over it by any craft of subreption or by force, except one whom the regular brothers, according to the fear of God, shall have chosen—either from among themselves, if they find such a person among them, or from outsiders, if necessary—with the counsel of the bishop who has been canonically elected and ordained by the Roman Church.

To ensure that all these provisions, with the Lord’s help, may always remain firm and unimpaired, we decree by the authority of this present document that no one at all may rashly disturb your canonical community, take away its possessions, retain what has been taken, diminish them, or harass them with rash vexations. Rather, both what you possess today from the donations of bishops and what you possess from the offerings of any of the faithful shall be preserved intact for you forever.

Among these, we have thought it right to specify the following by name: the parish church of Viliano with all its tithes; likewise the parish church of Saint Quiricus; the other tithes, both within and outside the city, granted to you by the bishops; the fourth part of the offerings which are made at the litanies; the tithes of Gropole and Collina; and the church of Saint Blaise with the lands situated at Aqua Vivola, Virsano, Falagrano, Barzani, and Glandaria, as Girard, son of Baconchus [Note: Perhaps Racontus; for Bacontus is indeed a celebrated name among the people of Pistoia.], and Ronaldus with his son-in-law Davizzo gave them.

We also confirm by the assertion of our authority what was established by your bishops: if any of the ordinary clergy who still remain in their own homes should depart from the world, whatever appears to belong to their order shall be converted to the use of the canons living according to the rule. This must be done with such diligence and care that you do not abuse the increase of possessions as an opportunity for the liberty of the flesh or a veil for wickedness; nor should you in any way increase your possessions while diminishing the number of the brothers. Rather, let the number of canons be maintained at whatever level the resources of your place appear able to support, lest the Church suffer harm to religion and due service.

We further add that whatever your canonical community lawfully possesses today, or may lawfully and canonically obtain in the future through the grant of bishops, the generosity of rulers, or the offerings of the faithful, shall always remain firm and unimpaired for you and your successors who remain in the same religious observance, and shall serve in every way the needs of those for whose support and administration these things have been granted.

You, therefore, dearest sons in Christ, ought diligently to devote yourselves to the institutions of regular life and to observe in all things the decrees of the apostolic see, so that, after the hardships of the present life, with the Lord’s help you may deserve to attain the glory of the heavenly expanse.

If, in the future, any archbishop or bishop, emperor or king, margrave, count, viscount, judge, or castaldus, or any person, great or small, knowingly attempts rashly to act against this page of privilege, and, after being warned a second and third time, does not correct himself by suitable satisfaction, let him lose the dignity of his power and honor, recognize himself as guilty before the divine judgment for the iniquity committed, be separated from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord and Redeemer Jesus Christ, and be subjected to strict punishment at the final judgment.

But let there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ for all who preserve justice toward this place, so that here they may receive the fruit of good action and may find, before the strict Judge, the rewards of eternal peace. Amen, amen, amen.

Given at Pistoia, by the hand of John, cardinal deacon of the holy Roman Church, 14 Kalends of January, indiction 3, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1094, in the seventh year of the pontificate of Lord Urban II, pope.

---

### CXIX. Letter of Urban II to Durannus, bishop of Clermont  
*He orders him to command that the monastery of Blessed Lupus be restored by the canons of Billom to the monks of Cluny. (Year 1094.)*

*[Mabillon, Benedictine Annals, vol. V, p. 336.]*

Urban, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Durannus, his dearest brother, bishop of Clermont: greetings and apostolic blessing.

A considerable complaint has arisen against your Fraternity concerning the canons of Billom, who are regarded as subject to your jurisdiction. Namely, they have seized the monastery of Blessed Lupus—which has been held under the jurisdiction of the monastery of Cluny for many years, beyond our memory—in a dreadful manner, intolerable to Catholic ears. Usurping it against all right and law, they destroyed the altar of that monastery, plundered the relics lying within it, and—and this is wicked to say or hear—did not hesitate to scatter upon the ground the very body of the Lord that had been placed upon the altar for the use of the sick and and was to be revered by the powers above the heavens. They also carried away for their own use the other ornaments and the entire equipment of the monastery.

We do not believe that your prudent mind is unaware how grave, how dreadful, and how intolerable to Catholic ears these things appear. We are therefore greatly astonished that your vigilance could have allowed them to remain unpunished, if the truth of the matter is indeed as reported.

By this present letter, therefore, we remind you of the duty of your office: see that you restore the aforesaid place and all the utensils taken from it to the monks of Celsinac. Once they have been reinvested, if the canons of Billom claim to have had any right in that place, let them, at a suitable time, present themselves with the monks of Celsinac before our presence.

But if the canons of Billom disdain to obey this command of ours, impose an interdict upon them from the divine office until, having come to their senses, they restore to the provost and brothers of Celsinac what they have plundered. If they disregard the judgment of episcopal authority, let them know that by our authority they are forbidden the divine offices, so that neither they themselves anywhere nor anyone else in their church may dare to celebrate them until they have fulfilled what we have ordered.

---

### CXX. Letter of Urban II to William, count of Toulouse  
*He rebukes him concerning the abbots expelled from Moissac and Lézat. (Around the year 1094.)*

*[Baluze, Miscellanea, Luc edition, vol. II, p. 181.]*

[Col. 0392D]

Urban, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to William, count of Toulouse: greetings and apostolic blessing.

We rejoice with the greatest joy and give the greatest thanks concerning the religious devotion and almsgiving which you are said to display toward God and his servants. There is something, however, that makes you . . . affect our goodwill, because we have heard that you are carrying out justice so thoroughly. This is increased by the fact that you could in no way tolerate the unjust expulsion of the abbots of the monasteries of Moissac and Lézat and the unlawful substitution of others in their places.

We make known to you that we have consecrated our venerable brother Ansquilinus as abbot of Moissac, while we have decreed that the usurper Hunald must withdraw from that monastery; and we have communicated the whole matter by our letters to the bishop of Cahors.

Let your religious devotion, therefore, labor diligently for the decrees of the apostolic see and apply itself to carrying out our commands in accordance with our wishes.

Since we have learned that you wholly love and honor the church of Saint Mary the Golden at Toulouse [Note: *History of the Counts of Toulouse*, p. 125], in response to your prayers and in agreement with your devotion, we grant you permission to construct a cemetery there for yourself and your descendants and to have it blessed. And so that you may devote yourself with dutiful service to blessed Mary and blessed Peter the apostle, we absolve you, and all who may wish to be buried in that place for the sake of religion, through the grace of blessed Peter, from every bond of sin.

You shall command the bishop of the city, in our name, to consecrate it.

---

### CXXI. Letter of Urban II to William [Gerald?], bishop of Cahors  
*He orders him, after expelling Hunald, to restore Ansquilinus to the monastery of Moissac. (Around the year 1094.)*

*[Baluze, Miscellanea, Luc edition, vol. II, p. 181.]*

[Col. 0393C]

Urban, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to William, bishop of Cahors: greetings and apostolic blessing.

Although Hunald, from the monastery of Moissac, has raised his heel against his mother, the Roman Church, mother of all Churches—having become abbot in that monastery and having expelled Ansquilinus contrary to the will of the Roman Church—we have nevertheless, through the kindness and patience of the apostolic see, suspended the sentence and spared so great a presumption.

We command you to expel Hunald from that monastery and to restore our venerable brother Ansquilinus to the same place as abbot, within forty days after you have received our letters. If you do not complete this within the prescribed period, we shall suspend you from every office, even against your will.

But so that you may strive with all diligence, know that you will obtain the blessing of the mouth of our Lord through the disposition of our hand. If, therefore, you obey our commands, you will be judged favorably by us. But if not, we shall strike you with our arrows. As you conduct yourself, so shall you have us.

---

### CXXII. Letter of Urban II to Godefrid, bishop of Lucca  
*That those who kill excommunicated persons out of zeal for the Church are not to be regarded as murderers. (Between 1088 and 1095.)*

*[Mansi, Councils, vol. XX, p. 713.]*

[Col. 0394A]

As you know to be the custom of the Roman Church concerning the killers of excommunicated persons, impose upon them, according to their intention, a suitable form of satisfaction. For we do not consider them murderers if, burning with zeal for the Catholic mother, it should happen that they slaughter any of those who are excommunicated.

Nevertheless, lest the discipline of that same mother Church become excessively harsh, impose upon them, in the manner we have stated, an appropriate penance, through which they may be able to please the eyes of divine simplicity toward themselves, if perhaps, through human frailty, they have contracted some duplicity in the same offense.

[Note: Gratian excerpted these very words from Urban’s letter to Sancius, *Decretum* 32, question 2, canon “De neptis.”]

---

### CXXIII. Letter of Urban II to Cyriacus, bishop of Genoa  
*Who must establish kinship by oath. (Between 1090 and 1095.)*

*[Gratian, *Decretum*, C. XXXV, question 6, canon 3.]*

We notify you that, after three or two of the closer relatives of the deceased wife of the man who is accused, or of the living woman, have confirmed this kinship by oath—or after three or two of the older Genoese, to whom this kinship is known, who are of good reputation and truthful testimony, having put aside affection, fear, payment, and every evil motive, have confirmed the consanguinity in the aforesaid manner—the marriages are to be dissolved without any delay.

But if relatives or outsiders merely testify to the kinship in words and either refuse or are unable to prove it by oath, the marriage is not to be dissolved in any way. Rather, a suitable penance is to be imposed upon them for the infamy or stain of sin, if perhaps they have contracted some such fault in this matter.

---

### CXXIV. Letter of Urban II to the brothers Roger, duke, and Bohemond  
*He defends the monks against usurpers. (Between the years 1094 and 1095.)*

*[Mansi, Councils, vol. XX, p. 647.]*

Urban, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Roger, duke, and Bohemond, his brother: greetings and apostolic blessing.

Before our presence, Abbot Urso of Bantinus made a complaint concerning certain counts and barons who, seduced by the crafty and envious [or: envious and crafty] machinations of bishops, are now disturbing him and his monastery, consecrated by our hands, even more severely.

Since it is not unknown to you that the aforesaid monastery belongs by right to blessed Peter, by the authority of blessed Peter and our own we commend the monastery and its abbot to you, so that you may guard and assist them and faithfully defend them from evil men as the property of blessed Peter. Do not permit anyone to inflict either plunder or any diminution of its rights.

[Col. 0395A]

Always remembering that [perhaps: and] at the consecration of that monastery we specially commended the abbot and the monastery itself into your hands, defend our monastery from everyone, and especially from Goffredo, son of Count Amicus, as faithful men of blessed Peter, both by that former commendation and by the command of this letter.

That man, accompanied by robbers, confronted the abbot—even though the abbot was traversing the coastal regions in defense of his own property and the Church’s possessions—and, having snatched from him by fraud [perhaps: having stolen] our precious privilege, obtained at your petition, together with other documents, plundered his goods and, after his companions had heaped insults upon him, left him on foot. From there he wickedly reclaimed for his own sacrilegious hands whatever had previously been donated by his father, the count, to the same monastery as a restoration.

If that sacrilegious man refuses to return the privilege and whatever he has plundered, and to make worthy satisfaction to the abbot and brothers, we command you to compel him. Otherwise he and his supporters shall be subjected to anathema.

---

### CXXV. Letter of Urban II to Beringer, abbot of Saint Lawrence of Liège, persecutor of the Simoniacs and Wibertists, expelled by Emperor H[enry] and Bishop Obert  
*(Between the years 1094 and 1095.)*

*[Mansi, Councils, vol. XX, p. 915.]*

Urban, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved brother in Christ, Beringer, abbot: greetings and apostolic blessing.

[Note: Beringer, formerly prior of the monastery of Saint Aubert at Andain, became the first prior of Saint Lawrence of Liège and was afterward made abbot in place of Abbot Wolbod, who had been deposed by Bishop Henry. He was appointed by the votes of all the brothers in the year 1075. Martène.]

[Col. 0395C]

We give thanks to God for you, for the grace of God that has been given to you. In this evil time, when almost all Gaul lies submerged in the darkness of error, he has enlightened the eyes of your mind to the knowledge of truth, so that the fire of his Spirit might kindle your heart to love justice and defend the Catholic faith.

We give thanks to him who has intoxicated you with the splendid cup of his grace, who has made the Spirit of the Lord, fervent in your reason, ready to endure manifold injury, and who has roused you to undergo labors and dangers in defense of the truth.

We do not doubt that this is a special gift of God, who, through the provident grace of his dispensation, usefully tests and examines his elect in a time of persecution. Yet, lest they stray completely or, shaken, be utterly cast down, he sustains them by the power of his strength, so that they may become readier to endure all things for his sake and may be made stronger.

As we know for certain, previously, when others were laboring in defense of truth and justice, you used to assist them with every office of charity, with great joy of heart and cheerfulness of countenance, ministering beyond your strength to the needs of the saints; to attack the Simoniacs and Wibertists, the Church’s new enemies, with powerful verbal arrows; to batter the trembling wall of their reasoning with the ram of faith; and to strengthen the athletes of God who had fallen in the battle-line of Christian religion.

Now divine mercy has looked upon your devotion, and at last the lofty Majesty deigns that you should suffer for him who was not ashamed to bear the disgrace of the cross for your glory. Your prudence ought to respond in some measure to so great a benefit of heavenly grace: having gratefully accepted the cup of salvation, you should seek the glory and honor of the eternal King and, in every condition of your life, invoke, praise, bless, and magnify the name of him who has granted you understanding.

Nor should the losses of temporal goods trouble you, nor the fact that H. [Note: Henry IV, king of the Romans, the third emperor of that name, who created a schism in the Church by elevating Wibert to the see of Saint Peter and expelling the most holy Gregory VII. ID.], a man who overturns Christian peace, a sacrilegious seller of churches, destroyer of the Roman Empire, author and defender of heretics, expelled you from your church through his henchman, Bishop Obert [Note: Otbert, provost of Holy Cross at Liège, fled to King Henry after Bishop Henry died in 1090 and purchased the bishopric from him for a large sum of money; he immediately expelled Abbot Beringer and restored Wolbod, as the contemporary author of the *History of Saint Hubert* relates. ID.].

For if he called (the printed *invocavit*, “invoked,” should read *vocavit*, “called”) the master of the household Beelzebub, how much more his household servants? (Matthew 10:25.) If he inflicted deadly hands upon the holy and apostolic Roman Church, should it seem strange to you that the sword of his madness reached even to you?

If he tyrannically expelled from the pontifical chair the supreme priest to whom the almighty Lord, through Peter, had granted by singular privilege the power of opening and closing the gates of the heavenly kingdom to whomever he wished, and in his place erected a golden statue in the holy place and compels as many as he can to worship them, why are you troubled that he violently expelled you and caused a clay and molten idol of abomination to be placed in your position?

Rather, rejoice, because God wishes you to be a companion of the labors of his saints. If you are unwilling to endure the plundering of temporal goods for Christ, how would you rejoice to endure the harshness of death for Christian truth?

I believe that it is God’s will—or rather, the work of divine mercy—that some human force compels you to leave that pit of curse and wickedness, lest righteous Lot perish with the unjust, lest the mirror of your holiness admit some contamination from dwelling together with the surrounding wickedness.

For what wall would stand unshaken, what mind would remain immovable in its firmness, where coarse swine grunted continually, where a crowd of evildoers besieged the simplicity of your innocence?

[Col. 0396D]

Obert, standard-bearer of Antichrist, beast of burden of Satan, manifest follower of Simon’s treachery, despiser of apostolic judgments, and, insofar as he is able, trampler upon the Church; the robber, destroyer, and profane seller of the churches which he rashly seized for his own destruction—now he would thunder threats, now with devilish flatteries and cunning strive to bend the head of your firmness.

We have already excommunicated him, condemned by the authority of God, blessed Peter, and the holy Roman Church, which, under God’s guidance, I serve, in accordance with the decree of the council recently held by us. Together with his Wibert, that terrible and many-formed beast which rises from the sea and makes war upon the saints, whom those whose names are not written in the book of life and of the Lamb worship, we have assigned him a portion of the curse because he is a Simoniac, because he usurped the bishopric by paying money, because at the command of his king he unjustly expelled you from your place, because, after accepting money from him, he installed one who had been publicly adjudged and condemned for contumacy and disobedience, and because he laid hands upon a certain Lupus [Note: Or Luponus, abbot of Saint Trond, who had been expelled from his dignity by Henry of Liège. See the *Chronicle of Saint Trond*, *Spicilegium*, vol. VII. ID.], who had been publicly and justly condemned for the Simoniacal heresy and other capital offenses.

Likewise, we have condemned and excommunicated that profane invader of the Church, Wolbod, because by Simoniacal and tyrannical power, through ill-gotten money, he invaded your abbey and the place from which, through his insolence, he had fallen like the devil from heaven.

[Note: Concerning him, an ancient author of the *History of Saint Lawrence*, which we shall publish [the work was published in vol. IV of the *Ancient Monuments*], says: “He borrowed a great deal of money from the merchants of this country, to be repaid from this church; from it the king received three hundred marks, while Obert received no small part.” ID.]

Together with him we expel, anathematize, condemn, and judge as sacrilegious all his military retainers, helpers, and supporters, and all those to whom he has sold or given the offerings of the faithful, the property of the Church, and the things previously dedicated to divine use, until they restore them to the Church.

But you, dearest brother, rejoice, because the King of Israel wishes his son to sit and weep beside the rivers of Babylon and to sigh with a free affection of heart for the return to the land of promise, not to perish entangled in those rivers and worldly pursuits.

The sum of our desire is that your prudence should hold fast what reason persuades, divine Scripture bears witness to, the order of holy religion requires, the blood of martyrs intimates, and our mother, the holy Church, commands and commends. Truth itself willed to die in order to turn us toward the truth; nothing except Truth alone will free our souls from the power of the devil.

The brothers who are presently gathered here with us—bishops, clerics, abbots, and monks—salute you in Christ and those who are with you. We earnestly ask you to remember us in your holy prayers and to pray fervently for our peace and that of the holy Church to him who brought peace to the earth at his birth and betrothed the Church to himself with his own blood.

Our dearest son Gerbert, bearer of this letter, will secretly inform you when, where, how, and with whom you may come to us without Satan’s hindrance.

Farewell.

---

### CXXVI. Bull of Pope Urban II for the monastery of Saint Peter at Puteoli, in the diocese of Lucca  
*(Year 1095.)*

*[Mittarelli, Camaldolese Annals, vol. III, Appendix, p. 114.]*

[Col. 0398A]

Urban, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son Martin, prior of the monastery of Saint Peter, situated in the parish of the Church of Lucca, in the place called Puteoli, and to his successors forever.

A desire which is shown to pertain to a religious purpose and the salvation of souls ought, with the Lord as its author, to be fulfilled without any delay. Therefore, dearest son in Christ, granting your petitions, we fortify by the authority of this present decree the monastery of Saint Peter, over which, with the Lord as its author, you preside.

For we establish that whatever the same monastery lawfully possesses today, or may lawfully and canonically obtain in the future through the grant of pontiffs, the generosity of rulers, or the offerings of the faithful, shall remain firm and unimpaired for you and your successors. We also wish you to possess forever, without any molestation, the tithes of the possessions contained within the property of the monastery.

We further decree that the burial ground of the same place shall be entirely free, so that no one may obstruct the devotion and final wishes of those who decide to be buried there, saving the due rights of the parish church.

Therefore, we decree that no person at all may rashly disturb the same monastery, take away the possessions subject to it, retain what has been offered, diminish it, or harass it with rash vexations. Rather, everything shall be preserved intact and shall serve in every way the needs of those for whose support and administration it has been granted, saving the due and canonical reverence owed to the Church of Lucca.

If, in the future, any archbishop or bishop, emperor or king, count or viscount, judge or castaldus, or any person, great or small, knowingly attempts rashly to act against this page of our privilege, and, after being warned a second or third time, does not correct himself by suitable satisfaction, let him lose the dignity of his power and honor, recognize himself as guilty before the divine judgment for the iniquity committed, be separated from the most sacred body of God and of our Lord and Redeemer Jesus Christ, and be subjected to strict punishment at the final judgment.

For all others, etc.

Blessed be God and the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ. Amen.

Given at Florence by the hand of John, cardinal deacon of the holy Roman Church, on the Kalends of February, indiction 3, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1095, in the seventh year of the pontificate of Lord Urban II, pope.

---

### CXXVII. Bull of Urban II for the monastery of Saint Giles, confirmed at the Council of Piacenza  
*(Year 1095.)*

*[Baluze, Miscellanea, Luc edition, vol. II, p. 177.]*

[Col. 0399A]

Urban, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to all the faithful throughout the Gothic province: greetings and apostolic blessing.

We wish all of you to know that our beloved son Raymond, count of Toulouse, moved both by our admonitions and those of other religious men, and struck by the fear of almighty God, has returned to God, to holy Mary, the Mother of God, to the holy princes of the apostles Peter and Paul, and to blessed Giles the confessor the share—or rather, the plunder—which he had been accustomed to possess on the altar of Saint Giles and on the other church altars belonging to that altar, as a result of the seizure by his parents.

This restoration or renunciation took place at the synod of Toulouse in the presence of our legate Bernard, archbishop of Toledo, and many bishops and abbots. Likewise, on the feast of Saint Giles, in the presence of the same legate and very many other bishops and abbots, he confirmed the same restoration with his wife Hervira and his son Bertrand upon the altar of blessed Giles, placing there two coins of Giles’s currency.

Therefore, at the request of that count, we confirm this act by apostolic authority, undertaken for his salvation and that of his parents, and we beseech the mercy of almighty God that, by his favor, he may forgive them what they have hitherto committed through the usurpation of ecclesiastical property and, through the merits and prayers of the holy apostles and Saint Giles, absolve them from the bonds of their sins.

Furthermore, we subject both him and all his descendants to anathema and exclude them from the entire fellowship of the Church if they should thereafter attempt to seize the offerings of the altars. Whoever, whether from that count or from anyone else, holds a fief from those offerings shall likewise, once he has learned the force of this decree, be subject to the same anathema unless he restores it entirely to the Church.

We also forbid the monks themselves, under anathema, ever to permit any layperson to possess a share in the offerings of those altars. Otherwise, both the one who gives and the one who receives shall be subject to the anathema we have pronounced.

[Col. 0399D] Given at the hand of John, cardinal deacon of the holy Roman Church, at Cremona, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of March, in the third indiction, in the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1095, and in the seventh year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Urban.

> **[Note: Col. 0399D]** The following additions were made later.

It was reread and confirmed in the council which the same pope held at Piacenza.

I, John, cardinal bishop of Porto, have subscribed.  
I, Albert, cardinal, have subscribed.  
I, Richard, cardinal priest of the holy Roman Church and abbot of Marseille, have subscribed.  
[Col. 0400A] I, Bonus the Elder, cardinal priest, have subscribed.  
I, Teuzo, cardinal priest, have subscribed.  
I, Gregory, cardinal deacon, have subscribed.  
I, Daibert, archbishop of Pisa, have subscribed.  
I, Rodulf, archbishop of Tours, have subscribed.  
Hugh, cardinal deacon of the holy Roman Church, has subscribed.  
Hermann, cardinal.  
I, Philip, bishop of Luni, have subscribed.  
I, William, bishop of Orange, have subscribed.  
I, Roger, deacon of the holy Roman Church, have subscribed.  
I, John, cardinal bishop of Porto, have subscribed.  
[Col. 0400B] I, William, archbishop of Auch, together with my suffragans—namely Dodo, bishop of Bigorre; Sancho, bishop of Lescar; Otto, bishop of Oloron; and William, bishop of Couserans—have subscribed.  
I, Otto, bishop of Imola, have subscribed.  
I, Rodulf, archbishop of Reggio, have subscribed.

Peter the Venetian, patriarch; Peter, archbishop of Milan; Gotafrid, bishop of Maguelonne; Berengar, bishop of Fréjus; Amatus, archbishop of Bordeaux; Aldebert, archbishop of Bourges; Peter, archbishop of Aix; and Fulco, bishop of Beauvais, were present.

Tetbald, abbot of Vercelli, approved it. Poncius, abbot of La Chaise-Dieu, and Frotardus, abbot of Saint-Pons, also approved it.

These men, together with all the archbishops, bishops, and abbots [Col. 0400C] sitting in the synod at Piacenza, approved and confirmed this charter of relinquishment at the command of the lord pope. They also subjected forever to anathema anyone who thereafter invaded or usurped what had been relinquished, and ordered that, if an invasion should ever occur, the entire monastery should cease from every divine office by being placed under interdict.

## CXXVIII. Pope Urban II receives the monastery of Saint George in the Black Forest under his protection and grants it notable liberties. (Year 1095)

*[Schoepflin, Alsat. dipl., vol. I, p. 177.]*

**URBAN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son Thoger, abbot of the monastery of Saint George, [Col. 0400D] situated in the Black Forest beside the river Brigach, and to his successors regularly appointed, forever.**

The desire which is shown to belong to a religious purpose and the salvation of souls must, with God as its author, be fulfilled without any delay. Therefore, since the noblemen Herilo and Hesso, in the diocese of Constance, in the district called Baar, in the county of Ascheim, in the forest which they call the Black Forest, beside the river Brigach, built a monastery in honor of Saint George the martyr, and entrusted that same monastery, together with everything they had offered there, to the blessed apostle Peter, we, in accordance with their devotion, receive the aforesaid place under the special protection of the apostolic see, so that it may be fostered.

Therefore, by the text of the present privilege, we establish by apostolic authority that whatever estates or possessions the aforesaid men or anyone else has offered from his own right to the aforesaid monastery, and whatever it may hereafter justly and canonically obtain through the concession of pontiffs, the liberality of princes, or the offering of the faithful, shall remain secure and unimpaired for you and your successors.

Moreover, no priest, king, duke, count, or any other person may claim for himself in that place any condition of ownership—whether hereditary right, advocacy, or the usurpation of any power—that might harm the liberty of the monastery. The abbot and his brothers shall have free power to appoint as advocate whomever they wish. If that man later proves useless to the monastery, they shall remove him and appoint another.

When you, the present abbot of that place, or any of your successors dies, no one shall be placed over it through any device of subreption or violence, except one whom the brothers, by common agreement, or the sounder-minded part of the brothers’ council, shall have elected according to the fear of God and the Rule of Saint Benedict.

So that the brothers gathered in that place may devote themselves more freely to the service of almighty God, we decree that no human being may rashly disturb that monastery or take away, diminish, or harass with reckless vexations the possessions subject to it. Rather, everything shall be preserved intact, so as in every way to benefit the uses of those for whose support and administration they were granted.

[Col. 0401C] You, however, beloved sons in Christ, ought diligently to adhere to the institutions of regular discipline and to aspire to every virtue of soul and mind, so that, walking along the narrow way, you may be able to please almighty God and reach heavenly blessedness.

As a sign of the liberty received from the Roman Church, you shall pay each year one gold Byzantine coin to the Lateran palace.

If, in the future, any archbishop or bishop, emperor or king, duke or margrave, count or viscount, or any ecclesiastical or secular person knowingly attempts rashly to act against the text of this constitution of ours, then, after being warned a second or third time, if he does not make amends by suitable satisfaction, let him lose the dignity of his power and honor, recognize himself to be guilty before the divine judgment of the iniquity committed, be separated from the most sacred body of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ the Redeemer, and be subject to strict punishment at the final judgment.

But let there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ for all who preserve what is just toward that place, so that both here they may receive the fruit of good action and, before the strict Judge, find the rewards of eternal peace. Amen, amen, amen.

Given at Piacenza through the hand of John, cardinal deacon of the holy Roman Church, on the eighth day before the Ides of March, in the third indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1095, and in the seventh year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Urban II.

> **[Note: Col. 0401D]** Those are mistaken who persuade themselves that Eugene IV was the very first to use the Incarnation era in his rescripts, and who therefore render suspect as interpolations all bulls dated by the years of the Incarnation before Eugene IV. Popes had already occasionally used the Incarnation era from the time of Leo IX onward, but under Eugene IV and his successors that usage began to become constant. *(Mabillon, De re diplomatica, book II, chapter 25; Pagi, Vitae pontificum, vol. II, p. 356.)*

## CXXIX. The monastery of Hirsau in the diocese of Speyer is received under the protection of the apostolic see, and all its possessions are confirmed to it. (Year 1095)

*[Cocquelines, Bullar. collect., II, 80.]*

**URBAN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son Gebehard, abbot of the monastery of Hirsau, [Col. 0402B] and to his successors regularly appointed, forever.**

Although we are indebted to all the sons of the holy Church through the authority and benevolence of the apostolic see, nevertheless we ought to devote ourselves with more eager charity to those places and persons which adhere more specially and intimately to the Roman Church and which excel through a greater grace of religion.

Therefore, following the example of our predecessor of blessed memory, Gregory, we grant and confirm to you and your legitimate successors the same things which he granted and confirmed to your predecessor William and to that monastery at the petition of Count Adalbert. Inflamed by love of eternal recompense, Adalbert had repaired attractively, in his estate called Hirsau, a monastery built long ago by his ancestors, restoring what had recently been lost; and he had enlarged it with many possessions and revenues for the use of the brothers serving God there.

He requested that this arrangement of his liberality be fortified by a privilege of apostolic authority and strengthened by the protection of the holy Roman Church, so that no audacity of wicked men might thereafter diminish or violate it. For this reason, embracing the aforesaid monastery especially under the protection and guardianship of the apostolic see, we establish by the text of the present privilege that whatever the same monastery justly possesses today, or may hereafter justly and canonically obtain through the concession of pontiffs, the liberty of princes, or the offering of the faithful, shall remain secure and unimpaired for you and your successors.

[Col. 0402D] Among these we have thought it appropriate to specify by name: the cells of Saint George, called Richenbach, and of Saint Martin, called Vischbahajo, and the estate called Gilstein, which was given for the cell of Saint Peter. We establish that neither you, beloved son Gebehard, nor any of your successors may presume to destroy the aforesaid cells or rashly diminish what has been or shall be granted to them.

Moreover, we decree that no human being may rashly disturb that monastery or take away, diminish, or harass its possessions with reckless vexations. Rather, everything shall be preserved intact, so as in every way to benefit the uses of those for whose support they were granted.

We also carefully establish, for the protection of posterity and to ward off the assaults of aggressors, the provisions concerning immunity and liberty which the aforesaid illustrious Count Adalbert inserted in the written charter of his donation and caused to be impressed with the royal seal, so that nothing of what was promised may be neglected and nothing of what was forbidden may be attempted.

When you, the present abbot of that place, or any of your successors dies, no one shall be placed over it through any device of subreption or violence, except one whom the brothers by common agreement, or the sounder-minded part of the brothers’ council, shall have elected according to God and the Rule of Saint Benedict.

The consecrations of altars or basilicas, the ordinations of clerics, holy oil, and the other matters belonging to episcopal office you shall receive from the bishop of Speyer, in whose diocese you are, provided that he is catholic, maintains communion with the apostolic see, and is willing to provide these things freely and without simoniacal depravity. Otherwise, you may approach any catholic bishop whom you wish and receive from him the sacraments of consecration; supported by apostolic authority, he shall grant what you have requested.

Moreover, we appoint as your advocate or protector Godfrey, the son of the aforesaid Count Adalbert, provided that, by God’s favor, he proves to be such a man as will show due honor to the Church and to the servants of God and will be a useful and diligent defender of the aforesaid monastery. If not, it shall be in your power to choose a suitable protector for your church, one who will vigorously and reverently perform that service of divine worship without demanding secular profit.

You, therefore, beloved sons in Christ, ought to pursue more anxiously and devotedly the institutions of regular discipline and to aspire to the virtues of mind and soul, striving especially to observe the venerable decrees of the Roman Church, by whose patronage, with the Lord’s assent, you have been fortified against every yoke of the living.

As a token of the liberty received from the Roman Church, you shall pay each year one gold Byzantine coin to the Lateran palace.

If, in the future, any bishop or archbishop, emperor or king, count or viscount, judge, or any person, great or small, knowingly attempts rashly to act against the text of this privilege of ours and renders void anything that has been granted or established, then, after being warned a second or third time, if he does not make amends by suitable satisfaction, let him know that he is bound by eternal anathema and separated, by the authority of apostolic power, from the body of Christ and from the Church.

But for those who preserve these things, may peace from God and mercy be preserved in the present and future ages. Amen.

## CXXX. Letter of Urban II to the clergy and people of Noyon.—He sends back to them, with the fullness of his favor, Bishop Radbod, who had attended the council of Piacenza, and confirms the privileges granted to the Church of Noyon by his predecessors. (Year 1095)

*[D. Bouquet, Recueil, vol. XIV, p. 712.]*

[Col. 0404B]

**URBAN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons, the clergy and people of Noyon, greeting and apostolic blessing.**

Let your love know that our brother Radbod, your bishop, reached the council which, with the Lord’s assent, we held at Piacenza.

> **[Note: Col. 0403D]** The council of Piacenza was held in the year 1095, on the Kalends of March, according to the Chronicle of Berthold.

While he was with us, no one brought forward anything against him.

> **[Note: Col. 0403D]** Radbod had confessed himself guilty of simony to Hugh, bishop of Die and legate of the apostolic see, as Hugh himself relates in his letter to Gregory VII. When the matter was brought before the Council of Poitiers in 1078, the decision was left to the judgment of Gregory VII, who appears to have decided nothing. Urban, however, left the matter unresolved in this letter.

> “When it had been judged that he should clear himself of simony with two bishops,” says Hermann in *The History of the Restoration of the Church of Saint Martin of Tournai*, no. 72, “Master Anselm, then the foremost teacher of the school of Laon and the most renowned throughout France for his learning, withdrew the assistance of the bishops from him by his counsel, being aware that they could not safely swear him innocent. When, after many interventions, he was permitted to clear himself by his own hand, Hugh, archbishop of Lyon and legate of the apostolic see, seeing that he wished to swear, rose before everyone and said: ‘What are you doing, wretched man, who by swearing falsely seek to kill your soul? Stop this oath, and we shall obtain that you not be deposed for the present, but, having a delay of two years, you will afterward voluntarily resign the pontificate honorably, as though on account of religion or old age. For if you swear, behold, I foretell you that you will not leave this year with honor.’ The bishop, as he had begun, placed his hand upon the Gospel text and, swearing himself innocent of simony, left the council confident and returned to Tournai. A few days later he went to Bruges, etc., where he died a sudden death on a Sunday within the octave of Epiphany in 1097, or 1098 according to the French reckoning.”

Therefore we send him back to you with the fullness of our favor. Nevertheless, if any complaint should arise against him, whether concerning his entry into the episcopate or for any other reason, let it be heard more carefully before Hugh, the legate of Lyon.

We decree that the authentic privileges of his Church, which his predecessors obtained from our legitimate predecessors, shall remain valid and be preserved undisturbed.

Given at Piacenza, on the seventh day before the Ides of March.

## CXXXI. Bull of Urban II for the abbey of Saint Peter in the Black Forest. (Year 1095)

*[Schoepflin, Historia Zaringo-Badensis, Karlsruhe 1763, quarto edition, V, 29.]*

**URBAN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons in Christ who are striving under the Rule of Saint Benedict in the place called the Cell of Saint Peter, and to their successors regularly appointed, forever.**

[Col. 0405A] The desire which is shown to belong to a religious purpose and the salvation of souls must, with God as its author, be fulfilled without delay. Therefore, since the man of distinguished nobility, Duke Berthold, built a monastery in the county of Breisgau, in the diocese of Constance, in the forest called the Black Forest, in honor of Saint Peter, prince of the apostles, and also subjected that allod to the jurisdiction of the Roman Church, we, confirming his devotion by our authority, have received that place under the special protection of the apostolic see, so that it may be fostered.

Therefore, by the text of the present privilege, we establish by apostolic authority that whatever estates or possessions the aforesaid duke, or other men from their own right, have offered to your monastery, and whatever you may hereafter justly and canonically obtain through the concession of pontiffs, the liberality [Col. 0405B] of princes, or the offering of the faithful, shall remain secure and unimpaired for you and your successors.

We decree, therefore, that no human being may rashly disturb that monastery or take away, diminish, or harass with reckless vexations the possessions subject to it. Rather, everything shall be preserved intact, so as in every way to benefit the uses of you and your successors.

When the man who performs the ministry of abbot among you dies, no one shall be placed over it through any device of subreption or violence, except one whom the whole community of your fellowship, or the sounder-minded part of it, shall have elected according to the fear of God and the Rule of Saint Benedict.

The advocate whom you establish for your rights shall have no power to dispose of anything in your monastery. No secular person may reside in that place.

[Col. 0405C] You, however, beloved sons in Christ, ought diligently to adhere to the institutions of regular discipline and to aspire to every virtue of soul and mind, so that, walking along the narrow way, you may be able to please almighty God and reach the heavenly expanse.

As a token of the liberty received from the Roman Church, you shall pay each year one gold Byzantine coin to the Lateran palace.

If, in the future, any archbishop or bishop, emperor or king, prince or duke, count or viscount, judge, or any person, great or small, secular or ecclesiastical, knowingly attempts rashly to act against the text of this constitution of ours, then, after being warned a second or third time, if he does not make amends by suitable satisfaction, let him lose the dignity of his power and honor, recognize himself to be guilty before the divine judgment, be separated from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ the Redeemer, and be subject to strict punishment at the final judgment.

But let there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ for all who preserve what is just toward that place, so that both here they may receive the fruit of good action and, before the strict Judge, find the rewards of eternal peace. Amen.

Given at Piacenza through the hand of John, cardinal deacon of the holy Roman Church, on the sixth day before the Ides of March, [Col. 0406A] in the third indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1094, and in the seventh year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Urban II.

## CXXXII. Letter of Urban II to Robert, count of the Flemings, and his nobles.—He urges him to assist Lambert, bishop of Arras, in recovering the possessions of the Church. (Year 1095)

*[Mansi, Concilia, XX, 675.]*

**URBAN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son Robert, count of the Flemings, and to his nobles, greeting and apostolic blessing.**

In repeated letters we exhort and beseech you on behalf of our beloved brother Lambert, bishop of Arras, to extend to him the hand of your counsel and assistance in restoring the dignity of the renewed bishopric, and to labor in every way, for the remission of your sins, to wrest from the hands of their holders and restore to that Church the possessions of the same bishopric which were wrongly alienated by the bishops of Cambrai, to whom that Church had been entrusted.

Moreover, we wish and command by apostolic authority that at no time hereafter you allow the aforesaid Church to be subjected to or harassed by any Church. Rather, honor it as your mother and lady, while preserving the rights of the Church of Reims; take care to protect and defend it from injuries.

Given at Piacenza, on the fifth day before the Ides of March.

## CXXXIII. Letter of Urban II to Walter, bishop-elect of Cambrai.—He urges him not to injure the rights of the Church of Arras. (Year 1095)

*[Mansi, Concilia, XX, 675.]*

[Col. 0406C]

**URBAN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son Walter, bishop-elect of Cambrai, greeting and apostolic blessing.**

You ought to remember that you promised by oath faithfully to observe the decrees of the apostolic see. Therefore, take care not to attempt, on any pretext, to disturb what the apostolic see has established concerning the Church of Arras.

Indeed, we wish and command you to permit all those things which you recognize, according to our privilege, to belong to the right of that Church to be peacefully possessed by it and to remain undisturbed.

## CXXXIV. Letter of Urban II to Guido, archbishop of Vienne. (Year 1095)

*[D. Ruinart, Vita Urbani, p. 363.]*

[Col. 0406D]

**URBAN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Guido, archbishop of Vienne, greeting and apostolic blessing.**

In providing for the need and utility of the Church, we tolerated in your promotion what was lacking in age. Contrary to the custom of our Church, we granted you the pallium while you were absent, and we also granted a privilege. In it, however, your legate caused to be entered through subreption something which, until your time, the bishop of Grenoble had possessed; we hold him in very great affection in the Roman Church.

Since our venerable brother, the aforesaid bishop, had often complained to us and to our legate concerning this matter, you, forgetful of such great benefits, obeyed neither our letters nor those of our legate, nor our command.

Recently, when that same bishop came to the council which, with God’s assent, we held at Piacenza, he complained publicly about the same matter—namely, the district of Salmoriac—and it was also made clear by the assertions of many that that district had belonged under certain bishops to the Church of Grenoble.

Therefore, we decree that the act of subreption by which you claim, as though by privilege, the property placed under complaint is invalid and has no force. Accordingly, by synodal judgment, we reinvested him in that district, without prejudice to the justice of your Church, and by the authority of these present letters we command you to complete that reinvestiture and allow him to possess it peacefully until the matter is decided by canonical judgment either before us or before our legate.

If you disregard this, know for certain that you will lose the favor of blessed Peter and of us.

Given at Piacenza, on the fourth day before the Ides of March.

## CXXXV. Pope Urban II confirms the transfer of the bishopric of Oca and the division of parishes made at the council of Fusella. (Year 1095)

*[Flórez, España sagrada, XXVI, 463.]*

**URBAN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved brother Gomesanus, [Col. 0407C] bishop of Burgos, and to his successors canonically appointed, forever.**

That many cities once flourished in Spain through the glory of the Christian religion and the dignity of episcopal sees is shown by the monuments of holy martyrs and confessors and is indicated by the numerous councils of Toledo. We know that some of these cities were destroyed. Nevertheless, through the mercy of almighty God, many were afterward restored to Christian rule and received again the insignia of their former dignity. The dignity of others, which had been utterly destroyed, was transferred to neighboring cities.

Thus, when the episcopal city of Oca had failed, so that the whole diocese belonging to it might not lack the consolation of its own shepherd, the city of Burgos was established by the Christian princes as the substitute of Oca. There, in fact, our beloved son King Alfonso built an episcopal church at his own expense. So that this institution may remain permanently stable, with the Lord’s help, we confirm it by apostolic authority through the text of the present decree.

We also order that the divisions of parishes which were established between the churches of Burgos and Osma before Richard, cardinal priest and legate of the apostolic see, and the abbot of Husillos, in a synod at the monastery of Fusella, shall have perpetual force, as we have learned from the statement of that same brother of ours.

Moreover, we establish that both Valeránica and the other monasteries or villages [Col. 0408A] which are known to have been granted to the Church of Burgos through the wills of catholic princes shall always remain under the administration and possession of you, beloved brother, and your successors.

Whatever the same Church of Burgos may justly and canonically obtain in the future, whether through the liberality of princes or the offering of the faithful, we command by the authority of the present decree that it possess forever by right.

If, in the future, any archbishop or bishop, emperor or king, prince or duke, count or viscount, judge, or any secular or ecclesiastical person knowingly attempts rashly to act against the text of this decree of ours, then, after being warned a second or third time, if he does not make amends by suitable satisfaction, let him lose the dignity of his power and honor, recognize himself to be guilty before the divine judgment of the iniquity committed, be separated from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ the Redeemer, and be subject to strict punishment at the final judgment.

But let there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ for all who preserve what is just toward that place, so that both here they may receive the fruit of good action and, before the strict Judge, find the rewards of eternal peace.

Given at Piacenza through the hand of John, cardinal deacon of the holy Roman Church, on the day before the Ides of March, in the third indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1095, and in the eighth year of the pontificate of Lord Urban II.

## CXXXVI. Bull of Urban II confirming the canonical life established in the Church of Maguelonne. (Year 1095)

*[Gallia Christiana nova, vol. VI, p. 352.]*

[Col. 0408C]

**URBAN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons in Christ Orgerius, archdeacon; Raymond, priest; and Deodatus, subdeacon; and to the others professing the canonical life in the Church of Maguelonne, and to their successors who shall live in the same religious observance, forever.**

The disposition of pious will ought to be fostered by attentive zeal, so that ecclesiastical utility may receive strength and increase through the favor of the apostolic see.

We give thanks to almighty God, whose mercy is better than lives, because you are the ones who have resolved to renew the exemplary life of the holy Fathers and, at the prompting of the Holy Spirit, to revive the institutions of apostolic teaching which were unfamiliar to the beginnings of the holy Church but, as the Church grew, had almost been entirely destroyed.

Therefore, by the authority of our office we confirm your vow and your purpose. We exhort you to remain firm in it, and, as though God were exhorting through us, we beseech you to do so.

For this reason, to all those in your monastery who profess the canonical life according to the Rule of Saint Augustine and who remain in it with the Lord’s help, we, although unworthy vicars of the apostles, grant their blessing and ours, together with the absolution of sins, by the power granted to us by the Lord. We establish that no one at all may alter this condition of your order.

[Col. 0409A] We also establish that no one who has professed the canonical life, after having [uncertain: “deifice”] placed a man upon his head, may, prompted by any frivolity or under pretext of a stricter religious life, dare to leave that cloister without the permission of the provost and the whole congregation. No abbot, bishop, or monk shall receive the person who departs without a common letter of security.

By apostolic authority we prohibit you from placing over yourselves a provost, archdeacon, or minister of any ecclesiastical administration unless he is one whom the common election of the brothers living according to the rule has regularly chosen according to God.

Since some among you still have not chosen the canonical life, but support you with brotherly charity as though you were among the last, we do not compel them to adopt your way of life. But when they either convert to the regular life or depart from the world, we decree by the present authority that their honors and ecclesiastical possessions, together with their increases or improvements, and the lands thereafter given to your Church, shall pass into the possession of the regular brothers. No one shall thereafter be made or ordained a canon there unless he has professed that he will live canonically.

Moreover, whatever our brother Godefrid, your bishop, has given for your use—namely, the churches of Villeneuve, Montpellier, and Gigean, with the tithe of the village of Paderne; the churches of Saint Eulalia and Saint Leocadia of the Valley; Saint Michael of Montel; Saint John of Cucon; Saint Marcellus of the Brothers; Saint Andrew of Mauron; Saint Peter of Mont-Arbedon; Saint Hilary of Centraneges; Saint Stephen of Bézénac; Saint John of Vedace; Saint Felix of Véruna; Saint Stephen of Pignano; Saint John of Buia; and Saint Andrew and Saint Dionysius of Montpestelleret; Saint Martin of Prunet—all with their chapels, tithes, offerings, and allods—and whatever he may thereafter give, we grant you shall remain secure and intact.

We also command that henceforth the bishop may not, without your counsel, grant to any monk or canon anything belonging to the right of the mother Church. Any such grant made otherwise shall be considered invalid.

When the bishop dies, everything belonging to him shall remain under your care until another is canonically substituted in his place; and we especially wish that this substitution be established by your election.

So that, with the Lord’s help, you may hold perseveringly and inviolably the purpose of canonical life which you have begun, we confirm by the authority of the present decree, for you and your successors who remain in the observance of canonical life, all the immunity generally decreed to churches by the sacred canons and laws, all the liberty granted by catholic princes, and especially the liberty granted to your Church by the commands of Emperor Louis addressed to Bishop Argimirus.

In addition, we establish that near Villeneuve, which belongs to your property, no one may ever build on the bend of the island any fortification that could harm you or your successors.

If, in the future, any archbishop or bishop, emperor or king, prince or duke, count or viscount, judge, or any person, secular or ecclesiastical, knowingly attempts rashly to act against the text of this decree of ours, then, after being warned a second or third time, if he does not make amends by suitable satisfaction, let him lose the dignity of his power and honor, recognize himself to be guilty before the divine judgment of the iniquity committed, be separated from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ the Redeemer, and be subject to strict punishment at the final judgment.

But let there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ for all who preserve what is just, so that here they may receive the fruit of good works and, before the strict Judge, find the rewards of eternal peace. Amen, amen, amen.

Given at Piacenza through the hand of John, cardinal of the holy Roman Church, on the day before the Ides of May, in the third indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1095, and in the eighth year of the pontificate of Lord Urban II.

## CXXXVII. Privilege for the monastery of Cluny. (Year 1095)

*[Bibliotheca Cluniacensis, p. 516.]*

**URBAN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his most reverend brother Hugh, abbot of the monastery of Cluny, and to his successors regularly appointed, forever.**

Although we are indebted to all the sons of the holy Church through the authority and benevolence of the apostolic see, nevertheless we ought to devote ourselves with more eager charity to venerable persons and places, especially those which have always adhered more specially and devotedly to the apostolic see and which excel through the greater glory of religion.

Therefore, most reverend and beloved brother, on account both of the ancient familiarity of the apostolic see and of the most noble reverence due to your religious life and that of your monastery, a special prerogative of affection is owed to you by us.

Whatever liberty, whatever immunity, and whatever authority is known to have been granted by the privileges of our predecessors to you and your successors, and to your monastery, we too grant, deliver, and confirm through the text of this decree of ours.

[Col. 0410D] For this reason, to that chapel which your vigor built outside the town, on its eastern side, in honor and under the name of Saint Odo, we grant by the authority of the present decree the complete liberty and immunity which our predecessor Gregory of apostolic memory confirmed by his privilege for the other chapels of that same town.

To this we add that the monastery of Saint Stremonius of Mauzaca, Saint Mary of Verziac [Vizeliac], Saint Peter of Alta-Petra, and the monastery called Sales shall never be withdrawn from the ordering and governance of you or your successors. We decree the same concerning all the monasteries and churches written below, namely:

In the diocese of Lyons: the church of Saint Justus and Saint Desiderius; the church of Frontenaic and that of Rorterius.

In the diocese of Mâcon: the church of Meletum, Otgers, Saviniac, Seniciac, and Berziac; the church of Saint Hippolytus, Saint Martin, and Saint Mary of Casella.

In the diocese of Autun: the church of Monrisalt, Pulignium, Blanchiaca, Monte Saint John, Luciacum, Crupella, and Milpont; the church of Saint Mammes and Saint Christopher.

In the diocese of Langres: the church of Saint Eulalia; Saint John of Laon, Trualt, Arcus, Vandovra, Marmaissa, and Altars.

In Basila,* the church of Saint Alban.

In the diocese of Chalon: the church of Viniules.

In the diocese of Clermont: the church of Saint Amandus, the Holy Sepulchre of Lavenna, Saint Mary of Castello, Canaries, Montania, Nigro-Stapulo, Angeroli of Arumna.

In the diocese of Vienne: the church of Artaz, Moras, Mantula, Loteng, and Monte-Castaneto.

In the diocese of Grenoble: the church of Alavart, Avalun, Teies, Valbones, and Visilia.

In the diocese of Valence: the church of Cabetul, Castelli, Ales, and Urz.

In the diocese of Die: the church of Saint Sebastian, Saint Euphemia, Saint Peter of Trefrort, Arun, Aurel, Calciun, and New Castle.

In the diocese of Toul: the church of Our Lady and that of Frondonis villa.

In the diocese of Metz: the church of Tihencurt.

In the diocese of Limoges: the monastery called Boort.

In the diocese of Beauvais: the church of Saint Lupus and Saint Christopher.

In the diocese of Meaux: the church of Saint Mary of Nantolium.

In the diocese of Paris: the church of Saint Mary of Longpont and that of Alnes.

In the diocese of Amiens: the church of Saint Peter of Lehun.

In the diocese of Thérouanne: the church of Saint Michael.

In the diocese of Soissons: the church of Saint Peter of Cusiacum.

In Lombardy: the monastery of Saint Valerian of Castello Rothobio, Saint Maiolus of Pavia, Saint Michael of Mucharion, Saint Maiolus of Castemola, Saint Mary of Ferrara, together with everything that Gonteranus gave at Lomello and in the Lomellina; the church of Saint Mary of the Lake.

In the diocese of Vercelli: the monastery of Saint Peter of Castellitio, Saint John of Baina, Saints John and Paul of Sandaliano, Saint Martin of Salamone, and Saint Mary Ferminiana; the church of Parione, Calvallium, and Saint Peter of Sade.
