### CLXIV. Urban II’s synodal letter to the clergy and people of Cambrai. (Year 1095.)

[Mansi, Councils XX, 917.]

[Col. 0437C]

Urban, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to all the clergy and people of Cambrai: greeting and apostolic blessing.

When, at the council celebrated at Clermont in Auvergne, the question concerning the election made by you of our beloved son Manasses and likewise of Gualcherius had been raised and carefully investigated, it became clear that Manasses had indeed been canonically elected by you, whereas Gualcherius had intruded himself into your church contrary to the authority of the holy canons.

Therefore, by the judgment of the whole council, it was decided that Gualcherius, as an invader, should be expelled from your Church, and that Manasses should be restored to his election and to your Church. Gualcherius, however, withdrew from the council of his own conscience. After he had been summoned a third time and had altogether evaded appearing, we regarded his flight as a confession and, in accordance with the universal sentence of the council, issued on the authority of the holy canons, deposed him from the entire episcopal order. We restored Manasses to his election and to your Church, with the praise and confirmation both of your metropolitan, the archbishop of Reims, and of all the suffragans of that metropolitan see.

Now, by these letters, we admonish you and command by apostolic authority that you presume no longer to receive Gualcherius, but render fuller obedience to Manasses as your truly catholic bishop. [Col. 0438A] Nor should it escape your notice that Gualcherius is subject to anathema if he should thereafter attempt, with profane presumption, to interfere in the government of your Church.

Therefore, if anyone henceforth should presume to oppose these commands of our decrees, he shall encounter the indignation of almighty God and his apostles and shall be struck by the sword of apostolic vengeance. By apostolic authority we also absolve all who have sworn fidelity to Gualcherius from the bond of that oath.

Given at Auvergne on the second day before the Kalends of December.

### CLXV. Pope Urban II’s decree concerning the primacy of Lyon. (Year 1095.)

[Mansi, Councils XX, 828.]

[Col. 0438B]

Urban, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother Hugh, archbishop and primate of Lyon, and to his successors who shall be canonically promoted, in perpetuity.

By the duty of the apostolic see and the authority of the holy canons, we are compelled to correct throughout all the Churches of the world what has been wrongly done and to confirm what has been rightly established. Therefore, when the favor of the heavenly disposition granted that we come into the regions of Gaul, we took care to summon a general council at Clermont in Auvergne.

There, among the other matters brought forward for synodal hearing and discussion, your fraternity presented a complaint concerning the primacy of the holy Church of Lyon, a matter already disputed in many earlier provincial councils. At that gathering, privileges of Roman and apostolic authority affirming that primacy were read.

When Richer, archbishop of Sens, had therefore been ordered to respond on the following day concerning this matter, but had offered no legitimate reason for excuse, it nevertheless pleased us, out of the abundance of apostolic gentleness, to grant a postponement until the third day for deliberation concerning this subjection. On the third day, when he had withdrawn from the synodal assembly, partly because of the gravity of the matter and partly on account of illness, he was summoned through legates; but, refusing to obey, he still requested time for deliberation.

As the decision was already imminent, the suffragans of the church of Sens again obtained a postponement until the following day, so that they might approach him more privately. This promise was made beforehand: if he should then still obstinately resist, they themselves would nevertheless unanimously obey the council’s decision.

When the sixth day of the council had passed and he still resisted by requesting postponements, it was established, with the favor and judgment of the entire synod, that the archbishop of Sens owed subjection and obedience to the archbishop of Lyon as primate, because both the authority of the catalogues and the authority of the apostolic see bore witness to the same. Each of the suffragans of the church of Sens declared in his own voice that he would humbly obey that judgment.

The same was also confirmed concerning the church of Rouen. As for Tours, because it had already obeyed without resistance from earlier times, no question was raised.

On the eighth day of the council, your fraternity again complained that the archbishop of Sens, although admonished by your legates—namely Agano, bishop of Autun, and Lambert, bishop of Arras—still professed no reverence toward the Church of Lyon on account of its primacy. Therefore, with the entire council consenting, we forbade the archbishop of Sens the use of the pallium and the obedience of his suffragans until he obeyed.

We promulgated the same sentence against the archbishop of Rouen, who was absent, unless within three months after learning of the sentence he promised in writing the subjection that was due, if he could not do so in person. His suffragans who were present received our sentence with due humility and promised obedience. Thus, with the Lord’s assent, the long-standing complaint of the Church of Lyon was finally concluded.

Therefore, by the text of this present privilege, we confirm to your Church of Lyon the primacy over four provinces, and through it to you and your successors—but only to those who have been elected or promoted in that order and according to that form which was established and prescribed by the privilege of Gregory VII of holy memory for your predecessor Gibuinus.

The provinces that we confirm to you are Lyon, Rouen, Tours, and Sens, so that these provinces may render fitting obedience to the Church of Lyon and, with devotion and humility, offer the honor which the Roman pontiffs have prescribed in their own writings as due, while preserving in all things reverence and authority for the apostolic see.

If in the future any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowingly confronting this privilege, should attempt to act against it, then, after being admonished a second or third time, unless he corrects his conduct by making appropriate satisfaction, let him lose the dignity of his power and honor, acknowledge himself condemned by divine judgment for the iniquity committed, be excluded from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord and Redeemer Jesus Christ, and be subject to strict punishment at the final judgment.

But let there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ for all who preserve what is just for that Church, so that both here they may receive the fruit of good action and, before the strict Judge, find the rewards of eternal peace. Amen.

Twelve archbishops of various provinces were present at this decision, together with eighty bishops, ninety abbots, and more.

Given at Clermont in Auvergne by the hand of John, cardinal deacon of the Holy Roman Church, on the Kalends of December, in the third indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1095, in the eighth year of the pontificate of Lord Urban II, pope.

### CLXVI. Privilege for the church of Saint James of Compostela. (Year 1095.)

[Flórez, Sacred Spain, XX, 21.]

[Col. 0440A]

Urban, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved brother Dalmatius, bishop of Compostela, and to his successors who shall be canonically promoted, in perpetuity.

The sequence of ancient synodal decisions and pontifical acts acknowledges that it has always been permitted to the apostolic see, as circumstances required, to separate things joined, join things separated, and exchange one see for another.

Strengthened, therefore, by this authority of our predecessors, by the authority of the present decree we grant to you, dearest brother in Christ Dalmatius, and to your successors, out of reverence for blessed the apostle James, that just as your predecessors held the episcopal chair in the city called Ilia [Note: It is written Ilia or Hilia in various places; in this same codex it is called Iria, as are the terms “Irienses” and “port of Iria”], so henceforth you shall hold it perpetually in the place called Compostela, which contains the church in which the body of blessed James is believed to rest.

We have therefore decreed that everything belonging to the diocese of the aforesaid city of Ilia shall always remain entire and inviolate for you and your successors. Furthermore, out of singular devotion to blessed James, we grant that both you and your successors shall henceforth be subject to no one except the Roman metropolitan; and that all who succeed you in that see shall be consecrated by the hand of the Roman pontiff as special suffragans of the Roman see.

Moreover, by a decree that shall remain in force forever, we establish that whatever has hitherto been lawfully offered to the church of blessed James in royal charters, whatever is contained in legitimate catalogues, and whatever the see of Iria is known to have lawfully possessed from its parishes shall always be preserved secure and intact for you and your legitimate successors remaining at Compostela.

It is fitting, moreover, for your holiness to observe in all things the decrees of the Holy Roman Church and to shine inwardly and outwardly with the light of virtues, so that all may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven.

If in the future any archbishop or bishop, emperor or king, prince or duke, marquis, count, viscount, judge, or any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowingly confronting this decree, should rashly attempt to act against it, [Col. 0440D] then, after being admonished a second or third time, unless he corrects his conduct by making appropriate satisfaction, let him lose the dignity of his power and honor, acknowledge himself condemned by divine judgment for the iniquity committed, be excluded from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, and be subject to strict punishment at the final judgment.

But let there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ for all who observe these provisions and venerate the aforesaid church of blessed James, so that both here they may receive the fruit of good action and, before the strict Judge, find the rewards of eternal peace. Amen, amen, amen.

[Col. 0441A] Given at the town of Privata [Note: It is called Privatium elsewhere, in the Vivarais region of Gaul, not far from the Rhône], by the hand of John, cardinal deacon of the Holy Roman Church, on the Nones of December, in the third indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1095 [Note: In the manuscripts that I have been able to see, the year 1116 is written; this is certainly corrupt, since Urban died before the year 1100. I have inverted the numbers CX for XC and added not VI but V, so that the year is 1095, which alone is established by the accompanying evidence—namely, the Council of Clermont, the third indiction, and the eighth year of his pontificate; he ascended the chair on 12 March 1088], in the eighth year of the pontificate of Lord Urban II, pope.

### CLXVII. Pope Urban II’s letter to Hugh, abbot of Cluny.—He grants the Cluniac monks permission to retain the altars and tithes which they had acquired by purchase and to withdraw tithes from the hands of laymen, if this can be done according to God’s will. (Year 1095.)

[D. Bouquet, Collection, XIV, 716.]

Urban, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother Hugh, abbot of Cluny, and to the brothers placed under his governance: greeting and apostolic blessing.

The benevolence of the apostolic see has always been accustomed to cherish the servants of God as a mother cherishes her children, and to extend the hand of consolation mercifully and eagerly to those placed in difficulties. Since, therefore, through the grace of almighty God, you have for a long time flourished far and wide in outstanding religious observance and have sprinkled many with the fragrance of a good reputation, it is fitting for us to provide henceforth for your tranquillity and to set the shield of apostolic protection against the attacks of your rivals over your monastery, both its head and its members.

Therefore, by the authority of the present decree, we establish that no bishop shall henceforth have the power to inflict any burden or trouble concerning the altars, churches, or tithes which, before our prohibitions or those of Pope Gregory, you are known to have possessed, or which you acquired afterward by the concession of bishops. Rather, just as you held some of them in part and others in their entirety by their permission, so you shall possess them perpetually in the future [Note: The second canon of the recent Council of Piacenza had decreed that whatever had been acquired in the sacred orders or in ecclesiastical matters, whether given or promised for money, was invalid and would never have any force. Hence the disturbances which the Cluniacs suffered from the bishops, against which Urban judged it fitting to set the shield of apostolic protection].

As for the tithes of those churches which you do not possess but which are held by laymen, if the reverence of your religious life is able to withdraw them from their control according to God’s will, you may possess them for the governance of yourselves and of the poor.

To ensure that all these provisions remain wholly firm and unshakable, we confirm them by the power of the almighty Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, and by apostolic authority. But if anyone, having learned the tenor of this decree, should obstinately presume to oppose it, let him encounter the indignation of the same Father and Son and of their apostles and be struck by the sword of the Holy Spirit. But upon all who cherish you and what belongs to you, may mercy, peace, and grace from the Author of all things be bestowed throughout perpetual ages.

Given at the town of Brive, by the hand of John, cardinal deacon of the Holy Roman Church, [Col. 0442A] on the Nones of December, in the third indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1095, in the eighth year of the pontificate of Lord Urban II, pope.

### CLXVIII. Diploma of Pope Urban II confirming all the privileges and possessions of the priory of Marcigny. (Year 1095.)

[Cluniac Library, Appendix, p. 86.]

Urban, servant of the servants of God, to the nuns of the monastery of Marcigny: greeting and apostolic blessing.

We recognize that, by the Lord’s arrangement, we have been promoted to the service of the apostolic see for this purpose: that we should effectively assist those who implore its help and, as the Lord grants, guard and protect those who obey it. [Col. 0442B] Therefore we ought to extend the hand of protection to venerable places and to provide with particular care for the tranquillity of those who serve God.

Accordingly, both on account of your special religious observance and because of our affection for our venerable brother Hugh, abbot of Cluny, under whose care your place belongs by right of the Cluniac monastery, we assent to your prayers, dearest daughters in Christ, and fortify your monastery by the authority of the present decree.

We decree that whatever that monastery justly possesses today, or may in the future justly and canonically acquire through the concession of pontiffs, the generosity of princes, or the offering of the faithful, shall always remain secure and inviolate for you and for those who succeed you in the same place and religious observance.

Among these possessions we have decided to specify the following by name:

In the diocese of Autun: the church of Varennes; those of Brian and Sarory; that of Bessay; that of Camboliac; the churches of Saint Nicetius, Saint Faith, Saint Christopher, Saint Leodegarius, and Saint Mary outside the town of Semmur, with their tithes and cemeteries; and one quarter of the church of Saint Martin outside Semmur.

In the diocese of Mâcon: the church of Saint James.

In the diocese of Lyon: half the village of Vitry; the church of Saint Martin; the church of Saint Reverian at Briançon; the church of Saint Romanus; the chapel of Celerias; and the land of Hugh Letbald, together with certain other possessions at Casiotum.

In the diocese of Clermont: the church of Saint Peter of Lodda; Saint Vincent of Lodessa, with its tithes and cemeteries; and Saint Nicholas at the Three Fountains.

In the diocese of Die, at the town or territory of Orello, four churches. In the diocese of Valence, the church of Saint Stephen of Balma. In the county of Béarn, the church of Saint Faith at the village called Furcas. In the diocese of Poitiers, two churches. In Saintes, the church of Montoso. In Liège, the village called Argules, with its church and tithes, and another called Raicampas. In Rouen, the village called Aqua-Bella. In the Périgueux region, fifteen mansi belonging to Prioress Agilmodis, at the village of Maurense. In Cahors, the church of Saint Constantius. In the diocese of Vivarais [Vaurais], three villages—Villeta, Ataid, and Glangla—with all their possessions and appendages.

Moreover, we decree that no one at all shall be permitted rashly to disturb that church, or to take away its possessions, retain what has been taken away, diminish them, or harass them with reckless vexations. Rather, everything shall be preserved intact and shall in every way benefit the uses of those for whose support and governance it was granted, without prejudice in all things to the due reverence owed to the abbots of Cluny.

We establish that the burial of that place shall be entirely free, so that no one may resist the devotion and final wish of those who decide to be buried there, unless they happen to be excommunicated. We also add to this present chapter that no one shall henceforth be permitted to impose upon your congregation the burden of excommunication, prohibit the divine office, prevent due burial, or inflict the trouble of any interdict, because you have been enclosed for fear of God and have already died to the world, so that, secure from every assault and removed from the burden of worldly oppression, you may always yearn with all the strength of your mind and soul for the desirable vision of the eternal Bridegroom.

If in the future any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowingly confronting this constitution of ours, should rashly attempt to act against it, then, after being admonished a second or third time, [Col. 0443C] unless she or he corrects the conduct by making appropriate satisfaction, let that person lose the dignity of power and honor, acknowledge before divine judgment the guilt of the iniquity committed, be excluded from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord and Redeemer Jesus Christ, and be subject to strict punishment at the final judgment.

But let there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ for all who preserve what is just for that place, so that both here they may receive the fruit of good action and, before the strict Judge, find the rewards of eternal peace. Amen, amen, amen. Blessed be God, the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ. Amen.

Given at the town of Saint-Flour by the hand of John, cardinal deacon of the Holy Roman Church, in the third indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1096, in the eighth year of the pontificate of Lord Urban II, pope, on the seventh day before the Ides of December.

### CLXIX. Pope Urban II’s letter to Ademarus, bishop of Angoulême.—He compels the monks of Saint-Eparchius, by the penalty of excommunication, to obey the abbot of Saint-Jean-d’Angély. (Year 1095.)

[D. Bouquet, Collection, vol. XIV, p. 717.]

Urban, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother Ademarus, bishop of Angoulême: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Our most beloved son in Christ, Ausculfus, abbot of Saint-Jean-d’Angély, reported to us in person that the monastery of Saint-Eparchius, once subjected through your favor to the monastery of Saint-Jean-d’Angély, had been taken away through the presumption of wicked monks. We have learned that these monks were excommunicated in certain councils for that same presumption, as our venerable brother and legate Amatus, metropolitan bishop, has testified.

Therefore, by these present writings, we command your vigor to ensure that this excommunication is observed in your diocese until those monks consent to obey the aforesaid abbot according to the rule.

Given at Limoges, on the fourth day before the Kalends of January, by the hand of John, cardinal deacon.

### CLXX. Pope Urban II’s bull for the monastery of Tulle. (Year 1096.)

[Baluze, History of Tulle, Appendix, p. 437.]

[Col. 0444B]

Urban, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son William, abbot of the monastery of Tulle, and to his successors who shall regularly be appointed, in perpetuity.

The pious petition of a willing heart ought to be brought to completion by the fulfillment that follows, so that both the sincerity of devotion may shine forth commendably and the benefit requested may undoubtedly gain strength. Since, therefore, your affection, fleeing to the harbor of the Apostolic See, sought its protection with due devotion, we have graciously assented to your supplication and, by the authority of this decree, fortified the monastery of Saint Martin of Tulle, over which, with God’s authorization, you preside. We establish that whatever the same monastery justly possesses today, or may thereafter justly and canonically acquire [Col. 0444C] through the grant of pontiffs, the generosity of princes, or the offering of the faithful, shall remain secure and unimpaired for you and your successors.

We therefore decree that no person whatsoever be permitted rashly to disturb the aforesaid monastery, or to take away its possessions, or to retain what has been taken away, diminish them, or harass them with reckless vexations. Rather, let everything be preserved intact, so that it may in every way serve the uses of those for whose support and administration it was granted. Since certain churches or estates belonging to the monastery of Tulle have hitherto been given to laymen by irreligious abbots or monks, or have been usurped by laymen for the benefit of other monasteries without lawful possession, we order that they be restored wholly to your monastery. In addition, we establish that the monastery itself shall not be excommunicated on account of the misdeeds of the soldiers residing in the castle of Tulle, on the condition, however, that if those same soldiers have been excommunicated, they shall not be admitted there to the divine offices. By apostolic authority we also prohibit the lands of the monastery of Tulle from being devastated or harassed on account of offenses committed by those soldiers.

Moreover, we decree that burial at that place shall continue according to the ancient and canonical custom, without prejudice to the respect due to the bishop of Limoges. When you, the abbot of that place, die, or any of your successors, no one shall be placed there through any stratagem of deceit or by violence, except one whom the brothers shall have elected by common consent, or the more prudent part of the brothers’ council, according to the fear of God and the Rule of blessed Benedict. Therefore, under the prohibition of a strict anathema, we decree that no person whatsoever shall have the power to obstruct the regular election of an abbot or to demand any gift on its account, so that the brothers of that monastery, freed from every burden of worldly oppression, may strive, diligent and undisturbed in the observance of holy religion, to please almighty God with all the powers of mind and soul.

If, in future, any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowingly attempting to act rashly against this page of our constitution, does not correct the offense with suitable satisfaction after being warned a second or third time, let that person be deprived of the dignity of his power and honor, recognize himself as liable before the divine judgment for the iniquity committed, be separated from the most sacred body and blood of God and our Lord and Redeemer Jesus Christ, and be subject to strict punishment at the final judgment. But let there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ for all who observe what is just toward that place, so that both here they may receive the fruit of good action and, before the strict Judge, find the rewards of eternal peace. Amen, amen, amen.

Given at Limoges, by the hand of John, cardinal deacon of the Holy Roman Church, on the fourth day before the Nones of January, in the fourth indiction, in the year of the Incarnation of the Lord 1096, and in the eighth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Urban II.

Farewell.

### CLXXI. Letter of Urban II to the suffragans of the Church of Reims

He exhorts them to obey Manasses, appointed in place of the deceased archbishop Rainold. (Year 1096.)

[Baluze, *Miscellanea*, edition of Lucca, II, 138.]

[Col. 0445C]

Urban, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his most beloved brothers and fellow priests, the suffragans of the Church of Reims, greeting and apostolic blessing.

After the death of our venerable brother, the archbishop of your metropolitan church, we have learned that Manasses, the provost of that same church, was advanced to govern the metropolis by the common consent of the clergy and people, in accordance with the decrees of the Apostolic See. Since this advancement plainly appears to conform to the holy canons, it cannot fail to be pleasing to us. Confirming it, therefore, by the weight of our authority, we exhort your affection by this present letter not to withhold from the person of the elected man anything that belongs to your office through any form of evasion. Rather, make every effort so that what has been well begun may, by the Lord’s generosity, be brought to a better completion, lest so great a Church remain any longer deprived of the exercise of episcopal duties.

Given at Angers, on the eighth day before the Ides of February.

### CLXXII. He exhorts the clergy, order, knights, and people of Reims to show fidelity to Manasses, the elected archbishop

(Year 1096.)

[Baluze, *Miscellanea* II, 139.]

Urban, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons—the clergy, religious order, knights, and people residing at Reims—greeting and apostolic blessing.

The depths of our affection, most beloved sons in Christ, have been constricted, because we know that you have been deprived of the solicitude of a shepherd, and we of the consolation of our brother and fellow bishop Rainold. Yet in this tribulation the inner chambers of our charity are enlarged by the grace of almighty God, because we have learned that you have chosen a shepherd from among the sons of your Church with due care, attentive affection, without deceit, and without wickedness. The consensus of your unanimity confirms the confidence of your hope. For where the petition of all is in agreement, we ought in no way to doubt that the Lord Jesus is there both the author of the will and the arbiter of the petition, the director of the appointment, and the giver of grace.

We therefore congratulate your worthy efforts with still greater devotion, and what you have begun justly and holily according to the decrees of the Apostolic See, we confirm by the grace of almighty God through the declaration of the Apostolic See. You have risen into the liberty of the Apostolic See, so that, just as you are the head of the kingdom, so also you may be the beginning of religion and Catholic authority in that same kingdom. Therefore let no words of the wicked prevail against you, and let no perversity of earthly intention obscure anything. For we trust that what the almighty Lord anticipated by inspiring you, through the merits and prayers of blessed and glorious Mary ever-virgin and of your holy father Remigius, he will continue to bring to completion by assisting you.

Trusting in him, take care to pursue what you have [begun] simply and without wickedness. For in this matter the arm of the Apostolic See will not be withdrawn from you. Let no disguise of idolatry intrude in this affair; let no threats or terrors move your nobility away from this liberty—lest, God forbid, having begun in the spirit, you should be brought to completion in the flesh. We have sent letters of our authority to the suffragans of your Church, so that they may not neglect to fulfill toward the elected man whatever belongs to their office. But if they should perhaps withdraw from him through some wickedness—which we do not believe—present him to our presence at a suitable time. For the liberty and grace of blessed Peter knows how not to fail those who trust in it.

We have judged it unnecessary to exhort you at length to display lively affection and obedience toward him. For we do not doubt that the one who inspired in you such unanimity, such zeal, and such ardor in his election will also illumine your minds with the fervor of his spirit, so that you may love, obey, and serve him. May he himself bless you by his grace, strengthen you, and lead both shepherd and flock into the pastures of eternal refreshment.

Given at Angers, on the eighth day before the Ides of February.

### CLXXIII. He congratulates Manasses, the elected archbishop of Reims

He warns him: “Take great care and keep watch lest you be subjected, through any instability, to royal pride.” He promises assistance. (Year 1096.)

[Baluze, *Miscellanea* II, 139.]

[Col. 0447A]

Urban, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son Manasses, elected archbishop of Reims, greeting and apostolic blessing.

We give thanks to almighty God because we have learned that your person, whose integrity we trust greatly, has been elected without wickedness to govern the Church of Reims. Now, therefore, visiting your affection with a letter of apostolic grace, we exhort you to strive to raise good beginnings to better advances. Let no threats or terrors impede your prudence, so that you may persist in the simplicity and liberty with which you began. Take great care and keep watch lest you be subjected, through any instability, to royal pride, lest, having begun in the spirit, you be consumed in the flesh. Do not doubt at all the assistance of the Apostolic See, because if you remain in its liberty, you will be fortified in all things by its help.

Given at Angers, on the eighth day before the Ides of February.

### CLXXIV. Letter of Urban II to Philip, bishop of Châlons

He commends to him and to his brother Hugh, count of Champagne, the monks of Saint Vanne of Verdun, expelled by his parishioners from the church of Saint Nicholas in the forest of Lugolli. (Year 1096.)

[Dom Bouquet, *Recueil*, XIV, 719.]

[Col. 0447C]

Urban, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved brother Philip, bishop of Châlons, greeting and apostolic blessing.

This brother, the bearer of the present letter, has complained to us that both he and his brothers have suffered many injuries at the hands of certain of your parishioners, clerical as well as lay, in the church of Saint Nicholas built in the forest called Lugolli, and that their prior has been driven out of that church. For this reason we direct this letter to your affection, ordering you to compel those same parishioners to make satisfaction to the brothers for such injuries and to cease from them in the future. We also ask that, for love of blessed Peter and of us, you protect these brothers beneath the shelter of your wings and make them remain peacefully and securely under the governance of the venerable Rodulf, abbot of Verdun. We also wish your brother Hugh, count [of Troyes], to be requested by us as well as by you to protect and defend that place for the salvation of his soul and to restrain its attackers by the power of his authority.

Given at Angers, on the fifth day before the Ides of February.

### CLXXV. Privilege granted by Urban II to the monastery of Saint Nicholas, without prejudice to the canonical respect due to the bishop of Angers

(Year 1096.)

[Petit, *Theodori Poenitentiale*, II, p. 612.]

[Col. 0448A]

Urban, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son Natalis, abbot of the monastery of Saint Nicholas situated near Angers, and to his successors to be regularly appointed.

It is fitting to offer favorable consent to religious desires, so that a faithful donation may attain a heavenly effect. Therefore, lending an ear to your devotion and to the requests of the distinguished Fulk, count of Anjou, we fortify by the authority of this decree the monastery of Saint Nicholas, which, by the Lord’s arrangement, we consecrate with our own hands. We establish that what the aforesaid count offered at the dedication of that church, at our exhortation and through our hands—namely, as much land at Silvacane as ought to suffice for three, and the land at Avallo, which Count William of Orléans had given—as well as whatever exemption or gift his predecessors, the counts Geoffroy and Fulk, conferred upon that church from their own right, and whatever it justly possesses today or may thereafter justly and canonically acquire, shall remain secure and unimpaired for you and your successors.

Among these possessions we have decided to specify the following by their proper names: the church of Ariac, of Sainte-Comma, of Castillon, Segregio of Bulleio, of Paucio, of Aracaio, and of Cupollio; in the district of Poitiers, the churches of Monasterolo, Alaneio, Rilliaco, Borchiaco, and Pusanviis; in the bishopric of Le Mans, the churches of Geprona and Potroniaco; in the bishopric of Saint-Malo, the church of Saint Paternus; in Naunoton, the church of Saint Lambert and the chapels of Donacelli, Cornioquense, and Prugniaco; [Col. 0448C] in England, in the bishopric of Lincoln, the church of Guiongta, and Spalmeta with its dependent churches at Guilguenna; in the bishopric of Chester, the church of Quircheberia; in Wales, in the bishopric of Glamorgan, the church of Caillone with its appurtenances and possessions.

We therefore commend this place to all the faithful for visitation, honor, and protection. Trusting in the benefit of their devotion, in the mercy of almighty God, and in the authority of the holy apostles, and through the merits of blessed Michael, we remit one-seventh of the penalty incurred for sins to those who take care to gather here with devout hearts on the day of the dedication; specifically on the condition that on that day the abbot and monks feed the poor, and on the following day chant seven psalms with litanies in the assembly and celebrate a public Mass. We order that all who do so be secure from adversaries both on their journey there and on their return. [Col. 0448D]

In addition, we decree that no person whatsoever be permitted rashly to disturb that monastery, or to take away its possessions, or to retain what has been taken away, diminish them, or harass them with reckless vexations. Rather, let everything be preserved intact, so that it may in every way serve the uses of those for whose support and administration it was granted, without prejudice to the canonical respect due to the bishop of Angers.

Given at Sablé, by the hand of John, cardinal deacon of the Holy Roman Church, on the sixteenth day before the Kalends [Col. 0449A] of [March—see note below], in the fourth indiction, in the year of the Lord 1096, and in the eighth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Urban II.

[Note: [Col. 0449D] March appears to be missing.]

### CLXXVI. Letter of Urban II to the suffragans of the Church of Reims

(Year 1096.)

[Baluze, *Miscellanea* II, 139.]

Urban, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved brothers and fellow bishops Hugh of Soissons, Lambert of Arras, Philip of Châlons, Gerard of Thérouanne, and the other suffragans of the Church of Reims, greeting and apostolic blessing.

We recently wrote to your fraternity, and behold, we write again, lest under the pretext of any occasion you withhold from our venerable brother Manasses, elected by divine grace archbishop of your metropolis, what you recognize as belonging to your office. Therefore, by the obedience which you do not fail to recognize that you owe to the Apostolic See, we order your affection that whenever he summons you to his ordination or consecration, you hasten eagerly and promptly to that very duty, as you desire both the integrity of your order and the fullness of our grace.

Given at Tours, on the fourth day before the Nones of March.

### CLXXVII. Letter of Urban II to the clergy of Tours

He confirms the privileges of the Church of Tours. (Year 1096.)

[Mansi, *Concilia*, XX, 656.]

[Col. 0449C]

Urban, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to all the sons of the holy Church, greeting and apostolic blessing.

We wish it to be known to those present and to those who will come that God, the giver of all good things, in his mercy led our devotion to visit the tomb of blessed Martin. Since certain practices had arisen in the church of that same blessed confessor which seemed to require advancement for the better and eradication with the sickle of salvation, we remained there for seven days and more, administering medicine for souls as we entered and left among them frequently. With God inspiring and working together with us in them, we found them obedient and well disposed toward us in all things.

But since it had reached our ears that they had ceased to receive the legates of the Roman Church with the courtesy of a procession, and that the authority of this Church was not known to those legates through knowledge of its privileges, we became angry and severely rebuked them for incurring so great an offense of disobedience. When they humbly presented to us the writings of our fathers, the Roman pontiffs, we carefully examined their privileges. We noted with particular attention that, apart from the pope, the king, and the archbishop of Tours, they admitted no one to be received in procession, save once during his lifetime. Our cardinals Teuzo, Albert, Gregory of Pavia, and Rausger, Hugh, primate of Lyon, and other persons, both bishops and holders of other dignities, were present, as were Bishop Bruno of Segni and Ingelram, archdeacon of the Church of Soissons.

We, therefore, strengthened by such authority, supported their ancient custom by their written documents and reinforced it by our authority in the presence of the brothers mentioned above. Since our son Amatus, archbishop of Bordeaux, was one of the legates of the Roman Church sent into Gaul by our predecessor Gregory VII and had not been received by this Church with the solemnity of a procession, he was consequently moved to severe anger against those same clerics and had struck them with excommunication at the Council of Exoudun. We restored him to concord and peace with them. We neither compelled them to offer any satisfaction, since they had fortified themselves with effective authority, nor judged that they needed to be cleansed by absolution for such an excess. Finally, since in certain privileges of their church it has been granted to them to have their own bishop, we decree that, in his place, they shall adhere in a special manner to the Roman pontiff, and that their more serious cases shall depend upon his judgment.

If, in future, any cardinal, legate, bishop, or anyone sent from our side, knowingly attempting to act rashly against this page of our confirmation and violating our authority, seeks a procession from the church of that holy confessor, and does not desist when warned, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and honor, and recognize himself as liable before the divine judgment for the presumption committed. But let there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ for all who observe these provisions. Amen, amen, amen.

Given at Tours, in the castle of Saint Martin, by the hand of John, cardinal deacon of the Holy Roman Church, on the second day before the Ides of March, in the fourth indiction, in the year of the Incarnation of the Lord 1097 [1096], and in the ninth year of the pontificate of Lord Urban II.

### CLXXVIII. Letter of Urban II to the monks of Saint Peter of Bainson

He protects by the authority of the Apostolic See the church of Bainson, donated by his parents to the monastery of Cluny, and determines the rights of the Church of Soissons. (Year 1096.)

[Dom Bouquet, *Recueil*, XIV, p. 720.]

[Col. 0450D]

Urban, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the monks of Saint Peter at Bainson, greeting and apostolic blessing.

The authority of our office impels us both to increase religion and to provide for the peace of religious persons. Therefore, for the sake of preserving religion, we place under the authority of this decree the place of Bainson, in which you live by God’s grace, which comes to us by right of our parents, by transferring it to the monastery of Cluny. We thus fortify both you and your successors.

We have decreed that this place, like the other members of the monastery of Cluny, shall remain perpetually free, so that whatever it justly possesses today, whether from the gift of our parents or from the offering of other faithful persons, or will possess in the future, or may justly and canonically acquire, shall remain secure and unimpaired for you always. Neither the bishop of that parish nor the bishop’s archdeacons shall be permitted to inflict any trouble or injury upon you or your chaplains, or to demand anything at all beyond the twenty annual solidi which were established, with the consent of the preceding bishops and of my father, to be paid to the canons of Soissons. In all other respects, both you and your chaplains shall remain always undisturbed and free, subject to the duty of episcopal respect.

If anyone, having learned the force of this command, should presume to act contrary to it, let him, as a despiser of the Apostolic See, be struck by the judgment of the Church and by the sword of the Holy Spirit.

Given at Tours, by the hand of John the cardinal, on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of April, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1096, in the ninth year of the pontificate of Lord Urban II, in the fourth indiction.

### CLXXIX. Pope Urban II receives all the goods and rights of the monastery of Trenorci under the protection of the Apostolic See

(Year 1096.)

[Coquelines, *Amplissima Collectio*, II, 87.]

[Col. 0451C]

Urban, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son Peter, abbot of Trenorci, and to his successors to be regularly appointed in perpetuity.

The pious petition of a willing heart ought to be brought to completion by the fulfillment that follows, so that both the sincerity of devotion may shine forth commendably and the benefit requested may undoubtedly gain strength. Since, therefore, your affection, fleeing to the harbor of the Apostolic See, sought its protection with due devotion, we have graciously assented to your supplication and received the monastery of Trenorci, over which, with God’s authorization, you preside, together with everything belonging to it, under the protection of the Apostolic See.

Therefore, by this page of the present privilege, we establish by apostolic authority that whatever goods and possessions presently belong to the same monastery through the generosity of Catholic emperors or other princes, through the concession of bishops, or through the offering of other faithful persons, or whatever it may justly acquire in the future, shall remain secure and unimpaired for you and your successors. We therefore decree that no person whatsoever be permitted rashly to disturb that monastery, or to take away its possessions, or to retain or diminish its offerings, or to harass it with reckless vexations. Rather, let everything be preserved intact, so that it may in every way serve the uses of those for whose support it was granted.

We also confirm the other matters that were confirmed to the monastery of Trenorci by the privilege of Pope John, of revered memory. As for the complaint of the monks of Saint Florentius concerning the churches of Lausdun—namely, those of the Holy Cross and Saint Nicholas—which they bring against you and your Church, and which we carefully examined in our presence at Tours, we bring it to its proper conclusion, with God’s authorization. We again command by apostolic authority that they presume to inflict no trouble on you or your Church because of these matters, but that you and your successors possess the aforesaid churches perpetually by right, without their disturbance.

If any ecclesiastical or secular person should attempt to act contrary to this page of our constitution, let that person be deprived of the dignity of his power and honor, and be separated from the most sacred body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ until he repents with worthy satisfaction. But let there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ for all who observe what is just toward that place, so that both here they may receive the fruit of good action and, before the strict Judge, find the rewards of eternal peace. Amen, amen, amen.

### CLXXX. Privilege for the monastery of Saint Vincent at Metz

(Year 1096.)

[Dom Calmet, *History of Lorraine*, Documents, p. 507.]

Urban, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son Lanzon, abbot of the monastery of Saint Vincent situated at Metz, and to his successors to be regularly appointed in perpetuity.

The pious petition of a willing heart ought to be brought to completion by the fulfillment that follows, so that both the sincerity of devotion may shine forth commendably [Col. 0452C] and the benefit requested may undoubtedly gain strength. Since, therefore, your affection, fleeing to the harbor of the Apostolic See, sought its protection with due devotion, we have graciously assented to your supplication, both out of devotion to blessed Vincent the martyr and out of respect for your religious life, and by the authority of this decree we fortify the monastery of that same martyr, over which, with God’s authorization, you preside. We establish that whatever gifts and possessions the same monastery justly possesses today, or may thereafter justly and canonically acquire through the concession of pontiffs, the generosity of princes, or the offering of the faithful, shall remain secure and unimpaired for you and your successors.

[Col. 0452D] We therefore decree that no person whatsoever be permitted rashly to disturb the aforesaid monastery, or to take away its possessions, or to retain what has been taken away, diminish them, or harass them with reckless vexations. Rather, let everything be preserved intact, so that it may in every way serve the uses of those for whose support and administration it was granted, without prejudice to the canonical respect due to the bishop of Metz.

When you, the abbot of that place, die, or any of your successors, no one shall be placed there through any stratagem of deceit or by violence, except one whom the community shall have elected by common consent, or the more prudent part of the brothers’ council, according to the fear of God and the Rule of blessed Benedict. Moreover, according to the statutes of our venerable predecessors John and Benedict, we grant that, if the bishop of Metz is absent, you and your successors may on feast days go to the episcopal see and celebrate the solemnities of Mass there wearing the dalmatic and sandals.

If, in future, any archbishop or bishop, emperor or king, prince or duke, count, viscount, judge, or any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowingly attempting to act rashly against this page of our constitution, does not correct the offense with suitable satisfaction after being warned a second or third time, let that person be deprived of the dignity of his power and honor, recognize himself as liable before the divine judgment for the iniquity committed, be separated from the most sacred body and blood of God and our Lord and Redeemer Jesus Christ, and be subject to strict punishment at the final judgment. But let there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ for all who observe what is just toward that place, so that both here they may receive the fruit of good action and, before the strict Judge, find the rewards of eternal peace. Amen, amen, amen.

Given at Tours, by the hand of John, cardinal deacon of the Holy Roman Church, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of April, in the fourth indiction, in the year of the Incarnation of the Lord 1096, and in the ninth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Urban II.

### CLXXXI. Urban II confirms to the abbey of Saint Bertin, of the Order of Saint Benedict, at Saint-Omer, all its altars and possessions

(Year 1096.)

[Miraeus, *Diplomatic Works*, III, 21.]

[Col. 0453C]

Urban, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son Lambert, abbot of the monastery of Bertin the confessor of Christ, and to his successors to be regularly appointed in perpetuity.

The pious petition of a willing heart ought to be brought to completion by the fulfillment that follows, so that both the sincerity of devotion may shine forth commendably and the benefit requested may undoubtedly gain strength.

Since, therefore, your affection, fleeing to the harbor of the Apostolic See, sought its protection with due devotion, we have graciously assented to your supplication and received under the protection of the Apostolic See the monastery of blessed Bertin the confessor, over which, with God’s authorization, you preside. That monastery is known to have been founded by the same blessed Bertin in honor of the holy apostles Peter and Paul, together with everything belonging to it. [Col. 0453D] Therefore, by this page of the present privilege, we establish by apostolic authority that whatever your monastery justly possesses today, or may thereafter justly and canonically acquire through the concession of pontiffs, the generosity of princes, or the offering of the faithful, shall remain secure and unimpaired for you and your successors.

Since, however, a branch of Simoniacal wickedness has already grown for a long time in the regions of Gaul, so that churches which among you are commonly called “altars” are frequently sold to monasteries by bishops under the guise of avarice, namely when the clerics whom they call “persons” die or are changed, we, by God’s authority, drive away every form of sale both from ministers and from ecclesiastical goods, and by apostolic authority prohibit this from happening any further.

Moreover, whatever altars or tithes the monastery is known to have possessed for thirty years or more under such a redemption, we confirm as henceforth to be possessed peacefully and without any disturbance by you and your successors, subject, of course, to the annual episcopal payment which they have hitherto received from them. Namely: the church of Stenkerca in the parish of Thérouanne; the church of Gueninga; the church of Brogurgh with its chapels; the churches of Saint Margaret, Saint John, and Saint Martin; the churches of Pitarnesse, Longanessa, Gisnes, [de] Poparingehem with the town itself, Arcas, Arbella, Coiea, Helcin, Gueserna, Aquina, Bofrichem, Scasas, and Hunela, with their towns; and the church of Turboteshem. In the parish of Noyon, the church of Calmunt; in the parish of Tournai, the churches of Rukeshem, Hetlingehem, Huminkehem, and Guestkercke. In the parish of Cologne, the churches of Frekena and Gildesdorp. In the territory of Beauvais, the land called Huboisin, with all their appurtenances or dependencies.

We therefore decree that no person whatsoever be permitted rashly to disturb your monastery, or to take away its possessions, or to retain what has been taken away, or to harass it with reckless vexations. Rather, let everything be preserved intact, so that it may in every way serve the uses of those for whose support [Col. 0454C] and administration it was granted, without prejudice to the canonical respect due to the bishop of Morini.

When you, the abbot of that place, die, or any of your successors, no one shall be appointed there through any stratagem of deceit, except one whom the brothers shall have elected by common consent, or the more prudent part of the brothers’ council, according to the fear of God and the Rule of blessed Benedict. Therefore, beloved sons in Christ, take care always to have the fear and love of God in your hearts, so that, the freer you are from worldly tumults, the more earnestly you may strive with all the powers of mind and soul to please God.

If, in future, any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowingly attempting to act rashly against this page of the privilege, does not correct the offense with suitable satisfaction after being warned a second or third time, let that person be deprived of the dignity of his power and honor, recognize himself as liable before the divine judgment for the iniquity committed, be separated from the most sacred body and blood of God and our Lord and Redeemer Jesus Christ, and be subject to strict punishment at the final judgment. But let there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ for all who observe what is just toward that place, so that both here they may receive the fruit of good action and, before the strict Judge, find the rewards of eternal peace. Amen.

Given at Tours, by the hand of John, cardinal deacon of the Holy Roman Church, on the ninth day before the Kalends of April, in the fourth indiction, [Col. 0455A] in the year of the Incarnation of the Lord 1096, and in the seventh year of the pontificate of Lord Urban II.

### CLXXXII. Privilege of Urban II for the church of Marbach

(Year 1096.)

[New *Gallia Christiana*, V, p. 474.]

Urban, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons who have professed the canonical life in the church of Marbach, and to their successors who will remain in the same religious life in perpetuity.

It is fitting to grant a ready assent to religious aspirations, so that faithful devotion may attain a distinguished result. Accordingly, acceding to your prayers through our familiar, your provost Manegaldus, we receive both you and all that belongs to you under the protection of the Apostolic See, and fortify you by the authority of this present privilege.

For we decree that no one among you, once profession has been made, may possess anything as private property, nor may anyone freely depart from the cloister without the permission of the provost or of the community. If anyone should depart and disdain to return, the provost and his successors shall have the power to prohibit such a person anywhere from his offices; and no one shall absolve a person interdicted by bishops or abbots without his consent.

Furthermore, by the authority of the Apostolic See, through this present privilege we decree that whatever your church justly possesses today, or may hereafter lawfully and canonically acquire through the grant of pontiffs, the generosity of princes, or the offering of the faithful, shall remain secure and unimpaired for you and your successors. Therefore we decree that no one at all may rashly disturb this same Church, remove its possessions, retain what has been removed, diminish them, or harass them with reckless vexations; rather, everything shall be preserved intact, wholly serving the needs of those for whose support and administration they were granted.

In addition, we decree that no one may be imposed upon you as provost by violence or by any form of cunning, except one whom all the brothers by common agreement, or the sounder part of the brethren according to the fear of God, shall have regularly judged should be elected. You shall receive chrism, holy oil, the consecrations of altars or basilicas, and the ordinations of clerics from the bishop in whose diocese you are situated, provided that he possesses the grace and communion of the Apostolic See and is willing to provide these things freely and without corruption. Otherwise, you may approach whichever Catholic prelate you prefer and receive from him the sacraments of consecration.

If, indeed, any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowingly attempting to act against this page of our constitution, should be warned once, twice, or three times and fail to correct the matter by suitable satisfaction, let him lose the dignity of his power and honor, recognize that he stands guilty before the divine judgment on account of the iniquity committed, be excluded from the most sacred body and blood of God and our Lord and Redeemer Jesus Christ, and at the final judgment be subjected to strict punishment. But for all who observe what is just toward this place, let there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that both here they may receive the fruit of good action and before the strict Judge find the rewards of eternal peace. Amen, amen, amen.

Given at Tours, by the hand of John, cardinal deacon of the holy Roman Church, on the ninth day before the Kalends of April, in the fourth indiction, in the year of the Incarnation of the Lord 1096, and in the ninth year of the pontificate of Lord Urban II, pope.

### CLXXXIII. *Urban II confirms the privileges of the monastery of Corbie.* (1096)

[Mabillon, *Annales Benedictini* V, 372.]

### CLXXXIV. *He grants Gerard, the new abbot of the monastery of Saint-Maur of Glanfeuil, “the most ample privilege.”* (1096)

[D. Ruinart, *Vita Urbani*, p. 254.]

[Col. 0456B]

### CLXXXV. At the Council of Tours Urban settles the dispute between the canons of Saint Martin and the monks of Cormery, judgment being rendered in favor of the canons; he decrees that the abbots of Cormery are to take the pastoral staff from Saint Martin’s tomb at the command of the dean and chapter. (1096)

[Mansi, *Concilia* XX, 926.]

**URBAN**, bishop, servant of the servants of God.

We command that, by a letter of our authority, it be recorded for the perpetual peace of both parties how the dispute concerning the monastery of Cormery, long agitated between the canons of Saint Martin and the monks of that place, was settled in our presence by the judgment of the archbishops and abbots.

For when the privileges of Saint Martin and also the records of that monastery had been read publicly in our presence, it became clear that the place had been built from the revenues of the aforesaid church through the efforts of those canons. Later, on the pretext of advocacy or defense, it was taken from the authority of the canons by the count of Anjou. Accordingly, by the deliberation and judgment of the assembled brothers who had come with us to Tours to settle ecclesiastical affairs, Guido, abbot of Cormery, returned to the canons of Saint Martin the staff he had received improperly. It was immediately placed upon Saint Martin’s tomb; afterward, however, it was restored from that same tomb to the same abbot, since he was regarded as a man of religious conduct.

We therefore command by perpetual decree that henceforth no one be elected at the monastery of Cormery in any other manner than is contained in the privilege of the aforesaid church. The person elected according to that provision shall take the staff from Saint Martin’s tomb. Likewise, when the abbot has died, the staff shall always be returned to the same place, so that upon those most holy members of the apostolic confessor, at the command of the dean and chapter, that sign of pastoral government may always be received—without prejudice, of course, to the right of the archbishop of Tours, which is to be exercised in the ordination of the abbot according to the common custom of the Church.

If anyone should attempt to oppose this holy constitution and to withdraw the monastery of Cormery from the Church of Saint Martin, let him be struck by the sword of apostolic indignation and by the judgment of the Holy Spirit.

Sign of Urban, pope. Sign of Hugh, archbishop of Lyon. Sign of Ralph, archbishop of Tours. Sign of Guido, archbishop of Vienne. Sign of Hildebert, archbishop of Bourges. Sign of Amatus, archbishop of Bordeaux. Sign of Heuzon, cardinal. Sign of Albert, cardinal. Sign of Gregory, cardinal. Sign of Ivo, bishop of Chartres. Sign of Goffred, bishop of Angers. Sign of Hoel, bishop of Le Mans. Sign of Morvan, bishop of Vannes. [Col. 0457B] Sign of Benedict, bishop of Nantes. Sign of William, bishop of Clermont. Sign of Bruno, bishop of Signi. Sign of Marbod, elected bishop of Rennes. Sign of the monks of Cormery, Simon the prior and Bernerius. Sign of Burchard, precentor of Saint Martin. Sign of Fulcher, provost. Sign of Matthew, provost. Sign of Sichard, provost. Sign of Alexander, subdeacon.

Given at Poitiers, by the hand of John, cardinal deacon of the holy Roman Church, on the third day before the Kalends of April, in the fourth indiction, in the year of the Lord 1096, in the ninth year of the pontificate of Urban, pope.

### CLXXXVI. Letter of Urban II to the canons of Saint Martin of Tours—Against the Simoniacs. (1096)

[Mansi, *Concilia* XX, 658.]

[Col. 0457C]

**URBAN**, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons, the canons of the Church of Saint Martin, present and future, forever.

We give thanks to God, the giver of every good, who in his mercy led us to visit the tomb of Saint Martin. Since, however, in the church of that blessed confessor a corrupt practice of this kind had taken root, so that all honors and prebends were acquired for a price, we desired to cleanse the holy place from this detestable plague and resolved to send religious men ahead to admonish you. Under the inspiration of the Lord, you faithfully promised them that you would obey our commands in every respect and abandon the contamination of Simoniacal wickedness.

By God’s grace you fulfilled this promise in our presence, confirming it as though in the hand of Saint Peter: that you would neither sell nor buy any further honors or prebends, nor ever consent to their being sold or bought. You also added that henceforth no one should be admitted to the number of the canons unless he had confirmed the same promise by oath. We have confirmed all these matters by the authority of the holy apostles and have pierced all violators with the sword of anathema.

Responding, therefore, to past favors and cherishing a far better hope for the future, according to the privileges of our predecessors, the pontiffs of the Roman Church, we have taken you as spiritual sons of the Apostolic See. By that same authority we decree that no pontiff, no king, and no person of any rank or order, except your provosts, may exercise power or lordship in your Church or its dependencies, so that, by observing the commands of the Roman Church, you may enjoy the perpetual liberty of the Roman Church—without prejudice, naturally, to the right or custom that the archbishop of Tours is known hitherto to have exercised toward you.

Whatever that venerable Church of Saint Martin possesses by legitimate right, whether through the grant of pontiffs, the generosity of kings and princes, or the offerings of the faithful, or whatever it may justly and canonically acquire in the future by the Lord’s favor, shall always remain secure and unimpaired for you. No one in the villages, estates, territories, churches, or districts belonging to your Church may presume, against your will, to hold courts, constrain free persons or serfs by secular authority, or demand tolls or transport dues.

The tithes or ninths of your possessions shall be devoted entirely to the use of the poor. The bishop in whose diocese those possessions lie shall have responsibility only for the ordination of clerics; he shall impose no other burden upon the clerics, nor presume to give, sell, or alienate in any way the altars of the churches or other goods that were formerly granted to you by royal commands and confirmed by the privileges of the Roman pontiffs.

Whatever liberty or immunity our Roman pontiff predecessors, the archbishops of Tours, or the general synod of the churches of Gaul assembled at Tussiacum in the diocese of Toul for the reverence of the blessed apostolic confessor Martin granted to your Church and to your predecessors, we confirm by the page of this present decree.

And because certain of your Church’s privileges have granted you your own bishop, we decree that in his place you shall adhere especially to the Roman pontiff and that your more serious cases shall depend upon his judgment. If in the future any archbishop or bishop, emperor or king, prince or duke, count, viscount, judge, or any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowingly attempting to act rashly against this page of our constitution, should be warned once, twice, or three times and fail to correct the matter by suitable satisfaction, let him lose the dignity of his power and honor, recognize that he stands guilty before the divine judgment on account of the iniquity committed, be excluded from the most sacred body and blood of God and our Lord and Redeemer Jesus Christ, and at the final judgment be subjected to strict punishment. But for all who observe what is just toward this Church, let there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that both here they may receive the fruit of good action [Col. 0459A] and before the strict Judge find the rewards of eternal peace. Amen, amen, amen.

Given at Poitiers, by the hand of John, cardinal deacon of the holy Roman Church, on the fourth day before the Kalends of April, in the fourth indiction, in the year of the Incarnation of the Lord 1097 [1096], in the ninth year of the pontificate of Lord Urban II, pope.

### CLXXXVI bis. Privilege of Pope Urban II for the canons of Saint Martin of Tours. (1096)

[Launoi, *Opera*, vol. III, part II, p. 59.]

**URBAN**, bishop, servant of the servants of God, sends greetings and apostolic blessing to the venerable brothers, the archbishops and bishops established throughout Gaul.

How great a glory Christ bestowed upon the blessed confessor Martin throughout the entire expanse of Christian peoples is attested even by the ferocity of barbarian nations, and the unanimous veneration of both the Greek and Latin languages affirms it. Among these peoples, that same blessed confessor, according to the preaching of the holy teacher Ambrose, is regarded as the apostle’s vicar. For he truly deserved to hold the place of an apostle among the peoples of Gaul, whose teaching and virtues in particular converted them to the faith, and through whose merits after the holy martyrs they are protected by the Lord.

Therefore the venerable pontiffs of the Apostolic See have taken care to protect with greater benevolence and to fortify with more distinguished privileges the church in which, by the Lord’s arrangement, his most holy body rests. Burning with devotion to this most holy man in the same spirit, when we crossed into Gaul for ecclesiastical business, we took care to visit his venerable tomb and to commend our frailty to his merits as though he were more immediately present.

With his favor, when we earnestly desired to cleanse that distinguished dwelling of his from the filth of the Simoniacal plague, we found the brothers of the community obedient. We therefore wish it to be known to all our fellow bishops that, according to the ancient privileges of the Roman pontiffs, we have taken them as special sons of the Apostolic See and have decreed to protect them with Roman protection as they observe the decrees of the Roman Church.

For this reason, through this present letter we ask your charity to protect everything belonging to them throughout your dioceses, and not to allow injuries or troubles to be inflicted upon them either by you or through any other persons. Whoever, out of devotion to the blessed confessor of Christ Martin and reverence for the Apostolic See, becomes their helper and protector shall merit the favor of the Apostolic See; but whoever presumes to attack them or what belongs to them shall be struck by the sword of apostolic indignation.

Given at Poitiers, on the third day before the Kalends of April, by the hand of John, cardinal deacon of the holy Roman Church, in the fourth indiction, in the year of the Lord 1096.

### CLXXXVII. Letter of Urban II to Richer of Sens and the other bishops of the Franks—On not absolving an excommunicated king. (1096)

[Mansi, *Concilia* XX, 665.]

[Col. 0460A]

**URBAN**, bishop, servant of the servants of God, sends greetings and apostolic blessing to his beloved brother Richer, bishop of Sens, and to the other bishops of the Franks.

It has been reported to us that certain of our fellow bishops have proceeded to such audacity that they assert that they will by no means abstain from association with the king, and even that they will release the king himself from the bond of excommunication, although he has not abandoned that woman on whose account he was excommunicated by us. Those who say this either plainly do not know the Scriptures or are not at all afraid to transgress obstinately.

The authority of the holy canons has decreed, and the custom of the Church everywhere observes, that no one may presume to absolve a person justly excommunicated by a bishop. The bonds of suffragans themselves, imposed by the metropolitan—who is their superior—are likewise forbidden by the institutions of the holy Fathers to be absolved.

If this is observed by any bishops whatsoever, let our venerable brothers consider how they could dissolve the acts of the Apostolic See, when it is already clearer than daylight that, by divine institution, not only bishops and primates but the patriarchs themselves are subject to the pontiff of the Apostolic See. They know that everyone appeals to him, while no one appeals from him; they know that he alone has the right to judge concerning the whole Church, whereas he himself is subject to the judgment of no one.

Nor do we believe that they are unaware that the Apostolic See alone, without any preceding synod, can restore to their former state those whom a synod has unjustly condemned, while no one may overturn its judgments. Certainly, when the Lord spoke to Moses about leprosy—that is, the varieties of sins—he said: “The priest shall examine the leper and judge him unclean” (Leviticus 13); and afterward he adds: “He shall be kept shut up at the discretion of the priest” (ibid.). You see, therefore, that he is commanded to be kept shut up at the discretion of the priest by whose judgment he was declared unclean.

How, then, will they stretch out a hand to release one against whom they did not dare to open their mouths to confine him? When the Lord raised Lazarus, who had been dead four days, no one among those standing around is read to have intervened to absolve him. Rather, at the command of the Savior himself, the disciples absolved the man who was already alive and standing, so that an example might plainly be given for those who would follow: even a penitent is not to be absolved except by the judgment of him by whose voice or lament the guilty man is brought out of the tomb.

Nor do we think that this is unknown to our venerable brothers: God resists the proud, but he is near to the brokenhearted. “Upon whom shall I look,” says the Lord, “if not upon the humble and quiet one who trembles at my words?” (Isaiah 66). Let them therefore see how they may attempt to absolve a sinner in the absence or without the command of the one by whose judgment he was shackled in a general synod.

It became plainly evident to us and to all who, by God’s favor, assembled with us at Tours, from the testimonies of the Law, the Gospel, and the holy canons, that your fraternity possesses no power to absolve one whom we have bound. Therefore we declare our son, the king of the Franks, excommunicated until he satisfies God through us and the holy Roman Church; and we decree that both bishops and all others who obstinately communicate with him are to lose the privilege of their power if any of them presumes to misuse his authority in granting him an unauthorized absolution.

Furthermore, we invite all of you to the council at Arles on the octave of the apostles Peter and Paul, with every excuse set aside.

[Note: [Col. 0461] It was held at Nîmes in the month of July, in the year 1096.]

### CLXXXVIII. Bull of Pope Urban II for the New Monastery at Poitiers—He receives the New Monastery, whose church he had dedicated, under the protection of the Apostolic See and subjects it to the monastery of Cluny. (1096)

[Dom Martène, *Thesaurus Anecdotorum* I, 267.]

**URBAN**, bishop, servant of the servants of God, sends greetings and apostolic blessing to his most reverend brother Hugh, abbot of Cluny.

We recognize that, by the Lord’s arrangement, we have been promoted to the service of the Apostolic See for this purpose: that we ought effectively to assist its sons when they implore help, and to guard and protect those who obey it, insofar as the Lord grants us strength. It is therefore fitting for us to extend the hand of protection to venerable places and to provide more attentively for the peace of God’s servants.

Accordingly, for the venerable monastery that William, count of Poitiers, of blessed memory, built in the suburb of that city in honor of blessed Mary ever-virgin and of the holy apostles John and Andrew, we grant this privilege through the benevolence of the Apostolic See, both out of devotion to our same Lady and the holy apostles and out of love for your exceptional religious discipline.

For we decree that whatever goods and possessions the aforesaid count or other faithful people have bestowed upon the same monastery from their own rights, and whatever it justly possesses today or may hereafter justly and canonically acquire, shall always remain secure and unimpaired, to be possessed, governed, and administered in perpetuity without any disturbance, both by you and by those who succeed you in your office and place, as was established by our predecessor, Gregory VII of holy memory, at the petition of the aforesaid count.

Therefore we decree that no one at all may rashly disturb this same church, remove its possessions, retain what has been removed, or harass it with reckless vexations; rather, everything shall be preserved intact, wholly serving the needs of those for whose support and administration it was granted.

We also establish that, when the abbot dies, no other person shall be placed there through any stratagem of deception or violence, except one whom you and your successors shall have chosen according to the fear of God. The person elected shall be consecrated by the bishop of Poitiers, with every demand for a profession set aside.

They shall receive from that same bishop the consecrations of altars and basilicas and the ordinations of monks or clerics who are to be advanced to sacred orders, provided that he possesses the grace and communion of the Apostolic See and is willing to provide these things freely and without corruption. Otherwise, they may approach whichever Catholic prelate they prefer and receive from him the sacraments of consecration.

Since, by the Lord’s favor, the church of this same monastery has been consecrated by our own hands, we add this to the present chapter: neither the bishop nor anyone acting in the bishop’s ministry shall have the power to impose an excommunication upon that place rashly, without the permission of ourselves or our legate. Thus its abbots and monks may remain secure from every disturbance of service, removed from every burden of worldly oppression, diligent in the observance of holy religion and remaining in peace, subject on no occasion to anyone other than the abbot of Cluny.

If any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowingly attempting to act against this page of our constitution, should be warned once, twice, or three times and fail to correct the matter by suitable satisfaction, let him lose the dignity of his power and honor, recognize that he stands guilty before the divine judgment on account of the iniquity committed, be excluded from the most sacred body and blood of God and our Lord and Redeemer Jesus Christ, and at the final judgment be subjected to strict punishment. But for all who observe what is just toward this place, let there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that here they may receive the fruit of good action and before the strict Judge find the rewards of eternal peace. Amen, amen, amen.

Given at Angoulême, by the hand of John, cardinal deacon of the holy Roman Church, on the seventh day before the Ides of April, in the fourth indiction, in the year of the Incarnation of the Lord 1096, in the ninth year of the pontificate of Lord Urban II, pope.

### CLXXXIX. Bull for the monastery of Saint Martial of Limoges. (1096)

[Baluz., *Miscellanea*, edition of Luc, II, 178.]

[Col. 0462D]

**URBAN**, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son Ademar, abbot of the monastery of Limoges built in honor of blessed Martial, and to his successors regularly appointed, forever.

It belongs to the care and benevolence of the Apostolic See both to increase religion and to extend the assistance of its protection to religious places and persons. Therefore, dearest son in Christ, Ademar, abbot, we greatly rejoice in your devotion, since, chiefly through you—at the command and through the diligence of the most reverend abbot Hugh of Cluny—the state of religious observance in the monastery of Saint Martial at Limoges has, by the Lord’s favor, been restored.

Desiring this restoration to be increased and advanced through the merits of the blessed apostolic confessor Martial, by the page of this present decree we establish that the place itself, as it exists today and as it is known to have been constituted by the bishop and canons of the Church of Limoges, shall always remain under the discipline, administration, and custody of the abbot of Cluny. When the abbot dies, no one shall be placed there through any stratagem of deception or violence, except one whom the aforesaid abbot of Cluny or his successors shall have chosen there according to the fear of God.

Since, by the Lord’s arrangement and through the favor of his holy confessor, we have been granted the opportunity to visit his tomb ourselves and to consecrate the church of that place in honor of the holy Savior, out of devotion to that apostolic confessor, out of love for our most reverend fellow brother Hugh, abbot, and at your own request, we receive both the monastery itself and everything belonging to it for perpetual protection under the guardianship of the Apostolic See. Among these possessions we have thought it right to list the following by name:
