In the county of Limoges: the monastery of Saint Valeria; Saint Valeric; Saint Mary, called Subterranea; the chapel of Buxus; the churches of Valera, namely Saint Sulpicius, Saint Mary, and Saint Martin; the church of Saint Martial of Rociacum; Saint Mary of Clairvaux; at Pairac, the churches of Saint Martin and Saint Dionysius; likewise Saint Dionysius of Murs; Saint Mary of Roera; Saint Peter of Parazol; Saint Silvanus of Castel; Saint Martial of Rot; [Col. 0463C] Saint Martial of Roser; Saint Peter of Vernol; Saint Alpinian of Tarne; Saint Martial of Manave; the abbey of Saint Peter of Vosius; the monastery of Saint Pardulf of Arnac; the chapels of Colret and Monzac; the church of Sirac; Saint Mary Magdalene of Quadris; Saint Martial of Cosei; the chapel of Saint Michael called Anteana; and the castle surrounding your monastery with all its dependencies, just as the religious emperor Louis is known to have handed it over to blessed Martial.

In the county of Saintes: the monastery of Saint Martial at the castle of Colesium; Saint Peter of Mont-André; Saint Martin of Salion; Saint Savior, called Eternal Life; Saint Peter of Anesium; [Col. 0463D] and the church of Doaz.

In the county of Auvergne: the church of Saint Martin of Vernojol.

In the county of Bourges: the monastery of Saint Martial at Rosiacum; the church of Saint Leodegarius of Malvera; and Saint Martial of Duno.

In the county of Poitiers: at the castle of Monmorde, the church of Saint Martin of Monzac; and, beside the new castle, the church of blessed Martial.

In the county of Rodez: the church of Teuciac; Saint Mary of Panesa; and Saint Martial of Rivo-Petrosus.

In the county of Béziers: the churches of Laurenc and Paimolo.

In the county of Narbonne: the church of Saint Cassian.

In the county of Périgueux: the monastery of Saint Martial at Palnat.

In the county of Angoulême: the churches of Saint Martial of Multene and Cantrazac; a chapel in the forest of Biarga; another in the wood of Nigretus; and Saint Hilary in the castle of Roca.

In the county of Bordeaux: the churches of Saint Peter of Tortirac, Fornel, and Petraficta.

In the county of Die: the churches of Saint Mary of Sermea and Soant, with their dependencies and appendages.

Moreover, whatever your monastery justly possesses at present or may hereafter justly and canonically acquire shall remain secure and unimpaired for you and your successors.

Therefore we decree that no one at all may rashly disturb this same monastery, remove its possessions, retain what has been removed, diminish them, or harass them with reckless vexations; rather, everything shall be preserved intact, wholly serving the needs of those for whose support and administration it was granted.

This is without prejudice to the canonical reverence due to the bishop of Limoges, provided that he is Catholic and possesses the grace and communion of the Apostolic See. Otherwise, for as long as—God forbid—the Church of Limoges should lack a pastor, you and your successors may, for the sake of whatever ordinations or consecrations are required, approach whichever Catholic bishop you prefer and receive from him what is necessary.

We also establish that, according to the manner of the ancient custom, in the absence of the bishop the abbot of Saint Martial shall exercise primary care together with the principal canons of the Church of Limoges, and that the election of the bishop shall be arranged chiefly according to his judgment. When the bishop is present, the more serious affairs of that Church shall not be conducted without the counsel of the same abbot.

We add this also to the present chapter: your monastery shall not be subjected to an interdict or excommunication on account of a general interdict or excommunication of the parish, although those who have been excommunicated or placed under interdict shall in no way be admitted there to the divine offices.

If any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowingly attempting to act rashly against this page of our constitution, should be warned once, twice, or three times and fail to correct the matter by suitable satisfaction, let him lose the dignity of his power and honor, recognize that he stands guilty before the divine judgment on account of the iniquity committed, be excluded from the most sacred body and blood of God and our Lord Jesus Christ the Redeemer, and at the final judgment be subjected to strict punishment.

But for all who observe what is just toward this place, let there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that here they may receive the fruit of good action and before the strict Judge find the rewards of eternal peace. Amen, amen, amen.

Given at Saintes, by the hand of John, cardinal deacon of the holy Roman Church, on the second day before the Ides of April, in the fourth indiction, in the year of the Incarnation of the Lord 1097, in the ninth year of the pontificate of Lord Urban II, pope.

### CXC. Letter of Pope Urban II to Raymond, archbishop of Auch—Against the clerics who had violated the cemetery of Saint Orientius. (1096)

[Dom Bouquet, *Recueil*, vol. XIV, p. 725.]

**URBAN**, bishop, servant of the servants of God, sends greetings and apostolic blessing to his beloved brother Raymond, archbishop of Auch.

[Col. 0465A]

Since you have recently been ordained in the metropolitan church of Auch by the Roman Church, you must obey the decrees of the Apostolic See without reservation. We therefore command your fraternity to ensure, according to canonical equity, that justice be done concerning the clerics of your see who violated the cemetery that had been confirmed to the Church of Saint Orientius by the decree of blessed Pope Leo and by our own decree. For the rest, guard both yourself and the clerics of your see in such a way that, by the Lord’s favor, the decrees of the Roman Church may be preserved among you unshaken and intact.

Given at Rome, on the third day before the Kalends of May.

### CXCIII. Letter of Pope Urban II to Ansculf, abbot of Angély—He confirms for him the church of Bury, acquired as a gift from the bishop of Beauvais and secured by the assent of the king of the Franks. (1096)

[Dom Bouquet, *Recueil*, vol. XIV, p. 724.]

[Col. 0465C]

**URBAN**, bishop, servant of the servants of God, sends greetings and apostolic blessing to his beloved sons Ansculf, abbot of Angély, and his brothers.

Since, by the Lord’s arrangement, we were granted the opportunity to visit your place ourselves, we have considered it fitting to provide for your peace by a letter of our authority. We therefore decree that everything which you presently appear to possess justly shall remain secure and intact for you forever.

Among these possessions, we confirm to you by name the church of Bury, so that, just as Wido, bishop of Beauvais, of reverend memory, granted it to your monastery—with the consent, of course, of the canons of the Church of Beauvais—and just as the king of the Franks secured the same donation by his assent, so you may possess it forever, by the strength of our authority and without disturbance by any person, without prejudice, naturally, to the canonical reverence due to the bishop of Beauvais.

[Note: [Col. 0465D] The church of Bury (Bury-sur-le-Térain) was granted in the year 1084, on the sixth day before the Kalends of March, and therefore in the year 1085, to the monks of Angély in Saintonge; [Col. 0466D] Mabillon mentions this grant, as well as the confirmation by the king of the Franks, in *Annales Benedictini* XCV, p. 144.]

### CXCVI. Bull confirming the privileges of the monastery of Moissac. (1096)

[Baluz., *Miscellanea* II, 179.]

**URBAN**, bishop, servant of the servants of God, sends greetings and apostolic blessing to his beloved brothers and fellow bishops Isarnus of Toulouse, Simon of Agen, Gerald of Cahors, and Raymond of Lectoure.

We believe your Fraternity is not unaware [Col. 0466B] that the monastery of Moissac was once of great religious devotion, great renown, and great excellence. Later, however, when the glory of religion had declined through the negligence of those dwelling there, its abundance of possessions was diminished and reduced almost to nothing. But thanks be to God, who in our times has deigned, through the diligence of the abbots of Cluny, to restore the religious observance abolished in that place. It is therefore fitting that your Fraternity also, out of devotion to the blessed Peter and Paul, to whose name this place itself is dedicated, should labor so that it may deserve to recover the substance of its ancient possessions and firmly retain those which it presently holds, for the use of the servants remaining there.

Accordingly, we confirm to the church of Moissac, by apostolic authority, the monasteries or abbeys which they have hitherto held or now hold, so that they may possess and retain them under the authority of the abbot of Cluny: namely, in the diocese of Toulouse, the abbey of Lézat; in that of Agen, the abbey of Saint-Gervais of Exiens; in that of Elne, Saint Mary of Arles; and in that of Girona, Saint Peter of Camprodon. But concerning the latter, we establish and command that no abbot shall henceforth be appointed there; rather, the abbot of Moissac shall place a prior over it.

We also wish and command that the priories of Saint Mary at Toulouse, Saint Peter of the Coquins, Saint Genesius of Lectoure, Durivolus, and Villeneuve in the district of Rodez, together with Conques and its dependencies, and everything which they presently hold, be possessed by them in peace forever. And this we add by the authority of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul: in the abbeys listed above, no abbot may in any way be elected or appointed by anyone without the counsel and consent of the abbot of Moissac. If anyone should rashly attempt to do this, both the elected candidate and the electors, both the appointed man and the appointer, shall be excommunicated and, by the authority of blessed Peter, deposed from their orders under threat of anathema.

The brothers of Moissac also complain that very many churches belonging to their jurisdiction are occupied by laymen. In the diocese of Toulouse: the church of Saint Martin of Melzago [Col. 0467A] [variant: Mansacho], Saint Julian, Saint Rusticus, the church of Affiniano, of Corduba, of Bisingis, and of Monte Berterio; in the diocese of Agen: the churches of Saint Amantius of Trangon [variant: Tairago], of Verbegaria, and of Angairiago; in the diocese of Cahors: the churches of Saint Martin and Saint Vincent of Antejago, Saint Peter of Biolo, Saint Stephen of Liciaco, Saint Liberata, Saint Amantius, Saint Martin, Saint Mary, Saint Peter of Casces, Saint Saturninus of Bos, Saint John of Pertica, the church of Saint Saturninus joined to the church of Saint Peter, and the church of Antiago; Saint Peter of Brugarias, Saint Mary of Troilo, and the church of Cogornago, of Gratacumba, Saint Lupus of Malausa, the church with the court called Sals, and the church of Arduno; [Col. 0467B] the church of Saint Sulpicius and Saint Maurice; likewise, in the diocese of Lectoure, in the parish of Lomagne, the church of Sarraciago, of Flamalingis, of Aliciano, and of Oriols; the churches of Saint Martin, Saint Quiriacus, Saint Hilary, and Saint Saturninus of Mancion’s village.

We therefore exhort and command your Prudence by letter, as required by your office, to admonish the occupiers of the aforesaid churches and compel them to restore whatever they themselves or their parents have unjustly taken from the servants of God. If they should refuse to obey your admonitions, let them know that they have incurred the indignation of the blessed apostles as usurpers of ecclesiastical property, since they persist obstinately in that usurpation, and that they are excommunicated.

[Col. 0467C] Given at Toulouse on the Nones of May, in the fourth indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1097, by the hand of John, cardinal deacon of the holy Roman Church.

### CXCVII. Letter of Pope Urban II to Hugh, abbot of Cluny. (Year 1096.)

[Dom BOUQUET, *Recueil*, vol. XIV, p. 322.]

URBAN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother HUGH, abbot of Cluny, greetings and apostolic blessing.

The solicitude of the Apostolic See admonishes us to provide with particular attention for the peace of religious places. Therefore we have judged that your petitions, dearest brother, presented through our common son Guido, prior of Saint Orientius, and his brothers, should by no means be disregarded—both in view of the demands of justice generally and because of that special affection which, for the greater advancement of religious observance, we owe to you—under whose care the rights of that monastery rest—and to all your brothers.

Accordingly, we confirm to your Cluniac monastery, by the present decree, the monastery of Saint Orientius, situated in the suburb of Auch, over which you preside by the command and arrangement of your experience, together with everything belonging to it, and we fortify it by the authority of the Apostolic See. We establish especially and distinctly that the ancient arrangement of that cemetery must not be disturbed by any attack from its rivals, but, as was decreed by the authority of our most holy predecessor Leo IX, must continue undisturbed forever.

Therefore neither outside nor within the city may the archbishop of Auch and his canons establish a new cemetery. Rather, archbishops as well as regular or irregular clergy, and laypeople who have hitherto followed this custom, shall in future obtain a place of burial among you, etc.

Given at Moissac, by the hand of John, cardinal deacon of the holy Roman Church, on the third day before the Ides of May, in the fourth indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1097 [Note: [Col. 0467] The year 1096, which according to the computation customary among the Pisans was reckoned as the year 1097, having begun on 25 March of that year], in the ninth year of the pontificate of the lord Pope Urban II.

### CXCVIII. Diploma of Pope Urban II concerning the donation of the abbey of Bellus-Locus. (Year 1096.)

[*Bibliotheca Cluniacensis*, p. 525.]

[Col. 0468B]

URBAN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother HUGH, abbot of Cluny, greetings and apostolic blessing.

The monastery of Bellus-Locus had for a long time been without the discipline of the monastic rule, and had been exposed both to losses of temporal goods and to the destruction of souls. For the monks had expelled their abbot, relying on secular protection, while the abbot continually lodged complaints against the monks. For this reason that place had also for some time been subjected to excommunication by our brother, the archbishop of Bourges; and that knight Hugh, who was unlawfully in charge of the same monastery, had likewise acted as a patron of the monks in their wicked way of life. After our second or third gentle admonition, he was struck by the sword of blessed Peter and by the punishment of canonical discipline.

Now, according to the disposition of almighty God, that brother whom the wickedness of the monks had driven from the monastery has been taken from human affairs; and the knight who occupied the monastery by secular power, in the presence of his lord, Count Raymond, renounced into our hands whatever authority he had hitherto exercised, and restored the place itself through us to God and blessed Peter, asking and entreating that, through your solicitude and that of your brothers, the vigor of the monastic order might be restored there.

Granting his petition, we entrust that place, by the authority of the present decree, to be governed and administered perpetually under your care and that of your successors. We ask and command that from now on you diligently govern the monastery of Bellus-Locus as a member of the Cluniac monastery, and always appoint an abbot there from the Cluniac congregation, so that, with the Lord’s help, through your solicitude the vigor of regular discipline may be restored and preserved there.

Given at Toulouse, on the tenth day before the Kalends of June.

### CXCIX. At the council held at Nîmes, having abolished Gregory VII’s decree, Urban forbids the monasteries of Figeac and Conques to be united. He orders each monastery to be governed by its own abbot. (Year 1096.)

[MABILLON, *Acta Sanctorum Ordinis Benedicti*, Third Age, part II, p. 448.]

[Col. 0469A]

URBAN, bishop, servant of the servants of God.

When we had come into the regions of Gaul on ecclesiastical business, by the Lord’s favor we convened a plenary synod at Auvergne. There the brothers of the monastery of Conques presented letters of Gregory VII of revered memory, ordering that the monastery of Figeac be united to the monastery of Conques. Since at that time each place was presided over by its own abbot, the survivor was to be placed over both monasteries after the death of either one.

Accordingly, the abbot of the monastery of Conques, because he had been substituted contrary to the tenor of those letters, was deposed in the same council, and the abbot of Figeac, who had survived, was placed over both places. Discord then began to arise between the two monasteries to such an extent that many goods were dissipated and the salvation of souls was gravely endangered.

Moreover, when this arrangement came to the ears of the abbot of Cluny, he began to denounce the aforesaid letters of the pope as having been obtained by deception, and to testify that the decision in this matter had been carried out differently in his presence—especially since the place of Figeac had been confirmed to the Cluniac monastery by a privilege of the same pontiff.

Therefore, when, by the Lord’s favor, a third synod had assembled at Nîmes at our insistence, the question of this matter began to be seriously debated. After a lengthy discussion by the bishops and abbots, it was decided, both for the preservation of the apostolic privilege and for the common welfare of the monasteries, that a proper abbot should be restored to each place, as had formerly been the case, and that the monks of Figeac should henceforth remain under the care and provision of the abbot of Cluny.

We, therefore, confirming the common decree of the council with the weight of apostolic authority, ordered that the course of this decision should be recorded in letters bearing our name as something to remain forever, and that it should be secured by the impression of our seal. If anyone should rashly attempt to violate the tenor of this decision, let him know that he will incur the vengeance of apostolic indignation and suffer the loss of his order or office.

Done in the council at Nîmes, in the church of Saint Mary, on the seventh day before the Ides of July, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1096 [read: 1096], in the fourth indiction, and in the ninth year of the pontificate of the lord Pope Urban II.

Given at Flavian Valley, in the monastery of Saint Giles, on the Ides of July.

### CC. Bull of Pope Urban II for Saint Martin of the Fields. (Year 1096.)

[FÉLIBIEN, *History of Paris*, proofs, vol. III, p. 12.]

[Col. 0470A]

URBAN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother HUGH, abbot of Cluny, greetings and apostolic blessing.

A pious request of the will ought to be fulfilled by the accompanying effect, so that the sincerity of devotion may shine forth with praise and the benefit requested may undoubtedly acquire strength. Therefore, assenting to your will and to the petitions of our common son Ursio, the prior, we fortify by the authority of the present decree the monastery of Saint Martin called “of the Fields,” situated in the parish of Paris, so that, like the other members of the Cluniac monastery, it may always remain under the protection of the Apostolic See.

We likewise confirm everything which presently appears to belong to that place: namely, the churches of Agonville, Neuville, Marcy, Montmartre, Louvres, Châtenay, Noa of Saint Remigius, Noa of Saint Martin, Renzé, Bolbigny, Cale, Conflans, Copeyo, Fontaines, Flammarègue-Ville; Valle-Villaris, Moncy, the village called Bonzeia, large Noisy, small Noisy, Anet, Majoriolas, Sainte-Gemme, Rodanville, Ursionville, Clamart, Sorville, Pentin, Ceurennes, Saint Hilary with their churches and appurtenances, and also the churches of Cona, Bonella, and Pringy.

[Col. 0470C] Furthermore, whatever the same place now justly possesses, whether by the gift of Henry, king of the Franks, of blessed memory, who was its founder, or by the donation of his son Philip, through whose gift this cell is known to belong to your monastery; whatever has been bestowed upon that place by any of the faithful from their own property, or may in future happen to be bestowed, shall always remain firm and inviolate, to be perpetually possessed, governed, and administered both by you and by those who, through you or your successors, are placed over that place.

We therefore decree that no human being whatsoever may rashly disturb the same monastery, take away its possessions, retain what has been taken away, diminish them, or harass them with rash vexations. Rather, everything shall be preserved intact and shall in every way benefit the uses of those for whose support and governance it was granted.

If, therefore, in the future any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowingly disregarding this decree, should rashly attempt to act against it, then, after being admonished a second or third time, if he does not make suitable satisfaction and correct his conduct, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and honor, acknowledge himself guilty before the divine judgment of the iniquity committed, be separated from the most sacred body and blood of God and our Lord and Redeemer Jesus Christ, and be subjected to strict vengeance at the final judgment.

But let the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with all who observe justice toward that place, so that both here they may receive the fruit of good action and before the strict Judge find the rewards of eternal peace. Amen, amen, amen.

Given at Nîmes by the hand of John, cardinal deacon of the holy Roman Church, on the second day before the Ides of July, in the fourth indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1097, in the ninth year of the pontificate of the lord Urban II.

### CCI. Urban subjects the church of Burgos directly to the Roman Church, releasing it from obedience to other metropolitan churches. (Year 1096.)

[FLOREZ, *España Sagrada*, XXVI, 464.]

URBAN, bishop, servant of the servants of God.

After, by the grace of almighty God, a plenary synod had been celebrated at Nîmes while we presided, a complaint of Bernard, archbishop of Toledo, was brought to our hearing. He demanded the obedience of the bishop of Burgos as his own suffragan, on the grounds that Burgos had been built in the parish of Osma, since Osma is known without doubt to be part of the province of Toledo.

The bishop, however, protested that his church belonged rather to the metropolitan church of Tarragona. We had decreed that the city of Burgos was to be regarded as the vicariate of Auca, which, as is said, had anciently been subject to the metropolitan of Tarragona by metropolitan right. Alfonso, moreover, king of Further Spain, by no means allowed the bishop of Burgos to be subject to the metropolitan of Tarragona, for the reason that Burgos lay within the boundaries of his kingdom, whereas Tarragona was under the authority of the count of Barcelona.

[Col. 0471C] For these reasons, therefore, it seemed to our judgment and that of the brothers who were present with us, in order to calm the dispute between those churches, that henceforth the bishop of Burgos should be governed only by the hand of the Roman pontiff, and that that church should receive the consecration of its bishops from the Apostolic See, unless the archbishop could prove by an authoritative argument that it belonged to him. In the meantime, we release it from the obedience and subjection of both metropolitan churches.

After this, Gomizo, bishop of Burgos, brought a complaint against the same archbishop because, after the first decision of the abbot of Marseille, who at that time had exercised the office of the Apostolic See in those regions, the archbishop had usurped a certain part of the parish of Burgos. More specifically, he had occupied the village called Fenicularis, the monastery of Valeranica, and the cell of Saint Mary of Ravenaria, as property and domain belonging to the church of Burgos.

Concerning these three matters, the archbishop himself conceded that they were the property of the church of Burgos or Auca, and in our presence he restored them to the bishop. At our request, however, and with the bishop’s consent, we permitted the same metropolitan to retain the monastery of Valeranica for three years. Let him hold the village of Fenicularis and the cell of Saint Mary of Ravenaria for as long as he retains the church of Osma in his hands, in whose parish those places are situated, although by decree they have been assigned as property to the church of Auca. But if a proper bishop is restored to the church of Osma, [Col. 0472A] the property belonging to it shall return to Auca.

Moreover, concerning the part of the parish which the bishop of Burgos claimed had been taken from him after the legate’s decision, the same archbishop asserted that it had been voluntarily renounced by the bishop himself into his hands and by the judgment of the bishops. Since the bishop replied that he had been burdened and compelled in that matter, we nevertheless, lest we appear to oppress our brother Bernard, the archbishop, too severely, allowed the matter to remain as it was, until he could prove before our hearing, by suitable witnesses, that the renunciation had been carried out voluntarily and in judicial order.

Given at Flavian Valley, in the monastery of Saint Giles, on the Ides of July, in the fourth indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1097, in the ninth year of the pontificate of the lord Pope Urban II, by the hand of John, cardinal deacon of the holy Roman Church.

### CCII. Pope Urban II confirms the possessions of the monastery of Ripoll and grants it certain privileges of immunity and exemption. (Year 1096.)

[COCQUELINES, II, 90.]

URBAN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son BERNARD, abbot of the venerable monastery of Saint Mary called Ripoll, situated in the county of Osona between two rivers, and to his successors regularly appointed in perpetuity.

We are compelled by the authority and duty of the Apostolic See to labor for the condition of all churches and, with the Lord’s help, to provide for their peace. Therefore we have rightly judged that your petitions, dearest son in Christ Bernard, should be granted, so that we might fortify the monastery of Ripoll, over which by God’s authority you preside, with the privilege of the Apostolic See, following the example of our predecessors Sergius and Agapitus.

By the present decree, therefore, we establish by apostolic authority that whatever the same monastery justly possesses today, or may in future justly and canonically obtain through the grant of pontiffs, the generosity of princes, or the offering of the faithful, shall remain firm and inviolate for you and your successors. Among these we have judged that the following should be recorded by name:

The church of Saint Peter adjacent to the same monastery, together with the other churches subject to it; in the castle of Cervaria, the church of Saint Martin, the chapel of Saint Nicholas, the cell of Saint Peter with the church of the castle of Montpalau, the cell of Saint Quintin, the monastery of Saint Mary called Gualter’s, Saint Andrew between the bridges, Saint Mary of Panizars, Saint Mary of Montserrat, the church of Saint Stephen of Granyanella, Saint Stephen of Ripa with the allods of Bernard the viscount, which he assigned to the monastery.

We also confirm to you and your successors the toll and every right of justice belonging to the market customarily held at that monastery; likewise the castle of Menslei with its boundaries and appurtenances, the castle of Torsa with its churches and demesnes, its sea-ports, fisheries, and [Col. 0473A] everything belonging to it; the fisheries of the waters of Tezer from Ripa Mala to Spata, and of the river Frever from the bridge of Corba to Tezer; and all the demesne which Bernard of Besalú gave to Saint Mary, both in the valley of Ripoll and in other places.

Furthermore, whatever possessions, villages, or churches, with their tithes, first fruits, or offerings, you possess in any regions by the privileges of our predecessors; whatever you now possess justly and lawfully by authentic writings of pontiffs, princes, or any of the faithful, or may in future, by the Lord’s generosity, possess, we confirm to the monastery of Saint Mary aforesaid.

We therefore decree that no human being whatsoever may rashly disturb the same monastery, constrain its dependents by secular judgment or power against the will of the abbot and brothers, take away its possessions, retain what has been taken away, diminish them, or harass them with rash vexations. Rather, everything shall be preserved intact and shall in every way benefit the uses of those for whose support and governance it was granted.

When you, the abbot of that place, die, or any of your successors, no one shall be placed there through any trickery of concealment or violence, except the person whom the brothers by common agreement, or the sounder part of the brothers’ council, shall elect according to the fear of God and the Rule of Saint Benedict.

You shall receive chrism, holy oil, the consecrations of altars or basilicas, and the ordinations of the clergy of your place, or of monks who are to be promoted to holy orders, from whatever Catholic bishop you choose. We further add that no bishop may rashly excommunicate the cloister itself or those serving the Lord there, nor may he place under interdict or excommunicate the chapels situated around the monastery’s enclosure without a hearing before the Roman pontiff or his legate; nor may he inflict the prejudice of canonical punishment upon other places belonging to you without certain cause.

We decree that burial in that place shall be entirely free, so that no one may oppose the devotion and final will of those who decide to be buried there, unless they should happen to be excommunicated. We also forbid a bishop to celebrate public Masses in the same monastery or hold stations there against the will of the abbot and brothers, lest any opportunity for popular gatherings be provided in the retreats of God’s servants.

If, therefore, in the future any archbishop or bishop, emperor or king, prince or duke, count, viscount, judge, or any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowingly disregarding this decree, should rashly attempt to act against it, then, after being admonished a second and third time, if he does not make suitable satisfaction and correct his conduct, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and honor, acknowledge himself guilty before the divine judgment of the iniquity committed, be separated from the most sacred body and blood of God and our Lord Jesus Christ, and be subjected to strict vengeance at the final judgment.

But let the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with all who observe justice toward that place, so that both here they may receive the fruit of good action and before the strict Judge find the rewards of eternal peace. Amen.

Given in the monastery of Saint Giles, by the hand of John, cardinal deacon of the holy Roman Church, on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of August, in the fourth indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1096, in the ninth year of the pontificate of the lord Urban II.

### CCII bis. Privilege of Pope Urban II for the monastery of Banyoles. (Year 1096.)

[COCQUELINES, *Collection of Roman Pontiffs’ Bulls*, II, 91.]

URBAN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son BENEDICT, abbot of the venerable monastery of the holy protomartyr Stephen, situated in the place called Banyoles, in the county of Besalú, and to his successors regularly appointed in perpetuity.

We are compelled by the authority and duty of the Apostolic See to labor for the condition of all churches and, with the Lord’s help, to provide for their peace. Therefore we have rightly judged that your petitions, dearest son in Christ Benedict, should be granted, so that we might fortify the monastery of Banyoles, over which by God’s authority you preside, with the privilege of the Apostolic See.

By the present privilege, therefore, we establish by apostolic authority that whatever the same monastery justly possesses today shall remain firm and inviolate for you and your successors: namely, the parish of the valley of Banyoles itself; the churches of Saint Benedict and Saint Peter of Agemal, Saint Romanus of Millanicas with its cemetery, Saint Christopher, Saint James with its tithes and first fruits, and with half the tithes or first fruits of the village of Figeroles and of the Hermitages; the church of Saint Mary; Saint Lawrence with the cemetery of Porqueres; the church of Saint Maurice of Caldes, Saint Quiricus, Saint Martin of Campo Maior in the valley of Millars; the church of Saint Peter; Saint Andrew of Rituls; Saint Vincent of Salient; Saint Julian of Augustí; Saint Mary of Vila-rodona; Saint Martial of Quarantella; the cell of Saint Mary of Riu d’Àlser, with its tithes, offerings, and other appurtenances.

In the county of Peralada: the churches of Saint Martin and Saint Sylvester. In the valley of Mala: the cell of Saint John of Croce, Saint Cyprian of Pineda, with their tithes, offerings, and other appurtenances. In the county of Empúries: the cell of Santa Creu; Saint Nicholas with its cemeteries and allods; and the castle of Collepodium with its appurtenances. In the county of Girona: the church of Saint Mary of Fenestre, Saint Felix of Buada with their tithes, offerings, and other appurtenances. In the county of Barcelona: the monastery of Saint Martial of Montseny; in Tazilano, the church of the Savior.

We also confirm to you and your successors the toll and every right of justice belonging to the market customarily held at your monastery. Furthermore, whatever has been justly and lawfully bestowed upon your place through the privileges of pontiffs of the Apostolic See, our predecessors, through authentic writings of kings or princes, or through offerings of any of the faithful, or whatever you may in future possess by the Lord’s generosity, we command to be preserved for you as valid and intact.

We therefore decree that no human being whatsoever may rashly disturb the same monastery, constrain its household by secular judgment or power against the will of the abbot and brothers, take away the possessions of the monastery, diminish them, or harass them with rash vexations. Rather, everything shall be preserved intact and shall in every way benefit the uses of those for whose support and governance it was granted.

When you, the abbot of that place, die, or any of your successors, no one shall be placed there through any trickery of concealment or violence, except the person whom the brothers by common agreement, or the sounder part of the brothers’ council, shall elect according to the fear of God and the Rule of blessed Benedict.

You shall receive chrism, holy oil, the consecrations of altars or basilicas, and the ordinations of the clergy of your place or of monks who are to be promoted to holy orders, from whatever Catholic bishop you choose, just as certain of our predecessors granted to your monastery and the bishops of the province confirmed.

We further add that no bishop may rashly or without a hearing before the Roman pontiff or his legate place under interdict or excommunicate the cloister itself or those serving the Lord there, nor may he inflict the prejudice of canonical punishment upon other places belonging to you without certain cause.

We forbid public Masses to be celebrated in the same monastery by a bishop against the will of the abbot and brothers, or stations to be held there, or popular assemblies to be gathered for the hearing of cases, lest any opportunity for popular gatherings be provided in the retreats of God’s servants.

We also decree that burial in that place shall be entirely free, so that no one may oppose the devotion and final will of those who decide to be buried there, unless they should be excommunicated.

If, therefore, in the future any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowingly disregarding this decree, should rashly attempt to act against it, then, after being admonished a second or third time, if he does not make suitable satisfaction and correct his conduct, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and honor, acknowledge himself guilty before the divine judgment of the iniquity committed, be separated from the most sacred body and blood of God and our Lord Jesus Christ, and be subjected to strict vengeance at the final judgment.

But let the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with all who observe justice toward that place, so that both here they may receive the fruit of good action and before the strict Judge find the rewards of eternal peace. Amen, amen, amen.

Given in the monastery of Saint Giles, near Flavian Valley, by the hand of John, cardinal deacon of the holy Roman Church, on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of August, [Col. 0476A] in the fourth indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1096, in the ninth year of the pontificate of the lord Urban II.

### CCIII. Privilege of the monastery of Juvigny. (Year 1096.)

[MABILLON, *Annals of the Benedictines*, V, 658.]

URBAN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved daughter GALBURGA, abbess of the monastery of Juvigny, and to the others who are to be regularly appointed after her in the governance of the same monastery.

We are compelled by the authority and duty of the Apostolic See to labor for the condition of all churches, and especially to provide, with the Lord’s help, for the peace of those which adhere more particularly to that See and are subject to it as by its own right.

Therefore, dearest daughter in Christ Galburga, we mercifully assent to the petitions of your devotion, and by the authority of the present decree we receive under the special protection of the Apostolic See the monastery of the blessed virgin Scholastica, over which by the Lord’s authority you preside, situated at the village called Juvigny.

The illustrious Boniface, marquis of revered memory, and his wife Beatrice, together with their distinguished daughter, the lady Matilda, offered this monastery to blessed Peter and to the bishops of the holy Roman Church.

By the present privilege, therefore, we establish by apostolic authority that whatever goods were given to the same monastery by the aforesaid princes shall always remain firm and inviolate: namely, the entire village of Juvigny [Col. 0476C] with both of its halves, one of which the aforesaid marquis and his wife are known to have given to it during their lifetime, and the other of which Countess Matilda gave to Saint Scholastica after their death; the village of Remon with its appurtenances and revenues; half the village of Greater Verinole; Yreia with two churches; the village of Boson with its dependencies; all of Lesser Virolin; twelve holdings in the village of Vismol; three holdings with a church at Marcey; land with one quarter of a church at Clémencey; four holdings and one third of a church with a mill at Hastoit; two holdings with a church at Betrui; two and a half holdings at Vellans, and one-sixth of a church holding, mill, and fishery; one holding at Gualkering; land at Ase near Masencey; one quarter of a holding at the other Ase; a holding at Nemachy; and a holding with one quarter of a church and mill at Ham.

We also confirm to you the church of Surre with its allod and municipal rights; nine *perticata* of vineyards at Laesura; and forty-seven days’ ploughland for oxen at Remonville, which your Prudence purchased from Arluin for a price.

Furthermore, whatever the same monastery of Saint Scholastica justly possesses, or may in future justly and canonically obtain through the grant of pontiffs, the generosity of princes, or the offering of the faithful, we decree that it be preserved for you as valid and inviolate.

We therefore decree that no human being whatsoever may rashly disturb the congregation of the aforesaid monastery, take away its possessions, retain what has been offered [variant: taken away], diminish them, or harass them with rash vexations. Rather, everything shall be preserved intact and shall in every way benefit the uses of those for whose support and governance it was granted, without prejudice to the canonical reverence due to the church of Trier.

When you, the abbess of that place, die, or any of those who succeed you in the governance of that place, no one shall be placed there through any trickery of concealment or violence. Rather, the person whom the sisters, by common agreement or the sounder part of the sisters’ council, shall deem fit to be elected according to God and the Rule of blessed Benedict shall be appointed, with the counsel also of the diocesan bishop, if he proves to be Catholic and religious. Thus, no one shall henceforth be permitted within the abbey itself to claim any act of violence or wicked custom, or to impose any burden that would impede the peace of the handmaids of the Lord God.

We further establish that the advocate of that place shall be no one other than the person whom the abbess, with the consent of her religious sisters, requests as useful to the monastery. Neither he nor the abbess, nor any minister of the place, shall have the power to give the church’s goods to secular persons in fief, place them under a rent, or alienate them in any way.

Furthermore, we do not permit any cleric to minister in your monastery except from the number of the more regular canons whom your religious solicitude has established at the church of Saint Montanus [Note: [Col. 0477] Not far from Juvigny there is the church of Saint Montanus, who foretold the birth of Saint Remigius, where two hermits live under the monastery’s patronage]. To them we forbid anyone in future to withdraw the sustenance assigned from a portion of your resources.

As a token of the liberty received from the Roman Church, you shall pay six silver coins of Verdun currency each year to the Lateran palace.

Therefore, if in future any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowingly aware of this page of decree, should rashly attempt to act against it, then, after being admonished a second or third time, if he does not make amends by suitable satisfaction, let him lose the dignity of his power and honor, acknowledge himself to be guilty before the divine judgment of the iniquity committed, be alienated from the most holy body and blood of God and our Lord and Redeemer Jesus Christ, and be subjected to strict punishment at the final judgment. But let there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ for all who observe what is just toward that place, so that both here they may receive the fruit of good action and, before the strict Judge, find the rewards of eternal peace. Amen, amen, amen.

Given in the monastery of Saint Giles, at Flavinian Valley, by the hand of John, cardinal deacon of the Holy Roman Church, on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of August, indiction 4, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1096, in the ninth year of the pontificate of the lord Pope Urban II.

## CCIV. Privilege for the monastery of Saint Giles. (Year 1096.)

[MANSI, *Councils*, XX, 938.]

URBAN, bishop, servant of the servants of God.

[Col. 0478A] Just as no effect ought to be granted to those asking for what is unjust, so the petition of those desiring what is legitimate ought not to be delayed. Raymond, count of the Toulousains and Rouergue, and marquis of Provence, retaining a share of his power from the Roman Church, abandoned, for the honor of God and reverence for blessed Giles, all the rights belonging to Saint Giles, both in Flavinian Valley and outside it, whatever he appeared to hold justly or unjustly, and all the rightful or wrongful customs that his predecessors or he himself had possessed. He made this cession to Abbot Odilo and his brothers, swearing it into our hand before the council at Nîmes, as he was about to depart on the expedition to Jerusalem; and, should he or any of his successors attempt to invalidate this gift, he imposed condemnation and a curse upon himself and all his successors, insofar as it lay within his power.

At his suggestion, therefore, and at the monks’ petition, we confirmed this in the presence of the entire council, and we also establish it by the letters of our authority. If, therefore, any ecclesiastical or secular person should presume to nullify or pervert the aforesaid count’s renunciation and our confirmation, as well as that of the entire council, let him be subjected to excommunication and anathema until he makes satisfaction, and let him be punished by the loss of his honor and office.

After this, by the disposition of the divine will, it came about that at the monastery of Saint Giles we dedicated with our own hands the altar of the new basilica to almighty God. Therefore we have decreed and do decree, and we designate this in writing for future remembrance, that no archbishop [Col. 0478C] or bishop may thereafter dare to issue a sentence of excommunication or interdict against that same church, so that the same monastery, subjected by the gift of Saint Giles himself to the proper jurisdiction of the Holy Roman Church, may always enjoy the privilege of Roman liberty.

But if anyone, having learned the tenor of this decree, should attempt to oppose it, let him suffer the loss of his honor and office, be alienated from the most sacred body and blood of God and our Lord and Redeemer Jesus Christ, and be subjected to strict punishment at the final judgment. But let peace and mercy from God our Father and our Lord Jesus Christ be preserved for all ages, present and future, for all who observe what is just toward that place. Amen, amen, amen.

[Col. 0478D] Given by the hand of John, cardinal deacon and librarian of the Holy Roman Church, at Avignon, in the monastery of Saint Andrew, on the eleventh day before the Kalends of August, indiction 4, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1096, in the ninth year of the pontificate of the lord Pope Urban II.

## CCV. Bull for the church of Saint Saturninus at Toulouse. (Year 1096.)

[BALUZE, *Miscellanea* II, 179.]

URBAN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons in Christ, the canons professing the regular life in the church of blessed Saturninus [Col. 0479A], and to their successors who will live in the same religious observance, forever.

Just as no effect ought to be granted to those asking for what is unjust, so the petition of those desiring what is legitimate ought not to be delayed. The dispute that had for a long time been conducted between you and our brother Isarnus, bishop of Toulouse, concerning the fourth part of the offerings of the altar and church has, by the grace of almighty God, been heard in our presence [Note: [Col. 0479D] Namely, at the council of Nîmes.] and settled by synodal judgment and by the sworn testimony of legitimate witnesses who had heard and seen the matter.

For it became clear that certain clerics who, before your time, had lived at the church of blessed Saturninus contrary to canonical discipline had held both the fourth and all the other full portions of the offerings of the altar or church. The bishop himself had already acknowledged that this had been done at that time, even before the proof supplied by the witnesses [Col. 0479B]. For before Peter Roger, bishop of Toulouse, who gathered all the offerings for the purpose of building a new basilica, the clerics living in their own houses freely enjoyed the offerings of blessed Saturninus.

It therefore seemed unjust that what earlier bishops had permitted secular clerics should now be taken away from you, who by God’s grace live together under regular discipline. Accordingly, our same brother Isarnus, in the presence of the provost and certain members of your community and of the brothers who were present with us, renounced before us that fourth part which he held, and earnestly requested that this be confirmed by our privilege.

Therefore, in accordance with his petition and yours, by this present decree we permanently confirm by apostolic authority, in their entirety, both that fourth part and all the other portions of the offerings of the altar or church for your use and that of your successors; and we prohibit any bishop from demanding them thereafter.

Furthermore, since, by the Lord’s favor, we consecrated the church of blessed Saturninus with our own hands, we have decreed and do decree that no bishop or archbishop may dare to issue a sentence of interdict or excommunication against that place without a hearing before us or our legate. Nor may anyone alter the order of things that is maintained there today; and after the canons have taken possession, no one may have property of his own or leave the cloister without the permission of the provost or the community.

If anyone should leave and, after being admonished, refuse to return, it shall be within the provost’s authority, if he judges it appropriate, to prohibit him from exercising his offices anywhere. But no one may lift an interdict imposed by bishops or abbots without the provost’s permission.

When the provost of that place dies, no one may be placed over it through any trickery or violence, except one whom the regular brothers, by common agreement or by the decision of the wiser part of the brothers, shall have provided to be regularly elected according to the fear of God.

If any clerics, with the permission of their bishops, should come to that place for the sake of conversion, it shall be lawful for the provost to receive them, despite every objection by the bishop of Toulouse [Col. 0480A], so that no cause of disobedience or pride toward their provost may remain for them.

Moreover, we confirm to you and your successors the provostship, deanery, sacristy, office of cantor, and all the other possessions of your church. We also confirm the dignity of the archdeaconate and the cemetery, as contained in the charter of the bishop and canons of Saint Stephen.

We likewise prohibit anyone from thereafter daring to demand the wax candles that our son Raymond, count of Toulouse, renounced in our presence at the dedication of the church.

We also prohibit anyone from violently entering the cloister of that church or daring to commit robbery or injury within it.

In addition, we confirm to you and to your successors living under regular discipline the churches of Saint Peter of Valeriis and of Artaxena, the abbey of Saint Avitus, the church of Saint Cyprian, the church [Col. 0480B] of Saint Peter of Slaniacum and of Mascaranum, and whatever else that same church justly possesses or may in future justly and canonically acquire.

If, therefore, in future any archbishop or bishop, emperor or king, prince or duke, count, viscount, judge, or any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowingly aware of this page of decree, should rashly attempt to act against it, then, after being admonished a second or third time, if he does not make suitable amends, let him lose the dignity of his power and honor, acknowledge himself to be guilty before the divine judgment of the iniquity committed, be alienated from the most sacred body and blood of God and our Lord and Redeemer Jesus Christ, and be subjected to strict punishment at the final judgment.

But let there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ for all who observe what is just toward that place, so that both here they may receive the fruit of good action and, before the strict Judge, find the rewards of eternal peace. Amen.

Given at Mont Andaon, in the monastery of Saint Andrew, by the hand of John, cardinal deacon of the Holy Roman Church, on the eleventh day before the Kalends of August, indiction 4, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1097, in the ninth year of the pontificate of the lord Urban II.

## CCVI. *Urban confirms the privileges and possessions of the monastery of Saint Andrew at Avignon.* (Year 1096.)

[RUINART, *Life of Urban*, p. 270.]

[Col. 0480D]

## CCVII. Letter of Pope Urban II to Coloman, king of Hungary, against Guibert the antipope, or Clement III. (Year 1096.)

[MÉNARD, *History of Nîmes*, Paris, 1750, quarto, vol. I, Proofs, 15.]

URBAN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son in Christ, COLOMAN, illustrious king of the Hungarians, greetings and apostolic blessing.

When we heard that, by the disposition of almighty God, your Illustriousness had been raised to govern the kingdom of Hungary [Col. 0481A], we rejoiced with no little gladness. For our venerable son Odilo, abbot of Saint Giles, reported to us that, besides the ability in secular affairs in which you excel, your vigor is also learned in the ecclesiastical Scriptures and—what especially befits judicial authority—is endowed with knowledge of the sacred canons.

Therefore, dearest son in Christ, you ought to take greater care than those who preceded you in governing that kingdom, both for your own salvation and for that of the peoples entrusted to you. For, as divine Scripture declares, the powerful will suffer powerful torments; and from the one to whom more is given, more is certainly required.

Raise, therefore, O king, the glorious standard of the catholic faith, which ought to win victory and glory over the secular standards of your kingdom. For a long time [Col. 0481B] the peoples of the Hungarians have followed the byways of error; abandoning the shepherds of their salvation, they have clung to the footsteps of alien flocks.

Let your vigor then remember the religious prince Stephen, the first of your race to receive from the holy Roman and apostolic Church the religion of the faith and to merit the rights of regular dignity. For the more you understand yourself to have been advanced on earth in dignity by the disposition of divine judgment, the more humbly ought you, dearest son, to obey the divine princes Peter and Paul and faithfully display toward their church the submission and honor established by the aforesaid prince.

Let none of the poisons of the false apostles who invaded their church corrupt you; let no perversity lead you away from the true religion. For we believe that you cannot be unaware of the heresiarch Guibert [Col. 0481C], excommunicated and condemned by all Catholics everywhere, who, contrary to the commands of divine law, contrary to the ordinances of the Gospel, and contrary to the decrees of the holy canons, mounted the bed of the living father and lord, invaded the chair of Gregory VII, the pontiff of blessed memory, and committed incest against the Roman Church, the mother of all the faithful. But nearly the whole world now recognizes him as a thief and robber, through the revelation of God’s judgment.

What the justice of the divine majesty has done and is doing against Henry, the author of this iniquity and presumption, we think has also come to your attention. Given over to a debased mind and doing things that are unbefitting—indeed, things detestable to God and human beings—he has been exposed to public disgrace.

In him, that saying of divine Scripture seems in a certain manner to have been fulfilled: “Why does earth and ashes take pride?” For during his lifetime he casts out his innermost parts. Those whom he had held closest, whom he loved as his own entrails—not merely his intimates, but even his son—having execrated him for his abominations, withdrew themselves from his company.

Already, by God’s mercy and judgment, he has lost that principal part of his kingdom by which he oppressed the Roman Church. Amid these storms of diabolical persecution, your kingdom has for a long time withdrawn from obedience to the apostolic see; surrendered to the leaders and agents of this error, it has been led astray along the byways of the broader road.

Nor, finally, has divine grace, as we believe, raised up your person in order to remove the veil from that people [Col. 0482A]. Therefore, since we—although unworthy—are responsible, in the service of the apostolic see, for the care of all the churches, and since we are debtors to Greeks and barbarians, to the wise and the foolish, we have judged it necessary to admonish your prudence in this matter: namely, to learn the intention of your mind as to whether you consent that representatives of the apostolic see be sent for the salvation of your kingdom and the instruction of your people.

For this work we have appointed the aforesaid abbot of blessed Giles as collaborator. Concerning this matter, therefore, do not delay to inform us by your reply, through the bearer of this letter, of your firm intention.

Moreover, we wish Your Excellency to trust us in this way: whatever honor and dignity your predecessor Stephen is known to have deserved from our apostolic Church, seek them with certain devotion and receive them with complete generosity and kindness, provided that you remain firmly established in the unity of that same apostolic Church and, with faithful devotion, render to it whatever honor and reverence the aforesaid king established.

Given on the sixth day before the Kalends of August.

## CCVIII. Letter of Urban II, Supreme Pontiff, to Gebehard, bishop of Constance, directing him to ensure that a certain monk is restored by the monks of Reitenbuch to the monks of Schaffhausen. (Year 1096.)

[PEZ, *Thesaurus Anecdotorum* VI, I, 297.]

URBAN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother G., bishop of CONSTANCE, greetings and apostolic blessing.

It is plainly evident to your fraternity why and how long there has been discord between the communities of Schaffhausen and Reitenbuch. Recently, when we were at Tours, we had heard through our son Manegold, master of the schools, that they had been reconciled. But our common son Gerard, a monk of Schaffhausen, came and repeated the same complaint before us: namely, that those brothers had refused to return the monk.

We therefore command Your Affection to continue diligently, together with the religious, to restore concord between them. But if they now refuse to obey and, after receiving our letters, do not restore within thirty days to the abbot of Schaffhausen the monk on whose account their discord arose [Col. 0482D], know that thereafter they are interdicted by our sentence.

Given on the seventh day before the Ides of August at the Forum of Cholcherius.

## CCIX. Letter of the same pope to Odalric, or Udalric, provost of Reitenbuch.—On the same matter. (Year 1096.)

[PEZ, cited above, p. 298.]

URBAN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons O., provost, and M., dean of Reitenbuch, greetings and apostolic blessing.

For a long time we have exhorted Your Affection, through letters repeatedly sent and resent, and have added our prayers, that you return to complete peace with the venerable abbot or community of Schaffhausen, after restoring to them the brother whom you deceitfully removed from their cloister.

But you have done what was wholly unbecoming to your religious profession: you have disregarded our prayers and treated lightly the authority of the apostolic see in us. Indeed, you offended God, who is charity, when you presumed to mock the religious men gathered for your reconciliation, and the venerable abbot of Schaffhausen, who had humbled himself before you solely out of charity, and to frustrate him with the promise you had made.

We do not doubt that you can read on the tablet of your heart the guilt of disobedience and deceit—a guilt that we ought to pursue with whatever severity.

After receiving this letter, therefore, unless within thirty days [Col. 0483B] you make satisfaction to the same abbot, thereafter the celebration of the divine offices [lacuna]

## CCX. Letter of Pope Urban II to the people of Bologna.—He praises their faith and offers remission of sins to all who take part in the war of Jerusalem. (Year 1096.)

[SAVIOLI, *Bolognese Annals*. Bassano, 1784, quarto, I, II, 137.]

URBAN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved catholic sons among the clergy and people of Bologna, greetings and apostolic blessing.

We give thanks for your goodness, because, although situated among schismatics and heretics, some of you have always remained in the catholic faith, while others, having by God’s grace discovered the truth, have abandoned the byways of error [Col. 0483C] and now understand what belongs to the catholic faith.

We therefore exhort you, most beloved, in the Lord, to walk manfully along the path of truth and strive to add better outcomes to your good beginnings. For it is not the one who begins, but the one who perseveres to the end, who will be saved.

We earnestly commend to your charity our venerable brother and fellow bishop Bernard, whom divine providence has deigned to give you as shepherd through our hands, so that, if you love God, you may show it in his representative. For he himself said concerning such men: “Whoever hears you hears me.”

We have heard that some among you have conceived the desire to go to Jerusalem; know that this pleases us greatly. You should also know that, to all who go there not out of desire for earthly advantage [Col. 0483D], but solely for the salvation of their souls and the liberation of the Church, we remit, by the mercy of almighty God and the prayers of the catholic Church, through the authority both of ourselves and of nearly all the archbishops and bishops in Gaul, the entire penance for the sins of which they have made a true and perfect confession, since they have exposed their possessions and persons for the love of God and neighbor.

We do not, however, grant clerics or monks permission to go there without the authorization of their bishops or abbots. Moreover, bishops must take care not to send their parishioners away without the advice and provision of the clergy. Provision must also be made for young married men, so that they do not rashly undertake so great a journey without the consent of their wives.

May almighty God strengthen you in his fear and love [Col. 0484A], and, absolved from all sins and errors, lead you to the vision of supreme charity and true piety.

Given at Pavia, on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of October.

## CCXI. Bull of Pope Urban II confirming all the rights of the nuns of Saint John the Evangelist at Cremona. (Year 1096.)

[MURATORI, *Italian Antiquities* V, 809.]

URBAN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved daughter GISILA, abbess of the monastery of Saint John the Evangelist near Cremona, and to those who are regularly appointed to succeed her in that place, forever.

A desire that is shown to pertain to a religious purpose and the salvation of souls ought, with God as its author, to be fulfilled without any delay. Therefore, with fatherly affection, we incline the ears of apostolic kindness to the wishes of you and your sisters, and we strengthen with the privilege of Roman authority the monastery of Saint John the Evangelist, over which, by God’s favor, you are known to preside.

That monastery was built at their own expense by Count Bernard and his wife Berta, and they offered it into the hands of Gregory VII, of most reverend memory, our predecessor, to blessed Peter and his holy Roman Church.

We therefore decree that whatever possessions were offered to that place by the aforesaid counts or by any other faithful people from their own right, or that may in future, by the Lord’s generosity, happen to be offered, shall always remain firm and inviolate for you and for those who succeed you [Col. 0484C].

We decree, moreover, that no human being whatsoever may rashly disturb that place, remove or diminish the possessions subject to it, or harass it with presumptuous vexations. Rather, let everything be preserved intact and serve in every way the needs of those for whose support and governance it was granted, without prejudice to the canonical rights of the bishop of Cremona, provided that he is catholic and enjoys the communion and favor of the apostolic see.

Even so, he may in no way burden that monastery or impose upon the sisters living there any exaction or custom harmful to monastic liberty and peace.

As a sign of the protection received from the Roman Church, you shall pay each year twelve denarii of Milanese coin to the Lateran [Col. 0484D] palace.

If, therefore, in future any archbishop or bishop, emperor or king, prince or duke, count, viscount, judge, or any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowingly aware of this page of our constitution, should rashly attempt to act against it, then, after being admonished a second or third time, if he does not make amends by suitable correction, let him lose the dignity of his power and honor, acknowledge himself to be guilty before the divine judgment of the iniquity committed, be alienated from the most sacred body and blood of God and our Lord and Redeemer Jesus Christ, and be subjected to strict punishment at the final judgment.

But let there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ for all who observe what is just toward that place, so that here they may receive the fruit [Col. 0485A] of good action and, before the strict Judge, find the rewards of eternal peace.

I, URBAN, bishop of the catholic Church, have subscribed.

Given at Cremona by the hand of John, cardinal deacon of the Holy Roman Church, on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of November, indiction 5, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1096, in the ninth year of the pontificate of the lord Urban II.

## CCXII. Letter of Urban II to Alexius, emperor of Constantinople.—Concerning the expedition to the Holy Land and the taking of the cross. (Year 1096.)

[MANSI, *Councils* XX, 660.]

[Col. 0485B] Urban II, Roman pontiff, to Alexius, emperor of Constantinople, etc.

When it had been decided at Clermont in Auvergne that, by common vows, war should be waged against the Saracens, so great a multitude of people took the cross that they were reckoned at three hundred thousand men. The enthusiasm of the bravest leaders is likewise so great that we ought to hope much for the recovery of Jerusalem.

Peter the Hermit was the first of all to offer himself as leader to countless men. Godefrey, Eustace, and Baldwin, brothers and counts of Boulogne, joined him and prepared even larger forces. From there came the bishop of Le Puy, leader of the army, and Raymond, count of Saint Giles; then Hugh the Great, brother of Philip, king of the French; Robert of Normandy; another Robert of Flanders; and Stephen, count of Chartres [Col. 0485C].

What should I say of Bohemond himself, who with immense greatness of spirit joined their company with seven thousand chosen Italian youths, leaving the care of all his possessions to his brother, with whom he had long contended in war?

For these great preparations for war, one thing above all is necessary: that such forces be assisted by your protection and supplies. I therefore ask you most earnestly to support this most just and glorious war by whatever means you can.

Although I do not doubt that you will take care of this, I nevertheless wished you to know by our letter that this would be exceedingly pleasing to me and to the entire Christian commonwealth. Farewell.

At Rome, etc.

## CCXIII. Letter of Urban.—Contemptors of the canons must be excommunicated. (Between 1088 and 1097.)

[IVO, *Decretum*, IV, ch. 219.]

[Col. 0485D]

Those who despise the canons must be excommunicated and condemned, since one who refuses to obey the sacred canons must be excluded from the sacred mysteries of the altar.

## CCXIV. Urban confirms and enlarges the liberties and privileges of the monastery of Cluny. (Year 1097.)

[*Cluniac Bibliotheca*, p. 520.]

URBAN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother HUGH, abbot of Cluny, and to his successors to be regularly appointed, forever.

Since the grace of apostolic charity ought to assist the petitions and needs of all the faithful, the mercy of its beneficence must be bestowed all the more upon those whom the Roman mother Church rejoices to have as her special sons.

Among these, the congregation of Cluny, more fully imbued with the divine gift than others, shines upon the earth like another sun, so that in these times the saying of the Lord applies especially to them: “You are the light of the world.” Therefore, dearest brother Hugh, the authority of the apostolic dignity is compelled all the more to assent to your petitions, since we know that, on account of the holiness of your life, the Author of all things wishes your desires to be fulfilled.

Accordingly, whatever liberty, protection, or authority our predecessors, the pontiffs of the Roman Church—especially Gregory VII, of apostolic memory—have conferred upon your monastery and the places belonging to it, we too, by the present decree and with God as author, confirm: namely, that all places and monasteries belonging to the monastery of Cluny, which have been granted to that place by Christian faithful—kings, bishops, dukes, counts, or princes—and acquired by your predecessors, and whatever appears in any way to belong to that same place or may in future be given to it, whether lands, churches, tithes, or any other gifts of the faithful, may be possessed by you and your successors forever, without anyone’s opposition, in great peace and security [Col. 0486C].

We further strengthen this by the promulgation of divine judgment, by confirmation, and by the prohibition of anathema. We decree that no bishop or any priest may presume to come to that venerable monastery, or to any place subject to it, to perform any ordination or consecration of an altar or church, or of priests or deacons, or to celebrate Masses, unless he has been invited by the abbot of that monastery or by the priors subject to it.

But let your monks, wherever they may be, receive whatever degree of ordination they wish, wherever it pleases you and your successors [Col. 0486D].

Under a similar promulgation of anathema, we prohibit the imposition upon Cluny or upon any place belonging to it, anywhere, of an episcopal or priestly interdict, excommunication, or anathema. For the authority of the holy apostolic see does not permit the power of liberty granted by it to be cut down by the bond imposed by any person whatsoever.

Therefore, let your brothers and monks, wherever they may be, not be held bound by the curse, excommunication, or interdict of any bishop.

If anyone, knowingly aware of this page of ours, should presume to act against it, then, by the authority of blessed Peter, to whom the Creator of all things entrusted the power of binding and loosing [Col. 0487A], let your church and the monks themselves be absolved.

But whoever he may be who wishes, contrary to our decree, to bind or curse a son of the apostolic see, let him be bound by an everlasting curse, anathematized, and condemned.

If some competent cause should arise against any matter, and it cannot otherwise be determined or defined, let the apostolic judgment—which permits no prejudice to be inflicted upon anyone—be patiently awaited and humbly sought.

It shall also be lawful for you or your brothers to choose priests in your churches, provided that they receive the care of souls from the bishops or their vicars without purchase. If, God forbid, they should perversely refuse to entrust the care of souls to them, then, through the kindness of the apostolic see, let the priests obtain permission to celebrate the offices [Col. 0487B].

The brothers of your places shall receive the consecration of churches or altars from the bishops in whose dioceses they are located, provided that those bishops are willing to provide it freely and without corruption. Otherwise, let them receive the sacrament of those consecrations from whichever catholic bishop they prefer.

We decree, and by the authority of the one whose office we perform, although unworthy, we establish that this place and the places subject to it shall be a bosom of mercy and a harbor of complete piety and salvation for all who flee there for safety.

Let the just find a place there, and let the unjust who wishes to repent not be rejected. Let mutual fraternal charity be offered to the innocent [Col. 0487C]; let hope of salvation and the indulgence of mercy not be denied to offenders.

Even if someone bound by an anathema should seek that place or the places subject to it, whether for burial of the body or for some other benefit or reason of salvation, let him not be excluded from pardon and the mercy he desires. Rather, let him be kindly bound up and cared for with the oil of saving medicine, because it is also just that, in a house of mercy, holy fraternal love be shown to the just, and that the medicine of indulgence and salvation not be denied to the sinner who flees there for pardon.

Let this be for all who come there, here and forever, a refuge of divine compassion and mercy and a safeguard of apostolic blessing and absolution.

We also grant you this prerogative: if a monk from another monastery should transfer to you for the improvement of his life [Col. 0487D], let him be freely received, regardless of the complaints of his former place, so that, by the Lord’s generosity, he may obtain among you the salvation he appears to seek.

We likewise grant permission to receive regular clerics, whom they call canons, who either cannot be saved in their own places or flee to your places out of necessity, and to admit them to your way of life.

We further decree and establish absolutely that, when the abbot of the aforesaid place dies, no one is to be appointed there through the violence of any person. Rather, the congregation of the place itself shall elect, according to the fear of God and the rule of the legislator Benedict, the Father who is to preside over it; and whatever bishop they prefer shall be invited to ordain him [Col. 0488A].

We further establish that no human being whatsoever may rashly disturb your venerable monastery or the places subject to it. Their churches, tithes, possessions, and other goods, which have already been donated for the salvation of souls or which, by the Lord’s mercy, may in future be donated, shall remain firm and inviolate for you and your successors.

If, therefore, any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowingly aware of this constitution of ours, should rashly attempt to act against it, then, after being admonished a second or third time, if he does not make amends by suitable satisfaction, let him lose the dignity of his power and honor, acknowledge himself to be guilty before the divine judgment of the iniquity committed, be alienated from the most holy body and blood of God and our Lord and Redeemer Jesus [Col. 0488B] Christ, and be subjected to strict punishment at the final judgment.

But let there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ for all who observe what is just toward that monastery and its places, so that here they may receive the fruit of good action and, before the strict Judge, find the rewards of eternal peace. Amen.

Given at the Lateran on the fifth day before the Ides of January, indiction 5.

## CCXV. Letter of Pope Urban II to the clergy and people of the church of Trani. (Year 1097.)

[*Acta Sanctorum*, vol. I, June, p. 249.]

URBAN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the clergy and order, the nobles and people residing at Trani, greetings [Col. 0488C] and apostolic blessing.

Recently, when by the Lord’s generosity we were holding a synodal council with a large gathering of bishops and abbots, our venerable brother Bisantius, archbishop of your city, read aloud before the entire council several miracles of the venerable man Nicholas—who among you is called Pilgrim—which had been set forth in writing; and he earnestly requested that, by our authority, this man of God be enrolled in the catalogue of the saints.

We therefore entrusted the matter itself to that same brother of ours, having no hesitation concerning his integrity and knowledge, so that he may determine, with more mature deliberation, whatever the Lord, by revealing it, should show him—unto the praise and glory of him who, through gratuitous mercy, is accustomed wonderfully to enrich his servants with grace.

## CCXVI. Letter of Urban II to Hugh, archbishop of Lyon. (Year 1097.)

[BALUZE, *Miscellanea*, Luc. edition II, 180.]

[Col. 0488D]

URBAN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother and fellow bishop HUGH, legate of the apostolic see, greetings and apostolic blessing.

What you have indicated to us concerning the bishops Guapicensis—or Diensis—you have dealt prudently with the bishops of Guapicensis and Diensis; and, if more had already been done, we would have been still more pleased: so that Guapicensis might be rescued from the jaws of the encroaching boar, and Diensis might enjoy the shepherd whom he desires.

In the Church of Limoges, understand that we have granted our fellow-bishop A. no authority, except that, when he petitioned us on behalf of that Church, we instructed him to make representations to the count of Limoges for the sake of greater friendship. We therefore regard the election or consecration there as not lawfully performed and indeed invalid; nevertheless, at the request of our revered father, the abbot of Cluny, we have deferred judgment. For he earnestly entreated us not to act impatiently toward that brother.

For our part, with the Lord bringing it about, we shall diminish nothing of the right of your legation, and whatever justice dictates from our mouth shall in no way cease to possess its force through us. Concerning Orléans, what you have decided we also decide, provided that what has been alleged concerning him both before us and before you is found to be true.

What you requested concerning the clerics of Sens we shall more willingly carry out if those clerics should perhaps come to us on behalf of their elected candidate. Nor are we at all displeased with what you have done concerning Beauvais, since we neither wish nor, with the Lord’s help, will tolerate the holy canons being trampled with impunity on behalf of any persons.

We wish your energetic efforts to be diligently concerned for the cause of the monastery of Cluny, so that, when you have been summoned by the lord abbot, you may administer appropriate justice concerning the duke of Burgundy and Aimo of Bourbon, who are grievously harassing them.

Give thanks to God with us for our circumstances: for we have come peacefully as far as Rome with Count M.; we entered the city most honorably, accompanied by a very large procession; and we now possess the greater part of the city itself. We solemnly celebrated the synod at the Lateran. We have bound the citizens and all the surrounding regions by oaths. Thanks be to God, we are honorably, safely, and cheerfully situated.
