Give thanks to God with us, and pray for his mercy on our behalf; nor, amid these matters, neglect to attend more earnestly to assisting your mother, the Roman Church.

### CCXVII. Urban II commends the Church of Pamplona to Peter, king of the Aragonese and Pamplonese, and to the other faithful of those regions. (Year 1097.)

[Ruinart, *Life of Urban*, p. 282.]

### CCXVIII. Urban restores the monastery of Glanfeuil, which had been assigned to the monks of Fossé, to Oderisius, cardinal of the Roman Church and abbot of the monastery of Monte Cassino, consecrated by Urban himself. (Year 1097.)

[Mansi, *Councils*, XX, 928.]

[Column 0489D]

Urban, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his most reverend and beloved brother Oderisius, consecrated by our hands, through the grace of God, as cardinal-priest of the holy Roman Church and as abbot of the monastery of Cassino, and to his successors, regularly appointed in perpetuity.

Benedict, the father and founder of monastic discipline, illustrious both in grace and in name, sent his most blessed disciple Maurus into Gaul, in order that, through his zeal for religious observance, he might teach and extend it, as we find with the greatest clarity in the account of their deeds. When Maurus reached the places appointed for him, he built, with divine grace assisting him, the monastery called Glanfeuil in the diocese of Angers. He entrusted it to the monastery of Cassino, from which he had come. After shining there, with the Lord’s cooperation, through many outstanding virtues, he appointed his disciple Bertulf as abbot and instructed the Cassinian monks who had come with him to watch over him with particular care, lest he deviate in anything from the straight path of regular discipline. Thus he met the end of his temporal life and was buried.

After a number of years had passed, that same monastery, once destroyed by Gaidulf, was later restored through the efforts of religious men, sins so requiring. At that time Pope Adrian of revered memory, together with Charles, king of the Franks and patrician of the Romans, restored the aforesaid monastery of Glanfeuil to the venerable Theodemar, abbot of Cassino, who had brought a complaint concerning it; having examined the matter, he also confirmed it by apostolic authority.

But because the judgments of God are a great abyss, the aforesaid monastery is said to have been again devastated and destroyed by the incursion of barbarians. While the desolation of that barbarous depopulation continued, distinguished princes took measures so that the place of Glanfeuil, then unsuitable for monastic peace, might be administered by the monks of Fossé. This arrangement continued immovably down to our own times.

After the place of Fossé, too, had ceased to observe religious discipline, the church of Glanfeuil appeared for a long time to have been not so much administered as dissipated by the superiors of that place. By the disposition of divine mercy, however, it happened that, when we had crossed into Gaul on ecclesiastical business, we visited that place with our fellow bishops and cardinals of the Roman Church.

A crowd of brothers serving God there, together with noble men living in the surrounding area, gathered around us, complaining of the many forms of dissipation inflicted by those whose diligence ought to have governed them. To these were added the petitions of our common son John, cardinal deacon of the holy Roman Church, and of your monks of the Cassinian monastery, submitted on your behalf and on behalf of our venerable brother Goffrid, bishop of Angers, and our son Fulk, count of Angers. They requested that, by the authority of the apostolic see, a proper abbot for that place be restored under the jurisdiction of the Cassinian Church. They hoped that the place would make considerable progress in a short time, and that the number of monks—then thirty—would suddenly become greater, if, rescued from the tyranny of the monks of Fossé, they were permitted to enjoy the governance of their own abbot.

Accordingly, we appointed a fixed day for the monks of Fossé, on which they were to appear before our hearing if they possessed privileges to present.

When forty-four archbishops, bishops, and abbots were seated with us in the church of Tours, and the matter had been investigated, the aforesaid brothers presented to us, in a public hearing, a document allegedly belonging to the Roman pontiff Adrian. This was proved by clear indications to be entirely false.

Therefore all the brothers who were seated there agreed that, since the observance of religious discipline had already failed for a long time in the monastery of Fossé, and the place of Glanfeuil appeared to have been exposed by them not to improvement but to deterioration, the effect should cease when its cause ceased, and the monks of Glanfeuil should be restored to the support of a cardinal abbot.

Accordingly, by common decree we then enacted—and now, by the text of this present privilege, establish perpetually by apostolic authority—that a cardinal abbot shall always be maintained in the aforesaid venerable place, while in every respect the reverence and obedience owed to its mother church, Cassino, remain intact.

Following, therefore, in the footsteps of our predecessors, the Roman pontiffs Adrian and Nicholas, we confirm by this text of our privilege the aforesaid monastery of Glanfeuil, with all its dependencies, to you and to your monastery of Cassino, preserving the freedom and dignity of that place, together with all its possessions. Among these we have judged that the following should be recorded by their proper names: first, the village of Blazon, and so forth.

We also establish that, when Girard, now abbot of that place, dies, no one shall be placed over it through the trickery of subreption or by force, except one whom the brothers shall elect by common agreement, or whom the sounder part of the brothers’ council shall elect according to the Rule of Saint Benedict, to be blessed at Cassino in accordance with the terms of their privileges.

If, however—a circumstance we scarcely believe could occur—no one suitable for this office is found within the congregation itself, let them choose an abbot from the monastery of Cassino, to be blessed there in the same manner. He shall then receive the Cassinian superiorship and the vicariate of that abbot throughout Gaul and return to his own monastery.

Every five years he shall visit the threshold of Saint Benedict at Cassino, and he shall reside in the place of Maurus at Cassino. In all its cells no other abbot shall sit over him, and he shall be subject to no other place except Cassino alone. If anything concerning the monastic order must be dealt with, it shall be arranged according to the judgment both of the Cassinian superior and of the abbot of Saint Maurus.

Moreover, by this present privilege we strengthen the aforesaid place, together with all that belongs to it, its churches and possessions throughout the world; and by apostolic authority we forbid it to be subjected to the jurisdiction of any other church or bishop except the Church of Cassino.

Whatever in the future you may justly and canonically acquire, whether by the concession of pontiffs, the generosity of princes, or the offerings of the faithful, shall remain firm and unimpaired for that place.

We therefore decree that no human being whatsoever may rashly disturb that monastery, seize its possessions, retain what has been seized, diminish them, or harass them with presumptuous vexations. Rather, all things shall be preserved intact and shall in every way serve the uses of those for whose support and governance they were granted.

We also establish that burial in that place shall be free, so that no one may oppose the devotion and final wish of those who decide to be buried there.

If, in the future, any ecclesiastical or secular person knowingly attempts rashly to act against this page of our constitution, and, after being warned a second or third time, does not make amends by suitable satisfaction, let that person lose the dignity of his power and honor, recognize himself, by divine judgment, as guilty of the iniquity committed, be excluded from the most holy and sacred body and blood of God and our Lord and Redeemer Jesus Christ, and be subject to strict punishment at the final judgment.

But let there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ for all who preserve what is just for that place and for your monastery, so that both here they may receive the fruit of good action and, before the strict Judge, find the rewards of eternal peace. Amen, amen.

Written by the hand of Peter, scrivener of the sacred palace.

[Column 0492B] Given at Terracina by the hand of John, cardinal deacon of the holy Roman Church, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of April, in the fifth indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1097, and in the tenth year of the pontificate of our lord Pope Urban II.

### CCXIX. Pope Urban II confirms the sacred monastery of Cassino and its possessions free from every jurisdiction under the protection of the holy Roman Church, and declares that it is to be preferred to the other monasteries of the West. (Year 1097.)

[Margarini, *Cassinian Bullary*, II, p. 119.]

Urban, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his most reverend and beloved brother Oderisius, consecrated by our hands, through the grace of God, as cardinal-priest of the holy Roman Church and as abbot of the monastery of Cassino, and to his successors, regularly appointed in perpetuity.

Beyond the general obligation of charity, and beyond the particular prerogative of your monastery—which, in the promulgation of monastic law and through its most holy lawgiver Benedict, was established by the Lord as the head of all monasteries throughout the West—the magnificent benevolence by which your congregation has always, and especially in our own times, assisted the holy Roman Church compels us to be greatly indebted to that place.

For that place has remained, and continues to remain, the relief of our poor, the refuge of those who flee, and the tireless rest of the weary sons of the apostolic see. Therefore, responding both to the sweetness of the divine constitution and to fraternal benevolence, we decree that the place itself and everything belonging to it shall always remain undisturbed and free from the yoke of all mortals, and shall perpetually be held under the sole right and protection of the holy Roman Church.

But let the safeguards granted to the monastery of Cassino by our predecessors retain their proper force. Following in their footsteps, we declare that the monastery of Cassino is to be preferred to all other monasteries throughout the West. We also decree that you and your successors shall sit above all abbots in every assembly of bishops or princes, and that in all judgments you shall present the knowledge of law before the other members of your order.

If, in the future, any archbishop or bishop, emperor or king, prince or duke, count, viscount, judge, or ecclesiastical or secular person knowingly attempts rashly to act against this page of our constitution, and, after being warned a second or third time, does not amend himself by suitable satisfaction, let him lose the dignity of his honor, recognize himself by divine judgment as guilty of the iniquity committed, be excluded from the most sacred body and blood of God and our Lord Jesus Christ our Redeemer, and be subject to strict punishment at the final judgment.

But let there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ for all who preserve what is just for that place, so that both here they may receive the fruit of good action and, before the strict Judge, find the rewards of eternal peace. Amen, amen.

[Column 0493B] Written by the hand of Peter, scrivener of the sacred palace.

Given at the Lateran by the hand of John, cardinal deacon of the holy Roman Church, on the fourth day before the Kalends of April, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1097, and in the tenth year of the pontificate of our lord Pope Urban II.

### CCXX. Privilege of Pope Urban II to Saint Hugh concerning the immunity of the Cluniac cells, the interdict, and the freedom to summon to Cluny whichever bishop he wished to confer the chrism and bless the oil. (Year 1097.)

[*Cluniac Bullary*, 28.]

Urban, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his most reverend brother Hugh, abbot, and to all the brothers of the monastery of Cluny, greeting and apostolic blessing.

Since, as iniquity increases, the charity of many grows cold, it is necessary that, for the governance of the place divinely entrusted to us, we provide more attentively for the religious observance of the few—that is, of the servants of God. For in many places the servants of God and monks are disturbed by those through whom it would especially be appropriate for them to be supported and protected.

This fault concerns certain bishops of our time, who, while they covet earthly things, disturb those who appear to have despised earthly things. We have judged that their vexations must be countered through the dispensation of the apostolic see, so that, with God’s help, you may be free from secular tumults and able to pray more earnestly both for us, for them, and for all the faithful of Christ.

By this present constitution, therefore, we decree that, wherever your cells are situated, the brothers shall not suffer the suspension of divine offices because of an interdict or excommunication imposed by neighboring dioceses. Rather, both the monks themselves and their servants—namely, those who have devoted themselves to the monastic profession—shall celebrate the offices of divine service with the doors of the churches closed and the diocesan clergy excluded, and shall perform the obligations due to burial.

Moreover, we grant to you who reside in the monastery of Cluny permission to summon whichever Catholic bishop you prefer to prepare the chrism or bless the oil for your use and that of your brothers. Supported by our authority, he shall grant what is requested.

But if any bishop, or any minister of a bishop, presumes to cause you trouble in these matters and to oppose our constitutions, then, for his contempt of the apostolic see, according to the judgment of blessed Gelasius, he shall be a destroyer of his own order and honor.

Written by the hand of Lanfranc, notary of the sacred palace.

Given at the Lateran by the hand of John, cardinal deacon of the holy Roman Church, on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of May, in the fifth indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1097, and in the tenth year of the pontificate of our lord Pope Urban II.

### CCXXI. Urban II confirms the privileges and possessions of the Church of Auvergne and “establishes that the bishop of that Church shall hold the first place in the ordination of the metropolitan of Bourges.” (Year 1097.)

[Ruinart, *Life of Urban*, p. 285.]

### CCXXII. Letter of Pope Urban II to Raymond, archbishop of Auch—against the clerics who had violated the cemetery of Saint Orientius. (Year 1097.)

[Dom Bouquet, *Collection*, XIV, p. 725.]

[Column 0494B]

Urban, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved brother R. [Raymond], archbishop of Auch, greeting and apostolic blessing.

Since you have recently been ordained in the metropolitan church of Auch by the Roman Church, you must obey the decrees of the apostolic see without resistance. We therefore command your fraternity to ensure, with canonical equity, that justice be done concerning the clerics of your see who violated the cemetery that had been secured to the church of Saint Orientius by the decree of the blessed Pope Leo and by our own decree.

For the rest, so guard both yourself and the clerics of your see that, with the Lord’s generosity, the decrees of the Roman Church may be preserved among you unshaken and intact.

Given at Rome, on the third day before the Kalends of May.

### CCXXIII. The district of Salmor is asserted to belong to the Church of Grenoble. (Year 1097.)

[Ruinart, *Life of Urban*, III, 366.]

Urban, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his most reverend brother and fellow bishop Hugh, vicar of the apostolic see, greeting and apostolic blessing.

How arrogantly and unworthily our brother Guido, archbishop of Vienne, has behaved toward us and the holy Roman Church is by no means unknown to your knowledge. Among other things, he raised his neck against our humility to such a degree that he re-entered the abbey of Romans, which had been placed under interdict by us, and took back without judgment from our brother, the bishop of Grenoble, the churches that he himself had restored together with us.

We therefore command your fraternity to be stirred entirely to justice on our behalf. Let him feel that your face is like adamant and flint; and, setting aside the reverence due to your former leniency, restore altogether, according to justice, the rights belonging to the Church of Grenoble, and avenge the injuries inflicted upon the apostolic see.

Until now, out of the grace of apostolic gentleness, we have yielded excessively to the petitions of the Gauls in changes of bishops. Henceforth, however, we command that this be wholly avoided. For we shall no longer permit the authority of the Council of Nicaea—which we venerate no less than the holy Gospel—to be annulled on such pretexts.

Given at the Lateran, on the second day before the Nones of June.

### CCXXIV. Letter of Pope Urban II to Bertran, archbishop of Narbonne—he confirms the privileges of the Church of Narbonne. (Year 1097.)

[D. Bouquet, *Collection*, XIV, p. 727.]

[Column 0495B] Urban, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved brother in Christ Bertran, archbishop of Narbonne, perpetual salvation in the Lord.

The Church acknowledges that the power of binding and loosing in heaven and on earth was principally entrusted by God to blessed Peter and his successors, in the words with which the Lord addressed Peter: “Whatever you bind on earth shall be bound also in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth shall be loosed also in heaven” (Matthew 18:8).

The firmness of Peter’s own faith and the strengthening of the faith of others were likewise granted by the same Lord, when he said to him: “I have prayed for you, that your faith may not fail. And you, once converted, strengthen your brothers” (Luke 22:32).

It is therefore necessary that we, who, although unworthy, see ourselves seated upon Peter’s chair, correct what is wrong, strengthen what is right, and arrange in every Church what must be arranged according to the judgment of the eternal Judge, so that judgment may proceed from his countenance and our eyes may behold equity.

Therefore, assenting to the just petitions of your fraternity, we confirm by the text of this present decree the holy Church of Narbonne, over which, by the clemency granted by God, you preside, for you to possess, govern, and administer.

For we consecrated you bishop in the Church of Nîmes and, when necessity required it, permitted you by letters of our authority to be transferred to your metropolitan see through the election of your suffragans. We decree that henceforth this is not to be permitted to anyone.

We decree that the following cities shall be subject to the fraternity of your Church: Toulouse, Carcassonne, Elne, Béziers, Agde, Maguelonne, Nîmes, Uzès, and Lodève, while the right of the apostolic see remains intact in all matters.

Moreover, we decree by the text of this present decree that the primacy of the metropolitan Church of Aix, which is Narbonensis Secunda, and whatever dignity or honor that same Church of Narbonne is found to have possessed by ancient right, shall remain perpetually secure and inviolable.

We grant the pallium to your fraternity, according to custom, solely for the celebration of Mass, and you may use it only on the following days: Epiphany; all the feasts of blessed Mary; the Lord’s Supper; the Resurrection of the Lord for two days; the Ascension of the Lord; Pentecost; the Nativity of blessed John; the feasts of all the apostles; the feast of blessed Martin; the solemnities of the holy martyrs Justus and Pastor; and of Paul the Confessor; at the consecration of bishops and churches; and at the ordination of clerics.

You should carefully consider how much weight and responsibility are imposed upon you by this. For the honor of this garment is humility and justice, and so forth.

Written by the hand of Peter, scrivener of the sacred palace.

Given at the Lateran on the eighth day before the Ides of November, by the hand of Lanfranc, acting in place of the chancellor, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1097, in the sixth indiction, and in the tenth year of the pontificate of our lord Pope Urban II.

### CCXXV. Letter of Pope Urban II to Peter Goffrid, archbishop of Aix—he commands him to show reverence to the archbishop of Narbonne as his primate. (Year 1097.)

[D. Bouquet, *Collection*, XIV, p. 728.]

[Column 0496B]

Urban, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved brother, the archbishop of Aix, greeting and apostolic blessing.

Our brother, the archbishop of Narbonne, has complained about you, because you refuse to obey him according to the right of primacy. By this present letter, therefore, we command your affection to render the reverence owed to the Church of Narbonne; otherwise, as a contemptor of the apostolic see, you will be subject to the judgment of the apostolic see.

### CCXXVI. Letter of Pope Urban II to Hugh, archbishop of Lyon—so that he may compel the archbishop of Aix to obey his primate, the archbishop of Narbonne. (Year 1097.)

[D. Bouquet, *Collection*, XIV, p. 728.]

[Column 0496C]

Urban, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the venerable Hugh, vicar of the apostolic see, greeting and apostolic blessing.

Our brother, the archbishop of Narbonne, has complained about the archbishop of Aix, because he refuses to obey him according to the right of primacy. Therefore we send this letter to your fraternity, commanding you to compel that same archbishop of Aix to obey his primate in accordance with the ordinances of the apostolic see. Farewell.

### CCXXVII. Privilege for the Church of Veroli. (Year 1097.)

[Ughelli, *Sacred Italy*, I, 1390.]

[Column 0496D]

Urban, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved brother Albert, bishop of Veroli, and to his successors, canonically appointed in perpetuity.

It is fitting that we grant assent to just wishes and lend our ears to just petitions—we who, although unworthy, appear by the Lord’s arrangement to have been placed as guardians and heralds of justice upon the lofty watchtower of the princes of the apostles, Peter and Paul.

Therefore, dearest brother in Christ Albert, assenting to your just petitions, we fortify by the authority of the apostolic see the holy Church of Veroli, over which, with God as its author, you preside.

We establish that whatever has already been donated to that venerable place by any persons from their own right, or whatever in the future may be granted to it, through the mercy of God, by the concession of pontiffs, the generosity of princes, or the offerings of the faithful, shall remain firm and unimpaired for you and your successors.

That is: the valley of Literana with its dependencies; the lake with its dependencies; Astianum, Pattena, Mundezanum, Paternus, the estate, the Crypt of Anselm, and Cassianum with their dependencies; the church of the Holy Cross; Saint Mary’s, called the Rotunda; the church of the Holy Archangel; Saint Mary’s of Paretis, with its dependencies; the mill situated at Masena, with its dependencies; the church of Saint Stephen; and that of Saint Vitus, with their dependencies; the church of Saints Cosmas and Damian, with its dependencies; the church of Saint Angelus of Forgna, with its woods and territories; and the church of Saint John in the territory of Frusino, situated beside the river Casam, with everything belonging to it.

The lake of Mascianum, and whatever is known from authentic documentary records to belong to the Church of Veroli in the territory of Sora.

We grant and confirm these possessions, to be governed and administered perpetually by episcopal right by you and your successors: the city of Veroli with all the neighboring churches, inside or outside it; Frusino with all that belongs to it; the towns of Turricis, Larnaria, and Paphen, with the churches of Saint Peter and Saint Columba; the monastery of Saint Sylvester; Ripas; Castrum; Monte Nero; Fabrateria with their boundaries and dependencies; Ceperannum; Cannetum; Castellum Novum; Strangulagallum; Carpenum; Monte San Giovanni, with the monastery of the same name; the church of Saint Peter of Arenula; Saint Pudentiana’s; Babucum, with all the churches adjacent to that castle.

In addition, two monasteries of canons: one of Saint Paternianus, the other of Saint Peter of Canneto; the church of Saint John at Ceprano; Saint Magnus, with all the others; and the church of Saint Benedict situated between Castrum and Monte Nero, with all its dependencies.

We decree that the church of Saint Angelus of Meruleta and that of Saint Stephen, with all the others, shall perpetually be subject to the administration of you and your successors.

In the monastery of monks called Saints John and Paul, whatever canonically belongs to the ancient right of the bishop of Veroli shall be preserved intact for you perpetually, while the reverence due to our holy Roman Church remains secure.

Moreover, by the text of this present privilege, we decree by apostolic authority that no human being whatsoever may rashly disturb that Church, seize its possessions, diminish them under any pretext or occasion, appropriate them for his own uses, or grant them to others under the guise of pious purposes as an excuse for his own greed. Rather, all things shall be preserved intact, to be wholly useful both for your needs and those of the clerics and the poor.

If, therefore, any priest or cleric, emperor or king, prince or duke, count, viscount, judge, or any person of great or small rank, knowingly presumes rashly to act against this page of our constitution, let him lose the dignity of his power and honor, recognize himself by divine judgment as guilty of the iniquity committed, and, unless he restores what he has wickedly taken away or mourns his unlawful conduct through worthy penance, let him be excluded from the most sacred body and blood of God and our Lord Jesus Christ, our Redeemer, and be subject to strict punishment at the final judgment.

But let there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ for all who preserve what is just for that place, so that both here they may receive the fruit of good action and, before the strict Judge, find the rewards of eternal peace. Amen, amen, amen.

Written by Albanus, and given by the hand of Lanfranc, acting in place of the chancellor, in the year of the Lord 1097, in the sixth indiction, and in the tenth year of the pontificate of Pope Urban II.

### CCXXVIII. Urban II takes the Church of Saint Mary of Buron under his protection, confirms its possessions, and establishes privileges, imposing upon the brothers an annual census of a gold bezant. (Year 1097.)

[Petrus, *Ecclesiastical Swabia*. Augsburg and Dillingen, 1699, folio, p. 212.]

Urban, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son Berthold, superior, and to his brothers professing the canonical life in the church called Saint Martin’s, which is to be consecrated in honor of blessed Mary the Virgin, at the place called Buron, between two mountains, on the bank of the Danube River, in the territory of Constance, and to their successors in perpetuity.

Just as assent ought to be denied to those who ask for unreasonable things, so a kindly assent ought to respond to the wishes of those who ask for what is just.

Therefore, dearest son Berthold in Christ, assenting to your just petitions, we receive under the special protection of the apostolic see the church of God’s Mother and ever-Virgin Mary—which our son Peregrinus built on his own estate and offered as his own allod to blessed Peter and his holy Roman Church, and over which, with God as its author, you preside—as a proper right of the apostolic see, and we fortify it against the wickedness of all evil persons by the privilege of its authority and ours.

By this present decree, therefore, we establish that whatever your church justly possesses today, or may in the future justly and canonically acquire through the concession of pontiffs, the generosity of princes, or the offerings of the faithful, shall remain firm and unimpaired for you and your successors, always under the protection of the apostolic see.

In addition, we decree that no one among you who has made his profession may possess anything as his own, nor may anyone leave the cloister without the permission of you, dearest son Berthold, or of those who succeed to authority in the same government, or without the common permission of the congregation.

If anyone should leave and, after being warned, refuse to return, you and your successors shall have the power to prohibit such a person from his offices wherever he may be. Nor shall one so interdicted accept an interdict from any bishop, abbot, or superior.

When you, the present superior of that place, or any of your successors dies, no one shall be placed over it through any kind of subreption or force except one whom the brothers elect by common agreement, or whom the sounder part of the brothers’ council, in the fear of God, chooses from that congregation or from another congregation of the same profession.

We therefore decree that no human being whatsoever may rashly disturb that church, seize its possessions, retain what has been seized, diminish them, or harass them with presumptuous vexations. Rather, all things shall be preserved intact, to benefit you, your successors, and the poor, while the canonical right and reverence of the bishop of Constance remain secure, provided that he is Catholic.

As a sign of the liberty received from the Roman Church, you shall pay each year to the Lateran palace one gold bezant, or silver of the same value.

If, therefore, in the future any archbishop or bishop, emperor or king, duke, count, viscount, judge, advocate, or person of any rank violates this page of our decree or knowingly attempts to act against it, and, after being warned a second or third time, does not amend himself by suitable satisfaction, let him lose the dignity of his power and honor, recognize himself by divine judgment as guilty of the iniquity committed, be excluded from the most sacred body and blood of God and our Lord Jesus Christ, our Redeemer, and be subject to strict punishment at the final judgment.

But let there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ for all who preserve the rights of that place, so that both here they may receive the fruit of good action and, before the strict Judge, find the rewards of eternal peace. Amen, amen, amen.

Written and given by the hand of Lanfranc, acting in place of the chancellor, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1097, in the fifth indiction, and in the tenth year of the pontificate of Pope Urban II.

### CCXXIX. Letter of Urban II to Manasses, archbishop of Reims. (Year 1097.)

[Dom Marlot, *Metropolis of Reims*, II, 221.]

[Column 0499D] Urban, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother Manasses, archbishop of Reims, greeting and apostolic blessing.

The case of the abbot of Saint Remigius was examined in our presence and in that of our fellow bishops and cardinals through a more careful investigation, and was finally brought to this conclusion.

You should know that the judgment pronounced by the bishops against him was rejected for this reason: after a son has been emancipated from his father, he is not compelled by the strictness of the laws to return under his father’s care and authority, unless he himself should voluntarily ask to do so. For we understand the promotion of an abbot as emancipation, and therefore judge that he ought not to return under the authority of an abbot.

[Note: See Saint Bernard, Letter 87.]

### CCXXX. Letter of Pope Urban II to Bernard, bishop of Bologna—he commends certain brothers who were ordained unwillingly by heretics. (Year 1097.)

[Savioli, *Bolognese Annals*, I, part II, p. 138.]

Urban, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother Bernard, bishop of Bologna, greeting and apostolic blessing.

Concerning ordinations performed by the heresiarch Guibert after he had been condemned by Pope Gregory of blessed memory and by the Roman Church, and concerning those also carried out by the false bishops subsequently ordained by him, it was defined by the general judgment of the Council of Piacenza [Col. 0500B] that they be regarded as invalid, unless they should wish to prove that, when they were ordained, they did not know that those men had been condemned.

But because you assert that the brothers about whom you ask are religious men, and openly confess that they suffered force and were dragged into ordination, while you also complain of the great need of your Church, we entrust to your prudence the question whether they should be treated with leniency in the priestly order, according to the more serious necessity. Let your experience, however, take care that the Church suffer neither scandal nor disgrace on their account. In the case of others, when they cannot be excused by the same religious motive and the application of force, you should pursue the sentence of the synodal judgment without exception. If, nevertheless, you restore any of them because of pressing necessity, you shall not permit this without the remedy of daily penance; and you shall command those very men to be present among those upon whom you impose hands for ordination, [Col. 0500C] while the solemnity of the prayers is being performed. Yet we absolutely command that this not be presumed under any circumstances without the Church’s more serious necessity and the merit of the persons concerned.

Given at the Lateran, on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of May.

### CCXXXI. Urban asserts to Jarenton, abbot of Saint Benignus of Dijon, that the monastery of Saint Vigor of Bayeux was donated by Bishop Odo. (1098)

[Ruinart, *Life of Urban*, p. 292.]

### CCXXXII. Letter of Urban to Udalric, abbot of the monastery of Saint Michael on the Meuse.—He grants permission to establish a cemetery beside the new church. (1098)

[Baluz., *Miscellanies*, Lucerne edition, III, 61.]

[Col. 0500D]

Urban, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son Udalric, abbot of Saint Michael, greetings and apostolic blessing.

We give thanks for your kindness, because you open the embrace of brotherly charity to our venerable brothers and fellow abbots, namely Rodulf and Lanzon, and protect them, as we have learned from their report, with the shelter of your tranquility while they labor amid the heat of persecution. We therefore ask that you pursue more vigilantly and devotedly what you have begun, out of reverence for our request. As for what you have presented to us through your petition—namely, the construction of a cemetery around the new church of your monastery—since, as you have written, it is burdensome and contrary to religious observance for the brothers to carry the bodies of the dead to the site of the old church, because it is farther away, we grant this by the authority of the present letter.

Given at the Lateran, on the seventh day before the Kalends of April, in the year from the Incarnation of the Lord, according to Dionysius, 1098; but according to the more certain reckoning of the Gospel, 1121; indiction 6, epact 15, concurrent 4.

### CCXXXIII. Bull of Pope Urban II for the monastery of Wiblingen. (1098)

[D. Gerbert, *History of the Black Forest*, III, 34.]

[Col. 0501B]

Urban, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son Werner, abbot of the monastery called Wiblingen, and to his successors who shall regularly be promoted there, forever.

It is fitting to grant a ready assent to religious desires, so that faithful devotion may obtain a swift result. Since, therefore, Count Hartmann and his brother Otto, sons of the Roman Church, have handed over to Saint Peter and the apostolic see the church of Saint Martin, built at their own expense in the place called Wiblingen, we receive it into the right and protection of the apostolic authority and strengthen it by the privilege of this authority. We decree that whatever estates and whatever gifts the aforesaid church of Saint Martin now possesses, or may thereafter justly and canonically acquire—whether from the generosity of those brothers or from the offerings of faithful devotees—shall remain secure and inviolate for you and your successors.

We decree, therefore, that absolutely no person shall be permitted rashly to disturb the same monastery, take away its possessions, retain what has been taken away, diminish them, or harass them with reckless vexations. Rather, everything shall be preserved intact for the uses of those for whose support and administration it has been granted, while the canonical reverence due to the bishop of Constance is preserved; yet he shall in no way be permitted to impose any exaction or custom harmful to the peace of the religious.

After the religious Count Hartmann, the heir whom the abbot and brothers shall choose shall administer the advocacy of the monastery. If he should later prove unsuitable for the monastery, they shall remove him and appoint another. We also decree that burial in the same place shall be entirely free, so that no one may obstruct the devotion and final wish of those who have decided to be buried there, unless they happen to have been excommunicated.

Furthermore, by a decree that shall remain perpetually in force, we establish that no living person shall be permitted to claim in your monastery any conditions of ownership—whether hereditary right, investiture, or any other power—that might harm the liberty and peace of the brothers.

You shall receive chrism, holy oil, the consecrations of altars and basilicas, and the ordinations of monks who are to be promoted to sacred orders from the bishop in whose diocese you are situated, provided that he possesses the grace and communion of the apostolic see and is willing to provide these things freely and without corruption. Otherwise, you shall be permitted to approach whichever Catholic bishop you prefer and receive from him the sacraments of consecration; supported by the authority of the apostolic see, he shall grant what is requested.

When you, the abbot of that place, die, or any of your successors, no one shall be placed over it through any stratagem of deception or violence except one whom the brothers unanimously, or the sounder part of the brothers’ council, shall elect in the fear of God and according to the Rule of Saint Benedict. As a payment for the liberty received from the Roman Church, you shall pay one gold Byzantine coin each year to the Lateran palace.

[Col. 0502B] If, therefore, any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowingly attempting to violate this page of our constitution, should rashly act against it, then, after being warned a second or third time, if he does not correct himself by suitable satisfaction, let him lose the dignity of his power and honor, recognize himself as guilty before the divine judgment of the iniquity committed, be separated from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord and Redeemer Jesus Christ, and be subject to strict punishment at the examination of the final judgment.

But for all who preserve justice toward that place, may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that both here they may receive the fruit of a good deed and, before the strict Judge, find the rewards of eternal peace. Amen, amen, amen.

Written by the hand of Peter, notary of the sacred palace.

[Col. 0502C] Given at the Lateran, on the third day before the Nones of April, through the hand of John, cardinal deacon of the holy Roman Church, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1098, and in the eleventh year of the pontificate of our lord Pope Urban II.

### CCXXXIV. Bull of Urban II for the Church of Urgell. (1098)

[Marca, *Hispanic March*, Appendix, p. 1207.]

Urban, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved brother Odo, bishop of Urgell, and to his canonically appointed successors forever.

It is fitting for us, who, although unworthy, appear by the Lord’s arrangement to have been placed as guardians and heralds of justice upon the lofty watchtower of the chief apostles Peter and Paul, to grant assent to just vows and lend an ear to just petitions. Therefore, dearest brother in Christ Odo, assenting to your just petitions, we fortify by the authority of the apostolic see the holy Church of Urgell, over which by God’s authority you preside.

We decree that everything known to belong justly to that same Church, whether by parochial or proprietary right, shall always be preserved freely and inviolate for you and your successors: namely, the county of Cerdanya, Libia, Berguedà, Pallars, Ribagorza, Gistau, Cardós, Àneu, Tirvia, and the place of Santa Deodata with its boundaries; the castle of Gissona with all its territories; the castle of Lanera with its boundaries; the castle of Solsona and the church of Saint Mary of Solsona with everything belonging to them; the castle of Aguda de Vallearia with its boundaries; the castle of Clusa with its boundaries; the castle of Figerola and Fontanet with all their appurtenances; the castle of Perarua; the castle of Sallent; the village of Montaniocel and Cubilar with their boundaries; the castle of Corneliana with its territories; the village of Tossen with its boundaries; the castle of Turris, the village of Biscaran, and the village of Archavel with their appurtenances; the valley of Andorra with all its boundaries; the castle of Riu de la Matriu, the castle of Colomers, the castle of Sarred, the castle of Arnoll, and the castle of Archalis with all their appurtenances; the village of Saort, the village of Languanes, the village of Aquatepida, Calbiciniano and Feners; Submonte and Alass, Leton, Clopedera, Ges, Sardine, both Nocolona, both Boxedera, the village of Saint Stephen, and the village of the see of Urgell, with all their appurtenances.

In the parish of Ausona: the castle of Turizella and the small castle below Manresa, while the parochial right of the bishop of Ausona is preserved.

We also confirm to you and your successors a third part of the toll or market dues in all places belonging to your bishopric, as well as firstfruits and tithes to be distributed according to canonical enactments. Moreover, whatever your Church now justly possesses, or may hereafter justly and canonically acquire, shall always remain secure and whole for you and your successors.

In addition, we decree that the clergy of your parishes shall not be subjected to the coercive authority of any secular power, but shall always be subject to episcopal discipline according to the institutions of the holy canons.

If, in the future, any archbishop, emperor, king, prince, duke, margrave, count, viscount, judge, or any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowingly attempting to violate this page of our constitution, should rashly act against it, then, after being warned a second or third time, if he does not correct himself by suitable satisfaction, let him lose the dignity of his power and honor, recognize himself as guilty before the divine judgment of the iniquity committed, be separated from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord and Redeemer Jesus Christ, and be subject to strict punishment at the final examination.

But for all who preserve justice toward that place, may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that here they may receive the fruit of good action and, before the strict Judge, find the rewards of eternal peace.

Written by the hands of John, notary of the holy Roman Church, son of Constantine, in the month and indiction written below.

Given at the Lateran through the hand of John, cardinal deacon of the holy Roman Church, on the eighth day before the Ides of April, indiction 6, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1098, and in the eleventh year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Urban II.

[Giulini, *Memoirs of Milan*. Milan, 1760, quarto edition, vol. IV, p. 542.]

[Col. 0504A]

### CCXXXVI. Bull of Pope Urban II for the monastery of Jesus of Nazareth (Mount Aragon). (1098)

[Aynsa, *Foundation, excellences, greatnesses, and memorable things of Huesca*, p. 455.]

Urban, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his dearest son Eximino, provost, and to the other brothers, the canons of Our Lord Jesus of Nazareth, and to their successors forever, etc.

(“Its date is … at the Lateran, through the hand of John, cardinal deacon of the holy Roman Church, on the fourth day before the Nones of May, indiction 6, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1099, and in the eleventh year of the pontificate of our lord Pope Urban II.”)

### CCXXXVII. Letter of Urban to Peter, bishop of Huesca.—He establishes the Church of Huesca as the head of the Church of Jaca. (1098)

[Mansi, *Councils*, XX, 702.]

Urban, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother Peter, bishop of Huesca, and to his canonically appointed successors forever.

We give manifold thanks to the mercies of the Lord, because, after the passage of many years, he has deigned in our own times especially to relieve the hardships of the Christian people and exalt the faith. In our days, by the strength of the Christians, he has defeated the Turks in Asia and the Moors in Europe, and with greater favor restored formerly famous cities to the worship of their religion.

Among these, he restored Huesca, the city of the pontifical see, liberated from the tyranny of the Saracens, to its Catholic Church through the efforts of our dearest son Peter, king of Aragon. We therefore judged it right that we too should pursue the goodness of almighty God, who has granted this through his generosity, by the liberality of the holy apostolic see, and restore the dignity of the episcopal see to the one to whom, through manifold mercy, he himself has restored the liberty of his faith.

By the authority of this decree, therefore, we establish that henceforth and perpetually the same church of Huesca shall be regarded as the head of the entire parish now subject to the Church of Jaca, and of the Church of Jaca itself. The episcopal seat shall be maintained in that great mosque which the canons of Our Lord Jesus Christ of Nazareth had possessed by the gift of King Sancho during the time of the Saracens, but which Peter, his son and king, granted to your fraternity after the capture of the city.

We do not, however, confirm by the authority of this present decree the other gifts granted to your church; but all the estates, possessions, and revenues from tolls or taxes that King Ramiro of blessed memory, the grandfather of the present King Peter, granted to the Church of Jaca by royal charters with his son Sancho, we decree, by the Lord’s generosity, shall remain forever inviolate for the aforesaid Church of Huesca, just as King Peter is known to have desired and established in his letter of donation, except for those things that the aforesaid King Sancho, his son, together with his own son Peter, named above, altered from that settlement of Ramiro their father, with the consent of your predecessors Sancho and Garcia and with your own confirmation of the same.

Likewise, for you, your successors, and your Church, we establish forever whatever is known to have been offered by the distinguished King Sancho, except for those things that the aforesaid king, Sancho’s son, altered from his charter with the consent of the clergy of your church and of the distinguished provost of the canonry of Our Lord Jesus of Nazareth, and with your confirmation of the same.

For when Lupus, the archdeacon of your see, and that distinguished provost of the Church of Our Lord Jesus of Nazareth came to us, they commended in our hearing and by mutual consent requested that the settlement made between you and our son Peter, king of Aragon and Pamplona, at the castle of Calasanz, concerning the property and revenues of your church and of the canonry of Our Lord Jesus of Nazareth, be confirmed.

Your affection, with the intervention of the aforesaid king, granted to the clergy of that canonry a fourth part of the tithes from the whole of Mount Aragon, and whatever belonged to it by episcopal right apart from the care of souls and the consecration of churches or clergy, and secured this by a written guarantee. They, however, restored to your authority and that of your successors half of the tithes which they had been accustomed to receive from the city of Huesca through the hand of that same king.

As for the labor dues owed to the royal household, half of the tithes was assigned by mutual charity to you and the clergy of the episcopal see, and the other half to the canons of Our Lord Jesus Christ. You established all the remaining matters by common agreement according to the charter of King Sancho of blessed memory and that of the son named above, and through the messengers mentioned above you asked us to confirm the same.

In addition, we decree that the boundaries of the parishes which are still held under the oppression of the Saracens, and which by ancient right belong to the Church of Huesca, shall be restored to it when the favor of almighty God returns them to Christian rule.

We also entrust to you, your successors, and the canons of your church, provided that they observe the decrees of the apostolic see and retain its favor, the administration and disposition, according to the founder’s wish, of the canonry of Hasien, belonging to our jurisdiction, which Sancho the count, son of the aforesaid King Ramiro and maternal uncle of King Peter, built through his own efforts and offered to the holy Roman Church.

This is to be done on the condition that you take care to preserve regular discipline there more diligently and pay from that place an annual census of half an ounce of gold to the Lateran palace.

[Col. 0506A] Besides this, we confirm to you, your canonically ordained successors, and the clergy of that see all the tithes and firstfruits owed both from the city of Huesca itself and from all the other territories established as belonging to it by episcopal right, except for that portion of the revenues which your fraternity, at the request of the aforesaid King Peter, granted with generous kindness to the canons of Jesus of Nazareth. If any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowingly attempting to violate this page of our constitution, should rashly act against it, etc.

Given at the Lateran through the hand of John, cardinal deacon of the holy Roman Church, on the fifth day before the Ides of May, indiction 6, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1098, and in the eleventh year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Urban II.

### CCXXXVIII. Urban writes to William, king of the English, “that he should make Anselm’s affairs free in his kingdom and restore to him all his possessions.” (1098)

[See Eadmer, *New History*, book II, p. 51.]

[Col. 0506B]

### CCXXXIX. Letter of Urban II to Roger, count of Sicily.—Concerning the privilege of the Sicilian monarchy. (1098)

[Mansi, *Councils*, XX, 659.]

Urban, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his dearest son Roger, count of Calabria and Sicily, greetings and apostolic blessing.

[Col. 0506C] Since the favor of the heavenly majesty has exalted your prudence with many triumphs and honors, and your integrity has greatly extended the Church of God in the lands of the Saracens, and has always shown itself devoted in many ways to the holy apostolic see, we have adopted you as a special and dearest son of that universal Church.

Therefore, placing great confidence in the sincerity of your integrity, just as we promised in words, so by the authority of this letter we confirm that throughout your lifetime, and throughout the lifetime of your son Simon, or of any other legitimate heir of yours, we shall appoint no legate of the Roman Church in any land under your authority without your will or counsel. Indeed, whatever we intend to undertake through a legate, we wish to have carried out through your diligence in the legate’s stead.

Whenever we send someone from our side to you [variant: “whenever we shall have sent”], it shall be for the welfare of the holy churches [variant: “namely”] that are under your authority [variant: “exist under your authority”], for the honor of blessed Peter and of his holy apostolic see, which you have hitherto devoutly obeyed and which you have vigorously and faithfully assisted in its necessities.

If a council is held and I command you to send me the bishops and abbots of your land, you shall send whichever ones you wish [variant: “whichever ones you may send”], while retaining others for the service of your churches [variant: “and for their protection”]. May almighty God direct your actions according to his good pleasure and, having absolved you from sins, lead you into eternal life.

[Col. 0507A] Given at Salerno through the hands of John, deacon of the holy Roman Church, on the third day before the Nones of July, indiction 7, in the eleventh year of our pontificate.

### CCXL. To Alphano, archbishop of Salerno, and his successors, he asserts primacy over the provinces of Acerenza and Cosenza, at the request of Duke Roger. (1098)

[Ughelli, *Sacred Italy*, VII, 393.]

Urban, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved brother Alphano, archbishop of Salerno, and to his canonically appointed successors forever.

[Col. 0507B] The singular privilege of the apostolic see has always been evident: to govern the Churches subject to it throughout the world by its authority and to cherish them with more indulgent kindness. Those to whom the favor of the heavenly majesty has granted a fuller abundance of grace, it has also been accustomed to endow with more distinguished dignity.

For this reason, we rightly judge that Salerno should be honored with greater gifts of our kindness, since almighty God has exalted it through the prerogative of his exceptional gift and gratuitous mercy. From the farthest regions of the earth he permitted the body of blessed Matthew the apostle and evangelist to be brought to this place and preserved here by the gracious favor of his most merciful providence. The excellence of that apostle’s glory in God and in the Church, enriched by the grace of divinely bestowed gifts, is demonstrated by the following.

He was the first among the others to begin writing the sequence of the Gospel under divine inspiration. In the fruitfulness of the divine seed he alone received the hundredfold crown of three orders, so that he was at once an apostle, evangelist, and martyr. Almighty God added to this by honoring the same Church with both the triumphs and the bodies of the glorious martyrs Fortunatus, Gaius, and Anthes.

He added also the glory of a third gift, by illuminating it in our own times through the exile and tomb of Pope Gregory VII of apostolic memory. How outstanding his life, how distinguished his teaching, and how admirable his steadfastness were, the Roman Church proclaims and the whole West acknowledges; the persistence of tyrants, endured and trampled underfoot, bears witness to it.

Nor do we pass over, as ungrateful, the fact that amid the manifold persecutions which the same apostolic see has suffered in our times, through the devotion and zeal of the most glorious dukes Robert and his son Roger, and through the efforts of the sons of the apostolic see, it has sometimes also been a place of rest and refuge for us ourselves.

Since, therefore, by the grace of almighty God, although unworthy, we hold the governance of the apostolic see, we have judged that such benefits of divine grace and services of your devotion should be met and answered by the liberality of the judgment of the Roman Church. Accordingly, out of reverence for Saint Mary, ever-glorious and Virgin Mother of God, and for blessed Matthew, apostle, evangelist, and martyr; out of devotion to our most reverend father and predecessor Gregory; also at the petition both of yourself and of our dearest son Duke Roger, who has always faithfully obeyed the apostolic see; and instructed by the records of the ancient privileges of your Church, we grant to you and henceforth to your successors, by the liberality of the apostolic see, primacy over the Churches of Cosenza and Acerenza and their suffragans.

These Churches, or rather the cities whose privileges belong to your Church, were formerly subject to your metropolitan Church by concession of the apostolic see. Yet, for reasons unknown to us, they have in past times obtained from the apostolic see both the dignity of the pallium and the authority of privileges.

But because we wish the enactments of our predecessors to remain unshaken and undefiled, we preserve for them the grace of their proper dignity, so that they may enjoy archiepiscopal honor and title. We restore to your Church the integrity of its privileges in the following manner: whatever reverence or subjection the decrees of the sacred canons establish as due to primates shall henceforth be rendered to you and your legitimate successors by the archbishop of Cosenza and the archbishop of Acerenza.

Moreover, from the abundance of fuller grace, we add that, even when a legate of the Roman Church is present in the aforesaid two metropolitan cities, the archbishops shall be elected always with your counsel or that of your successors; the men to be consecrated shall be sent to the apostolic see with your letters or those of your messengers; and they themselves shall likewise be summoned to the election of your successors.

After their consecration, or after receiving the pallium from the apostolic see, they shall promise and render obedience to you and your successors as primate, while in all things preserving the authority of the Roman Church according to canonical enactments, and while the privileges of those cities retain their own force.

It is therefore fitting that you henceforth show greater devotion and obedience to the apostolic see and observe its decrees more effectively, so that, the more highly you are raised above others through it, the more humbly you may submit to it both in the affection of your heart and in the performance of your duties.

You must also regulate your life and conduct with more watchful care, so that, having been chosen as judges of others, you may first judge yourselves more strictly according to the Apostle’s teaching. Preserve the Lord’s commandment spotless and irreproachable, so that, when the Prince of Shepherds appears, you may receive the unfading crown of glory.

May the favor of heaven preserve your fraternity unharmed for many years. But if anyone knowingly attempts rashly to act against this page of our constitution, then, after being warned a second or third time, if he does not correct himself by suitable satisfaction, let him lose the dignity of his power and honor, recognize himself as guilty before the divine judgment of the iniquity committed, and be subject to strict punishment at the final examination.

But for those who preserve these provisions, may the peace and mercy of our Lord Jesus Christ be preserved, so that here they may receive the fruit of good action and, before the strict Judge, find the rewards of eternal peace. Amen, amen, amen.

Saint Peter. Saint Paul. Urban, Pope II.

Given at Salerno through the hand of John, cardinal deacon of the holy Roman Church, on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of August, indiction 6 [variant: 7], in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1099, and in the eleventh year of the pontificate of Lord Urban II.

### CCXLI. Urban confirms the possessions granted to Bruno and Lanuin, hermits, by Count Roger and John, bishop of Squillace. (1098)

[Ughelli, *Sacred Italy*, IX, 427.]

Urban, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons in Christ Bruno and Lanuin, greetings and apostolic blessing.

Since it belongs to our office to provide, insofar as it is possible in the Lord, for the peace and welfare of the servants of God, we mercifully assent to your petitions, dearest and most reverend sons in Christ.

By this page of the apostolic privilege, therefore, we grant by apostolic authority and confirm as firm, stable, and perpetual the donation of the lands given to you in the territory of Squillace, written down, bounded, and marked out by fixed limits by our beloved son R., the count, with the grant and confirmation of our fellow brother John, bishop of Squillace.

Accordingly, by the aforesaid authority we command, establish, and forbid that from this day forward neither the count himself nor any of his heirs may violate or restrict the donation made to you or this our confirmation. Nor may anyone interfere with any of the things we confirm without your consent, so that you may devote yourselves with unencumbered minds to the contemplation of almighty God and, by his favor, be able to reach the sweetness of his face.

But if any person or heir of the count should violate it, unless he comes to fitting satisfaction, we decree that he shall be subject to the peril of his honor or office; separated from Christ and from the body of the Church, he shall be strictly subject to punishment at the eternal judgment, without interruption or remedy.

But for those who piously preserve these provisions, may God and his mercy preserve them in the present and future ages. Amen.

If, however, the lawful count or his heir should wish to add anything to this donation, we establish that it shall be valid under this our confirmation.

Urban, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, Cardinal Rainerius, have subscribed. I, Cardinal John, have subscribed. I, Alphano, archbishop of Salerno, have subscribed. I, Amatus, chaplain and priest, have subscribed. I, Dis, chaplain, have subscribed. I, Constantine, bishop of Catanzaro, have subscribed.

Given at Salerno in the month of September, indiction 6, in the year from the Lord’s Incarnation 1098.

### CCXLII. Urban confirms to Gerland, consecrated bishop, the boundaries of the restored Church of Agrigento. (1098)

[Mansi, *Councils*, XX, 951.]

[Col. 0510A]

Urban, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved brother Gerland, bishop of Agrigento, and to his canonically appointed successors forever.

By the disposition of almighty God, times are changed and kingdoms transferred. Hence we sometimes read that nations of great renown have been ruined and brought low, while insignificant and small ones have been exalted. Hence in some regions the ferocity of pagans has seized the power of the Christian name, while in others the dignity of Christian power has trampled down pagan tyranny.

Thus in our own times, through the strength of the most glorious rulers Duke Robert and Count Roger, the mercy of the supreme Majesty has conquered every Saracen assault on the island of Sicily and restored the ancient state of the holy Church according to his good pleasure.

We therefore give thanks for his ineffable mercy, implore his grace upon those distinguished brothers—one already dead, the other preserved alive by his action—and, as our office requires, hasten toward the restoration and ordering of the churches on that island.

Just as, with God’s assent, we have already arranged the other parishes, so by the authority of this present decree we arrange the diocese of Agrigento. We establish, dearest brother Gerland, whom almighty God has deigned to consecrate in that very Church through the hands of blessed Peter, that henceforth and forever whatever is contained within the boundaries written below shall remain under your episcopal right and that of your legitimate successors, to be governed and administered:

namely, from the place where the river rises below Corleone to the rock above Zinet; from there it extends along the boundaries of Jatina and Cefalà, and then to the boundaries of Vicari; from there as far as the Salt River, which is the boundary between Palermo and Termini; and from the mouth of that river, where it falls into the sea, this parish extends along the sea as far as the Tortus River.

From there, from the place where it rises, it extends to Pyra below the Rock of Elia, and thence to the high mountain above Pyra; from there to the Salt River, where it joins the River of the Rock of Elia; and from this river, following its descent, to Lympiadum, the place that divides Agrigento and Butera; and thence along the coast to the River Bilichi, which is the boundary of Mazara; and it continues still as that river runs to below Corleone, where the boundary begins, excepting Vicari, Corleone, and Termini.

As property, the estate of Cathal with one hundred villagers shall be preserved under the right of you and your successors, just as it was handed over by our aforesaid son Count Roger.

Moreover, whatever the same Church of Agrigento may hereafter justly and canonically acquire through the generosity of rulers or the offerings of the faithful shall remain secure and inviolate for you and your successors.

We therefore decree that absolutely no person shall be permitted rashly to disturb that Church, take away its possessions, retain what has been taken away, diminish them, or weary them with reckless vexations. Rather, everything shall be preserved intact for the uses of you, the canons, all the clergy, and the poor.

If any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowingly attempting to violate this page of our constitution, should act against it, then, after being warned a second or third time, if he does not correct himself by suitable satisfaction, let him lose the dignity of his power and honor, recognize himself as guilty before the divine judgment of the iniquity committed, be separated from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord and Redeemer Jesus Christ, and be subject to strict punishment at the final examination.

But for all who preserve justice toward that Church, may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that here they may receive the fruit of good action and, in the place of judgment, find the rewards of eternal peace. Amen, amen, amen.

Given at Bari through the hands of John, cardinal deacon of the holy Roman Church, on the sixth day before the Ides of October, indiction 8, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1099, and in the eleventh year of the pontificate of Pope Urban II.

### CCXLIII. Letter of Urban II to the brothers of Saint Hubert of Andage. (1098)

[Martène, *Most Extensive Collection*, IV, 1013.]

Urban, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the Catholic brothers of the Ardennes monastery of Saint Hubert, greetings and apostolic blessing.

We have heard—and cannot hear without grief—that through the violence of Otbert, the false bishop, our venerable son Theoderic, your abbot, has been expelled from your monastery for the sake of the Catholic faith, and that Wired, a false monk, has been imposed over you through that same Otbert’s violence. Know that this displeases us utterly. Therefore, greeting you by this present letter, we exhort you to preserve the steadfastness of your faith, and we grant you permission that, if you cannot live in your monastery according to the rule of blessed Benedict and apostolic truth, you may withdraw to whatever religious monastery you wish, until almighty God looks upon your place and restores it to its former condition according to his good pleasure. We notify you by this present writing that Wired, the invader of your monastery, together with all his subjects, is excommunicated by the holy Roman Church for as long as he does not desist from invading that monastery.

### CCXLIV. Letter of Urban II to the people of Liège on behalf of Abbot Theoderic. (Year 1098.)

[MARTEN., as cited above.]

**URBAN**, bishop, servant of the servants of God, sends greetings and the apostolic blessing to all Catholics among the clergy and people of Liège.

We grieve deeply on your behalf, dearly beloved sons in Christ, [Col. 0512A] because for so long the darkness of error has covered your Church and alienated it from the truth of the apostolic see. Therefore, as sons of my own heart, we correct you with paternal affection, admonishing and beseeching you to raise the eyes of your minds toward the light of pure truth. Remove the evil from among yourselves: I mean that wolf and thief who did not enter through the door for your salvation, but climbed in by another way, in order to slaughter, eat, and destroy.

Either, then, drive from among you—if this can in any way be done—the invader and occupier of the Church, namely Obert, the accomplice of Henry and Guibert; or withdraw your obedience and fellowship from him as one alienated from the holy Roman Church and excommunicated. We issue the same command concerning Wired, the false abbot, who [Col. 0512B] through the violence of that same false bishop occupied the Ardennes monastery of Saint Hubert. If anyone thereafter presumes to associate with them, until they abandon the oppression of the churches upon which they have encamped and make satisfaction to God and the apostolic see, let them know that they are bound by the chain of the same excommunication.

Let it be known to you and to everyone else that we have granted the religious Abbot Theoderic permission to absolve from the bond of excommunication those converts from the schismatics who take refuge with him.

Given at . . . .

### CCXLV. Rescript of Urban II on behalf of the monastery of Monte Cassino.

**URBAN**, bishop, servant of the servants of God, sends greetings [Col. 0512C] and the apostolic blessing to his dearest son Anso, lord of Benevento.

When we recently departed from you, you know with what affection we left you behind. We wish both to remain toward you in that same affection and benevolence, and for you to remain toward us in the same way, since we shall strive to preserve and increase your honor if you, for your part, take care to persevere in fidelity and love toward the apostle blessed Peter and toward us.

We do not think that you yourself are unaware how often, and for how long now, the monks of Monte Cassino have complained concerning the monastery of Saint Sophia. Recently, at the council of Bari, when they had been prepared to establish their rights by the writings and records of their church, the abbot of Saint Sophia, taking advantage of your involvement, evaded the proceedings of the case. When we also came to Benevento, in the very house of blessed Sophia, you heard how greatly the brothers themselves complained. You remember what we said to you about this matter; at that time you answered us according to your own pleasure.

We do not wish to endure any longer that the monastery of Monte Cassino should continue to suffer injury concerning the things that appear to belong to it. For that place, by the grace of God and through the merits of blessed Benedict, is useful and necessary not only to us, who are nearby, but also to all Italy. It would greatly become us if, were it possible, we were to devote that place even from our own resources, rather than allow it, with justice favoring it, not to receive what belongs to it.

Therefore, as our dearest and faithful son, we command you to render justice on our behalf to our venerable brother, the abbot of Monte Cassino, and to his brothers concerning the monastery of Saint Sophia. But if they excuse themselves from bringing the case before you as though before a secular authority, compel them to come into our presence. Beforehand, however, inform us at what appointed time they must appear before us for this case, so that we may likewise notify the abbot of Monte Cassino.

Moreover, whatever we decide thereafter, it will be your responsibility to carry out, even if they resist. Otherwise, we shall no longer be able to endure the injury done to our authority without fulfilling against the contumacious what belongs to our office and restoring to the abbot of Monte Cassino the things that are his. We believe that, so far as appears, he possesses full justice in this matter.

Given at Ciperano, on the third day before the Nones of November.

### CCXLVI. Bull of Pope Urban II on behalf of the monastery of Saint Cucuphas. (Year 1098.)

[MARCA, *Marca Hispanica*, Appendix, p. 1203.]

[Col. 0513B]

**URBAN**, bishop, servant of the servants of God, forever, to his beloved son Berengar, abbot of the monastery of Saint Cucuphas, called Octoviense, and to his successors regularly appointed in his place.

A pious petition should be completed by the support of its fulfillment, so that the sincerity of devotion may shine forth commendably and the benefit requested may undoubtedly acquire strength. Since, therefore, your devotion, taking refuge in the harbor of the apostolic see, has sought its protection with due devotion, we mercifully assent to your supplication. [Col. 0513C]

Accordingly, we decree that the venerable monastery of blessed Cucuphas, over which, by the Lord’s ordering, you are recognized as presiding as abbot, shall remain forever under the special protection of the apostolic see, according to the model of our venerable predecessors. We confirm to you and to your legitimate successors, to possess, govern, and administer, both that monastery itself and everything belonging to it: namely, the allod situated within the enclosure of the monastery itself, together with the churches of Saint Peter and Saint Severus, with all their boundaries and appurtenances, as contained in the privileges of our predecessors; the monastery of Saint Cecilia of Montserrat, with its boundaries, possessions, and appurtenances; the church of Saint Lawrence, together with the church of Saint Stephen [Col. 0513D] and the castle, with their boundaries, adjacent lands, possessions, and appurtenances; the church of Saint Paul outside the walls of Barcelona, together with the allod which Girbert and his wife offered there, and with everything that it now possesses or may acquire in the future; the church of Saint Mary of Font-Rubia, together with the allod which Gerald Mironis offered to you; the church of Saint Peter of Clariana; the church of Saint Vincent of Aqua-Obba; the church of Saint Mary and Saint Stephen of Palatium; the church of Saint Cucuphas of Rifano; the church of Saint Stephen of Ripoll; the church of Saint Acisclus of Villa Auziri; the church of Saint Martin and Saint Romanus of Montgat; the church of Saint Felix of Castellari; the church of Saint Sebastian of [Col. 0514A] Montmajor, together with the mountain itself; the church of Saint Mary of Toldelo; the church of Saint Felix of the Villa of Milanos; the church of Saint Mary and Saint Peter called Felix Castle; the church of Saint Mary and Saint John called Monasteriolum; the church of the Holy Cross and Saint Sylvester of Vallerana; the church of Saint Cucuphas of Moia; and another church of Saint Cucuphas of Garriga; the church of Saint Benedict of Spiseles; the church of Saint Stephen of Castellet; the church of Saint Julian of Santa Oliva, together with the castle; the church of Saint Saviour of Bacta, with its possessions and appurtenances; the church of Saint Peter and the Holy Cross of Mosquefa; the church of Saint Mary of Capellades; the church of Saint Felix of Castro Odilone; the church of Saint [Col. 0514B] Mary of the Castle of Clariana, together with the castle itself; the church of Saint Mary of Aqualata; the church of Saint Peter of Viri; the castle of Saint Vincent, together with the church itself; the castle of Albiniana, together with its church; the churches of the Holy Sepulchre and Saint Mary of Amposta, with all their possessions and appurtenances; the churches of Saint Martin, Saint Felix, and Saint Genesius, which belong to the court of Faio; the church of Saint Genesius and Saint Eulalia, called Tapioles; the allod within the walls of the city of Barcelona, namely, with houses, courtyards, gardens, and garden plots, or whatever the aforesaid monastery appears to possess within the territory of that city; the allod within the boundaries of the castles of Font-Rubia, Montacuto, and [Col. 0514C] Piniana, and of Carolo, and of the castle of Virli; the allod of Olorda, together with the tower itself; and the allod situated at Duodecimo or Misano; the allod which it possesses within the boundaries of Terrassa and Castellaro, and at Arraona, Barbarano, the palace of Ausit, and the palace of Palatano; in the village of Mogoda and of Moleto; in the palace of Aries; in upper and lower Lisiano; in the parish of Parietes; and of Gallegos, Plegarnanis, and Petiaco, which they call Bellum Ditinum; and of Bitilona, Palumbare, Otto, Ripoll, the valley of Ariolfo, Grannularios, Lerona, Moserata, Samatus, Canovas, and upper and lower Corrone; the allod of Turres Beses, together with another which Nelma, a woman, offered there; the allod of Ausona; the allod [Col. 0514D] of Storria; and all the allods which it has and ought to have in the aforesaid counties of Barcelona, Girona, Ausona, and in the county of Manresa, with all their boundaries; the church of Saint Quiricus, with its tithes, first fruits, and offerings.

We also decree that the tithes which, whether from these or from other places, your monastery possessed more than thirty years ago by concession of our predecessors, shall be preserved forever entirely free and intact for your use. Moreover, by the terms of this present privilege, we establish by apostolic authority that whatever goods or possessions your monastery now justly possesses, or may hereafter justly and canonically obtain through the concession of pontiffs, the generosity of princes, or the offerings of the faithful, shall remain firm and inviolate for you and your successors. [Col. 0515A]

We therefore decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb that Church, take away its possessions, retain things offered to it, claim for his own use things rightly given to it, diminish them, or harass them with presumptuous vexations. Rather, everything shall be preserved intact and shall in every way serve the use of those for whose support and administration it was granted.

We also decree that burial at that place shall be entirely free, so that no one may obstruct the devotion and final wish of those who have decided to be buried there, unless they happen to be excommunicated. Upon your death, or that of any of your successors as abbot of that place, no one shall be placed over it through any trickery of deception or violence, except one whom the brothers by common consent, or the wiser portion of the brothers’ council, shall elect according to the fear of God and the rule of blessed Benedict. The one elected shall be consecrated by the diocesan bishop, provided that he possesses the favor and communion of the apostolic see and is willing to perform this freely and without corruption. Otherwise, he shall have recourse to the Roman pontiff, or be consecrated by whatever other Catholic bishop he prefers.
