We establish the same concerning the ordinations of the brothers, chrism, and the consecration of altars or basilicas. As a sign of the liberty granted by the Roman Church, you shall pay one morabitin each year to the Lateran palace for the church of Saint Paul.

If any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowingly, should presume rashly to act against this page of our constitution, then, after being warned a second or third time, if he does not correct himself by suitable satisfaction, let him lose the dignity of his power and honor, acknowledge himself guilty before the divine judgment of the iniquity committed, be separated from the most sacred body and blood of God and our Lord and Redeemer Jesus Christ, and be subject to severe punishment at the final judgment. But let the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with all who preserve what is just toward that place, so that here they may receive the fruit of good action and find, before the strict Judge, the rewards of eternal peace.

Written by the hand of Gerard, regional notary and scrivener of the holy Roman Church, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1098, in the seventh indiction, on the first day of December. [Col. 0515D]

### CCXLVII. Bull of Urban II on behalf of the monastery of Monte Cassino. (Year 1098.)

[MABILLON, *Annales Benedictini*, V, 665.]

**URBAN**, bishop, servant of the servants of God, sends greetings and the apostolic blessing to his beloved sons, the monks of the monastery of Monte Cassino.

We are compelled by the duty and authority of our office to provide, insofar as the Lord grants us knowledge and ability, for the salvation and peace of the Churches—especially for your monastery, which has always adhered more familiarly and devotedly to our holy apostolic see and has shown itself readier and more generous whenever persecution has arisen. [Col. 0516A]

Therefore, at the request of our venerable brother Oderisius, your abbot, we have considered it appropriate to record in a future letter how the case of the cell of Cingoli, by which your monastery has long been troubled, was recently determined in our hearing by our judgment.

You know this matter more fully: the same case was often discussed in the Roman Church, during synodal proceedings, before our predecessors, by Desiderius of holy memory—Pope Victor III, cardinal priest of the apostolic see and abbot of Monte Cassino—who afterward, by divine favor, reached the summit of the pontificate but survived for only a short time.

In our own time also, during synodal proceedings, our fellow brother whom we named above, Oderisius, cardinal priest of our holy Church, repeatedly brought a complaint concerning this case before our presence. It happened that Count Robert, having turned more readily toward devotion to blessed Benedict, recognized that the place itself belonged by right to your monastery, and immediately returned that same place into the hands of our aforesaid brother Oderisius. At that time the abbess, who had entered the cell by force, had withdrawn out of fear of that count.

Meanwhile, while we were in the city, she began to appeal to the ears of our authority with repeated outcries. We therefore sent capable men from our own side as far as Capua, so that they might carefully investigate both sides of the case and settle it peacefully; but at that time, for various reasons, they could not bring it to completion. [Col. 0516C]

After some time, having left the city for ecclesiastical affairs—[Note: [Col. 0515] When he came into these parts several months earlier, at which time Capua was being besieged by Roger.]—and while we were examining the same case more carefully in the presence of both parties, we learned that our aforesaid venerable brother Oderisius, your abbot, had taken possession of that place not with malicious intent but out of regard for justice, as though it were his own property, concerning which he had often lodged a complaint.

Indeed, by pontifical decrees, royal documents, the writings of the rulers of the land, and the charter of the place’s founder, the cell was shown to belong to your monastery. Nevertheless, because he had taken possession of it without a prior judgment, it seemed equitable to us that the abbess who complained that she had been dispossessed should be reinstated; after our return, however, a lawful judgment should be conducted between both parties.

In those days, by the Lord’s favor, we were preparing to celebrate a plenary council in the city of Bari. After six months, therefore, we summoned that abbess by letter and by an invitation from our own mouth. She refused to come, but sent a messenger. Since she had given before the council no fully adequate or sufficiently reasonable grounds for her absence, we postponed the proceedings in this case until our return, lest she should complain that she had suffered some burden from us.

When we came to Benevento, we again sent her our letters, specifying the day and place at which [Col. 0517A] the case would be heard. Since she did not come then either, we summoned her a third time to another place. She came, but refused to undertake the case, asserting that she had by no means received all the documents and letters concerning the cell of Cingoli. Some of our brothers had been prepared to affirm under oath that they had found no more documents, nor any others, in that place than those they had returned.

Privately, she revealed her documents to some of the brothers who were with us, but refused to show them to us. Since she neither wished nor was able to conduct the case according to judicial procedure, we admonished her to seek agreement with the abbot and your brothers. She did not accept the admonition and completely evaded judgment.

Again we examined the documents of your monastery; again we inspected the privileges of the Roman pontiffs and the writings of the emperors; again we heard the charter of the place’s founder and the concession of the Beneventan ruler who held office at that time. Instructed by all these materials, we became convinced that the cell of Cingoli had belonged to the monastery of Monte Cassino from the very beginning of its foundation, and that a community of nuns had been established there by the will of the abbot of Monte Cassino.

Thus, after many delays, once the truth of the case had at last been ascertained, and after consultation with our brother bishops, the cardinals of the Roman Church, and the judges, we restored the monastery of Cingoli in its entirety to our venerable brother Oderisius, your abbot. We did so, however, on the condition that the nuns should not be expelled from the place, but that a congregation of maidens dedicated to God should always remain there, entrusted, as we hope, to the more religious care of a holier patron and monastery, with the reverence due to the apostolic see preserved in all things. [Col. 0517C]

We decree—indeed, we order—that this restoration, by the present letter, remain forever confirmed and inviolate. If anyone thereafter, having learned the substance of this proceeding, should rashly attempt to oppose our constitution, he shall be punished by the vengeance of apostolic indignation. But whoever proves himself its preserver shall enjoy the grace of divine blessing.

Written by the hand of Peter, our scrivener of the sacred palace, in the seventh indiction, on the seventh day of December.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, by the hand of John, cardinal deacon of the holy Roman Church, on the sixth day before the Ides of December, in the seventh indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1098, and in the eleventh year of the pontificate of the lord Pope Urban II. [Col. 0517D]

### CCXLVIII. Letter of Urban II to Manasses, archbishop of Reims. (Year 1098.)

[BALUZE, *Miscellanea*, Lucca edition, II, 144.]

**URBAN**, bishop, servant of the servants of God, sends greetings and the apostolic blessing to his most reverend brother and fellow bishop, Manasses, archbishop of Reims.

Although we do not doubt that the letters of the clerics of Noyon concerning the union of the Church of Tournai are partly false—for we had confirmed the unity of those Churches only during the lifetime of our venerable brother Rabbodus, and had decreed that only the authentic privileges of Noyon should remain valid—we have nevertheless decided that, for the present, nothing should be either changed or established concerning this matter.

We are sending back to your fraternity our brother Baldwin, the elected bishop of Noyon, whom you sent to us. Take care, with the diligence due to God and to the salvation of your soul and his, to provide appropriately for him and for the Church in which he was elected. Farewell.

### CCXLIX. Bull on behalf of the abbot of the Greater Monastery of Tours. (Around the year 1098.)

[BALUZE, *Miscellanea*, Lucca edition, II, 181.]

[Col. 0518B] **URBAN**, bishop, servant of the servants of God, sends greetings and the apostolic blessing to his venerable son Bernard, abbot of the Greater Monastery.

Among good men humility must be preserved in such a way that the authority of truth and justice is not abandoned. Accordingly, we receive your humility while upholding truth and justice. By the grace of almighty God, we regard you as Catholic and truly religious. If, however, at the beginning of your ordination you committed any fault, either through the fault of the one who ordained you or through your own negligence, we forgive you in the place and by the authority of blessed Peter, trusting in the merits of blessed Martin.

We impose this penance upon you: from now on, do not cease to attend more watchfully and fervently to the salvation of the brothers entrusted to you. In this matter, we remove from everyone any occasion for speaking against you and command perpetual silence.

By the authority of this present letter, we command all the brothers of your monastery to render you the reverence and obedience due to you with the fullest devotion, so that, with God’s consent, they may rejoice in the grace of your care and you likewise in their obedience.

### CCL. Letter of Urban II to the bishop of Magdeburg.—He exhorts him not to waver but to stand firm in a just cause. (Between 1098 and 1099.)

[MANSI, *Concilia*, XX, 711.]

**URBAN**, bishop, servant of the servants of God, sends greetings and the apostolic blessing to N., bishop of Magdeburg.

[Col. 0518D] We marvel at the remarkable vigor of your character, beloved brother in Christ; indeed, we fear somewhat for the inward affections of your piety, lest the persuasion of an approaching error may already have sprouted within your heart, which God forbid. For, through faithful religious persons of both sexes, we have several times sent our letters to your fidelity, as we hope, and you have given us no response—or an extremely rare one—such as befits a man so distinguished and vigorous.

Therefore, beware—beware, I beg you, meanwhile—that your neck be subjected to Pharaoh. When he falls, the ancient controversy—which, because our sins demanded it, had for a great span of time wearied the Church of God through the various regions of the world almost to its innermost marrow—will be ended; yet, with the inward man of a few preserved, Baal is gradually confounded and the fraudulent merchant of the holy bishop’s gifts is swallowed up by the world. [Col. 0519A]

You, therefore, who have received your eminence from God and also from men, must uphold what you promised to the teacher of the apostles, whose place you have assumed, and to his successors. If you are able to persevere, you will be safe. For no one who puts his hand to the plow and looks back, making a crooked furrow, is fit for the kingdom of God; and whoever touches pitch will be defiled by it.

There are other matters which should not be entrusted to a little sheet of paper; by God’s arrangement, the present legate will disclose them to you privately in words of gold. We ask that you send your reply honorably as soon as you can.

May the glorious God watch over your mind and provide for your actions.

### CCLI. Urban II appoints Hartmann, abbot of Göttweig, as assistant to Gebhard, bishop of Constance, in the apostolic legation. (Between 1088 and 1099.)

[See *Acta Sanctorum*, August, vol. II, p. 376, in the *Life of Altmann, bishop of Passau*.]

[Col. 0519B]

### CCLII. Urban II confirms the privileges of the monastery of Göttweig at the request of Abbot Hartmann. (Between 1088 and 1099.)

[See *Acta Sanctorum*, as cited above.]

### CCLIII. Privilege of immunity granted to the monastery of Schaffhausen at Hirsau. (Between 1088 and 1099.)

[MANSI, *Concilia*, XX, 706.]

[Col. 0519C]

**URBAN**, bishop, servant of the servants of God, forever, to his beloved son in Christ, the abbot of Schaffhausen, and to his successors regularly appointed in his place.

Although we are debtors to all the sons of the holy Church through the authority and benevolence of the apostolic see, we ought nevertheless to devote ourselves with a more generous zeal of charity to those places and persons which adhere more specially and familiarly to the Roman Church and which stand out through the excellence of their religious observance.

Therefore, assenting both to the pious wishes and petitions of you and your brothers and to those of the religious count N., we receive under the perpetual jurisdiction and protection of the apostolic see the venerable monastery of Saint Saviour, built by the former Count N. near the village H., under the honor of all the saints, and offered to blessed Peter, just as it is known to have been received by our predecessor Gregory VII of pious memory.

Whatever immunity that pontiff conferred upon the place itself, we likewise grant and confirm by this present decree. Accordingly, by apostolic authority we establish that everything which the aforesaid counts or any other faithful persons have contributed to your monastery from their resources, and whatever it now possesses or may hereafter justly and canonically obtain through the concession of pontiffs, the generosity of princes, or the offerings of the faithful, shall remain firm and inviolate for you and your successors.

Concerning the cells of Saint Agnes and Saint Mary in the village N., we expressly forbid anyone, for any reason, to dare to withdraw or alienate them from the ownership of the aforesaid monastery. Rather, they shall always remain in the order [Col. 0520A] in which they were established by you, dearest son N. Neither you nor any of your successors may dispose of them or rashly or violently diminish or remove their goods. If anyone has hitherto taken away any of their property, let him remain alienated from the grace of almighty God until he restores it.

Moreover, by a decree to remain permanently in force, we establish that no living person whatsoever may claim in your monastery any property right, personal status, hereditary right, advocacy, investiture, or any other power that might harm the liberty and peace of the brothers.

The abbot, together with the brothers, shall appoint as their advocate the person whom they judge most useful. If he later proves useless to the monastery, they shall remove him and appoint another in his place.

We have decreed that burial at that place shall be entirely free, so that no one may obstruct the devotion and final wish of those who have decided to be buried there, unless they happen to be excommunicated.

If, with the Lord’s consent, you are able to recover from laymen any tithes belonging to the churches which you possess or will possess, we decree that they shall be permanently assigned to your use, without contradiction from any bishop, while preserving episcopal reverence.

Let no bishop or provost’s opposition prevent you from receiving laymen or secular clerics into religious conversion. We further add that no bishop shall have the power, without the permission of the Roman pontiff, to subject your places or monks to an interdict or excommunication.

Moreover, no person may rashly disturb the aforesaid monastery, take away its possessions or other goods, retain what has been taken, diminish it, or harass it with presumptuous vexations. Rather, everything shall be preserved intact and shall in every way serve the use of those for whose support and administration it was granted, so that the brothers serving God there may, through the generosity of Rome, enjoy freedom from every power and, removed from secular tumult, be able to devote themselves more freely to the contemplation of almighty God.

Upon your death, or that of any of your successors as abbot of that place, no one shall be placed over it through any trickery of deception or violence, except one whom the brothers by common consent, or the wiser portion of the brothers’ council, shall elect according to the rule of blessed Benedict.

You shall receive the consecrations [Col. 0520D] of altars and basilicas, the ordinations of clerics, chrism, and the other matters belonging to episcopal office from the bishop of Constance, in whose diocese you are situated, provided that he is Catholic and possesses the favor and communion of the apostolic see. Otherwise, you shall be permitted to approach whatever Catholic bishop you wish and receive from him the sacraments of consecration, or have recourse to the apostolic see, which, supported by apostolic authority, may grant what is requested.

As a sign of the liberty received from the Roman Church, you shall pay one ounce of gold each year to the Lateran palace.

If any ecclesiastical or secular person thereafter, knowingly, should rashly attempt to act against this page of privilege, [Col. 0521A] then, after being warned a second or third time, if he does not correct himself by suitable satisfaction, let him lose the dignity of his power or honor, acknowledge himself guilty before the divine judgment of the iniquity committed, be separated from the most holy body and blood of God and our Redeemer Jesus Christ, and be subject to severe punishment at the final judgment.

But let the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with all who preserve what is just toward that place, so that here they may receive the fruit of good action and find, before the strict Judge, the rewards of eternal peace.

### CCLIV. Letter of Urban II to Count Rudolf.—On ecclesiastical immunity. (Between 1088 and 1099.)

[MANSI, *Concilia*, XX, 659.]

[Col. 0521B]

We wish you to know that no secular lord may exercise authority over clerics; rather, all clerics must be subject solely to the bishop. Whoever presumes otherwise will without doubt be subject to canonical judgment.

### CCLV. Letter of Urban II to Hugh, archbishop of Lyon. (Between 1088 and 1099.)

[MANSI, *Concilia*, XX, 677.]

**URBAN II TO HUGH**, archbishop of Lyon.

Your religious prudence may receive, with the honor of their orders, the clerics of the diocese of Lyon whom, as you have shown by the report of your letters, bishops of another diocese ordained contrary to the statutes of the canons, provided that it is established that they were otherwise canonically ordained and without any serious impediment, and provided that you judge their commendable life to have merited this indulgence.

For we read that the holy bishop Epiphanius ordained certain clerics from the diocese of Saint John Chrysostom; the holy man would certainly not have done this if he had perceived that they would suffer harm from it. Therefore, those whom your moderation judges should be received, after imposing a suitable penance as an act of satisfaction on behalf of the Church which they offended, receive each one in his own honor, out of consideration for mercy, while preserving in all things the discipline of the holy canons.

### CCLVI. Letter of Urban II to the bishops of Embrun, Gap, and Die.—Before they are reconciled, no one is compelled to remain faithful to the excommunicated. (Fragment.—Between 1088 and 1099.)

[GRATIAN, *Decretum*, C. XV, q. 6, c. 5.]

[Col. 0521D]

Forbid the soldiers who have sworn allegiance to Count Hugh to serve him while he remains excommunicated. If they plead their oaths, they should be warned that they ought to serve God rather than human beings. For no authority compels them to render the allegiance which they swore to a Christian ruler who opposes God and his saints and tramples upon their commands.

### CCLVII. Letter of Urban II to Hugh, bishop of Grenoble.—Unusual pollution in the natural acts does not impede marriage. (Fragment.—Between 1088 and 1099.)

[GRATIAN, *Decretum*, C. XXXV, q. 2, c. 11.]

[Col. 0522A]

Unusual pollution, occurring only in natural acts or repeatedly apart from marital affection, does not appear to impede marriage, provided that it has been established, on oaths tendered, to be as you reported to us in your letters, although the act itself is criminal and damnable.

### CCLVIII. Letter of Pope Urban II to Hugh, abbot of Cluny.—He grants him the monastery of Saint Bertin to be organized according to Cluniac customs. (Between 1088 and 1099.)

[D. BOUQUET, *Recueil*, vol. XIV, p. 737.]

[Col. 0522B]

**URBAN**, bishop, servant of the servants of God, sends greetings and the apostolic blessing to his venerable brother Hugh, abbot of Cluny.

Our ministry ought not to be lacking to just requests. For this reason, we have decided that the petitions which the countess of Flanders sent at the suggestion of the abbot of Saint Bertin should be admitted.

She requested that we entrust the monastery of Saint Bertin to your care and that of your successors, to be administered and governed. We have mercifully assented, since we, who by the office entrusted to us must provide for the salvation of all, are obliged to do so.

Therefore, by the authority of this present letter, we admonish your fraternity to receive that monastery henceforth under your care, and we freely permit you and your successors to remove the abbot if he should prove unsuitable for monastic discipline, while preserving the right of the diocesan bishop—namely, so that he may not be able to oppose your correction of the monastery.

[Note: [Col. 0521D] Clementia, who had previously called the Cluniacs to organize the Sithiu monastery of Saint Bertin, applied her strength and determination in the year 1112 to expel them from it. On this matter, Iperius should be read in Martene, vol. III of the *Anecdota*, col. 608.]

### CCLIX. Privilege of Pope Urban II granted at Rome to Rainer, abbot of the monastery of Saint Peter of Crispinium. (Between 1088 and 1099.)

[*Gallia Christiana*, vol. III, Instruments, p. 26.]

**URBAN**, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his dearest son Rainer, abbot of the monastery of Saint Peter, situated in the village called Crispinium on the river Hon, in the district of Hainaut.

[Col. 0522D] Therefore, dearest son in Christ, acceding to your just requests, by the text of this present privilege we confirm to you and to your legitimate successors the governance and administration of the monastery of Saint Peter, in which the blessed confessor of Christ, Landelinus, rests, situated in the village called Crispinium, on the River Hon, in the pagus of Hainaut. We likewise decree that the adjacent village named above, Novo Fossato, with all its possessions in meadows, cultivated or uncultivated fields, waters and watercourses, and the forest called Ambligis, just as they were restored to the blessed Landelinus by Count Baldwin, of good memory, and by his mother Richilde, and confirmed by the venerable Gerard, bishop of Cambrai, shall remain in perpetual possession of the aforesaid monastery of Saint Peter, wholly intact and free from every exaction.

Moreover, by apostolic authority we decree that whatever the same monastery justly possesses today, or may hereafter justly and canonically acquire through the concession of pontiffs, the generosity of princes, or the offering of the faithful, shall remain firm and inviolate for you and your successors, without prejudice to the canonical reverence due to the bishop of Cambrai. We decree, therefore, that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the same monastery, or take away, diminish, or harass with reckless vexations the possessions subject to it; rather, they shall be preserved wholly intact, so that they may in every way serve the needs of those for whose support and administration they were granted.

Indeed, if in the future any archbishop or bishop, emperor or king, prince or duke, count or viscount, judge, or any person, great or small, powerful or powerless, knowingly attempts to act against this text of our privilege, and, after being warned a second or third time, does not make amends with suitable satisfaction, we separate him from the body of the Church of Christ by the authority of apostolic power. But for those who preserve these provisions, may peace from God and mercy be preserved throughout the present and future ages. Amen.

### CCLX. Urban II receives the Generense monastery in Gascony into the right and ownership of the Apostolic See and secures it by a privilege, subject to an annual census of two ounces of gold. (Between 1088 and 1099.)

[Centii Camerarii *Liber censualis*, in MURATORI, *Antiquitates Italicae*, V, 885.]

[Col. 0523C]

### CCLXI. Privilege of Pope Urban II for the monastery of Lagny. (Between 1088 and 1099.)

[MABILLON and RUINART, *Ouvrages posthumes*, III, 401.]

URBAN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son ARNULPH, abbot of Lagny, and to his successors who shall be regularly promoted, forever.

A devout request ought to be brought to completion by a favorable outcome, so that the sincerity of devotion may shine forth laudably and the benefit requested may assuredly gain strength. Since, therefore, your election, taking refuge in the harbor of the Apostolic See, sought its protection with due devotion, we have graciously assented to your petition. We receive under the protection of the Apostolic See the monastery of Saint Peter of Lagny, over which by God’s authority you preside, together with both the village adjacent to it and all other possessions belonging to it.

By the text of this privilege, therefore, we decree by apostolic authority that both the aforesaid village of Lagny and all the other possessions which your monastery possesses today, or may hereafter justly and canonically acquire through the concession of pontiffs, the liberality of princes, or the offering of the faithful, shall remain firm and inviolate for you and your successors. We decree, therefore, that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the same place, or take away its possessions, retain what has been taken away, diminish them, or harass them with reckless vexations; [Col. 0524A] rather, everything shall be preserved intact, so that it may in every way serve the needs of those for whose support and administration it was granted. This is without prejudice to the canonical right of the Church of Paris, but in such a way that neither the bishop nor the archdeacon of that Church may inflict upon the brothers any burden of rash excommunication, enforcement, or customary demand.

When you, the abbot of the same place, die, or any of your successors dies, no one shall be placed over it by any deceitful trickery or violence, unless he is elected by the common consent of the brothers, or by the saner portion of the brothers’ council, according to the fear of God and the Rule of Saint Benedict. The elected man, however, shall be consecrated by the bishop of Paris.

As a token of the liberty received from the Roman Church, you shall pay one ounce of gold each year to the Lateran palace. [Col. 0524B] Therefore, beloved sons in Christ, strive to have the fear and love of God in your hearts, so that, the freer you are from worldly disturbances, the more earnestly you may aspire to please God through every virtue of mind and soul.

Indeed, if in the future any archbishop or bishop, emperor or king, duke, count, viscount, judge, or any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowingly attempts rashly to act against this text of our authority, and, after being warned a second or third time, does not make suitable amends, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and honor; let him acknowledge himself guilty before the divine judgment of the iniquity he has committed; let him be alienated from the most sacred body and blood of God and our Lord Jesus Christ the Redeemer; and at the final judgment let him be subject to strict punishment.

But for all who justly observe these provisions toward the same place, may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that both here they may receive the fruit of good action and, before the strict Judge, find the rewards of eternal peace. Amen.

### CCLXII. Letter of Urban II to Rotger, bishop of Soissons.—That regular canons be instituted in parish churches. (Between 1088 and 1099.)

[MANSI, *Concilia*, XX, 677.]

URBAN, pope, to ROTGER, abbot of Soissons.

It is fitting that we, who, although unworthy, by the Lord’s arrangement seem to have been placed as guardians and heralds of justice upon the lofty watchtower of the chief apostles Peter and Paul, should grant assent to just vows and lend our ears to just requests. Therefore, so that the brothers entrusted to you may be able peacefully to preserve the order of their way of life according to the Rule of Saint Augustine, without disturbance from worldly tumult, with the Lord’s favor we gladly assent to your petition. By the authority of these present letters, we grant that in the parish churches belonging to your monastery you may institute as regular clergy [canons] members of your cloister, who shall both serve those churches religiously and diligently care for the parish of the neighboring people according to the fear of God, without prejudice to the bishop’s right, [Col. 0525A] so that all that belongs to the house of God may be administered by the wise and wisely.

Given on the second day before the Ides of July.

### CCLXIII. Letter of Pope Urban to Bernard, archbishop of Toledo. (Between 1088 and 1099.)

[MANSI, *Concilia*, XX, 701.]

URBAN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved brother and fellow bishop BERNARD of Toledo, greetings and apostolic blessing.

The bearer of these letters came to us and confessed that he had received no order from the rank of exorcist through the priesthood. We were greatly astonished upon hearing this. Since his identity was unknown to us, and he presented himself before us without letters or any evidence, we have sent him back to your diligence, instructing you to investigate his case carefully. If it is established that his report is true, you shall order him to abstain for one year from the priesthood improperly and irregularly received, imposing whatever penance you deem appropriate. After the year has elapsed, if his life and conduct appear suitable, and no other impediment exists to make him worthy of such an honor, you shall restore to him all the orders he did not receive together with the presbyterate, provided that he assumed the presbyterate without payment.

### CCLXIV. Bull of Pope Urban II to Peter, bishop of Jaca. (Between 1088 and 1099.)

[MARTÍNEZ, *Historia de la fundación y antigüedades de San Juan de la Peña*. Zaragoza, 1620, folio, p. 235.]

[Col. 0525C]

URBAN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother PETER, bishop of Jaca, greetings and apostolic blessing.

Since you received the beginnings of monastic religion in a religious cloister, we are greatly surprised that you strongly oppose men of that same religion. Our venerable son, the abbot of Saint John of Peña, complains that you vigorously attack the cemetery of that place and withdraw laymen from it. How wickedly you act in this matter may also be learned from secular laws, which, consonant with holy monasteries, establish that the final wishes of the dying are to be held valid. He also says that you withdraw, by wicked persuasion, men devoted to the monastery. Greatly to be feared concerning these men is that, according to the Apostle’s statement, they may incur condemnation because they have invalidated their first faith.

Therefore, by these present letters we admonish and command your affection not to weary any further with such vexations that place, which is specially contained under the right of blessed Peter, through the persuasion of anyone whatsoever. Do not allow the devoted to be withdrawn from conversion, or the dead from the cemetery. Concerning the loss inflicted upon the monastery on these occasions, we further command that either full justice or a suitable settlement be rendered to the aforesaid abbot. Those who withdrew from the monastery contrary to their vow shall be compelled in every way [Col. 0526A] to return to the monastery and fulfill their vow.

Given, etc.

### CCLXV. Privilege of Pope Urban II for the Church of Jaca. (Between 1088 and 1099.)

[AYNSA, *Fundación, excelencias, grandezas y cosas memorables de Huesca*, p. 539.]

URBAN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to PETER, bishop of Huesca, and to his successors who shall be canonically promoted, forever.

The Roman See, mother of mercy and guardian of justice, has learned from the Lord Jesus Christ—who granted the blessed apostles Peter and Paul the power of binding and loosing—to observe justice and dispense mercy. Therefore, following the text of the constitution of our predecessor, Pope Gregory VII, concerning the boundaries of the bishoprics of Huesca and Jaca, which he himself, by virtue of ancient right and at the petitions of the glorious King Ramiro, granted in the eastern region to his son and our dearest Garsias, bishop of Huesca and Jaca: just as the River Cinca, descending from the Pyrenean mountains, runs through mountain and plain as far as the Valley of the Wolves; within these boundaries he also confirmed to that same predecessor of yours, O Peter, bishop of Huesca, by the assertion of a privilege, the churches of Bielsa, Gistain, Alquézar, and Barbastro.

We too, in the same spirit, confirm by this present authority those same boundaries, together with the aforesaid churches and their boundaries, and with your canons; and all the other churches that exist today between the two rivers, namely the Alcanadre and the Cinca, or that in the future, by God’s mercy, shall be built within the prescribed boundary. Thus the complaint which your archdeacons, Lupus Fortunionis and Lupus Enneconis, made to us concerning the churches that, at the worthy petitions of King Sancho, we had granted from the parish of your see to his chapel of Montearagón—because he had acquired the land by the sword—may thereafter be completely laid to rest.

And because your predecessor, Bishop Garsias, had been violently expelled from the aforesaid church, namely Alquézar, contrary to the sanction of the Roman privilege, may your Church thereafter, through our hand, freely and peacefully possess those churches with their appurtenances, without disturbance from any successors.

In the northern region likewise, under the same terms by which, at the similar insistence of that same King Ramiro, the boundaries assigned above were established, extending as far as the place commonly called Planamayor, there are included the whole land of Pintano and the Valley of Orsella, together with the churches of the castles situated below them, namely those of Us, Sos, Luesia, Biel, Agüero, and Morillo. And we [lacuna] grant the same to the Church of Huesca and Jaca in perpetuity, judging it right that these and all the other possessions which the aforesaid king, on the day when the canonical see was established at Jaca in the presence of nine bishops, freely gave to the bishop and canons for the support of their order—namely, the village of Lierta, Sesave, and the place called Seven Springs, with all their appurtenances, cultivated and uncultivated, and with the tithes of all royal revenues and of all revenues that for whatever reasons may ever be paid to kings at Jaca and throughout Aragon—should thereafter be held inviolate for the service of the canons throughout endless ages.

If in the future any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowingly attempting rashly to act against the tenor of this declaration, does not, after being warned a second or third time, make suitable satisfaction, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and honor [lacuna]; let him acknowledge before the divine judgment the iniquity he has committed, and let him be alienated from the most sacred body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ.

But for all who observe the rights set forth above of the Church of Huesca and Jaca, may there be the peace [Col. 0527B] of our Lord Jesus Christ and eternal life.

### CCLXVI. Urban absolves Petronius, bishop of León, born of an illegitimate mother, from the bond of this sin. (Between 1088 and 1099.)

[GRATIAN, *Decretum* I, distinction 56, chapter 14.]

Since you came simply to the Apostolic See and humbly confessed the sin which seemed to impede the office of your bishopric—namely, that you were born of an illegitimate mother, whom your father is known to have had intercourse with while his lawful wife was living—÷ we, instructed by the grace of apostolic gentleness, recognizing from both your confession and the testimony of the brothers who are with you that you are free from the other crimes that impede the priesthood, and hearing of your religious life, confirm you in the priestly office you have undertaken, absolved from the bond of this sin.

### CCLXVII. Pope Urban II entrusts Countess Matilda with the restoration of the church of Saint Florian, to be carried out by the bishop of Mantua in favor of the monastery of Saint Benedict of Polirone. (Between 1088 and 1099.)

[MARGARINI, *Bullarium Casinense*, II, 118.]

URBAN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the illustrious MATHILDA, the only daughter of blessed Peter, greetings and apostolic blessing.

Our son, the abbot of the monastery of Saint Benedict, has complained concerning a certain church of Saint Florian, founded by your father, B. of blessed memory, on the estate of the same monastery, and later restored by your devotion to that monastery. After that monastery had held it peacefully and had allowed it to be administered without molestation or dispute by its chaplains, who governed it as their own, an exchange was made between the bishop of Mantua and the monastery concerning the monasteries of the bishopric and the churches of the abbey, as your prudence well knows. When that arrangement was later destroyed and both parties received what belonged to them, the bishop retained for himself this one church, about which the complaint is made, and refused to restore it to the monastery.

When that monastery was also transferred by your grant to the Church of Saint Peter, over which, although unworthy, we preside, the abbot’s chaplain governed the people of that land, celebrated baptisms, and, with the permission of the bishops of Mantua, administered there whatever pertains to the care of souls.

Therefore we desire and command that our monastery receive in full what was its own and what it held by right, and that it suffer no diminution whatsoever of the goods it possessed. It is therefore necessary that, in the presence of the bishop of Reggio and other prudent men, you summon the bishop of Mantua and command him to restore to the monastery the things that belonged to it and to allow it peacefully to possess the other things.

### CCLXVIII. Letter of Urban II to the clergy and people of Salerno.—Concerning ecclesiastical immunity. (Between 1088 and 1099.)

[MANSI, *Concilia*, X, 660.]

[Col. 0528B]

URBAN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons, the clergy and people of Salerno, greetings and apostolic blessing.

Know that the priest Lanzone, who invaded the church of Saint Mary through a lay hand, expelling the man who lawfully possessed it, has by our sentence been prohibited from office and benefice. Moreover, all who have obtained churches, ecclesiastical benefices, or chaplaincies through a lay hand without the consent of their bishop, until they make satisfaction to their bishop according to the decrees of the holy canons, we prohibit from office and benefice.

### CCLXIX. Letter of Urban II to Godinus, bishop of Oria.—He orders him to restore to the city of Brindisi the episcopal see once transferred to the city of Oria. (Between 1088 and 1099.)

[UGHELLI, *Italia sacra*, IX, 30.]

[Col. 0528C]

URBAN II, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved brother in Christ GODINUS, bishop of Oria, greetings and apostolic blessing.

Since it has become known to us through the assertion of truthful men who carefully investigated the matter that your cathedra, now located in the municipality of Oria, formerly existed in the city of Brindisi, and that after the city had been deserted it was transferred to the municipality of Oria, while now, through the mercy of the Lord, the city of Brindisi has been restored, we desire and by the authority of this present document decree [Col. 0528D] that the same episcopal cathedra be returned to Brindisi, on the terms promised by our illustrious count and son in Christ, Goffridus, etc.

### CCLXX. Letter of Urban to Vitalis, priest [of Brescia].—Mercy may be shown to Simoniacs in preserving their dignity if their life commends them. (Between 1088 and 1099.)

[GRATIAN, *Decretum*, C. I, question 5, chapter 2.]

We permit those who have bought a church, if they are persons whose life commends them—namely, if they live regularly in canonries or monasteries—to minister in the office of their honor, by mercifully condescending to them, without prejudice, however, to the holy canons.

### CCLXXI. To the same.—Sons or daughters born before or after spiritual co-parenthood may be joined in lawful marriage. (Between 1088 and 1099.)

[GRATIAN, *Decretum*, C. XXX, question 3, chapter 4.]

Regarding the matters about which your affection consults us, this seems to us the answer that should be given: baptism is valid if, in pressing necessity, a woman baptizes a child in the name of the Trinity; and the sons or daughters of spiritual parents, born before or after their spiritual co-parenthood, may lawfully be joined in marriage, except with the person through whom the co-parents became spiritual co-parents.

### CCLXXII. To the same.—A wife should not receive another person’s child at baptism together with her husband. (Between 1088 and 1099.)

[GRATIAN, *Decretum*, C. XXX, question 4, chapter 6.]

[Col. 0529B]

No authority is found to prohibit a wife from receiving a child at baptism together with her husband. But so that the purity of spiritual fatherhood may be preserved free from every stain and disgrace, we decree that it is fitting that the two should by no means presume together to undertake this. Since he committed an abominable crime by marrying two spiritual co-mothers as though they were two sisters, great penance, proportionate to the fault, ought to be imposed upon him.

### CCLXXIII. To Lucius, provost of Saint Juventius.—Concerning the validity of baptism and the other sacraments conferred by criminal priests. (Between 1088 and 1099.)

[MANSI, *Concilia*, XX, 660.]

[Col. 0529C]

URBAN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son LUCIUS, provost of the church of Saint Juventius at Pavia, greetings and apostolic blessing.

The Savior foretold in the Gospel that, toward the end of the age, pseudo-Christs and false prophets would arise and lead many astray, and that his faithful would have many afflictions in the world; yet the gates of hell would not prevail against the Church. Therefore, since, as the Apostle says (1 Corinthians 11), heresies must exist so that those who are approved may become manifest, we must ascend against the adversary with the prophet, set up a wall for the house of Israel, and, with the same Apostle, enter the kingdom of God through many tribulations; for the sufferings of this present time are not worthy of comparison with the future glory that shall be revealed in us.

Since, then, you have made known to us the question put to you—whether selling an ecclesiastical thing is Simoniacal—it is plainly gathered that this is Simoniacal from what the Apostle Peter said to Simon: “Your money be with you for destruction, because you thought that the gift of God could be acquired with money” (Acts 8). The Holy Spirit is the gift of God, and the thing offered to the Church is also the gift of God.

And if you pay close attention, Simon Magus, who approached the faith hypocritically, did not wish to buy the Holy Spirit for the sake of the Holy Spirit itself, of which he was unworthy—for, as it is written, “the Holy Spirit of discipline will flee deceit” (Wisdom 1)—but wished, so far as it lay within him, to buy it in order to multiply through the sale of the signs performed through him the money he had offered. The Apostle did not abhor in Simon the purchase of the Holy Spirit, which he knew could not be made, but rather the ambition for such profit—that is, greed, which is the service of idols—and struck him with the dart of a curse.

Therefore, whoever sells or buys ecclesiastical things, which are gifts of God because they are given by God to the faithful and by the faithful to God, and are received freely from him and therefore ought to be given freely, believes, together with Simon, that the gift of God can be possessed with money. Whoever, therefore, gives or acquires these things not for the purpose for which they were established, but for his own profit, by a gift of speech, an illicit service, or money, is a Simoniac, since Simon’s principal intention was mere greed for money, that is, idolatry, as the Apostle Paul says.

Otherwise, why does the Council of Chalcedon prohibit the procurator or defender of the Church, or anyone subject to the rule, from being appointed through money to such an extent that it anathematizes even those who intervene in so great a crime, unless it judges them to be Simoniacs? If the aforesaid soldiers of the Church are so struck down on account of this crime, no wise person will deny that those who do not serve in the Church’s ranks ought to be struck down much more deservedly for this reason, namely, sale or purchase.

Moreover, our blessed predecessor Paschal [Note: [Col. 0529D] Paschal I.] affirms concerning consecration and the things that proceed from consecration that whoever sells one of them, without which he cannot possess the other, leaves neither one unsold. Accordingly, he understands the one who sells or buys a thing belonging to the Church to be a Simoniac.

By “procurator,” the aforesaid council understands any administrator of ecclesiastical things, for example, a provost, steward, or vice-lord; by “defender,” an advocate or castellan, and a judge; by “one subject to the rule,” an archpriest, archdeacon, canon, monk, or anyone bound to ecclesiastical office.

That the one who sells or buys a provostship or something of this kind sells or buys the Holy Spirit, so far as it lies within him, hear Augustine on John:

> “How many offices (*proposita*) they have made! Primian has one at Carthage, Maximian another, Rogatus another in Mauretania; in Numidia those men and those others, whom we can no longer even name, have others. So does someone go about to buy the dove? Each praises the office (*propositum*) that he sells,” etc.

Behold, venerable Augustine, speaking of the sale of a provostship, understands by the name of the dove of the Holy Spirit the sale or purchase of a provostship, as do all the interpreters of this Gospel passage.

It must also be considered by what penalty those are punished who sell or buy things already offered to God and his Church, since those who sold or bought what was to be offered to God were driven from God’s temple with whips. If it was said of the sellers or buyers of things to be offered, “You have made my Father’s house a house of commerce and a den of thieves” (John 2:16; Mark 11:17), what will be said now of the sellers or buyers of things offered to the Church?

And lest some madman object that the Lord rightly punished those people so harshly because at that time those things were traded in God’s temple, whereas ecclesiastical things are now traded outside the temple, let him consider that Augustine does not determine the place of sale or purchase of provostships, but speaks only without qualification: “Does someone go about to buy the dove?” Each person praises his own provostship, which he sells—he does not add “in the temple” or “outside the temple.” This is what concerns the sellers and buyers of sacred things.

As to the further question in your letter—whether it is wicked to obey those who attempt to kill, a question repeated near the end of the same letter—we answer with the words of blessed Peter: “We must obey God rather than men” (Acts 5). From this example it should be noted that men must sometimes be obeyed, but God must be obeyed more: men in matters that are not contrary to faith and religion. For we read that the citizens of Jerusalem served in the armies of the citizens of Babylon, as did holy Joseph and Daniel’s companions. The former, abhorring adultery with his mistress, and the latter, abhorring idolatry, nevertheless governed the affairs of state loyally under foreign princes.

In the Gospel also you have the command (Matthew 5) that with the one who compels you to go one mile, you should go another two, and that you should render to Caesar what belongs to Caesar, and to God what belongs to God.

Likewise Jerome, commenting on the Epistle to the Philippians, says:

> “If the lord commands what is not contrary to the holy Scriptures, let the servant submit to his lord; but if he commands what is contrary, let the spirit obey the Lord rather than the body’s lord.”

And below:

> “If what the emperor commands is good, carry out the will of the one commanding; if it is evil, answer: ‘We must obey God rather than men’” (Acts 5).

As to what is added in the same letter—whether one should use ordinations and the other sacraments administered by criminals, such as adulterers, violators of nuns, or people of this kind—we answer as follows: if they are not separated from the Church by schism or heresy, we do not deny that their ordinations and the other sacraments are holy and venerable, following blessed Augustine, who discussed this matter both extensively and truthfully in his commentary on John.

For he says:

> “Whether a good servant or a bad servant baptizes, let the one who is baptized not know himself to be baptized by one who has not denied himself the power to baptize.”

And shortly afterward:

> “Let the dove not shrink from the ministry of wicked men; let it regard the Lord’s power. If the minister is proud, he is counted with the devil, but through him Christ’s sacrament is not defiled. What flows through him is pure; what passes through him is clear.”

Likewise:

> “The spiritual power of the sacrament is like light, which is received pure by those who are illuminated and is not polluted if it passes through what is unclean. Those whom a drunkard baptizes, those whom a murderer baptizes, those whom an adulterer baptizes—Christ baptizes.”

And other statements of this kind.

Nevertheless, our predecessors Nicholas and Gregory decreed that the faithful abstain from the Masses of priests who were demonstrably such men, both to remove from others the license to sin and to recall such men to lamentation worthy of penance.

Our predecessor Gregory wrote this, among other things, to the dukes Rudolf and Berthold (GREGORY VII, book II, letter 45):

> “Knowingly receive the ministry of Simoniacs and of those lying in fornication in no way; and, as far as you can, prohibit such men by force, if necessary, from serving in the sacred mysteries,” etc.

Furthermore, concerning the matters posed to you syllogistically in the same letter—namely, if the body and blood of Christ and the other things mentioned above do not possess their own inherent sacramental powers, how do they harm those who perform or receive them; but if they do possess such powers, why are they rejected when they are presumed upon by an unworthy person?—we answer as follows:

They certainly possess their own inherent sacramental powers, as the aforesaid Augustine says in his discussion of John against the Donatists. But when those who perform or receive the same sacraments do so contrary to the institutions of the aforesaid pontiffs, [Col. 0532C] [Note: [Col. 0531D] Except in a case of necessity: “Whoever receives a sacrament from one cut off, outside a case of necessity, sins; but not one who receives it from a wicked man.” (THOMAS, part III, question 6, article 6, ad 2; and question 67, article 2.)] unless perhaps death alone intervenes—for example, lest someone depart this life without baptism or communion—they are harmed by them to such an extent that they are true idolaters. For the conferral of ordinations and sacraments by such men, and knowingly receiving them in a manner other than that stated above, are vehemently prohibited by the holy canons.

For the prophet Samuel says: “To resist is like the sin of divination, and not to acquiesce is like the crime of idolatry” (1 Samuel 15).

This concerns wicked Catholics who are within the Church. As for the sacraments of schismatics and heretics, since they are outside the Church, in accordance with the traditions of the holy Fathers—namely Pelagius, Gregory, Cyprian, Augustine, and Jerome—we profess that they possess the form of the sacraments, but not the effect of sacramental power, unless they themselves, or those initiated through their sacraments, return to Catholic unity through the laying on of hands.

It should be known, however, that the Apostolic Canons, by whose authority the Eastern Church and part of the Roman Church are united, and the illustrious martyr Cyprian, together with eighty bishops, call the baptismal washing of heretics the bath of the devil. Stephen and Cornelius, martyrs and Roman pontiffs, and the venerable Augustine in his book *On Baptism*, vehemently rebuke Cyprian and the aforesaid bishops on this account, affirming that baptism celebrated according to ecclesiastical custom, whether by a heretic or by a schismatic, is valid.

And rightly so, because one consideration applies to baptism and another to the remaining sacraments: baptism is prior in order and more necessary. For one who is about to die is provided first with baptism rather than with communion of the Lord’s body or with the other sacraments. And when a Catholic cannot be found, it is better to receive the sacrament of baptism from a heretic than to perish eternally.

In following this judgment of the aforesaid pontiffs Cornelius and Stephen and of Augustine were Innocent, Siricius, Leo, Anastasius, and the great Gregory, together with the entire Catholic Church.

And since the brevity of a letter may perhaps not suffice for the questions proposed to you, send the rashness of these men to the Apostolic See for instruction; or, according to the Apostle, avoid them as opponents of sound doctrine after the second and third admonition (Titus 3). But remain faithful unto death, so that you may receive the crown of life.

Given at Rome.

### CCLXXIV. Urban establishes privileges for the church of the Holy Trinity, in the place called Ponte Guinizeli, on the condition that the clerics pay “six coins of Milanese currency every four years to the Lateran palace.” (Between 1088 and 1099.)

[MURATORI, *Rerum Italicarum Scriptores*, V, 479.]

URBAN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son LIPRANDUS, etc.

[Col. 0533C] We decree that that church, together with the small estate on which it was founded [lacuna], or which may by the Lord’s favor have been granted there by other faithful people, shall remain forever peaceful and free from every secular opposition. We grant the clerics who are to live there the faculty of living according to a rule, and we decree that they receive from the archbishop of Milan their own ordinations, as well as the consecrations of altars and churches and the other gifts of the sacraments, provided that he is Catholic, has communion and the grace of the Apostolic See, and grants these things freely and not corruptly. Otherwise, they shall be free to receive the same sacraments from whichever Catholic bishop they choose.

We decree, therefore, that neither the archbishop of Milan nor anyone living may impose upon that church and the brothers who serve God there any yoke on any pretext, or sell their goods and apply them to his own uses, or harass them with reckless vexations. Rather, everything shall be preserved intact for you and your successors, so that it may in every way be beneficial to you, without prejudice to the Catholic reverence due to the same archbishop of Milan.

As a token of the liberty received from the Roman Church, you shall pay six coins of Milanese currency every four years to the Lateran palace.

If, therefore, in the future any ecclesiastical or secular person knowingly attempts rashly to act against the text of this decree, let that person be deprived of the dignity of power and honor, acknowledge before the divine judgment the iniquity committed, be alienated from the most sacred body and blood of Christ God and our Lord Jesus Christ the Redeemer, and be subject to strict punishment at the final judgment.

But for all who justly serve the same place, may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that here they may receive the fruit of good action and, before the strict Judge, find the rewards of eternal peace. Amen.

### CCLXXV. Pope Urban in a letter to the people of Saint Vincent of Volturno near Capua. (Between 1088 and 1099.)

[MANSI, *Concilia*, XX, 714.]

If adulterers or otherwise criminal persons are not separated from the Church by heresy or schism—that is, by cutting off or deposition—we do not deny that their sacraments are holy, following Augustine in this; but our predecessors Gregory and Nicholas ordered that people abstain from the Masses of such persons, so that by this terror they might remove from the others the license to sin, and recall the offenders themselves, through the shame of being despised, to the worthy lamentation of repentance. [Col. 0534B]

And shortly afterward:

“The sacraments of criminals possess their proper dignity of power,” as blessed Augustine says concerning John, against the Donatists; “but when such sacraments are performed or received contrary to the constitutions of the holy pontiffs—unless perhaps death intervenes, so that no one may depart from human affairs without baptism or communion—they are so harmful to those who perform or receive them that they are truly idolaters. With such persons, the conferral of ordinations and sacraments, and their reception otherwise than stated above, are strongly prohibited to those in the sacred orders.” [Col. 0534C]

Again, shortly afterward:

“These things concern wicked Catholics who are within the Church. But since the sacraments of schismatics and heretics are outside it, following the traditions of the holy Fathers—namely Pelagius, Gregory, Cyprian, Augustine, and Jerome—we profess that they possess the form of the sacraments, but not the effect of their power, unless they themselves, or those initiated by their sacraments, return to Catholic truth through the imposition of hands.”

### CCLXXVI. Urban II permits the daughter of Prince Jordan, a little girl betrothed to Rainald, son of Rodel, against the wishes of her mother and family, to be given in marriage to another man. (Between 1088 and 1099.)

[GRATIAN, *Decretum*, C. XXXI, qu. 5, c. 1.]

[Col. 0534D]

If it is established as true what the envoys of Prince Jordan reported to us—namely, that he, compelled and grieving, betrothed his unwilling young daughter, who was weeping and resisting with all her strength, to Rainald, son of Rodel, although her mother and family did not consent but were deeply distressed—since the authority of the canons and laws does not approve such a betrothal, as will be shown below, and lest what we say seem excessively harsh to those ignorant of the laws and canons, we temper our judgment as follows: if the prince wishes to complete what has been begun with the consent of his daughter, her mother, and her family, we grant permission. But if not, [Col. 0535A] let our legate hear both parties; and if there is nothing further on the part of the aforesaid Rainald that prevents it, let him receive from Jordan an oath that these matters stand as they have been stated. Then, following the decrees of the canons and laws, we do not henceforth prohibit his aforesaid daughter from marrying another man, if she wishes, provided that it be in the Lord.

### CCLXXVII. Another decree of Urban II. (Between 1088 and 1099.)

[GRATIAN, *Decretum*, C. XIX, qu. 2, c. 3.]

No bishop shall compel his clergy to swear an oath to him, except perhaps those entrusted with the administration of ecclesiastical property.

### CCLXXVIII. Another decree of Urban II. (Between 1088 and 1099.)

[MANSI, *Concilia*, XX, 714.]

[Col. 0535B]

Pope Urban II said:

“There are two laws: one public, the other private. The public law is that which has been written and confirmed by the holy Fathers, such as the law of the canons, which has indeed been given on account of transgressors. For example, the canons decree that a cleric must not pass from his own bishopric to another without letters of recommendation from his bishop. This was established on account of criminals, so that, evidently, infamous persons should not be received by any bishop. For they used to exercise their offices in another bishopric when they could not do so in their own; this has rightly been condemned by precepts and written enactments.

“But private law is what is inspired by the Holy Spirit; it is written in the heart, as the Apostle says of certain people who have the law of God written in their hearts, and who are themselves a law to themselves. If one of these retains his own position in his Church under his bishop and lives in the world, but, when the Holy Spirit breathes upon him, wishes to save himself in some monastery, then, since he is led by private law, no reason requires that he be constrained by public law [variant: “that he be constrained by the public law”]; for private law is more worthy than public law. The law is indeed the Spirit of God, and those who are led by the Spirit of God are guided by the law of God. And who can worthily resist the Holy Spirit? Therefore, whoever is led by this Spirit, even if his bishop objects, may go forth freely by our authority. For the law is not laid down for the righteous; and where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is freedom; and if you are led by the Spirit of God, you are not under the law.” [Col. 0535C–D]

### CCLXXIX. Urban II writes to certain regular canons concerning the restoration of canonical discipline. (Between 1088 and 1099.)

[MANSI, *Concilia*, XX, 712.]

[Col. 0535D]

It is fitting that we who, although unworthy, sit in the place of Peter should correct what is wrong, strengthen what is right, and ensure that in every Church our judgment proceeds as the decision of its judge, and that our eyes see equity. Therefore we give thanks to almighty God, whose mercy is better than life, because you are renewing the commendable life of the holy Fathers and, by the inspiration of the Holy Spirit, reviving the apostolic institutions of discipline that arose at the beginning of the holy Church [Col. 0536A] but have now, as the Church has grown, almost perished.

From the beginnings of the holy Church, two ways of life have been established for her children: one by which the weakness of the infirm is sustained, and another by which the blessed strength of the stronger is perfected. One remains small in Segor; the other climbs toward the higher places of the mountain. One redeems daily sins with tears and almsgiving; the other seeks eternal merits through daily perseverance. Those who hold to the former, lower way make use of earthly goods; those who follow the latter, higher way despise and abandon the good earth.

This latter way, which turns away from earthly things, is divided almost into two portions of one and the same purpose: namely, that of canons and that of monks. Of these, the second, by divine mercy, having become widespread, now shines sufficiently throughout the whole world. The first, however, as the fervor of the faithful has declined, has almost entirely ebbed away. This way was instituted by the martyr and pontiff Urban. Augustine ordered it by his rules. Gregory instructed Augustine, archbishop of the English, to establish it. Thus it should not be considered a lesser achievement to revive this life of the primitive Church, with the Spirit of the Lord inspiring and advancing it, than to preserve the flourishing religious life of monks through the perseverance of that same Spirit. [Col. 0536B]

### CCLXXX. Letter of Urban to Bernard, archbishop of Toledo.—Since Richard, bishop of Marseille, has been deprived of the legation, he himself should watch over everything; the archbishop of Compostela, released from his bonds, should be restored to his office. He is to advise whom he thinks should be entrusted with the legation. (Between 1096 and 1099.)

[MANSI, *Concilia*, XX, 697.]

[Col. 0536C]

You ought always to remember the blessing, grace, and outstanding generosity that you received from the apostolic see; and you ought always to show by your actions how highly you regard the dignity of your office. You should always demonstrate that you are a stream descending from the fountain of the Apostle Peter, and continually carry to higher things the flame that you received from the furnace of his fire.

Now especially it is necessary for your fraternity to instruct the princes in the fuller discipline of Peter and Paul and to display the vigilance of your office, particularly since there is no legate of the apostolic see in your regions. We have denied Richard the legation that he has hitherto held, [Col. 0536D] and we have entrusted the legation of your regions to no one else.

Therefore, as a prudent and religious man, we exhort and beseech you in the Lord diligently to put these things into practice: sharpen the good toward what is better, correct the wicked, and fervently and unceasingly ensure that canonical discipline is observed in all things, to the glory of the Roman Church and as the reward of your zeal. Be present, watch, and persevere with our brothers the bishops, kings, princes, and people, so that those who have gone astray may return to the right purpose, while those who remain in the truth of the faith may persevere manfully to the end.

We particularly wish and ask that you labor so that the bishop of Saint James, released from his bonds, may be restored to his office. Whatever you do concerning him, with the Lord’s help, you will report to us in your letters. Concerning other matters, and what you foresee should be arranged by us in the kingdoms of Spain, and whom you think should most suitably be entrusted with the legation of the apostolic see, you will inform us by your messages and letters. Do not in any way forget the labors that the princes of the apostles daily endure in their members; rather, carrying their mouth always in your heart and commending them to all the faithful, hasten to relieve them through the help of your consolations. [Col. 0537A]

### CCLXXXI. Letter of Pope Urban II to Galon, provost of Saint-Quentin of Beauvais.—He confirms the donation of the land of Alnella made by William, bishop of Paris. (Between 1096 and 1099.)

[DOM BOUQUET, *Recueil*, XIV, 734.]

[Col. 0537B]

Urban, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son Galon [Note: [Col. 0537D] Or Walon, disciple and successor of Ivo of Chartres, who himself later became bishop of Paris in 1104.], provost of the church of Saint-Quentin, situated at Beauvais, greeting and apostolic blessing.

Both the authority of the office entrusted to us compels us, and special charity exhorts us, to confirm what has been rightly established and to provide more generous protection for those things placed under the guardianship of our see. Therefore, by the confirmation of these present letters, we ratify the donation to your church of the land called Alnella, made by William, bishop of Paris [Note: [Col. 0537D] William of Montfort, brother of that famous Bertrada [Col. 0538D] who married King Philip. He was educated in the Church of Chartres under the discipline of Ivo and, through Ivo’s efforts, obtained the bishopric of Paris in 1096, although he was elected before reaching the required age.]. The aforesaid bishop had received this land from the canons of Saint-Germain of Auxerre, giving in exchange a prebend of the Church of Paris, in the presence of and with the subscriptions of the brothers of both chapters. Henceforth no one may violate this exchange, unless it is perhaps revoked by the judgment of our apostolic see. [Col. 0537C]

### CCLXXXII. Urban sends “letters in favor of the monks of Saint-André of Vienne, whom Guido, archbishop of that city, had harassed, along with their lay dependents, to such an extent that he even kept some of them in prison.” (Between 1097 and 1099.)

[See RUINART, *Vita Urbani II*, p. 292.]

### CCLXXXIII. Urban writes to Ivo, bishop of Chartres, and Ramnulf, bishop of Saintes, “in favor of the monks of Vendôme, whom he declares exempt from all subjection to bishops.” (Between 1097 and 1099.)

[See RUINART, cited above.]

[Col. 0537D]

### CCLXXXIV. The liberty of the monastery of Vendôme is confirmed. (Between 1097 and 1099.)

[Works of Sirmond, III, 468.]

Urban, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the venerable congregation of the monastery of Vendôme, greeting and apostolic blessing.

[Col. 0538A]

It has been reported to us that the bishop of Chartres exacted from our beloved son Gaufred, your abbot, a profession when he received consecration. Since we have recognized that this was done contrary to the authority of the Roman Church, know that we have mercifully forgiven the abbot this fault. But we annul the profession itself in such a way that it possesses absolutely no force. Moreover, we have established by the privilege of our authority, and we prohibit by these present letters, that henceforth the abbot of your monastery make a profession to the bishop. If anyone in the future attempts to act against these provisions, let him be barred from the thresholds of the holy Church and remain excommunicated until he comes to his senses and satisfies the Roman Church.

[Col. 0538B]

Given at Rome, on the eighth day before the Kalends of December.

### CCLXXXV. Letter of Urban to the archbishops and bishops of France.—He rejoices that King Philip, who had dismissed his wife and given himself to an adulteress, has returned to his senses. (Between 1097 and 1099.)

[DACHERY, *Spicilegium*, vol. III, p. 431.]

Urban, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his dearest brothers in Christ, Manasses, archbishop of Reims, and the other archbishops and bishops throughout France, greeting and apostolic blessing.

The envoy of our dearest son Philip, king of the Franks, came to the apostolic see bearing a letter of due humility and words of devotion; and concerning the guilt involving that woman, on account of which our venerable fellow-brother, the archbishop of Lyon, had pronounced a sentence of interdict against him, he made satisfaction according to the counsel of our brothers. [Col. 0538C]

For the king swore that, after he had rejected that woman into our hands—or rather, through us, into the hands of blessed Peter—he had never had carnal relations with her. Later, after taking counsel with our brothers, we decreed that the king should send to us, from among the bishops and leading men of his kingdom, several persons by the feast of All Saints who would affirm the same thing that his envoy had sworn.

Therefore, having accepted such satisfaction through his legate, we absolve the same son of ours, the king, from the bond of the interdict that had been pronounced against him for this cause, and we have granted him authority to use the crown according to the custom of the kingdom. [Col. 0538D]

Given at the Lateran, on the eighth day before the Ides of May.

### CCLXXXVI. Letter of Urban to Hugh, abbot of Cluny.—He informs him that “in the Roman synod recently” he decreed that the monastery of Saint-Germain of Auxerre, which had been “renounced” to him by its abbot at the Council of Nîmes, should be entrusted to him. (Between 1097 and 1098.)

[BALUZE, *Miscellanea*, Lucerne edition, II, 177.]

Urban, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother Hugh, abbot of Cluny, greeting and apostolic blessing. [Col. 0539A]

At the Council of Nîmes, the abbot of the monastery of Saint-Germain, situated at Auxerre, renounced that abbey into our hands; and although we were often asked by him, we were unwilling to restore the place to him. Moreover, our son Stephen, count, together with his wife, entreated us to entrust the same monastery to you. We recently established this very thing in the Roman synod, in the presence of the bishop of that city and the brothers of the aforesaid place.

Therefore, by these present letters we command your fraternity to accept the aforesaid abbey, henceforth and permanently to be administered under your care, and to establish there monastic religious life according to the manner of life of your brothers, [Col. 0539B] but in such a way that the place does not lack its own abbot.

### CCLXXXVII. Bull of Urban II by which the see of Barbastro is established. (Around the year 1099.)

[FLOREZ, *España Sagrada*, vol. XLVI, p. 245.]

Urban, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son Pontius, bishop of Barbastro. [Col. 0539C]

We owe abundant thanksgiving to the mercies of the Lord because in our times the Church is spreading, the dominion of the Saracens is diminishing, and, by the Lord’s favor, the ancient honor of episcopal sees is being restored. Among these, the parish of the city of Lleida has now been restored for the greater part to Christian rule through the zeal of Peter, king of Aragon. Therefore, yielding to the petitions of the same king, we have decreed that an episcopal see shall remain at Barbastro, the chief town adjoining Lleida.

We further decree that all the territories or boundaries of Barbastro belonging to the diocese of Lleida that have been or shall be brought under Christian power, together with the town of Alquézar, shall be subject by episcopal right to your administration and that of your successors. To ensure that this remains perpetually firm and inviolate, we confirm it by the authority of the almighty Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.

### CCLXXXVIII. Letter of Urban to Ingelrannus, bishop of Laon.—He urges him to restore the altar of Corbiniac to the brothers of Saint-Remigius. (In the year 1099.)

[MANSI, *Concilia*, XX, 678.]

[Col. 0539D]

Urban, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Ingelrannus, bishop of Laon, greeting and apostolic blessing.

The more familiarly you are loved by the Roman Church, the more graciously you ought to have favored and embraced those whom she herself loves. Therefore let your fraternity cease harassing the brothers of Saint Remigius, and restore to them the altar which those same brothers are known to have possessed in the village called Corbiniac. For we removed the persons, but we did not take away from the monasteries the right of their ancient possession. Indeed, in that change of persons, [Col. 0540A] the renewal of avarice and the alienation of ecclesiastical property were occurring. Moreover, we wish the altars that monasteries have possessed for eleven or thirty years, as was established in the synod, to remain undisturbed for them.

### CCLXXXIX. Urban II confirms the monastery of Blaubeuren in the diocese of Constance, together with all the donations made to it by Adelaide and her uncles. (In the year 1099.)

[COCQUELINES, *Bullarum Romanorum Pontificum Collectio*, II, 105.]

Urban, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved Azelin, abbot of the monastery of Blaubeuren, and to his successors regularly appointed in perpetuity. [Col. 0540B]

Just as assent ought to be denied to those making unreasonable requests, so we ought to respond with benevolent assent to the wishes of those making just requests. For this reason we have decided to yield to the desire and petition of our dearest daughter, Countess Adelaide. Coming to the threshold of the holy apostles, she earnestly sought to fulfill the devotion of yourself, her husband, and her father-in-law. For the church of Burron, over which your fraternity now presides by God’s authority, built from its foundations through the zeal of her father-in-law, she offered upon the sacred altar of blessed Peter according to their wishes and, by our hand, transferred it as the personal allod of the apostolic see. She requested that this offering be confirmed by the authority of our writings.

We therefore decree by the authority of this present document that both the aforesaid place and all the possessions granted there by the generosity of the aforesaid counts, Henry and Hugh, or of the aforementioned Countess Adelaide, or that may in the future be bestowed by their offerings or those of other faithful people, shall always remain whole and unimpaired under the protection of the apostolic see, serving in every way the needs of the servants of God who dwell there, without prejudice to the canonical reverence due to the bishop of Constance. An annual census of one bezant, however, shall be paid from that place to the Lateran palace. [Col. 0540C]

We therefore decree that no person at all may rashly disturb the same monastery, or take away, diminish, or appropriate its possessions for personal use under the pretext of pious causes. When you, the abbot of the place, die, or any of your successors, no one shall be placed over it by any act of deception [Col. 0540D] or violence except one whom the brothers, by common consent—or the sounder part of the brothers’ council—shall have elected in the fear of God and according to the rule of blessed Benedict.

If, therefore, any priest, cleric, duke, count, judge, or secular person, knowing this page of our constitution, attempts to act against it, and, after being warned a second or third time, does not make amends by suitable satisfaction, let him lose the dignity of his power and honor, recognize himself as guilty before the divine judgment for the iniquity committed, be separated from the most sacred body and blood of God and our Lord and Redeemer Jesus Christ, and at the final judgment be subjected to severe punishment.

But may the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ be upon all who preserve justice toward that place, so that both here they may receive the fruit of good action and before the severe Judge may find the rewards of eternal peace. [Col. 0541A]

Given at the Lateran through the hand of John, cardinal deacon of the holy Roman Church, on the eighth day before the Kalends of February, in the seventh indiction, in the year of the Incarnation of the Lord 1099, in the eleventh year of the pontificate of the lord Pope Urban II.
