### CCXC. Bull of Pope Urban II by which he receives the monastery of Saint Blasius under the protection of the apostolic see. (In the year 1099.)

[D. GERBERT, *Historia Nigrae Silvae*, III, 36.]

Urban, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable son Huto [Note: [Col. 0541] This is Udo, or Utto, the fourth abbot of Saint Blasius, successor of Gisibert from 1088 until 1108.], abbot of the monastery of Saint Blasius, [Col. 0541B] situated in the Black Forest, and to his successors regularly appointed in perpetuity.

A pious request ought to be completed by the fulfillment of the will that follows it, so that both the sincerity of devotion may commendably increase and the benefit requested may undoubtedly gain strength. Since, therefore, your affection, taking refuge in the protection of the apostolic see, requested its guardianship with due devotion, we have mercifully granted your supplication and receive the monastery over which you preside, by God’s authority, together with everything belonging to it, under the protection of the apostolic see.

Therefore, by the page of this present privilege, we establish by apostolic authority that whatever the same monastery possesses today, or may justly and canonically acquire in the future through the concession of pontiffs, the generosity of princes, or the offerings of the faithful, shall remain secure and unimpaired for you and your successors. [Col. 0541C]

We therefore decree that no person at all may rashly disturb the same monastery, or take away, retain after seizure, diminish, or harass through presumptuous vexations its possessions or offerings; rather, everything shall be preserved intact for the use of those for whose support and administration they were granted, and shall serve their needs in every way.

You shall receive the consecrations of altars or basilicas, the ordinations of monks, chrism, holy oil, and the other matters belonging to episcopal office from the bishop of Constance, in whose diocese you are, provided that he is Catholic, possesses the grace and communion of the apostolic see, and wishes to provide these things freely and without corruption. Otherwise, you may approach whatever bishop you wish and receive from him the sacraments of consecration, or have recourse to the apostolic see, which, supported by apostolic authority, will grant without hesitation what is requested. [Col. 0541D]

Moreover, we decree that the burial ground of the same place shall be entirely free, so that no one may obstruct the devotion and final will of those who have decided to be buried there, unless they happen to be excommunicated. Let no opposition from any bishop or provost prevent you from receiving laypeople or secular clerics for conversion.

When you, the abbot of the same place, die, or any of your successors, no one shall be placed over it by any stratagem of deception or violence except one whom the brothers, by common consent—or the sounder part of the brothers’ council—shall have elected according to the fear of God and the rule of blessed Benedict. [Col. 0542A]

If, therefore, any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowingly attempting to act against this page of our constitution, after being warned a second or third time does not make suitable amends, let that person lose the dignity of power and honor, recognize himself or herself as guilty before the divine judgment for the iniquity committed, be separated from the most sacred body and blood of God and our Lord and Redeemer Jesus Christ, and at the final judgment be subjected to severe punishment.

But may the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ be upon all who preserve justice toward that place, so that both here they may receive the fruit of good action and before the severe Judge may find the rewards of eternal peace. Amen, amen.

[Col. 0542B]

Written by the hand of Peter, regional notary and scrivener of the sacred palace.

Given at the Lateran through the hand of John, cardinal deacon of the holy Roman Church, on the seventh day before the Kalends of April, in indiction VII, in the year of the Incarnation of the Lord 1099, in the twelfth year of the pontificate of the lord Pope Urban II.

### CCXCI. Bull of Urban II for the monastery of Saint Saturninus in the district of Urgell. (In the year 1099.)

[MARCA, *Marca Hispanica*, p. 1208.]

Urban, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son Peter, abbot of the monastery of Saint Saturninus, situated near the river Valira in the parish of Urgell, and to his successors regularly appointed [Col. 0542C] in perpetuity.

A pious request ought to be completed by the fulfillment of the will that follows it, so that the sincerity of devotion may commendably shine forth and the benefit requested may undoubtedly gain strength. Therefore, accommodating your request with paternal kindness, we receive under the protection of the apostolic see the venerable monastery of Saint Saturninus, over which you preside by God’s authority, and decree that it shall always remain in the liberty established by the emperor Charles of illustrious memory, confirmed by Leo, venerable pontiff of the holy apostolic see, through the sanction of a privilege, and accepted by the provincial bishops through the affirmations of their documents.

The place itself shall always remain under the jurisdiction and ownership of the apostolic see. No layperson shall exercise dominion over it, but all pleas, judgments, and disciplinary penalties concerning everyone belonging to the monastery shall remain in the abbot’s power. Nor shall the diocesan bishop be permitted to impose any excommunication upon the monastery or inflict any trouble upon it. Rather, whatever it is known presently to possess peacefully in authentic possession, and whatever it may justly and canonically acquire in the future through the concession of pontiffs, the generosity of princes, or the offerings of the faithful, shall remain secure and unimpaired for you and your successors.

This applies especially to what Erimbaldus, bishop of Urgell, and Arnulf, bishop of Ribagorza, of venerable memory, are read to have given and granted at the dedication of the same [Col. 0543A] monastery: churches, church tithes, firstfruits, and offerings or cemeteries throughout the parish of Urgell or Ribagorza, throughout Cerdanya, Berguedà, or Pallars; and also the church of Saint Peter of Villanita, at which you have restored the state of monastic discipline. We grant that its castle, Carogio, and the rock called Saint Romanus, together with everything belonging to it, shall remain perpetually subject to your monastery, as it is today.

In addition, we decree that no person at all may rashly disturb the aforesaid monastery of Saint Saturninus, or take away, retain after seizure, diminish, or harass through presumptuous vexations its possessions; rather, everything shall be preserved intact for the use of those for whose support and administration they were granted, serving their needs in every way. [Col. 0543B]

When the abbot of the same place dies, or any of your successors, no one shall be placed over it by any stratagem of deception or violence except one whom the brothers, by common consent—or the sounder part of the brothers’ council—shall have elected according to the fear of God and the rule of blessed Benedict.

As a sign of the liberty received from the Roman Church, you shall pay each year one pound of silver to the Lateran palace.

If, moreover, in the future any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowingly attempting to act rashly against this page of our constitution, after being warned a second or third time does not make suitable amends, let that person lose the dignity of power and honor, recognize himself or herself as guilty before the divine judgment for the iniquity committed, be separated from the most sacred body and blood of God and our Lord and Redeemer Jesus Christ, and at the final judgment be subjected to severe punishment. But may the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ be upon all who preserve justice toward that place, so that both here they may receive the fruit of good action and before the severe Judge may find the rewards of eternal peace. Amen, amen, amen. [Col. 0543C]

Written by the hand of Peter, regional notary and scrivener of the sacred palace.

Given at Rome, in the portico of blessed Peter, through the hand of John, cardinal deacon of the holy Roman Church, on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of May, in indiction VII, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1099, in the twelfth year of the pontificate of the lord Pope Urban II. [Col. 0543D]

### CCXCII. Letter of Urban to Hugh, archbishop of Lyon.—He announces that his primacy has finally been recognized at Rome by Daimbert, archbishop of Sens. (In the year 1099.)

[MANSI, *Concilia*, XX, 877.]

Urban, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother and fellow bishop Hugh, primate of Lyon, greeting and apostolic blessing.

It is unnecessary to recall how many disputes and how many outcries, both in our time and that of our predecessors, have caused the apostolic see to be petitioned concerning the complaint that both your predecessors and your fraternity have until now vigorously pursued against the Church of Sens; the writings of our predecessors make this clear, and the common memory of the councils that we have celebrated in Gaul by God’s authority bears witness to it. [Col. 0544A]

This matter was treated and decided at the plenary Council of Auvergne. When Richerius, archbishop of Sens, refused entirely to accept the synodal decision, it was taken up again through your diligence at the Councils of Tours and Nîmes. The aforesaid Richerius died under interdict because of his obstinacy, while his suffragans had already professed obedience to you as primate and according to synodal judgment.

But our brother Daimbert, who now presides over that Church by the Lord’s will, received the grace of consecration through my ministry under the same complaint, as we informed you in our letters. Recently, when he had returned to the threshold of the apostles both to pursue this case and in response to a general synodical summons, in the presence of your legates—Ismeon, bishop of Die; Girinus, the dean; and another Girinus, the chaplain—the judgment of the apostolic see compelled him, and, after every evasion had finally been rejected, he professed into our hands that he recognized both you and the Church of Lyon as holding primacy over Sens, and that henceforth he would obey you and your legitimate successors as primates. [Col. 0544B]

He likewise promised that, at the time appointed by us—that is, by the next feast of Saint Denis—he would come to you and profess the same thing in his own voice in the presence of the Church of Lyon, unless a canonical impediment should arise; when that period had passed, he would take care to fulfill it within thirty days.

Thus we assigned this matter through your vicars, and through them into your hands and those of the Church of Lyon, in the presence of our brothers whose names are written below: Anselm, archbishop of Canterbury; Leodegarius, archbishop of Bourges; Amatus, archbishop of Bordeaux; Walter, bishop of Albano; Odo, bishop of Ostia; Guntardus, bishop of Fondi; Leutaldus, bishop of Senlis; Nunerius, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Clement; Teuzo, cardinal priest of the title of Saints John and Paul; John, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Anastasia, priests of our apostolic see; Peter Leonis and John Frangipane, Roman nobles. [Col. 0544C]

Therefore let your fraternity henceforth consider more carefully what it owes to the apostolic see, by displaying both greater love and greater service. [Col. 0544D]

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, through the hand of John, cardinal deacon of the holy Roman Church, in the seventh indiction, on the eighth day before the Kalends of May, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1099, in the twelfth year of the pontificate of Pope Urban.

### CCXCIII. * Urban orders that the institution of regular discipline which Andrew, founder of the monastery, had established according to the custom of the Vallombrosan brothers should always be preserved in the monastery of Casale Saint Peter. (In the year 1099.)

[See MABILLON, *Annales Benedictini*, V, 406.]

### CCXCIV. * At the request of Amatus, archbishop of Bordeaux, he confirms the possessions of the monastery of Holy Cross. (In the year 1099.)

[See MABILLON, cited above.]

[Col. 0545A]

### CCXCV. Letter of Urban to Hugh, archbishop of Lyon.—Concerning the recall of Robert, abbot of Cîteaux, from the hermitage. (In the year 1099.)

[MANSI, *Concilia*, XX, 666.]

Urban, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother and bishop Hugh, vicar of the apostolic see, greeting and apostolic blessing. [Col. 0545B]

We have received a great outcry in council from the brothers of Molesme, who are vehemently demanding the return of their abbot. For they said that their religious observance had been overturned and that, because of the absence of that abbot, they were hated by princes and by their other neighbors.

At last, compelled by our brothers, we command your affection by these present writings, informing you that it would please us if that abbot could be brought back from the hermitage to the monastery. If you cannot accomplish this, take care that both those who love the hermitage may be at rest and those who are in the monastery may serve regular disciplines.

### CCXCVI. Letter of Urban II on behalf of John, archdeacon of Arras. (In the year 1099.)

[DOM BOUQUET, *Recueil*, vol. XIV, p. 239.]

[Col. 0545C]

Urban, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son John, archdeacon of Arras, greeting and apostolic blessing.

Since it has been reported to our ears that you have been elected in the Church of Thérouanne by the common vote of religious men, both clergy and people, we rejoice greatly. Therefore, by the authority of the apostolic see, we confirm and strengthen that election, and, lest it be evaded on any pretext, by that same authority we altogether prohibit . . . .

### CCXCVII. * Urban confirms the liberty of the monastery of Psalmodi, “so that the people of Marseille may have no lordship there.” (In the year 1099.)

[See the account in MABILLON and RUINART, *Ouvrages posthumes*, III, 395, and below in the appendix to Urban’s letters.]

[Col. 0545D]

### CCXCVIII. Letter of Pope Urban II to the canons of Saint-André of Bordeaux.—He makes known that their dispute with the clergy of Saint-Seurin was so decided in the Roman council that the church of Saint-André should have its own cemetery in perpetuity. (In the year 1099.)

[DOM BOUQUET, *Recueil*, XIV, 736.]

Urban, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons, the canons of Saint-André, greeting and apostolic blessing.

Know, dearest brothers, that the dispute which the clerics of Saint Severinus had long maintained with you concerning the cemetery of your mother church, consecrated by us through the grace of God, we have brought to a just and lawful conclusion. For in the Roman council which, by God’s will, we solemnly celebrated before the body of the most blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, after your arguments had been set forth by Peter the dean and the objections of your adversaries had been carefully examined, the holy Synod decreed that your mother—the Church of Bordeaux, namely, our daughter, perpetually joined to us by the unique privilege of love—ought to possess forever the cemetery which she had claimed. Therefore, by the council’s common decree, we immediately restored to your church the cemetery which you had requested for the burial of the faithful [Col. 0546B], and granted it to be possessed in perpetuity by apostolic authority and right. Thereafter, in the sight of the council, we invested Peter, your dean, with our own hand. Accordingly, by the authority of almighty God, of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul and Andrew, and by our own authority, we absolutely forbid anyone ever to presume to act against this definition of the council and our grant.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, on the fifth day before the Nones of May, in the seventh indiction, in the year 1099 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the twelfth year of the pontificate of our lord Pope Urban II.

**CCXCIX. Letter of Pope Urban II to Peter, provost, and the canons of the Church of Rodez.** (Year 1099.)

[BALUZ., *Miscell.* III, 91.]

[Col. 0546C]

URBAN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Peter the provost and his brothers in the Church of Rodez who profess the canonical life, and to their successors who shall remain in the same religious observance, forever.

A pious request ought to be completed by the fulfillment of its purpose, so that the sincerity of devotion may shine forth laudably and the benefit requested may undoubtedly acquire strength. Since, therefore, dearest sons, inspired by divine grace, you have resolved to restrain your conduct under the discipline of the regular life and to serve almighty God together according to the institution of the holy Fathers, we rejoice in your wishes with paternal affection. Accordingly, with due kindness, we grant our assent to your petition [Col. 0546D]. For by the authority of this present privilege we confirm the canonical order of life which you have professed; and we forbid anyone, after making his profession, to possess anything as his own or to leave the cloister without the permission of the provost or the congregation. If anyone should leave and, after being admonished, disdain to return, you and your successors shall have the power to suspend such a person from his offices wherever he may be; and no bishop or abbot shall receive one so suspended, so long as, by the Lord’s favor, the discipline of the canonical order continues to flourish there.

We therefore decree that you and your successors who remain in the same religious observance shall possess perpetually all those things which you now appear to possess for the support of your common sustenance [Col. 0547A]: namely, the Church of Saint Savior of Veirieiras, the Church of Saint Peter of Colnac, and the Church of Saint Gerald of Salas; and, in addition, all the *paratae* or *symbolae*, as they call the synodal dues, belonging both to the churches already mentioned and to the other churches which the bishops of the Church of Rodez—Peter, formerly son of Berengarius; Pons, son of Stephen; Raymond Frotard; and Ademar, who at present presides over that Church of Rodez—have granted to you for the expense of clothing.

We also confirm for the use of your community the provostship, a dignitary office of the parish of Rodez, the archdeaconry, and the offerings of your mother church, which you possess by the gift of the aforesaid Ademar, our brother and fellow bishop; as well as whatever you or your successors may henceforth justly and canonically obtain by the grant of bishops, the generosity of princes, or the offerings of the faithful [Col. 0547B].

So that you may serve almighty God more peacefully and observe the discipline of the canonical order more strictly, we grant you, at the request of our aforesaid brother Ademar, your bishop, permission to have a cemetery at the mother church where you live together, in which the bodies of your brothers or of parishioners to whom, during their lifetime, you administer the divine mysteries may be buried.

If, moreover, any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowingly aware of this page of our constitution, should rashly attempt to act against it, and, after being admonished a second or third time, should not correct the offense by suitable satisfaction, let that person be deprived of the dignity of his power and honor, recognize himself as guilty before the divine judgment of the iniquity committed [Col. 0547C], be separated from the most sacred body and blood of God and our Lord and Redeemer Jesus Christ, and at the final judgment be subjected to strict punishment. But let the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with all who preserve justice toward that place, so that they may both receive here the fruit of good action and find with the strict Judge the rewards of eternal peace.

Written by the hand of Peter, regional notary of the sacred palace.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, through the hand of John, cardinal deacon of the holy Roman Church, on the Ides of May, in the seventh indiction, in the year 1099 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the twelfth year of the pontificate of the lord Pope Urban II.

**CCC. Letter of Urban to Alfanus, archbishop of Salerno.** (Year 1099.)

[UGHELLI, *Italia sacra*, VIII, 393.]

[Col. 0547D]

URBAN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Alfanus [Col. 0548A], archbishop of the holy Church of Salerno, and to his successors.

Because, at the request of P., abbot of the monastery of the Holy Trinity, we granted that monastery liberty for the sake of the brothers religiously living there, placed it under the protection and jurisdiction of the holy Roman Church alone, and granted to that abbot and his successors that they should receive the abbatial blessing only from the Roman Church, while receiving the consecration of churches, altars, and clerics from the archbishop of Salerno—if he were Catholic and enjoyed our favor and that of our successors; otherwise, the aforesaid abbot and his successors were permitted to receive these things from whatever bishop they wished.

Now, having seen the privileges of your Church, which we previously did not know, we have truly discovered that our predecessors granted to your Church all churches and all monasteries, both those already built and those to be built, whether within the city or outside it, so that they would be subject to your Church, with full rights over them and over their clerics, as the canons of the holy Fathers prescribe [Col. 0548B]. Finally, we have realized that we had been persuaded to act against the canons of the holy Fathers and against the authority of our predecessors concerning all the matters written above which we had granted to the aforesaid abbot and his successors.

Therefore, we recognize that all the foregoing was represented to us by concealment and deception, and, recognizing this, we decree that it shall henceforth be invalid [lacuna]. We restore in full to your Church, to you, and to your successors the canonical right over the aforesaid monastery, over the other monasteries, and over all their churches and clerics, according to the canons of the holy Fathers and according to the privileges granted to your Church by our predecessors [Col. 0548C].

Furthermore, if the aforesaid monastery or the other monasteries possessed any churches in your parish before the decrees of Pope Gregory VII, of venerable memory, our predecessor, let them retain them. But if the aforesaid monastery or the other monasteries acquired, or shall acquire, any churches in your parish after the decrees of that pope, whether by your grant or by that of your predecessors or successors, or in any other manner, we return those churches to your Church and establish them in its possession. Only if anyone should inflict any injustice upon the aforesaid monastery or the other monasteries, and they should thereafter flee for help to the Roman Church, do we not exclude them from our protection and that of our successors [Col. 0548D].

Given at Rome in the year 1098 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the month of May, in the seventh indiction.

## DOUBTFUL DOCUMENTS

[Col. 0549]

**CCCI. Bull of Pope Urban II declaring that the body of the most blessed legislator and patriarch of monks, Benedict, rests at Monte Cassino, on the revelation of the same holy Father and the sign of restored health.** (Between 1088 and 1099.)

[MARGARINI, *Bullar. Casin.*, I, 12.]

[Col. 0549A]

URBAN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to all the sons of the Catholic Church redeemed by the precious blood of our Redeemer, greeting and apostolic blessing.

It is written: “The gifts and calling of God are without repentance.” That gift, however, which almighty God granted to our most blessed Father Benedict and, through him, to his Casinense monastery, cannot by any means be torn away or altered by any violence, so that he himself, the Father of all monks, and his aforesaid Casinense monastery may perpetually be regarded as the head of all monasteries [Col. 0549B]. And rightly so: for from that place the venerable religion of the monastic order flowed, as it were, from the fountain of paradise, from Benedict’s breast; and the same venerable Father made that place memorable throughout the world both by his virtues and by his bodily repose.

When, following the custom of our predecessors, we had visited his most sacred threshold on the very day of that Father’s vigil, we were struck by our customary pain in the side. When every hope of recovery already seemed to have been entirely removed from us, and uncertainty had arisen in our mind concerning the bodily presence of that same Father Benedict in that place, on the night when his solemnity was being celebrated [Col. 0549C], the same most holy Benedict appeared visibly to our lowliness and said: “Why do you doubt our bodily presence?” When we asked who he was, the holy man of the Lord replied: “I am Brother Benedict, guardian and eternal inhabitant of this Casinense monastery. Because you have doubted that I rest here, this shall be a sign to you, so that you may doubt no longer and may believe that my little body rests here: as soon as the bell is rung for the nocturnal office, you shall suffer from this pain no longer.” Having said this, he disappeared.

When the appointed hour arrived, just as the holy man of the Lord had said, we were restored to our former health. Together with the bishops and cardinals, giving the greatest thanks to God and to the most holy confessor Benedict, we celebrated his feast with fitting [Col. 0549D] reverence.

For this reason we ask and implore in the Lord Jesus, who for our salvation deigned to become incarnate and die; and by the authority of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, in whose place we preside over the Roman Church; and by the power of the Holy Spirit we expressly command that no one thereafter presume to celebrate a false translation of Father Benedict. We pronounce divine judgment against those who contradict this apostolic ordinance of ours and bind them with the bond of anathema.

Because, by the dispensation of the most sacred see of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, which by God’s authorization—though unworthy—we administer, we are compelled by pastoral concern to care for the whole flock of the Lord [Col. 0550A], we know that we owe so much greater favor to the Casinense community, perpetually devoted by right to divine worship, because through Father Benedict we were restored to our former health. It is also fitting that they be removed from every worldly disturbance, so that the faithful mind, freed from worldly impediments, may devote itself even more intensely to the praises of its Creator [insist], and so that we may be relieved of the burden of our sins by the support of their holy prayers.

Therefore, following the statutes of our holy predecessors, we confirm in perpetuity for the holy Casinense monastery everything that, from the times of the emperors Justin and Justinian to this day, has been offered, granted, sold, or exchanged to that place throughout the world [Col. 0550B], as well as whatever it may henceforth and in future rightly and canonically obtain.

We further confirm all privileges of the Roman pontiffs; the decrees of emperors, kings, margraves, dukes, and princes; and the offerings of all the faithful whatsoever that have been granted to blessed Benedict and, through him, to the Casinense monastery.

If in the future any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowingly aware of this page of our constitution, should rashly attempt to act against it, and, after being admonished a second or third time, should not correct the offense by suitable satisfaction, let that person be deprived of the dignity of power or honor, recognize himself as guilty before the divine judgment of the iniquity committed [Col. 0550C], be separated from the most holy and sacred blood of God and our Lord and Redeemer Jesus Christ, and at the final judgment be subjected to strict punishment. But let the peace of the Lord Jesus Christ be with all who preserve justice toward that place, so that they may both receive the reward of good action in the future and find with the strict Judge the rewards of eternal peace.

Given, etc.

**CCCII. Urban grants to Peter, king of the Spaniards, and to his duly appointed successors, “that they may distribute among whatever monasteries they wish the churches of villages, both those which they may be able to capture in the lands of the Saracens and those which they themselves may cause to be built in the kingdom, except only episcopal sees”; and he grants the same permission to the nobles of the kingdom, “so that they may retain for themselves and their heirs, with the first fruits and tithes only of their own inheritances, the churches which they may acquire by right of war in Saracen lands or found on their own hereditary estates, or subject them to the jurisdiction of any chapels or monasteries.”** (Between 1088 and 1099.)

[ARRUEGO, *Catedra episcopal de Zaragoza*. Zaragoza, 1653, folio, 659.]

[Col. 0550D]

**CCCIII. [Note: [Col. 0551] This document, like the following one, was fabricated by Humbald of Limoges.] Urban orders the clergy and people of Limoges to obey Humbald, bishop, after he had been cleared of simony and fully restored by him.** (Year 1094.)

[BALUZ., *Miscell.*, II, 182.]

[Col. 0551A]

URBAN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to all the clergy and people of Limoges, greeting and apostolic blessing.

We believe that you all know how, in the preceding year, your bishop appeared before us after being accused on certain counts which, according to the rule of the holy canons, invalidated both his election and his consecration; the archbishop of Bourges, who had consecrated him, was also present [Col. 0551B]. Since he could not canonically clear himself of all these charges—for he had come unprepared and without defenders—he renounced the episcopate, though in hope of mercy, and set out for Jerusalem. On his return he implored mercy. We, moved by the prayers of many of our sons, entrusted the same case to our most reverend brother H., archbishop of Lyon, to be investigated by a more careful examination within the province, where the persons of the accusers were known and the bishop could in no way complain of the absence of witnesses.

After the case had been investigated more carefully, and since the accusers had been unable to prove him guilty of simony, in consideration of mercy and ecclesiastical peace he was granted the opportunity to clear himself of this charge together with suitable witnesses. Although the others assert only his deposition, by the compassionate kindness of apostolic gentleness, granted for the peace and tranquility of your Church, he swore an oath concerning the crime of simony that, in order to obtain the episcopate, he himself had neither given nor promised money, nor had anyone else done so with his knowledge [Col. 0551C].

Because, in the midst of the great difficulties of the present time, the bishops of the province could in no way be summoned into our presence [Col. 0552A], F., abbot of Stirpensis, and J., abbot of Fleury—men, certainly, of religious life and unimpaired reputation—together with three other clerics of theirs, affirmed the oath. We therefore send him back to you with the fullness of our favor and of his episcopal office, and by this letter admonish you to obey him as your proper shepherd. May divine mercy preserve you in obedience.

**CCCIV. He again commends Humbald, bishop, to the clergy and people of Limoges.** (In the same year.)

[BALUZ., *Miscell.*, II, 182.]

URBAN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to all the clergy and people of Limoges, greeting and apostolic [Col. 0552B] blessing.

Our brother Humbald, bishop of your city, came to us complaining that many injuries were being inflicted upon the mother Church by her sons. For certain soldiers violently abuse the goods of the churches, demand honors as though they were hereditary possessions, and impose troubles upon the bishop, as though he were an enemy, when he refuses to consent. Therefore, by this letter, we exhort and command your devotion to strive henceforth to abstain altogether from this presumption. If after this you should disregard our command, whatever sentence your bishop may pronounce against you by canonical authority, we confirm by the authority of our assent [Col. 0552C].

For we desire that all the churches of the diocese be subject to the bishop and show him canonical reverence, without prejudice to any privileges of the Roman Church, if there are such. We wish him to be commended to all, clergy and laity alike, as one returning to you with the favor of our kindness. May divine mercy preserve you in obedience to our admonitions.

Given at Pisa, on the sixth day before the Ides of October.

[Col. 0551]

# LETTERS OF VARIOUS PERSONS TO URBAN II

**I. Letter of Bohemond, prince of Antioch; Raymond, count of Saint-Gilles; Godfrey, duke of Lorraine; Robert, count of Normandy; Robert, count of Flanders; and Eustace, count of Boulogne, to Urban II** [Note: [Col. 0551] It appears in Fulcher of Chartres, chapter 15.]

(BALUZ., *Miscell.* Luc. edition, III, p. 60.)

[Col. 0551D]

To the lord and venerable Pope Urban: Bohemond and Raymond, count of Saint-Gilles; Godfrey, duke; Robert, count of Normandy; Robert, count of Flanders; and the count of Boulogne, greeting, faithful service, and, as sons to their spiritual Father, true submission in Christ.

[Col. 0552D] We all wish and desire that it be known to you how, by the great mercy of God and by his most evident assistance, Antioch was captured by us; how the Turks, who had inflicted many insults upon our Lord Jesus Christ, were captured and killed; how we avenged the injuries inflicted upon Jesus Christ, the supreme God, at Jerusalem; how we, who had previously defeated the Turks by besieging them, were later besieged by Turks coming from Chorasan, Jerusalem, Damascus, and many other lands; and how at last we were liberated by the mercy of Jesus Christ.

After Nicaea had been captured and, as you have heard, on the Kalends of June we had defeated that immense multitude of Turks in the valley of Dorylaeum, put the great Solyman to flight, and stripped his men, land, and possessions; after all Romania had been acquired and pacified, we came to besiege Antioch.

When it was besieged, we suffered many evils, both from battles with the supreme Turks and pagans, who attacked us so frequently and in such numbers that we might more truly be said to have been besieged than to have besieged those whom we held within the city of Antioch. At last, after all the battles had been overcome and the Christian faith had been exalted by their outcome, I, Bohemond, having made an agreement with a certain Turk who handed the city over to me, placed ladders against the wall shortly before dawn with many soldiers of Christ; thus, on the third day before the Nones of June, we captured the city which had previously resisted Christ [Col. 0553B]. We killed Cassianus, the tyrant of that city, together with many thousands of his men, and retained their wives, children, and households, along with their gold, silver, and all their possessions.

We were not able, however, to secure the citadel of Antioch, which had been fortified by the Turks. When on the following day we wished to attack it, we saw an infinite multitude of Turks, whom for many days we had been waiting for outside the city to come and fight us, running across all the fields. On the third day they did not besiege us; more than one hundred thousand of them entered the aforesaid citadel and tried to burst through its gate into the city situated below the citadel, which was held in common by us and them. But we took up position on another mountain opposite the citadel and guarded the road descending between the two armies toward the city, lest far more numerous forces break through against us. Fighting at the gates by night and day, both within and outside, we compelled them to re-enter the city of the citadel and return to their camp [Col. 0553C].

When they saw that they could harm us in no way from that side, they surrounded us on every side so completely that none of our men could leave or come to us. Thus we were so desolate and afflicted that, dying from hunger and many other hardships, many of our men killed and ate our starving horses and asses.

Meanwhile, when the most merciful kindness of almighty God came to our aid and watched over us, the Lord’s lance, with which the side of Jesus Christ was pierced by the hands of Longinus, was revealed three times by the holy apostle Andrew to a certain servant of God [Note: [Col. 0553D] See William of Tyre, book VI, chapter 14.], who also showed him the place where the lance lay. We found it in the Church of Blessed Peter, prince of the apostles. By its discovery and by many other divine revelations we were so comforted and strengthened that we who had previously been afflicted and fearful then urged one another on to battle, exceedingly bold and ready.

After being besieged for three weeks and four days, on the vigil of the apostles Peter and Paul [Note: [Col. 0553D] The same, chapter 220.], trusting in God and confessing all our iniquities, we went out through the city gates with our entire armed army to seek battle. We were so few that, as they themselves assert, we were not going out to fight them but to flee [Col. 0554A]. Having made all preparations and arranged both foot soldiers and knights in proper formations, we boldly attacked them where their strength and power were greatest, carrying the Lord’s lance, and forced them to flee from the first position of the battle.

They, as is their custom, began to scatter in every direction, occupying the hills and taking to the roads wherever they could, wishing to deceive us [the reading *gvrare* is uncertain], because they thought that in this way they could kill us all. But since we had been instructed by many battles in their deceptions and tactics, God’s grace and mercy came to our aid, so that although we were very few in comparison with them, we drove them all together into one place; and, once gathered, with God’s right hand fighting alongside us, we compelled them to flee and abandon their camp with everything that was in it [Col. 0554B].

After defeating them, pursuing them throughout the day, and killing many thousands of them, we returned joyfully and happily to the city. A certain Admirable, who was in the aforesaid citadel with a thousand men, surrendered it to Bohemond. Thus our Lord Jesus Christ delivered the whole city of Antioch to Roman religion and faith [Note: [Col. 0554D] The same, book VI, chapter 1.]. But because something sorrowful always tends to intervene in joyful affairs, the bishop of Le Puy, whom you had entrusted to us as your vicar, died on the Kalends of August, after the battle had been completed and the city pacified, in which he had conducted himself honorably.

Now, therefore, your sons, deprived of their Father, commend to you, our spiritual Father, that you who began this road, who by your words caused all of us to abandon our lands and whatever was in them, who commanded us to follow Christ by carrying the cross, and who urged us to exalt the Christian name, should come to us and complete what you encouraged us to undertake; and that you should urge as many as you can to come with you [Col. 0554C].

For here the Christian name took its beginning. After blessed Peter had been enthroned in the chair which we see daily, those who had previously been called Galileans were here first and chiefly called Christians. What, then, could appear more proper in the world than that you, who are the Father and head of the Christian religion, should come to the principal and capital city of the Christian name and complete on your part the war which properly belongs to you?

We have defeated the Turks and pagans [Col. 0554D], but we were unable to defeat the heretical Greeks, Armenians, Syrians, and Jacobites. Therefore we send and send again this message to you, our dearest Father: come, Father, to the place of your fatherhood; you who are the vicar of Saint Peter, sit in the chair of Saint Peter and keep us, your sons, obedient to you in all right actions; eradicate and destroy by your authority and our strength all heresies, whatever nation they may belong to; and thus complete with us the road of Jesus Christ begun by us and preached by you. Open also for us the gates of both Jerusalems, and make the Lord’s tomb free and the Christian name exalted above all [Col. 0555A].

For if you come to us and complete with us the road begun by you, the whole world will obey you. May the living and reigning God cause you to do this, throughout the ages of ages. Amen [Note: [Col. 0555D] This does not appear in Fulcher.]

I have indeed been told one thing which is strongly contrary to God and to all Christians: that those signed with the holy cross have permission from you to remain among Christians. I am greatly surprised by this. Since you are the initiator of the holy journey, those who delay that holy journey ought not to receive counsel or anything good from you unless they complete the journey they began. We do not need you to disrupt the good work which you began; rather, by your arrival, and by that of all the good men whom you can bring with you, you should strengthen us [Col. 0555B].

For it is fitting that we, who by God’s help and your holy prayers have acquired all Romania, Cilicia, Asia, and Syria, should have you, after God, as our helper and supporter. You, most pious Father, ought in every respect to separate us, your sons obedient to you, from the unjust emperor, who promised us many good things but did none of them. Indeed, he inflicted upon us every evil and hindrance he was able to cause.

This letter was written on the eleventh day in September, in the fourth indiction [or seventh].

**II. Supplicatory petition of Theodoric, abbot, and the sons of the Church of Blessed Hubert of Andage, to Pope Urban against Wiredus, the intruder.**

(MARTEN., *Ampl. Collect.* IV, 1010.)

To the lord and universal Pope Urban: the sons of the Church of Blessed Hubert, who have suffered dispersion in the sight of God for the defense of the true faith and its legitimate apostolate [Col. 0555C].

While the Lord Jesus slept, the apostolic ship was tossed amid the waves in the middle of the sea; and now, while he likewise appears to delay, because our sins demand it, the unity of the holy Church is disturbed by schismatics, and amid the most bitter storms of persecution truth and justice are everywhere confounded.

After enduring the storm of this persecution without resistance for seven years, we have at last fled for refuge to the counsel of the Roman Church. We delayed doing so for a long time lest we should be a burden to you, since we had not been of any use to you.

After the death of our lord Henry, the legitimate bishop of Liège, a certain Otbert, by the gift of Henry, the aforesaid king, with whom he had been staying on campaign against the Roman Church, seized the bishopric; and he did so without the canonical election of clergy and people. Since he publicly boasted of being the supporter and defender of Guibert, the heresiarch, and rashly brought many things not belonging to our accusation into disorder against the sacred canons, it seemed to us, out of fear of God and reverence for your apostolate, that we should withdraw ourselves from subjection to him, since we could not resist his violence.

Taking some of our brothers with us, we withdrew to our cells which we possessed in the dioceses of Reims and Laon. There, meanwhile, through Lord Ragenold, bishop of Reims, and through the venerable Hugh, primate of Lyon and legate of this Roman Church, we were confirmed in the position which we held [Col. 0556A]. We provoked Otbert’s anger against us so greatly that he publicly excommunicated us as though we were disobedient to him and, after convening a tribunal of certain abbots and archdeacons of his, completely forbade us the office of abbot.

He then substituted in our place a certain young man from the monastery of Lobbes, without a regular election, and forcibly imposed him despite the opposition of the brothers. Because of this man’s youthful and therefore undisciplined conduct, during the nearly two years in which he presided, the ecclesiastical possessions were dissipated, and the religious observance which had flourished gloriously in that place also declined.

Thus, compelled by Duke Godfrey and other princes of the province, who were troubled by the dispersal of that place, Otbert expelled his appointee from it [Col. 0556B]. When the place was therefore open for our return, as we were returning to our brothers at their summons, Otbert became angry with us. On hearing that we were perhaps weakened, he forbade us a common burial if we should die, prohibited the abbey’s ministers from obeying us, and swore that, unless we withdrew, he would expel the monks, replace them with clerics, and divide the ecclesiastical possessions among his soldiers.

We, however, giving way to anger, and lamenting the danger threatening our Church to Lambert, bishop of Arras, and to our lord Rodulf, abbot of Verdun, and to many other men of sound counsel, finally reached this decision: of our own accord we would relinquish the pastoral staff and return it to the brothers in our place [Col. 0556C], lest, because of us, what we feared should happen to them.

Nevertheless, the following condition was attached to this relinquishment on the advice of the aforesaid men and confirmed in sealed letters: I consented to be deprived on the understanding that the common agreement of the brothers would elect in my place a certain Beringer, abbot of Saint-Laurent, who had previously been a monk of our monastery and appeared to defend the same position which we upheld.

We judged that this should be done so that Beringer, having been consecrated abbot by Lord Henry, the venerable pontiff, might avoid the necessity of receiving a second consecration from Otbert. When he absolutely refused to do this, and Otbert, weary of the delay, ordered the brothers to elect an abbot, and they jointly elected one of his men [Col. 0556D], Brother Wiredus—who had formerly left the monastery with us for the defense of the faith and had then been Otbert’s most vigorous opponent, and who had also voluntarily supported the aforesaid election—persuaded the elected man to remain at home for the time being, lest he contaminate the favor of his election by the gift of one who had been excommunicated.

Wiredus himself went to Otbert and, without our knowledge or that of the brothers, seized the abbey from Otbert’s hand, contrary to the election. But when his thoughts began to accuse one another, and he for some time held back from receiving consecration from Otbert, while Otbert, understanding this, repeatedly summoned him to be consecrated, the brothers opposed their communion and submission to him if he allowed himself to be consecrated by Otbert.

In addition to all that we have said above, a certain castle not far from the church was burdening it. Bishop Henry had destroyed it and had condemned it under perpetual anathema so that no one should rebuild it. Setting aside this anathema, Otbert restored it for the oppression of the monastery, and when the brothers carried the body of Blessed Hubert there in their own hands, as though to obtain mercy, he slaughtered them with his own hand, even to the shedding of blood [Col. 0557A].

Although Wiredus knew all these things about Otbert, he nevertheless feared losing the honor he had once seized. Changing the position which he had held with us, he disregarded the glory of God and sought his own; and thus, consecrated by Otbert against the will of the brothers, he violently thrust himself into the place of a father.

Because of this indignation, the brothers dispersed. When he pursued them with certain secular men hired, they fled for aid to the Churches of Reims and Laon. When he pursued them there as well, the matter of what had taken place between us was examined in the presence of our lord Manasse, bishop of Reims, and Engelram, bishop of Laon. By the decree of both, the following judgment was confirmed: we were to seek a hearing from the Roman See and await your judgment and justice concerning these matters.

We have therefore come here, moved by the counsel of many religious men, whose greatest expectation depends upon what they see in us, so that either, through our consolation, they may advance in defense of the true faith and your fidelity, or—God forbid—through our desolation and defection they too may fall away.

Therefore take thought for your justice, your reputation, and your authority; and do not allow the violence of the faithless or rebellious to grow through impunity [Note: [Col. 0557D] When this page of the complaint had been recited in the presence of Pope Urban and had been repeatedly and carefully discussed by the Romans, they expressed compassion for the abbot thus deprived because of his fidelity to the Roman Church. They decreed that W., unless he repented and withdrew from the place, should be excommunicated without delay. With the support of Rainer, who succeeded Urban in the pontificate, this sentence of excommunication was at that time postponed until the day appointed for the discussion between the parties, in case, when Wiredus arrived, a more certain hearing could be held concerning the matter. Since he remained at home, he was judged to have evaded the hearing assigned to him, as though conscious of guilt. Therefore, on the solemnity of All Saints, the pope pronounced the excommunication, and the letter of that excommunication was delivered in his presence.]

**III. Letter of the nuns of Blasilia in Auvergne to Pope Urban II** [Note: [Col. 0558D] See Book I of the *Genealogical History of the People of Auvergne*, chapter 1.]

(BALUZ., *Miscell.* Luc. edition, II, 181.)

To the most exalted lord, Pope Urban of the Roman Church: the humble flock of nuns, or clerics, of the monastery of Blasilla in the Lord offers the best grace and salvation, together with obedience and service to him in all things.

Let your apostolic and venerable dignity, lord Father, know and believe clearly that every day, on bended knees, we pray God to preserve you and yours safe and unharmed, and also to grant that your worthy and praiseworthy rule may flourish over and preside over the whole Church. [Col. 0557D] For your shield ought to be for us an invincible weapon and protection. The authority of your privilege ought forever to keep us safe and free from every servitude to others.

In former times, therefore, a certain noblewoman named Ermengard, countess and wife of Bernard, count of Poitou, established the monastery of Blasilla on her estates for her own salvation and that of both [utriusque sui: uncertain], and for the souls of her deceased sons—Warine, namely, and William—and endowed nuns serving God there with an inheritance from the surrounding fields, villages, and churches, from which they might live. Then she carefully travelled to Rome and granted that monastery, as its own right, to the blessed apostle Peter and to the bishop who at that time presided over the apostolic see. The pope, kindly approving this gift, decreed that five Poitevin soldi should be given once a year to Saint Peter; moreover, by the authority of an apostolic privilege, he permanently constituted that monastery an abbey of nuns, and sent us the altar that we still possess, consecrated by his own hand, [Col. 0558B] through that same noblewoman. In his own letters he also always marked out for us apostolic absolution and blessing for our benefactors, and excommunication and anathema, accusation and disturbance, for those who inflicted these upon us.

With these firmest decrees and constitutions, our monastery, built with all its appurtenances, long remained in peace and great prosperity. As soon as Rome, our head and our protection, began to be troubled and disturbed, the monks of La Chaise-Dieu rose up and, acting with the force and violence of a certain powerful man, Stephen of Mercœur, took from us, despite our opposition, the church of Saint Stephen the Protomartyr and of Saint Leo, pope of the city of Rome—the one whom the Romans blinded because Emperor Charles had chosen him—and whose body, as we believe, rests there. With the help of lord Durand, bishop of Clermont, they held it for as long as the aforesaid Stephen lived.

After his death, by judgment of the provost and abbot of Clermont, seven of our priests swore that the property was Saint Peter’s, as was the altar of Blasilla, and the bishop accepted this oath. Yet those monks, still rebellious, retain the right that they established through seven knights; and, by the bishop’s excommunication, they leave that church deprived and without ministry, while also placing its minister outside the church like a sacrilegious person.

Therefore we humbly and kindly ask and beseech you to do what your predecessors did, and to rescue from the invasion and seizure of the aforesaid monks the church that they loved and our monastery with all its possessions, and forever protect and defend us from servitude to everyone else. Farewell.

[Col. 0557] (See, among the writings soon to be published, the letters of Saint Anselm of Canterbury, Ivo of Chartres, Hugh of Lyons, Hugh of Cluny, Rainald of Reims, Lambert of Arras, and Geoffrey of Vendôme to Pope Urban.)

## [SERMONS.]

[Col. 0559]

## NOTICE CONCERNING THE FOLLOWING SERMONS OF URBAN

*(Histoire littéraire de la France, vol. VII, p. 546.)*

Some of Pope Urban’s speeches, whether whole or in part, have been collected; it is our purpose to provide an account of them. If people had taken care to transmit all those that he delivered during the course of his pontificate, there would doubtless be enough material for an entire volume. It is in fact known that he did not dedicate a church, or even simple altars, without addressing those present on some edifying subject. He acted in the same way at the opening of the councils over which he presided, and even spoke thus on various occasions while the same assembly was in progress.

Nevertheless, we possess very little of all these speeches, and perhaps none of them in its entirety. Only a very small fragment remains of the speech he delivered at the consecration of the high altar of the church of Cluny *(Clun. Bib. app., p. 98)*. One readily recognizes in it the gentleness of his style, and it is unfortunate that it was not printed in full.

Foucher of Chartres preserved for us a much more substantial portion of another speech that Urban delivered at the opening of the Council of Clermont *(FULC., Gest. Fr., book I, pp. 816–817)*; but he reports it only in a foreign style, which diminishes its merit. In it the author addresses the prelates of the assembly and, after setting before them the sad condition to which the Church had then been reduced, exhorts them passionately to apply an effective remedy, since they are the salt of the earth. Among the means most suitable for this purpose that he proposes, he insists chiefly upon good example, without which one rarely succeeds in recommending the practice of virtue and the avoidance of vice.

The same Foucher and the other historians of the crusade have preserved six or seven other speeches, or rather fragments of speeches, most of them delivered on the occasion of, and concerning the plan for, that great event which had so many consequences in this century, and still more in the two that followed. In reporting them, these historians imply, or even expressly say, that all were delivered at the Council of Clermont. But it is much more likely that most of them were delivered at other assemblies, such as that of Piacenza and those that followed it, whether in France or in Italy; for it is known that our pontiff preached the crusade everywhere from the time when it was solemnly resolved upon.

There are, however, three of these speeches that certainly were delivered at Clermont. This is shown by the fact that one is reported as such by William of Tyre, a judicious, exact, and faithful writer, and the other two by Baudri, then abbot of Bourgueil, and by Robert of Saint-Remy of Reims, who were members of the assembly. It would otherwise be very difficult to determine definitively which of the three preceded the others. But there seems to be no difficulty in recognizing them as three speeches distinct from one another, although we lack sufficient grounds for asserting that they are complete—at least those reported by William of Tyre and Baudri. As for the one reported by Abbot Robert, it is plainly only a fragment of a longer work *(ROB., Gest. Fr., book I, pp. 31–32)*.

This one appears to have been intended particularly for the French, whom the pope addresses and whose valor he greatly praises. It was in fact from them that he expected the greatest assistance for this great undertaking. The motives he employs are drawn from that same valor; from the reputation they had formerly acquired under Charlemagne and Louis the Pious; from the extreme sufferings endured by the faithful of the East, their brothers, under the tyranny of the Turks; from the holiness of the places that God had chosen for his inheritance and that Jesus Christ had consecrated by his presence, death, and burial; and finally from the merit they would gain through this expedition, in which they would find a sure means of expiating their sins.

The speech reported by Baudri *(Gest. Fr., book I, pp. 86–88)* is the same as the second printed in Baronius *(year 1095, nos. 43–49)* and in the General Collection of Councils *(vol. X, pp. 514–516)*, and as the first in the appendix to Dom Ruinart’s Life of Pope Urban *(Urb. Vit. app., pp. 369–373)*. It is one of the most prolix of all and begins with the words: “We have heard, dearly beloved brothers.” The motives that the pope sets forth to persuade his listeners are partly the same as those in the preceding speeches, but more extensive and treated more pathetically, with still others added. He speaks neither of valor nor of reputation, because he is not addressing a particular nation, as in the preceding speech, but all Christians generally, in the persons of those listening to him. In addition to the cruel oppression suffered by their brothers in the East, the profanation of the holy places, their ancient dignity, and the means of expiating their sins, he tells them that, by driving the Turks from Palestine, the crusaders will fulfill the figure of what happened among the Israelites when they destroyed the Jebusites. He flatters them with the hope of the spoils of the enemy of the Christian name—a motive, in any case, quite misplaced. Finally, he promises the crown of martyrdom to those who die in this war. Urban recalls there the miracle of the candles kindled by divine intervention and ends by exhorting the bishops and priests also to preach the crusade in their churches.

The style of this speech, as we possess it, represents our pontiff’s style quite naturally; from this it follows that there can be no doubt that it was recorded almost as he delivered it. We enter into these details only so that the speeches may be better distinguished from one another, and so that it may be judged that their diversity arises rather from their multiplicity than from the fact that each historian who reports them made the pope speak according to what seemed most plausible to him.

The speech copied by William of Tyre *(book I, no. 15)*—the same as the first in Baronius *(ibid., nos. 35–42)* and in the General Collection of Councils *(ibid., pp. 511–513)*, and the second in Dom Ruinart *(Urb. Vit. ibid., pp. 373–377)*—begins as follows: “You know, dearly beloved brothers.” The pope delivered it after the reading of the letter from the patriarch of Jerusalem, which Peter the Hermit had brought. The motives he employs are substantially the same as some in the preceding speeches, but differently expressed and sometimes supplied with more circumstances. Such, in particular, are the motives drawn from the consideration that the holy places were the Lord’s inheritance and from the oppression suffered there by Christians. Urban not only exhorts them but also commands them to undertake this holy war in order to obtain remission of their sins, promising the crusaders that both they and their possessions would be under the protection of the Holy See. The style of the speech appears very consistent with that of the other works of our pontiff.

[Col. 0561] William, monk of Malmesbury *(De Reg. Angl., book IV, chap. 2, pp. 131–132)*, incorporated a fourth speech into his History of the Kings of England, which was reprinted from him by Dom Ruinart *(Urb. Vit. ibid., pp. 377–381)*. This speech is the longest of all and differs greatly from the other three. But one does not recognize Pope Urban’s style in it. We must therefore say that the person reporting it paid attention only to the substance and did not copy it as it had been delivered. The pope begins by describing the flood of sins inundating Christendom, for which the war against the Turks would become the remedy, adding that the labors accompanying it are far greater than those required for committing sin. After this he enters into a detailed account of all the countries the Turks had invaded: Asia, Africa, Spain, the Balearic Islands, and contrasts these vast regions with the small territory occupied by Christians. He then contrasts the courage and valor of the Europeans with the cowardice and timidity of the Turks, and says a word in particular about the bravery of the French. But he dwells chiefly on raising the crusaders above the fear of death, even inspiring them with contempt for it and making them regard it as a great advantage, and he ends by fixing their departure for the following spring.

Guibert, abbot of Nogent *(Gest. Fr., book II, chap. 2)*, presents a fifth speech by our pope, again different from all the others. He is right to warn that, if he does not report it as it was delivered, it nevertheless contains what Urban intended to establish in it. Indeed, it is obvious that this is not the manner in which that pontiff expressed himself. Instead of the clear, flowing, natural style that was his, this is confused, harsh, and affected. The motives that the author advances in this speech are drawn from the excellence of the Church of Jerusalem above all others, as their mother; from the example of the Maccabees, who so generously endured many battles on behalf of their nation and its temple; from the almost complete extinction of Christianity in the East; from the hope of restoring it there and repopulating that part of the world with Christians in order to combat the Antichrist, who was to arise there; and finally from the crushing contributions demanded from the few Christians who remained there, and the cruel outrages inflicted upon those who went to visit the holy places. The author dwells principally on these last two motives, and especially on the final one, which he treats in a detail implying horrible cruelties on the part of the Turks.

“Frizon *(Gall. purp., pp. 20–22)* and François du Chesne *(History of All the French Cardinals, vol. II, pp. 43–44)* present a sixth speech, which they drew from the Chronicle of John Nauclerus, but which appears to have been unknown to all the ancient historians of the crusade. In any case, it differs from all the others not only in its subject matter but also in the order and manner of its expression. There is none in which there is so much elegance and such grand strokes of eloquence. Its opening indicates that it was delivered at the Council of Clermont; this also appears from what follows in the speech. After a brief but vivid description of the unheard-of sufferings that the Turks and Saracens inflicted upon the Christians of the region and upon those who came there from elsewhere on pilgrimage, Urban proceeds to enumerate the various regions of Europe that these unbelievers had ravaged: Spain, part of Aquitaine, and Italy as far as Rome. Then, addressing the principal Christian nations—the French, Germans, Saxons, Poles, Hungarians, and others—he points out to them that their countries would already have undergone the same fate without the empire of Constantinople, which served them as a kind of defensive wall and sheltered them from the same incursions. The pope has also introduced into this speech the motive of spoils taken from the enemy. He ends by granting plenary indulgence to those who take the cross and assuring them that both they and their possessions will be under the protection of the Roman Church.

“Foucher of Chartres *(ibid., pp. 817–818)*, following the example of the other historians of the crusade, also inserted in his work a portion of a speech by Urban on this subject. But the style of this shapeless piece bears no resemblance to the manner of expression of our pontiff, although the motives employed in it are found, though expressed somewhat differently, in the other speeches we have just discussed. One cannot therefore avoid judging that this piece was composed afterward from Urban’s other speeches, either by Foucher himself or by someone else who communicated it to him. It is the same piece, but somewhat abbreviated, that is reported by the anonymous author *(Gest. Dei per Fr., vol. I, p. 561)*, who, in Bongars’s collection, follows immediately after Abbot Guibert.

“Peter Tudebode *(Gest. Fr., book I, p. 777)*, another historian of the crusade, cites a simple passage that is found somewhat more fully in the anonymous work published by Dom Mabillon *(Mus. It., vol. I, p. 139)*, as forming part of our pope’s speech at the Council of Clermont. But this passage, as it is reported, is not found in any of the preceding speeches.” Louis Jacob, author of the *Pontifical Library* *(book I, p. 222)*, asserted that one of these speeches is found in the chronicle of Berthold of Constance. But if he had looked more closely, he would have seen that there is none.

[Col. 0561]

# THE SERMONS OF POPE URBAN II

## I. SERMON AFTER THE CONSECRATION OF THE CHURCH OF CLUNY

*(Bibliotheca Cluniac., 518.)*

[Col. 0561] In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1095, indiction 3, on the eighth day before the Kalends of November, lord and venerable Pope Urban II consecrated the first and largest altar of our new monastery in honor of God and in memory of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul. He also personally consecrated [Col. 0562] the second altar, that of the morning Mass. The archbishop of Lyons, Hugh; the archbishop of Pisa, Daibert; and Bruno, bishop of Signi, consecrated three altars in the monastery itself on that same day, at the pope’s command, in the first three choir screens. Then, while consecrating and celebrating Mass, after other exhortations concerning salvation, [Col. 0563A] the pope delivered the following speech to the people in the presence of the bishops, cardinals, and many others:

“Holy Fathers and our elders, the Roman pontiffs who have presided over the holy apostolic see, from the time when Cluny was established and this monastery founded, have loved, cherished, and cared for this place and its rulers and inhabitants with particular devotion. And rightly so. For that pious William, formerly the founder of this monastery, entrusted its care and protection to no advocate, patron, king, or prince, but only to God and blessed Peter and his vicars, namely, the Roman pontiffs. Among their number and succession divine favor, though I am unworthy, has joined me, formerly a monk and prior of this monastery under lord and venerable Hugh, who by God’s mercy still survives and prospers.

“Therefore, just as the supreme pontiffs before me succeeded one another in the apostolic see, so they also succeeded one another in protecting and caring for this place with particular devotion. Yet none of them has until now visited this place in his bodily presence. To me, however, as you see at this moment, divine mercy has granted that privilege. Indeed, among the other reasons that moved us to visit Gaul, this was the first and chief: that by our presence we might gladden this place and this congregation, bound to us by a special kinship; that by our arrival and our address we might assist them; and that we might devote our labor to their every advantage and benefit.

“Thus, present here with you today, we consecrate the first and largest altar, together with the others that have been prepared, of this new monastery, [Col. 0563C] and we encourage your hearts toward the remaining construction of the same monastery. It also pleases us—and we urge you to let it please you, for this appears both good and just—to assign on every side certain limits of immunity and security around this place, which ought to be held in veneration and good care by you and by all other Christians, and to establish these limits as the boundary of the sacred ban.

“Within these boundaries, no person, whatever his condition or power, shall ever dare or attempt to make any great or small invasion, or to set fire, or to carry off booty or plunder, or to abduct a person, or to strike anyone on the road, or—which is much graver—to commit homicide or [Col. 0563D] mutilate a person’s limbs, since sacred authority forbids it.

“Therefore, these are the boundaries of the sacred ban. Toward Berzé, the boundary is at the crossroads this side of Sarrat; from there one road comes to Cluny and the other goes to Mâcon. On the road toward Beaulieu, the boundary is opposite the crossroads situated above the cellarer of Cluny’s mill, this side of Viengues. Beyond Cluny toward Mâcon, the boundary is at the crossroads from which one road leads to Mâcon and the other to Saint Mary of the Woods. Above Rufiaco, the boundary is at the summit of the fortified place, at the crossroads from which one road leads to Bezorgny and the other to Carelle. Toward Saitg, the boundary is within the crossroads, this side of the place called Adturgum. On the road toward the territory of Chalon, the boundary is at the great Cassania above Marziac. Toward Brancedun, the boundary is on the road above Bosc Banned. Toward Trinorch, the boundary is on the stream called Long Water, between Blanosc and Donziac. Toward Perron or Laziac, [Col. 0564B] the boundary is at the Three Beeches, where our wood of Cluny and the count’s wood are divided. Toward Igiac, the boundary is at Carmos, on the middle mountain.

“We therefore establish these boundaries of the sacred ban for this monastery of Cluny, and likewise for the village and borough; we assign these limits with full certainty, commanding in the name of the Lord God almighty and by the authority of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul, and calling upon all of you and every person who shall read or hear this, that you knowingly do not violate this ban, but that each and all of you observe its law.

“If anyone knowingly violates it in any one of the matters forbidden above, and, after being summoned by the abbot, prior, chamberlain, or dean of the Cluniac community, and granted whatever period of grace they deem appropriate, does not make suitable satisfaction and repair the offense, then, whoever he may be, he shall be subject to excommunication. Moreover, if any of you are summoned by the abbot or brothers against such a person, you shall be obliged to restrain him and compel him to make amends. Anyone excommunicated for breaking the ban shall be absolved once he has made suitable satisfaction.

“The law of this ban is established not only for you who are present, but also for all who are absent, and for your sons and descendants.

“But let us now consider the conclusion of the matter for which we are striving. All who do harm to this place of Cluny and act unjustly against this congregation shall be worthy of anathema and shall be struck by the sword of blessed Peter until they have made suitable amends. But all who do good to this place of Cluny, act rightly toward this congregation, [Col. 0564D] and preserve peace, may obtain forever the grace and mercy of Christ, our Lord and God, and have the blessed apostles Peter and Paul, first and foremost, as their helpers before God. Amen.”

## II. ADDRESS TO IVON AFTER HIS CONSECRATION

[Col. 0563]

[Col. 0563D] “Since, as we believe, the clergy and people of that city, summoned by the divine will, unanimously elected you as their ruler, and brought you all the way to us asking that you be consecrated bishop, and since, with God’s consent, you have been consecrated bishop through the laying on of our hands, know now, dearest brother, that you have taken upon yourself a very great burden of labor: the responsibility of governing souls, serving the interests of many, becoming the least and servant of all, and rendering an account on the day of divine judgment for the talent entrusted to you.

“For if our Savior said, ‘I did not come to be served, but to serve,’ and laid down his life for his sheep (Matthew 20), how much more ought we, idle servants of the supreme master of the household, with the greatest exertion, labor to lead the Lord’s sheep entrusted to us by the supreme Shepherd into the Lord’s fold, with the help of divine grace, without sickness and without blemish [macula]?

“We therefore exhort your affection to keep undefiled and inviolable the faith that we briefly and clearly set forth at the beginning of your consecration, because faith is the foundation of all virtues. We know that from infancy you have been instructed in sacred letters and taught the ordinances of the canons; nevertheless, a brief address from us must be directed to you.

“Let no favor exalt you, and let no adversity wear you down—that is, let not your heart be lifted up in prosperity, nor be cast down in any way by adversity. Rather, we wish you to act in all things cautiously and with discretion, so that you may be proved to live without reproach before everyone.

“May the Holy Trinity guard your fraternity with its protection, so that, when you have fulfilled in our Lord, with such moderation, the burden you have undertaken, you may on the day of eternal recompense deserve to hear him say: ‘Well done, good and faithful servant: because you have been faithful over a few things, I will set you over many things; enter into the joy of your lord’ (Matthew 25).”

## III. ADDRESSES DELIVERED AT THE COUNCIL OF CLERMONT  
### Concerning the Expedition to Jerusalem

[Col. 0565]

## I.

*(From volume X of Labbe’s Councils, col. 514, and D. Ruinart, Life of Urban, Appendix, p. 369.)*

[Col. 0565B]

“We have heard, dearly beloved brothers—and you have heard it as well—that we cannot discuss this without profound sobs: with what calamities, what hardships, what dreadful afflictions our Christians, our brothers, the members of Christ, are scourged, oppressed, and abused in Jerusalem, Antioch, and the other cities of the eastern region. They are our true brothers, your companions and your kindred—for you too belong to the same Christ and are sons of the same God. In their own hereditary homes they are enslaved by foreign masters, or driven from them; they beg among you; or, what is more grievous, they wander as exiles and suffer blows for sale in their own patrimonies. Christian blood, redeemed by Christ’s blood, is poured out, and Christian flesh, kindred to Christ, is enslaved to unspeakable follies and wicked servitudes.

“In those cities there is mourning everywhere, misery everywhere, groaning everywhere. I say this with a sigh: the churches in which divine sacrifices were once celebrated—alas! behold, they are now stables for animals. Wicked men have occupied the holy cities. Filthy and unclean Turks rule over our brothers. Blessed Peter presided as bishop at Antioch; behold, in that very Church the gentiles have installed their superstitions and have shamefully expelled the Christian religion, which they ought above all to have honored, from the hall dedicated to God.

[Col. 0565D] “The estates assigned for the support of the saints, and the noble patrimonies entrusted for sustaining the poor, have been subjected to pagan tyranny, and their cruel masters abuse them after turning them to their own uses. God’s priesthood has been trampled into the ground; God’s sanctuary has everywhere been profaned by sacrilege. If any Christians still lie hidden there, you have heard how they are sought out with tortures.

“Of holy Jerusalem, brothers . . . . . we have refrained from speaking, because we greatly fear to speak of it, since that city in which, as you all know, Jesus Christ suffered for us, because of the demands of our sins, has been reduced beneath the filth of the pagans and, to our shame, withdrawn from the service of God. What little remains of our empire is a disgrace to us Christians, who have deserved these things.

“To whom does the church of blessed Mary now belong, the church in which she herself was buried in the Valley of Jehoshaphat? But why do we pass over the temple of Solomon—or rather, of the Lord—in which barbarous nations now venerate their idols, placed there contrary to right and law? We refrain from recalling the Lord’s sepulchre because you have seen with your own eyes to what great abomination it has been handed over.

“From there they violently remove the offerings that you have so often brought for its worship. There, indeed, they heap upon our religion countless and innumerable mockeries. And yet in that place—what I say I know well—God rested; there he died for us. Nor does God fail each year to perform a miracle there: on the days of his Passion, after all the lights in the sepulchre and throughout the surrounding church have been extinguished, the extinguished lamps are rekindled by divine radiance. Whose breast, turned to stone, would not be softened by so great a miracle? Believe me, the man whose heart is not struck by such an immediate divine power toward faith is bestial and dull-witted; and yet, although gentiles and Christians alike see this, they are not reformed.

“They are indeed terrified, but they are not converted to the faith; and this is not surprising, because blindness of mind dominates them. You yourselves know best how many afflictions they have inflicted upon you who are here and have returned, you who sacrificed your possessions and your blood to God there.

“We have said these things, brothers, so that we may have you yourselves as witnesses to our speech. There are still more sufferings of our brothers and devastations of God’s churches that we could recount individually; but tears and groans press upon us, and sighs and sobs press upon us. Let us weep, brothers—come, let us weep—and, weeping from the depths of our being with the Psalmist, let us lament: miserable and wretched are we, in whose time this prophecy of God has been fulfilled:
