“‘O God, the nations have entered into your inheritance; they have defiled your holy temple; they have made Jerusalem a place for guarding fruit. They have given the corpses of your servants as food to the birds of the sky, and the flesh of your saints to the beasts of the earth. They have poured out their blood like water around Jerusalem, and there was no one to bury them’ (Psalm 78).

“Woe to us, brothers, who have now become a reproach to our neighbors, a mockery and derision to those around us (ibid.). Let us grieve and sympathize with our brothers, at least in our tears. We, who have become the rejected of the people and worse than all others, let us mourn the monstrous devastation of the most holy land.

“Rightly do we call it holy land, for there is not even a footprint that has not been illumined and sanctified either by the body or shadow of the Savior, or by the glorious presence of the holy Mother of God, or by the embrace-worthy passage of the apostles, or by the blood of the martyrs, which must be drunk. How blessed, O Stephen the Protomartyr, were the stones that crowned you with laurel! How happy then, O John the Baptist, were the waters of the Jordan that served you in baptizing the Savior!

“The sons of Israel, led out from Egypt, who prefigured you by crossing the Red Sea, won that land for themselves by arms under the leadership of Jesus; they expelled the Jebusites and other foreigners from it, and cultivated the earthly Jerusalem in the likeness of the heavenly Jerusalem.

“What we say, brothers, hear and understand. You, girded with the belt of military service, with great arrogance tear your brothers apart and cut one another to pieces. This is not the army of Christ, which destroys the Redeemer’s fold. The holy Church has reserved military service for the assistance of her own—if we speak the truth—and we ought to be its heralds.

“You are not truly following the road by which you may proceed to salvation and life. You are oppressors of orphans, plunderers of widows, murderers, sacrilegious men, robbers of what belongs to others; you await the pay of brigands for shedding Christian blood, and, just as vultures scent corpses, so you anticipate and pursue wars in distant lands. Certainly this is the worst possible road, because it is utterly removed from God.

“Therefore, if you wish your souls to be cared for, lay down the belt of this kind of military service as quickly as possible, and hasten to defend the Church of the East. For from her have flowed the joys of your entire salvation; she poured into your mouths the breasts of divine milk and gave us the sacred teachings of the Gospels.

“We say these things, brothers, so that you may restrain your murderous hands from fratricide, oppose yourselves for the sake of the faith to foreign nations, and, under Jesus Christ as your leader, let the Christian army—an invincible army—fight better than the ancient Israelites for your Jerusalem, and attack and conquer the Turks who are in it, more wicked than the Jebusites.

“May it be a beautiful thing for you to die for Christ in that city in which Christ died for you. But if it should happen that you die earlier, consider it the same as dying on the road, provided that Christ finds you in his own army. For God is the rewarder of the denarius at both the first and the sixth hour.

“It is dreadful, brothers, dreadful, for you to extend your greedy hand against Christians. To brandish the sword against the Saracens is a singular good, because it is love to lay down one’s life for one’s brothers. And so that you may not be anxious about tomorrow’s outcomes, know that those who fear God lack nothing, nor do those who love him in truth.

“The resources of our enemies will also be yours, for you will strip their treasures, and either return home victorious or, purpled with your own blood, obtain an everlasting prize. You ought to serve such an emperor, one for whom bread cannot fail and for whom no rewards of service are lacking.

“The road is short, and the labor very great, yet it will bring you an unfading crown. Now, therefore, let us speak with prophetic authority:

“‘Gird yourself, every man, with your sword upon your thigh, O most powerful one’ (Psalm 44).

“Gird yourselves, gird yourselves, I say, and be powerful sons, for ‘it is better for us to die in battle than to see the evils of our nation and of the holy places’ (1 Maccabees 3).

“Let not the seductive allurements of women and of your possessions soothe you into staying away; nor let the hardships that must be endured frighten you into remaining behind.”

You, brothers and fellow bishops, fellow priests and fellow heirs of Christ, announce this very thing throughout the churches entrusted to you, and preach the way to Jerusalem to everyone with full voice. Those who confess their ignorance of their sins should confidently obtain swift forgiveness through Christ. You who are going to depart will have us as your intercessors; let us have you as fighters for the people of God. Our task is to pray; yours is to fight against the Amalekites. We shall stretch out our tireless hands with Moses, praying toward heaven; you, fearless warriors, draw and brandish the sword against Amalek. Amen.

## II.

*(Council, same place, col. 501; D. Ruinart, same place, p. 373.)*

You know, dearest brothers—and it is expedient that your charity should know it too—how the Restorer of the human race, assuming flesh for the salvation of us all and living as a human being among human beings, illumined by his own presence the promised land which he had long ago promised to the patriarchs, and rendered it especially distinguished both by the works of the dispensation he had assumed and by the frequent display of miracles. For this is taught by the sequence of both the Old and the New Testament in almost every syllable.

It is certainly established, by a particular privilege of love, that he loved this land, so much so that he deigned to call it a portion—indeed, a fragment—of the world his inheritance, although the whole earth and its fullness belong to him. Hence through Isaiah he says: “Israel is my inheritance” (Isaiah 14). And again: “The vineyard of the Lord of hosts is the house of Israel” (Isaiah 5). Although from the beginning he consecrated the whole land to himself as a special portion, he nevertheless adopted the holy city more particularly as his own, as the prophet bears witness, saying: “The Lord loves the gates of Zion above all the dwelling-places of Jacob” (Psalm 86). Of this city glorious things are proclaimed: namely, that in it the Savior, teaching, suffering, and rising again, accomplished salvation in the midst of the earth. From the ages it was chosen to be conscious of and a familiar chamber for such great mysteries. It was chosen, certainly, because he who chose it himself testifies, saying: “And from Jerusalem, the city which I chose, a Savior will come to you.”

Although, because the sins of its inhabitants demanded it, the Lord has often permitted it in his just judgment to be delivered into the hands of the wicked, and has allowed it for a time to bear the yoke of harsh servitude, it must not therefore be thought that he cast it away as though he had rejected it. For it is written: “The Lord scourges every son whom he receives” (Hebrews 12); but to the one of whom it is said, “My zeal has departed from you; I will no longer be angry with you” (Ezekiel 16), he stores up wrath.

He loves it, therefore, and the fervor of his love for it has not grown cold, for he says to it: “You shall be a crown of glory in the hand of the Lord and a royal diadem in the hand of your God; and you shall no longer be called Forsaken, but you shall be called My Delight, because the Lord has been pleased with you” (Isaiah 62).

Yet these cradles of our salvation, the Lord’s homeland, the mother of religion, are violently possessed by a godless people—the son of the Egyptian slave-woman—and, having enslaved the freeborn children, impose upon them the harshest conditions, although in turn they deservedly ought to have been subject to them.

But what is written? “Cast out the slave-woman and her son” (Genesis 21). For the impious race of the Saracens, followers of worldly traditions, has for many years now oppressed the holy places—where the Lord’s feet stood—with violent tyranny. Having subdued the faithful and condemned them to servitude, dogs have entered the holy places; the sanctuary has been profaned; the people who worship God have been humbled; the chosen race suffers shameful forced labor; the royal priesthood serves in mud and brick; the city of God, once mistress of provinces, has become tributary.

Whose soul would not melt? Whose inward parts would not waste away when these things return to the mind? Who can hear such things with dry eyes, dearest brothers? The temple of the Lord—from which the zealous Lord drove out the sellers and buyers lest it become the den of thieves belonging to his Father—has become a seat of demons. This very circumstance also inflamed Mattathias the high priest, the ancestor of the holy Maccabees, to commendable zeal, as he himself bears witness, saying: “The temple of the Lord has become like a dishonorable man; its vessels of glory have been carried away captive” (1 Maccabees 2).

The city of the King of all kings, which handed on to others the rules of undefiled faith, is compelled unwillingly to serve the superstitions of the nations. The church of the Holy Resurrection, the resting-place of the sleeping Lord, endures their rule; it is defiled by the impurities of those who will have no share in the resurrection but will be assigned, like stubble, to the everlasting fires of eternal punishment.

The venerable places devoted to divine mysteries, which received the Lord as a guest in the flesh, saw his signs and experienced his benefits, and which display within themselves the full evidence of all these things in firm faith, have become sheepfolds and stables for beasts of burden. The praiseworthy people whom the Lord of hosts blessed groan, exhausted beneath the burden of forced labor and filthy exactions. Their sons—the dear pledges of Mother Church—are seized so that they may serve the impurities of the nations; they are compelled either to deny the name of the living God or to blaspheme it with sacrilegious lips. Those who detest their impious commands are cut down by the sword like two-year-old sheep, to be joined to the holy martyrs. For the sacrilegious there is no distinction between places, no regard for persons. Priests and Levites are killed in the sanctuaries; virgins are forced into prostitution or compelled to perish under torture; even more mature age does not protect married women.

Woe to us, who have descended into the misery of so perilous a time! Foreseeing it in the spirit, David, chosen by the Lord, the faithful king, laments, saying: “O God, the nations have entered into your inheritance; they have defiled your holy temple” (Psalm 78). And again: “They have humbled your people and afflicted your inheritance. Why, Lord, are you angry forever? Shall your wrath burn like fire?” (Psalm 93.) “Where are your ancient mercies, Lord?” (Psalm 88.) Is it true what is said: “God will not forget to show mercy; he will not restrain his mercies in his anger”? “Remember, Lord, what has happened to us; look and see our disgrace” (Lamentations 5). Woe to us! Why were we born—to see the corruption of our people and the ruin of the holy city, and to sit there while the holy things are delivered into the hands of enemies? (1 Maccabees 2.)

Therefore, beloved, arm yourselves with the zeal of God; let each one gird his sword upon his thigh most mightily (Psalm 44). Gird yourselves and be mighty sons, for it is better for us to die in battle than to see the evils of our people and of the holy places (1 Maccabees 3). If anyone has zeal for the law of God, let him join us. Let us aid our brothers; let us break their bonds and cast their yoke from us (Psalm 2).

Go forth, and the Lord will be with you. The weapons which you have illicitly stained with one another’s blood, turn against the enemies of the faith and of the Christian name. Theft, arson, robbery, murder, and all the other deeds by which those who commit them will not possess the kingdom of God—redeem these through this service pleasing to God, so that these works of piety and the prayers of the saints offered for you may obtain swift forgiveness for the offenses by which you provoked the Lord to anger.

We therefore admonish and exhort you in the Lord, and impose upon you, for the remission of sins, that, sympathizing with the affliction and labors of our brothers and fellow heirs of the heavenly kingdom who dwell in Jerusalem and its territories, you check with due punishment the insolence of the unbelievers who strive to subject kingdoms, principalities, and powers to themselves, and that you confront with all your strength those whose purpose is to destroy the Christian name. Otherwise it will soon happen that the Church of God, bearing the yoke of unlawful servitude, will suffer loss of faith, as the superstition of the gentiles prevails.

Some among you know in what great affliction they are placed, for they have seen with their own eyes the things of which we speak; and the letter brought to us by the hand of the venerable Peter, who is present, makes their present condition known. We, relying on the mercy of God and the authority of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul, release from the immense penances owed for their sins all faithful Christians who take up arms against them and assume upon themselves the burden of this pilgrimage.

Those who die there in true repentance should have no doubt that they will obtain both forgiveness of sins and the reward of eternal recompense. Meanwhile, those who, fired by the ardor of faith, undertake this labor to conquer them, we receive as sons of true obedience under the protection of the Church and of the blessed Peter and Paul; and we decree that they shall remain secure from every disturbance, both in their property and in their persons.

But if anyone should rashly dare to harass them, let him be struck with excommunication by the bishop of the place, and let the sentence be observed by all until both what was taken has been restored and suitable satisfaction has been made for the damage inflicted.

But bishops and priests who do not firmly resist such acts shall be punished by suspension from office until they obtain the mercy of the apostolic see.

## III.

*(From William of Malmesbury, book IV, chapter 2, p. 74.)*

You recall, dearest brothers, the many things spoken to you in these days, some commanded and some forbidden in our council. The chaotic and confused mass of crimes demanded an interval of many days; an old disease required cautery. For while, with the indulgent rope of mercy, we loosen the line, many things have offended the duty of our apostolate which it ought to cut away, and none which it ought to spare.

Let it have been human weakness, then, that you sinned; that, lulled to sleep by the wrappings of temptations, you provoked heavenly mercy by treating lightly the suspended anger. Let it have been worldly drunkenness, that, disregarding lawful marriages, you did not consider the injury done to another’s marriage-bed. Let it have been excessive greed, that, ensnaring your brothers—who were bought by that great and identical price—as each of you could, you shamefully drained them of their money.

Now, as you stand amid these shipwrecks of sin, a harbor of peaceful rest is opened to you, if only you do not neglect it: for a small labor against the Turks, in a brief undertaking, an everlasting station of salvation will be repaid to you. Compare the labors you endured in practicing crimes with those you are going to endure on the journey I command.

The contemplation of adultery or murder produces many fears—for, as Solomon says, nothing is more fearful than wickedness (Wisdom 17)—and many labors; for what is more laborious than injustice? “But whoever walks simply walks confidently” (Proverbs 10:9). The outcome of those labors and fears was sin. “The wages of sin is death” (Romans 6:23), and “the death of sinners is most evil” (Psalm 33:22).

Now an equal labor and fear are demanded of you for a better price. The cause of these labors will be charity, if, admonished by the Lord’s command, you lay down your lives for your brothers (1 John 3:16); the wage of charity will be the grace of God, and eternal life will follow the grace of God.

Go, therefore, happily; go confidently to pursue the enemies of God. For they have long ago—what enormous shame for Christians!—occupied Syria, Armenia, and finally all of Asia Minor, whose provinces are Bithynia, Phrygia, Galatia, Lydia, Caria, Pamphylia, Isauria, Lycia, and Cilicia. Now they insolently trouble Illyricum and all the lands farther south, as far as the sea called the Arm of Saint George.

What shall we say of the fact that they claim for themselves the Lord’s tomb, the unique pledge of faith, and sell our pilgrims entrance to that city, which ought to be open to Christians alone if any trace of their customary valor remained in them? This alone would suffice to burden our brows with shame. But who, unless utterly inactive or envious of Christian glory, can bear the fact that we have not divided the world equally?

They inhabit Asia, the third part of the world, as their hereditary nest. Our ancestors rightly judged it equal to the remaining two parts both in the length of its regions and in the greatness of its provinces. There the branches of our devotion once put forth shoots; there all the apostles except two consecrated their deaths. There now the worshipers of Christ, if any survive, eking out a famine on poor farming, pay tribute to those impious men, or with silent sighs long for your liberty, because they have lost their own.

They hold Africa, another part of the world, possessed by arms for two hundred years and more. I declare this a danger to Christian honor because that land was once the nurse of brilliant minds, and through divine writings it will repel every mark of antiquity from itself so long as there is anyone who reads Latin letters. The learned know what I mean.

Europe remains as the third climate of the world. We Christians inhabit only a very small part of it; for who would call all that barbarism Christian which inhabits the frozen Ocean in distant islands and lives like beasts?

The Turks and Saracens therefore oppress this small portion of our world by war. For three hundred years now they have subjugated Spain and the Balearic Islands, and in their hope they devour what remains—utterly sluggish men who, lacking the confidence to fight at close quarters, prefer a war of flight.

A Turk never dares to engage in hand-to-hand combat; driven from his position, he stretches his bowstring from a distance and entrusts his wounds to the winds. And because his arrows are drunk with deadly poison, it is not valor but venom that brings death to the man he strikes. Whatever he does, therefore, I would attribute to fortune, not courage—to flight and poison rather than combat [variant: “to flight and poison”].

It is plainly established that every people born in that region, dried out by the excessive heat of the sun, has indeed more intelligence but less blood; and therefore they flee close combat, because they know that they have little blood. By contrast, a people born amid the frosts of the north and removed from the sun’s heat is less prudent, certainly, but, proud of its abundant and luxuriant blood, fights with the greatest readiness.

You are a people born in the more temperate regions of the world. You are both lavish with blood, scorning death and wounds, and not lacking in prudence; for you preserve discipline in the camp and employ deliberation in battle. Therefore, endowed with knowledge and courage, undertake a memorable journey, to be proclaimed throughout all ages if you rescue your brothers from danger. To those present I command in God’s name; to those absent I give orders.

Since you are going to defend Christianity, let them mark their garments with the sign of the cross, so that outwardly they may display their love for the inward faith. By God’s grant and through the privilege of blessed Peter, they will possess the absolution of all crimes; and in the meantime let them lighten the labor of the journey with this joy, knowing that after death they will receive the reward of blessed martyrdom.

Therefore, putting an end to crimes, so that at least in these regions Christians may be permitted to conquer peacefully, go forth, pouring into a more just battle that strength and prudence which you have been accustomed to possess in civil conflict. Go, soldiers worthy of praise throughout the world; go and overthrow the cowardly nations. Let the renowned valor of the Franks, together with the peoples attached to them, rouse the whole world by the mere terror of its name.

But why do I delay you longer by diminishing in words the strength of the gentiles? Rather, set this divine saying before your minds: “Narrow is the way that leads to life” (Matthew 7:14). Let the path of travelers therefore be narrow, full of deaths and fraught with dangers; nevertheless, this same path will lead you to your lost homeland, for “through many tribulations we must enter the kingdom of God.”

Consider in your hearts crosses, if you are seized; consider chains and, finally, whatever tortures can be inflicted. Endure dreadful punishments for the strength of your faith, so that, if necessary, at the cost of your bodies you may bring healing to your souls. Do not fear death, bravest men, outstanding in courage and boldness. Certainly, human wickedness will be unable to devise anything against you for which the glory above may be an adequate recompense.

“For the sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the future glory that will be revealed in us” (Romans 8:18). Do you not know that for human beings life is calamity and death happiness? This teaching, if you remember it, was poured into you with your mothers’ milk through the word of the priests; your forefathers, the martyrs, displayed it by their example.

Death frees souls from their foul prison, so that according to their merits they may fly to their proper place. Death hastens the good toward their homeland; death cuts off evil from the guilty. Through death, therefore, liberated souls either rejoice in delights, anticipating better things in hope, or enjoy punishments, fearing nothing worse.

But while they are entangled in the bonds of their bodies, they draw from them the contagions of earthly things and, as someone might truly say, are dead. For what is of clay does not fit well with what is heavenly, nor what is divine with what is mortal.

Yet the soul, even now joined to the body, can accomplish very much: it gives life to its instrument, moving it secretly and carrying its actions beyond mortal nature. Nevertheless, when it has been released from the burden by which it is dragged toward earth and has received its proper place, it shares a blessed strength, free in every respect, communicating in some manner with the invisibility of the divine nature.

Thus, fulfilling a twofold office, it supplies life to the body when it is present, but causes its transformation when it departs. You see how pleasantly the soul keeps watch in a sleeping body and, withdrawn from the senses, foresees many future things because of its divine kinship.

Why, then, do you fear death, you who love the rest of sleep, which is like death? It is surely madness, for the sake of a brief life, to begrudge yourselves eternity. Rather, dearest brothers, if it should happen, lay down your lives for your brothers; empty the sanctuary of God of the impious, drive out the robbers, and bring in the devout. Let no affection of kinship restrain you, because the first human devotion is devotion to God.

Let no love of your native soil impede you, because, from different perspectives, the whole world is exile and the whole world is homeland to a Christian—so that exile is homeland and homeland exile. Let the extent of your inheritances not delay you, because what is promised is greater; nor let those things flatter the wretched with empty hope or soothe the idle mind with the lazy medicine of possessions, but let what is displayed by frequent examples and confirmed by constant use guide you.

These things are sweet, certainly, but fleeting, and, together with their seasons, they bring a hundredfold price. This I declare; this I command; and I set the deadline at the beginning of next spring. God will be present with those who go, so that the year may smile favorably upon them, both with abundance of crops and with fair weather.

Those who are going to die will enter the banquet hall of heaven; those who are going to live will see the Lord’s tomb. And what greater happiness could there be than for a person living on earth to see those places in which the Lord of heaven lived as a human being? Happy are those who are called to these duties, so that they may obtain those rewards; fortunate are those who contemplate these battles, so that they may attain those prizes.

## IV.

*(D. Ruinart, *Life of Urban*, Appendix, p. 381, from the *History of Italy* of Jerome Briani, book VII.)*

I give the greatest thanks to God because you show that you are going to take up arms for Christ your Redeemer with such unanimity of soul and eagerness. We, for our part, relying on the mercy of God and the authority of the blessed Peter and Paul, so far as we can assist your zeal, release from all penances for their sins all who go forth to this war. We receive them as sons of true obedience under the protection of the Church and the patronage of the blessed Peter and Paul, and decree that they shall be safe from every harassment of body and property.

## V.

*(Duchesne, *Script. Franc.*, IV, 816; Fulcher of Chartres, *History of Jerusalem*, book I, chapter 1.)*

Dearest brothers, by God’s permission placed at the head of the world as the supreme apostle, and with a necessary occasion presenting itself, I, Urban, have come down to these regions to you as an envoy of divine admonition. Those whom I judged to be stewards of God’s mysteries, I wished to find equally faithful, once the foulness of hypocrisy had been driven off.

If anything crooked or twisted stands against the law of God, after the modesty of rational justice has been set aside, I shall diligently strive to set it right, with divine assistance present. For the Lord has appointed you stewards over his household, so that you may provide it with food seasoned with a moderate flavor at the proper time. You will be blessed, however, if the exacting master of the stewardship finally finds you faithful.

You are also called shepherds; see to it that you do not act like hirelings. Be true shepherds, therefore, always holding your staffs in your hands, and, without sleeping, preserve on every side the flock entrusted to you. For if through your carelessness or negligence a wolf carries off even one sheep, you will surely lose the reward prepared for you with our Lord; first you will be scourged most harshly with the lashes of your sins, and afterward you will be violently thrust down into the custody of a fatal way of life.

According to the evangelical saying, you are the salt of the earth. But if you fail, it is doubtful how anything will be salted. O what a salting! It is truly necessary for you, by correcting with the salt of wisdom the ignorant populace that craves the world’s wantonness beyond measure, to salt it, lest, having been putrefied by sins, it stink when the Lord wishes at some time to address it.

For if he finds worms—that is, sins—in it, owing to the negligence of your care, he will immediately command that, having been despised, it be driven into the abyss of filth. And because you will not have been able to restore to him what was so greatly lost, he will utterly banish you, condemned by his judgment, from the intimacy of his love.

But such a salter must be prudent, watchful, moderate, instructed, peaceful, investigative, devout, just, fair, and pure. For how will the unlearned make the learned learned, the immoderate the moderate, or the impure the pure? If someone hates peace, how will he make peace? Or if someone’s hands are dirty, how will he be able to wipe away another’s filth and defilement?

It is also written that if the blind leads the blind, a pit will be open for both. Therefore correct yourselves first, so that you may amend your subjects without reproach. If you wish to be friends of God, willingly practice what you perceive to be pleasing to him.

Above all, ensure that ecclesiastical property remains under its proper law. Take care that the Simoniac heresy never takes root among you, lest sellers and buyers alike, scourged with the Lord’s whips, be pitifully driven through the alleyways to the destruction of confusion. Maintain the Church entirely free, in its own orders, from every secular power, and faithfully see that tithes belonging to God are given from all the cultivations of the earth; let them neither be sold nor withheld.

Whoever captures a bishop is to be considered wholly outside the law. Whoever captures or despoils monks, clerics, nuns, or their servants, or pilgrims or merchants, is to be anathema. Raiders, those who burn houses, and those who consent to them are to be expelled from the Church and struck with anathema.

It must therefore be considered with the greatest care what punishment should be imposed upon one who seizes another’s property, if the one who does not give away his own is struck with the condemnation of hell. This is what happened to the rich man mentioned in the Gospel: he was not punished because he had taken another’s property, but because, having received possessions, he abandoned himself to evil.

You have seen the world for a long time grievously disturbed by these iniquities, dearest brothers, to such an extent that, as has been made clear to us by those who reported it, in some of your provinces no one perhaps dares, through the weakness of your administration of justice, to travel along the road by day without being seized by plunderers, or by night by robbers, either by force or by malicious cunning, at home or away.

Therefore the truce (*trevia*, as it is commonly called), long ago established by our holy fathers, must be restored. I earnestly exhort each of you to ensure that it is most firmly observed in his bishopric. If anyone, whether led by greed or pride, should willingly violate it, let him be anathematized by the authority of God and by the sanction of the decrees of this council.

Since, sons of God, you have promised God more manfully than usual that you will maintain peace among yourselves and faithfully preserve the rights of the Church, it is worthwhile that you now turn the strength of your probity toward another matter of God and of your own, recently invigorated by the Lord’s correction.

It is necessary that you hasten to aid your brothers living in the East, who have often proclaimed their need of your assistance. For, as has already been said to many of you, the Turks and Arabs have invaded them as far as the Mediterranean Sea, specifically to the place they call the Arm of Saint George, near the borders of Romania. By occupying more and more of the lands of those Christians, they have defeated and overcome them in war seven times over, killing or capturing many, overthrowing churches, and laying waste to the kingdom.

If you allow them to remain undisturbed in this way for any length of time, they will overrun many more of God’s faithful. Therefore I urge you with humble prayer—not I, but the Lord—that you, preachers of Christ, frequently proclaim to all, of every order, infantrymen and cavalrymen, poor and rich alike, that they should promptly strive to assist the Christians in exterminating that wicked race from our regions.

To those present I speak; to those absent I command. Christ, however, commands. To all who go there, if they end their life either by walking, by crossing the sea, or by fighting against the pagans, forgiveness of sins will immediately be granted. I grant this to those who go, invested by God with so great a gift.

What immense disgrace it would be if a race so despised and degenerate, enslaved to demons, should thus overcome a people endowed with faith in the almighty God and made splendid by the name of Christ! What great reproaches will be charged against us by the Lord himself if you do not help those who are reckoned Christian by profession, as we are!

Let those who once customarily prolonged private conflict abusively against the faithful now go forth against the unbelievers to a battle worthy to be begun and completed with a trophy. Let those who were formerly plunderers now become soldiers. Let those who once fought against brothers and kinsmen now fight properly against the barbarians. Let those who once served as mercenaries for a few coins now obtain eternal rewards. Let those who exhausted themselves to the detriment of body and soul now labor for a double honor.

Indeed, here they will be sorrowful and poor; there, rich. Here, enemies of the Lord; there, his friends. Let no delay postpone the journey of those who are going: after arranging their affairs and gathering their expenses, when winter has ended and spring has followed, let them enter the road cheerfully, with the Lord going before them.

## VI.

*(The Deeds of God through the Franks, in the works of Guibert, abbot of Saint Mary of Nogent, edited by Dachery, p. 377.)*

If, among the churches spread throughout the whole world, some deserve greater reverence than others because of their persons and places—because of their persons, I say, when greater privileges are granted to apostolic sees; because of their places, when royal cities are accorded the same dignity as persons, as is the case with the city of Constantinople—we ought to show particular honor to that Church from which we received the grace of redemption and the origin of all Christianity.

For if what is said by the Lord is true—namely, that “salvation is from the Jews” (John 4:22)—and if it is established that the Lord of hosts left us a seed, lest we become like Sodom and resemble Gomorrah (Romans 9:29), and if Christ is our seed, in whom there is salvation and the blessing of all nations, then the very land and city in which he lived and suffered are called holy by the testimony of Scripture.

If this land, the inheritance of God and the holy temple, is read of in the sacred and prophetic pages as holy even before the Lord walked and suffered there, what holiness, what reverence is it believed to have obtained when the God of majesty was there embodied, nourished, grew to maturity, and in bodily growth walked about or was carried here and there?

And, to compress into suitable brevity all that could be recounted in a long circuit of words: where the blood of the Son of God, holier than heaven and earth, was poured out; where his body, dead while the elements trembled, rested in the tomb—what veneration do we think that place deserved?

If, when our Lord had only recently been killed and the city was still possessed by the Jews, the holy city is called holy by the evangelist when he says, “Many bodies of the saints who had fallen asleep rose and came into the holy city and appeared to many” (Matthew 27:53); and if the prophet Isaiah says, “His tomb shall be glorious” (Isaiah 11:10), then, since the holiness once bestowed upon the city by God himself as its sanctifier cannot be nullified by any supervening evil, and since the glory of the tomb likewise remains undivided, you must strive with the greatest zeal, dearest brothers, so that the holiness of the city and the glory of the tomb—which the frequent presence of the gentiles continually pollutes as far as lies within their power—may be cleansed, if you aspire to the Author of that holiness and glory, if you love the signs of his footprints upon the earth, and if you desire them, with God going before you and fighting on your behalf.

If it once benefited the Maccabees to the highest praise of piety that they fought for the ceremonies and the temple, and if it is lawfully granted to you, Christian soldiers, to defend the freedom of your homeland through the pursuit of arms; if you consider the thresholds of the apostles or of any of the saints worthy of being sought with such great sweat, why do you shrink from recovering and visiting the cross, the blood, and the tomb, or from spending the price of your souls to recover them?

Until now you have waged unlawful wars; at times, driven by mere greed or pride, you have hurled mad weapons into mutual slaughter. For this you have earned perpetual destruction and certain ruin through condemnation. Now we propose to you wars that contain within themselves the glorious gift of martyrdom and that leave behind the title of present and eternal praise.

Let us now suppose that Christ was neither dead nor buried in Jerusalem, nor had ever lived there. Certainly, if all these things were absent, that one fact alone ought to rouse you to aid the land and city: that “the law went forth from Zion and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem” (Isaiah 2:3). For if whatever belongs to Christian preaching flowed from the Jerusalem fountain, let the streams scattered in every direction throughout the whole world turn back the hearts of the Catholic multitude, so that they may carefully consider what they owe to so abundant a fountain.

If rivers return to the place from which they flow so that they may flow again, according to Solomon’s saying (Ecclesiastes 1:7), it ought to seem glorious to you if you can offer cleansing to that place from which it is evident that you received the purification of baptism and the teaching of faith.

Moreover, you must weigh with the greatest deliberation whether, if through your efforts the very mother of the churches—the Church itself—should flourish again in Christian worship, with God acting through you, God might perhaps will, as the times of Antichrist draw near, that some regions of the East be restored to the faith.

For it is clear that Antichrist will not wage war against the Jews or against the gentiles, but, in accordance with the etymology of his name, will attack Christians. And if Antichrist finds there no Christian at all, as scarcely anyone is found there today, there will be no one to oppose him or whom he may rightfully attack.

For, according to Daniel and Jerome, the interpreter of Daniel, he will pitch his tents on the Mount of Olives; and it is certain, as the Apostle says, that he will sit in Jerusalem, in the temple of God, as though he were God (2 Thessalonians 2:4). According to the same prophet, he will undoubtedly kill first the three kings—namely, those of Egypt, Africa, and Ethiopia.

But this cannot happen at all unless Christianity comes to exist where paganism now is. Therefore, if you devote yourselves to the practice of pious warfare, so that, just as you received from Jerusalem the seedbed of knowledge of God, you may there repay and restore a corresponding return of grace, then through you the Catholic name may spread and oppose the faithlessness of Antichrist and of the antichrists.

Who could not infer that God, who surpasses the hope of all by the abundance of his power, might through your spark consume such vast reed-beds of paganism, so that he might enclose Egypt, Africa, and Ethiopia—which have departed from communion with our faith—within the beginnings of this law, and so that the sinful man, the son of perdition, might find some rebels opposing him?

And behold, the Gospel cries out that Jerusalem must be trampled by the nations until the times of the nations are fulfilled (Luke 21:24). The “times of the nations” can be understood in two ways: either because they have dominated Christians at will, pursuing every kind of disgraceful excess according to their own desires, and encountering no obstacle in any of this—for those are said to have their time to whom everything is available according to their wishes, as in the passage: “My time has not yet come, but your time is always [Col. 0579A] ready” (John 7:6). Hence it is also customary to say to pleasure-seekers: “You have your time.”

Or again, the “times of the nations” are the fullness of the Gentiles, which will enter before Israel is saved. These times, dearest brothers, may perhaps now be fulfilled, while, with God’s cooperation, the power of the pagans is driven back through you, and while the end of the world is already near—even if the nations cease to be converted to the Lord, because, according to the Apostle, “the apostasy from the faith must come” (II Thess. 2:3). Yet it is first necessary, according to the prophets, that before the Antichrist’s coming the rule of Christianity be renewed in those regions, either through you or through whomever God chooses, so that the head of all evils, who will have his throne of kingship there, may find some nourishment of faith against which to fight.

[Col. 0579B] Consider, then, within yourselves that perhaps the Almighty has providentially appointed you for this purpose, so that through you he may restore Jerusalem from such great trampling. I beg you, weigh in your minds with what feelings those joys will be conceived when we see the holy city raised up through your aid, and the prophetic—or rather, the divine—utterances fulfilled in our own times. Let what the Lord himself says to the Church stir your memory: “From the East I will bring your seed, and from the West I will gather you” (Isa. 43:5).

God brought our seed from the East, because that eastern province in two ways produced the first beginnings of the Church for us. But he gathers her from the West, when through those who were the last to undertake the proofs of faith—that is, through Westerners, which we think can be accomplished through you by God’s favor—he restores the losses of Jerusalem.

[Col. 0579C] If the words of Scripture do not rouse you, and if our admonitions do not penetrate your hearts, let at least the great misery of those who desire to visit the holy places rouse you. Consider those who make pilgrimage and travel there across the Mediterranean lands. If they are wealthier, to how many exactions and acts of violence are they subjected, while they are compelled to pay charges and tribute at almost every mile, and to make payments for admission at every city gate and at the entrances to churches and temples? At every migration from one place to another, when any accusation has been brought against them, they are compelled to buy their release. And when they hesitate to give gifts, how brutally do the pagan governors, as is their custom, press them with beatings?

What shall we say of those who possess absolutely nothing and, trusting only in their poverty, undertake that journey because they seem to have nothing except their bodies to lose? When money that they do not possess is demanded from them through intolerable tortures; when the calluses of their heels are cut open and torn away to search whether they may have sewn anything inside them; when the cruelty of the wicked is carried so far that, believing the wretched to have swallowed gold or silver, or having given them scammony to drink, they force them to vomit—or even to expel their entrails—then, with iron, which it is shameful even to mention, they cut open their bellies and stretch apart the folds of their intestines, exposing by horrible mutilation whatever nature keeps concealed.

Recall, I beg you, the thousands who have perished in this detestable manner, and act for the sake of the holy [Col. 0580A] places from which the beginnings of your piety came. Believe without doubt that Christ will go before you as standard-bearer when you are sent into his wars, and that he will be your inseparable herald.

## VII

*(Peter Tudebode, priest of Sura, History of the Journey to Jerusalem, book I, chapter 1, in Duchesne, Script. Franc. IV, 777.)*

Brothers, we must suffer many things for the name of Christ: the miseries of poverty, persecutions, want, illness, nakedness, hunger and thirst, and other things of this kind, as the same Lord says to his followers: “You must suffer for my name”; and: “Do not be ashamed to speak before the faces of men. I myself will give you a mouth and wisdom,” and afterward a generous reward will follow you.

## VIII

*(Duchesne, History of All the French Cardinals, vol. II, p. 43, and Frizo, Gallia purpurata.)*

Perhaps you, true Christians, who have been summoned here and gathered before us, have supposed that the sole reason which compelled me to come from Rome was the regulation of ecclesiastical affairs and the arrangement of religion according to the standard of faith. Certainly that was partly a reason, but another, more urgent, and one greater than which none can be named or imagined, drew us here.

A few years ago, a people from Persia—the Hagarenes whom you corruptly call Saracens—invaded and captured the holy city of Jerusalem and the holy land. They plundered and burned them, and profaned the most sacred tomb of the Lord—which we cannot mention without tears. They also polluted the chapels of the churches, while the temples of our rite were either leveled to the ground or converted to profane uses.

The Christians who were driven from there suffered different fates. The weaker and less able to endure torture renounced their salvation and, after circumcising their foreskin, became Saracens. Others, steadfast in the faith, were torn and mangled through various forms of death; and the one whom the executioner struck down with the sword was fortunate.

Christian women, extremely numerous in the cities and towns—women whom the devotion of some of you present here had drawn across so many lands from your own cities and towns to see and venerate the holy places—suffered everything that the cruel enemy of Christ could devise which was obscene to describe, not merely to satisfy his own lust, but also to bring disgrace upon Christians. And if you are Christians—indeed, if you are men—you cannot hear these things with an untroubled spirit or endure them patiently.

In order that you may provide for all these matters as befits the name of Christian, the examples of your ancestors, the greatest danger that threatens the negligent, and the hope of rewards ought to lead—or rather drag—you forward. For we are certain that there is none among you who does not know that cities once subject to Roman rule, and the holy land, are possessed by the Turks and Saracens, our enemies.

As for the provinces of Europe and the cities that these same infidels oppress, occupy, and tear apart: if you are all ignorant of them together, each person knows what is happening in his own province—unless perhaps you, Gauls, being more remote, do not feel these things, although you ought to hear day after day the cries and lamentations of the Spaniards and Aquitanians who are oppressed by that people, seized into slavery, and carried off to Africa.

But what of you, Germans, Saxons, Poles, Bohemians, and Hungarians? Even if you have not yet felt the Turks and Saracens raging within your own entrails, do you not know how far they are from you, whether by straits or by rivers?

Now I address Italy, which the Saracens seized almost halfway many years ago. They penetrated so deeply into it that they invaded and besieged Rome, the head of the Christians and the seat of Peter, still wet with the blood of martyrs, and polluted the captured basilicas of the apostles Peter and Paul.

Here I see Venetians, Dalmatians, and other inhabitants of the shores of the Adriatic Gulf, who, while waging continual battles with the Saracens in order to defend themselves, are defending what remains of Italy.

Why say more? Until now, in the far northern regions of Europe, the empire of Constantinople was a barrier and, as it were, a wall that held back and prevented the Turks and Saracens from first overwhelming the Hungarians, Poles, Bohemians, and Germans themselves, and then the remaining Christians. But the emperor was driven out of Asia a few years ago, and he is struggling to retain the European territories of Constantinople.

If now you look upon and consider only what lies before your eyes, and if you do not continue to resist the Turk and Saracen who will soon invade, then you will soon feel them rushing upon your own heads. For you have neglected for so many years the sacred tomb of the Lord and the holy land of Jesus Christ, trampled underfoot and polluted by the foulest people. You will see, grieving and mourning, your wives torn from your embraces, your maidens from their mothers’ bosoms, and your boys and young men carried away with you into slavery.

Our forefathers, with greater success and glory, raised the dignity begun in Rome, Italy, and throughout Europe to rule over the whole world; through all its provinces and regions the Christian name flourished. In our times we see it contracted into a small corner of the world and endangered each day by destruction.

But let us come closer to home. This Charles, called the Great, was almost of your ancestral stock, Germans; he was your king, Franks, and your immense glory. He drove off countless multitudes of Saracens who pressed upon Spain, Aquitaine, and even the borders of France. Charles expelled the Saracens from Italy—as popular tradition reports—and from the holy land and Jerusalem.

How, after this, will you dare say that France alone, or primarily France, is the nation that may truly be called Christian, if, amid the wealth that surrounds you, you allow the Saracens and Turks, after capturing and polluting the Lord’s sacred tomb, to seize and oppress through your cowardice even the remnants of the Christian people?

Awaken, we implore you, and, by the compassion of our God, we entreat you: become strong men, destined to be an example and an incentive to the Christian world. Take up arms; bring out your troops, cohorts, and legions. You will have as many followers as you show yourselves willing to undertake this with fervent spirit.

The almighty God will be with you. He will send his angels from heaven before your face to direct your steps. Take up and seize your weapons, then, Christians, to liberate the Lord’s tomb. In it you will all obtain everlasting glory for yourselves, and you will also acquire incomparable riches in the things of this world.

Finally, trusting in the mercy of God and in the authority of the blessed Peter and Paul, we release from all penances for their sins those faithful Christians who take up arms against the pagans occupying such venerable places. Meanwhile, those who undertake this labor in the ardor of faith we receive under the protection of the Roman Church as sons of true obedience, and we decree that they shall remain secure from every disturbance, both in their persons and in their possessions.

[Col. 0581]

## Epitaph of Simon, Count of Crépy

Written on his pyramid by Pope Urban, called Odo.

*[Note: This epitaph is also found in the same manuscript of the monastery of Clarimaris in Flanders, together with Simon’s Life. However, the six later verses seem to belong to the author of the Life, who added them to the earlier verses published by Pope Urban.]*

[Col. 0581D]

Simon is my name; sprung from the noble blood  
of the great men of France, I was a significant one among them.  
Loving poverty, I abandoned my homeland and the world,  
preferring Christ to all riches.  
Afterward, the exceptional love of so great a Father  
led me to the apostolic court of the heavenly Prince.  
Under his guidance, may I at last deserve to be raised above the stars:  
here I dwell, buried before the sacred gates.

[Col. 0582D]

Once, renewing my father’s deeds at my brother’s bidding,  
I wrote for the disciples a rule in humble form.  
But since God neither rejects these things nor those more humble,  
Moses shows that lesser things suffice for undertaking the work.  
Therefore, desiring the reader to be my helper,  
I ask him to read me, absent and lacking strength.

## A Double Epitaph of Blessed Urban

*(D. Ruinart, Life of Urban, Appendix, p. 280.)*

### I

[Col. 0583A]

Odo, canon of Reims, whom Hugh of Cluny  
made a monk—does he become an outstanding pope?  
While he lived, he was the light of the City; in death, an everlasting night.  
The City stood while Urban stood; when he fell, it fell [another reading: when he collapsed, it collapsed].  
By ruling according to law and fostering you in peace, Rome, he blessed you,  
keeping you inwardly from vices and outwardly from the enemy.  
Neither wealth, fame, nor power ever bent or exalted him,  
whether through gifts, praise, or threats.  
Eloquence adorned his tongue, wisdom his breast,  
uprightness his character, and dignity his outward bearing.  
Behold: through him the holy city shines forth, our law triumphs,  
[Col. 0584A] nations are conquered, and faith increases throughout the world.  
But the rose that blooms most richly in the garden is taken away most quickly;  
so fate also carried off this flourishing man.  
Death released the body, rest the soul, the cistern the corpse;  
the hard place set him free, the pleasant one shelters him, the deep one covers him.  
He receives him; among us nothing remains except his fame.

### II

Urban, the pope whom France called Odo,  
the region that had brought forth the tender child—  
the vital breezes abandoned him as he was dying.  
In him the world’s eloquent tongue collapsed,  
so that, while such a teacher is gone, the world lacks his equal.  
Here, weeping, Rome laid her own to rest.

## Eleventh-Century Authors of Uncertain Date; Anonymous Writings Follow

### Valcandus, Monk of the Monastery of Moyenmoutier in Lorraine

[Col. 0583]

## Notice Concerning Valcande

*(Literary History of France, vol. VII, p. 239.)*

Valcande, unknown to all our biographers, nevertheless deserves to hold a place among ecclesiastical writers. Little is known about his person, but we are better informed about the works of his pen. He was a monk of Moyenmoutier, in the diocese of Toul in Lorraine, and was still flourishing after the year 1014 (Martène, Anecdota, vol. III, pp. 1109–1124).

The evidence for this is drawn from his own writings. When speaking of Saint Hidulphus, the founder of this abbey, he calls him his father and nourisher. Elsewhere he reports several miracles performed under the episcopate of Berthold and during the government of Abbot Nardulphus, which began in 1011 and ended in 1026 or the following year. Among these events is one that occurred in 1014, showing that the author wrote only after that date (Calmet, History of Lorraine, vol. IV, part II, p. 61).

If, however, one relied on another passage in which Lambert, one of Nardulphus’s successors, is mentioned—around the middle of the same century—one would think that Valcande lived until that time (Martène, ibid., p. 1121). But Dom Calmet, having printed this passage within brackets and in italics (ibid., p. 56), leads us to judge that it was an addition made afterward. This is also plainly apparent from a reading of the work. Our author’s name did not become known to the public until 1724.

As for his writings:

1. We have from him a Life of Saint Hidulphus, first bishop of Trier and afterward founder and abbot of Moyenmoutier. In the manuscripts this work bears the name of no author. Jean-Jacques Chifflet attempted to attribute it to Bruno, later pope under the name Leo IX; Dom Martène and Dom Durand, the first editors, do not seem far from accepting this attribution. But it is a wholly conjectural opinion and cannot be maintained. Bruno was not yet old enough to write for posterity when the work left its author’s hands. It is more reasonable to follow Dom Humbert Belhomme, abbot of Moyenmoutier, who, having worked on the history of his abbey and conducted particular investigations for that purpose, discovered that the author whom he had initially believed anonymous was none other than Valcande.

[Col. 0585] His work is properly a commentary on a Life of Saint Hidulphus composed in 964, based on another much older and very prolix Life of the same saint, of which it is merely an abridgment. That first Life, believed to have been the work of Saint Hidulphus’s disciples, and which Dom Mabillon earnestly desired to recover, has been lost since it was abridged. Thus all that remains is the abridgment made in 964 by the monks of Moyenmoutier and the commentary with which Valcande illustrated it, preserving almost the whole text of the abridgment made by his confrères. There is, in truth, another much shorter abridgment, but it scarcely deserves mention.

This shorter work, whose date and author are unknown, was first printed in Mosander’s supplement to Surius by his confrère, who altered its style (Surius, Supplement, 11 July, p. 575–576). In 1723 the continuators of Bollandus reprinted it in the third volume of their July collection, using a manuscript from Utrecht through which they restored its original integrity. The following year Dom Belhomme incorporated it into the first part of his History of Moyenmoutier, published at Strasbourg in a single folio volume.

In both editions this shorter abridgment is preceded by the one composed around the year 964 and followed by Valcande’s work. The former is presented from a manuscript of Moyenmoutier at least seven hundred years old, and the latter from manuscripts of Moyenmoutier, Echternach, and Paderborn.

The whole is accompanied by extensive and learned preliminary observations and by historical and critical notes composed by Dom Belhomme and the other editors. They undertake to demonstrate and correct the enormous errors—especially chronological ones—found in both works. As early as 1717, Dom Martène and Dom Durand had published Valcande’s work from the Paderborn manuscript just mentioned.

2. In the single manuscript of Moyenmoutier, this work is immediately followed by a sermon by the same author, which the editors did not consider it appropriate to include in their collections. It is an invective against the corruption of the morals of that age, from which Valcande takes occasion to exhort his confrères to imitate the virtues of Saint Hidulphus and his disciples.

3. In place of this sermon, the manuscripts of Paderborn and Echternach immediately contain a treatise on the successors of Saint Hidulphus in the Vosges. There is no doubt that this other writing belongs to the author of the preceding work, who explicitly promises it there.

*[Note: The History of the Abbots of Moyenmoutier, situated in the Vosges and now called Moyenmoutier, together with the Life of Saint Hildulphus, founder of that monastery, has been carried only to the time of Hardulphus, the abbot said to have been deposed in 1016. Therefore Belhomme incorrectly concluded that the work had already been completed before 1020 and should be attributed to a certain monk named Valcande. Rivet agrees with him in the Literary History, VII, p. 240, where he judged the matter too lightly. For that writer lived during the time of Bruno of Toul and explicitly mentions the year 1043; an ancient manuscript, nearly contemporary, prevents us from thinking with Belhomme that this material was added later. It is certain that the same author was responsible for an interpolated Life of Saint Deodatus, which must have been presented for approval in 1049 to Bruno, already ordained pope. Whether he was abbot or monk of Moyenmoutier, it is therefore likely that the author composed both works at approximately the same time and sent them to Pope Leo IX.

He enlarged and interpolated the older Life of Saint Hildulphus and added a second book to it, in which he narrated both the deeds of the successors and the miracles performed by the saint himself. In doing so he followed an ancient tradition of the monastery and was later well informed about events that had occurred there. Yet the book commends itself neither by the importance of the events it contains nor by its manner of narration. Richerius in his History of Senones and John of Bayon, who in the fourteenth century wrote a larger history of Moyenmoutier, drew very extensively from this source. (G. Waitz, Preface to the Book on the Successors of Saint Hidulphus, in Pertz, Monumenta Germaniae Historica, Scriptores, vol. IV, p. 86.)]*

We have three editions of this work of Valcande. Dom Martène and Dom Durand first published it after the Life of Saint Hidulphus. But they removed several chapters near the end because they seemed to them of little interest. In fact, they contain only a few miracles. Dom Belhomme later inserted it into the second part of his History of Moyenmoutier, and finally Dom Calmet included it among the proofs of the History of Lorraine. The work is complete in both of the latter editions.

Valcande uses it to give the succession of the abbots of his monastery, from Saint Hidulphus to Nardulphus, together with several details from their lives. He added other material concerning the various conditions in which Moyenmoutier found itself during that period. If he reports no more, he says that the reason is the lack of records that could have informed him. His work, moreover, is not free from errors. Speaking of a Fortunatus to whom Charlemagne gave the abbey of Moyenmoutier, Valcande represents him as patriarch of Jerusalem. But scholars are convinced that he was patriarch of Grado and the same man who, pursued by the Venetians, withdrew to France around 803.

4. It is believed with considerable probability that Valcande also revised the Life of Saint Dié, or Diey, first bishop of Nevers and afterward founder and abbot of the monastery bearing his name in Lorraine (Bollandists, 19 June, p. 883, note). What supports this opinion is that the author of the Life as we possess it refers his readers to the Life of Saint Hidulphus revised by Valcande, as we have seen; moreover, the same chronological errors occur in both works. One may add that the dates are compatible, since the author or reviser wrote only a few years after the elevation of Saint Dié’s body, which took place in 1003 (Spicilegium, vol. III, p. 313).

Looking further back, one finds that this Life of Saint Dié must have undergone the same vicissitudes as that of Saint Hidulphus (Bollandists, ibid., pp. 870–871, nos. 3, 6). The tradition of the eleventh century indeed held that the acts of this saint had originally been collected by his disciples and afterward revised by a holy and learned abbot of Moyenmoutier. The latter detail cannot, it is true, be maintained in every respect, but it remains true in substance. The text clearly shows that the final reviser preserved the notable circumstance that the acts were revised not by an abbot of Moyenmoutier but by a monk of Val-Galilée, now Saint-Dié. He must therefore have done this before 980, the date when the canons took the place of the monks.

Finally, Valcande revised the acts in his turn and made them what we now possess. He promises there an account of the saint’s miracles. But this projected work remained merely an idea—or else it is still hidden or has been entirely lost. Later these acts were sent to Pope Leo IX, who approved them at a council held in Rome in 1049, the first year of his pontificate.

We have several editions and some translations into our language. Mosander included them in his Supplement to Surius (Surius, Supplement, 19 June, pp. 539–546). But besides altering the style, he omitted the preface and conclusion from his edition. In 1619 (Bollandists, ibid., p. 870, no. 3) they were reprinted in full at Nancy. As early as 1594, Jean Ruyr, secretary of the chapter of Saint-Dié, had translated them into French and [Col. 0587] published them at Troyes. He later inserted them into his work on the Saints and Antiquities of the Vosges, printed at Épinal in 1634. François Riguet, grand provost of Saint-Dié, published them again in 1679, based on the Nancy edition. Finally, the successors of Bollandus published them from several manuscripts, collated with the earlier editions, and enriched them with learned notes and preliminary observations.

[Col. 0587]

# Life of Saint Hildulphus, Bishop of Trier and Founder of Moyenmoutier

*(Martène, Anecdota, III, 1093.)*

## Chapter One

### The Origins of Saint Hildulphus

[Col. 0587A]

Since all who have been baptized have put on Christ (Gal. 4:27), and have longed in spirit for the inheritance of eternal salvation so that they might one day attain it, they have made use of the light of charity. Through charity, the only-begotten Son of God—although he alone existed in the kingdom of the eternal Father—adopted human beings as brothers so that he might establish dwelling places for them in his Father’s house.

Therefore, as they hastened toward that destination, the men of God were ashamed to go there alone, knowing that a sure reward awaited those who drew others along with them, so that the more people they carried, the greater the reward with which they would be crowned. They trusted in the testimony by which that evangelical servant who returned the talent entrusted to him with profit was admitted to the joy of his lord.

Accordingly, that good master of the household, wishing to bring everyone into the ineffable sweetness of this joy, sent his servants into the world and commanded that all be invited. And so that they might not fail or go astray on the journey, he ordered them to be sustained by the wheat of life and the lamp of twofold charity.

When it had pleased the Almighty’s divinity to continue this work for a long time, distributing to his fellow servants the measure of wheat at the proper time, he commanded that a future shepherd of peoples, named Hildulphus, come forth for the labor of this present life. Born of the noble stock of the Nervians, he was nourished among the wings of the schools for the sacred warfare.

*[The following passage is enclosed in brackets in the edition: Around the time of his youth, Garibaldus ruled the same people of Noricum—that is, the Bavarians. His daughter, named Theudelinda, was taken as wife by Agilulfus, king of the Lombards. The most distinguished lord, Pope Gregory, also mentions this Agilulfus hastening to besiege a city (in his Commentary on Ezekiel). At that same time Theudebertus, born from Childebert through Brunhild, ruled the Austrasians. In his court the blessed Arnulfus was raised, the son of Arnoaldus or Arnoldus, an illustrious man under Chlothar or Dagobert, who afterward was appointed bishop of the city of Metz from the office of mayor of the palace. In the end, renouncing the summit of so great a pontificate, he became a devoted follower of the eremitical life. But Hildulphus, a boy mercifully chosen by the Creator himself and soon to become a defender and teacher of the Christian religion, was entrusted to literary studies and, with divine grace cooperating, quickly distinguished himself most effectively.]*

From this point, while many fall headlong down the steep paths of vices and roll into the mire of pride—especially if they have touched upon some part of worldly knowledge—this boy, still of good character, advanced day by day, becoming superior to all and remaining free from the vices that entangle youth.

While many such people were astonished by the disputes of the law courts, others by countless games, and a very few by investigating the complexities of secular disciplines, he was ever-watchful in prayer and constant in reading. Beyond his strength, he devoted himself to works of mercy, taking pleasure in helping those who labored, bringing aid to the needy, and standing beside the miserable. Through the growth of such virtues he showed beforehand what he would do as a future shepherd of the Church.

## Chapter Two

### He Becomes a Cleric and Soon afterward a Monk

[Col. 0588B]

Meanwhile, having been trained in ecclesiastical conduct, he was invested with the dignity of the clergy in the city commonly called Regensburg.

*[Note: An old manuscript reads “Regenesbuorch.”]*

Because the almighty Farmer had once sown the seed of right intention in the good soil of his heart, the stalk of vigorous action gradually rose within him. He was an astonished and eager hearer of the Gospel, not deaf to it; he burned to become an obedient listener, continually impressing upon himself the Lord’s saying: “Whoever has left house, or father, or mother, or brothers, or sisters, or fields for my name will receive a hundredfold and possess eternal life” (Matt. 19:29).

For he considered the possessions he saw before him a serious obstacle to his perfection. The question of a wife and children, however, did not trouble his mind, since he had thus far been without them.

Moreover, in those days ecclesiastical orders were not distributed as indiscriminately as we see them distributed in our own age; rather, they were reserved permanently for professors of chastity or virginity. But this blessed man, anticipated by the grace of the Holy Spirit, preserved his breast undefiled by the corruption of the flesh from the cradle, and in its hidden chamber he shaped and nourished his mind.

After considering these and other words of evangelical instruction, he wisely recognized that such sayings and gifts had been addressed not only to the holy apostles but to everyone. Firmly grounded in the apostolic teaching and following the example of faithful Abraham, he left his land, his kindred, and his ancestral home. He set out toward Sicambria and entered the city of Trier, which at that time was inhabited by a numerous population. The city was also adorned by a community of monks who spread around them the fragrance of a good reputation.

[Col. 0589A] Joining them, this fearless champion of Christ mocked the hope of the world and fulfilled the monastic rule both by profession and by deeds. The fire of holy zeal for monastic perfection burned his heart so intensely that he became an object of terror and an example to his juniors, but of reverence and love to his seniors.

Thus Milo, the son of the venerable Lutroinus and at that time archbishop, perceiving that this holy man was supported by knowledge, mature in discernment, angelic in conduct, and advancing by the steps of various virtues toward the summit of perfection, wished to withdraw him from the monastery and retain him with himself. He granted him a second seat beside him, so that Hildulphus might perform the pastoral office in his place, bearing the burden of the sheep entrusted to him and giving counsel to the sound and the weak according to what he judged appropriate.

How piously and energetically he carried this out, the continuation of the narrative will make clear.

*[Note: This Milo was a pseudo-archbishop and lived too late for Hildulphus to have succeeded him. Thus the author has made a mistake in the name of the bishop.]*

## Chapter Three

### He Is Appointed to the See of Trier

At this time, in Gaul, the kings of the Franks were degenerating from their customary strength and wisdom. Those who appeared to be the royal mayors of the palace began to exercise the power of administering the kingdom and to do whatever it was customary for kings to do, since heaven had ordained that the kingdom of the Franks would pass to their descendants.

In those days Angisus, son of Arnulfus, was in the royal palace. He was said to have been named after Anchises, once a Trojan, and he administered the principality under the title of mayor of the palace. His era also reached the time of Heraclius, Augustus of the Roman state, who brought back the wood of the most holy Cross from the territories of the tyrant Chosroes.

*[The following passage is enclosed in brackets in the edition: After a long time, Pippin succeeded his father Angisus and governed the state of Gaul with great distinction. He was a man of great power, remarkable piety, and courage, who very often crushed his enemies by attacking them at once. Once, having crossed the Rhine against one of his adversaries, he attacked with only a single companion and slaughtered him, while he sat in his chamber, together with his men. He also waged many wars against the Saxons and especially against Rathbodus, king of the Frisians. He had other sons as well, but the foremost among them was Charles, who later succeeded him in the principality.

This has perhaps been pursued at greater length than necessary so that the similarity of names and the passage of time in what follows may not cause the reader difficulty: the aforementioned duke Charles was the grandfather of Charles the Great, the first emperor from among the Franks.]*

While the aforementioned Angisus was vigilant over the public welfare—

*[Note: For the material enclosed in parentheses, only the following is found in the manuscript Life: “Pippin, then a man of great piety, namely the father of Charles the Great, was governing the state of Gaul with the greatest distinction.”]*

—and while Milo, archbishop of Trier, had departed from human affairs, the people of Trier were in need of a bishop. The Lord’s flock, deprived of a shepherd, turned to the Lord and applied itself with all its prayers, asking him to provide a ruler for his Church, which was tossed about by the storm of the world.

Then suddenly the name of Hildulphus sounded from everyone’s lips. He was a noble man, learned in knowledge, polished in speech, and composed in life and character—

*[“pleasing to God, approved by men, and ordered in a manner useful and appropriate to the clergy and people”]*—

The report soon spread through the royal court, and an edict went out that such a great man should undertake the pastoral ministry.

When this had been accomplished, the man of God, intent on fleeing in another direction—

*[“he took flight toward the land of his birth; anxious and fearful of being elevated to a suspected honor, he sought refuge in foreign lands, thinking that there he might conceal himself as an obscure man among his own people”]*—

for he had longed for the desert, unless the devotion of the people had prevented him by forestalling him.

He was therefore seized from Istria and brought as far as Belgic Gaul.

*[“Although his desire was delayed, it was not taken away.”]*

A gathering of the whole kingdom was held. Princes came running with the bishops; groups of clergy and monks arrived with crowds of people. There was one cry from everyone: Hildulphus was most worthy of episcopal honor, while the man of God, on the contrary, protested that he was wholly unworthy.

For he was often a strong examiner of his own weakness and feared himself when he measured himself against himself, reflecting on what and how great an account of souls he would have to render.

If people would now consider this, while they can live freely and peacefully, they would certainly not rush to purchase with money ecclesiastical rule, to which holy men were scarcely compelled even then.

But at last the faithful and devoted acclamation of the people prevailed, and, in all things conformed to the apostolic faith—

*[“the thirty-third bishop after the blessed Eucharius, disciple of the Apostle Peter”]*—

he was confirmed by the common will of all as bishop of Trier.

What he was from that time and how he presented himself to everyone will be difficult to explain; nevertheless, we shall attempt it.

## Chapter Four
### His Virtues as Bishop

Accordingly, the blessed man not only diminished nothing of the purpose of good works [or of monastic rigor] that he had once undertaken, but increased it as though a hundredfold. Indeed, as though he had committed every crime lying anywhere, whether as a boy or as a young man, he turned to repentance and rose up against himself. You would have seen a man consumed by fasts, scarcely clinging to his bones, lying tirelessly before the memorials of the saints, assiduously drenched in floods of tears, and passing sleepless nights.

What shall we say of the way he cared for the poor, the ordinary, and the rich with the utmost zeal and every diligence? Whatever he possessed, he made common to all; for rich and needy alike he was always the same. He instructed them not to be arrogantly minded or to set their hope on the uncertainty of riches, but in the Lord, “who gives all things abundantly to everyone” (I Tim. 6:17), and that the abundance of their possessions should supply the poverty of the poor, so that in the future the abundance of the poor might become a provision for the poverty of the rich (II Cor. 8:14). He especially admonished the poor to know that they were poor in spirit and to give thanks to God in humility, as the Lord himself says: “Blessed are the poor in spirit” (Matt. 5:3).

He sought to discover which of the saints he might imitate in some good quality, complaining that he had lost any day on which he had made little or no progress in his conduct or in God’s commandments. He never failed on any day to offer God a sacrifice for the salvation of the whole world and for the repose of the dead, knowing that he was saying to the Lord: “I will bless the Lord at all times; his praise shall always be in my mouth” (Ps. 33:2); and: “I will freely sacrifice to your name, O Lord, for it is good” (Ps. 53:8).

Whatever the man of God wanted done for himself, he refused to no one, in accordance with the evangelical command, but most willingly granted it to everyone who asked him: he was a harbor for the weary, a consoler of the sorrowful, a covering for the naked, and a host to travelers. Who ever sought him and did not experience his goodness?

Daily concern for souls compelled him to groan whenever anyone was perishing; yet he was so compassionate that, whenever anyone caused him offense, he believed that he himself had given offense. And because he knew that he was a resident and a stranger here below (Ps. 118:19), where he knew that he had no abiding city (Heb. 13:14), he never closed his door to a traveler, nor did he eat his morsel alone.

[As a most gentle father, he never ceased gently admonishing his spiritual sons to long for the inheritance of their heavenly homeland; he carried the grace of the divine law in his breast, and with its salt seasoned the speech of his mouth. He so abhorred the vanity of the world that he believed and professed its lovers to be wretched. He labored especially in almsgiving and devoted himself most generously to hospitality, as though he were offering it to Christ himself. Whoever he saw sad and grieving, he gladdened with a word of consolation and the necessary assistance; those who were at odds he restored to harmony.]

Moreover, he became all things to all, “that he might save all” (I Cor. 11:22); and, like a good shepherd, he showed by the performance of his works whatever he told the flock ought to be done.

## CHAPTER V

### He Transfers the Body of Saint Maximin

Since such eminence in this and in his other virtues befitted the bishop, he was revered with wondrous devotion by all. He was a man noble by birth, distinguished in religion, cautious in counsel, and renowned for his works.
