Among the magnificent works that he accomplished, he transferred the body of the most blessed [and most glorious] bishop Maximin [of whom he was then regarded as the twenty-ninth successor] from the crypt where Saint Paulinus, a bishop of great merit, had buried it after bringing it back from Aquitania, into the church in which it is now venerated.

For that crypt was vomiting forth unusual waters, which had covered the entire surface of its pavement to a depth of more than three cubits; yet they had no access to the mausoleum of the revered limbs, but touched it solidly on either side like a wall. The blessed man, understanding from this sign and from many other revelations that he was being admonished to transfer the holy body after a basilica had been built, judged that the work must be completed with every diligence.

Accordingly, after an oratory had been built at enormous expense and brought to completion through vigilant labor, the entire clergy arrived with the people. Without delay the venerable bishop, together with his fellow bishops Clement and Chotbert, laid hands upon a cover of extraordinary size. It was lifted with such speed that one would have thought it had no weight; yet that same cover, after having been tested by three hundred men and forty pairs of oxen, had remained unmoved.

At last, after the revered limbs had been honorably placed, as was fitting, in a cypress coffin and then in a marble one, he brought them into the oratory on the fourth day before the Kalends of June. He had taken this oratory from its foundations and brought it to completion. The bodies of three hundred martyrs of the Theban Legion were likewise placed there. He so ennobled that place with furnishings and lands and filled it with monks that from then on it appeared in no respect inferior to the episcopal residence of that city.

While the blessed man devoted himself day after day to that place with an excessive affection of piety, foreseeing the future with a discerning spirit and fearing the unnecessary tyrannies of successors, he transferred the whole aforesaid property by royal right to the nobility, as it remains at the present time.

## CHAPTER VI

### He Resigns the Bishopric

After so many and such varied labors for Christ’s flock, although, once placed in the episcopate, he had wished to possess nothing [Note: In the old manuscript: “although in his whole life he possessed nothing”], nevertheless, whatever it was that he seemed to have acquired [on the occasion or pretext of his administration] [or to have presumed to claim for himself], he abandoned; and, as he had formerly conceived in his mind, he resolved to seek the wilderness.

[Not forgetting his monastic vow,] he considered that his deeds could provide him with insufficient means of salvation, since the Lord had said: “Unless someone renounces all that he possesses, he cannot be my disciple” (Luke 14:33). [Keeping, as it were, the watchfulness of a keen-eyed heavenly creature,] he did not turn back as he went forward, but, forgetting what lay behind, pressed on toward what was ahead (Phil. 3:13).

Indeed, he knew that many appeared to stand upright before human judgment through the performance of good works, yet had fallen before the eyes of almighty God through their deliberation about better things. For the good work of such people was less pleasing to God because, by the deliberation of their minds, they had unmistakably placed themselves in a better state. Therefore, lest it later be vainly sought whether such a loss had crept into his own mind, he hastened to complete the one resolution that he sighed to himself was still lacking.

When rumor first carried this news to the ears of the common people, every age and sex rushed into the city as though barbarians were pursuing them. When they saw the man of God, a cry was raised to heaven, and almost everyone’s grief was borne along as though destruction threatened the entire province.

“Why do you abandon the guardianship of the flock entrusted to you? Why, why do you not fear the danger that such a thing will bring? Who, do you think, will be the most savage devastators of this Church? For ravenous wolves will tear your flock apart.”

Moved by such lamentations, and especially by those of the pious sheep of the aforesaid place, the holy man, full of compassion, dissolved in tears. At last he turned to the people and said:

“You are the people of God and his pasture’s sheep. He himself will guard you, for he promises us, saying: ‘Behold, I am with you all the days, even to the consummation of the age’ (Matt. 28:20). Until now my guardianship has benefited no one, because I have watched over myself too little. But if there is still any time remaining, allow me to complete what will benefit both me and you.”

Thus, having hardened himself against the mournful complaints of the flock that followed him—as though against stronger chains attempting to subjugate the freedom of his soul—and having broken them, he designated Nicomadus as his successor and pastor for his sheep [Note: A more recent manuscript reads “Weomadus”]. After his final farewell, he gave his mind, eyes, and feet to the journey.

He departed exalted in knowledge, taken up into life, and bitter in the indignation of his spirit; groaning, he asked that wings might be given him like a dove, so that he might fly to rest and, fleeing far away, remain in solitude (Ps. 54:7–8).

As the worthy pope Gregory says: “It is sweet to be amid human affairs, but only for one who has tasted none of the joys of heaven. Yet if someone has already tasted with the mouth of his heart what the sweetness of heavenly rewards is, then, the sweeter that which he sees within is, the more all that he endures without is turned into bitterness.”

He contended with himself over the sins he remembered, reproached himself for his thoughts, pursued himself for his words, and punished himself for his deeds by weeping. Therefore, unless the Holy Spirit had moved this man’s mind in this way to bitterness toward temporal things and delight in eternal ones, he would not have sought a deserted and trackless land with such fervor of heart.

## CHAPTER VII

### With the Support of the Bishop of Toul, He Withdraws into the Vosges

At that time Jacob, a man admirable in conduct and character, governed the city of Leuca [that is, its churches]. Since he was held in everyone’s esteem because of his holiness, he was also an object of wonder to kings. When the man of God Hildulph came to him, Jacob most willingly cooperated in providing him, through charity, with a secluded place.

For, formerly, under his predecessor in the episcopate, a man named Girbaldus [Note: The old manuscript reads “Garibaldus”], a man equally most holy, Deodatus, a bishop of Nivernum and a man of supreme holiness, had renounced the world and obtained a place in the forest of the Vosges. There he lived most holily, established monasteries, and, after a long military service in Christ’s struggle, entered crowned into the senate of life. There were also cells of holy men in that forest.

[Finally, Sanctivagium had already been organized at that time for the spiritual exercise of monks. Moreover, Lord Gundelbertus, formerly the distinguished archbishop of Sens, around that time named the monastery at Grandiavium, which he had built, after the name of the abandoned city of Sens. Bodo, the first predecessor of the aforesaid Jacob, also wished Christ’s handmaid Tietberga—whom he had received before his episcopal dignity as a daughter born of lawful wedlock—to preside over the virginal bands with whom he had filled a place brought to completion through his own care and which he had decided would be named after himself.]

Among these, therefore, the athlete of Christ Hildulph, with the counsel and assistance of the aforesaid Jacob, chose a place of habitation.

## CHAPTER VIII

### He Founds Medianum Monastery

There is a place in the Vosges surrounded on every side by mountains, past which a certain river flows with a strong current, called Rabado [Note: The beginning of this chapter is read thus in the older codex: “This place, surrounded on every side by mountains, is passed by a certain little stream, which, because of its strong current, is called Rapido.”]. Under the direction of the Holy Spirit, the holy man founded churches there: the first, in the name of the blessed Mother of God and ever-virgin Mary, which he dedicated on the eighth day before the Kalends of March; and another, consecrated in honor of blessed Peter, prince of all the apostles, on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of November. He called the first Medianum Monastery.

After establishing these things, he began to live for God and for himself. As the fame of his holy name carried his renown far and wide, powerful and noble men frequently flocked to him for the sake of visiting him. Since many came running from different regions, some, inflamed with the desire for the way of life, decided to remain with the man of God.

When the man full of God saw this, he judged that it was being brought about by the Lord. And since he himself had formerly professed to be a monk, he began to build habitations suitable for monks. When the people learned of this, they increased in devotion and gathered in greater numbers than usual; for through the merits of the holy man and of those subject to him, the blind were enlightened there, the lame recovered, and demons were driven away.

Unable to bear the crowds that were gathering, he built and dedicated outside the enclosure a church of Saint John the Baptist, and established houses in which those arriving might be received.

## CHAPTER IX

### After Gathering the Disciples, He Appoints Leubald Abbot

Meanwhile, the faithful servant of the Lord saw that a considerable part of that solitude had gradually been cultivated through the occasion of his arrival and had become, as it were, clothed all around with spiritual sons like young olive trees. His soul conceived the greatest delight in the presence of the Lord his Savior.

For although the formerly deserted and tangled wilderness sustained the poor of Christ through the produce of each year, so that they would not fail on the journey of this world, he rejoiced to see fulfilled even literally what the prophet had once foretold concerning the mysteries of the old law and the nourishment of the new people: “The deserted land, turned into fruitfulness, will be eaten by the strangers.”

The frequent crowd of the faithful who diligently came to visit the man of God had also built numerous dwellings around the cells of the saints, because of their proximity or the suitability of the places.

But because the man of God had already tasted and seen that the Lord is sweet, he held nothing dearer than to be free for contemplation and to see that God is ineffably . . . surpassing. [The supplied text here contains a lacuna.]

As the number of our brothers there increased, that holy man, always watchful and fearful for his own safety, was afraid of being separated in any way from the beloved quiet of his contemplation by responsibility for them or by the frequency of worldly visitors. Therefore he designated the venerable man Leubald as abbot. He understood him to be endowed with no small knowledge of divine and human matters, so that he might preside over the brothers with pastoral vigilance and attend to the affairs of those who arrived.

How devoutly and energetically he administered this office is made clear by the authority of the one who promoted him, which satisfies the minds of believers: the holy bishop would never have promoted him over so great a company of monks unless he had judged him more worthy than the others for this task.

## CHAPTER X

### He Receives the Pious Men Spinulus, John, and Benignus

As the number of the brothers there increased, three lovers of the heavenly life came among the others. The first was Spinulus; the remaining two, who were brothers in flesh and spirit, were called John, the elder, and Benignus, the other.

[They are reported to have come from the monastery of the most blessed Maximin, which the aforesaid Father had founded, and to have decided to live with the man of God because they took great delight in his way of life and charity. We shall explain some of their miracles in greater detail below, so that it may become perfectly clear how great their merit is before God.]

Received kindly by the man of God, instructed by him as a father, and themselves living devoutly, they yearned for the way of life. Although each wished to outstrip the others in every work of virtue, they hastened nevertheless to surpass one another in humility and obedience. Christ was constantly in their mouths, and the proclamations of eternal life continually resounded from them. As is fitting for monks, they did everything according to the Father’s command [without faintheartedness, resentment, or bitterness; subject in the fear and love of Christ, they chastened themselves with fasts and vigils, were contrite in prayers, and devoted themselves tirelessly to humility of heart. They preferred to endure whatever is considered intolerable anywhere rather than offend Christ in anything].

And because “through the envy of the devil death entered the world” (Wis. 2:24), Hildulphus, the athlete of God, knew that he and his companions would one day have to pay Adam’s debt. He therefore resolved to seek a place of burial.

But because, as commonly happens in valleys, there was an abundance of water around the monastery, he judged the site quite unsuitable for a cemetery. To the south, however, a hill rises above the monastery. Upon it the holy man built a church, consecrated it in the name of blessed Pope Gregory, and blessed a cemetery around it.

## CHAPTER XI

### He Is Visited by Bishop Erardus

Meanwhile, the fame of his proclamation flew across the surrounding lands and penetrated even to more distant regions. As many came to the man of God from different places, Erardus, also most holy in life, related by blood to the blessed Hildulphus but, in rank, his fellow bishop, summoned by his renown [ascitus; Note: The old manuscript reads “excitatus,” “roused”], came running to him.

When he had found the man whom he had long sought, he rejoiced in his labor and said:

“Behold, brother, God has granted you the desire of your heart and has not deprived you of your will (Ps. 20:3). You have found a place suitable for your way of life, which you long desired for a long time. Stand firm, therefore, manfully in the faith, and take courage in the Lord (Ps. 26:14), confident in the power of his strength that ‘whoever perseveres to the end will be saved’ (Matt. 24:13).”

For several [continuous] years, they remained together, mutually proclaiming eternal life, [and together they provided what was necessary for life to the brothers gathered there and erected their shelters. The old manuscript reads “for days” instead of “to the brothers.”]

## CHAPTER XII

### He Restores the Sight of Otilia, Daughter of Duke Eticho, and Gives Her Baptism

To display their merits, God renewed wondrous miracles. [While the men of God were still living together there,] Otilia, daughter of Duke Eticho of Alsace, was brought to the men of God, having been born blind; her sorrowful parents humbly begged them to have pity on her.

When they learned that she was still a pagan [Note: The author improperly calls her “pagan,” not as though she worshiped idols, but because she had not yet been baptized], they catechized her according to ecclesiastical custom. Prostrating themselves in prayer, they begged the Lord’s mercy for the girl’s salvation.

After she had been instructed in the teachings of the Catholic faith, Saint Hildulphus baptized her. The blessed Erardus received her from the sacred font, enlightened in mind and body, and, giving her a name, called her Otilia.

[She remained in the holiness of religious life, was no ordinary imitator of what is good and right, and now, reigning with Christ, grants daily on earth miracles of innumerable signs.]

This event had such an effect that not only people of modest standing but also powerful persons revered and loved the man of God Hildulphus and supplied assistance for the enlargement of the place. [For he was composed with the beauty of every virtue and showed himself equally approachable to all.]

## CHAPTER XIII

### The Gifts of Bego and the Pious Death of Saint Spinulus

A certain man named Bego, sharing in the needs of the holy man, decided to assign some of his possessions for the use of the brothers serving God under the blessed man. He designated the place that is still called Bego’s Cell and the part of the Vosges called Folchodi-Rupes.

Finally, in the cell just mentioned, dedicated to the holy cross, the man of God Hildulphus appointed a man of supreme humility and obedience named Spinulus. Serving God faithfully there, after many labors in Christ’s struggle and numerous signs of miracles, he obtained the rewards of eternal life.

The almighty Trinity, wishing to show him glorified on earth and glorious in heaven, made his death known to blessed Hildulphus through angelic ministry, so that he might bring the saint’s body to the monastery for burial, [just as the blessed man himself, while still living, had earnestly charged the brothers to do].

Without delay, the old man obeyed the command, shook out the ashes in which the weary limbs had rested, and, summoning the brothers, announced the death of the man of God. Although they mourned, deprived of such great assistance from their brother, they nevertheless rejoiced in his glory. Lighting candles, they hastened to the funeral of the blessed man’s [body].

## CHAPTER XIV

### Miracles Occur at His Tomb

The force of the winds had grown more violent than usual, so that it uprooted not only shrubs but also ancient oaks and lofty fir trees. In such a tempest, however, the burning candles were carried before the body of the holy man all the way to the place of burial.

After he had been buried in the earth, God wished to show that he was living with him in heaven and chose to assist all the sick who came to the holy man’s tomb. How many paralytics were strengthened there when their veins were restored cannot easily be explained in speech or writing. Every blindness was illumined, and, astonished by the light, marveled at the day. Every weakness there, its functions restored, felt the strength it had lost return.

As a result, when the crowds rushed in, extremely salty water was found.

## CHAPTER XV

### Saint Hildulphus Orders It to Cease, Lest the Brothers’ Tranquility Be Disturbed

Because of their desire for healing, and because of the site’s suitability and abundance of water, the people who flocked there attempted to establish a market. The man of God Hildulphus felt this disturbance and grieved.

[With a staff supporting his limbs,] he entered the church of Saint Gregory to pray, as was his custom. When he had completed his prayer, he rose and went to the tomb of Saint Spinulus. As befitted his pious mind, his face covered with tears, he said:

“Brother Spinulus, we give thanks to God that we believe you rest in the region of peace and that we trust you have great influence with almighty God. We also know how and why we, desiring to devote ourselves more freely to prayers and to the service of God, left the tumult of the people and came to this solitude.

“Therefore, since you possess tranquility, have mercy, we beg you, on us who are on the road of death and tossed amid its dangers. Indeed, if it is lawful, we demand it by that very virtue of splendid and supreme obedience which shone forth in you while you lived in time, and by whose merit you now rejoice eternally, as is clear from evident and daily signs: do not raise against the monastic religion a storm of unspeakable danger through the affairs of the people.

“For if we are pressed by this gathering of people, we shall deviate considerably from our purpose. Little by little, as though infected and defiled by the excessive dust of worldly quarrels and lawsuits, we shall fail to cling to the all-pure Creator; and—God forbid!—the monastic order, now established here by God’s favor, will be utterly destroyed.

“For although, with God cooperating, bodily provisions are being brought to our place, we fear dangers to souls. Therefore restrain the crowds of those who are rushing here, and implore God, the cheerful and generous giver, so that we may experience the grace of his blessing. Thus, once the scarcity of necessary food and clothing has been driven away, and the opportunity for the envious devil to set the snares of deception has been removed, we may fulfill the vows of our profession.”

Then you would have seen a spirit released from the flesh and endowed with life obeying a mortal, as though still held by the bond of death. For when the signs ceased and the veins of the salt springs were restrained, the crowds of people also ceased.

Nevertheless, to refute the shameless chatter of the envious and unbelieving, very clear traces of the three former wells are still shown there to this day.

Finally, when the saint had ended his prayer and complaint, lively and confident that he had already obtained what he desired, he returned to the brothers, who were anxious, and urged them to persist in watchful prayer, so that, after the crowd’s rush had been restrained, the consolation of voluntary poverty might be directed to them from elsewhere by the Almighty.

## CHAPTER XVI

### Gifts Are Made to the Monastery; Saint Hildulphus Mortifies Himself and Seeks Flight

Through the prayers and merits of blessed Spinulus and the holy man, the Lord’s blessing followed immediately. For before seven days had passed, an illustrious man named Hagio, also accustomed to be called Flariulphus [Note: A more recent manuscript reads “Hariulphus”], arrived and contributed to the church of Saint Peter a large part of a certain noble estate called Berchem [Note: This is how it is read in the manuscript of Medianum Monastery, and likewise below in chapter 19; the Paderborn codex, however, reads “Berenfini”]. After the conveyance had been solemnly carried out, it was immediately put into writing, and the documents were entrusted to Leutbald, then abbot, so that they might refute any dispute of violent men that might at some time be contrived concerning it.

Afterward, many noblemen transferred estates belonging to their own legal rights to the aforesaid place, and not long afterward some portion of the village called Hundinis-Heym likewise passed to that place by the right of its possessor.

Let whoever is able duly consider how profoundly this man had mortified himself and clung to God and to his life. He appears crucified to the Apostle—or, what is more excellent, to Christ himself—able to say in the true words of his heart: “The world has been crucified to me, and I to the world” (Gal. 6:14). And: “I live, yet it is no longer I; rather, Christ lives in me” (Gal. 2:20).

The world, which lies in wickedness (I John 5:19), had indeed been crucified to him: he neither feared adversity nor desired prosperity. Then he, who abhorred the world, was dead to the world. He avoided the devil’s flattering birdlime and did not dread his raging assault. Fearing to be honored in his own country, he entrusted himself to foreigners. When he understood that he was being glorified among them, he sought flight; but in the end, glory pursued him and, though he wept and resisted, forcibly held him back.

Not long afterward, however, freeing himself from it, and distrusting that this wilderness would be his permanent dwelling, he explored trackless places. Even there glory, not yet wearied of pursuing so praiseworthy a fugitive, sought to steal upon him in the garb of divine signs [Note: The manuscript reads “sought it”], as though it could thereby more easily persuade him—though he was utterly destitute of all resources, including, what was more, the money of his dependents, and was not moved by persuasion. The syntax of this corrupt passage is uncertain. Thus he might fear being blamed if he rejected support apparently provided by God.

Who, I ask, among the religious of our time would not desire his possessions to be increased through worldly affairs and his reputation raised by the crowds of those arriving? Who, seeing such things supplied to him, would not believe that he was being honored from heaven, counting—or rather imagining—great things about himself that are already known before God to be small or nothing?

But this worshiper of God, like blessed Abraham, was tested by the Lord and did not fall. The Lord knew both what he himself would do and what lay hidden in his servant, so that his innermost mortification might be revealed to us. But now let the pen return to the work begun.

## CHAPTER XVII

### After the Death of Abbot Leutbald, He Resumes Pastoral Care of the Monks

At last Lord Leutbald, having faithfully and prudently administered the office of stewardship entrusted to him, was taken from the slippery ground of this life. He gave his limbs to the earth and his spirit to heaven, to cling eternally to the Lord, whom he had preferred to nothing in the world.

Immediately, the anxious crowd of monks, deprived of the timely provision of a suitable pastor, hastened back to the bishop of piety and sought by mournful entreaty to turn him back, lest he disdain to resume the burden of the sheep for whom the Shepherd of shepherds had embraced the outrage of an infamous death.

But the teachable man, knowing how to yield to God’s mercy, judged that he ought by no means to refuse what he perceived Christ commanding through the heartfelt plea of his own people: to be their poor pastor, despite his now spent old age. Accordingly, after once again accepting the heavy burden of the flock, during the only three years he remained alive in this world he diligently extended to the brothers the rod of correction together with the staff of support.

In measuring out the small remainder of his journey, he was made more cheerful because, having traversed that stretch, he had begun to draw nearer to the prize.

## CHAPTER XVIII

### Saint Erardus Bids Him Farewell

Then blessed Erardus, having built a church in the name of Saint Aper the Confessor not far from the monastery, on the left bank of the aforesaid river, said to his brother, the man of God, after exhorting him in the service of the Creator:

“The Lord has taken possession of this place for you, and he will be present in all that you do. Nevertheless, I warn and beg you always to remember the last things and us. I must indeed be separated from you in sight, though not in heart, in face, though not in mind. May the good angel of the Lord, according to his good pleasure, accompany me as I prepare to return to my own proper dwelling.”

[In reply, the blessed bishop entrusted to his brother, amid other conversations concerning heavenly mysteries, the brothers whom he had gathered under God and under the venerable patron Maximin, so that, as far as possible, he might provide them with faithful and continual protection both within and without. The man full of God most willingly agreed.]

At last they rushed into a tender embrace, covering one another with mutual and abundant tears. After praying together, they parted from one another’s sight with no small contrition of heart.

Blessed Erardus, having forded the Rhine, entered his own city, Regensburg [Note: The Median manuscript reads “Renesbuorch,”], destined to become renowned as the seat of so holy a bishop. There, after not many cycles of time, he passed from death to life on the sixth day before the Ides of January.

Saint Hildulphus, however, did not cease from the work of God. He compelled limbs wearied by fasts and labors to serve the spirit. He rejoiced to see the brothers subject to him, especially John and Benignus [whom we mentioned above], advance daily toward better things. He admonished them, not only in public exhortation but sometimes in private and friendly conversation, to remember him; he urged them to pray for the state of God’s churches, for the peace of kings, and for the salvation of peoples; to run faithfully along the way of life that they had once undertaken; and knowingly to long for the prize of heavenly reward, constantly repeating with attentive hearts the Lord’s saying:

“No one who puts his hand to the plow and looks back is fit for the kingdom of God” (Luke 9:62).

He said:

“God is faithful and does not know how to lie. Let them strive to become accustomed to good conduct; let them learn to be content with modest food and clothing; let them offer one another humble and careful obedience; let them follow Christ’s footsteps before all else; let them labor eagerly in the instruction of blessed Benedict; and let them keep watch over discretion in all things.”

He frequently impressed this upon them, teaching that discretion is the mother of virtues [Note: The Paderborn manuscript reads “reward”]. He said that the evil of murmuring, ill-temper, excessive talk, detraction, and idleness ought not to be found even among the body of the faithful, much less in the cloisters of monks.

Thus, arranging everything in due order and instructing the brothers more by his example than by his word, the blessed old man made them ready and eager for every good work. He obtained food for his holy old age by the labor of his hands, continually impressing upon himself and upon others that apostolic saying:

“Whoever is unwilling to work should not eat” (II Thess. 3:10).

## CHAPTER XIX

### The Illustrious Theudoald Submits to His Discipline

As the radiant splendor of his exemplary life shot the light of virtues everywhere, like the passage of the true sun, to rebuke the darkness of mortals, some worldly men, mocking the world that falsely smiled upon them lest they themselves be truly mocked by the world, shortly afterward handed over their possessions to the poor and to the legal authority of Saint Peter. Having subdued the obstinacy of foolish wisdom, they took up the wise foolishness of Christ, intending to serve under the blessed man.

In those days a certain man named Theudoald was considered illustrious among the nobles of the kingdom. Prudently turning aside from the world’s tenacious glue—which softly but ruinously seeks to bait precious souls—he, with the consent of his wife, who had already undertaken a religious way of life, laid aside his military belt and submitted himself to the teaching of the blessed man, together with his natural son named Abbo.

Among the other gifts of his offering, he also bestowed upon this monastery a basilica dedicated to the honor of the ever-virgin Mary. It stood on the aforesaid estate of Berchem and was especially distinguished by the multiplicity of its revenues.

## CHAPTER XX
## The Death and Burial of Saint Hildulph

As this distinguished Father devoted himself to this undertaking, sparing neither his years nor his own body, he labored with the greatest care to provide for the needs and peace both of the monks living there at that time and of those who would come after them, lest lack of anything whatsoever should enable them to offer even the slightest excuse for being unable to serve the regular discipline. This is especially characteristic of the sluggish and of those who observe the strict life laxly. And when, although his body was already exhausted by labors, his spirit was more fervent than ever, merciful God wished to call him to the crown of righteousness.

While he was therefore engaged in vigils, he was seized by a fever. As it grew worse over several days, the troubled brothers hurried to the old man’s bed—for he always proclaimed Christ as best he could. When they became sorrowful and grieved that they were being left desolate, all the mourners and supplicants had one cry: that the shepherd of the sheep [f.: “sheep”] should not abandon them. Moved by these complaints and tears, and already dead in the extremities of his body, he sat up at the foot of the bed. Looking around at the brothers, he said, “Peace be with you.”

Then, raising his hand, he blessed them with these words:

> O almighty God, mercifully bless and preserve your servants who are here present forever.

When this was finished, with the deepest humility and in the humblest prayer he earnestly entreated the brothers continually to retain the memory of his name at Christ’s altar and in every divine office, lest he and those whom he had governed here for a time should be deprived of the companionship of the blessed Father Benedict. Having diligently provided for the repose of his little sheep through the matters mentioned above and a thousand other consolations, the venerable Father, full of virtues and days, was withdrawn from a world that no longer deserved to possess such a man. Secure at the gate of the kingdom, he will be numbered among the senators of the earth, among whom Christ, the noble man of the holy Church, will be held.

This blessed man Hildulphus had scattered the seed of right intention in the field of a contrite and humbled heart, following the example of the Lord’s parable. The seed, bearing fruit of its own accord, first produced the blade of tender action, then the ear of advancement, and finally reached the grain of perfection under the divine sickle. Thus, when his life in time had been brought to an end, he was brought, like grain selected from the refuse of the chaff, into the granaries of eternal life.

Our most merciful shepherd and nourisher, Saint Hildulphus, shone forth from the sorrowful dwelling-place of this exile on the fifth day before the Ides of July, when the year from the Incarnation of Jesus Christ was 707, during the consulship of Justinian the Younger Augustus, who had been disfigured by the cutting off of his nose by Leo, who had rebelled against him, in the fifth indiction, while the venerable Pope Sergius governed the Roman Church. His two immediate successors bore the name John; he was the one who found a remarkable portion of the saving wood in the shrine of blessed Peter.

[In his days Theudobald, king of the Angles, who had waged many wars in his homeland, was converted to Christ and hastened to Rome. He came through Cunipert, king of the Lombards, and was received with great honor. When he reached Rome, he was baptized by the aforesaid pope and was called Peter. While still in his white baptismal robes, he departed to the heavenly kingdom. **Note:** The sentences enclosed in brackets are absent from the Paderborn manuscript.]

At this time, too, the lord Bede, a distinguished man of monastic religion in learning and the art of calculation, flourished magnificently, and continued to flourish long after the death of our Father Hildulphus. Although you could see companies of disciples flocking eagerly from every side and surrounding the funeral of the pious Father and teacher with pious lamentation—for they rejoiced devoutly that the heavenly patronage of so illustrious an instructor would not be lacking to them, yet they mourned devoutly that the customary human consolations had been taken from them.

At last, after they had dutifully cared for the body of the Father who would always be remembered, they buried it in the basilica of the blessed Pope Gregory, on the right side of the altar, when daylight had fully come on the second day of the week. This was in the thirty-sixth year of his dwelling in the desolation of this dreadful wilderness and the fortieth after the glorious translation of the lord Bishop Maximinus, which had taken place under our archbishop, while Pippin, mentioned above, was already governing Gaul.

Nevertheless, when the glory of blessed Hildulphus shone forth through frequent miracles, his wondrous body was removed from the church of his burial and, through the devotion and zeal of the brothers, was brought into the church of the blessed Virgin Mary. There it lay for some time on the right beneath an elegant vaulted arch. May we now be occupied with his praises, be raised up by his merits, instructed by his footsteps, and joined to the joys of the future, through the most effective mercy and the most merciful efficacy of our almighty and most benevolent Creator and Restorer, who glorifies the followers of the bare cross, freed from worldly burdens, above the sons of men; and who declares that they will be not only secure because of their own merits but also judges of those of others.

## CHAPTER XXI

### On the Blessed Deaths of Saints John and Benignus

After the passing of the glorious blessed Hildulphus, Reymbertus, a man suitably endowed with the splendid adornments of character, assumed the office of governance by the unanimous vote of the brothers. His period and writings extended through the reigns of Kings Theodoric and the younger Childeric, and of Pippin, son of Duke Charles. There remain, in truth, very many deeds of our most worthy Father Hildulphus and of his successors, composed in accordance with his merits; because of the reader’s weariness, we have judged that these should for the present be deferred and assigned to another work.

But an exceptionally clear proof of invincible charity, preserved without extinguishing throughout life, in death, and after death, should not for the present be postponed. It is altogether sweet and profitable for all who love him chastely.

The two disciples of the praiseworthy teacher, John and Benignus, whom—as has been said—we know to have been brothers in flesh and spirit, the former serving as priest and the latter as deacon, were accustomed continually to attend his service. Offering daily to God the sacrifices of our redemption and of their own mortification, and joining a more praiseworthy end to a praiseworthy beginning, they followed their beloved teacher to the heavenly kingdom. On the day before the Kalends of August they departed together to Christ, namely, twenty-one days after his departure.

No faithful person will deny that this was granted through the intimate charity of the three, and did not happen by chance, since we read that among others a brother, not summoned by the prayers of the venerable Anastasius, preceded his seventh day by his own death.

Although my pen is now too eagerly bent upon the matter, I am reluctant to recount the sequence of what happened more fully. When the blessed and ever-to-be-remembered teacher Hildulphus was about to leave the precariousness of this life and enter the senate of the kingdom, he admonished the beloved brothers and sons of the holy congregation of the blessed Bishop Maximinus to remember him, as was fitting, both spiritually and bodily, in the presence of Christ and his Church. In prophetic spirit he announced that these two brothers would follow him to heavenly joys.

Immediately both of them were overcome by illness and lay down upon their beds [**Note:** The manuscript of the Monastery of Mediana reads this passage somewhat differently and more briefly: “After Hildulphus had been taken from mortal life, the aforesaid two brothers, overcome by an equal illness, immediately lay down upon their beds.”] [that they would live with the Lamb].

As the illness increased over the course of several days, they sensed that the dissolution of their bodies was approaching. Suddenly Saint John, who was the elder by birth, sent one of the brothers to inquire how his most beloved brother, who was lying apart, was faring. The monk quickly carried out the order and found that the servant of God, strengthened by the Lord’s sacraments, had escaped the bonds of this mortality. He ran back and reported it.

But the blessed man, who had still been troubled by concern that his younger and beloved brother might die first and that he himself might remain for some time among human affairs, heard of his departure and said joyfully:

> I give the greatest thanks to your goodness, most merciful Maker of man, because I am sending my brother to your kingdom ahead of me; now, secure and joyful, I go after him from here to you.

When he had finished, the brothers asked him whether they should be buried separately. He replied:

> Far be it from us, my lords, that we should be separated from one another, either in the future or in the present! The womb of one mother brought us forth into this light; together and under one rule we were trained in monastic practices; one departure from this light commends us both to the one God; let one earth receive us in every respect and close the bosom of the mother of us all, until the Lord comes and awakens us.

When he had finished this speech, he also departed from temporal light. The holy man followed his holy brother, and both beloved men followed their beloved teacher, who had once urged them to long for heavenly things and who now offered them things greater than his promises.

But why should we linger here at length? They were placed together in a single honorable mausoleum and entrusted to burial in the oratory of Saint Gregory. This shared distinction is still granted to our own days and will be granted to those of the future.

## CHAPTER XXII

### A Nun’s Withered Hand Is Healed at Their Tomb

After their escape from this mortality, the almighty Majesty ennobled these saints through innumerable miracles, by which it became clear how good a treasure had lain hidden in the field of their hearts while they lived. But of the many miracles, let the few that follow suffice.

At that same time there was a certain nun named Hymeldrudis, poor in possessions but rich in faith. Whether because her sins demanded it, or so that heavenly power might manifest in her the merits of these friends of God, she had been deprived of the natural use of her hand and carried the useless and painful burden of a withered hand.

She kept watch diligently in the aforesaid oratory, where, prostrated before their tomb, she begged for help with prayer, tears, and insistent lamentation. One night, therefore, when this little woman had by no means ceased from what she had begun, a radiant man in monastic dress appeared before her and said:

> Hymeldrudis, heavenly medicine will come to your infirmity. Nevertheless, take care from now on not to become involved in any sins, lest you perish with them.

He touched her hand and healed her through his most excellent power. The same man declared that he was John; beside him appeared another, younger than he and exceedingly handsome, who stated that he wished to depart from that place.

## CHAPTER XXIII

### A Blind Woman Receives Her Sight

Another miracle was likewise displayed there. So that this may not seem burdensome to anyone, it should be approached in a concise narrative.

Not far from the monastery, scarcely half a mile away, there lived an old woman named Agnes who, after the passage of many years, had been deprived of her sight. She was accustomed to visit that church on a little donkey, guided by her companions.

One day, coming as usual and, after the completion of Mass, prostrating herself before the tombs of the saints, she remained at prayer for a long time. At last her companions, wearied by the length of her prayer, began to move her away from the place, saying that the hour for returning had passed.

She rose and declared that she could see her companions and everyone present perfectly. When all rejoiced and gave thanks to God, she herself then and thereafter returned to her own home, burning ever more intensely with the desire to please her Giver through upright action.

## CHAPTER XXIV

### A Third Miracle Is Added to the Second

A certain poet sang that the Lord delights in an odd number [Virgil, *Eclogues* 8.15].

As the fame of these righteous men spread everywhere—men whom eternal memory will always possess—the place was ordinarily called the estate of Saint Stephen of the Danes, although everyone living along the banks of the River Meuse now corruptly calls it Danobrium, a certain blind man joined the crowd of common people hurrying there. Driven by the grave affliction that afflicted him and encouraged by the hope of receiving a benefit, he came with a hand-offering.

He spent the night in prayer, but was not gladdened by the hoped-for healing. When morning came, he earnestly tried to return to his own home. But what could the wretched man do? While everyone else hurried back to their own homes, he remained dependent upon the assistance of others, anxious for two reasons: both because he had not received the benefit he had hoped for and because, cast out from his familiar hut, he had become the object of the mockery of foolish people.

One of the brothers, however, extended his hand to him and led him as far as the place called Vision-Valley. There the man finally burst into complaint and began miserably to curse his misfortune in these words:

> Alas, I am ashamed and distressed that I, wretched man, have come to these parts and visited patrons and Fathers so widely renowned! Everyone will say that I am the most wretched and worthless of mortals, just as I now experience and fully confess. Oh, how many people, detained by equal or even greater misfortune, have obtained benefits through those saints, while I alone, as is obvious, have been allowed to return more wretched than the wretched, without the fulfillment of my vow!

While he continued with these and many similar vehement complaints, the presence of the friends of God—whose power is most effective everywhere—prevailed. At a place called Coriletum, one of those who accomplishes all things with him and in him, who is everywhere present and powerful, removed the darkness of blindness. The man unexpectedly found himself restored to himself as his own guide along the road.

Forgetting his continual complaint and changing his words and emotions, he suddenly said joyfully to his guide:

> I see you, and the woods on either side; I feel that I am master of the entire road. With all my heart, therefore, I offer immense thanks to divine Omnipotence and to the effective merits of the saints whom, in my misery, I visited, because I recognize that I have been given back to myself.

The joyful brother then sent the joyful man on his way home. He himself returned to the monastery’s enclosure, and each made the monks and the people joyful—the one through his return, the others through hearing what had happened on the road.

Through this and countless other miracles, that place has until now shone through the assisting gift of divine favor. Because of the abundance of these events, the poverty of writers, and the apathy of readers, the earlier generation either shrank from touching upon them altogether or could scarcely bring itself to make them known, at least by means of a copy containing some unpolished account. But I, fearing to yield to disobedience, have by no means allowed what was to come to lie hidden under any sort of unadorned narrative.

[If anyone wishes to run through the book of miracles concerning these matters, he will be able to recognize from the clearest indications how great our blessed Father Hildulphus was and what sort of men, at the direction of the Holy Spirit, he educated for the holy Church.]

---

## On the Successors of Saint Hildulphus in the Monastery of Mediana

(See *Patrologia*, vol. CXXXVIII, col. 203.)

## Life of Saint Deodatus

### Preliminary Commentary on Saint Deodatus, First Bishop of Nevers, Then Abbot of the Valley of Galilee in the Vosges

(*Acta sanctorum* of the Bollandists, June, vol. III, day 19, p. 869.)

### On His Cult, Life, Age, and Monastery

#### 1

The Vosges is a mountain, woodland, forest, and wilderness extending along the borders of Alsace, Burgundy, and especially Lorraine. In former times it provided dwellings or monasteries for various saints, both hermits and coenobites.

Among these, five more important monasteries were considered to be arranged in the form of a cross. At the head, toward the north, stood the monastery of Bodo, constructed by Saint Bodo, Bishop of Toul, who will be discussed more fully below; it has now been destroyed.

To the east is the monastery of Senones, founded by Saint Gumbert, or Gundobert, Archbishop of Senones, as is reported more fully in his Life on 21 February. It now belongs to the Benedictine Congregation of Saint Vanne.

Opposite it, to the west, stands the monastery of Stinagium, commonly called Estinan, on the River Meurthe. It was later transferred to the Premonstratensian Order.

There is also found there the Middle or Mediana Monastery, erected by Saint Hildulphus after he had resigned the archbishopric of Trier. Much will be said below about it and its founder. It is now united with Senones in the Benedictine Congregation of Saint Vanne.

Finally, to the south, as though at the foot of the cross formed by these monasteries, stands the Monastery of the Valley of Galilee, formerly called Junctures. It was founded and cultivated by Saint Deodatus, whose Acts we are here illustrating, and became famous through his death, burial, and miracles. From him the town that gradually grew up beside it took its name; it lies on the River Meurthe and is now commonly called Saint-Dié-en-Lorraine. There is another place of the same name on the Loire, Saint-Dié-sur-Loire, where canons were introduced in the tenth century in place of monks and venerate the same Saint Deodatus as their patron.

#### 2

On the twelfth day of this month, June, Saints Nabor and Nazarius are celebrated. Saint Chrodegang, Bishop of Metz, brought their holy bodies from Rome. He placed the body of Saint Nabor in the monastery of Hilariacum, founded in present-day Lorraine by Saint Fridolin, as we stated in the Lives of both saints on 6 March.

In the manuscript Martyrology of that monastery, namely of Saint Nabor, the following is read under 19 June:

> On the same day, Saint Deodatus, bishop and confessor.

Grevenus, in the printed Auctarium of Usuard of 1515 and 1521, celebrates “Deodatus, bishop of Nevers and confessor,” whom Saussay adorns with a very long encomium in his *Gallican Martyrology*.

Trithemius writes the following in book III, chapter 304, of *On Illustrious Men of the Benedictine Order*:

> Adeodatus, abbot of the monastery of the Valley of Galilee and afterward bishop of Nevers, shone forth distinguished by great virtues and merits; and although he was a bishop, he violated in no respect the purpose of a monk. His feast is celebrated on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of July.

Wion and Dorganius follow Trithemius, as do Menardus and Bucelinus. They call him Deodatus and accurately show from his Acts that, after leaving the episcopate, he entered the monastic life.

Camerarius likewise assigned Adeodatus, Bishop of Nevers, to the Scottish Menology on 23 March and to this day; Fitz-Simon calls him Theodatus in the Irish Calendar. But these claims are readily refuted by the Acts themselves.

In the manuscript *Florarium*, the deposition of Deodatus, Bishop of Nevers and confessor, is celebrated on 2 January.

#### 3

We obtained his Acts transcribed by John Gamans from a paper manuscript of the Library of the Capuchin Fathers at Paderborn and collated with a parchment manuscript of the Passionary of the Monastery of Böddeken in the same diocese of Paderborn, belonging to the Canons Regular of Saint Augustine. In the latter, however, chapter 4 is missing.

We also had the same Acts in the Utrecht manuscript of Saint Saviour, but in it the material at the beginning of section 1 and that narrated from section 27 onward is absent.

Mosander possessed a similar copy, in which he published the same material, with the style somewhat corrected, as a supplement to Surius. These Acts were also published in their entirety at Nancy in 1619. From all these sources, following our custom, we present them with divisions and explanatory notes.

John Ruyrus, or Ruerus—for he had his name printed in both forms—later translated them into French. He was secretary of the church and chapter of Saint Deodatus and published the translation at Troyes in 1594. He subsequently inserted it into his likewise French work *On the Saints and Antiquities of the Vosges*, part II, book II, printed at Épinal in 1634.

In the dedicatory letter of the first edition, addressed to Gabriel de Reynette, grand provost, and the canons of the distinguished church of Saint Deodatus, he asserts that these Acts were later written from an original collection made by the disciples of Saint Deodatus by a certain learned and holy man, who was abbot of the Monastery of Mediana, after he had been divinely urged to do so by a third vision.

He states that this very fact is attested in a letter written in verse and sent together with these Acts to Waldrad, grand provost, and the venerable chapter of Saint Deodatus.

There exists a *History of the Abbey of Senones*, written by Richer, a monk of that monastery, and published by Luc d’Achery in volume III of the *Spicilegium*, and in part II, section III, of the Benedictine edition. From it we append some information about a miracle and the translation. The remaining material can be read there.

#### 4

A few years before his death, Henschenius had proceeded this far. Continuing his work, I note that “the lord Deodatus passed from death to life,” as section 20 says, “on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of July, on a Sunday, in the six hundred and seventy-ninth year from the Incarnation of Our Lord Jesus Christ.”

Since these dates agree extremely well with one another, I would not depart from them because of certain errors in other circumstances of the same Life concerning the names of bishops. I do not know whether these should rather be attributed to the Deodatian author or to the Medianan interpolator. Otherwise this death would have to be postponed by almost an entire century, as our Father Labbe postponed it, ordering that 769 be written instead of 679. Although such a conversion of numerals is easy to write, it is impossible to prove.

Nor would this have occurred to Labbe had he considered that Doublet’s *San-Dionysian Works* contains a diploma issued by Charlemagne at that time, in which he declares that he grants “to the house of Saint Denis the martyr … the little monastery called after Saint Deodatus, within the forest of the Vosges, just as Pippin, his father, is proven to have held it in his possession.”

Therefore the saint had died long before—even before Pippin’s reign—the little monastery being called by his name. We do not think that it was any other than the one under discussion, namely the Valley of Galilee.

Nor would I accept the claim that in the very year in which this saint is said to have died he was taken from his hermitage to travel to Rome with Saint Wilfrid. Charles le Cointe’s opinion was that for this reason he was compelled to postpone Deodatus’s death until 684.

He confused the Deodatus under discussion with Adeodatus, Bishop of Toul, who subscribed to the Roman synod in 680 and accompanied Saint Wilfrid, as Henschenius explained at greater length in the Life of Saint Wilfrid on 24 April, chapter 4.

The body of the former, as the aforementioned Ruyrus writes, was raised by Bertold, Bishop of Toul, in 1003, on 17 June, with the assistance of the blessed widow of Frederick, Duke of Lorraine, and her son Theodoric. The translation is described in chapter 15 of the *Chronicle of Senones*, which extends almost to the end of the fourteenth century.

#### 5

Francis Riguetus Magnus, provost of Saint Deodatus, had the Life of that saint reprinted according to the old Nancy copy. He sent the reprint to Henschenius in 1679, adding in his own hand, both in the margins and at the end of the booklet, observations in French that are by no means negligible.

In the following year he enlarged these with historical and chronological memoirs, also in French, and sent them to us at Antwerp with similar care. Henschenius had no leisure to revise this preliminary commentary and the notes prepared for the Life in light of them.

I am now doing so, while at the same time giving the author the acknowledgment due to his devotion toward his holy patron.

#### 6

In his initial observations he begins by saying that the author of the Life appears to him to have been “a monk of the Valley of Galilee,” who says in section 11, “of this monastery,” and in section 20, “into this Valley of Galilee.”

Since canons were introduced there in place of monks around the year 980, it seems to follow that the Life was written before that year, or even much earlier. The phrases mentioned above, to speak frankly, suit a monk of that monastery better than a monk of Mediana.

But when I read the note at the end of the Life stating that in 1049 it was read at a synod in Rome and that Pope Leo IX ordered it to be recited in the Church of God; and when I learn from Riguetus that in the Deodatian archive there is still preserved a parchment *Legendarium* in which the same Life seems to have been divided word for word into readings, with most of it still remaining there, I am compelled to think that we do not possess the original composition of the Deodatian monk.

That original may have been written in a much simpler style and, in all likelihood, obscured by no chronological errors or by fewer of them. The Medianan abbot, more holy than learned, may have accumulated these errors all the more laboriously because he tried to adapt himself to a certain, apparently very corrupt, catalogue of the bishops of Toul, from which he took the names inserted here. These matters will be discussed below in the notes.

Certainly that Provost Waldrad to whom Ruyrus says the Life was sent appears to be the same man about whom Pope Leo IX wrote to Udo of Toul in 1051:

> Our dearest brother Weldrad, provost of the monastery of Saint Deodatus, together with certain of his brothers, being present with us in the court of Henry III, at the time when we ourselves were elected pope there, implored our help.

On that same occasion, therefore, he may have presented to Leo the Life as he had received it from the Medianan abbot, for its initial approval at a Roman synod. In this way it may have passed into the aforementioned parchments, but without the letter mentioned by Ruyrus. If only he had published that letter! Riguetus now indicates that it can be found nowhere.

#### 7

For the present we must use this Life, whatever its quality, and the remaining details must be adjusted to the year of the saint’s death. That year, together with its accompanying indiction and Sunday letter, could have been known with greater certainty.

Thus, although the author or interpolator of the Life repeatedly says that the saint came to the Valley of Galilee in 669, he must nevertheless have come there a decade earlier. The cause of the error may have been a privilege discovered under the name of Saint Hildulphus, Bishop of Trier, supposedly issued in that year to Saint Deodatus for his monastery in the Valley of Galilee.

The author may have thought that this was the beginning of the monastery, while he had neither the donations of King Childeric, granted to the monastery when its construction had already begun around 660—which charters are not found even now—nor the older privilege of Saint Numerianus, Bishop of Trier before Hildulphus, issued no later than 665.

Riguetus congratulates himself on having found this privilege in the Monastery of Mediana, since it is the model after which the other privilege of Hildulphus was later either made or forged. It speaks of a monastery already fully established; to bring it to that condition, at least five or six years would have been required.

Moreover, others there held the following opinion—“to which,” says the author in section 14, “we neither object nor assent, since we are entirely unable either to refute or defend it”—namely, that blessed Deodatus entered this valley thirty years after leaving France.

Those thirty years, together with the preceding twenty, make fifty years spent amid the solitudes of the Vosges, not in one place or at the foundation of a single monastery.

In this way Deodatus may be understood to have come from France, where he had administered a bishopric for at least a few years, around the year 630, when he was approaching forty or was already older. Thus he truly died “very old,” as section 16 says, “a veteran of distinguished service,” having been born around 590.

All these points, in the notes we have made on the Life—much more extensive than those left by Henschenius—will be shown to cohere perfectly with the more reliable history, illuminated by Riguetus’s observations and memoirs.

#### 8

He begins by describing the present condition of his church, which it will not be inappropriate to append to this preliminary commentary:

> The present chapter consists of twenty-four canons, together with the major provost, who is the head of all. Their number includes the dean, the cantor, and the scholasticus; because of their greater dignity in relation to the others, they also have a larger prebend.
>
> Formerly there were thirty. But our predecessors obtained from Rome the suppression of three prebends, preserving an organ and supporting an organist, together with four choirboys and a music teacher. By papal authority our princes removed a fourth prebend for the erection of the new church of Nancy, which they call the primatial church.
>
> The canons perform the office in the church together with the vicars. Their number and stipend are now undefined; before the wars there were usually eleven or twelve.
>
> It is believed to have resulted from the institution of Leo IX—who at one time held among us the title and office of major provost—that his successors, when performing pontifical functions, should have a staff and mitre, together with a distinctive silk ornament covering the alb, tunicle, and dalmatic from the girdle to the feet in the form of a fisherman’s net. In common speech it is called *rete*; in Latin we might call it *retiatum*, “netted.”
>
> This opinion can also be confirmed from the privilege concerning the pallium and mitres that the same Leo IX granted, in memory of his predecessor Clement II, formerly Bishop of Bamberg, to the bishop and the more distinguished canons of that same Church of Bamberg.
>
> The provost appears in such attire at the offices of the more solemn days; otherwise he is not required to attend. If, however, he wishes to attend, he is obliged to come in episcopal dress: in winter, in a violet cope lined with Armenian mouse-fur (ermine); in summer, in linen, with a shoulder ornament and a pectoral cross.

#### 9

> The provost also possesses episcopal jurisdiction, not only in the town of Saint Deodatus but throughout the entire valley, which is separated from the neighboring dioceses of Strasbourg, Toul, and Basel, and includes twelve large parishes.
>
> I added a thirteenth for the greater convenience of the parish priests. I summon them to my synods and hold elections for their institution. I have ministers of my spiritual court—an official, a promoter, and others—plainly as bishops do. From my court there is no appeal except to Rome.
>
> In the bulls that come from Rome to us, we are simply called part of the province of Trier, with no diocese named. For functions requiring episcopal consecration, we are free to request any bishop, and no one refuses the letters of release for ordinands signed by us.
>
> Our territory, through a donation made by Theodoric II to Saint Deodatus, extends over the mountains seven leagues in length and four in breadth. Formerly it was entirely deserted; now, because of the monasteries and cells built by the saint, it is also crowded with the dwellings of laypeople. Our Church receives the tithes of all of them, although at present only a third part of the territory is subject to us by title of supreme jurisdiction.
>
> In earlier centuries, regalian rights also belonged to us, such as the right to mint coinage, levy troops, exact tribute, and other rights of this kind.
>
> We find in our registers that the title “Magnus” was given to the provosts as early as the thirteenth century, and that the Duke of Lorraine used it in a charter that he signed for us in 1272.

#### 10

Thus far he has spoken. He then introduces the later records as follows:

> I shall follow, as far as I can, the ancient Life approved by Leo IX. Nevertheless, I shall have to add certain matters omitted there and refute some things that are wholly incompatible with other passages of the same Life, being especially concerned to separate what is false from what is true.
>
> In this I hope for considerably better success than others have had—men more learned than I, to be sure, but occupied with greater studies or situated farther away, who had neither the leisure to weigh every circumstance nor the opportunity to investigate the records of our archive and personally visit the places where the events occurred. For this reason they could do nothing other than refer themselves to this Life as the sole source from which any information could be expected.

I therefore undertake to review and expand Henschenius’s notes with these resources.

---

# Life of Saint Deodatus

*First written by a monk of Deodatus, then interpolated by the abbot of Mediolanum*

From manuscript copies and the Nancy edition.

## CHAPTER I

### His Birth, the Bishopric of Nevers, and His Solitary Life

#### 1

The Catholic faith and Christian devotion fix the mind’s gaze upon invisible things with such greater vitality that they attend less closely to visible things, because they perceive that they could be blinded by their vanity. Nor are they charmed by whatever appearance belongs to things passing away—things that the outward curiosity of the flesh admires and pursues—for inwardly they know them to be sometimes foul and sometimes empty.

For this reason the faithful turn their eyes away from such things, so that they may enjoy forever the delight of true and solid goodness. They are so intoxicated by its sober wine that they do not know by what path they may return to these frail things. To this kind of wine the *Song of Songs* exhorts us:

> Drink, friends, and become intoxicated, beloved ones.  
> (*Song of Songs* 5:1)

There are two kinds of intoxication of the soul. Either it is intoxicated with love of the world and forgets its Creator, or it is intoxicated with the splendid cup of the love of God and clings so ardently to its Maker that it does not perceive anything belonging to the world.

We frequently hear and see this happen when certain people, out of desire for eternal life, flee from their fleshly parents and homeland, though no one compels them, in order to live under the rule of spiritual Fathers. Those who were once exalted now wish to become what they had shortly before despised, and begin to hate what they had been.

Things once sweet become bitter to them, and bitter things become sweet. They fear prosperity and desire adversity, forgetting their possessions and every carnal affection. They are not recalled by the importunate tears of their spouses or by the devotion owed to their little children, but hurry toward labor as though toward rest.

Filled with this new wine of the Holy Spirit, some have forgotten their wealthy cities in this poor Vosges, content to waste away from hunger and cold. Among their number our most devout Father Deodatus must be proclaimed to us with exceptional praise.

[**Note:** At this point the Utrecht manuscript begins, with these words: “Our most devout Father Deodatus, who today must be proclaimed to us with exceptional praise, who [was] of noble …,” etc. Mosander followed the same text.]

## 2

Blessed Deodatus, born of the noble blood of the western Franks, was the first in his line to distinguish himself within his family by the excellence of his character and actions, although in bodily age he was reckoned the youngest. Thus, advancing step by step from virtue to virtue as his years increased, he showed himself pleasing to God and to the people through a twofold love, indefatigably embracing, as an incorruptible treasure, the riches of salvation—namely, wisdom and knowledge, together with the fear of the Lord. At length, by the equal and unanimous consent of clergy and people, he was granted by God—to whom he had given himself entirely—the episcopal office at Nevers, so that his holy activity might no longer remain hidden under a bushel, like a most splendid lamp that ought to be set upon a most fitting lampstand, and that he might shine before all, in word as well as deed, in the sanctuary of the Lord. No one among those who came before us doubts how greatly and zealously he illuminated that office under the episcopal mitre, since his complete end sings all his praise. In this it is recognized more clearly than daylight that, in the episcopate, he sought not his own interests but only the things that belong to Jesus Christ. [Col. 0612B]

[Note: Charles le Cointe, under the year 657, no. 16, produces “the privilege which Emmo, archbishop of Sens, granted to Saint Peter of the Living in an assembled synod,” to which, among others, the bishop of Nevers subscribed. Le Cointe conjectures that this bishop was the present Saint Deodatus; but—if he departed from the episcopate, as Rignetus maintains, under the year 640, or, as I maintain, in 630—that conjecture is very far astray. [Col. 0612C] It is equally mistaken with that of the Sammarthani, who defer his episcopate until the year 668, preceded by Gilbert in the year 665, as is known from a manuscript of the Church of Nevers. I therefore think that Deodatus was appointed after Agricola, who, in the early years of his episcopate, was present at the Synod of Mâcon in 581 and could easily have prolonged his life beyond 620. [Col. 0612D]]

Nor did he desire from that honor, which he was able so perfectly to renounce, even the reverence due from men, but rather an unblemished reward from God.

## 3

Finally, the most holy bishop, salutarily wounded by the arrow of divine love, desired with his whole being to be drawn and to run after Jesus, [Note: Mosander adds the following: “Saying to him with the bride: ‘Draw me after you; we shall run together into the fragrance of your ointments’” (Song of Songs 1:3).] considering that the world lies in the Evil One (1 John 5:9), and that he himself was in the midst of scandals. For just as it is characteristic of the proud to do little—or certainly no—good and to regard themselves as perfect in the eyes of God, so it is truly characteristic of the humble to do all that has been commanded, and to declare themselves useless servants (Luke 17:10), lower and more contemptible than all human beings—not merely with their lips, but also to believe this in the inmost affection of their hearts. Indeed, turned away from wickedness and made little in their own eyes, they lament before the Lord, who guards the little ones (Psalm 114:6), with a supplicant mind: “Your eyes saw my unfinished state” (Psalm 138:16).

In this manner, Deodatus, a man of supreme holiness, rooted and founded in the city of God in perfect humility (Psalm 47:2–3), and struck with awe at the thought of the strict Judge and the final examination, knowing that from the one to whom more has been entrusted, more will be required (Luke 12:48), was perfectly inflamed to follow Christ. Having therefore firmly undertaken the deliberation of so great a matter, [Note: The printed edition has *abrepta*. I believe that the original read *adrepta*, in accordance with medieval usage, which wrote the preposition *ad* without alteration.] he renounced his own affairs and those of others, choosing a successor for the governance of his diocese, [Note: These words concerning the chosen successor are absent from the manuscripts of Bodec and Utrecht. According to Riguet’s view, the successor ought to be considered Rauracus, who subscribed to the Council of Chalon in the year 650. Nor is this an objection, etc. See the appendix, volume VI of June, p. 216, column 2.] so that the ship of Christ’s Church might not be endangered by being deprived of so suitable a helmsman.

Thus, taking leave of the crowds of his flock, armed with pious tears to retain him, he withdrew with several companions of like mind from the town of Nevers. He voluntarily became an exile from his native soil, enrolled as a fellow-citizen and co-heir with Christ. He desired to await him while remaining in the wilderness, safe and delivered from faintness of spirit and the storm of popular tumult (Psalm 54:9).

Here we may appropriately do what prospectors and excavators of precious metals are known to do. When the quality of an earthly vein pleases them and promises—or announces—that they will reach a rich mass by itself, they immediately drive their energetic spades [Note: So the manuscript reads. Consult what we discussed concerning *vangæ* on 11 April, in the Life of Saint Isaac, from the Third Dialogue of Saint Gregory. The same word also occurs on 14 January, in the Life of Saint Felix of Nola. A *vanga* is a kind of mattock. Mosander explains it as “mattocks and other tools.” The printed editions read *vasis*. Riguet further believes that in the author’s time there was a mine in these mountains: “We have seen,” he says, “people in our own age laboring in vain to excavate them. Meanwhile, our chartularies show that in the year 1290 the tithes of silver extracted there were paid to our church. I do not cite a copy of the document as one dated 989, because its authenticity is highly suspect to me.” Thus far he.] and mattocks into all the rubble until they reach the desired metal.

In the same way, if we can, let us measure and weigh the soul of this holy man, dead to this world and hidden with Christ in God, from the quality of his outward actions. Let us consider how highly he valued the present age, to which he bade farewell when it smiled upon him most favorably, following the Lord Jesus amid the lamentations of a troubled spirit and contrite heart (Psalm 50:19)—the Lord who descended into this valley of tears so that we might not perish here.

No poor little man ever left a wretched hut, covered with thatch and turf, with as much alacrity as this worshiper of God left the city of Nevers, [Col. 0613C] where, amid the greatest abundance of worldly possessions, he administered the episcopal office. [Col. 0614A] But because interior things are hidden within the innermost parts, let us now proceed to what follows.

## 4

It is reported, therefore, that these men, Arbogast and Florentius, clung above all others as companions to the blessed Deodatus—who was thrice and four times blessed, receiving from Christ a hundredfold and eternal life—and shared in so great a reward. [Note: Saint Arbogast is commemorated on 21 July and Saint Florentius on 7 November; both are entered in the Roman Martyrology. I have discussed what is said of them here in the *Dissertation on the Three Dagoberts*, book II, chapter 3. They flourished under Dagobert II, son of Saint Sigebert, who—as I explained in the revised *Dagobertine Dissertation*, printed before volume III of April—reigned from the year 661 in the Ardennes provinces, and, after Childeric was killed, over the rest of Austrasia until the year 680, when he too was killed.

Riguet nevertheless doubts whether these saints followed Deodatus to Nevers, and prefers to believe Richerius, author of the *Chronicle of Sens*, and others who assert that their friendship was formed in Alsace, when the saint was already occupying the third place of his anchoritic life. He is moved not only by the fact that both are said to have originated in Scotland, but especially because Saint Arbogast is said to have died in the year 668, after having governed Strasbourg for twenty-seven years, and therefore from the year 641. Yet he was not elected bishop until after his virtue had been tested for several years in Alsace; consequently, he could have come there before Saint Deodatus, even if he ought not to have done so. This may be examined more fully in his Life.]

The former of them lived an eremitical life in the sacred grove called in the Teutonic language *Heiligestorst*, and from there he was taken to the episcopate of the city of Strasbourg. When he died, a successor was brought from another solitude, Hasale. [Note: This was Saint Florentius, who had built himself an oratory near Hasel, a stream of Alsace, “and not far from the famous river Brusch,” as Gaspar Bruchius says in his account of the bishops of Strasbourg. But he places Rodtharius, taken from the equestrian order, between the two saints; and he declares that those who say this man occupied the third place are completely mistaken, and that this can be demonstrated with absolute certainty from ancient charters.]

After these men had displayed on earth many distinguished signs of their merits, they were called by the Lord and now rest in spirit in the court of heaven, while in body they lie in the places which, as we said above, they founded.

At that time Willigod, the little lord, and his namesake Deodatus, from whom no labor had separated them, by eagerly devoting themselves to his service and obeying his commands, judged it better to suffer tribulation with him among strangers than to rejoice with acquaintances in the land of their birth.

## 5

When, therefore, the most holy man Girbaldus presided over the diocese of the holy Church of Toul, Deodatus, the faithful servant of the Lord, renounced the world and resolved to choose a dwelling-place in the Vosges wilderness. [Note: Girbaldus must be assigned to the following century, and Bodo seems to have to be substituted for him. Richerius writes the following in book I, chapter 10 of his *Chronicle of Sens*: “After a short time had passed, when that most blessed man Deodatus had entered this Vosges region, there was an equally holy man named Bodo, bishop of Toul. Led by zeal for God, he established, on one of his estates, a cloister there for nuns, having assembled a considerable community; and, after many revenues had been bestowed upon that monastery in his name, the order of nuns continued there for a long time.” Saint Bodo is commemorated on 11 September, when these matters will be examined more carefully, as will also be done on 29 December in the Life of Saint Hilduard, whom some believe was called Girbaldus by others.]

At length, when he came with his companions to Romon, [Note: Commonly Romont, and Riverius likewise calls it so. Riguet adds that, in relation to the town of Saint-Deodat, it lies farther away than Rembert’s Village, at a distance of a small league, and therefore five leagues from the former.] an estate which two brothers had then divided between themselves by hereditary right, the kind of man he was was revealed by divine providence.

For there the elder of the brothers, named Asclas, having hired workmen, was engaged in building a new house. As they were approaching the final stage of the work, a timber beam had to be laid transversely at the very center of the summit, upon which the entire framework was to rest. Yet for three days it could not be fitted to the structure by any skill: sometimes its shortness prevented this, sometimes its curvature, or some other crookedness. Therefore the master of the estate, angry with the craftsmen, heaped abuse upon them, because, although they had a forest at hand, they had sweated for so long and so uselessly under that timber as though they were incapable men.
