But when they were already exhausted by their labor and went sorrowfully to eat, it happened that the holy man entered the same house and sat down there, weary from his journey. Having learned the whole matter from a certain boy, he was moved by the bowels of mercy that had grown with him from childhood and had come forth with him from his mother’s womb. He tried to help the grieving men; and, having summoned blessed Willigod and the others, he gradually fitted the timber into its proper place. [Note: Richerius, chapter 4: “He placed that great beam of the house high above, where it was supposed to be set, without any resistance of strength preventing it.”] He then immediately resumed the journey he had begun.

He had not yet gone far when he was brought back, the head of that estate having learned of his benevolent deed. When the man had inquired about the purpose of his pilgrimage and learned who he was, he granted the estate itself to him, retaining its use only for himself as long as he lived, and promising to pay the holy man five silver shekels each year. [Note: From Richerius, who was writing in 1203, and from the chronicle of the Monastery of Moyen, compiled in 1326 by John of Bayonne, Riguet proves that such a rent continued to be paid even in their own time. He nevertheless doubts whether this kind of rent belongs to a later period; indeed, he denies that ownership of the place was ever alienated by its lord, since it has always formed part of the marquisate of Gerbéviller. He says that the priory later established there by Saint Willigod belonged not to the Church of Saint-Deodat but to the abbey of Bèze.]

The poor man of Christ did not hesitate to accept another’s property, since he had renounced his own, so that the reward of the devout layman might be increased by the almsgiving from which he had foreseen that the poor whom he later gathered to Christ could be supported; or, at any rate, because he knew in spirit that the place would be ennobled by the burial of his beloved disciple Willigod. At whose lifeless body so many and such great miracles are still displayed there that it is plain that his spirit is perpetually rewarded with glory in heaven. [Col. 0615C]

[Note: It is therefore surprising that the name of Willigod is not found entered in the ancient calendars, since no memory of his cult remains there at present.]

## 6

From there the most devout bishop continued on and came to Argentilla, so called from its stream, although the rustic population now corruptly calls it Arentella. [Note: Ruyrus says that the place was situated between Mariville and Angiville. Riguet admits that its location is unknown, but says that the stream from which it took its name rises below Bruyères and passes through Granviller, Pierrepont, and Étang—so called because it was an estate belonging to the rights of the canons—as well as the villages of Sainte-Hélène and Gergonne, until it joins the larger river below Rembert’s Greater Village.]

Wearied there by the labor of so long a journey, he agreed to remain for a time and prepared the expenses for constructing a monastery there. When he had brought its foundations to some height, he began to be offended and injured by the wickedness and assaults of the inhabitants, who envied him, as though he were about to seize their estates day after day. They were also men of considerable military character, but they possessed liberty as a cloak for their malice.

As soon as the servant of God humbly avoided and fled their insolence, heavenly anger descended upon them so heavily that both they and all their descendants either failed to reach the youthful years that were then most sweet to them, or remained intellectually stunted, contemptible and ridiculous to their relatives, until that wicked stock had been removed from their midst.

## 7

From there, after making excessively long circuits through a difficult and winding wilderness, the venerable man entered Elisacium. [Note: Richerius, without mentioning Arentella, says that the saint first came “to a certain place called in the Teutonic language *Heligewoist*, in Latin ‘holy desert,’ near the town called Hagenau, situated on the borders of Lower Alsace. Believing that he had found there the rest for which he had vowed, he remained hidden for some time; but, driven from there by the assaults of envious men, he came to the cloister called *Abregennisten*,” where he formed his first close friendship with Saint Arbogast.

Meanwhile Riguet rightly judges that, through the ignorance of scribes who did not know the Teutonic language, *Ebersheim Münster*, that is, “Monastery of the House of the Boar,” became *Abresennisten*. This is the abbey whose first abbot some make Saint Deodatus, at a place formerly called Novietum. Atticus, who is said to have been the founder of this monastery, the father of Saint Odile, long after these events was rather its restorer than its founder, as Rignetus thinks probable for many reasons; especially because the body of Saint Deodatus is said to be kept there. This is Deodatus of Nevers’s companion and disciple, placed there by his master after the site had been organized in some fashion, and confused by many with him.]

There, between Amalricivillare and Ungisi Village, he settled at Wilram, having erected a dwelling for himself. Many ruins are still shown there, together with a clear and most healthful spring famous under his name. There, as though an intellectual sun were flashing rays all around him of actions pleasing to God, and drawing receptive religious minds to himself by the good fragrance of Christ, one of the more distinguished nobles, Hunus, who lived nearby with his wife Huna and served this world more from obligation than from intention, was joined familiarly in friendship to the servant of God. For like is united to like, while unlike commonly shuns unlike.

Their relationship was further brought to the fullness of firm affection by this: the holy bishop both baptized his child and received him from the bath of the saving font. [Note: Ruyrus, book II, chapter 1, says that the boy was named Adeodatus and later became a monk under this saint.]

But the devil, enemy of holy charity and every good work, when he saw that considerable fruits could rise up for the Lord through the saint’s word and example if so great a cultivator of religion remained any longer among that impious people, barren of good works, raised his wicked head to drive him away from there. Finally, by a sudden frenzy, he stirred up the foolish and unteachable populace against the saint as though he were an invader of another’s property; through them he inflamed the local patrons, until the saint, harassed by continual quarrels and threats, was compelled to leave the place.

When his sponsor Hunus humbly begged him not to abandon him and gladly offered him his own possessions in which to remain, the man of God replied tearfully:

“Why should I, an exile and fugitive for so many years, continue to wander through this province, when in it—because of my sins—I cannot find the desired rest for my foot? From now on I shall give myself over to a vast and unknown solitude, to die there. Let the Lord’s mercy see whose desire it was that I rejected my homeland and sought these borders.”

Having said this and exchanged the kiss of peace, they parted in mutual embrace, not without a great deal of weeping on both sides.

## 8

But divine compassion did not abandon its servant, who was suffering persecution for righteousness. It provided him with a suitable and desired place, and struck his persecutors with a shameful and miserable affliction in their offspring. For it cut short the days of their leading men and carried them away from this light in the very years that were sweetest to them.

It continued to exercise this judgment upon their descendants to such an extent that on several occasions distinguished nobles and three illustrious matrons, fearing for themselves such a lamentable condition in their genealogy, fined themselves and their estates for the benefit of this saint, lest, because of the iniquity of their fathers, they should deserve to be punished by God.

All the country people who were born in the same village while he remained there lived continually with swollen throats. [Note: Riguet now remarks that there is no village there. I fear, however, that something of the fabulous has been mixed into this narrative, perhaps arising from the saint’s frequent invocation against this kind of disease.] All who were able to be born on the farther bank of the intervening torrent were entirely free from that disgrace. Observing this, women in labor were accustomed to cross the torrent.

# Chapter II. Departure into the Valley of Galilee; the Church and Monastery Constructed and Fortified with Privileges

## 9

Then the soldier of Christ, tireless in spirit but excessively wearied in body, crawling through the rocky ridges of lofty mountains and the hollows of barren valleys, at last entered the place called the Valley of Galilee. [Note: Richerius describes this valley in chapter 6 as “beautiful and spacious, planted everywhere with woods, abundant in well-watered and fish-filled streams. When the man of God had carefully surveyed it, he finally settled in a certain place beside a mountain called Comberg; there he erected and consecrated an oratory in honor of Saint Martin, which remains to this day.” Riguet says that he first came to a place which still takes its name from a good man, perhaps from the saint himself, who stayed there.]

This occurred in the year 669 from the incarnation of the Word. [Note: Riguet points out that there is an error in the number, since the local chartulary shows that the monastery had been established before the year 664. Perhaps one *X* was added to the number when it was written out in letters by a monk of Deodatus, or the letters had been transposed and *649* was read.]

He entered breathless beside the Mortha, a broad and fish-filled river that flows through and waters it. [Note: Riguet says that the author must have seen few rivers, “to call the Mortha a broad river.” It has lost its name after flowing into the Moselle two leagues below Nancy.]

On its southern bank, having found a cave and a most pleasant spring, he remained hidden there for some time, relieving his bodily hunger only with the food of wild herbs and little fruits. He desired to live after the example of the holy Fathers who, dwelling in deserts, “wandered in mountains and caves and holes in the earth.” [Col. 0618A]

Meanwhile, the Lord, solicitous for his servant, who thought nothing of the morrow, deigned to address the religious man Hunus in another kind of dream:

“Why do you permit your sponsor, Deodatus, bishop of Nevers, to perish from hunger in the wilderness—a man who, for my sake, has become an exile and needy, and who, out of humility, scarcely allowed you to know even his smallest deeds?”

When Hunus replied that he did not know where he ought to seek him, the Lord commanded him, saying:

“Load your pack animals [Note: The printed edition reads *saginarios*. It is well known that from *sagma*, in rustic speech *saume*, meaning pack-saddles, horses, mules, and donkeys assigned to carry loads are called *sagmarii*.] with the good things I have granted you, invoke the divine majesty, and send them forth by themselves to undertake this journey. Believe me: a guide will not be lacking.”

Awakened by this, Hunus reported the matter to his devout wife and began to urge her in every way that they must hasten. What more is there to say? The pack animals, released as he had been commanded, passed through the pathless wilderness and reached the saint’s cave by a straight line. Their route was observed by those who had followed them there almost step by step, and the servant of God was found.

He first asked them why they had come and learned the whole matter in due order. Without delay he offered God thanks mingled with heartfelt tears, having discovered that God had not forgotten his own in their necessity. Then, after refreshing both the men and the animals with necessary food, he sent them back, giving thanks to their Lord.

Thus, after the men of God had discovered his hut, not only Hunus himself but also several other religious men later served him there. If we recall the lives of the ancient Fathers, we shall find the blessed Deodatus in this deed in no way inferior to them; for, as he did for the most holy Fronto, Benedict, and Columbanus, [Note: In the Life of Saint Fronto on 14 April, this is found in section 6. Benedict and Columbanus are also well known.] the Lord provided him with necessary nourishment.

## 10

By this kindness of the Lord, who was so solicitous for him, the very perceptive man, understanding that his steps had been divinely redirected there, was encouraged to establish a cell for himself. After erecting it there and dedicating it to the veneration of Blessed Martin the bishop, [Note: It is now called the Slope, or Hill, of Saint Martin, in French *la Côte Saint-Martin*.] he also placed there other most precious relics of the saints, brought with him from his native soil.

As the reputation of his holiness spread day by day—not only throughout our own neighborhood but eagerly across more distant lands—it happened that the faithful were drawn to him in crowds from every direction. Some of them gladly contributed estates; many supplied money for building the monastery and whatever other expenses they could; and at times they offered not only their possessions but also themselves, inflamed to imitate him, submitting themselves with great devotion to his discipleship. [Col. 0619A] For fame was not ashamed of the good things it spread about him while he was absent, since in his presence he still displayed better ones.

In those days the aforementioned Hunus devoutly granted him estates and the place called Hunivillare after himself, together with its church. Huna herself is shown buried there with her holy husband. [Note: Ruyrus discusses their holiness in book II, chapter 1, page 2, and asserts that Huna was enrolled among the saints by Pope Leo X in the year 1520, on 15 April. On that day Ferrarius records, in his general catalogue, the memory of Saint Huna in Alsace, citing the calendar of that region; Arturus follows him, as we said among the omitted notices.

Riguet confirms the same from Herculanus, cantor and canon of his church, who lived and wrote about the antiquities of the place shortly after the relics had been scattered by the heretics in 1540. He says that twenty years earlier these relics had been raised from their tomb by order of Leo X, at the request of Ulrich, duke of Württemberg, on 16 April.

Riguet also adds, from Herculanus, that Saint Huna’s charity toward the poor was so great that she herself regularly went to a spring far from her house to wash the poor’s linens. For this she deserved to have Saint Deodatus draw out another spring nearer to her; and in the saint’s church she is greatly venerated, with a relic kept on the altar that is customarily displayed to the people each year.]

But they are shown by miracles alike to live in heaven. At that time, too, the generous munificence of Childeric, the most excellent king, [Note: King Childeric began to reign in Austrasia after the death of Saint Sigebert, around the year 659, when Dagobert returned from Ireland, about the year 661. After some dispute, he left Alsace and the provinces beyond the Rhine to Dagobert, Sigebert’s son, while he governed the rest of Austrasia. Later, from the year 671, he also obtained Neustria and Burgundy, and was killed in 675.

Whatever he granted to Saint Deodatus must therefore have been granted around the year 660. We can say no more, since Riguet admits that neither the original nor a copy of Childeric’s charter survives. He proves its credibility from the privilege of Numerian of Trier, mentioned below, which he assigns to the year 664.

That privilege does indeed mention Theuderic, as the one under whom Trier was subject, but not as the donor. Hence nothing so far prevents those donations from having been made after Dagobert’s death and after the privilege was written by Numerian. Nevertheless, the earlier opinion is more pleasing, for Numerian seems unlikely to have granted such extensive privileges unless the monastery had already been established with royal authority. Consult our revised *Dissertation on the Three Kings Named Dagobert*.]

took that same Valley of Galilee from the royal treasury and, by his ring, confirmed it forever to the man of God and his successors in its entirety—from the rise [lacuna] of all the streams, or of all those entering the aforesaid valley, to their exit from it—so that he might build a monastery there and gather whatever number of servants of God he deemed appropriate.

They believed that, after so many hardships by which he had until then been surrounded and oppressed, while he wandered here and there, driven into exile, the Lord was now fully consoling his holy soul and speaking to him almost soothingly in the words of the holy prophet Isaiah:

“Poor little one, shaken by the storm and without any consolation, behold, I will set your stones in order” (Isaiah 54:11), “for for a brief moment I abandoned you, but with great mercies I will gather you” (ibid., 54:7).

## 11

Understanding this, the teachable man of God, as though seeing both divine and human assistance being offered to him, was laboring there to build a monastery near the little oratory of Saint Martin.

One of his disciples spent the day across the river at Urimont—now towering above the monastery—while workmen felled and smoothed the timber needed for that building, and returned to the cell in the evening. One evening, however, since he was reluctant to cross the Mortha and wished to return to his work earlier, it happened that he remained overnight on the hill called Juncturas.

That hill is thought to have received this name because the Robach and the Mortha join not far from its foot. As the brother lay there asleep, he received in a vision a command from the Lord that an oratory should be built there for blessed Mary, Mother of God and perpetual virgin.

When he reported this to his most holy master in the morning, Deodatus ordered a stone to be erected at the place indicated by the vision as a sign. Not long afterward, a basilica was built around it, an altar was installed, and it was consecrated in honor of the most merciful Mother of the Lord and of all the apostles, and likewise of the principal bishops of the city of Trier: Eucharius, Valerius, Maternus, [Note: We discussed these first three apostles of Trier on 29 January, in the Life of Saint Valerius. They are also commemorated separately: Saint Eucharius on 8 December and Saint Maternus on 14 September.] and Maximinus. [Note: We illustrated the Acts of Saint Maximinus on 29 May, together with the translation soon to be mentioned.]

Near this, another oratory was built and is known to have been dedicated to Saint Maurice [Note: Saint Maurice and his Theban companions are commemorated on 22 September.] and his most devout community. In this undertaking it is plainly evident that the most blessed archbishop Hidulphus [Note: We discussed the date of Saint Hidulphus, more correctly Hildulphus, in the dissertation cited above, book IV, chapter 5, and showed that it had wrongly been transferred to the time of King Pepin; this passage proves the point. He is commemorated on 9 July.] was an intimate friend of the most holy bishop Deodatus from the foundations of this monastery. He is believed to have endowed it with the relics of the aforementioned bishops of the people of Trier, especially Saint Maximinus, whose venerable remains he had very recently transferred to the church where they are now most worthily venerated—namely, when the year 667 from the incarnation of the Lord was passing and the servant of God Deodatus was staying at Elisacium.

For it is established that in the year 669 from the Lord’s incarnation he entered the Valley of Galilee. [Note: “On the contrary,” says Riguet, “it is certain from the privilege of Numerian dated 664 that the monastery had already then been fully founded.” But perhaps in that year, the one after Saint Maximinus’s translation, Deodatus had gone to Trier to greet the new archbishop and obtain from him a confirmation and enlargement of the privilege previously obtained from Saint Numerian.]

## 12

For it is not without reason that the bishop most devoted to God is recognized to have left behind so many and such precious protections of the saints in his own Francia.

Indeed, the man of God Hidulphus, intending to lead an eremitical life, could have sought the immense forests of the Ardennes—as some of his neighbors are found to have done—or revisited the deserts of Istria, [Note: It is said without any likelihood that Hildulphus was brought from Istria. Born in Bavaria, he passed directly from the schools of Regensburg to Trier. Whether, when he was younger, he saw Saint Deodatus in the Vosges and thereafter began to be attached to him, I leave undecided, since I have nothing by which to prove it.] from which he had once been taken to the episcopate of Trier. But he was drawn to our Vosges by the exceedingly intimate love he bore the most beloved Deodatus.

If anyone among the slanderers resists this opinion, he will be refuted by the privileges of the Valley of Galilee, in which the mutual charity of our dearest Fathers is clearly displayed.

But since an opportunity has presented itself, let something be inserted here concerning the ancient immunity or liberty of that place. In certain charters of the often-mentioned monastery, confirmed by royal and pontifical authority, the name of blessed Father Hidulphus is found prefixed, with twelve bishops subscribing beneath it.

There the archbishop—indeed, patriarch, since a company of bishops belongs only to a patriarch—of holy compassion declares that the holy, contrite, and religious petition of the venerable man Deodatus, bishop, had penetrated the innermost chambers of his ears and softened his heart through a visceral affection of piety by its charitable appeal, so that he would have judged it exceedingly irreligious not to fulfill his will most willingly.

13. Consequently, it is also recorded there [Note: [Col. 0621C] Riguet admits that no charter of this kind belonging to St. Hidulphus—whether genuine or forged—exists anywhere in the archive, but congratulates himself on having found at the Median Monastery an earlier charter of St. Numerianus in which these same matters are contained. Would that he had sent a complete copy of it, transcribed word for word, so that it could appropriately be inserted and examined here! For, insofar as I gather from the fragments sent by Riguet, King Childeric is indeed named there—obviously because Trier was subject to him when the privilege is said to have been granted—“so that the monks might be able to pray to the Lord more fully for the welfare of the Catholic Church and for the desirable salvation of Prince Childeric”; but the year of his reign is not expressed, still less the year of Christ, which was unknown to the Frankish kings of that period. Riguet’s entire basis for assigning it to the year 664 is therefore that it is subscribed by “Gisloaldus, bishop of Verdun,” whom Wasseburg dates as having died in 665. If this is correct, it proves only that the privilege was not written later, although it may have been issued in the year 660 itself, when Dagobert had not yet returned from Ireland, Childeric still held Alsace, and the bishops Numerianus and Gisloaldus had already long presided over their churches.], because the reverend Bishop Deodatus, inflamed by the ardor of a holy desire, was the first to build monasteries at Junctures (as we said above) in the Valley of Galilee, which he had obtained from the royal fisc.

[Note: [Col. 0622C] Riguet notes that those monasteries—or rather, hermitages—scattered throughout the Valley of Galilee were converted into parishes subject to a provost.]

There the devout man resolved to establish monks or pilgrims who would live under the most holy rule of Fathers Benedict and Columbanus.

[Note: [Col. 0622C] Riguet says that Numerianus’s charter, subscribed by six bishops, was the source and beginning of the almost episcopal jurisdiction which his abbots, and afterward his provosts, acquired and still possess. Charles le Cointe, under the year 671, no. 15, records this passage and adds: [Col. 0622D] “The Valley of Galilee is not far from Luxeuil, where the institution of St. Columbanus flourished; his memory was then celebrated throughout the neighboring regions. The name of St. Benedict, who was less known in that province, was inserted by a Benedictine author. We have already often exposed similar interpolations.” Thus le Cointe. Let the reader judge the truth of the matter after first reading what Mabillon has to say in defense of his own position, in his treatment of the spread of the rule before the Benedictine age, against le Cointe himself.]

At last, by common decree of the holy bishops, it was granted to him

[Note: [Col. 0622D] Riguet notes that, in a similar manner, Numerianus’s privilege was entrusted to the priest Blidoaldus and the deacon Vahinus for delivery to the absent bishops—namely, those of Toul, Metz, and Verdun. Thus the same names appear to have been corrupted by copyists, increasing suspicion that the document was fabricated for the sole purpose of making it appear that whatever rights the abbots acquired beyond Numerianus’s privilege had been granted by his successor, or that Hildulphus had been substituted for Numerianus as a saint known in the Vosges. Add also that Numerianus’s style, although more barbarous, is therefore more genuine. Indeed, Riguet doubts whether St. Hildulphus was ever more than a chorepiscopus of Archbishop Numerianus; we shall discuss this elsewhere.]

that no king, prince, bishop, or any cleric whatsoever should ever dare to usurp for his own use anything of what appeared to belong to the servants of God living there under evangelical perfection, nor anything acquired by Father Bishop Deodatus himself, whether by royal gift or by the contributions of the other faithful—whether in sacred books, altar gifts, and ecclesiastical ornaments, or in those things which the servants of God might thereafter add by their own labor.

And whenever the aforesaid Deodatus (who is now the father of that monastery) should be called by God, whoever that community should unanimously elect from among themselves was to be substituted as abbot. For the blessing of altars or the reception of holy orders, they were to seek whatever bishop they wished. No church living without privileges was to presume to hope for or take anything from them, and no one was permitted to enter the enclosure of that monastery

[Col. 0622B]

unless invited or permitted by the entire community. If any bishop, commonly requested by them, should come for their benefit, he was immediately to depart, once his ministry had been completed according to the community’s wishes, without demanding any gift, so that those living under the holy rule might, with the Lord’s help, rejoice through the ages in the peace they had received and might pray more fully to God for the welfare of the Catholic Church.

But if they should commit some violation of their rule and refuse to be rebuked by their own shepherd, and even if their bishop, who was also their abbot, were unable to quell the community’s dissension, then he was to summon other abbots who professed the same rule to that monastery, so that they might strive to suppress the scandal by a regular judgment.

Whoever should dare to violate this privilege was, by the authority of the bishops present, to be bound by anathema; and it was denounced by the venerable men Bibliobaldus the priest and Labinus the deacon, in the absence of the others, for subscription. It has already been said above that this was dutifully done. So much for this matter; let us now proceed to what remains.

## CHAPTER III. The mutual charity of Saints Deodatus and Hildulphus; the death and burial of the former, and the succession of the latter

[Col. 0623A]

14. Thus, in the year 671, and in the third year from the arrival of Lord Deodatus in Galilee

[Note: [Col. 0623D] Rather, easily the thirteenth.]

the ever-worthy Father Hidulphus—having renounced the archbishopric of Trier

[Note: [Col. 0623D] Or at least the vicarious administration of the diocese of Trier.]

and devoting himself to dying with Christ—came as the sweetest neighbor and most peaceful relative to his Deodatus in this arid wilderness, with the assisting support of Jacob,

[Note: [Col. 0623D] Here the author is completely mistaken concerning the bishops of the Leuci, that is, of Toul, and needlessly torments himself, having been led far astray by certain manifestly confused catalogues. The Jacob named here (as we shall say on his feast, 23 June) flourished under Pippin in the year 756 and subscribed the privilege of the church of Gorze. He had succeeded Girbaldus, or Garibaldus. Before him in that same century had come Saints Godo and Dodo. Blessed Bodo, also called St. Leudinus, had succeeded Theufredus, who is known from the year 640. After these, Eborinus, or Ebroinus, and then Adeodatus, mentioned under Pope Agatho in the year 680, are indicated by name alone; afterward Ermantheus and Magnaldus. Ruyrus thinks that Eborinus was the person who caused St. Hildulphus to withdraw. I would rather say that it was Bodo himself, who, as is stated below, was still living in the year 670.]

the most reverend bishop of the Leuci.

Lest anyone here become angry with us and object that two bishops of the Leuci—namely Godo and Bodo—stood between Girbaldus (during whose episcopate Blessed Deodatus is said to have abandoned the bishopric) and Jacob, in whose time Lord Hidulphus came, and that it is unreasonable for four bishops to have administered the bishopric in scarcely three years, we shall briefly answer the objection. Considering the brevity and vicissitudes of human life, we do not deny that even within a single year more than four men, succeeding one another in order, could have died.

But we do not derive an argument from uncertainty, especially since we know that Blessed Bodo presided over the bishopric for many years and founded a monastery of virgins in the Vosges. Therefore, it must be said that the deaths of the first three bishops intervened between the time when Blessed Deodatus left the episcopal dignity and the beginning of his third year in this Vosges region. Thus it happened that, in the first year of the episcopate of Blessed Jacob, the man of God Hidulphus came here after him.

[Col. 0623C]

This is demonstrated by the aforesaid privilege and by Blessed Bodo’s subscription, dated 670 from the Lord’s Incarnation, as well as by the statement that Lord Hidulphus came to us in the year 601. For Deodatus, the friend of God, remained for several years under the aforementioned three bishops

[Note: [Col. 0624C] Rather, under Eudolus, Theufredus, and Bodo.]

in the places from which, as we said above, he had been driven out, and at last entered the Vosges as though in the final days of his life. Thus it happened that, while the servant of God sometimes lingered and sometimes fled here and there, Girbaldus and Godo sought the man; and that, in the first year after his arrival among us, Bodo was completing the penultimate year of his priesthood.

[Col. 0624A]

When Bodo died, he received Lord Jacob as his successor in the following year. In the first year of Jacob’s episcopate—already Deodatus’s third year in this Vosges region—the champion of God, Hidulphus, entrusted himself to the wilderness. Some, however, maintain that Blessed Deodatus entered this valley thirty years after his departure from France; when those thirty years are added to the ten years completed here, the total is undoubtedly forty.

But we neither oppose nor support this opinion, since we are entirely unable either to refute or defend it.

[Note: [Col. 0624C] “A great service,” says Riguet, “has been done us by this author in reporting this opinion, while admitting that he has nothing with which effectively to refute it.” Unlike him, I am not concerned to determine how the ten-year period can be preserved which the author, by his own reckoning, adds to Deodatus’s time in the Valley of Galilee. I shall gladly grant that he spent twenty years there; added to the thirty years received from earlier authorities, these make fifty years spent among the solitudes of the Vosges, after he had come from France around the year 629.]

15. Thus the blessed and ever-to-be-remembered Fathers, Hidulphus and Deodatus, having become neighbors in the wilderness, as they had desired,

[Note: [Col. 0624D] Riguet writes that the monastery begun by St. Hildulphus at Medianum lies two leagues from the monastery of St. Deodatus, midway—whence it received its name—between the abbeys of Étival and Senones. From each of these, estates were taken and given to St. Hildulphus.]

did not sleep, but vigilantly watched over the preservation of their mutual and sincere love, becoming more intimate as they became nearer to one another.

For just as, to increase brilliance or heat, one adds a lamp to a lamp or fire to fire, so holy charity grew in these holy men through their proximity, their sight of one another, and their friendly conversation. Although it was their greatest delight always to live and remain together, it was nevertheless unworthy that such great guests—like two exceptionally bright lights of the world—should lie hidden in the narrow space of a single cell, when scarcely one person could fit in each cell, especially since they were able to lead many people with them to God.

Therefore, the beloved bishops decided that, once a year, while they remained in this life, each should visit the other’s cell and stay there overnight. They customarily spent the entire sleepless night in holy conversation and divine praises, returning to their own cells at dawn.

Their disciples, meanwhile, went back and forth, conveying to each other the wishes, needs, and abilities of the one and the other. Lord Hidulphus, with his companions, would meet Lord Deodatus and his companions not far from his cell as they came toward him.

[Note: [Col. 0624D] Riguet adds: “They also erected a chapel halfway along the road, at a place called Belli-Campus, where they customarily met one another; it still exists today. Only a few years ago the custom was interrupted by which the canons from one side and the monks from the other annually carried the bodies of their holy founding fathers to the aforesaid chapel, exchanged them with one another, and restored them only on the return journey, after many prayers had been sung by both sides.”]

Taking him by the hand, he led him to prayer according to the custom of the ancient Fathers and the institution of the most holy abbot Benedict. Thus, after pouring out their prayers together, they greeted one another with spiritual joy, and finally joined in the holy kiss of undisturbed peace and in every other duty of charitable affection.

16. The most devout Father Deodatus did the same most dutifully for his beloved Hidulphus. He would meet him and his companions after crossing the Meurthe, for, as long as he lived, he did not leave his earlier cell near the little oratory of St. Martin.

He was an exceedingly old man, a veteran already discharged from the service of Christ, and he could not endure the crowds of ordinary people or take part in the brothers’ external activities. He found nothing sweet except to be free for contemplation and to see that the Lord himself is God (Ps. 45:11), and to taste and see that the Lord is good (Ps. 33:9).

He was said to be very tall in stature, most elegant in appearance,

[Col. 0625B]

and most gentle in heart; but he was already exhausted and bent by excessive labor and by his years.

[Note: [Col. 0625D] According to our reckoning, he was nearly ninety when he died and not far short of seventy when he came to the Valley of Galilee, having left France at about forty, unless he had been a bishop for only a few years.]

At times he would go over to the brothers who were working; after inspecting and arranging each person’s work, he would return to his cell at night. The path by which he used to approach the monastery at Junctures is still pointed out today.

[Note: [Col. 0626D] Ruyrus says that this path no longer exists since the town of St. Deodatus was built.]

Hidulphus, by contrast, was of medium height, angelic in face, most contrite in spirit, and especially fond of voluntary poverty. His still-vigorous old age and soul suspended in God made him ready and cheerful for every good work; even in the final years of his life he lived by the labor of his hands.

In character the two were alike, but unequal in age. Each preferred the other to himself. The very humble Hidulphus considered the most holy old man Deodatus his senior because of his service to Christ and his venerable age; but Deodatus, most devoted to the Almighty, observed in the younger Hidulphus the dignity of a patriarch and maturity of character.

[Note: [Col. 0626D] Riguet firmly believes, after seeing Apri-Monastery and carefully considering the traditions and monuments of the place, that St. Deodatus truly lived there for many years and eventually settled there a disciple who shared his name. The relics of that disciple, who died there, may have occasioned the confusion of saints bearing the same name. Other places have been discussed above.]

17. How sweet and delightful it was for devout souls continually to contemplate two columns of the heavenly structure, fittingly raised by God and lifted up—not against God, but toward the Lord in holiness. With solid and unbending strength of mind they stood before the supreme Craftsman, so that they desired a heap of little stones to be placed upon them, according to the part in which they had been found worthy to be set.

Indeed, as though competing with one another in the multitude of Christ’s little ones, both present and future, they rejoiced to have their architraves—that is, their capitals—burdened, provided that there were people whom they could win for the Lord. They accepted, within the breadth of their charity, the weakness of others’ faith and the weight of others’ sins, so that, raised by the strength of their merits and by the labor of their perseverance, they might carry them to the heavenly building.

One might have thought that these holy Fathers were intellectual hens, defending their little chicks with the wings of their merits and the beaks of their prayers against the rapacity of invisible kites, providing them with food by their hands and feet, and warming those who were cold toward God by nurturing them with many examples.

Moreover, they sometimes loved to extend their wings beyond their own nest, as they mutually strove to benefit each other’s chicks through love of God and neighbor. Changing their voice and with their bodily appearance worn away, they became weak with the weak, as you find in the Apostle’s words: “Who is weak, and I am not weak?” (2 Cor. 11:29).

Thus our Fathers lived for a time, anxious that their children, both present and future, might eventually be secure. They were not wearied by their own labor and sweat, so long as their successors remained safely established. This was demanded by their buildings; this was sought by their flight—especially by our blessed Father Deodatus, who exchanged so many places built by him with great toil until he found a quiet dwelling for his spiritual children.

For if they had sought only their own interests, they would have rested very easily. Having food and clothing, they would have been content with these (1 Tim. 6:8), especially since, by renouncing riches, they had hastened toward poverty with the greatest longing. But this belongs elsewhere.

Thus these bishops, most worthy of God, persevering in their spiritual work, never withdrew from what they had begun or deviated from their purpose, becoming better from day to day. They grew more cheerful for labor in proportion as they drew nearer to rest, and in Christ’s vineyard they did not feel the burden of the day and the heat, since the payment of the denarius was already near.

18. Finally, when together in this Vosges region they had completed seven continuous years and six months, with one heart and one soul, God, the generous rewarder, decreed that the most blessed Deodatus should receive the fruit of his labors.

Having completed the course of the present life, the vigorous champion already longed for the crown and the prize of heavenly reward. Therefore, summoned by the Lord and seized by an attack of illness, he was confined to his bed. When the sad report reached his disciples, who were absent, they immediately hurried sorrowfully to his cell. Their minds, foreseeing the grief to come, could not hear of his illness without being disturbed.

Weeping, they stood around the bed of their stricken master, lest so sweet a Father should abandon his sons; with a common wailing and groaning they cried out to him. But that holy man restrained them with words of salvation, encouraging them as far as he could to observe the holy rule and remember him, and above all commending them devoutly to Christ the good Shepherd.

[Col. 0627A]

19. After this event and the death of so holy a man, his dearest Hidulphus was divinely warned in a nocturnal vision to hasten to him as quickly as possible. It was fitting that a friend should bid farewell to a friend going before him to God, devoutly ask him not to forget him, perform the ecclesiastical commendation, provide him with viaticum, properly arrange his mouth and eyes, hands and feet, conduct his funeral with due reverence, and place him most carefully in the tomb.

All these things, God willing, are known to have been fulfilled by Lord Hidulphus for the most devout Father Deodatus. For as soon as he awoke, he hastened to the blessed man as quickly as the Lord had commanded him. He found him still alive. At the sight he had longed for, the saint was refreshed

[Note: [Col. 0627D] The old printed edition reads *optato vir sanctus creatus* (“the holy man, created according to his desire”); Riguet corrected it to *optato obtutu … recreatus* (“refreshed by the desired sight”).]

and rejoiced greatly in the Lord, who had deigned to reveal his death to his servant Hidulphus and send him to arrange his funeral.

Without delay, as he was about to depart from this life, Deodatus compelled his surviving friend to accept the governance of the sheep whom obedience and charity had until then nourished there, and he instructed his own followers to retain Lord Hidulphus as their father in his place for as long as he lived.

Thus, after Lord Hidulphus had fulfilled all that a beloved man owed his beloved friend departing from this world, he most joyfully sent to heaven, from between his hands, the holy soul—commended to God by many prayers, exercised and refined by countless unceasing labors for God’s kingdom and his righteousness, and filled and adorned with innumerable virtues—yet destined to be more joyful on arriving where it deserved to see God face to face without end.

As it is written in Ecclesiasticus: “He died, and as though he had not died, for he left behind him one like himself. In his life he saw him and rejoiced in him, and at his death he was not grieved, nor was he confounded before his enemies; for he left behind a defender of his house against his enemies, and one who would repay his friends” (Ecclus. 30:4–6).

20. The beloved Father, Lord Deodatus, passed from death to life and from exile to his homeland on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of July,

[Note: [Col. 0627D] The chronological indicators agree, including the Sunday letter B. If the author possessed these indicators from ancient tradition or writing, nothing more certain can be required in preference to any alternative date for the year 679. This certainty would be obscured only by his faulty arrangement of the episcopate of Garibaldus with Deodatus’s departure from France, and of Jacob with Hidulphus’s arrival in the Vosges.]

on a Sunday, in the year 679 from the Incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ, in the seventh indiction, and in the eleventh year, midway through, from his entrance into this Valley of Galilee.

[Note: [Col. 0627D] Rather, “the twenty-first year.”]

Theodoricus, son of Clovis and brother of Childeric, was reigning.

[Note: [Col. 0627D] Theodoricus was restored after Childeric’s murder in the year 675, became sole monarch from the year 680 onward, and died in 693.]

Under him the wicked apostate Ebroinus, after first torturing the most excellent martyr Leodegarius, bishop of Autun,

[Col. 0628A]

cut him down with a sword.

[Note: [Col. 0627D] Leodegarius was killed in the year 688, on 2 October, the day on which he is commemorated.]

After the funeral of so great a Father had been reverently prepared, his disciples carried him amid exceedingly tearful rites to the church of blessed Mary, Mother of God. There the most devout archbishop offered the saving sacrifice for him; and, after the rite of the Catholic Church had been completed, the most precious body was committed to the vilest earth.

[Note: [Col. 0627D] “Yet in a stone sarcophagus,” says Riguet, “which is still preserved, until the larger one should be completed. The latter had been begun in the church of St. Maurice, now called St. Deodatus; there the body was placed in the same sarcophagus before the altar of the Holy Cross.” But what if one believes that the body was first buried in bare earth and placed in this sarcophagus at the time of the translation? “Our church did not then have the cruciform shape it now has, which, as is established by the bull of Nicholas III, was the work of the year 1278,” says Riguet.]

This was because the cemetery of his earlier cell was waterlogged, being situated in a valley, and because it was necessary that the body of so great a patron should be present among the brothers as they offered praises and prayers to God.

Although the devout souls knew that he should not be mourned, they could not restrain the flood of tears which the spirit, not the impulse of the flesh, drew from the depths of their hearts. They did not mourn because he had died, but because he had gone before them to God, as the learned Father Ambrose was accustomed to say of himself. Nor did they envy his glory; rather, they desired to be with him, considering that they had remained behind in grief, knowing that they were seeking the homeland to come and had no abiding city here (Heb. 13:14).

Moreover, under the joy of the Holy Spirit they shed devout tears as they recalled the memory of his sweetest fatherhood and companionship. He had been for them a most kind chariot and charioteer (4 Kings 2:12), carrying them in his hands and urging them toward better deeds.

How far such tears differ from those which worldly people customarily pour out inconsolably for their loved ones or their losses, with unrestrained boldness daring to spring forth in open defiance of the divine judgments! Because they do not long for eternal goods, they do not know what they can hope for after temporal things have been lost. Therefore, those whom they love uselessly, while neglecting God, they do not want to be taken from this world, because they wish, if they could, to enjoy them forever in the pleasures of the flesh and the use of the world.

Against such people holy Jeremiah inveighs: “Cursed is the man who trusts in man, who makes flesh his arm, and whose heart departs from the Lord” (Jer. 17:5).

21. Thus the man of God Hidulphus obeyed the final request of his dying friend in such a way that, for twenty-eight and a half years—during which he survived him in this world—he watched over his flock, administering the affairs of that place through provosts. Although he had appointed an abbot over his own community

[Note: [Col. 0628D] Here the manuscript readings for the saint, distributed over the octave, come to an end; up to this point they agree word for word with the printed editions. The abbot appointed by Hildulphus was called Leutebaldus, but his death before Hildulphus obliged the saint to resume the governance during the final three years of his rule, as Ruyrus writes.]

[Col. 0629A]

because he was inflamed by the desire for heavenly contemplation and refused to be occupied with external affairs, nevertheless he did not remove the Valley of Galilee from his care as long as he remained in this light.

[Note: [Col. 0629D] Here the Utrecht manuscript and the Life published by Mosander end.]

The force of his perfect love for the most holy Deodatus made him endure these labors. He did not grow weary of caring for another’s affairs, although his own weariness had caused him to place his affairs upon another. For what weak old age refused to bear, and what a mind desirous of devoting itself to God alone sought to avoid, he eagerly embraced through fraternal affection and the virtue of holy obedience, as though he were continually exhorting himself: “With what face will you go to your friend if you refuse his final command?”

For the sake of his friend’s perpetual life and glory in heaven, in the first year after Deodatus’s burial he was accustomed to visit the monastery of the Valley of Galilee many times and frequently celebrate the solemnities of Mass at the saint’s body. He knew that it is written: “No one knows whether he is worthy of love or hatred, but all things remain uncertain for the future” (Ecclus. 9:1–2).

He also knew the saying of the most penetrating Father Augustine: “Woe to the praiseworthy life of human beings if it is judged without mercy. For who among human beings would dare to say, ‘The prince of this world is coming, and he has nothing in me’ (John 14:30), unless he is free among the dead?” (Ps. 87:6).

Therefore, he never ceased to transmit the only and singular benefit he knew to be available to the dead, after his friend had entered upon the way of all flesh. Although the pious mother Church sends this offering after all her children without distinction, because she has not yet penetrated God’s hidden judgments, the just Judge nevertheless accepts the prayers of his own in such a way that they do not grieve at being wholly frustrated.

According to the judgment of the holy Fathers, thanksgivings are offered for those who are very good, propitiatory prayers for those who are not very bad, and whatever consolation the living can provide for those who are very bad.

But since in this life all merit is acquired, by which each person is either relieved or burdened after this life, it is clear that the most devout servant of Christ, Deodatus, acquired pious merit here, so that every supplication offered for him might there become thanksgiving.

## CHAPTER IV. The veneration of Saints Deodatus and Hidulphus in their tunics and bodies; their elevation; the approved Life

22. At last, after a year had passed from the glorious death of Lord Deodatus, during which Blessed Patriarch Hidulphus, by constant visitation and frequent offering of the saving sacrifice, took care to benefit his spirit, the brothers of both places resumed their former institution.

As the holy bishops had previously been accustomed to visit one another’s cells once a year, so afterward they took pains to continue doing so. When the man of God Hidulphus visited the Valley of Galilee in place of Lord Deodatus, his disciples came out to meet him, carrying the tunic of their great master.

The holy bishop received it reverently, kissed and embraced it as the sweetest pledge of his friend, and venerated the name of that saint most tenderly in the garment. He seemed to see Deodatus himself in it.

He did the same when, at the appointed time, the disciples of the saint carried the tunic to the Median Monastery. Whatever veneration he showed to the lifeless tunic, he rejoiced to show to his beloved Deodatus. He believed that Deodatus perceived the devotion shown to him, and he prayed amid sweet sighs that, through his effective merits, he himself—still struggling in the course of this life and laboring in the spiritual arena—might be sustained.

For he trusted that Deodatus, having already struck down and trampled his adversary, had received victory and a crown from the Lord, and that he possessed great influence with him, having been indelibly enrolled in the ranks of the heavenly court.

But since, by God’s providence, the earthly life of the holy man was prolonged for many years, so that many might be kindled by his example toward eternal life, it happened that in his final years, already weighed down and broken by old age and weakened by continuous labor, he no longer left his cell even for his customary visit.

Nevertheless, the disciples of the most blessed Deodatus did not cease to bring him their master’s tunic, as they had been accustomed to do.

23. When divine mercy had decreed that its veteran soldier Hidulphus should rest eternally from his excessive labors, it deigned, through his beloved Deodatus, to announce to him the day of his departure and to urge him to arrange both of their cells as the occasion required.

The holy man therefore rejoiced greatly in the Lord, because he was soon to pass from the world’s turbulent conflict to the tranquility of perpetual peace, where every tear would be wiped from his eyes (Rev. 21:4) and he would be comforted forever.

Accordingly, after appointing Lord Raimbertus as abbot of his own cell and Lord Marcinannus over the Valley of Galilee, he sprang forth from this exile in the year 707 from the Incarnation of Jesus Christ.

Because the course of our narrative has led us to mention him here, we have scarcely touched upon his holy life except in summary, lest we be accused of gathering and forcing food upon ears weary of it. We nevertheless direct the eager reader to the saint’s Life.

[Note: [Col. 0629D] Riguet suspects that he himself composed the Life of Hildulphus published by Mosander. Certainly, either the interpolator of both works was the same person, or the author of the Life of St. Hildulphus, by making him succeed Milo and committing many other chronological errors, led the interpolator of this Life into the mistakes by which we have seen two centuries confused.]

Lord Marcinannus, whom we mentioned above as superior of the monastery of the most blessed Deodatus, was exceptionally zealous in providing for the monastery’s welfare. He survived for a long time under Kings Theodoricus and Childeric the Younger, and from the latter he also obtained at Aachen a royal confirmation of the description of his entire abbey.

24. Thereafter, the worthy successors of such holy predecessors, Raimbertus and Marcinannus, did not diminish the charitable fellowship received from their most holy masters and left to them almost as a hereditary law; rather, they increased it.

This was still demonstrated by the breviaries or written records of that period, in which the names of the brothers of both monasteries, both dead and living, were carefully recorded and preserved upon the altars. Concerning them, it was truly said during the solemnities of Mass, as is found throughout the sacramentary books: “And those whose names appear to be written upon your holy altar.”

Meanwhile, the most devout disciples inviolably observed what they remembered as having been handed down by their most pious masters: namely, that once a year each community should visit the other’s cells, carrying before them, as their chief pledges, the tunics of their masters. The disciples of Lord Hidulphus had likewise retained his tunic for themselves.

They went out to meet these tunics with such devotion and showed them such veneration that the sweetest Fathers seemed to have returned to their children after the long revolutions of the centuries.

25. Whenever, because of sins, heavenly anger raged against the people, and they were struck by drought, an excessive abundance of rain, pestilence, or any other affliction, the assembled community from both sides would immediately bring forth the tunics of their patrons and present them before the divine gaze amid mournful prayers. At once, mercy removed what impiety had deserved.

For against the assault of the raging scourge the merits of the saints and the faith of the people had such power that the most merciful Creator, without delay, restrained the severity of his just judgment from the people and caused the consolation of the desired mercy to distill upon them.

Thus the small and temporal consolation of faith became a great advancement. It urged each person, according to his capacity, to correct his depravity, imitate the saints, and rise toward the veneration owed to those whom they understood to have merited so greatly before God that they could turn his anger away from a sinful people. They desired to become such as divine kindness graciously deigns to regard.

Let us now consider, if we can, what merit or virtue these holy souls of our Fathers possessed inwardly, whose most contemptible tunics, outwardly presented before the eyes of God by a people full of sins, suspended his anger.

26. Therefore this custom, so pious and religious, was preserved with complete integrity between these two monasteries [Col. 0631D], until the holy bodies, manifested by very many miracles, were raised from the bosom of the earth by the ordering of divine grace. Then what they had been accustomed to do with the tunics of the saints they preserved, down to our own times, with their bodies also: they visit one another, or sweetly meet one another in a place pleasing to them. There, exchanging pious burdens among themselves, they love for a while to carry them as though they were their own lords; nor does either community believe that either saint is alien to it. Thus the congregation of the Valley of Galilee recognizes blessed Hidulphus as its own, since he presided over it for twenty-eight and a half years; while, conversely, the people of the Middle Monastery claim for themselves the distinguished confessor of Christ, Deodatus, to whom Lord Hidulphus had assigned the priorship of his own place, receiving him there with the greatest honor while he lived, and likewise receiving his tunic after he died.

Moreover, they add to this their mutual affection, through which it has come about that everything is common to them. As the philosophical saying declares: “Most things belonging to neighbors are common, but everything belongs to friends” (ARISTOTLE, *Ethics*, book VIII, chapter 9). Accordingly, just as they once used mutually to receive the tunics of these saints—that is, the remnants of their bodies—so now also they receive their bodies, which are, in truth, the remnants of their souls. Through whose merit may peace be ours, now and forever.

Let this now suffice for religious minds: in our poor discourse we have hastily explained what we could about the deeds of our most devout Father [Col. 0632B] Deodatus, scarcely touching upon a few things out of countless matters, the smallest out of the greatest—the matters by which the Holy Trinity glorified its beloved one on earth for the merits of his holy life. Besides these things, his venerable body is daily ennobled by so many and such great miracles that, as is thought, even some very eloquent person would scarcely be sufficient to relate them all.

[Note: [Col. 0631D] Theoderic presided from the year 720 to 737; and after an interregnum, Childeric, the last of the Merovingians, was appointed in 743 and deposed in 751. [Col. 0632D]]

27. So widely was he proclaimed that he became known throughout the world and had no need to be praised by this meager and barren account of ours. But since Christian discernment consists rather in seeking and attending to the works that make each person a saint than to those that display him as a saint, it certainly takes delight in the visible deeds of the saints, yet desires by every means to reach their invisible deeds; and, thirsting, it prefers to quench its thirst from the fountain [Col. 0632C] rather than from the stream. For from the Lord Jesus it learned what it ought to rejoice in. He said to his disciples: “Do not rejoice in this, that the spirits are subject to you; but rejoice that your names are written in heaven” (Luke 10:20).

May we deserve this through holiness of soul, not through a display of miracles—especially since, on the day of judgment, he will say to many who have performed many mighty works in his name: “I do not know you” (Matthew 7:22–23). Hence, when he invites to himself all who labor and are burdened, he does not say, “Learn from me to perform signs,” but rather, “because I am meek and humble in heart, and you will find rest for your souls” (Matthew 11:29).

What we have said from the Head we must also learn from his principal members, because the faith of the Church more ardently seeks to know what those whom it venerates were like in the invisible virtues of the soul than what they were like in visible signs, which are truly the milk of little ones, not solid food for the strong. But just as one proceeds from milk to solid food, so from signs, which nourish the imperfection of our faith, we are eventually led to the solid virtues of the soul, so that we no longer need to suck but only to chew the cud.

This, dearest ones, is why, although you were being nourished by the daily and extraordinary miracles of the most worthy confessor of Christ, Deodatus, you have been brought to such strength of mind that you are no longer content with these alone [Col. 0633A], but anxiously seek to have your holy hunger refreshed by his holy life. You know very well that the soul must be sought amid miracles, and that when the good itself is absent, miracles are nothing.

28. Let us now give thanks together to the most devout Creator of all, since you have not been altogether deprived of so good a disposition of mind. For from the few things we have set forth we recognize how good the treasure of his heart was (Ecclesiasticus 60:14). In his joy at finding the pearl, he sold everything he possessed (Matthew 13:46), even denying himself; and, an exile amid labor and hardship, many sleepless nights, hunger and thirst, and many fasts, amid cold and nakedness, he imitated the apostle Paul (2 Corinthians 11:27) and wandered for many years for Christ’s sake. Nor could any worldly pressure wrench from him the sweetness of the twofold love [Col. 0633B] on which the whole law and the prophets depend (Matthew 22:40).

Therefore, in accordance with the admonition of the Book of Ecclesiasticus, “Let us praise glorious men, our fathers in their generation” (Ecclesiasticus 44:1)—but let us praise them in such a way that, following their example, we may direct and shape the perversity of our own lives. For, as the most learned Father Augustine says: “To speak well and live badly is nothing other than to condemn oneself by one’s own voice.”

Above all, by contemplating the life of our fathers, let us arm ourselves for contempt of the world and imitate them in so perfect a work. Let us not love the world or the things that are in the world (1 John 2:15), because, as the blessed evangelist John declares, everything that is in the world is “the desire of the flesh, and the desire of the eyes, and the pride of life” (1 John 2:16), and these are not from the Father. These three are certainly the causes of the remaining vices; they grow so hot through love of the world that they prevail in separating an innumerable multitude from the love of Christ. We shall be wholly free from them if we exclude love of the world from our hearts [Col. 0634A].

When we have done this, let us not doubt that we are everywhere aided by the patronage of the saints, whose footsteps we eagerly pursue with willing hearts. Since external miracles bear witness to a good life, in what follows we shall try [Note: [Col. 0633C] Whether the author carried this intention of his will through to the accomplishment of the work, we do not know; Riguetus certainly found no miracles in the inscriptions, and Ruyrus very few, concerning which see below.], if God permits, to transmit some of them to posterity, so that from a few examples it may be gathered how greatly our most devout nourisher Deodatus is exalted in glory in eternal life, to whose dead bones so many heavenly consolations are brought for bodies and souls.

Finally, relying upon his merits and prayers, let us approach with confidence the throne of divine glory (Hebrews 4:16), asking that our debts be forgiven us (Matthew 6:12), and, following the example of the patron of this temple, let us persevere in girding ourselves for a manner of life pleasing to God. May the mercy of the eternal Father go before us and follow us, together with the Son consubstantial with him and the Holy Spirit, in the triune Unity and the one Trinity, which inseparably rules, lives, and reigns forever and ever. Amen.

29. [Note: [Col. 0633C] What follows was undoubtedly written in at a later time.]

In the year 1049 from the Incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ, in the second indiction, with the sixth concurrent year and the fourteenth epact, while Henry, son of the emperor Conrad, was reigning in his tenth year and exercising imperial authority in his third, these deeds, which were written concerning Deodatus, the bishop of blessed memory, were brought to the highest summit of the apostolic see. In a provincial synod of that same holy Roman Church it was decreed that they should be read in the presence of bishops, abbots, clergy, and laity; and, after they had been read, by authority granted by the supreme pope Leo IX [Note: [Col. 0634C] Pope St. Leo IX is commemorated on 19 April, on which day we supplied his Acts and showed that the synod indicated here was held at Rome after Low Sunday; all the chronological particulars reported here agree.], in the first [Col. 0634C] year of his apostolate, it was decreed that they should be read in the Church of God and preserved with the greatest firmness, for the praise and glory of our Lord Jesus Christ, for the honor of our most blessed patron Deodatus, and for the edification of many throughout all ages of ages.

GUDINUS OF LUXEUIL

GUDINUS’S RHYTHMIC LAMENT  
On the death of Constantius, a monk of Luxeuil.

(MABILLON, *Analecta*, new edition, p. 217.)

[NOTE.]

Gudinus, the author of this rhythmic lament, is as unknown as Constantius, whose death he mourns here. Both were undoubtedly monks of Luxeuil under King Robert, during the abbacy of Milo; and Constantius was indeed placed in charge of the schools at Luxeuil, as is clear from the fact that he was famous.

[Col. 0635A] Therefore mourn the pious master by singing, O cantor;  
Until now I have stretched my lyre along the paths of music.  
Now I shall extend my course toward the dear obsequies,  
Which the love of my sorrowful heart presses down with lamentation.

A great burden, a great force of grief constricts my former power,  
And I cannot complete what I had previously resolved to do;  
Nevertheless, I shall speak in the bare words of an oppressed heart.

Heaven, stars, earth, sea, human beings, and beasts,  
Extend your hearing to the lament of this poem,  
And return faithful laments to Constantius the philosopher.

I never pronounce his name without a grieving mind;  
I form in my mind an image of his face, a likeness not unlike him;  
I embrace him, and I am joined to him with an ever-watchful heart.

His death, which must be mourned, encompasses the whole world,  
Imposing a cessation of public business upon the wise of kingdoms,  
By which both princes and common people are greatly disturbed.

[Col. 0635B] Never have I seen, nor shall I see, so pious a philosopher,  
Who, becoming food for his disciples after the Lord,  
Administered learning with gentleness, not with terror.

While I lament these two matters with great grief and summon tears,  
Full of the languor of an implanted sorrow, I waste away,  
Deprived of so distinguished a man and such counsel.

Let the excellent books mourn with me,  
Which the beautiful hand of illustrious Constantius copied,  
Lamenting that they are to be neglected under a teacher like him no longer.

O Jesus, Redeemer of the world, what offense has the age committed,  
When you took from the earth life’s supreme delight—  
And indeed the hope of pure learning, the son of philosophy?

A region of the world would have perished in a great catastrophe,  
And the sun’s brightness would have grown pale in its appearance,  
Before the pious master was carried away by death.

Night and day would have exchanged the qualities of their seasons,  
The waves of the sea would have driven back the sailors’ sails,  
So that Gudinus might not have lost his lord Constantius.

I believe heaven grieved at such a death,  
When the moon, changing the former appearance of her shining sphere,  
Signaled to the world that so grave a shipwreck was coming.

The East and the South mourn, the West and the North.  
[Col. 0636A] Cities and castles mourn for the pious Constantius.  
Everywhere the monks are overcome by tearful compassion.

The people of Luxeuil grieve with continual tears;  
The pious abbot Milo mourns with most devout lamentations,  
Since he will no longer possess the radiance of so great a lamp.

Now exhausted by grief, the city of Chrysopolis mourns [Note: [Col. 0635C] Besançon.],  
Firm in the triumphs of Stephen and surrounded by the rampart of its river.  
The people of Strasbourg touch heaven with their prolonged complaints.  
Lyons too is stunned, the glory of great cities;  
Chalon and Mâcon marvel greatly,  
Bending pious ears toward so harsh a report.

Robert, the glory of kings and the crown of the world,  
Lays aside his royal countenance at the funeral of Constantius,  
Whom he knew to be prudent through his service to the Lord.

[Col. 0636B] France, ornament of kingdoms, is happy and flourishing,  
Shining more brightly through Constantius than through the strength of its power;  
By the lot of his burial she has remained most beautiful.

You have lost, people of Langres, the joy of fellowship,  
Now learning that the distinguished philosopher has died,  
The pearl of monks, the treasure of clerics.

Autun, in no way inferior to any in the gift of piety,  
With willing devotion, open the depths of your compassion,  
And kindly care for Constantius, now dead.

Henry, residing in the Roman palace,  
And approving by his intellect the secret matters of the wise,  
Grieves that no one like Constantius can be found.

The princes of Burgundy stand in mourning and lamentation.  
The prelates of Germany mourn the world’s loss.  
The Alemanni and Lombards yield their place to sorrow.

[Col. 0636C] Who could hear the fame of so great a man, who hear his name,  
And not bless him and visit him with affection?  
No one, I believe, except the one to whom Christ is displeasing.

Who, man or non-man, speaks more pleasantly?  
Who will be a more brilliant rhetorician in beloved discourse?  
Who will excel him in the teaching of mathematics?

O my Constantius, eloquent one, supreme part of my soul,  
Inexhaustible care of my heart and study,  
Why do you lie as the prey of death beneath the closure of the tomb?

You always made promises to me, whom in mourning I desire;  
Now, wretched and unhappy, I lack you even in those promises [reading uncertain].  
[Col. 0637A] Alas for the grief! Why, while I live in this age, do you not live?

You, master of masters, more learned, most learned,  
Better from virtue to virtue, and in goodness the best,  
Have rightly, through your merits, become most steadfast—*Constantissimus*.

I praise all the wise, but I place you before them all.  
I commend your soul to the most holy Spirit (*flamen*),  
That under his guidance you may enjoy the fellowship of the saints.

May you be blessed, and happy a hundred and a thousand times.  
May the court of beautiful paradise become your rest.  
May the right hand of Christ protect you a thousand and a thousand times.

Behold, I have offered a lament on my lyre for the one dearest to all.  
Now I ask those who hear to offer prayers to the Lord,  
That he may grant Constantius forgiveness of his sins.

Through the favor of the Lord Jesus Christ, to whom are honor and glory throughout the ages of ages. Amen.

CIRCA A.D. 1000. WIDO, A MONK

WIDO’S LETTER TO HERIBERT, ARCHBISHOP OF COLOGNE

(BALUZE, *Miscellanea*, Lucerne edition, vol. II, p. 114.)

[NOTE.]

We possessed three ancient copies of the following letter, which was also published by Ivo in the second part of the *Decree*, chapter 84: one from the Royal Library and the others from the Colbert Library. In one of these it has no title; in another it bears this title: “Letter of Pope Paschasius to the archbishop of Milan, suffering under the heresy of simony.” It is certain that in the age of Paschal II—who was also called Paschasius by some—Peter Grosolanus, archbishop of Milan, was accused of having bought the archiepiscopal dignity for money.

But since this letter is not concerned with that sort of simony, and since it appears to have been written by a man of lower rank than the person to whom it was addressed, I am readily led to believe that the inscription found in the Royal Codex is more authentic. It reads: “Letter of Wido the monk to Heribert, archbishop”—namely, the archbishop of Cologne, whom Rupert, abbot of Deutz, shows to have been attacked by various calumnies. For this reason above all we wished to reproduce it here, so as to restore it intact to its author.

[Col. 0637A] Whoever, when able, fails to defend his brother from death incurs the guilt of fraternal death. We too, who have heard of the supreme danger threatening your eminence, incur the penalty of the gravest guilt if we remain silent, since the Lord solemnly testifies through the prophet [Note: [Col. 0637C] “Solemnly testifies”: in one Colbert codex *intestante* is read, and in another *intonante*. In both, however, the word *terribiliter* is absent.] that he surely sheds blood who silently conceals the iniquity of the wicked.

For we have heard—and we greatly marvel at it—that sacred orders among you are being sold for money, although all who attempt such a thing are rightly proved to be heretics; the Holy Spirit thundering through Gregory that whoever is ordained through money is promoted in order to become a heretic.

And to show that the cause of this little page of ours was not presumption but fear, the same blessed man continues (St. Gregory, book IV, letters 51, 55, and 56, and book VII, indiction II, letter 810; *Decree*, I, question 1, chapter 5, “Whoever”): “Whoever, according to the place of his office, has not burned vehemently against the heresy of simony and of the newly ordained, may be certain that he will have a share [Note: [Col. 0637C] “Will have a share”: the same copies read “will have a share.”] with the one who first committed this abominable crime.” [Note: [Col. 0637C] “Whoever”: in the Colbert copies it is written, “For whoever.”]

Since these words expressly name the heresy as heretical, simoniacal, and that of the newly ordained [Col. 0638A], they make it utterly clear that this is a crime deserving eternal death. The divine oracle, speaking through Augustine, bears witness and says (Fulgentius, *On the Faith to Peter*, chapter 391): “Hold most firmly, and doubt in no way, that every heretic or schismatic—even if he gives many alms or even sheds his blood for Christ—is to be handed over with the devil and his angels to the fire of eternal burning, unless before the end of this life he has been incorporated into and restored to the Catholic Church.”

Hence the Lord drove the buyers and sellers from the temple; the earth swallowed Dathan and Abiram when they sought office; Peter condemned Simon when he made his attempt [Note: [Col. 0637C] “Condemned”: this word and those that follow up to *condemnavit* are absent from the same copies and appear superfluous.]; and Peter condemned all who practice simony in this matter with an everlasting ecclesiastical anathema.

And it is exceedingly shameful that, when the Church has already been confirmed in complete strength [Note: [Col. 0638C] “In complete strength”: thus the Colbert codices. The Royal Codex has “in complete strength” with a different grammatical form.], it should succumb to so savage an enemy—an enemy over whom it triumphed with such power at the beginning of its infancy.

But if someone should object that not consecrations, but the things resulting from consecration, are being sold, he seems [Note: [Col. 0638C] “Are being sold, he seems”: we have retained the reading of the Royal Codex. One Colbert copy reads, “To seem to be sold—what is it to say something other than to understand absolutely nothing?” In the other, where the word “sold” is absent, this passage reads: “What is it for anyone to say something else, unless indeed to understand absolutely nothing?”] indeed to say something [Col. 0639A], but in reality understands absolutely nothing. For since the bodily Church, whether a bishop, an abbot, or something of that kind, can in no way prosper without bodily and external goods—just as the soul does not live in time without the body—whoever sells one of these without which the other cannot be possessed leaves neither unsold [Note: [Col. 0639B] “Leaves neither unsold”: thus the Colbert copies. The Royal Codex reads, “does not sell either and does not leave it unsold.”].

Yet the sacred canon utterly destroys this objection (Council of Chalcedon, chapter 2), since it forbids a procurator or defender of a church, or one subject to a rule, to be appointed through money, and even strikes down with the sword of anathema those who intervene in so great a crime.

What more need be said? If those who have been anathematized and excommunicated, and who, as true heretics, are simoniacs and newly ordained, have been separated from the number of the Church’s faithful, who does not see that the Masses and prayers of such priests [Col. 0639B] or clerics provoke God to anger against the people, whereas we thought that by such means he would be appeased?

For it is written: “Everything that is not from faith is sin” (Romans 14:23). And again: “There is no place for a true sacrifice outside the Catholic Church” (*Decree*, I, question 1, chapter 71, “Outside”). Hence it is also said: “After the first and second admonition, avoid a heretical person” (Titus 3:10).

How, then, do we avoid such bishops, abbots, or other clerics if we hear their Masses, when, if we pray even once with them, we incur excommunication? [Note: [Col. 0640B] “If we pray once”: the Colbert copies simply read “if we hear.”]

To believe that such men are at least priests is wholly erroneous, since Peter says to Simon: “May your money be with you for destruction, because you thought that the gift of God could be possessed through money” (Acts 8:20). When it says “you thought,” it is clear that he is condemned not because he had done the deed, but because he believed that he could do it, although thinking it possible is less than believing it.
