Since, therefore, being any kind of heretic entails certain and indubitable condemnation, what benefit is there in having driven the impious Arians, Sabellians, Photinians, and Manichaeans from the world, if the heresy of simony and of the newly ordained—which, as blessed Gregory says, first crept into the Church through the devil’s fraud—defiles the Church’s original and greatest chastity with utterly foul pollution? [Col. 0640B]

Therefore, for God’s sake, and for the sake of your eminence and all Christ’s faithful, we beg and implore you: if you desire to have a share in Christ, strive with all your strength to destroy completely, by your authority and example, so savage a plague, which by its ravages has already inflicted eternal death everywhere upon countless peoples. lest, God forbid, there be any further sin against the Holy Spirit—a sin forgiven neither in this age nor in the age to come.

RAYMUND ARNALLI

LETTER OF R., A MONK OF SAINT-VICTOR, TO B., HIS ABBOT  
He excuses himself for not yet having returned from Italy and asks permission to devote himself to the study of law.

(Dom MARTÈNE, *Amplissima Collectio*, I, 469.)

NOTICE.

(*Literary History of France*, vol. VII, p. 570.)

This letter is interesting for the early period in which the study of jurisprudence was revived. Its inscription shows that it was written to an abbot of Saint-Victor of Marseille, whose name is represented only by a B, and that the author, whose name is designated only by an R, was a monk of the same monastery. Yet it is highly probable that B represents Abbot Bernard, and R Raymond Arnalli, a monk under the same abbot. On this supposition—which is anything but rash—the letter was written in 1065, the year of Bernard’s election, or the following year; for the text clearly shows that this abbot had only recently come to preside over the community of Saint-Victor.

Raymond’s principal purpose is to obtain permission to study jurisprudence, and the means of subsistence during the course of his studies. He himself frankly explains what gave rise to this plan. Having been sent to Rome on some important business of his house, and having lost his mount on the way, he stopped at various places in Italy. There he witnessed the extraordinary gathering of students whom this new kind of study attracted from every direction—from Provence as well as from other countries—and what impressed him still more was that monks themselves increased their number. Struck by their example, he conceived the desire to imitate them. Accordingly, he informs his abbot that he is going to Pisa to await his reply. But, so that Bernard would be less hesitant to grant his request, he takes care to assure him that, far from using the knowledge he hoped to acquire to practice as an advocate in secular courts, as some monks then customarily did, he would use it only to uphold and defend the rights of Saint-Victor against anyone who attempted to violate them.

LETTER OF R., A MONK, TO HIS ABBOT B.

[Col. 0641]

[Col. 0641A] To B. [Note: [Col. 0641] Perhaps Bernard, who governed the monastery of Saint-Victor of Marseille from 1065 to 1079], his most reverend lord and most worthy of highest praise, the excellent dispenser of the divine bounty of the monastery of Marseille, R., his servant, humblest of all who serve him, though not least in affection, offers the service of due obedience.

As the evangelist bears witness, it is clear that the angels declared that “on earth there is peace to people of good will.” And elsewhere it is written: “Good will is sufficient.” Rightly, therefore, just as the will to accomplish a good deed is said to be sufficient even when it cannot advance to completion, so too the same good will that I have always had toward you should undoubtedly be considered sufficient for me.

For after I was deemed worthy to see with bodily eyes the fame of your greatness, which for a long time had resounded in my ears, I strove, as many have been able to know, to apply the small measure of my ability inseparably to the immensity of your love. Yet I used often to desire that the proof of the affection which lay hidden, burning within the confines of my heart, might at some time give off its fragrance through the exhibition of a deed.

Nor is it because God has visited his people—because he has raised you to the better part which Mary chose for herself—and because he has wonderfully adorned the monastery of Marseille, already completely darkened by the lack of a ruler, through the illumination of your virtues. If all my limbs were turned into tongues, it would be impossible for anyone to express how greatly I rejoice.

But if it pleases your accustomed goodness, attend: when I learned that, under God’s guidance, you had been advanced to the aforementioned rank, I am prepared to give an explanation, though not a sufficient one, of why I delayed coming to obey your commands.

Let your clemency, most desired Father, know that I once began to go to Rome, with the permission of the brothers of the aforesaid monastery, on account of a certain pressing and intolerable matter—one which, as I believe, has already been sufficiently reported to you. Because of extreme poverty, I dismissed my own companion at Pavia [Col. 0642A] and proceeded to Rome with strangers. But since it did not please the divine will that I should complete the journey I had begun, the animal whose conveyance I was attempting to use to reach Rome first fell ill on the way and then failed me completely there.

Therefore, since I could not go farther, and since I was exceedingly ashamed to return immediately with the business unfinished, I first began to hesitate, but finally resolved to devote myself to the study of letters. After a few delays had intervened there, by God’s grace, I have remained until now, exercising my mind in this way.

This, therefore, sweetest lord, is the reason why, after I began to realize that what my soul had long desired had come about, I delayed hastening to you. Indeed, I resolved to study more and more, so that henceforth, with life as my companion, I might be able to serve you better.

Now, however, since throughout almost the whole of Italy I continually see scholars—especially men from Provence, and also men of the order to which I belong—devoting themselves in crowds to the study of law, and since I observe that our monastery is incessantly harassed by clerics and laymen through litigation and suffers the loss of its rightful possessions, I desire to acquire a little knowledge of this kind.

For if, by the gracious gift of God, I should be able to achieve anything in this work, I would not covet secular lawsuits, but would assist, as far as I could, only the justice of our monastery. If it therefore pleases your dignity, most exalted Father, that I devote myself as far as I am able to this work, I ask and humbly entreat you to grant me charitable permission in this matter and to arrange to instruct the prior at Pisa by your letter to assist me.

If I obtain from your mercy what I hope for, I shall go to Pisa, God permitting, to pursue my studies there. In the meantime, I shall await your consoling command until the feast of Saint Michael. Farewell.

ALWALO

ALWALO’S LETTER TO L., A PONTIFF

(MARTÈNE, *Thesaurus Anecdotorum*, I, 105.)

[NOTE.]

We have extracted this and the following letter from an old manuscript codex of the Oratory of Troyes, whose script appears to be more than six hundred years old. I have not yet been able to determine who the author of the first letter, Alwalo, was, nor who the supreme pontiff L. was to whom he writes. If conjecture may be allowed some weight, L. was not a Roman pontiff but an ordinary bishop. Certainly, in the following letter he is addressed simply by the title of bishop.

Nor are examples lacking in which ordinary bishops are called supreme pontiffs. Thus Bruno, archbishop of Cologne, is called “supreme pontiff” by Widricus in the *Life of Saint Gerard, Bishop of Toul*. The abbot Heldricus to whom this man writes also appears to be Hel., the father of the monastic congregation to whom there survives a fragment of a letter from Bishop Bruno. Bruno ascended the throne of the see of Langres in 980; Heldricus, namely the abbot of Saint-Germain at Auxerre, was presiding in 990.

I. ALWALO’S LETTER TO L., THE PONTIFF  
He asks to be absolved from the excommunication imposed because of injuries inflicted upon the provostship of Capuleia.

[Col. 0643A]

Alwalo, more wretched than all other mortals and weighed down by the burden of sins, to L., the supreme pontiff, almost the sole administrator in our times of the Lord’s vineyard: whatever a son owes to his father or a servant to his master.

Struck by the vengeance of the Lord’s correction, which my own sins have demanded, terrified by the fear of death, and desirous only of the salvation of my soul, I flee to you, the one physician of souls, and ask that you mercifully make known what remedies ought to be applied to my wounds.

For you yourself know under how great a bond of excommunication I am held on account of the provostship of Capuleia [Col. 0643B]—that is, the authority of Saint Martin. Therefore, if days are prolonged for me in this life, I have resolved to seek the judgment of the canons of that saint, and I promise that in all things I shall act according to your counsel’s decree.

But if I should prove disappointed in the hope of life, I commit these matters, under Christ’s witness, to my wife and children in their faith, on this condition: that you do not permit them to deny me the services that ought to be rendered to Christians who are dying.

II. LETTER OF L., BISHOP, TO HELDRICUS, THE ABBOT  
He explains how he absolved Alwalo from excommunication.

To Heldricus, an abbot fervent in the love of Christ, and to his whole congregation [Col. 0644A], Bishop L., a sinner, sends greeting and health.

I give thanks to you, dearest brothers, because, fervent in your love of sacred authority, you were unwilling to receive Alwalo, deprived of communion with the holy Church, for burial. But I shall make known to you the terms on which I absolved him.

His wife, together with his sons, sent two men to seek the favor of our majesty. They brought letters promising every amendment and asking that absolution be granted. I did not believe their words and refused to consent until they themselves swore under oath that the wife and sons would, up to the feast of Saint Martin, make right in good faith before blessed Martin and his canons whatever the judgment of the princes determined that they ought to make good, and would pay it according to the custom of the law.

If they refused to do this, these two men who had requested absolution would, on the feast of Saint Andrew, surrender themselves as hostages to the canons and place themselves in their power.

On this condition, therefore, we absolved Alwalo by the authority of the Father, the Son, the Holy Spirit, Saint Martin, all the saints, and ourselves, and we grant you permission to receive him for burial. We also command you to absolve him, and so may God bless you.

But know that his wife and sons have not been absolved until the amends have been made and paid. Without the presence of his wife and sons we order him to be put into the earth, so that through this they may know themselves to be excommunicated.

ANSELM THE SCHOLASTIC

NOTICE

(MANSI, in Fabricius, *Bibliotheca medii et infimi latini*, vol. I, p. 111.)

[Col. 0643] I believe this Anselm was a monk. His short work is found in codex 57 of Saint-Illidius of Clermont, in P. Montfaucon, *Bibliotheca manuscriptorum*, p. 1263. The title of the work is: “Vision of a certain monk in the monastery of Saint-Remigius, written down by Anselm, disciple of Saint Abbo, abbot of Fleury, at the command of Abbot Odo.”

VISION OF ANSELM THE SCHOLASTIC

(Published by D. Edelestand du Méril, *Popular Latin Poems*, vol. I, p. 200.)

[Col. 0643] In Solomon’s litter,  
Which he constructed from Lebanon  
Of wondrous woods,  
Signifying deeper mysteries,  
Where he built  
A most excellent resting place  
Of gold,  
And purple ascent,  
For the daughters of Jerusalem,  
Who signify the Church,  
You may find  
A spiritual banquet  
In the greatest abundance.

There, with a full horn,  
He brings in provisions,  
So that he may lighten our complaints  
And satisfy us with various foods,  
That the human race may cease  
To weep over its miserable ends.

But as you pluck sweet fruits  
[Col. 0644] And lilies of the valleys  
Among the sweetest flowers  
And the pleasant tastes of honey,  
You will find one particular thing  
Which you will taste with delight.

There is a metropolitan city,  
Called Rheims, most noble,  
Which a certain Remus founded,  
[Col. 0645] Who was the brother of Romulus,  
The founder of the Roman city.

Of this distinguished city,  
Once great in glory,  
There was an excellent bishop,  
The great Remigius of old.

When he was chosen as bishop  
And duly blessed,  
When the bishop lacked the oil  
With which his sacred head  
Was to be anointed by the bishop,  
A dove, flying through the air,  
Very swiftly carried in its beak  
A flask full of oil;  
With the gentlest mouth it carried  
That with which the bishop was anointed. [Note: [Col. 0645] Historians place this miracle at the baptism of Clovis: “When the font had finally been sanctified, the chrism was lacking by divine will. But the holy bishop, raising his eyes to heaven, is said silently to have prayed with tears; and suddenly a white dove—or snow—flew in, carrying in its beak a flask filled with the chrism of the heavenly gift.” Flodoard, *History of Rheims*, book I, chapter 13; see also Hincmar, *Works*, vol. I, p. 744. [Col. 0646]]

Remigius, always worthy.

While the people devoutly celebrate  
His feast  
On the Kalends of October,  
And come dancing in procession,  
Among the other faithful  
And Catholics in Christ,  
A certain monk was present.  
He came diligently to pray,  
That, lamenting his wicked deeds,  
He might mourn his sins.

While this man possessed lodging  
Within the monastery,  
Was joined to the brothers  
And united with them in charity,  
While he placed his limbs upon a bed  
And slept in the dormitory,  
In a peaceful vision  
He revealed in this way  
What he had seen:

“Be present now to me, O God,  
Who are one and three,  
And who open  
The pregnant visions of Ezekiel  
And illuminate  
The hidden visions of Daniel.

Reveal the way of salvation,  
So that I may proclaim your praises:  
How, when the lower regions were broken open,  
You brought souls out from there,  
At the time of the Passion,  
And on the holy day of Easter,  
On which the whole world  
Rejoices and resounds together.

While sleep weighed upon my eyes  
And my body lay upon the bed,  
I suddenly saw myself transported  
To the pulpit of Remigius,  
The distinguished bishop,  
And ministering the office of a deacon  
Before the assembled people.

It was the Lord’s Day,  
On which there was a great multitude of Jews—”

The crowd came out to meet

Christ, the Son of Man,

and truly the Son of God—

the Gospel does not relate,

after he came into the world,

that such great honor

was ever bestowed upon him by the peoples

as there was on that day.

“Hosanna!” the children cry;

“Blessed is he who comes

now in the name of the Lord!”

Because of this honor,

the envious Jewish populace,

condemning Christ to the cross

and subjecting him to suffering,

his side is pierced by a lance [text uncertain: “blood is poured out”?];

blood and water are poured forth,

the soul leaves the body,

and he departs into the Father’s hands.

While I devoutly recall

this passion in fear,

and mourn its completion,

and descend from the pulpit,

carrying the Gospel

in my own arms,

I seem to see

an image of Christ himself

descending from the cross,

and carrying in his strong hand

the sign of victory,

which today is called the cross,

and addressing me in these words:

“If you faithfully believe

what you, brother, recently read?”

I, suppliant and humble,

gave the true answer:

“Although I am insignificant dust

and earthly ash,

as I have read with my mouth, Lord,

so know that I believe with my heart;

and there is no doubt

in the innermost part of my heart

that I believe you to be the true God,

born, having suffered and died,

and having risen again on the third

day—I believe this through all ages.”

He immediately commands:

“Follow me without delay

where you see me proceeding.”

[Col. 0646] Then immediately—beyond what I could have hoped for—he proceeds to the regions below, carrying the cross in his hands.

I followed fearlessly,

having nothing to fear,

trusting in so great a leader.

Then the princes of darkness,

the leaders of pale death,

the fiercest torturers,

and the swift ravagers

fled away with the greatest speed,

not daring to pay attention,

nor daring to gaze upon

the appearance of so great a thunderbolt

and of so brilliant a light.

Across the fields and valleys

the savage demons scatter,

blacker than soot,

most dreadful in their darkness,

and discolored in appearance.

They howl and bellow,

and roar with dreadful voice;

they rage like savage lions

when they lose their cubs.

They weep through night and day,

and from their foul throats

pour forth a pitiable song.

[Note: This is a reminiscence of the *Georgics*, book IV, verse 515:

“He weeps through the night, and, sitting on the branch, renews his pitiable song and fills the places far and wide with mournful complaints.”]

Then angels also come to meet us;

they applaud the joyful Judge,

receiving the souls.

Christ, freeing them from darkness,

leads them to joys.

Then praises resound in heaven

and melodies ring out:

what no eye has seen,

nor ear has heard,

nor can enter the heart—

how great the joys were,

or how immense the happiness,

when they return to the heights,

rescued from the tomb of death.

O Jesus, good Lord!

Who anywhere can or will be able

to praise you fittingly—

you who have mercy on the wretched,

you who lead the ungrateful

and the lost back to heaven?

Let us turn the pointer of our pen

toward the dream of the vision,

which truly recounts

the order of the marvelous vision.

While, then, I was seeing these things

and proceeded joyfully on foot,

thinking that I had already been freed

from the burden of the flesh

and released from the body,

the Lord, calm and peaceful,

looked upon me with serene countenance:

“Where are you proceeding so joyfully?”

“—I am following you, Radiance of light,

admiring such great glory,

of which I desire to become

a participant and companion.”

He kindly replied:

“—Stop your step as quickly as possible;

do not proceed farther.

But return to the monastery;

your time has not yet come.”

I dared to say nothing.

For what could I contradict,

or what could I wish to mutter?

With one word I fell silent;

I trembled utterly within myself:

“—By what way shall I go, Lord?”

“—Return by the way

by which you came.”

“—So many enemies block the roads!

If I return from here alone,

I shall not return to the heights.”

Then, quicker than speech,

he looked toward the left side

and saw a grim figure,

black and diabolical.

He beckoned to it with his finger:

“—Come here, worthless servant!

Bad servant, do this!”

He commanded with authority:

“—Return this brother

safe and unharmed to his homeland,

and quickly return this monk

to holy Remigius.

See that no one harms him,

but that he returns without fear,

and that none like you

touch him even lightly.”

Thus, accompanied by the devil,

I was dismissed by the Lord.

He had entrusted the sheep to the wolf,

but had clenched its evil jaws

and bound Leviathan,

whose most savage jaws

and wicked throat

he had pierced with his hook.

Then, entering together

the chaos of Erebus,

the evil and most wicked spirits,

returning to their own seats,

find them empty;

and so they languished

all the more in the darkness.

They gnash their teeth with a roar,

and with groaning give forth harsh voices;

with a dreadful cry

they summon their companions in torment,

so that with hooked hands

and glowing hooks

they might seize me more intently,

so that one head might, on behalf of many,

suffer undeserved penalties.

But even if the broken world should fall,

and heaven should collapse with earth,

and everything should perish together

that nature, joining it together,

holds fast with an unloosable bond,

in a fourfold connection,

the ruins would strike me,

unafraid—

the deacon of Christ the King.

[Note: Ansellus recalls here stanza 2 of ode 3 in book III of Horace’s *Odes*:

“Neither the stormy ruler of the restless Adriatic,

nor the mighty hand of thundering Jove,

if the shattered world should fall,

will the ruins strike the fearless man.”]

Then the evil leader

terrifies them with these words:

“If you wish to harm this man alone

with evil effort,

what will you do, wretches,

when Christ returns here?

I forbid you to touch him;

I prohibit you from injuring him.

Permit him to proceed

where he has been ordered by the prince,

who terrifies us with his cross,

whose power is terrible

and frightening to us,

which we cannot endure

nor wish to name.

Our foolish prince,

when he saw the covering of flesh,

thought him to be merely a man,

not knowing that the Son of God

was concealed in the flesh.”

By these words he calms the harsh ones

and inspires such great fear

that, through the most dreadful fires,

through ranks of weapons,

and through black chasms,

I arrive uninjured and unharmed

inside the boundaries of the monastery

of holy Remigius,

through the aid of that most evil guardian

who had not yet abandoned me.

Upon the altar of the bishop

I place the Lord’s text;

then I place the chasuble

upon the altar-table,

together with the stole

and likewise the alb;

then I put them down quickly.

[Col. 0648] The evil leader does not leave me

until the place of my bed.

Immediately and on the spot

I lay my body upon the bed.

He stands there with black teeth,

with loosened hair,

with blood-red eyes,

resembling a bear in his feet,

imitating the claws of lions,

and wearing a black goat’s fleece:

“Make me your companion in bed,

since I was the leader of your journey.

Do not fear to receive a companion

into your embrace:

he who did not harm you on the road

will not be able to harm you in bed.”

I, bold and unafraid,

trusting in Christ rather than in strength,

turn onto my right side.

I make room as quickly as possible.

He places his foot upon the straw;

his mouth is almost joined to mine,

and we speak in turn.

Secure in my Christ,

I fear him not at all:

“Tell me, fellow [or: ‘I pray you’],

most evil leader,

enemy of the truth [perhaps: ‘contrary to the truth’]:

what causes have now arisen,

or what reason has there been,

why Christ descended to hell,

so that he might take away from you

the wretched souls

and make so many free

from the yoke of servitude,

and lift from your throat

those weighed down by the burden of sin?

I am exceedingly amazed

that such a powerful authority

should bear iron gates

broken by the finger of one man, Christ.”

He, gnashing his teeth,

begins with a barbarous,

horrible, resounding, dreadful voice;

with distorted mouth

and trembling lips he growls:

“Listen now, evil monk,

and perceive with the ear of your heart

the truth which, unwillingly,

I cannot conceal within myself.

For it is not mine to say

what is wholly true:

sacrilegious bishops,

abbots ignorant of the rule,

unhappy priests,

most wicked fornicators,

lying deacons,

and new little prostitutes

with their young clerks,

and sufficiently envious monks,

turbulent murmurers,

persist day and night,

from the celebrated course of Easter

until your Easter returns,

always praying to the Lord,

with the solemnities of Masses,

for lost souls.

And evil laborers

give their alms

to the needy and the poor.

These take souls away from us;

their works have made them ours.

[Note: The word *quae*, found in manuscript 4587, is necessary for the sense; but unless it is removed by an entirely exceptional elision, it gives the verse one syllable too many.]

By their prayers appeased,

[Note: In the time of Saint Gregory, who died in 604, the efficacy of the sacrifice of the Mass for delivering souls from purgatory was already believed in; *Dialogues*, book IV, chapter 55, vol. II, col. 464, Paris edition, 1705.]

and by their evil works,

Jesus is good to you but evil to us,

sufficiently our rival.

Thus he takes away from us

the souls whose deeds

have made them pleasing.

After rising from the dead—

alas, grief!—and conquering us,

he weakened our authority

and took away our glory.

[Note: The origin of this popular belief is in the *Gospel of Nicodemus*: “And while Satan and the prince of hell were speaking these things to one another, suddenly there was a voice like thunder and a spiritual cry: ‘Lift up your gates, princes, and be lifted up, eternal gates, and the King of glory shall enter.’ When the prince of Tartarus heard this, he said to Satan: ‘Depart from me and go out from my seats. If you are a powerful warrior, fight against the King of glory; but what have you to do with him?’ And he cast Satan out from his seats. And the prince said to his impious ministers: ‘Shut the cruel bronze gates and put iron bars beneath them; resist firmly, lest we be led captive into captivity.… The Lord of majesty has come in the form of a man, has illumined the eternal darkness, broken the indissoluble bonds, and visited with unconquerable power those sitting in the depths of the darkness of sins and in the shadow of the death of sinners.’” 6 (*Gospel of Nicodemus*, chapter 21, in Fabricius, *Codex apocryphus Novi Testamenti*, p. 282.) There can be no doubt about the wide circulation of this passage, since part of it entered the Sunday office for Palm Sunday. We shall cite several further proofs drawn from different languages:

“Then the prince of the abyss seeks his accustomed weapons,

by which he himself had subjected the human race to himself;

but as soon as he saw the threshold collapsing, broken,

terrified and stunned, he fled to the depths of the house.

Yet the tyrant did not escape through the dark caverns.

A stronger one entered, who carried away his vessels.

Dragged out, captured, bound, and held fast with tightened chains,

subdued and driven from the citadel

where once the prince of the world had sat exalted—

the savage, greedy, long-unsubdued beast.

But the victor of the world, alone superior to all,

struck down and shattered his entire head.”

John Scotus, *Christ’s Descent into Hell*, v. 5; in Mai, *Classicorum auctorum fragmenta*, vol. V, p. 439.

“Into the midst of hell Satan has put him;

he lays a chain around his neck.

He has bound his feet and hands tightly,

and hurled him into the midst of hell.”

*Gospel of Nicodemus* in Provençal verse, in Raynouard, *Lexique Roman*, vol. I, p. 511.]

While the Paschal solemnities return,

pleasant to you,

but always fearful to us,

he is accustomed to do this,

not fearing to conquer us.

[Note: We have nowhere encountered this particular idea, but it was generally believed that, in memory of Christ’s resurrection, the sufferings of the damned were suspended:

“There are also, for spirits often harmful,

celebrated holidays of punishment beneath Styx,

on that sacred night when God returned

from the waters of Acheron to the heights.

…

Tartarus grows languid beneath gentler punishments,

and the people of the shades rejoice

in the leisure of their prison, freed from the fires;

the rivers do not boil with sulfur as usual.”

Aurelius Prudentius, *Cathemerinon*, hymn V, verses 125 ff.]

But there is one thing praiseworthy

and pleasing to us envious ones:

that he did not take away

those who are held fast

by dreadful crimes,

bound by evil deeds—

murderers, adulterers,

robbers, hot for plunder,

and most wicked sodomites,

accustomed to perjuries,

who were not ashamed to do

what your law forbade,

nor repented of it.

He neither took nor freed them,

so that he might remain just:

he promised rewards to the just

and punishments to the worst;

if he were to change his judgment,

he would commit injustice.”

“—O lost one!” I reply.

“Why are you so forgetful of yourself?

Why do you not bend in repentance?

And why do you not ask pardon,

so that, humbled,

you may possess what you lose

through pride

and the boldness of arrogance,

and, by seeking pardon,

may regain

your lost dignity

and even your fair glory?”

He, scorning these admonitions,

again answered as follows:

“You are mistaken; you do not know

what you are advising;

you do not know what you are urging.

Listen: I shall explain briefly

what my position is.

Misfortune made me illustrious.

But I lost my dignity

and was deprived of my inheritance.

You, who were born from earth,

mortal and foul,

pay the debts of death;

you, offspring of earth’s refuse,

take possession of the inheritance

which ought to have been ours.

He who ought to have served

now rules over us.

O shame! O misery!

That the master should serve beneath

and the servant carry out commands.

Between servant and master,

if the servant takes the reward,

tell me what peace can exist,

or what concord can be made?

Between us and you, know this

and hold it for certain:

there will always be discord

and the greatest madness,

as long as your Lord

is our rival,

prefers you to us,

and makes you more beloved.”

To this the monk replied,

steadfast and fearless:

“Through your pride,

the boldness of your heart,

and your vain exaltation,

you lost the heavenly things,

while thinking that through pride

you could become like God.

From a bright archangel

you became a black Ethiopian.

If the goodness and mercy

of our God grants us

what you, swollen with pride,

lose in your arrogance,

then let us, the humble, acquire it.

What does it matter if you grieve

that we become what you were?”

We have scattered many speeches

and lamented many things

that dreams brought

and were handed over

to oblivion from the memory of the heart.

One thing still remains,

which my pen will bring before you,

so that you may hear it attentively,

if it pleases you, lords.

Then the wicked spirit said:

“Now the end of the night is approaching;

Remigius is drawing near,

so that he may receive your praises

and hear the lessons.

But some wicked custom,

I do not know what,

advises you that, after the ringing

has struck your ears,

you immediately leap from bed,

and, if you can, quickly be first

in the church.

For while you can rest,

and surrender your limbs to sleep,

and rest sweetly,

like a fool you seek

to be first at the monastery entrance.

While the *Venite* is being prolonged,

and the ninety-fourth [Psalm]

is being sung slowly,

then you may rise quite sufficiently

to meet the appointed order.”

[Note: For the sense it would be better to change the order of these two verses:

“While the *Venite* is prolonged,

which is sung slowly,

the ninety-fourth [Psalm],

then you may rise sufficiently.”

But both manuscripts place them in the same order, and at that time the grammatical order of words was departed from without any scruple.]

“O wicked chastiser,

may the Lord command you;

may you nowhere fare well,

but always lack good things,

you who advise me to act while asleep

against the rule

which orders us to rise immediately

when the ringing has sounded

in our ears.”

[Note: It is probably necessary to read *auditus* (“heard”) instead of *auritus*. *Signierit*, “has sounded,” derives from the Old German *sing*, “bell,” which has survived in *tocsin*.

“The clerks with high and clear voice

sang *Te Deum laudamus*;

the *seins* [perhaps “breasts”; the reading is uncertain] and the bells rang.”]

“Then it is necessary for the brothers

to come as quickly as possible.

If you, evil and sleepless one,

advise anything bad

while they are sleeping,

let them mourn it with tears

before the sight of the Lord.

But what business is it of yours

to sing our song,

most savage and wicked wolf?”

[Note: In the hymn of Flavius, *Ad lotionem pedum in Coena Domini*, in the works of St. Gregory, vol. III, p. 334, the text reads:

“Savage wolf, wicked Judas,

you bear kisses to the gentle lamb.”]

“I run everywhere

and wish to move swiftly through the air.

I am swifter than the East Wind,

and I roam through the monasteries.

If I find one of my own,

let him do whatever I wish.”

“—At last, wicked one, put an end

to your deceit,

and cease from blasphemies.”

We cease speaking in turn.

He vanishes from my eyes;

heavy sleep leaves me.

Joined with the others,

I pray to the God of Remigius

to make the dream of the vision

correspond to the vision itself.

**[BERNELINUS.]**

[Col. 0651]

## Notice concerning the following musical treatises

*(Dom Gerbert, Ecclesiastical Writers on Music, vol. I, Preface.)*

“We close,” says D. Gerbert, “this first volume of our Collection with various measurements of the monochord. That instrument, whose name derives from its single string, was, in the theory of ancient music, after the hammers of Pythagoras, a sure and infallible foundation for discovering and demonstrating musical consonances and intervals.

From this, musical science rises to mathematical certainty and displays to us the rays of divinity in the works of nature—namely, in all sounding bodies, in which the same ratios are consistently found, both harmonic and arithmetic, and with the same evident force of demonstration in weight and measure as is found in geometry. Through all these things we are raised toward God, the creator of all things, who has ordered everything in measure, number, and weight (Wisdom 11:21).”

[Col. 0653]

## Bernelinus’s Exact and True Division of the Monochord in the Diatonic Genus

### [Notice]

We publish the following short work from a parchment codex of Christina, Queen of Sweden, preserved in the Vatican Library, formerly numbered 480 and now 1661. On its front it bears the title *Rules of the Abacus and Certain Other Matters*. In a more recent hand is added: “G. the Scholastic’s Abacus. Bernelinus’s Abacus, music, arithmetic, and geometry. Certain matters of Gerbert to Adalbold,” namely to that Adalbold who, while still a scholastic and later made bishop of Utrecht, in turn dedicated a small book to Gerbert, already pope under the name Sylvester II.

Gerbert calls himself a scholastic in the rule concerning the abacus of computation, which is read in the aforementioned codex after Bede’s verses *On the Preparation*, and so forth. On page 18 follows the preface to the *Abacus* that the younger Bernelinus published at Paris: “To Lord Amelius, Bernelinus’s gift of eternal happiness.” “I never cease to wonder, holy Father, at the urgency of your demand,” and so forth. In the same preface Amelius is called a venerable priest and monk; mention is also made of the work of lord pope Gerbert. On page 34 the present *Exact and True Division of the Monochord* is immediately appended to the short work on the *Abacus*.

[Col. 0653A] Half of the *proslambanomenos* is the *mese*; half of the latter is the *nete hyperboleon*. A third part of that, added to itself, is the *nete diezeugmenon*. Half of the same *nete hyperboleon*, likewise added to it, is the *paranete diezeugmenon*. A fourth part of this, [Note: Add: “taken away from the same.”] is the *paranete hyperboleon*. Half of the latter, added to itself, is the *trite diezeugmenon*. A fourth part of this, [Note: Here again one must add: “taken away from the same.”] is the *trite hyperboleon*.

A third part of the *nete diezeugmenon*, added to itself, is the *paramese*. Behold, you have eight divisions; if to each of them you add its octave—that is, as far as the *proslambanomenos*—you will have fifteen sounds, arranged within two octaves.

The first species of the diatessaron consists of a tone, a semitone, and a tone. [Note: This and what follows should be compared with Guido’s *Monochord*, so that they may be understood more easily.] The second consists of two tones and a semitone. The third consists of a semitone and two tones.

The first species of the diapente consists of the first species of the diatessaron with a tone added above. The second consists of the second species of the diatessaron with a tone added above. The third consists of the third species of the diatessaron with a tone added below. The fourth consists of the first species of the diatessaron with a tone added below.

The *protus* consists of the first species of the diapente and the first species of the diatessaron above it; its *subjugalis* consists of the same species of the diapente and the same species of the diatessaron above it. [Note: Read: “below.”]

The *deuterus* consists of the second species of the diapente and the second species of the diatessaron above it; its *subjugalis* consists of the same species of the diapente and the third species of the diatessaron below it. [Note: Better: “the second, or the same.”]

The *tritus* consists of the third species of the diapente and the third species of the diatessaron; [Note: Add: “above.”] its *subjugalis* consists of the same species of the diapente and the same species of the diatessaron below it.

The *tetrardus* consists of the fourth species of the diapente and the first species of the diatessaron above it; its *subjugalis* consists of the same species of the diapente and the same species of the diatessaron below it.

Every *tropus subjugalis* has the same diapente and diatessaron as its authentic mode. It differs in this: the authentic mode has the diatessaron above the diapente, while the *subjugalis* has it below.

The *protus* and *tetrardus* are opposites, because the diapente of the *protus* first has two tones, then a semitone, and finally a tone; whereas the diapente of the *tetrardus* [Col. 0654A] first has a tone and a semitone, then two tones. They agree in the first species of the diatessaron, except that in the *tetrardus* it is lower. [Note: Better: “higher.”]

The *deuterus* and the *tritus* are altogether opposed: the diapente of the *deuterus* first has three tones and then a semitone, whereas the diapente of the *tritus* first has a semitone and then three tones; and the diatessaron of the *deuterus* consists of two tones and a semitone, whereas that of the *tritus* consists of a semitone and two tones.

If you invert the diapente of the *protus*, it becomes the diapente of the *tetrardus*. Again, when the diapente of the *tetrardus* is inverted, it sounds as the diapente of the *protus*. Their diatessaron, however, cannot be inverted.

If you invert the diapente of the *deuterus*, it becomes the diapente of the *tritus*. Again, when the diapente of the *tritus* is inverted, it sounds as the diapente of the *deuterus*. Their diatessaron likewise can be inverted.

## Measurement of the Pipes and the Monochord

[Col. 0654B]

Since I have often been asked by many people, according to the capacity of my understanding, to demonstrate what the reason is that the measurement of the monochord cannot be matched by the measurements of the pipes—or, if this matter, intercepted among the secrets of still-hidden nature, should fail, at least to offer some other rule for discovering their measurements, so that we may not entrust the matter solely to the judgment of the ears and appear to approach Aristoxenus, while being condemned by Boethius and the Pythagoreans—I shall first say that Boethius should not be blamed as though he spoke without having tested the matter, especially since he seems to have followed the discoveries of Pythagoras.

Macrobius also, and Censorinus in his work to Cerellius on his birthday, seem to have left statements agreeing with these. But perhaps the holes of the pipes were formed among them in another manner for blowing into them. Whether or not we have examined this matter with the required curiosity, we shall refrain from saying.

But since many will perhaps read this, and since for some even the commensurability of the monochord itself will be unknown, we shall briefly set out the numbers that constitute the rule of measurement and explain how one gradually reached that plurality. Thus the numbers and measurements of the pipes will become clear to anyone who adds the appropriate elements, and those will be refuted who think that Boethius invented larger numbers than were necessary for measuring the harmonic rule.

For the numbers that would display the symphonies discontinuously could be found almost within twelve, or at most within twenty-four, as the description placed below shows. [Note: The description is missing. Perhaps it ought to have been something like the following.]

But for continuing the fifteen sounds, or even all the tetrachords of the three genera, much larger numbers are necessary.

For discovering two consecutive tones in the diatessaron, or three in the diapente, or six [Note: Supply: “in the diapason.”]—contrary to Aristoxenus—or any other superparticular ratios, the readings of Boethius, whether in his *Music* or in his *Arithmetic*, may suffice.

But in order to proceed gradually and arrive at 2,304, which is the first number of the three genera, the process began as follows.

The first and smallest number that forms an *epogdoos* is eight. An eighth added to itself produces nine, which immediately ceases to be epogdoic; and therefore, if [Note: Better: “nor.”] two consecutive tones follow one another here, multiplying them by any numbers up to eight will accomplish nothing more.

Now, eight times eight makes sixty-four; an eighth of this, namely eight, added to it makes seventy-two, [Note: Since 72 is epogdoic, the following must be supplied here: “if an eighth of these—namely nine—is again added to them, 81 is produced, which itself,” and so forth.] which likewise lacks an epogdoic ratio.

But to complete the diatessaron, which consists of two tones and a semitone, or four terms—that is, three intervals—these numbers, 64, 72, and 81, would suffice, except that the first of them lacks its third part, which, added to it, ought to constitute the fourth term.

Therefore, when the numbers are multiplied by three, they produce those numbers which Boethius is known to have borrowed from Plato’s *Timaeus*: 192, 216, and 243. If you add to the first its third part, 64, you supply the fourth term, 256, so that the complete diatessaron is 192, 216, 243, 256.

The first of these is secured either by two times eight taken twelve times, by three times eight taken eight times, or by four times eight taken six times—all of which agree with musical relations—or, if there is some other method deriving from its nature, it will become clear as Calcidius teaches. [Note: Better: “by calculation.”]

Other numbers may then be fitted to these by the epogdoic ratio up to the complete diapason, except that the seventh term cannot be divided by a whole number.

Let such numbers be placed in order to infinity, so that it may be evident at a glance how long it was necessary to extend them, until both the *trite synnemmenon* or the *paramese*, and the tone—not only of the diatonic genus but also of the chromatic and enharmonic genera—could be represented by whole numbers.

[Note: To make the following table clearer, I have expressed the same numbers in a second column with Arabic numerals and inserted between each pair of numbers the individual differences, so that both the progression of the tones and the reduction of the differences and fractions may be more evident. I also thought it useful to place here the signs for the fractions that occur below, from the Rules of Lord Oddo concerning the Abacus, adding the value of each in Arabic numerals. I have also supplied above them other signs that are used below because of the lack of other typefaces.]

[Col. 0655]

[Col. 0655B] Numbers displaying the two-octave span five times, with their differences.

[Col. 0656B] The same numbers in Arabic numerals.

[Col. 0657] Do not complain, or think that we were unaware that we have not placed the letters or signs used by Boethius. We did this for ease and so that they might be recognized more clearly: we marked these numbers instead with the letters by which our instruments are labeled.

Since, because of the fractions of numbers—namely two-thirds (*bisse*), halves, thirds, quarters, and the rest—it is already clear that Boethius, or rather the ancients, devised very large numbers, each of these numbers will not readily lend itself to division unless one begins with the larger numbers.

For example, begin with 9,216, upon which let F be placed. Upon its half let another F be placed, namely upon 4,608. Upon its quarter let a third F be placed, 2,304. Upon its eighth let a fourth F be placed, 1,152. Upon its sixteenth let a fifth F be placed, 576. Upon its thirty-second let a sixth F be placed, namely 288. Upon its sixty-fourth let a seventh F be placed, namely 144. Upon its one-hundred-and-twenty-eighth let an eighth F be placed, namely 72. Upon its two-hundred-and-fifty-sixth let a ninth F be placed, namely 36. Upon its five-hundred-and-twelfth let a tenth F be placed, namely 18. Upon its one-thousand-and-twenty-fourth let an eleventh F be placed, namely 9.

These examples, given with whole numbers, show that the same can also be done with those whose final reductions are in fractions. Such are the numbers marked above with *a* and *d*, because, owing to the semitones, they have more difficult divisions: as the denominators increase, the quantity diminishes.

In the squares of three terms, two differences are enclosed. In the larger numbers they are distinct; in the smaller numbers, however, because of the fractions introduced by the semitones, they are not easily discerned and are everywhere joined through the semitone and tone. For it often happens that, if one contains two-thirds (*bisse*), the other contains a third, and together they restore one whole—such as ς and ς, and ςσ and ςς, and so forth according to the ratio of the *unciae*.

A diligent calculator will be able to separate them by applying the appropriate method: beginning with the larger numbers, where they are distinct, and descending by division through the halves, quarters, eighths, and the rest, according to the preceding notation of similar letters *a*, *b*, *c*, and *d*, reducing them as far as indivisible quantities.

## Notation of the Preceding Numbers

Since the description of the preceding numbers proceeds almost in such a way that sometimes two tones, sometimes three [Note: It is preferable to read: “a semitone follows,” etc.] follow one another, it has seemed appropriate to add here examples in which tetrachords consisting continuously of two tones above and a semitone are displayed. By their analogy, anyone can continue any fivefold notation of two octaves, either by ascending according to the rule given above to doubles, quadruples, octuples, and the rest, or by descending to subdoubles, subquadruples, suboctuples, and so forth, so that either the denominator increases while the quantity diminishes, or, while the quantity increases, the denominator diminishes.

[Col. 0659B] Thus those whose beginning is 192, 216, 243, 256 fill out the complete diatessaron. But for the diapente to be completed thereafter in whole numbers, so that the diapason may be filled by the two symphonies, it is impossible.

The next number is 288, which is completed by 256 together with its eighth. With its own eighth it completes the number 324. Since an eighth of this cannot be found, the preceding number, namely 288, is multiplied by eight and rises to 2,304.

This is not because other numbers could not be found before these—namely, before 2,304—in which the diapason might appear in whole numbers, but because before these numbers neither the chromatic nor the enharmonic genus, nor even at least the *trite synnemmenon* or the diatonic *paramese*, can be found completely, that is, in 2,304.

Moreover, 288 is such a number that, when divided by halves, quarters, eighths, and so forth, it has nine as its thirty-second part. This is joined by the epogdoic ratio to the thirty-second part of the preceding number, 256, which is eight. Between these two numbers, 256 and 288—which are recognized as Platonic numbers—the former is the end of the diatessaron and the latter the beginning of the diapente; together they complete the diapason symphony.

When the first diapason begins at 192, its sixth term appears, namely 324, which has no eighth. When another diapason begins at 884, [Note: It should read: 768.] or when the fourth diapason begins at 1,536, the *paramese* appears in none of these, just as it does not in the first; that is, the two conjunct tetrachords, *hyperboleon* and *diezeugmenon*, cannot be continued.

Likewise, when the diapason begins at 288, or another diapason at 576, the *trite synnemmenon* appears in neither. When this happens, the diligent calculator will foresee it in the numbers arranged in order: either because, for forming the diatessaron, the fourth number before the place of the *paramese*—that is, the *nete diezeugmenon*—does not have a third part, or because, for forming the diapente, the immediately preceding number cannot be divided by an eighth—that is, the *trite diezeugmenon*—nor the fifth number, the *trite hyperboleon*, by a half. [Note: I think one should read: “But when …”]

When 2,304 is reached, all symphonies and all tetrachords or pentachords of every genus will occur to infinity.

Someone more attentive might say that, beginning even at 1,152, all the tetrachords of every genus would also succeed properly; and we grant this. But perhaps because the number of the *trite synnemmenon*, namely 2,187, would fall odd, the author avoided these subduples, just as he avoided the preceding subquadruples and suboctuples, since when one begins at 2,304 none of their succeeding terms, eighths, or differences falls upon an odd number.

This must be shown briefly by the numbers written below: which of the numbers arranged above, by means of any one common number, produces most nearly the differences of the fifteen tones in every genus. Let that common number be twelve, which is unquestionably musical, so that, by the same analogy, with the same number slightly increased for purposes of estimation—namely twelve—each of the prescribed numbers belonging to the diapason or double diapason may display the configurations of the pipes.

[Col. 0661]

But let us call this eighth part of the first number, as it were, the common diameter of the pipes, just as was said of the strings, so that the mass itself may descend all the way into silence and, at the highest pitch, the strings, excessively tightened, may break through the thinness of the voice. The middle term in each diapason, both in the numbers and in the measurements either of the monochord or of the pipes, is the one that is fifth in relation to the first or eighth, and fourth-from-the-end in relation to the eighth or fifteenth, so that in relation to one it is sesquialteral, or a diapente, and in relation to the other sesquitertian, or a diatessaron. One is called sescuplar, the other triple; but when the two diapasons are compared with one another, the ratio is double. For just as the eighth stands to the first, and the fifteenth to the eighth, so the twelfth has the ratio of doubleness to the fifth. That the middle terms in each diapason are the fifth and the twelfth can be shown either by the differences or by the numbers that produce the same differences when multiplied by twelve. Thus four differences or numbers from the first to the fifth, or from the eighth to the twelfth, when joined together, do not amount to more than three equal numbers or differences when these are joined together either from the fifth to the eighth or from the twelfth to the fifteenth.

This has been said because, however much the eighth exceeds the first in the measurements of the pipes, or the fifteenth exceeds the eighth by more than double, it nevertheless requires the whole difference either from the first to the eighth or from the eighth to the twelfth [Note: [Col. 0664D] Perhaps “the fifteenth.”]. Divide the fifth in the first diapason, or the twelfth in the second, into middle portions, and leave an equal part of it to each portion [Note: [Col. 0664D] I cannot understand what the author intends by this; perhaps something has been omitted.].

When, therefore, any length has been assigned to the first or smaller pipe—but it seems better to assign eight times the diameter of the opening to the length—wherever a tone is next to be made, let the larger have the whole smaller pipe, together with its diameter and one-eighth of its diameter. In a diatessaron, let the larger have the smaller and one-third of it, and in addition one-third of the diameter. In a diapente, let the larger have the smaller and one-half of it, and in addition one-half of the diameter. In a diapason, let the larger have the smaller twice over, and in addition the whole diameter. The remaining intervals will easily follow from the numbers.

The diameter is either half of the circle in the opening, measured from the broader side, or the transverse width of the opening on the narrower side through which the pipe is blown, and beneath which opening one [unit] lies. To show this with smaller numbers, though still broken up according to the consonances, it should be represented as follows.

That is, between the first and the eighth stands the fifth; between the eighth and the fifteenth stands the twelfth. And just as the eighth surpasses the first not only by doubleness but also by the diameter, so the fifteenth surpasses the eighth not only by doubleness but also by twice the diameter and, in addition, by one-eighth of that diameter. Consequently the fifteenth will surpass the first not only fourfold, but also by four diameters and, in addition, by one-eighth of the diameter. ]. For greater clarity I append individual examples, which should be compared with the table of the pipes in cols. 665–666.]

If you seek a tone, let the larger pipe have the smaller and its eighth. If a diatessaron, let the larger have the smaller and its third, and a tenth of the third, and a sixth of the eleventh. If a diapente, let the larger have the smaller, and its half, and an eighth of the half, and an eighth of the eighth. If a diapason, let the larger have twice the smaller and, in addition, one-eighth of it and an eighth of the eighth. If a diapason and diapente, let the larger have three times the smaller and its two eighths, that is, a fourth. If a bis diapason, let the larger have four times the smaller and, in addition, its three eighths.

**THE SAME, IN ANOTHER WAY.**

If the pipes are of equal thickness, let the larger contain the length of the smaller four times within itself, and, in addition, the diameter [Note: [Col. 0672C] Which constitutes one-eighth of the length.], so that the hollow part contains four measures [Note: [Col. 0672D] Add: “together with an eighth of the diameter.”]; it will sound the consonance of a bis diapason. [Col. 0671B] If the larger contains the smaller twice in its length and, in addition, once the diameter of its hollow, they will sound a diapason with one another. If the larger contains the entire smaller and, in addition, half its length together with half the diameter of the hollow, it will sound a diapente. Likewise, if the larger pipe contains the entire smaller pipe and, in addition, one-eighth of its length together with one-eighth of the diameter, it will sound a tone. Again, if the larger pipe contains the entire smaller and, in addition, one-sixteenth of its length together with one-sixteenth of the diameter, it will produce approximately a semitone. Nevertheless, it is better to obtain the semitone by means of the diatessaron than by sixteenths.

**MEASUREMENT OF THE MONOCHORD AND OF PIPES IN GENERAL, IN THE DIATONIC GENUS, IN THE FIRST DIAPASON.**

[Note: [Col. 0672D] In these and the following passages compare the table in cols. 667–668.] E has all of F and its eighth, that is, the sesquioctave. D has all of E and its eighth, that is, the epogdous. C has all of F and its third, which is the sesquitertian or epitrite, that is, the diatessaron. B has all of C and its eighth, which is a tone; or all of E and its third, which is a diatessaron; or all of F and its half, which is a diapente. G. G. A. B. C. D. E. F.

**MEASUREMENT IN THE SECOND DIAPASON.**

F has all of G, [Note: [Col. 0672D] Paramese.] and its eighth, which is a tone; or all of B and its third, which is a diatessaron; or all of C and its half, which is a diapente; or another F twice over, which is a diapason. E has all of F and its eighth, which is a tone; or all of A and its third, which is a diatessaron; or all of B and its half, which is a diapente; or another E twice over, which is a diapason. D has all of E and its eighth, which is a tone; or all of G trite synemmenon and its third, which is a diatessaron; or all of A and its half, which is a diapente; or another D twice over, which is a diapason. C has all of F and its third, which is a diatessaron; or all of G paramese and its half, which is a diapente; or another C twice over, which is a diapason. B has all of C and its eighth, that is, a tone; or all of E and its third, which is a diatessaron; or all of F and its half, which is a diapente; or another B twice over, which is a diapason; or another F three times over, that is, a diapason and diapente. A has all of B and its eighth; or all of D and its third; or all of E and its half; or another A twice over. G has all of C and its third; or all of G paramese twice over. F has all of G and its eighth; or all of B and its third; or all of C and its half; or another F twice over; or a third F four times over.

**INSTRUCTION FOR FINDING THE SEMITONE.**

From any given total subtract a twenty-seventh; from what remains seek an eighteenth [Col. 0673A], add the result to the whole total, and you will have a semitone.

**FOR FINDING THE APOTOME.**

Next, if you wish to find the apotome, add to the final term one-third of the semitone’s difference and one one-hundred-and-fourth of that third, or one three-hundred-and-twelfth of the whole difference, together with the whole difference itself. Without any ambiguity you will find the tone at the first term and the apotome at the second.

**FOR CONTINUING A TONE AND A SEMITONE.**

[Col. 0674A]

Take a sixth of any given term, then a ninth of that sixth; add these parts to the whole total, and you will have a tone with a semitone.

**FOR CONTINUING TWO TONES.**

[Note: [Col. 0673A] Better: “Two.”]

From any given number take one-fourth of it, then one-sixteenth of that fourth, or one sixty-fourth of the whole; add these parts to the whole total, and you will find two tones.

[Col. 0673]

**ANONYMOUS I. MUSIC.**

**NOTICE.**

From the manuscript of our library at St. Blasien we present certain writings by an Anonymous author. The first, although brief, touches, besides the diatonic genus, which is devoted solely to ecclesiastical use, also upon the chromatic and enharmonic genera. To the second is appended a fairly extensive tonary, which we would have preferred to publish above others of its kind, if our printing types permitted us to reproduce the ancient musical signs with which it is written throughout. A poem follows continuously, explaining how the eight musical tones or modes are suitably arranged on the fingers of the hand. Next comes a description and division of the monochord. The explanation of the eight tones that follows in the same codex seemed to us best omitted, since for the most part it is copied from Aurelianus. Nor is the material that follows under the title “What are those words Nonenoeane?” unrelated. Next comes a Fragment of Music, in which certain canons of Boethian music are elucidated. There follow measurements of the monochord by Boethius himself and others of the same kind, as well as those of Guido and Otbert of Regensburg, from the Ottoburan manuscript; finally, diagrams of Boethius’ monochords in the three genera—diatonic, chromatic, and enharmonic—and likewise those of Odo, in the manner of enchiridial notation, and of Guido of Arezzo.

**CONTENTS.** — 1. Division of the three genera on the monochord. 2. The diatonic genus. 3. The chromatic and enharmonic genera. 4. The names of the strings. 5. The five tetrachords. 6. The consonances. 7. Their species. 8. The eight modes of chant.

[Col. 0673A]

1. Two hemispheres, which they call *magades* [Note: [Col. 0673B] *Magade*, μαγάδιον. Du Cange, *Glossarium mediae et infimae Latinitatis*, s.v.], are placed from either side upon a hollow instrument. Between them, across the projecting surface, divisions are drawn by lines stretched above it like strings. If you intend to measure the three genera of the monochord, divide the surface extending from one *magas* to the other into three by means of stretched lines, and arrange the diatonic below, the chromatic in the middle, and the enharmonic above, according to the rule.

But before I begin their measurement, I shall briefly explain the meaning of the terms. The diatonic is so called because it is determined by the measurement and composition of tones; the others do not possess this characteristic, since the diatonic is marked out by semitones, whereas the other is marked out by dieses, as will become clear below. This genus is judged stronger and harder. And so that the minds of listeners or singers may not be softened by the sweetness of the song, it is chosen for ecclesiastical use. Everyone can experience for himself that minds are changed by the sweetness or languor of music, and we know that the writings of the wise bear witness to it.

The chromatic is called, as it were, “colored,” because, departing first from the diatonic, it is of another, as it were, color; for *chroma* means “color.” This genus is judged the softest, and therefore is not applied to ecclesiastical use. The enharmonic, however, which is moderately composed and tempered from both of these, takes its name from *harmony*, [Col. 0674A] which is the concordant fitting-together of different things. This genus occupies, as it were, the middle position, so that it is neither hard nor soft, but, composed from both, is sweetened.

2. Let us now begin the measurement of the diatonic. Divide the projecting surface stretched from the right hemisphere, which is T., to the left, which is A., into four parts, and mark the lines drawn with these letters: S. for the first on the right-hand side, II. for the middle, and D. for the third. Then, from T. to S., add a fourth to a tripartite interval, and mark the drawn line P. Again, over the surface from T. to S., divided into two parts, add a third, and mark that line O. Likewise divide the surface from T. to O. into four parts; where the third falls, add the line B. Once this is done, let the breadth of the interval from II. to O., in which the diatonic is measured, be divided by equal lines; let the upper part of the bisected line O. be designated L., while the lower part retains the designation O. Next let the interval from T. to R. be divided in two, and let a transverse line be drawn, with a third added, and divided into two; let its upper part be marked K. and its lower part N. Again, divide the interval from T. to N. or K. into four; where the third falls, mark the line Q. From here, divide the interval from T. to P. into three, add a fourth, and mark the transverse line, which does not cross over but is drawn below, M. Then divide the surface from T. to Q. into two, add a third, and mark the transverse line, which does not cross over but occupies the upper part, I. Again, divide the interval from T. to II. into three, add a fourth, and mark the line E. Then divide the surface from T. to E. into three unequal parts, add a fourth, and mark the line B. From here divide the interval from T. to D. into four; where the third falls, inscribe G. Again, divide the surface from T. to G. into two and add a third, where C. is to be placed. From here divide the interval from T. to C. into four, mark the third, and add F. Thus the diatonic is drawn.

3. From here, draw the lines marked B. and C. for the chromatic, and divide the interval between D. and E. into two; then, placing a half backward between D. and C., draw a line. In the same way draw E. and F., and, placing a half backward in the interval between O. and H., draw a line between G. and F. Then draw H., I., and L. as in the diatonic, and in this genus also; draw a dividing line from H. to I., and draw M. and N. beneath it. Likewise divide the interval between K. and L., and, placing a half backward between K. and L., mark a transverse line crossing over. From here place half the interval between P. and L. between I. and K., and draw a line beneath the transverse line. In the same way draw P. and Q.; and, placing a line in the middle of the interval between R. and S., draw a line backward between R. and Q.; then draw the final S. and complete the chromatic.

Next, draw B. and C. in the enharmonic as in the diatonic and chromatic, and divide their interval with a middle line. Again draw E. and F., and divide the semitone into two dieses. After H. has been drawn, draw the dividing line and L. as in the other genera, toward II. and L., and place a middle line between H. and L. Thus, after drawing M. and N. beneath the transverse line, insert the middle line. In the same way draw P., Q., and S.; placing a middle line between P. and Q., complete the enharmonic.

Thus the diatonic is drawn through tones and semitones; the chromatic through a semitone, a semitone, and an incomposite triemitone; and the enharmonic through a diesis and a diesis—that is, half a semitone—and an incomposite ditone.

4. But since we have given the rule for measuring them, we do not consider it superfluous to add the names of the strings. The first, therefore, which is designated A., is called *proslambanomenos*; B., *hypate hypaton*; C., *parhypate hypaton*; D., *lychanos hypaton*; E., *hypate meson*; F., *parhypate meson*; G., *lychanos meson*; H., *mese*; I., *trite synemmenon*; K., *paranete synemmenon*; L., [Col. 0675D] *nete synemmenon*; M., *paramese*; N., *trite diezeugmenon*; O., *paranete diezeugmenon*; P., *nete diezeugmenon*; Q., *trite hyperboleon*; R., *paranete hyperboleon*; S., *nete hyperboleon*.

These are their names; Boethius also explains fully in his *Music* the order of their discovery and the rationale of their names. Since we are aiming at brevity, and since these matters provide little or no usefulness, they seem to us best omitted, so that more useful things may be said in their place. For as far as usefulness is concerned, if you call the first string *proslambanomenos*, it is just as useful to call it A. Therefore, leaving these matters aside, let us look at others.

5. Five tetrachords are found in the measurement of the monochord. Each is likewise completed by a semitone—that is, not a half but an imperfect tone (for the Greeks call “imperfect” *semum*)—and by two tones. By “tone” we mean the sesquioctave proportion, which they also call the epogdous. For if you divide the interval from T. to S. into eight parts and add a ninth, you will see that you have found a tone between S. and R. Thus the interval from T. to R. will contain the whole interval from T. to S. and, in addition, its eighth; for if you compare nine with eight, it contains the whole of it and its eighth, namely one unit. Thus, to describe the tone simply and briefly, it is found in the sesquioctave proportion.

The tetrachords, therefore, are completed by two tones and a semitone; and they derive their name from being contained under four strings or notes. The first is B C D E, called *hypaton*, that is, “principal,” because it occupies the first position among the *hypatai*, and sounds lower and more grave than the others. The second is E F G H, called *meson*, that is, “middle.” For on one side it is joined to what we called *hypaton*, and on the other it is connected with what is called *synemmenon*. *Synemmenon*, that is, “joined,” is contained under H I K L; it is so called because it is joined to the middle, specifically in distinction from the fourth, M N O P, which is called *diezeugmenon*, that is, “disjoined,” because it is separated from the middle by an intervening tone. The fifth, P Q R S, is called *hyperboleon*, that is, “highest” or “excellent,” because it is found among the higher and therefore more excellent notes. These five tetrachords are each completed in the same way by a semitone and two tones.

[Col. 0676C] 6. Having briefly touched upon these matters, let us come to the consonance. Consonance is the concord of different notes, occurring sweetly and uniformly to the ears—for example, when on a lyre or some other musical instrument, with the strings carefully tightened and slackened, you strike the first and fourth, or the first and fifth, or the first and eighth notes together. The first of these, which is also the smallest, is called a diatessaron; the second is a diapente, greater by a tone; the third, composed from these two, is a diapason; the fourth is a diapason and diapente; and the fifth is a bis diapason, or disdiapason. If, following Ptolemy’s rational judgment, you add the diapason and diatessaron, you will have six consonances. But since this receives both the name and definition of its genus, reason does not explain why it should be excluded. For if a horse is an animate, sentient substance, it certainly belongs among the species of animal; and if a diapason and diatessaron is the concord of different notes occurring sweetly and uniformly to the ears, it should rightly be included among the species of consonance. No one will be able to deny that it is this; therefore it belongs among the consonances.

The first, therefore, which we called a diatessaron, consists in the sesquitertian proportion, as when four is compared with three. The diapente consists in the sesquialteral proportion, as when six is compared with four. The diapason is in the double proportion, as when the same six is compared with the aforementioned three. The diapason and diatessaron is in the double-sesquitertian proportion, as when fourteen is compared with the same six. The diapason and diapente is in the triple proportion, as when nineteen is compared with the aforesaid six. The bis diapason is in the quadruple proportion, as when you compare XXIV with the same six. But we seek no other order for them than that according to the drawing of the monochord and the simpler number—for example, the numerical comparison [Col. 0678A]—of which you may have the following subscription.

[Col. 0677A] No one, however, should think that the diatessaron is the same thing as the sesquitertian, the diapente as the sesquialteral, or the diapason as the double. For what mathematicians call sesquitertian, musicians call diatessaron, which means “from four,” because such a proportion is contained under four notes. The diapente means “from five,” because it is contained under the same number. The diapason means “from all,” either because it contains all the notes of these two, or—which I consider the better explanation—because it encloses within itself the intervals of all the notes. For there are only seven distances of notes, namely A B C D E F G; and if you strike the eighth, which is H, you will find it the same as the first. Hence Virgil says, not ignorant of any science:

> It resounds against the seven distinctions of the notes.

The names of the others are clear to anyone who knows them.

7. Now that these matters have been set out in advance, let us show their species. The diatessaron, which is the smallest, has only three species, each one note short of four. The first consists of a tone, a semitone, and a tone, namely A B C D. The second form is B C D E, which consists of a semitone and a ditone. The third is C D E F, which consists of a ditone and a semitone. Thus, counting by fours through the entire series of strings, except between F and M and between I and P, you should know that you will find these three forms alternately.

The diapente, which has one more note, has one more species. The first is D E F G H. The second is E F G H M. The third is F G H M N. The fourth is G H M N O. If you examine these carefully, you will find that the positions of the tones and semitones are different and arranged alternately through the sequence of notes, except in three places, namely between B and F, E and I, and M and Q.

The diapason, since it is completed by these two consonances, will have as many forms as the two embrace. It therefore contains seven species: four on account of the diapente and three on account of the diatessaron. The first is contained between A and H. The second extends from B to M. The third ends at C and N. The fourth stretches from D to O. The fifth is bounded by E and P. The sixth rises from F to Q. The seventh descends from R to G. If you examine the arrangement of the tones and semitones in all of them, you will see that they differ from one another. If you add an octave to H, ascending through M and N to S., you will see that it does not differ from the first. If you ascend from H through I and K to S., you will observe it to be the same as the fifth. Thus the diapason has seven species, one fewer than the notes in which the seven modes have different positions; the following account will make this clear.

8. We know from Boethius in his *Music* that there were originally only seven species of the diapason, but that Ptolemy added an eighth. Since we have promised brevity and simplicity, let us explain their names and differences according to ecclesiastical usage.

The ecclesiastical order uses eight modes of chant, which it improperly calls “tones.” Four of them, having obtained the higher notes of the monochord, are called as follows: *authenticus protus*, that is, “first master”; *authenticus deuterus*, that is, “second master”; *authenticus tritus*, that is, “third master”; *authenticus tetrardus*, that is, “fourth master.” For the Greeks call masters *authentoi*, as though they were “authorized,” that is, endowed with authority—namely, those whose authority is pre-eminent. Hence, by comparison with a higher rank, these modes came to be called this way.

The other four, occupying the lower positions, are called *plagis proti*, that is, “of the side of the first,” with *authenticus* understood—as though it were contained at its side and were lower; and similarly *plagis deuteri*, *plagis triti*, and *plagis tetrardi*. But since we are giving their rules, let us use Latin names and call the higher ones masters, and the lower ones disciples.

[Col. 0679B] But before we begin their ascents or descents, let us display the final strings of them all. There are four notes called finals, because in each of them the regular chants end: D, E, F, G—that is, lychanos hypaton, hypate meson, parhypate meson, and lychanos meson. They were chosen as finals from among all the notes for this reason: among the distinctions of the seven notes they are found to be more sonorous. If any old or new chant is made outside them, it is undoubtedly judged irregular.

The chant of the first master and of his disciple ends on D; that of the second and his disciple on E; that of the third and his disciple on F; that of the fourth and his disciple on G. We call the first master the first mode, and his disciple the second; the second master the third, and his disciple the fourth; the third master the fifth, and his disciple the sixth; the fourth master the seventh, and his disciple the eighth.

But since we have stated their names and finals, let us disclose the limits of their ascent and descent. The first master ascends to P and descends to A; his disciple rises to II or M and descends to the same A. The second master ascends to Q and descends to B; his disciple rises to Q and descends to the same B. The third master ascends to R and descends to C; his disciple rises to O and descends to the same C. The fourth master rises to S and descends to D; his disciple rises to P and descends to the same D.

For this is their ancient rule of ascent [Col. 0679D] and descent, which can be proved in many chants. If, however, they exceed these limits upward or downward, no one should argue that they ought not to be corrected. But the Juniors, judging more subtly and acutely, and distinguishing more certainly and more lawfully, neither agree entirely nor disagree entirely. For they say that there ought to be definite differences between the modes, so that we may be able to recognize to whichever mode the chants belong.

But if the first mode descends to A, while the second descends from M to the same A, and a chant that does not exceed the interval between H and A is composed and regularly ends on the final D of both, it is uncertain to which of the two it should rather be assigned. Similarly, if the third is lowered from Q to B, while the fourth descends from N to the same B, a chant composed within M and B and ending [Note: [Col. 0679D] Supply: on E] is considered uncertain as to which of the two it belongs. The same occurs in the other cases. To drive away this uncertainty, we approve the rule of the Juniors; since its treatment is more probable, let it be made more exact.

Let the finals, as we stated above, be preserved. Let the ascents and descents vary somewhat. The first mode rises to O, though rarely to P; it descends to C, containing the fourth species of the diapason between D and O, with a string both above and below. The second mode ascends to H, though rarely to M or I; it descends to A, possessing the first species of the diapason between A and H, with a note above, though rarely. These are the first master and his disciple.

The chant of the master begins on six strings, namely C, D, E, F, G, H; on these it has its cola and commas—that is, its members and cuts, which we call the divisions of the chant. The disciple’s chant has four lawful beginnings, A, B, C, D, but six commonly used ones, on which it also has its cola and commas: A, B, C, D, E, F.

If you begin the first chant on C, D, E, or F, you must ascend no less than to H, so that by ascending you may discern to which mode it belongs. If you begin the second chant on any of the same notes, you must descend no less than to B, so that by descending you may show to which it belongs. In this judgment, however, only four beginnings will be assigned to each disciple.

[Col. 0680C] The third mode rises to P, though rarely to Q; it descends to D. Its chant has six beginnings and divisions: D, E, F, G, H, M. It possesses the fifth species of the diapason between E and P, with a note both above and below.

The fourth mode ascends to M, though rarely to N; it descends to B, containing the second species of the diapason between B and M, with a string above. According to many, its chant begins on six strings; according to the lawful rule, on four: B, C, D, E. It has six divisions: B, C, D, E, F, G, or H. These are the second master and his disciple.

If you begin the master’s chant on D or E, the mode’s ascent must be no less than to O. If the disciple’s, its descent must be no less than to C, so that by rising or falling you may discern to which mode it belongs.
