[Col. 0680D] The fifth mode rises from E to Q, though rarely to R, containing the sixth species of the diapason between F and O, with a note both above and below. Its chant has six beginnings and divisions: E, F, G, H, M, N.

The sixth mode ascends from C to N, though more rarely to O, possessing the third species of the diapason between C and N, with a string above. Its chant has four lawful beginnings, C, D, E, F, and six divisions, C, D, E, F, G, H. These are the third master and his disciple.

If you begin the master’s chant on E or F, its minimum ascent should be to R, though more rarely to P [Note: [Col. 0680D] Supply from the preceding: “you begin”]. The disciple’s minimum descent should be to D, so that by this distinction it may become clear to whom it ought to be assigned.

[Col. 0681A] The seventh mode rises from F to R, though rarely to S, containing the seventh species of the diapason between G and R, with a note both above and below. Its chant has six beginnings and divisions: F, G, H, M, N, O.

The eighth mode ascends to O, though rarely to P, possessing the fourth species of the diapason from D to O according to the first master, with a string above. Ptolemy added N to it. Since the diapason lacks an eighth species, it obtained the fourth, like the first. Although it possesses the same species, it has a different final and does not descend to the same C.

Its chant’s lawful beginnings, like those of the other disciples, are four: D, E, F, G. Its divisions are six: D, E, F, G, H, M, or I. These are the fourth master and his disciple.

If you begin the master’s chant on F or G, its minimum ascent should be to Q; but the disciple’s, because of the difference stated above, should descend to E.

[Col. 0681]

## ANONYMOUS II: TREATISE ON MUSIC

[Col. 0681B] There are five musical consonances: the diatessaron, which is also called sesquitertia; the diapente, which is also called sesquialtera; the diapason, which is called dupla; the diapente and diapason together, which is called tripla; and the bis diapason, which is called quadrupla.

We make more frequent use of two of these, namely the diatessaron and diapente; we use the third, the diapason, rarely; the others we do not employ in our chants.

The diatessaron consists indeed of four notes, because it consists of four strings, but of three intervals. It is composed of two tones and a minor semitone. A tone is also called a sound; a semitone, however, is major or minor. It is called a semitone not because it is half a tone, but because it is not a complete tone.

The diapente consists of five notes, because it consists of five strings, and of four intervals, because it is composed of three tones and a minor semitone. The diapason, in turn, consists of a diatessaron and a diapente—that is, of five tones and two minor semitones, which do not complete a tone.

These three principal consonances—the diatessaron, diapente, and diapason—are suitably distinguished among eighteen strings by tetrachords, pentachords, and octachords. For everything that is a tetrachord gives the consonance of the diatessaron. There are five principal tetrachords: hypaton, meson, synemmenon, diezeugmenon, and hyperboleon. In the diatonic genus of melodies they give the consonance of the diatessaron.

There are three genera of melodies: diatonic, chromatic, and enharmonic. The diatonic is harsher and more natural than the others; therefore, as though the others had been rejected, it is the more commonly used. It is called diatonic because in every tetrachord it proceeds by tone, tone, and semitone.

This same consonance, the diatessaron, has three species. The first proceeds by tone, tone, and semitone; the second is sung by tone, semitone, and tone; the third is sung by semitone, tone, and tone.

The consonance of the diapente is distinguished by pentachords, which themselves also have four species. The first proceeds by tone, tone, semitone, and tone; the second by tone, semitone, tone, and tone; the third by semitone and three continuous tones; the fourth by [Col. 0682B] three continuous tones and a semitone.

The consonance of the diapason is also distinguished by eight strings. For, as stated, it consists of five tones and two minor semitones, containing within itself a diatessaron and a diapente. It also has seven species, but since these are rarely used, we shall omit them for the sake of brevity.

The names of the strings on which these consonances are distinguished are as follows. The first and lowest of all is proslambanomenos. It is immovable for two reasons: either because it is the foundation of the other notes, or because in the three genera of melodies—diatonic, chromatic, and enharmonic—it remains uniform in sound and name.

The following hypate hypaton bears to it the proportion of a tone and is likewise immovable for two reasons: either because it is similar in all three genera, or because without it a chant cannot rise from the first preceding note to the third following one, nor descend from the third following note to the first without it.

The third following these is parhypate hypaton. It is neither wholly movable nor wholly immovable, because in the diatonic and chromatic genera it is uniform, but in the enharmonic it varies. Again, without this third, a chant can rise from the preceding second to the following fourth, or descend from the following fourth to the preceding second. There is a semitone between hypate hypaton and parhypate hypaton.

After these comes the fourth, lychanos hypaton, entirely movable, because it varies in all three genera. Without it, the path of singing in ascent from the lower notes to the higher, or in descent from the higher to the lower, is readily apparent. There is a tone between parhypate hypaton and lychanos hypaton.

Thus, from the first, proslambanomenos, to the fourth, lychanos hypaton, the consonance of the diatessaron ascends; and from that fourth back to the first it descends by tone, semitone, and tone.

The fifth then follows, hypate meson, immovable like hypate hypaton. It is separated by a tone from lychanos hypaton; with hypate hypaton it produces the consonance of the diatessaron, and with proslambanomenos the consonance of the diapente, whether the chant descends from the higher notes to the lower or rises from the lower to the higher.

Next, in sixth place, comes parhypate meson. It is neither wholly movable nor wholly immovable, like parhypate hypaton, and it too differs from hypate meson by a semitone. With parhypate hypaton it produces the consonance of the diatessaron, whether ascending or descending.

In seventh order comes lychanos meson, entirely movable like lychanos hypaton. It is separated from parhypate meson by a tone; with lychanos hypaton it produces a diatessaron, and with parhypate hypaton it forms a diapente.

In eighth place is mese, which is the middle of the higher and lower notes. It is itself immovable, like proslambanomenos, because without it there is no open descent from the higher notes to the lower, nor an easy ascent from the lower to the higher.

It is again separated by a tone from lychanos meson; with hypate meson it forms a diatessaron, with lychanos hypaton a diapente, and with proslambanomenos a diapason. Here it is clearly understood what was stated above: that the diatessaron and diapente are contained within the diapason.

For from mese to hypate meson there is a descending diatessaron, and from hypate meson to proslambanomenos a descending diapente. Likewise, there is a descending diapente from mese to lychanos hypaton, and from that same note to proslambanomenos a descending diatessaron. Conversely, from proslambanomenos to lychanos hypaton there is an ascending diatessaron, and from that note to mese an ascending diapente. Again, from proslambanomenos to hypate meson there is an ascending diapente, and from that same note to [Col. 0683C] mese an ascending diatessaron. Thus, from mese down to proslambanomenos there is a diapason.

Next follow two tetrachords, partly synemmenon and partly diezeugmenon. The synemmenon tetrachord is joined to mese by a semitone, which lies between mese and trite synemmenon; the diezeugmenon tetrachord, however, is separated from mese by a tone, which lies between mese and paramese. Hence the former is called synemmenon, “joined,” while the latter is called diezeugmenon, “separated.”

If, then, from mese, which is the eighth, you ascend by a semitone, the ninth, trite synemmenon, will be encountered. It is neither wholly movable nor wholly immovable, and with parhypate meson it produces a diatessaron. If from it one again ascends by a tone, the tenth, parahete synemmenon, will be encountered. It is entirely movable and produces a diatessaron with lychanos meson by tone, semitone, and tone; with parhypate meson it produces the consonance of the diapente.

After this, by ascending a tone, comes the eleventh, nete synemmenon, which with mese produces a diatessaron and with lychanos meson a diapente.

But if one ascends a tone from mese, paramese will be encountered. Having left the synemmenon tetrachord, it seems to be the ninth after mese, but when properly arranged it is shown to be the twelfth. It too is immovable, like hypate hypaton, and with it produces the consonance of the diapason.

This same paramese descends to hypate meson by a diapente, through three continuous tones and a semitone; but it cannot descend to parhypate meson by a diatessaron. Hence it appears removed from the meson tetrachord and is altogether opposed to trite synemmenon, so much so that if either of them is uttered in a chant, the other is in no way introduced.

From the same paramese, by ascending a semitone, comes the thirteenth, trite diezeugmenon. It is neither wholly movable nor wholly immovable, like parhypate hypaton, and with it produces the consonance of the diapason. It is consonant with paranete synemmenon, differing from it only in name; and the ascent from mese to the former is by tone and semitone, while to the latter it is by semitone and tone.

From it, by ascending another tone, the fourteenth, paranete diezeugmenon, is encountered. It is entirely movable, like lychanos hypaton, and with it produces the consonance of the diapason. In its own sound and proportion of sounds it equals nete synemmenon. For just as the ascent from mese to that note is a diatessaron by semitone, tone, and tone, so also to this one it is by tone, semitone, and tone. It also descends, like the other, by a diapente to lychanos meson.

Again, from the same paranete diezeugmenon, by ascending a tone, comes the fifteenth, nete diezeugmenon, immovable like hypate meson, and with it produces the consonance of the diapason. This tetrachord, beginning at paramese, produces the consonance of the diatessaron, like the others. When the tone between mese and paramese is added to it, the consonance of the diapente is formed.

The tetrachord hyperboleon is joined to this. For by ascending a semitone from nete diezeugmenon, the sixteenth, trite hyperboleon, arises. It is neither wholly movable nor wholly immovable, like parhypate meson, and with it produces the consonance of the diapason.

From it, by ascending a tone, follows the seventeenth, paranete hyperboleon, entirely movable like lychanos meson, and with it produces the consonance of the diapason.

From this, by ascending another tone, follows the eighteenth, nete nete hyperboleon, immovable like mese, and with it produces a double sound. For just as proslambanomenos ascends a diapason to mese, so mese ascends a diapason to nete hyperboleon. Therefore proslambanomenos and nete hyperboleon form a bis diapason, which is also called quadrupla. But this, as stated, is not employed in our chants.

From the species of consonances mentioned above, therefore, arise eight modes or tropes, by which every chant is regulated. The first and lowest of all is called hypodorian; the second, hypophrygian; the third, hypolydian; the fourth, Dorian; the fifth, Phrygian; the sixth, Lydian; the seventh, mixolydian or hyperdorian; the eighth, hypermixolydian.

The first is exceeded by the second at the summit by a tone; the second by the third by a tone; the third by the fourth by a semitone; the fourth by the fifth by a tone; the fifth by the sixth by a tone; the sixth by the seventh by a semitone; and the seventh by the eighth by a tone. This is readily seen in the division of the monochord, where [Col. 0685A] the mese of the hypodorian, in its arrangement, corresponds to the lychanos meson of the hypophrygian, to the parhypate meson of the hypolydian, and likewise to the hypate meson of the Dorian.

The mese of the hypophrygian is the paramese of the hypodorian. The mese of the hypolydian is the trite diezeugmenon of that same hypodorian. Likewise, the mese of the Dorian is the paranete diezeugmenon of that same hypodorian. The mese of the Dorian therefore stands at the consonance of a diatessaron [Note: [Col. 0685C] Supply: “from the mese of the hypodorian”].

Thus the succeeding tropes surpass one another in height, so that the nete hyperboleon of the hypodorian is found to be the mese of the hypermixolydian. This same hypermixolydian produces a diapente with the mese of the Dorian, and with the mese of the hypodorian it produces a diapason. Indeed, the note that is the middle of the first is also the first of the eighth.

Consequently, it often happens that the chants of the higher tropes are loosened from the regularity of their position into lower strings. Of these, therefore, four are called authentic—that is, masters or principal modes—and four others are placed beneath them in turn. These are called plagal, that is, lateral or particular modes [Note: [Col. 0685C] A tonary for all eight modes, written in ancient musical notation, is preserved here in the manuscript. Because of the lack of those signs, however, as noted above, it was necessary to omit the tonary. It proceeds afterward in this manner [Col. 0686C]: “The index…”].

The first, taking its beginnings from the summit of the index,

Places its ending at the first bend of the little finger,

Where stands the seat that is the beginning and end of the second.

The third again takes its rise from the summit of the index,

Distinguishing its ending at the summit of the little finger.

Here the beginning and ending of the fourth are recognized.

The fifth takes its narrow beginning at the middle of the index,

And fits the ending of its melody into the nail:

This position guards the beginning and ending of the sixth.

From here the base of the index finger supplies the beginning of the seventh;

Its final occupies the uppermost tip of the middle finger.

In this position the eighth places both its beginning and its ending.

[Col. 0686A] First the whole line must be divided into four parts by three points, always proceeding from the right-hand side—that is, from the right magada. At the first point place P, the string called nete hyperboleon. At the second place H, called mese. At the third, D, called lychanos hypaton. At the fourth, place A, or on the left magada, whose string is proslambanomenos.

Then divide by eight parts up to P, and place nine up to O; this will be a tone, whose string is called trite hyperboleon. Again divide by eight parts up to O and nine up to N; this will be a tone, and its string is called trite hyperboleon. These are sesquioctave proportions.

Then divide up to P into three parts, and at the fourth place M; this will be the consonance of the diatessaron, whose string is called [Col. 0686B] trite diezeugmenon. Divide again into two parts up to P, and at the third place I; this will be the consonance of the diapente, whose string is called paramese.

Next divide from I up to H, and halfway between them place the figure trite, whose string is called trite synemmenon. Likewise, divide up to I into two parts, and at the third place G; again there will be the consonance of the diapente, whose string is called lychanos meson.

Divide again into two parts up to H, and at the third place F, whose string is called parhypate meson. Divide again into two parts up to I, and at the third place E, whose string is called hypate meson.

Likewise, divide up to F into three parts, and at the fourth place C; this will be the consonance of the diatessaron, whose string is called parhypate hypaton. Divide again up to E [Col. 0686C] into three parts, and at the fourth place B, whose string is called hypate hypaton [Note: [Col. 0686C] This appears defective at the end. What follows from there, concerning the eight tones, is found above in Alcuin and in Aurelianus; so that it would not be repeated, we have omitted it].

[Col. 0685]

## ANONYMOUS III: FRAGMENT OF MUSIC

[Col. 0685D] “If from every superparticular proportion one subtract the superparticular proportion immediately following it,” and so forth. It is as though he had said: If the smaller proportion is subtracted from the larger proportion, what remains, when doubled, does not produce the completeness of the smaller proportion that was subtracted.

For example: subtract the diatessaron from the diapente—that is, two tones and a semitone from three tones and a semitone—and a tone remains. When doubled, it does not produce a complete diatessaron; a semitone remains.

Again, let a sesquiquarta be subtracted from a sesquitertia; a semitone remains, for a sesquiquarta consists of two tones. If that semitone is tripled, the sesquitertia does not reach the completeness of the sesquiquarta.

The same applies to the others: let a sesquiquinta be subtracted from a sesquiquarta [Col. 0686D]; a diesis remains, that is, a quarter of a tone. For a sesquiquinta consists of a tone, a semitone, and a diesis. When the diesis is quadrupled, since it is a sesquiquarta, it produces a complete tone, and a semitone and a diesis remain, or more.

Nevertheless, if you do this with arithmetic proportions, it proceeds to infinity. For if you subtract a sesquitertia from a sesquialtera, and double what remains, you will not reach the sesquitertia, because the sesquioctave proportion that remains, when doubled, cannot complete the sesquitertia. This can also be proved in the cases of the sesquiquarta and sesquiquinta.

“If from every superparticular proportion one subtract the superparticular proportion immediately following it.” This statement can be proved by the following examples.

Let one and the same term be proposed, to which a sesquialtera and a sesquitertia proportion are related. Let it be VI, to which VIIII is sesquialter and VIII sesquitertius. They are arranged in this way: VI, VIII, VIIII.

Since these two continuous superparticular proportions are constituted in three terms—VI, VIII, VIIII—let us remove the first term, to which VIII is sesquitertius and to which VIII is sesquialter. VIII and VIIII remain, and they are sesquioctaves. But the sesquioctave proportion is not half of the smaller proportion, that is, of the sesquitertia, because when doubled it does not produce it; it is smaller.

Let us therefore double the sesquioctave proportion. Let three numbers be arranged so that they do not depart from the proportion of VIII and VIIII. Let eight times VIII, eight times VIIII, and nine times VIIII be made: that is, LXIIII, LXXII, LXXXI; or two [sesquioctave proportions], since the first to the second and the second to the third constitute the sesquioctave relation. But the third to the first is less than a sesquitertia.

The sesquioctave is therefore not half of the sesquitertia. This must be considered in all continuous superparticular proportions: if the smaller is subtracted from the larger, what remains is less than half the proportion subtracted, because when doubled it does not equal it, as the diagram below shows.

The explanation of this diagram is as follows. X and VII, and X and VIII, have between them a sesquiseptimadecima proportion, which is understood as a single sesquiseptimadecima only in unity. If I add another sesquiseptimadecima proportion, there will be two. If I then add two to X and VII—that is, twice a sesquiseptimadecima—there will be X and VIIII. But X and VIIII do not establish a sesquioctave proportion with X and VII, for an eighth part of the unit is lacking. From this it is understood that two sesquiseptimadecimae do not make a complete tone.

Of X and VII, two and an eighth part of one are the eighth part. If these two and an eighth part of one are added to X and VII, they produce X and VIIII and an eighth part of the unit; this is sesquioctave in relation to X and VII. This reasoning is necessary for the first chapter of the following book.

“If a superparticular proportion is multiplied by two, what results is neither superparticular nor multiple,” and so forth [Note: [Col. 0687] See Boethius, pp. 1093 and 1130 of the Basel edition of 1546].

A proportion is said to be multiplied by two when it is doubled, and the first relation is reproduced in the second: that is, as the first term relates to the second, so the second relates to the third.

Let the superparticular proportion be, for example, IIII to VI. Since this is one [such proportion], let it be multiplied by two; for twice one makes II. Therefore, as IIII is to VI, so VI must be to some other number; here it is VIIII. Two [such proportions are present], because nine in relation to four is neither multiple nor superparticular.

Although what arises from such multiplication is neither multiple nor superparticular, nevertheless the thing that is multiplied is either superparticular or of another kind, but not multiple.

What arose from the previous multiplication is a double sesquiquartus, as VIIII is to IIII. It is neither multiple nor superparticular, but a multiple of a superparticular. And what has been multiplied by two is not of the multiple kind, but either superparticular or of another kind. Here, however, it is neither multiple nor of another kind, but a multiplication of a defined sesquialtera proportion [Col. 0688C]. This reasoning is necessary for the tenth chapter of this book.

[Col. 0687]

## BOETHIUS’ MEASURE OF THE MONOCHORD

From the twelfth-century Benevento–Burano manuscript.

[Col. 0687D] First divide the whole monochord into four, and at the beginning of the monochord place F. At the first step make B; at the second, F mese; at the third, F; the fourth ends there. Then from the end make three steps to the lowest F, two to the highest, and at the fourth step you have upper c.

Again, from the end make two steps to the same F, and at the third you have upper b. Then from that b make four steps to the end; the first of them ends at upper e. Again, from the end make two steps to the same e, and backward at the third you have upper a.

Then from that a make four steps to the end; the first ends at upper D [d]. From the end make three steps to upper C [c], and backward at the fourth you have upper G [g]. From the end make two steps to upper D [d], and backward at the third, G synemmenon.

Afterward double the space of each letter into its corresponding equivalent: that is, make one step from the end—from the high end—to each of the upper letters, and the second step to its corresponding low letter.

## MEASURE OF THE MONOCHORD

From the twelfth-century manuscript of St. Blasien.

Divide the whole surface into nine parts. At the first point of the left-hand section mark F; at the second, A; at the fourth, D; at the fifth, F; at the sixth, A [a]; at the seventh, D [d]; at the eighth, a [a].

Likewise, divide the line up to A into nine parts. The first point from A will yield A, the second B, the third E, the fifth [a] square, the sixth e, and the seventh [].

Then, with the whole surface divided into four, the point on the left of the second section gives C; in the third, G; in the fourth. Divide up to G into four and it yields c. Divide up to E into four: at the second point, b flat; at the third, F. From F, divided into four toward the end, it gives b [b] synemmenon modern; from g, divided into three, it gives d [d]; from c, divided into two, c [c].

The end.

## ON THE MEASURE OF THE MONOCHORD

From the same manuscript of St. Blasien.

If you wish to know the regular division of the monochord according to the authentic system of Boethius, I shall try to make it clear to you in simple language. When you have placed the magada at both ends of the monochord, divide its entire length between the magada into four equal parts. It is appropriate to mark these points, or these letters: F, B, F, F, C.

Then divide the fourth part that meets the divider on the right—that is, F–Z—into eight, and add a ninth to it; place E there, so that E–Z is separated from it by a sesquioctave proportion, that is, by a tone.

Again divide E–Z by eight, and, adding an eighth, mark D; you will have the second tone. Then divide the original fourth part, F–Z, by three, add three to it, and place C there. C–Z will be separated from F–Z by a sesquitertian or epitritic proportion, that is, by the consonance of the diatessaron, and from D–Z by a semitone.

Behold, you have the tetrachord hyperboleon, consisting of tone, tone, and semitone. Next you can find B, which ought to be separated from C by a tone, either by adding an eighth to C–Z—that is, a sesquioctave—or by adding it to E–Z itself—that is, an epitritic—or by increasing half of F–Z—that is, a hemiolic or sesquialteric relation. This produces the consonance of the diapente.

Likewise, make A, which is separated from B by a tone, either by adding an eighth, a sesquioctave, to it; or by adding a third, a sesquitertia, to D–Z; or by adding a sesquialtera to half of E–Z.

Immediately place G, which is separated from A by a semitone, one third of the way before it; make C–Z sesquitertian to it there, and the second tetrachord, diezeugmenon, consisting likewise of tone, tone, and semitone, will properly end. Thus you will find that a tone remains up to the second F, placed in the middle of the monochord.

At this point you must join the synemmenon tetrachord, whose highest string is joined to the B mentioned above. Its second is joined to the A mentioned above; its third ought to be separated from A by a tone and from the second F by a semitone. You may obtain this either by making A–Z sesquioctave to it, or by making half of D–Z hemiolic and sesquialteric to it.

When this has been done, you will see that this tetrachord also consists of tone, tone, and semitone up to the second F. Behold, we have completed the consonance of the diapason from the first F to the second, consisting of a dupla proportion.

To this you must attach another diapason up to the third F, using the same method of measurement from the second F, with the same arrangement of the letters recurring and the same order of tones and semitones.

Find E, which is separated from F by a tone, either by adding a ninth to E–Z by the eighth method, or by adding a fourth to A–Z by the third method, or by adding a third to half of B–Z, or by doubling another E–Z.

Find D, which is separated from E by a tone, either by adding a ninth to E–Z by the eighth method, by adding a third to half of A–Z, or by doubling another D–Z.

Then find C, which is separated from D by a semitone, either by adding a fourth to F–Z by the third method, by adding a third to half of G–Z, or by doubling another C–Z.

Thus this meson tetrachord, from F to C, consists of tone, tone, and semitone, like the preceding ones. Next B, which is separated from C by a tone, is encountered at the fourth part of the entire monochord, although it can also be found in many other ways.

Seek A, which likewise differs from B by a tone, either by placing a ninth, the upper note, above B–Z by the eighth method; or by joining a fourth to D–Z by the third; or by adding a third to half of E–Z toward the high end; or by doubling another A–Z.

Then find G, which is separated from A by a semitone, either by adding a fourth to C–Z by the third method, or by doubling another G–Z. Thus you will complete this hypaton tetrachord from C to G in tone, tone, and semitone, like the preceding ones.

A tone still remains from C to the third F, at which the second diapason ends; and the entire measurement of the monochord is fully completed in the diatonic genus of melodies.

But so that you may more easily retain this measure in memory, let us briefly add a universal rule concerning what has been stated. Any sounds that correspond to one another by a tone are separated by a sesquioctave or epogdous interval. That is, divide the sharper or shorter string into eight equal parts, and make the lower or longer string exceed it by a ninth, so that the smaller has eight parts and the larger nine.

Any sounds that are joined by the consonance of the diatessaron differ by two tones and a semitone, in an epitritic or sesquitertian interval: the shorter string has three parts, the longer four.

Any sounds that agree in the consonance of the diapente—that is, in three tones and a semitone—differ in a hemiolic, sescupla, or sesquialtera proportion: the shorter string has two parts, while the longer has three.

Any sounds that agree in the consonance of the diapason—that is, in five tones and two semitones—are separated in a diplasic, that is, double, relation: when the shorter string is doubled, it produces the longer one.

In this H diapason consonance there are seven distinctions of different notes. The eighth is the same as the first. Therefore, above also, when indicating the measure of the monochord in the diatonic genus, we marked it with only seven letters.

But if you also wish to measure the chromatic and enharmonic genera, you can be instructed generally in a single tetrachord of the diatonic genus. To measure the chromatic, take the smallest and highest tone in any diatonic tetrachord and divide it in two. Then turn the compass toward the following, larger tone, and, having made a mark, encompass the three semitones together; distinguish the remaining two semitones from the tetrachord by lines.

To measure the enharmonic, encompass two continuous tones of the diatonic genus and divide only the following semitone into two equal parts by drawing a line. In this way measure these two genera in all the tetrachords of the diatonic genus.

## ANOTHER RULE FOR THE MONOCHORD
The organum measurement requires this: below the finals there should be a tone, above a ditone—that is, from A to G—arranged as follows. I inscribe A wherever I wish, at the beginning or in the middle of the monochord, though preferably at the midpoint between the low and high notes. From that A I make four steps to the right, toward the end; the first step will terminate at D, while the others remain unused. Again, from the same A I extend three steps toward the end; the first of these will terminate at E, while the others remain unused. From the end I return three steps to that same E, the fourth [step] ending at B. From that B I extend three steps toward the end, and the first ends at F, while the others remain unused. From the end I return three steps to that same F, the fourth [step] ending at C. From C I extend three steps toward the end, and the first ends at C. From D I extend four steps toward the end, and the first will terminate at S *synemmenon*; and the measurement is complete.

## GUIDO’S MEASUREMENT

From the Benedictine-Burana manuscript of the twelfth century. [Note: [Col. 0691B] See Pez, vol. V of the *Anecdota*, p. 225.]

When you first divide the monochord from G to the end into nine steps, the first step will terminate at A; the second is unused; the third at D; the fourth is unused; the fifth at upper a; the sixth at d; the seventh at a; the remaining steps are unused. [Col. 0692A]

Likewise, when you divide from A to the end into nine steps, the first step will terminate at B; the second is unused; the third at E; the fourth is unused; the fifth at square [B]; the sixth at e; the seventh at [unclear]; the remaining steps are unused.

Then divide from G to the end into four parts: the first will terminate at C, the second at G, the third at g, and the fourth ends [at the end].

Similarly, from C to the end in four steps, the first will terminate at F, the second at c, the third at e, and the fourth ends [at the end].

From F, however, to the end in four steps, the first will terminate at round b, the second at upper f; the remaining steps are unused.

[Col. 0692B] From round b to the end in two steps, the first will terminate at excellent round b. From upper d to the end in two steps, the first [will terminate at] excellent a or b.

Then finally make one step from the end to upper round b. The second step [goes] backward to low T *synemmenon*, which is to be inserted between low A and low B; and it is complete.

[Col. 0691]

## THE MEASUREMENT OF THE FOUR-PART FIGURE OF OTKER, A MONK OF REGENSBURG, OF UNCERTAIN DATE

From the Benedictine-Burana manuscript of the twelfth century.

[Col. 0691C] A certain monk of Regensburg named Otker devised this four-part measurement and called it the “Theorem of the Modes,” which we may call the sieve of the monochord. For in it you can see clearly how all the low notes, all the finals, all the upper notes, and all the excellent notes correspond; at the same time you can see all the species of the fourth and all the species of the fifth, and in what direction the course of each tone proceeds, upward or downward. You should arrange this measurement as follows.

Divide one side of the monochord into four parts, leaving a space above or below, alongside the width of one stalk, in which you can write the letters of the measurement on either side. Once one side has thus been divided into four, measure it according to Guido’s method. Mark the points on the upper line with their letters, and mark the same points and letters on the lower line. Assign each part to one authentic tone and its plagal, as follows: assign the uppermost part to the Tetrardus and its plagals—that is, to the seventh and eighth tones. Assign the part before the penultimate to the authentic Tritus and its disciple—that is, to the fifth and sixth tones. Assign the penultimate part to the Deuterus and its subordinate—that is, to the third and fourth tones. Assign the last, namely the lowest, part to the Protus and its lateral—that is, to the first and second tones. Give the uppermost part, which belongs to the Tetrardus, the name TE; give the part before the penultimate the name TR; the penultimate part the name DE; and the last part the name PR.

Once Guido’s measurement has been made and the points with their letters have been placed above and below, put a ruler transversely from point to point and cut it according to this monogram, beginning from G. The following chant shows which part you should cut:

TE. TR. TE. TR. SY, that is, *synemmenon*. TE. DE. SE, that is, *semitone*. TE. TR. TE. DE. PR. TE. TR. DE. PR. TE. TR. PR. TE. DE. PR. TE. TR. DE. PR. TE. [Col. 0692D] TR. PR. SY. TE. DE. PR. SE. TE. TR. TE. SY. TR. DE. PR. SE. TR. SE. DE. PR. TE. TR. SE. PR. TE. DE. PR. TE. TR. DE. PR. TE. TR. PR. SE. PR. TR. DE. PR. PR.

Then measure from low A of the Tritus to the end in nine steps, and the first step [is] y. y. [Note: [Col. 0691] The remainder is missing; everything is explained more distinctly in the *Music of Saint William of Hirsau*, which we shall provide below.]

[Col. 0693]

## THE MONOCHORD OF THE *ENCHIRIADIS*

(Edited by D. Ravaisson, *Rapports sur les bibliothèques des départements de l’Ouest*, Appendix, p. 370.)

[Col. 0693A] The monochord of the *Enchiriadis* consists of eighteen strings: namely, four low notes, four finals, four middle notes, and four excellent notes, together with two super-excellent notes. They are composed of a tone and a semitone and two tones. The division of this monochord is arranged as follows.

First divide the entire board into four sections. The first, on the left, is designated by the name of the first low *magoda*. The second is called the fourth low note. The third is called the fourth final. The fourth bears the name of the third excellent note. Then divide the same board into nine parts, and place the ninth part on the left at the protus. This string itself is called the second low note.

Next divide the distance from the right-hand *magoda* to the fourth low note into eight parts, and take the ninth part, extended forward, as the third low note. Likewise, measure to the same fourth low note in nine parts. The ninth part will be the first final string; measure to that final itself in nine parts. By doing this, the ninth part will produce the second final at a semitone. From there, laying out eight parts as far as the fourth final mentioned above, the ninth part extended forward displays the third final. Then divide again to that fourth final in nine parts, and the ninth part will indicate the first middle note.

From there divide to the first middle note in nine parts, and the ninth part will disclose the second middle note at a semitone. Backward from the fourth final to the third excellent note already mentioned, divide the distance in half; [Col. 0693C] and at that midpoint place the third middle note. Then measure to that third middle note in nine parts, and place the fourth middle note at the ninth part. Dividing to the fourth middle note in nine parts, establish the first excellent note at the ninth part. Moreover, divide that first excellent note into nine parts; at the ninth part will be the second excellent note. Measuring to the third [excellent note] mentioned above in nine parts, the ninth part will show the fourth excellent note.

Multiply by nine twice, and at the end multiply the last excellent notes: first low, second low, third low, fourth low; first final, second final, third final, fourth final; first middle, second middle, third middle, fourth middle; first excellent, second excellent, third excellent, fourth excellent; and two super-excellent notes.

The first final has an inclined S at the head, thus: S. The second final has an inverted E at the head, thus: E. The third has a simple iota and an inclined [sign], thus: I. The fourth final has half an E at the head, thus: E. The low notes have reversed finals, thus: . . . . . The upper notes have lowered final heads, thus: . . . . . . The excellent notes have lowered low-note heads, thus: . . . . . ., except the Tritus, which has the sign H among the low notes, inclined. Among the upper notes, H is inverted and inclined . . . . . .; among the excellent notes, an iota is prefixed +. The two remaining signs belong to the recumbent Protus and Deuterus. There are twenty-eight in all, so that each may reach its extreme consonance, namely the fifteenth note.

[Col. 0693]

## A LETTER OF A., A CITIZEN OF SPIRES, WRITTEN ABOUT THE YEAR M.A. [uncertain], TO HERIBERT, ARCHBISHOP OF COLOGNE

### Against Hasty Absolutions of Sinners

(Edited by Martene, *Amplissima Collectio*, I, 357.)

[Col. 0693D] To H., archbishop of a most noble see, still nobler, A., a resident citizen from the city of Spires, [sends] the fullness of eternal happiness. [Note: [Col. 0693D] We found this letter in a very old manuscript of the monastery of Tuitium near Cologne, at the end of the *Life of Saint Heribert*, and therefore judged that it had been written to him.]

I know certain men of your order, and indeed men sufficiently upright and learned, who, whenever they distribute spiritual wheat to God’s people in their churches, after completing everything they understand to pertain to the fruit of holy edification, order the people to raise their hands and confess their sins. Thereupon they immediately grant them absolution and remission of all their sins with as much ease as they might perhaps be unwilling to remit three obols of their own money to anyone.

On hearing this, some of the brethren who, by divine gift, possess a certain knowledge of sacred Scripture, yet dare say nothing in opposition because of their reverence, are gravely scandalized. They know that something wholly unlawful is being done, something which cannot be defended by the authority of any of the holy Fathers, and which is a diabolical snare leading the ignorant multitude to destruction. For the multitude supposes that it will afterward need no confession, but that all its crimes have been forgiven, as though those people had been baptized anew. Having accepted this deadly security, they do not incur dangers to their souls and consider it of no account to repeat their offenses or add even graver ones, since they trust that these too will be forgiven them again and again with such ease.

You see, therefore, my lord, how widely this evil extends—how wicked, how full of blasphemy, and altogether unlawful it is—which the evangelical trumpet proclaims and displays to the whole world. For who can forgive sins except God alone? To him every human being truly says: “Against you alone I have sinned.” They suppose, however, that they have received this power in what the Lord said to his disciples: “Whatever you bind on earth will be bound also in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth will be loosed also in heaven.”

But our holy teachers wish this to pertain to the duty of administration, not to a right of power: what is invisibly decreed concerning human acts before the tribunal of divine judgment, that the priest himself, as a kind of mortal god, may carry out among human beings under a visible form. Whoever searches the sacred writings knows that priests are called gods; but this earthly Church also bears a certain likeness to that blessed city. Thus whoever has been exiled from it because of the enormity of some crime must likewise be separated from this Church, like a leper outside the camp. When he appears to have returned there by way of legitimate satisfaction, he is then restored to this Church through the priestly ministry as one cleansed.

Finally, the priests of the Old Testament did not cleanse lepers; they led those already cleansed into the temple. With what slightness [read: recklessness], then, do the priests of the New Testament claim to cleanse spiritual leprosy? Which of the saints do they ever find saying to a sinner, “I forgive your sins,” rather than, after joining their fasts and prayers, obtaining from the Lord what they wished to provide as assistance? We read in ecclesiastical history that the apostle John did this for that young man whom he had recalled from brigandage and was bringing forth again for Christ. The Son of Man himself, although he had power on earth to forgive sins, avoiding an explicit assertion of his own person, did not say, “I forgive your sins,” but rather, as though modestly: “Man,” he said, “your sins are forgiven you.”

He plainly knew that that paralytic, purified by long and most bitter suffering, deserved pardon, just as did the man who, as the Gospel testifies, had been ill for thirty-eight years and whom he healed at the pool of the sheep-gate. Yet the sons of men dare to forgive the unknown and unexamined sins of others, although they themselves are neither conscious of them nor witnesses to the penitence of those persons. Is this not what the Lord complains through his prophet about false prophets, saying: “They put to death souls that do not die, and give life to souls that do not live”?

By what order this power ought to be administered, he clearly declares through another prophet: “I have appointed you as an assayer among my people, a strong one, and you shall know and test their ways.” The steps of each person must certainly be tested, to determine how they have walked along the path of conduct; and before a human judgment is pronounced, one must watch carefully toward what direction the divine sentence tends.

Finally, Lazarus was first brought to life by the Lord and afterward loosed by the disciples. If they had loosed him before the Lord’s command, he would nevertheless have remained senseless and stinking in the grave. Thus the lifeless soul must first be aroused, when the Lord calls the sinner from the underworld, and then absolved through the ministry of priests. Whoever acts otherwise certainly accomplishes nothing for another person, but does himself great harm; for, as Blessed Gregory says, the one who exercises this power according to his own desires and not according to the merits of his subjects deprives himself of the very power of binding and loosing.

It must therefore be considered, according to the rule of the holy Fathers, what fault preceded and what satisfaction followed. After careful discernment has been exercised, the power of the office is then to be applied cautiously and humbly. One must not say, “May the Lord forgive your sins, and I forgive you,” unless perhaps the offense is personal, inflicted by the guilty person upon the priest himself. Of such a sin he may confidently say: “May the Lord forgive you, and so may I.”

But just as no one is so righteous, no one so holy, that he would presume to say, “I am righteous; I am holy,” so this blasphemy against the Holy Spirit must be avoided all the more—the forgiveness of sins being his proper work—lest any human being dare say to another human being: [Note: [Col. 0695] From the entire sequence of this letter it appears that its author admitted no other formula of absolution in the sacrament of penance than one expressed as a prayer.] “I forgive your sins.”

For if he can say this, he can consequently say: “I justify you.” Then we shall no longer speak only of God, “God who justifies the ungodly”; and it is as impious to conceive this in one’s heart as it is sacrilegious to utter it with one’s mouth.

Those who act in this way could easily avoid this slander and conduct all the rest much more simply if they were willing to imitate the examples of the venerable teachers whose fruitful sermons they hear daily. When those teachers prepared themselves to expound the divine word, they first of all prepared the attention of their hearers with a gentle and kindly address. Then, having begun an exposition of the Gospel, the apostolic writings, or even the prophets, they strove, according to the capacity of popular understanding, to clarify the obscurity of mystical meanings. Above all, they sought to instill fear in the sinner: through confession and penitence to promise forgiveness; to exhort the righteous toward improvement; and then to speak of the instability of present things, the brevity and uncertainty of this life, the severity of the future judgment, and finally the ineffable blessedness of the saints and the most wretched damnation of the impious.

On these and similar matters, our Catholic preachers composed ecclesiastical sermons—some more extensively and sweetly, others more briefly and severely, according to the measure of divine grace granted to each. But these strange new absolutions—which we more truly call public deceptions—we find neither in their writings nor, we believe, in their practice, except on that one day when, according to an ancient custom, they restored ecclesiastical communion to penitents.

I thought that this ought to be written to your eminence boldly, but faithfully and in no way arrogantly. I know that by the sword of your authority this heresy, which is still emerging and hidden, can be cut away more easily, since among many people a judgment carries as much weight as does the power of the secular person who pronounces it. Your prudence, however, does not think in this way; nor does it measure reason by a person’s fortune, but measures the person by the force of reason. May almighty God increase your ability to understand and carry out his will.

[Col. 0697]

## A LETTER OF A CERTAIN MONK, AROUND THE YEAR 1057, TO ODERIC, ABBOT OF THE MONASTERY OF VENDÔME

### On Haymo’s Homiliary

[Note: [Col. 0697B] Although this letter may not appear to be of great importance, it seems worth including here, since it makes clear how expensive books were at that time and how highly this Homiliary was valued.]

(At Mabillon, *Annales Benedictini*, book LXI, vol. IV, p. 574.)

[Col. 0697A] To his lord, Abbot O., Brother R. [sends] prayers in Christ.

Dearest father, we wish you to know that the countess bought from Martin, who is now bishop, the codex about which you have heard, at a great price. On one occasion, on account of the book, she gave him one hundred sheep; on another occasion, on account of that same book, one modius of wheat, a second of rye, and a third of millet. Again, for the same reason, one hundred sheep; on another occasion, certain marten skins. When he separated from the count, he received from her four pounds for the purchase of sheep. But when he afterward demanded denarii, she began to complain about the book. She immediately remitted to him what he owed her.

[Col. 0698]

## LETTER OF THE CONGREGATION OF SAINT ALBINUS OF ANGERS TO P., THE POPE’S NEPHEW

### Complaint Concerning the Injustice of the Apostolic Legate in the Case of the Church of Saint Clement of Credon

[Note: [Col. 0697C] V. C. Étienne Baluze published the acts of the dispute that was conducted between the monks of Saint Albinus of Angers and those of Vendôme concerning the church of Saint Clement of Credon, in book II of his *Miscellanea*. This letter refers to that dispute.]

(Martene, *Anecdota*, I, 201.)

[Col. 0697C] To Lord P., the pope’s nephew, the congregation of Saint Albinus [sends greetings].

We have been most anxious, most noble lord, to inform your dignity how carefully Lord G. [Gerard], bishop of Ostia, obeyed the apostolic command. Certainly, Lord Pope, unless our memory deceives us, had ordered—through the intervention of your prudence—that if the party of the legates had gone to Rome while the others were returning, he should return promptly, examine our case through careful investigation, and settle it with a just conclusion; or, if this could not be done because the delay of the aforementioned party hindered it, he should report to him the truth of the matter ascertained by testimony.

After reading the apostolic letters, he first gave our legate no definite reply. Later, having entered our region and lingered several days at Tours, he refused even when entreated to hear our case, and instructed us to follow him outside our borders. He said he would hear our account at Vendôme or at Chartres. Both places were exceedingly disadvantageous to us.

At the one place, because, with enemy ambushes threatening us on every side, it was either impossible or extremely difficult for us to bring there a sufficient number of both the resources and the persons appropriate to such a case. At the other, our adversaries had the opportunity—as lords or householders of that region—not only to bring money for corrupting the minds of judges, but also to bring friends for perverting justice itself through the shameless loquacity of cunning men rather than through honorable eloquence.

What, then, happened? With scarcely any support, after passing Vendôme, we entered Chartres. In the court of Bishop A. [Artaldus], formerly a monk of Vendôme, before many persons living both under monastic and clerical habit, we presented our account to G. himself, while the opposing side raised no objection of any weight. We argued the case with complete clarity for two days or more. Everyone, except their supporters, whispered or openly affirmed that Saint Albinus had the most just and honorable case, and that the others had the opposite.

We were awaiting the judges’ decisions on the authority of the canons and the cardinal’s determination, in accordance with the pope’s command, no opposing force hindering him except the bishop of Chartres, a man said to be a master of cunning. The cardinal and the aforementioned A. then led one another from the assembly to a certain lodging for consultation.

When we refused, on the basis of their request, to allow our stable hereditary possession of the church to be alienated for money paid out, the cardinal asserted that he would impose no decision concerning the case in the present session. He ordered us to go with him to another council that would meet at Paris a few days later.

On the journey itself he seized us and, persuading each one individually to accept money, spent such an amount on entreaties and threats, now flattering and now intimidating, that it cannot be written in a letter. From this alone it became clearer than daylight that he was more prepared to defend their side in particular than to judge impartially between the parties, although secular laws prohibit a person from being both advocate and judge.

At Paris too, much and by many [lacuna]xatus before [lacuna] and several bishops who were present, [he was urged] to put an end to our labor. Our witnesses were present and ready to affirm our right. Yet he replied in great anger that we would accomplish nothing and invited us to that unspecified council which would be held in foreign parts, on the condition, however, that if the dispute were not settled there either, we should again return to Rome. Although we openly demonstrated to many that we could not be taken away with him for three weeks, he refused to acknowledge necessity as an impediment.

What more can I say? The joy obtained from your apostolic majesty through your kindness is being turned into grief. How harshly—indeed, how cruelly—he deterred and exasperated us; how he contended publicly with certain people and insulted them; and how he often promised in secret that he would render judgment if we sought a Roman synod! How dishonorably he himself drove Frotmund, well known to you, from his lodging, pushing him out with his own hands! Fearing that we would become a burden to you, since we did not dare approach a man occupied with such great matters, he cut off every hope of obtaining justice.

As we were returning, bound by sadness, Bishop A. seized the opportunity and, with many entreaties, persuaded us to accept two hundred pounds for the church, contrary to the prohibitions of the canons. Alas, in his capitol, compelled by our flight from justice, we sorrowfully agreed. Moreover, he extorted from our abbot that he should have that agreement confirmed by his monks in the chapter at Angers. Since the consent of the congregation of Saint Albinus had not yet been heard, he ordered that a charter be made at Chartres contrary to custom.

Our abbot, therefore, with his prior absent and without summoning either the deans or men of greater understanding and age, compelled the smaller number who happened to be present in the chapter—childish in either judgment or age—to consent to the agreement according to his own will. Some openly resisted, while nearly everyone cried out that they were agreeing to such a pact unwillingly and under compulsion.

As a result, a dispute broke out among us worse than civil sedition; and you should know that from this present evil a considerable future detriment to the Church is springing up. For no ministers of the Church who retain authority from an apostolic legate will henceforth fear selling or giving anything away, making light of the complaint of the poor who await alms from the Church’s inheritance.

Know this with certainty: from now on, no one, once he has heard the outcome of our case, will travel to Rome in pursuit of justice. For everyone repeats that Jugurtha’s proverb: “Rome is for sale, if it finds a buyer”—and everyone who departs from Rome repeats it.

Therefore, most prudent man, resist the growth of so great an illness, lest what has been laboriously established remain in force. Bring this to the attention of the apostolic authority, so that it may be reduced to nothing.

[Col. 0699]

## ANONYMOUS FISCANNENSIAN BOOKLET ON THE REVELATION, CONSTRUCTION, AND AUTHORITY OF THE MONASTERY OF FISCANNUS

(R. P. Art. du Monstier, *Neustria Pia*, Rouen, 1663, p. 193.)

### PRELIMINARY NOTICE

Some have thought that the abbey of Fiscannus is among the more recent foundations that began toward the end of the second dynasty of the kings of the Franks. How far they are mistaken will become clearer from the fact that this same abbey was previously a monastery of holy women, begun by Blessed Waningus, a most distinguished man, in the time of Saint Audoenus, archbishop of Rouen, and of Dom Wandregisilus, abbot of Fontenelle, around the year of Christ 662.

But in order that the proper order may be preserved in the many records of this renowned abbey which we shall soon produce, we first judged it worthwhile and appropriate to bring to light and illustrate with certain scholia an old manuscript work of venerable antiquity, an excellent little document of historical truth, so that the entire sequence of the history might be confirmed and supported, and the kindly reader’s understanding might be greatly assisted. It is preserved at Fiscannus by Dom Nicholas of Marseilles, infirmarian and monk of this abbey.

## THE PROLOGUE BEGINS

Here begins the booklet on the revelation and authority of the monastery of Fiscannus; in this booklet, if you read attentively, you can find how the church called Fiscannus was built and dedicated in the name of the holy and undivided Trinity.

[Col. 0701]

[Col. 0701A] I have composed, illustrious Father William, a booklet on the revelation, construction, and authority of the monastery of Fiscannus, and I have sent the completed work for correction and confirmation to the sincere judgment of your affection, so that the approval of your eminence may both command the booklet to be published and grant weight and authority to the published book.

For my part, illustrious Father, I would rather have concealed my ignorance under such silence than publish it to the judgment of anyone presumptuously through writing. But because of the persistent command of our brethren, and their insistence that commands, our mind is compelled to exceed its capacity and unexpectedly expose its own inadequacy to the view of many people. I say, it is compelled to disregard its ignorance and to offer obedience to the commanding request of our brethren; [Col. 0701B] yet in offering that obedience, neither the judgment of the mind in any way assents nor the shamefacedness of the undertaking ceases entirely to object.

Nevertheless, since holy obedience excuses—and ought to excuse—no work as difficult or impossible, after hesitating for a long time and inventing delays upon delays, under the pressure of the continual command of fraternal affection I finally undertook the burden imposed upon me. In the following booklet I have disclosed and explained the beginnings of the monastery of Fiscannus [Col. 0702A] in a rustic and undistinguished style.

In this booklet I have inserted no falsehood deceptively. Rather, I have written the sacred histories known through the faithful account of ancient men, preserved in the tenacious memory of their descendants, and transmitted to our own time through the careful report of succeeding men. I have published what I have written for the authority of the church of Fiscannus and for the benefit of the brethren who read it.

At the beginning of this booklet, following not the authority of all but of a few reasonable reporters, I set forth the miracle of the stag. In accordance with the exact care of the chronicles, I determined that this was the first revelation of Duke Ansegisus.

As for my account that from its ancient beginning the church of Fiscannus was marked not with the title of the glorious and undefiled Virgin Mary, as some wish, but with that of the holy and undivided Trinity, the reason was that, regarding an ambiguous matter, I should incline toward an opinion that would incur the disgrace of no falsehood. For every church, although it is distinguished by the title of this or that saint, is principally founded, constituted, and dedicated under the name and patronage of the holy and undivided Trinity.

**The prologue ends.**

## THE TREATISE BEGINS

[Col. 0701]

[Col. 0701C] After the ineffable Trinity of the supreme divinity, by the secret counsel of its clemency, resolved to liberate human nature and expose the poisonous persuasions of the ancient serpent, it ineffably took from the undefiled body of a certain virgin an undefiled portion, excluding the work of a man. It divinely fashioned this portion according to the structure of the human species, vivifying it with a rational soul made fruitful by the abundance of all heavenly grace, and composed and perfected it into the substance of a complete man.

This man, therefore, a man without a man, from the womb of the incorrupt Virgin, the whole holy and immutable Trinity composed and sanctified; but the sublimity of the Word alone personally associated and united him with the person of its own proper nature. [Note: [Col. 0701C] These words must be read cautiously.]

For it was fitting that one person should obey two, so that by the example of his humility he might instruct creatures how those inferior to their Creator should obey, when they recognized that such great obedience and humility were being offered by an equal to equals. The Son of God demanded this work of humility from God, as though by a privilege of love, so that, having become man, he might reconcile human beings whom he had created from nothing by his power and wisdom.

Thus, in mercy, the Word of God made manifest to human beings the sweetness of its love, the abundance of that sweetness, and the greatness of that abundance. It became flesh, was conceived from the undefiled womb of a virgin, and came forth from its bridal chamber—not converting God into man, but personally joining man to the immutable God and constituting him gracious toward God and human beings.

Therefore Christ, perfect man, emptied himself of the form of his majesty and assumed the nature of his servants; he assumed weakness so that he might preach the forgiveness of sins more readily to the human beings who were to be redeemed, persuade them more convincingly of the usefulness of conversion and return, and join to their nature and weakness a form of divine sublimity, which he did not disdain to do.

He could plainly have condemned Satan in many other ways and excluded his evasive ambushes and ambushing evasions, either by commanding with a mere nod or by employing the service of angels. But the way of return had to be shown to human beings, so that power might be preceded by endurance and endurance followed by power.

The merciful God, therefore, secretly providing for human beings through a human being, condemned pride through humility and death through death. Trampling upon the curse of original sin, he mercifully bestowed upon those reborn in faith the blessing of new grace through the outpouring of his blood.

To the joy of the solemn banquet of this incomprehensible grace, the ineffable kindness of the supreme Trinity summoned—and decreed that there should be summoned—guests whose hungry minds it might abundantly satisfy with heavenly food and intoxicate with the delightful drink of its torrent.

The chosen disciples are therefore sent throughout the whole world, bearers of the heavenly treasure, announcers of restored blessedness, and faithful messengers of promised grace. The excess of love is preached, the humility of the Incarnation, the cruelty silently endured in the Passion, and the harshness of death gladly accepted.

The perfect forgiveness of sins to be granted to converted sinners is preached; the correction of the former life is enjoined; the building and construction of a new life are proclaimed. The falsehoods of demons are exposed, and the errors of those who serve demons are refuted.

Abundant flashes of miracles accompany the voluntary rain of heavenly clouds. Through them the service of powerful idolatry is shattered, and hearts that serve Christ are strengthened and uplifted. By the rains of heavenly grace, therefore, the cultivation of the whole world is made fruitful; the ancient, obstinate roughness of the thorns is uprooted and cut down. The flowers of a joyful harvest spring forth, and the ripened sheaves of blessed sowing are gathered into sacred granaries.

The fullness of the promised time, once completed, enriches the wedding feast of the heavenly sacrament with the delights of every kind of wealth. In that feast the Church, an immaculate virgin, is joined to the most beautiful Bridegroom of all things in spiritual bridal chambers.

Therefore the nations of all peoples, invited, gather together and sing to the banquet of the heavenly Bridegroom the sweetness of heavenly harmonies. The royal halls are filled with ranks of those reclining at table, whose attention, raised up by the joys of the everlasting court, forgets temporal pleasures. Thus the heavenly attendants resound on the tambourine and in the choir, on the lyre and psaltery, on strings and organ; through the measured harmony of their unceasing praise, the whole world is gathered and the choir of angels is joined to the heavenly court.

## CHAPTER ONE

### Here ends the explanation of why the basilicas of the saints are built.

[Col. 0704A]

The sublime divinity of the incorrupt Trinity, seeing the people of its grace attending upon divine praises and scorning the business of temporal affairs, commands sacred buildings to be constructed. It decreed that these should be closed to earthly business and opened only to its own praisers.

Sacred temples are therefore built, glorious buildings of sacred temples, in which the ecclesiastical sacraments may be celebrated with greater reverence, the mysteries of the legal Scriptures revealed, and the teachings of the holy Gospels recited and heard.

The holy basilicas of blessed peoples arise, consecrated to spiritual offices. The eternal providence of the supreme Emperor decreed that they should be distinguished by the names of exalted men and called by their titles. [Col. 0704B] When holy churches have been consecrated to holy men, holy men are entreated and venerated; and God alone is worshiped and adored.

In their appointed places, therefore, blessed apostles, martyrs, and confessors, as well as glorious virgins, receive their basilicas as their portion and dwell in the portions assigned to them. They behold the devotion of those who gather there, hear their prayers, and mercifully grant the benefits they request.

## CHAPTER TWO

### How God Chose the Valley of Fiscannus to Be Consecrated to His Name
Having therefore built and consecrated dwellings of supreme veneration for holy men, reason demanded that a temple should be built more gloriously than the others for the triune and one God, the almighty Creator of all things—a temple which he would mark with the royal privilege of his name [Col. 0704C] and adorn and protect by the presence of his unique majesty.

For the dwelling of so great an Emperor, the maritime borders of Gaul are chosen: there the territory of the Calciacens, looking toward the left, eight miles distant from the Seine, exposes its waters to the devouring western Ocean from a certain lofty promontory, where two small rivers discharge their waters. There, then, Fiscannus of the territory of Calciacum is chosen—a maritime valley which, dark with the density of forests and thickets and surrounded by the towering height of immense trees, was believed to offer a hiding-place not for the Creator of all things but for wild beasts and sea-robbers.

O greatest humility of divine majesty! O image of the greatest humility to be set before mortals! It is not a city, not a cultivated field; [Col. 0704D] rather, by the special privilege of so great a title, a shadowy and dreadful valley is distinguished as Fiscannus.

It is asked what words of revelation or signs of miracles became manifest by which the eternal and unchangeable Trinity judged that the aforesaid place should be set apart for its service and honored by the oracle of its name. We learned the solution to this question from the frequent account of our predecessors, and, once learned, we have taken care to explain it in the diligence of what follows.

## CHAPTER III—On Duke Ansegisus

From the faithful narration of men, therefore, we learned that Ansegisus ruled the Gauls in ancient times. The distinguished vigor of his noble deeds commended him outwardly to the world, while the renowned virtue of his great devotion commended him inwardly to God.

With a bold sword he held back the terrifying ranks and savage incursions of the barbarians from the borders of Gaul; and, keeping the subject provinces secure in peace, he commended them by the praises of justice and adorned them with holiness of conduct. Through his ambition, neighboring kingdoms were not weakened or devastated for the sake of his own realm; rather, by the counsel of his virtue they flourished and were brought to peace.

By secret counsels of avarice he did not plunder his provincials in a hostile manner; instead, with the resources at his disposal, he royally increased the wealth of his nobles, while mercifully supporting the needs of the poor.

To a man of such great merits, the first indications of the revelation concerning the Fiscannense church were granted, and the revelations of those first indications were made manifest. For the aforesaid duke, established in this world as though outside the world, by the privilege of a certain contemplation, [Col. 0705B] was not nourished by the glory of the kingdom entrusted to him; rather, he meditated on the abiding riches of the heavenly empire. Because of the sweetness of those riches, he handled temporal affairs unwillingly and withdrew from them willingly. Devoting himself intensely to hunting, he delighted in the solitude of the forests and was exercised by the opportunity for frequent labor.

For this reason he often visited the maritime part of the territory of Calciacum, which, rich in ancient woodland, provided hiding-places for various kinds of wild animals.

## CHAPTER IV—On the Dogs and Horses That Were Struck with Contracture

One day, then, Duke Ansegisus, rising early as usual, summoned his huntsmen and ordered the dogs to be coupled. He commanded that nets, hunting spears, and the other instruments of the hunt be carried to the woods of Fiscannus, its deep valleys, [Col. 0705C] and its steep mountains.

The huntsmen obeyed their lord’s orders: they summoned the dogs, entered the appointed forest hiding-places, stretched the nets, set guards, and with the greatest care searched through the places that had been reconnoitered and designated.

At last, while the duke and his huntsmen were burning and panting with great exertion and an intense desire to find their quarry, a stag of extraordinary size appeared. Its entire body was white as snow, and it was marked by no spot of any other color.

Immediately the vast space of the air was filled with the great shouts of the astonished huntsmen and the discordant barking of the rushing dogs; the wooded hills echoed with the cry. The dogs were released from all their couplings, and, their reins loosened, the horses were urged forward with all their strength.

But the handsome stag, protected by an almighty patron, easily mocked the fury of its pursuers. It either leapt over the nets placed before it or tore them apart unharmed by the force of its breast.

Thus, in vain the dogs’ keenness was spurred on, the horses’ speed driven by repeated blows of the spurs, and a great cloud of weapons sent after the stag. The animal, running without turning aside and turning aside while running, proceeded calmly at a leisurely pace, faithfully leading its pursuers to the place it had chosen.

At last it came to the aforesaid valley, to that part of the valley where the eternal and unchangeable Trinity was preparing an altar for the future title of its name. When it arrived there, it stopped; lowering its antlers, and displaying, after the manner of its kind, a certain expression of gentleness, it calmly looked back at its pursuers. [Col. 0706A]

There divine vengeance overtook the innocent creature surrounded by barking guilty dogs. Contracting all their limbs, it swiftly deprived them of every strength. You could see some gaping without barking; others unable to draw back the tongue they had thrust out; others remaining motionless even as they rushed forward.

At the spectacle of so great a miracle the duke and his huntsmen gathered there, and, their feet burning, congratulated one another from the depths of their hearts as though the animal had already been captured.

A wondrous event! Sudden vengeance seized the duke and his huntsmen, contracted all the limbs of their horses, and stripped them of every strength, just as it had done with the dogs.

When the great hero saw this miraculous sign—or the miracle of this sign—and, with the liveliness of his mind, contemplated the silence of the hidden mystery, [Col. 0706B] he exclaimed:

“Stop, stop, my huntsmen! You are not driving or pursuing a stag, but a messenger of the Most High God! This white stag,” he said, “indicates to us the place appointed, and a certain inhabitant and patron of the appointed place, one of supreme virtue.

“Therefore, hastening down from our horses, implore with humble devotion the most powerful Creator of all things, that he may deign to reveal to our ignorance what we perceive to be signified by a stag of such extraordinary form and by the evidence of this unusual event.”

They dismounted, therefore, and humbly prostrated themselves on the ground; and, prostrate, they reverently entreated the most powerful Lord of all things. When he looked upon their devotion, [Col. 0706C] he revealed the meaning of the present miracle and restored their horses and dogs to their former health.

For when they had finished praying, rose, and eagerly turned their eyes again toward the stag, the stag, with its head lowered, made a circuit in the same place like a sphere. By this silent movement it indicated that there, in its name, a dwelling should be built for the one whose power of greatness governed the whole world.

After this the stag vanished. None of those standing by observed whether it had ascended upward, entered the earth, or turned away by some other route.

The duke, therefore, rejoicing and understanding the meaning of the present miracle, gave thanks to divine providence. He ordered branches to be cut and the cut branches to be carried there, and hastily fitted together with twigs and branches a sort of model of a church at the place indicated by the stag. In his mind he resolved that he would soon build there, on a considerable scale, an oratory for the triune and one God.

But since God had ordained otherwise, and had destined the glory of so great a work for another king, Duke Ansegisus put off his human nature; and, as many years passed, the place mentioned above remained uncultivated, unknown, and unhonored.

## Annotation

Who or what sort of duke this Ansegisus was is not precisely stated, unless one turns one’s eyes to Trithemius and others, with their endless genealogies of the ancient kings and princes of Gaul. I willingly pass them over. [Note: [Col. 0705D] Trithemius, *On the Origin and Kings of the Franks*; Annius of Viterbo, in the same work; Charron, in the *Universal History of Gaul*. [Col. 0706D] Wasseburg, in *The Antiquities of Belgic Gaul*.]

As for the stag, however, which appeared to the same Duke Ansegisus in the wondrous sequence of the event, nothing unusual or new occurred, since very similar—and indeed much greater—events happened to the blessed Eustace, Hubert, and others. John Roberti discusses and reviews these matters learnedly, following Saint John Damascene, Book III, *On Images*. [Note: [Col. 0707D] In *The History of Saint Hubert*, Part III, Question 3.]

## CHAPTER V—On Blessed Vaningus and How He Was Seized by a Fever

Many days and years had passed, and no one worthy was found either to build the oracle that had been signified or to whom the ineffable Trinity of supreme mercy might disclose the command to build. For the exaltedness of divine providence was waiting for a man whom, freed from the prison of carnal desire, it might consecrate and preserve as a pleasing temple of the Holy Spirit.

It was fitting that a man who was himself the spiritual temple of God should build a bodily temple for God—a man who, having considered the image within himself, might understand how he ought outwardly to arrange and build a temple for the Creator of all things.

For this reason Saint and glorious confessor Vaningus was at last chosen for the building of so great an oracle, and, once chosen, was instructed. The nobles of Gaul admired the excellence of his noble deeds, and the heavenly court rejoiced in the grace of his celestial conduct.

He possessed what not many, but only a few rich men, are accustomed to possess: both a desire for eternal things and an abundance of temporal goods. In the merciful expenditure of these goods he looked for neither the favor nor the repayment of mortals.

Because of such merits he was both a friend of God and renowned in the world, and he was a familiar and confidant of King Lothair. King Lothair had entrusted Blessed Vaningus with the greater part of his kingdom; nevertheless, in arranging or administering the whole, he followed and listened to the prudent counsel of the blessed man.

I say that King Lothair had entrusted to Blessed Vaningus the territory of Calciacum. Because of its abundance of ancient forests and the pleasant hunting of various wild animals, Vaningus loved its valleys and reasonably judged that they should be entrusted to no one except a familiar and faithful man.

Faithfully guarding the forests entrusted to him, Blessed Vaningus frequently visited them and, by visiting, inspected them. He did not rejoice so much in the sport of capturing or the profit from captured animals as he sought relief from the turmoil of the flesh in the shade and solitude of the forests.

With this purpose he judged the woods of Fiscannus more suitable and, having judged them so, visited them frequently, unaware of Duke Ansegisus’s earlier revelation, of the manifestation of the holy place, and of the reverence due to the future oracle.

For Blessed Vaningus showed no reverence to the holy place. Rather, there he frequently coupled his dogs, stretched his nets, drove fleeing beasts, or stripped captured animals of their hides. Divine majesty, in its mercy, corrected this transgression arising from excessive ignorance of the law: it chastised the holy man and gave a clear indication that the miracle would be fulfilled.

Suddenly the holy man was seized by the burning heat of an immense fever. It weakened the structure of his whole body, cruelly deprived all his limbs of every strength, threatened to take away his life, and seemed to bring immediate death.

As the affliction grew heavier, his vital strength was entirely confined; once confined, it was extinguished. While his outward man was consumed, his inner man was extended and carried away in a kind of great ecstasy.

I say that Saint Vaningus was led to the glorious places of the blessed and to the cruel torments of miserable human beings. On his return he recounted the crowns of the righteous and the punishments of the rejected, and clearly set them forth with the evidence of his own experience.

After he had seen the everlasting dwellings of blessedness and misery, Blessed Vaningus was presented to a certain judge and brought and placed before the lofty throne of his majesty. [Col. 0708B]
