But as he contemplated the immeasurable radiance of the seat, the terrible appearance of the one seated upon it, and the innumerable multitude standing around—and as he was terrified by what he contemplated—he fell. Prostrate with his whole body, he lay before the Judge’s presence as though lifeless and bewildered.

Then the Judge said:

“How is it, Vaningus, that you are ignorant that the valley of Fiscannus is to be consecrated to my name, and that through your ignorance you dishonor it? Why, by paying no attention to the place of my consecration, do you not shrink from defiling it? Do you not fear incurring my ancient anger, when you faithfully recognize my omnipotent will?”

He had spoken, and the chorus of elders standing around confirmed the judgment of their Emperor with grave severity on their faces.

But Saint Vaningus, greatly terrified, did not dare to open his lips at all, [Col. 0708C] nor to raise his head from the ground. In the purity of his heart, however, he both confessed his guilt and sought pardon, offering only the excuse of ignorance.

While all those standing by remained silent, and by their silence testified both to the discipline that should be imposed and to the indulgence that should be shown, only Saint Eulalia the virgin rose. Taking up the cause of the man lying there, she softened the severity of the merciful Judge, entreated that his ignorance be pardoned, and by her intercession prolonged the present life of Saint Vaningus, her familiar and friend, for twenty years.

Saint Eulalia was therefore heard, and the saint was entrusted to her, so that she might instruct him fully concerning how he should establish the holy oracle and to what persons he should entrust it once established.

The virgin said to him:

“You will recover, Vaningus, and live; you will be restored to your possessions and return to the valley of Fiscannus. In the valley of Fiscannus, diligently inquire from the inhabitants about the place revealed to Duke Ansegisus. When you have found it, hasten to cultivate it; there faithfully build a suitable temple for the supreme and undivided Trinity.

“When the temple is completed, you shall entrust it to holy virgins, and you shall take care to place over them Childemarcha, a virgin of Bordeaux, a renowned abbess and mother there of many virgins.”

## CHAPTER VI—On the Fiscannense Church, First Founded by King Lothair and Endowed with Very Rich Estates

When the words of so great a revelation had ended, Saint Vaningus received life together with health, and health together with life. As all his limbs recovered equally, he sought King Lothair and explained the whole course of his revelation.

The king, moved and terrified by these things, said:

“Hasten, my son Waningus, return, and diligently seek the holy place according to the truth of your account. With my resources and your own, build there, as quickly and gloriously as you wish, a palace for the Most High Emperor.”

Hearing this with a joyful heart, Blessed Vaningus immediately returned to the territory of Calciacum. Entering the forest of Fiscannus, he sought out, found, and cultivated the place mentioned above.

Workmen were brought in. Ancient oaks were cut down and felled; twigs and thorns were uprooted and burned; and the site of the heavenly dwelling was cleared and freed from the brambles and briars of its ancient solitude. [Col. 0709B]

Foundations were laid, and with ineffable speed the sacred walls rose. As though by the almighty operation of divine power, the roofs were put in place, and the buildings described in the revelation were completed.

When the building had been finished and completed, King Lothair of Gaul was invited. Holy Fathers from many cities were summoned and assembled, and the oracle that had been made was marked and consecrated under the title of the Creator and governor of all things. Once consecrated, it was generously endowed with royal treasures and estates, and was enriched and enlarged still more abundantly by a mass of wealth.

## CHAPTER VII—How King Lothair Entrusted the Care of the Temple to Childemarcha and Numerous Virgins, with Saints Audoenus and Wandregesillus as Administrators

[Col. 0709C]

King Lothair ordered that holy virgins be gathered. When they had assembled, he ordered Childemarcha, a virgin of supreme holiness, to be placed over them according to the command of Blessed Eulalia; and he entrusted and committed the general administration of the whole Church to the holy and blessed confessors Audoenus and Wandregesillus.

## CHAPTER VIII—How Ebroinus Cut Out Blessed Leodegarius’s Tongue and How He Later Recovered It by Divine Power

The devout holy virgins assembled. They wrote immutable charters of their promised virginity to their heavenly Bridegroom. By the aromatic fragrance of their conduct they admonished and inflamed all the surrounding provinces to serve the almighty God. [Col. 0709D]

The blessed Trinity, the unchangeable God, rejoiced both in the completed temple and in the service of the assembled virgins. Beholding the continuous praises by day and night of the three hundred and sixty-six virgins, it promised them deliverance from death and prepared for them, in the enduring city, the unfading crown of blessed reward. [Col. 0710A]

At that time Blessed and glorious martyr Leodegarius was brought to Fiscannus. The savage and impious apostate Ebroinus had unjustly expelled him from the seat of his bishopric, stripped him of much property, and, after cruelly cutting out his tongue, deprived him of the entire function of speech.

But when the glorious martyr and bishop entered the sacred house of the supreme and almighty God and heard the angelic voices of the singing virgins, he recovered the use of the tongue that had been taken from him. For the course of two years he lived among the holy virgins, displayed a model of humility and patience, and watered and made fruitful the hearts of those who heard him with the dew of heavenly teaching.

When Blessed Vaningus saw the unexpected glory of the temple, the devotion of the holy congregation, and its heavenly multitude, he reviewed all the wealth of his property and assigned it for the use of the holy virgins. Throughout the whole course of his life he displayed, in that church, the humility and obedience of one who serves, according to the rule and custom of those who minister there.

## Annotation

From this account several points should be noted.

1. Clotharius, or Lotharius, of whom mention is made, was the third of that name, the son of Clovis II. He assumed the reins of the kingdom after the year 662 and reigned for four years. [Note: [Col. 0709D] Sigebert, under the year 662; Peter Roverius, note 1 to the *History of the Monastery of Saint John of Réomé*, under the year 660; Nicholas Gillius, in the *History of the Franks*, under the year 662; Carion, in the *Chronicle*, and Corrozet, Book I of the *Treasury of French History*, title 1, under the year 663; Baronius, volume VIII of the *Ecclesiastical Annals*, under the year 664.]

By the royal generosity with which he enriched that monastery, he is rightly recognized as its founder.

2. Saint Audoenus, archbishop of Rouen, labored greatly, by his episcopal authority and pastoral vigilance, for the foundation of this abbey. For this reason he too is found called its founder by Ordericus, who consistently writes that he “founded one monastery of nuns at Fiscannus.” [Note: [Col. 0709D] Ordericus, Book III of the *Ecclesiastical History*, under the year 678; Coenalis, in *Saint Audoenus, Archbishop*; Nicholas Gillius, under the year 698; Charron, chapter 103 of the *Universal History of Gaul*.]

Nicholas Gillius accepts this; but both men are mistaken in assigning the date.

3. Saint Wandregesillus, abbot of Fontanella, also deserved the title of founder, both because of the illustrious nobility of his lineage and the immense wealth he possessed, which was doubtless bestowed upon this same abbey, and because of the spiritual direction and discipline of monastic observance that he taught there, according to Sigebert:

“Saint Wandregisillus,” he says, “also called Wando, the nephew of Ansegisus, mayor of the palace, through his brother Walchiso, flourished at this time. He built the monasteries of Fiscannus and Fontanella for God.” [Note: [Col. 0710D] Sigebert, in the *Chronicle*, under the year 492; Belforest, Book I of the *Frankish Annals*, chapter 41; Theuntus, volume II of the *Cosmography*, Book XV, chapter 9; Nicholas Gillius; Charron; Corrozet, title 29 above; Quercetanus, Book VII of the *Antiquities of the Franks*, chapter 6; Choppinus, Book II of the *Monastic History*, title 2, §20.]

He is mistaken, however, when he says that this saint died in the year 665. [Note: [Col. 0710D] Surius, on 22 July, and Gazetus; Baronius, in the same place, in his notes on the *Roman Martyrology*, and volume VIII of the *Annals*.]

We therefore say that this monastery of Fiscannus was built after the year 662, not in 659, as Antonius Yeppes maintains, nor in 660, as the *Chronological Treasury* believes. [Col. 0710D]

Furthermore, since it is certain that Saint Leodegarius, bishop of Autun, stayed at Fiscannus during his exile, it follows that he remained there before the year 685, when he was crowned with martyrdom by the impious Ebroinus, mayor of the palace of King Theuderic I, according to Sigebert, Baronius, Surius, and others. [Note: [Col. 0710D] Part II of the *Annals of the Benedictine Order*, century 2, under the year 659, chapter 2.]

Finally, it appears that the aforesaid Saint Waningus died around the year 685. For, as is confirmed by the heavenly vision granted to him, his life was prolonged for a period of twenty years—namely, from the beginning of the construction of this abbey, around the year 662, until about 682.

Ferrarius must therefore be corrected when he says that he flourished around the years 707 and 730. It is no more true than the statement he adds: “At Caletes, in Gaul, Saint Waningus, monk of Fiscannus.” [Note: [Col. 0711D] Ferrarius, in the *Catalogue of the Saints*, 9 January; likewise in the new *Topography* under the *Roman Martyrology*, entry “Fisci-campus.”]

I am not unaware that the Benedictine Martyrology speaks of him; but without identifying him as a monk, it says: “At Fiscannus, Saint Waningus, confessor.”

Hugo Menardus, an otherwise pious and learned man, noticed this and aptly drew the following conclusion:

“It is said in the same Legendary that the blessed Waningus had resolved to give himself to the monastic order, but that God provided otherwise. Although this is true, he should not on that account be removed from the Benedictine order, since he lived for many years with the nuns of Fiscannus, and, as is credible, according to a regular observance. For, since he desired the monastic life with his whole heart, nothing prevented him from living according to the manner of those same virgins.” [Note: [Col. 0711D] Menardus, Book I of the *Observations on the Benedictine Martyrology*, 8 January.]

Accordingly, Molanus spoke of him absolutely and clearly in these words:

“In Normandy, the deposition of blessed Waningus, confessor: he founded the noble monastery of Fiscannus and sheltered Leodegarius in exile.” [Note: [Col. 0711D] Molanus, additions to Usuard, 9 January.]

Saussayus agrees with him. [Note: [Col. 0711D] Saussayus, in the *Gallican Martyrology*, on the same day.]

Moreover, in the monastery of Ham, belonging to the regular canons of the Order of Saint Augustine in the diocese of Noyon, his sacred relics are preserved with the greatest worship and veneration. His reliquary was opened in the year 1199, in the presence of Odo III, lord of Ham, and John, the abbot. At that time a document was placed inside it to testify to the memory of the event for posterity. It was opened again in 1382 and, for the third time, in 1562, while a very large assembly of both orders looked on. The citizens of Ham and the neighboring people venerate his feast with pious devotion on 9 January. [Note: [Col. 0711D] Hemeraeus, in *Augusta Veromanduorum Illustrata*, under the year 1108, p. 142.]

Finally, it must be concluded that Saint Hildemarcha arrived at Fiscannus before the year 665, when—as we recently said—Saint Wandregesillus, the archimandrite, died. She had been divinely sent to him so that she might undertake the governance of the new monastery and the care of the nuns living there. She was placed over them by Saint Audoenus, archbishop of Rouen, and blessed as abbess.

She herself eventually departed this life on 25 October, after the year 685, when Saint Leodegarius was carried into heaven crowned with the laurel of martyrdom. On the same day her memory is commemorated in the Benedictine Martyrology:

“On the same day, Saint Hildemarcha, first abbess of Fiscannus.” [Note: [Col. 0711D] *Benedictine Martyrology*, 25 October.]

Saussayus also inserted her into the Gallican Diptychs. [Note: [Col. 0711D] Saussayus, in the supplement to the *Gallican Martyrology*, on the same day; Ferrarius, in the new *Topography*, entries “Fontanella” and “Rouen.”]

It is therefore erroneous to write, concerning Saint Eulalia, virgin and martyr, who appeared to Blessed Waningus, that she was the first abbess of this place. [Note: [Col. 0712D] *Manuscript Antiquities of Normandy*, p. 52, in the possession of D. Bigot.]

## CHAPTER IX—On the Invasion of the Barbarians, the Destruction of the Temple, and the Expulsion and Slaughter of the Holy Virgins

[Col. 0711D]

After Blessed Vaningus had died and many days had passed, the pagan people of the Seine invaded the lower provinces of Gaul. With cruelty they destroyed cities, overturned fortresses, devastated towns and villages, and carried away and consumed the spoils and accumulated wealth of many peoples whom they had killed or driven into flight. [Col. 0712A]

In the most cruel storm of that age, the Fiscannense church was invaded and seized, and the holy virgins of so many merits were expelled and driven away.

Alas! The lofty structures of the oracle of so great a name were burned; the straight walls were pierced; and the very foundations of the temple were drawn out from their hidden places and shattered.

Many holy virgins whom excessive love of the glorious temple had held there fell beneath the hostile sword before the sacred altar itself. By pouring out their own blood they uselessly delayed the violence of the destroyers and, by delaying it, struggled to extinguish it.

Why say more? When the flames prevailed, the sacred temple was burned; the buildings adjoining the sacred temple were destroyed; and the ruins that alone remained testified that works of great preparation had once stood there. [Col. 0712B]

O divine patience! O patient deity! O greatness of patience worthy of admiration! O most almighty God! Although mad barbarism may devastate all the provinces of Gaul because of the sins they have deserved, at least let the house of your majesty, distinguished by its unique privilege, be spared and protected.

For what you accomplish by destroying your temple—whether you correct guilt, exercise patience, or punish the impurity of hidden disgrace—we do not know at all. Because we are wholly ignorant, we do not presume to investigate what preceded; that too is hidden from us.

We have nevertheless heard and learned that the confusion of the holy place, together with the return of the ancient thickets and its solitude, continued until the time of William II, duke of the Normans.

## Annotation

It is not expressly stated here who those pagans were who destroyed the monastery of Fiscannus. Yet they were without doubt the Normans, still pagan at that time, as the authors themselves acknowledge. [Note: [Col. 0712D] Above, in the abbey of Saint Audoenus, chapter 3, and in the chapter on Fontanella, chapter 9.]

In their time, around the year 842 and thereafter, when they were devastating everything throughout Neustria and Gaul by frequent raids and plundering, the monastery of the virgins itself was exposed to their fury. Many of the virgins were killed for Christ and were therefore rightly counted by Menardus among the holy virgin martyrs of the Order of Saint Benedict, in these words:

“Many nuns of the monastery of Fiscannus were slain by the Danes, that is, by the Normans.” [Note: [Col. 0712D] Menardus, in the Second Appendix to the *Benedictine Martyrology*, under the letter S, from the manuscript codices of Fiscannus; Yeppes, volume II of the *Chronicle of the Order of Saint Benedict*, century 2, under the year 659, chapter 2; Saussayus, in the Appendix to the *Gallican Martyrology*, under the letter S; Charron, chapter 114 of the *History of Gaul*.]

After peace had been restored to the Church and kingdom in the year 912, when Rollo, duke of the Normans, submitted his neck to Christ God through baptism, the aforesaid place of Fiscannus was again cultivated and inhabited by some nuns until about the year 989—not, however, 990, 996, or 999—when the virgins were thereafter transferred and settled at the monastery of Mont-Villare, already built there since the year 675, in the same diocese and in the region of Caletes. [Note: [Col. 0713D] The same Yeppes; Quercetanus, Book VII, *Antiquities of Gaul*, chapter 6; *Chronicle of Chronicles*, Part II, fol. 20, under Richard I, duke of Normandy; Grisius, *On Regular Clerics*, section 13, §9; Lanovius, in the *Historical Syntagma on the Chancellors of the Saints of France*, notes on the *Life of Saint Audoenus, Archbishop of Rouen*; *Manuscript Antiquities of Normandy*, pp. 225–226, in the possession of D. Bigot; Coenalis, volume II of the *Hierarchy of Neustria*, under the fourteenth bishop of Avranches.]

From this transfer Antonius Yeppes wrongly concluded that there had been two monasteries of virgins at Fiscannus. His interpreter Matthaeus Oliverius rightly rebukes him, since the two places and towns are entirely different.

It is therefore established that the monastery of Fiscannus was first inhabited by virgins. After they had been transferred elsewhere, regular canons succeeded them under William I Longsword, duke of Normandy. Let us hear the history of what happened from the manuscript already cited so many times.

## CHAPTER X—On the Restoration of the Fiscannense Church Under Duke William

After the long misery of wars had worn down and exhausted the provinces of Gaul, divine severity was at last appeased, remembered its ancient mercies, and granted suffering peoples the consolation of unexpected assistance.

Through the abundance of divine graces the erring pagans were pierced with remorse; and the minds of the barbarians, once remorseful, were converted. They pursued and venerated with the greatest devotion the truth of the Christian religion, which shortly before they had persecuted and abominated with savage madness.

Thus it happened that, by the gift and concession of Charles, king of Gaul, they received the seven farthest and maritime provinces. [Note: [Col. 0714D] By “provinces” he means the bishoprics of Neustria, which are seven.]

They were to cultivate these provinces by foreign settlers who would inhabit them through their labor, and to defend and protect them from the invasions of the attacking barbarians.

Once the peoples had been reconciled by divine power, peace was restored to the world; the cities that had been destroyed were fortified; the overturned fortresses were surrounded with suitable walls and embankments; and, as the colonists returned, the villages and fields were filled and cultivated.

Finally, the Normans, renewed by the grace of the spiritual sacraments, called the provinces they had received Normandy, after the name of their northern wind. Rollo I held the duchy of this land, and William, Rollo’s son, held it second.

In the time of this duke, the oracle of the eternal and undivided Trinity was discovered; once discovered, it was restored to the knowledge and use of many peoples and renewed.

Duke William ordered his servants to restore the town of Fiscannus and, in the restored town, to build a palace of great beauty and size.

His servants obeyed and undertook the work assigned to them. After restoring the town, they began to build a palace of lofty grandeur. While moving about there and striving to find stones and mortar for the construction of the palace, they discovered the ruins of sacred buildings. They decided to transport the ruins they had found into the building intended for human habitation.

But, suddenly inspired by a divine impulse, they summoned the ancient inhabitants and natives of that place, questioned them about the cause of the ruins they had found, and carefully investigated for what emperor or other power those ruins had once stood amid the lofty palaces.

“This place,” replied the natives when questioned, “was once a famous and celebrated valley, distinguished by the title of the Emperor of all things. It provided quiet and secluded habitation for many virgins.” [Col. 0714A]

When the holy workers heard this, they mourned the destruction of the sacred buildings, recoiled from the inhumanity of their paganism, and, granting freedom to the holy ashes, sought elsewhere for material for the work they had undertaken.

Once this material had been sought and easily found, they raised a palace of great magnificence. Fulfilling their duke’s command, they completed the extensive work they had undertaken within a short time.

When the task of so great a labor had been completed, they invited Duke William. They presented the completed fortress and palace to his judgment and authority.

Duke William praised their skill and the form of the completed works, but reproached their negligence because he had found no oracle of a church in the fortress beside the palace.

Rebuking his builders for this negligence, he said:

“Go and build a church at the site of those ruins, so that the sight of it may restore to those who behold it the memory of the holy temple, and at some time inspire me or one of my heirs with the desire to restore the ancient church.”

Hearing the duke’s command, the workmen approached the sacred places. Amid the very confusion of the fire and destruction, they laid the foundations of a small church. Having marked the site of the first altar, they raised walls of modest height from the stones and fragments of the ruins; they brought the walls they had raised to the intended dimensions without any interval.

When the walls had been completed, only the roof was lacking. Once its protective covering had been conveyed there, it would be necessary to keep the harshness of the air away from the entire building. [Col. 0714C]

Accordingly, carpenters were sought and, once found, brought in; responsibility for making the roof was assigned and entrusted to them. The carpenters seized their tools, adapted them to the work they had been ordered to enlarge, and prepared to enter the selected forests without delay.

## CHAPTER XI—On the Roof That the Sea Brought from the Territory of Coutances, and on the Two Beams That Were Missing
But as the interval of deliberation proceeded, divine omnipotence both released the craftsmen from the sweat of their appointed labor and recalled them, and declared and demonstrated its presence in the aforesaid little church through the glorious testimony of an extraordinary miracle (in the manuscript codex of the lord Bigot, the reading is: “in the district of Coutances, near a certain island in the sea” [Col. 0714D]). For the people of the province of Coutances had prepared a roof for a certain church of Saint Marculf and were preparing to place the roof upon that church. The sea, however, passing over it, seized and carried away that roof and, borne along by the service of a gentle wave, conveyed it to the shores of Fécamp; and—wondrous to relate!—in the presence of the erected walls of the holy little church, it dutifully set it down, then withdrew in an unharmed course into the channel of its own shore.

The workmen marveled at the receding sea, at the roof that remained, and at the fact that, although the roof had been battered by the force of storms, no loosening of any nail could be seen in the roof that had remained. A greater miracle followed. For when they placed the foreign roof upon its walls, they found it to possess such equality and correspondence of size that the most exact measuring lines or rods could scarcely have expressed a closer agreement. Two beams were missing. The sea had not withheld them when it carried off the roof; rather, the hands of the men of Coutances had not yet joined them to the other beams of the roof. The craftsmen were ordered to cut beams and, having cut them, to use their skill to supply and complete the roof’s deficiency. They obeyed: they cut the beams, measured what they had cut, and repeatedly attempted to fit them to the other members of the roof, which had already been set in place.

Yet the labor of the sweating craftsmen and their careful skill were wholly frustrated: no lines drawn by human craftsmanship could join the work of their labor [Col. 0715B] to the work of heavenly grace. While the distressed and anxious craftsmen were in this difficulty, someone who arrived relieved them and announced that two beams were lying on a distant shore; he asserted that, by placing them in position, the imperfection could be entirely completed. The craftsmen therefore rejoiced; the beams were carried over, and, once all the measuring had been dispensed with, they were easily placed in their proper positions. With its natural members thus supplied, the entire construction of the roof was completed and finished.

### CHAPTER XII  
### Concerning the angel, the knife, and the footprints remaining on the same stone upon which the angel ascended

Thus stirred by so great a multitude of miracles, the workmen sought Duke William, reported to him the extraordinary events concerning their work, and summoned him, with only a few words of persuasion, to the dedication of the church that had been built. [Col. 0715C] Then the duke, who deserved to be praised for the abundant wealth of heavenly graces, summoned many bishops and nobles. Accompanied by their multitude, he came to Fécamp, entered the new church, and ordered all that was necessary for the dedication to be prepared.

When these things had been sufficiently prepared and assembled, the duke and the bishops, together with many nobles, entered the church to be consecrated and carefully considered under whose saintly title it ought to be distinguished. While they held differing opinions, defended different judgments, and, according to the devotion each of them had toward particular saints, contended over the saint to whom the church should be consecrated, a man of exceptionally handsome face and clothing entered the church. His head and long beard were covered with brilliant white hairs. Without turning his eyes anywhere, he proceeded directly to the altar that was to be consecrated. Reverently bending over it, he placed a knife upon it; without breaking his silence by a single word, he turned and left the church. He entered a courtyard almost adjoining the church, climbed upon a millstone that lay there, and, lifting himself from it into the air, disappeared.

### CHAPTER XIII  
### How the duke and the bishops marveled that the angel vanished so suddenly

Many who had gathered at Fécamp that day for the dedication followed the departing angel and crowded around the stone upon which he had climbed. On that stone they found the angel’s footprints impressed as though in sand or dry dust. Disturbed by their astonishment at this event [Col. 0716A], they went to Duke William’s presence, and, as though he knew nothing of the miracle’s greatness, each one in turn hastened to recount to him what had happened.

They all rejoiced and surrounded with a gathered throng the altar upon which they had seen the knife placed by the angel’s hand. They all sought to explain what the deposited knife signified. Then the holy prelates took up the knife and found writing upon it. By its indication, the dispute among the nobles came to an end, and it was revealed under whose title the church ought to be dedicated.

The knife bore this inscription:

> In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity.

When the illustrious Duke William heard this, he leapt for joy and ordered the present church to be dedicated in honor of the holy and undivided Trinity. He confirmed this with an oath and with many promises: that the church would one day be enlarged through his work and that a church resounding with the privilege of so great a name would be magnified and raised up. But while divine providence arranged otherwise, the aforesaid duke was killed through the deceit and treachery of the Flemings, and the glory of enlarging the holy temple was transferred and granted to his son Richard.

### CHAPTER XIV  
### How Duke Richard, while standing at a certain lofty window of his palace, asked what church was situated there

One day, therefore, when the aforesaid Duke of Fécamp was leaning at a certain lofty window of his palace and could see far below the church of the holy and undivided Trinity, he questioned the nobles standing near him, as though he did not know, and inquired in the pleasing language of his gentleness about the name of the church before him. They replied:

“Father, your father founded this church and ordered it to be distinguished and dedicated under the title of the divine Trinity.”

When he heard this, the glorious duke was pierced by a great dart of grief. Streams of falling tears wet his rosy face and snow-white beard. After remaining silent for a long time and shaking his head, he finally broke into speech amid his sobs:

“O how ill it accords that I, a man of such ambition, should live in a palace, while almighty God lies beneath such a little hut! O, I say, how ill it accords that the heavenly Lord above should have a hut below, while the earthly servant below should possess a palace above! How much more reasonably would it be arranged for me to have a small dwelling—or none at all—and for the Lord of all things to possess the sole and greatest one!”

He had spoken, but he could neither restrain nor dry the waves of tears that poured forth, either by any strength of spirit or by the frequent deliberation of his hands. Then he added:

“Let many masons be sought and, once found, brought here, so that, in comparison with that little church which you despise, I may make this palace appear as nothing.”

### CHAPTER XV  
### Why Duke Richard, when rebuilding the church at Fécamp, placed with his own hand in the church’s foundation a stone upon which the angel had climbed

When the duke’s order had been received, faithful servants sought masons; by seeking, they found them; and, once found, they brought them [Col. 0717A] to the desire and presence of their lord. Carefully examining their skill, the duke said:

“Go everywhere through the mountains and valleys, seek stone suitable for building a temple of the one and triune God, and build a church of exceptional beauty and size on the site of that little church.”

[Note: The same account is given in the manuscript codex of the lord Bigot. [Col. 0717D]]

Without delay, stones that had been found were transported; a great multitude of pyres was burned; and a large quantity of material for the future temple was prepared and assembled. At last, when the foundation was to be laid, the holy duke was present. Taking up a mattock, he was the first to open the earth, and at the very beginning of the foundation he first laid down one part of the stone upon which, in the time of Duke William, the angel had climbed.

It was a source of immense delight to those who watched when so great a duke—conspicuous with his snow-white head, long beard, and tall body—went around among all the workmen, admonishing some, correcting others, urging on those who were idle, helping those who were laboring, and, by the example of his own fervor, equally kindling them all toward the completion of the work they had begun. Through the burning desire of this great and illustrious duke, the glorious temple of the holy and undivided Trinity was completed within a short time. It was beautiful in the quality and size that the diligent skill of expert craftsmen at that time was able to conceive as greater and more beautiful.

The interior walls of the holy sanctuary were painted with scenes from history, while the ceilings were ornamented with flowers joined together in a marvelous interlacing and distinguished by varied workmanship. After the adornment of the entire structure had been elaborately completed, each wall of the temple was polished and brought to, and finished in, its proper and perfect beauty.

Therefore the duke, rejoicing and marveling at the appearance of the completed work, which answered to the judgment of his will, richly endowed the new church with golden and silver vessels and ornaments. He clothed it most abundantly with a threefold adornment of silk, linen, and woolen curtains, and in a marvelous manner honored and enlarged it with both the ornaments of the sacred altar and priestly garments of gold and gems.

When all these things had been arranged and completed through the duke’s excessive generosity, the princes and bishops of all Normandy and of other provinces were summoned and assembled. The completed church was dedicated and given its title in the name of the holy and undivided Trinity. The aforesaid manuscript codex of the lord Bigot records that fourteen bishops were present at that time. [Col. 0717D]

### CHAPTER XVI  
### A remarkable miracle concerning the body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ

At that time a miracle worthy of being reported occurred near Fécamp. A certain priest named Isaac, when, after completing the prayers, he was about to receive the most holy sacraments of the Lord’s body and blood, found the substance of the body and blood covered not under the appearance of bread or wine, but plainly displaying the color and quality of flesh and blood.

Disturbed by the novelty of this event, the priest hurried to Duke Richard and to the assembly of the holy bishops [Col. 0718A] and disclosed the greatness of the unprecedented miracle. Then the duke, all the bishops, and a very great multitude of the people went there. According to the priest’s account, they found the event to be true; reverently lifting up the mysteries of such great significance, they carried them to the consecrated church. There, sealing the paten to the sacred chalice, they enclosed and deposited the most holy mysteries upon the altar of the holy Trinity, after the likeness of the angel’s knife, which they had enclosed in the crucifix.

The prudent duke, carefully joining the greatness of the present miracle to the multitude of ancient miracles, and balancing the authority of the church to be consecrated by the correspondence of both miracles, chose many canons. To the canons he had chosen he entrusted the holy church, so that they might dwell there devoutly and offer eternal praises and spiritual services to the Creator and Lord of all things.

When all the services had at last been completed, and the condition and supreme ordering of the entire church had been arranged and determined, the duke, now more eager, was recalled to the administration of his duchy, while the bishops returned more watchfully to the care of the sheep entrusted to them.

### NOTE

Robert of Torigni records this miraculous event in this manner, in the appendix to the chronicle of Sigebert, under the year 1182:

> “This also happened to a certain most holy priest near Fécamp, while he was singing Mass on the day of the dedication of the church of the Holy Trinity at Fécamp. Sending his deacon, he summoned the bishops who had gathered for the dedication. They came, and the priest took it in his hands, in the chalice, as it was vested, and they placed it upon the altar. The Lord’s goodness did this to confirm in us faith in his sacraments, upon whom the ends of the ages have come.”

The manuscript codex of the lord Bigot, cited above, commemorates the event as follows:

> “In those days there was a certain priest named Isaac, a man of good life, who frequently celebrated the solemnities of Mass at the altar of Saint Machutus, bishop and confessor, situated not far from Fécamp, at a distance of two miles. One day ...”

See, concerning this event, the entry for 27 March in *Neustria Sancta*. Rolliardus writes in his *History of Melun*, pages 406 and 407, that other similar events occurred elsewhere in Gaul.

### CHAPTER XVII  
### How Duke Richard caused the canons to be expelled from the church itself and introduced monks there

Meanwhile it happened that the canons of Fécamp imitated the conduct of other canons, entered the broad roads of perdition [Col. 0718D], and pursued the luxuries and laziness of temporal possessions with indulgence. When the most prudent Duke Richard heard of the canons’ wretched life and the misery of those who lived it, and learned of it by hearing, he grieved greatly. Abhorring the conduct and way of life of wicked men, he promptly sent a messenger to Cluny and summoned Saint Majolus to Fécamp with entreaties of great humility. He begged him to arrange and order the new church according to the rule and institution of Saint Benedict.

Saint Majolus replied:

“I will undertake the greatness of this labor, dearest son Richard, on this condition: that throughout your entire duchy you grant to God the custom commonly called *Pasnagium*, and that you decree that no prince under your authority may ever again exact it.”

Duke Richard, however, not through the disease of avarice, but because hidden divine providence was arranging matters and transferring to Abbot Saint William the glory of ordering the holy church, followed the counsel of his own men and did not heed the holy intervention of Saint Majolus. Thus it happened that Saint Majolus returned to Cluny, and the correction or expulsion of the canons was postponed for some time.

### CHAPTER XVIII  
### How Duke Richard, lying on a bed of sickness, appointed his son Richard as his heir and entrusted the church of Fécamp to him

[Col. 0719B]

At last the illustrious Duke Richard, worn out by the holy old age of a long life, was seized by the immense distress of a certain illness. His body weakened and all his strength exhausted, he was brought to his end. When he recognized, as his suffering grew worse, that his final hour was approaching, he summoned Richard, his son, in the presence of all the assembled nobles of his duchy and appointed him heir and successor to all his possessions.

“Son Richard,” he said, “I appoint you heir and successor to my duchy and name, and I entrust and commit the Fécamp church of the Holy Trinity to your vigorous protection and administration, so that you may fulfill in it my ardent purpose, exclude and drive away from it the filth and uncleanness of the canons, and hand over and entrust the holy Church to a multitude of holy monks who imitate the apostles. You shall not bury my body inside the holy church; instead, outside it, beneath the dripping eaves of the roof, you shall give me a common burial, so that the sacred roof’s flowing infusion of falling drops may wash the bones of one lying there—bones which my negligent and neglected life has defiled and stained with the pollution of all sins.”

When he had finished these words in a gentle and cheerful manner, he grew pale, as though lightly overcome by sleep. Having attained his desire, he returned, sent forth, and entrusted his soul to the Judge most powerful over all things, to be nourished by the bread of life and understanding and crowned with the glory of eternal blessedness.

When Richard saw the death and absence of the holy father, he became rigid like a stone and filled the entire hall with lamentations and cries [Col. 0719D]. At last, when he had regained his strength, he threw himself like a madman upon the lifeless body. He kissed it for a long time, struggling in astonishment as though he could call back one who was departing. Later, restored in spirit and relieved by the consolation of the surrounding nobles, Richard celebrated the funeral rites of the holy father for many days. Finally, in accordance with the order that had been given, he buried him beneath the dripping eaves of the holy church. Over his father’s tomb he built a basilica in honor of Saint Thomas the Apostle; and there, in honor of God and in recognition of the holy confessor, glorious miracles frequently shine forth and most clearly reveal to understanding minds the merits of the buried duke.

### CHAPTER XIX  
### How Richard II assigned the church of Fécamp to the use of the monks

[Col. 0720A]

Richard, the son of Richard, having assumed the duchy of all Normandy, at the very beginning of his duchy wisely withstood his rebellious Normans, successfully overcame them, and powerfully restored and subjected them to the customs of his father’s yoke. Once the seditions of his citizens had suddenly been calmed, and the neighboring provinces had been pacified and allied through the image of his father’s virtue, the illustrious Duke Richard began to shine forth and to spread the fragrance of his virtues, as it rose, through the various regions of the world.

By the incomparable nobility of his deeds he surpassed and overshadowed the renown and distinction of his predecessors, and he fashioned and presented to some of his successors an imitable model of life [Col. 0720B]. He demanded the brotherhood of holy communities from almost the entire world and paid each holy community whose fraternity he had received a voluntary annual tribute of great generosity, according to the amount he had prescribed.

His devotion is said to have been so excessive that, whenever he entered a city, he would not leave it before making the rounds of all the city’s churches before dawn, celebrating sacred vigils in each church, and pouring out and leaving behind streams of many tears. If by chance he found people praying there, he filled them with the immense gift of his generosity; by his arrival he awakened and summoned many needy people to nocturnal prayers.

When the illustrious Duke Richard, shining before almost the whole world with the radiant lamp of such graces [Col. 0720C], recalled the glorious command of his father, he proved by the result and evidence of his work that he had remembered it. For he assembled workmen of the highest skill, came to Fécamp, and with his own mouth marked out, arranged, and built the cloisters, the workshops, and all the other houses suitable for the use of the monks.

When all the workshops had been completed, only a supply of water was lacking. He laboriously diverted it and, leading it beneath the castle through suitable channels, caused it to flow through the rear towers of the church into the courtyard and to run abundantly through all the monastery’s workshops.

Meanwhile he carefully investigated and, while investigating, inquired whom above all he should trust and commit with the task of arranging and governing the church of the holy and [Col. 0720D] undivided Trinity according to the rule and institution of Saint Benedict.

At that time the abbot William, of blessed memory, was illuminating all the regions of the Roman Empire with the abundance of his profound religious life and was restoring and inflaming the hesitant spirits of many abbots through the image of his fervor. Highly educated in the liberal arts, trained in ecclesiastical disciplines and all spiritual duties, and likewise imbued and enlightened by the grace of almost every virtue, he had appointed and established Saint Majolus as abbot and master of the church of Divion.

To this illustrious and exceptional man the illustrious Duke Richard sent his envoys. He disclosed the purpose of his intention and entreated him with prayers of great humility to arrange and instruct the church of Fécamp according to the rule of Saint Benedict [Col. 0721A].

Abbot William of blessed memory is said first to have replied:

“Dearest sons, we have heard that the Norman dukes, barbarous and savage men, overthrow holy temples rather than build them; destroy and drive away rather than gather or nurture holy congregations of spiritual men. Therefore return to your duke and tell him that we are wholly unprepared for this undertaking, since we lack horses for conveying the brothers and pack animals for meeting the expenses of bringing in the brothers.””

When the illustrious duke learned this from the report of the envoys who had returned, he was alarmed and promptly prepared many horses and pack animals. When the envoys returned, he humbly sent them to Abbot William of blessed memory. [Col. 0721B]

Then the blessed abbot, weighing the duke’s persistence and importunity, and balancing against that importunity and persistence the intention and devotion of his spirit, gathered a very large multitude of spiritual brothers and set out. After a few days had passed, he presented himself and the presence of many brothers to the desire of the eager duke.

The excellent duke received him with the sincerity of his entire spirit and the love of complete sincerity, as though he had received Christ. Sending away the other servants, he himself served with his own hands. Within a short time he led him to Fécamp, gave and handed over to him the church of the Holy Trinity, and begged him to arrange and order the church that had been given and handed over according to the rule and institution of Saint Benedict.

The excellent Duke Richard, I say, gave and handed over the Fécamp church of the Holy Trinity to William, the abbot of blessed memory. He expelled the enormous multitude of carnal canons, retaining and restoring to the church all their possessions; and, for the canons who had been expelled and refused conversion, he provided suitable compensation elsewhere.

On the night before the day on which the church of Fécamp received spiritual monks and expelled the carnal canons, the entire roof of the church appeared to the canons to be covered with eagles. By these eagles the assembly and spiritual flight of the monks entering, and thereafter the descent and habitation of the protecting angels, are fittingly represented.

Thus the blessed and glorious Abbot William began to govern and administer the church he had received [Col. 0721D], to arrange and correct it according to the institution of Saint Benedict, and to summon truly faithful men from various provinces, uniting and confirming them in heavenly services.

By this sudden transformation the church of Fécamp burned and blazed with the zeal of heavenly men, and surpassed and overshadowed the surrounding churches in the glory of its much-praised reputation. Through its instantaneous transfer, the church of Fécamp attained such a summit of greatness that, just as it surpassed all the churches of Gaul in fact and in the appearance of the highest religious life, so it surpassed them in its name and in the special privilege of its designation.

The church of Fécamp shone greatly with frugality, chastity, and the abundance of voluntary poverty: with the light of virtues whose visible evidence revealed to others the hidden beauty of its form and kindled and urged the minds of those who looked upon it to adopt and imitate the rule of its way of life, as an example of perfect virtues.

At that time the church of Fécamp knew nothing of individual private ownership in anything; it knew only the united love of common possession. By distributing different portions according to the different needs of the needy, it renewed and represented the primitive image of the holy apostles.

For these excellent goods, maintained with outstanding perseverance, Duke Richard was wholly bound to the church of Fécamp, and all the diligence of his providence was directed toward the church’s interests. He loved and diligently frequented the regular life and true religious observance of the illustrious men of the church of Fécamp [Col. 0722B] to such an extent that he served the heavenly congregation with, so to speak, the gathered richness of his entire duchy. He himself often served the multitude of attendants who waited upon the brothers as they feasted; and, when this ministry of such great humility had been completed, he sat down last of all the brothers and rejoiced to be refreshed by the delightful nourishment of their regular meals.

### CHAPTER XX  
### Concerning the freedom of the monastery of the church of Fécamp, or how the duke freed it from every episcopal yoke

The illustrious duke therefore perceived the criticisms and disparagements of certain clerics, as well as their foreboding of future troubles. Because of the duke’s excessive devotion and his great reverence for the holy Church, the disease of envy had infected them and tormented those infected with the cruel distress of inward rancor [Col. 0722C].

When the duke learned of the malevolence of these detractors and recognized the arrogant presumptions and presumptuous arrogance of the clerics, he promptly summoned the bishops and nobles of all Normandy to Fécamp. He wrested and freed the Fécamp church of the Holy Trinity from every episcopal yoke and custom, whether just or unjust.

The archbishop of Rouen established this freedom and desired that it be established. He also freed and released fourteen other churches, on account of the memory of his father and the command and will of his present brother, from every episcopal custom and exaction. The archbishop and the other bishops strengthened the charter of the granted freedom by their signatures and consent, and, once strengthened, delivered it with the endorsements of noblemen [Col. 0722D].

The prudent duke, therefore, desiring in every way to confirm and secure the holy church, summoned King Robert and many nobles of Gaul to Fécamp. Through royal charter and authority, and with the consent and endorsement of his peers, he wrested and freed the Fécamp church from every episcopal yoke and custom, and confirmed and strengthened his own charter and ordinance and those of his nobles.

### CHAPTER XXI  
### How Abbot William went at the duke’s command and obtained privileges from the lord pope

The duke Richard rejoiced over the freedom established for the church of Fécamp and, with the living attention of his mind, considered its future perpetuity. He addressed William, the abbot of blessed memory [Col. 0723A], and, assigning him the duty of an embassy, sent him to the apostolic authority of the Roman see, laden with many gifts.

After completing his journey, Abbot William arrived in Rome. He explained to Pope Benedict, of pious memory, the reason for his arrival and the will of the duke who had sent him. With a prayer of great humility, he suitably requested confirmation of the charter that had been made and the authority of an apostolic privilege.

Pope Benedict, marveling at the duke’s diligence and at the supreme excellence of the friend whose presence he had received, confirmed the requested privileges and willingly handed them over. He freed and rescued the Fécamp church of the Holy Trinity from every episcopal yoke, subjection, and custom, and established and received it under the sole governance and protection of the Roman Church [Col. 0723B].

He established, I say, that Fécamp should be subject only to the Roman Church and immune, released, and completely free from the power of every other church, while the form of the monastery of Cluny remained in force.

Having received the carefully drafted privileges of apostolic authority, William, the abbot of blessed memory, returned swiftly to Normandy. He explained and demonstrated to Duke Richard that the duke’s desire had attained its intended result and that the duty of the embassy entrusted to him had been successfully completed [Col. 0724A].

The duke, therefore, made ineffable rejoicing and gave thanks to the triune and one God with the fervor of his whole devotion. By the hidden counsel of divine providence, God was freeing and releasing from the yoke and authority of all men, through the concurrence of so many persons, the church that Richard’s father had founded and that Richard himself, at his father’s request and command, had completed and arranged.

Afterward he honored his most beloved abbot William with great gifts and sent him, so honored, back to the church of the Holy Trinity at Fécamp. Again and again he earnestly entreated him to guard the church entrusted to him according to the religious discipline of the order he had begun, and, by guarding it, to complete and confirm it.

The blessed abbot received these holy prayers and the excessive humility of these holy requests as though they were oracles of God. He entered Fécamp and, through the turning of many years, governed the church of Fécamp until the duchy of Robert of Jerusalem. He kindled and reformed his subjects by word and example according to the image and likeness, honor and glory, of almighty God, who lives and reigns forever and ever. Amen.

[Col. 0723]

## A SUPPLICATION OF THE MONKS OF ARLES

To the Fathers assembled in council at Saint Tiberius in the year 1050, against the invaders of the monastery’s possessions.

*(Mansi, Councils, XIX, 793.)*

[Col. 0723C]

To the orthodox Fathers worthy of every kind of veneration, whom holy faith has gathered together from different regions, and whom the bond of brotherly affection rightly joins in the double bond of charity—to the pontiffs, that is, to whom the care of God’s churches has been entrusted—the very small flock of the monastery of the blessed Mary, Mother of God, at Arles, sends this petition to your clemency. In it are recorded the estates which it complains have been taken away from its rightful possession by unjust and wicked men, whether by force, by unlawful donations, or under the pretext of any kind of fraud.

For let your holiness know that, because of the loss of so many estates, we are unable to bring to completion the monastery whose construction has recently begun, since the necessities required to sustain human weakness are lacking [Col. 0723D]. Therefore the aforesaid monastery, wearied by such varied misfortunes, implores almighty God and your collective clemency: for love of that glorious Mother, may you, by pontifical authority, strike the holders of the aforesaid estates with the bond of just condemnation and excommunication, until they restore them to the aforesaid Virgin.

These, then, are the names of the estates and of the knights who possess them.

First, the freehold of Saint Mary which she has in the county of Berchita, namely at Marola with the church itself; and at Avisano, a woman of the late Reynald holds it with her son.

Raymund, son of Arnold, holds the freehold of Orlarios; Gausbert, that of Pidre and Ursiniano; William, son of Oliba, that of Corneliano; William, son of John, holds Saint Mary of Panisar and the vineyards of Clusa.

William, son of Dalmatius, holds the freehold of Maras, of the Field of Eldric, of Tressera, of the village of Mulacha, and that of Keixanos.

Bernard of Oliva holds the freehold of Rutmors, of Kastellone, and of Rodas.

Aicard, son of Odo, holds the freehold of Rabdos.

Bernard, son of Adalbert, holds the church of Chasamori.

Arnold, son of John, holds the freehold of Elsinas.

Seniofred, son of Miro, holds the freehold of Terradas and, at Pines, half a mansus.

Deusdefranc holds one mansus at Terrodas.

Segarus, son of Berard, holds those mansus and freeholds at Terradas; at Cirasia, three mansi; those mansi together with the freehold of Ortos; those mansi together with the freehold of the village of Rubeo; those at Vilaro Castellano; and the freeholds of Costa, Felgus, Valedella, and Campo Sambuce.

Seguinus holds at Albiniano seven mansi and bordas together, as well as the tenth share of Rabugadas with half a mansus, and many other things he takes away from us.

Udalgerius, the viscount, holds the entire freehold of Alleles.

### The synod pronounces an anathema against the invaders of the monastery’s possessions.

When holy faith compelled us to gather together from various regions for the celebration of a holy synod [Col. 0725A] on the Ides of July at the church of Blessed Tiberius, amid a multitude of religious abbots and most honorable men and women of every age and rank, a written complaint was brought before our eyes by monks of the monastery of holy Mary the Virgin at Arles, together with the estates listed above, which unjust men were taking from them. Because of this loss of property they were compelled to approach our presence and seek our assistance; to deny it to them is neither proper to our office nor right, since we ought to help those in danger and administer justice to those in need.

Therefore we, humble bishops of Jesus Christ, observing so great and unheard-of a complaint by the servants of God, are moved by the prompting of the same Spirit to restrain it, insofar as we can, in accordance with the decrees of the canons. Accordingly, I, Wifredus, metropolitan of holy Narbonne, confirm this.

+ Hugo, bishop of Uzès.  
+ Arnaldus, bishop of Maguelonne.  
+ Berengarius, bishop of Béziers.  
+ Bernardus, bishop of Lodève.  
+ Gontarius, bishop of Agde.  
+ Berengarius, bishop of Elne.

[Col. 0725B] We, together with the legates of our other fellow bishops and with religious abbots from various orders of Gothia and Spain, unwilling to depart from the rules of the holy Fathers and inflamed by the fire of the Holy Spirit, strike those involved in the destruction of Malo, Saint Mary, and Riarde—namely Roland and the others who consented—who are or shall be entangled in the fault and negligence written above, according to the degree to which they are or shall be implicated in the fault, by the sword of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, and by the anathema [Col. 0725C] of all the faithful of God who are, were, and shall be.

Unless they come to true repentance and amend their conduct as far as they can, let them be excluded from the thresholds of the holy Church of God. Let all those named above be under anathema, and let us multiply upon their heads all the curses of the Old and New Testaments.

Cursed be they in the city; cursed in the countryside; cursed be their barns and their storehouses; cursed be their food and their leftovers; cursed be the lower parts of their bellies and the produce of their lands, their herds and their flocks; cursed be those entering and those departing. May the Lord send upon them hunger, pestilence, and rebuke in all the works they undertake, until he crushes and swiftly destroys them because of their wicked devices, by which they abandon the Lord.

May the Lord bring pestilence upon them until he wipes them from the land they possess. May he strike them with poverty, fever, cold, burning heat, oppressive warmth, corrupted air, and blight, and may he pursue them until they perish. May the Lord deliver them, falling before their enemies. May their corpses become food for birds and beasts of the earth, with none to drive them away.

May they be struck with blindness, madness, and derangement of mind; and at midday may they grope as a blind man is accustomed to grope in darkness, and may their steps not be directed. Cursed be their heads [Col. 0726B] through the seven gates—that is, through their nostrils, ears, eyes, and mouth.

Cursed be their brains, hair, shoulders, arms, hands, fingers, forehead, eyebrows, tongues, teeth, throats, chest, back, heart, belly, navel, inward parts, outward parts, hind parts, vital organs, groins, buttocks, knees, shins, ankles, feet, soles, joints, veins, articulations, entrails, bones, and marrow.

Let all these things named above be accursed in them unless they come to their senses and return to true repentance. Let this rule of cursing and anathematizing be observed and remain in all the principal churches.

Therefore, whoever knowingly speaks with the men named above, unless he has urged them to amend; or eats, drinks, sleeps, or shares anything with them, unless he repents—if he is a cleric, let him fear that he will imperil his own order; if he is a layman or woman, unless poverty or fear has compelled him, let him fear that he is to be destroyed by the condemnation stated above, anathematized, and excommunicated.

The synod was enacted on the Ides of July, in the year 1050 of the Incarnation of the Word, in the third indiction, the twentieth year, while King Henry was reigning in France; the sixth year of the eighteen-year cycle. Written by the hand of Oliva. + Guislibertus, by the grace of God bishop of Barcelona. Wifredus, bishop. +.

[Col. 0725]

# Sermon on Saint Marculfus, Abbot of Nantes and Confessor

*(Mabillon, Acts of the Saints of the Benedictine Order, sixth century, part II, p. 517, from a manuscript of the monastery of Saint Vincent at Laon.)*

[Col. 0725D] **1.** Venerable Fathers and beloved brothers, whom God makes to dwell together in his house in unity, may your kindly ears receive the words of our exhortation—or rather, the marks of divine power displayed through the merits of blessed Marculfus.

With Solomon bearing witness—or rather, with the Holy Spirit speaking through Solomon’s mouth—we have learned that “it is the glory of kings to conceal a word, but the glory of God to search out a matter” (Proverbs 25:2) [Col. 0726D].

[Note: [Col. 0725] This passage is expressed today in our Vulgate with the opposite meaning: “It is the glory of God to conceal a word, and the glory of kings to search out a matter.”]

Therefore, most beloved, let your affection know that we have investigated certain works of our Savior God—works which his Father by nature, and our Father by grace, continues to perform to this day, and which the same Son does not cease to perform with the Father. Thus, from the report of a faithful man of good repute, we learned what we have endeavored to commit to writing for the glory of God and the honor of his saints [Col. 0727A].

**2.** On the night following the day of the Lord’s Annunciation, in the church where blessed Marculfus rests bodily, we believe that God performed the following miracle.

That same night, when it was already well advanced, the light of the lamp in the church went out, and the familiar darkness of night returned. The sacristan, awakened from sleep, looked around and realized that the basilica lacked visible light. He left his bed in the dormitory and, without fear, went to the brothers’ kitchen so that he might light a candle there and restore light to the holy house.

But in the dormitory too he found the lamp extinguished, and in the kitchen itself he found the coals dead—not by accident, as we suppose, but so that the works of God might be made manifest. What, then, was the sacristan to do? [Col. 0727B] He did not know. Finally, stunned by extreme sorrow, he returned to the oratory. There he prostrated himself before the altar and devoted himself to prolonged prayer, begging the divine majesty to come to his aid, through the merits of its saint resting there, in this moment of need, lest light be lacking to the brothers who were soon to sing the morning office.

The Almighty did not delay hearing and receiving the tears of the poor man crying out to him in affliction. For, overcome by grief and also wearied by the prayer itself, while Elbertus—for that was the name of the sacristan mentioned above—was returning to the small space of his bed, he was still weeping. Believing that through his own negligence the church was deprived of light, he looked around by a divine prompting and saw the entire basilica shining with heavenly light.

Suddenly rejoicing with great joy, he approached the lamp that had gone out shortly before and found it burning most brightly. At once, pouring tears of joy over the tears of his sorrow, he offered to God and blessed Marculfus hymns of praise and jubilation, and then went to sleep more securely.

In the morning, when the veil of night had been removed and the day was shining clear, he summoned the brothers of the place, namely the monks of the most blessed Remigius, and, in my presence—I who wrote these things—revealed to them what had happened. He affirmed that the power of God and the authority of his saints confirmed everything he said, as well as what we have decided to insert in this little document.

**3.** Even in our present sorrowful age, almighty God displayed a no less remarkable miracle in the same church, so that, since he had ineffably glorified his chosen one in heaven, he might deign to make him wondrous on earth as well, for the understanding of mortals [Col. 0727D].

For the healing of that illness which they call the royal disease [Note: [Col. 0727D] You see here the disease of scrofula—for Saint Marculfus presides over its cure—which was formerly called “royal.” Otherwise, the ancients use this name for leprosy.] such grace was bestowed upon him as a heavenly gift that crowds of sick people continually flock to him, no less from distant and barbarous nations than from neighboring ones.

One day, then, because of this grace, a certain man came to the church and offered a gift of his devotion. He explained the reason for his arrival to the man whose office it was to receive such matters. This custodian of the sacred affairs of the church was a man of great reverence in Christ. He had fled from the waves of the world to the harbor of the monastery and had served there for several years.

After receiving from that same lord Robert—for that was his name—everything customarily provided for his healing, the sick man added:

“Indeed, Father, since I come from far away, I now intend to return to my homeland. But I ask this as an act of devotion: may this candle which I have offered burn before this most sacred tomb for as long as it can last, until it is completely consumed. For when I was in my own country, I often offered it to blessed Marculfus, if not in action, certainly in desire.”

It was of no small size, sufficient to provide light in the church for three full days; and already, before the altar that is in honor of the same confessor of Christ, it lay burning across the pavement [Col. 0728B]. After the monk had promised that he would fulfill what the pilgrim had requested, the pilgrim departed.

Then Elbertus, whom we mentioned above, as though wishing to do something else, placed his foot upon the candle and extinguished it. He set it aside, extinguished, beside the coffin and went away, intending to close the church doors behind the pilgrim.

Immediately, once the doors had been secured and before he returned, the candle was kindled by divine power. So great a flame sprang from it that it suddenly reduced the coffin and the garments laid upon the coffin to ashes. The candle itself, just as the poor man had asked of the saint, was immediately consumed.

It is a wondrous thing that, in what was almost two moments, both a many-branched flame grew up and completely consumed whatever it seized. But if we consider the devotion of one man and the negligence of the other, it is entirely clear that, in response to the fraud committed, a just divine punishment followed [Col. 0728C].

You would have seen, I confess, a miracle involving insensible things, intended to rebuke the greed of sensible beings—that is, of human beings. The brothers who were nearby came running, for they had heard the crackling of the fire and the custodian shouting. They did not know what to say or do, since nothing remained that they could rescue from the flames.

But he confessed amid deep sobs that he was guilty and responsible for this danger. After the brothers had imposed a penance upon him, it was established in common and confirmed by the bond of anathema that the lights offered by the faithful should never thereafter be expended for any purpose other than the uses of that church and of the brothers serving there.

[Col. 0728D] **4.** Dearly beloved brothers, it is necessary to commit to memory, in praise of this most holy patron and protector of ours, Marculfus, what, by God’s gift, was displayed before our eyes: the man whom almighty God has deigned to give as a special intercessor for us.

He is the one who continually prays for his people and for the inhabitants of this holy monastery of his. At the time when those who were present at the miracles of this blessed man at the fortress of Péronne, who saw him shine with miracles and touched him with their hands, revealed to us, who had remained at his glorious seat, how greatly he was honored there through his wondrous works [Col. 0729A], there was a lamp burning before the altar where he rests in his precious body.

It was never extinguished by day or night, because although he was bodily absent by a short distance, he was not spiritually absent. The man in charge of the church’s service began to say to himself in thought that the lamp was burning in vain, since the body of blessed Marculfus was not present. He failed to consider that the Lord’s body was there [Note: [Col. 0729C] In the archive of the monastery of Saint Remigius I read a letter from Abbot Simon attesting that Odo of Sarcey, a monk, had acquired revenues with his consent and had established from those revenues that a candle should burn perpetually in the church of Saint Remigius before the high altar, upon which the body of the Lord is placed. This was done under William, archbishop of Reims, around the year 1165.

A century earlier, Paul, abbot of Saint Alban’s in England, had done the same. According to Matthew of Paris, he gave a [piece] of silver so that a candle might be kept continually burning before the high altar. Aimoin observes that at Fleury it had been established by the ancient Fathers as a custom that the church should be illuminated both day and night by the light of three lamps. Lamps, therefore, were commonly used in former times; candles more rarely, for continuous light in basilicas.]

—and that the greater and more excellent presence was guarded by angels.

When he had entertained this foolish and empty thought, he extinguished the lamp and went away. But after an hour had passed, he returned because some necessity compelled him. Wonderful to relate, it immediately appeared before his eyes. He saw the same lamp shining with angelic brightness, suspended in an ineffable manner so that it was held neither by a rope above nor supported by the ground below [Col. 0729B].

It was a great miracle to see that there was a cubit’s space between the rope and the lamp, and likewise a cubit’s space between the lamp and the ground. As I said, it had been kindled by heavenly light and burned wondrously.

Perhaps your mind would not have been sufficient to believe it, had not the gathering of the brothers and the people established its testimony. For, seized by fear and wonder alike, the man summoned from the entire village a great assembly of the people to see the extraordinary sight.

Many overflowed with tears, saying: “Since the most merciful confessor of Christ, Marculfus, their most vigilant guardian after God and their powerful advocate before God, although he had been elsewhere for a short time, has nevertheless deigned to console and visit his sons by displaying this miracle.”

This took place at Corbiniac [Col. 0730A], in the year 1085 of the Incarnation of the Word.

**5.** Therefore, beloved, you who have not refused to hear this and, as we suppose, to believe it, know that God has deigned to perform this so evident a miracle for the honor of his saint and also for our benefit. And not without reason.

For blessed Marculfus, while he dwelt in the flesh in this valley of tears, cast away the works of darkness and, clothed in the armor of light, bravely served the prince of that same light. Rightly, therefore, freed from the burden of the flesh and, as we believe, carried to the heights of heaven, he deserved to cling to the author of brightness.

We must therefore not doubt that he restored the extinguished light, since he could not tolerate the darkness of night in his basilica. Nevertheless, since nothing happens on earth without a cause, and since, as blessed Gregory teaches, we have learned that God and our Lord sometimes admonishes us to do good by words and sometimes by the very examples of miracles, let us seek the protection of this holy and blessed patron of ours, Marculfus, before whose sacred ashes we keep vigil and whose memory we solemnly celebrate today.

Let us seek, I say, his patronage, beseeching him that by his devout prayers he may drive away the darkness of our blindness and ignorance and obtain for us the light of heavenly grace. Enlightened by that light, may we cast away the works of darkness and, intent upon pious deeds, clothe ourselves in the armor of light. Armed with these things, may we trample the prince of darkness; and, having thus gained the victory, may we deserve to cling to the Creator of light, who lives and reigns, one God in Trinity.

[Col. 0729]

# A Short Work on the Seven Liberal Arts

*(Edited by D. Ravaisson, Reports on the Libraries of the Departments of the West, Appendix, p. 404, from a twelfth-century manuscript in the library at Alençon.)*

[Col. 0729C]

Run, thirsty ones, to the table of philosophy,

and drink the seven streams of its threefold flavor,

flowing forth from one spring, though by no single path,

which Pythagoras, having explored it, awakened for physics;

then Socrates and Plato ennobled it for ethics,

and Aristotle wedded it to eloquent logic.

From these, manifold schools, having found their material at Athens,

watered all Greece with this liquid;

and, overflowing, it poured without limit into Hesperia.

Yet not without a guide or a safe oar,

for Maro and Cicero, steering the ship,

each enlisted a hundred sailors for his own discipline.

[Col. 0729D]

Thus true philosophy conquered the threats of the sea,

taking our letters in place of Greek letters,

and at last, rejoicing, came to Rome through the waters of the Tiber.

For Rome was powerful through victories in war,

and just as she subjected all peoples to her commands,

so she said that she surpassed them with philosophical jewels.

Tullian eloquence bent these things to itself,

and his threefold rhetoric thunders with great force.

The Mantuan pipe, imbued with these things, strikes the stars.

From this point, after not a few cycles of years had passed,

Severinus succeeded, unlike them in nothing,

who adorned philosophy, inferior to none in merit.

Besides him and those mentioned above, there were many others:

[Col. 0730D]

teachers, poets, and writers of history,

[Col. 0731A]

some of whom we shall name here, as the order requires.

They are Plautus, Naso, Flaccus, Naevius, Terence,

Livy, Lucan, Varro, Statius, Sallust,

Pliny, Quintilian, Juvenal, Persius,

Ennius, Cato, Catullus, Macer, and Macrobius,

Martianus, Victorinus, Donatus, and Servius,

Priscian, the energetic restorer of the first art.

Yet we have passed over and left behind many distinguished men.

Now we shall try to taste here something from the arts,

something that will benefit students of these disciplines.

Grammar, presiding over the foundation of the first seat,

is divided into thirteen parts;

at the beginning, divided into five parts of two fours,

it is learned in the earliest toys of study.

With the help of its instrument it prepares the way for the others,

forming and teaching through countless rules.

[Col. 0731B]

To it is joined, second, civic rhetoric,

wordy above all, with five parts,

whose subject matter comprises three kinds of causes.

It calms forensic disputes, pleads causes, cries out,

judges by distinguishing, rejecting, and defending,

and turns laws wherever it wishes; it speaks, denies, and entangles.

From its kind comes dialectic,

which by nature is prior even to grammar,

while binding and loosening everything, though difficult to perceive.

[Col. 0732A]

It defines and distinguishes, divides and asserts,

able to reason, unconquerable in victory,

which the lamp of Manlius’s light has illumined.

He transferred it by explaining it in the two Analytics,

introducing the Isagoge in two commentaries,

and likewise the Categories together with *On Interpretation* (*Peri Hermeneias*),

the Topics with the Syllogisms and Differences.

He explained the book of Definitions together with the Divisions,

adding one book on Propositions.

From this point the quadrivium teaches abstract quantities,

proper to numbers, harmonies, and measures,

and weighs the courses of heaven, their paths, and the stars.

Its science is divided into four parts,

to be explained in two forms beneath its essence.

Here the diligent skill of Severinus bears witness:

[Col. 0732B]

the first of these, mother of the others, is arithmetic;

then music, mistress of the seven voices;

third, geometry; and thereafter the art of astrology.

It weighs heaven, earth, the sun and the zodiac, the moon, and the poles,

the parallels, the axis, and the ten circles,

and knows the positions of the stars in their two settings.

Rejoice, citizens of illustrious Pavia,

among whom rest the bones of the renowned Boethius;

you, made famous by these streams, are rightly outstanding thereafter.

[Col. 0731]

# Form of Excommunication

*(Mabillon, Analecta, new edition, p. 162.)*

## Note

This excommunication was issued toward the end of the tenth century, at approximately the time when Ragenardus, count of Sens, was excommunicated together with Gauzfridus and Geilo, canons of Sens. An example of that excommunication was first printed in volume X of the *Spicilegium*, and later by Étienne Baluze in the appendix to Regino. For various formulas of excommunication used in the ninth century, see Regino, abbot of Prüm, *On Ecclesiastical Disciplines*, book II, chapters 407 and following.

[Col. 0731C]

This is the excommunication under which Saint Theutbaldus, archbishop of Vienne, and Isarnus, bishop of Grenoble, stood.

Whoever among the inhabitants of Arles reads this document, I admonish, beseech, and adjure you, by the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, by the one God and Creator of all things, by blessed Mary, Mother of God, and by all the saints of God who stand in his presence: do not fail to announce it openly to everyone. Let no one remove it from the altar of Saint Stephen until it has been read and heard, and until you hear that the persecutors of the Church of God, whose case is at issue, have come to make satisfaction.

Let the prudence of all God’s faithful therefore know how I, Aimo, by the grace of God the most humble bishop of the see of Valence, made my complaint before the presence of our lord King Gondrad: namely, that Aikardus was unlawfully holding the land of blessed Apollinaris, the distinguished confessor of Christ, and of blessed Cyprian, the glorious martyr, and was possessing it with cruel boldness against God and his saints.

And since I could not in any way persuade him to do what was right, I judged it proper to seek the judgment of the eternal King, our Lord, and to entreat his ineffable mercy. For we truly know that the sword and fire of the heavenly Emperor work vengeance against the sons of unbelief.

With this necessity pressing upon us, and with the Lord our Savior protecting us, we sought counsel and assistance from our senior bishops living around us, and we obtained their support according to the desire of our heart.
