We have the excommunication of Lord Theutbaldus, archbishop of Vienne; Lord Amblardus, archimandrite of Lyon; Lord Wido, bishop of Le Puy; Lord Isarnus, bishop of the see of Grenoble; and also Lord Gerauldus, bishop of Geneva [Col. 0732D]. In this matter, their judgment and agreement are one.

And since Arles is and ought to be the head of this Gaul, we have decided to bring our complaint before its ruler, so that he may not disdain to lend his support to such great patrons as those mentioned above.

Let Aikardus, that cruel violator of the Church of God, therefore be excommunicated, together with all those who consent to him in so unjust a matter, by the authority of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, of all the saints of God, of the angels and archangels standing in the presence of God, and by the authority of all bishops, until they come to make satisfaction.

May all the curses that are read in the Old and New Testaments be upon them, so that they may swiftly perish by the sword of God and be led to the infernal place where their lamp may be extinguished forever, unless they come to amendment. Amen.

[Col. 0733]

# Diptychs of the Church of Arles

*(Mabillon, Analecta, new edition, p. 220.)*

## Note

In an extremely ancient sacramentary book of Pope Gregory, a book once used by the Church of Arles, the following names of the bishops of Arles are written at the end of the canon of the Mass, where the saints are designated by the sign of the cross. This list differs greatly from the commonly published lists, with which scholars may compare it.

Caesarius is included, but no bishop of the eighth century appears, contrary to Sigebert and others, who assign Saint Giles to that period. We have no doubt that this is the same Giles, the abbot who presented a petition to Pope Symmachus together with the notary Messianus on behalf of the Church of Arles. The pope replied to that petition in a letter addressed to Caesarius, bishop, during the consulship of Flavius Senator—that is, in the year 515.

# Names of the Bishops of the Holy Church of Grenoble

*(Mabillon, as above.)*

## Note

This catalogue will be of great assistance, both for supplying several bishops of Grenoble who are absent from the printed lists and for distinguishing the periods in which they lived; the same is true of the archbishops of Vienne.

Antonius Vionius Herovallius, auditor of the chamber of accounts, a man highly distinguished in the republic of letters, extracted this catalogue together with the form of excommunication printed above from an ancient manuscript and generously communicated them to me.

[Col. 0735A]

Bishop Domninus. Bishop Diogenius. Bishop Amicus. Bishop Sebastianus. Bishop Vitalianus. Bishop Ciratus. Bishop Viventius. Bishop Victor. Bishop Ursolus. Bishop Siagrius. [Col. 0735A] Bishop Isicius. Bishop Clarus. Bishop Ferreolus. Bishop Boso. Again Bishop Isicius. Bishop Austrobertus. Bishop Ramnoldus. Bishop Ragnomarus. Bishop Austoricus. Bishop Corbus. [Col. 0736A] Bishop Leopertus. Bishop Ardincus. Bishop Odolardus. Bishop Radoldus. Bishop Suipertus. Bishop Ebroardus. Bishop Adalulfus. Bishop Ebbo. Bishop Bernerius. Bishop Isaac. [Col. 0736A] Bishop Alcherius. Bishop Isarnus. Bishop Umbertus. Bishop Mallenus. Bishop Artaldus. Bishop Pontius. Again Bishop Pontius. Bishop Hugh.

## Series of the Archbishops of Vienne and the Bishops of the See of Grenoble

Archbishop Barnardus.

Archbishop Agilmarus, whose contemporary was Ebbo, bishop of Grenoble; and that same bishop Ebbo was contemporary with Saint Ado, archbishop [Col. 0735B].

Archbishop Ottrannus, successor to Saint Ado, whose contemporary was Bernerius, bishop of Grenoble.

Archbishop Barnoinus, successor to Ottrannus, whose contemporary was Isaac, bishop of Grenoble.

Archbishop Raganfridus, successor to Barnoinus, whose contemporary was Isaac, bishop of Grenoble.

Archbishop Alexander, whose contemporary was Isaac, bishop of Grenoble.

Archbishop Sobo, whose contemporary was Alcherius, bishop of Grenoble [Col. 0735C].

Saint Theutbaldus, archbishop, whose contemporary was Isarnus, bishop of Grenoble.

Archbishop Brocardus, whose contemporary was Humbertus, bishop of Grenoble.

Archbishop Leodegarius.

Archbishop Artmannus.

Archbishop Gormundus.

Archbishop Guido.

### Another Series

Saint Barnardus.

Ebbo, bishop of Grenoble, was contemporary with Archbishop Agilmarus, as is found in the catalogue in the book of the Church of Lyon, in the time of Charles, son of Emperor Lothar.

In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 860, Agilmarus, archbishop of Vienne, and Remigius of the holy Church of Lyon died. Ebbo, bishop of Grenoble, together with the clergy and people of Vienne, elected Saint Ado archbishop, while the aforementioned Charles was reigning.

In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 876, in the ninth indiction, Saint Ado, archbishop, died. The clergy and people elected Ottrannus archbishop of Vienne, and Bernerius, bishop of Grenoble, took part in his consecration during the reign of King Charles [Col. 0736B].

After Ottrannus, Barnoinus was elected and consecrated archbishop. His contemporary was Isaac, bishop of the holy Church of Grenoble, as we find in the books of the Church of Lyon, in the time of King Boso and his son Louis.

In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 890, in the second indiction, while King Louis was reigning, Lord Barnoinus, archbishop of Vienne, departed to Christ.

In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 898, in the second indiction, on the fifth day before the Kalends of February, a Sunday, Raganfridus was consecrated archbishop. Isaac, humble bishop of the holy Church of Grenoble, took part in his consecration during the reign of Louis, son of Boso [Col. 0736C]. We find this in the books of the Church of Lyon.

After Raganfridus, archbishop, his successor was Alexander, archbishop of Vienne. His contemporary was the aforementioned Isaac, bishop of Grenoble, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 912, in the fifteenth indiction, as we find in the charters of the Church of Valence.

After Alexander, archbishop of Vienne, his successor was Archbishop Sobo. His contemporary was Alcherius, bishop of Grenoble, as we find in the election of the aforementioned Bishop Alcherius, in the time of King Gondrad.

[Col. 0737A] After Sobo, archbishop of Vienne, while no other archbishop had yet been elected in his place and the Church of Grenoble was without a pastor, we find in the charters of the Church of Valence that Odilbertus, bishop of Valence, together with the other fellow bishops who were suffragans of the Church of Vienne, and with the agreement of the clergy of Vienne, ordained Isarnus bishop of the Church of Grenoble as successor to Alcherius, bishop of Grenoble. This same Bishop Isarnus was contemporary with Saint Theutbaldus, in the time of King Gondrad.

[Col. 0738A] After Isarnus, bishop of Grenoble, his successor was Bishop Humbertus, who was contemporary with Saint Theutbaldus, in the time of the aforementioned King Gondrad.

After Saint Theutbaldus, archbishop, his successor was Archbishop Brocardus, whose contemporary was the aforementioned Humbertus, in the year 1012 from the Incarnation of the Lord, as is found in a charter of Saint Lawrence in the monastery of Grenoble.

[Col. 0737]

*(Mabillon, as above, from the manuscript of the illustrious Boherius, president in the senate of Dijon.)*

2. Almus.  
3. The just and holy Eusebius.

7. Saint Decius, again.  
8. Gundulfus, called bishop.  
9. Adalramnus.  
10. Braidemus.  
11. Bernardus.  
12. Lambertus.

# Some Documents Concerning the Truce of God

*(Marca, On the Harmony of the Priesthood and the Empire, book IV, chapter 14, edited and annotated by Baluze.)*

## Notice

[The supplied source ends here.]

The truces that were commonly called the Truce and Peace were decreed everywhere, he noted, not only by bishops but also by the nobles of each region. The illustrious man [De Marca, book IV, chapter 14, *On the Concord of the Priesthood and the Empire*] also adduces the example of the people of Barcelona. In the first edition of these dissertations that we prepared, we published several monuments from those times showing that, along the same maritime coast of Tarraconensian Hispania and Narbonensian Gaul, a truce and peace had been sanctioned by bishops and nobles: namely, the Council of Tuluges in the territory of Roussillon; the Synod of Elne, under Oliba, bishop of Ausona, acting in place of Berengarius, bishop of Elne, who at that time was a pilgrim in overseas regions; the Council of Narbonne held in the year 1054; excerpts from the council held at Saint-Gilles in the First Narbonnese province in the year 1056; and the Council of Troy in Apulia, celebrated by Urban II in the year 1093.

But the year in which this Council of Tuluges was finally held is not so well established. Formerly I intended to assign that synod to the year 1045, because I saw that in that year Guifred, archbishop of Narbonne, and Oliba, bishop of Ausona, had performed the consecration of the church of Saint Michael of Flaviana among the Emporitans, and that Poncius, count of Empúries, had been present at this consecration. I also observed that Gauzfred, count of Roussillon, who lived at precisely that time, had subscribed the acts of that dedication, drawn up by Guifred and Oliba. What still makes me persist in that opinion is that Oliba, bishop of Ausona, whose decree published at the Synod of Elne confirms what had been established concerning the truce and peace by the bishops assembled in the meadow of Tuluges, died in the year 1047, as is attested by an old manuscript authority, *On the Deeds of the Counts of Barcelona*. Moreover, Guillelmus, count of Besalú, who attended the Council of Tuluges, died in the year 1052, as the same old authority attests. Finally, the acts of the council held at Narbonne in the year 1054 seem to speak of the regulations of the Council of Tuluges. These things, I say, suggest that the Council of Tuluges was held in the year 1045, as we maintained.

But many considerations prevent us from holding that view. First, Raymundus was not yet bishop of Elne, since he reached that see only around the year 1064. For I have established from very certain evidence that Berengarius was bishop of Elne from at least the year 1032 until the year 1053; that Arnaldus succeeded him, and attended the Council of Toulouse in the year 1056 and the dedication of the church of Barcelona in the year 1058, on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of December; and that Berengarius succeeded Arnaldus, whom I find seated at Elne in the year 1058, on the fourth day before the Ides of December. Finally, I see that Raymundus was bishop of Elne in the years 1064 and 1084, on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of June. From these arguments I think it may be proved that the Council of Tuluges was not celebrated in the year 1045, since Raymundus, who attended the synod, reached the see of Elne only about twenty years later.

Moreover, Berengarius, bishop of Girona, who likewise attended the Council of Tuluges, became bishop only in the year 1050—as Franciscus Didacus noted in his catalogue of the bishops of Girona—and therefore could not have attended this Council of Tuluges in the year 1045 as bishop of Girona. But if this is so, what shall we do with the decree of Oliba, bishop of Ausona, who in the acts of the Synod of Elne explicitly mentions what had been established concerning the truce and peace by the bishops who assembled in the county of Roussillon, in the meadow of Tuluges? Shall we say that Oliba was speaking of some earlier Council of Tuluges at which the matter of the truce and peace had been dealt with? Or shall we say that Oliba’s decree is false and spurious? I see that the matter is exceedingly difficult, and perhaps another place will be more suitable for explaining it.

It remains, therefore, for us to publish here once again the same ancient monuments that, as we said, we made public in the first edition of these dissertations—provided that I first inform the reader that Tuluges is a town in the territory of Roussillon, not far from Perpignan, specifically three miles from that city. Around the year 880 it is called the village of Tuluges, and *de Tulugiis*, in the county of Roussillon, as the ancient acts preserved in the cartulary of the church of Elne attest. Today it is called Tuluges by the inhabitants of those regions.

Concerning the Council of Troy, which we also wished to publish here, I thought it should be noted that it was copied into the register of Urban II, as Ivo attests in part IX, chapter 53, together with two ancient collections of canons, one of which belonged to the illustrious man Peter de Marca, archbishop of Paris, and the other to the distinguished man Claudius Puteanus. The latter collection is now preserved in the Royal Library. This council was celebrated in March of the year 1093, as is clear from the material we now publish and from a bull of Urban preserved in the archive of the archbishop of Narbonne, dated at Troy on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of April, in the year 1093. Those who think that Urban II celebrated two Councils of Troy are mistaken. The Anianus manuscript, now preserved in the Colbert Library, assigns the Trojan canons to a single synod. The illustrious Cardinal Baronius had already suspected that this was correct. That Gerard was bishop of Troy during this period is clear from the Chronicle of Cava, which Ferdinand Ughellus published in his catalogue of the archbishops of Salerno, and likewise from the subscriptions to the privilege of the monastery of Cava in Baronius under the year 1092.

## I. Council of Tuluges held under Guifred, archbishop of Narbonne

[Col. 0739A]

This is the truce and peace confirmed by Guifred, lord archbishop of Narbonne; by Berengarius, bishop of Girona; by Raymundus, lord bishop of Elne; by the counts of Roussillon, namely Gauzfred and Guilabert his son; by Poncius, lord count of Empúries; by Guillelmus, lord count of Besalú; by Raymundus, lord count of Cerdanya; by Gauzbertus, lord viscount of Castellnou; and by the other nobles of the bishopric of Elne, in the meadow of Tuluges, which is in the county of Roussillon.

The aforesaid bishops therefore established, with the consent of the other nobles, that in the counties of Roussillon, Conflent, and Vallespir no one should violate a church, nor the cemeteries or sacred precincts extending thirty ecclesiastical paces around each church, except a bishop on account of an excommunicated person or on account of his dues. If, however, anyone should otherwise violate a church or the thirty-pace space surrounding that church in the aforesaid bishopric of Elne, he shall make whatever restitution is just to the person against whom he committed the wrong, shall make lawful satisfaction to the church in which he committed it, and, in addition, shall pay the composition for sacrilege to the bishop of Elne.

As for those churches where castles have been built, or where thieves and plunderers have gathered their stolen goods, booty, or misdeeds, the aforesaid bishops placed them under the protection of the prescribed peace until the complaint concerning those churches should be brought before the bishop of Elne. Then, according to his judgment, either what had been committed in those churches should be justly repaired, or those churches should be removed by that bishop from the protection of the aforementioned peace.

[Col. 0739B]

The same bishops mentioned above also established that in the aforesaid bishopric of Elne no one should violently violate the estates of canons or monasteries, nor seize anything from them. No one should apprehend a cleric who was not carrying arms, or a monk, or a nun, or a widow, nor inflict any injury upon them. No one should apprehend a male or female villein except for an offense that the villein himself or herself had committed. And if anyone apprehended them, he should not distrain them except according to law.

No one should carry off booty in the aforesaid bishopric consisting of mares or their one-year-old foals, or of mules, or of oxen, cows, or their calves, or of male or female asses or their foals, or of sheep, rams, he-goats, goats, or their young. No one should burn or overturn the dwellings of villeins. No villein should work lands under dispute after being warned by the person before whom the justice of the case was pending. If, however, after being warned three times he worked there, and consequently suffered loss, no claim should be brought against him for breach of the peace.

If anyone had stood as surety and failed to fulfill his pledge, he should be distrained from his own property and should not be considered to have broken the peace. If anyone broke the aforesaid truce and peace, he should make only single compensation to the person against whom he had broken it, within the first fifteen days. If he did not make simple compensation within the first fifteen days, he should pay double compensation for the wrong he had inflicted, so that half of this double compensation should go to the complainant, and the other half to the bishop and to the count who had assisted that bishop in carrying out this justice.

If anyone broke the aforesaid peace or truce and refused to render justice for it, and if, within fifteen days after the complainant had presented his complaint before the bishop, his clerics, and the count, the wrongdoer, his counselors, and his helpers refused to make amends, they should depart from the truce and peace, and no evil inflicted upon them on that account should be claimed as a breach of the peace or truce. If afterward, during the truce, the wrongdoer and his helpers inflicted any harm upon the complainant, they should make compensation for breach of the truce and peace.

The aforesaid bishops also established the Lord’s truce, namely, that it should be observed at all times by all Christians from sunset on Wednesday—that is, the day of Mercury—until sunrise on Monday—that is, the day of the Moon. It should likewise be observed continuously from the first day of Advent of the Lord until the octave of the Epiphany of the Lord, when the feast of Saint Hilary is celebrated. It should similarly be observed continuously from the Monday preceding the beginning of the fast until the Monday that is the first after the Sunday of the octave of Pentecost.

It should also be observed on the three feasts of Saint Mary together with their vigils; on the Nativity of Saint John together with its vigil; on the feast of Saints Justus and Pastor; of Abdon and Sennen; of Saint Felix; of Saint Gennesius; of Saint Nazarius; of Saint Laurence; of Saint Michael; of All Saints; of Saint Martin; on the two feasts of the Holy Cross; on the Chair of Saint Peter; and on the feast of Saint Ennesius, which is on the twelfth day before the Kalends of September; and on the Beheading of Saint John the Baptist, together with the vigils and all the nights of the aforesaid feasts. It should also be observed on all the days and nights of the Ember seasons.

If anyone inflicted any harm upon another during this aforesaid truce of the Lord, he should pay double compensation to him, and afterward make satisfaction for the Lord’s truce by the judgment of cold water at the see of Saint Eulalia.

[Note: That is, in the cathedral church of Elne.]

If anyone killed a man during this truce without any accident, it was determined, with the agreement of all Christians, that he should be condemned to exile for all the days of his life. If he had done this accidentally, he should nevertheless leave the land for as many years as the bishop or the canons judged should be imposed upon him.

If anyone during this truce had set himself in ambush—*aguit* [“had laid an ambush”]—or had firmly established an ambush for the death or apprehension of any man, or for the capture of another castle, and yet had been unable to carry out the attempt, he should likewise make satisfaction for the Lord’s truce according to the judgment of the bishop and his canons, just as he would have done had he accomplished what he had attempted.

They also prohibited anyone from building a castle or fortification during these periods of continuous truce, namely during Advent of the Lord or Lent, unless he had begun the construction fifteen days before the aforesaid continuous truces commenced.

A complaint or prosecution concerning the aforesaid truce or peace could always be brought before the bishop or his canons; and what is written above concerning peace in the case of churches should likewise apply here. Those against whom the bishop or the aforesaid canons had brought proceedings concerning the violation of the aforementioned peace or the Lord’s truce—whether sureties or hostages for the Lord’s peace or truce—and who acted in bad faith toward the bishop or his canons, should be excommunicated by the bishop or by the canons of that see, together with their protectors and helpers, for as long as they persisted in their position as violators of the peace or the Lord’s truce. Neither they nor their property should be considered to be under the Lord’s peace and truce.

[Col. 0742A]

I, Gauzfred, count, swear to you, Peter, bishop of Elne, and make myself your hostage: twice each year, namely at the dedication of Blessed Eulalia, on the eighth day before the Ides of October, and at the beginning of the fasts, I shall return each year, for as long as you live, to this see of Blessed Eulalia. I shall not depart from here without your permission or that of those clerics to whom you entrust the matter. If I do not have money, I shall remain; and if I have money, after it has been spent I shall return within eight days. I shall not depart from here without your permission or that of those clerics to whom you entrust the matter—by God and these holy things.

## II. Synod of Elne under Oliba, bishop of Ausona

[Col. 0742B]

In the year 1027 from the Incarnation of the Lord, on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of June, Oliba, bishop of Ausona, acting in place of Berengarius, bishop of Elne, who at that time was a pilgrim in overseas regions, assembled together with Udalcherus, archpriest of the holy church of Elne; Gancelinus, archdeacon; Ellemarus, sacristan; Coraule; Gauzbertus; and the other canons of the aforesaid see. He also assembled a company of sacred leaders and a multitude of the faithful, not only men but also women.

They assembled in the county of Roussillon, in the meadow of Tuluges. When they had gathered there, they first entreated the mercy of the Lord to turn the hearts of his faithful toward him and to direct their minds and actions. Then they inquired whether the regulations previously established by the aforesaid bishops were being observed.

[Col. 0742C]

But when they found that almost everything had been not only trampled underfoot but also consigned to oblivion, they endeavored to restore it again in the same form in which it had previously been established. Therefore the aforesaid bishops, together with all the clergy and the faithful people, decreed that no one living in the whole of the aforementioned county or bishopric should attack any enemy of his from the ninth hour of Saturday until the first hour of Monday, so that every person might pay the honor due to Sunday.

Nor should anyone in any way attack a monk, or a cleric walking without arms, or any person going to or returning from a church with a council, or anyone traveling with a small basket, or anyone traveling with women. No one should dare to violate or attack a church or the houses situated around it within thirty paces.

[Col. 0742D]

They established this pact or truce because the divine law and almost the whole of Christian religion had, as is written, been reduced to nothing: iniquity abounded and charity had grown cold. Therefore we, the aforesaid bishop, the clergy together, and every order devoted to divine worship, solemnly forbid before God that any man or woman should willingly presume to violate or break any of the foregoing provisions, or invade the property owed to the holy mother church of Elne or to the other churches or monasteries.

Nor should anyone knowingly remain in incest as far as the sixth degree. Nor should anyone dismiss his own wife or take another woman. If anyone has done this, or should do it in the future, unless he repents, makes reparation as far as he is able, and comes before the aforesaid canons within a period of three months to make full satisfaction to the holy mother Church, let him remain excommunicated from the thresholds of the holy Catholic Church and from the assembly of all Christians.

And so that all may know what a grave sin it is to associate with the excommunicated, no Christian should eat or drink with them, offer them a kiss, or speak with them except concerning satisfaction. Nor, if the excommunicated have died, should they be buried in churches; nor should any cleric or faithful person pray for them.

If they regard excommunication as nothing, then, after three months have passed, let them be condemned by the bond of anathema—that is, let them be damned as lost like Judas the betrayer. And if, God forbid, they die in this treachery, let their bodies not be carried to burial with psalms, hymns, or spiritual songs, nor let their names be recited at the sacred altar among the faithful dead. Since they have committed a sin leading to death, unless they repent, let them be condemned without end to eternal damnation.

We forbid all the canons of the aforesaid see, before God and his saints, that any of them should dare to release anyone from these penalties without the consent of the aforesaid archpriest, or of the archdeacons, or of the sacristan and the schoolmaster, or of the other canonical brothers.

The divine offices should nevertheless be performed without interruption for the excommunicated during the period of three months, so that God may grant them repentance and they may recover from the snares of the devil, by whose will they are held captive. Whoever refuses to carry this out shall know that, unless he repents, he is to be punished by the aforesaid excommunication.

But to all who observe the foregoing, peace and mercy shall be granted by the Lord Jesus Christ, here and forever. Amen.

## III. Council of Narbonne held in the year 1054

In the year 1054 from the Incarnation of the Lord, in the seventh indiction, with a ninth epact and concurrent V, on the eighth day before the Kalends of September, ten venerable bishops assembled at the city of Narbonne: Bernard of Béziers, Gonterius of Agde, Rostagnus of Lodève, Arnaldus of Maguelonne, Froterius of Nîmes, Guifred of Carcassonne—or rather, Berengarius of Girona—Guifred of Barcelona, and Guillelmus of Albi. Among them were the representatives of Guillelmus, lord of Urgell, namely Berengarius and Hugo of Uzès.

The assembly was presided over by Guifred, lord archbishop of that city. Through his efforts, with the assistance of Peter Raymond, count, and Berengarius, viscount, and together with a very considerable multitude of abbots, clerics, and certain nobles and commoners, the synod came together to confirm and preserve the truce, peace, and charity that the universal Church had unanimously instituted, and to restore its condition, which wicked men had trampled underfoot. Obeying the Lord’s commands, with temporal benefits bestowed upon the people entrusted to their care, they might deserve to obtain from the supreme Shepherd of all eternal rewards throughout the ages.

First, therefore, of all the regulations that are to be written in this volume, we warn and command, according to the commandment of God and our own, that no Christian kill any other Christian, because whoever kills a Christian without doubt sheds the blood of Christ. If anyone, which we do not wish, unjustly kills a man, let him make legal compensation for him.

Again we command and confirm that very Truce of God which had formerly been established by us and now appears to have been broken by wicked men, so that henceforth it may be firmly observed by all. Therefore we beseech and admonish, by God, that no Christian seek out any other Christian in order to do him harm from sunset on Wednesday until sunrise on Monday.

We also command that from the first Sunday of Advent of the Lord until the octave of the Epiphany has passed; from the first Sunday before the beginning of the fast until the octave of Easter has passed; from the Sunday before the Ascension of the Lord until the octave of Pentecost has been completed; on the feasts of Saint Mary and their vigils; on the vigil and feast of Saint John the Baptist; on the vigils and feasts of the apostles; on the vigil of the Chains of Saint Peter and its feast; on the vigil and solemnity of Saints Justus and Pastor; on the vigil and feast of Saint Laurence; on the feast of Saint Michael; on the vigil and feast of All Saints; on the feast of Saint Martin; and during the fasts of the four Ember seasons—during all the aforesaid fasts, feasts, and vigils—no Christian should harm any other Christian, nor presume to dishonor or plunder his property.

We command that this Truce of the Lord be firmly observed. Let all who maintain and faithfully observe it receive everlasting blessing from Jesus Christ our Lord and Savior himself, and possess the inheritance of eternal life without end. But let those who rebel or transgress, and those who provide them assistance in any way, remain subject to the bond of anathema until they make worthy satisfaction according to the judgment of their own bishop.

If anyone voluntarily or knowingly kills or apprehends a man during this truce, or takes or destroys anyone’s castle, or is proved to have wished, by plotting or by setting an ambush, to act within the proclaimed truce [lacuna], it has been determined by the whole assembly of Christians that he shall be condemned to perpetual exile for the entirety of his life.

If anyone otherwise inflicts any injury or damage upon another, he shall make restitution according to the measure of his fault, by the judgment of his own bishop or of the clerics whom that bishop has appointed, either by the judgment of cold water or by exile, as has been established.

Whoever, when the season of Lent, or the Ascension of the Lord, or Pentecost, or Advent of the Lord—which is covered by the Lord’s truce—is approaching, wishes to construct a castle or fortification may not do so unless he begins it two weeks before the aforesaid period, with everyone aware of it.

Concerning debtors and sureties, we command that if they dispute the things they owe, they be expelled from the Church, and that no one perform a sacred ministry in their parishes until the aforesaid debtors repay what they owe.

We place the olive trees under such firm protection of peace—for through their fruits we read that peace was restored to the earth in the flood of waters, and from their oil holy chrism is made and the holy altars are illuminated—that no Christian should dare to cut them down, mutilate them by cutting off their branches, or seize their fruit. Whoever does this shall make compensation under the Truce of God, according to what has been determined concerning other offenses.

The sheep and their shepherds who guard them shall likewise remain under the Truce of God on all days and in all places, so that no Christian shall presume to plunder them, injure them, or attack either them or their shepherds. Whoever does this shall make full reparation under the Truce of God.

## Concerning the Peace

We command and confirm the peace formerly established by us or by the princes, so that from this day forward no man may violate a church, the dwellings that are or shall be situated around churches, or anything among all the things that are or shall be within thirty paces of a church. No one may violently carry anything away or presume to do so—except a bishop, or someone whom he has commanded, on account of his dues or an excommunicated person, except for a fortification situated within the aforesaid thirty paces of a church—in order to stir up wars and disputes.

We again decree that no one should presume to claim the lands or property of any church without the gift and permission of the person to whom that church belongs. No layman should retain synodal revenues for his own use without the consent of the bishops or clerics; he must restore them completely to those to whom they are legally owed.

We again warn that no layman should retain for his own use the first fruits, offerings, cemetery fees, or eggs, or those things given to them by the sprinkling of salt and water on the Lord’s Supper, or the *trigintarii*—the thirty-day offerings—which clerics rightly receive for prayers for the faithful dead. He must leave these for the use of the clerics who preside over those churches. Nor should anyone presume to diminish anything from the fief that he holds for the same church.

Likewise, no one should seize or carry off anything from the possessions of clerics, monks, nuns, or their companions who do not carry military arms. No man or woman should presume to invade, seize, or carry away those possessions, lands, vineyards, and other things that canons, monks, and nuns possess or are known to possess by right and ownership; nor should anyone usurp anything from them, whether by force, by *vicaria*, or by distraint; nor should anyone take lodging there by any means, unless he has been able to acquire it through the permission or gift of the bishops, canons, and abbots to whom the property properly belongs.

Moreover, no person should dare to possess or retain, whether by *vicaria*, by fief, by stewardship, or under any other pretext, those villages, manses, lands, vineyards, or churches that appear to have been granted by God’s faithful for the use of the canons, so that they might live from them in common, and which are truly known to have been given for this purpose. This may not be done without the express will of the bishop and the canons, or of the abbots, canons, or others known to have rights in those properties, with the consent of their canons, except to the extent that the aforesaid canons and the aforesaid superiors have jointly determined.

We establish among you, by the authority of God and our own, concerning disputes over lands and concerning debtors and sureties, that no one should take vengeance upon any of them until he has come into the presence of his own bishop and of the authority under whose jurisdiction he falls and has presented his case, so that it may be settled and determined by the judgment of one of them. The bishop and the prince of that region, to whom the matter belongs for enforcement, shall harm the person who resists and assist the person who obeys.

No Christian should seize any property of a villein, except his body alone for an offense that he himself has personally committed; and no one should distrain him except according to law. No one should seize a mounted man in order to impose or exact a *redut* [Note: A corrupt word], nor should he take any of his property, except according to law.

No man or woman should commit robberies or plunder against any Christians. We also command that no one seize mares unless an armed man is found upon them. No one should burn *aleses* [the term is uncertain in the source]. No one should knowingly offer assistance to a notorious and public thief, robber, or plunderer, or hire him to carry out such an act, until they come to satisfaction. No one should seize the property of merchants or messengers carrying baskets.

We jointly warn and beseech that all men and women living in the aforesaid counties or bishoprics firmly maintain and carefully observe this institution according to their ability. If any of those men or women presumptuously violates the aforesaid peace and institution and does not make amends within eleven days, let him know that he is to remain excluded from the fellowship of Christians and separated from the thresholds of the holy Church of God until he restores double to the person whom he has harmed and pays forty solidi to the authority of the land in which the act was committed.

He must also make compensation to the bishop of that land, swearing with his own hand upon the altar of the see, or upon whatever altar the bishop orders, that he ought not to make further compensation for the violation of excommunication; or he may pay him forty solidi without an oath.

We say again that this institution is to be firmly observed by all as it is written above, except by those who have been its institutors from their own allod, fief, or stewardship. Whoever transgresses this institution and refuses to obey the regulations set out above shall have no priest sing Mass for him, perform any sacred office for him, give him communion, or bury him, if the priest knows of his disobedience.

If from this day forward any man or woman becomes, through reckless audacity, a violator of this institution, let him be struck by the bond of anathema, driven far from the holy Church of God, and separated from the whole assembly of Christians until he unquestionably comes to make satisfaction.

## IV. Excerpts from the council held at Saint-Gilles in the year 1056

[Col. 0747B]

From the council completed at Saint-Gilles, where a synodal conference of the Fathers was held—namely, of twenty-two Gallican bishops—whose unanimous agreement and equal vote determined the following. We order that this decree, here set out under its heading, be remembered, together with the persons named.

They are: Raimbaldus of Arles; Laudegarius of Vienne; with the legates acting in place of the archbishop of the First Narbonnese province; Froterius of Nîmes; Hugo of Uzès; Wilelmus of Albi; Bernard of Lodève; Geraldus of Viviers; Petrus of Vaison; Udalricus of Die; Franco of Vence; Clemens of Cavaillon; Petrus of Aix; Pontius of Marseille; Deodatus of Toulon; Gaucelinus of Fréjus; Andreas of Nice; Durandus of Vence; Bertrandus of Riez; Hugo of Senez; Pontius of Glandèves; and Hugo of Digne.

All these, assembled together, issued the following decree.

1. We promulgate the canonical judgment that no person of any condition may invade the places belonging to canons, the monasteries of monks, or the villages designated for the sacred orders of the churches, from today and forever—not for the sake of lodging, nor through the ingenuity of an ingrained evil custom—unless necessity compels it, and then only insofar as the use of nature requires, without destroying the place.

[Col. 0747D]

2. Concerning churches founded within a castle or city, or in villages or fields—namely, those in which no building exists for waging war, with which no sedition is practiced, and in connection with which no incursion of evildoers is known to occur for repairing civil or communal losses—they unanimously wish and define that the following power shall apply: no one may presume to seize anything within the limit of thirty *dextra* around the churches, nor inflict harm upon any person, guilty or innocent, unless the wrongdoer has caused damage within that very boundary. They place the offenders under excommunication and perpetual anathema.

3. They command both greater and lesser soldiers that from today until the Nativity of Saint John no one should presume to carry arms for any reason, unless released by his bishop.

Given on the day before the Nones of September.

## V. Council of Troy held by Urban II in the year 1093

In the year 1023 from the Incarnation of the Lord [the date is printed thus], in the first indiction, during the first week of Lent, on the sixth day before the Ides of March, a council of approximately seventy-five bishops and twelve abbots assembled at Troy in Apulia. On the second day, after the matter of certain persons joined within the prohibited degrees of consanguinity had been dealt with, all finally agreeing, this chapter was promulgated concerning them.

1. Let the bishops in whose dioceses they are summon them three times up to Pentecost. Then, if two men [Note: In Gratian, 35, question 6, chapter “If two.”] or three confirm the consanguinity by oath, or if the persons themselves should happen to confess it, let the marriages be dissolved.

But if neither of these things occurs, let the bishops adjure them by the baptism of Christ, by the faith of Christ, and by the judgment of Christ, in true obedience, to make openly known whether they acknowledge themselves to be related by blood, as is reported. If they deny it, they are to be left to themselves, but in such a way that, if they hold something else in their conscience, they should know themselves to be separated from the thresholds of the Church, from the body and blood of the Lord, and from the communion of the faithful, and to have become infamous, until they desist from the crime of incest.

If they have separated themselves by the judgment of the bishops, and if they are young, they should not be prohibited from contracting other marriages.

2. If anyone breaks the Truce of God, let him be admonished by the bishop to make satisfaction up to three times. If he does not consent to make satisfaction even after the third admonition, let the bishop—or with the counsel of the metropolitan, or with that of two or one neighboring bishops—pronounce a sentence of anathema against the rebel, and announce it in writing to the bishops all around.

Let no bishop receive anyone so excommunicated into communion; rather, after receiving the written notice, let each bishop confirm the sentence. If anyone should presume to act otherwise, he shall be subject to the peril of his order.

All replied: “Let it be done.”

## VI. Synodal Decree concerning the Peace Commonly Called the Truce of God

[Note: [Col. 0747D] As the line of Charlemagne was declining toward its end, the counts, who governed their provinces, began to appropriate them to themselves as private possessions and hereditary estates. The transfer of the kingdom to Hugh greatly advanced their efforts: the provinces were no longer administered on the authority of the earlier laws [Col. 0748D], but each man was eager to arrange matters according to advantage rather than equity. [Col. 0749C] Neighbor envied neighbor, quarrels were stirred up, and mutual fighting became customary. Following the example of the magnates, the battles and wars of private persons became almost domestic; the feud, which had previously been nearly extinguished, revived, and whenever someone had killed another, his relatives began to avenge the slaughter and, in retaliation, to kill with impunity either the murderer himself or anyone of his family. [Col. 0749D] Since so grave an evil could not be remedied immediately, the following measure was adopted to remove it. Certain days were appointed on which there was to be rest from such wars: no one was to dare pursue another, but each person was to enjoy the security of public peace. These truces were called the Truce of God, or the Lord’s Truce; they are frequently mentioned by authors of that period. The Truce was celebrated and approved by decrees of councils and letters of the supreme pontiffs. Those who rashly dared to violate this law of truce were punished by death, exile, or excommunication [Col. 0750C]; indeed, the writers of that age report that many were struck down by God himself in vengeance. It was not adopted everywhere at the same time. In 997 Dagbert, archbishop of Bourges, confirmed with Theobald, archbishop of Vienne, a charter concerning the truce and peace made by Wido of Anich and other bishops [Col. 0750D]. In 1033, throughout the provinces of Arles and Lyons, and indeed throughout all Burgundy, the bishops issued a decree for the restoration of the peace, or Truce of God, which everyone accepted with willing minds. According to Glaber Radulfus, book IV, chapter 5, in the year 1041 the Truce of God was re-established, chiefly through the agency of Odo, abbot of Cluny, as Abbot Hugh of Flavigny bears witness. The Austrasians approved it, and finally the Neustrians did so at councils held at Caen in 1043 and 1061.]

Established by William the Elder, king of the English and duke of the Normans, together with the bishops of Normandy, at Caen in 1042 [Note: [Col. 0748D] The title is restored from the manuscript of Saint Michael, with which the remaining text was compared, as well as with Bigot.] (Mansi, *Councils*, vol. XIX, col. 597, from Bessin, *Provincial Councils of Rouen*.)

Dearest brothers in the Lord, concerning the peace commonly called the Truce of God, which begins at sunset on Wednesday [Col. 0749A] and ends at sunrise on Monday, you must henceforth observe the following provisions with the greatest readiness of mind.

No man or woman shall ever assault, wound, or kill any man or woman; nor, during this period of four days and five nights, shall anyone assault, plunder, seize, or burn a castle, town, or village by any device, violence, or fraud. If anyone—God forbid—breaks this command by failing to observe what we have prescribed, then, unless he performs thirty years of penance in exile and, before leaving our episcopate, makes reparation for whatever he has done against the peace, let him be excommunicated by the Lord God and separated from all Christendom.

Whoever communicates with him in any matter, or gives him counsel or assistance, or has any conversation with him except in order that he may come to penance and, as stated, depart from this episcopate, shall likewise be excommunicated until he comes to make reparation. If that most wretched violator of the holy peace dies in exile before undertaking the thirty years of penance, no Christian shall presume to visit him, remove his body from the place where it lies, or take anything from his possessions. [Col. 0749B]

Moreover, brothers, you shall maintain this peace and Truce of God among yourselves concerning lands, animals, and all possessions that can be held. If anyone takes from another any animal, or even a coin or a garment, during this peace, let him be excommunicated until he comes to make reparation. If he wishes to come to make reparation, he must first return what he stole, or the full value of what he took. Thereafter he shall do penance for seven years within the episcopate. If he dies before making satisfaction and undertaking penance, he shall not be buried, nor shall he be moved from the place where he died, unless his relatives make satisfaction on his behalf to the person whom he injured. [Col. 0749C]

Furthermore, during this peace no one except the king or the count of this region shall undertake a mounted expedition or military action. Whoever is engaged in the king’s mounted expedition or military action shall take in this episcopate nothing more than what is necessary for himself and his horses to live on. [Col. 0750A] Merchants, moreover, and all persons who pass through your territory from other regions shall have peace from you.

You shall also maintain this Truce of God every day from the beginning of Advent of the Lord until the octave of Epiphany, from the beginning of Lent until the octave of Easter, and from the beginning of the Rogation days until the octave of Pentecost.

Priests are commanded on feast days and Sundays to bless all who have observed this peace, offering prayers for them; but those who have broken it, or who have consented to its violators, they shall curse. If anyone says that he has broken the peace unknowingly, he must first take an oath and carry the hot iron of judgment. [Col. 0750B]

[Note: He must carry the judicial iron. In a *Pontifical* written before the year 1000 and preserved in the library of Jumièges, the rite of judgment by red-hot iron is described as follows: The iron is brought forward, and the accused takes it before everyone and carries it for a measure of nine feet. His hand is sealed and kept under the seal, and after three nights it is opened. If it is clean, he is to give thanks to God; [Col. 0750D] but if festering matter is found developing in the mark left by the iron, he is to be considered guilty and impure.]

## VII. Council of an Uncertain Location in Germany, at Which the Pious and Holy Institution of the Truce of God Was Confirmed, Held about the Year 1041

(Mansi, *Councils*, vol. XIX, col. 593, from the manuscript of Talavera.)

[Col. 0750B]

In the name of God the almighty Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit.

Raginbald, archbishop of Arles, together with Benedict, bishop of Avignon, and Nithard, bishop of Nice, as well as the venerable abbot Lord Odilo, together with all the bishops and abbots and the entire clergy residing throughout Gaul, to all archbishops, bishops, priests, and the entire clergy dwelling throughout Italy: grace to you and peace from God the almighty Father, [Col. 0750C] who is, and who was, and who is to come.

[Note: Hugh, abbot of Flavigny, expressly asserts in his *Chronicle* that the Truce, first firmly established through Saint Odilo, was confirmed in the year 1041, and that it was strengthened not only by human authority but also by divine terrors. Martène.]

We beg and entreat all of you who fear God, believe in him, and have been redeemed by his blood, to take care and provide for the salvation of your souls and bodies, and to follow the footsteps of God, having peace with one another, so that you may deserve to possess peace and perpetual tranquility with him.

Receive, therefore, and hold fast the peace and that Truce of God which we too, by the divine mercy inspired and sent to us from heaven, have now received and firmly maintain. It has been established and arranged as follows: from the evening hour of Wednesday, among all Christians, friends and enemies, neighbors and strangers, there shall be firm peace and stable truce until the second day of the week—that is, Monday at sunrise—so that throughout these four days and nights they may at every hour be secure and do whatever is necessary, freed from all fear of enemies and strengthened in the tranquility of peace and of this truce. [Col. 0751A]

Whoever observes and firmly keeps this peace and Truce of God shall be absolved by God the almighty Father, by his Son Jesus Christ, and by the Holy Spirit; by holy Mary with the choirs of virgins; by Saint Michael with the choirs of angels; by Saint Peter, prince of the apostles, with all the saints; and by all the faithful, now and forever and throughout all ages of ages.

But those who have pledged the truce and knowingly intend to violate it shall be excommunicated by God the almighty Father, by his Son Jesus Christ, and by the Holy Spirit; and by all the saints of God they shall be excommunicated, cursed, and detested here and forever. They shall be condemned like Dathan and Abiram and like Judas, who betrayed the Lord, and they shall be cast into the depths of hell like Pharaoh in the midst of the sea, unless they come to make reparation, as has been established. [Col. 0751B]

That is to say, if anyone commits murder during those days of the Truce of God, he shall be made an exile and driven from his native land; while making his way to Jerusalem, he shall endure a distant exile there. If, however, he breaks the aforesaid Truce of God and peace in any other matter, he shall be examined according to the decrees of secular laws and compelled to pay according to the measure of his offenses; and by the rules of the sacred canons he shall be judged to a doubled penance. [Col. 0751C]

We consider this fitting so that, if we presume in any way to corrupt the promise made there, we may be condemned twice over, both by worldly and by spiritual judgment. For we believe that this matter was divinely inspired in us from heaven with God’s assistance, because, as we believe, no good was being done among us when it was sent by God to his people. The Lord’s appointed day was not being celebrated; rather, all servile work was being done on it. [Col. 0752A]

Therefore we promised and devoted to God the four-day period mentioned above: Thursday on account of the Ascension, Friday on account of Christ’s Passion, Saturday in reverence for his burial, and Sunday so that the Resurrection might be celebrated inviolate. On all these days no rural labor was to be performed at all; no enemy was to fear an enemy, in accordance with the authority bestowed by God and handed down by the apostles.

We bless and absolve all who love this peace and Truce of God, as stated above. But those who oppose it we excommunicate, curse, and anathematize, and we expel them from the thresholds of holy Mother Church. [Col. 0752B]

When it happens that someone wishes to take vengeance upon those who have presumed to violate this charter and the Truce of God, those who exact vengeance shall not be held liable for any guilt; rather, as worshipers of God’s cause, they shall go forth and return blessed by all Christians.

But if something has been taken during the remaining days and is encountered during the days of the truce, it shall not be retained at all, lest it appear that an opportunity has been given to the enemy.

Moreover, brothers, we ask you that, on whatever day the aforesaid peace and truce has been established among you, you devoutly commemorate that day in the name of the Holy Trinity. Drive all robbers from your region, abhor them, curse them, and excommunicate them on behalf of all the saints written above. [Col. 0752C]

Offer your tithes and first fruits from your labors to God. Bring offerings from your goods to the churches for the salvation of the living and the dead, so that God may free you from all evils in this life and, after this life, lead you to the kingdoms of heaven—he who with God the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns as God throughout the ages of ages. Amen.

[Col. 0751]

# SATIRICAL RHYTHM ON THE TIMES OF KING ROBERT

(Mabillon, *New Analecta*, new edition, p. 366.)

[Note.]

The venerable Godefridus Hurmannus, canon of Beauvais, extracted these verses from a manuscript of Beauvais. Landricus, the principal craftsman of the stage, was the son of Bodo, count of Nevers, and lord of Donzy, against whom Fulk Nerra waged serious conflicts. Landricus is said to have been an unjust man, filled with deceit and every kind of wickedness, in chapter 7 of *The Deeds of the Counts of Anjou*. These characteristics suit the present passage well.

Here he is also called Ahithophel, Crassus, the Master of the Feast, and Eglon. His adversary, Odo, count of Champagne, is called the Stone in Zion. Nabuzardan, his supporter, appears to be Hugh of Beauvais, who sowed an evil seed of hatred between King Robert himself and his wife and, for the sake of his own advantage, made the queen hateful to him. He obtained such favor from the king that he was regarded as count palatine, as is shown by the same deeds in volume X of the *Spicilegium*, p. 466.

Adalbero, bishop of Laon, otherwise called Ascelinus, is described as an old traitor and false bishop of Laon because he betrayed Charles, duke of Lorraine, whose counselor he was and to whose word he had sworn allegiance. On the day of the Lord’s Supper, in the year 990, he opened the gates of Laon by night to Hugh, king of the Franks. Previously, through the favor of King Lothair in 977, he had succeeded Rorico in the see of Laon. He lived until about the year 1030.

At that time he designated as his successor Wido, a cleric and nephew of Berold, bishop of Soissons, contrary to the prescriptions of the canons. On this matter serious letters of Gerold, bishop of Cambrai, survive, addressed both to Adalbero himself, to Ebalus the metropolitan, and to Berold of Soissons. Perhaps this is the Wido whom Landricus is here said to have deprived of favor either with the king or with Queen Constance. The same cleric is called “sad” because he had fallen from royal favor.

Hence envoys were sent to Chela, then from Chela to Worchies and to Paris, where the king was staying, so that he might restore his favor. The same Landricus takes the woman from Henry—that is, Constance, his mother, the queen, who opposed Henry. Constance seeks Gascony.

Meanwhile Ahithophel, or Landricus, restored Berta to the royal bed, although she had previously been separated from Robert by the judgment of Gregory V because of a bond of consanguinity and affinity. He was plotting to make Robert’s sons Hugh a monk, Henry a sacristan, and Robert a bishop, having himself been deceived by Berta’s promise at Provins because of his wicked schemes.

This seems to me to be the meaning of this enigmatic satire. If it pleases some people less, they may offer another interpretation—a better one, if they can. Certainly, the fact that Landricus was contemplating making King Robert a bishop can scarcely be interpreted as referring to anyone other than Robert, the son of King Robert; the remaining circumstances hardly allow any other interpretation. For to plot this against the father would have been far from Landricus’s intention, since he had reconciled Berta to him.

Hugh appears to be called Absalom because of his handsome appearance and hair, and because he rejected Landricus’s plans. The Stone in Zion that spiritually crushed Landricus was no one other than Odo, count of Champagne, Landricus’s adversary and conqueror, as I have already said, from book 8 of *The Deeds of the Counts of Anjou*, chapter 8.

Nor is it surprising that Landricus, Odo’s rival, tried to drive Queen Constance, Odo’s sister, from the court, and finally actually accomplished it. In any case, Berta was considering returning to Robert’s love, according to Odorannus, when Robert undertook his journey to Rome. But the event mentioned here by the author of these verses seems to have been different, since the time and other circumstances do not agree.

[Col. 0753A]

The deceit of Landricus strives solemnly  
To overthrow the monarchy of the great world  
By an energetic campaign.

There is one stone in Zion, which they call the stone of stumbling,  
Which has fallen upon the head of Ahithophel seven times.  
But when the stone falls once, it falls with sevenfold force:  
We have seen the Burgundian spiritually crushed.

Ahithophel has restored Burgundy to our age;  
The very long-haired Absalom spurned his counsel.  
The shape-shifter often enters royal palaces;  
He hides his nose beneath skins, concealing his breast under deceits.

Now, worse than Catiline, he offers a kiss to his friends;  
But he holds out traps drunk with the flavor of gall.  
Another Jugurtha speaks—not in good faith, but about faith—  
Returning enmities in place of true friendships.

[Col. 0753B]

Going to the throne of kings, he greets Ceges but does not love him;  
Yet it is like a hut in a lofty cucumber garden.  
He was not heard in Thebes, nor found in Corban,  
While an earlier laughter appeared on faces unknown to his friends.

But the bishop learned that the cleric had become sad:  
They go from Chela to Worchies, and from Worchies to Paris.  
The laughter of Crassus is the agitation of the kingdom;  
He who knows how to seduce kings goes beside the hedge to urinate.

He overturns the position of princes, the enemy of the Frankish nobles;  
Running with spread-out ships, like fox-like Crassus.  
Adalbero does not understand why Ahithophel laughs:  
He carries a fox in his breast, though he does not know how to spare his own people.

[Col. 0753C]

The justiciar, armed with wiles [perhaps: *furcifer*, “gallows-bird”], takes the woman from Henry,  
[Col. 0754A]  
First taking away Wido’s favor, fearing the bride’s prudence.  
The wife seeks Gascony; Ahithophel seeks wickedness,  
While through the burden of oath-taking he throws the whole country into confusion.

He pours out the boundary of honor, entering the king’s palace;  
“Let Henry be sacristan,” says the son of Bodo.  
“Let Hugh the monk be king; let Robert be bishop”—  
One possessing a simple life, the other sweetness of speech.

A dark legion of frauds reigns in Landricus’s stomach,  
Whose statements the authority of Nabuzardan fortifies.  
With guffaws he displays deceit, regard, and danger;  
Sharp is the razor of treachery’s hardness.

The tearing-up of a promise, brought forward in deceit,  
Amid a little covering of words, in a lying wallow.  
His saliva, mixed with deceits, moves amid deceits;  
[Col. 0754B]  
His speeches, together with dangers, move in his syllables.

There he renewed the unlawful marriage of Herodias:  
Because of incestuous kisses, may the walls of Provins perish.  
The impious Master of the Feast rejoiced over the walls;  
Because of the marriage he believed himself to have become more powerful.

The king slept in the little bed under Landricus’s pontificate;  
Berta’s promise sleeps, while the Burgundian grows angry.  
Our latter-day Eglon—[the sense of *cujus ut non turpissimus* is uncertain]—  
Puffed up by many banquets, is displeasing to the people of Provins.

He endures a second moon; he is broken by shifting hope;  
He never lost Provins, because he could not possess it.  
Let it be written on a sheet of lead, so that memory may not pass away,  
That later generations may be prudent if he rises after death.

The prosperity of Ahithophel is the captivity of Europe,  
[Col. 0754C]  
He grows worse each day, destined to perish only very slowly.

[Col. 0755]

# ANCIENT RHYTHMS

## I. The Rhythm of the Mutinensian Soldiers

## II. The Rhythm on the Capture of Emperor Louis II by Adelchis

Preceded by L. A. Muratori’s Dissertation on the Rhythmic Poetry of the Ancients

(*Antiquities of Italy*, III, 664.)

## [Dissertation]

[Col. 0755A]

The Italian language owes its origin no less than Italian poetry does to the barbarous age, although the foundations of the latter must be investigated more deeply by us.

At the beginning of the *Poetics*, Aristotle, inquiring into the origin of poetry, held that it arose from the love of imitation, which is implanted in human beings, and from the love of harmony and rhythm. In particular, he says:

> Κατὰ φύσιν δὲ ὄντος ἡμῖν τοῦ μιμεῖσθαι, καὶ τῆς ἁρμονίας, καὶ τοῦ ῥυθμοῦ (τὰ γὰρ μέτρα ὅτι μόρια τῶν ῥυθμῶν, ἐστὶ φανερὸν) ἐξ ἀρχῆς οἱ πεφυκότες πρὸς αὐτὰ μάλιστα κατὰ μικρὸν προάγοντες, ἐγέννησαν τὴν ποίησιν ἐκ τῶν αὐτοσχεδιασμάτων.

These words mean in Latin:

> “Since imitation, harmony, and rhythm are natural to us—for it is clear that meters are parts of rhythms—those who were naturally most fitted for these things, advancing little by little from the beginning, produced poetry by improvising verses.”

It is remarkable how much the interpreters of Aristotelian poetry, especially the Italians, have lingered over, disputed, and strained their ingenuity upon these words, since they could not adequately grasp the force of the word *rhythm*, and explained the word *harmony* in one way here and in another way there.

But the genuine meaning of the Philosopher is this: by the institution of nature we take pleasure not only in imitation but also in harmony—that is, in modulation and musical harmony, whether it arises from the singing or voice of living creatures or from the sound of musical instruments—and, in addition, in rhythm, that is, in the ordering and arrangement of words joined together or ending in such a way that the sounds, even without singing and merely when pronounced, produce consonance and, so to speak, a kind of melody, striking the ears of the hearers with a pleasurable and delightful sensation.

By the name “meter” is meant speech so bound and fashioned by the invention and establishment of certain rules that it consists of a definite number of feet, with exact attention in those feet to the syllables that are long and short.

Poets’ verses are called meters because *metron* (μέτρον) means the same as “measure.” In verses constructed and bound according to poetic rules, the measure of time is preserved so that the same pattern always recurs in verses of the same kind, whether they consist of long feet, short feet, or mixed feet.

Quintilian writes in *The Orator’s Education*, book IX, chapter 4, that everyone, even children, knows that a long syllable consists of two time-units and a short syllable of one. Accordingly, in the periods of rhetoricians, elaborated by hidden art, a certain harmony is heard; for this reason both Cicero and Quintilian command that rhythm, not meter, be cultivated in prose.

Aristotle had already preceded them, writing in *Rhetoric*, book III, chapter 8:

> Ῥυθμὸν δεῖ ἔχειν τὸν λόγον, μέτρον δὲ μή.

That is: “Speech ought to have rhythm, but not meter.” Otherwise, he adds, it will be a poem.

Referring to this passage, Cicero, speaking of Aristotle himself, says: “He therefore forbids verse in prose and commands number.” He translated μέτρον as “verse” and ῥυθμόν as “number,” from which prose with numerical rhythm was also called “numerous prose.”

Thus poetry arose, as the Philosopher rightly observed. At first certain peoples—whether Hebrews, Greeks, or anyone else, for this does not concern me—when they devoted themselves to harmony during sacrifices, weddings, banquets, victories, or other occasions of public or private dancing and rejoicing, using pipes or strings, gradually began to join voice and song to the sound of the pipe or lyre.

For this purpose they employed a particular arrangement of diction and feet, in whose structure rhythm, or harmony, was heard, since in one phrase the connection of words and feet responded to the phrase that followed. But at that time there was no, or at least very little, concern for the shortness or length of syllables. It was enough to construct the brief speech in such a way and to establish some sort of number and measure of feet that a certain modulation and harmony would arise for the judgment of the ears.

The structure of such brief speech came to be called a verse. It was poured forth not by reflection but by the spontaneous force of talent, just as in our own time rustic people make verses extemporaneously.

These were the beginnings of poetry. But when considerable pleasure began to flow from it into the ears and minds of hearers, learned and excellent men gradually perfected the imperfect work: they introduced certain rules according to which verses would thereafter be constructed and applied a more exact measure of feet, so that the reckoning and uniformity of time would be strictly maintained in the use of short and long syllables.

The earlier verses were called rhythmic; the later, metric. Hence we understand why Saint Augustine wrote in book III, chapter 2, of *Music*:

> “Therefore every meter is rhythm, but not every rhythm is also meter.”

For example, in the hexameters of Virgil or Homer one hears not only rhythm, or something melodic, but also meter—that is, an exact observance of time—since, whether the poet forms the verse with short or long feet, twenty-two time-units of the voice always occur in each hexameter.

The same proportion applies to the other kinds of verse among the better poets. But in rhythmic verses, although from the joining of words and feet—and often from an observed numerical pattern—some harmony arises that produces pleasure in the hearer, the craftsman is little or not at all concerned whether he uses short or long feet; he rejects the law and the fetters that poets of long ago imposed upon themselves.

For example, the penultimate foot of the hexameter requires a dactyl, that is, three syllables, of which the first is long and the remaining two short, as in *carmina* and *turgidus*. But, as Quintilian notes in book IX, chapter 4, rhythm is indifferent to whether that dactyl has its short syllables before or after the long one. Therefore, for one producing rhythm, it is the same whether he uses a tribrach, composed of three short syllables, as in *macula* and *canimus*; an anapest, formed from two short syllables and a long one, as in *rutilans* and *Erato*; or a cretic, composed of a long, a short, and a long syllable, as in *Achates* and *fulgidis*.

These words too produce a sound similar or close to that of a dactyl. Anyone who has only his ears as judge detects little or no difference among the sounds of these feet, although metric poets regard them as entirely different.

I confess that I do not know by what art or striking of the voice the ancient Greeks and Romans distinguished, especially in disyllabic words, the shortness and length of syllables. For in vain, even now, with attentive ear, I ask why the word *mala*, meaning “evil,” or *res malae*, “evil things,” should have a different measure of time from *mala*, meaning “apples,” or *gena*, “cheek,” when the sound of each word seems identical to me, although according to the rules of prosody one is treated differently.

Thus two kinds of poetry arose in ancient times: one older but lowly and plebeian; the other noble and cultivated only by learned men. The former was called rhythmic, the latter metric.

But the most important point to observe is this: although metric poetry gained the first place, and was approved by the judgment and usage of all better writers and everywhere adorned with praise, rhythmic poetry did not therefore disappear among the Greeks and Romans.

Whenever the unlearned common people and rustic folk wished at times to play the poet but were not equal to learning the rules of meter, they continued to form whatever verses they could—that is, contenting themselves with rhythm, they disregarded meter. By meter I mean the strict rules of prosody followed by perfected poetry.

Nevertheless, in a broader sense I sometimes see rhythmic verses also given the name “meter,” because in them too some measure of feet and time was observed.

The first rhythmic verses, and indeed poetry itself, were introduced among the Latins by rustic people, although the Greeks had preceded them. It was their custom after the harvest to amuse themselves by striking one another with alternating insults and competing in rhythmic verses, which were also called Fescennine verses.

Horace describes the practice in book I, epistle 1, attributes its origin to the ancient farmers, and finally says:

> Fescennina per hunc inventa [or rather, “introduced”?] licentia morem,  
> Versibus alternis opprobria rustica fudit.

“Through this custom Fescennine license, newly found [or rather, introduced?], poured forth rustic insults in alternating verses.”

Tibullus expresses a similar thought in book II, elegy 2:

> Agricola assiduo primum lassatus aratro  
> Cantavit certo rustica verba pede.

“The farmer, first wearied by the unceasing plow, sang rustic words in a fixed foot.”

Livy also, speaking at the beginning of book VII of the *Annals* about the Etruscan performers, says:

> “Then the young men began to imitate them, pouring forth among themselves crude jests in verses.”

Livy calls their verses “crude,” as Virgil does in the second Eclogue and in book II of the *Georgics*, where he calls the verses of rustic people “unadorned,” because they were rough and did not proceed according to any fixed rule of prosody.

Below Horace calls this kind of verse “harsh,” that is, rough and unpolished:

> [lacuna] Thus that harsh  
> Saturnian rhythm flowed away [lacuna]

The Latin word *numerus* expresses the Greek *rhythmus*. Horace continues:

> [lacuna] And a grave poison  
> Drove out refinement. Yet for a long age  
> The traces of the countryside remained, and remain today.

That is: although we learned the rules of meter from the Greeks and now compose corrected and polished verses in place of the rough rhythms of rustic people, rhythmic poetry nevertheless always endured and still flourishes among the common people.

The commentators on Horace cite at this passage the words of Servius. Explaining the unadorned verses mentioned by Virgil in book II of the *Georgics*, Servius says that they were poems composed in Saturnian meter, which the common people were accustomed to compose only according to rhythm.

From this we may conjecture that Saturnian and Fescennine verses were once the same. Asconius, however, presents an obstacle, since he mentions the hypercatalectic senarius, which is also called Saturnian; this may indicate that the verse was not rhythmic but metric.

Nevertheless, let us hear Livy again. Writing in the same seventh book that poetry gradually acquired polish, he says:

> “Not as before, in a verse resembling the Fescennine—thrown out alternately, haphazardly uncomposed and crude.”

By these words he describes the first verses of the Latins: uncomposed, that is, poured forth extemporaneously and improvised, fashioned without exact observance of order and time, such as we perceive in meters composed according to the laws of prosody, and therefore unpolished and crude.

When such Fescennine or joking verses descended into excessive mockery and satire, their license was restrained by Roman laws, so that it was permitted to use them only to taunt at weddings and triumphs. See Ferrarius, book VI of *On Ancient Acclamations*, chapter 10, who explains the matter and supplies examples.

As the Roman Empire declined, the people were also evidently entertained by rhythms of this kind, as Vopiscus sufficiently reveals in his *Life of Aurelian*, whose words Salmasius has extensively illuminated.

Under the Christian emperors, and especially under the barbarian kings, rhythms were widely used—not for cursing or reproach, but for all sorts of honorable subjects, especially the praises of God and the saints, and also of living persons.

Although metric poetry never at any time failed, and every century could show its own poets, using bound speech and not all to be despised, nevertheless, after a great wound had been inflicted upon good letters and ignorance had taken hold of most people, few devoted themselves to the laws of prosody. It was easier for them to exercise themselves in rhythms, since that sort of little composition required less care and labor.

Accordingly, one finds medieval writers mentioning and distinguishing both rhythmic and metric compositions.

Saint Boniface, bishop of Mainz, writing around the year 740 in letter 4, says:

> “I beg you to be so kind as to send me some little works of Bishop Aldhelm, whether in prose, meter, or rhythm.”

Writers of literary history mention a book by this Aldhelm, *On the Kinds of Meter*, or *On the Art of Meter*.

Thus Alvarus, a Spanish writer of about the year 847, has the following in his *Life of Saint Eulogius*:

> “We conducted our correspondence with one another, and softened ourselves with praises in rhythmic verses.”

Ekkehard, in the *Life of Blessed Notker Balbulus*, in Goldast, volume I, p. 237 of the *Alamannic Affairs*, chapter 16, writes:

> “He sent by a messenger to Pope Nicholas and to Liutward, bishop of Vercelli, the sequences that the same holy Father had composed; this was at the time of Charlemagne the emperor—that is, Charles the Fat, about the year 883. That venerable pontiff of the apostolic see canonized everything that Blessed Notker had dictated, namely the hymns, sequences, tropes, litanies, and all the songs that he had composed, whether rhythmically, metrically, or in prose.”

Moreover, Ekkehard himself, or another writer, in chapter 1 of *The Misfortunes of Saint Gall*, speaking of Salomon, abbot and bishop of Constance, writes:

[Col. 0760A]

> “He passed by the schools, opened the door, and entered. It was indeed their right, just as it is today, since they are outlaws: when guests enter, they seize them and, once captured, hold them until they ransom themselves.”

See how ancient is the abuse that is said still to persist in the school at Ticinum. They call it *spupillare*. After much else, the middling students speak rhythmically, while the rest speak metrically:

> What have we done to you, that you should treat us badly?  
> We appeal to the king, whom we have made our law.

But another versifier says:

> We had no pious hope, since you are a new guest,  
> That you yourself would wish to turn old law into something worse.

Thus Hermannus Contractus, in Pez’s preface to the *Treasury of Anecdotes*, has this rhythmic verse:

> I beg you: compose a song in meter, or in melodious rhythm.

Orderic Vitalis also praises rhythmic verses in the twelfth century. Around the year 1145, Silvester Giraldus the Briton, in *The Mirror of the Church*, book IV, chapter 16, reports the following about a certain Golias:

> “A man abundantly learned, but neither well behaved nor trained in the disciplines, he spewed forth against the pope and the Roman court many and repeated notorious poems, both metric and rhythmic, no less shamelessly than imprudently.”

All these examples sufficiently indicate how widely rhythmic poetry was once used, and that even learned men did not always shrink from it.

Bede explained how rhythms differ from meters in the eighth century, in his book *On Meters*, as follows:

> “Rhythm appears to be similar to meter. It is a measured composition of words, examined not according to a metrical rule but by the number of syllables, according to the judgment of the ears, as are the songs of vernacular poets. Rhythm can exist without meter, but meter cannot exist without rhythm. This may be defined more clearly as follows: meter is measure together with modulation; rhythm is modulation without measure.”

Isidore likewise distinguishes rhythms from meters in book I, chapter 38, of the *Etymologies*.

Let us now see what the course of the rhythms was. Most completed their course in a few steps, imitating the movement of distichs, epigrams, odes, or hymns—that is, they were content with a short or at least moderate series of verses. Yet there were also those who advanced beyond these limits, as the subject matter or the poet’s purpose required. If I say that the rhythm-makers once employed every kind of verse with which poetic art has been adorned, I shall perhaps not be speaking without justification. Indeed, it seems likely that lyric poetry first learned such a variety of songs from the practitioners of rhythm, and gradually perfected it by adding meter. For dithyrambic poetry, instituted in the earliest times, was composed of various kinds of rhythms, as Proclus also testifies; and just as tragedy and comedy are believed to have originated from it, so too lyric poetry must be regarded as having arisen from it. The commentator on Aristophanes also seems to agree on this point. But I shall pass over these matters.

Only this should be noted: although Anacreon excels among the Greek lyric poets in sweetness and grace, he is nevertheless carried along in his verses with great license, so much so that he approaches rhythmic freedom. Moreover, the words of Horace that I quoted above were spoken of the dithyrambs formed in his age, in Book IV, Ode 2. He says:

> Whether through bold dithyrambs  
> He rolls forth novel words,  
> And is borne along in rhythms  
> Freed from law.

Spartianus also quotes certain verses of the emperor Hadrian, namely:

> I do not want to be Florus,  
> Wandering through taverns,  
> Lurking through cookshops,  
> Suffering round mosquitoes.

I scarcely doubt that these should be classified among rhythmic verses, as should others said to have been uttered by the same emperor at his death. Certainly, one finds in them no exact metrical pattern. Nevertheless, to speak frankly, the rhythms themselves were so formed that they often displayed some appearance of meter. For if what Quintilian states in Book IX, chapter 4 of the *Institutio oratoria*, is true:
