> Metrical feet are indeed found so abundantly in speech that verses of every kind frequently slip from it without our noticing.

And conversely, nothing is written in prose that could not be reduced to certain kinds of little verses. How much more easily, then, must the same thing occur in rhythms?

Leo Allatius, in his *Diatribe on Simeon*, testifies that the use of rhythms continued among the more recent Greeks as well. They called these *political verses*, which, as he himself writes, consist for the most part of iambics and Anacreontics, but in such a way that no account is taken of syllable quantity—which the ancients observed with the greatest precision. Attention is paid only to their number and to the changes of accent. This method of composing poems, moreover, was not first introduced among that people in recent times, but is found to have been in use for many centuries, as we see in the verses of the patriarch Photius, Christopher the *a secretis*, Psellus, and others. Vossius likewise, in Book I, chapter 8 of his *Institutiones poeticae*, observes that rhythm, not meter, is present in the political verses of Constantine Manasses, Tzetzes, and their like. He then adds:

> There is no doubt that those verses are older in which rhythm alone is present.

He adds also:

> Some poets were content with rhythm alone, and differed in no other way from ordinary speech. Others animated rhythm with poetic language. Finally, others added meter as well.

He learned this from Bede, in the book *De arte metrica*. His words, joined to those I quoted shortly before, are these:

> Yet generally, by some chance, you will also find a pattern in rhythm—not preserved by the discipline of art, but led by sound and by the modulation itself—which uneducated poets of the common people necessarily produce in a rustic manner, though learnedly.

In this way, too, that famous hymn was most beautifully fashioned in the likeness of iambic meter:

> Eternal King and Lord,  
> Creator of all things,  
> Who were before the ages,  
> The Son ever with the Father.

And there are many other Ambrosian hymns of the same kind. Likewise, in the form of trochaic meter, they sing the hymn on the day of judgment alphabetically:

> Suddenly the day will appear,  
> The great day of the Lord, a thief in the darkness,  
> Seizing the unsuspecting as though by night.

This is Bede. If countless examples of these rhythms had not perished—for they were not preserved with the same care as metrical verses—we should now discern in these verses an immense variety. For my part, I transcribed from a manuscript of the Ambrosian Library the Antiphonary of the monastery of Bangor and published it in Volume IV of the *Anecdota Latina*. Its date seems to belong to the eighth century of the Christian era. Several hymns occur there, and the fact that the metrical pattern is only loosely observed persuades me that all of them should be assigned to the category of rhythmic compositions.

Above all, however, the catalectic trochaic verse was frequently used in rhythms, as Terentianus Maurus calls it in his book *De litteris et metris*. Indeed, he himself left a number of verses of this kind composed by him. Let us offer an example from him:

> I have brought forward the syllables which agree with heroic meter,  
> As my ability allowed, I have set them forth after discussion, etc.

> That swift little vessel is the one you see, guests.

Verses of this kind were used especially for taunts, as in that celebrated song of the soldiers against Julius Caesar while he was leading his Gallic triumph:

> Caesar conquered the Gauls; Nicomedes conquered Caesar.  
> Behold, Caesar now triumphs, who conquered the Gauls;  
> Nicomedes does not triumph, who conquered Caesar.

Suetonius supplies another example: verses then produced against the same Caesar:

> Guard your wives, city men: we are bringing the bald adulterer.  
> You fucked away gold in Gaul; here you borrowed it.

In both passages the meter is the same, with a dactyl at the end and fifteen syllables in each verse; but the short and long syllables are not observed in the same way. I say fifteen syllables because the ancient rhythm-makers almost always took care to preserve equality of syllable-count when such verses were sung to musical tunes. Dancing was even added, together with a kind of striking of the fingers, as Cicero, Quintilian, and others indicate.

This appears to have been done earlier by the Jews as well. For taunts were not used in rhythmic form only among the Romans, but also among the Jews, and long before they were adopted by the Romans. See the First Book of Kings, chapter XVIII, verse 6. When David returned after striking down the Philistine, the women, singing and leading choruses to meet King Saul, sang:

> Saul has struck down a thousand,  
> And David ten thousand.

The stinging rhythm displeased the king. The most ancient translator rendered its words in such a way that he formed from them a trochaic verse, as were many of the rhythms of antiquity. This was done because in Hebrew that gibe is expressed in two eight-syllable little verses as follows:

> Icchà Saùl balafaju [Saul by his thousands],  
> Vedavìd berivvodaju [and David by his ten-thousands].

Here, I would have you notice at once the rhyming syllables at the ends of such little verses, which Italians call *rime* (“rhymes”). Whether this happened by chance or by art, let others decide. There will be discussion of it below.

Thus, just as our songs consist of fixed feet in each stanza, so that the same musical harmony is maintained throughout, so too did the rhythms of the ancients proceed. Christians retained the same practice in barbarous times when they composed hymns, as will also be clear from the Bangor examples mentioned shortly before. I shall cite only these, dividing one verse into two little verses:

> You are found among the prophets,  
> Born in our age.  
> You existed before the ages,  
> Maker of the first age, etc.

> When he commands the little ones to be killed,  
> The crowd made martyrs.  
> The infant to be hidden is carried  
> To the river Nile, where it flows.

The aforementioned Allatius also observed that in the political verses of the Greeks, as he himself writes, the syllables never exceed fifteen; and if any appear to go beyond that number, they shorten and remove them by aphairesis or synaloepha.

The same meter is found in the *Rhythmic Lament on the Death of Constantine, Monk of Luxeuil*, composed by the monk Gudinus, and in the alphabetic rhythms of Adelmann the Scholastic, *On the Illustrious Men of His Own Time*, which the most distinguished Mabillon published among the ancient *Analecta*, composed in the eleventh century. See also, among the works of Saint Fulbert, the rhythms printed without division into verses. He too flourished in the eleventh century. Landulf the Elder, the historian of Milan, likewise exhibits a similar rhythm, which I published in Volume IV of the *Rerum Italicarum*. I shall speak of it again below. See another, too, which I made public at the end of Part II of Volume II of the *Rerum Italicarum*, in the *Paralipomena* of the Anonymous of Salerno.

But perhaps the following rhythms should be valued above all the others, since they are the most ancient and highly useful for history. The first, comprising a eulogy of Verona, Mabillon likewise added to his *Analecta*. The second, composed in praise of Milan, I published in the same Part II of Volume II of the *Rerum Italicarum*. Each owes its birth—or at least the life it now enjoys—to the Veronese rhythm-maker, since both were finally brought to light through our efforts after being taken from Veronese manuscripts. Indeed, for this principal reason, both Mabillon and I hoped that we would win the favor of the most illustrious man, the marquis Scipione Maffei of Verona, who continues to glorify both his homeland and ancient learning with the highest distinction.

But, astonishingly, he found in our undertaking scarcely anything other than a cause for anger and criticism. What our friend found so displeasing, and what he wrote in his dissertation on rhythmic verses published in 1727, I shall report frankly.

First, he objects that we published such rhythms as we found them in the manuscript codices—that is, full of errors. Then he accuses us of having submitted both rhythms to the press not in verses separately distinguished, but in continuous prose-like form, preserving only the order of the stanzas:

> Such monuments, he writes, should not be printed like inscriptions or like old legal instruments, without changing a letter, since one thing is an original document of an ancient notary, where the errors themselves teach many things; and another is a history or composition transmitted to us by copyists who have foolishly deviated from the author’s mind and writing. In the latter case it is necessary to use the critical lamp, and to recognize and emend wherever we can do so securely.

He then reprints the rhythm edited by Mabillon, distinguishing the individual verses and removing every error he can eliminate by emendation.

I certainly approve and commend the critical lamp of this most learned man—indeed, I approve it for correcting and purifying these same rhythms. But perhaps no one will applaud a man who rises up, not against me—for that is of no importance—but against Mabillon, a man who has deserved so extraordinarily well of letters and of the republic of learning, and who is worthy of the highest reverence from everyone.

When an ancient monument is transcribed and published from a single very old manuscript, an editor properly performs his duty if he faithfully reproduces whatever the manuscript contains, except for certain gross errors that strike everyone’s eyes and therefore permit all to excuse their removal, even without warning the reader. I never deceive the reader, provided that I myself have not been deceived in correctly understanding and rendering the writing of that ancient codex.

Afterward, however, every critical reader is free to suggest better readings, correct corrupt passages, and supply what is missing. Indeed, it might seem dangerous to do otherwise, especially when dealing with the poems of the ancients, among which these rhythms belong. Their art is delicate, and one must not venture too boldly in correcting them unless the reader is informed of the remedy applied; for, while reflecting on the passage, he may perhaps conceive a better one.

If the rule that my friend Maffei has now devised for the first time had any validity, we could already call wretched all those scholars who, especially in our own age, have rescued the monuments of antiquity from darkness without lighting the critical lamp over every individual passage. My own fortune above all would have to be lamented, since I have introduced so many previously unpublished histories into my *Collection of Italian Things* and have given them as I received them from manuscripts, often disfigured by the faults of ancient copyists. But the judgment of the learned world will certainly be otherwise.

Mabillon, I, and the other editors of unpublished materials have generally had, and shall continue to have, one purpose: to bring to light for the benefit of scholars what lies hidden in manuscripts, not to stop and subject everything to severe meditation, purifying it as though we were conducting a meticulous anatomical examination of a diseased and disordered body. That is the work of men who enjoy greater leisure—or, indeed, of anyone who wishes afterward to make use of the benefit we have supplied.

Let him therefore be exceedingly captious who takes it upon himself to rebuke that most celebrated man and me because we rescued from destruction and oblivion the rhythms as we found them in a single ancient codex, even without distinguishing the verses and even though we did not remove every error in them.

But why say more? I shall place our critic before an excellent judge, whose verdict will show how lightly grounded this novel criticism is. That judge is none other than the learned Maffei himself. When he published the *Complexiones* of Cassiodorus at Florence in 1721, he appended a letter of his own, previously published in Volume V of the Venetian edition of *Italia Sacra*. In that letter he printed the very rhythm *On the Praises of Verona*, edited by Mabillon, not once but twice, in copperplate type, using precisely the words found in Mabillon and without distinguishing the verses or employing any critical lamp. Yet in the same book he had printed, in ordered verses, the sepulchral rhythm for Pacificus the archdeacon, which is of the same meter and which I too shall republish below in this work, Dissertation XLIII, *On the State of Letters*.

Why, I ask, was what Maffei himself considered permissible and praiseworthy in 1721 regarded as unlawful and blameworthy six years later? Behold how he fights against himself with his own weapons.

If I see correctly, the only conclusion that can be drawn from his recently devised opinion—not from what he contrived against Mabillon and me—is that suspicion has been cast into the minds of readers, and will scarcely ever be removed: whenever Maffei himself publishes something new from ancient codices, we shall not receive it as it stood on the parchment, but as it appeared to the learned man’s critical lamp. Consequently, we shall no longer be certain whether, in many places, we possess the words and thought of the ancients or Maffei’s ideas, with which he makes the ancients speak as he himself judges best. What confidence, then, should be placed in him in the future?

These, I believe, are the legitimate rules of genuine criticism. When ancient monuments are first published, especially if they are taken from some single ancient manuscript—and all the more if they are poems—there is no need to depart from the reading of the codex. Indeed, the circumstances demand that the same reading be retained as far as possible, excluding only the most obvious errors of the copyist, which anyone can recognize.

If, however, the editor intends to alter, delete, or supply anything more substantial, he may not do so secretly and without the readers’ knowledge. Nor is it sufficient to justify such license by saying: “I have applied the happiest conjectures and the most suitable remedies in accordance with the authors’ intention and the laws of meter.” For however abundant anyone may be in intellectual acumen—and I unquestionably acknowledge this praise in the most illustrious Maffei—the reader’s judgment must always remain free, so that he can see whether the critic has applied his medical hands correctly or incorrectly to the ancient codices and the works of the ancients.

Indeed, however great critics may be in correcting ancient books, they often serve us not the authors’ words but their own reflections and conjectures—things that the ancients never even dreamed of.

In the rhythm edited through Mabillon’s efforts, the verse stood as follows:

> From the East he has the first martyr Stephen.

Maffei restored it by his own conjecture as follows:

> From the East you have the first proto-martyr Stephen.

If the author had used *primum* not as an adverb but as an adjective—which one may quite reasonably suppose, since otherwise he would have said *primo*, not *primum*—he would, I think, now laugh on seeing himself compelled by such an emendation to call Stephen “the first martyr” twice. Why, then, may I not restore that verse by a lighter addition and write:

> From the East you have, for, the first martyr Stephen.

When we undertake to put displaced bones back into their places, it is better to complete the treatment than to inflict new wounds.

The verses of these rhythms consist of two little verses, of which the first contains eight syllables and the second seven, provided that the ordinary laws of that rhythm are observed. If we read “the first proto-martyr Stephen,” the number of syllables will run beyond the limits. It is therefore more reasonable to supply the verse by writing “for, the first martyr Stephen.”

But what am I saying? In correcting the writings of barbarous times we must proceed in darkness, and we shall often be mistaken whenever we attribute to the carelessness and ignorance of copyists faults that ought rather to be attributed to the uneducated authors themselves. We see the laws of meter—that is, the number of syllables—neglected in these rhythmic verses. Who assures us that the copyist, rather than their author, committed the error?

Consider these other monstrous verses:

> John the Baptist the precursor, and Nazarius the martyr.

> Mamas, Andronicus, and Probus, with forty martyrs.

> In the times of princes, kings Desiderius and Adelchis.

I omit the rest. We have a similar example in the epitaph of Pacificus the archdeacon, which the same marquis Maffei nevertheless copied from the marble:

> In the twenty-seventh year of the age of Caesar Lothair.

The distinguished marquis advises that in Mabillon one should write *Adelchiis* [or, perhaps more correctly, *Adelchii*], and likewise *Baptismium* and *Ravennia*, since that kind of rhythm requires a dactyl, Cretic, or anapaest at the end. Quite so. Yet it remains uncertain whether the common rhythm-makers of those times allowed themselves to be bound so strictly by these laws. We have just seen what happened in the observance of syllables.

Vopiscus also records a military rhythm in his *Aurelian*, composed in these words:

> A thousand, a thousand, a thousand, a thousand, a thousand we beheaded.  
> One man: a thousand, a thousand, a thousand we beheaded.  
> A thousand, a thousand, a thousand—long live the man who killed a thousand.  
> No one has as much wine [or: drinks as much wine] as the blood he shed.

I think these verses should be written in this way. The third, it seems, closes contrary to the rules with the word *killed*. But even hexameters among the better poets sometimes close not with a dactyl but with a spondee.

As for the rhythm *On the Praises of Milan*, which I published, the learned critic complains that it was incorrectly transcribed from a very old Veronese codex. In these words he seems silently to accuse the most learned Bartholomeo Campagnola, chancellor of the chapter of the canons of Verona and now archpriest of the church of Saint Cecilia in that same city, by whom the little work was transcribed and sent to me.

It is surprising that a man otherwise so perceptive did not first consider whether he might incur the reproach of a rash judge, since he had to pass judgment on an unknown matter without having inspected the manuscript codex. Yet the rhythm is full of errors. I do not deny it. But what follows from this in the judgment of a cautious critic? No fewer faults occur in Mabillon’s rhythm, although no one would deny that he was an incomparable man and supremely skilled in ancient writing.

“But,” Maffei replies, “very few people now understand the characters of the ancients,” which he calls *antico corsivo*, “ancient cursive.” But what if Campagnola himself should not be excluded from the ranks of those few? Maffei himself is now free—for formerly he was not—to examine that same codex, at the place where it contains the rhythm published by me. He will then judge more prudently whether the things that remain corrupt or obscure in this rhythm should be attributed to the ancient copyist—not to mention the author of the rhythm itself—or to the exceptionally capable Campagnola.

For my part, I took care to have the same rhythm transcribed with the greatest exactness and to reproduce it from the manuscript in precisely the same forms of the letters, as though I had inspected the codex with my own eyes. I also touched it with my own hand, and nothing in the copy once sent to me by the most accurate Campagnola differed from the fidelity of that codex.

Whatever differs in my edition from the codex was altered or emended by me alone. It is permissible—and I repeat this, and the distinguished Maffei himself also prescribes it—for one transcribing ancient monuments from manuscripts, few of which are free from copyists’ errors, to remove manifest faults, but only those that can rightly be conjectured to have arisen from the scribes’ negligence.

I left the rest untouched, being occupied and preoccupied with other matters by the magnitude of the undertaking. Nor would I have considered it permissible to venture on greater changes without informing the readers. I now also observe that there was no need to write *quaestu* in place of *quaestum*. But I have no time to dwell further on these minor disputes or trifles.

I shall add only this: we are forced to believe that our friend Maffei was driven by an immense itch to wield the censor’s rod when he wrote these things. Not content with this, and straying beyond the proper path, he also attacked a fragment of the *Life of Saint Geminianus, Bishop of Modena*, which I had excerpted from another Veronese codex and published in the same Part II of Volume II of the *Rerum Italicarum*, believing its author to have flourished around the year 910.

If I were possessed by the same desire, and wished to repay like with like, I would not lack material in the books of the learned critic that might be subjected to more equitable criticism. But, not forgetting the laws of friendship, I shall use a shield here, not a sword.

He therefore writes that the aforementioned fragment of the *Life of Saint Geminianus* was taken from a Lectionary written around the fourteenth century. Very well. Codices of that century, themselves copied from older ones, have sometimes preserved even rarer gems for us.

He adds:

> Little account can be made of it, since the Lives in that Lectionary contain very inept interpolations; among others, the Life of Saint Zeno.

That interpolations occur in the *Life of Saint Zeno* does not prove, as I think learned men will agree, that all the other Lives in that codex are likewise teeming with interpolations. More than this: no one will point out a single interpolation in the aforementioned *Life of Saint Geminianus*. Why, then, does Maffei say this?

He continues:

> The author of the addition mentions the ancient incursion of the Hungarians; but he does not show that he lived at the time of that incursion, but rather during some other one of those made by that people.

Yet all learned men will be certain that this same Life, together with the fragment published by me, was committed to writing before the middle of the tenth century.

“I had persuaded myself,” he adds, “that this addition had hitherto remained unknown because I had noticed that it was missing from the Life published by the distinguished Father Bollandus for 31 January. But while writing this, I now discover that the same Bollandus had long ago printed the identical fragment from the Bodec manuscript in the additions at the end of the volume for that day, although with such differences that I do not at all regret having published it again.”

We therefore now have evidence that the fragment was not derived from a single Veronese codex. In that manuscript, however, it is written:

> But since we have composed, as best we could, the Life of so great a father, the lord Geminianus, in writing, it is also fitting to explain more truthfully something about the location of the city in which he served as bishop.

These words plainly show that the material concerning the site of the city of Modena was added not by another hand but by the author of the Life himself.

At what time that author flourished can be gathered most clearly from his other words, where he speaks of the most savage people of the Hungarians, feared by almost everyone, whom, he says, “we have experienced in our tribulations.” He then adds that they entered Italy from the north, crossed as far as Verona after devastating the Friulian march, and ravaged the whole region, attacking without resistance all the strongest city walls, all fortified places, and every walled town.

Finally he writes:

> And so that plague—which, would that we had never known it!—not merely of battle but of an unaccustomed death, etc., at last reached the episcopal city of Modena, etc.

Everyone sees that these words were written by a man who had not merely seen but had also experienced how furiously the savage Hungarian people had torn Italy apart, or had torn it apart only a few years before. They had come from Scythia into Pannonia, which they had previously subjected, around the year 889 of the Christian era.

According to Hermannus Contractus, the Continuator of the *Annals of Fulda*, and others, their first incursion into Italy appears to belong to the year 900. The Saxon Annalist, published by Eckard and following Regino, describes either the same or another invasion under the year 901 in these words:

> They also entered Lombardy, mingling slaughter with fires. When the inhabitants of the land gathered together and attempted to resist, many bishops and counts, together with an innumerable multitude of people, were slaughtered by arrows. Liutward, bishop of Vercelli, fled with the treasures, encountered them, and was immediately killed.

There is an indication of how far that most savage people had penetrated in that year or the preceding one. Their incursion into the territory of Modena, and the devastation of the celebrated monastery of Nonantola carried out by them, seems to belong to those same years, as Pagius rightly observed.

In the following years, Italy suffered new wounds from them. After the Christian army that Berengar I, king of Italy, had led against them was defeated, there was no one, as Liutprand of Cremona reports in Book II, chapter 6 of his *History*, who could await their arrival except perhaps in the most strongly fortified places.

According to the same Liutprand, in the year when Emperor Louis III paid the penalty for violated faith after being captured by Berengar—that is, either in 902 or later, as he shows elsewhere—the fury of the Hungarians spread throughout Italy without anyone being able to resist them.

Richard of Cluny, and Bonfinius after him, report that from then on the Hungarians were accustomed to return to Italy almost every year for the purpose of plundering, so that they might wipe out whatever remained. In the year 905, Sigonius writes, those same barbarians made a new incursion. Then, in 921 and the following year, Italy was drenched in blood by their swords and arrows.

In 924 their power and fury increased so greatly that they compelled Ticinum, the splendid seat of the kingdom, to surrender and consumed it with fire. In 937 the same people traversed Alamannia, Gaul, and Burgundy, and returned through Italy to their own kingdoms.

Lupus Protospata likewise records that they harassed Italy in 920, then in 936, 940, and 947 invaded Apulia, besieged Capua, and inflicted innumerable disasters on those regions.

There is also a marginal note in a manuscript of the Casanatensian Library at Rome, where the Paschal Cycle of Dionysius Exiguus is recorded in these words:

> In this year—that is, in the year of Christ 922—the Hungarians came into Apulia on the fourth day of the month of February.

But such a disaster does not seem to have concerned Lombardy, since the Hungarians could have reached Apulia not by land but by sea.

After the death of Hugh, king of Italy, the same Hungarians again invaded the heart of Italy, but withdrew after being appeased by gifts from Berengar, marquis and later king. Baronius and Pagius think this occurred in the year 949. Yet from the historian Liutprand one might perhaps infer that it happened earlier.

Finally, Frodoard, in his *Chronicle* under the year 951, reports that the Hungarians advanced from Italy into Aquitaine. Perhaps Italy also saw Hungarians fleeing from Gaul in 954; but after that we do not read that the most savage people again invaded these regions. For the warlike peoples of Germany, after inflicting many massacres, finally taught them to keep within their own boundaries.

The entire period of the sufferings that Italy endured from the Hungarians therefore truly falls between the years 900 and 950.

Since it is established, as we have seen above, that the author of the *Life of Saint Geminianus* flourished during that very period, I ask whether there was any just ground for criticism because I wrote that its author flourished around the year 910.

But my friend Maffei says:

> That author does not show that he lived when the Hungarians made their incursion against the people of Modena in 900 or 902, but rather during one of the other invasions made by that people while it was raging.

And what of it? Is it not enough for me that he lived while the Hungarians were roaming about and making incursions into Italy? But why could he not also have lived earlier? Here we are both dealing with conjectures. Let him deny, if he can, that this writer might have flourished even in the year 900 itself. If that could have happened, it is enough for me, and there is no reason for Maffei to prefer his conjecture to mine.

This is especially so since the distinguished Bollandus appended the following note to the words “whom we experienced as most savage in our tribulations”—for, using the Bodec manuscript, he reads the passage somewhat differently:

> This appears to have been the Hungarian incursion mentioned by Liutprand, *History*, Book II, chapters 4, 5, and 6, at the beginning of the tenth century.

I was all the more entitled to write this because I did not assign the writing of the *Life of Saint Geminianus* precisely to the year 900, but to the year 910; and even that I did not specify with certainty, for I added the word “around,” thereby indicating to the reader that the writer’s date could also be placed later.

But if I were to add more, I would show that I had no regard either for time or for the patience of others. It is therefore better to resume the journey that has been interrupted.

To make it still clearer that Campagnola should not have been accused of ignorance of ancient writing in the matter mentioned above, and that the errors with which ancient little works abound should be assigned to ancient authors who were poorly acquainted with the Latin language and to copyists who stumbled most disgracefully, it is useful to add here another rhythm of the same meter, never before published, excerpted by that same Campagnola from a very ancient Veronese codex.

I removed no fault from it, although many things immediately strike the eye. The first letters of the stanzas form an acrostic, namely **GAIDHADLUS**, who seems to have been a parish priest in the city of Verona and the author of the rhythm itself:

> Let us likewise render exalted thanks to the King,  
> Who gathered us together as one; we praise you, Lord,  
> So that we may find rest forever.  
> Let us petition the most high Son of God on high,  
> That he may deign to send his radiant angel  
> To defeat and drive away the most ancient enemy.  
> That envious tempter, deceitful and ruined,  
> Always desires to set brothers who agree at odds.  
> So that he may be able to earn grace before the wicked Prince.  
> The Lord and Savior, who redeemed his own with his blood,  
> May always preserve souls in his power,  
> So that no one except him may possess authority.  
> Honor and power remain with him forever,  
> Who deigned to appoint us shepherd over the flock,  
> So that we may present the saved sheep before his eyes.  
> That kindly watchman, the priest among the people,  
> Always stands by, stands above the flock, and fights against the impious,  
> So that no single one may snatch the sheep from the flocks.  
> Coming together in the divine temples, let us sigh together,  
> Supplicating for the flock of peoples on account of our sins,  
> So that the merciful One himself may grant forgiveness.  
> Let us strive to offer God a sacrifice for the brothers,  
> So that it may deserve to carry sheaves before him,  
> And so that we may render a double profit from the talent.  
> Let each of us watch and pray for the other,  
> So that we may find rest forever,  
> And possess the life that the Lord has sent.  
> Let us ask the supreme King on behalf of the guilt of all,  
> And through him let us deserve to find forgiveness  
> Who always lives and reigns forever.  
> I ask you, dear brother, who sing this little verse,  
> To seek out the initial letters in order.  
> Thus one finds the name of the one who composed this.

How many errors you encounter here! Am I to be blamed because I publish this? Or Campagnola, because he transcribed it faithfully? From fair-minded readers I certainly do not expect such a reward.

Thus far we have observed the trochaic verse preserved in rhythms, although prosody is neglected. It remains to say that in barbarous times the authors of rhythms also turned to imitation of other kinds of verse.

Saint Boniface, bishop of Mainz and martyr, around the year 740, wrote the following in Letter 65:

> I send and dedicate to you, most discerning sower, a third poem, worked out not according to the measurement of feet but composed with eight syllables in each verse, fitted by one and the same letter into corresponding lines, and traced in a continuous course of the pen [that is, written out], which I have engraved and transmitted to you.

He describes a rhythm composed by himself, and also provides an example of it in the preceding letter, where these verses are found:

> For me I seek prayers.

Of prayers: it will set forth the principal matters, etc. But the rhythm-makers also imitated the hexameter, though sometimes with such an appearance of harshness that only someone who already knows to look for rhythms there will recognize the wretched attempt of an unlearned people to emulate the noble meter. If you seek examples of this rhythm, see Inscription VII, Christian, p. 1061 of the old edition of Gruter’s *Thesaurus* [Col. 0772A], and also, in volume IV of *Italia Sacra*, among the bishops of Vercelli, the epitaph of Bishop Flavian, who is thought to have occupied the see of Vercelli around the year 540.

But I should like you to behold an even more ancient and altogether clearest example of this shapeless poetry in the poem of Commodianus, a rough Christian poet. It was once published by Rigaltius and later included in volume XXVII of the *Bibliotheca Patrum*. He is believed to have flourished at the beginning of the fourth century of the Christian era; indeed, some have thought that his lifetime should be assigned to the third century. He carries out his acrostic *Instructions* in no other verses than hexameters, but without observing any of the laws of meter, as a few examples will make clear. Thus, in *Instruction* XV:

> Hercules, who dashed down the monster of Aventine Mountain,  
>   
> Of Evander, who was accustomed to steal cattle,  
>   
> The rustic mind of men, unlearned even in praise,  
>   
> When they wished to give thanks to the absent Thunderer, etc.

He continues in this manner, being a common man, and closes these most useful teachings in verses suited to the understanding of the common people. It is certain that poets who accommodated themselves to the common people afterward employed such license, and employed it for a very long time.

At this point two examples present themselves to me, belonging to the period of the Lombard kingdom. The first is an epitaph placed around the year 722 in the church of the celebrated monastery of Bobbio, during the reign of King Liutprand, for Saint Cumianus, bishop of the Scots, who ended his life there. Ughellius published it in volume IV of *Italia Sacra*, among the bishops of Bobbio. Since I once copied it more carefully from the marble itself, I present it again to readers:

### Epitaph of Saint Cumianus, bishop, inscribed on a marble tablet at Bobbio

> + Here the sacred limbs of blessed Cumianus are laid to rest; his soul, penetrating heaven, rejoices with the angels. He was great in dignity, birth, and appearance. Scotland sent this old man to the Italian borders. He is placed at Bobbio, constrained by love of the Lord, where, observing the venerable teaching of Columbanus, ever watchful, fasting, unwearied, continually praying, he lived happily for four Olympiads and one year’s cycle, so that he may now rightly be believed blessed: gentle, prudent, pious, and peaceful toward all his brothers. He had completed ninety years of age, together with one lustrum and four months. But, O excellent and powerful Father, become an intercessor for the most glorious King Liutprand, who, devoted to you, adorned your tomb with a precious stone, so that it might be manifest where the nourishing body is buried. D.P.  
>   
> [Note: That is: “Here was laid to rest the lord Cumianus, bishop, on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of September,” etc.]  
>   
> Here is the lord Cumianus, bishop, [buried] on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of September. John the master made [this].

[Col. 0773B] P. Romualdus of Saint Mary, of the order of the Discalced Hermits of Saint Augustine, also reports in his *Papia Flavia*, part I, p. 131, the epitaph of Theodata—that is, of the woman to whom the oldest as well as noblest monastery of consecrated virgins at Ticinum owes its origin, now called della Posterla, which is mentioned by Paul the Deacon. That fragment of Lombard learning, written at the beginning of the eighth century, deserved to be transmitted to us more accurately from the stone. I shall indicate only the first verses:

> Dweller in heaven [Note: [Col. 0773B] Perhaps *caelicam*, “heavenly.”]—thus at last I shall weave her lineage. She lived as mother of virgins for exceedingly many years, feeding Christ’s little sheep in the Lord’s flock; cherishing them, teaching them, reproving them, correcting them, and loving them, etc.

See also, in the *Life of Saint Felix, archbishop of Ravenna*, in volume II of *Rerum Italicarum*, p. 164, an epitaph formed in hexameters and pentameters of this kind, though strangely disfigured by a copyist. It was composed around the year 716. Nor was the eternal city itself without such poetic graces. Turrigius, part II, p. 539, of *De cryptis Vaticanis*, reports the epitaph of the girl Elisabeth, buried on the sixth day before the Kalends of September, in the fifth indiction—a formula that belongs to a remote age.

> Here lies the body of the girl Elisabeth in a tomb, which remains in the holy hall of the most blessed John. Hildebrand, her offspring [Note: [Col. 0775C] Perhaps *genitor*, “father,” for *genita*.], and Theodora, her mother. She passed away at twice six years and ten months; [the remaining wording is corrupt: “John, yours, and Paul, duly led beneath the gracious [one] …”], etc.

But above all, among rhythms of this kind, the epitaph of Thomas deserves to be read. He assisted Pope Honorius I around the year 636 in removing the schism of the Church of Aquileia. It is presented by the cardinal of immortal name, Baronius, in the appendix to volume XII of the *Annals*, among the additions to the *Ecclesiastical Annals* for the year 638. This, I think, was the reason why the other cardinal of the Holy Roman Church, Henry Noris, whose praise can never be sufficient, never noticed this monument when, in his *Dissertation on the Fifth Synod*, §6, he discussed the date on which that schism was abolished. The opening verses, composed in the form of hexameters, run as follows:

> Who will grant me that the immense weeping may cease,  
> and give the mourning of my soul a place for speaking truth?  
> Although, amid tears, sobbing words burst forth,  
> I, your most certain disciple, speak of you.  
> The nobility of your parents, minister of Christ,  
> and your pure conduct, Thomas,  
> showed you to be honorable.  
> Virginity lived with you from the cradle, etc.

Nor were the pagan age and its common people without these disordered verses. I am now pleased to produce an example that, as I believe, has not yet been published. From the manuscript papers of the most eminent Cardinal of the Holy Roman Church, Domenico Passionei, I copied the following poem. It lies in the village of Salsola in the county of Urbino, engraved on an ancient stone, displaying unmistakable barbarism both of language and of lettering.

> To the divine Manes. Gaius Arrius Victorinus, husband, [set this up for] Vttidia Titianeni. While you were among the gods above, no woman was more beautiful to me than you. Now you lie prostrate, undeserving, surrounded by earth; you who were deprived of the way, having followed the light. Thus, with reason, I would inscribe such verses about you, not composed by study but given by the mind and compelled by grief. You, Titiana, were first joined to me in marriage; you were the first and sweeter part of my sorrow. [Uncertain: *ut mei te repellat*]; suddenly snatched away, you left [me] forever, [a joy] which I was not permitted to enjoy for years, by final fate. You were cruelly snatched away from [your] mother [or: “by death”?], as a little lamb; just as that wretched one is snatched and vowed upon altars, so you quickly made me, still a child, sorrowful. Your wretched parents suffer this grief with me through life. As a rose is lovely in the new spring for a short time, so this unfortunate woman, my dearest wife, lived for me seventeen years, eight months, [and] days [lacuna]. Felix, stone-[lacuna].

[Col. 0775C] Add to these the Christian epitaph of Catervius, whom the people of Tolentino venerate as a saint. Mabillon published it in his *Itinerarium Italicum*, and Fabretti subsequently edited it more accurately in chapter 10, no. 505, of his *Inscriptiones Antiquae*, as follows:

> Those whom the almighty Lord joined through equal merits in a sweet marriage, this tomb guards forever. Catervius, Severina joined to you rejoices; may you rise together, blessed through Christ’s favor.

Below:

> Whom the priest of God, Probia[nus], washed and anointed.

For a long time the use of such plebeian verses continued; this is shown by an inscription placed at Rome around the year 1014 and published by the distinguished Marco Antonio Boldetti in his excellent work *On the Cemeteries of the Martyrs*, book II, chapter 5.

> Here, buried, lie the limbs of Petrocius. He was good and wise; for he was of great birth, handsome, distinguished, generous to his friends. He always possessed grace, worthy conversation, lovable to all, kindly, ready, and bold; loving the heavenly kingdoms, always a lover of them, gentle in character, and a defender of the poor. All of you who read, I beg you, say together: Most merciful God, have mercy on your servant. Virgin Mother of God, with all the saints, have mercy on Petroccius. He died in peace in the time of Benedict VIII, on the eighteenth day of January.

Fabretti also reports the following in chapter 3, p. 146, of his *Inscriptiones Antiquae*:

> A name was her name: both [names] clung to Cosuccia at her birth. By this inscription I signify the names. I lived a little and was sweet while I lived for my parent. By this inscription I am covered. Whoever reads the inscription, you perceive how little I lived. This alone I ask: now say, “May the earth be light for you.”

See also other similar examples, indeed ones composed with still greater hostility toward the Muses, in the same Fabretti, chapter 4, pp. 329, 418, 419, and 421. See also the epitaph of Boni, consul and duke of Naples, who flourished in the ninth century of the Christian era, in volume II of *Rerum Italicarum*, p. 342.

So much for hexameter and pentameter rhythms.

We must now append the hendecasyllables, dodecasyllables, heptasyllables, and others that were in use among the ancients. I do this all the more willingly because Italian poetry in the vernacular derived from them, above all, examples for its own compositions. Before showing this, it is useful to bring forward another very ancient practice of rhythmic, indeed also metrical, poetry.

Some believe that even the ancient Romans and Greeks found pleasing the modulation of consonant syllables—what we now call *rhyme*, the word *rhythmus* having been transformed into *rima*—especially when sought at the ends of verses, so that the final syllable of one verse or member answered the final syllable of the following one. Such an arrangement, or figure, of words is said to have pleased poets themselves. It certainly pleased orators, provided that it was used sparingly. The Greeks called this figure ὁμοιοτέλευτον (*homoioteleuton*), “ending alike”; the same thing was called *similiter cadens* in Latin.

Two verses of Cicero, quoted by Quintilian in book XI, chapter 1, are widely known, although many mocked them even during Cicero’s lifetime:

> Let arms yield to the toga; let laurels yield to the tongue.

> O fortunate Rome, born under my consulship!

Varro too, in the *Funeral of Menippus*, brought forward:

> Nor did the orthophallic psalteries bring forth  
>   
> those sayings that resound in Greece,  
>   
> which place the beginnings of stories.

Here I think *exodia* should be read.

Even the most ancient Ennius appears to have delighted in this device. Cicero reports these verses of his in the *Tusculan Disputations*, book I:

> I saw all these things set ablaze,  
>   
> life being taken from Priam [or rather, “being unmanned”?],  
>   
> the altar of Jupiter defiled with blood.

Cicero also records the following in the same *Tusculans*—whether they belong to someone else or to himself, I do not know:

> The sky growing bright, the trees putting forth leaves,  
>   
> the joyful vines swelling with tendrils,  
>   
> the branches bending beneath the abundance of berries.

Similar verses of the ancients led Stilianus, writing on the art of versification, to persuade himself that rhythms—now called *le rime*—were used in the finest age of Latin. For, as he writes, Virgil, *Aeneid* VI.165, has:

> To stir the men with bronze and kindle Mars with song.

And Ovid:

> As many stars as the sky, so many girls your Rome possesses.

And Propertius:

> No, no—such gifts are not won by human means;  
>   
> the months of the gods did not produce these blessings.

So Horace, in *The Art of Poetry*:

> It is not enough for poems to be beautiful: let them be pleasing,  
>   
> and let whatever they wish move the minds of their hearers.

And Ausonius likewise, in *Idyll* II:

> Whether drinking three, or multiplying three by three.

Yet it could scarcely have happened that such verses did not occasionally escape ancient versifiers even when they were thinking of nothing of the kind. Accordingly, I will certainly not oppose those who judge that these things arose by chance rather than by art, or were produced unintentionally. Nevertheless, since I have said that *homoioteleuton* did not displease orators, it cannot stubbornly be denied that poets too may sometimes have delighted in the same figure. This was especially possible among rustic and popular poets, for whom consonance of words might have sounded more pleasing to the ear.

Had so many rhythms and poems of plebeian poets of that age not perished, perhaps we would possess more verses taken from Latium itself that ended alike. Similar examples also occur among the Greeks, as in the *Anthology* and elsewhere.

There are also those who think that the Hebrews sought similar pleasures for the ear in their poetry, either in the middle of verses or in their endings. I see this asserted especially by the most distinguished Huet. You can indeed sense it in the Hebrew rhythm that the women sang in David’s praise, which I cited above. The distinguished Father Martinaceus, a Benedictine monk of the Congregation of Saint Maur, also shows, by examples brought forward in his *Prolegomena to the Divine Library of Saint Jerome*, that rhythms occur in the Song of Deuteronomy and in the Lamentations of Jeremiah—that is, equal endings of sound at the end of cola.

But I leave the controversy concerning Hebrew poetry to others. Perhaps in some passages of it a similarity of sounds entered by chance rather than by art. Especially in the barbarian centuries, however, it was customary to add this embellishment both to rhythms and to meters. In my judgment, the unlearned did so in order at least by these decorations to compensate for the quantity of feet that they neglected; the learned did so so that verses ending alike might more easily be retained in the memory of the people.

At first they established this slight shadow of modulation in the final syllable of one verse, which would be consonant with the final syllable of the following verse or verses. Sometimes alternating verses also answered one another. If a verse ended in a dactyl, some became accustomed to placing the same final two syllables in the succeeding verses. Finally, the practice was carried so far that at the end of a verse two entire syllables, if long, answered the subsequent verses in letters and sound; three syllables answered in the same way if the penultimate syllable of the verse was short, as it is in a dactyl. The poets of our vernacular language adopted this practice and still retain it.

Verses in which this final *homoioteleuton*, or *similiter cadens*, occurred—more pleasing than what came before it and striking the ears of men—were once called Leonine. Scaliger did not know why they had been so called, in *Poetics*, book II, chapter 29. Stephanus Guazzius foolishly thought that they were so named from a lion’s tail. René Moreau, a Parisian physician, in his commentary on the *School of Salerno*, and du Cange in his *Latin Glossary*, suppose that they may perhaps have been so called because they were invented by a certain poet named Leo, who lived around the time of Louis VII or Philip Augustus, kings of France.

Du Cange adds that this was also the opinion of Stephanus Paschasius, book VII, chapter 2, of his *Investigations into French Matters*, who produced some very elegant verses by this poet Leo. The learned Papebrochius likewise accepted this opinion in the *Acta Sanctorum* for 1 June, in the *Life of Saints Gratianus and Felinus*, judging only that these verses were brought to their highest perfection by Leo, a French poet of the twelfth century.

Indeed, Aegidius of Paris, in du Chesne, volume V of the *French Writers*, p. 323, mentions among other poets of his time—that is, from 1191 to 1198:

> Nor less, in sacred song, Leo, playing  
> with history in melodious language.

He is the same man praised by du Cange and Papebrochius. Therefore Polycarpus Leyserus was mistaken to regard these as different poets in his *History of the Poets of the Middle Ages*, nos. 79 and 95.

My once highly learned friend D. Gaspar Berettus, a Benedictine, often praised by me in this work, discussed Leonine verses in the *Prolegomena to the Chorographic Map* that I published in volume X of *Rerum Italicarum*. There, no. 62, p. 117, he judges that Leonine verses began to be composed in Italy only after the arrival of the Normans, that is, in the eleventh century of the Christian era. Accordingly, both he and Papebrochius, Eccardus, and others assigned certain inscriptions believed to belong to earlier centuries [Col. 0780B] to no earlier than the year 1000 of the Christian era, because they consisted of Leonine verses.

Let the reader now learn my opinion on this matter. First, I firmly maintain that the origin or invention of the verses which the ancients called Leonine, and which we call rhymed verses, cannot in any way be attributed to that Leo—or Leoninus—the Parisian poet and Benedictine monk of the monastery of Saint Victor, who flourished around the year 1091, as du Cange, Jacobus Perizonius, and others judged. For there were predecessors who played with verses of this kind, composing either rhythms or meters.

Second, I maintain that it is still uncertain whether he at least perfected this manner of versifying. But if we wish to confer some glory upon him, it is permissible to suppose either that he composed a poem so harmonious and elegant, and so sonorous in the concert of mutually answering words, that it became an object of popular admiration; or that he constructed his verses so that, although he produced a long work, he nevertheless preserved in the endings of the verses a continuous order and the similar ending of two syllables—something perhaps no one before him had fully dared.

For, as I have said, most of the ancients placed the concord of their rhythms or meters in a single syllable consonant with another. Most also sought this pleasure for the ears not at the end of pairs of verses, but within the verse itself, whose first member answered the following one. All this is confirmed by examples.

At the end of the sixth century after Christ, Saint Columbanus flourished, that most celebrated founder of the monastery of Bobbio. Among his works is a rhythm *On the Vanity of Life*, in which we see most of the verses ending alike. For example:

> Death, uncertain, snatches life from those who differ;  
>   
> sorrow of death seizes all the proud and wandering, etc.

> Most have endured the fires of punishments,  
>   
> unwilling to suffer the losses of slippery desire, etc.

I omit the remainder. If they truly have Columbanus as their author, they provide the most ancient form of verses ending alike.

Thus, among the works of Bede, verses *On the Rules of Computus* are read in which one hears Leonine harmony. Take the opening ones:

> It is not right to celebrate the Lord’s coming in December  
>   
> after the third day before the Nones, nor before the fifth day before the Kalends, etc.

Saint Boniface of Mainz, bishop and martyr, whom I praised above, also produced, in his first letter, written around the year 780, a rhythm distinguished by consonant words:

> Farewell, brother, with the flourishing  
>   
> strength of youth,  
>   
> so that, flourishing with the Lord,  
>   
> you may be in the eternal throne, etc.

In letter 69, four poems of his are also reported, with paired verses answering one another in similar sound, though, although a dactyl almost always closes the verse, only the final two syllables are alike. I offer a specimen:

> The supreme Sower sits upon the heavenly thrones,  
>   
> through the ethereal realms,  
>   
> surrounded by the threatening citadels  
>   
> of high Olympus, etc.

Surely, by God’s love, someone might wonder whether such poems should be assigned so great an antiquity. But all doubt will end if you consult the Bangor Antiphonary, which, as I said above, I published. It was certainly in use in the seventh century, or at the latest the eighth, at that famous monastery situated in Ireland, and was later transferred to the library at Bobbio and finally to the Ambrosian Library.

There one encounters a hymn of Saint Comgall divided into strophes, each of which begins with a letter of the alphabet, and whose individual verses end in the same syllable:

> Let us remember the justice  
>   
> of our radiant patron,  
>   
> in the name of holy Comgall,  
>   
> resplendent in his work, etc.

The verses of the second strophe all end in *a*:

> Hear, all, the deeds  
>   
> brought to the angelic [realm],  
>   
> the hidden things of God’s athletes,  
>   
> from a flourishing youth, etc.

The rest proceed in the same order.

There are also verses of the Bangor community, many of which display the complete form of those later called Leonine. Let the reader test the matter:

> Truly a royal hall,  
>   
> adorned with varied gems,  
>   
> and a fold of Christ’s flock,  
>   
> guarded by the supreme Father.  
>   
> A very fruitful virgin,  
>   
> both mother and undefiled,  
>   
> joyful and trembling,  
>   
> subdued by the Word of God.

These things are so clear that anyone can now understand that the ancient rhythm-makers and poets did not wait for the time of Leo, the Parisian poet, to be taught by him how to form verses ending with similar harmony. Nor should poems constructed in this manner too readily be judged to have been composed only after the year 1000 of the Christian era.

Cardinal Baronius reports in his *Annals* for the year 808 that verses were still preserved at Rome in the church of the Crucifers, which is said to have been founded by Belisarius during the reign of Justinian I. The learned cardinal believes that they were composed and inscribed on marble at that very time. I too present them for the reader’s inspection:

> This church, the patrician Belisarius, friend of the city, founded to obtain forgiveness for his fault. Therefore, you who set foot in this sacred building, often pray to God that he may have mercy on him.

If anyone should assign this inscription to after the tenth century, I would not oppose him. Nevertheless, there are considerations suggesting that it was set up in the sixth century of the Christian era itself. For, after many centuries had passed, the people would hardly have needed to be asked to obtain mercy from God for Belisarius through repeated prayers.

But we have another, whatever its worth, and even earlier example of words ending alike. Around the year 393 Saint Augustine composed a psalm against the party of Donatus, which is nothing other than a rhythm. Each verse consists of two eight-syllable verses. Some contain more syllables, but perhaps they should be corrected. Look for this psalm among Augustine’s works, in the opening pages of volume IX of the latest edition.

He himself writes of it in book I of the *Retractations*, chapter 20:

> I composed, in Latin letters, a psalm to be sung by the uneducated and ignorant. Such works are called abecedaries.

The rhythm of Milan mentioned above is of this kind, as is also the other one by Adelmannus the Scholastic mentioned earlier. Mabillon called that one alphabetical; Augustine called his an abecedary. I shall also give below a similar work, copied from the manuscript at Vercelli, concerning the capture of Louis II Augustus.

In addition, I possess a rhythm in honor of Saint Zeno, sent to me by the Campagnola mentioned above and excerpted from the same very ancient manuscript in which the praises of Milan, already published above, were read. This too is an abecedary. Here is its beginning:

> Let princes hear, let peoples hear, etc.

There one finds:

> The chaste daughter of the emperor had remained, etc.

> The empire asks you; it summons you to itself, etc.

There *empire* stands for *emperor*.

But let us hear Augustine himself again speaking of that psalm:

> I did not wish this to be done in any particular kind of poem, so that metrical necessity would not compel me to use words that are less common among the people.

From these words, and from those quoted above, we therefore understand that rhythms were once composed to be sung by the uneducated and ignorant. The works I mentioned a little earlier—on the praises of Milan, on Louis II, and so forth—were composed for the same purpose. In those times too there were people like those of our own day who sang crude poems, especially rhythms, either at home for amusement or in the streets for profit before an assembled crowd.

At least the semilearned understood such songs. No one had yet dared to use the vernacular for poems or rhythms; or, if anyone did use it, not even a fragment has come down to us.

I return to Augustine’s psalm. There the endings of the individual verses end in *e*, as I have also observed in other rhythms. Many consonant words ending in *-are* and *-ore* also occur, but I think that they came together by chance rather than through a deliberate search for such euphony. At least it is clear that, even in the fourth century of the Christian era, the African populace took pleasure in a certain consonance of words, so to speak, in rhythms—a consonance that later centuries enlarged and adorned more carefully.

Commodianus, whom I mentioned above, had also preceded them in his final poem, where you can sense that each verse ends in *o*.

To the Bangor rhythms and other eighth-century compositions with consonant words that I recently cited, I add the epitaph of Lantfrid, abbot of Buria in Bavaria, which Mabillon published in his *Analecta*. He flourished under Pippin and Charlemagne, kings of the Franks, and seems to have died around the year 790.

> Behold Lantfrid, the lord, born from his first beginnings,  
> paid what was owed to the earth, which man owes to himself.  
> In the flower of age, running in the fragrance of his espousals,  
> he himself offered an example of goodness to many, etc.

The remaining verses continue with the same harmony. If they were truly composed at that time, as seems very likely, they confirm what I said about minds delighted by such music in the eighth century of the Christian era.

Another example is provided by the bronze doors of the basilica of Saint-Denis at Paris, made around that period. The author wished his name to be inscribed there—Airadus the monk—in two pairs of verses engraved on the doors, which the same Mabillon attributed to the year 780 in his *Benedictine Annals*:

> This work Airadus, relying on a heavenly gift,  
> behold, offers to you, Dionysius, with a gentle heart.

Moreover, how much the sought-after harmony of consonant words was prized in the following ninth century by certain poets in weaving verses, I could demonstrate with many more examples.

An ancient mosaic is still seen in the church of Saint Mary Nova at Rome, according to Ciampinus, part II, chapter 28, of *Ancient Monuments*. There are these two verses:

> The sacred tree of the Cross becomes for the world a pathway of light;  
>   
> Christ, who bore it, raised us to the stars.

As Anastasius reports, the author both of that church and of the mosaic work was Pope Leo IV, in the year 848, or Pope Nicholas I, around the year 860. If this is certain, we already have evidence that in Rome itself, nearly nine centuries ago, consonant harmony of words was in use in verses.

If the epitaph placed on the tomb of Louis the Pious Augustus at Metz had been composed in the same century in which he died—that is, in the year 840—we would have another clear testimony to the harmony of sound then beloved in verse. It is read in volume II, p. 320, of du Chesne’s *French Writers*, and in the *Annals* of Cardinal Baronius. I offer only four verses from it:

> The lightning of empire, the noble summit of the Franks,  
>   
> Louis the king, raised from the age, is buried in this tomb;  
>   
> so great a friend of piety,  
>   
> who is called pious by the people and by the inscription, etc.

An epitaph was also placed for Drogo, archbishop of Metz and brother of that same Louis the Pious, published by the same du Chesne. Here are its opening verses:

> In this tomb is buried Bishop Drogo, carved in sculpted marble;  
>   
> his spirit, rejoicing in rest, triumphs with Abraham, etc.

Moreover, in the monastery at Lorsch the tomb of Tassilo, duke of Bavaria, whom Charlemagne deposed from his throne, is still seen, with these verses:

> In this pit is buried he whom, merciful Christ, bless:  
> Tassilo, first duke, afterward king, but finally a monk.  
> He died on the third Ides of December.

Since, however, it is possible to doubt whether verses of this kind were added to such tombs much later, let us present more certain examples. Gaspar Barthius, a man of distinguished learning, produces in book XXXII of his *Adversaria* a rhythmic poem by the monk Erinfred from a manuscript. He lived in the year 806, as his *Life* testifies. Here are only two strophes of that poem:

> The order of felicity  
>   
> always stood firm at this end.  
>   
> When it came to its appointed points,  
>   
> it collapsed, rolled back into itself.  
>   
> Whatever life brought forth—  
>   
> uncertain things, joyful and sad—  
>   
> wherever hope raised itself,  
>   
> unfaithful, hard, credulous, etc.

Especially in that century and the two following it, many took care to insert into each verse a harmony of similar words, with the verses divided, as it were, into two members whose final syllables answered one another.

The often-mentioned Mabillon published in his *Benedictine Annals* for the year 827 some verses written around that time in a very old manuscript at Hautvillers. From them what I have just said will be understood more easily:

> Ebo, glory of Reims, bishop and shining shepherd,  
>   
> evangelical teacher, friend of the exalted King,  
>   
> he ordered this book to be made, full of lofty inspiration,  
>   
> in the love of God and in honor of blessed Peter, etc.

Here, apart from the consonance of each verse’s cola, the end of one verse also rhymes with the end of another, though only in a single syllable.

Likewise, in the mosaic still surviving in the Basilica of Saint Ambrose at Milan, which Puricellus reasonably judges to have been made around the year 835, this quatrain is read:

> Martin dies, but deserves the gifts of life;  
>   
> the world grieves, while heaven rejoices.  
>   
> His death is reported as fittingly celebrated for the good patron,  
>   
> while the spirit of Ambrose ministers there.

Mabillon also reports verses of Milo, a monk of Saint-Amand, composed with equal harmony in the year 855, in his *Benedictine Annals* for the year 872. See also formulas XIV and XV in volume II of Baluzius’s *Capitularies*, p. 565. They are not formulas, however, but two rhythms breathing the utmost barbarism and, in my opinion, strangely deformed by unlearned copyists.

[Above I mentioned Notker Balbulus, a monk of Saint Gall, who, toward the end of the ninth century and the beginning of the tenth, published a book of Sequences, praised by the ancients and most recently edited by the distinguished Father Pez in part I of volume I of the *Thesaurus Anecdotorum*. Such Sequences—though I would rather call them hymns—were composed with rhythmic license in various meters. I select one of them:]

> The renowned merits  
>   
> of blessed Benedict,  
>   
> of revered holiness  
>   
> and ruler of monks—  
>   
> may our instruments  
>   
> according to our ability  
>   
> and knowledge resound together.  
>   
>   
> Blessed Nursia  
>   
> bore him as a son;  
>   
> Rome, mistress and nourishing mother of the world,  
>   
> cherished him.  
>   
>   
> He, therefore, having been endowed beforehand with the best gift  
>   
> of the Holy Spirit, etc.

The same Notker ended his life in the year 812. We owe his metrical epitaph to Mabillon, published in the *Benedictine Annals*, in these words:

> Behold the glory of his homeland, Notker, the teaching of wisdom:  
>   
> although a mortal man, he is buried in this tomb.  
>   
> On the eighth Ides of April, released from the flesh here,  
>   
> he is carried into the heavens and received in song.

I have no doubt that we would possess many more works of this kind, written even long before Notker, if the age that destroyed so many precious things had not deprived us also of these slight compositions.

That single famous monastery of Saint Gall, in which Notker lived, can here supply others published by Henry Canisius and afterward included in the *Bibliotheca Patrum*. There you may read a hymn composed by the monk Hartmann, who flourished around the year 870. These are its opening verses:

> When the Lord had been born,  
>   
> the unbelieving king was troubled;  
>   
> the Magi brought gifts,  
>   
> whom the guiding star led.

The remaining verses proceed in the same order of consonant words. There are also other hymns and other poems displaying the same texture of words, composed either in the same ninth century or in the tenth. Thus there is now abundant evidence to make the opinion seem badly put together—that whenever someone hears a trace of Leonine harmony, he immediately persuades himself that it belongs to the eleventh century or later.

Canisius also published a poem of Solomon, bishop of Constance, who flourished in the year 895:

> Excellent bishop, Dado, receive these greetings,  
>   
> written to you in sorrow by Solomon, etc.

The same artifice continues in the remainder.

Add to these the inscription placed for Emma, queen of the Franks, in the year 954, which the same Mabillon, recently praised, reports. I give only its opening verses:

> Here lies a noble offspring of Caesarean blood,  
>   
> issued from Charles for the people of the Franks, etc.

If you desire more epitaphs of this kind, consult the *Analecta* of the same Mabillon. Consult also Brower’s *Trier Annals*, which offers many works composed in the eighth, ninth, and tenth centuries.

In that same tenth century flourished Frodoard of Reims, who inserts many verses of the same workmanship into his poem on the *Life of Saint Columbanus*. Roswitha, the incomparable holy woman of that same century, did the same in her poem on the deeds of Otto. Here are only two of her verses:

> After the King of kings, who alone reigns forever,  
>   
> by himself transforming the times of all kings, etc.

Saint Gebehard, bishop of Constance, ended his life in the year 993, and an epitaph was then placed for him, reported by Canisius and Surius:

> Reject the deceitful times, the portion owed to earth,  
>   
> and remember the road that this ash testifies to.  
>   
> Here lies the honor of our people, and also the grief of our people;  
>   
> he presided over this city, but benefited the whole world, etc.

I mentioned above the alphabetical rhythm of Adelmannus the Scholastic, published by the much-praised Mabillon among the *Analecta*. It belongs to the eleventh century and was composed around the year 1035. Three verses form a strophe, and the ending of each consists of a similar syllable, as will be clear from the first strophe:

By the grace that inspires harmonic skill,

I recount illustrious men, luminaries of letters,

whom a mind wounded by recent grief recalls, etc. You will also find corresponding sounds at the ends of the rhythms that Saint Fulbert composed before Adelmann. A similar rhythm was fashioned around the year of Christ 1075 by Landulf the Elder, the Milanese historian, at the end of Book I of the *History* published by me in Volume IV of *Rerum Italicarum*. Here is the first stanza:

> Jesus Christ, splendor of the Father, way, life, and truth,  
> Gracious Redeemer of all, righteousness of everyone,  
> Your love fills all who seek you.

In the first verse one should read “life and truth.” The remaining verses proceed in the same meter.

The same Landulf, in Book III, chapter 16, also reports a song—that is, a rhythm—about the condition of King Albert; in describing it, the ancient scribe made mistakes more than once. I scarcely doubt that such a rhythm was composed when Adelbert, son of Berengar II and king of Italy, was expelled from the kingdom of Italy, that is, around the year 962. Observe these verses, sung at Milan in his contempt, after the custom of the ancient Romans:

> You, Albert, are suited to the grove,  
> While honor awaits Otto.  
> In place of Walpert’s disgrace,  
> The seaweed of the kingdom suits you.  
>   
> In place of the Latin queen,  
> Now use the maritime one.  
> In place of our royal scepter,  
> Enjoy the ship’s beak, etc.

Landulf’s contemporary was Benzo, pseudo-bishop of Alba, who took particular pleasure in such rhythms in his muddy *Panegyric of Henry IV, King of Germany*, in the first volume of Menken’s *Scriptores Rerum Germanicarum*. Indeed, in the same eleventh century people were so captivated by the harmony of such rhyming verses that few devotees of the Muses could be found who wished to leave their poems deprived of this ornament, as they believed it to be.

[Col. 0788A–B] I shall offer a striking witness to this custom in Othlo, a monk of Saint Emmeram, whose works were published by the previously praised Father Pez in Part II of Volume III of the *Thesaurus Anecdotorum Novissimus*. This monk flourished in the year of Christ 1050 and left behind several poems in which one finds very many rhyming verses. In his poem *On Spiritual Instruction* he speaks as follows:

> Moreover, because I sometimes append **CONSONANT WORDS**,  
> which **THE EXCESSIVE FASHION NOW PREVAILING AMONG MANY** demands,  
> I have also done this, beyond the more fitting arrangement of words,  
> **FROM AN ANCIENT CUSTOM**.

As you see, among the ancients *consonant words* was the name given to what we now call rhymes; and this kind of poetry was an established ancient custom during the eleventh century. It is therefore no wonder if, in the following twelfth century, the same pursuit became familiar also among cultivated lovers of the Muses in Italy.

[Col. 0788C–D] See Donizo, who composed a poem in 1115 about the life of Countess Matilda. Observe the verses with which William of Apulia concludes Book V of his work on the Normans. See also the anonymous author who, around 1127, composed a poem about the destruction of the city of Como; likewise Radulf of Caen, to whom we owe the *Deeds of Prince Tancred*, written around the same period in both meter and prose; finally, Godfrey of Viterbo’s *Pantheon* and Geoffrey Malaterra’s *History of Sicily*. All these works are included in my *Collection of Italian Matters*, especially Volume V.

I would also have you read certain rhythms composed around the year of Christ 1130 by the venerable Peter, abbot of Cluny, in which you will find the same concord of sounds. I pass over innumerable other meters and rhythms elaborated by the same art and collected by me from monuments of the ninth, tenth, and later centuries, lest I become excessive.

[Col. 0789A] Nothing, however, should be concealed. Most of these poems, whether rhythmic or metrical, consist of this art alone: a single syllable placed in the middle of the verse produces a sound similar to that of the syllable at the end, or merely a pair of syllables occupies the ends of two verses. But when, as I indicated above, verses were perhaps called *Leonine* by a special designation if two long syllables—or three, if the penultimate syllable was short—answered one another with equal sound in the middle and at the end of the verse, or at the end of two verses, doubt may still remain whether the invention or perfection of this art should be attributed to Leo the Parisian poet, who flourished around 1190.

Yet I do not see on what just grounds such glory should be transferred to this Leo, when so many others come before me who composed meters or rhythms with the same art. For as regards individual verses woven with consonant words, many preceded Leo in composing them.

[Col. 0789A–B] Italy herself immediately presents us, first of all, with Master Moses of Bergamo, author of the poem *On the Praises of Bergamo*, published by me in Volume V of *Rerum Italicarum*. He was writing around the year of Christ 1120, and certainly pursued at the ends of his verses a continual concord of two syllables. Thus he begins his poem:

> Nourishing God, ruler who governs the reins of the world,  
> And do not allow the heavenly seats to drift without order, etc.

The remaining verses proceed in the same measure.

There are also older verses which William of Malmesbury, in Book I of *On the Deeds of the Kings of England*, said around 1127 that he had heard from childhood, written in honor of Saint Lullus, bishop of Mainz:

> Bishop Lullus, than whom no one is holier,  
> Powerful in divine medicine, granted by God,  
> He meets diseases, as the whole world proclaims.

[Col. 0789B–C] There is also a very ancient verse used by not a few of the German emperors on their seals. I shall give an example taken from an original diploma preserved in the archive of the chapter of canons at Lucca.

### Diploma of Conrad I Augustus, by which he confirms the privileges of the canons of Lucca, in the year 1038

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity. Conrad, by the favor of divine clemency, Augustus, emperor of the Romans. Since imperial magnificence ought to enrich and venerate holy places and to exercise care and concern for the souls of all Christians, we therefore judged it fitting at the present time to enrich in some measure the place of the most holy bishop Martin situated at Lucca, so that it may contribute both to refreshment for those for whom it was given and to everlasting remedy for us.

Therefore, considering this and turning it over in our mind, at the request and admonition of our beloved wife and fellow-partner in our kingdom, Gisla, we confirm to the aforesaid holy place, just as formerly Hugh, Lothair, and the first, second, and third Otto, as well as Henry, our predecessors as kings and emperors, gave for the remedy of their souls and those of Margrave Adelbert and Countess Berta, and likewise for those of their own, to blessed Bishop Martin, his church situated at Lucca, and his faithful, etc.

Seal of Lord Conrad, most serene Augustus, emperor.

Kadeloh, chancellor, acting in place of Hermann, archbishop and archchancellor, authenticated this.

Given on the seventh day before the Kalends of March, in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1038, indiction VI, in the fourteenth year of Lord Conrad’s reign and the thirteenth of his empire.

Done at the Venarian Way in the county of Lucca, successfully. Amen.

[Col. 0790A–B] A leaden bull hangs not in the middle but at the outer edge of the parchment. On its obverse can be seen the images of two men, one holding an orb in his hand and the other a scepter; between them are read the letters:

> HENRICVS REX — “Henry, king.”

Around it, however:

> CONRADVS DI GRA IMP AVGVSTVS — “Conrad, emperor Augustus by the grace of God.”

On the reverse there is an image of Rome, sculpted with this verse:

> Rome, head of the world, governs the reins of the round earth.

[Col. 0790C] Robert, abbot of Saint-Remi, who committed his *History of Jerusalem* to writing around 1110, published in the first volume of *The Deeds of God through the Franks*, likewise interspersed his prose with similar verses, part of which is read in the margin and part in the text itself. I shall quote several:

> Nor was Raynald lightly touched, having become an apostate;  
> By abjuring God, he proves himself guilty.  
>   
> What could the Turk, and that people filthy in every respect, do,  
> If he did not turn his back and return whence he had come?

So too Geoffrey Malaterra, who wrote his *History of Sicily* around 1099, published in Volume V of *Rerum Italicarum*, gives us equivalent verses in Book III, chapter 23. Hear these few:

> Nor do I blame this too much, although here I carve such things.  
> Nor do I forbid or avoid it: when she is joined to her husband,  
> Let her love him justly, gracefully keeping faith with the bond.  
> For those whom the law joins, no judicial sentence sunders, etc.

An epitaph was also placed on the tomb of Beatrice, duchess of Tuscany, who died at Pisa in 1076:

> Although I am a sinner, I am called Lady Beatrice;  
> Sent into the tomb, I lie here, who was countess.

[Col. 0790D–0791] The distinguished Mabillon likewise published a poem about Ivo the Dionysian abbot, killed in 1094, in which the first part of each verse answers the following part. I select only a few:

> He who did not yet know under what Charybdis he labors,  
> Hiding it, let that condemned ash be made;  
> And, like sparks, let him fall from the straw, etc.

His epitaph likewise reads:

> Ivo, burdened by fate, cruelly overwhelmed by death,  
> Whom this stone covers—may you be happy in the ether, etc.
