[Col. 0791A–0792A] In addition, in Dissertation XXXVII, *On Hospitals*, I published the foundation of a foundling hospital established at Milan by the archpriest Datheus in the year of Christ 787. Two verses are inscribed on the floor of that building:

> Holy God, remember that this Datheus founded  
> This hall to aid wretched children.

I cannot establish that these little verses were inscribed there in that same year, 787; nevertheless, the words “this Datheus” seem to indicate that he was still alive. Once this is established, you now understand what antiquity belongs to the verses which we call Leonine.

Even more ancient, though lacking a date, are the verses written in mosaic which Panvinio read in the cloister of the Lateran monastery, already worn away and collapsing:

> Taking up the canonical form, declare the rule  
> Which you promised when you sought this cloister.

The remainder continues in the same harmony.

I shall restrain myself from piling up further examples. As for the other method of versification—namely, placing consonant words at the ends of paired verses—examples from long before the age of Leo of Paris are not lacking here either.

Indeed, around the year 1055, more than a hundred years before that Leo gave his name to Parnassus, the celebrated holy man Peter Damian, later bishop of Ostia, was composing verses in Italy. From him we have many poems, hymns, and rhythms in various meters, and nearly all of them are woven with consonant words. We should especially consider his rhythm on the Angelic Salutation, number 63, in which perfect Leonine verses occur:

> Hail, daughter of David, holy, born for the world,  
> Wise and temperate Virgin, betrothed to Joseph,  
> Given as an example for the salvation of all,  
> Now proven a companion of the heavenly citizens.  
>   
> Through you, Mary, misery comes to an end,  
> And through you mercy is recalled, etc.

Hear also his poem 64, addressed to the same most holy Virgin:

> O merciful one—O mistress—command by your word,  
> Lest we be devastated—lest we be struck—by the blow of hail, etc.

Let those who contend that our ancestors learned the use of consonant words from the Provençals consider this.

Mabillon also reported in the Benedictine *Annals* an epitaph, still carved in marble, for Albert, abbot of Micy, who died in 1036. It is distinguished by a similar arrangement of words:

> Here lies Albert, once scorning royal things,  
> Prudent and pious, seeing only heavenly things.  
> He spurned the foremost riches of the world, together with royal dominion and *gemetica* [reading/word uncertain], for religion, etc.

[Col. 0791C] Baldric, abbot of Angers, flourished in 1095; his poems were published by du Chesne in Volume IV of the *French Historians*. Some of them display a concord of sounds at the ends of the verses. The first two verses of the first epigram are these:

> On the roll many, with a certain solicitude,  
> Always measure the sequence of their speech from Adam, etc.

The same concord occurs in poems composed on the death of Matilda, abbess of Condé, in 1012, and published by the previously praised Mabillon in Volume V of the Benedictine *Annals*:

> If tears could prepare the heavenly kingdoms for anyone,  
> If our songs could help anyone who had died, etc.

[Col. 0792C] In the same eleventh century of Christ there flourished Gualdo, a monk of Corbie, who composed in meter the *Life of Saint Anscharius, Bishop of Hamburg*, published by Lambecius. In his preface he played with verses distinguished by the same final consonance. Here is the beginning:

> Sweet honor to your people, Albert, radiance of fiery lights,  
> Tower of the Church, splendid diadem of the kingdom,  
> Glory of bishops, venerable power of kings—  
> What your mother Corbie has initiated in you, take up this volume, etc.

See also the epitaph of the blessed Lanfranc, the celebrated archbishop of Canterbury, composed by Saint Anselm, likewise archbishop, around 1089. Here are the first verses:

> Lanfranc did not undertake the riches or honors of an archbishop,  
> But cares and labors.  
> Born in Italy, from the region of Pavia,  
> Among distinguished citizens and in an honorable condition, etc.

[Col. 0791D–0792D] See also the rhythms of Peter, abbot of Cluny, mentioned recently. Among the others I shall mention one *On the Resurrection of the Lord*, in which these verses occur:

> The bright light of darkness’ dwellings shone forth,  
> While he willed to save and restore what he had created;  
> Hence the Creator dies, so that the sinner might not die.  
>   
> By whose death, through a new lot, life arises for us, etc.

There is also another similar rhythm in honor of the Mother of the Lord, published under the name of prose. These were written around the year of Christ 1130.

Thus John Severanus, in his book *Sacred Memories of Rome*, page 314, reports an inscription placed in 1128 for John of Crema, cardinal-priest of the title of Saint Chrysogonus. These are its words:

> O good Savior, lover of our salvation,  
> Son Christ of God, spare him, Redeemer.

[Col. 0794A] And in Canisius, *Antiquarum Lectionum*, Volume III, Part II of the latest edition, poems are read by Metellus, a monk of Tegernsee, who flourished at least in 1160—that is, before Leo, or the Gallic Leonine poet. There are many rhythmic verses there. Hear a few:

> Let others praise a famous lineage; for me the gentle  
> Yoke of Christ gives words to my song.  
>   
> He sought to abolish the citizens of the starry homeland,  
> Through whom he possessed peace in worldly affairs.  
>   
> A spark nevertheless lived on, though the ember was cold;  
> At last, stirred from afar, it shines, etc.

But two similar verses appear to have been composed long before these times; they can still be read at Capua:

> This pious bishop, Otto, light of the clergy, prepared this;  
> Father of the Church, he enlarged its possessions and customs.

If the inscription refers to Otto, bishop of Capua, whom Ughelli believes to have flourished toward the end of the ninth century, you see once again that the antiquity of such verses is confirmed.

Thus, according to Mabillon’s testimony, in the Benedictine *Annals* under the year 707, these verses were read on a silver-covered reliquary in which the relics of Saint Hidulf, bishop, appear to have been placed in the year of Christ 946:

> By whose gift I am clothed with such honor;  
> May they be rendered worthy always by divine love.

Likewise, at the end of the *Chronicle of Centula* in Dacherius’s *Spicilegium*, Hariulf, its author, appended a poem in 1088, of which here are only the first verses:

> With all my heart I have loved you, mother Centula;  
> Given to you from childhood, I bound my neck beneath you, etc.

The remaining verses proceed with the same weaving of sounds.

Consult also, if you wish, William of Malmesbury, who quotes a poem composed in honor of King Athelstan, long before Leo of Paris was born. Here is a specimen:

> Royal offspring produced a noble lineage,  
> When a splendid jewel shone upon our darkness, etc.

See also Radevicus, Book II, chapter 2, *On the Deeds of Frederick I*; Henry of Huntingdon’s *History*, Book V; the School of Salerno; Godfrey of Viterbo; and a poem published by me in the *Chronicle of Casauria*, Part II of Volume II of *Rerum Italicarum*, page 785; as well as the preface of the distinguished Father Pez in the *Thesaurus Anecdotorum*.

But above all, recall what I previously brought forward from the very ancient Bangor Antiphonary; for nothing is lacking there for a complete example of the Leonine melody. The hymn of Hartmann, a monk of Saint Gall, in Volume XXVII of the *Bibliotheca Patrum*, page 517, will further confirm that the antiquity of this art is much greater than is commonly believed. I have already stated that he flourished in the year 870.

> With three signs,  
> Worthy of God,  
> This day is celebrated.  
>   
> Three signs,  
> Worthy of praise,  
> This assembly follows.  
>   
> The star led  
> The wandering Magi  
> To the Lord’s manger, etc.

The remaining stanzas produce the same harmony of sounds.

I pass over other monuments of the ancients of the same kind, and shall finally say that I can scarcely understand why Leo of Paris, the poet said to have flourished around the year of Christ 1190, is believed to have invented Leonine verses, when we possess so many much older examples that composed rhythms and meters with precisely the same art and ringing of consonant words.

Certainly we must depart from the opinion of Papebrochius, who, under 19 May in the *Life of Saint Pudentiana and Praxedis*, assigns the rhythmic verses in the church of Saint Pudentiana to the time of Pope Innocent II, around the year 1130, giving this reason: “No learned man would place the beginning of Leonine verses earlier than the twelfth century.” In the future, I believe, learned opinion will be different.

So much for the rhythmic poetry of the ancients. I now turn to the origin of Italian vernacular poetry.

There is no room for doubt that the poetry used by poets in the vernacular languages owes its birth to the rhythmics of the ancients. For the vernacular languages—Italian, French, Spanish, and so forth—pay no attention in composing verses to the quantity of syllables, or prosody, as was done by the ancient Greeks and Latins.

Although the Italian language favors two kinds of words, namely short and long, this quantity occurs only in the penultimate syllables when the words are of three syllables, etc.; moreover, no account is taken of the quantity of these short or long syllables except insofar as the arrangement of words demands it for a fuller pleasure of the ear in hearing the verse.

The poems of more recent times are therefore nothing other than rhythms. Just as many of the ancient writers of rhythms sought only the number of feet or syllables, not the observance of temporal quantity, and considered it sufficient in composing them to charm the listeners’ ears with a certain concord arising from the arrangement and equality of the feet in each verse, so too did the poets of the vernacular languages.

Thus, when the Italians, French, and others first began composing verses in their own vernacular languages, they called them *rhythms*. This word, with slight alteration, was called—and is still called—*rima* among the Italians, French, English, and other peoples.

I am not unaware that by this word *rima* some writers of the Italian language, both recent and ancient, mean the Greek term *homoioteleuton* (ὁμοιοτέλευτον), “ending alike,” by which vernacular poets in particular were accustomed to adorn their verses.

Yet by its original institution, *rhythmus*, or *rima*, came to be the name for a complete vernacular verse—that is, a song or poem—composed in imitation of the Latin rhythms discussed above. For this reason Petrarch sang:

> You who listen to the sound in scattered rhymes.

For, as we saw above from Othlo, an ending alike was formerly called a consonant word, or concordance of sounds, as Antonius de Tempo testifies.

I mentioned this author’s book long ago, still unpublished and preserved in the Este and Ambrosian libraries, in Book I, chapter 3, *On Perfect Italian Poetry*. Its title is: *Summary of the Art of Vernacular Rhythmic Composition, composed by Antonio de Tempo, judge and citizen of Padua, for the illustrious Prince Albert della Scala. In the year of the Lord 1332.*

He therefore preceded Petrarch’s poems in his own work. He enumerates seven kinds of vernacular rhythms: the sonnet, the ballata, the extended canzone, and so forth. From this you see that the poems themselves were given the name *rhythms*.

Again, in rubric I he writes:

> Vernacular rhythm is a certain kind of composition, etc. Literary rhythm—that is, Latin rhythm—according to the grammarians, is a consonant equality of syllables contained within a fixed number. The same arrangement occurs in every vernacular rhythm, especially in a movement that has been completed, etc.

Below he adds:

> Let every rhythm have at least one consonance with a word that has a different meaning, etc.

There are nevertheless other passages in which the word *rhythm* seems to mean the same thing as *rima* does for us.

But when, and among whom, was Italian poetry born?

It has now been established by the common judgment of all learned men that the Sicilians were the first in Italy to use the vernacular language—Italian, that is—in composing verses. The oldest surviving poems in the Italian language are attributed to Sicilian poets.

Moreover, Petrarch, when listing Italian poets in *The Triumph of Love*, chapter 4, mentions the Sicilians:

> Who were once the first, and there they were at the end.

From whom, however, did the Sicilians derive the form of vernacular verses and the use of consonant words? This has previously been debated among Italian scholars.

Giovanni Mario Crescimbeni, to whom the history of Italian poetry owes more light than to anyone else, states in his *Commentaries*, Volume I, chapter 2, as though it were an entirely obvious matter, that the Sicilians borrowed the whole structure of poetry from the Provençal poets, whose lives Nostradamus left in writing, since those poets flourished earlier.

Indeed, nearly all Provençal poems are contained in the precious handwritten codex of the Este library, written in 1254; and we know that they wrote verses from 1110 through that same year. By contrast, we scarcely now find any trace of Italian poets before the year of Christ 1200, and the few verses of theirs that survive are entirely unfinished and crude, displaying the infancy of poetry at its birth.

The distinguished Fontanini, however, in Book I, chapter 7 and following chapters of *On Italian Eloquence*, relying on the authority of Brunetto Latini, shows that in the year 1260 the vernacular Provençal or French language was “the most delightful and the most common of all the other languages”; and therefore his opinion is not only that the Italians derived from that language the art of vernacular rhythms, but also that “the Provençal language was in reality, to a great extent, the mother of Italian after the eleventh century.”

I suspect that Fontanini will find no one willing to agree with so extravagant an opinion, although Varchi too judged that the Provençal language was, to a great extent, the mother of Italian after the year 1200.

For Italian did not emerge so late or then acquire its form. Rather, it borrowed only a few words from the Provençals, as has already been made clear above in Dissertation XXXII, *On the Origin of the Italian Language*.

And even if we were to concede that many words migrated into Italian from French or Provençal, it would not therefore follow that the rights of a mother should be assigned to that language.

Huet himself, a man of outstanding learning, although French, laughs at our writers in his book *On the Origin of Romances* because, with excessive generosity, they attribute many words of our language to the Provençals as though received from them, although both they and we owe those words to Latin. I have also given examples in my notes to Petrarch’s Italian poems.

Finally, Dante Alighieri too condemned those who preferred the Provençal language to Italian in his *Convivio*.

As for Italian poetry, however, it was not without reason that Mario Equicola, Pietro Bembo, Speroni, Sansovino, and, to omit others, the previously praised Crescimbeni and Fontanini believed that its origin must be traced entirely to imitation of the Provençals.

Nevertheless, allow me to add that this is plausible, but by no means certain.

I have already quoted in Book I, chapter 3 of *Della perfetta poesia* Petrarch’s words, which deserve to be considered again here. In the preface to his familiar letters, when speaking of the books he had composed, he describes his works in the vernacular rhythm in these words:

> The part devoted to soothing the ears of the common people followed its own laws as well. This kind, as is reported, was reborn among the Sicilians not many centuries ago and soon spread throughout Italy and beyond; it had once been celebrated among the most ancient Greeks and Latins, since we are told that even the Roman common people were accustomed to use only rhythmic poetry.

Petrarch wrote this around the year of Christ 1360. These words, long ago noticed by Ludovico Castelvetro of Modena in his *Additions to the First Book of Bembo’s Prose*, persuaded him that Provençal poets were wrongly imposed upon us as the parents or teachers of Italian poetry.

Crescimbeni opposed this view; but although he produced many arguments, no one so far seems to have weakened, much less demolished, Castelvetro’s position.

The fact that we possess no Sicilian vernacular poems written before the year 1200 certainly does not imply that none were actually composed before that year. Only someone entirely unfamiliar with learning could be unaware of how many and how great things time has taken from us, to say nothing of the many works that could have been composed without ever being committed to writing.

Petrarch, having spent several years in Provence, had a very clear knowledge of how many poets that region had produced and when they had flourished. Nevertheless, he writes that the Sicilians did not learn the art of rhythms from them, but rather from the Latins and Greeks, among whose common people he himself had learned that rhythms had once been in use.

Why should we assert what he, who was much closer to the Provençal poets and is counted among the fathers of Italian poetry, did not know?

Especially since Leonardo of Arezzo, in his *Life of Dante*, wrote, on Dante’s own authority, that the art of Italian vernacular rhythms had originated approximately one hundred and fifty years before Alighieri himself. This period falls precisely within the years when the first Provençal poets also flourished.

What is more, Crescimbeni himself states in Part II of Book II of his *Commentaries* that Tuscany did not lack vernacular poets even in the year 1200.

Since, according to Petrarch, the Sicilians preceded the Tuscans, it remains that, during the period when Provençal poetry was flourishing, Sicilian poetry too was in common use among the vernacular population. It is therefore grounded in truth that Petrarch says the art of rhythms was reborn among the Sicilians not many centuries earlier—at least two centuries earlier.

Nor does he unjustly add that the Sicilians learned this kind of poetry from the Greeks and Latins, since we have already seen that rhythms were familiar both to Greeks and to Latins, and, in addition, that the use of consonant words—which we now call rhymes—was commended in late antiquity.

I shall briefly show that among the Sicilians themselves, during the twelfth century, such verses were cultivated by Latin poets.

A tomb was erected at Mileto for Roger I, the renowned count of Sicily and Calabria, who died in the year 1101; it was adorned with this inscription, according to Rocco Pirro in his *Chronology of the Kingdom of Sicily*:

> Leaving earthly things, the duke Roger migrated  
> To pleasant seats, for he occupies the dwellings of heaven.

There is a similar epitaph for Count Raynald, who was taken from human affairs in 1126, in the same Pirro’s *Account of the Church of Catania*.

Likewise, this inscription was carved on the tomb of King William I in 1170:

> Here the tomb holds your bones, Roger, once duke in the time of your father;  
> It lies beside your mother’s tomb.  
> Eleven times a hundred, ten times six, and twice more years  
> Had passed since Christ was born under the tyrant Herod, etc.

The remaining verses proceed in the same rhythm.

There is a similar inscription, placed in 1183, for Queen Margaret:

> Here you lie, queen, Margaret, born from royal wombs;  
> Margaret is the name given to you, equal to your character, etc.

There was therefore no need for the Sicilians to submit themselves to Provençal instruction in order to be taught the art of composing verses with *homoioteleuta*—verses ending alike.

It should also be added here that not only Latins and Greeks supplied examples of rhythmic poetry to the Sicilians, as Petrarch learnedly observed; other peoples too could have held the torch of this art before them and before the other Italians.

For Sicily groaned under the yoke of the Saracen Arabs for more than two centuries, until the year 1060, when Messina was taken from them. In 1091 the entire island came under the rule of the Norman princes.

It is certain, however, that the Arabs too delighted in rhythmic verses, which they ended, according to our custom, with consonant words. Among them are very ancient poems which still bear witness to this fact.

This was familiar even in the time of Muhammad himself. For, as Marracci testifies in his *Prodromus*, where he discusses the Qur’an, chapter 2, the signs, or little verses, of that impious book end in rhythm, which is generally consonant, with a vowel supplied and one of the three quiescent letters preceding it, such as *una*, *ina*, *ano*, and so forth.

The matter is so certain that the highly learned Huet, in his book *On the Origin of Romances*, held that we received from the Arab people the art of rhyming—that is, the use of consonant words in verses—from the time when that wicked nation began to press the greater part of Spain beneath its yoke, which occurred at the beginning of the eighth century.

In the ninth century it likewise established its seat in Sicily and Calabria.

I have said that poems of the Arab people still exist, and Derbelot has taught us the same. Indeed, Spanheim states that in invention, as well as in the number of poems and the abundance of verses they wrote, those poets far surpass every other people.

It seems entirely plausible to me that we may reasonably attribute the rhythmic art—or the use of consonant words at the ends of verses—to the Arab people, since learned men testify that the custom of rhyming is most ancient among them, that they still retain it, that their name was once celebrated for literary studies, and that they had extensive dealings with Europeans, especially with Italians.

Perhaps we also received from them the various forms of verse described by Agapitus of Valle Flemmarum, of the Order of Friars Minor, in his little book *On the Metrical Art of the Arabs*.

Among other books of that people, a celebrated work on this subject is the treatise of Badr al-Din al-Damamini, the foremost prince of poets among the Arabs, who wrote carefully about the use of rhythms.

In ancient centuries, after the Greek empire had been driven out of Italy, Arab learning was held in such honor among the Italians that Arabs were regarded above all as teachers of letters. I shall also have to mention this below, in Dissertation XLIV, *On the Fortune of Letters*.

I add that we have no slight reason for suspecting that the Arabs learned the art and use of rhythms from the most ancient Jewish people.

Above we saw the taunting song of the Hebrew women concerning Saul, on the occasion of the victory won by David. There was consonance of words there.

In recent years this subject has been debated between the most learned Blasius Garofalus and other scholars. As far as I know, Augustine of Eugubium, Meibomius, Ludovicus Capellus, Clericus, Huet, and others held that the Jews had used this concord of words in their poems, hymns, and songs from the most ancient times.

What is more, Fourmont, a very distinguished scholar, published in Paris in 1714 a dissertation on this subject, printed in that same city in Volume VI of the *Mémoires de l’Académie des Inscriptions*. On page 160, with considerable learning, he showed that in the poetic books of the Old Testament such a concord occurs at the ends of verses.

I shall spare the examples.

Once we establish these points, it is now clear that the use of consonant words in verse is far more ancient than is commonly believed, since it seems to have passed from the Jews to the Syrians and Arabs. Next, it seems probable that the peoples of the West learned this art from the Arabs, unless they had previously learned the same art from the northern peoples.

For we must also turn our attention to them in investigating these matters. Certainly, after the Arabs, the Northmen—counts, dukes, and kings—seized dominion over Sicily: a people formerly poured forth from the icy North into Gaul and eventually into Great Britain, Apulia, and Sicily, establishing their rule most firmly in those places. [Col. 0799D] The power and seat of the Northmen kings among the Sicilians lasted until the year 1094. [Col. 0800A]

From this people, too, the Sicilians could have learned—if we are unwilling to suppose that they received from the Arabs the art of vernacular poetry—the art of poems composed in the vulgar tongue. The use of rhythms composed in the vernacular among the northern peoples is certainly older than that of the Provençals and Italians.

The Germans show us Gospels rendered from Latin into Germanic rhythms by the monk Otfrid around the year 880. These songs consist of short verses ending in consonant words. He also produced other poems of the same kind, which are still preserved in manuscripts in the most ancient codices of the Imperial Vienna and Vatican libraries; indeed, they have also been issued in copperplate print by Johann Schilter. There are likewise among the Danes, Swedes, and other Germans extremely ancient poems of this kind.

[Col. 0800B] George Hickes, likewise, a man of the highest learning among the Britons, writes in the *Thesaurus of the Ancient Northern Languages* that in the most ancient Anglo-Saxon works pseudo-rhymes—that is, rhymes—are nowhere found. Nevertheless, in chapter 24 of his *Anglo-Saxon Grammar* he gives specimens of poems which he himself calls semi-Saxon, in which a similar cadence occurs, such as we use at the ends of verses.

Usser also, in chapter 17, page 450, of the *British Ecclesiastical Antiquities*, cites the following from the *Life of Saint Albe*:

“Then Saint Patrick, archbishop and patron of all Ireland, sang the following verse in the Scottish language, possessing, as it were, the force of a certain legal oracle. The family of Saint Albe and the family of Saint Declan did not wish us to render this verse into Latin for them either rhythmically or metrically; but, in order to confer upon it greater authority, we shall bring it forward in the very language, proper and genuine, in which it was pronounced and composed by Saint Patrick. Thus that verse is sung in Scottish:

> Ailbe umal, Patric Muman, mo gach rath  
> Theclan Patric Nandeisi, ag theclan go brath

The approximate sense is: ‘Humble Ailbe; Patrick of Munster, my every blessing; Declan, Patrick of the Déisi, with Declan for ever.’”

To this Mabillon, in volume III of the *Benedictine Annals*, page 684, adds a rhythm composed in the Germanic language, in which one will find the same consonance of words. These examples clearly demonstrate that vernacular rhythms are much older than many have supposed.

The Franks themselves seem to have composed verses of this kind before the celebrated company of Provençal poets arose. Bulaeus, in his *History of Paris*, reports an epitaph in French rhymes placed upon Frodoard, the historian of Reims, who died in the year 965. Take from it only these two lines:

[Col. 0800] “A worthy cleric, a good monk, the best abbot,  
And of Agapit the Roman was the abbot,” etc.

[Col. 0799D] Mabillon himself, in the fifth volume of the *Acts of the Benedictine Saints*, judges these verses to have been written not long after that period. Let them have the authority they deserve.

Here, then, is another source from which the Sicilians might have drawn the pattern of vernacular rhythms: namely, from the Northmen who themselves ruled Sicily, or from other Germanic peoples, before poets in Provence sought fame for themselves through their poems. Since the Northmen were well acquainted with the customs and language of the Franks, Germans, and Britons, they may rightly be thought to have brought this poetic practice into Sicily as well.

How greatly Geoffrey Malaterra, a Northman by birth but recently become a Sicilian, delighted in such rhythms around the year of Christ 1100, I have indicated above.

[Col. 0801A] As for the form of Italian vernacular poems, it was not necessary even here for the Sicilians and other Italians to borrow it from the Provençal poets. Crescimbeni had written in book I of his *History of Vernacular Poetry*: “It is a clear fact that the Italian hendecasyllable came into Italy from Provence.” But, after examining the matter more carefully, he abandoned this opinion in book I, chapter 5, of his *Commentaries*, where he expressly admits that he too recognizes Italian verses as having developed through imitation of Latin verse.

Before him, our own Castelvetro and Jacobus Mazzonius had already noted this learnedly, the latter in book II, chapter 33, of his *Apology for Dante’s Comedy*. I add that the Italian form could have been derived not only from the measured and perfected verses of the Latins, but also from their unadorned and rough rhythms.

I have already shown, and could easily show more clearly again, that Latin rhythms were composed in four-syllable, five-syllable, and other forms, and that they existed long before the age of the Provençal poets. But this dissertation has now grown sufficiently, and more than sufficiently. I shall therefore pursue only one matter: namely, the hendecasyllabic verse, in which Italian poetry chiefly delights, and which, besides occurring among the Greeks and Latins, was also cultivated by poets who composed rhythms and by metric poets while the barbarian age was passing.

Among the works of Walafrid Strabo, whose fame is celebrated among the writers of the ninth century, there is a pious prayer of his, from which I select several verses:

> O dread Creator of all things,  
> While, innocent, you endured the penalties of the cross;

[Col. 0801C] In which you find nothing except ruin, etc.

In these lines one finds not only the feet but also the number of the Italian hendecasyllable. The same occurs in that Horatian line:

> Now enough snow and dreadful storms have fallen upon the earth, etc.

And since our poetry can use a dactyl instead of a spondee at the end of verses of this kind, such verses then become dodecasyllables, though belonging to the same period as the hendecasyllables—those which we call *sdruccioli* in Italian, whose invention I do not know why Varchi, in the *Herculanus*, attributed to Sannazaro. I draw a specimen of these verses from Walafrid’s own poems:

> You have read; your sagacity remembers;  
> But though I myself am covered with many stains,  
> I believe that I shall cleverly be granted pardon, etc.

Certainly, in these hendecasyllables of the ancients one rarely detects the placement of accents—the *posature*, as we call them—which is easy and evident in Italian verse. Nevertheless, when the first vernacular poets devoted themselves chiefly to verses of few syllables and later sought a verse that would acquire a certain majesty from the movement of several syllables, they found none more suitable than the hendecasyllable, whether it is formed from two shorter verses or coalesces in some other arrangement. They had an example of it before them in the writers of rhythms.

Here I wish to make public a rhythm that has hitherto remained unknown, which I mentioned in Dissertation I, concerning foreign peoples. I copied it from a very ancient manuscript codex of the chapter of the canons of Modena. Both what precedes it and the antiquity of the codex sufficiently indicate that it was composed at the beginning of the tenth century after Christ; at that time, as I stated in my preface there, the Hungarians made many incursions into Italy, especially into the territory of Modena.

The verses are dodecasyllables, but, when their temporal quantity is counted, they correspond to hendecasyllables. Among them, however, one can recognize certain verses so constructed that one detects in them the familiar structure and sound of our verses. In addition, each verse has something Leonine about it, since they end on one and the same vowel and with an equal consonance. Try it yourself.

## Rhythm to be sung by the soldiers guarding the city of Modena, around the year 925

[Col. 0801]

> O you who guard these walls with weapons,  
> Do not sleep, I warn you, but keep watch.  
> While Hector remained awake in Troy,  
> Deceitful Greece did not capture it.  
> While Troy slept during the first watch,  
> The treacherous Sinon loosened its faithless gates.  
> Hidden troops, sliding down by a rope,  
> Invade the city and set Pergamum aflame.  
> By its watchful voice the white goose  
> Drove the Gauls from the Roman citadel;  
> For this deed it was made of silver  
> And worshiped by the Romans as a goddess.  
> Let us worship the exalted power of Christ;  
> Let us offer him our melodious jubilees.  
> Trusting in his great protection,  
> Let us sing these songs while keeping watch.  
> O Christ, divine guardian, King of the world,  
> Preserve this camp beneath your watchful care.  
> Be an impregnable wall to your people;  
> Be a terrible enemy to their enemies.  
> While you keep watch, no force harms us,  
> You who drive all weapons of war far away.  
> Encircle these fortifications of ours, Christ,  
> Defending them with your strong spear.  
> Holy Mary, radiant Mother of Christ,  
> Obtain this with John, O Mother of God:  
> Here we venerate their holy pledges, that is, relics,  
> And to whom these sanctuaries are consecrated.

[Col. 0803A] [Note: Or “walls” (*moenia*)?]

> Under whose leadership the right hand is victorious in war,  
> And without whom arrows have no power.  
> Brave youth, daring military strength,  
> Let your songs be heard along the walls,  
> And let alternating watch be kept under arms,  
> So that hostile deceit may not invade these walls.  
> Let the companion echo resound: “Hey, keep watch!”  
> Along the walls let the echo say: “Hey, keep watch!”

I shall place the final hand upon this dissertation by adding a colophon of no ordinary value: namely, by publishing a historical rhythm which the aforementioned Bartholomeus Campagnola—who has deserved well of me in many respects—copied and sent to me from that same very ancient codex of the chapter of the canons of Verona from which the other work, *On the Praises of Milan*, was extracted.

In the year of Christ 871, all Italy, and indeed the remainder of the Frankish empire as well, was shaken by the detestable crime of Adelgis, prince of Benevento. He dared, after provoking a rebellion, to seize and imprison Louis II Augustus, although Louis was illustrious for the many benefits he had bestowed upon the Beneventans, having broken the horns of the Saracen people and turned their swords away from their throats.

Some excuse the man and lay the blame upon Augustus himself and his wife, as can be gathered from Erchempert, the *Bertinian Annals*, and the anonymous writer of Salerno, published by me in part II of volume II of *Italian Matters*. And indeed, since Adelgis had no intention of attempting anything against Louis’s life, but wished only to inflict fear and force upon him so that he would leave the city and territory of Benevento, it may be supposed that the Beneventan prince had not lacked some cause or occasion for justified anger.

Nevertheless, scarcely anyone failed to shudder on hearing that Augustus—a most holy man, the savior, naturally, of the province of Benevento, dwelling within the walls of Benevento and resting securely—had been loaded with so many insults and deceitfully captured, as Erchempert writes. Yet the same Erchempert by no means recognizes this holiness in Louis below.

[Col. 0804B] The author of the alphabetic or abecedarian rhythm now to be published therefore describes this crime. He was certainly contemporary, as both the event and the narrative itself suggest, but at the same time was extremely unskilled in the Latin language.

I have decided to present the rhythm itself to the reader exactly as it is found in the Verona manuscript, without changing even a single letter, merely distinguishing the verses, which are undivided in the manuscript, so as to lighten this burden for the most illustrious Marquis Maffei. But I also wish him to observe here how many errors this little piece of antiquity contains, attributable partly to the author and partly to the ancient copyist.

## Rhythm concerning the capture of the emperor Louis II by Adelchis, or Adelgis, prince of Benevento, composed in the year 871 or 872

[Col. 0803]

> Hear, all the ends of the earth, in error with sadness [Note: I think it should be read “with horror” (*horrore*).],  
> What sort of crime was committed, O city of Benevento.  
> They seized Louis, the holy and pious Augustus [Note: If Maffei’s rules are to be followed, *Augustio* ought to be written; but the ancients do not seem to have bound themselves rigidly by those rules.].  
> The Beneventans gathered themselves into one council.  
> Adalferius [Note: Adalferius, one of the Beneventan nobles.] was speaking, and they said to the prince:  
> If we release him alive, surely we shall perish.  
> He prepared a great crime [Note: I think *celus* stands for *scelus*, “crime.”] against this province.  
> He takes our kingdom from us; he regards us as nothing.  
> He has done many evils [Note: Write *plura*, “many things,” rather than *plures*.] to us. It is right that he should die [Note: That is, *moriat*, with Priscian’s gracious permission.].  
> They took the holy and pious man [Note: For *sanctum pium*, that is, Louis Augustus, whom Erchempert also calls “most holy.”] down from his palace;  
> Adelferius led him as far as the Praetorium.  
> But he went joyfully [Note: Perhaps “he went rejoicing.”], as though to martyrdom.  
> Sado and Saducto [Note: Sado, or Sadoan, Sugdan, a Saracen prince then held captive at Benevento. The anonymous writer of Salerno also relates that Adelgis used his counsel for this deed.] were coming to meet the emperor [Note: *Saducto inoviabant*. What should be written here may be left for those with more leisure to guess. Perhaps “those who were meeting the emperor.”].  
> And the holy and pious man himself began to say:  
> You have come with swords and clubs as against a robber.  
> There was once a time when I raised you up in everything;  
> But now you have risen up against me in conspiracy.  
> I do not know for what reason [Note: A Ciceronian elegance: write *pro qua causa*, “for what cause.”] you wish to kill me.  
> A cruel generation, I have come to destroy [Note: “I have come to kill him who came here in order to rescue God’s holy churches from the yoke of the Saracens. I have come to avenge the blood of your enemies which has been shed upon the earth.”];  
> I have come to cherish the holy churches of God;  
> I have come to avenge the blood that has been poured out upon the earth.  
> That hot-tempered tempter [Note: Who is this tempter? Adelgis, Seodan, or someone else? The words *ratum adque*—for *atque*—make the expression obscure.] will place [Note: For *ponit*, “places.”] the imperial crown upon his head  
> And was saying to the people:  
> Behold, we are emperor; I can rule you [Note: In trying to express in Latin the Italian *vi posso regere*, he did not know whether *vi* answered to an accusative rather than a dative.].  
> He was going away with a happy spirit because of what he had done [Note: I think this should be *abibat*, “he was going away,” happy about what he had done.].  
> He was tormented by a demon and had fallen to the ground [Note: Here too it is uncertain whether the prince Adelchis or Seodan was meant, tormented by a demon.].  
> Many troops came out to see the marvels.  
> The great Lord Jesus Christ judged judgment [Note: I would write *domnus*, so that the meter of the preceding verse would proceed more correctly. But I see that the syllabic rules are neglected elsewhere as well. It should also be written *judicat judicium*.].  
> A multitude of pagans came out into Calabria [Note: Instead of *e Calabria*.].  
> They reached Salerno to possess the city [Note: At the end of the aforementioned year 871, Salerno was besieged by the Saracens, who were finally compelled to raise the siege when Louis Augustus returned against them. Instead of *possidere*, I would write *obsidere*, “to besiege.”].  
> It was sworn by the holy relics of God [Note: This stanza, corresponding to the letter I, is missing above. I do not know whether it should be restored in its proper place. It seems to indicate the oath by which Louis bound himself never to exact some vengeance for the slander he was then suffering, as Regino writes. In any case, this stanza is incomplete, and other complete stanzas may perhaps be missing; for the rhythm does not proceed through the remaining letters of the alphabet.].  
> He himself was to defend the kingdom and seek another.

## Song concerning the patriarch Joseph

*(Edited by D. Ozanam, *Unpublished Documents for Use in the History of Italy*, etc., p. 46, from Vatican codex no. 3325.)*

[Col. 0805]

> Joseph, beloved of God,  
> Sweet and capable to his father,  
> A handsome boy of excellent character  
> And of manifold grace! [lacuna]  
> Hence new dreams  
> Revealed the stars of heaven to him,  
> As signs of what was to come,  
> To him almost as punishments. [lacuna]  
> He is attentive to the omen,  
> As though to God’s business;  
> Envious fraternal hatred  
> Observes this with such a spirit.  
> Joseph, remaining at home,  
> Providing for the private matter,  
> Is soon ordered to visit  
> Whether all things are proceeding well. [lacuna]  
> No delay: when they see him,  
> “Here is the Dreamer,” they say;  
> “Bring death, so that it may be clear  
> Whether what he dreams has helped him.” [lacuna]  
> They avoid the guilt of the crime,  
> So that they may not be accused of bloodshed;  
> Taking a weight of coin,  
> Thus they sell him to the Hagarenes. [lacuna]

Segardus composed this poem.

# Liturgical monuments of the eleventh century

[Col. 0807]

## Sequences composed up to the eleventh century

*(Daniel, *Hymnological Treasury*, vol. II, p. 49, from Munich codex 6.)*

### I. On the Assumption of the Blessed Virgin

[Col. 0807A]

“Hail, Mother of the Most High God, ever-virgin Mary,” etc.

### II. On the Holy Trinity

[Note: We should not be correct in assuming that this sequence belonged specifically to the feast of the Holy Trinity and was first sung on that feast; for it is not sufficiently clear at what time this festival was established in the Roman Church and prescribed for all. Although Benedict XIV, in his book on feasts, judges that the solemnity was established by John XXII in the year 1334, nevertheless no trace of that festival appears either in the Venetian Missal published in 1469 or in the Missal of the Order of Friars Minor published at Rome in 1482.

The Missal of the Hermits of Saint Augustine, which appeared in Venice in 1497, commands the following: “On the first Sunday after Pentecost, the office of the Holy and Undivided Trinity is celebrated, with a commemoration of the Lord’s Day. Seek the Mass at the end of the book under votive Masses.”

In Germany, however, the first indications of this feast are said to be found already in the tenth century, and we know that afterward the festival was celebrated in all dioceses, though in some—Magdeburg, Halberstadt, Minden, and others—it was observed on the Monday after the octave of Pentecost.

If we ask why this feast was received so late, and especially at Rome, the reason seems to lie in the character of the ancient Church, and particularly of the Roman Church, which on feast days presents for recollection before the mind and spirit not so much doctrines as sacred histories, perceptible as it were through the bodily ears and eyes. Hence all feasts in which doctrines are taught—such as those of the Trinity, the Body of Christ, and the Conception of Mary—were not discovered in the very metropolis of the Church but introduced there from elsewhere.

Moreover, it must also be considered that all Sundays were regarded almost as feasts of the Trinity; therefore the most ancient Preface of the Trinity was sung on them as well. We also possess a votive Mass and votive office of the Trinity of considerable antiquity, to which the prose written above seems to belong.

Later it was read on the very feast of the Trinity, but not, as Adelphus says, throughout the entire world; for other sequences besides this one were also used. The author of this sequence is usually, and recently by Rambach, called Notker, but the matter is very uncertain, since it is absolutely certain that in Munich codex 5 this sequence was added later together with two other poems.

There is no need to point out that many things in this prose are translated from the Creed of Saint Athanasius.

1. Thus the Introit of the Mass of the Trinity: “Blessed be the holy Trinity and undivided unity.” The reading adopted by us is found in codices 5 and 6; in the remaining books, “the deity, namely, unity.” The Athanasian Creed: “equal glory, coeternal majesty.”

2. Codices Pm.: “but one and the same.” A solemn term, a word in the doctrine of the Trinity. Adelphus: “How this should be understood is shown by that common saying: Snow, ice, and water are three names, yet the thing is one. They are distinct things, nevertheless they merge into one watery nature.”

3. Pm., Md., Rambach: *socia*, “associated.”

4. The Athanasian Creed: “And yet there are not three gods, but one God.” Manuscript 5: “truly one”; perhaps the poet wrote it thus. Adelphus: “and the Son and the Holy Spirit.” Manuscript 16: “the Son, the Holy Spirit.” Ludovicus: “the Spirit, the Lord.” Clichtoveus: “After this verse some books—for example Pm.—immediately have the following: ‘Yet the Son himself is true God from the Father, and therefore the glorious Spirit proceeds from both,’ or, as in Pm., ‘proceeding.’ This has the flavor of the dispute between the Eastern and Western Churches, whether the Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son or not.”

5–6. We have presented the passage as it stood in codices 5 and 6. The others read: “and it is”; manuscripts 16, Md., Pm., Pt., Torr., Lud., and Rambach. Manuscript 16: “honor also.” Pm.: “the Trinity is in the persons.” Preface of the Trinity: “[...] distinction in the persons, unity in essence, and equality in majesty is to be worshiped.”

7. Manuscripts 10: “similarly also.” Pm.: “contains.”

8. James 2:19. Adelphus: “Throughout the entire universe there is a threefold place that recognizes the triune and one God: the highest, such as heaven; the middle, such as earth; the lowest, such as Tartarus. The first is good, because there is supreme joy there. The second is of an intermediate character, because there are hope and fear there. But the third is worst, because there is supreme sadness there.”

9. Manuscripts 5, 16, Nb., Pt., Torr., Adelphus, and Clichtoveus: “they praise.” Manuscript 10: “the angels worship.” Some of Clichtoveus’s books have “the plurality of angels.” In Torr., the eighth stanza follows the ninth.

10–11. We have given the passage as it stood in codices 5 and 6. The others read: “And let us all now sing with exalted voice, in harmonious songs with sweet melody: ‘Hey and hey, now together let us jubilate praises in the heights to the high-throned Lord,’” though they differ somewhat in each case. Manuscripts 10, 12, 16, Nb., Md., Pm., Lud., and Cl. omit *nunc*, “now.” Manuscript 16: “in the highest place.” Clichtoveus notes that individual books have the writing *Altithroni*, etc. “Organic songs” are either simply musical, as in Lucretius III, 133, “the musical dance of Helicon,” or songs recited with the sound of instruments.

12. Thus manuscripts 5, 6, 10, 12, and 13. The others: “O, O, O, Trinity, O, O, blessed unity.” Pm.: “O wondrous Trinity.”]

1. May the holy Trinity always be blessed, namely, the one deity, equal in glory:

2. Father, Son, Holy Spirit: three names, all of one substance.

3. God the begetter, God begotten; in both, the Holy Spirit is associated with the Godhead.

[Col. 0808A] 4. Yet there are not three gods: there is one true God—thus the Father, the Lord Son, and the Holy Spirit.

5. Distinction in the persons, unity in essence:

6. Equal majesty and power, dignity and honor alike in everything.

7. Containing the stars and seas, the fields together with all created things.

8. Whom impious Tartarus trembles at, whom the lowest abyss also worships.

[Col. 0809A] 9. Now let every voice and tongue confess him, now with due praise,

10. Whom sun and moon praise, whom angelic dignity adores.

11. Now let us all jubilate praises in the heights to the high-throned Lord:

12. Hey and hey, let us all together sing harmonious songs with sweet melody.

13. O venerable Unity,

14. O adorable Trinity:

15. Through you we were created, true eternity;

16. Through you we were redeemed, supreme charity.

17. Protect the entire people; save, free, rescue, and cleanse them.

18. We adore you, Almighty; to you we sing, to you [Col. 0809B] praise and glory.

19. Through infinite ages of ages.

### III. On the octave of Pentecost

“Let us give thanks to God, blessedly,” etc.

### IV. On the Saturday of Septuagesima

[Note: A very distinguished poem, composed according to the pattern of Psalm 148, is sufficiently rare in Missals and Sequentiaries. We transcribed it from Munich codices 6 and 11; the Palatine Vienna codex no. 1485, folio 50 a–b, also agrees with these books, and supplied Wolf with the sacred dithyramb.

The learned man also found it in a liturgical book adapted for the use of children, published at Basel in 1516, and in another very ancient Hymnary. It seems that both books read the closing stanza 21 as follows: “Praise to the eternal Trinity. Alleluia, alleluia, alleluia, alleluia, alleluia, alleluia.” The alleluiatic sequence, as it is called, was sung on the Saturday of Septuagesima before the Alleluia was laid aside or buried.]

1. Let us all now sing a melodious Alleluia.

2. In praises of the eternal King, let this people resound: Alleluia.

3. Finally, let the heavenly choir sing this aloud: Alleluia.

4. Throughout the paradisal meadows, let the company of the blessed sing this psalmody: Alleluia.

5. Let the shining lights of the stars also jubilate the lofty Alleluia.

6. The courses of the clouds, the flight of the winds, the flashing of lightning, and the sound of thunder, let them all sweetly harmonize together: Alleluia.

7. Waves and billows, rain and storms, tempest and calm, heat, ice, snow, hoarfrost, wooded heights, and groves, let them compose the Alleluia.

8. From here, various birds, sing praises to the Creator together with the Alleluia.

[Col. 0810A] 9. But there let the high voices of various beasts respond: Alleluia.

10. From there let the lofty summits of the mountains sound the Alleluia.

11. From here let the depths of the valleys dance the Alleluia.

12. You too, jubilant abyss of the sea, say Alleluia.

13. And likewise the immense vastnesses of the earth: Alleluia.

14. Now let the entire human race rejoice in praise: Alleluia.

15. And, frequently giving thanks to the Creator, let it harmonize: Alleluia.

16. This name itself delights in hearing it continually: Alleluia.

17. Christ himself also approves this heavenly song: Alleluia.

[Col. 0810B] 18. Now, companions, sing joyfully: Alleluia.

19. And you, little boys, always respond: Alleluia.

20. Now sing together the Alleluia to the Lord, Alleluia to Christ the Spirit: Alleluia.

21. Praise to the eternal Trinity, which is glorified in the baptism of the Lord. Hence let us sing: Alleluia.

### XI. On the feast of Saint Dionysius and his companions

[Note: In codex 5 the poem was added by a second hand. In the margin is written: “The unconquered king of kings, Arnulf, had transferred the most holy body of Dionysius into this monastery.” On the famous controversy concerning the body of Saint Dionysius between the monks of Saint Emmeram at Regensburg and the monastery of Saint Dionysius at Paris, consult Rader, *Bavaria Sancta* I, 119 ff.

This prose of the eleventh century, from Munich codex Emmeram E. CXIII, sings of this transfer of the sacred bones—or, more correctly, this sacred theft. A fragment of it is found in Wolf, p. 466:]

> Hear, faithful peoples, the cause of the greatest rumor,  
> Which occurred in modern times in the Noric lands.  
> For the most blessed Dionysius, once bishop of Athens,  
> Whom Saint Clement sent into Gaul for the sake of preaching,  
> Was there crowned with martyrdom and found buried.  
> He was later transferred from there, in an age now near our own,  
> To the monastery of blessed Emmeram, very celebrated and famous.  
> But in what manner this was accomplished, I shall briefly tell you.  
> There was a certain distinguished emperor, whose name was Arnulf,  
> From the family of that glorious bishop Arnulf of old,  
> Possessing the most illustrious origin in the flesh and following his virtue.  
> He, therefore, invited, set out toward the western borders,  
> To wage war against certain peoples already oppressing the Frankish kingdoms,  
> Whom the inhabitants of that province were unable by themselves to overcome.  
> And when, with the help of the Almighty, he had so destroyed the strength of the enemy  
> That not one man remained from their immense army,  
> He returned with the glory of so great a triumph to the city of Paris.  
> After he had remained there for several days  
> And had discussed various matters,  
> He also began secretly to consider and investigate by every means  
> How he might obtain the body of the most holy Dionysius.  
> In response, many people gave many and varied counsels;  
> But finally a certain man [lacuna] ...

“Let us rejoice in this solemnity, brothers; let the whole Church rejoice together,” etc. “But no less let blessed Ratisbon rejoice, which, by heavenly command, now possesses these same bones,” etc.

### XII. On Saint James the Apostle

[Note: Nothing in this poem is read concerning James’s journey to Spain or the transfer of his bones to Compostela. The final stanzas mention Saint Christopher the Martyr, whom Catholic people were accustomed, and still are accustomed, to commemorate on this very feast of the Apostle.]

“Rejoice, bride of Christ, virgin mother Church,” etc.

### XXIV. At the Nativity of the Lord, at cockcrow

[Note: The prose is found in Munich codex 6 and in the Palatine Vienna library codex no. 1845, folio 47a, from which Wolf communicated it to readers. It also appears in Clichtoveus. I have nowhere investigated the poem in Missals.]

1. At the birth of the Lord, all devout companies sing.

2. Touching the organic melodies syllable by syllable.

3. This is the consecrated day on which new joys have been fully given to the world.

4. On this exalted night, glory resounded in an angelic voice.

[Col. 0812A] 5. At midnight immense lights shone for the shepherds,

6. While they tended their flocks, divine commands suddenly proclaimed:

7. “There is immense glory in heaven, and peace on earth;

8. He has been born from a gracious virgin who exists before the ages.”

9. Therefore let the company of heaven jubilate most exaltedly,

10. So that the lofty structure of the heavens trembles at so great a song.

11. The most cruel dominions of the enemy have been shattered.

12. All human things resound with the God born on earth.

13. Peace has been restored on earth; now let all things rejoice in the beginnings of the birth.

14. Let glory, restored in a clear voice, sound everywhere on this day.

[Col. 0812B] 15. He alone who watches over all things,

16. He alone who governs all things,

17. May he himself, in his mercy, save all peaceful kingdoms.

# An ancient collection of ecclesiastical hymns

*(Edited by D. Ozanam in the book entitled *Unpublished Documents for Use in the Literary History of Italy*. Paris, 1850.) (C)*

## Hymn I of Saint Nicholas

[Col. 0813A]

> Singing the praises due to the Lord,  
> Let us all celebrate with devoted mind  
> This sacred day on which Nicholas  
> Ascends to heaven;  
> He who, worthily meditating on God’s law,  
> Ever watchful, by attaining the kingdom of heaven,  
> After conquering the enemy, shone brilliantly  
> As a holy man in the world.  
> For when, as a shepherd worthy of goodness,  
> He was sought for the renowned city of Myra,  
> At last he deserved to be called from heaven  
> Its excellent ruler.  
> Having become a bishop, kind toward the people,  
> He was gentle, peaceful, and merciful;  
> Through the practice of piety he provided everyone  
> With worthy benefits.  
> Filled with Christ’s saving grace,  
> He utterly rejected the worship of demons;  
> With the darkness driven away, he showed  
> How to walk along the way of light.  
> He preaches to all that serving Christ  
> Raises up the sorrowful from fear of hunger,  
> Providing benefits and distributing grain,  
> Without diminishing anything.  
> Called by prayer when people were sinking amid the waves,  
> He was present, calming the waters,  
> Prudently showing, through the liquid of oil,  
> How to despise the flames.  
> The gracious father, I say, terrifies the Augustus,  
> So that he may release the wretched men bound in vain;  
> By blessed warnings concerning cruel death  
> He wipes away their bonds [sic].  
> Thus, often performing deeds of piety  
> In serving Christ with devotion,  
> He deserved to ascend, renowned,  
> To the sacred kingdom of heaven.  
> Your distinguished people applaud, Blessed One;  
> Greece rejoices, crowned with festivals,  
> Because by your holy merits you shatter  
> The crimes of the wicked.  
> Protect the people singing praise to you,  
> Shaking off the deceits of the hostile enemy,  
> So that we may deserve to despise  
> The dark waves of the world.  
> We beseech you, most holy and blessed one:  
> Pray for us, entreating the Lord,  
> So that we may all deserve  
> To behold his true light.  
> Let us all resound glory to the Father,  
> And to you, Christ, begotten from above,  
> With whom the Holy Spirit, likewise Creator,  
> Reigns.

## HYMN II OF THE SAME SAINT NICHOLAS

[Col. 0813]

The solemn season returns  
in which Bishop Nicholas,  
laying down the burden of the flesh,  
freed, crossed beyond the heavens.

Born of illustrious stock,  
he adorned his lineage with his conduct.  
Obedient to the holy commandments,  
he was consecrated bishop from heaven.

With gold he redeemed his father’s disgrace,  
the violation of virgins;  
flowing forth in words and teaching,  
he destroyed the rites of demons.

He supplies the measure of grain taken  
to the royal servants;  
distributing wheat to the people,  
he removed the want caused by famine.

The sailors oppressed by the waves  
seek his power;  
at once the very fierce storm  
and threatening whirlwind are stilled.

Present, he rebukes the consul;  
in a dream he terrifies Augustus;  
he immediately commands  
those unjustly bound in chains to be released.

All devoted Greece  
applauds with great rejoicing,  
because the honor of her foster-child and bishop  
shines with noble beauty.

And, radiant with a blessed crown,  
he possesses the gifts of grace,  
granting to his suppliants  
what they ask with a pure heart.

Therefore we pray, bowed down,  
all of us, most holy father,  
that we may always enjoy abundantly  
your patronage.

Bend beneath our feet  
the neck of the treacherous tyrant,  
lest he compel us to serve  
the deceptive allurements of the world.

May no final encounter, we ask,  
disturb us;  
nor may the opposing party  
deliver our spirit to eternal fires.

But let us freely sing forever  
the glory of praise to Christ,  
to the Father, and to the holy Spirit,  
through infinite ages.

## HYMN I OF SAINT SYLVESTER, POPE

[Col. 0814]

Let the Christian people sing  
with harmonious voice  
the triumph of the holy bishop Sylvester,  
the distinguished glory of the city of Rome.

The savage and cruel prefect Tarquinius  
assailed him with imprisonment,  
he raging in his brutality,  
while Sylvester suffered for the Lord.

But, remaining steadfast and unmoved,  
the noble athlete conquered;  
through the wicked man’s downfall  
this bishop was chosen.

Through his chaste words  
Constantine Augustus then,  
exhorted to believe in Christ,  
was reborn through baptism.

When Sylvester anointed him with chrism,  
he was immediately cleansed  
of the disease of elephantiasis  
by the power of the Holy Spirit.

Then, contending fearlessly  
against the troublesome Jewish philosophers  
concerning the heavenly mystery,  
he conquered them.

For he restrained  
the savagery of the poisonous dragon,  
and led innumerable peoples  
to the Lord of heaven.

[Col. 0816]

He freed us also from the bonds of sin  
through his prayers;  
for the glory of the Thunderer  
we sing his annual praises.

To God the Father . . . .

## HYMN II OF THE SAME SAINT SYLVESTER

[Col. 0815A]

Let us all resound with joyful voice,  
bringing devotion through holy praises;  
let us celebrate in song  
Sylvester, father of the Roman city.

This pious shepherd and guardian of the flock  
was light for the blind and a staff for the lame,  
and performed many signs  
like those of paradise upon earth.

He showed everyone the perfectly straight way,  
restored health to the stricken king,  
and thereby enabled those who saw  
to behold the light of the heart.

Through him the highest splendor  
of virtues flourished,  
radiating throughout the whole world;  
and thus he watered dry hearts  
with the faithful bath of Christ.

He joined many souls  
to the company of angels and to the Church,  
and caused the Lord’s temple to resound  
day and night  
with the ten-stringed harp.

Let us all resound the glory of the Father,  
and to you, holy heavenly Begotten One,  
with whom the holy and Creator Spirit  
reigns together.

## HYMN III OF THE SAME SAINT SYLVESTER

Christ, King of kings, great governor,  
eternal offspring of the boundless Father,  
mercifully receive the vows of suppliants  
and their songs as well.

Cleansing the world’s harmful reproaches,  
and shining moreover with wondrous splendor,  
mercifully grant the outstanding gifts  
of heavenly goodness.

Among these highest gifts we venerate the holy one;  
the great city granted us this distinction.  
The entire Roman people, father of the world,  
honors him throughout the earth.

After he had been poured forth  
in the holy waters,  
imbued with sacred letters and instruction,  
burning in spirit, at the Lord’s command (sic),  
“always accumulate” [corrupt text].

[Note: The passage is corrupt, like very many others.]

“You rightly—[corrupt reading *parchus*]—holy father, I say:  
‘Fool, you will breathe out your soul tonight.  
Why do you not cease torturing  
the worshipers of Christ with punishment?’”

And immediately, the shepherd worthy of holiness,  
at last chosen by the Roman people,  
withdrew into hiding from the savage tyrant,  
together with his clergy.

[Col. 0816A]

Augustus, horrified at so monstrous a crime,  
released the happy mothers and their children,  
and, in his goodness, bestowed  
the benefits of life upon all.

Truly inspired by Christ’s grace,  
he instructed Peter and Paul  
that healing and salvation for him  
should be sought in the water of the pool.

He was called the kindly bishop of the people;  
he proved gentle and merciful toward the king.  
Immediately, he showed holy *loquoris* [corrupt reading]  
by Christ’s power.

He proclaims that the people should serve Christ,  
raising up those who had long been grieving  
by his exhortation,  
continually granting benefits to the faithful,

[Col. 0816B]

always praying.

And thus, devoted, frequently giving  
the deeds of truth, serving heaven,  
he deserved, illustrious,  
to ascend to the kingdom of blessed life.

His distinguished, consecrated people rejoice;  
renewed by the waters, the Roman people applaud,  
because through your ancient holy merits  
he destroys deceit.

Favor all who serve you,  
shaking off the deceits of the wicked enemy,  
so that we may all deserve  
to behold the true light.

We ask, most holy and blessed father,  
pray for us to the Lord,  
that we may all be able  
to drive the evils of the world far away.

To you, immense Trinity, be praise,  
in whom the heavenly host now rejoices;  
grant us true grace  
forever and ever.

## HYMN OF SAINT SEVERINUS, ABBOT

[Note: See the Bollandists under 8 January.]

Singing a hymn of praise to the Lord,  
let us all celebrate this solemn day,  
on which blessed Severinus entered  
the heights of heaven.

Who, rich in literary skill  
and modulating the plectrum,  
could recount all the signs  
which powerful Christ, in his generous purposes,  
bestowed upon him?

The renowned and exceedingly blessed seer,  
to whom God often revealed  
many future events  
for the salvation of the oppressed people,

uncovering by prophetic voice  
the snares of robbers  
and the schemes of marauders,  
strongly protected the weary towns  
with heavenly warnings.

Bringing sweet comfort to the wretched,  
he cut off the dreadful plague of famine;  
victorious over the savage cruelty of many barbarians,  
he freed them from the enemy.

Great confessor, humble teacher,  
you gave the monks their rule,  
showing your followers by a sober path  
how to ascend to heaven.

In your holy hands  
heavenly light shone forth;  
and the flowing supply of oil increased  
at your draughts, like a spring.

[Col. 0817B]

Pitying all the poor, he cherished them;  
healing the weak, he relieved the sick.  
Everyone who approached  
received salutary healing from him.

And you caused Sylvinus, lying in a coffin,  
after prayers had been performed before the brothers,  
to return, death conquered,  
to the joys of lif—.

As the flame of faith burned the candles,  
the holy father rebuked the unbelievers;  
and our cold hearts  
glow with the fire of the Godhead.  
[The printed *Nosque* is uncertain.]

At his sacred funeral,  
the mute received the power of speech;  
the blind rejoiced to see acquaintances  
walking from afar.

Naples, rejoice, adorned with festivals;  
applaud while retaining your heavenly patron,  
whom the Founder granted you  
as your highest honor and help.

[Col. 0818B]

O merciful Creator of his merit,  
grant us glory and forgiveness,  
so that we may always enjoy  
the light of your worship above the stars.

## HYMN OF SAINT MARK THE MARTYR

[Note: See the Bollandists under 25 April.]

[Col. 0817]

Let us celebrate the feast  
of the blessed martyr  
with harmonious songs,  
whom the providence of the heavenly King  
sent to the world.

In the fourfold faces  
the prophet, foreknowing the future,  
once saw the illustrious formula  
of the lion’s mystery.  
[The printed *mysteriarchis* is corrupt.]

Sent by a heavenly gift  
to the land of Alexandria,  
he shone among its learned inhabitants  
as a noble evangelist.

Scattering among the people  
the bright seeds of the word of salvation,  
for the name of the exalted King  
he became crowned with blood.

With his consecrated limbs,  
Christ, the author of all salvation,  
in our own time adorned  
the soil of Germany.

Rejoice, happy Reichenau,  
endowed with such honor;  
cherishing your beloved patron on earth,  
you possess him also in heaven.

We, lost through our sins,  
ask you, Mark, with humble prayer:  
mercifully release your servants  
from the evil of sin.

To the Trinity be glory  
and the greatest praise and honor,  
which grants the martyr his crown,  
now and throughout every age.

Amen.

## HYMN II OF THE SAME SAINT MARK

[Col. 0817B]

Now throughout every age  
the light shines forth—  
that light which shines from the Father’s throne,  
the fountain, source, and splendor  
of golden light,  
always possessing unfailing brightness.  
It makes heaven serene,  
driving away the world’s darkness.

From the sacred vibration of this light  
Mark received a blessed ray  
within his breast.  
The blessed evangelical teacher,  
made a lamp through love of such light,  
burning, drove away  
the gloom of the age.

One of seven white columns,  
one of seven golden lampstands,  
it surrounds the whole world  
with a radiant star.  
It strives beneath the summit of the churches  
and supports the foundations  
of the structure on high.

What Ezekiel had once seen,  
the holy prophet,  
the most excellent living creature,  
John saw also,  
as one reclining with Christ:  
in the form of the typological lion  
he roared loudly through the wilderness.

Thus, sent by blessed Peter,  
he approached the once most famous  
city of Aquileia.  
He scattered the sprouting seeds  
of the sacred word,  
and, blessed, carried  
the hundredfold fruit  
to Christ’s high granaries.

Soon there he dedicated a church to Christ,  
for he had fixed the strongest foundation of faith  
upon a single clear rock,  
which no surging river,  
no thunderbolt of winds,  
no torrents of rain  
can shake.

Then, returning again with a crown,  
Christ’s athlete, adorned with beautiful lilies  
and mixed with palms, laurel, and little roses,  
joyfully carried the diadem upon his head.  
With Christ as his companion,  
he entered the city of Rome.

After these deeds he proceeded to Alexandria.  
Filled with the most joyful Holy Spirit,  
throughout all the Memphite regions  
he continually proclaimed  
that the only Son of the dread Father  
had come for the world’s salvation.

The cruel crowd, swelling against Christ’s soldier,  
then prepared the darts of torture.  
They bound him with chains, pierced him with hooks,  
tore his holy entrails with whips,  
and sent him into the phantasmal shadows of prison.

Mark first gave the city of Alexandria  
knowledge of the heavenly name.  
Soon he dedicated a basilica to Christ there,  
which he purified with precious blood  
and fortified with the protection of blessed faith.

[Col. 0819A]

Glory to the Father, honor and dominion!  
Son, may honor and power  
always be yours above the stars;  
and to the Holy Spirit  
be the indivisible power of the Trinity  
through infinite ages of ages!

## HYMN OF SAINT FLAVIAN THE CONFESSOR

Blessed confessor, bishop of the highest King,  
hear the voice of your servants,  
who entreat you.

Renowned in faith, pure in life,  
a true preacher,  
whose inspiration the Holy Spirit bestowed upon him.

O good shepherd, holy Flavian,  
protect the people entrusted to you,  
the athletes of God.

Your enemies fight on every side;  
help us, Father, your servants and dependants.  
[The printed wording is corrupt.]

You despised the doctrines of the heretics  
and refuted them—*uticeque probat* [corrupt text].  
[Note: The text is corrupt . . . .]

O holy Father.

Enter into joy, and present  
to your Lord the sheep entrusted to you,  
faithful servant.

You became a son who suffered for Christ;  
there you ended your life in the flesh  
and were received into heaven.

You adorned the land of Aprutium;  
the Lord did not wish  
to deprive us of our own patron.

He who once was bishop of the city  
remains so;  
through God’s help he shines miracles  
from his tomb for us.

Praise, honor, and power be to him  
who, seated upon the heavenly throne,  
is Three and One. Amen.

## HYMN OF SAINT JUVENAL, BISHOP OF NARNI

[Note: See the Bollandists under 4 May.]

### I

May Juvenal’s glory shine upon earth,  
he who rejoices among the holy companies of heaven;  
through whose sacred merits  
the city of Narni shines secure.

Africa divinely brought forth  
this prudent man, most gentle in conduct,  
an outstanding student of sacred Scripture,  
beautiful in mind.

Yet divine Providence did not wish  
to leave him fertile without fruits;  
it compelled him to hasten to Rome  
with Christ as his oarsman.

Behold the beautiful matron Philadelphia;  
she then received Juvenal as her guest.  
Ever solicitous for the brethren,  
she fulfilled her name, Philadelphia [“brotherly love”].

When she learned the kindness of her guest,  
she petitioned the Roman Pontiff  
with humble prayer  
that he be consecrated bishop  
to be sent to Narni.

There were abominable idols. The citizens worshiped  
Jupiter and Mercury, Mars, Saturn, Minerva, and Venus,  
blinded by their light.

When the servant of Christ entered,  
he showed the city, already deceived  
by its wandering error,  
the bright, open path of truth to Olympus.

He overthrew the filthy worship of idols;  
breaking the little stones  
at Christ’s command,  
he raised many sons of Abraham  
with beautiful speech.

You, Juvenal, we all ask  
with humble prayers:  
intercede with the Lord Christ for us,  
that he may free us all  
from the second death.

Let us all resound the glory of the Father, etc.

### II

When he was spreading the words of life  
among the citizens,  
a former sacrilegious priest of demons  
urged him to take the sacrificial victim  
and taste it with his own mouth.

Juvenal, the greatest bishop of Christ,  
with steadfast face and purest mind,  
refused the outrage,  
as a very blessed disciple of Christ.

Then the judge, angered, dared  
to thrust inside his holy teeth  
the knife with which he gave meat  
to the sacrifices,  
by wicked craft.

Juvenal, filled with the divine Spirit,  
refusing to taste the impious victim,  
kept his lips pure for Christ’s body,  
free from the filth of evil.

The judge, inflamed by manifold fury,  
pulled the sword from the bishop’s mouth;  
in that very assault  
he killed himself in the throat  
by a mortal wound.

When a great part of the citizens  
saw the miracle, they demanded  
to be washed in the flood of Christ’s baptism  
and to follow the commands  
of the holy and blessed bishop.

[Col. 0820D]

After these people had been received  
into the Lord’s sheepfold,  
Juvenal approached the altar of the martyr Valentine  
to offer sacred victims  
to the Almighty.

While he was presenting to all the people  
the crystal chalice filled with blood,  
the sacred offerings increased  
and were wondrously enlarged from heaven.

You, Juvenal, etc.

Glory to the Father, etc.

### III

So that Christ’s athlete might engage in battle,  
the city was held under siege  
for a long time and could not be rescued [lacuna]  
from the plague it had received.

Then, through the great prayers  
and tears of the supreme bishop Juvenal,  
the earth swallowed the enemies of the citizens  
with its open mouth.

When he had increased his victory  
over the proud enemy,  
the crowd of citizens, from the least to the greatest,  
followed the remarkable bishop of Christ,  
who bore the signs.

Thus one enemy, slain by his own sword,  
fell, so that many might rise  
through baptism;  
and when all had been destroyed,  
everything arose.

The shepherd strove to aid  
not only his own sheepfold,  
but also sailors shipwrecked at sea,  
near death amid wind  
and immense storms.

[Col. 0822A]

Juvenal shone through exalted signs,  
showing himself to be a disciple  
of the All-Powerful,  
who overcame Saul with his sword  
and bestowed love.

With Christ’s blood increased in the chalice,  
he served the very author of all,  
who fed many crowds in the wilderness  
with a small loaf.

With his broad jaws the earth swallowed  
the enemies,  
as we read that Dathan and Abiron of old  
were always subject to the Lord,  
proud in the same manner.

Through the whirlwind of the wind  
and stormy clouds,  
the sailor, whom Juvenal’s prayer frees,  
follows the Master  
who rescues his dependants  
from the plague of the sea.

You, Juvenal, etc.

Glory to the Father, etc.

## HYMN OF SAINT APOLLINARIS

[Col. 0821B]

the sacred feast  
of Bishop Apollinaris the martyr,

and the fame of the signs

of the tyrant Saturninus, then judge,  
whose savage greed  
raged against the martyr,

At once Boniface,  
a citizen of Classis, became mute.  
Words placed upon his lips

Amid these events he proceeded  
to Emilia;

he restored health to the sick.

He delivered the daughter of the patrician Rufus,

## HYMN OF SAINT JUSTUS THE MARTYR

[Note: See Baronius’s Roman Martyrology under 2 November.]

The sacred festivity is here,  
on which Justus endured dangers,  
for Justus, a citizen of heaven,  
endured them for heavenly rewards.

The avenging decree  
of the most wicked rulers was burning,  
compelling them to burn  
filthy victims in silent shrines.

In the territory of Praeneste [printed *Pregestinis 2*],  
the illustrious martyr Justus shone,  
in name and deed Just,  
from the flower of his youth.

When the impious Magnatius  
heard the report of his salvation,  
he thrust the martyr,  
his nerves exhausted,  
into a foul prison.

Standing firm as an athlete,  
rejecting the tyrant’s threats,  
he sang with blessed voice  
thanks to the eternal Judge.

Then the mad Magnatius  
changed the sentence;  
laughing, he ordered  
the consecrated neck  
to be pressed beneath a weight.

For he fastened a mass of lead  
to him bound with linen thread,  
restrained his blessed shoulders,  
and plunged him into the depths  
of the river.

to the shore;  
the presbyter Sebastian  
committed it to the tomb.

Glory to the Father, etc.

## HYMN OF SAINT CLEMENT

[Col. 0821B]

Clement’s feast is celebrated today.  
Come, peoples, and behold the prince,  
the follower of Peter, the Lord’s apostle,  
the bishop of the entire Roman see,  
whom Christ consecrated as his martyr.

While living in the city of Romulus,  
by proclaiming Jesus Christ the Lord  
he enlightened Theodora and Sisinnius,  
when she saw Peter in a dream.

Thus Sisinnius, baptized by Clement,  
believed.

By preaching Christ’s Gospel,  
he was led by Trajan’s command  
into exile beyond the Pontic Sea,  
into a rugged wilderness.

[Col. 0822B]

There he performed a notable miracle.

who were cutting marble

he was sunk into the deep sea  
with an anchor;  
there he was enclosed  
in a burial chamber.

The church now stands there  
for his reception.

through the ages.

[The printed text is corrupt:]  
“which, at the course of the year, covered by mighty water, demands that the naked be submerged in the deep sea.”

When the annual feast returns,  
the sea withdraws for three miles  
and, for seven days,  
provides shining paths.

Let us all learn,  
as approved followers of yours,  
to despise the world in our conduct,  
to tame anger,  
and to reject the fleeting things of the flesh.

and entreat the blessed Holy Spirit,

and thereby let us escape

To you, Son, be honor and dominion;
