## THE ANCIENT SACRAMENTARY

Now published for the first time from an eleventh-century parchment manuscript, with observations and notes by the distinguished gentleman Octavius Turcius, canon of the very notable collegiate church of Pyrensis.

## PRELIMINARY NOTICE CONCERNING THE FOLLOWING ANCIENT SACRAMENTARY

(D. Giovanni Benedetto Mittarelli and D. Anselmo Costadoni, *Annals of Camaldoli*, Venice, 1756, vol. II, Appendix, p. 397.)

[Col. 0823B]

We make public an ancient sacramentary that was formerly used by the monks or hermits of the church of the Most Holy Trinity on Mount Suavicino—or, if we listen to the persistent popular tradition, which is almost always in some way a companion of truth, it was used by Saint Dominic Loricatus, to whom it was given by his holy master, Saint Peter Damian.

For this reason it has enjoyed immemorial sacred veneration among the people of Frontal Castle, situated in the diocese of San Severino and not far from the monastery of Suavini. It is still guarded with the greatest reverence in the parish church of that castle.

The script of this manuscript sacramentary indicates the eleventh century, in which both Dominic and Peter Damian lived; nor can anything be brought forward that would compel us to assign it to a later period.

The distinguished Octavius Turcius, canon of Pyrensis, who published in print seven years ago the Life of Saint Dominic Loricatus and who examined this sacramentary almost to the point of superstition, gave us his learned annotations, printed below, in 1752, when we visited that very friendly man and together examined the antiquity of the codex. He is entirely of the same opinion.

The same judgment was held by the very learned Dom Gabriel Guastuccius, a monk of Classis, who was then with us, and by our earlier and most learned superior, Dom Maurus Sartius, who carefully examined the manuscript several times when it was placed before him.

In his preliminary observations, which follow immediately, Turcius thinks that this codex formerly belonged to the famous monastery of Saint Apollinaris at Classis outside Ravenna, or to some place subject to Classis, because in the litanies, in the order for assigning penance, Saint Apollinaris is invoked, whose title and sacred body belong to the basilica of Classis. Saint Severus, Saint Vitalis, and Saint Guido are also named there, all Ravennate saints.

While not rejecting this very reasonable observation, we add that the manuscript might have been copied from a similar codex that was used in the monastery and hermitage of the Holy Cross at Fonte Avellana, which Saint Peter Damian governed. The litanies in the ancient rituals and liturgical books of that monastery are almost identical, and there too the names of Saints Apollinaris, Severus, and Vitalis occur, although Guido is absent. Indeed, in one of those codices there is an office with proper hymns for Saint Apollinaris.

Peter Damian, a native of Ravenna and also for a time an inhabitant of the monastery of Classis, maintained the greatest connection and communication between the monks of that monastery and those of Avellana. He introduced the veneration of his Ravennate saints among his Avellanese, giving particular observance to Saint Apollinaris, who, long ago—at the very time when the beginnings of the Avellanese monastery were emerging—had appeared visibly near Catria, where the Avellanese hermitage was founded, to Saint Romuald, our father, as Damian himself recounts in his Life.

Damian may have granted Guido, abbot of Pomposa, a place in the litanies of our sacramentary because, before his administration of Avellana, he had instructed the monks of Pomposa for two years during that abbot’s rule. He may therefore have arranged for this man, recently numbered among the saints, to be inserted into the liturgical missal.

The Suavicino Sacramentary is enclosed in covers consisting of two plates, embossed in relief and skillfully worked in gilded silver, within which is set an ivory panel surrounded by a small ebony border.

It would be superfluous to observe here that gospel books, sacramentaries, missals, and other codices intended for altar use were customarily adorned with the noblest and most precious coverings. Others have discussed this, and our canon Turcius does so learnedly as well.

We also dealt with the matter in our observations on an ancient ivory panel, and in the brief record of Boniface, abbot of Pisa, which appears in the Appendix to this second volume, one reads: “One very well-written text of the Gospels, with a very fine silver panel.”

In a manuscript catalogue of possessions drawn up on 28 April 1317, according to the constitution of our congregation and the command of Bonaventure, the general superior, Dom Bartholus, abbot of the monastery of Saints Justus and Clement near Volterra, recorded among the other treasures of his monastery “one four-Gospel book with silver panels, weighing nineteen pounds and eight ounces.”

There was likewise a practice of enclosing carved ivory panels between silver plates. In the museum of our monastery we preserve a thirteenth-century ivory panel on which the image of the most holy Savior is carved; along the borders of its two sides are images of the holy martyrs Gervasius and Protasius. We sent a copy of it to the distinguished Antonio Francesco Gori for insertion in his precious treasury of ancient ivory works.

But let us describe the plates and panels of our sacramentary. Several small circles are represented on each plate. On the first plate there is an image of an angel, as indicated by the wings and the letters placed beside it: Μιχαήλ, “Michael.”

In another circle opposite the first is a similar image with the letters Ο Αρχάγγελος ΓΑΒριήλ, “the archangel Gabriel.” Both angels raise their hands toward an altar placed in the central circle between the lateral circles.

Upon the altar lies a gem-encrusted codex, representing the sacred book of the Gospels. Beneath it is a cloth, and beneath the cloth a cushion, visible only from its left side.

Behind the cushion rise a reed with a sponge on one side and a lance on the other—the well-known instruments of the Lord’s Passion. Behind the codex rises the double cross called the Jerusalem, patriarchal, apostolic, and commonly Greek cross.

Among the Greeks of a later age we find the custom of this symbolic altar. We saw a similar altar in the mosaic of the cathedral of Torcello, and also on a gilded wooden panel of the fourteenth century preserved in the sacristy of the canons of the principal basilica of Treviso.

Some difference can nevertheless be observed between these and the more ancient symbolic altars of earlier periods, as may be seen in Ciacconius and Ciampini’s mosaics of Saint Mary Major in Rome and Saint Mary in Cosmedin at Ravenna, which belong to the fifth and sixth centuries. We have discussed elsewhere the worship of Gospel books upon altars, in imitation of the book seen by the Apostle John.

In the fourth and fifth circles, halfway along the plate, are images of Saint Peter the Apostle and Saint Paul, his fellow apostle, with the letters Α. ΠΕΤΡΟC and Α. ΠΑΥΛΟC.

Finally, along the lower edge of the plate three further circles are carved. On one side is Saint Mark, Α. ΜΑΡΚΟC; on the other, Saint Luke, Α. ΛΟ8ΚΑC; in the middle is an angel standing and holding a bare globe in his left hand, while with his right he presses something that cannot clearly be seen because of corrosion on the plate. Beside him are the letters Ο ΑΡχάγγελος ΓΑΒριήλ, “the archangel Gabriel.”

We attribute the repetition of the bust and letters of the archangel Gabriel, and the omission of the image and letters of the archangel Raphael, to the craftsman’s error, and believe that the matter has no symbolic significance.

On the ivory panel enclosed by the silver plate described above is carved the image of Saint George, Ο ΑΓΙΟC ΓΕΟΡΓΙΟC, “Saint George.” He holds a cross in his right hand and raises his left, covered with his cloak, as craftsmen customarily represented it in other ancient and later images, both Greek and Latin. A hand wrapped in a cloak indicated either prayers poured out to God or something received with humble reverence.

The other cover, by which the sacramentary codex is closed on the lower side, retains a similar ivory panel on which Saint Theodore is visible, with the letters Ο ΑΓΙΟC ΘΕΟΔωΡΟC, “Saint Theodore.” His hands are raised, but without any symbolism, unless according to the craftsman’s intention.

Since the craftsman was Greek, he selected two Greek saints who enjoyed the greater veneration of that church, and whose images are therefore more frequent in Greek-style paintings and carvings.

In the upper circle on the right side of this second plate is Saint Matthew, with the letters Ο ΜΑΘΕΟC. On the left is Saint John the Apostle and Evangelist, here called “the Theologian,” Ο Ιωάννης ΘΕΟλογος.

This may illuminate the dissertation of Christoph August Heumann, published at Eisenach in 1715, *On the Title “Theologian” Given to John the Prophet*.

Between these two circles, in a square, is an image of Saint Michael holding a bare globe in his left hand and a spear in his right.

The middle circles show Saint James, Ο ΙΑΚΩΒΟC, and Saint Andrew, Α. ΑΝΔΡΕΑC. The final two, at the lowest edge, show Saint Bartholomew, Ο ΒΑΡΘΟλημηοC, and Saint Simon, Ο CΙΜων. In the middle is another circle with an image of the great Saint Nicholas, Ο ΝΙΚΟΛΑΟC, who likewise receives supreme veneration among the Greeks.

There is nothing else in these images that deserves particular comment, except that the customary sign Α. ΑΓΙΟC, “saint,” is placed before the apostles, evangelists, confessors, and martyrs. It is denied, however, to the archangels on these covers.

The entire workmanship is Greek in character, as is clear from the Greek letters themselves. In the Middle Ages and later, mosaics, paintings, carvings, and other works of this kind were the work of Greeks, since the arts in Italy had either miserably perished or were extremely rudimentary.

The mosaics of the ducal basilica of Saint Mark at Venice, those of the cathedral church of Torcello, and many Roman works impressed in bronze all bear a Greek character—indeed, they are thoroughly Greek.

The arts later flourished again in Italy during the fifteenth century. Therefore the plates we have described thus far were made before that century. Indeed, if the form of the Greek letters in the two ivory panels is examined, since they are more elongated than round, these covers may be assigned to the fourteenth century or the end of the thirteenth, whereas the Greek letters of earlier centuries were formed with greater roundness and breadth.

But let us now proceed to the second preface by the distinguished Turcius.

[Col. 0825]

## PRELIMINARY OBSERVATIONS OF OCTAVIUS TURCIUS

[Col. 0825D]

At that time, most courteous reader, when I turned my attention to illustrating the Acts of blessed Dominic Loricatus—which, as I desired, have now been completed and also published in print—I sought above all to gather together everything that might contribute to their dignity, to the glory of the blessed man, and to the usefulness of lovers of learning.

As soon as I learned that a missal was preserved in the parish church of Saint Anne in Frontal Castle, in the diocese of San Severino, and that, sealed under episcopal insignia, it was annually displayed for the veneration of the assembled people; that it had once belonged to the use of the most holy Peter Damian and had later been given by him to blessed Dominic Loricatus for the use of the monastery or hermitage of Suavicinio, according to the ancient and continuous tradition of the inhabitants, confirmed also by letters of the bishops of San Severino—I judged that I would perform a worthwhile service if I brought such a venerable monument of antiquity out of darkness and arranged for a copy of it to be published for the advancement of sacred liturgy.

Dionysius Pieraugustinus, bishop of happy memory and a most distinguished man, approved these plans and further encouraged me to carry out the work.

Accordingly, by a letter, that exceedingly courteous prelate instructed the parish priest of Frontal to break the seals and hand the codex over to me for copying. He did so without hesitation. This is the very codex that I now place before your eyes, with certain observations of my own added, which I judged should appropriately be inserted.

No sooner had I brought the sacred codex out of its custody than, at first sight, I recognized from the covers themselves that it was one of those sacred diptychs which learned men and students of antiquity, if they happen to find them, kiss as though they were most precious treasures and believe that they have discovered something very important.

A diptych, generally speaking, is nothing other than two folding panels suitable for receiving sculptures or inscriptions, as the distinguished Negelein neatly defines it in his dissertation *On the Consular and Ecclesiastical Diptych* (§ 3, p. 3). The most learned Johann Andreas Schmidt, in another dissertation on diptychs, says that the term derives its etymology from the same Greek word that means “double” (p. 3).

Kuster likewise believes (*On Diptychs*) that any book with jeweled covers may be called a diptych, even though its interior consists of several leaves or panels. He says that this terminology depends more on the double covering than on the number of pages or panels contained within it.

The more precious diptychs were of gold, silver, ivory, and cedar, and these themselves were of various kinds.

Passing over those that do not pertain to our subject, and which the distinguished Negelein and Schmidt enumerate, it is useful to mention only those called sacred and ecclesiastical.

These displayed sacred images and various symbols of our most holy religion, and enclosed sacred and divine books.

For in those ancient times there was an enormous cult and reverence for sacred codices, especially missals and Gospel books. In the capitulary of Charlemagne, by decree of the Council of Aachen, it was ordered that missal books be written with every care by men of mature ability. Cardinal Bona observes this (*Liturgical Matters*, book I, chapter 25, no. 10).

Monks were particularly occupied with this devotion, copying sacred books and taking care also to enrich them externally with as much ornament as they could provide.

The same honor was shown to Gospel books, and therefore we read in the ancient Chronicle of Fontenelle that he ordered “the four Gospels to be written in purple parchment in gold, in Roman letters” (chapter 16).

[The supplied source ends here.]

A lectionary of this kind, written on purple parchment in silver letters and provided with an ivory cover, is described by Cangius in his *Glossary* (vol. II, p. 513). Likewise, in the Vatican Library there is preserved a codex containing the Gospels of Saints Luke and John, covered with an ivory diptych, of which only one half remains. Carved upon it are Christ the Lord, with two angels attending him, and the three holy Magi speaking with Herod and offering gifts to the newborn Lord, as Cardinal Quirinus wrote to Monsieur de Boze in a letter (letter 24). Wiltemius likewise reports in the Appendix to the *Liège Diptych* that the Epistles of Saint Paul preserved at the monastery of Saint Maximinus near Trier were covered with an ivory diptych.

From this we believe that a custom universally received in the Church prevailed: namely, that sacred books or codices intended for divine worship—such as missals, Gospels, and others of this kind—were furnished with various ornaments of gold or silver, and that the external pages of the books themselves were gilded. Our Suavicinian sacramentary is covered with two finely worked silver covers, on which are depicted numerous images of angels, apostles, evangelists, and saints of the Greek Church, together with Greek captions.

The book is written on parchment and is entirely intact, displaying a clear and very large script. Its pages—only one or two of them being slightly worn—are polished, neither consumed nor soiled by use or any other defect. All these features are indications of the very ancient esteem in which it was held and of the uncommon care bestowed upon it. It contains 126 pages, comprising prefaces, prayers of the Mass, the canon for consecration, and certain other prayers; it therefore deserves to be counted among the more distinguished diptychs.

I now turn to the period in which this sacred codex was perhaps written. Everything accords with the antiquity of the eleventh century, in which Saint Peter Damian lived. I find a still more specific indication in the invocation made in the litanies read in the rite for giving penance, of Saint Wido. I believe this to be none other than the celebrated abbot of Pomposa, through whose prayers Saint Peter Damian, while he was still a pupil living in the monastery of Avellana, went to that monastery in order to instruct its monks.

Saint Peter himself bears witness to Wido’s glorification in his letter to Henry, archbishop of Ravenna, where he mentions Romald, or Romuald of Camerino, of Rombibona—or, as Philippus Bonarota more accurately reads it (*Ditt. sacro*, p. 28), Rambona; Wido of Pomposa; Firmanus of Fermo; and many others enrolled in the lists of the saints, in accordance with the custom of those times.

Since it is certain that Saint Wido departed to God in the suburbs of Parma in the year of the Lord 1046—as is evident from his Life, written by an anonymous contemporary and reported by Mabillon in the *Acts of the Saints of the Order of Saint Benedict* (sixth century, p. 509)—there is an appropriate period in which our book may have been written: namely, after the year 1046, in which Saint Wido died, and before the year 1060, in which, according to my hypothesis, followed by the writers of the *Camaldolese Annals*, Saint Dominic Loricatus died, to whom Damian had given the book as a gift.

If, however, as reason requires, we should not believe that Saint Wido was enrolled in the lists of the saints in the very year of his death, but rather that some time elapsed—as five years elapsed between Saint Romuald’s death and his glorification, according to Damian himself—and if, moreover, it may be conjectured that the monastery of the hermitage of Mount Suavicinium was built around the year 1049, and that Saint Dominic Loricatus was appointed prior there by Damian, the founder of the hermitage, then Blessed Dominic must be thought to have acquired possession of our missal only after the construction of that hermitage, and not before—around the year 1050.

It is furthermore certain that this book of the sacraments is entirely monastic and belonged to monks of the Benedictine order. This is shown both by the Mass of Saint Benedict itself and by the preface for his particular passage from this life, as well as by the two prayers for clothing a monk, in the second of which we read:

> We beseech you, Lord, that, through the intercession of your confessor, blessed Benedict, this servant of yours, upon whom we are placing the habit of holy religion, etc.

The same is evident from the litanies in the rite for giving penance, in which several holy Benedictine monks are invoked. On account of those invocations, and especially the invocation of Saint Apollinaris—whose sacred body rests in the basilica at Classe and who is placed before the other martyrs after Saint Clement the pope—I would not hesitate to attribute the use of this book either to the monastery of Classe itself at Ravenna or to another monastery of the same order subject to Classe.

Such was formerly the judgment of the most learned Peter Pollidorius, and it is supported by the opinion of the distinguished bishop of Auximum and by that of Pompeius Compagnoni of Cingoli. The evidence is strengthened by the Mass that we have for the dedication of a church, occurring after the feast of Saint Mark and before the nativity of Saint John the Baptist. Now the dedication of the basilica of Saint Apollinaris at Classe is celebrated every year on the seventh day of May. I might therefore almost say that this missal belonged to the monastery at Classe, and that it was first given by the monks of Classe to Saint Peter Damian, and by him in turn presented as a gift to Saint Dominic Loricatus.

This sacramentary begins with the common preface and proceeds through the entire Mass in honor of all the saints, for the living and the dead. The materials preceding and following the Mass—the prefaces and prayers written in a different script—are nothing other than two appendices; nevertheless, according to the judgment of learned men, and especially of Sartius, the most learned Camaldolese bishop and a highly experienced scholar in these matters, they too were written in the same eleventh century. We submitted the autograph itself to their inspection.

Each Mass contains only three prayers: the first, called the Collect; the second, called the Secret; and the last, called the Postcommunion. All ecclesiastical historians know, and ancient monuments demonstrate, that Gelasius was the first author of the Collects used in the Mass, as Franciscus Pagius writes in his *Breviary of the Roman Pontiffs* under Gelasius (no. 13).

Here we have neither the Introit nor the Graduals, nor the Epistles or Gospels, nor, finally, the Offertories and the verses after Communion. I may therefore reasonably suspect that this sacramentary served only solemn Masses, at which the celebrant formerly recited the three prayers preserved here, together with the preface and the canon, while the ministers sang the remaining portions.

It must therefore be said that the churches formerly used two sacramentary books in the sacrifice of the Mass. One was called the plenary book, which Leo IV ordered to be kept in every church:

> Let every church have a plenary missal, a lectionary, and an antiphonary.

Perhaps this is the plenary missal that priests now use for celebrating private Masses. It was called “plenary” because whatever is contained separately in the lectionaries and antiphonaries is collected and found there in full. The other was a book of the same kind as ours, assigned only to solemn Masses. In addition to it, a lectionary—containing the Epistles and Gospels—and an antiphonary—containing the Introits, Graduals, Offertories, and verses after Communion—would have to be acquired.

To make the truth of this ancient custom clearer, we must recall that Saint Gregory the Great selected from the psalms that Pope Celestine had decreed should be sung alternately before Mass certain verses for the Introit and the Responsories, others for the Offertory and Communion, and gathered still others into a single book, which he called the antiphonary. It was therefore called Gregorian, and was published in print by the late Cardinal Tommasi.

Because some of those antiphons that are sung after the Epistle used to be sung in a more elevated place, to which the singers ascended by steps, they were called Graduals, as Cardinal Bona maintains (*Book II*, chapter 3, no. 4), against those who think that they were so called from the steps of the altar.

Formerly both the Epistles and the Gospels were always sung in the ambo or pulpit; the Gospels in the higher place and the Epistle in the lower, according to the prescriptions of the Roman Order. The books containing the Epistles and Gospels were called lectionaries. One of these, under the title of *Comes*, Jerome compiled at the command of Damasus.

Lectionaries were also called by another name, *passionaries*, because the deeds and martyrdoms of the saints were written in them as well. The books in which the canonical Epistles were written were called epistolaries. Desiderius, abbot of Monte Cassino and later supreme pontiff Victor III, wished one of these to be adorned with jewels, one panel being silver and the other gold, as is recorded in the *Chronicle of Monte Cassino* (book III, chapter 3).

There was also a book of the Gospels called an evangeliary. Among the faithful it was held in such esteem and honor that, according to Baronius and Bona, whenever general councils were held it was placed beneath the royal throne in the midst of the assembled Fathers.

The remaining prayers said in the sacrifice of the Mass, which are absent here—such as the *Kyrie eleison*, the *Gloria in excelsis*, the Apostles’ Creed, and the other prayers before the canon and before Communion—may perhaps have been written on those tablets that, according to current custom, are placed on the altar before the celebrant’s eyes and that bishops and others possessing episcopal rights now read from the book commonly called the canon.

Finally, I observe that this missal agrees in many respects with the sacramentary of Saint Gregory, although frequent variations are found in accordance with the usage of the eleventh century. Whatever I found in the missal worthy of note I briefly append below in its proper places.

[Col. 0829]

This is the public copy of a certain very ancient manuscript Missal, written on parchment, consisting of 126 pages, thirteen inches in length and nine and a half inches in width. It is covered on the front and at its clasps with green silk velvet, with covers made of silver plates lined with gold and finely embossed, bearing here and there certain small circular images. Around them appear certain Greek characters; in their midst are seen other images, likewise embossed and carved in ivory, bordered with ebony, as they are shown in the drawing attached on the following leaf and on another leaf, placed at the beginning and end of this present copy. The inner side of the covers is entirely covered with silk cloth, likewise green in color. Its contents are as follows.

[Note: [Col. 0829D]]

These three prefaces, written in this first Appendix, are mentioned in the manuscript *Customs of Saint-Germain-des-Prés*. At the end of them the following is read in Martène (*On the Ancient Monastic Rites*, book II, chapter 4, no. 29):

> It remains to see when the preface is said on the vigil of the Nativity of the Lord, on the day itself at the three Masses, on the Nativity of Saint Stephen, of Saint John the Evangelist, and also of the Holy Innocents.

Our preface for Saint Stephen is entirely singular. It is not repeated in the other sacramentary books published by Tommasi, nor in Pamelius’s Gregorian sacramentary, nor finally in the books on the ancient discipline of the Church published by Martène.

The second preface, for Saint John, is found in the sacramentary books published through the work of Menardus and Pamelius (vol. III, col. 10, p. 551); with their assistance the deficiencies in our preface can be supplied.

The preface for the day of the Holy Innocents occurs alone, without a Mass or prayer in the body of our missal. It should be noted that the institution of this festive day is earlier than the third century. Origen, who flourished in that century, has a sermon on the Holy Innocents (*Homily 3 on Matthew*), as does Saint Augustine, as Baronius writes in his notes to the Martyrology.

Martène reports that this solemn feast day was forbidden at the Council of Basel because of the many abuses that had then crept in, especially because in various places it was celebrated by children with childish games. Since in this preliminary Appendix there is only a preface for the Holy Innocents, without a Mass, it may to some extent be inferred that around the middle of the eleventh century the observance of this feast had spread among Benedictine monks.

The Mozarabic Missal contains a Mass for the Holy Innocents. See, among the works of the venerable Cardinal Tommasi, the *Order of the Gothic Divine Office of the Mozarabs* (vol. I, chapter 35), and the treatise on the ancient Hispanic Liturgy written by Pinius (chapter 20, § 4).

From this preface it cannot be conjectured on which day the monks celebrated the feast, whether before or perhaps after Epiphany. The Greeks celebrated it before Epiphany, according to their menologion as reported by Canisius (vol. III, fol. 941), namely, on 29 December.

In the *Gothic-Hispanic Book of Prayers* published by Tommasi (vol. I, p. 165), this feast day is placed after Epiphany:

> On the day of the slaughter of the infants.

The latter custom seems more consistent, since the slaughter of the Innocents was preceded by the adoration of the Magi, which is commemorated at Epiphany. See the material collected with great learning in his notes to that book by the distinguished Joseph Blanchinius.]

## At the Feast of Saint John the Evangelist

+ Eternal God. As we commemorate the venerable birthday of your blessed apostle and evangelist John, who, having accepted the call of our Lord Jesus Christ, rejected his earthly father so that he might find a heavenly one, he obtained in the kingdom of heaven the seat of apostolic eminence. He had despised the bodily nets of his father, and was so familiarly received by the Only-Begotten as the beloved disciple and approved by gifts of immeasurable grace, that the same Lord, already placed upon the cross, [lacuna] entrust him as a son to his Virgin Mother [lacuna]. Thus [lacuna] the virginity of the beloved disciple, approved by his love, might serve the integrity of the blessed Mother. For at the sacred banquet of the mystical Supper he had reclined upon the very source of life, namely, upon the eternal breast of the Savior. Drawing from it the heavenly streams of teaching that flowed perpetually, he was so filled with profound and mystical revelations that, surpassing every created thing, he contemplated it with exalted mind and proclaimed with evangelical voice:

> In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.

And therefore, with the angels—

## At the Nativity of the Innocents

+ Eternal God. And in the precious deaths of the little children whom Herod wickedly slew with bestial cruelty because of the infancy of our Savior. In [lacuna] there is more grace than will, and the confession is clear before speech, and suffering precedes limbs capable of suffering. They become witnesses of Christ who had not yet known him; and the merit of glory for those slaughtered in his name is not allowed to perish. Rather, salvation through regeneration is granted to those drenched in their own blood, and the crown of martyrdom is reckoned to them. And therefore, with the angels and archangels—

[Note: [Col. 0831D]]

The missal book begins with the common preface. The particular prefaces assigned to the more solemn feast days are found in their proper places, in the respective Masses.

Some attribute the institution of the prefaces to Saint Gelasius I. Cardinal Bona (*Book II*, chapter 10) grants that several prefaces were added, but maintains—and supports the claim with many proofs—that their use is to be traced back to the very beginnings of the Church and to the apostles or apostolic men.

Formerly there were many and diverse prefaces, according to the variety of seasons and feast days; indeed, there were as many prefaces as feast days, as the same cardinal notes (ibid., chapter 10, no. 14).

We have a letter of Pelagius II to the bishops of Germany and Gaul, reported by Baronius. They had asked the pontiff to send them the order of the prefaces that the holy Roman Church then observed. In reply he lists only nine prefaces to be retained:

1. One for the Paschal season in white garments;
2. another for the Ascension of the Lord;
3. a third for Pentecost;
4. a fourth for the Nativity of the Lord;
5. a fifth for the Epiphany;
6. a sixth for the Apostles;
7. a seventh for the Trinity;
8. an eighth for the Cross;
9. a ninth for Fasting and Lent.

Nevertheless, Cardinal Bona (as above, no. 33) believes that this letter was wrongly attributed to Pelagius, and adduces many highly worthy arguments in support of his view. Finally, he concludes:

> If my conjecture does not please the impartial reader, he will at least be unable to deny that the usage of the Roman Church which Pelagius attests had fallen into disuse after his death, and that his decree concerning the nine prefaces was nowhere received or put into practice except in the tenth and eleventh centuries. It is evident, in fact, that in the ancient sacramentary books bearing the title of the Roman Church more prefaces are found, and scarcely any Mass lacks its own particular preface. When the number of so many prefaces ceased is unclear, except that in missals written after the year 1200 only the nine enumerated by Pelagius are found, with only two added: one, the very ancient common preface, believed to be that of Gelasius or Gregory; the other, that of the Blessed Virgin, instituted by Urban II. These eleven are those now used by all the Churches adhering to the Roman rite.

That Pelagius II’s decree was put into practice in the tenth or eleventh century is, however, contradicted rather than confirmed by our missal. For here 27 prefaces are read in various Masses, among which there is neither a preface of the Cross nor one of Fasting in Lent. A special preface of the Apostles is read on the feast day of the holy apostles Peter and Paul.

Martène finally reports (*On the Ancient Monastic Rites*, book II, chapter 4, no. 34) that the number of prefaces was reduced at the Council of Westminster.]

Through all ages of ages. Amen.

Many things have been said by many authors about the author of the canon, whom Pagius lists under Gelasius I (no. 15). Bishop Adelmus (*On the Praise of the Virgin*, chapter 23) attributes it to Saint Gregory the Great. Gregory himself, however, writes (*Letters*, book VII, letter 64) that it was composed by a certain scholasticus.

Whoever this scholasticus may have been, the following must be held as certain: he was earlier than Gelasius, who was not the author of the canon. Polydore Vergil (*On the Inventors of Things*, book V, chapter 10) writes that it was assembled by many pontiffs, but this is incorrect.

Although some added certain words to the canon—Pope Saint Leo, “the holy sacrifice” and “the spotless victim”; Saint Gregory the Great, “And order our days in your peace,” and “command that we be snatched from eternal damnation and numbered among the flock of your chosen”—as is shown from the *Book of the Pontiffs* and Bede (*Ecclesiastical History*, book II, chapter 10), and as John the Deacon also asserts in his Life of Gregory, nevertheless, as Pope Vigilius says in his letter to Eudocius, “we have received it from apostolic tradition.” The sacred Council of Trent repeats the same teaching (session 2, chapter 4), stating that it was composed from the very words of the Lord, the traditions of the apostles, and the constitutions of the supreme pontiffs.

After Saint Gregory the Great, nothing was added to or altered in the canon by the Roman pontiffs, as the aforementioned Bona observes (chapter 11).

There is very little worthy of note in the canon of our missal, since it is almost entirely identical with the one we use. The proper name of the supreme pontiff and bishop is not prescribed; only the words “together with your servant, our pope, and our bishop” are given.

Perhaps the monks for whose use this book was intended pronounced the names of the pope and bishop according to some particular rubric. For it is a very ancient apostolic rite to mention the pontiff and bishop in the canon, and this occurs in all manuscript sacramentary books and in the liturgies of the Greeks. So Bona states (chapter 11).]

The institution of the Mass to be celebrated everywhere on this holy night is attributed to Saint Telesphorus, and the decree is reported by Gratian (*On Consecration*, distinction 1). But that decretal of Telesphorus is spurious. This is clearly demonstrated by the fact that the vigil and keeping of the night, and indeed the feast day of the Nativity of the Lord itself, were fixed for celebration on 25 December many years after this Roman pontiff, under Julius I.

Florentinius proves this in exercise 2 of his notes on the Hieronymian Martyrology, as does Pagius in his *Breviary* (nos. 1 and 11) under Telesphorus and under Julius I. Pagius refutes Nicephorus, who wrote that the emperor Justin had established the feast of the Nativity to be observed throughout the world. We know that long before Justin it had been instituted in the West and East, either on 25 December or on 6 January; and that it was Justinian, in the year 557—not Justin—who assigned 25 December for universal celebration.]

## MASS DURING THE HOLY NIGHT

O God, who have made this most holy night shine with the illumination of the true light, grant, we beseech you, that, having come to know on earth the mysteries of that light, we may also enjoy its delights in heaven. You who live and reign with him.

**Secret.** May the offering of today’s feast be acceptable to you, Lord, we beseech you, so that, through these holy exchanges, by the gift of your grace, we may be found in the likeness of him in whom our substance is with you. You who live and reign with him.

[Col. 0836B]

**Postcommunion.** Grant us, we beseech you, Lord our God, that we who rejoice to celebrate repeatedly the nativity of our Lord Jesus Christ may, through worthy conduct, deserve to attain fellowship with him. You who live and reign with him.

## ON THE HOLY DAY OF THE NATIVITY OF THE LORD

[Note: [Col. 0836D]]

We have only two Masses for the feast day of the Nativity of the Lord: one during the holy night and the other on the day itself. The Mass at dawn is absent.

It certainly should not be believed that the Benedictine monks omitted it on that day. The distinguished Joseph Blanchinius teaches us in his notes on the ancient Gothic-Hispanic prayers (vol. I, p. 168) that only one Mass is assigned in the Gothic Missal, in the Sacramentary, and in the Gallican Lectionary published by Mabillon, and likewise in the Mozarabic and Ambrosian Missals published by Pamelius.

In the Gelasian and the New Ambrosian, however, three Masses are assigned. Therefore, since our sacramentary follows the Gregorian one, and since three Masses are found in the Gregorian, the only reasonable explanation for the absence here of the Mass at dawn is that our missal contains only solemn Masses. The Mass at dawn is consequently omitted because it was less solemn and was not sung.]

Receive, O Lord, the gifts that we offer you on his solemn feast, whose patronage we trust will deliver us. Through him.

### Communion

Refreshed by heavenly food and drink, we humbly beseech you, our God, that, having received these gifts in commemoration of him, we may be fortified by his intercession. Through him.

## On the Octave of the Lord

O God, who grant us to celebrate the eighth day of the birth of the Savior, make us, we beseech you, continually protected by his divinity, through whose sharing in human flesh we have been restored. Through him.

### Secret

Grant, we beseech you, O Lord, that through these gifts, which we present in the mystery of the hidden birth of our Lord Jesus Christ, we may attain understanding with a purified mind. Through him.

### Communion

Grant, we beseech you, O Lord, that what we have received in the repeated solemnity of our Savior may bring us the remedy of everlasting redemption. Through him.

## On the Epiphany of the Lord

O God, who on this day revealed your Only-Begotten Son to the nations, with a star as guide, mercifully grant that we who have already come to know you through faith may be led onward to contemplate the appearance of your majesty. Through him.

### Secret

Mercifully regard, we beseech you, O Lord, the gifts of your Church: no longer are gold, frankincense, and myrrh brought forward, but what is signified by those same gifts is offered and received. Through him.

### Preface

+ Eternal God, because when your Only-Begotten Son appeared in the substance of our mortality, he restored us by the new light of his immortality. And therefore.

### Within the Canon

Joining in communion and celebrating the most sacred day on which your Only-Begotten Son, coeternal with you in your glory, visibly and bodily appeared in the reality of our flesh, and also venerating the memory, [Col. 0838B] etc.

### Communion

Grant, we beseech you, O Lord our God, that through the understanding of a purified mind we may attain what we celebrate in solemn worship. Through him.

[Note: [Col. 0837D] The blessing of candles on the day of Mary’s Purification is considerably later than the time of Saint Gregory the Great. Neither Amalarius nor Walafrid, nor the spurious Alcuin—who nevertheless mentions the blessed candles distributed by the supreme pontiff—makes any mention of it. Still less is this blessing discussed in the Gelasian, Gregorian, Gellone, or other sacramentary books. In an ancient missal of the Church of Tours, written around the [Col. 0838D] tenth century, only one prayer is repeated for blessing the lights; and in another very ancient book of the monastery of Saint Theodoric, likewise only one prayer occurs for blessing candles. Martène reports these prayers (vol. III, *De antiquis ecclesiae ritibus*, book IV, no. 5), together with certain genuinely ancient rites for blessing candles. Moreover, there is no mention of the blessing itself in the ancient booklet of Gothic-Hispanic prayers mentioned elsewhere.] 

## Blessing of Candles on the Purification of Saint Mary

Hear, we beseech you, O Lord, your people, and grant by the light of your grace that inwardly we may attain what outwardly you grant us to venerate each year with devotion. Through him.

The Lord be with you. And with you. Lift up your hearts. Let us give thanks to the Lord our God.

+ Eternal God, creator of heaven and earth, King of kings and Lord of lords, graciously deign to hear us, your suppliants, as we cry out to you, because you created all things from nothing and, by your command, caused the work of bees to produce this liquid for the perfection of the candle, and on this day fulfilled the petition of the righteous Simeon.

We humbly beseech you to bless and sanctify by your mercy these candles for human use and for the health of bodies and souls, which any of your faithful may carry in their hands for a blessing, whether on land or on the waters, through the invocation of your most holy name, the intercession of Saint Mary, the mother of your Son, whose purification we celebrate today with devoted minds, and the prayer and merits of all your saints. May you deign to bene+dict and sancti+fy them, so that your people, who honorably carry these candles in their hands and sing your praises with psalmody, may have you hear their voices from your holy heaven and from the seat of your majesty; and may you be merciful to all who cry out to you, whom you have deigned to redeem by the precious blood of Christ your Son, who lives with you.

Let us pray. Instructed by saving commandments, etc. Our Father, who are in heaven, etc.

### Another Prayer

Bless+, O Lord Jesus Christ, this substance of a candle through our supplications, and pour into it, through the power of the holy Cru+ss, a heavenly blessing, so that, since you have granted it to the human race for dispelling darkness, whoever receives it may receive through the sign of your Cross such strength and blessing that, wherever it is lit or placed, the devil may depart and tremble, and may flee pale-faced from dwellings with all his servants, nor dare any longer to mock those who serve God.

Therefore we beseech you, O Lord, send your holy angel Raphael, who tore away from Sarah and Tobiah the deadly demon that was afflicting them. May he crush that demon and destroy it from all the dwellings of those who worship God—from houses, corners, beds, dining rooms, and every place in which those serving God live, rest, sleep, keep watch, walk, or stand. May that evil one no longer be able to trouble those whom you have fortified with the anointing of your holy chrism.

I bless these candles in the name of God + the almighty Father, and of his Only-Begotten Son +, and of the Holy + Spirit, the Comforter, so that everywhere there may be the flight of the devil and the destruction of all his companions, with the help of that same holy and undivided Trinity, which forever remains in the essence of Unity, for ages of ages. Amen.

The priest should first light a candle and distribute it to the others; after the lighting he should say this prayer:

Almighty and everlasting God, who on this day presented your Only-Begotten Son to be received in your holy temple in the arms of holy Simeon, we humbly beseech you [Col. 0839C] to bless+ and sanctify+ these your candles, which your servants desire to receive and carry, lighted with every magnificence; and to kindle them with the light of your heavenly bene+diction, so that, by offering them to you, the Lord our God, we may be worthy to be presented in the holy temple of your glory, kindled by the holy fire of your sweetness and love. Through him.

## Mass on the Holy Day

Almighty and everlasting God, we humbly implore your majesty that, just as your Only-Begotten Son was presented on this day in the substance of our flesh, so you may cause us to be presented to you with purified minds. Through the same.

### Secret

Hear our prayers, O Lord, and grant us the assistance of your mercy, so that the gifts we offer to the eyes of your majesty may be worthy. Through him.

### Communion

We beseech you, O Lord our God, that through the intercession of the blessed Virgin Mary you may make the holy mysteries, which you have bestowed for our restoration and protection, both a present and a future remedy for us. Through him.

[Note: [Col. 0839C] The feast of the Chair of Saint Peter is observed in our missal after the feast of the Purification of the blessed Virgin Mary, and therefore in February. This most clearly shows that in the time of Saint Peter Damian the feast of the Roman Chair, which is observed in January, had not been included in the Roman Ordo. Indeed, I possess an ancient parchment breviary written in the fourteenth century in which the Chair of Saint Peter does not occur on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of February. It should not, however, be thought that the feast celebrated here concerns only the Chair of Antioch, which is celebrated in February—especially since no mention of the Roman Chair is found in the sacramentary books of Gelasius and Gregory. Menardus, with sound judgment, thinks that on this day the Church commemorates both Chairs; this is in fact confirmed by the authority of our missal, where a Mass is provided for the Chair of Saint Peter without specifying whether it is the Roman or Antiochene Chair.

Much support for this view is supplied by the learned notes of Father Blanchini on the booklet of Gothic-Hispanic prayers. There, in February, on the eighth day before the Kalends of March, the Chair of Saint Peter is observed as in our book; yet the hymn found there clearly demonstrates that the feast was established to commemorate both Chairs, since it says:

> The day is here on which  
> you were consecrated in the Romulean city.

That most learned man appropriately adds (vol. I, p. 172): “Here is the commemoration of the Roman Chair together with the Antiochene on the seventh day before the Kalends of March.” Pinius also discusses the Chair of Saint Peter (no. 444), as does another author at length in his chronological treatise *On the Ancient Hispanic Liturgy.] 

## On the Chair of Saint Peter

O God, who entrusted to your blessed apostle Peter, when you gave him the keys of the heavenly kingdom, the authority to bind and loose souls, grant that by the help of his intercession we may be freed from the bonds of our sins. [Col. 0840B] Through him.

### Secret

May the prayer of the blessed apostle Peter commend to you, O Lord, the prayers and offerings of your Church, so that what we celebrate for his glory may benefit us for pardon. Through him.

### Communion

May your holy things, O Lord, which we have received, give us life, and, through the intercession of your blessed apostle Peter, prepare us, once purified, for everlasting mercy. Through him.

[Note: [Col. 0840D] As I have already said, this Mass of Saint Benedict the abbot makes it clear that this missal was intended for the use of monks of the Order of Saint Benedict, especially from the first and second prayers, in which God is entreated that the monastic community’s offering may be commended through the paternal intercessions of the magnificent shepherd Benedict. At his passing there is a proper preface, written in the final Appendix.] 

## On the Feast of Saint Benedict

Almighty and everlasting God, who through the glorious examples of the blessed abbot Benedict’s humility have shown us the triumphant path, grant, we beseech you, that, aided by his outstanding merits, we may follow without error the way of obedience pleasing to you, along which the venerable Father Benedict went unharmed before us. Through him.

### Secret

Through the paternal intercessions of the magnificent shepherd Benedict, we beseech you, almighty God, commend the offering of your household, which is adorned by his life-giving examples. Through him.

### Communion

Having received the saving sacraments, we humbly beseech you, Lord our God, that, through the intercession of the blessed abbot Benedict, what we perform in reverence for his death may advance our salvation. Through him.

[Note: [Col. 0840D] The feast of the Annunciation of the blessed Mary [Col. 0841C] is observed here in the month of March. Saint Augustine bears witness to its antiquity (*On the Trinity*, book IV, chapter 5). It is likewise discussed in the Council of Toledo held in 656 as a feast already long established and universally received by all the Churches. That same Church of Toledo, which celebrates this feast eight days before the Nativity of our Lord Jesus Christ, renews its commemoration again on 25 March, as Bollandus notes (vol. III). Other Churches later followed this practice.

Rodulfus Glaber, a writer of the eleventh century, relates that several councils were held to determine the date of the feast of the Annunciation of the blessed Virgin outside Lent; among the Fathers many difficulties and disagreements arose. In the very ancient Roman Calendar edited by Martène (*Anecdota*, vol. V), an order is given for celebrating this feast one week before the Nativity of the Lord, and, he says, this custom is still observed in the Church of Milan. Blanchini makes the same assertion, saying that the Church of Milan commemorates the fourth Sunday of Advent under the title “On the Incarnation of the Word,” or “On the Annunciation of Mary.”

The most recent Roman order observes both feasts: one on 25 March under the title “The Annunciation of Mary,” and the other on 18 December under the title “The Expectation of Childbirth.” In this Sacramentary Codex we have both Masses: the first in March, the second in the final Appendix, though without a title. Nevertheless, the prayer itself shows that the latter concerns the expectation of the Virgin’s childbirth.] 

## On the Annunciation of Saint Mary

O God, who on this day willed your Word to be joined to the womb of the blessed Virgin, make us conduct ourselves in such a way that we may be able to please you. Through the same.

### Secret

Strengthen in our minds, O Lord, the sacrament of true faith, so that, confessing that the one conceived from the Virgin is true God and man, we may deserve to attain eternal joy through the power of his saving resurrection. Through the same.

### Communion

Pour your grace into our minds, O Lord, so that we who learned of the incarnation of Christ your Son through the angel’s announcement may be led through his passion and cross to the glory of the resurrection. Through the same.

## First Sunday in Lent

O God, who purify your Church each year through the observance of Lent, grant to your household that what it strives to obtain from you by abstinence it may accomplish through good works. Through him.

### Secret

We solemnly offer the sacrifice marking the beginning of Lent, beseeching you, O Lord, that, while restricting bodily food, we may also restrain ourselves from harmful pleasures. Through him.

### Communion

May the holy sharing in your sacrament restore us and, cleansed from our former state, make us pass into the fellowship of saving service. Through him.

[Note: [Col. 0842C]

The blessing of palm and olive branches is not an institution of Gregory. Martène and Meratus disagree about its origin. The former asserts (*On the Ancient Discipline of the Church*, chapter 20) that no author before the eighth and ninth centuries mentions the blessing of palms. The latter attempts to refute this view in his notes on Gavanti’s *Sacred Rites Treasury* (vol. I, p. 1003). But the distinguished Joseph Blanchini (vol. I, p. 202) reconciles both opinions, saying that the Sixth Sunday of Lent was called “in the branches of palms” long before the rite of blessing them existed. Yet before the eighth century there are no documents sufficient to prove that the blessing of palms was contemporary with Saint Gregory or even older. Accordingly, he concludes: “To summarize briefly, whatever the distinguished Meratus sets forth in his lengthy refutation of Edmund Martène, I wish to regard as firmly and certainly established.”

All the authorities brought forward against any writer from before the eighth century establish only that the name “Palm Sunday” is very ancient; they do not at all persuade us that the rite of blessing, which is in dispute, had already been instituted at that time.

The prayers found in the following Mass are the same as those that Meratus cites from the Ottobonian Sacramentary, except for the prayer over the people, which is lacking here.]

## The Blessing of Palm and Olive Branches Begins

Increase, O God, the faith of those who hope in you, mercifully hear the prayers of your suppliants, and let your manifold mercy come upon us. Let these branches of olive trees also be blessed; and just as, as a figure of the Church, you multiplied the human race when Noah came out of the ark and when Moses went out from Egypt with the children of Israel, so may we, carrying palms or olive branches, go out to meet Christ through good works and, through him, enter into eternal joy. Through him.

### Another Prayer

O God, who gather what is scattered and preserve what is gathered, who blessed the peoples carrying branches to meet Jesus, bless+ also these branches of palm and olive, which your servants faithfully receive for the blessing of your name. Wherever they are brought, may they obtain your blessing; every adverse illness being driven away, may your right hand protect those whom you have redeemed. Through the same.

### Reading

“Tell the daughters of Zion.”

According to Matthew: “At that time, when he had drawn near…”

### Another Prayer

Holy Lord, almighty Father, everlasting God, who commanded olive trees to produce branches in your creation for preparing the lights of the altar, we therefore ask in humble prayer that you deign to bless+ and sanctify+ these branches of palm and olive, so that your servants, carrying them in their hands, may be sanctified in soul and body and filled with your blessing as they say: [Col. 0842B] “Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord. Hosanna in the highest.”

Then it is said: The Lord be with you. And with your spirit. Lift up your hearts. We have them toward the Lord. Let us give thanks to the Lord our God. It is fitting, etc.

(+) Eternal God, we praise and bless you among all your wonders: you gave Lamech righteous offspring; you revealed to Noah, foreknowing through him the future waters of the flood; for our salvation a spiritual dove brought to his ark a fruitful olive shoot. Noah joyfully received it as it returned to him with its spiritual fruit.

From the anointing of that branch, chosen Jacob set up a title, made a vow, and poured oil upon it. This is the sign of that branch, from which grace flows down from heaven, and which also fills the vessels of the people. This is the grace that blessed the widow in her oil. This is the sign of that branch planted beside streams of water, whose leaf does not wither. Through it the Church daily brings forth the washing of baptism, and our sins are blotted out.

This is your good planting, exceedingly good, and you are the life and resurrection of the dead. You raised Lazarus, dead four days; and if you had not called him by his own name, all would have risen from the dead. Therefore the crowd also, coming to meet [him] with palm branches, cried: “Hosanna, blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord, the King of Israel.”

Therefore we ask your mercy: rescue and strip us, your servants who receive the grace and faith of this mystery, from the mouth of hell; and deign to grant us the help of your grace, so that, living justly, devoutly, and holily, you may grant us fellowship with the elect. Through him, O Lord, you always create, sancti+fy, vivi+fy, bene+dict, and lavishly bestow all these good things upon us, your servants. For ages of ages. Amen.

### Another Prayer

O God, who sent your Son, our Lord Jesus Christ, into this world for our salvation, so that he might humble himself toward us and call us back to you, and who, when he was coming to Jerusalem to fulfill the Scriptures, the most faithful crowd of believing peoples spread their garments on the road with palm branches, grant, we beseech you, that we may prepare for him the way of faith. With the stone of offense and the rock of stumbling removed, may branches of righteousness put forth leaves in our works, so that we may deserve to follow his footsteps. Through him.

### Another Prayer

We ask you, holy Father, almighty, everlasting God, to deign to look upon this creation of olive and palm, which you commanded to arise from the substance of wood, and which the dove, returning to the ark, brought in its own beak. Deign to bless+ and sanctify+ it, so that whoever takes anything from it may receive it for the perfection of soul and body; and may it become, O Lord, the remedy of our salvation and the sacrament of your grace. Through him.

## The Mass on the Day Begins

Almighty and everlasting God, who willed our Savior to assume flesh and undergo the cross for the human race, as an example of humility to be imitated, mercifully grant that we may deserve both to possess the lessons of his patience and to share in his resurrection. Through him.

### Secret

Grant, we beseech you, O Lord, that the gift offered before the eyes of your majesty may obtain for us the grace of devotion and acquire the effect of blessed perpetuity. Through him.

### Preface

(+) Eternal God, through whom forgiveness is granted to us and peace is proclaimed throughout every age. The discipline is handed down to all believers, so that the coming day may receive us as sanctified. And therefore with the angels.

### Communion

Through the working of this mystery, O Lord, may our vices be cleansed and righteous desires fulfilled. Through him.

## Thursday, at the Lord’s Supper

O God, from whom Judas received the punishment of his guilt, while the thief received a reward through his confession, grant us the effect of your mercy, so that, just as Jesus Christ our Lord in his passion brought different recompense according to the merits of each, so, when the error of our former state has been removed, he may bestow upon us the grace of his resurrection. He who lives with you.

### Secret

May he himself, holy Lord, almighty Father, make our sacrifice acceptable to you—he who today showed his disciples, by his institution, that this should be done in remembrance of him. He who lives with you.

### Within the Canon

Joining in communion and celebrating the most sacred day on which our Lord Jesus Christ was handed over for us, and also venerating the memory…

### Communion

Refreshed by saving nourishment, we beseech you, O Lord our God, that what we carry out in the time of our mortality we may attain through the gift of your immortality. Through him.

## On Good Friday

Let us pray, dearly beloved, for the holy Church of God, that God and our Lord may deign to grant it peace and protection throughout the whole world, subjecting to it principalities and powers, and granting that, while living a quiet and peaceful life, we may glorify God the almighty Father.

Let us pray. Let us bend our knees.

Almighty and everlasting God, who revealed your glory in Christ to all the nations, preserve the works of your mercy, so that the Church, spread throughout the whole world, may persevere with steadfast faith in confessing your name. Through the same.

Let us also pray for our most blessed pope N., that God and our Lord, who chose him for the episcopal order, may keep him safe and unharmed for his holy Church, to govern the holy people of God.

Let us pray. Let us bend our knees.

Almighty and everlasting God, by whose judgment all things are established, mercifully regard our prayers and preserve, by your goodness, the bishop whom you have chosen for us, so that the Christian people, governed by such a leader, may increase in the merits of their faith under so great a pontiff. Through him.

Let us also pray for all bishops, priests, deacons, subdeacons, acolytes, exorcists, readers, doorkeepers, confessors, virgins, widows, orphans, and for all the holy people of God.

Let us pray. Let us bend our knees.

Almighty and everlasting God, by whose Spirit the whole body of the Church is sanctified and governed, hear us as we make supplication for all orders, so that through the gift of your grace you may be faithfully served by every rank. Through him.

Let us also pray for our most Christian emperor N., that God and our Lord may subject all barbarian nations to him for our perpetual peace.

Let us pray. Let us bend our knees.

Almighty and everlasting God, in whose hands are all powers and all rights of kingdoms, look favorably upon the Roman empire, so that the peoples who trust in their own ferocity may be restrained by the right hand of your power. Through him.

Let us also pray for our catechumens, that God and our Lord may open the ears of their hearts and the door of mercy, so that, having received remission of all sins through the bath of regeneration, they too may be found in Christ Jesus our Lord.

Let us pray. Let us bend our knees.

Almighty and everlasting God, who always make your Church fruitful with new offspring, increase faith and understanding in our catechumens, so that, reborn from the baptismal font, they may be joined to the children of your adoption. Through him.

Let us pray, dearly beloved, to God the almighty Father, that he may cleanse the world of all errors, remove diseases, drive away famine, open prisons, break bonds, grant travelers a return, the sick health, and those at sea a safe harbor.

Let us pray. Let us bend our knees.

Almighty and everlasting God, consolation of the sorrowful and strength of those who labor, may our prayers reach you as we cry out from every tribulation, so that all may rejoice that your mercy has been present to them in their needs. Through him.

Let us also pray for heretics and schismatics, that God and our Lord may rescue them from every error and deign to recall them to the holy mother Church, catholic and apostolic.

Let us pray. Let us bend our knees.

Almighty and everlasting God, who saves all and wills no one to perish, look upon the souls deceived by the devil’s fraud, so that, having laid aside every heretical depravity, the hearts of those who have gone astray may come to their senses and return to the unity of your truth. Through him.

Let us also pray for the faithless Jews, that God and our Lord may remove the veil from their hearts, so that they too may acknowledge you, Jesus Christ our Lord.

Here “Let us bend our knees” is not said.

Almighty and everlasting God, who does not even reject Jewish faithlessness from your mercy, hear our prayers, which we offer for the blindness of that people, so that, having recognized the light of your truth, which is Christ, they may be rescued from their darkness. Through him.

Let us also pray for the pagans, that God may remove iniquity from their hearts, so that, abandoning their idols, they may be converted to the living and true Lord and to his only Son Jesus Christ, our God and Lord, with whom he lives and reigns, God, with the Holy Spirit, for ages of ages.

Let us pray. Let us bend our knees.

Almighty and everlasting God, who always seek not the death but the life of sinners, receive our prayer, free them from the worship of idols, and gather them into your holy Church for the praise and glory of your name. Through him.

[Note: [Col. 0845D] Martène includes a blessing of incense, but it is later than the time of Saint Gregory and is found in no other ancient sacramentary book of the eleventh century. In the Mozarabic Missal this rubric occurs: “Then let him bless five grains of incense to be inserted into the candle.” Blanchini notes in the margin that this rite began in the tenth century. But in that Mass there is no mention of blessing incense or of burning it.]

## Blessing of Incense on Holy Saturday

I beseech your eternal and most just mercy, holy Lord, almighty Father, everlasting God, that you deign to bless+ this kind of incense, or whatever kind it may be, so that it may be incense acceptable to your majesty as an aroma of sweetness. May it be blessed by you, O Lord, so that wherever its fragrance reaches, every kind of demon may be expelled and driven away, just as the smoke of the fish’s liver, which your archangel Raphael taught your servant Tobiah to burn for holy deliverance.

May a full bene+diction descend upon this kind of incense, so that it may be acceptable to you, as your prophet David sang, saying: “Let my prayer be directed like incense in your presence.” May it be for us a fragrance of consolation, sweetness, and grace; may its smoke drive away every fantasy of mind and body, so that, in the words of your Apostle, we may be a good fragrance to God. May every attack of demons flee from the presence of this incense like dust before the wind and smoke before the fire.

Grant this, most merciful Father, through your Only-Begotten Son, with whom you live and reign, God, with the Holy Spirit, forever and ever. Amen.

## Blessing of the New Fire

[Col. 0846B]

Almighty, everlasting, eternal God, creator of all things, we humbly beseech you to deign to sanctify+ and bless+ this new fire, bestowed by heaven upon the earth. Just as at your coming you promise to cleanse the elements polluted by the contagion of sins, so may this new fire, kept in the dwellings of your faithful, obtain perfect purification and, undefeated by obstacles, be made effective against every wickedness of the evil spirit. Through him.

### Reading I

“In the beginning he created…”

### Prayer

O God, who wondrously created humanity and more wondrously redeemed it, grant us, we beseech you, to stand firm through reason of mind against the allurements of sin, so that we may deserve to attain eternal joys. Through him.

### Reading II

“It happened in the vigil.”  
Response: “Let us sing to the Lord.”

### Prayer

O God, whose ancient miracles we perceive still shining in the present age, grant, we beseech you, that just as you freed the former people from the Egyptians, so you may accomplish this for the salvation of the nations through the waters of baptism. Through him.

### Reading

“Seven women shall take hold…”  
Response: “A vineyard was planted.”

### Prayer

O God, who instruct us to celebrate the paschal mystery through the pages of both Testaments, grant us to understand your mercy, and may the expectation of future things be made firm through our reception of present gifts. Through him.

### Reading

“This is the inheritance…”  
Response: “Attend, O heaven.”

### Prayer

O God, who always multiply your Church through the calling of the nations, mercifully grant that those whom you wash with the water of baptism you may guard with continual protection. Through him.

Response: “As the deer longs…”

### Prayer

Grant, we beseech you, almighty God, that we who celebrate the paschal feasts, kindled by heavenly desires, may be satisfied at the fountain of life. Through him.

[Col. 0847A] [Note: [Col. 0847C] Two points in this Mass deserve particular attention. First, after the blessing of the incense and the new fire, the singing of the angelic hymn “Glory to God in the highest” is prescribed. There was once such reverence for this hymn that its recitation at Mass was permitted to bishops alone during the year; other priests were permitted to recite it only on the solemn day of Easter. This custom is thought to have continued until the eleventh century, precisely until the year 1040.

Second, the Mass we have here, by the privilege of the Paschal Resurrection of the Lord, was celebrated at night, as is clear from the prayers. This solemn day should therefore rightly be counted among the *polyliturgical* days, like the Nativity of Christ the Lord. Polyliturgical days are those on which several Masses are celebrated by one priest; in our missal we have two such days, namely the Nativity of the Lord and the day of the Resurrection.

Ecclesiastical histories provide various examples of this very ancient rite. The Council of Mérida, under Pope Vitalian after the middle of the seventh century, stated in canon 19 that a priest who had several churches under his governance should celebrate the sacred rites in each of them on Sunday. The Council of Seligenstadt, held in 1022, fixed the number of Masses and decreed that no one should presume to celebrate more than three Masses. Cardinal Bona (book I, chapter 18; book II, chapter 5) collects examples of saints who celebrated Mass several times each day, and there he introduces the custom of the holy Roman Church of offering sacrifice twice or three times on certain feast days.

The Council of Oxford, in the time of Honorius III, ordered that only one Mass should be said on the same day, except on the days of the Nativity and Resurrection of the Lord and at the funerals and burials of the dead. In the kingdom of Valencia and other regions of Spain, priests celebrated twice or three times on the Day of the Commemoration of All the Dead, whether by privilege or by custom. His Holiness Benedict XIV, Supreme Pontiff, confirms and extends this custom in a decree most recently published.

For these reasons, therefore, I do not hesitate to count the feast of the Resurrection of the Lord among the polyliturgical days, just as the Nativity of the Lord. But if anyone should say—as some do not hesitate to assert—that on those feast days on which two Masses are recorded the sacrifice was offered not by one priest but by several, let him, I ask, read Cardinal Bona in his liturgical books (no. 8), where with the greatest learning he refutes this opinion.] 

At Mass is said: “Glory to God in the highest.”

O God, who illumine this most sacred night with the glory of the Lord’s resurrection, preserve in the new offspring of your household the spirit of adoption that you have given, so that, renewed in body and mind, they may offer you pure service. Through the same.

### Secret

Receive, O Lord, we beseech you, the prayers of your people together with the offerings of sacrifices, so that, initiated through the paschal mysteries, they may, by your working, advance toward the healing of eternity for us. Through him.

### Preface

(+) It is truly fitting and salutary to proclaim you, O Lord, at all times, but especially to glorify you on this night, when Christ our Passover was sacrificed. For he is the true Lamb who took away the sins of the world; by dying he destroyed our death, and by rising he restored life. And therefore.

### Within the Canon

Joining in communion and celebrating the most sacred night of the resurrection according to the flesh of our Lord Jesus Christ, and also venerating especially the memory of the glorious ever-virgin Mary, mother of the same God and Lord of ours Jesus Christ, and of the blessed apostles.

Therefore, O Lord, we beseech you, graciously accept this offering of our service and also of your entire household, which we offer to you for those whom you have deigned to regenerate from water and the Holy Spirit, granting them remission of all sins. Through him.

### Post-Communion

Pour into us, O Lord, the Spirit of your love, so that those whom you have satisfied with the paschal sacraments you may, through your mercy, make united. Through … in the unity of the same Holy Spirit, God.

## On the Holy Day of the Lord’s Easter

O God, who on this day, through your Only-Begotten Son, opened for us the entrance to eternity after death had been conquered, continue to assist by your help the vows that you inspire beforehand. Through the same.

### Secret

Receive, O Lord, the prayers of your people together with the offerings of sacrifices, so that, initiated through the paschal mysteries, they may, by your working, advance toward the healing of eternity for us. Through him.

(+) “It is fitting and salutary. You indeed”; look back.

“Joining in communion”; see on the holy night.

“This offering”; likewise.

### Post-Communion

Pour into us, O Lord, the Spirit of your love, so that those whom you have satisfied with the paschal sacraments you may, through your mercy, make united. Through him.

## Monday in Easter Week

O God, who have bestowed remedies upon the world through the paschal solemnity, accompany your people with a heavenly gift, so that they may deserve both to attain perfect freedom and to advance toward eternal life. Through him.

### Secret

As we renew the paschal offerings, we beseech you, O Lord, that what we perform outwardly we may grasp inwardly. Through him.

### Post-Communion

May the holy sharing in the paschal sacrament be fulfilled in us, we beseech you, O Lord, and may it transfer us from earthly desires to a heavenly way of life. Through him.

## Tuesday in Easter Week
God, who ever multiplies your Church with new growth, grant your servants that by their manner of life they may hold fast the sacrament which they received by faith. Through him.

**Secret.** Receive, O Lord, the prayers of the faithful together with the offerings of sacrifices, so that through these services of devout worship we may pass over to heavenly glory. Through him.

**Postcommunion.** Grant, we ask, almighty God, that the reception of the paschal sacrament may continually endure [Col. 0848C] in our minds. Through him.

## ON THE OCTAVE OF EASTER

Grant, we ask, almighty God, that, having completed the paschal festivals, we may, by your generosity, preserve them in conduct and life. Through him.

**Secret.** Receive, we ask, O Lord, the gifts of your rejoicing Church, and grant perpetual fruitfulness of joy to her to whom you have granted the cause of so great a gladness. Through him.

**Postcommunion.** We ask, O Lord our God, that the most holy mysteries which you have bestowed for the protection of our restoration [Col. 0849A] may make them for us both a present and a future remedy. Through him.

[**Note:** [Col. 0849D] In the first prayer of this Mass, Saint Mark is adorned with the glory of martyrdom, against certain persons who remove him from the number of martyrs, although Pope Gelasius clearly calls him a martyr. Their opinion rests chiefly on these arguments: namely, that neither Eusebius, who wrote his acts (*Book II*, chapters 14 and 15; *Book III*, final chapter), nor Isidore calls him a martyr, nor says that he suffered martyrdom. Therefore Mark—and the same should be said of Luke—is not inscribed in the canon of the Mass, since it is uncertain whether he died [Col. 0850D] a martyr. For in the canon there is a place for holy martyrs, while confessors are always excluded, as Bona testifies (*Book II*, chapter 12, no. 11). Nevertheless, Gelasius possesses such authority in the Church that he removes every suspicion, since he says: “Sent into Egypt, he preached the word of purity and gloriously completed his martyrdom.” To the authority of Gelasius is added that of our Sacramentary, in which he is called a martyr in the eleventh century. According to the testimony of Pinius, in the fifth or sixth century he is read of in a fragment of the Mozarabic Calendar at the sixth day before the Ides of February as “Saint Mark the evangelist and martyr.”]

## ON THE BIRTHDAY OF SAINT MARK THE EVANGELIST

God, who consecrated this day to us through the martyrdom of your glorious blessed evangelist Mark, grant, we ask, that he who deserved to become the evangelical preacher of your Only-Begotten Son may stand before you as our chief intercessor. You who live and reign with him.

**Secret.** Receive, we ask, O Lord, the offerings graciously presented, and grant that, through the assisting merits of blessed Mark the evangelist, they may advance toward the aid of our salvation. Through him.

**Postcommunion.** Refreshed, O Lord, by heavenly gifts, we humbly beseech you that we may be protected by the assistance of blessed Mark your evangelist and martyr, whose [Col. 0849B] triumph we celebrate with devout hearts. Through him.

## ON THE DAY OF THE ASCENSION OF THE LORD

Grant, we ask, almighty God, that we who believe that on this day your Only-Begotten Son, our Redeemer, ascended into heaven may ourselves also dwell in heavenly things in mind. Through the same Lord of ours.

**Secret.** Receive, O Lord, the gifts which we bring for the glorious ascension of your Son, and mercifully grant that we may be freed from present dangers and reach eternal life. Through the same.

**Preface.** (+) Eternal God, through Christ our Lord. After his resurrection he appeared manifest to all his disciples, and, while they looked on, he was raised into heaven, so that he might grant us to share in his divinity [Col. 0849C]. And therefore—

**Communicantes.** And celebrating the most sacred day on which your Only-Begotten Son, our Lord, placed in the glory at your right hand the substance of our frailty united to himself. Let its memory be kept.

**Communion.** Grant us, we ask, almighty and merciful God, that what we have received to consume through visible mysteries we may obtain through an invisible effect. Through him.

## HOLY SATURDAY BEFORE PENTECOST

**Lesson:** “God tested.”  
**Response:** “Let us sing to God.”

**Prayer.** O God, who through the deed of your servant Abraham gave the human race examples of obedience, grant us to break the perversity of our will and [Col. 0849D] fulfill in all things the uprightness of your commandments. Through him.

**Lesson:** “Moses wrote.”  
**Response:** “Attend, O heaven.”

**Prayer.** O God, who through the mouths of the prophets commanded us to leave temporal things and hasten toward eternal things, grant your servants that, by heavenly inspiration, we may be able to fulfill what we have recognized as commanded by you [Col. 0850A]. Through him.

**Lesson:** “Seven women shall take hold.”  
**Response:** “As the hart.”

**Prayer.** O unchangeable power of God, eternal light, look mercifully upon the wondrous sacrament of your entire Church, and carry out the work of human salvation more peacefully through the effect of your eternal ordering.
