“The righteous man will flourish like the palm.”

Prayer: May the distinguished prayer of blessed John the Baptist, who foretold that our Lord would come, accompany us, we ask, O Lord, and may he ask Christ our Lord to favor us in his mercy.

Antiphon: “Peter,” etc.

Prayer: Grant, we ask, almighty God, that you permit no disturbances to shake us, whom you have made firm upon the rock of apostolic confession. Through [Christ our Lord].

The antiphon and prayer for peace are as in the printed editions.

Antiphon for all the saints: “The righteous will shine like the sun in the kingdom of my Father,” says the Lord.

“Wonderful is God.”

“In his saints.”

Prayer: O God, who grant us to celebrate the commemoration of blessed Mary ever-virgin and all your saints, grant us to rejoice in their fellowship in eternal blessedness. Through [Christ our Lord].

At Terce the following prayer is appointed: Extend your right hand, we ask, O Lord, in mercy to your people who seek it, so that it may both avoid human errors, receive the consolations of immortal life, and grasp eternal joys. Through [Christ our Lord].

At Sext, prayer: Hear us, O God our Savior, and order our days in your peace, so that, freed from all disturbances, we may serve you in tranquil devotion. Through [Christ our Lord].

At None, prayer: Grant, we ask, O Lord, to your people the Spirit of truth and peace, so that they may know you with their whole mind and pursue with all their heart what is pleasing to you.

At Vespers, prayer: As darkness is born, O Lord, may the dawn of righteousness arise in our hearts, so that, when the day is completed, we may humbly give thanks and, in the morning also, you may graciously look upon us as we fulfill our vows. Through [Christ our Lord].

The suffrages mentioned above are said at Lauds. At Vespers, however, the following are said at all times, both on weekdays and feast days.

Antiphon: Save us, Christ our Savior, through the power of the holy cross. You who saved Peter on the sea, have mercy on us.

“The whole earth.”

Prayer: “Perpetually [protect us],” etc.

Antiphon: Holy Mary, Virgin of God, always intercede for us with the Lord our God.

“Grace has been poured out.”

Prayer: Grant, merciful God, etc., to our weakness.

Antiphon: “Michael,” etc.

Prayer: Grant us perpetual assistance from your mercy, O Lord, to whom you have also granted that angelic aid not be lacking. Through [Christ our Lord].

The suffrages of Saint Benedict the Father are as in the printed editions.

The antiphon and versicle for Saint John the Baptist are as at Lauds.

Prayer: Almighty, everlasting God, give our hearts that uprightness of your paths which blessed John the Baptist, the voice of one crying in the desert, taught. Through [Christ our Lord].

Antiphon: “Glorious princes.”

Prayer: Raise us up, we ask, O Lord, by the protection of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul, so that, the more fragile we are, the more powerful the assistance may be by which we are supported. Through [Christ our Lord].

The antiphon for peace is as at Lauds.

Antiphon: All you saints of God, deign to pray and intercede for the salvation of us all.

“Rejoice in the Lord.”

Prayer: Almighty God, protect us, your servants, from every danger by the right hand of your power; and, with blessed Mary ever-Virgin interceding together with all your saints, make us rejoice in present and eternal prosperity. Through the Lord.

## WEDNESDAY AT THE BEGINNING OF THE FAST

For the blessing of the ashes, only the prayer “O God, who do not desire death,” etc., is read. Then the following rubric follows:

[Col. 0955D] Then let them be sprinkled with holy water; they must not be incensed. Immediately the priest shall begin placing ashes upon the heads of each of the brothers in the form of a cross, saying: “Remember, man,” etc. And the one who receives them shall say: “May the sprinkling of these ashes, O Lord, be for me a healing remedy.”

After Lauds on Wednesday of Holy Week the following is given.

Here all lights are extinguished.

Antiphon at the Benedictus: “The betrayer.”

After these words, let two go before the altar and say in a clear voice: “Lord, have mercy; Christ, have mercy; Lord, have mercy.” And let all the others answer in the same way. Let those before the altar say: “Christ God became obedient unto death.” Let the others answer: “Lord, have mercy; Christ, have mercy; Lord, have mercy.”

And let those before the altar say: “Jesus, Lord, who came to suffer for us.” And let the others answer: “Lord, have mercy; Christ, have mercy; Lord.”

And let those before the altar say: “You who prophetically promised: ‘I will be your death, O death.’” And the others: “Lord, have mercy; Christ, have mercy; Lord, have mercy.”

And let those before the altar say: “Life dies upon the wood, and death is emptied by death.” And the others: “Lord, have mercy; Christ, have mercy; Lord.”

And let those before the altar say: “Christ the Lord became obedient unto death.” And the others: “Even death on a cross.”

Our Father.

Chapter: I said: O Lord, heal. Turn again, O Lord. And be entreated. Let your mercy, O Lord, be upon us. As we have hoped in you. Your priests. And your saints. Send them, O Lord. And from Zion. O Lord, hear. And let my cry.

Psalm: “Have mercy.”

Chapter: O Lord God of hosts. And show your face, without “The Lord be with you.” But it is said silently: Let us pray.

[Col. 0956B] Look upon us, we ask, O Lord.

These prayers are recited after Terce, Vespers, and Lauds on the three days of Holy Week, namely Maundy Thursday, Good Friday, and Holy Saturday. After the antiphon at the Benedictus of Holy Saturday, the following is provided: “Here let the Kyrie eleison, the verse, the chapter, and the prayer be said as at the Lauds of the Lord’s Supper.” Prime, Terce, Sext, and None are as on that same day. On this day, before Terce, the crosses and panels that had been veiled throughout the Passion are uncovered. Between Terce and Sext, the altar is honorably adorned.

At Vespers, an antiphon is said, and this antiphon is sung at Vespers throughout the week until Saturday:

“Crucified, he rose on the third day from the tomb, alleluia, alleluia.”

Psalm: “Praise, servants.”  
Psalm: “Praise the Lord, all nations.” [Col. 0956C]  
Psalm: “Behold, how good!”  
Psalm: “Praise, Jerusalem.”

Reading: “If you have risen with Christ.”  
R\. “The angel of the Lord.”  
V\. “You seek Jesus.”

Hymn: “At the supper.”  
V\. “Christ our Passover has been sacrificed.”

At the Magnificat, an antiphon: “But in the evening.”

Prayer. O God, who enlighten this most sacred night with the glory of the Lord’s resurrection, preserve in the new offspring of your family the spirit of adoption which you gave, so that, renewed in body and mind, they may present pure service to you. Through the same Lord.

Antiphon of the Cross until the octave:

“Let us praise him crucified in the flesh, and glorify him buried for our sake. Come, let us adore him rising from the dead, alleluia, alleluia, alleluia.”

[Col. 0956D]

Antiphon of Saint Mary until the octave of Pentecost:

“Queen of heaven.”  
“She has been poured out.”  
“Therefore.”

Prayer. O God, who apply healing to wounded nature through virginal beauty, grant that, through the prayers of blessed Mary ever-virgin, we may utterly cast away the leaven of conceived depravity and pass from the old into the unleavened bread of newness. Through him.

## SUNDAY OF THE RESURRECTION

The vigils begin according to the custom of the canons, namely: “O Lord, open my lips.”

At Sext on this day the following prayer is provided:

Grant, we beseech you, almighty God, that we who celebrate the solemnity of the Lord’s resurrection may deserve to receive the joy of our deliverance. Through him.

At the Magnificat, an antiphon:

“After the Lord’s Passion, the assembly gathered, because his body was not found in the tomb. The stone held everlasting life; the tomb gave back the heavenly pearl, alleluia.” [Col. 0957A]

Throughout the Temporal Office nothing worthy of note is found in the codex, except that the Office of the Trinity is placed after the Twenty-Fourth Sunday after Pentecost.

## ON THE FEAST OF SAINT ANDREW THE APOSTLE

Invitatory. Let us adore Christ the King, the Lord, who glorified the blessed apostle through the martyrdom of the cross.

### Hymn at Matins

Andrew’s feast is celebrated;  
A clear light rises for the faithful.  
Through him they abandon darkness  
And return to the true light.

Aegeas rages in a threatening spirit  
Against the apostle;  
Through him he sees the people of Achaea  
Go after the Lord.

He does not know how to fear threats;  
He cannot yield to torments.  
The burning ardor of faith  
Does not feel the force of punishment.

Bound to the cross’s gallows,  
He hung joyfully for two days.  
Placed amid death itself,  
He pours forth the utterance of life.

When heavenly light descended  
And suddenly surrounded him,  
He who was worthy thus to die  
Sought the Author of light.

To the unbegotten Father be praise;  
To the Only-begotten be honor;  
To the equal Majesty of both,  
The supreme glory of the Spirit. Amen.

### Hymn at Vespers

Once a catcher of fish,  
Now a fisher of human beings,  
Andrew, by your nets  
Snatch us from the waves of the world.

Peter’s brother in the flesh,  
Not unlike him in the manner of death:  
Those whom one flesh begot,  
The cross gave as brothers to heaven.

O truly noble offspring,  
O equal crown of glory!  
The devout Fathers of the Church  
Are equally children of the cross.

Go before your brother to Jesus,  
Brave judge of life;  
For us also, wretched ones,  
Be the blessed guide of the journey.

To the unbegotten Father be praise, etc.

## ON THE FEAST OF SAINT AMBROSE, CONFESSOR

Prayer. Almighty and everlasting God, who through the mouth of blessed Ambrose the bishop opened to us the hidden things of your words, grant us to apply the ear of our heart to his teachings, so that, through his intercession, we may deserve to reach that homeland for which he himself yearned with all his desires. Through him. [Col. 0958A]

## ON THE FEAST OF SAINT ZENO

Prayer. O God, who grant that this venerable day be celebrated in devotion to your blessed confessor and bishop Zeno, preserve your mercy in us, and deign in your goodness and clemency to be present to our prayers, so that, just as you granted grace to blessed Zeno the priest, you may likewise deign to grant it to us. Through him.

## ON THE FEAST OF SAINT SYRUS

Prayer. O God, most powerful enlightener of your bishops, grant, we beseech you, that, instructed by the magnificent examples of your most blessed priest and confessor Syrus, we may pass through the darkness of this age without danger. Through him.

## ON THE PURIFICATION OF BLESSED MARY THE VIRGIN

[Col. 0958B]

At Vespers. Antiphon: “With you is princely rule.”  
Psalm: “The Lord said.”  
Antiphon: “Redemption.”  
Psalm: “I will confess.”  
Antiphon: “Light has dawned.”  
Psalm: “Blessed is the man.”  
Antiphon: “From the fruit.”  
Psalm: “Remember.”

Prayer. Fulfill in us, we beseech you, O Lord, your grace, which you fulfilled in the righteous Simeon, so that, just as he did not see death before he deserved to see Christ the Lord, we too may obtain eternal life. Through him.

After Terce on this day the following is read for the blessing of candles:

“After this, let the candles be blessed,” and let the priest say in a loud voice: “The Lord be with you.” “Hear us,” etc.

Prayer. Almighty and everlasting God, who through your Word—namely, the true Light—enlighten every human being coming into this world, with the inextinguishable grace of your visitation illumine our hearts through and through, and sanctify these candles, suited to visible light, with heavenly blessing +, so that, in reverence for the present solemnity and in memory of blessed Mary ever-virgin, who offered in the temple her Son and Lord, the Author and Observer of the Law, those who offer them, when they have been offered by your servants and devoutly dedicated to your name, may forever possess the radiance of your blessing. Through the same Lord.

Another prayer. Almighty and everlasting God, who on this day, as in the printed editions.

Another prayer. Bless +, Lord Jesus Christ, this creature of wax through our supplications, and pour into it, through the power of your holy cross, a heavenly blessing +, so that the one which you have given to the human race for driving away darkness may receive in such a way the strength and blessing of the sign of your cross that, wherever it is lit or placed, the devil may depart and tremble, and may flee in fear with all his ministers from those dwellings, and may no longer presume to disturb or mock those serving God.

Therefore we humbly beseech you, O Lord, to send your holy angel Raphael, who drove out and repelled from Sarah and Tobias the deadly demon that afflicted them, so that he may crush and destroy him from all the dwellings of those who worship the Lord: from basilicas, houses, corners, beds, refectories, [Col. 0959A] and from every place in which those serving God dwell, rest, sleep, keep watch, walk, and stand. May he no longer be able to disturb them or send terrors upon those whom you have made secure through the anointing of your holy chrism.

I bless + you, wax, in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ and of the holy Trinity, so that you may be the destruction of the devil and of all his companions. Through the same Lord of ours, who lives and reigns.

Then let them be sprinkled with blessed water and incensed, and let the antiphon be sung:

“A light for revelation to the nations,” etc., except for the canticle “Now you dismiss,” in whose place “May God have mercy” is said.

Prayer at Sext. May the prayer of blessed Mary ever-virgin, we beseech you, O Lord, be present with us everywhere; and may your people, who venerate her with devoted service, experience her obtaining aid for them through loving assistance. Through him. [Col. 0959B]

Prayer at None. May the venerable intercession of holy Mary ever-virgin help us, we beseech you, O Lord, and, having been freed from the bonds of sins, make us rejoice in your peace. Through him.

## ON THE FEAST OF SAINT BLAISE, BISHOP AND MARTYR

Prayer. O God, who exalted your blessed martyr and bishop Blaise through the office of the episcopate and the gift of faith, grant to your suppliants that whatever has been contracted in us through the contagion of sin may, through his intercession, be loosed. Through him.

## ON THE FEAST OF SAINT GREGORY, POPE AND CONFESSOR

Prayer. O God, who through your blessed confessor and bishop Gregory gave us to drink the sweetness of heavenly speech, mercifully grant to your family both to preserve what he taught and to follow where he proceeded. [Col. 0959C]

## ON THE FEAST OF SAINT BENEDICT

### Hymn

Precious heavenly jewel,  
Rule of the just King,  
Way of monks,

Benedict, draw us away  
From the filth of the impure world.

You alone despising it,  
Fixing your heart on the stars,  
You compelled heirs  
To become parents.

A vessel full of God,  
You deserved to restore  
Fruitfulness.

Great among the small,  
A beardless hermit,  
You surpassed your age,  
You overcame toil.

You fervently fulfilled  
The beginnings of a strict  
And disciplined life.

When you prayed  
Over the boy slain  
By the falling stones,  
You raised him by your prayers.

His spirit to his flesh,  
And his flesh equally  
To health.

Under the gentle appearance  
Of a dove,  
You saw the soul of your sister,  
Who knew no bitterness,  
Penetrating the highest heights  
Of the starry heaven.

You yourself, after bringing back  
A bright triumph,  
Seek the lofty stars,  
With the world overcome.

As they lay down cloaks  
For the path blazing  
With radiant light.

Praise and honor to the Father,  
To the equal Son,  
One majesty,  
The same power,  
With whom the holy Spirit  
Together fills the whole world. Amen.

The hymns at Matins and Lauds are the same as those in the Little Office of blessed Benedict.

Prayer. Almighty and everlasting God, who through the glorious examples of blessed Benedict the abbot showed us the triumphant path of humility, grant, we beseech you, that, aided by his illustrious merits, we may follow without error the way of obedience pleasing to you, along which that venerable Father went unharmed before us. Through him. [Col. 0960C]

Prayer at Sext. Grant us, O Lord, to be fostered by the supplications of your holy confessor and abbot Benedict, so that we, who celebrate his venerable solemnity with acts of service, may be commended by his intercessions and merits. Through him.

Prayer at None. O God, who willed that we be instructed by the teachings of your blessed confessor Benedict, deign through his merits to protect us from every deception of the enemy. Through him.

## ON THE FINDING OF THE HOLY CROSS

### Hymn at Vespers

Cross, salvation of the lost world,  
Life of the world that was slain,  
At whose victory the underworld trembles  
And the armies of heaven stand in awe.

While life dies upon you,  
The chain of death is loosed.  
Freed from Egypt’s yoke,  
They are truly children of light.

The Judge of all sets you up  
When the judgment seat is judged.  
Already then he separates  
The goats from the sheep among the robbers.

You mock the prince of the world  
While punishing the Impassible One.  
You, accustomed to offer the guilty,  
Now take away the spoils.

Upon you the Victim is sacrificed  
Who cleanses the world’s offenses. [Col. 0961A]  
To you the talent is entrusted  
That released Adam’s debt.

Protect us with the sign of life  
By which the King of glory triumphs.  
Through you bring to the kingdom  
Those whom he frees from servitude.

To the unbegotten Father be praise;  
To the Only-begotten be honor;  
To the equal Majesty of both,  
The supreme glory of the Spirit. Amen.

### Hymn at Lauds

Cross, blessing of the world,  
Hope and certain redemption,  
Once the bearer of Gehenna,  
Now the shining gate of heaven.

Upon you the Victim is raised,  
And drew all things to himself.  
The prince of the world attacked him  
And found nothing belonging to him.

That, older than the Law, cancels  
The old legal document;  
Ancient servitude perishes,  
True freedom is restored.

The abundance of your fragrance  
Overcomes all perfumes;  
The sweetness of your nectar  
Fills the secret places of the heart.

Through the Cross, O Christ, we beseech you,  
Transfer to the reward of life  
Those whom, fixed upon the wood,  
You deigned to redeem.

Praise to the unbegotten Father, etc.

## ON THE FEAST OF THE APOSTLES PETER AND PAUL

### Hymn

A happy feast, throughout all the world’s compass,  
Shines forth in splendor:  
The feast of blessed Peter  
And most holy Paul,  
Whom Christ consecrated  
With his gracious blood  
And appointed as princes of the churches.

These are the two olive trees before the Lord  
And the two lampstands radiant with light,  
The two illustrious lights of heaven.

They powerfully loose the bonds of sinners  
And open Olympus’ gates to the faithful.

They have heavenly power  
To close the dwellings by their word  
And to open the shining lights of the heavens.  
Above the lofty stars, their tongues  
Have become the keys of heaven;  
They drive demons beyond the world’s boundaries.

Blessed Peter miraculously broke  
The snares of chains at Christ’s command.  
Guardian of the fold and teacher of the Church,  
Shepherd of the flock and keeper of the sheep,  
He holds back the savage fury of wolves.

Whatever you bind with chains on earth  
Will be firmly bound in the stars;  
And whatever you loose on earth by your decision  
Will be loosed beneath heaven’s rays. [Col. 0962A]

At the end of the world you will be judge of the age.

Paul, teacher of the nations,  
Was not unequal to him:  
Most sacred temple of election,  
His companion in death and sharer in the crown.

Both lamps and ornaments of the Church,  
They flash throughout the bright world  
With radiant splendor.

O happy Rome,  
Which, robed in the precious blood  
Of such great princes,  
Surpasses all the world’s beauty—  
Not through your own praise,  
But through the merits of the saints  
Whom you slaughtered with blood-stained swords.

Therefore, now, glorious princes—  
Blessed Peter, Paul, lily of the world,  
Triumphant soldiers of the heavenly court—  
By your loving prayers protect us  
From every evil, and carry us above the heavens.

Glory to God throughout endless ages;  
To you, Son, be honor and dominion, etc.

## ON THEIR FEAST

Invitatory, as in the printed editions.

Antiphon. “In the streets the sick were placed on beds, so that when Peter came …”

And the other antiphons of the first and second nocturns, which are taken from the history of the Acts of the Apostles.

Antiphon at the canticles. “The Lord signified to Peter by what death he would glorify God, alleluia.”

Responsory of the twelfth reading. When Peter was on the cross, a great crowd came, cursed Caesar, and made a great lament before the cross. Peter exhorted them from the cross, saying: “Do not weep, but rejoice with me, because I am going to prepare a place for you.” “I give you thanks, good Shepherd, because the sheep whom you entrusted to me suffer with me forever.” And when he had said this, he added: “Do not …” [Col. 0962C]

## ON THE FEAST OF SAINT MARY MAGDALENE

### Hymn at Vespers

Mary took a pound  
Of precious pure nard,  
Anointed the blessed feet of the Lord,  
And washed them with her tears.

Honor, glory, etc.

Invitatory. Let us praise the eternal, triune, and one God, who carried Mary, holy to himself, into heaven.

### Hymn

With harmonious songs  
Let us venerate Christ,  
Celebrating this feast-day,  
Rejoicing throughout the world  
Now in Mary Magdalene.

She once anointed  
The Lord’s head and washed his feet,  
Wetting them with tears  
And wiping them with the hair of her head,  
While humbly groaning in her heart.

Then Christ immediately granted  
Forgiveness of all guilt  
To the suppliant,  
Showing through his gracious mouth  
A worthy example to Simon.

She brought myrrh at dawn  
To anoint the Lord in the tomb,  
And deserved to be the first blessed woman  
To see him risen.

After these things,  
By Christ’s granting,  
We believe that she penetrated  
The summit of heaven  
Through this favor.

Have mercy on us, Creator of the world.

Let us sing glory to the Father,  
Glory likewise to the Son,  
And to the gracious Spirit;  
Let us all resound it  
Always, throughout every age.

Antiphon. When the Lord Jesus, the glory of the world, had reclined in the house of Simon, a certain woman who was a sinner brought fragrant ointments of nard.

Antiphon. Standing beside the Lord’s feet without ceasing, she kisses his sacred footprints with her mouth, full of tears. [Col. 0963B]

Antiphon. Thus she watered the Lord Jesus’ feet; when the alabaster had been broken with the most precious perfumes, the whole house was fragrant, and she wiped them with the service of her hair.

Antiphon. But Simon said within himself: “If he were a prophet, he would certainly know what sort of woman she is who touches him, because she is a sinner.”

Antiphon. And the Lord turned and said: “After I came into your house, this woman has not ceased kissing my feet with her loosened hair.”

Antiphon. “Because you had loved greatly, know that your sins are forgiven you; and by the faith in which you abound, I mercifully forgive you in peace.”

R\. Let every age rejoice in the solemnity of holy Mary, whom Jesus loved greatly with eternal love.

V\. This was Mary, most pleasing to the Lord, who anointed his feet with precious ointment.

R\. Mary chose the best part for herself, and it shall not be taken from her forever.

V\. Loving the Lord with a most perfect heart, she obtained the dignity of heaven.

R\. Most powerful one, intercede with the Lord, rejoicing because you have been carried triumphantly to heaven. Obtain that we may forever enjoy with you the divine joys.

V\. Because, with our sins erased, we seek your merits.

R\. Who was more sinful than Mary Magdalene, who went after every evil? Called a sinner, full of guilt even in her name, she was as though named for sin.

V\. Yet when she moved God by the tears that flowed from the affection of her heart, she deserved to be freed from sin.

Antiphon. Martha, the sister of Mary Magdalene, was busy with the tasks of service, while Mary, sitting beside the Lord’s feet, listened to the words of his mouth.

Antiphon. “Lord,” she said, “do you not care that my sister has left me alone to serve? Tell her to help me.”

Antiphon. Immediately the Lord answered her: “One thing alone is certainly necessary. She has chosen the best part, which shall not be taken away.”

Antiphon. When the Pharisee had asked the Lord to dine, she enjoyed bodily food while giving spiritual things.

Antiphon. Behold, the pious sister of Lazarus, once sinful but now pious, brought the precious weight of fragrant ointment.

Antiphon. Greatest hope of forgiveness, help the people who ask, so that through you they may deserve to receive forgiveness of their sins.

R\. O happy watering of the sacred feet with tears, through which Mary deserved to be called and to be his beloved; and where the saints are nourished in heaven.

V\. She and they possess angelic beauty through Christ.

R\. Blessed Mary, who wiped away the stains of your sins in streams of pious tears, we earnestly ask you to pray for our transgressions.

V\. Gathered among the highest citizens of heaven and now clothed in eternal immortality.

R\. Mary Magdalene came announcing to the disciples: “I have seen the Lord.” We ask to be helped with him by your prayers, most merciful Redeemer.

V\. For just as a woman in paradise gave death to a man, so from the tomb a woman announced life to men.

R\. Immense King and Creator of the world, receive the devout prayers of the clergy praying in the present.

V\. May it always be able to offer you worthy praises.

Antiphon at the canticles. O lamp and brilliantly shining pearl of the world, who, by announcing Christ’s resurrection, deserved to become the apostle of the apostles, Mary Magdalene, always be a loving intercessor for us before God, who chose you.

R\. Mary, burning in her inmost heart, anointed with consecrated ointment the holy feet of Jesus, whom she had addressed with intimate gifts. Thus she deserved forgiveness of her sins.

V\. By your most loving intercessions, may he wash away the filth of our sins in the divine fountain.

R\. Mary, standing at the tomb and weeping, saw two angels seated in white, where the body of Jesus had been placed.

V\. And when she was weeping, she bent down and looked into the tomb.

R\. You who brought exalted joys to Christ’s disciples when they were exceedingly sorrowful over the death of the Master, join heavenly life’s joy to us.

V\. So that, made like him whose mercy healed you, we may deserve to become one with the blessed in their lot.

R\. O wonderful and great miracle: a sinful woman dared to touch the Redeemer of the world, and by weeping and wiping with her hair she washed away her sins. Therefore many sins were forgiven her, because she loved greatly.

V\. Mary saw the Lord and believed, and received him with joy, rejoicing and weeping because she recognized herself to be a sinner.

At Lauds, an antiphon. “In those days, a woman who was a sinner in the city, when she learned that Jesus had reclined in the house of Simon the leper, brought an alabaster jar of ointment.” This antiphon alone is read at Lauds.

### Hymn

Let the devotion of the faithful bring forth  
A hymn to the Lord,  
Who gave Mary Magdalene  
A dwelling in heaven.

In her he showed  
What piety was  
By his goodness,  
And by his clemency revealed  
What repentance gives.

For she who had previously committed  
Countless crimes,  
Having received the peace of forgiveness,  
Obtains the kingdom of glory.

Mary, falling at Christ’s feet  
With her hair wiped clean,  
While she wets them with tears,  
Washes herself from the filth of sin.

Having thereby attained  
Very great love for the Lord,  
She rejoices in the palace of heaven  
With an everlasting reward.

Therefore we ask you, Lady:  
Erase our sins,  
And by your holy prayers  
Join us to the citizens of heaven.

To the Father, Son, and Spirit  
Be praise forever;  
To him who is supreme Divinity,  
The Trinity in Unity. Amen.

At the Benedictus, an antiphon. Holy Mary, joined in devotion to Jesus, kissing his feet and piously wetting them, wipe away our sins, always praying to him for us.

## ON THE FEAST OF SAINT APOLLINARIS, BISHOP AND MARTYR

[Col. 0965B]

At the Magnificat, an antiphon. Rise, receive the Holy Spirit and likewise the episcopate, and go to the city called Ravenna.

Commemoration of Magdalene, antiphon. O venerable seat of God, illustrious hope of ours, O most celebrated vine of Christ, bearing powerful fruit, the drachma that was found, but the sheep brought back from death: pray earnestly to God for us; we earnestly pray.

Antiphon. Blessed Peter the apostle said to the Jews: “For I too am a Hebrew, but I have come because of love for the brothers.”

Antiphon. A multitude of Hebrews, doing penance, were baptized, believing that Jesus Christ truly is the Son of God.

Antiphon. Blessed Peter the apostle said to Apollinaris, who was serving him: “Why are you sitting with us? Behold, you have been instructed in all that Jesus did.”

Antiphon. Blessed Peter said to his disciple Apollinaris: “You have been instructed in all things to preach Jesus the Son of God at Ravenna.”

Antiphon. “May Christ the Lord send his angel, who will prepare his way, and may he grant what you have asked.”

Antiphon. Blessed Apollinaris, born at Antioch, was sent to Ravenna to preach the baptism of repentance for the forgiveness of sins.

R\. Blessed Peter said to his disciple Apollinaris: “Why are you sitting with us? Behold, you have been instructed in all that Jesus did.”

V\. Rise, receive the Holy Spirit and likewise the episcopate, and go to the city called Ravenna.

R\. Blessed Peter the apostle said to his disciple Apollinaris: “Rise, go to Ravenna. A multitude of people dwells there; preach to them the baptism of repentance in the name of Jesus.”

V\. Behold, you have been instructed in all that Jesus did.

R\. O God, who are not in one place but everywhere, introduce into this city knowledge of your Son, our Lord.

V\. So that, knowing Jesus your Son, a place of preaching may be granted to me with great devotion.

R\. O God, who work together with Peter, my teacher, work also with me, so that all may know that you alone are God forever.

V\. O God, who are not in one place but everywhere.

In the second nocturn, an antiphon. When blessed Apollinaris reached the city of Ravenna, making the sign of the cross, he was received into the house of the soldier Irenaeus.

Antiphon. O God, who work with Peter, my teacher, work also with me, so that your name may be glorified. [Col. 0966A]

Antiphon. Blessed Apollinaris entered the tribune’s house and said: “May the peace of the Lord and of our God Jesus Christ remain in you.”

Antiphon. “May the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ remain in you,” through which blessed Apollinaris healed the tribune’s sick wife.

Antiphon. “There is no other power than that of our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom blessed Apollinaris healed that blind son of Taurus.”

Antiphon. The pagans reported this to Caesar: someone from Antioch had introduced the name of Jesus into the city of Ravenna, and a great multitude obeyed him, including the household of Rufus the patrician.

R\. The tribune said to him: “You have arrived well, physician.” Blessed Apollinaris answered him: “May the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ remain in you.”

V\. When he had entered the tribune’s house, he was received with the greatest courtesy, and he said: “May it remain.”

R\. Open, O Lord, immediately the mouth of the mute, so that they may confess your name, you who live forever.

V\. At once the bond of his tongue was loosed, and he cried out.

R\. Lord Jesus Christ, my God, who granted to my teacher, your apostle Peter, the privilege of obtaining from you what he desires: raise up this girl, who is your creature, and there is no other God besides you.

V\. Then, taking the woman’s hand, he said: “My Lord and my God.”

R\. Now that I have been led into the capitol of the governor, be confident that I shall not place incense in my hands for demons, but offer incense to my Lord Jesus Christ.

V\. I confess that the Lord Jesus Christ is the living God, and I say that there is no other besides him.

At the canticles, an antiphon. Most holy Apollinaris, conversing with angels, receive the prayers and petitions that we offer to you, and return a hymn for us to the Savior, so that he may save us.

R\. “Strip him and, while beating him, say: ‘Look and sacrifice to the gods.’” But he answered: “I am a Christian; do what you wish.”

V\. There is one Lord God, invisible, through whom demons are cast out.

R\. This is the priest of the Lord who meditates on his commands day and night. He was sent by the apostle Peter to Ravenna to preach the baptism of repentance.

V\. Blessed is the man who has not walked in the counsel of the wicked.

R\. I served Christ as a good soldier; I fought the good fight. I pleased God, who tested me, and the Lord gave me the crown of life.

V\. I have fought the good fight, I have finished the course, I have kept the faith.

R\. With beautiful face and cheerful countenance, blessed Apollinaris, behold, your sheep run to you with devoted mind—those whom you acquired for the Lord. Pray, I beg you, good shepherd, to Jesus Christ for them.

V\. That we may be made worthy of his promises.

At Lauds, an antiphon. Hear, Judge, what I say courageously: Jesus was God and remains forever in a pure body, but he willed to suffer in the flesh for all.

This is the only antiphon provided at Lauds for this office.

At the Benedictus, an antiphon. Weighed down by the burden of iron, he is sent into exile from the city, and after three years he returns to his holy city, Ravenna. When the Christians saw him, they received him with joy. [Col. 0967A]

At Prime, an antiphon. The angel of the Lord visited blessed Apollinaris in prison, fed him in the sight of the guards, and strengthened him.

At Terce, an antiphon. Suspended on the rack, blessed Apollinaris cried out: “I confess that the Lord Jesus Christ is the true God.”

At Sext, an antiphon. Our guardian and protector, Lord Jesus Christ, whom blessed Apollinaris foretold, we bless you and sing a hymn to you, our God.

Prayer. On this day the confession of blessed Apollinaris, your priest and martyr, has given us saving joy through your power, O Lord. Grant, we beseech you, that we may continually glory in imitation of his praiseworthy way of life and in his intercession, pleasing to you. [Col. 0967B]

At None, an antiphon. Holy Apollinaris, priest and martyr of Christ, pray for your people whom you acquired from the nations; but we are your people and the sheep of your flock. Intercede for us with the Son of God.

Prayer. Terrible God, unconquered strength, and power greatly to be feared, grant us through the prayers of your blessed martyr and priest Apollinaris the resources of eternal salvation, so that, bearing pure hearts, we may return praises of your clemency while celebrating his solemnity.

At the Magnificat, an antiphon. Receive the Holy Spirit and likewise the episcopate. Rise, go to Ravenna; a multitude of people dwells there. Preach Jesus to them, that he truly is the Son of God.

## ON THE FEAST OF SAINT AEMYGDIUS, BISHOP AND MARTYR

At the Magnificat, an antiphon. O glorious martyr Aemygdius, commend us continually to God by your prayer—you who gave birth to your children in Christ by shedding your blood. [Col. 0967C]

At the Benedictus, an antiphon. Holy bishop and martyr of God, Aemygdius, who, born in western France and coming to Rome, were appointed by God’s arrangement and sent by the Roman pontiff as preacher to the city of Ascoli, intercede with God for us, whom by words and miracles you caused to come to the knowledge of the Christian name.

## ON THE VIGIL OF THE ASSUMPTION OF THE HOLY VIRGIN MARY

At Vespers, an antiphon. Mary the Virgin, rejoice always, you who deserved to bear Christ, Creator of heaven and earth, because from your womb you brought forth the Savior of the world.

Psalms of the weekday.

### Hymn

Joy of the world, new star of heaven,  
Bringing forth the sun, giving birth to the parent,  
Give your hand to the fallen, bring help to the failing,  
Virgin Mary.

It is clear that you were made a ladder for God:  
By which the lofty One reaches down to the lowest,  
Grant that we may return to the heights,  
To the summits of heaven.

The chorus of the blessed angels,  
The order of prophets and apostles,  
Beholds you placed first among them,  
After the Godhead.

Beautiful heavenly palace of the King,  
Supported by the seven columns of Wisdom,  
You enclose in your womb  
Him whom the whole world cannot contain.

Him whom the heavens tremble at,  
Whom the abysses fear,  
Whom the setting sun praises  
And the rising sun venerates,  
You hold in your arms.

He whom the angels feed with food,  
A girl bears in her unwedded womb,  
He who by his broad dominion  
Balances the burdens of the earth.

Let supreme honor without end be given to Christ,  
Whom holy Mary the Virgin bore,  
Who, equal to the Father and the holy Spirit,  
Reigns forever. Amen.

## ON THE ASSUMPTION OF THE HOLY VIRGIN MARY

Invitatory. Your fragrance, holy Mother of God, is like the fragrance of balsam. You flower like a lily, Virgin Mother of God. [Col. 0968B]

### Hymn

Let all earthly things rejoice;  
Let the stars resound with praises;  
Before the Virgin’s bridal chamber  
Let them sing an alternating hymn.

This Virgin, pregnant with the Word,  
Becomes the gate of paradise.  
She who gave God back to the world  
Opened heaven for us.

Happy is this mother,  
Freed from Eve’s law:  
She conceived without intercourse  
And brought forth without a groan.

Mary’s womb, rich beyond measure,  
Carried the price of the world,  
By which we rejoice to be redeemed,  
The debt’s yoke having been loosed.

The Son of the Father fills her;  
The Holy Spirit overshadows her;  
The most chaste womb of the sacred maiden becomes heaven.

Praise to you, most high King,  
Who were born of the Virgin.  
Praise be to the ineffable Father  
And to the holy Spirit.

### Hymn at Lauds

Like a shining dawn  
She makes her way to heaven’s heights,  
And Mary, radiant as the sun,  
Is like the fairest moon.

Today the Queen of the world  
Ascends the throne of glory,  
She who gave birth to that Son  
Who existed before the morning star.

Taken above the angels,  
You surpass the archangels;  
One woman transcends  
All the merits of the saints.

Him whom she had cherished in her womb  
And laid in a manger,  
She now sees as King over all  
In the glory of the Father.

For us, Virgin of virgins,  
Ask your Son,  
Through whom he had received our things  
And bestowed his things upon us.

Praise to you, most high King, etc.

## ON THE OCTAVE OF THE HOLY VIRGIN MARY

Antiphon at the Magnificat. Under your protection we flee, Mother of God; do not despise our prayer in our necessities, but always free us from dangers, glorious Virgin.

Final antiphon of the First Nocturn. A mother in giving birth, a virgin in childbirth: rejoice and be glad, Virgin, Mother of the Lord.

## ON THE FEAST OF SAINT MARTIN

### Hymn at Vespers

King Christ, glory of Martin,  
Here is your praise, and he is yours.  
Grant that we may worship you in him,  
Since you grant us to find him in you.

You give throughout the world’s compass  
What shines like a jewel among bishops.  
Grant that those weighed down by grave sins  
May be released through his great merit.

Behold, poor and humble,  
He enters heaven rich.  
The cohorts of heaven go out to meet him;  
Tongues, tribes, and nations rejoice.

As his passing shines forth like life,  
Splendid in heaven and on earth,  
It is right for all to rejoice;  
May this day be salvation for all.

Martin, equal to the apostles,  
Foster those who celebrate your feast.  
You who wished to live for your disciples  
And did not refuse to die.

Do now what you once did:  
Now glorify the bishops,  
Increase the Church’s honor,  
Shatter Satan’s deceptions.

You who three times empty the abyss,  
Raise up those sunk in guilt.  
As you had divided your cloak,  
Clothe us in righteousness.

So that you may remember  
Your former special glory,  
Now help the monastic order,  
Already almost fallen.

Glory be to the Trinity,  
As Martin confessed it;  
May he himself strengthen in us  
The faith he demonstrated through works. Amen.

## ON THE DEDICATION OF A CHURCH

### Hymn at Vespers

Christ, loving ruler of all,  
Begotten from the mouth of the eternal Father,  
Look kindly upon the prayers of suppliants  
And upon their hymn as well.

See what your people, O God,  
Humbly resound in this pure hall of honor,  
Whose annual festivals  
Return to be celebrated in their season. [Col. 0970A]

This house, duly dedicated to you,  
Is recognized as the place where the people  
Receive the sacred Body, drink,  
And partake of the blessed Blood.

Here the holy liquids wash away  
Ancient sins and destroy offenses;  
And through chrism a race of worshipers  
Of Christ is created.

Here there is salvation for the sick,  
Medicine for the weary,  
Light for the blind, forgiveness  
For our offenses, and every fear  
And sorrow is driven away.

Here the savage plunder of the demon perishes;  
The stubborn monster is afraid,  
And, abandoning the bodies it had seized,  
Quickly flees into distant shadows.

This place is rightly called  
The hall of the eternal King,  
And of the snowy heaven;  
It receives all who seek  
Their homeland, the gate of life.

No whirlwind shakes it,  
Nor do wandering winds or clouds  
Overthrow it;  
Horrible Tartarus does not harm it  
With its gloomy, pitch-black darkness.

Therefore we beseech you, O God,  
To look upon your servants  
With a serene countenance,  
Who celebrate the highest joys  
Of your temple out of love for you.

May no troubles of life torment us;  
May our days be joyful and our nights peaceful;  
May none of us, as the world perishes,  
Feel the fires.

May this day, on which you behold  
The altar consecrated to you,  
Grant us everlasting joy,  
And may it remain strong  
Through the long passage of time.

Let us resound glory to the highest Father,

Let us sing glory to the Son, and likewise

To the Holy Spirit, with a sweetly modulated hymn,

To be forever. Amen.

At the end of the aforementioned breviary the office of blessed Mary is written.

# THE OFFICE OF BLESSED MARY THE VIRGIN BEGINS, ACCORDING TO THE CUSTOM OF THE MONKS OF THE MONASTERY OF HOLY CROSS OF THE FOUNTAIN OF AVELLANA

[Col. 0970D]

## At Matins

O Lord, open my lips, etc., through the lessons.

**First lesson.** Holy Mary, Virgin of virgins, mother and daughter of the King of kings, bestow upon us all your consolation, so that we may deserve to possess the reward of the heavenly kingdom and reign forever with God’s elect.

**Response.** That among us, etc.

**Second lesson.** Holy Mary, most holy of the devout, intercede for us, holiest of the holy, so that through you he who was born for us and reigns above the heavens may receive our prayers, and through your goodness may erase our sins.

**Response.** For blessed indeed, etc.

**Third lesson.** Holy Mother of God, who deserved worthily to conceive him whom the whole world cannot contain, we ask that through your intercession you wash away our sins, so that, redeemed through you, we may deserve to ascend to the everlasting seat of glory, where you dwell with that same Son of yours without end.

[Col. 0971A]

**Response.** Blessed are you, etc.

**Hymn.** *Te Deum laudamus*—“We praise you, O God.”

**Versicle.** The Lord be with you.

**Continuation of the holy Gospel according to Luke.** At that time: As Jesus was speaking to the crowds, etc.

**Response.** Amen.

To you praise is due, etc.

**Antiphon at the Benedictus.** Who is this that comes down like the rising dawn, beautiful as the moon, chosen as the sun, terrible as an army arrayed for battle?

Lord, have mercy, etc.

Our Father.

**V.** Let us bless the Father and the Son with the Holy Spirit.  
**R.** Let us praise and exalt him forever.

**V.** After giving birth, you remained an inviolate Virgin.  
**R.** Mother of God, intercede for us.

**V.** Wonderful is God.  
**R.** In his saints.

**V.** The Lord be with you.  
**R.** And with …

**Prayer.** O God, by whose gift we confess the Trinity in persons and Unity in the divine substance, mercifully grant that, protected by this faithful breastplate, we may also deserve to be freed from every adversity.

**Another prayer.** O God, who in your goodness sent your Son to us through the Virgin, grant that, aided by the prayers of that same blessed Mary, we may continually hasten toward you.

**Another prayer.** Mercifully bestow your help upon us, O Lord, and, through the intercession of blessed Mary, Mother of God, together with all your saints, make us free from every adversity and rejoice in eternal happiness. Through the Lord, etc.

### Suffrages at Matins

**Antiphon.** Among those born of women, etc.

**V.** The righteous shall flourish like a palm tree.  
**R.** Like a cedar.

**Prayer.** O Lord, we ask that blessed John the Baptist, etc.

**Antiphon.** Peter the apostle.

**V.** Into all the world.  
**R.** And to the ends.

**Prayer.** Grant, we ask, almighty God, that no ..., etc.

**Antiphon.** Give peace.

**V.** Let there be peace.  
**R.** And abundance.

**Prayer.** O God, from whom come holy desires, etc.

**Antiphon.** The righteous shall shine.

**V.** Wonderful is God.  
**R.** In his saints.

**Prayer.** O God, who grant us, etc.

## At Prime

**Hymn.** *Beata Dei Genitrix*, etc., from the works of Saint Peter Damian.

**Antiphon.** From you, Mary the Virgin.

**Psalm.** Blessed is the man who has not walked.

**Psalm.** Why do the nations rage?

**Psalm.** O Lord, rebuke me not in your anger.

**Antiphon.** From you, Mary the Virgin, God and man proceeded; from you, O holy Virgin, Christ was cut out as a stone, whom the prophet Daniel had foretold.

**Lesson.** And thus in Zion, etc.

**R.** Blessed are you among women, etc.

**V.** Hail, Mary, full of grace, etc.

**Prayer.** Of the blessed and glorious one, etc.

**Another prayer.** Grant, we ask, almighty God, that your holy men and women may continually pray for us and that they may be mercifully heard. Through the Lord, etc.

## At Terce

**Hymn.** *Maria, decus omnium*, etc.

**Antiphon.** Through you, Mary the Virgin.

**Psalms.** As in our office.

**Antiphon.** Through you, Mary the Virgin, all the proclamations of the prophets have been fulfilled—the proclamations that said: “A virgin, you conceived; a virgin, you gave birth.”

**Lesson.** I have inherited among the people, etc.

**R.** In your beauty.

**V.** Blessed are you.

## At Sext

**Hymn.** *Maria, templum Domini*, etc.

**Antiphon and psalms.** As in our office.

**Lesson.** Like a cedar.

[Col. 0972A]

**R.** He will help.

**V.** Like myrrh.

**Prayer.** O God, who have revealed to us the mystery of the Holy Trinity, grant, we ask, that we who have now come to know you through faith may grow through the increase of good works.

**Another prayer.** Grant, we ask, almighty God, that we may be sustained by the prayers of blessed Mary, ever Virgin, through whose ineffable childbirth you provided the remedy of human salvation.

**Another prayer.** Mercifully appeased by the supplication of all your saints, O Lord, grant us pardon and bestow everlasting remedies.

## At None

**Hymn.** *O singularis Domina*, etc.

**Antiphon, psalms, and lesson.** As in our office.

**R.** God chose her, etc.

**V.** You have been made beautiful.

**Prayer.** O God, who [the virginal …], etc.

[Col. 0972B]

**Another prayer.** Stretch out your right hand to us, O God, and through the intercession of blessed Mary, ever Virgin, and of all your saints, bestow upon us the help of heavenly strength.

## At Vespers

**Antiphon.** Before the bridal chamber.

**Psalm.** The Lord said.

**Antiphon.** Many waters.

**Psalm.** I was glad.

**Antiphon.** Rise up, north wind, and come, south wind; blow through my garden, and let its fragrances flow.

**Psalm.** Unless the Lord builds.

**Antiphon.** Return, return.

**Psalm.** Remember, O Lord.

**Antiphon.** In giving birth, Mother; in childbirth, Virgin: rejoice and be glad, Virgin, Mother of the Lord.

**Psalm.** Praise Jerusalem.

**Lesson.** I am like a vine, etc.

**R.** You have been exalted, holy Mother of God.

**Hymn.** *Sidus Mariae splendidum*, etc.

**At the Magnificat.** Mary the Virgin, no woman born in the world is like you: flowering like a rose, fragrant as a lily, pray for us to your Son.

Lord, have mercy.

Our Father.

# THE MICROLOGUS ON ECCLESIASTICAL OBSERVANCES

A short work written six hundred years ago by a man devoted to ecclesiastical antiquity; first published through the efforts of James Pamelius of Bruges, Licentiate of Sacred Theology, and now revised a second time by him from manuscript copies.

(*Bibliotheca Patrum* XVIII, 469.) (G)*

## JAMES PAMELIUS OF BRUGES TO THE CANDID READER, GREETINGS

[Col. 0973B]

While I was wholly occupied in seeking everywhere the books of Rabanus Maurus, archbishop of Mainz, a man beyond all doubt most learned and exceptionally skilled in the interpretation of sacred Scripture—for he compiled the most exact commentary on the whole of the sacred Bible from the monuments of the ancient theologians—a *Micrologus on Ecclesiastical Observances* was sent to us from the library of the Seven Fountains under the name of Rabanus.

When I first examined it and learned the subject of the entire work from the very titles of its chapters, I rejoiced extraordinarily at the discovery of such a treasure, especially since a firm hope shone forth that I might at last restore to its true author the book which I had found cited elsewhere under an uncertain author, since I knew that Rabanus had written on the divine offices.

But when shortly afterward I examined the codex more thoroughly and saw that it mentioned Pope Gregory VII and the bishops Amalarius of Trier and Anselm of Lucca, who lived several centuries [Col. 0973C] after Rabanus, I discovered with certainty that it was not his. Nevertheless, this did not deter me from the edition I had once conceived; rather, because I had persuaded myself that you, Reader, would find it pleasing, I undertook at last to rescue it from bookworms and moths. I also thought that by this small literary gift I might win the goodwill of learned men, so that, if they possess anything of Rabanus by which they could advance this pious undertaking of mine, they might not be reluctant to share it. I earnestly—and indeed urgently—beg all of them to do so.

Another occasion also impelled me to this decision with all possible force, as the saying goes, with sails and oars. The fathers of the most recent Council of Trent selected a certain number of men who, to avoid that discrepancy in ecclesiastical rites which the Aristarchuses of our age reproach us for, were to compose a Breviary and Missal, [Col. 0974B] complete in all their parts, and propose them for observance throughout the Christian world by apostolic authority.

Since I had no doubt that they would restore everything to the ancient rite of the Roman Church, and since I believed that our *Micrologus* could contribute not a little to that task, I considered that it should be published at the earliest opportunity, since I thought that almost anything altered from that original institution of the Roman order could be repaired from it.

Although it must be admitted that Amalarius, Walafrid Strabo, and the *Gemma of Honorius* also contribute greatly to this purpose, nevertheless I believe that the authority of this work should not be neglected, indeed that it ought even to be preferred to the others, because through long experience of these matters and careful reading not only of Amalarius, who easily holds first place among them, but also of much earlier authors, whose authority ought to be sacred to everyone, it acquired an exceptional knowledge of ecclesiastical affairs.

[Col. 0974C]

These are the Sacramentary and Antiphonary of Gregory the Great, and the Lectionary of Jerome, which he entitled the *Comes*. He always kept them before his eyes when establishing the divine offices, and thought that he must always look to them, just as sailors look to the Pole Star.

Since they are of the greatest importance for correctly establishing ecclesiastical offices, we shall shortly bring them to light and, with God’s approval, share them with everyone. In my judgment, everything can be restored more correctly to its former integrity from these works than from the Missals or Breviaries now in circulation. Although these sometimes bear the title of the New and sometimes of the Ancient Roman Order, the authors cited above, as well as our present author, make it clear that they do not agree with it in every respect.

What I say could be demonstrated by examples, both concerning the Gospel for the First Sunday of Advent and the insertion of the wandering Sundays after Pentecost, and concerning the exact concord between the Gospels and the prayers which Saint Gregory prescribed.

[Col. 0975A]

But I have decided to pass over this here, lest I annoy anyone with excessive length or seem to claim for myself the office of censor. If anyone is more curious about the matter, let him consult chapters twenty-one, thirty-one, forty-one, and the final two chapters of the *Micrologus*.

I shall not hesitate to say this much: there will be less novelty throughout the other Churches of the world if the fathers follow that ancient Roman rite than if they preserve this more recent one unchanged in every respect. For almost all the Roman Churches throughout the world, including our own Church of Bruges—now a cathedral, but for seven hundred years distinguished by its college of canons—come very close to it.

[Col. 0975B]

The instituted Franciscan fathers borrowed this rite from the papal chapel not many centuries ago, if history is to be trusted, and afterward almost the Romans alone adopted it for use.

About two hundred years ago, around the year of the Lord 1380, Radulphus de Rivo, dean of Tongeren, left testimony to this in a book which I possess in manuscript, *On the Observance of the Canons*. In his twenty-second proposition the title is as follows:

> “The order of the holy Roman Church is to be gathered not from the usage of the Friars Minor, but from the sacred canons, authoritative Scriptures, ancient books, and the general and proportionate custom of places.”

After asserting this throughout his work by many arguments drawn from the matter itself and by comparing the rites with one another, he develops it extensively here by a twofold historical argument; we have condensed it into a summary.

The first argument is that he himself had learned in Rome that, in the papal chapel at the Lateran, the ecclesiastical offices were not usually [Col. 0975C] performed as fully as in the other collegiate churches of the City. Indeed, that chapel office—as he calls it—was customarily shorter and was more frequently altered by the pontiffs. This was the office which the Friars Minor undertook to observe, since he himself had seen its ordinary collected at Rome from the time of Pope Innocent.

The second argument is that Pope Nicholas III, around the year of the Lord 1277, after removing the older books from the other churches of the City as well, introduced the Breviaries and Missal books of the order of the Friars Minor for use and ordered them to be observed in all the churches of the City, so much so that in his own day Radulphus found all the books in Rome to be new.

But these matters are outside our purpose. What is more relevant to our undertaking is what he says:

> “The other nations of the Roman world have their books and offices directly from the Roman churches themselves, and not from the pope’s chapel, as is clearly gathered from the books and treatises of Amalarius, Walafrid, the *Micrologus*, [Col. 0976A] the *Gemma*, and the other writers on the divine office.”

We have quoted these words here all the more willingly because they explain in a few words the subject of our *Micrologus*. He valued it so highly that, above all others, he relies especially upon its authority and sometimes transcribed entire pages from it into his own work. From this source we have also restored certain passages, so that it may be clear that the *Micrologus* was not first valued by me, but was already held in esteem long ago by him. No one, therefore, should find it strange that I was not afraid to publish it without the author’s name, since even at that time its author was unknown to so vigilant an investigator of antiquity itself.

But I—returning to our author—believe that, whoever he may finally have been, he omitted his name out of humility, as we find many others doing. The claim made by some that he was Bernold of Constance rests on conjecture, [Col. 0976B]

because Trithemius testifies that Bernold described the Roman Order; the chronology, however, does not fit sufficiently well.

Others entitle it *The Micrologus of John*, but I do not know which John this was. It is nevertheless certain that the author lived in the age of Pope Gregory VII, whom he rather clearly indicates as having presided over the Roman See in his own time, although already dead when he wrote. He also indicates that he had been acquainted with Anselm of Lucca, who was an indefatigable associate of Gregory VII. Both of them flourished, and so did our author, around the year of the Lord 1080, nearly five hundred years ago.

Since at that time communion of the Eucharist under both kinds was still observed in certain places, no one should be surprised if he finds something written in the *Micrologus* about that kind of communion. Nevertheless, it can be sufficiently inferred from chapter seventeen that communion of the sick under one kind—namely, bread alone—[Col. 0976C] was already customary.

But perhaps I shall discuss these matters more fully elsewhere, as well as the public and private Masses, both of which the *Micrologus* acknowledges in more than one place.

Whatever else it contains that deserves notice, you will find noted at the foot of the page. Moreover, if anyone should say that I am publishing the *Micrologus* a second time, since he has already seen it published by others, I reply that those editions contain only mere fragments, whereas ours is augmented by forty chapters. Those deal only with the proper celebration of Mass; ours treats also of the other offices of the entire year.

Since I consider that I have satisfied you, Reader, abundantly, and do not wish to seem to exceed the proper bounds of a preface, I shall draw in the sails of my discourse. Please judge whatever it may be favorably and kindly. Certainly, if I learn that it has pleased you, I intend shortly to bring to light several other booklets on the same subject which have not yet been seen. Meanwhile, farewell and enjoy it.

# ON THE AUTHOR OF THE *MICROLOGUS*

## I. From the Master of the Sacred Palace

[Col. 0975D]

Some think that the author of this book was Guido of Arezzo, a monk of Saint Benedict, a distinguished musician, who first devised those musical notes—ut, re, mi, fa, sol, la—and published a book on music called the *Micrologus*. At its conclusion he ended with these words:

> “The *Micrologus* of Guido concludes, in the thirty-fourth year of his age, while John the twentieth governs the Roman Church.”

That is the account of the man; more about him may be found in volume XI of the *Annals*, under the year of the Lord 1022, and in Possevinus’s *Sacred Apparatus*.

But since the writer of this *Micrologus on Ecclesiastical Observances*, [Col. 0976D] in chapters 14, 17, 24, 25, and 43, expressly states that he composed this commentary after the time of Saint Gregory VII, I judge that if that Guido of Arezzo, who was thirty-four years old during the time of John XX, who succeeded Benedict VIII, was the author of this book, he must have written it when he was more than ninety years old. For John XX died in the year of the Lord 1035, whereas Saint Gregory VII died in 1085, according to the more reliable chronology of the annals.

It is beyond dispute, however, that the *Micrologus* on music written by Guido for Theobald, bishop of Arezzo, is [Col. 0977A] entirely different from this *Micrologus* presented here. Moreover, the author of this *Micrologus* declares in chapter 14 that he lived in the time of Saint Gregory VII, in these words:

> “For in our time he placed upon that apostolic See such a governor—Gregory, I mean, the pope, whose memory is revered—etc.”

## II. From Father Theophilus Raynaud, S.J., in the *Questions on Good and Bad Books*

The book called the *Micrologus* was falsely attributed to Berno, abbot of Reichenau; that is the title of the book, not—as some have fabricated—the surname of its author, whom they imagine to have been called John Micrologus.

Claudius Expensus, in his treatise *On the Public and Private Mass*, which is found at the end of his work *On the Adoration of the Eucharist*, says that the author of this book was Berno of Reichenau. He reports that the book appeared under Berno’s name at Paris in the year 1518, with the title *On the Office of the Mass*, [Col. 0977B] and that Trithemius counts it among Berno’s works.

Nevertheless, the *Micrologus* cannot plausibly be attributed to Berno, since Berno testifies in his book *On Matters Pertaining to the Office of the Mass* that he attended the coronation of Henry I by Benedict VIII in the year 1014. But the author of the *Micrologus*, in chapter 34, states that he is writing after the death of Gregory VII, who died in 1085. It would therefore be necessary to admit that Berno undertook the writing of the *Micrologus* when more than decrepit.

[Col. 0978A]

There is someone who writes that the author of the *Micrologus* was Guido, abbot of Holy Cross of Avellana near Arezzo, who devised figured chant and those solemn notes—ut, re, mi, fa, sol, la. For the priest Domnizo, in his poem *On the Deeds of Countess Matilda*, speaking of Theobald, bishop of Arezzo, sings as follows:

> “Guido, a skilled musician, monk, and blessed hermit,  
> Dictates the book *Micrologus* for him.”

This *Micrologus*, however, is entirely different from the work *On Ecclesiastical Observances*, or *On the Office of the Mass*. For Cardinal Baronius, in the year 1022, when recounting its preface addressed to the aforementioned Theobald, shows that it was a book *On Music*, which is said to have been written in Guido’s [Col. 0978B] thirty-fourth year, under John the Roman pontiff—namely John XX, who died in the year 1033.

From this comparison of dates we are brought almost to the same difficulty into which those who attributed that work to Berno fell. For if Guido was thirty-four years old during the time of John XX, as the old codex of the musical *Micrologus* testifies—the work being attributed to him, as Baronius reports—while the author of the *Micrologus on Ecclesiastical Observances* wrote after Gregory VII, whom we have noted as dying in 1085, it will be necessary to suppose that Guido wrote this work on ecclesiastical observances when he was more than ninety years old.

Did Guido experience what the next century experienced in Martin Navarro: namely, that even at ninety years of age and more he still continued to write?
