# CHAPTER I — On the Introit of the Mass

[Col. 0979A]

When the priest prepares for Mass, according to Roman custom he chants these psalms: “How lovely,” “You blessed,” “Incline, O Lord,” and “I believed” (Psalms LXXXIII, LXXXIV, LXXXV, CXV); then *Kyrie eleison*—“Lord, have mercy”—and the Our Father, together with prayers and a petition for sins, namely, that inwardly and outwardly he may be able to please the High Priest, whom he desires to placate for himself and for all Christians through the most holy offering.

When prepared, he enters the altar area and makes confession, because it is written: “The wise man is his own accuser at the beginning” (Proverbs XII); and the priests of the ancient Law were accustomed to offer first for themselves, then for the people (Hebrews VII; Leviticus XVI).

Meanwhile the antiphon for the Introit is sung. It earned this name from the entrance of the priest to the altar.

[Col. 0979B]

[Note: [Col. 0979D] Amalarius likewise says this in book III, chapter 5.]

Pope Celestine, forty-fifth in order, instituted that it should be said at the Introit. Until his time, only Paul’s Epistle and the Gospel had been read before the sacrifice. The Litanies that follow are believed to have been adopted from the Greeks because of the Greek words themselves.

# CHAPTER II — On the *Gloria in Excelsis* and *Dominus vobiscum*

On every feast that has a complete office, except during Advent, Septuagesima, and the feast of the Innocents, both priest and bishop say the *Gloria in excelsis*. It is never prescribed to be read after midday, except on Maundy Thursday, where the chrism is prepared, and on the Saturdays of Easter and Pentecost.

Then, turning toward the people, he says: “The Lord be with you.” The response is: “And with your spirit.”

It should be noted from these words that there ought to be several responding and one giving the greeting. For just as “And with your spirits” would be an inept response when there was one person giving the greeting, so “The Lord be with you” is incongruous when only one person or no one at all is present.

The most blessed apostolic Fathers, Anacletus—fifth after blessed Peter—and Soter, thirteenth in order, confirmed this by their decrees, so that the priest should always be at least the third person when celebrating Mass.

Zacharias, an apostolic man, ninety-third in order, decreed that priests should not enter to celebrate the solemnities of Mass carrying a staff, nor stand at the altar with covered heads.

The holy Fathers also, at the Council of Orléans, chapter 3, decreed that at the priest’s greetings not only clerics and those dedicated to God, but the entire people as well, should respond with one voice.

# CHAPTER III — On the First Prayer at Mass

There follows the prayer which they call the Collect, because the priest, who acts as an ambassador for the people before the Lord (2 Corinthians V), gathers and concludes everyone’s petitions in that prayer.

Those prayers, however, seem more particularly to be called Collects which are offered among the Romans over the gathering of the people while they assemble to proceed from one church to another in order to celebrate the station. Thus, on the Beginning of the Fast, the prayer “Grant, we ask” is said at Saint Anastasia over the gathering of the people who are going to celebrate the station at Saint Sabina.

# CHAPTER IV — On the Number of Prayers at Mass

According to the Roman Order, we ought to say only one prayer before the reading, as Amalarius admits that he learned from the Romans themselves in the preface to his book *On the Offices*.

The institution of the offices also seems to require this: just as at one Mass we read only one reading and one Gospel, and sing one Introit—indeed, one office—so likewise we should say one prayer.

But now few observe this. Rather, many multiply the prayers to such an extent that they make their hearers displeased with them and turn the people of God away instead of drawing them to make the sacrifice.

This greatly displeases wiser men. Although at times, in accommodating themselves to others, they exceed the ancient tradition, even in their excess they generally observe moderation and pay attention to some rationale.

Therefore, even if at Mass they are not always content with only one prayer, they rarely exceed the number seven in their prayers. That number is not exceeded even by the Lord’s Prayer, which, with only seven petitions, includes everything necessary for body and soul.

They generally observe this most carefully: at Mass they say either one, three, five, or seven prayers.

One, because of the Roman tradition;

three, because the Lord is read to have prayed three times before his Passion;

five, because of the fivefold division of his Passion, in whose commemoration we celebrate these same offices;

seven, because the apostles too are read to have frequently used the seven petitions of the Lord’s Prayer for the consecration of these mysteries.

At the Nativity of the Lord, however, at the morning Mass the Romans add the prayer of Saint Anastasia, because at that same Mass they celebrate the station in the church of that martyr.

We imitate them in this addition, although we do not seem to have the same reason for making it.

The more diligent observers of the offices very rarely admit other numbers in the prayers, except those which we have noted above as marked by an appropriate mystery.

# CHAPTER V — On Authentic Prayers

They also admit other prayers only with great difficulty, unless they are ancient and Gregorian, since these are found especially in the older and more carefully corrected Sacramentaries.

For the eighth council of the African province, at which Saint Augustine—in fact, two hundred and fourteen holy Fathers—were present, decreed in chapter twelve as follows (Council of Milevis, canon 12):

> “No petitions, prayers, Masses, prefaces, commendations, or impositions of hands are to be said unless they have been approved in council.”

Likewise, the Third Council of Carthage, at which Saint Augustine was also present, says in chapter twenty-three:

> “No one at the altar shall name the Father on behalf of the Son, or the Son on behalf of the Father, but shall always direct the prayer to the Father; nor shall anyone use a prayer unless it has been approved.”

The prayer is indeed to be directed to the Father, in accordance with the Lord’s command. When the disciples asked him how they ought to pray, he instructed them:

> “When you stand to pray, say: ‘Our Father, who are in heaven’” (Matthew XI), etc.

# CHAPTER VI — On the Conclusion of Prayers

We conclude the prayers with “Through our Lord,” praying to the Father through the Son, in accordance with the command of that same Son, who instructed us in the Gospel:

> “Until now you have asked nothing of the Father in my name; ask, and you will receive” (John XVI).

He also promises the fulfillment of our petitions if we ask through him, saying:

> “Whatever you ask the Father in my name, he will give you” (John XVI).

Therefore we conclude many prayers, or nearly all of them, quite appropriately in this way: “Through our Lord.”

Very few are found that, because of the suitability of their meaning, end with another conclusion. For example:

> “Grant, we ask, almighty God, that the Savior who was born, etc. He who lives and reigns with you.”

Likewise:

> “O God, whose Son is in the heights of heaven, etc. Our Lord Jesus Christ, who lives with you, etc.”

In every conclusion we are accustomed to observe a commemoration of the Holy Trinity, as we find expressed in the more carefully corrected Sacramentaries.

[The holy Fathers observed the invocation of the Holy Trinity in prayers and blessings so diligently that they did not consider even those sacraments valid in whose making lacked the invocation of the Holy Trinity, as in the sacred rites of the Paulianists, whose baptism and ordinations they judged should be repeated when converts were received (Council of Nicaea, canon 19, and the Sixth Council, canon 97).]

It should also be known that in the customary conclusion “Through our Lord,” the Roman Order and the most ancient copies insert the name of God where it says:

> “Who lives and reigns with you, God.”

Modern usage, however, generally adds this after the name of the Holy Spirit.

This custom has become so widespread even among the Romans that carrying out the ancient tradition can now take place only with scandal. According to the Apostle (Romans XIV) and the Gospel (Matthew VIII), we ought to avoid this with the greatest care in matters so trivial.

# CHAPTER VII — Again, on the Conclusion or Confirmation of Prayers

[Col. 0981D]

According to Roman authority, we conclude no prayer with “Through him who is to come,” unless it is an exorcism, in which the devil is exorcised or adjured by divine judgment so that he may depart from God’s creature.

In the other prayers, which we conclude with “Through our Lord,” we implore the Father to assist us through the love of his Son.

In an exorcism, however, we rebuke the devil by God’s judgment so that he may flee.

All those standing present, in accordance with the ancient tradition of the holy Fathers, ought to add “Amen” as a sign of confirmation, so that they may confirm the common prayer which the priest has offered to the Lord on behalf of everyone.

Therefore, in the Secret itself he says “Through all ages of ages” more loudly, so that the preceding prayer may be confirmed by the people through “Amen.”

# CHAPTER VIII — On the Epistle to Be Read at Mass
Only to subdeacons among the lower orders does Roman authority grant permission to read the Epistle at Mass while vested in sacred vestments. Yet they earned this privilege not by their consecration, but rather by ecclesiastical concession. Hence it seems more reasonable that the priest himself read the Epistle than that he summon someone not yet ordained to read it for him. For blessed Hormisdas, the fifty-third pope after Saint Peter, deposes in chapter three anyone who, though unordained, has usurped the office of one who is ordained—an office which he certainly had never earned either by consecration or by ecclesiastical custom. [Col. 0982B] The canons have also forbidden in various councils that anyone not ordained for this purpose should read in church, chant publicly from the pulpit, say the Alleluia, or perform an exorcism anywhere.

Nothing, however, prevents a priest from carrying out the duties of the lower orders at Mass if necessity requires it; and it is evident that he holds all the lower orders, since at Mass he is vested in sacred vestments, without which, according to Roman practice, we ought not to minister at the altar. Therefore it is more fitting that he himself perform the office of subdeacon than that he permit some unordained person, not vested in sacred vestments, to perform it.

## CHAPTER IX — In which part the Gospel is to be read

[Col. 0982C]

The deacon, too, will more appropriately perform his own office at Mass than someone who is not vested in sacred vestments. For the deacon must also be clothed in an alb at the time of the oblation and the reading, according to chapter forty-one of the Fourth Council of Carthage, which Saint Augustine—in fact, two hundred and seventeen holy Fathers—attended. According to the decree of Pope Anastasius, no one sits while the Gospel is read (the text has *donec*, “until,” for *dum*, “while”); and, they say, this reverence is also shown to the apostolic reading among the Greeks.

[Note: [Col. 0981D] “Ambo” is the term used here for what was previously called the pulpit.]

When the deacon reads the Gospel, according to the Roman Order he turns in the ambo toward the south, where the males gather, not toward the north, where the women stand. For he rightly turns toward the principal sex, to which, as the Apostle ordained, the weaker sex is entrusted for instruction at home.

[Col. 0982D]

That priests do not turn toward the south when reading the Gospel, we believe to have arisen for this reason: the Order did not command them to ascend into the ambo to read, as deacons do, where they would necessarily have to turn toward the males rather than toward the females. For according to ecclesiastical custom they read at the altar, where no difference among the hearers approaches that would require those reading to turn more toward one side than the other. No women are permitted to stand there, but only the religious, on the right and on the left.

They have the book at the left corner of the altar when they read the Gospel, or when they offer the sacrifice, so that on the right side they may be freer to receive the offerings or to accomplish the altar’s sacraments.

[Col. 0983A]

Thus they appear to be turned more toward the north than toward the south when they proclaim the Gospel. From this, then, that usurpation seems to have arisen by which deacons also, contrary to the Roman Order, turn toward the north in the ambo and are not ashamed to turn toward the side of the women rather than toward that of the men. This usurpation has now become so entrenched that among most people it is held almost as an ordinance. But because it is certainly contrary to the Order and dishonorable, it is rightly rejected by the more diligent guardians of the Order.

The Order also prescribes that the one who is going to read the Gospel should make the sign of the cross on his forehead—that is, according to Augustine, on the seat of shame—in order that, with all shame cast out, he may not be ashamed, with the Apostle (Rom. 1), of the Gospel of Christ, who foretold that he would be ashamed of anyone who here was ashamed of him or of his words before human beings.

[Col. 0983B]

He should also make the sign of the cross on his breast, lest any suggestion of the devil hinder him from being able to proclaim the Gospel of God with a pure heart.

When the priest reads the Gospel, in the Roman manner he lifts the chasuble onto his right shoulder, to show that he is free from earthly attachments for evangelizing. For the same reason, deacons also, when they read, appear to place the chasuble only on their left shoulder.

Likewise, the Roman Order prescribes that incense should always precede the Gospel when it is carried to the altar or into the ambo. It does not, however, permit the offering to be incensed on the altar; Amalarius also admits in the prologue of his book *On Offices* that the Romans avoid this, although now it is practiced by many—indeed, by almost everyone.

[Col. 0983C]

[Col. 0983D]

## CHAPTER X — On arranging the offering on the altar

When the Gospel has ended, the offering is immediately to be made, while the *offerenda* is sung, which derives its name from the offering. For in an inverted order it is offered afterward, once the offering has been placed on the altar and the priest exhorts the people to pray.

Saint Alexander, fifth pope after blessed Peter, decreed that only bread and wine mixed with water should be offered in the Lord’s sacrifice, because blood and water flowed together from the Lord’s side. Hence Saint Cyprian writes in his letter to Caecilius, *On the Sacrament of the Chalice*:

> “Water must not be lacking in the Lord’s chalice together with wine, lest the people, who are signified by water according to the Apocalypse, appear to be separated from Christ.”

According to the Roman Order, the elements are to be arranged on the altar as follows: once the offering—that is, the host—has been placed on the corporal, the chalice is to be placed on the right side of the offering, as though it were to receive the Lord’s blood, which we believe flowed from the Lord’s side. For we do not doubt that the offering, or bread, is changed into the true body of Christ, just as the wine is changed into the Lord’s blood.

When priests offer without ministers, they customarily place the offering on the altar and conceal the paten beneath the corporal, perhaps because according to the Order the acolyte is to hold it wrapped during the sacrifice. The chalice is also covered, not so much for the sake of the mystery as for protection, until, after the Canon has ended, the words are said: “Let us pray, instructed by saving commandments.” It is uncovered, however, when the words are read: “Taking also this noble chalice,” and there: “Through him, and with him, and in him”; perhaps because it is lifted more safely without its covering than when covered.

[Col. 0984A]

## CHAPTER XI — What is to be said over the offering

Once the offering has been arranged on the altar, the priest says this prayer according to the Gallican Order:

> Come, almighty sanctifier, eternal God; bless this sacrifice prepared for your name. Through Christ our Lord.

Then, bowing before the altar, he says this prayer—not from any established order, but from ecclesiastical custom:

> Receive, holy Trinity, this offering, which we present to you in memory of the Passion, Resurrection, Ascension, etc.

This prayer alone is regularly used by the more diligent observers of the Order and of approved custom, both for the dead and for the living. Although they often yield to the custom of many, they nevertheless avoid what is superfluous with the greatest care.

[Col. 0984B]

The Roman Order, however, has established no prayer after the *offerenda* and before the Secret. Once the priest has risen, he exhorts the people to pray; and after the Secret has ended, he begins the Preface leading into the Canon. In it the orders of the citizens above are rightly included, because, according to the testimony of the holy Fathers, they are believed to participate in the same mysteries that are accomplished there.

Hence the angelic hymn follows, namely, “Holy, holy, holy,” which blessed Pope Sixtus, eighth in order, established should be said before the sacrifice. The priest himself must necessarily say this hymn with the others, lest he appear to have deprived himself by his own prayer—he who, in the Preface, pleaded that both his own voice and those of others might be admitted among the praises of the angels.

According to the Roman Order, we never celebrate Mass [variant: “Masses”] without light—not, indeed, to dispel darkness, since it is broad daylight, but rather as a figure of that light whose mysteries we accomplish there, without which even at midday we would grope as in the night.

[Col. 0984C]

[Col. 0984D]

## CHAPTER XII — What has been added to the Canon

We do not read explicitly who composed the prayer which, because of the regular confection of the sacraments, we call the Canon, or the Action, according to Roman usage, except that Saint Gregory testifies that a certain scholar composed it.

Nevertheless, we read that many things were inserted into this Canon by the holy Fathers. Thus Saint Alexander, fifth in order among the popes, commanded that a commemoration of the Lord’s Passion itself be inserted. Likewise Saint Pope Gregory the First added: “And order our days in your peace,” through “Through Christ our Lord.” And Leo the Great added to the Canon: “A holy sacrifice, an immaculate offering.”

Gregory himself also asserts in his *Register* that he added the Lord’s Prayer to the Canon (*Register*, book VII, letter 63, to John of Syracuse). When certain people murmured about this, he satisfied them with a humble reply, asserting that it was inappropriate for the prayer composed by a scholar to be said over the offering while the prayer which the apostles themselves, by the Lord’s institution, were believed [variant: “are believed”] to have used in the confection of these same sacraments was omitted.

[Col. 0985A]

On the chief feast days we also insert certain additions into the Canon at the place where “In communion” or “This offering, therefore” is said. We learned, however, from the more ancient and more accurate Sacramentaries that they are to be inserted on the Nativity of the Lord, on the Epiphany, at the Supper, at Easter, at the Ascension, and at Pentecost.

[These insertions cause us to understand “In communion” more clearly in itself—as though we were remaining in Catholic communion—than if we referred it to the communion of the saints mentioned afterward.]

It appears exceedingly rash for us to add anything to the Canon at our own discretion, except what we know was added, or ought to be added, by the holy Fathers—especially since among the holy Fathers themselves none are reported to have added anything except those who, endowed with apostolic authority, were able to do so.

It therefore seems best that in this matter we should not exceed the limits of our fathers, nor make ourselves guilty of opposing apostolic authority by daring to enlarge the Canon with additions of our own, since this belongs exclusively to apostolic authority.

[Col. 0985B]

[Col. 0985B]

## CHAPTER XIII — What is superfluous in the Canon

Some customarily insert their own prayers where it says, “Remember, Lord, your male and female servants,” and before the commemoration of the dead. Likewise, after the name of the lord pope or of one’s own bishop, they add: “And all orthodox people and those who cultivate the Catholic and apostolic faith,” but this is superfluous.

For the Order immediately grants us, in the following verse, where it says, “Remember, Lord, your male and female servants,” permission to commemorate all the living whomsoever we wish.

After a short interval they also add: “For whom we offer to you,” whereas in the more ancient and more reliable Sacramentaries those offering there are found written only in the third person.

Likewise, at the words “Therefore, mindful, Lord, we your servants,” they commemorate the Nativity of the Lord, although according to the Apostle in such a sacrifice we ought to proclaim not the Nativity of the Lord but his death. Hence Saint Ambrose writes in his books of the Sacraments:

> “Whenever the sacrifice is offered, the Lord’s death, the Lord’s resurrection, and the Lord’s ascension are signified.”

Saint Augustine also confirms this by his testimony.

[Col. 0985C]

Therefore we commemorate there only the Passion, Resurrection, and Ascension.

Whoever carefully examines the more ancient and more accurate Sacramentaries will unquestionably judge all the additions that we have marked as superfluous and worthy of erasure.

It should be understood, however, that Roman authority permits the names of living faithful people to be included where it says, “Remember, Lord, your male and female servants”; likewise the names of the dead where it says again, “Remember also those.” But we ought not to include the names of other saints except those whom we find written in the Canon from ancient times, with the exception of the prayer after the Lord’s Prayer, where according to the Order we may include the names of as many saints as we wish.

[Col. 0986A]

It should also be noted that the persons of prelates and subjects are distinguished in the Canon. When we mention the name of the apostolic lord or of our bishop, we appear to be speaking of prelates. We speak of subjects in the following verse, where we say: “Remember, Lord, your male and female servants.”

Likewise, the words “This offering of our service” refer to prelates. What follows—“and also of your entire family”—appears to indicate subjects. Again, “Therefore, mindful, Lord, we your servants” refers to prelates, while “and also your holy people” unquestionably speaks of subjects.

[Col. 0985D]

[Col. 0986B]

## CHAPTER XIV — On the signs made over the offering

Regarding the signs that different people make differently over the offering, we have decided to take our form above all from the apostolic see, from which we received the order and origin of the entire Christian religion.

In our own time God placed over that see such a governor as Pope Gregory—of venerable memory, I say—[Note: Gregory VII.] who, having been raised and educated at Rome from childhood under ten of his predecessors, investigated all the apostolic traditions with the greatest diligence and took the greatest care to put what he had investigated into practice. We have therefore decided above all to imitate this teacher, pre-eminent in religion and authority—or rather, through him, the apostolic tradition—in the consecration of the mysteries.

[Col. 0986C]

As we ourselves received from him and from the bishops who imitated him, we always observe an odd number in the administration of the signs over the offering: namely, by making one cross, or three, or five. This is certainly not without a definite mystical reason.

In one and three we signify the one and triune God. In five we signify the Lord’s fivefold Passion. An odd number is rightly used frequently in ecclesiastical offices, unity preventing it from ever being divided into two equal parts, just as the unity of the holy Church does not permit it to be divided into two.

At the beginning, where it says, “These gifts, these offerings, these holy sacrifices,” we make only three crosses together over the bread and wine. We never separate the bread from the chalice in making the sign, except where they are named separately in the Canon.

We make the sign over them together in such a way that the upright part of the cross extends only over the bread, while the transverse part extends over the chalice. For the upright part of the cross supported the Lord’s body, while the transverse part stretched out his arms. Hence the chalice is fittingly placed beneath his arm, as though it were to receive the Lord’s blood from his side.

[Col. 0986D]

When we say, “This offering, therefore,” we bow toward the altar, after the example of Christ, who humbled himself for us unto the death of the cross. When we rise, at the words “blessed, inscribed (*adscriptam*), ratified,” we make three crosses over both together. For here not only the offering is to be signed, as some do; both are signed in the offering.

For it follows that it may become for us the body and blood—“this offering” being understood. When this is said, the fourth cross is made separately over the bread and the fifth over the chalice.

We fittingly made only three crosses over both earlier, although we had five words equivalent for making the signs: “blessed, inscribed (*adscriptam*), ratified, reasonable, acceptable.” This was so that we would not exceed the number five and could appropriately make the fifth cross over the chalice as an indication of the fifth wound, from which blood flowed.

[Col. 0987A]

## CHAPTER XV — On taking the offering into the hands

Next the bread is taken into the hands and blessed before it is placed back on the altar. The chalice, too, is blessed after being lifted and before it is set down. For the Lord himself is also read in the Gospel to have blessed both before releasing them from his hands: “Having taken it in his hands, he blessed it; afterward he gave it to the disciples” (Matt. 26).

[Col. 0987B]

Likewise, where it says, “A pure victim, a holy victim, an immaculate victim,” we make three crosses over both together, because we understand both together in the same words. We make the fourth cross over the bread and the fifth separately over the chalice, again signifying the Lord’s blood flowing from the Lord’s side.

## CHAPTER XVI — On the commemoration of the Lord’s Passion

It should be noted that throughout the entire Canon the commemoration of the Lord’s Passion is especially enacted, according to the Lord’s command in the Gospel: “Whenever you do this, you shall do it in memory of me” (Matt. 26; Luke 22); and according to the Apostle: “Whenever you take this, you shall proclaim the Lord’s death” (1 Cor. 10).

[Col. 0987C]

Hence throughout the entire Canon the priest himself, by extending his hands, signifies not so much the devotion of the mind as Christ’s extension on the cross, according to the words: “I stretched out my hands all day long” (Isa. 65).

The fingers therefore should not always be contracted, as some do out of excessive caution. We are poorly cautious if we do not strive above all to imitate Christ. It is therefore fitting that we extend our hands during the Canon, while observing this precaution: that we touch nothing with our fingers except the Lord’s body.

It should also be noted that the words “Through Christ our Lord” occur five times in the Canon; and in this fivefold conclusion the Lord’s five wounds are not unfittingly signified.

The priest customarily withdraws his hands only rarely, except when he must necessarily bless the offering placed before him. As we said earlier, the priest also indicates the Lord’s humiliation unto the cross when he bows down to the altar, saying: “This offering, therefore.” Immediately afterward the account of the Lord’s Passion is arranged, and its type is observed up to the words “We humbly beseech you.”

There, as the priest bows toward the altar, he signifies that Christ, with his head bowed on the cross, gave up his spirit.

[Col. 0987D]

## CHAPTER XVII — On the commemoration of the dead and the other observances up to the end of the Canon

After Christ’s death on the cross comes the commemoration of the dead,

[Col. 0988A] because no other dead [variant: “deceased”] are to be commemorated except those who were redeemed in Christ’s death and ended this life in Christ.

When the priest raises his voice, saying, “And also for us sinners,” he signifies that centurion who, having seen Christ’s death, raised his voice, saying: “Truly this was the Son of God.”

He makes three crosses together over the body and blood when he says, “You sanctify, enliven, and bless,” in honor of the holy Trinity.

Afterward, with the Lord’s body, we make four crosses over the chalice, saying, “Through him, and with him, and in him,” and a fifth on the side of the chalice, again signifying the wound of the Lord’s side. Hence, according to the Roman Order, we touch the chalice from that same side with the offering.

Many, however, make only three crosses over the chalice and two on its side. But this seems inappropriate, since Christ had only one wound in his side.

[Col. 0988B]

As we said earlier, Pope Gregory of venerable memory established this practice; blessed Anselm, bishop of Lucca, testified that he had learned it from Gregory and always observed it in this way, firmly impressing upon us that we too should observe it.

When we say, “World without end,” we lift the body together with the chalice and immediately place them on the altar and cover them. For Joseph also lifted the Lord’s body from the cross and, once it had been placed in the tomb, covered it with a stone.

Up to this point the chalice appeared to be covered for protection; from then on it is covered more for the sake of the mystery. For just as Christ was covered in the tomb for three days, so we cover the Lord’s body and chalice until we complete the three parts of the prayer: namely, the Preface of the Lord’s Prayer, the Lord’s Prayer itself, and the prayer that follows, which is called the embolism of the Lord’s Prayer.

[Col. 0988C]

According to the Roman Order, when the words “and secure from every disturbance” are said, the archdeacon receives from the subdeacon the uncovered paten, which the acolyte had held wrapped. After kissing it, he gives it to one of the deacons to hold, so that the breaking may be performed upon it.

Therefore, a priest who is offering the sacrifice without a minister takes it again from the same place, where it had been hidden beneath the corporal, and, after kissing it, places it on the altar in order to break the host upon it.

When he says, “Through our Lord,” he breaks the host on the right side, according to the Order, to signify the piercing of the Lord’s side. Then he breaks the larger portion in two, so that he can make three portions from the Lord’s body.

[Col. 0988D]

For he must place one into the chalice, making the sign of the cross, when he says, “The peace of the Lord be always with you,” to signify the union of body and soul in Christ’s resurrection.

He himself, the priest, must take another before partaking of the chalice, according to the Lord’s institution. He necessarily leaves the third for those who are to receive Communion or for the sick. This too is not without a definite mystical reason.

For the Lord’s body is understood in three ways: one is that which rose from the dead, signified by the particle placed into the blood; another is that which still lives on earth, signified by the particle consumed by the priest; the third is that which already rests in Christ, aptly represented by the third particle preserved on the altar, which we customarily call the viaticum of the dying.

## CHAPTER XVIII — On the breaking of the bread and Communion

[Col. 0989A]

After the bread has been placed into the chalice, according to the Roman Order the priest says silently:

> May there be a mingling and consecration of the body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ.

Blessed Pope Innocent, forty-fifth in order, established that the peace should be given after the sacraments had been accomplished.

When we give the peace, we customarily say:

> Peace be with you.

The response is:

> And with your spirit.

Peace is fittingly given before Communion, because whoever presumes to receive Communion without first being reconciled to his brother eats and drinks judgment upon himself.

Pope Sergius, eighty-sixth in order, established that during the breaking of the Lord’s body the *Agnus Dei* should be sung by clergy and people, so that the one whose body we see and believe to be broken there may be merciful to us.

[Col. 0989B]

Once the breaking has been performed, all should receive Communion while the antiphon is sung, which derives its name from Communion; a psalm with the *Gloria Patri* is also to be added if necessary.

It should be understood that this same Antiphon always has the same psalm as the Introit, if it does not have its own psalm from which it appears to have been taken.

The prayer that we say while bowing before receiving Communion is not from the Order but from the tradition of religious people, namely:

> Lord Jesus Christ, who by the will of the Father …

Likewise, there is the prayer:

> The body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ,

which we say when we distribute the Eucharist with others.

[Col. 0989C]

There are also many other prayers which they frequently use for the peace and for private Communion. But the more diligent observers of ancient traditions have taught us to pursue brevity in such private prayers and have preferred that we occupy ourselves with the public prayers in the office of the Mass.

For blessed Pope Innocent, writing to Saints Augustine and Aurelius, bishops, asserts that we can profit more from common and public prayers than from individual and private prayers.

[Col. 0989D]

## CHAPTER XIX — On avoiding intinction

It is not authentic for certain people to dip the Lord’s body and distribute it dipped to the people as the completion of Communion. For the Roman Order contradicts this: on Good Friday it commands that unconsecrated wine be consecrated [the Roman Order reads not “consecrate” but “sanctify,” and rightly so: on Good Friday the wine is not consecrated, but sanctified by the insertion of the Lord’s body] with the Lord’s Prayer and the placing of the Lord’s body into it, so that the people may be able to receive Communion fully.

It would certainly command this superfluously if the dipped body of the Lord from the previous day were preserved and the dipped element appeared sufficient for the people to receive Communion.

Pope Julius, thirty-sixth in order, also, writing to the bishops of Egypt, completely forbids this kind of intinction and teaches that the bread separately and the chalice separately are to be received, according to the Lord’s institution.

Hence blessed +Gelasius, fifty-first in order [forty-ninth], writing to certain bishops, commanded that those who, after receiving the Lord’s body, abstained from participation in the chalice be excommunicated.

[Note: You have the true meaning of Gelasius’s words in Algerus, chapter 8.]

[Col. 0990A]

For in the same decree he himself asserts:

> Such a division of the sacraments cannot occur without great sacrilege.

[Col. 0990B]

After everyone has received Communion, the priest says this prayer silently, according to the Roman Order:

> What we have taken with our mouth …

When this has ended, the prayer or prayers to be said after Communion follow. They should correspond in number and order to the prayers said before the reading, or to those said as the Secret before the Preface.

These prayers are not offered for those who are about to receive Communion, but for those who have already received it, according to the proper meaning of their name. Therefore, those who desire to be strengthened by the blessing of these prayers should not neglect to receive Communion before them.

When these things have ended, the following is said:

> Let us bless the Lord,

or:

> Go, the dismissal is made,

provided, however, that it is a feast which ought to have the *Gloria in excelsis*.

Everyone responds:

> Thanks be to God,

according to the Apostle, giving thanks for the benefits bestowed.

[Col. 0990C]

## CHAPTER XX — A recapitulation of what precedes in the Mass

To repeat briefly what has preceded: after the priest has signified the Lord’s resurrection through the joining of the Lord’s body and blood, he must next offer peace to the people, just as Christ offered peace to his disciples after the resurrection, saying:

> Peace be with you.

The breaking of the offering suggests to us the breaking of bread which the Lord performed before his disciples after his resurrection.

The Communion of the people represents that banquet which the Lord is read to have held with his disciples after his resurrection—not just once (Luke 24).

Before departing from them for heaven after the final banquet, he also blessed them, just as the priest blesses the people with the prayer after Communion. He is now about to depart from them shortly; yet first, by the words “Go, the dismissal is made,” he announces that he is departing, as a figure of the angels who, when the Lord had departed from the disciples, said to them:

> Men of Galilee, why do you stand looking into heaven?

and the rest (Acts 1).

When they heard this, the disciples, worshiping the Lord, returned to Jerusalem with great joy. In the same way, after rendering thanks to God, the people return home with joy.

## CHAPTER XXI — On the blessing after Mass

[Col. 0990D]

First, however, the people are blessed by the bishop, if he is present; otherwise, by the priest who celebrated the Mass. Yet blessed Pope Damasus says that this is not permitted to priests, when he discusses the empty superstition of chorepiscopi—provided that the corruption of the exemplar has not deceived us.

But Pope Leo the Great and blessed Pope Gelasius, his successors, eminently instructed in ecclesiastical offices, in their decrees—in which they describe with the greatest care what is and is not permitted to priests—by no means forbid them to give the blessing, except when a bishop is present.

[Col. 0991A]

Blessed Jerome also, cardinal presbyter of the holy Roman Church, who under blessed Damasus and after him, down to Sixtus, his successor, watched over ecclesiastical institutions with the greatest zeal, states—writing to Rusticus, bishop of Narbonne, about ecclesiastical orders—that priests should not be forbidden to bless the people:

> “If a priest consecrates Christ, when he blesses the sacraments on God’s altar, ought he not to bless the people, since he has been deemed worthy to consecrate Christ?”

And shortly afterward:

> “Let the priests do this in your churches [variant: ‘their churches’], as they do at Rome, or in the East, in Africa, in Spain, in Britain, in Gaul, and in all places where humility endures.”

[Col. 0991B]

From these statements we can infer that blessed Pope Damasus either did not say that such a blessing was unlawful for priests, or, if he did say it, that ecclesiastical custom nevertheless prevailed in this matter. His words can especially be understood in such a way that he was teaching priests that they could not usurp this as something belonging to their own office, while they did not fail to recognize that it could be granted to them by episcopal authority.

For the confirmation of neophytes has likewise been completely separated from the office of priests, although blessed Pope Gregory the First is read to have granted it to certain priests when writing to Januarius, bishop of Cagliari:

> “Likewise, priests earned the right to receive penitents, not from their own consecration, but from the concession of bishops. This will not be hidden from anyone who carefully examines their order of consecration or the statutes of the holy Fathers.”

[Col. 0991C]

The Council of Agde, in chapter forty-four, also appears to forbid priests to bless the people. But they interpret this prohibition as concerning only episcopal blessing. This blessing, according to chapter eighteen of the Council of Toledo [Note: This canon is now numbered 30. Gratian nevertheless cites it under title C. 44.] and the testimony of Saint Augustine to Bishop Paulinus, ought [variant: “is customarily”] to be given to the people before Communion by bishops alone.

But if anyone should think that this was said about the very blessing under discussion, the judgment of a provincial council nevertheless cannot prejudice so general an ecclesiastical custom.

[Col. 0991D]

Perhaps this kind of blessing was formerly forbidden to priests because it appeared to belong to the episcopal office and was not yet considered so necessary for the ecclesiastical assembly. For in ancient times only those who received Communion took part in the confection of the sacraments; and the prayer after Communion, which was instituted for communicants alone, could serve them as a blessing.

Among modern people, however, once the people had ceased to receive Communion but did not withdraw from the divine mysteries, it was necessarily permitted that they be blessed by a priest, lest they appear to depart deprived both of blessing and of Communion.

Whether this was permitted to priests by bishops for that reason or for another, it has nevertheless now become so universally customary that it cannot in any way be omitted by priests among the people without grave scandal, unless perhaps the apostolic see should wish to prohibit it generally and synodally.

[Col. 0992A]

## CHAPTER XXII — What the priest should do after Mass

When everything has ended, the priest [variant: “presbyter”] kisses the altar, saying:

> May it please you, holy Trinity.

Then, removing his sacred vestments, he sings the hymn of the three boys, according to what the Fathers decreed in chapter fourteen of the Fourth Council of Toledo—namely, that any priest who neglected to say this hymn after Mass should be subjected to examination.

He also adds the psalm “Praise the Lord in his holy places” in thanksgiving, together with the Lord’s Prayer and the verses appropriate to it, and concludes it with the prayer:

> O God, who [didst act for] the three boys …

[Col. 0992B]

It should be understood, according to the decrees of the pontiffs, that a priest is not permitted in the presence of a bishop—unless the bishop commands it—to celebrate the sacrifice, bless the people, greet them, or exhort them.

Therefore, when he reads the Gospel in the presence of a bishop, he asks him for a blessing. Likewise, when he wishes to celebrate the sacrifice, he bows to the bishop for permission; the bishop also bows with the people for the final blessing.

## CHAPTER XXIII — A brief description of the celebration of Mass

When the priest prepares for Mass, he first sings the psalms “How beloved,” “You have blessed,” “Incline,” and “I believed, therefore …”

Then:

> Lord, have mercy.  
> Our Father.  
> And lead us not into temptation.  
> Verse: I said, Lord.  
> Turn again, Lord.  
> Let mercy be shown.  
> Priests.  
> Look upon our Protector.  
> Lord, hear us.

[Col. 0992C]

Prayer:

> Take away from us, Lord, our iniquities and our sins, so that we may be worthy to enter with pure minds.

Another:

> We ask, Lord, that you both go before our actions by your inspiration and accompany them by your assistance, so that every work of ours may always begin through you, and, once begun through you, be brought to completion. Through our Lord, etc.

Once prepared, he comes to the altar, saying:

> Antiphon: I will go in to the altar of God.  
> Psalm: Judge me, O God, and discern …

And he makes confession:

> I confess to almighty God, to these holy ones, to all the saints, and to you, brother, that I have sinned in thought, in speech, in deed, and in the pollution of mind and body. Therefore I beg you: pray for me.

> May almighty God have mercy on you, forgive you all your sins, deliver you from every evil, strengthen you in every good work, and bring us together—Jesus Christ, the Son of the living God—into eternal life. Amen.

[Col. 0992D]

> May almighty and merciful Lord grant us indulgence and remission of all our sins. Amen.

When the priest receives the offering, he says: “May our sacrifice be acceptable to almighty God.” Then, having placed the chalice on the altar to the right of the offering, he says: “Come, almighty Sanctifier, eternal God, and bless this sacrifice prepared for your name. Through Christ, etc.” And, bowing before the altar, he says: “Receive, holy Trinity, this offering which we offer to you in memory of the passion, resurrection, and ascension of our Lord Jesus Christ, and in honor of holy Mary, Mother of God, Saint Peter, Saint Paul, and these and all your saints, so that it may profit them for honor and us for salvation, and so that they may deign to intercede for us, whose memory we commemorate on earth. Through Christ, etc.” Then: “Pray.” The secret prayer follows.

The Canon according to Roman authority is as follows:

In the first place, those which we offer to you for your holy Catholic Church: may you deign to grant her peace, guard her, unite her, and govern her throughout the whole world, together with your servant, our pope, and our bishop.”

They offer you this sacrifice of praise for themselves and all their own, for the redemption of their souls, and for the hope of their salvation and well-being; to you, the eternal, living, and true God, they render their vows.

Whenever you do this, you will do it in memory of me.’”

## CHAPTER XXIV — On the Spring Fast

[Source column anchors: 0995D, “first week of Lent”; 0996A, “the fast precede it”; 0996B, “June, September, and December”; 0996C, “twelve bishops assembled at Mainz”; 0996D, “within Lent”; 0997A, “observed with Lent according to the lunar month”; 0997B, “we must observe this without any doubt.”]

Pope Gregory VII, when he presided over the Apostolic See, decreed that the fast called the March fast should be celebrated every year in the first week of Lent, just as the holy Fathers are said to have instituted it. For Saint Gregory I, pope, assigned the offices of this fast to the first week of Lent both in the Sacramentary and in the Gradual and Antiphonary books. Likewise, Saint Jerome, in the Book of the Comes, assigned readings and Gospels concerning this fast to that same week. The vacant Sunday itself, which Saint Gregory wished to be the second Sunday in Lent, clearly indicates that the March fast must nevertheless precede it every year in the first week. For that Sunday would not properly be called vacant if it were not immediately followed by the Saturday of eleven readings, which is characteristic of all vacant Sundays: since they lack their own office, they are supplied from the preceding week, if it is necessary that they be taken. Hence this Sunday of which we are speaking borrowed the office of the fast from the preceding Wednesday. It is therefore necessary that the fast precede it, since that Sunday receives its name and office from nothing other than its precedence.

Moreover, the younger Pope Gregory, writing concerning the ordination [order] of Saint Boniface, archbishop to the people of Mainz, commanded that the ordination assigned to the March fast should always be celebrated at the beginning of Lent together with that fast. The most blessed Pope Leo I also, in his sermon on the fast of the seventh month, declared that the spring fast should be celebrated in Lent, the summer fast at Pentecost, and the autumnal fast in the seventh month. Likewise, blessed Pope Gelasius, in his decretals, chapter 11, decreed that the ordinations of priests and deacons should take place only at fixed times—namely, during the fasts of the fourth, seventh, and tenth months, that is, June, September, and December, and also during the fast at the beginning of Lent, which is undoubtedly understood to be the March fast.

Do you see, then, how clearly this fast is assigned, together with its ordinations, to the first week of Lent, since it is so emphatically called the fast at the beginning of Lent? This beginning of Lent, however, is to be reckoned not from the first day of the fast but from the following Sunday. For although we begin from the first day of the fast, as a kind of completion of Lenten abstinence, nevertheless, according to the assertion of Saint Ambrose, Saint Gregory, and other holy Fathers, we properly begin Lent from the following Sunday.

Let no one be disturbed by the fact that, in the time of the Emperor Henry II, twelve bishops assembled at Mainz are said to have decreed otherwise concerning this fast. Since considerable disagreement concerning such fasts had arisen among them, because they paid insufficient attention to the ancient tradition of the holy Fathers on this matter, they proposed this rule for correcting the confusion: thereafter, every year they would fast on the first Wednesday of March, the second Wednesday of June, and the third Wednesday of September. But this rule neither ought nor can prejudice apostolic authority, especially since it plainly appears to conflict with the decrees of the holy Fathers. If we observe the aforesaid rule annually, we will often fast not only during Lent but even before Lent, whereas the decrees of the apostolic men and the institution of the offices, as stated above, determine that it should always be celebrated within Lent, indeed in the first week of Lent.

We must therefore reject without hesitation whatever we see so clearly opposing apostolic authority, from which the whole beginning and form of the Christian religion and order have proceeded. Nor should it surprise you that this fast is assigned to March rather than February, although it sometimes occurs in February together with Lent. For this fast always falls either on the Kalends of March or within the lunar month of March, or on both together; it never reaches the lunar month of February. It is therefore assigned much more appropriately to March, which it never leaves, than to February, which it often does not touch at all.

This fast is indeed observed with Lent according to the lunar month, just as Easter is. Hence it is not inappropriate to assign it to March because of the lunar month, although it occurs in February. Easter likewise is always assigned to April, although it often occurs in March. Nor will this lack a plausible example, since the conferral of sacred orders sometimes takes place in February when the beginning of Lent has been moved earlier for this reason [source *praemutatio*; bracketed variant *ratio*, “reason”]. For our most reverend Fathers, distinguished in holiness and apostolic authority—namely, Simplicius, Gelasius, Symmachus, and Felix—are said to have carried out ordinations in February, after the holy Roman Church had decreed that the Ember fasts should be observed at ordinations and had promulgated that other churches should observe them in the same way.

Therefore, we must observe this without any doubt. We have, accordingly, sufficiently certain precepts and examples of the holy Fathers endowed with apostolic authority, especially since it is easier to observe what provident antiquity and authority instituted than what inconsiderate novelty and weakness devised. No one can doubt that it is easier to celebrate the same March fast every year in the same week with the same offices, without confusion, than to shift it from week to week annually amid confusion of the offices, as many are accustomed to do.

## CHAPTER XXV — On the Summer Fast

[Source column anchors: 0997C, “summer fast should be celebrated annually”; 0997D, “Saturday of twelve readings”; 0998A, “fourteen weeks between these fasts”; 0998B, “judge its decrees”; 0998C, “how rational, how canonical”; 0998D, “Lenten fast that follows Pentecost”; 0999A, “summer fast at Pentecost”; 0999B, “Saint Jerome compiled”; 0999C, “summer fast within Pentecost”; 0999D, “summer fast is always observed”; 1000A, “lunar month of May.”]

Pope Gregory VII, presiding over the Apostolic See, decreed that the summer fast should be celebrated annually within the octave of Pentecost. This easily persuaded the more discerning because of their reverence for the Apostolic See, but some doubt about the promulgation of this decree remained among the simpler-minded. For it differs considerably from the custom they had derived from certain writings that were not especially authoritative, namely, from the Council of Mainz held in the time of the Emperor Henry II. That council established this rule for the Ember fasts (canon 3): every year there should be fasting on the first Wednesday of March, the second of June, and the third of September.

Furthermore, they take into consideration what they find in certain Sacramentaries: that we should fast on the first Saturday of March, the second of June, and the third of September. They also observe the rule, attributed to Amalarius, that fourteen weeks are counted from one Saturday of twelve readings to the next. “If, then,” they say, “you fast annually within Pentecost according to the decree of the apostolic lord, you will not always be able to observe either the second Wednesday or the second Saturday of June.”

But why, like the Pharisees, do we strain out the gnat while swallowing the camel? Why, I ask, should we fear transgressing such writings more than the decree of the Apostolic See, especially when their mutual contradiction prevents them from being observed together? For if one fasts every year according to the Council of Mainz on the first Wednesday of March, the second of June, and the third of September, one cannot annually observe the first Saturday of March, the second of June, and the third of September, nor can one count fourteen weeks between these fasts according to Amalarius. This will be clear to anyone who carefully counts the intervening weeks each year.

Such rules can never be observed together except in a year when the Kalends of September fall on a Wednesday or Thursday. But Amalarius should not be criticized too severely in this matter, since he was accustomed not so much to institute a custom as to draw an appropriate pattern from one already instituted.

Why do we go over these matters again, when even if the aforesaid rules agreed with one another each year, they could nevertheless in no way prejudice the authority of the Apostolic See? We owe complete and unquestioning obedience to that authority. We never render it due obedience if we are more concerned to judge its decrees than to fulfill them. For this is the privilege of obedience: not to judge the decision of one’s teacher, at least in matters which we do not see to contradict the canonical Scriptures, but immediately to carry out what is commanded. Whoever refuses to do anything unless he has first proved by his own reasoning that it ought to be done will be judged to have satisfied not so much his teacher as the judgment of his own will.

We must therefore owe this pure obedience to all our spiritual teachers, but above all we owe it from the depths of our heart to the Apostolic See, which is the head and origin of the whole Christian religion. Since this reasoning perhaps does not satisfy the simpler-minded, it seems worthwhile to discuss the preceding decree more fully and to clarify how rational (*rationale*; bracketed variant *rationabile*, “reasonable”), how canonical, and how consonant with the holy Fathers it proves to be.

The most blessed Pope Leo I, forty-seventh in succession, by whose authority the holy Council of Chalcedon was assembled and confirmed, declared in his book of sermons that the fast of the fourth month should be celebrated only in the week of Pentecost. Nor did he say this in only one sermon, but in several, which he is recorded to have delivered on Pentecost in different years. This cannot escape the notice of anyone who carefully reads the same book. For it will be taught there most clearly that the observance of this fast descends from apostolic tradition and that it ought to be celebrated not separately but continuously [variant: “divided, but contiguous”] after the day of Pentecost.

But lest anyone think that he had ordered this concerning the Lenten fast that follows Pentecost rather than concerning the fast of the fourth month, he subsequently makes the matter clear by decreeing that fasting should take place on Wednesday and Friday within that same week and that vigils should be celebrated at Saint Peter’s on Saturday. He maintained nearly this same mode of proclamation in all his sermons when he announced the Ember fasts. For that Lent after Pentecost is imposed for observance not on everyone, as this fast is, but only on penitents. Nor is it commanded to be kept only during this three-day period within Pentecost, but during all three-day periods, or even on the six days of the weeks.

Moreover, the same apostolic man says in his sermon on the fast of the seventh month: “Let us celebrate the spring fast in Lent, the summer fast at Pentecost, and the autumnal fast in the seventh month.” There he clearly indicated that the fast of the fourth month must be celebrated only in the week of Pentecost. For if he had decreed that this fast should always take place in June, just as the autumnal fast takes place in September, he could have named June no less than September. Therefore, according to the judgment of this apostolic man, just as the autumnal fast is always to be celebrated in September, so the summer fast must always be celebrated at Pentecost.

Saint Gregory I, pope, from whom we have nearly all the ecclesiastical offices, agrees perfectly with blessed Leo. In both the Sacramentary and the daily Antiphonary, he assigns no prayers or chants to this fast except those to be said within Pentecost. The Book of the Comes, or Lectionary, which Saint Jerome compiled, likewise assigns to this fast readings pertaining to the feast of the Holy Spirit.

Just as the fast of December borrowed its offices from the Advent of the Lord, and the fast of March from Lent, so the fasts of those months are never celebrated at another time except at the time from which they also appear to derive their office. Finally, before the decree of our Pope Gregory, when the March fast sometimes occurred before Lent according to the Council of Mainz, it was nevertheless postponed until Lent because of its Lenten office. It would be inappropriate for readings specifically indicating Lent and prayers over the people belonging to the same fast to be said outside Lent.

For the same reason, then, we appropriately observe the summer fast within Pentecost, because it has borrowed its offices from that solemnity. Those who observe it outside Pentecost cause great confusion among the offices, associating Lenten chants and prayers with readings from Pentecost. They disrupt the harmony of the Pentecost offices, which the holy Fathers especially sought to preserve in such offices. Since they find no office for this fast outside Pentecost, they rashly presume to compose offices for themselves—or rather, to confuse them.

Nor should it surprise you that they prefer to find this fast assigned to June rather than May, although, according to the preceding discussion, it is celebrated more often in May. For Pentecost itself, with which this fast is always observed, is celebrated more often in May than in June, yet according to the reckoning of the moon it is always assigned to June. This feast, like Easter, is observed annually not according to the reckoning of the months but according to the lunar months. Easter is always assigned to April, and Pentecost to June, because of the observance of the lunar months belonging to those months, although they often anticipate those months, as the lunar months themselves do.

For the same reason we assign this fast to June, since we must observe it every year with Pentecost under the same lunar month. This fast always observes the lunar month of June and often also its Kalends, but never the lunar month of May, nor does it always reach its Kalends. It always possesses either the Kalends or the lunar month of June, whereas it very often possesses neither the Kalends nor the lunar month of May. It is therefore more appropriately assigned to June, which it never leaves, than to May, which it often entirely bypasses.

Whoever wishes faithfully to consider these reasons, setting aside the spirit of contention, will undoubtedly judge that the apostolic lord, in instituting the spring or summer fast, instituted not so much his own decree as that of the holy Fathers. He will also have no doubt that the same decree, confirmed by authoritative arguments, must be observed universally.

## CHAPTER XXVI — On the Autumnal Fast

[Source column anchor 1000B: “Leo, Gelasius, and the others.”]

According to the decrees of the holy Fathers Leo, Gelasius, and the others, we must celebrate the autumnal fast in the seventh month. Yet neither the institution of the offices, nor the assignment of the vacant Sunday, nor the decrees of the holy Fathers appear to assign it to any particular week as specifically as they assign the other fasts. It is, however, the ecclesiastical custom to fast on the third Saturday of September. This custom ought certainly to suffice for us, especially since it nowhere appears to contradict the apostolic institutions.

## CHAPTER XXVII — On the Winter Fast

[Source column anchor 1000C: “called the following Sunday vacant.”]

According to the tradition of the holy Roman Church, the winter fast must always be celebrated in the third week of the Advent of the Lord, just as the holy Fathers instituted it. They assigned the offices of this fast to that same week and called the following Sunday vacant. We require no special decree for this, since in it we do not depart from the footsteps of the saints.

## CHAPTER XXVIII — On the Offices of These Fasts

[Source column anchors: 1000D, “on Wednesday and Friday”; 1001A, “following readings are to be read”; 1001B, “Gospel: ‘The fig tree’”; 1001C, “holy Church supplicates in the gradual”; 1001D, “the salvation of the people is requested”; 1002A, “fuller office than the others”; 1002B, “hymn of those same children.”]

As for the annual shifting of the offices in the spring fast, over which we have labored so fruitlessly until now, it is not necessary for us to labor any longer. According to the ancient institution, we must observe all the offices of this fast in their proper place and order, just as they were instituted.

In the summer fast, however, we appropriately observe each year the order of the offices which our predecessors maintained in the same fast when they observed it within Pentecost. Namely, on Wednesday and Friday, the chant and reading assigned to those days in that week are to be used.

On Saturday, together with the office appointed there, the following readings are to be read:

Reading: “Love justice”; “Hear, Jacob”; “Rejoice”; “I will pour forth.”

At Mass: “Justified.”

These all correspond most suitably to the feast of the Holy Spirit.

The Gospel is “Jesus went out,” as we also find it arranged in the ancient Breviaries. This too must be observed: on Wednesday or Saturday we should not say the Lenten offertories—namely, “I meditated” and “Lord God of my salvation”—but, in honor of the Holy Spirit, we should sing “Alleluia,” then the offertory “Send forth your Spirit,” for both days.

Nor should we add the Graduals, but rather Alleluia [Note: [Col. 0999] A word appears to be missing; this Alleluia is sung after Reading IV] to the aforesaid readings: “The Spirit of the Lord”; “The Paraclete”; “Send forth”; “Come, Holy Spirit.”

In the autumnal fast we observe everything as it was instituted.

On Wednesday: antiphon, “Rejoice”; gradual, “Who is like”; gradual, “Tribulations”; offertory, “I meditated”; communion, “Eat.” Readings: “Behold, days are coming”; “He was gathered.” Gospel: “One answering.”

On Friday: antiphon, “Let the heart rejoice”; gradual, “Turn”; offertory, “Bless”; communion, “Take away from me.” Reading: “Turn.” Gospel: “He was asking Jesus.”

All these have great harmony with one another.

On Saturday: antiphon, “Come, let us adore”; offertory, “Lord God of my salvation”; communion, “In the seventh month.” Readings: “On the tenth day”; “On the fifteenth”; “Our Lord God”; “It came to pass.” Gospel: “The fig tree.”

The Graduals are the same as those in the spring fast. Although different books assign these differently, they are found in very many books as follows: “Protector”; “Propitious”; “May it be directed”; “Save your people.” These are arranged in the autumnal fast as in the spring fast, except that in the autumnal fast “Protector” is sung after the gradual “Propitious.”

This appears to be demanded by the harmony of the offices. For in the spring fast the first reading, “Look, Lord, from the sanctuary, and bless your people,” corresponds extremely well to the gradual “Our protector,” from which the following prayer, “Protector,” also begins. The gradual “Propitious” is not incongruously adapted to the second reading. For what is promised to the people of Israel in the reading concerning bodily deliverance, the holy Church supplicates in the gradual to be fulfilled spiritually for us, so that the nations of demons may not prevail over us, just as the nations of the pagans did not prevail over them.

In the autumnal fast, “Propitious” is placed first because it also better suits the first reading, which prescribes for us the day of propitiation and that God be propitious to us. The gradual “Protector” more aptly suits the second reading, in which the children of Israel are commanded to celebrate annually for seven days under the protection of booths.

The third gradual, “May it be directed,” corresponds excellently to the third reading in both fasts, because in the spring fast Jonathan, and in September Micah, direct their prayers to the Lord for the people of God. The fourth gradual likewise corresponds to the fourth reading. For in the spring fast the salvation of the people is requested, while in the autumnal fast it is promised to the people, provided that they have not departed from the truth.

It therefore seems sufficiently appropriate that we follow the tradition of those books which assign the same Graduals equally to the spring and autumnal fasts. For, as we have said, they have great harmony with the readings of both fasts, and the holy Fathers taught us to attend to this harmony above all in the arrangement of the offices.

In the winter fast, which must always be observed on the Saturday immediately before the vigil of the Nativity of the Lord, nothing in the offices is changed. It should be noted that all the apostolic men, from blessed Peter through Pope Simplicius, celebrated ordinations only during the December fast, as is read in the Roman Pontifical. Hence this fast not undeservedly has a fuller office than the others. For the offices of the others are now supplied entirely, now in large part, from elsewhere through their weekdays.

In every Ember fast, except within Pentecost, we bend the knees. On Wednesday, this is done only at the first prayer, which is spoken without a salutation. The second is spoken with a salutation and without genuflection. On Friday the prayer is recited with a salutation and genuflection. On Saturday, all the prayers are preceded by genuflection without a salutation, except the prayer concerning the furnace, which requires a salutation without genuflection.

We omit bending the knees at that prayer, following the example of the three children who refused to adore the statue with the pagans. The order also commands that we should not sit during the hymn of those same children, lest, while they were laboring in the furnace, we appear devoted to the inactivity of sitting.

Although this Saturday has only six readings, it is nevertheless called a Saturday of twelve readings because in ancient times the same readings were read twice, namely in Greek and in Latin.

It should also be known that Pope and martyr Callistus established that such fasts should be celebrated four times a year; previously they had been celebrated only three times a year. The same apostolic man testifies to this in his letter to Bishop Benedict, his first decretal epistle.

## CHAPTER XXIX — On the Vacant Sundays

[Source column anchors: 1002C, “preceding Wednesdays of the fasts”; 1002D, “attributed rather to Sunday”; 1003A, “canons of Nicaea entirely forbid on Sunday.”]

The four Sundays which immediately follow these fasts are called vacant in the Book of Sacraments because they lack their own offices. Hence, according to Roman custom, they are supplied from the preceding Wednesdays of the fasts, as are the two Sundays which follow the spring and winter fasts.

The Sunday after the summer fast is supplied not from Wednesday but, much more suitably, from the office of Pentecost, since it is its octave. After the autumnal fast, some supply the following Sunday from Wednesday, in order by this supplement to remedy the scarcity of Sunday offices in summer. The Romans, however, remedy this deficiency by repeating Sunday offices. Hence they usually omit there the aforesaid compilation [or: completion] from Wednesday as unnecessary.

These Sundays were anciently vacant from the office because, according to the decrees of the holy Fathers, the celebration of ordinations took place so late on Saturday that it was attributed rather to Sunday than to Saturday. For the most blessed Pope Leo I testified that ordinations could lawfully be celebrated until the morning of Sunday, provided that the Saturday fast continued. Indeed, writing to Dioscorus the bishop, he ordered that levitical and priestly ordinations should never be celebrated except on Sunday:

“Let no benediction,” he says, “ever be given for those being consecrated except on Sunday, which begins from Saturday evening.”

Likewise, blessed Pope Gelasius, his successor, writing to all the bishops, decreed that ordinations should be celebrated toward evening on the Saturdays of the Ember fasts. Hence the Roman Order forbids the prayer over the people on the Saturday of ordinations in Lent, at which the ancients bent not only their heads but also their knees, something which the canons of Nicaea entirely forbid on Sunday.

Saint Gregory likewise marked the days of ordinations in his homilies as Sundays. In particular, he expounded these two Gospels—“In the fifteenth year” and “The fig tree”—to the people. Saint Pope Leo also expounded the Gospel “Jesus took” concerning the spring fast, as though providing for the Sunday within which he had always established that ordinations should take place.

## CHAPTER XXX — On the Advent of the Lord

[Source column anchors: 1003B, “Sometimes (*aliquando*; variant *aliquanto*)”; 1003C, “Christ’s infancy, rather than his passion.”]

From the Advent of the Lord until his Nativity, we omit *Te Deum laudamus*, *Gloria in excelsis Deo*, and *Ite missa est*, because the glory of the New Testament is greater than that of the Old, whose type we observe during the Advent of the Lord. Sometimes (*aliquando*; variant *aliquanto*, “somewhat”) we receive the Nativity of the Lord more festively, if on that day we begin anew these glorifications that have been suppressed for some time.

Some use chasubles instead of dalmatics during the Advent of the Lord. Others vest in the customary manner, because they say Mass at terce and the *Alleluia*, as throughout the whole summer. Nevertheless, at the nativity of the apostles or at the dedication of a church, we do not omit the aforesaid glorifications. From this point until after the octave of Pentecost, we are accustomed to omit the customary commemoration of the holy cross at vespers or matins, on Friday, and of the Holy Trinity on Sundays. For some people resume the commemoration of the holy cross during the very brief interval that sometimes separates the Purification of Saint Mary from Septuagesima; this does not seem especially fitting, since at that time Christ’s infancy, rather than his passion, is sung and read.

## CHAPTER XXXI — On the Gospel: “When he drew near”

On the First Sunday of Advent some read the Gospel, “There will be signs,” because Saint Gregory placed it first in his Book of Homilies. But they pay little attention to the fact that the same apostolic man did not observe such an order in that book, in which he omitted several Gospels altogether; moreover, in what he expounded, he was accustomed many times to place later passages before earlier ones. Others read the beginning of the Evangelist Mark, but because this is unusual, few agree with them.

We, however, following ancient tradition, read “When he drew near” (*Cum appropinquaret*), not preaching anything contrary to the Apostolic See if it should command otherwise [folio addition: *contraria*], but meanwhile following the authority of the holy Fathers. Saint Jerome arranged it in this way in the *Comes*, whose order Saint Gregory also followed most diligently, both when he adapted the missal prayers to the readings and Gospels in the Sacramentary, and when he arranged antiphons from those same Gospels for many days in the Antiphonary.

The Gospel itself, “When he drew near,” although historically it appears to concern the Lord’s journey toward his Passion, does not entirely forget this Advent, since the children of the Hebrews, in his praise, loudly proclaim that saying of the Psalmist: “Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord” (*Benedictus qui venit in nomine Domini*) (Psalm 117). The author of the Antiphonary undoubtedly understood this as referring to this Advent, when from it he composed a responsory for the history of the Lord’s Nativity [Col. 1003D–1004A].

## CHAPTER XXXII — On the History “Cry Out”

Some begin the history “Cry out” (*Clama*) every year on the Wednesday of the winter fast, even when twelve days still remain until the Lord’s Nativity. They suppose that this history was instituted for that same fast, but they are mistaken. For if Roman authority had instituted it for this purpose, it would have placed it before the vacant Sunday—that is, “Blow the trumpet” (*Canite tuba*)—just as it places the daytime offices of that same fast. In all such fasts this is observed: their offices always precede the vacant Sunday, which is also always observed after them, in accordance with the statutes of the holy Fathers, or is omitted altogether.

A Sunday is not properly called “vacant” unless it follows such offices of the fast without interruption; and, if necessary, it too is deprived of its office so that the fast may be observed. Furthermore, if the same history had been instituted for the fast, it would be superfluous for the second, third, fourth, and fifth days to be deprived of their offices in the same way as the sixth day, since the aforesaid fast has no connection with those days.

It is therefore clear that this history was instituted not for the fast, but rather so that, in the week immediately preceding the Lord’s Nativity, just as before Easter, the offices might be observed with greater solemnity in proportion as the Sunday feast drew nearer. The Antiphonary also seems to indicate this: it calls “Blow the trumpet” the Sunday immediately preceding the Nativity, and subsequently indicates that this history, “Cry out,” is to be sung during the week of that same Sunday [Col. 1004B–C], assigning one nocturnal praise to each weekday.

They are written out in such a way that they apply to the year in which the Lord’s Nativity falls on a Sunday and the vigil on a Saturday. This is also shown by the antiphon “Do not fear,” assigned to the preceding Wednesday, and by the antiphon “Let it be awaited,” assigned to the canticle of the vigil on Saturday. Consequently, it was not necessary for that Saturday itself to be marked by a special nocturnal praise. For every year it will have either the office of that vigil or that of whatever weekday the same vigil occupies in that year. Care must be taken, however, that the Saturday always retain from the vigil a ferial psalm, canticle, and antiphon [Col. 1004D].

## CHAPTER XXXIII — On the Seven Days before the Lord’s Nativity

It must therefore be understood that the aforesaid offices belong not to the fast, but to the Sunday, the five weekdays, and the vigil. Accordingly, each year we appropriately begin those same offices on the eighth day before the Lord’s Nativity, so that we may celebrate the entire week with its appointed offices, without for our part assigning any day to this celebration beyond the institution of the holy Fathers.

This too should not be noted without reason: although the offices of this week were not instituted specifically for the fast, as has been demonstrated, they never entirely abandon it except in the year when the Nativity falls according to the canonical arrangement. Then the vigil falls on Saturday, and this compels the fast to be celebrated on the preceding Saturday, outside this week. For the office of the vigil and of the fast cannot suitably be observed together on a single day.

In all other years, however, the same fast is included either wholly or in part within the aforesaid week and is celebrated on its appointed weekdays. Thus, although the antiphons from the Gospels of this fast are often brought forward together with the fast itself, they are rightly assigned to the Wednesday, Friday, and Saturday of that week, because the fast so regularly occupies those weekdays that it scarcely leaves them entirely unused in any year.

It must also be provided that when the vigil falls on a Sunday, it takes six responsories from the Sunday history together with the Sunday psalms; but it concedes the final three [Col. 1005A] and the nocturnal praises to Saturday with the ferial psalms. At Mass everything is from the vigil, but festively and with the Alleluia, “Come, Lord” (*Veni Domine*).

## CHAPTER XXXIV — On the Nativity of the Lord: Why at the First Mass “Let us go, the Mass is ended” Is Not Sung, but “Let Us Bless the Lord”

On the Nativity of the Lord, after the ninth responsory has been completed, the Gospel “The book of the generation” (*Liber generationis*) is read. Then “We praise you, O God” (*Te Deum laudamus*) is said with the ringing of bells.
