When the nocturnal vigils have thus been completed, the Mass “The Lord said” (*Dominus dixit*) is concluded before the morning lauds with “Let us bless the Lord” (*Benedicamus Domino*), not with “Go, the Mass is ended” (*Ite missa est*), lest we appear to have given the people permission to depart during the nocturnal praises, which we customarily begin immediately after Mass, with the bells ringing again.

## CHAPTER XXXV — On the Second Vespers of Saint Stephen

[Col. 1005C]

All authoritative Antiphonaries grant the second Vespers entirely to Saint Stephen. Accordingly, following this example, we grant the second Vespers in full to the other feasts throughout the year, even when a greater feast follows. For it is not appropriate to assign the evening psalms only to the preceding feast and everything else to the following one. The holy Fathers left us no example of this; rather, they taught us above all, with singular diligence, to preserve harmony among the offices.

Nevertheless, if a very great feast follows a lesser one, it may not inappropriately claim the entire second Vespers of the preceding feast—for example, the Lord’s Octave may claim the second Vespers of Saint Sylvester [Col. 1005D]. We complete Vespers for any feast in the same manner; afterward, if necessary, we commemorate the other feast after “Let us bless the Lord,” as we observe for Saint Stephen and Saint John.

## CHAPTER XXXVI — On the Holy Innocents

On the Nativity of the Holy Innocents, according to the established order, we omit “Glory to God in the highest” (*Gloria in excelsis*) and the Alleluia. Likewise, we omit “We praise you, O God” (*Te Deum laudamus*) and “Go, the Mass is ended” (*Ite missa est*), which, together with “Glory to God in the highest,” are customarily admitted or omitted according to Roman usage. All these, I say, are omitted unless the feast falls on a Sunday.

We never omit “Glory be to the Father” (*Gloria Patri*), except on a feast of the Lord’s Passion [Col. 1006A]. It is fitting, however, that the Passion of the Holy Innocents should be celebrated less festively than that of other saints, because although they were crowned with martyrdom, they had not yet departed to glory, but to infernal punishment [Note: Properly understand “infernal punishment” as the prison of the Limbo of the Fathers, or Abraham’s bosom, to which the innocent martyrs descended before Christ’s death; nevertheless, through Christ’s death they were received into heaven.] [Col. 1005D–1006D].

For before Christ’s descent into hell, none of the saints attained that glory to which Christ led the ancient saints and to which he has not ceased to lead his followers thereafter. But because they deserved to be liberated and glorified with the other saints at the Lord’s resurrection, they too will most appropriately receive the customary glory in the offices together with the other saints if their feast reaches the day of the resurrection, that is, Sunday.

We also celebrate their octave in the same way as that of the other saints, because, the day of the resurrection having already passed, we do not doubt that they rejoice in glory with the other saints [Col. 1006B].

## CHAPTER XXXVII — On the Office “While Deep Silence”

If the Lord’s Nativity or any of the subsequent solemnities falls on a Sunday, the office “While deep silence” (*Dum medium silentium*) is suitably observed on the ordinary days after the feast of the Holy Innocents, just as we do on other Sundays if we happen to have a more solemn feast on them. Thus the same office is also repeated according to Roman usage whenever a Sunday occurs between the Lord’s Octave and Epiphany [Col. 1006C].

Every Sunday from the Lord’s Nativity to Epiphany will have this office by ancient tradition, unless it is occupied by a more solemn feast. Since this office concerns the Lord’s Nativity, it is most appropriately adapted to those Sundays that customarily receive the remaining offices of the same solemnity.

We should not listen to those who think that this office, because it concerns the Nativity, should never be sung after the Lord’s Octave, since they themselves customarily—and ought to—give the vigil of Epiphany the office of the Lord’s Nativity in full. If a Sunday falls within the octave of Saint Stephen or of another saint, they likewise deprive that Sunday of its office and assign it the office of the octave, provided that the ecclesiastical solemnity is celebrated not as the octave of Saint Stephen but as the octave of the Lord.

In arranging the offices, the holy Fathers took the greatest care that the office should always correspond to the feast then being celebrated, so that the clergy would not observe something different from the people in the ecclesiastical celebrations [Col. 1006D].

Moreover, all Sunday solemnities related to one another have this privilege: their observance continues from one into another. Thus we commemorate the Resurrection until the Ascension, and the Ascension until Pentecost, and we assign to all the Sundays falling between those solemnities their offices. In the same way, we commemorate the Lord’s Nativity until Epiphany, except insofar as we are compelled to satisfy the feasts or octaves of the saints. Sundays occurring within this period will likewise possess the office of the Nativity.

## CHAPTER XXXVIII — On Repeating the Same Office on Another Sunday

[Col. 1007A]

Although two Sundays often occur during that period, feasts of the saints will never permit both to be occupied by a Sunday office, except in the one year when the vigil of Epiphany falls on a Sunday. Thus Saint Gregory quite appropriately arranged one Sunday office for that period, since in almost every year only one Sunday occurs that requires such an office.

Nor did Saint Gregory take care to preserve this arrangement after Epiphany or after Pentecost, so that we would always have as many offices as Sundays might occur. He foresaw very well that such inequality could easily be corrected by repeating offices. Accordingly, when the vigil of Epiphany falls on a Sunday, we repeat the office of the preceding Sunday in full [Col. 1007B].

We ought to do the same on the Sundays after Epiphany and after Pentecost whenever necessary, according to Roman custom. For just as we repeat the histories of the Sundays insofar as the season permits, so too we may repeat their offices. A Sunday office can be assigned no less appropriately to another Sunday that has the same observance than to individual ordinary days, which, when they receive Sunday offices, turn their ferial offices into festive ones. This, however, we practice everywhere not so much from the necessity of the ecclesiastical assembly as from personal devotion.

It should therefore not seem more incongruous for the same office to be repeated on another Sunday in order to satisfy the ecclesiastical assembly [Col. 1007C].

## CHAPTER XXXIX — On the Lord’s Octave

On the Lord’s Octave, according to Roman authority, we sing not the office “A child is born to us” (*Puer natus est*), but “Your countenance” (*Vultum tuum*), as it appears in the Gradual, with the Alleluia “After childbirth, a virgin” (*Post partum virgo*). We say the Gregorian prayer “O God, who are the salvation of eternal life” (*Deus qui salutis aeternae*), not “O God, who in the Nativity…” (*Deus qui nos Nativit.*).

It should be noted that the office of this octave clearly concerns Saint Mary. Thus on that day the Romans hold the station at Saint Mary’s, and not without reason. Recently, when we were celebrating the Lord’s Nativity, we could not assign any office so particular to his Mother. Accordingly, we fittingly venerate her more especially on the Lord’s Octave, lest she appear to be excluded from the solemnity of her Son, although we do not doubt that in that solemnity she is to be honored above all after the Lord [Col. 1007D].

The nocturnal praises of this octave also speak most explicitly of Saint Mary. Thus the responsories from the Lord’s Nativity that commemorate Saint Mary are appropriately assigned to this day, so that we may not differ in anything from the Gregorian office for that day.

Everything may suitably be arranged as follows:

At Vespers:

- Antiphon: “With you is dominion” (*Tecum principium*), with the remaining items.
- Responsory: “Rejoice together” (*Congratulamini*).
- Hymn: “From the rising of the sun” (*A solis*).

At the Gospel:

- Antiphon: “A great inheritance” (*Magnum haereditatis*).

Invitatory:

- “Christ is born” (*Christus natus est*).

Antiphons and responsories:

- “The Lord said” (*Dominus dixit*).
- “In the sun” (*In sole*).
- “You have raised up” (*Elevamivi*).
- Responsory: “He descended” (*Descendit*).
- Responsory: “O great mystery” (*O magnum*) [Col. 1008A].
- Responsory: “Holy and undefiled” (*Sancta et immaculata*).
- Antiphon: “Beautiful” (*Speciosus*).
- Antiphon: “King of all” (*Rex omnis*).
- Antiphon: “We have received” (*Suscepimus*).
- Responsory: “Blessed and venerable” (*Beata et veneranda*).
- Responsory: “Rejoice together” (*Congratulamini*).
- Responsory: “He contains in his womb” (*Continet in gremio*).
- Antiphon: “A man is born” (*Homo natus*).
- Antiphon: “They will rejoice” (*Exsultabunt*).
- Antiphon: “He has made known” (*Notum fecit*).
- Responsory: “It has been confirmed” (*Confirmatum est*).
- Responsory: “A mother who did not know” (*Nesciens mater*).
- Responsory: “The Word became flesh” (*Verbum caro*).

Nocturnal praises:

- “O wondrous” (*O admirabile*), in order.

The same antiphons are read over the psalms at the second Vespers, from the Lord’s Nativity. At the Gospel there is the antiphon “He who is of the earth” (*Qui de terra est*).

On the Sunday after the Lord’s Nativity the arrangement will be as follows:

- Invitatory: “Christ is born” (*Christus natus est*).
- Sunday psalms, with three antiphons from the Lord’s Nativity.
- Responsory: “He descended” (*Descendit*).
- Responsory: “Whom did you see?” (*Quem vidistis*) [Col. 1008B].
- Responsory: “O great mystery” (*O magnum*).

In the second nocturn:

- Responsory: “He contains in his womb” (*Continet in gremio*).
- Responsory: “It has been confirmed” (*Confirmatum est*).
- Responsory: “This one who has come” (*Hic qui advenit*).

In the third nocturn:

- Responsory: “Behold the Lamb of God” (*Ecce Agnus Dei*).
- Responsory: “Blessed” (*Benedictus*).
- Responsory: “O King” (*O regem*).

Nocturnal praises:

- “Whom did you see?” (*Quem vidistis*).

At the Gospel:

- “While deep silence” (*Dum medium*).

It should be noted that the nocturnal chant of the Lord’s Octave speaks greatly of Saint Mary, since the daytime office also appears to have been instituted in her honor. On the Sunday night, however, we concern ourselves not so much with Saint Mary as with the Lord’s Nativity, because in the daytime office too we commemorate the Lord’s Nativity specifically.

It is a tradition of the holy Fathers that at such solemnities the remaining offices should correspond with the office of the Mass.

## CHAPTER XL — On Epiphany

[Col. 1008C]

If the vigil of Epiphany falls on a Sunday, we sing at night as stated above. During the day also we observe the office “While deep silence” (*Dum medium*) in full, as on the preceding Sunday.

If it falls on another day, we sing the same office, but with the reading “We know” (*Scimus*) and the Gospel “When Herod had died” (*Defuncto Herode*); accordingly, we sing the Communion “Take the child” (*Tolle puerum*). This office was formerly sung there on the occasion of this vigil, as the Sunday of that same week; similarly, “The voice of rejoicing” (*Vocem jucunditatis*) is sung at the vigil of the Ascension, and the Communion is taken from the Gospel of that day.

On Epiphany at the nocturnal office, according to the Roman Order, we omit the invitatory, so that we may differ from Herod’s deceitful invitation [Col. 1008D]. We begin that night with the antiphon “Bring forth” (*Afferte*). The antiphon “Of the river” (*Fluminis*) is deferred with the psalm to the third nocturn, because a greater praise than the Alleluia resounds under grace, which is represented by the third nocturn; the preceding nocturns signify the time before the Law or under the Law. Therefore all histories that claim the Alleluia for themselves use it more frequently in the third nocturn [Note: See William Durandus on the same matter.] [Col. 1007D–1008D].

If Epiphany falls on a Sunday, we touch nothing of the Sunday office on that day. We customarily observe this during its octave, however, so that the ferial readings and Gospels concerning the Lord’s Baptism may be recited at the time when the feast of the Lord’s Baptism is also celebrated.

## CHAPTER XLI — On the Sundays after Epiphany

[Col. 1009A]

If a Sunday occurs during the intervening days between Epiphany and its octave, we necessarily satisfy the ecclesiastical assembly on that day with the Sunday office, since we know that the assembly has gathered for the Sunday, not for Epiphany. The Sunday psalms are also to be recited with the chant from Epiphany.

In this way we customarily assign to every Sunday falling between the Sunday solemnities, but not occupied by a more solemn office, the offices of those same solemnities. We also observe the ordinary days intervening between solemnities in such a way that we say the invitatory and one antiphon over the ferial nocturn, and likewise the verse, responsory, nocturnal praises, and the other elements from the feast.

According to the Roman Order, we never omit the ferial nocturn when we say only three responsories, except during the weeks of Easter and Pentecost [Col. 1009B].

Therefore the office of the first Sunday within this octave is properly observed every year, even if, because of the number of weeks, it appears necessary to repeat it up to Septuagesima. The same applies to the other two offices, “All the earth” (*Omnis terra*) and “Adore” (*Adorate*), even when six weeks frequently occur that must be supplied with these offices.

When only one Sunday occurs between Epiphany and Septuagesima, whoever wishes to omit none of the appointed offices in that year ought to join two offices into one week, although no ecclesiastical assembly requires this. We therefore repeat the same office on another Sunday no less appropriately when we have no more solemn office with which we can properly satisfy the ecclesiastical assembly [Col. 1009C].

The ordinary days themselves also receive, according to Roman usage, the office of the preceding Sunday if they cannot suitably be supplied from another source. Nevertheless, we do not omit the sprinkling with blessed water, according to the decree of Pope Saint Alexander, nor “I believe in one God” (*Credo in unum*).

## CHAPTER XLII — On Two Feasts Falling on the Same Day

When two feasts requiring nine readings fall on the same day, each of which independently demands a complete office, we observe the more solemn one in full and afterward make only a commemoration of the other.

If both appear to require complete observance, either separate offices should be performed for both on that day—just as Saint Gregory assigned two offices to a single day several times in the Sacramentary and the Gradual—or one of them should be deferred to the following day, as Pope Saint Gregory wished the feast of Saint Paul to be observed after the feast of Saint Peter [Col. 1009D].

The practice of combining two offices into one disordered office on a single day is not admitted by the authority of the holy Fathers, who always warned us to preserve harmony in the offices—namely, that we should observe one nocturn from one feast and the remaining nocturns from the other. For if we attempted in this way to satisfy both feasts, we would be shown to have celebrated neither with the proper reverence owed to its offices.

Whether the offices of two feasts are completed separately on one day or one of them is deferred to another day appears to depend not so much on the general observance of the whole Church as on the private leisure of religious persons who do not wish to omit any of the appointed offices [Col. 1010A].

## CHAPTER XLIII — On Roman Pontiffs Who Were Martyrs

Gregory, the seventh pope of that name presiding over the Apostolic See, decreed that the feasts of all holy Roman pontiffs and martyrs should everywhere be celebrated solemnly with the full office. For if every church solemnly observes the feast of its patron, even if he was a confessor, how much more should it honor those who were not merely patrons but Fathers of the whole Church, and who did not cease to instruct it by words and examples even unto martyrdom? [Col. 1010B]

Note that Pope Gregory the First instituted pontifical offices for these martyrs in the Gradual, just as for confessors: for Saint Marcellus, the antiphon “He established” (*Statuit*), and for Saint Felix, the antiphon “Priests” (*Sacerdotes*). This is entirely appropriate because of the excellence of their apostolic dignity.

Our predecessors, considering this, also appear to have observed for these same saints the offices of confessors for the course of day and night. These likewise indicate the dignity of a pontiff, but in no way prejudice their martyrdom. The Gradual shows that the same is to be observed for Saint Apollinaris.

For these saints the hymn, the invitatory, and the verses “With glory and honor” (*Gloria et honore*), “You have placed” (*Posuisti, Domine*), and “Great is his glory” (*Magna est gloria ejus*) are sung as for martyrs [Col. 1010C]; the remaining elements are taken in order as for confessors.

Some moderns, paying less attention to harmony among the offices, observe all the chant for them as for martyrs, except at Mass, asserting that it is fitting that at night their martyrdom should be treated, but at Mass their priestly dignity. The practice of the earlier authorities, however, appears more appropriate, since the Mass at every feast ordinarily gives form to the remaining offices.

## CHAPTER XLIV — On the Octaves of the Saints

According to Roman authority, we ought to observe the octaves of no saints unless we have a definite tradition concerning them from the holy Fathers. Even for those whose octaves we celebrate, we make no daily commemoration during the intervening days, because we have no authority for doing so, except in the case of Saint Mary and Saint Peter, whose memory we do not cease to celebrate at other times [Col. 1010D].

On the feast of any saint with three responsories, we do not omit the nocturn. To the saint, however, we grant the invitatory, responsory, nocturnal praises, and the other elements through the end of Mass; the remaining elements are ferial.

According to Roman custom, we make no commemoration of any saint with three responsories after Mass, whether that Mass is sung at Terce or at Sext. Indeed, once the Mass itself is finished, the commemoration of the saint is finished.

On a feast with nine readings, however, we perform everything from the feast through the second Vespers.

## CHAPTER XLV — On the First Sunday Vespers

[Col. 1011A]

After the octave of Epiphany, whether the day is ordinary or a Sunday, the Epistles of Paul are read up to Septuagesima.

The first Vespers of every Sunday requires the prayer of the following day, because the chapter before the Magnificat is assigned to the following Sunday, as is demonstrated in the Sundays of the Lord’s Advent and of Lent, or of the Lord’s Passion. This practice is also followed almost everywhere on other solemnities.

The responsories and antiphons indicate the same thing, since they are customarily anticipated at first Vespers from the history of the following day. Sometimes, however, the final antiphon from the Gospel of the preceding Sunday is reserved for the aforesaid Vespers, as on the Sundays after Epiphany and Easter. These practices nevertheless agree so well that the antiphon of the preceding Sunday fits the prayer of the following one perfectly [Col. 1011B].

## CHAPTER XLVI — On the Water for Sprinkling, “Glory to God in the Highest,” “Go, the Mass Is Ended,” and “I Believe”

Pope Alexander, fifth after blessed Peter, decreed that salt and water should be blessed for sprinkling the people and their dwellings. We too follow this practice every Sunday according to the canons.

Pope Symmachus, fiftieth in order, decreed that on Sundays and on the birthdays of martyrs the hymn “Glory to God in the highest” (*Gloria in excelsis*) should be sung. We observe this every Sunday and on feasts with nine readings, except during the Lord’s Advent and from Septuagesima to Easter. On those days, however, the birthdays of the apostles and the feasts of Saint Mary receive “Glory to God in the highest” according to Roman custom [Col. 1011C].

Whenever “Glory to God in the highest” is said, we also recite “We praise you, O God” (*Te Deum*) and “Go, the Mass is ended” (*Ite missa est*), except at the night of the Lord’s Nativity, on Maundy Thursday, and at the vigils of Easter and Pentecost.

“Go, the Mass is ended” is appropriately said on feast days as well, because then the general assembly is customarily celebrated, and through this announcement it customarily receives permission to depart. For the daily solemnities of Mass, not everyone generally assembles, but religious persons do—those who attend more diligently to spiritual than to worldly matters and who, when permitted, also attend the remaining offices daily.

It is therefore appropriate that after Mass they be told not to depart immediately but to bless the Lord. Ecclesiastical custom also seems to support this assertion. When we say “Go, the Mass is ended,” we turn toward the people and order them to depart; but when we say “Let us bless the Lord,” we turn not toward the people but toward the altar, that is, toward the Lord, and exhort ourselves not to depart but to bless the Lord [Col. 1011D].

It must nevertheless be understood that “Go, the Mass is ended” is not recited during the Lord’s Advent and Septuagesima—not because no assembly occurs at that time which ought to be dismissed, but rather to signify the sadness of the season. “Glory to God in the highest” is likewise omitted.

“I believe in one God” (*Credo in unum*), according to the canons, ought to be sung on every Sunday and at all Sunday solemnities, likewise at the feasts of Saint Mary, the apostles, the holy cross, All Saints, and the dedication. This is not without reason, since each of these is commemorated in some way in the same Creed [Col. 1012A].

It should also be noted that whenever “Glory to God in the highest” is sung, dalmatics and the subdeacon’s vestments are resumed.

## CHAPTER XLVII — On Septuagesima

At Septuagesima they begin the Heptateuch. Accordingly, Pope Alexander II decreed that the responsories from that history should begin on that Sunday and be repeated on the following Sunday.

He also ordered that the Alleluia be omitted at Vespers on the Saturday before Septuagesima. From that point until Maundy Thursday, “We praise you, O God,” “Glory to God in the highest,” and “Go, the Mass is ended” are omitted. Likewise, dalmatics and the subdeacon’s vestments are omitted according to ancient custom.

In a leap year, we celebrate the Nativity of Saint Matthias the Apostle on the day immediately following his vigil, not on another day that, because of the leap year, is repeated in that year’s calendar [Col. 1012B].

## CHAPTER XLVIII — On Feasts Occurring during Septuagesima or Quinquagesima

If the Purification of Saint Mary falls during Septuagesima, we change nothing in it according to Roman custom except the Alleluia among the customary expressions of rejoicing.

Pope Sergius, eighty-sixth after blessed Peter, decreed that on the days of the Annunciation of the Lord, the Dormition and Nativity of Saint Mary, and Saint Simeon—which the Greeks call *Hypapantē* (ὑπαντή)—the Litany should depart from Saint Adrian’s and the people should assemble at Saint Mary’s.

It is called *Hypapantē*, meaning “meeting” or “encounter,” because on that day the venerable persons Simeon and Anna met the Lord when he was presented in the temple.

We also celebrate the Chair of Saint Peter, even during Septuagesima, and the Annunciation of Saint Mary, even during Lent, with the greatest solemnity, with dalmatics and “Glory to God in the highest,” according to Roman custom [Col. 1012C].

It should be understood that the Council of Laodicea, chapter 51, decreed that the birthdays of martyrs should not be celebrated during Lent, but that their commemoration should be made on Saturdays or Sundays. The reason that only martyrs are named here is that among the ancients the memory of confessors was not yet so celebrated.

The holy Fathers also decreed in the Council of Toledo that the Annunciation of Saint Mary should be transferred from Lent to the fifteenth day before the Kalends of January, where it could be solemnly and appropriately celebrated each year before the Lord’s Nativity [Col. 1012D]. Thus all the offices of that season might resound with the same Annunciation, as is observed in the Ambrosian Church.

But we, following more closely the custom of the holy Roman Church, celebrate it during Lent, as we do the feasts of certain other saints. A synodal decree is also read to the effect that if the same Annunciation falls during the three days before Easter, it should be anticipated on the Saturday before Palm Sunday. That day also lacks an office of its own and throughout the year customarily serves the veneration of Saint Mary.

This anticipation would appear necessary every year when the same feast follows that Saturday, since the two subsequent weeks are so occupied by their own offices that they cannot suitably serve so great a solemnity. But we have found nothing in this edition that has been rashly established as canonical [Col. 1013A].

When we celebrate feasts with nine readings during Lent, we perform everything from the feast, day and night, and celebrate the Mass of the feast festively at Terce. From Lent, however, after “Let us bless the Lord,” we say the ferial antiphon with the prayers and collect, and this only at Matins and Vespers; we also celebrate the Mass of Lent at None, with genuflection.

## CHAPTER XLIX — On the Beginning of the Fast

At the Beginning of the Fast (*Caput Jejunii*) we celebrate Mass at None and do everything as during Lent. Since those four days are received as completing the Lenten fast, they necessarily observe the Lenten discipline: namely, that the fast is finally [read: only] broken after Vespers, as the canons prescribe [Col. 1013B]. At other times, however, the fast is broken immediately after None, when Mass is celebrated at Sext.

The Lenten fast differs from the other days in this respect: on the others we should eat after None, but on this day after Vespers. According to the canons, we are not considered to be fasting in the Lenten manner if we eat before Vespers. Therefore we must fast in the same way on these four days if we wish to complete the forty-day fast with them. Accordingly, Mass is rightly celebrated on those days not at Sext but at None.

It is an ecclesiastical custom to eat at None when Mass is celebrated at Sext, and at Vespers when we offer the sacrifice at None. Thus, in order that we may fast until Vespers on those days also, it is canonical that we defer Mass to None.

It should be understood that not only moderns, as some think, but also the ancients began at the Beginning of the Fast, since Saint Gregory too appears to have begun the Lenten offices there. This is made entirely clear in the Gregorian Sacramentaries and Graduals.

The following Sunday, however, is properly called the beginning of Lent. Hence forty-two days are counted up to Easter; when the six Sundays are subtracted from these, only thirty-six days are observed in abstinence. Therefore we necessarily begin at the Beginning of the Fast if we wish to complete with the Lord a fast of forty days.

From that point we also begin the prayer over the people according to Gregory’s institution. We never say it except when we must also fast in the Lenten manner [Col. 1013C].

## CHAPTER L — On Lent

[Col. 1013D]

During Lent the preface “Who by bodily fasting” (*Qui corporali jejunio*) is said, according to the decree of Pope Pelagius, no less on Sundays than on their weekdays.

From Palm Sunday, however, because on that day we begin to read the Passions, we say the preface of the Cross until Maundy Thursday—that is, through those five days, signifying the fivefold Passion of the Lord—and we adorn the same week, which the holy Fathers call the Great Week, with that preface. It is most appropriate that it be said at that time, when the Lord’s Passion is treated so particularly.

In the first week of Lent the spring fast is to be celebrated, as the holy Fathers—Leo the Great, Gelasius, Pope Gregory I, Gregory II, and Gregory VII—are read to have established [Col. 1014A].

The Tract “O Lord, not according to…” (*Domine, non secundum*), which we frequently use during Lent, we adopt not so much from the Roman Order as from our own custom.

Pope Melchiades, thirty-third after blessed Peter, decreed that no one should fast on Sunday or on Thursday. Therefore Saint Gregory, in arranging the offices, left Thursday vacant during Lent, so that, because it was festive like Sunday, it might also be honored with the Sunday office.

But because that weekday was later assigned to the fast, like the others, Gregory the Younger established it as solemn, with offices collected from various sources and especially from the summer Sundays. Thus antiphons from the Sunday Gospels are still found assigned to Thursdays, such as those from the Gospels “There was a certain rich man” (*Homo quidam erat dives*) and “Jesus was going” (*Ibat Jesus*). In the week of Pentecost also, Thursday is supplied with the Sunday office [Col. 1014B].

The Saturdays before Lent and before Palm Sunday receive the offices of their respective Sundays, and not without reason, since every ordinary day is customarily supplied from its own Sunday.

At all the Lenten hours we kneel. Likewise at Mass, even if a greeting precedes the prayer, unless another prayer without a greeting has preceded; then we kneel only at the first. The exception is the Wednesday after Palm Sunday, when, according to the Roman Order, we kneel at both.

## CHAPTER LI — On the Prayer over the People

[Col. 1014C]

The prayer over the people is frequently used in Lent because, since we undertake a greater struggle in fasting and prayers against spiritual wickedness, we must necessarily commend ourselves to God more earnestly. For the prayer after Communion ordinarily prays only for those who have received Communion. But although the people assemble daily in Lent, they do not receive Communion daily, as they ought. Therefore, lest the people should be deprived of prayer as they are of Communion, the prayer over the people was added; in it, prayer is offered particularly not for Communion but for the protection of the people.

On Sundays, however, it is not said, because the genuflection is avoided which in ancient times was performed by the people for this prayer; or rather, because, according to the testimony of Saint Ambrose, everyone ought to receive Communion on Sundays, for whom the prayer after Communion could suffice as a blessing. It should also be known, according to the ancient Fathers, that ordinarily only those who received Communion used to remain for the divine mysteries. Hence, before the offering, the catechumens and penitents—namely, those who had not yet prepared themselves to receive Communion [variant: *ut qui*, “as those who”]—were ordered by the canons to leave.

The very celebration of the sacraments also indicates this: in it the priest prays not only for his own offering and Communion but also for those of others, and especially in the prayer after Communion he seems to pray only for those who have received Communion. Nor can it properly be called Communion unless several persons partake of the same sacrifice. Among the Greeks, moreover, as one reads, anyone who has not received Communion until the third Sunday is to be excommunicated. Our most blessed Fathers, Ambrose and Augustine, also exhort us to daily Communion.

But since this practice is observed neither by all priests in Lent, much less by laypeople, the prayer over the people was appropriately added, so that at least at that time the people would not be deprived of the final blessing, even though they ordinarily did not receive Communion. Hence that custom among moderns—which was not found among the ancients—also seems to have arisen: even at other times priests bless the people at the end of Mass, so that they do not allow the people to depart deprived of a blessing as well as of Communion.

## CHAPTER LII — On the Days of the Lord’s Passion

From Passion Sunday until Easter, *Gloria Patri* is not said at the responsories, at the introits, or at the psalm *Venite*. The repetition of the invitatory is also customarily changed: that is, the first verse is repeated from the middle, but the second from the beginning, and so the alternation continues to the end. In the psalms of the third nocturn, a homily is read from the Gospel: “When he drew near.”

According to the Ordo, the greeting is not omitted at the Passions, except on Good Friday, where the priestly office is also left unsaid [or: the office by the priest is omitted]; but we do not add “Glory to you, O Lord.” It should be known, however, that whenever during the Lord’s Passion we celebrate the feast of a saint, we do not omit *Gloria Patri*.

On the Monday and Tuesday after Palm Sunday, two lessons are read continuously at Mass, as at the Nativity of the Lord. Likewise, on the Saturday in the middle of Lent and on the Wednesday after Palm Sunday, two lessons are read, and each receives its own genuflection [variant: “each receives them”]. This is not without reason: for on that same day the Apostle, in the antiphon at the Introit, urges all heavenly, earthly, and infernal beings to genuflect because of the Lord’s Passion. On this day the plotting of the Jews is read as having taken place; what the Jews plotted on this day was carried out on Good Friday.

Therefore, just as Good Friday is celebrated with more solemnity in genuflections than the other Fridays, so on this Wednesday we ought rightly to genuflect more than on the others. For since we observe every Wednesday because of the Lord’s Passion, who would deny that we ought especially to observe the Wednesday that annually represents that same Passion more particularly to us? According to the Roman Ordo, we must also say on Wednesday the same prayers with genuflections that the holy Church customarily observes on Good Friday before the greeting of the cross.

Moreover, according to the Roman Ordo [or: Roman authority], this week is called “Great,” because, by reason of the most holy sacrament of the Lord’s Passion, it is regarded as more distinguished than the others. Rightly, therefore, we celebrate it more solemnly than the other weeks, in lessons, genuflections, and other observances.

According to the Roman Ordo, on Maundy Thursday, Good Friday, and Holy Saturday, after the *Benedictus* at the morning praises, the *Kyrie eleison*, prayers, and orations are to be said in silence. On Maundy Thursday, *Gloria Patri* and *Gloria in excelsis* are omitted, except where the chrism is consecrated; nevertheless, the deacons wear dalmatics and the subdeacons their subdeaconal vestments.

On that day it is forbidden under anathema for anyone to break the Lenten fast, as the Priscillianists do. For our holy Fathers are said to have established this in the Council of Laodicea and in the Council of Toledo. Hence blessed Leo says in his sermon on Lent:

> “Whoever,” he says, “omits one day in Lent has violated the whole of Lent, especially that day which, since it is the end of Lent, ought to be observed more than the others, because all praise is sung especially at the end.”

On Good Friday the office begins with a lesson, not with a prayer, according to the Ordo. For prayer is customarily the conclusion rather than the beginning of offices, as is evident in the Mass itself and in the individual courses.

On that same day, before each prayer, except the prayer for the Jews, we say “Let us bend our knees,” and immediately afterward “Arise”; then we add the prayer, according to Roman custom, continuing as on the other days.

## CHAPTER LIII — On Holy Saturday

On Holy Saturday Pope Zosimus decreed that a large candle should be blessed. It is to be lit before the blessing and distributed among the people during the octave of Easter for fumigating their possessions; after receiving the blessing from a priest, the deacon is to bless it.

According to the Roman Ordo, twelve lessons are to be read without titles before the baptism. After the baptism, the priests may at last celebrate Mass privately, if necessary, because those who have been reborn are now present, and we ought to deal with them particularly at Mass. Afterward, however, we customarily begin not with the lessons that we have already heard, but with the litany.

## CHAPTER LIV — On the Observance of Easter

According to Roman authority, the lamb is blessed at Easter, not at the altar but at the common table. We say *Credo in unum* and other things of this kind every day until the octave, as on the holy day.

We appropriately say the Gradual verse “Blessed is he who comes” on Thursday, and “The stone” on Friday, on which the Lord was rejected by the Jews. On the Saturday within the octave of Easter, the antiphon “When it was evening” is sung at Vespers, because among the ancients the same Gospel was read on that Saturday up to “But Thomas,” as the Gospel breviaries still testify.

At these Vespers the ferial psalms are said with *Alleluia*, and during the night of Sunday the nocturn and nine lessons are said according to the Roman Ordo. Thereafter we say the ferial psalms at Vespers and at the nocturn with *Alleluia*, unless a feast with nine lessons occurs. At Matins, however, we always recite “The Lord reigns.”

But since many people wish to observe all the days from this point until the octave of Pentecost with three psalms and lessons, it seems worthwhile to consult the authority of the apostolic see and learn from it what we ought to do, since from there we received the pattern of the whole Christian religion.

Pope Gregory, established in the apostolic see, promulgated the following rule in this matter:

> “From the day of the Resurrection until the Saturday in White, and from the day of Pentecost until the Saturday of that same week, we sing and read at the Nocturns only three psalms and three lessons, according to the ancient custom. On all other days throughout the year, if it is a feast, we say nine psalms, nine lessons, and responsories; on other days we recite twelve psalms and three lessons. On Sundays we say eighteen psalms and nine lessons, except on Easter Day and Pentecost. We also decree that this be done everywhere according to the Roman Ordo, as we have noted above. On the octave of Easter we begin, according to the Ordo, the history ‘Worthy are you, O Lord,’ and the Apocalypse.”

## CHAPTER LV — On Feasts during Eastertide

From the octave of Easter until Pentecost, on a feast with three responsories we sing only one *Alleluia*; on a feast with nine lessons we sing two *Alleluias* at Mass, whether the feast concerns the Resurrection or something else. When we say two *Alleluias*, we repeat not the first but the second.

We also do not omit the Preface until the Ascension of the Lord, because we celebrate the Easter office day and night. For it would be incongruous if only the Preface were observed in a ferial manner while everything else was observed as at Easter.

At the Nativity of the Apostles Philip and James, however, we say the Preface of the Apostles, as we say the Preface of the Cross at its Invention. During this period we are not ordered to fast or observe the vigil of any feast except the Ascension and Pentecost.

The following is also appropriately observed at all vigils: if the vigil is postponed until after Mass, the Ninth Hour is celebrated from the forthcoming feast. That is, once we begin the feast after Mass, we should not thereafter create any discord of offices with None, something which the holy Fathers especially took care to avoid in their arrangements.

It should also be known that in ancient times people customarily sang of saints collectively during Eastertide. Hence even now items pertaining to several persons are sung of one, such as the *Alleluia*, “Rejoice”; the Offertory, “They will confess”; and the Responsory, “In his servants.” This is because, in the universal resurrection typified by that season, the joy and festival are common to the righteous.

For this reason the feast of Saints James and Philip, and of all the Apostles, is also found in Martyrologies and Sacramentaries. Pope Eusebius, thirty-second after blessed Peter, decreed that all Christians should solemnly celebrate the Invention of the Holy Cross on the fifth day before the Nones of May [3 May].

Therefore we too ought to observe it with a complete office, which we may appropriately arrange as follows:

- Antiphon: “Helena.”
- Invitatory: “Alleluia, the crucified King.”
- First nocturn: antiphon, “Let us adore”; antiphon, “We adore”; antiphon, “Your cross.”
- Psalms: “O Lord our God” [variant: “The earth is the Lord’s”]; “Preserve me”; “O Lord, in your strength.”
- Verse: “All the earth.”
- Responsory: “This sign of the cross.”
- Responsory: “Christ, the Lamb of God.”
- Responsory: “Behold, the Lion has conquered.”

In the second nocturn:

- Antiphons: “The holy cross”; “Through the sign of the cross”; “But as for us.”
- Psalms: “The earth is the Lord’s”; “The Lord is great”; “Shout joyfully.”
- Verses: “Declare among the nations”; “The Lord reigns from the wood.”
- Responsory: “Worthy are you, O Lord.”
- Responsory: “I heard.”
- Responsory: “Sweet wood.”

In the third nocturn:

- Antiphons: “Savior of the world”; “Save us”; “O great [mystery].”
- Psalms: “Sing,” first; “The Lord reigns, let [the earth] exult”; “Sing,” second. Verse: “But far be it from me to glory.”
- Responsory: “It is good to confess to the Lord.”
- Responsory: “Let them say now.”
- Responsory: “O blessed cross.”

At the morning praises:

- Antiphon: “Helena of Constantine.”
- Antiphon: “Then he commanded.”
- Antiphon: “Holy Helena.”
- Antiphon: “And when he had ascended.”
- Antiphon: “Judas was praying.”
- Gospel antiphon: “When Judas had prayed.”

After the *Benedicamus*, we customarily commemorate Saint Alexander and his companions. The Exaltation of the Holy Cross, however, is not celebrated so universally and solemnly, perhaps because no statute concerning it as specific as that concerning the Invention is found.

## CHAPTER LVI — On the Annual Easter

The Romans call the annual Easter “Easter as an anniversary,” because in ancient times those who had been baptized at the preceding Easter assembled in church on the same day of the following year and solemnly celebrated the anniversary of their rebirth with offerings.

The office for that day was as follows: “I have risen,” throughout; lesson, “I saw a door”; Gospel, “There was a man of the Pharisees,” with the appropriate prayers. All these things seem most clearly to concern the grace of those who have been reborn.

Although this kind of anniversary is now observed by few anywhere, authoritative books nevertheless indicate that it ought to be observed: they prescribe for us each year a lesson and Gospel under the heading “Annual Easter.” For if everyone observes the birthday on which he was born for eternal death, how much more ought he to observe the day on which he was reborn for eternal life?

## CHAPTER LVII — On the Litanies

The Greater Litany was instituted by blessed Pope Gregory I because of the pestilence of his time. Writing to John, bishop of Ravenna, he also calls the day of the Litany the time of ashes and haircloth.

The three-day Litanies before the Ascension of the Lord are not Roman but Gallican, because Saint Mamertus, bishop of Vienne, is said to have instituted them. The holy Fathers decreed that they should be observed—not by riding on horseback or wearing splendid clothing, but in ashes and haircloth, just as the Greater Litany is observed.

On the final day of these litanies, that is, on the vigil of the Ascension of the Lord, the following are sung:

- Office: “The voice of rejoicing.”
- Offertory: “Men of Galilee.”
- Communion: “Father, while I was with them.”

## CHAPTER LVIII — On Pentecost Week

The summer fast must always be celebrated within Pentecost. For the prayers and lessons of that fast concern the Holy Spirit [variant: “the feast of the Holy Spirit”]. Therefore, just as the spring fast must always be celebrated within Lent because it has Lenten offices, so this fast is appropriately celebrated within the feast of the Holy Spirit, from which it derives its offices. For the holy Fathers are said to have established the same arrangement for both fasts.

During the Pentecost fast we do not genuflect, according to the Roman Ordo. Some people also do not omit *Gloria in excelsis* at the Mass of the fast, but this is incongruous, since that Mass is transferred from the Third to the Sixth Hour.

There are three hours of the day consecrated by the Lord’s Passion to the celebration of the mysteries: the Third Hour, when he was crucified by the tongues of the Jews; the Sixth, when he was crucified by the hands of the Gentiles; and the Ninth, when he gave up his spirit. Of these, the Third Hour is observed most particularly on feast days, perhaps because among the hours of the Passion it seems closer to the time of the Lord’s Resurrection or Nativity. The Sixth and Ninth Hours are assigned to the offices of the fasts.

Except on Maundy Thursday and on the holy Saturdays of Easter and Pentecost, *Gloria in excelsis* is never assigned to a Mass unless it is one that we ought to celebrate festively at the Third Hour. Therefore, it is not incongruous that we omit *Gloria in excelsis* from the Masses of this fast, which we customarily observe not festively at the Third Hour but at the Sixth.

Some people, however, sing two Masses quite appropriately during this fast: one solemnly at the Third Hour, with *Gloria in excelsis*, in order to satisfy the feast of the Holy Spirit; the other after the Sixth Hour for the fast. The same is done for the feast of Saint Thomas during the winter fast, for the feast of Saint Matthew during the autumn fast, for Saint Mark during the Greater Litany, and for the Annunciation of Saint Mary in Lent: the first Mass satisfies the feast, while the second satisfies the fast.

At this Mass [variant: “at which”] we sing not Graduals, as in ancient times, but *Alleluia*.

## CHAPTER LIX — On the Octave of Pentecost

The vacant Sunday follows, to which the lesson “I saw a door” is assigned. It borrowed the prayer—that is, the supplication—from Lent, and the Gospel from the Annual Easter; but it appropriately receives the office of Pentecost itself, since it is its octave.

At the Nocturn we say nine lessons according to the Roman Ordo, although we do not find an equal number of responsories concerning the Holy Spirit in the ancient Antiphonaries. This is perhaps because the Romans do not always append one responsory to each lesson, and frequently omit the third or the ninth.

We, however, attach to the nine lessons mentioned above an equal number of alleluiatic responsories, gathered from various sources, according to the Gregorian custom; that is, we use Communions in place of responsories, as is found in certain books.

On the following day we read and sing from the Books of Kings at the nocturn, and at Mass the office “Lord, in your …,” unless we have to celebrate a feast [variant: “unless we ought to celebrate a feast”].

We may also repeat this office on the following Sunday according to Roman custom, provided that in that year there are several weeks remaining until the Advent of the Lord. Otherwise, the ferial days alone suffice with the office “Lord, in your …,” just as ferial days suffice with any Sunday office whose Sunday has been occupied by another office.

## CHAPTER LX — On the Office of the Holy Trinity

Some people establish an office of the Holy Trinity on the octave of Pentecost, although it is not alleluiatic, and think that it should be observed throughout the following week as well. But this is not authoritative.

For a certain Stephen of Liège is said to have composed this office, as well as the history of the Invention of Saint Stephen; both are rejected by the apostolic see. Therefore Pope Alexander, of pious memory, when questioned about this matter, replied that according to the Roman Ordo no day should be specially assigned to the solemnity of the Holy Trinity, any more than to the holy Unity, especially since the memory of both is celebrated on every Sunday, indeed every day.

It should also be known that a certain Albinus, master of Emperor Charles, is said, at the request of Saint Boniface the archbishop, to have composed Mass prayers for the Holy Trinity: for Monday, prayers concerning wisdom; for Tuesday, concerning the Holy Spirit; for Wednesday, concerning charity; for Thursday, concerning the angels; for Friday, concerning the cross; and for Saturday, concerning Saint Mary.

This was done so that the priests of that time, recently converted to the faith, not yet instructed in ecclesiastical offices and not yet supplied with many books, would at least have something with which they could complete their office on each day. Hence even now some people refuse to omit these same prayers daily, although they abound in their own office [+ *proprio*; variant *propria*] [*officio*; variant *officia*].

Almost everywhere, Friday of each week is observed with the office of the cross and Saturday with that of Saint Mary, not so much by authority as by devotion. Therefore, just as such observances are assigned to no week more than to another, so too is that office of the Holy Trinity.

It thus seems incongruous to celebrate one Sunday with Albinus’s prayers and Stephen’s chant concerning the Holy Trinity, since all Sundays abound in authoritative offices that no less communicate to us the honor of the Holy Trinity.

The Preface of the Holy Trinity, however, which we frequently use on Sundays, was received not from Albinus but from Roman authority. For it is one of the nine Prefaces which Pope Pelagius, Gregory’s predecessor, established as the only ones to be observed.

Nevertheless, that same Albinus performed a work in the holy Church that should not be despised. He is said to have collected the Gregorian prayers in the Sacramentary books, adding a few others, which he nevertheless indicated should be marked with an obelus. He then collected other prayers or Prefaces which, although not Gregorian, were nevertheless suitable for ecclesiastical celebration, as the prologue testifies—the prologue that he placed in the middle of the same book after the Gregorian prayers.

## CHAPTER LXI — On the Harmony and Order of the Offices

It should be known that Saint Gregory arranged the ecclesiastical offices in such a way that the first prayer at Mass always agrees with the office, the lesson, and the Gospel, as can be observed in all solemnities.

But those especially disrupt this harmony in the summer Sundays who improperly adopt the prayers of vacant Sundays. For example, the prayer “Supplication,” although it is legitimately placed on the octave of Pentecost after the Ember fast, is nevertheless often found among the Sundays in third place. This happens because the aforesaid fast is sometimes celebrated in the second week after Pentecost, although inappropriately.

Whoever therefore applies the aforesaid prayer to the third Sunday office will disturb the harmony of the offices in due order until the Advent of the Lord.

In the same way, anyone will err who, after the autumn fast, adapts any Sunday office to the prayer of the vacant Sunday, or to the prayer “Absolve,” which precedes the fast.

With these matters established, the Mass prayers should be joined successively to the individual offices in such a way that the prayer “Almighty and everlasting God, who, in the abundance of your mercy …” is joined to the Gospel “Two men.” These agree with one another so closely that the devotion of the publican seems to be expressed in the prayer itself.

Likewise, the Secret “O God, who … [by] the distinction [+ *differentia*] of legal sacrifices” [variant: *differentiam hostiarum*, “the distinction of offerings”] should always be joined to the Offertory “As in a holocaust.” For although other prayers of this kind undoubtedly agree with their offices, a more evident harmony is marked in the examples mentioned above. Whoever observes this carefully will not disturb the harmony of the offices either before or afterward, if he wishes to associate the prayers individually with the offices in their proper order.

## CHAPTER LXII — On Not Easily Omitting the Sunday Office

According to Roman custom, every Sunday we satisfy the ecclesiastical assembly with the Sunday office, unless a particularly distinguished feast occurs on that day, such as the feast of John the Baptist or of Saint Peter the Apostle. For the people usually assemble for these no less than for Sunday, and we would celebrate them with the greatest solemnity on other days as well.

Likewise, since there are more Sundays than offices, we do not postpone them as some people do, but repeat certain offices whenever necessary, observing only this rule: the final office is to be sung only on the nearest Sunday before the Advent of the Lord.

For this is the preparation for the Advent of the Lord, which must always begin on the fifth Sunday before the Nativity of the Lord. Just as the ancient Fathers were taught about Christ’s Advent through the five ages or through the five books of Moses, so we too are to be instructed about his Advent through five Sundays, so that, according to the Gospel of that day, we may deserve to be satisfied with five loaves among five thousand people.

[Col. 1021] Here ends the *Μικρόλογος* (*Mikrologos*, “Little Discourse”).

# ELEVENTH-CENTURY DIPLOMATIC MONUMENTS

## DIPLOMAS AND ECCLESIASTICAL CONSTITUTIONS OF THE EMPERORS OF GERMANY AND OF THE FRANKISH KINGS

## RADULF III, CALLED THE PIOUS, KING OF BURGUNDY  
*(994–1032)*

# DIPLOMAS OF RADULF

## I. He confirms what his father Conrad had granted to the monastery of Saint Andrew at Vienne  
*(Year 994)*

[Edited by Achery, *Spicilegium*, vol. III, p. 380.]

[Col. 1021C]

In the name of the Lord, the eternal God, King Radulf.

[Col. 1022C] If, following the example of the preceding Catholic kings, we strive to confer some benefit upon holy places, by which the life of those serving God there may be sustained, we trust that we shall not only reign prosperously for a longer time in this life but also receive recompense from God in the eternal life.

Therefore let the whole of the holy Church of God and of our faithful, both present and future, know that the venerable abbot Haimoinus of the monastery of the Apostle Saint Andrew, situated in the city of Vienne, together with the monks entrusted to him, brought before our presence a charter of our father and requested that we deign to confirm, by a charter of our authority, the properties that he [that is, our father] had long before granted to the aforesaid monastery, which he had restored, for the remedy of the soul of our mother, Queen Matilda, and of his own soul.

These properties are situated in the county of Vienne: the church in the village of Vitrosco with its appurtenances; everything that our father and mother acquired in that village or at Arelo; one mansus at Arcas; and one tenant holding at Masiano.

We, however, not only grant our assent to this request but, moreover, with the counsel of our beloved wife, Queen Agildrudis, and of our brother Burchard, archbishop of Lyons, return and grant to Saint Andrew and Saint Maximus a certain village called Crisinciacus, together with its families of both sexes and every age and all its possessions. This village had long ago been taken away from the aforesaid monastery and was returned by our father at the end of his life for the salvation of his soul.

By this charter of our authority we decree that henceforth no duke, margrave, count, or any great or small person of our kingdom dare demand from the aforesaid properties any toll or other payment. They are to remain perpetually for the support of the monks serving God in the aforesaid monastery, free from the disturbance of all men.

If anyone should violate this charter of ours, let him know that he will pay thirty pounds of the finest gold, one half to our palace treasury and one half to the aforesaid monks.

To make it more truly believed that this was done by us, and to ensure that it be observed more carefully in succeeding times, we strengthened it with the subscription of our hand and ordered it to be marked with the impression of our seal. To confirm further the confirmation already made, we add the church of Masclatis with its appurtenances for the support of the aforesaid monks.

Sign of Lord Radulf, most noble king.

I, Paldolfus, chancellor, have reviewed this.

[Col. 1023D] Given on the second day before the Ides of January [12 January], in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 994, in the fifth indiction, and in the first year of the reign of Lord Radulf the king.

Done at Vienne, happily, in the name of God. Amen.

## II. He grants the county of the city of Tarentaise to Amizo, archbishop of Tarentaise  
*(Year 996)*

[Muratori, *Antiquitates Italicae*, I, 415.]

In the name of the holy and indivisible Trinity, Radulf, king by the mercy of the eternal Judge.

When kings were established at the beginning of the Christian religion, they considered the solicitude and care of the bishops serving God. By increasing bishoprics through gifts of land, many brought them to the highest dignity. We, therefore, weighing the examples of our predecessors and the burden of our sins, lest we be condemned in fear by the anger of the strict Judge, grant a county to the archbishopric that had been utterly devastated by Hibernian incursions and that Amizo has invested and ordered as far as his strength permits. By the authority of this charter of ours, we confirm that it has been given justly and lawfully, so that just as it had repeatedly fallen beneath the fury of the aforesaid wicked incursions, so it may be raised by the honor of our assistance.

We commit this matter to our heart with every consideration and, bending our knees, implore the Lord Christ Jesus that, after these things have been accomplished, we may be carried into the kingdom of the heavenly homeland. To the holy Church of God at Tarentaise we grant in full the county belonging to it; we present this county to God, prince of the most blessed Apostles, so that the aforesaid archbishop himself may have full power in all matters to entrust the administration or governance of his bishops for such times as he wishes.

Therefore, whoever presumes with reckless boldness to violate the terms of this donation of ours shall be subject to all the curses of God and, bound by the knots and bonds of all the holy Apostles, shall be condemned by perpetual anathema.

Let this authority of ours remain firm and stable forever. Moreover, let the violator know that he must pay one hundred pounds of the finest gold, one half to our treasury and one half to the archbishop or his successors.

But so that you may believe this more surely, we have confirmed the present charter and ordered it to be marked with our seal.

[Col. 1024C] Sign of Lord Radulf, most serene king.

Anselm, the king’s chancellor, wrote this charter in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 996, in the tenth indiction, and in the third year of Radulf’s reign.

Done at Agaunum, happily.

## III. He grants the church of Saint Nicholas at Poligny to Saint Odilo and the monastery of Cluny  
*(Year 1029)*

[Dom Martène, *Thesaurus Anecdotorum*, I, 147, from the archives of the Chamber of Accounts at Dijon.]

In the name of the holy and indivisible Trinity, Radulf, king of the Burgundians by the grace of God.

Just as it is certain that the almighty God does not … [lacuna]—indeed, without him there is no power— so it is also clear that he will call the works of the powerful to account. For this reason we must take the greatest care that, whenever by his dispensation we are able either to help or to harm, we completely subject our power to his will and eagerly do whatever may advance the honor of his holy Church.

Accordingly, considering the sequence of ancient custom and the royal practice of the Christian religion, we desire with all our strength and with the whole devotion of our mind to imitate them. What they devoted to the care of ecclesiastical eminence, we too undertake with spiritual weapons and the shield of the Lord’s protection, taking up that same solicitude of care, like those who mercifully rendered themselves pleasing to God’s servants.

Therefore let it be known to all, both kings and persons of every other rank, present and future, that our faithful Reinaldus, count, son of Otho called William, a most illustrious man, requested us to grant by this charter of our authority to the monastery of Cluny, constructed in honor of the first princes of heaven, namely Peter and Paul, over which the reverend Father Odilo presides, a church or monastery consecrated in honor of God and Jesus Christ the Savior, his Mother Mary, Saint Peter the Apostle, and Saint Nicholas the holy confessor, so that Cluniac monks might dwell there and continually offer prayers and vows to God for our salvation and that of all people.

We therefore grant to the aforesaid monastery the said place, situated in the diocese of Besançon near Poligny, established in a place properly called the Valley, together with its land and tithes and everything belonging to it; whatever was or will be granted there by Otho of blessed memory, called William, or by his son Reinaldus, or by any possessor; and everything acquired there from any source in our kingdom or to be acquired there perpetually.

At present we also grant four iron cauldrons and their sites in the saltworks, and the vineyards that once belonged to Beatrice, and everything that the Cluniac monks have acquired in the aforesaid borough.

In the borough of Gysans, whatever they have acquired there or may acquire in addition; and finally the village of Glenon, with its church and tithes, servants and maidservants, vineyards, small woods, meadows, rural holdings, fields, pastures, and every kind of land, cultivated and uncultivated, together with absolutely everything situated anywhere that belongs to the same little village.

We also grant the village of Milan and its church, with the tithes and all its appurtenances, especially the perpetual customary right in the forest of Maydun; likewise the village of Vesan, with its church and tithes and everything belonging to the same village; also the place called Mutua and everything belonging to it.

We further grant Gunther of Popilianum, with everything that he is seen to possess, both in allods and in the benefices of counts, and his entire possession without exception; also the fishery of Guiriacum, with all the land belonging to it.

Therefore, in response to the request of the aforesaid Count Reinaldus and of our other faithful, and with the consent of our wife Yrmengardis, we grant to the monastery of Cluny, as stated, everything mentioned above and everything that is to be acquired thereafter, to hold and possess by perpetual right, without contradiction from any person, whether from us, from anyone who succeeds us in the kingdom, or from anyone of any other order or dignity, and without any customary due retained there by anyone.

And so that this may be believed more certainly to have been done by us and not be broken by our successors, we have strengthened it with our own hand and ordered it to be marked with the impression of our seal.

Sign of Lord Radulf the king.

Done at Logis, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1029, in the thirty-fifth year of the reign of King Radulf.

# HENRY I, KING OF THE FRANKS  
*(1031–1060)*

[Col. 1025]

# DIPLOMAS

## I. For the monastery of Saint Salvus at Montreuil — Henry confirms the donations made to that place by his grandfather Hugh and his father Robert  
*(Year 1042)*

[Dom Mabillon, *Annales Benedictini*, vol. IV, Appendix, p. 733, from the cartulary of Saint Salvus.]

[Col. 1025C]

In the name of the holy and indivisible Trinity, I, Henry, king of the Franks by the grace of God, etc.

Therefore, for the place of Saint Wingaloeus situated at Monsterolum, endowed by many persons, we confirm by our authoritative command and order that it be marked with the impression of our seal. First, those things which were granted to the aforesaid place by our generosity, or by my father Robert, or by my grandfather Hugh: namely, two mills serving the purposes of brewing beer—one granted by me, with five inhabitants, and the other by my aforesaid grandfather Hugh, together with a tenth of the bridge toll—and two churches consecrated in memory of Saint Judocus, one of which is within the fortification and the other above the river [lacuna], together with the fishery of the water from Atimacum as far as [lacuna]. Moreover, in confirmation, we add those things which my father conferred: three churches, one consecrated in honour of Saint Peter, another in honour of Saint Wingaloeus, and the third in honour of Saint Salvius; and the passage of the new town [lacuna].

We further emphasize, in confirmation, those things conferred by the place’s first founders: namely, by Count Hilgod, who, receiving the aforesaid saint—recently brought from the regions of Brittany because of fear of pirates—with hospitality, generosity, and munificence in the time of Emperor Louis, son of Charles the Bald, gave him, first, a public courtyard, that is, a burial place for foreigners and pilgrims; then nine manses below La Ferté [lacuna]. To these, by our authority, we add those things conferred by Count Herlewin, Raynerus, Hato, Scylaldus, Wenerannus, Clarboldus, Aldo the count, Anscerus, Saleco, Count Arnulf, Count Baldwin, Gonfridus, Benzelinus, Alfridus, Hagano, the cleric Autgerus, Margrave Baldwin, Count Ingerannus, Rodulfus, Landricus-Largus, Hato, Framericus, Hugh, Walterus, and Herleboldus. The first of these, Count Herlewin, gave in the village of Sguira one church in honour of Saint Vedastus, and the village called Long Meadow, with woodland, arable land, and meadows. Finally, he gave the village of Silviniacum, and so forth.

Enacted publicly at Monsterolum in the year 1042 of the Incarnation of the Word, and in the eleventh year of the reign of King Henry. I, Baldwin, the king’s chancellor, have subscribed after rereading it.

[Note: The charter of Wido, count of Ponthieu, follows in the cartulary. He grants to the monastery of Saints Salvius and Wingaloeus all banns and all jurisdictions over whatever offenses, which his predecessors held, and so forth; in the year 1100, while Lord Pope Raynerus, surnamed Paschal, presided over the Roman See, Manasses held the archbishopric of the church of Reims, Perrevinus [read: Gervinus] was bishop of the church of Amiens, Normannus was abbot of this place, and King Philip, with his son Louis, held the scepter of the Franks in the fortieth year. I, Wido, count of Ponthieu, and so forth. The sign of my daughter Agnes.]

## II. Legal judgment for the monastery of Saint Medard against Robert of Coudray. (Year 1047)

[Dom Mabillon, *De re diplomatica*, book VI, p. 604, from the cartulary of Saint Medard.]

We see the customary human vice of habit spread so far that it obscures what is fundamental in nature with its own mists, and, having cast aside the purity of simplicity, it gladly bears the circle of toil beneath the yoke to which it has voluntarily submitted. Hence rare simplicity necessarily needs to be strengthened by testimony, since otherwise it cannot overcome the multiplied cunning of human wickedness.

For this reason, the long dispute between Rainoldus, abbot of Saint Medard, and Robert of Coudray, having been brought before the presence of Henry, the most invincible king of the Franks, was ended by his just judgment and royal authority. Concerning the many things which Robert had been unjustly able to do in the abbey by tyrannical force, the matter was settled by the king’s command, and the conclusion of the dispute was set out and confirmed in these letters [Col. 1027C] as a testimony to the truth, so that henceforth neither the aforesaid knight nor his descendants might murmur about anything, as the insatiable greed of mortals very often does concerning churches.

Let it therefore be known to all the sons and faithful members of the holy Church of God, present and future, that Rainaldus, by the grace of God constituted abbot of the monastery founded outside the walls of the city of Soissons in honour of Saint Medard, compelled by great necessity, approached King Henry in the abbey of Saint Stephen, at the place called Coudray, before the bishops, abbots, and many nobles listed below, for the purpose of establishing the truth. He brought to the ears of the most pious king complaints against Robert concerning numerous customary exactions, which Robert himself had levied in the same abbey contrary to law and right.

Robert, compelled by royal command, appeared. Although for a long time he had striven in vain to defend the things he had unjustly presumed to do and levy, at last, overcome both by the order of the most powerful prince and by the firmest reasoning of the nobles present, he was compelled, repenting of the past, to acknowledge that only what we have written below was owed to him in the abbey.

If any powerful person or neighbour should do anything unjust to the abbot or his agents concerning outsiders—for example, concerning levies or other wrongs—and the abbot or his agents are able by themselves to obtain and receive justice, Robert and his descendants shall have no claim in this matter. But if the abbot or his agents lack the strength to obtain justice, and for that reason Robert himself or his descendants are warned and summoned by the abbot or his agents to provide defense, then, if they obtain justice through them, they shall receive only one-third of the justice which is commonly called the Law.

Since, therefore, by the testimony of many he was brought to acknowledge this alone among the just and unjust customary exactions, we have written below the names of the suitable witnesses in whose presence this matter was conducted and confirmed, so that—something we believe will never happen hereafter—neither he nor any of his descendants would dare to breathe a word about seeking anything further.

And so that it might not happen again, all the bishops whose names are subscribed below, at the king’s command and in his presence, pronounced an anathema; the king confirmed this with his own hand and ordered it to be marked with the seal of royal authority.

The sign of Wido, archbishop of Reims. The sign of Beraldus, bishop of Soissons. The sign of Walterus, bishop of Meaux. The sign of Gibuinus, bishop of Laon. The sign of Drogo, bishop of Beauvais. The sign of Roger, bishop of Châlons. The sign of Frolandus, bishop of Senlis. The sign of Count Rainaldus. The sign of Guido, his son. The sign of Drogo. The sign of Godefridus. Of the knight of Saint-Quentin. The sign of Baldwin. The sign of Walter Albanus. The sign of William, his brother. The sign of Wido, viscount. The sign of Guido of Cerchia. The sign of Wazelin of Chasney. The sign of Wido, marshal. The sign of Drogo, provost. The sign of Odardus. The sign of Odelinus, chamberlain. The sign of Gunzelinus. The sign of Fulco. The sign of Everaldus, son of Hesselinus. The sign of Gerardus. The sign of Vivienus. The sign of Aeilbertus. The sign of Henry, the most invincible king of the Franks.

Written in place of Chancellor Rainoldus, at the order of Abbot Rainaldus, in the year 1047 of the Incarnation of the Word, in the fifteenth indiction, and in the nineteenth year of the reign of King Henry.

[Note: In the cartulary it was written “in the year 1049 of the Incarnation of the Word”; but it must be restored to “1047,” if the indiction is correctly written here, calculated according to the years of Henry’s reign from his coronation, which took place in 1027. Compare the legal judgment of King Philip against Alberic of Coudray. Here the sign of King Henry is placed out of order, whereas it ought to have been first.]

## III. King Henry I of the Franks grants the free fisc of Unigradus to the canons of Chartres. (Year 1048)

[*Gallia Christiana*, vol. VIII, p. 300]

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, namely, of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, I, Henry, king of the Franks by the grace of God.

If the institution of the ancients wished us to be devoted to the worship of the saints and the usefulness of churches, how much more ought we to be devoted to the singular memorial of our salvation, namely, the Mother of God, whom after God we believe and trust to be not only the aid but also the full realization of our salvation! Therefore, being greatly concerned with acquiring eternal happiness, I looked around to see whether I possessed anything that I could expend for her service and for earning her favour.

While I was reflecting on this for some time, the request of the canons of the church of Chartres came back to mind—a request they had often pressed—which asked that I grant the fisc called Unigradus [alternative: Ingreium] free and exempt henceforth from the various payments and exactions commonly called the vicaria.

I, however, increasing the weight of their petition, grant everything that any land of the aforesaid fisc had until now been accustomed to pay to me and mine, so that those dwelling there may live more securely and therefore be able to render more fully whatever they owe from those lands to the canons. I except four sextarii of wine from each arpent, which I have retained for the sake of advocacy, so that if anyone in the future should attempt to wrong that fisc, with the aid of the heavenly King he may find me a hostile advocate on its behalf.

And so that the munificence of our generosity might be known to all the faithful of holy Mother Church and to our own people, we command this to be written out with the greatest care and diligence and marked with the impression of our seal, so that what we have established with our own hand by impressing the sign of the cross may remain unshaken through the succession of time.

If anyone should attempt to violate this agreement—which God forbid—let him incur the wrath of God, depart convicted by the authority of us and our successors, and pay one hundred pounds of gold to the royal fisc for his unlawful presumption.

Enacted publicly at Paris in the year 1048 of the Incarnation of the Word, in the first indiction, in the eighteenth year of the reign of King Henry, on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of May.

## IV. Privilege for the monastery of Saint Thierry near Reims

The king, aided by Abbot Albert in the capture of Château-Neuf, frees his monastery from the yoke of advocates and the vexations of archdeacons. (Around the year 1050.)

[Dom Martène, *Amplissima Collectio*, I, 422, from a manuscript of Saint Thierry.]

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity. I, Henry, king of the Franks by the grace of God, offer peace and salvation to my successors, the kings.

Everyone who succeeds another in any rank of dignity ought to imitate him in every honourable purpose, since by succeeding him he has willingly bound himself to his office. For he ought not to seek by usurpation the place of office or the seat of exalted dignity if he does not dare to claim its effect. Therefore, carrying out as far as we can the generosity and munificence of kings and emperors whom, by the preceding grace of God, we have succeeded both in office and in dignity, we wish to be such generous and devoted servants toward the places of the saints and the communities of the faithful serving the divine Majesty that we may not appear sluggish or degenerate in comparison with their excellence and liberality.

Although we ought to do this generally for all churches, judging it right to support and assist them, nevertheless we owe a more attentive consideration, by duty and reason, to those whose members have laboured in our service and have happened to work especially hard in our faithfulness.

It is known to nearly all the inhabitants of the kingdom of the Franks how much labour we expended in capturing the castle called Château-Neuf. In carrying this through vigorously and courageously, the place of Saint Bartholomew gave us great assistance, since Albert, then abbot of that place, worked so diligently and steadfastly that I was often reminded by my own men to repay him suitably and grant him a worthy reward for his merit.

Moved by this persuasion from my men, I decided to seek what I might provide to the aforesaid place and abbot as a reward for his service and labour. But when I learned from the abbot and the inhabitants of the place that the advocacy of the abbey, which castellans had held, had been hostile to them and theirs, because they had suffered many public and private injuries through it, then, with the counsel and support of my men, we wholly granted the aforesaid advocacy, together with the benefice belonging to it, to the said place.

[Note: The place of Saint Bartholomew is the monastery of Saint Thierry near Reims, whose principal patron is still recognized as that apostle.]

Afterward they informed our serenity that they were suffering many adversities at the hands of the archdeacon, who ought to have been the administrator and provider of that place for its benefit, under the pretext of canonical institution. Although they repeatedly complained about this to the archbishop, they did not obtain the peace they desired and needed, because the archbishop was frequently occupied with secular affairs.

Compelled by this necessity, they made known to us what adversities they were suffering. Taking pity on this complaint, I approached the archbishop amicably together with the ecclesiastical ministers, asking that they entirely refrain from what was plainly injurious and contrary to the statutes of the canons and the decrees of the apostolic see, and that, out of love for us and at our request, they wholly frustrate whatever evils might be exacted under the appearance of good.

When I did not obtain this condition of our request from them voluntarily, we publicly granted to the aforesaid church the written agreement, bearing the impression of our seal and confirmed by the hands of our faithful men, and, with the assent of all who were present, forbade it.

We therefore ask our successors that, whatever they establish for the salvation of their souls and wish to remain perpetual, they preserve this our statute unshaken through the course of time against the dependants of the bishops.
