We confirmed this precept of our authority in the assembly of our bishops, lest anyone’s rashness should presume to violate it contrary to law and rights; we strengthened it by their excommunication and ordered it to be presented to the pope, so that he might do the same.

[Note: Without doubt this was Pope Leo IV, when he came to Reims and held a council in the church of Saint Remigius, which he had consecrated.]

Finally, we decided to insert into our written precept the agreement which the archbishop and archdeacon confirmed and made with us, so that no one might arise in the future who could add anything to it, subtract anything from it, or alter it.

## V. Privilege of Henry I, king of the Franks, for the monastery of Casa Dei. (Year 1052)

[*Gallia Christiana*, II, 1031.]

In the name of the Lord, and so forth.

We wish it to be known [lacuna] that the venerable and God-worthy man Robert, canon and treasurer of Brioude, having approached our clemency, sent by Lord Renconus [lacuna], bishop of Auvergne, and commended by letters, informed us that he wished to raise to the dignity and honour of an abbey, by command and authority of our generosity and with the permission of his bishop, a certain church situated in a wilderness in the territory of Auvergne and greatly enlarged by honours, called Casa Dei.

Therefore, having taken common counsel with the nobles and leading men of our palace, we decided to grant his requests and, both by our own [possibly: our] indulgence and that of our fathers, authorize this by a precept of our confirmation; we ordered and permitted it to become an abbey, and so forth.

We omit many details concerning this new abbey, subject to the church of Clermont, with the obligation of paying as a census one pound of incense on the feast of the Assumption of the Blessed Mary. We have transcribed the remaining material, which contains a catalogue of the possessions of the newly founded monastery.

We have also marked with the authority of our power and confirmed with the royal seal the gifts granted for the love and fear of God to the aforesaid church, namely: in the same village, a church consecrated in honour of the holy martyrs Vitalis and Agricola. In the territory of Brioude, one church in honour of Saint Andrew of Comps, with everything belonging to it. In the village of Tuniacum, the church of Saint Germanus the martyr, together with the village itself and everything belonging to it. In the territory of Fornoliacum, a church together with the village itself and everything belonging to it. The church of Bellum-Pomerium together with the village itself and everything belonging to it. The chapel of the Castle of Bullion. In the village of Luziliacum, three churches together with the village itself and everything belonging to it. In the village of Saint Domninus, two churches and half of the village itself. In the castle of Monte-Vasconum, a chapel. In the village of Saint Victor, two churches. In the territory of Rocense, the church of Saint Desiderius, bishop and martyr. In the territory of Lyon, in the village called Sociacus, the church of Saint Mary together with the village itself and everything belonging to it, as well as many other estates of villages, cultivated and uncultivated lands, woods, vineyards, waters, and pastures.

Whoever should presume to bring any dispute or claim against this donation [lacuna], let his petition be rendered void by our precept, and let the bishops of the region inflict full vengeance. Let the aforesaid church have permission, by order of our majesty, to enlarge and increase its possessions.

Whatever its rectors acquire in any part of our realm, saving ecclesiastical right, whether in villages, estates, or any goods, we have marked with the firmness of our majesty. Both goods to be acquired in the future and goods previously acquired and possessed we have transferred and authorized, and so forth.

So that this precept might rest upon firmer confirmation, we have strengthened it below with our ring and commanded the bishop of Auvergne and the other bishops of our kingdom by the authority of our office.

Enacted publicly at the palace of Vitry, at the request of Lord and Venerable Hugh, bishop of Nevers, in the month of September, on the eleventh day of the moon, in the year 1052 from the Incarnation of the Lord, and in the twenty-first year of the reign of our lord and most invincible King Henry.

The following prelates subscribe this precept: Aymo, archbishop of Bourges; Renconus, bishop of Auvergne; Hugh, bishop of Nevers; Mainardus, archbishop of Sens; Arnulfus of Tours; Isambardus, bishop of Orléans; Enzelinus, bishop of Paris; Agobertus, bishop of Chartres; Heribertus, bishop of Auxerre; Helmuinus, bishop of Autun; Gutdo, bishop of Chalon.

Among the princes and nobles: Robert, duke of Burgundy, the king’s brother; Odo, the same king’s brother; William, duke of Aquitaine; William, duke of Normandy; the counts William, Rodulfus, Theobaldus, Rainaldus, and Seguinus. Sciolus wrote this on behalf of Baldwin, the king’s chancellor, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of October.

At nearly the same time Pope Leo received the same monastery under the protection of the Apostolic See, by a diploma issued on the sixth day before the Nones of May, in the fourth year of his pontificate, in the fifth indiction. Later, through so many diplomas of this kind, whether papal or royal, and so forth, the abbey of Casa Dei was endowed that a large volume could easily be compiled from them; but we refrain from recounting them. Its first benefactors were Stephen of Mercœur, Gerard of Turlande, and William of Baffie, but especially Guido called William VII, duke of Aquitaine.

## VI. Charter for the monastery of Saint Victor of Nevers

The abbey of Saint Victor of Nevers, taken from lay hands, is restored. (Year 1055.)

[D. Martène, *Amplissima Collectio*, vol. I, p. 434, from the archives of Saint Victor of Marseilles.]

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, Henry, king of the Franks by the grace of God.

Let all posterity know that things recognized as pertaining to the restoration of the holy Catholic Church are proved beyond doubt to prepare a great support for the royal eminence; this not only strengthens the condition of the kingdom in the present, but also gains for itself the reward of eternal recompense in the future.

Therefore we make known to all the sons of the holy Church of God, present and future, that a certain cleric named Belinus approached our majesty, asking that we confirm by the privilege of our authority a gift made to him by William, count of Nevers, and certain other leading men of Nevers: namely, a certain church consecrated in honour of Saint Victor in the suburb of Nevers, an exceedingly ancient church and, in the earliest times, one of the first abbeys of the aforesaid city, wealthy, endowed, enlarged, and enriched by many gifts.

Later, when the world had been placed in evil, it was partly left desolate through the neglect of pastoral care in the curia, partly destroyed by the barbarity of the worst Christians, and, to speak more accurately, everywhere bent and humbled beneath the hands of the impious.

This church, emancipated from royal dominion like many others and handed over by our royal predecessors to the count of Nevers by beneficiary right, was subsequently held by a certain Frotmundus. He had distributed it among knights, had given more away, had given less to himself, and had retained less for himself.

Thus the church, desolated and reduced to nothing, was almost destroyed [lacuna], plainly a church overturned from its foundations. But Almighty God, unwilling that the honour of the martyr and the name of the church should be diminished, chose a certain cleric who had burned with love for that church from his earliest cradle. There he served God under the clerical profession in childhood, in adolescence, and up to mature age.

He helped and enlarged the captive church, which after God he loved uniquely, as far as he could; and he prayed and pleaded without ceasing that God might deign to visit it, rising from on high.

With the assent of Bishop Hugh and Count William, he approached the aforementioned Frotmundus and prayed that he redeem the captive church from its captors and from captivity itself, and urged him to restore the generosity that had been freely bestowed. He laboured in his exhortation and, through the mercy of God, obtained what he had sought.

Therefore the aforesaid Frotmundus, inwardly touched by the love of charity and inflamed by the words of the venerable man, approached the count and relinquished to him what he appeared to hold from him, namely, the church of Saint Victor.

The count, for his part, judged that the venerable man’s ardour ought to be fulfilled. He summoned him and, for the love and fear of God and for the repose of the souls of our royal predecessors, gave him the church as a gift and accepted nothing in exchange.

Not long afterward the aforesaid count approached the greatness of our authority with the priest just mentioned, reported this deed to our ears, and asked—pleading at length with the priest—that, for the repose of my soul and those of our parents, we authorize this gift [lacuna] and confirm it by our majesty.

We gladly assented to their request and confirmed the gift as it stood. We also decreed that that church should return to its former condition and that the abbey should be restored; the properties and churches divided among many persons and taken away from the aforesaid church [lacuna] should be restored by our authority, and no one should be permitted thereafter to seize or remove anything from its goods.

We decree and establish that whoever wishes to enlarge that church from our benefice, or to restore any of the goods anciently taken from it, whether by God’s arrangement or from his own resources [lacuna], shall, by the favour of our authority, have free power in all things.

It also pleased us that no archbishop, no bishop, no provost in holy Church, no duke, no count or viscount, and no secular person, powerful or powerless, should [lacuna] any secular matter in that church [lacuna].

A worthy abbot of God shall therefore be instituted there free from every form of venality—not through the favour or will of any powerful person, but by the election of the brothers serving God there. He shall not be sought because of secular lineage, nor one who delights in secular affairs, nor one who is bound to secular people in a worldly manner. For, as Blessed Gregory says, “he who, when invited, refuses, and when sought, withdraws, ought to be promoted to the sacred altars”; but he who thrusts himself forward uninvited and importunately and seeks the abbey for himself is in no way worthy of this honour.

Let that church remain free from every secular yoke. Let no one [lacuna] presume to institute a pastor there; let no one be received except one whom the brotherhood, unanimous and prudent through the mercy of God, has elected.

Let the aforesaid abbey therefore have free power to acquire or exchange [lacuna]. Whatever it has or shall have, whatever it acquires while preserving ecclesiastical right, preserving due reverence for us and for the mother church, let it remain unshaken, firm, and stable [lacuna].

But if anyone should intrude himself [lacuna], let the abbot of that place not doubt that he will receive full vengeance from the royal [lacuna]. Let the crafty person gain nothing from this, but pay one hundred pounds of gold to the royal fisc [lacuna].

Let this grant of our munificent authority always possess, in the name of God, the strength of firmness. We confirm it below with our own hand and strengthen it with the impression of our ring.

I, Baldwin, the chancellor, have subscribed after rereading it.

Enacted at the palace of Carisiacum, with the army in attendance, in the twenty-second year of the reign of King Henry, on the Kalends of May, on the tenth day of the moon, in the sixth indiction.

[Note: William, count of Nevers, subjected this church of Saint Victor of Nevers to the monastery of Sainte-Marie at La Charité on the Loire in the year 1085, with Hugh III, bishop of Nevers, subscribing.]

## VII. Charter concerning the freedom granted to a certain Ainardus. (Year 1056)

[D. Martène, *Thesaurus Anecdotorum*, I, 183, from the original.]

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, I, Henry, king of the Franks by the grace of God.

I wish it to be known to all my faithful, present and future, that Gausbertus, a cleric of Sainte-Maure, through the release granted by Count Goffridus, with the assent of his mother Aremburga, his brother Hugh, and his sister Jachelina, asked that, for the salvation of the soul of his recently deceased brother William, I grant the gift of freedom to one of his men named Ainardus.

I did so in royal fashion, namely, by striking him free from the palm-denarius, on the following condition: that the roads of the four quarters of the world be open to him as to a free man.

If anyone should attempt to rise against this freedom, let him be compelled to pay one hundred pounds of gold to the king, and let his claim remain void forever.

And so that it might remain firm and stable, I ordered it to be marked with my seal.

Enacted at Tours on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of February, in the year 1056 of the Incarnation of the Word and in the twenty-sixth year of the reign of King Henry.

I, Baldwin, the chancellor, have subscribed after rereading it.

## VIII. Diploma of Henry, king of the Franks, abolishing an unjust custom

That the gates of the city of Orléans should not be closed during the grape harvest, nor guards employed. (Year 1058.)

[Achery, *Spicilegium*, vol. III, p. 401.]

In the name of Christ, I, Henry, king of the Franks by the grace of God.

I wish it to be known to all the faithful of the holy Church of God, present and future, how Isambardus, bishop of Orléans, together with the clergy and people entrusted to him, approached our serenity, bringing a complaint concerning a certain unjust custom which appeared to exist in that city—namely, concerning the guarding of the gates, which were guarded and closed to the citizens during the grape harvest, and concerning the impious exaction of wine which our agents imposed there.

He earnestly and humbly begged that, for the love of God and for the salvation of our soul and those of our parents, I forever pardon that impious and unjust custom to the holy Church of God and to him, the clergy, and the people.

Kindly assenting to his request, I have perpetually pardoned to God, to him, and to the aforesaid clergy and people the aforementioned custom and exaction, so that no guards may thereafter be stationed there, nor the gates be closed throughout that season as had been customary, nor wine be taken from or demanded of anyone.

Rather, let entry and departure be free for all, and let each person’s property be preserved for him according to civil law and equity.

So that this pardon might remain firm and stable forever, we wished this testament of our authority to be made concerning it and confirmed it below with our seal and ring.

The sign of Isambardus, bishop of Orléans; the sign of King Henry; the sign of Gervasius, archbishop of Reims; the sign of Hugh Bardulfus; the sign of Hugh, the butler; the sign of Henry of Ferrières; the sign of Malbertus, provost; the sign of Hervaeus, the road-warden; the sign of Herbertus, deputy road-warden; the sign of Gislebertus, cupbearer; the sign of Jordanus, cellarer. Baldwin, the chancellor, subscribed.

Given publicly at Orléans on the sixth day before the Nones of October, in the year 1057 from the Incarnation of the Lord, and in the twenty-seventh year of King Henry.

## IX. Charter of King Henry for the monastery of Saint Peter. (Year 1058)

[*Gallia Christiana*, VIII, 301.]

Henry, king of the Franks by the grace of God.

Although the royal throne of dignity is adorned by the manifold cultivation of virtues, generosity and munificence nevertheless hold the foremost place among them.

Let it therefore be known to all that a certain faithful man of mine named Albertus, son of the most noble man Ribaldus, approached our serenity, earnestly asking that, by the royal piety of our munificence, we might assent to his requests and incline our ear to them.

His request was that a certain church, which his faithful father Ribaldus had built in the village of Bruerolum in honour of the blessed Germanus, bishop of Auxerre, for the salvation of his soul, might be enriched by him and his faithful men, through royal clemency, for the apostle Saint Peter in the monastery in the suburb of the city of Chartres, together with the property which he appeared to possess from our benefice.

Judging his request just, with Bishop Agobertus, in whose diocese the church is situated, and with our nobles, we considered it worthy, for our salvation and the integrity of our kingdom, to grant our assent.

We therefore give him permission to enlarge the aforesaid church from the benefice of ours which he possesses, and whatever he wishes to confer upon it shall be free and released from every judicial authority, just as our faithful Albertus has until now held it from us, and so forth.

It also pleased our piety to add to this work some of the possessions which Albertus himself gave to the aforesaid church, and so forth.

I, Albertus, son of the most noble Ribaldus, desiring to attain fellowship with heavenly beings, with the favour of my beloved wife Adelaisa, grant to Saint Peter of Chartres, free from every human claim, the church of Bruerolum, which my father built in honour of Saint Germanus the bishop, together with its courtyard, burial ground, and the tithe of the church which appears to be in our hand, so that the monks may hold that church, as well as the altar of the same church, which I had held in fief from the bishop of Chartres.

To this gift, Lord Bishop Agobertus, with the consent of the canons who were with him at Drocis in the king’s court, added, at the request of Abbot Landricus and moved by our request, the census of the village itself together with the market tithe, and so forth.

Likewise, I grant to the monks of Saint Peter free passage throughout the whole land, so that no customary payment may ever be demanded from them for fish, crows, or any goods shown to belong to the monks.

I could add what my faithful men have conferred upon the aforesaid place, but since it has been written elsewhere, I hasten to strengthen this charter with the king’s seal and the names of the nobles, and so forth.

The sign of Count Radulfus; the sign of Walterus, count and son of Radulfus; the sign of Count Hugh; the sign of Albertus; the sign of Theudo, his brother; the sign of Guarinus, his brother; the sign of Fredericus; the sign of Baldwin; the sign of Simon; the sign of Bishop Agobertus; the sign of Hugh, dean; the sign of William, provost; the sign of Sigo; the sign of Ascelinus; the sign of Gencelinus, dean.

## X. King Henry I introduces regular canons into the church of Saint Martin at the Fields, which he restored. (Year 1060)

[ *Gallia Christiana*, VII, 32.]

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, and so forth.

Therefore I, HENRY, by the grace of God king of the Franks, recalling with diligent thought how I loved the beauty of the house of the Lord and the place of his habitation [alternative: of those inhabiting it], wished it to be known to all, present and future. Now, before the gate of the city of Paris, there was recognized as having been an abbey in honor of Christ’s confessor Martin. This, utterly destroyed by tyrannical fury—as though it had never existed—I restored from the foundations and enlarged. Seeking to give back to the heavenly Bridegroom a church that, long barren and deprived of offspring, had mourned, I appointed there, on the advice of religious men, canons serving God according to a regular way of life, so that, living without anxiety and devoting themselves more to divine than worldly concerns, they might be able to live. I endowed the church with property for the remedy of the souls of my father and mother, and for the salvation and peace of myself, my wife, and my offspring; I grant them these possessions to hold in perpetual right:

First, the altar of the same basilica, endowed with complete freedom; the lands that I previously held around the same church, and those which Ansoldus, together with his nephews, namely Milo and Warinus, gave me, with the consent of Count Hugh, on account of the reconciliation of the aforesaid Milo, who was then accused of a great crime against me. But when, at the entreaties of Bishop Ymbertus, I accepted the cultivation of the land from the aforesaid soldiers, I remitted that offense, for which he would have paid one hundred pounds according to a just judgment.

These lands, situated around the church’s walls, I grant to the same church with this freedom: that no one presume to exact any payment from them. At Paris, one mill; in the village called Alberti Villare, the land that I held there; Noisiacum, situated on the Materna, with all the revenues and payments from the land, woodland, vineyards, and meadows; in the territory of Meaux, the village called Anethum, with all the revenues and payments from the land, woodland, vineyards, and meadows; from the revenues of the pasture, woodland, and *liegium* [alternative: *leigium*], the entire tithe. Likewise, in the county of Paris, Bongeias, with all the revenues and payments freely adjoining it. Also, in the county of Laon, let them have, hold, administer, and possess half of Disiaci, except for the altar, together with the aforesaid possessions.

I absolutely do not wish this to be omitted: I fortify the aforesaid church with such security that it shall forever be granted freedom by royal right from everyone, both within the circuit of its fortification and outside it, in its surrounding district—in tolls, fines, judicial matters, and everything whatsoever that the right of our fisc requires. Let no one ever dare to disturb it.

The canons shall also have this authority: when the abbot dies, they may, with the consent of the brothers and without anyone causing disturbance, restore a man of good reputation. Moreover, so that these fiscal rights may be held securely, I have confirmed below with my seal this charter in which, at my command, all these matters have been written. I myself, King Henry, together with the queen, and my son Philip with his brothers, have strengthened it by hand. Mainardus, archbishop of Sens, together with Ymbertus, bishop of Paris, and very many others, both bishops and lay princes, confirmed and strengthened it, approving all the matters stated above.

If anyone should thereafter presume to violate this privilege, let him first, as guilty of sacrilege or of negligence toward so great an authority, be struck with a harsh anathema; then, as punishment for his impious presumption, let him be condemned to a grievous loss of property.

In the twenty-seventh year of the reign of the aforesaid king.

[Note: The twenty-seventh year of Henry’s reign and the year of Christ 1060 do not agree; moreover, there is an error in the indiction [Col. 1038D], which was not XV, as in the charter, but XIII in the year 1060.]

Executed publicly at Paris in the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1060, indiction XV.

The sign of Henry the king. The sign of Philip the king. The sign of Queen Anne. The sign of Mainardus, archbishop of Sens. The sign of Gervasius, archbishop of Reims. The sign of Ymbertus, bishop of Paris. The sign of Odolricus, archdeacon of Paris. The sign of Baldwin, chancellor. The sign of Voizelinus, chaplain. The sign of Richardus, chaplain. The sign of Count Radulfus. The sign of Theobaldus of Montmorency. The sign of Rainaldus, chamberlain. The sign of Albricus, constable. The sign of Willelmus, seneschal. The sign of Hugh, butler. The sign of Robert, cook. The sign of Radulfus of Beauvais. The sign of Yvo, under-chamberlain. The sign of Walter, son of Bernerus. The sign of Amalricus Rufus. The sign of Willelmus, brother of Baldricus. The sign of Wido, bishop of Amiens. The sign of Walter, bishop of Meaux. The sign of Elinandus, bishop of Laon. The sign of Frollandus, bishop of Senlis. The sign of the bishop of Troyes. The sign of Robert, son of Count Baldwin. The sign of Wido, count of Ponthieu. The sign of Baldricus. The sign of Engenulfus. The sign of Amalricus of Montfort. The sign of Stephanus, provost. The sign of Framericus, cook.

## XI. King Henry grants the churches of Saints Stephen, Julian, Severinus, and Bacchus to the canons of Paris

*(Undated.)*

*[Gal. Chr. VII, 31.]*

[Col. 1038D]

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, HENRY, by the grace of God king of the Franks.

Let the posterity of all the faithful of holy Mother Church and of our own people know that a certain Imbertus, bishop of the Church of Paris, came into the presence of our serenity, asking and earnestly requesting that we grant to the aforesaid congregation certain churches in the Parisian suburb, anciently subject to our authority and that of our predecessors—namely, Saint Stephen, Saint Julian the martyr, Severinus the solitary, and Saint Bacchus. Some of these had once been elevated to the dignity of abbeys and therefore provided a lodging and station for the congregation of canons of Saint Mary; but, having been stripped of their granted possessions because of the disturbance of the kingdom and left vacant in desolation, they retained little or none of their ancient possessions.

Since the aforesaid bishop was highly esteemed by us for his merits, and since we did not wish to detract in any way from his desire, we granted his request concerning the aforesaid places by royal command and generosity, on this agreement and condition: that for as long as Giraldus the cleric, their possessor, lives, he shall hold them without disturbance, with the consent of the canons of the entire congregation; after his death, they shall be assigned without objection to the use of the canons. Canons shall be gathered there for the remedy of my soul and those of my parents; praying for the stability and security of our kingdom, they shall be sufficient both to render the customary station to the church and to live together in canonical service.

## XII. King Henry grants the small abbey of Saint-Germain in Laia to the Church of Paris

*(Undated.)*

*[Gal. Chr. VII, 31.]*

Since, in truth, the joys of the saints’ immortality are undoubtedly acquired through the services of virtues, and souls advance through the presentation of alms; and since the office of royal dignity always requires that it remove whatever danger threatens holy Mother Church and extend far and wide the benefit bestowed by the piety of departed fathers, we hope that we shall in no way escape the fire of eternal punishment if, insofar as our ability permits, we cease to fulfill divine service.

Set aflame, therefore, by these admonitions, I, Henry, prince—though unworthy—established by God’s will in the kingdom of the Franks, assented to the petitions of Lord Imbertus, bishop of Paris. I resolved to make known to all Christ-worshipers, present and future, who honor the reverence due to the Christian religion with fitting and worthy veneration, that I would grant to the Church of Paris, holy Mother happily nourished from the breasts of her infancy, a certain small abbey in the forest called Laia, built by the clemency of my father Robert in honor of Saint Germanus.

Because this seemed worthy, I assented and received the request with a kindly heart; with the consent and will of the bishops and abbots, and of all my counts and soldiers, I granted that small abbey to the holy Mother of God, together with everything belonging to it, so that, for as long as the superiors of that place live, they may hold, administer, and possess it, with none of our successors taking it away. These possessions are: the land of Filiolicurtis; in the county of Pincerais, the altar of Aurea Vallis; in the county of Valois, the altar of Treci; in the county of Beauvais, the altar of Borreti; and the church of Saint Marina on the island of Paris. Likewise, I grant to the aforesaid bishop, although they do not belong to the church itself, four arpents of vineyards in the Parisian suburb.

But so that this gift of our clemency may remain firm in our time and in that of our successors, it pleased us to order that a charter be made concerning it, so that neither in our time nor in any future time may anyone presume to inflict any impediment upon it concerning these possessions. And so that the authority of this command of ours might be more secure, we have confirmed it below with our hand and marked it with the impression of our seal.

# CHUONRAD II, EMPEROR, SECOND OF THIS NAME AMONG THE KINGS, FIRST AMONG THE AUGUSTI, CALLED “THE SALIAN”

*(1024–1039.)*

[Col. 1039]

## Constitutions of Chuonrad II

*(D. Pertz, Monumenta Germaniae historica, Leges, vol. II, p. 38.)*

### I. Edict concerning the serfs of churches

[Note: It now appears for the first time from the royal archive at Hanover, where it is preserved among the charters of the bishopric of Verden, authenticated and marked with the imperial seal. A copy of it exists in the Verden cartulary, where, however, *Heinricus* is written in place of *Chuonradus*.]

*(Around the year 1031.)*

[Col. 1039C]

CHUONRADUS, by the grace of God Roman emperor Augustus, to Duke Berinhardus, Count Sigifridus, and Margrave Bernhardus, greetings and grace.

Although, for the long-range and widespread administration of the welfare of the entire commonwealth, we ought to maintain constant vigilance, nevertheless we recognize that we are under an even greater obligation to watch diligently over the condition of the churches of God. Therefore, because we have heard that the serfs of the holy Church of Verden have hitherto been sold like brute animals for any trifling price, we not only marvel at that wicked custom but also condemn it as a matter detestable to God and humanity—especially since, according to canonical authority, the lands or serfs of no church may be exchanged for any other return except lands for lands and serfs for serfs, of equal or better quality.

Accordingly, by our imperial authority we forbid such a practice, contrary to the traditions of the holy Fathers, to be carried on there any longer. To you, to whom we have entrusted the government of these provinces, we command under the protection of God and our favor that wherever serfs of that church are found to have been sold in this manner, whether among your own people or others, they shall be restored to the bishop of that place with your assistance. The bishop shall then return to the purchaser only as much as he paid for them and shall receive back the serfs of his church.

But if anyone refuses to obey these orders, restrain him by your judicial authority until, compelled if necessary, he obeys this most just edict of ours. Therefore, as a most evident sign, we have ordered the seal bearing our image to be displayed to all.

*(L. S.)*

### II. Chapters concerning benefices

[Note: They are found in Book II, chapter 40, of the Feudal Books, embedded in a commentary, which we present separately in the notes attached to the text. From the inscription of the title, it seems quite plausible that the chapters should be referred to Chuonrad II and that they were promulgated in the fields of Roncaglia in May 1037, when the emperor, after capturing the bishops of Vercelli, Cremona, and Piacenza, was gathering an army to renew his expedition against Heribert, archbishop of Milan.

We present the text as it is found in manuscript 2, the Halle manuscript, parchment, folio, fourteenth century, collated with manuscript 5, the Göttingen manuscript, formerly Schwarzian, folio, fourteenth century, and manuscript 0 of the Frankfurt public library, parchment, folio, fourteenth century.]

*(Year 1037, May.)*

These are the chapters that Conrad made at Roncaglia concerning benefices. For he established that:

[Note: The heading reads “which King Conrad made” in manuscript 5 and in Spang’s edition.]

[Note: *Ictalia* corrected to *runcalia* in manuscript 5.]

1. If, after the death of the lord, the vassal, or after the death of the vassal, his heirs, remain for a year and a day without approaching the lord or his heir to promise fidelity—if it is a benefice for which fidelity must be rendered by seeking investiture—let him lose that benefice.

[Note: “As was also the ancient custom, but not among the Milanese. Moreover, see the Feudal Books.” One manuscript omits the words “his heir”; another omits “by seeking investiture.”]

2. Let lords be permitted to revoke all alienations made of a fief, notwithstanding any prescriptive limitation.

3. Likewise, when the *ostandicia* are demanded—

[Note: Manuscript 5 reads *hostendiciis*; manuscript 6, *hostandiciis*. *Ostandicia* are said to be the aid rendered to the Romans by vassals who do not go with them when they march to war with the king; for example, in Lombardy, the aid of Milan. The manuscripts read: “the twelfth denarius” in manuscript 2; “twelve denarii” in manuscript 5 and manuscript 6. Manuscripts 7 and 8 also appear to read this. One edition reads “the twelfth denarius of Milan”; another, “the third of Roncaglia.” Rebdorf reads “twelve denarii from a modius”; Spang’s edition reads “twelve denarii from a modius”; another edition reads “twelve denarii per modius.” The meaning appears to be that in Lombardy the Milanese paid the twelfth denarius, that is, a twelfth part of their resources—German *den zwölften Pfennig*—whereas the Germans paid only a third of the year’s produce.]

—the twelfth denarius; in Germany, only a third part of the produce of the year in which they undertake military service.

[Note: *Feudal Books*.]

4. Likewise, if a cleric holding a benefice granted by the king—granted not merely to the person but to the church—loses it through his own fault, while he lives and holds ecclesiastical office it shall belong to the king; after his death, however, it shall return to his successor.

### III. Edict concerning benefices

[Note: For example, a bishop or abbot.]

*(28 May 1037.)*

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, Chuonrad, by the grace of God the most glorious emperor of the Romans Augustus.

[Note: The manuscripts read variously: *In the name of the Lord* in manuscript V; *In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity* in manuscripts Vn and Cas.; and *Chuonrad, the most glorious emperor* in manuscript Cr.]

We wish it to be known to all the faithful of holy Church and to our own people, present and future, that, in order to reconcile the minds of lords and soldiers so that they may always be found in agreement with one another, and so that they may serve faithfully and steadfastly both us and their lords with devotion, we command and firmly establish that no soldier of bishops, abbots, abbesses, margraves, counts, or of any persons who now hold or have held a benefice from our public property or from the lands of churches, or who have unjustly lost such a benefice up to this time—whether they are among our greater vassals or among their soldiers—shall lose his benefice without a definite and proven fault, except according to the constitution of our predecessors and the judgment of his peers.

[Note: Some manuscripts read “custom” instead of “constitution”; others read “judges” instead of “peers.” The form *beneficia* is found in one witness for “benefice.”]

If a dispute arises between lords and soldiers, even if the peers have adjudged that he ought to be deprived of his benefice, if he says that this was done unjustly or out of hatred, he shall retain his benefice until the lord and the man whom he accuses come with their peers into our presence and the case is there justly concluded.

[Note: Other witnesses read “until his lord and the man whom he accuses”; one reads “and there the case shall be justly settled.”]

But if the peers of the accused fail the lords in judgment, the accused shall retain his benefice until he comes with his lord and his peers before our presence.

[Note: Some witnesses read “if his peers fail in judgment”; others, “if they fail the lord.” The final word is found in the Florentine manuscript.]

The lord or soldier who is accused and who decides to come to us shall notify the person with whom he has litigated six weeks before beginning his journey.

[Note: Other witnesses read “who has litigated” and “shall inform him.”]

[Note: The best edition of this law is found in Muratori’s *Italian Antiquities*, vol. I, p. 609 folio; vol. II, p. 287 of the Arezzo edition, taken from a very old parchment in the archive of the chapter of the canons of Cremona. We reproduce it here collated with eleventh-century manuscripts from Florence, London, Vienna, another Viennese manuscript numbered 39, Verona, and the Casino manuscript numbered 328 from the end of the eleventh century, as well as with the Este manuscript used by Muratori. Since the later manuscripts of the Feudal Books do not even approach these, I did not think it necessary to record the readings of the Halle manuscript, from the fourteenth century, which otherwise holds the first place among them.]

Let this provision be observed concerning the greater vassals.

[Note: One witness reads “let it be held.”]

As for the lesser vassals, let their case in the kingdom be settled either before their lords or before our envoy.

We also command that, when any soldier, whether one of the greater or lesser vassals, departs from this world, his son shall have the benefice.

[Note: Some witnesses read “his sons shall hold the benefice.”]

If he has no son but leaves a grandson through a male son, let him likewise have the benefice.

[Note: Some witnesses read “let them have the benefice”; another gloss explains *abiatici* as “grandsons,” literally descendants through a son.]

Let the established custom of the greater vassals be observed in supplying their lords with horses and arms. If by chance he leaves no grandson through a son but has a legitimate brother on his father’s side, and if he has offended his lord, yet wishes to make satisfaction to him and become his soldier, let him have the benefice that belonged to his father.

[Note: One witness reads “that belonged to his father or brother.” Another adds: “let him have it, with the custom of the greater vassals observed in supplying their lords with horses and arms.”]

Moreover, we absolutely forbid any lord to make an exchange, grant a precarious tenure, or issue a lease concerning the benefice of his soldiers without their consent. As for those goods that he holds by proprietary right, or by charters, or by a lawful lease, or by a precarious tenure, let no one dare unjustly dispossess them.

We wish to receive the fodrum from the castles that our predecessors possessed; but we demand in no way what they did not possess.

[Note: Some manuscripts omit “from the castles”; others omit the words from “which our predecessors possessed” through the repeated phrase “which they possessed.” In their place, manuscript V II has the rescript of Chuonrad printed below.]

If anyone violates this command, let him pay one hundred pounds of gold, half to our treasury and half to the person who has suffered the injury.

[Note: Some manuscripts read “transgresses” instead of “violates.” In the Halle manuscript the remainder is lacking. Another tradition continues: “But if anyone does not possess gold, let him be punished by our judgment as shall please us.”]

The sign of Lord Chuonrad, most serene Roman emperor Augustus.

Kadolohus, chancellor, acting in the place of Herimannus, archchancellor, recognized this.

Given on the fifth day before the Kalends of June, indiction V, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1037, and in the thirteenth year of Chuonrad’s reign and the eleventh of his empire. Done successfully during the siege of Milan. Amen.

### IV. Rescript concerning Roman law

[Note: In the Casino manuscript no. 328, parchment, from the end of the eleventh century, containing three books of Lombard laws, I found this rescript written on a thin parchment. Earlier, the learned Senckenberg had published it from the Leipzig manuscript in the appendix, section 17, page 109, of his *Method of Jurisprudence*. It is also found in manuscript no. 39 of the Imperial Library at Vienna among the manuscripts of civil law, from which the late Pirsner made a copy.]

*(Year 1038.)*

The emperor Chuonrad Augustus to the Roman judges.

[Note: One witness reads *Choradus*; another, *Conradus*. One omits *Augustus*; another adds “greetings.”]

Having heard the controversy that has hitherto persisted between you and the Lombard judges and has found no settlement, we decree that, from now on, whatever disputes arise, whether within the walls of the city of Rome or outside them in Roman territories, whether the plaintiff or defendant is a Lombard, shall be settled by you Romans according to Roman laws alone and shall never again revive.

[Note: One witness reads “having heard” in the plural; another omits “and the Lombard judges.” The Casino manuscript omits “whether the plaintiff or defendant is a Lombard.” Another witness adds “Roman or Lombard.” One reads “shall not revive.”]

# Diplomas of Emperor Chuonrad II

## I. Privilege of Chuonrad II for the abbey of Vuiscbiki

*(1025.)*

*[Erhard, Codex diplomaticus historiae Westphalicae, p. 87.]*

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, Chuonrad, by the favor of divine clemency, king.

Let all our faithful, present and future, know how a certain venerable abbess named Abug brought before our presence writings of our predecessors, kings or emperors, granted to her church situated at Vuiscbiki, and most humbly requested that they be confirmed and strengthened by our royal authority. Granting her petition the assent it deserved, for the love of God and for the remedy of our soul, and through the intervention of Sigebert, venerable bishop of the holy Church of Minden, as well as of Duke Berinhardus and our other faithful, we have wholly received the aforesaid abbess, together with the congregation subject to her and everything properly belonging there, under our protection and defense.

Therefore we command and order that no public judge, nor anyone exercising judicial authority, presume to constrain in any matter the free men, *coloni*, *liti*, or serfs of the aforesaid church, except only the advocate of that place. Let those holy women have free power, as time passes, to choose an abbess from among themselves or from elsewhere, subject to no secular authority except ours; for, with God’s consent, we wish to be their defender.

These are the estates belonging to the aforesaid church of Vuiscbiki. At that place, six full manses. In addition, at the places named as follows: Vuendredesa, one; Vuigbaldeshusun, four manses; Benneshusun, one mansus; Haddeshusun, one mansus; Tiadanhusun, one mansus; Hainanhusun, two manses.

And in other places belonging to the service of the church of Vuiscbiki: twenty-nine manses in the county of Tilithi, in the county of Count Herimannus; likewise, in the county of Merstem, in the county of the same count, eight manses; in the county of Laginga, six manses, in the county of Dodican; in Westphalia, in the county of Count Henry, eighteen manses; and in the county of Hrodwerc, six manses. In the village called Hramnesberg, two manses; at Fiahtthorpe, one mansus; at Anion, four manses; and in the county of Wirinhardus, a curtis called Thuliberh, five manses. At Tundirin, seven manses. At Hartingehusun, an entire village.

And so that this confirmation of ours may remain firm and undisturbed, we have strengthened this charter of our command, written for this purpose, with our own hand and ordered it to be marked with the impression of our seal.

The sign of Lord Chuonrad, most glorious king.

Odalricus, chancellor, acting in the place of Aribo, archchaplain, recognized this.

Given on the second day before the Ides of January, indiction VIII, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1052, and in the tenth year of the reign of Lord Chuonrad II. Done at Corbie.

## II. Privilege of Chuonrad II for the monastery of Corbie, at the request of Abbot Truchtmarus

*(1025.)*

*[Erhard, cited above.]*

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, Chuonrad, by the favor of divine clemency, king.

Let all the faithful of Christ and of ourselves, present and future, know how the venerable abbot named Truchtmarus came into our presence, humbly asking that, through our magnificent generosity, we look favorably upon the monastery over which he appeared to preside. It is built on the River Weser, in the place called New Corbie, in honor of God and Saint Stephen the Protomartyr, where the precious relics of the blessed martyr Vitus are also known to be preserved.

Granting his reasonable petition out of divine love and reverence for the blessed martyrs, we ordered these letters of our serenity to be made concerning the monastery. By them we decree and command especially that the monks shall have, when necessity arises, the power to choose an abbot from among their brothers; and that no bishop, public judge, or anyone exercising judicial authority—except solely the administrator and advocate of that place and of the aforesaid monastery—may ever dare to enter the churches, places, fields, or other possessions of the aforesaid monastery, which it is seen justly and reasonably to possess at the present time, in order to hear cases, demand fines, impose lodgings or provisions, take sureties, demand any payments or unlawful services, or unjustly constrain the monastery’s people, whether free, serfs, or *liti*; nor may anyone presume to demand or carry out any of the matters mentioned above.

Moreover, concerning the demesne manses, whether now held or acquired later, let the same monastery have complete immunity from the payment of tithes. As has hitherto been the custom, let them be delivered at the gate for the reception of guests and pilgrims, wherever they are located—in bishoprics, counties, or territories—or whatever may be granted there for the love of God and in reverence for that holy place. Thus let those serving God there be permitted, under the protection of our immunity, to live and remain in peaceful order, and let them be more eager at all times to implore the Lord’s mercy for us, our wife, and the stability of the kingdom granted to us by God.

Moreover, let them hold and administer tithes and tithe-churches in whatever bishoprics in the same manner as they are seen to have held and administered them under our predecessors, namely kings and emperors, by virtue of charters. To the bishops to whom they owe service and lodging during their circuits, let them pay these obligations each year according to their written agreements.

And so that the authority of this grant and confirmation of ours may be more secure and, in future times, may be more readily believed and more diligently observed by all the faithful of holy Church and of ourselves, present and future, we have confirmed it below with our own hand and ordered it to be marked with the impression of our seal.

The sign of Lord Chuonrad, invincible king.

Odalricus, chancellor, acting in the place of Aribo, archchaplain, recognized this.

Given on the eleventh day before the Kalends of February, indiction VIII, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1025, and in the first year of the reign of Lord Chuonrad II.

Done at Goslar.

## III. Diploma of Chuonrad II, king of Italy, by which he confirms the rights of the monastery of Saint Pontianus at Lucca

*(1025.)*

*[Muratori, Italian Antiquities I, 93.]*

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, Chuonrad, by the favor of divine clemency, king, etc., how Lord Ambrosius, venerable abbot, came humbly into our presence, asking that, for the love of God and at his petition, we confirm the monastery restored by a certain noblewoman named Willa, mother of the illustrious margrave Hugh, for her own soul and for the souls of all the faithful Christians. By God’s favor, it lies outside the walls of the city of Lucca, in honor of the holy apostles Philip and James and of Saint Pontianus, martyr of Christ, whose glorious body rests there, etc.

The sign of Lord Chuonrad, most invincible king.

Hugh, chancellor, acting in the place of Aribo, archchancellor, recognized this.

[Gap: the wax seal is lost.]

Given on the ninth day before the Kalends of May, indiction VIII, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1025, and in the first year of the reign of Lord Chuonrad II.

Done in the city of Augusta.

## IV. Diploma of Chuonrad I, Roman emperor, by which he confirms to Guido II, abbot of Farfa, and to his monastery all their possessions and rights

*(1027.)*

*[Muratori, Rerum Italicarum Scriptores II, II, 561.]*

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, Chuonrad, divine Roman emperor Augustus.

Let everyone’s prudence learn how Guido, venerable abbot of the monastery of Saint Mary built in the county of Sabina, in the place called Acutianus, came into our presence, showed us the charters of our predecessors, kings or emperors, made for that monastery, and humbly requested [lacuna] that we confirm those same charters by our imperial authority and command. We, assenting to his just petitions, confirm to the aforesaid monastery whatever is contained in the earlier charters, insofar as we can do so justly and lawfully—namely, whatever it appears to possess in the same territory of Sabina; that is, [lacuna] in the county of Horta; [lacuna] in the county of Viterbo, the cell of Saint Mary beside the River Mignone; [lacuna] in the county of Spoleto; [lacuna] in the county of Assisi; [lacuna] in the county of Osimo; [lacuna] in the county of Senigallia; [lacuna] in the county of Camerino; [lacuna] in the county of Fermo; [lacuna] in the county of Ascoli; [lacuna] in the county of Aprutium; [lacuna] in the county of Penne; [lacuna] in the county of Balva; [lacuna] in the county of Marsica; [lacuna].

Within the city of Rome, the church of Saint Mary and that of Saint Benedict, with their crypts and walls, and with their entrances and exits, and the field of Agones. In the city of Tivoli, [lacuna]; in the county of Rieti, [lacuna]; at Amiternum, in the county of Forcona, [lacuna].

Everything that appears justly and lawfully to belong in its entirety to the aforesaid monastery, or that it may acquire from other people fearing God, or from those who now unjustly hold ecclesiastical property; and whatever it appears to possess or may acquire in the city of Rome or in any part of our Italian kingdom—we confirm to that holy place by this charter, together with lands and vineyards, [lacuna]. For the love of God and the salvation of our soul, we pardon to those serving the monastery by this charter whatever is due, so that none of them, nor any of their people, shall thereafter pay fines or tribute, be compelled to provide lodging, become a surety against his will, or pay any toll on goods, river toll, pasture fee, acorn-pasture fee, or bridge toll—whether the persons concerned are monks, clerics, or people residing on their lands, whether free, leaseholders, or serfs.

We receive them under our protection. Therefore we command and order that no duke, margrave, bishop, count, viscount, or any of our traveling envoys, *sculdasius*, *gastaldius*, nor any great or small person of our empire, presume to disturb or harass the aforesaid monastery, its monks, or any faithful person, or to dispossess them without legal judgment of the things written above. [lacuna] Whatever our fisc might have hoped to obtain from the possessions of the aforesaid monastery, all of it we grant to that monastery as a reward for eternal recompense. [lacuna]

The sign of Lord Chuonrad, most serene emperor Augustus.

Hugh, chancellor, acting in the place of Lord Aribo, archchancellor, recognized this.

Given on the fifth day before the Kalends of March, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1027, and in the third year of Lord Chuonrad’s reign and the first of his empire.

Done successfully at Rome.

## V. Command of Chuonrad II, king of Italy and first among the Augusti, by which he confirms all the rights and privileges of the Lucca nuns’ monastery of the Lord Savior

*(1027.)*

*[Muratori, cited above, Italian Antiquities II, 95.]*

[Col. 1048C]

In the name of almighty God, Chuonrad, by the eternal gift of the Bestower, king.

## Full textual apparatus: Chapters II–IV

Source column anchors for this apparatus and its surrounding charters: [Col. 1037B], [Col. 1037C], [Col. 1037D], [Col. 1038A], [Col. 1038B], [Col. 1038C], [Col. 1038D], [Col. 1039], [Col. 1039A], [Col. 1039B], [Col. 1039C], [Col. 1040A], [Col. 1040B], [Col. 1040C], [Col. 1041], [Col. 1041A], [Col. 1041B], [Col. 1041C], [Col. 1041D], [Col. 1042A], [Col. 1042B], [Col. 1042C], [Col. 1042D], [Col. 1043], [Col. 1043A], [Col. 1043B], [Col. 1043C], [Col. 1043D], [Col. 1044A], [Col. 1044B], [Col. 1044C], [Col. 1044D], [Col. 1045A], [Col. 1045B], [Col. 1045C], [Col. 1045D], [Col. 1046A], [Col. 1046B], [Col. 1046C], [Col. 1046D], [Col. 1047A], [Col. 1047B], [Col. 1047C], [Col. 1047D], [Col. 1048A], [Col. 1048B], [Col. 1048C].

**Earlier charter.** The printed alternatives are *habitantium* / *habitationis*, *Has ego* / *ergo*, and *liegii* / *leigii*. Its tithe is from the distinct revenues of *passionis*, *vieriae silvae*, and *liegii*; *vieriae* is retained as an uncertain technical term, not silently made “woodland.”

**II. Chapters concerning benefices.** *que rex coradus* (“which King Conrad made”) is the reading of 5 and Spangenberg; 5 corrects *ictalia* to *runcalia*. In c.1, 2 omits *vel heredem ejus* (“or his heir”) and 6 *investituram petendo* (“by seeking investiture”); the appended reference reads “as also the ancient custom was, but not among the Milanese; moreover, see the Feudal Books.” In c.3, 5 reads *hostendiciis*, 6 *hostandiciis*. *Ostandicia* is the aid vassals give Romans who march to war with the king while they do not go, e.g. Milan’s Lombard aid. The readings are *medio XII denarium* (2), *medio XII den.* (5,6, apparently 7,8), “*de mediolan. XII de roncalia tertiam*” (edition 1 apud Spangenberg), *de modio XII denar.* (Rebdorf apud Spangenberg), *de modio XII denarios* (Spangenberg), and “twelve denarii per modius.” The gloss explains the Milanese twelfth-denarius, a twelfth of resources—German *den zwölften Pfennig*—against the Germans’ third of annual fruits. In c.4, 5 omits *non solum personae sed ecclesiae datum*; 6 has *propter* for *per*; H has *v. eo p.*

**III. Edict concerning benefices.** V, Vn, Cas: *domini* for *sanctae*; Cr: *Chuonradus gloriosissimus imperator*. L,V,Vn: *tam praesentibus quam et futuris*; Cr omits *semper*; Herold: *beneficiis*; V II: *praesidiis*; V,V II,Cas: *perdiderit*. Recorded *walvassores* forms: *walvasoribus* Cr, *vavassoribus* L,V,V II, *vavasoribus* Cas, *vassalloribus* Vn. L,V,Vn,Cas have *consuetudinem* for *constitutionem*; Cr *judicum* for *judicium*; L,V,Vn,Cas *Et si*; V,Vn,Cas *emerserit*; L,V,Vn,Cas singular *seniorem et militem*. V II has *suus senior vel ille qui culpatur* and *et illa causa ibi juste*; L,V,V II,Vn *terminetur*. L,V,Vn have *pares ejus culpati* and L *seniorem defuerint*; the final word is Florentine. L,V,V II,Vn,Cas read *vero*; L,V,Vn,Cas *litigavit*; V II *intimet*.

The cited edition is Muratori, *Antiquitates Italicae* I.609 fol. and II.287 Arezzo, from Cremona, collated with Florentine, London, Viennese, Vienna 39, Veronese, Casino 328, and Este witnesses; later Feudal-Book witnesses, including Halle XIV, are excluded. L: *teneatur*. L,V,V,Vn,E,Cas: *filios ejus beneficium tenere*; L,V,Vn,E,Cas: *filios*; L,Cas: *abiaticos*, V,Vn: *abbiaticos*, corrected to *abbiaticum*; Casino gloss: *id est nepotes* (“that is, grandsons”). L,V,Cas: *habeant*; L,V,Vn,Cas add *et*; Cas: *patris sui vel fratris*; Herold adds the greater-vassals horses-and-arms clause. V II: *Ille vero qui*. L,V,Vn,Cas omit *de castellis*; V II omits from *de* through repeated *habuerunt*, substituting the printed rescript; V omits from *habuerunt* through repeated *habuerunt*. V,Vn,Cas: *preterierit*. Halle lacks the remainder; L,V,Vn,E add *At si quis aurum non habuerit, nostra sententia feriatur ut nobis placuerit* (“if one has no gold, let him be punished by our judgment as shall please us”). One Cremona witness preserves the remaining signature; the date is corrected, while Cremona reads 1038.

**IV. Rescript concerning Roman law.** Casino 328, a late-eleventh-century Lombard-law parchment, preserves the rescript; Senckenberg printed the Leipzig witness (*Method of Jurisprudence*, Appendix III §17 p.109), and Pirsner copied Vienna Imperial Library civil-law no.39. Cas reads *Choradus* (a spelling of “Chuonradus/Conrad”); S and V II read *Conradus* (“Conrad”). V II omits *Augustus* (“Augustus/emperor”) and adds *salutem* (“greetings”). V II reads *Auditi* (“having heard,” masculine or plural) for *Audita* (“having heard,” feminine, agreeing with *controversia*, “controversy”). Cas omits *et Langobardos judices* (“and the Lombard judges”). V II has *amodo* (“henceforth/from now on”) for *admodum* (“further/thereafter”), omits *mota* (“raised, brought”), and reads *vel Romanus vel Langobardus* (“whether Roman or Lombard”) for the specification *actore Langobardo vel reo* (“with a Lombard plaintiff or defendant”). Cas omits *mota fuerint* (“shall have been raised”), *actore Langobardo* (“with a Lombard plaintiff”), and *vel reo* (“or defendant”). S has the same *reviviscant* (“shall revive again”); it is the transmitted wording, not a contrary reading.

**Glosses for the preceding textual forms.** *que rex coradus* means “which King Conrad [made]”; *ictalia* and corrected *runcalia* are the erroneous and corrected place-names “Italy/Roncaglia.” *hostendiciis* and *hostandiciis* are variant spellings of *ostandiciis*, “military aid/service.” The forms *medio XII denarium*, *medio XII den.*, and the *de modio* readings all concern “the twelfth denarius” or “twelve denarii per modius.” *beneficia* means “benefices”; *praesidiis*, “protections/guardianships”; *perdiderit*, “has lost.” The *walvassores* forms (*walvasoribus*, *vavassoribus*, *vavasoribus*, *vassalloribus*) are spellings of “vassals.” *consuetudinem* is “custom,” *constitutionem* “constitution”; *judicum* means “of judges,” contrasting with *judicium*, “judgment.” *emerserit* is “has arisen”; singular *seniorem et militem* is “lord and soldier”; *terminetur*, “be concluded”; *teneatur*, “be held/observed”; *abiaticos* and *abbiaticos* mean “grandsons,” as Casino’s gloss says. *preterierit* means “has transgressed/passed over.” The added sentence *At si quis aurum non habuerit, nostra sententia feriatur ut nobis placuerit* means: “But if anyone has no gold, let him be punished by our judgment as shall please us.”

If we bestow something upon places devoted to divine worship through the gift of our generosity, or confirm what has been bestowed, we have no doubt that this will greatly benefit us as a reward for eternal recompense. Therefore, let it be known to all the present and future faithful of the holy Church of God how, at the intervention of our beloved wife Gisla, through this page of our decree, insofar as we are able justly and lawfully, we confirm and [Col. 1048D] strengthen for the monastery of the Lord Savior, which has been built within the walls of the city of Lucca, and for the abbess of that place, named Alperga, and for all the nuns serving the Lord there, [lacuna] its possessions and properties, both those it now has and those it may have in the future, with cultivated and uncultivated lands, vineyards, meadows, pastures, woods, fisheries, male and female slaves, waters and watercourses, mills, and every substance that the same place appears to possess.

We also decree that from now on and in the future, whatever shall have been bestowed upon the aforesaid monastery through the gift of religious men or devoted women shall remain under the confirmation of our decree. We further wish that the aforesaid monastery, in our times and in those to come, together with all its property and dependents, remain immune from every public service and exaction. And whenever the abbess dies, let them choose from among the same women whomever they find to be of good character.

We command, moreover, that no public judge, or anyone exercising judicial authority, presume to enter that monastery or its churches, villages, or other possessions that it now has or may acquire in the future, in order to demand lodging or compulsory maintenance, take hostages, unjustly constrain the monastery’s people—whether free or enslaved—or enter it under the pretext of seeking unusual services. Rather, let the aforementioned abbess, and those who after her shall have governed the same monastery, together with the handmaids of God dwelling there, live peacefully, quietly preserve the purpose of monastic life, and implore God’s mercy for our salvation and [Col. 1049B] the stability of the kingdom.

If anyone, therefore—which we do not believe will happen—should prove to be a violator of this decree, let him acknowledge that he must pay one thousand pounds of the finest gold: half to our treasury and half to the aforesaid abbess Alperga and her successors. And so that this may be believed more truly and observed more diligently, we have confirmed it with our own hand and ordered it to be marked with our seal.

**The sign of Lord Conrad, most serene king.**

**The place of the seal; the +wax is lost.**

Hugh, chancellor, acting on behalf of Lord Aribo, archbishop and archchancellor, examined and authenticated this.

Given in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1027, in the ninth indiction; in the second year of the reign of Lord Conrad II.

[Col. 1049C] Done at Verona.

### VI. Decree of the Emperor Conrad I confirming all rights and possessions to Guinizon, abbot of the monastery of Saint Savior in Amiata, in the diocese of Chiusi. (Year 1027.)

[MURATORI, *Antiq. Ital.*, V, 449.]

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, Conrad, by the favor of divine clemency, emperor augustus.

It is fitting that those who prudently strive to order the service of God, and request that we confirm this for our stability, should be obeyed all the more willingly because we understand that their requests are pleasing to God, and because, with God’s protection, we have endeavored to bring them to fulfillment through good purpose. Therefore, let the diligence of all the faithful of the holy Church of God and of our own people, both present and future, learn that when we entrusted to our beloved and faithful Guinizon, abbot of the monastery of the Lord and Savior built on Mount Amiata, the administration of that monastery, he found that the service of God there and the care of those serving God there had, through the negligence of his predecessors, been neglected in many ways. He therefore strove with particular zeal to correct according to the rule the congregation of monks serving God there, and to make them devoted solely to divine service. [lacuna] we should grant sufficient provision for their needs, so that the prelates of the aforesaid monastery of the Lord Savior who shall exist in succession, and his successors, the abbots or provosts, together with the monks subject to them, may in the future have sufficient food for those serving God there [Col. 1050A].

For the love of God and the remedy of our soul and of the souls of our successors, whether kings or emperors, we grant them, for their sufficient provision: the cell of Saint Benedict at Bucino; the estate and parish of Saint Mary at Lamule; the estate of Saint Stephen at Monticolo with the castle of Montelatronis; the estate of Mustra with the castle of Montenegro; the estate of Laminiana with the castle of Montepenzutulo, as Ubertus held it in his possession; the estate of Saint Miniatus; the estate of Saint Quiricus at Piscinule; and those of Saint Simeon and Saint Peregrine; the estate of Saint Mary of Offena with the fortress called Sanine; the estate of Palea and that of Saint Sebastian; the estate of Saint Stephen at Tutona; the estate of Saint Clement at [Col. 1050B] Titiniano with its lands and *angariae*; the estate of Mussona with the land of Greater and Lesser Redula, and Bitena, Canneta, and Herminula; half of the estate of Saint Lazarus with its church; the estate of Feroniano; the estate of Citiliano; the estate of Saint Savior at Vigugnano; the estate of Saint Severus above Latum; the small estate of Bisenzo; the estate of Saint John at Vafriano and that of Saint Saturninus; the estate of Saint Columbanus; the estate of Saint Savior in the village of Racana; the cell of Saint Mary at Valeriano; the small estate at Cartutule with the land and vineyard near the Varano River; the estate of Saint Savior at Campagnatico; the estate of Saint Peter at Cervaria; the estate of Saint Stephen at Viniano; the estate of Saint Severus at Paterna with the field of Albiniono; [Col. 1050C] the small estate called Croscule; and the small estate at Cursiniano with all its appurtenances and dependencies; the cell of Saint Peter at Latera; the cell of Saint Peter at Garmarita with Saint Anastasius; the cell of Saint Sabinus; and those of Saint Restituta, Saint Peter, and Saint Stephen at Terquinum; and the cell of Saint Mary at Corgnitu, within the boundaries described as follows: on one side, the bank with the rock which is separated from the bank; on another side, the public road that comes through the gate, and the land of Azo, son of Benzo, with his partners; and on the fourth side, the land of the sons of Alon.

This is on the condition that from now onward the aforesaid holy congregation may possess all the named cells and estates, with all their appurtenances and dependencies, solely for its own use, receiving food and clothing according to the rule without delay, persevering solely in divine service by day and by night, and striving to pray for the stability of the entire empire entrusted to us by God.

But so that what we have done with good purpose and good will may possess enduring stability, the monastery requested our piety that we confirm this same arrangement in a written instrument; and so we have done. Finally, we also grant to the aforesaid monastery all tithes, *frea*—that is, fines—and judicial revenues, as well as every public composition and exaction from all the inhabitants of the aforementioned cells and estates, to be delivered at the gate of the monastery [Col. 1051A] for the support of pilgrims, as sustenance and for the increase of our soul, on account of the offenses of wicked and evil men, which they had been entirely unable to endure or sustain.

Therefore, we ordered this decree to be made for the same holy place, by which we command that from now onward the same holy congregation, in complete peace and without any public exaction, and with the local rector excluded, may possess, administer, carry out, and dispose of these cells and estates for its own uses and needs, so that, having sufficient provision from them, they may persevere in divine service, and their service to us may bring about everlasting remedy. But if any person, great or small—which we very much do not believe will happen—should act against this decree of ours, etc.

[Col. 1051B]

**The sign of Lord Conrad, the most unconquered emperor augustus.**

Hugh, chancellor, acting on behalf of Lord Aribo, archbishop and archchancellor, examined and authenticated this.

Given in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1027; in the third year of the reign of Lord Conrad II; in the first year of his empire; in the tenth indiction.

Given in the city of Leoniana, on the nones of April.

### VII. Privilege of Emperor Conrad for the Church of Paderborn. (Year 1027.)

[ERHARD, *Cod. diplom. Westph.*, p. 89.]

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, Conrad, by divine grace, emperor augustus of the Romans.

We have weighed and considered that, for our souls, darkened by the stains of sin, it can be of great help if we exalt, build, and enrich the churches of Christ from our possessions for the majesty of divine honor and glory. We also know that it belongs to the dignity of our imperial power to offer a worthy recompense of service to those who have served us well at home or in war.

Therefore, let all the faithful of Christ and of ourselves know how, through the intervention of our most beloved wife Gisla, and also of our son King Henry, Bruno, bishop of Augsburg, Margrave Hermann, and his brother Egilhard, for divine grace and glory and for the remedy of our soul, we have given to the Paderborn Church, consecrated in honor of Saint Mary, Mother of God, Saint Kilian the martyr, and Saint Liborius the confessor, and to its administrator Meinwerk, who has often, frequently, and faithfully served us, an estate named Ervitte, belonging to our imperial right, situated in the district of Engern and in the county of Count Marcward, to be held perpetually, together with all male and female slaves legally belonging to it, and with all its other appurtenances, namely, courtyards, buildings, cultivated and uncultivated lands, meadows, pastures, woods, hunting rights, roads and trackless ways, exits and entrances, waters and watercourses, fisheries, mills, things acquired and things to be acquired, together with the ban and the market also [Col. 1052A] customarily held at that estate, and with every benefit that may arise from it.

And so that the authority of this grant of ours may remain firm for all time, we have confirmed with our own hand the page written concerning it and ordered it to be marked with our seal.

**The sign of Lord Conrad, the unconquered Roman emperor augustus. (L. M.)**

Odalric, chancellor, authenticated this.

Given on the seventh day before the ides of April, in the tenth indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1027, in the third year of the reign of Lord Conrad II, and in the first year of his empire.

Done at Rome.

### VIII. Privilege of Conrad for the monastery of New Corbie. (Year 1028.)

[ERHARD, *Cod. diplom. Westph.*, p. 90.]

[Col. 1052B]

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity. Conrad, by the favor of divine clemency, emperor augustus of the Romans.

If we lend a gracious ear to the pious petitions of our faithful, especially those which they pour into our ears on behalf of the churches entrusted to them, we believe without doubt that this will benefit both the present condition of our empire and the reward of eternal blessedness. Therefore, let the prudent diligence of all our faithful, present and future, know that the venerable Druthmar, abbot of New Corbie, approached the eminence of our majesty and complained that an estate called Godelvesheim had previously been unjustly taken from the same monastery. He also brought with him an imperial decree of our deified predecessor Arnulf, which contained a settlement concerning that estate between the same emperor and Bovo, the abbot of the aforesaid monastery.

Trusting his representation, we ordered a certain matron named Alvered, who at that time possessed the estate as though by hereditary right, to be summoned to our palace. Since she was unable to refute the evidence produced, she returned the aforesaid estate, with all its appurtenances, to the aforementioned venerable abbot without dispute, with the assistance of her son Osdag and her patron, Count Fritheric. Hiddi, the monastery’s advocate, received it by our command [Col. 1052D].

Afterward, however, moved by our clemency, the abbot granted the same matron the aforesaid estate, another called Gimundian, and certain dependents in the village of Brumerinchthorp, on the condition that if anything should be found after her death in those possessions, it should be disposed of at the abbot’s discretion. To her son he granted an estate named Imminghusun on the condition that he hold it during his lifetime, unless our munificence should first promote him elsewhere; afterward, it was to return to the monastery’s ownership.

And so that the authority of this restitution may forever be considered more secure, we have confirmed it beneath with our own hand and ordered it to be marked with the impression of our seal.

**Witnesses:** Hunfrid, archbishop; Meinwerk, bishop; Godehard, bishop; Sigifrid, bishop; [Col. 1053A] Odalric, chancellor; Asculf; Sigibert; Bernhard, duke; Adalbero, duke; Ernest, duke; Liudulf, count and stepson of the emperor; Hiddi; Count Amulung and his brother Ecbert; Wigger; Gerlo; Uffo; Tiammo; Poppo; Bern; Thiathard; Brun; Gebo.

**The sign of Lord Conrad, the unconquered Roman emperor augustus. (L. M.)**

Odalric, chancellor, acting on behalf of Aribo, archchancellor, authenticated this.

Given on the kalends of July, in the eleventh indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1028, in the fourth year of the reign of Lord Conrad II, and in the first year of his empire.

Done successfully at Magdeburg. Amen.

### IX. Privilege of Conrad for the Church of Saint Gorgonius. (Year 1028.)

[ERHARD, *Cod. diplom. Westph.*, p. 90.]

[Col. 1053B]

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, Conrad, by the favor of divine clemency, emperor augustus of the Romans.

Let the diligence of all the faithful of the holy Church of God and of our own people, present and future, know how, at the intervention and petition of our beloved wife Gisla, empress augusta, and of our most beloved son King Henry, as well as of Bruno, venerable bishop of Augsburg, we granted to our faithful Sigibert, bishop of Minden, and to the church over which, by God’s gift, he presides, constructed in honor of Saint Peter, prince of the apostles, and Saint Gorgonius, martyr [Col. 1053C] of Christ, a certain forest situated exclusively within the property of the estates of that same Minden Church, in the district of Entergow, and in the county of Duke Bernhard, with the consent and approval of the aforementioned Duke B., his brother Detmar, and the other citizens who until now had shared the right of hunting in that forest.

The forest lies in woods, fields, and marshes between the rivers Ossembeke and Alerbeke, extending to the middle of the River Wermon, and from there to Northsulerecampon, and belongs to an estate called Sulegon. We granted it as a forest and surrounded it with the constraint of our ban, on the condition that thereafter no one should have the power in that forest, without the permission of the aforementioned bishop and his successors, to hunt, shoot, set nets or snares, or deceive wild animals by any device—rights which properly fall under the authority of the ban.

If anyone should prove to be a reckless violator of this imperial decree, let him know that he must pay the prescribed compensation to the bishop and his advocate under our ban. And so that this may be believed more truly and observed more diligently throughout the years to come, we have ordered this charter, written concerning it and confirmed below with our own hand, to be marked with the impression of our seal.

**The sign of Lord Conrad, the unconquered Roman emperor augustus. (L. M.)**

Odalric, chancellor, acting on behalf of Aribo, archchaplain, authenticated this.

Given on the third day before the kalends of April, in the twelfth indiction, in the year of the Lord’s [Col. 1054A] Incarnation 1028, in the fifth year of the reign of Lord Conrad II, and in the first year of his empire.

Done at Regensburg.

### X. Decree of Conrad for the monastery of Saint Kilian. (Year 1030.)

[ERHARD, *Cod. diplom. Westph.*, p. 91.]

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, Conrad, by the favor of divine clemency, emperor augustus of the Romans.

Let all the faithful of Christ, present and future, know how, at the intervention and petition of our beloved wife Gisla, empress augusta, and of our most beloved son King Henry, as well as of Meinwerk, bishop of the Paderborn Church, we gave to the monastery at Paderborn, consecrated in honor of Saint Mary and Saint Kilian the martyr and Saint Liborius the confessor, a certain estate of Count Bernhard, called Badperch, with ten holdings adjoining the same mountain, situated in the district of Nichter and in the county of Count Hahold. It came into our power by hereditary right because that same Count B. was illegitimate, which is commonly called “Wanburtich.”

We granted it with male and female slaves, villages, courtyards, buildings, fields, cultivated and uncultivated lands, roads and trackless ways, meadows, pastures, woods, hunting rights, waters and watercourses, fisheries, mills, exits and entrances, things acquired and things to be acquired, and all appurtenances legally belonging to the same estate, on the condition that it remain perpetually under the authority of the aforesaid monastery.

And so that this grant of ours may remain stable and unshaken for all time, we have ordered this page, written concerning it and confirmed below with our own hand, to be marked with the impression of our seal.

**The sign of Lord Conrad, the most unconquered emperor of the Romans. (L. M.)**

I, Odalric, chancellor, acting on behalf of Aribo, archchaplain, authenticated this.

Given on the kalends of June, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1030, in the thirteenth indiction, in the sixth year of Lord Conrad’s reign, and in the fourth year of his empire.

Done successfully at Merseburg. Amen.

### XI. For the Paderborn Church. (Year 1031.)

[ERHARD, *Cod. diplom. Westph.*, p. 91.]

[Col. 1054D]

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, Conrad, by the grace of divine providence, emperor augustus of the Romans.

We wish it to be known to the whole community of God’s faithful and of our own people how, for love of the heavenly homeland, at the intervention and petition of our beloved wife Gisla, empress augusta, and of our dear son King Henry, and because of the constant and devoted service rendered to us by Meinwerk, venerable bishop of the holy see of Paderborn, [Col. 1055A] we have given in perpetuity to the church over which, by God’s gift, he presides, built in honor of Saint Mary, Mother of God, Saint Kilian the blessed martyr, and Saint Liborius, confessor of Christ, the estates possessed by Bernhard and his sister Hazecha in the places called Alflaan and Etlinun, situated in the district of Paderborn and in the county of Amulung, together with everything else belonging there, and with every benefit that can in any way be written down or named, with male and female slaves, courtyards, buildings, fields, open fields, cultivated and uncultivated lands, meadows, pastures, woods, hunting rights, waters and watercourses, fisheries, millstones, mills, roads and trackless ways, exits and entrances, things acquired and things to be acquired.

This is on the condition that the aforesaid bishop and his successors thereafter have free power over these estates by imperial hereditary right to do whatever they wish, provided that it is for the benefit of their church and without anyone’s opposition.

And so that the authority of this grant of ours may remain stable and unshaken for all time, we have confirmed with our own hand the page written concerning it and ordered it to be marked with our seal.
