For since the divine Justinian rightly decreed [Note: “Had decreed that they should swear,” V II.] that the canons of the Fathers ought to have the force of laws (Julian, 119, 1), and since it is found in none of the canons of the Fathers [Note: “Is found,” V II.] that clerics may dare to swear, it is certainly fitting that the entire clerical order be considered exempt from taking an oath.

Therefore, in accordance with the intention of both divine and human law, we decree and irrevocably define by imperial authority that no bishop, no priest, no cleric of whatever order, no abbot, and no monk or nun shall be compelled for any reason to undertake an oath in any controversy, whether criminal or civil; rather, they may delegate this duty to suitable advocates.

## II. The Assembly of Zurich

*[Note: We present the laws promulgated at that assembly, both general and Lombard, with the aid of the London, Vienna, Vienna II (Civil Law no. 39), and Veronese manuscripts, and the Este manuscript published by Muratori. We have added the law against those who despise the emperor, which is found only in the Vienna and Veronese manuscripts.]*

*(Year 1054, February.)*

[Col. 1082C]

### Constitution on Marriages

Henry, by divine piety the second Roman emperor Augustus, to all.

Because we believe that the providence of divine mercy [Note: [Col. 1081] *p.* is present in L.] has entrusted us with the care of the imperial office, we too must constantly concern ourselves with matters pertaining to Christian religions and the cultivation of justice. Therefore, when we were sitting at the universal assembly of our Italian faithful at Turegi [Note: “in the kingdom,” V; “in the kingdom,” Vn; “of the kingdom,” editions and the Brancacciana manuscript of the Neapolitan library of Lombard laws.] [Col. 1083A] [i.e. princes, V II.], a question arose concerning unlawful marriages. With the counsel of our princes, archbishops, bishops [Note: Omitted in V II.], margraves, and counts, and by the judgment—or, rather, with the consent—of all those sitting in judgment, we defined the following sentence.

We confirmed with the highest authority everything that the holy canons or the sacred laws of our predecessors establish on this matter [Note: “ordain,” V II.], and we added to it, moreover, by our imperial law [Note: “and also, if anything remains,” V II.], that whoever, whether of legitimate age or below legitimate age [Note: That is, legally; gloss.] shall have married or betrothed a woman [Note: The remainder is lost in the London manuscript], if he should be overtaken by death, none of his relatives shall be permitted to marry his widow or betrothed.

If anyone does so, both the woman and the man shall by this law be disinherited; half of all their goods [Note: Thus our manuscripts; the printed editions have the opposite arrangement: “they shall lose their property, and one half shall pass by hereditary right to their near relatives, while the other half shall go to the treasury.”] shall go to the treasury, while the other half shall pass by hereditary right to their legitimate near relatives. Whoever is born from such a marriage shall likewise, just as his parents, be disinherited by this law.

## Constitution concerning those who despise the emperor

HEINRICUS, by the divine favor the Second, Roman Emperor Augustus, to all.

It is fitting that imperial prudence condemn with a capital sentence anyone who despises its presence [Note: Herold gives the text as follows: “It is fitting to condemn with a capital sentence every despiser of imperial dignity, prudence, and presence.” The law, however, is absent from the Vienna manuscript II.].

## Lombard constitution concerning poisonings

[Col. 1083C] HEINRICUS, by the divine favor the Second, Roman Emperor Augustus, to all Lombards [Note: “Longobards,” L, V, Vn.].

It is fitting that imperial prudence administer the affairs of the commonwealth in such a way [Note: “and thus be concerned for the present,” V II.] that it may be solicitous for the present while also diligently providing for those things that will be useful and beneficial to posterity. This is properly accomplished when the reward of virtue is repaid to the good, and a fitting punishment to the wicked—punishment for their correction and an example to others [Note: “is repaid,” V II.].

But since the human race surpasses all that the world possesses [Note: “surpasses,” V II.], its salvation must be cared for especially, in proportion as it is more clearly established [Note: “that it is,” V II.] that Almighty God also sent his only-begotten Son from the eternal seat of his divinity into the world for its redemption.

Therefore, since we have heard that many people—alas!—have perished through poisoning [Note: “through beneficence,” V II.; the same reading occurs below.] and through various kinds of secret death, while we were sitting at the universal assembly of the Lombards at Turegi [Note: “at the kingdom,” V; “at the kingdom,” corrected to “of the kingdom,” Vn.], we approved and sanctioned the following law with the agreement and authority of the bishops, margraves, counts, and many other of our faithful.

Whoever kills someone by poison or by any other form of secret death, or consents to such a killing, shall incur the death penalty and shall lose all his movable and immovable property. The price of ten pounds of gold [Note: Omitted in L.] shall nevertheless first be given to the relatives of the slain as a lawful wergild [widrigild]. Of the remainder, one half shall again go to the same relatives [Note: “of the same,” L?], while the other part shall go to the treasury.

If anyone accused of the aforesaid crime, whether as its perpetrator or as one who consented to it, wishes to deny the charge, he shall defend himself by trial by combat if he is free, and by ordeal if he is a slave; otherwise he shall incur the same sentence.

Moreover [Note: “Further,” V II.], we wish and sanction by our imperial authority [Note: Omitted in L.] that whoever provides refuge or any assistance to persons guilty of the aforesaid offense shall have all his property transferred to the public treasury, and shall incur our indignation and that of all our people, unless he defends himself in the manner we have stated [Note: Thus L, V, Vn, E. The words “unless he defends himself as we have stated” are absent from V II.].

## III. Fragments of constitutions concerning the loss of benefices

[Note: Both fragments were preserved by Jacobus de Ardizone in his *Summa juris Feudorum* and from there transcribed into the book of Jacobus Alvarotus on feudal matters; they were also inserted by Cujas in Book V of the *Feuda*, chapters 2 and 3. We reproduce them on the basis of the Cologne edition of 1563, octavo, the Lyon edition of 1535, folio, and the edition of Spangenberg. The first fragment appears, from its heading, to belong to Henry III, and its style does not contradict this, except for the word *dominus*, in place of which *senior* was most commonly used in that period. I have attempted to extract again the opinions of the glossators that were inserted into the text. We add the second fragment, preserved by the same glossators and inserted by Cujas in Book V of the *Feuda*, chapter 3, using the editions cited above and the text as Spangenberg received it from Cujas. Its authorship is much disputed. After weighing what the most learned men have argued on the subject (see Eichhorn, *Deutsche Staats- und Rechtsgeschichte*, 4th ed., 1835, vol. II, p. 280; Dieck, *Litterargeschichte des Longobardischen Lehnrechts*, 1828, p. 168; Laspeyres, *Über die Libri Feudorum*, 1830, pp. 224–297), we agree with Eichhorn on the basis of the word *senior*, which is used from ancient times down to Conrad II and occurs for the last time in 1136 in the constitution of Lothair III. We also believe that the word *feudum*, unusual in the eleventh century and appearing here for the first time in the constitutions of Lothair III as alternating with *beneficium*, may perhaps be due to Jacobus de Ardizone.] (1039–1056.)

### Constitution of Henry concerning the causes for losing a fief

The august Emperor Henry II.

Since we have learned that there are doubtful and various causes concerning the benefices of military men in our kingdom, we have therefore established certain provisions for the condition of the commonwealth [Note: One or more words are missing here.].

If, then, anyone kills his lord, wounds him, besieges the lord himself or his lady, or has “cucurbitated” him (*cucurbitaverit*; sense uncertain) [Note: *Eam*, “her,” in Ard. and Alv.], or acts against those things that are named in the oath of fidelity [Note: Omitted in Alv.], or gives counsel for the acts mentioned above, let him lose his benefice by the judgment of his peers.

If he wishes to defend himself against the foregoing accusations, and witnesses on the lord’s side are lacking, let him purge himself with three peers; but if he cannot have peers, let him defend himself with twelve of his closest relatives [Note: According to ordinary court practice, he may defend himself alone. *Feud.*].

If one of his peers, nevertheless a qualified one, says that he knows the truth of the matter and wishes to challenge him to combat, we decree that he defend himself by combat [Note: “we say,” Ard. and Alv.].

If anyone has failed to serve his lord [Note: “has done that which,” Alv.], let him lose his benefice by the judgment of his peers [Note: “Let him not lose his benefice,” Alv.] [Note: According to court practice, he may redeem it for half of whatever amount he wishes. *Feud.*].

But if he wishes to defend himself against this charge [Note: Thus Ard. and Alv.; “if he does not wish,” Sp.], let him produce two peers, or at least one, and swear with them that he has served. If he cannot have peers or a peer, let him swear with three or two of his closest relatives that he will render service within the year [Note: Thus Ard. and Alv.; “that he had served,” Sp.] [Note: According to court practice, he is permitted to swear alone. How he swears—whether alone or with others—is immaterial, provided that he names the services. *Feud.*].

But if he has maintained a harmonious relationship with his lord, frequently seeing him, we decree [Note: Thus corrected by the editor; “we say,” Ard., Alv., Sp.] that he prove by witnesses that he performed the service and that the failure did not lie with him.

If there has been any discord between lord and vassal, or if they have their residences far apart [Note: “if he has,” Alv.], the vassal, presenting himself to his lord, shall promise service; and, if necessary, he shall prove this by oath [Note: “to prove,” Ard. and Alv.], at least until the end of the dispute, as assigned to the vassal by his peers.

If he has served within the year, however slight the service may have been, and the lord has imposed another service which the vassal has neglected, thereby causing harm to the lord, the feudatory shall make good the damage, up to the harvest, according to the assessment of his peers [Note: “estimation,” Alv.].

For other faults through which the benefice is not lost, let him defend himself by the judgment of his peers, as above, or make compensation [Note: “make amends,” Ard. and Alv.].

### Another constitution of Henry concerning a vassal who rejected one of his lords

Emperor Henry.

If it should happen that a fief, through negligence or the neglect of a vassal [Note: “not fidelity,” Sp.], is assigned to co-heirs, let no relief be granted to one who has been displaced, lest the contempt shown to his lord be made a mockery, on account of which he had lawfully relinquished the fief [Note: “let no one of them accept relief,” Ard. and Alv.].

Let those who act otherwise than the intention of our most salutary constitution requires know that they will be deprived of their benefice, so that they may no longer hope to recover it. The lord shall have the right to claim the aforesaid benefice from them and their descendants, as well as from all other possessors.

# Diplomas of the Emperor Henry III

## I. Privilege for the monastery of Corvey and the convent of Herford (1039)

[ERHARD, *Codex diplomaticus Westphaliae*, p. 102.]

[Col. 1085C]

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity. HEINRICUS, by the favor of divine clemency, king.

If we bring the just and reasonable petitions of the servants of God to fulfillment, we undoubtedly hope that this will benefit us both in passing through this life more happily and in more easily obtaining the eternal one. Therefore we wish it to be known that the venerable abbot Truchtmarus approached our highness, humbly asking that our generosity take thought for the monasteries entrusted to him. One of them is called New Corvey, where he also serves as abbot under a regular constitution; the other is the convent of nuns called Herford [Col. 1086C], subject to its own abbess, whose name is Gotesdiu. In accordance with the custom by which provosts from the ecclesiastical order are accustomed to administer communities of the servants of God, we entrusted it to the aforesaid abbot, so that he might assist the abbess of the place in discipline and serve as their provider and patron in all matters which the handmaids of Christ could not carry out on account of their sex and profession.

He therefore asked our highness to remember that our predecessor, the Emperor Louis, of pious memory, ordered both monasteries to be built according to the model of the principal monasteries in Gaul: New Corvey in the likeness of Old Corvey, and the Herford monastery after the example of the convent of nuns built in the city of Soissons. In order that the perfection of those institutions might be completed as an alms for himself and his entire family, the aforesaid Louis gave to New Corvey the church under his jurisdiction called Meppia, with its tithes, possessions, and everything else belonging to it, as well as the church of Eresburg, which Charles, when he first built it in Saxony, endowed with the tithes of the inhabitants throughout a distance of two Saxon *rastae*.

For the assistance of the Herford monastery he gave, in the diocese of Osnabrück, the church of Buginithi with the churches subject to it; and in the parish of Mimigernaford, the church of Reni with the churches belonging to it. He stipulated that all the revenues of the tithes and other income should go to the aforesaid monasteries, and that they in turn should provide for the dependent populations in baptism, the Eucharist, burial, and hearing the confession of sins. The priests who held the principal churches were to perform the office of archpriests, carrying out everything that the archpriests of bishops customarily perform.

When the bishops themselves were required to make their visitations there, they were to receive for their lodging what is prescribed in the capitularies of our predecessors. Since, however, the expenses for the bishop’s ministry had to be increased on account of the illness and old age of the bishop then in office, Gauzbert, he wished, at the request of the first abbot of the same place, Warinus, that these expenses be regulated in such a way that, once what was sufficient for the bishop’s service had been specified, nothing would be withdrawn, while the bishop in turn would demand no greater amount and would come with no more people than could be adequately supported.

The aforesaid bishop agreed before our predecessor Louis, Archbishop Rabanus, and the others who were acting with him in synod that the following would be sufficient: for each church, four pigs, each worth twelve denarii, or eight rams of the same value; four piglets; four geese; eight chickens; twenty buckets of mead; twenty of honeyed beer; of unhoneyed beer, [lacuna]; 120 loaves; 100 *modii* of oats; 600 bundles. It was to be within the bishop’s power whether he wished to receive these provisions from each church as one lodging payment or as two.

So that the total obligation might be fulfilled neither in excess nor deficiency, he established and ordered this by his authority. It also pleased him to grant freely to both places the right to choose from their own community a suitable person to govern them for all future time. We confirm and strengthen this arrangement; and, so that every doubt might be removed, we have ordered it to be authenticated by our own hand and marked with the impression of our seal.

Sign of the lord Henry III, most invincible king (L. M.).

The chancellor Theodericus, acting in place of Bardo, archchaplain, examined and approved this document.

Given on 3 September, in the seventh indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1039; in the twelfth year of the ordination of the lord Henry III and the first of his reign.

Executed at Goslar, successfully. Amen.

## II. Privilege for the Church of Paderborn (1039)

[ERHARD, cited above, p. 103.]

[Col. 1088A]

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity. HEINRICUS, by the favor of divine clemency, king.

Since the providence of divine disposition has raised us, through the magnificence of its immeasurable mercy, to govern the monarchy of the entire commonwealth, we must first of all strive to ensure that he who granted us the crown of an earthly kingdom may, after we have completed the course of this life, also permit us to be crowned with one that will never be taken away.

We judge that this can be accomplished above all if places devoted to ecclesiastical service are strengthened by our authority, so that, once every external disturbance has been removed, they may remain in tranquility. In this way we may be assisted by the prayers of those who are obliged to devote themselves there day and night to prayer in the service of God, and may obtain through the pious intercession of those who serve the holy Church of God what, being troubled in conscience, we do not dare seek by ourselves.

Therefore we wish it to be known to all our faithful how Ruodolfus, venerable bishop of the holy Church of Paderborn, approached us with pious devotion and humbly entreated us, for the honor and indeed the greatest advantage of his church, to strengthen by our royal authority the Church over which he presides with pastoral care.

Since his petition seemed reasonable, we freely assented to it. Whatever the same Church ought to possess by right, whether through the donation of our predecessors, kings or emperors, or through our own gift, or through what has been bestowed there by other faithful persons—whether in goods, territories, counties and jurisdictions, or any kind of equipment—and whatever Bishop Megenwercus, the predecessor of the aforesaid Bishop Ruodolfus, contributed there from his own inheritance, or lawfully acquired elsewhere by exchange or lease, we once again grant as a stable gift and confirm by royal authority.

If anyone should thereafter attempt, through any presumption, to violate the edict of our confirmation, let him be fined one hundred pounds of gold according to our standard, half to be paid to our treasury and the other half to the same Church which he has rashly attempted to disturb.

And so that this confirmation may remain stable and unshaken through the succession of time, we have ordered this page of royal command to be written and, after confirming it with our own hand, to be marked with our seal.

Sign of the lord Henry III, most invincible king (L. M.).

The chancellor Theodericus, acting in place of Pardonis, archchancellor, examined and approved this document.

Given on 19 September, in the eighth indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1039; in the twelfth year of the lord Henry III and the first of his reign.

Executed at Bothtfelht, successfully. Amen.

## III. Privilege for the monastery of Corvey and the convent of Herford (1040)

[ERHARD, cited above, p. 103.]

[Col. 1089A]

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity. HEINRICUS, by the favor of divine clemency, king.

If our generosity grants some immunity to places devoted to divine worship, so that those dwelling there may serve the tranquility of heavenly life more securely and conveniently, we believe that we thereby make better use of the present and enjoy more blessedly the things that endure. Therefore let the vigilance of all Christ’s and our faithful, both present and future, know how, for the salvation of our soul and those of our parents, and also at the request of Gotesdie, abbess of the Herford Church, our beloved, we entrusted to the abbot of Corvey the grant of the Emperor Louis which he had made to the monasteries—one for monks, called New Corvey, the other for nuns, called Herford—which Louis, that emperor of pious memory, had built according to the model of the principal monasteries in Gaul: Corvey after the likeness of Old Corvey, and Herford after the likeness of Soissons.

In accordance with the custom by which provosts from the ecclesiastical order are accustomed to administer communities of the servants of God, he was to serve as their provider and patron both in discipline and in all matters which the handmaids of Christ could not carry out on account of their sex and profession.

As an alms for his family, Louis gave New Corvey the cell called Meppia, with its tithes and possessions belonging to it on every side, and the church of Heresburg, throughout a distance of two Saxon *rastae*. To the Herford monastery he gave, in the diocese of Osnabrück, the church of Buinidi with the churches subject to it, and in the parish of Mimigernaford the church of Reni with the churches belonging to it.

He stipulated that all the revenues from tithes and other income should go to the aforesaid monasteries, and that they in turn should provide for the dependent communities in baptism, the Eucharist, burials, and the hearing of confessions. The priests who held the principal churches were to perform the office of archpriests, carrying out everything customarily performed by the archpriests of bishops.

When the bishops themselves were required to make their visitations there, they were to receive for their lodgings what is prescribed in the capitularies of our predecessors, namely as much as was sufficient for them; and the bishops were not to demand more or come with more people than could be supported by it.

So that the bishops’ service might not be demanded in excess of what was necessary, the bishops of the aforesaid churches, with synodal consent, established before our predecessor, the Emperor Otto, Archbishop Rabanus, and the others who were acting with him in synod, that the following should be given for each church: four pigs, each worth twelve denarii, or eight rams of the same value; four piglets; four geese; eight chickens; twenty buckets of mead; twenty of honeyed beer; sixty of unhoneyed beer; 120 loaves; 100 *modii* of oats; 600 bundles. It was to be within the bishops’ power whether they wished to receive these provisions from each church as one lodging payment or as two.

Our aforesaid predecessor, the Emperor Otto, therefore established for both places the free right and authority to choose from their own community a suitable person to govern them for all future time. He also ordered that no public judge should have judicial authority over the people belonging to the aforesaid Herford monastery; rather, all their cases were to be settled before their own advocate.

We too confirm and strengthen this constitution of our predecessors as just and reasonable for the aforesaid Herford monastery by our royal command. And so that the authority of our confirmation may remain stable and unshaken forever, we have ordered this page to be written and, after confirming it with our own hand as appears below, to be marked with the impression of our seal.

Sign of the lord Henry III, most invincible king (L. M.).

The chancellor Eberhardus, acting in place of Bardo, archchancellor, examined and approved this document.

Given on 22 December, in the eighth indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1040; in the thirteenth year of the ordination of the lord Henry III and the second of his reign.

Executed at Herford, successfully. Amen.

## IV. Decree of King Henry III prohibiting Waldericus, abbot of the monastery of Saint Lawrence at Cremona, from alienating or leasing the goods of that monastery without the consent of the bishop of Cremona (1040)

[MURATORI, *Antiquitates Italicae*, VI, 217.]

[Col. 1090C]

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity. HEINRICUS, by the favor of divine mercy, king of the Franks and Lombards.

If we strengthen the holy Churches of God, etc. Therefore let it be known to all our faithful, both present and future, that the venerable man Hubaldus, bishop of the holy Church of Cremona and in every respect a most faithful man, reported to our moderation that a certain abbey, subject to his bishopric, dedicated to Saint Lawrence and situated within his city, was being diminished by a certain abbot named Waldericus through the granting of benefices and the drawing up of harmful instruments—namely, unjust leases, exchanges, and *libellaria*. On this account the provisions of the brothers were being withheld and the benefits of the servants reduced; thus the prayers and almsgiving that ought to be offered for the soul of the man who founded it and for the souls of all Christians appeared to be diminishing.

Struck inwardly with grief of heart on account of this matter, we began to consider what was being done. By the inspiration of divine grace, and with the salutary counsel of our beloved kinsman Herimannus, archbishop of Cologne, and likewise of our dearest cousin Bruno, bishop of Würzburg, as well as of Bishop and Chancellor Kadelous, we ordered a command of our royal authority to be issued, one that was to be held inviolable forever.

Its provision was that neither the present abbot nor any future abbot should thereafter have power to diminish the goods belonging to the aforesaid abbey, whether by granting benefices or by making exchanges, leases, or *libellaria*, without the permission of the aforesaid Bishop Hubaldus and his successors who may hold office in due course.

If any abbot should act against this authority of ours, all such acts shall remain invalid, void, and without force; the abbot shall be deprived of his honor and dignity; and whoever presumes to accept an investiture or any written instrument shall know that he must pay one hundred pounds of the finest gold, half to our treasury and half to the abbey which he attempted to damage.

So that this may be believed with greater certainty, etc.

Sign of the lord Henry, most glorious and invincible king.

I, Kadeolus, bishop and chancellor, acting in place of the lord Herimannus, archbishop and archchancellor, have examined and approved this document.

Given on 17 January, in the seventh indiction, in the year 1040, in the year of the lord Henry [remainder missing].

Executed at Augsburg, successfully. Amen.

## V. Diploma granted by Henry III, king of the Romans, to Abbot Poppo: confirmation of all the monastery’s possessions and immunities (1040)

[MARTENE, *Amplissima Collectio*, III, 59.]

[Col. 1091C]

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity. HEINRICUS, by the favor of divine clemency, king.

The exaltedness of royal prudence must in every way look after the peace and tranquility of those who serve God. Therefore let the diligence of all our faithful, both present and future, know that, being present at the consecration of the monastery of Stavelot, situated under our authority [Note: From this it is clear that the consecration of the church of Stavelot took place in 1040, under Saint Poppo, abbot, who restored discipline in the monastery and also restored the collapsed buildings, including the church. This is further evident from the account of the dedication itself (MARTENE, *Ampl. Collect.*, II, 60).], and since the reverence of its abbot, Poppo, stood high in our presence, at the request of the same abbot, we confirmed by our royal authority the grants and valid title to the goods attached or given to that church from the time of Saint Remaclus, in accordance with the enactments of the ancient kings Sigibert, Childeric, Clovis, and Dagobert, who were the founders of the aforesaid place, and likewise of the emperors Charles, Louis, the three Ottos, Henry, and also Conrad, our father, of most serene memory.

We have therefore established by our favor that whatever was given or granted to that place in the time of its predecessors, as well as the benefice which Emperor Henry granted to the same abbot from Hasbania for the sake of his soul’s reward, and whatever was restored to it by our father, of divine memory, after having been unjustly withheld for some time by Count Hermann from a deceased heir—namely, Scaletin and Palisiol with all their appurtenances—and whatever he purchased for that place, namely the sixth part of Amblava and Tumbis from Count Godefrid of Zingeis, or what was acquired by exchange from the church’s property—Wendengias and Corworonnon—with the villa of Astebronna given by the abbot of Saint Maximin in exchange, shall remain unbroken and undisturbed.

Since our predecessors, kings and emperors, established for that place, by the firmness of their authority, that the advocate of the same church should not presume, in the courts belonging to that place, to make lodging or provisioning arrangements, exact payments or fines, hold a court, or take *parafredi* for himself without the permission and consent of the abbot, we too strengthen and confirm this for the same abbot. By imposing our ban we reinforce it, so that no one may thereafter dare to violate these provisions.

Whatever he has acquired or is found to have acquired, in whatever goods belonging to the church, is likewise strengthened by the valid command of our authority, and he shall possess immunity from every disturbance by advocates.

Since the enactments of the ancient kings and emperors did not suffice for the monks of the other monastery, namely Malmedy, and since under two abbots they attempted to divide these same monasteries, although what had remained unbroken from the time of Saint Remaclus still endured, we have therefore decreed—as it is established that this occurred in the time of the lord Emperor Otto II—that, in accordance with the edict of our clemency, both monasteries shall remain subject to the rule of one abbot, as they have continually remained.

And so that the authority of our grant and confirmation concerning all these matters may be complete, we have confirmed this command below with our own hand and ordered it to be marked with the impression of our seal.

Sign of the lord Henry, invincible king.

The chancellor Theodericus, acting in place of Bardo, archchaplain, examined and approved this document.

Given on 5 June, in the eighth indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1040; in the thirteenth year of the ordination of the lord Henry III and the second of his reign.

[Col. 1092D] Executed at Stavelot, successfully. Amen.

## VI. Privilege for the convent of Saint Mary at Mimigardeford (1040)

[ERHARD, *Codex diplomaticus Westphaliae*, p. 107.]

[Col. 1092D]

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity. HEINRICUS, by the favor of divine clemency, king.

Let the careful diligence of all our faithful, both present and future, know how we, moved by divine admonition and also greatly encouraged by the most faithful and constant service of Herimannus, venerable bishop of the Church of Mimigardeford, granted and transferred to this church, for the salvation of the soul of our beloved father, Conrad, the august emperor, for the pious remembrance of the soul of our wife, Queen Chunehild, and likewise for the stability of our own life and that of our mother, the Augusta Empress Gisila, and from desire for divine recompense, a certain estate belonging to us called Harvia, situated in the district of Livegau and in the county of Count Dietbald.

This church was begun from its foundations at Mimigardeford by the aforesaid Bishop Herimannus, who completed it and, in our presence, solemnly consecrated it in honor of holy Mary, Mother of God. We granted and transferred the estate with all its appurtenances: serfs of both sexes, plots, buildings, cultivated and uncultivated lands, fields, meadows, pastures, open country, woods, hunting rights, waters and watercourses, mills, millworks, fisheries, exits and returns, roads and roadless places, things acquired and to be acquired, and every benefit that can be written or stated.

We gave it as a permanent possession so that the abbess of that church and the other nuns of God and of holy Mary, the Mother of God, might henceforth be able to fulfill more abundantly, day and night, the service of God in remembrance of us and our parents.

In making this transfer we made the following firm reservation: neither the present Bishop Herimannus nor his future successors should thereafter have any power to withdraw the aforesaid estate from the church or claim it for their own uses, except by an exchange or restitution that might appear more convenient or useful to the abbess of that church and all her nuns, whether because of proximity or because of the greater extent of its usefulness.

And so that the authority of this transfer and gift of ours may now and throughout the succeeding courses of time remain stable and unshaken, we have ordered this page to be written and, after confirming it with our own hand as appears below, to be marked with the impression of our seal.

Sign of the lord Henry III, most invincible king (L. M.).

The chancellor Eberhardus, acting in place of Bardo, archchancellor, examined and approved this document.

Executed on 29 December, in the ninth indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1041; in the thirteenth year of the ordination of the lord Henry III and the second of his reign.

Executed at Mimigardeford. Amen.

## VII. Diploma of the Emperor Henry II concerning the exchange made between the abbey of Saint Maximin at Trier and the abbey of Stavelot (about 1042)

[MARTENE, *Amplissima Collectio*, II, 64.]

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity. HEINRICUS, by the favor of divine clemency, emperor.

The sublimity of imperial prudence ought in every way to provide for the peace and tranquility of those who serve God, so that, whenever necessity requires or usefulness demands that a lease or exchange be made involving the estates or possessions of churches, it may record in writing by whose authority this is done. Thus, after the persons responsible for or guaranteeing the transaction have died, if any of their successors should wish to violate or alter it, the authority of the written record itself, brought forward publicly—and especially if it has been confirmed by imperial dignity—may serve as a witness for invalidating the efforts of the opposing party.

Therefore, let it be known to Christ’s faithful and to ours, both present and future, what sort of exchange was made concerning the property of Saint Remaclus at Wendengias. This property had formerly belonged to the abbey of Saint Maximin and, in exchange for Astenebruno, had been given, along with other exchanges, to the monastery of Stavelot and [Col. 1094B] sanctioned and confirmed by the imperial authority of my father, the Emperor Conrad, of blessed memory. A certain estate called Inkesengias belonged to the bishopric of Bamberg and pertained to the prebend of Saint George. Since it lay far from the aforesaid city, Luitpald, the provost of that place, with the consent of his lord, Bishop Sugerius, thought it appropriate to exchange it for another property. He therefore asked the venerable Poppo, abbot of the monastery of Stavelot, to accept this estate for himself, since it was near his abbey, and to give him in return the property at Wendagias, which was nearer to that place than the estate in question. So that the exchange might be equal on both sides, he was also to add two manses at Andernach and Nonam of Buobardium.

[Note: [Col. 1093D] Suggerus, or Suiggerus, or Suidigerus, said to have been Chancellor of the Emperor Saint Henry, was elected bishop of Bamberg in 1042 and, four years later, elevated to the supreme pontificate under the name Clement II.]

Accordingly, at Utrecht, in our court, we confirmed and strengthened the right of the aforesaid venerable abbot, who had been called upon to make the exchange, to hold and possess the property thereafter for the church of Saint Remaclus. By imposing our ban, we publicly reinforced the arrangement, so that no one thereafter might dare to take it away or appropriate it for himself, or to inflict any injustice or violence. And so that the authority of this confirmation and concession of ours concerning the exchange might be regarded as more complete—or rather, more certain—we have appended below, in our own hand, this written charter of command.

The sign of Lord Henry II, the unconquered emperor.

## VIII. Privilege for the monastery of Saint Peter at Minden. (Year 1043.)

[ERHARD, *Codex diplomaticus Westphaliae*, 110.]

[Col. 1094D]

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, Henry, by the favor of divine clemency, king.

If we apply ourselves to the founding of monasteries, or grant our assent to other faithful persons who wish to do the same, we do not doubt that this will benefit us not only for the advantage of the temporal kingdom but also for that of the eternal kingdom. Therefore, let all worshipers of the Christian religion, present and future, know how Bruno, bishop of Minden, approached us and obtained from us permission to build a monastery from the hereditary property belonging to him, on a certain island situated in the river Weser near Minden and placed under the authority of the apostle Saint Peter, in honor of the martyr Saint Maurice and his companions and of the other saints, for the commemoration of our father, the Emperor Conrad, who raised him to episcopal dignity, for our welfare and the stability of our kingdom, and for himself, his predecessors, his successors, and also his parents. He asked us to establish there a monastic way of life and to permit him to appoint an abbot there.

Since he had not previously presumed to initiate anything new in this matter or to ask anything from us before adding some supplement to the monasteries he had found, he requested that we receive this place under our protection. Because his petition was just and religious, we did not oppose it. At the intervention of our kinsmen Hermann, archbishop of Cologne, and Hunfrid, bishop of Magdeburg, and also with the consent of the other faithful of ours who were present at that time, we permitted him to build the aforesaid monastery and to establish there a monastic life and an abbot.

Although we rightly granted this to his desire, we consented to his request with all the greater confidence because, as we have said, the same bishop had first generously increased from his hereditary property the principal church of his see and the refectory of his brethren serving God and Saint Peter there. His predecessor, Bishop Sigebert, had begun two monasteries, namely those of Saint Mary and Saint Martin. Bruno completed one of them, that of Saint Mary, both in construction and in consecration; he had also devoutly enlarged the other, that of Saint Martin, in part. He likewise supplied, with faithful charity, the other monasteries under his authority in his bishopric and the refectories of those serving God there, so that he might later carry out his purpose in this monastery with the greater confidence that he had previously benefited the churches he had found.

For the same monastery he gave, from his hereditary property and from other donations that he had been able to acquire, eighty manses, with slaves, estates, plots, buildings, cultivated and uncultivated lands, roads and trackless places, outgoings and incomes, things acquired and to be acquired, meadows, pastures, woods, waters and watercourses, fisheries, mills, and the use of the woods. He also gave all appurtenances that can be stated or named, to remain there perpetually, except for those things that he might later acquire, with God’s help, or that might come to this church through the donations of the faithful. Moreover, he donated thirty manses and eighty plows in tithes from the property of the monastery of Saint Peter as an endowment for the same monastery.

He also established that every year, on the feast of Saint Maurice, the bishop of that see should come with the brethren of the monastery of Saint Peter to the aforesaid monastery, celebrate the solemn rites of Mass there, and fulfill the obligation of charity by dining there. If anything prevented the bishop from attending, the brethren were nevertheless to assemble there in the same spirit of charitable fellowship, so that through this concord and affection they might be united in greater devotion to God’s service.

And so that the same church, with the possessions now bestowed upon it by Bruno and those to be bestowed later by his successors or by others, might stand more securely, he placed it under the mundeburdium of Saint Peter, under our protection, and under the authority of the bishop of that place. Therefore, let everyone know that we wish to defend that monastery, its abbot, and the brethren residing there under the royal or imperial protection of ourselves and our successors, in such a way that no successor of the same bishop shall have the power in any manner to destroy or diminish the possessions of that monastery.

Therefore, whether he or anyone else should become a destroyer of this monastery and a dissipator of its possessions, let him know for certain that the abbot and brethren serving God there have a secure refuge in us and in our successors. And so that this decree of our concession may remain stable and unshaken for all time, we ordered this charter, written for that purpose and confirmed below by our own hand, to be marked with the impression of our seal.

Given on the tenth day before the Kalends of February, in the year of the Incarnation of the Lord 1043, indiction XI; in the fifteenth year of Lord Henry’s ordination and the fourth of his reign.

Enacted at Goslar, happily, in the name of God. Amen.

Adelger, chancellor, recognized it in place of Bardo, archchaplain.

## IX. Privilege for the monastery of Herford. (Year 1044.)

[ERHARD, *Codex diplomaticus*, 111.]

[Col. 1096C]

C. In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity. Henry, by the favor of divine clemency, king.

If by the munificence of royal generosity we confer something upon places dedicated to God, we confidently believe that this will benefit us both in temporal life and in eternal life. Therefore, let the understanding of all Christ’s faithful and ours, future as well as present, know how, especially for the love of God and for the remedy of our soul, and also at the intervention of our beloved wife, Queen Agnes, we wished by written authority to renew and confirm certain possessions given by our royal or imperial predecessors to the monastery of Herford, built in honor of holy Mary, Mother of God and perpetual Virgin, and of blessed Bosinna, who rests there bodily.

These possessions were two estates, Overanberh and Liutwinesdorf, given for the use of the nuns serving God there. They are situated in the district of Angeresgau and in the county of Count Witechind, with all their appurtenances: slaves of both sexes, plots, buildings, cultivated and uncultivated lands, meadows, pastures, waters and watercourses, millstones, mills, fisheries, woods, hunting rights, outgoings and incomes, roads and trackless places, things acquired and to be acquired, and every profit that could in any way proceed from them.

This was to be done on the following condition: that the aforesaid places should be held perpetually, without any opposition, for the use of all the nuns serving God there, and should be granted to no one as a benefice. We also generously grant and confirm, with the tradition and guarantee of our predecessors, that the nuns serving God there shall have the right and power to choose an abbess whenever one of them has died and thereby vacated the office.

No judicial official, tax collector, or public judge shall presume to conduct legal proceedings or exact fines in matters that appear to belong to the same church, or to compel its people to provide lodging or perform any service, except the advocate whom the abbess of that place shall have chosen. The people of these places shall be free from the jurisdiction of all others.

And so that the authority of this royal grant and confirmation may remain stable and unshaken for all ages, we ordered this charter, written for that purpose and confirmed below by our own hand, to be marked with the impression of our seal.

The sign of Lord Henry III (L. M.), the unconquered king. + CR. +

Theoderic, chancellor, recognized it in place of Bardo, archchancellor.

Given on the seventh day before the Kalends of October, in the year of the Incarnation of the Lord 1044, indiction XII; in the seventeenth year of Lord Henry III’s ordination and the sixth of his reign.

Enacted at Aachen, happily, in the name of God. Amen.

## X. Confirmation of the privileges and rights of the Church of Mantua, made by Henry III, king of Germany and Italy. (Year 1045.)

[MURATORI, *Antiquitates Italicae* VI, 415.]

[Col. 1097C]

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity. Henry, by the favor of divine clemency, king.

If, out of pious favor, we grant an increase of restoration to places consecrated to almighty God that have been desolated by various persons, we believe that this will benefit us both for the strengthening of our empire and for the reward of eternal recompense. Therefore, let the whole community of the holy Church of God and of our faithful, present and future, know that Marcianus, bishop of the holy see of Mantua, approached our clemency and asked that, for the love of God and for the remedy of our soul, we might deign to grant our Church a decree of our authority for the confirmation or restoration of all its possessions.

Moved by his prayers, and also through the intervention of our most beloved archbishop and archchancellor Hermann and our most loving bishop Bruno, we willingly assented. Since it is right that the property of the Churches of God should not be plundered by anyone, and that whatever is wicked should be removed from their control, we decreed for the Mantuan bishopric all the possessions that it now holds from gifts of our royal or imperial predecessors, or in any other manner, and all those which it appears to have lost through a lawless exercise of power or by force.

Namely: the monastery built in honor of the saints Memorius, Probus, and Rufinus, with all its appurtenances, including the water called Mulinelles, with its watercourses from the place where that water rises to the river Mincio, and twelve feet on each side of its bed; with all the possessions of the same monastery; and also estates situated in the counties of Verona, Vicenza, Mantua, Brescia, Piacenza, Modena, and Cremona, called Bagnolo, Colonia, and those around the river called Caput Alponis—Puliana, Alonte, Leonigo, and Sablone—or situated in the judicial district of Garda, with the male and female slaves belonging there; and all the other possessions of the same monastery situated in the aforesaid counties or within our Italian kingdom, whether obtained through concessions, grants, alienations, purchases, exchanges, the drafting of charters or any other royal documents, or through emphyteutic leases or emphyteusis.

We therefore confirm to it the parish of the city of Mantua, together with the parish of Sasselli, which is at Porto; the parish of Suave; the parish of Maurus; the parish of Saint Metrius; the parish of Octavo; the parish of Riverso; the parish of Goti; those of Volta, Bonago, Corte of Cauriana, Calziago, Gussenago, Caput Tartari, Margareja, Ludolo, which is in Scorzarolo, Turiselle, Saviola, Castellione of Mantua, Boneficio, Bigarello, Saint George, Ponterioli, Barbasio, Carisedolo, [Col. 1098C] Saint Cassian, Saint Martin of the estate of Barbasi, Saint Lawrence in the estate, Gubernule of Septingenti, Sermide, Saint Mary of Bagnolo, Castellucchio, Campedello, and Radaldesco; likewise the parish in Flumine Novo; the parish of Pletule; together with all the other parishes and chapels, cultivated and uncultivated lands, woods and hunting rights, tithes, estates, occupied and unoccupied manses, fields, meadows, pastures, and all the islands in the river Po, from Zara to Burana and to Vizanum, as the Po flowed in ancient times; with fisheries, fish-traps (*caretis*), marshes, mills, waters and watercourses, banks—everything in its entirety that can be said or named, wherever it is known that the same holy Church of Mantua was invested, by whatever arrangement or lawful authority.

Moreover, we renew the charter of the abbey of Saint Cassian, devastated by the pagans, bounded by these borders: from Agritia Major to the road commonly called Viscovilis, then to Agritia Minor; from there the boundary runs to Verenscula; thence it is diverted through the ditches of Paluti into the lake of Mantua; from there to Fissaro, and through Fissarum to Agritia Major, where the beginning of the boundary was established; together with all appurtenances and adjoining possessions that appear to belong to that abbey. Thus Marcianus, the bishop, and his successors may perpetually possess all these things for the benefit of their bishopric, without anyone’s hindrance or the harassment of opposition.

We also confirm to the same Church all tolls, banks and bank dues, and the fixing of posts on the bank of the city and harbor of Mantua, as well as the entire public revenue, the island of Reveris and the royal estate, and also the island called Suzaria, and so forth.

The sign (+) of Lord Henry III, the unconquered king.

Adalberius, chancellor, recognized it in place of Hermann, archchancellor.

Given in the year of the Incarnation of the Lord 1045, indiction XIII; in the fifteenth year of Lord Henry III’s ordination and the sixth of his reign.

Enacted at Augsburg, happily. Amen.

## XI. The Emperor Henry II decrees that what had been taken from the Church of Cremona by Gerard, nephew of Heribert, archbishop of Milan, be restored to it. (About the year 1046.)

[MURATORI, *Antiquitates Italicae* VI, 217.]

[Col. 1099B]

In the name of the eternal Lord God. Henry, by the favor of divine clemency, emperor augustus.

If we grant to the pastors of the holy Churches of God what our faithful properly request from our majesty, we do not doubt that this will contribute to the merit of eternal recompense for us. Therefore, let the diligence of all the faithful of the holy Church of God and of ours, present and future, know that Hubaldus, venerable bishop of the holy Church of Cremona and our beloved faithful, humbly reported to our royal authority through Lord Hermann, most reverend archbishop of Cologne and our dearest cousin, how he had found his Church almost desolate and worn down by many calamities and miseries.

For in the time of the Emperor Conrad Augustus, of blessed memory, our father, Lord Landulfus, who had always been entirely faithful to the aforesaid Church and to the Roman Empire, was seized by a serious illness and prolonged his life through that illness for a long time. During his long sickness, his Church suffered no small loss, especially at the hands of Gerard, nephew of Heribert, archbishop of Milan. Inflated with pride by the audacity of his uncle, who was arranging the whole Italian kingdom according to his own will, Gerard did whatever pleased him in the kingdom by force of authority, whether just or unjust.

He therefore seized the estate and parish of Arciacum against the will and without the permission of the bishop, who had long been gravely ill. When the bishop had left this lower world and departed to the heights, Bishop Hubaldus, our entirely faithful servant, succeeded him. When Hubaldus needed to approach the archbishop in order to receive episcopal consecration, he was entirely unable to obtain consecration from him unless he granted his nephew the parish and estate that Gerard had unjustly and coercively seized.

Since his consecration was prolonged for a long time because of this demand, he granted what Gerard had requested, not willingly but under compulsion, and obtained consecration only on that condition. Because he deeply regretted what he had done, he repeatedly complained to the majesty of our father that he had not done this willingly. When our father wished to restore the aforesaid estate and parish to him, he often and repeatedly instructed Gerard by letter to leave them in the possession of the bishopric.

Gerard could never be persuaded to do so. Instead, by diabolical prompting—for, as is evident to all Italians and Germans, he had served the devil from the cradle—he despised the emperor’s command, retained the possessions mentioned above, and did not hesitate to seize other, much greater properties, to the disgrace and humiliation of our father: namely, the parish of Misianum with all its possessions; the tithe from the castle of Aganellum belonging to the aforesaid parish of Arciacum; the tithe of Mauringum belonging to the parish of Fornovo; and half of the castle of Corteganum belonging to the abbey of Saint Lawrence.

When our father came into the kingdom and discovered that the archbishop, having violated the oath of loyalty he had given him, was attempting to seize the kingdom for himself, he rightly took all the aforesaid possessions from Gerard, who had instigated the archbishop and given him every support, as from one guilty of treason and deserving proscription, and restored them to the bishop. But when our father departed from the kingdom, Gerard did not fear to seize everything again, disregarding his reverence and his fear.

We, however, grieving over the diminution and misery of the bishopric and considering our father’s disgrace, grant all these possessions to the bishopric to be held perpetually. Moreover, by the authority of our decree, we establish that they are to be retained, on the condition that no archbishop, bishop, duke, margrave, count, viscount, or person of high or low rank in our kingdom shall dare to dispossess that Church.

But if anyone should do so, and so forth.

I, Raimundus, notary of this copy, saw and read the exemplar.

## XII. Diploma of King Henry III, the second emperor, by which he confirms all the possessions of the Veronese monastery of Saint Zeno. (Year 1047.)

[MURATORI, *Antiquitates Italicae* VI, 221.]

[Col. 1100C]

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity. Henry, by the favor of divine clemency, Roman emperor augustus.

It is fitting for imperial sublimity, and so forth: how Walter, bishop of the holy Church of Verona, together with Alberic, abbot of the monastery of the martyr Saint Zeno, humbly approached our clemency, entreating us, for the love of almighty God and the reverence of blessed Zeno, and so forth.

We, assenting to their just petitions, for the remedy of our soul and at the intervention of our most beloved wife, the Empress Agnes, grant and confirm to the aforesaid monastery, and so forth:

Namely, in the territory of Verona, the monastery built in honor of Saint Peter, called Mauritica, with its tithes and boundaries extending from the end of Fissaro to the Mantuan Ditch, on one side from Agricia to Finale, and reaching in Agricia as far as Trivularia; at one end, Castellione and Silvatico; also the castle in Vallepicta with its tithes and appurtenances; the castle of Mauriatica with the church in honor of Saints Firmus and Rusticus, with its tithes, judicial claims, jurisdictions, and all its possessions, just as it was granted and offered to the monastery of Saint Zeno by the most pious Emperor Charles, of good memory; the castle of Herbetum with all its possessions and appurtenances; the castle of Trebunciolum; the castle of Vicoaderis; the chapel of Saint Lawrence situated on the bank of the Po, called Ostiglia, with its tithes and all its possessions; Campolane, the field of Palliarium, Novoletum, and three hundred jugera at Gajo; the place called Casale-Orci; the estate called Aspo; the castle of Romanianum, with the artificial works of Saint Zeno, and the mountain called Alferia; at Lisino, in the place called Melario, two fields; at Clariano, three fields; at Crodano, two fields; at Laupha, one field; the castle of Saint Vitus with its possessions; Parona; Cassianum; the cell of Saint Peter within the city of Verona with its possessions; at Cavi, the cell of Saint Andrew with its possessions; at Venti, the chapel of Saint Vitus with its possessions; at Puviniaca, one small estate, and an estate at Rivariola with all its possessions; and at Pualo, three fields.

Also, together with all possessions belonging to the aforesaid monastery, including churches, castles, villages, tenant farmers, slaves, commendatory holdings, artificial works, and so forth.

We also admonish and forbid the abbot who presides over the monastery, and his successors, from taking from the monastery’s resources the provision-property dedicated to feeding the monks and granting it as a benefice to secular persons. Pious religion protests when the servants of God waste away in poverty while those who have no right grow rich from their abundance.

If any abbot should carelessly or rashly violate what we decree, let him justly take back what he unjustly granted and restore the broken member to the body of the Lord. If he should wish to purge his evil deeds but be unable to do so, then his successor, strengthened by the judgment of us and our successors, shall make good what his predecessor lost.

Finally, we decree by command that no duke, margrave, bishop, count, viscount, and so forth, shall do so. If anyone within the jurisdiction of our kingdom should rise against these royal letters or attempt to violate them in any respect, let him know that he shall pay thirty pounds of the finest gold, half to the aforesaid monastery and half to our palace. And, in the name of God, we order this decree of ours to be made more secure, and so forth.

The sign of Lord Henry III, the unconquered king, the second Roman emperor augustus.

Henry, chancellor, recognized it in place of Hermann, archchancellor.

Given on the eighth day before the Ides of May, in the year of the Incarnation of the Lord 1047, indiction XV; in the eighteenth year of Lord Henry III’s ordination, the eighth of his reign, and the first of his second imperial rule.

Enacted at Foligno, happily, in the name of God. Amen.

## XIII. King Henry III, the second emperor, renews the privileges of the canons of Padua and of their Church. (Year 1047.)

[MURATORI, *Antiquitates Italicae* I, 1001.]

[Col. 1102A]

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity. Henry, by the favor of divine clemency, Roman emperor augustus.

If we act for sacred and venerable places, and so forth, let the diligence of all the faithful of the holy Church of God and of ours, present and future, know that Arnold, venerable bishop of the holy Church of Padua, and also Bernard, our chaplain and archdeacon of that Church, humbly entreated our clemency to confirm by our authority, for the love of almighty God and for the remedy of our soul, and also at the request of Henry, our most beloved chancellor, all the decrees issued by our predecessors and all the charter instruments recently granted by faithful men to the holy Church of Padua.

Freely granting their request, both for the love of God and for reverence toward that Church, we confirm by this authority of ours everything that had formerly been granted to the aforesaid Church of Padua through decrees of other kings or emperors, as well as through charter instruments donated by faithful men.

We also establish that the canons of that Church who are now serving, and their successors, shall have, with the consent of the bishop who is in office at the time, free power to divide among themselves, as has been customary, everything that appears or shall appear justly and lawfully to belong to them, with all opposition from authorities removed.

Namely, the tithes of the city in their entirety, together with the churches and estates belonging to that city: first, the estate called Limena; the estate called Arzere; Autikeria; Turre; Noenta; the estate called Bergomi; Roncalia; Ronco Liuteri; the estate called Casale; another called Publitiano; and the estate called Albignaseca and Masserata, and so forth.

We also grant to the same Church that no duke, margrave, count, viscount, sculdassio, gastald, dean, or any minister of the public authority, and so forth, shall do so.

The sign of Lord Henry, the unconquered Roman emperor augustus.

Henry, chancellor, recognized and subscribed it in place of Hermann, archchancellor.

Given on the fifth day before the Ides of May, in the year of the Incarnation of the Lord 1047, indiction XV; in the eighteenth year of Lord Henry III’s ordination, the eighth of his reign, and the first of his imperial rule.

Enacted at Trent, happily, in the name of God. Amen.

## XIV. Diploma of Henry III, the second among the emperors, by which he confirms all rights and possessions to the canons of Saint Saviour at Turin. (Year 1047.)

[MURATORI, *Antiquitates Italicae* V, 195.]

[Col. 1103A]

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity. Henry, by the favor of divine clemency, Roman emperor augustus.

Let the whole community of the holy Church of God and of our faithful, both future and present, know how, for the love of God and for the remedy of our soul, by this decree of our confirmation we grant, confirm, and establish, insofar as we can justly and lawfully do so, to the canons of the Church of Turin, in the canonical church and cloister built within the city of Turin in honor of the Lord Saviour, and also to the canons serving there at the time, everything bestowed by Regnimius, bishop of that see and founder of the canonical church of the Lord Saviour, of blessed memory, as well as everything previously granted or to be granted through the decrees of kings and emperors, through the confirmations of successive bishops, or through the donations of religious men.

Namely, the churches within the same city of Turin: one in honor of the holy apostles Philip and James; another in honor of the holy apostles Simon and Jude; a third in honor of the holy martyr Stephen; a fourth in honor of Saint Martinianus; a fifth in honor of Saint Eusebius; and a sixth in honor of Saint Martin.

Also, the castle above the gate of the same city called Turrianica; the entire tithe both within and outside the city; and the mills and fisheries in the river Turia.

Moreover, all the possessions of the same canonical church, both within and outside the city, with their dwelling-sites, houses, gardens, approaches, lands, male and female slaves, and everything belonging to the aforesaid canonical church.

We also grant all the demesne tithes of the same bishop’s see and the tithes of all the bishop’s faithful who hold benefices. Also, the principal church in honor of Saint Maximus at Quinctum; the church of Saint Stephen at Maliascum; the church of Saint Mary; the church of Saint Peter; and the church of Saint Lawrence, with the entire tithe of the aforesaid estate.

An estate at Alpinianum, with its castle and the chapel of Saint Peter situated within that castle; another estate across the river Turia, belonging to Saint Mary, with mills, fisheries, and all appurtenances belonging to it; an estate at Lifiniascum, with its castle and the chapel of Saint Maurice in that castle, with everything belonging to it; the church of Saint Victor and Saint Corona, with the entire tithe at Marcomeda and with the lands and manses belonging to the aforesaid canonical church; the church of Saint Macharius at Vilascum, with the lands and tithes of that estate.

Also, the parish at Durionum of Saint Mary, with the entire tithe belonging to it in the plains, houses, lands, and vineyards; and the chapel of Saint Solutor on Mount Pharratus.

The church of Saint Vitus in the estate called Arsitias, with the whole estate, its tithe, ports, fisheries, and everything adjoining it; the church of Saint George with the mountain on which it stands at Villaparso, with the entire tithe of that estate and the manses belonging to the same canonical church; the tithe at Malavasius, with two churches, one in honor of Saint Mary and the other in honor of Saint Martin; and the entire tithe at Valleplana, Vallesurda, and Milionico, and from there at Ligadino, with the lands and vineyards belonging to the aforesaid canonical church.

An estate at Saxinas, with a church in honor of Saint John, with its entire tithe, mills, woods, brushlands, pole-lands, and all appurtenances; and the entire tithe of that estate.

An estate at Martiriascum, with the chapel of Saint Martin, woods, brushlands, and all its appurtenances; an estate at Pavatianum with all its possessions; a chapel at Romanianum in honor of Saint Remigius; an estate at Pavariolum with its castle and a chapel in that castle in honor of Saint Secundus, with all its possessions; an estate at Audisellum and Mandegum, with their possessions; an estate at Patianum with a castle and two chapels; an estate at Balbianum with one chapel; an estate at Alinianum with a castle and a chapel in that castle in honor of Saint Remigius.

Also, a chapel, manses, vineyards, and houses at Orsenascum; an estate at Santena with a castle and a chapel in that castle in honor of Saint Paul, with the entire tithe of that estate; an estate at Bulgare and a portion of the castle, with ports, mills, fisheries, woods, and everything belonging to it; half of the estate of Buriadis, with half of the chapel in honor of Saint Michael.

An estate at Scandalticum, with a parish church in honor of Saint Dalmatius and four chapels in the same estate: one in honor of Saint Michael, another of Saint John, a third of Saint Andrew, and a fourth of Saint Martin; with the entire tithe, mills, woods, pastures, common and private meadows, and everything belonging to the aforesaid canonical church.

A chapel at Polengaria in honor of Saint Remigius, with everything belonging to it at Sablone; five manses and half the tithe of that estate; together with lands, castles, chapels, vineyards, fields, meadows, pastures, woods, mills, ports, bank dues, waters and watercourses, fisheries, male and female slaves, persons of half-free status, tithes, rents, revenues, common and non-common marshes, banks, cliffs, cultivated and uncultivated lands, movable and immovable property—in its entirety, everything belonging or pertaining by the authority of our confirmation to the rights of the aforesaid canonical church and to the use and sustenance of the canons who may be in office at the time.

We grant, bestow, and establish all that has been granted and all that is to be granted, with every human dispute removed and banished far away.

Furthermore, by this page of our decree we prescribe and order that no bishop, even a public judge, nor any itinerant royal envoy, margrave, count, sculdahis, gastald, or person of whatever high or low authority dare to invade, plunder, or by any device wickedly remove from the authority of the canons—who serve the Lord there—any property belonging to the aforementioned canonry, nor give it as a benefice to anyone without the consent of the aforesaid canons; nor at any time dare to enter it in judicial fashion to hold proceedings or to inflict any of the aforesaid or other violence. Rather, let them, together with all their property and dependants, remain under our protection and the safeguard of immunity.

If complaints should arise against the aforesaid canons, whether concerning free men, servants, or property, we order that they be settled and brought to a final conclusion before the provost and canons of that same church. Therefore, if anyone should at any time attempt to act against this page of our decree and the authority of our command, or presume to violate anything written above, let him know that he must pay two hundred pounds of the finest gold, half to our treasury and half to the aforesaid canons, and that he has moreover incurred the offense of our majesty. And so that this decree of our immunity may possess inviolable and unshaken firmness, we have confirmed it below with our own hand and ordered it authenticated by the impression of our ring.

Sign of the lord Henry, most invincible emperor of the Romans.

I, Henry the chancellor, have examined and approved this document as deputy of Herimann, the archchancellor.

Issued on the Kalends of May, in the year of the Incarnation of the Lord 1047, in the fifteenth indiction, and in the eighteenth year of the lord Henry’s reign—or ordination—and the first of his imperial rule.

Done at Mantua, prosperously, in the name of God.

## XV. Decree of Emperor Henry concerning the liberty and possessions of the monastery of Casauria. (Year 1047.)

[MURATORI, *Rerum Italicarum Scriptores* II, II, 357.]

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity. Henry, by the favor of divine clemency, emperor Augustus of the Romans.

If we grant assent to the petitions of God’s servants, we do not doubt that this will contribute to our hope of divine recompense. Therefore, let the diligence of all Christ’s faithful and ours, both future and present, know how, for the love of God and the remedy of our soul, both at the petition of the venerable monk Adelbert and of his brother Guimarius, concerning the Church of the Holy Trinity and of Saint Quiricus the martyr, at the place called Placentro, in the county of Balbense, where Finianus is said to be located, we grant to them for holding and possessing that aforesaid place, both to them and to their abbot. Let no duke, margrave, bishop, count, viscount, or person of high or low rank presume to inflict any disturbance or invasion upon it.

Moreover, we grant them the aforesaid place of Finianus with its entrance and exit, bounded on one side from the head by the Serra de Barbarano, at the lower end by the Rigo of Placentro, on one side by the valley of Fuge, and on the other side by the Serra of Corviano, together with the fork and all its appurtenances. In the aforesaid boundaries there are four hundred *modia* of land; and if more should be found, let it belong to the same aforementioned church, together with lands, vineyards, waters and their courses, fisheries, mills, cultivated and uncultivated land—in every respect and in all things. Whatever our treasury might hope to obtain from the possessions of the aforesaid monastery, we grant to them as the reward of eternal recompense. And so that no one may pay the *mallatura* to its advocate, etc., as in the privileges above.

Sign of the lord Henry II, most invincible emperor Augustus of the Romans.

I, Henry the chancellor, have examined and approved this document as deputy of Herimann, the archchancellor.

Issued on the Kalends of January, in the year of the Incarnation of the Lord 1047, in the fifteenth indiction; in the eighteenth year of the ordination of the lord Henry III, in fact the eighth of his second reign, and the first of his imperial rule.

Done at the city of Columna, prosperously, in the name of God. Amen.

## XVI. Decree of Emperor Henry concerning the liberty and possessions of the monastery of Casauria.

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity. Henry, by the favor of divine clemency, emperor Augustus of the Romans.

If we grant assent to the petitions of God’s servants, we do not doubt that this will contribute to our hope of divine recompense. Therefore, let the diligence of all Christ’s faithful and ours, both future and present, know how, for the love of God and the remedy of our soul, and at the petition of the venerable abbot Dominic of the said monastery of the Holy Trinity and of Saint Clement the martyr, who rests there, in the county of Pinna, on the island called Casa-Aurea, in accordance with the decrees of our predecessors, kings and emperors, we have decreed by our imperial authority to strengthen and confirm whatever it is seen to possess justly and lawfully—namely, whatever the same monastery appears to possess within the city of Rome, etc., as above in the other privileges.

Sign of the lord Henry II, most invincible emperor Augustus of the Romans.

I, Henry the chancellor, have examined and approved this document as deputy of Herimann, the archchancellor.

Issued on the third day before the Ides of March, in the year of the Incarnation of the Lord 1047, in the fifteenth indiction, and in the eighteenth year of the ordination of the lord Henry III, in fact the eighth of his second reign, and the first of his imperial rule.

Done at Saint Flavianus, prosperously, in the name of God. Amen.

## XVII. Henry, the second among the emperors of that name, grants Bernard, bishop of Padua, the right to mint money. (Year 1049.)

[MURATORI, *Antichità Italiane* II, 711.]

[Col. 1107A]

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity. Henry, by the favor of divine clemency, emperor Augustus of the Romans.

If we grant beneficial gifts to sacred and venerable places, we have no doubt that this will contribute to the benefit of our soul. Therefore, we wish it to be known to all Christ’s faithful and ours, both future and present, how, at the intercession of our spouse and partner in the kingdom, namely the empress Augusta Agnes, and also on account of the devoted service to God and the petition of Bernard, bishop of Padua, we perpetually grant and permit to him and to his Church the license and power to make coin in the city of Padua, according to the weight of Veronese coinage.

And so that the authority of this concession of ours may appear more certain, we ordered that on one face of the denarii there be stamped the impression of our name and image, and on the other the figure of that same city. And since, in accordance with the imperial authority of our predecessors, kings and emperors, we deliver the aforementioned gift to the holy Church of God by a firm condition, for the remedy of our soul, we firmly desire and command that no person, greater or lesser, presume to deprive or harass the Church of God, or its custodian—namely Bishop Bernard—and his successors, with respect to this gift of our benevolence. And so that all may believe it more truly and observe it more diligently throughout the ages to come, we have confirmed this decree of our donation with our own hand and ordered it marked below with the impression of our seal.

Sign of the lord Henry III, most invincible king, second emperor Augustus of the Romans.

I, Herimann, archbishop of Cologne and archchancellor, have examined and approved this document.

Issued on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of May, in the year of the Incarnation of the Lord 1049, in the second indiction, in the year of the lord Henry III, king and second emperor, the twentieth of his ordination, the tenth of his reign, and the third of his empire, in the name of the Lord.

Done at Goslar, prosperously. Amen.

## XVIII. Privilege for the Church of Bremen. (Year 1049.)

[LAPPENBERG, *Hamburg Urkund*, 874.]

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity. Henry, by the favor of divine clemency, emperor Augustus of the Romans.

Since, by the duty of governing the kingdom, we owe paternal care to all the churches of the Roman Empire, we wish to exalt each one, insofar as it is granted to us by the gift of divine grace, and to advance it for the better through the gifts of our beneficence. Therefore, let all Christ’s faithful and ours, both future and present, know how, at the petition of our spouse and partner in the kingdom, namely Augusta Agnes, the empress, and on account of the devoted service of our faithful and beloved Adelbert, archbishop of the Church of Bremen, with the consent of Duke Berenhard and Count Udo and the other co-heirs, we have transferred to the altar of that same church, in honor of Saint Mary, Mother of God and perpetual virgin, and of Saint Peter, prince of the apostles, a forest together with the lawful right of the ban, in the district called Lara or Steiringa—namely, in the duchy of Duke Berenhard—and situated within the boundaries that we name below.

It begins at the bridge which in the vernacular is called Buribruc; from there it descends alongside the river Hunta as far as the bed of the river called Aldena; from there it proceeds along the course of the river to the place where Aldena flows into the Weser; from the confluence of these rivers it ascends along the bank of the Weser as far as the place where the boundaries of the archbishopric of Bremen and the bishopric of Minden meet; and again, along the boundary of those same bishoprics, it runs westward as far as the aforesaid bridge.

This is granted on the following condition and under the following provision: no one, without the permission of the aforesaid archbishop and his successors, may presume to capture or ensnare in that forest, by the skill of the hunting craft, any kind of wild animal whose taking is prohibited by the law of the ban. Whoever hunts within the defined boundary of that forest against this condition of our imperial decree shall be subject to the same law of compensation toward the archbishop as is established by law for all who hunt in our forest contrary to prohibition.

And so that this gift of our authority may remain firm throughout all ages, we have confirmed this charter, written in duplicate, with our own hand and ordered it marked with the impression of our seal.

Sign of the lord Henry III, most invincible king, second emperor Augustus of the Romans.

I, Uvinitherius the chancellor, have examined and approved this document as deputy of Pardo, the archchancellor.

Issued on the . . . Kalends of June, in the year of the Incarnation of the Lord 1049, in the second indiction, and in the twenty-first year of the ordination of the lord Henry III, king and second emperor, the tenth of his reign and the third of his empire. In the name of the Lord.

Done at Minden, prosperously. Amen.

## XIX. Diploma of Henry, second among the emperors of that name, by which he grants the monastery of Saint Zeno at Verona two advocates with various rights and privileges. (Year 1050.)

[MURATORI, *Antichità Italiane* V, 291.]

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity. Henry, by the favor of divine clemency, emperor Augustus of the Romans.

It befits imperial majesty that, the more exalted it is honored above other dignities, the more kindly and merciful it should be found toward the just petitions of those who serve God. Therefore, let it be known to all the faithful of the holy Church of God and to ours, both future and present, how Abbot Michael of the monastery of Saint Zeno the martyr approached our clemency in humble prayer, earnestly entreating us, for the love of almighty God and reverence for the blessed martyr Zeno, because the property of the church of the monastery of Saint Zeno—which our piety had granted to it—was suffering considerable loss at the hands of invaders.

He therefore petitioned us to grant him two advocates from among our faithful, namely Berifred and David, to administer the monastery’s affairs by virtue of their advocacy.
