We, consenting to his just petitions, grant and confirm them to the aforesaid monastery, for the remedy of our soul, at the intercession of our most beloved wife, the empress Agnes, and for the advancement of our son, King Henry IV; and we have ordered our letters of serenity to be drawn up. By these we command that our aforesaid vassals be its advocates in whatever counties or districts, with respect to the property of the aforementioned church—castles, *arimanni*, or servants—and wherever necessity may require; and no one shall presume to oppose them in carrying out this duty. But they shall attend to this matter in such a way that the resources of the aforesaid church are not diminished by any injury.

We further order that, wherever necessity requires and utility dictates, neither duke, margrave, count, nor any person, greater or lesser, shall in any way have the power, in those estates, possessions, *arimanni*, or servants, to hold a court, exercise jurisdiction, or draw up notices or charters, except the aforementioned advocates of Abbot Michael and of his successors. We grant them the power to hold courts and draw up notices or charters concerning all the property and possessions of the monastery of Saint Zeno, but only in this order: from every general court held once a year, the aforesaid advocates shall receive a third portion as a benefice for their military service, except at Parona, Cassano, and Villa.

If, beyond this benefice, they should attempt by any importunity or device to harass or disturb the monastery, the abbot, relying upon the strength of our authority, shall undoubtedly have the power to deprive them both of their authority and of their benefice, and to grant them to other faithful men by prudent disposition. Moreover, for their insufficiently restrained importunity, let them know that they must pay fifty pounds of gold, half, etc.

Sign of the lord Henry III, most invincible king, second emperor Augustus of the Romans.

I, Gunter, the chancellor, have examined and approved this document as deputy of Herimann, the archchancellor.

Issued on the third day before the Ides of November, in the year of the Incarnation of the Lord 1050, in the fourth indiction, in the twenty-fourth year of the ordination of the lord Henry III, king and second emperor, the thirteenth of his reign and the fourth of his empire.

Done at Verona, prosperously in the name of God.

## XX. Diploma of Henry III for Saint Maximin. — Through the intervention of Pope Leo IX he restores the estate of Prichina to the monastery and confirms several villas for the brothers’ use. (Year 1051.)

[MARTENE, *Amplissima Collectio* I, 425, from the chartulary of Saint Maximin at Trier.]

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity. Henry, by the favor of divine clemency, emperor Augustus of the Romans.

[Col. 1110B]

If we do not grant benefits to places dedicated to God, but at least restore what was previously bestowed by others and unjustly withdrawn or taken away, we trust that God will undoubtedly reward us. Therefore, let the diligence of our faithful, both present and future, know how, for the love of God and through the intervention of our spiritual father, namely the lord Leo, [Note: [Col. 1109D] the ninth of that name, who, having been made supreme pontiff after serving as bishop of Toul, visited his native land after attaining possession of the papacy, met the emperor Henry, who was residing in Saxony, then came from there to Cologne and held a council at Reims in Gaul. Afterwards, returning to Germany, he was able to visit Trier.] supreme pontiff and universal pope of the Holy Roman Church, we return to the monks of Saint Maximin—who rests bodily in the suburb of Trier—a certain estate called Prichina, situated in the district of Cinridke, with all its appurtenances and every utility that can either be written or named. We had unjustly ordered Abbot Theoderic to grant it as a benefice to a certain Anshelmo; but now, with justice dictating it, we have returned and confirmed that same estate, together with all property in whatever places that justly and lawfully belongs or pertains to it, to Saint John [Note: [Col. 1110D] For the basilica of the monastery recognizes Saint John the Evangelist as its principal patron.] and Saint Maximin and the brothers serving them, and, with God as author, have established it forever.

This is on the condition that neither the aforesaid Abbot Theoderic nor any of his successors ever presume to grant or sell it to anyone; rather, the brothers, being provided for from it, shall obtain their provisions, leggings, and also mantles (*mantelas*) [Note: [Col. 1110D] *Mantela* here seems to be the same as *mantellus*, a type of garment, French *manteau*.] and table-garments (*mensalia*) [Note: [Col. 1110D] *Mensalia* were over-tunics which the ancients wore at table in order to spare more precious garments.] for necessary use; they shall receive guests and faithfully provide from it for the needs of pilgrims and the poor. We have also decreed by this imperial authority to strengthen for the provision of those same brothers the churches, villas, and possessions which, under the times of the kings and emperors Dagobert, Pippin, Charles, and our other predecessors, down to our own time, appeared to belong to their private holding, so that from them they may obtain food and clothing. These are Apula, etc. (forty-nine villas are enumerated), and in the city of Metz and its surroundings, houses and fields, vineyards, small plots, Brisanga, Weinareskiricha, Crufta, Seranna, and the church at Steinsicla and Diedenhoium.

Therefore, we assign and confirm these places and all the churches of Saint Maximin, with their tithes, endowment, and dower-rights, together with all the *salic* tithes that we have established for the use of pilgrims, the poor, and guests, to the private holding of the brothers serving God there, in accordance with the custom of our predecessors, kings and emperors, and on this condition: just as our predecessor Henry, Augustus of blessed memory, established after removing from that abbey what pertained to military expeditions or royal service, no emperor, no king, and no abbot shall presume to grant any benefice from those places and churches to any of those who are called free men, or to a servant or minister of another church or lord, or to withdraw anything from their right. Rather, the abbots shall be permitted to restore the church lights, repair the buildings, and faithfully provide the brothers with what is necessary.

And so that this decree, written for that purpose, may always remain firm and stable, we have not only confirmed it with our hand and ordered it marked with the impression of our seal, but also obtained for that venerable place a privilege, drawn up for this purpose, of our aforesaid spiritual father—namely the lord Leo, most holy pope—so that, if anyone should wish to violate these provisions, they may have the aid of apostolic protection.

Sign of the lord Henry III, most invincible king, second emperor Augustus of the Romans.

I, Winnitherins the chancellor, have examined and approved this document as deputy of Bardo, the archchancellor and archbishop.

[Col. 1111C]

Issued on the twelfth day before the Kalends of February, in the year of the Incarnation of the Lord 1051, in the nineteenth year of the reign of the lord Henry III, king and second emperor, and the fifth of his empire.

Done at Trier, prosperously in the name of God. Amen.

## XXI. Privilege of the lord Henry III, king or emperor, concerning Clotten. — He confirms to the monastery of Brunweiler the donation made by Richeza, queen of Poland. (Year 1051.)

[MARTENE, *Amplissima Collectio* I, 427, from the Brunweiler manuscript.]

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity. Henry, by the favor of divine clemency, emperor Augustus of the Romans.

If we do not grant benefits to places dedicated to God, but at least confirm what has been bestowed by other faithful Christians, we trust that God will undoubtedly reward us. Therefore, let the community of our faithful, both present and future, learn how a certain venerable lady named Richeza, formerly queen of Poland, freely and entirely transferred to God and Saint Nicholas, for the remedy of her soul and that of her brother, Duke Otto of blessed memory, and of her other relatives buried in the monastery of Brunweiler, through the hand of Henry, count palatine, the son of her paternal uncle, under whose protection she then remained, her estate called Clotten, together with the other places listed below—namely Comenheim, Elre, Brembe, Asche, Masbrech, Wernus, Tanelach, Wilre, Pulego, Chucomo, Chundedo, Merle, Ryle, Erichriche, Lutzenrodo, Dreise, and Ottingin—with mansions and dependants, and with its entire integrity: in villages, plots, dwellings, vineyards, *arpents*, woods and fields, meadows, waters and their courses, pastures, roads and roadless places, cultivated and uncultivated lands, outgoings and incomings, things acquired and to be acquired, and all its appurtenances, without any diminution.

She also established the boundary and ban of that estate, as she had previously held it, from the river Andrida to the river Elza, so that no one there should possess any authority except the abbot of that place and the steward whom he appoints.

She also granted certain *arpents*, that is, vineyards, as benefices to certain servants of hers: two to Provost Rupert; two to Weringer of Salevelt; two to Sigebodo of Odendorff; three to Sigifrid the cupbearer; two to Eppo of Aldendorff; and chambers beside the lord’s court, two to Albert, brother of Winbold; two to Embrico of Geldestorp; thirteen mansions with their dependants at Lutzenrode, and the wine called *Srozwin*, to her clerk Ansfrid; two mansions with their dependants at Clotten to Ernest, her brother; and at Dreise she also transferred Wolfer with his possession to that place.

This was on the condition that, for as long as they lived, they should hold the church’s property or benefices; but after their death none of their heirs should claim or possess any of these things as if by hereditary right. Rather, they should return to the right and lordship of Saint Nicholas, his abbot, and the brothers serving him, so that the abbot might do and arrange whatever he judged more useful for himself and the brothers.

She also transferred the men whom she gave to Saint Nicholas on the following condition: none of them should take a wife from outside, unless she were free or belonged to the authority of Saint Peter of Cologne. If they should take foreign wives, all their inheritance and everything they possessed should pass to the monastery of Saint Nicholas, and none of their heirs should have any claim to it. But if they took wives from the authority of Saint Peter of Cologne, their sons should in turn take wives from the authority of Saint Nicholas; and if they failed to do so, all their inheritance and everything they possessed should return to the lordship of Saint Nicholas and the abbot.

At her request, Abbot Tegeno of the aforesaid monastery also permitted the same estate to him, after he had brought it under his own lordship. He immediately transferred to him the court of Caneda and a household paying five pounds there, which had been Ello’s benefice; six *arpents* at Clotten, which had been the benefice of Count Sico; and two small mansions that Wecelmus had possessed and in which he had lived.

She also transferred her castle of Chucomo to Henry, count palatine, the son of her paternal uncle, on the condition that, for as long as he lived, he should be defender and advocate over Clotten itself. After his death, if he had no heirs, the nearest heir of Queen Richeza should possess the advocacy over the same property; but if they too should lack heirs, the archbishop of Cologne should grant that advocacy to whomever the abbot and brothers requested.

To Count Sico, who had received that advocacy from the count palatine at the request of the aforesaid Queen Richeza, and to the advocates who would succeed him, she established the following service for only three periods of the year: at each court, one *modius* of wheat and one of rye and five solidi of light coin of current value should be given to the advocate; and as much should be given to one man as was appropriate for this service—five *modia* of oats, that is, ten *modia* of oats for two courts. At the Nativity of Saint John the Baptist, in the meadow called Summunt, fodder should be given to him in the grass, together with one *modius* of oats.

But if the steward should hold a court there concerning buildings or agriculture, the advocate should claim no portion or due from it; likewise from the court called Ludine.

She made this transfer, together with the coin and the market, through the hand of Henry, count palatine, under whose protection she then remained, in our presence and that of Hermann, the venerable and pious archbishop of the holy Church of Cologne, and many princes of the kingdom. Abbot Tegeno of the same monastery and the aforesaid Count Sico and advocate accepted it there, entreating our imperial clemency to confirm the same property to God and Saint Nicholas, and to grant the ships and goods of the abbot, the brothers, and the household of Clotten and Mesenich free passage and landing along the channels of the Rhine or Moselle, whenever necessity should require, without any levy of toll.

Granting their petition, we ordered this charter to be written, and, confirming it with our own hand as appears below, ordered it marked with the impression of our seal. If anyone should attempt to violate it, let him incur first the anger of God and Saint Peter, and likewise of all the saints.

Sign of the lord Henry III, most invincible king, second emperor Augustus of the Romans.

I, Winther the chancellor, have examined and approved this document as deputy of Bardo, the archchancellor.

Issued on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of August, in the fourth indiction, in the year of the Incarnation of the Lord 1051, and in the twenty-fourth year of the ordination of the lord Henry III, king and second emperor, the thirteenth of his reign and the fifth of his empire.

Done at Comphingin, prosperously. Amen.

The witnesses to this matter are Hermann, archbishop of Cologne; Henry, count palatine; Count Sico; Count Starchri; Gerard; Berenger; Gozwin; Rutger; Embrico; Eppo; Winbold; and Ansfrid.

## XXII. Diploma of Henry III for the monastery of Brunweiler. — Concerning confirmation of the monastery’s foundation by Hermann, archbishop of Cologne, and Richeza, queen of Poland, and concerning the right of the advocates. (Year 1051.)

[MARTENE, *Amplissima Collectio* I, 430.]

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity. Henry, by the favor of divine clemency, emperor Augustus of the Romans.

We wish it to be known to those present and to those to come that our dearest Hermann, the venerable and pious archbishop of the holy Church of Cologne, and his sister, the lady Richeza, formerly queen of Poland, came into our presence and claimed by law for themselves the abbey at the place called Brunweiler, first founded by their parents, namely the lord Ernfrid, count palatine, and his wife, the lady Mathilde; which, after their death, had devolved upon them by hereditary right. They likewise claimed by law the estate of Brunweiler itself with all its appurtenances, as it had been devoutly transferred by them to God and Saint Nicholas and first established by their pious administration.

A court having therefore been summoned before me and the legal questions examined, the sons, by a judgment of the princes and as justice dictated, obtained their parents’ inheritance. Immediately, admonished by fear and love of God, for themselves and for their parents, brothers, and sisters buried in the bosom of that same church, they transferred with equal devotion, for eternal remembrance, the said estate of Brunweiler with all its appurtenances and in its entirety—to wit, its fields, meadows, waters, pastures, and woods—to God, Saint Nicholas, and the brothers serving God there, to be possessed forever, in accordance with the determination and free transfer of their parents.

They also defined for the aforesaid monastery the boundary and ban of that estate, as their ancestors are known to have held it: from the road called Jacobs-wech to the road of Hespath, and again from the road of Hespath to the royal road, and from the royal road along the course of the stream called Visbach, as far as across the river called Arnese. They established that no one there should have any right or authority except the abbot of that place and whatever steward he should appoint.

For greater security, they transferred the same monastery and the said estate, without any exception, into the ownership of Saint Peter, supreme patron of the holy Church of Cologne, into the hands of Christian, the advocate of Cologne, by a ratified and perpetual donation, so that that place, free from the dominion of all present and future pontiffs, kings, and emperors, might serve more happily both our salvation and theirs.

But since it often happens that God’s servants are oppressed by the violence of wicked men and wearied by injuries or losses, they established, with prudent deliberation, that the archbishop of Cologne, with the counsel and consent of the abbot, should appoint the advocate of that church, provided that the abbot wished him to be suitable; and that no one called the second advocate should in any way be substituted after him.

They likewise arranged the service to be rendered to such an advocate as follows: during the three periods of the year in which the lawful courts are to be held, the advocate shall come to the place with twenty horses, and on the first night of his arrival and on the following day the abbot shall provide him with service sufficient for so many men. Then, in the morning of the third day, he shall receive only a meal and depart. The advocate himself shall also take care not to exact or demand anything excessive beyond the service established for him. If he brings more men with him, it shall be at the abbot’s discretion whether to give them anything or nothing.

The household of the same church shall likewise attend the advocate’s court three times a year and no more. Whenever the abbot or his steward wishes to hold a court at Brunweiler, or anywhere within the boundaries of the abbey, a court commonly called a *Buding*, this shall be entirely within his authority, and the advocate shall demand nothing at such a court or presume to claim anything for himself.

Therefore, so that the charter of this constitution, which at the request of the aforementioned archbishop of Cologne and his sister, Queen Richeza, was justly and reasonably established in the presence of us and the foremost men of the kingdom, may remain ratified and unshaken forever, we have confirmed it with our own hand, as appears below, and ordered it marked with the impression of our seal. If anyone should attempt to violate it, let him incur the anger of almighty God, Saint Peter, and all the saints; and, as the violator of our constitution, let him lose that advocacy and know that he must pay one hundred pounds of the purest gold, half to our treasury and the other half to the archbishop.

Sign, etc., as above.

## XXIII. Diploma of Henry III for Saint Maximin. — Against the advocates, whose rights and privileges he limits.

[MARTENE, *Amplissima Collectio* II, 432, from the manuscript of Saint Maximin.]

[Col. 1115C]

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity. Henry, by the favor of divine clemency, emperor Augustus of the Romans.

If we provide churches or monasteries dedicated to divine worship with the aid of some protection or defense against the insolence of wicked men, we undoubtedly believe that God will reward us. Therefore, let the discernment of all the faithful of the holy Church of God, both present and future, learn how, for the remedy of our soul and those of our ancestors, and also through the intervention of our most beloved wife, Augusta Agnes, the empress, and of our dearest son Henry IV [Note: [Col. 1115D] In the year 1054 Henry, son of the emperor Henry III, was anointed king of the Romans at Aachen, as Sigebert records in his *Chronicle*.], king, we kindly received the frequent and importunate complaint of Theoderic, abbot of the monastery of Saint Maximin, and carefully examined it in the presence of our faithful. The complaint concerned, in particular, the many oppressions that the household of Saint Maximin was suffering at the hands of counts and advocates, to such an extent that it appeared to have been deprived of its ancient laws and reduced to servitude, not as the household of a royal abbey but as the advocates’ own maidservant.

Therefore, on the advice of our friends, we decreed by command that, in the presence of our legates—namely Bertolt, [Col. 1116A] count of Strumburg, and Dragebodo, our minister, together with our other envoys—and in the presence of the present abbot Theoderic and Count Giselbert, then advocate, the chief and oldest men of the household of Saint Maximinus should be summoned and, bound by oath, should confirm under which laws that household had been subject in the times of Duke Henry the Elder and Duke Henry the Younger, and how pleas and judgments were to be conducted, so that they and their descendants might thereafter enjoy the same right and the same law.

Accordingly, men were chosen to establish this law and justice between the abbot and the advocate, according to the rights of their predecessors and ancestors; they confirmed it over the relics of the saints and thereafter, at Trier, in the presence of the bishops Eberard of Trier, Liutbald of Mainz, Adalbero [Col. 1116B] of Metz, and Bishop Theoderic of Verdun, and of our other princes, they reinforced it by oath at the petition of the aforesaid abbot.

It was therefore confirmed by their oath that the advocate of that household was not to hold a plea at the abbey more than three times a year. Whatever each defendant should have wagered or incurred in those pleas was to be assigned, according to his guilt and ability, at the discretion of the abbot and his provosts and stewards, with two parts going to the abbot and one part to the advocate. And if anyone should incur guilt of theft or sedition, and the abbot should summon the advocate on account of rebellious presumption, two parts of the same security or fine should go to the abbot and one part to the advocate—provided, however, that if the advocate had received the ban from the royal hand, he was not to presume to hold a plea in the abbey in any other manner. [Col. 1116C]

The servants who receive provisions and those who serve the brothers within the cloister, as well as those who serve outside at the estates and are called *dagescalci*, shall be subject neither to any advocate nor to any *hunnus* [Note: [Col. 1115D] The *hunnones* were a certain kind of magistrate.], but shall answer only to the abbot and his provosts for whatever offenses they commit.

The advocate who has received the ban from the royal hand shall hold a plea, on the day after the feast of Saint Maximinus, concerning the estates and dependants of those who are called *scaramanni* [Note: [Col. 1115D] The *scaramanni* were servants or ministers of the judges.], and only on that day. If it is not a fast, a solemn feast, or a Sunday, he shall hold the plea; but if it is a fast, he shall enter the plea at the first sounding of the bell and keep it until the ninth hour. After that he shall not be able to compel anyone to remain there any longer. Whatever he acquires there shall be divided into two parts for the abbot and one part for himself, and he shall presume to appoint no one after himself who is to be called a “sub-advocate.” [Col. 1116D]

On that same day the abbot shall provide the advocate with two measures of bread, four *frizkingas* [Note: [Col. 1116D] Some interpret *friskinga* or *friscinga* as a calf, others as a full-grown pig, others as a piglet or the young of a pig or sheep, and others as a ham; concerning the word, see Du Cange.], and one *ama* of wine.

If a man of the church is killed, and the abbot or his steward can exact the *wergeld* from the killer, the whole amount shall belong to him by right. But if it is necessary to summon the advocate, a discretionary third part shall go to him.

We entirely forbid, by imperial authority, both counts and advocates to hold pleas throughout the abbey, to demand lodging or services from the peasants, to burden them with requests, to take away their cattle or packhorses, or to extort revenues from them. And so that the authority of our command concerning all these matters may remain firm, we have confirmed it below with our own hand and ordered it to be marked with the impression of our seal.

The sign of Lord Henry, third Roman emperor Augustus.

I, Gebehard, [Note: [Col. 1117D] Namely, the bishop of Eichstätt, who was then the king’s chancellor and counsellor and who, after the death of Pope Leo IX, was appointed supreme pontiff as Victor II in the year 1055.] bishop and chancellor, acting in place of Wezel, archbishop and archchancellor, have verified this.

### XXIV. Diploma of Henry III as king and II as emperor, by which he exempts the clergy of Volterra from the jurisdiction of the counts and confirms to the Church of Volterra all its rights and privileges. (Year 1052.)

[MURATORI, *Antiquities of Italy*, III, 641.]

[Col. 1117B]

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity. Henry, by the ordering of divine piety, second Augustus of the Romans.

We believe that the care of our office has been divinely entrusted to us on the condition that, keeping the zeal of the fear of God always before our eyes in all affairs, we should so concern ourselves with the ordering of the earthly kingdom that we may come secure before the King of kings when we render our account. Therefore, although we ought to care for all our subjects, we must care especially for the churches, since, when their safety is preserved and the duty owed to divine worship is [Col. 1117C] rendered, the integrity of the Christian religion is preserved.

Accordingly, we wish it to be known to all the faithful of the holy Church of God and to our own faithful, present and future, how Wido, bishop of the holy Church of Volterra, approached our clemency, making a pitiful complaint against the count and the other officers of the public jurisdiction: under the pretext of exacting what was legally due, they harassed and gravely afflicted the clergy and servants of the Church, as well as others residing on Church land, and most disgracefully dishonored the dignity of the holy Church.

Therefore, listening to his pitiful complaint with the ear of our piety, we decreed the liberation of the Church, so that we would no longer permit the treachery of wicked men to tear it apart under any pretext. Accordingly, through the intervention of our beloved consort, the empress Agnes, and of our chancellor Opizo, we grant to the aforesaid bishop and his successors the clergy and servants, as well as others dwelling on the land of his Church, under his authority, so that he may hear cases before himself and settle a dispute by duel or by any lawful judgment, without opposition from anyone.

Moreover, everything that Adelmus, of blessed memory, together with his wife, transferred to the Church of Volterra by a deed of donation—namely, the castle of Pulliciano with the monastery of the Holy Sepulchre and its other appurtenances; the castle of Monteacutulo with its appurtenances; his share of Rocca de Cori with its appurtenances; the share which the aforesaid bishop acquired from the castle of Montegabro; whatever the aforesaid Church held in the castle of Casallia; the judgment which Ugo, son of Cunizo, rendered for the aforesaid Church; and everything else that the same Church, with God’s favor, should justly and legally acquire—we confirm and establish for that Church by the authority of our command, in such a way that no duke, margrave, count, or any person, great or small, may presume to dispossess or trouble the aforesaid Church, or the bishops appointed there in the course of time by God’s gift, with respect to any of the things written above.

If anyone should presume to violate this charter of our donation and confirmation, let him pay one hundred pounds of the finest gold, half to our treasury and half to the aforesaid Church and its rectors. And so that this may be believed more truly and observed more carefully by all, we have strengthened this charter with our own hand and ordered it to be marked with the impression of our seal.

The sign of Lord Henry, second Roman emperor Augustus.

Opizo, chancellor, acting in place of Herimann, archbishop and archchancellor.

Issued on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of July, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1052; in the year of Lord Henry III, king and second emperor, the twenty-fourth of his accession and the sixth of his empire.

Issued at Turengo, happily, in the name of God. Amen.

[Col. 1118C] The signs of the notaries who copied this from the original follow.

### XXV. Henry, third among kings and second among Augusti, confirms all the goods and rights of the Church of Vercelli and of its bishop Gregory by his charter. (Year 1054.)

[MURATORI, *Antiquities of Italy*, VI, 319.]

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity. Henry, by the favor of divine clemency, Roman emperor Augustus.

Since no one can be saved outside the Church, it follows that everyone who labors faithfully in God’s field must devote himself without interruption to the advancement of ecclesiastical affairs. For it is certain that, just as the mother of all living things is exalted, so the rewards of all who serve her increase. [Col. 1118D]

Therefore, let the charity of all the same faithful, present and future, know that we, devoting ourselves to the advancement of the churches and lending the ears of our piety to the requests of our most beloved wife, the empress, and of our dearest son, King Henry, confirm by the stable foundation of this present charter to the holy Church of Vercelli all the goods formerly bestowed upon Saint Eusebius by our predecessors, kings or emperors, or by any of the faithful, to be held quietly and enjoyed peacefully forever.

But so that the minds of the faithful may rejoice more fully and plunderers may guard themselves more carefully, we confirm to the Church of Eusebius the county of Vercelli and that of Saint Agatha, together with its jurisdiction, toll, and every public levy, exaction, or payment.

We further confirm Buriela in its entirety—that is, Vernade, Clavasa, Bedolium, Galienicum, Ponderianum, Muliaria, Andurnum, Cisidula, Coracodium, Monte, and Cerisdiana, with all their appurtenances—together with Sextegnum, Rovisinda, Monte Cutimali, Pedrorium, the estate of the city of Vercelli with everything belonging to it, Carcuella in Ondevico, the estate of Causana, the estate of Cavalli, the monastery of Saint Michael of Lucedio, Firminiana, and the royal estate called Hortus, with the whole forest of Mialda and Fulgitio and with all the estates and villages in the valley of [Col. 1119B] Elivi.

Also the bridge of Notingus, which Bishop Notingus of the Church of Vercelli lawfully acquired by riding over it in a remarkable manner; Languscum; the estate of Antimiano with all its appurtenances; the water of Sicida; the water of Servo; the water of Hellero with both banks, from the place where they rise to the Po; the water of the Po with both banks, from Liomia to the parish of Maroae; and the water of the Duria with both banks, from Petra Grossa to the Po; Consado, Matascum, Caudelle, Trevere, Clevoli, Sulzatum, Silva Salva, the castle of Quirinus, and the estate of Torcellus.

The Church of Vercelli shall possess all these in perpetuity, together with all public jurisdictions, entrance dues, tolls, [lacuna], common rights, hunting rights, ports, mills, mountains and valleys, Alps, buildings, dependants of both sexes, waters, vineyards, chapels, meadows, pastures, woods, waters and watercourses, cultivated and uncultivated lands.

Moreover, by a special edict we decree that, in all the lands named above, no mortal may presume to establish a market, or to exact jurisdictional dues, tolls, fodder, any public levy, or payment, or to exercise fishing or hunting, except for the benefit of, or by the proper right of, that Church itself.

Whoever, therefore, acts against this confirmation of ours shall be guilty against our majesty. Furthermore, let him know that he must pay one thousand pounds of gold, half to the imperial treasury and half to the Church to which he has caused harm.

And so that this may be held more firmly and observed more carefully by all, we have confirmed below with our hands this charter made by our command and ordered it to be marked beneath with the impression of our seal; and we have granted it to our most faithful Gregory, by God’s dispensation bishop and vicar of Saint Eusebius, so that he may preserve the perpetual peace of his Church.

The sign of Lord Henry III (+), most invincible king.

Gunther, chancellor, acting in place of Herimann, archchancellor, has verified this.

Given on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of December, in the seventh indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1054; in the year of Lord Henry III, king and second emperor, the twenty-sixth of his accession, the seventeenth of his reign, and the eighth of his empire.

[Col. 1120A] Issued at Mainz, happily, in the name of God. Amen.

### XXVI. Henry III, king and second emperor, confirms the rights and immunities of the *Arimanni* of Mantua. (Year 1055.)

[MURATORI, *Antiquities of Italy*, IV, 15.]

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity. Henry, by the favor of divine clemency, Roman emperor Augustus.

If we assent to the just and reasonable petitions of our faithful and, in accordance with the duty of imperial excellence, relieve their unjust necessities and violent oppressions, we hope that we shall happily obtain a fitting reward from God, the rewarder of all good things. Therefore, let the diligence of all the faithful of the holy Church of God and of our own people, future and present, know how the citizens of Mantua approached our clemency, complaining of their miseries and long-standing oppressions.

We, sympathizing with their great necessities, through the intervention of our most beloved wife, the empress Agnes, and for the advancement of our dearest son, namely King Henry IV, decree and confirm by our imperial authority that all superstitious exactions and unwarranted acts of violence are henceforth to be completely abolished and uprooted from among them.

We further decree that no person, great or small, may presume, without legal judgment, to disturb, trouble, or dispossess the aforesaid citizens—namely the *Arimanni* residing in the city of Mantua—with respect to their persons; their male and female servants; the free men residing on their land; the *Arimannia* and common property belonging to the aforesaid city and situated on both banks of the river Mincio; their benefices, hereditary leases, and precarious holdings; or any of their movable or immovable property, lawfully acquired or lawfully to be acquired.

We also command that all the aforesaid citizens may safely go to and return from every market, by land or by water, whenever they wish, in such a way that they need pay neither bank toll nor toll at Ravenna, Argenta, Ferrara, or the Upper Lake, and that they enjoy the good and just custom possessed by every city of our empire.

Whoever becomes a violator of this concession and confirmation of ours shall pay one hundred pounds of the finest gold, half to our imperial treasury and half to the aforesaid citizens.

And so that the authority of this confirmation of ours may remain stable and firm, we have strengthened this charter, written for that purpose, with our own hand, as appears below, and ordered it to be marked with the impression of our seal.

The sign of Lord Henry III, most invincible king and Augustus, Roman emperor.

Gunther, chancellor, acting in place of Herimann, archchancellor, has verified this.

Given on the third day before the Nones of November, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation [Col. 1121A] 1055; in the eighth indiction; in the year of Lord Henry III, king and second emperor, the twenty-seventh of his accession, the seventeenth of his reign, and the ninth of his empire.

Issued at Guastalla [reading: Guarstalla], happily, in the name of God. Amen.

### XXVII. King Henry III, second emperor, confirms all their goods to the canons of the Church of Cremona. (Year 1055.)

[MURATORI, *Antiquities of Italy*, II, 75.]

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity. Henry, by the favor of divine clemency, Roman emperor Augustus.

If we kindly and benevolently show the favor of our imperial munificence in their petitions to those who have been assigned to holy places and serve in divine offices, we hope to receive from God, the examiner of all things, a fitting and worthy recompense. Therefore, let the careful diligence of all the faithful of the holy Church of God and of our own people, future and present, know how, for the remedy of our soul, through the intervention of our most beloved wife, the empress Agnes, and also for the advancement of our dearest son, namely King Henry IV, we have provided for the needs of the canons of the holy Church of Cremona, built in honor of the most blessed Mother of God, Mary.

We confirm and strengthen by our imperial authority their lands, which the prelates of the aforesaid canonry had forcibly and unjustly taken from that Church—namely Butaningum, Castrumvetus, Insula, Raduldiscum, Casanova, Butalianum, Fontanella, the chapel of Saint Saviour with its appurtenances, as well as the other lands which the aforesaid canons now hold or may in future justly and lawfully hold, together with jurisdiction, pigs and rams, labor services, and all *scufiae*.

Moreover, we decree and command that no bishop, count, administrator, or dean may presume to take fodder or any payment from that canonry, or in any way to trouble or dispossess it without legal judgment.

If anyone should become a rash violator against the authority of this confirmation of ours, let him pay one hundred pounds of the finest gold, half to our imperial treasury [Col. 1121D] and half to the aforesaid canons.

And so that this may be believed more truly and observed more carefully by all, we have strengthened below with our own hand this charter written for that purpose and ordered it to be marked with the impression of our seal.

The sign of Lord Henry III, most invincible king and second Augustus, Roman emperor.

Gunther, chancellor, acting in place of Herimann, archchancellor, has verified this.

Given on the Ides of October, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1055, in the eighth indiction; in the year of Lord Henry III, king and second emperor, the twenty-seventh of his accession, the seventeenth of his reign, and the ninth of his empire.

Issued at Mantua, happily, in the name of God. Amen.

### XXVIII. Privilege granted to the people of Ferrara by Henry III, king of Germany and Italy and second emperor. (Year 1055.)

[MURATORI, *Antiquities of Italy*, V, 753.]

[Col. 1122A]

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity. Henry, by the favor of divine clemency, Roman emperor Augustus.

Let all the faithful of the holy Church of God and of our own people, future and present, know how, for the remedy of our soul, through the intervention of our wife, the empress Agnes, and through the intervention of our dearest son, King Henry IV, we permit all the estate-holders of Ferrara, who have petitioned us on account of their faithful and devoted service, to be secure from the payment at the court-assembly called the Thirds.

We also grant that the peasants within the whole city of Ferrara, or wherever they dwell on their land, need not come to the public court-assembly, but that their lords may answer for them. They shall not be compelled to provide their ships and horses for the service of the *P.*, except when we come into the kingdom of Italy or our envoy comes.

Moreover, if anyone is summoned to the court-assembly and voluntarily confesses his debt, he shall be released from the penalty of the Thirds. Likewise, we release widows from the Thirds at the court-assembly.

Their ban shall be one hundred and eight denarii according to the ancient custom. They shall pay no bank toll except at Pavia, where they shall pay twelve denarii of the same coin.

At Cremona, if any merchant should remain and conduct a salt transaction elsewhere, he shall pay two *oralia*. For fish, he shall pay two Milanese denarii for each *vegeta*; at Ravenna, two Venetian coins; and at Venice, twelve of the same coin. Apart from these places named above, they may safely frequent every Italian market without any exaction.

Also, as the law commands, a respite shall be granted to them at the court-assembly, except when we or our envoy come into the kingdom of Italy.

They shall observe the general court-assembly twice a year, providing in the following manner: for three days, each day three pigs and one hundred loaves, one pound of pepper, another of cinnamon, and three *sextarii* of honey; and on those three days only one *vegeta* of wine. On the fourth day they shall provide the person holding the court-assembly with one boar and fifty loaves.

They shall pay the fodder-tax in full to us or to our envoy when he comes to Italy. All these matters, which have been prescribed and also granted, we establish and confirm for future times with this exception: unless we or our envoy are staying in the kingdom of Italy.

If anyone should become a violator of this concession and confirmation of ours, let him pay one hundred pounds of the finest gold, half to our treasury and half to the aforesaid people of Ferrara.

And so that the authority of this confirmation of ours may remain stable and firm, we have strengthened this charter, written for that purpose, with our own hand, as appears below, and ordered it to be marked with the impression of our seal.

[Col. 1123A] The sign of Lord Henry III, most invincible king and second Roman emperor.

Gunter, chancellor, acting in place of Herimann, archchancellor, has verified this.

Given on the eighth day before the Kalends of September, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1055, in the eighth indiction; in the year of Lord Henry III, king and second emperor, the twenty-seventh of his accession, the seventeenth of his reign, and the ninth of his empire.

Issued at the Bridge, happily, in the name of God. Amen.

### XXIX. Charter of Lord Henry III, emperor Augustus, for the monastery of Prüm.—He confirms its privileges and possessions. (Year 1056.)

[MARTEN, *Amplissima Collectio*, III, 443, from the Prüm cartulary.]

[Col. 1123B]

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity. Henry, by the favor of divine clemency, king.

If we apply care and diligence to places devoted to divine worship, and not only strengthen but also strive to increase the institutions of our parents and predecessors, we truly trust that this will profit us as a recompense in the reward of eternal life.

Therefore, we wish it to be known to all the faithful of the holy Church of God and to our own people, present and future, that the illustrious and venerable Robert, abbot of the monastery of Prüm—which King Pippin of blessed memory once built from its foundations, with the suggestion and consent of his wife, Bertrada Augusta, in honor of our Lord Jesus Christ and his most holy Mother Mary, as property under his own right—together with the community of monks living under him according to the rule, approached the clemency of our serenity.

He petitioned that we should deign to renew and again confirm by royal authority the records and authorities of the Augusti, beginning with Pippin and continuing thereafter, by which they had strengthened through their charters and edicts the condition and status of the aforesaid monastery.

We gladly assented to his petitions, and, recognizing the steadfastness of their provost in unwearied divine vigils, decreed that this should be done. We ordered this present charter of our protection to be written, by which all the faithful of God and of ourselves, future and present, may know that whatever all our most serene predecessors, the Augusti, have usefully and completely decreed concerning the status of the aforesaid place and everything belonging to it, we decree shall remain in every respect unshaken and stable through all successions, for the remedy of our father, Henry II, Roman emperor Augustus, and also through the intervention of our most beloved mother, namely the empress Agnes Augusta.

Therefore, according to the charter and edict of the aforesaid illustrious King Pippin and by the authority of all his imperial successors, let the monks of the aforesaid monastery have the privilege of choosing an abbot for themselves, according to customary practice, from within that community, and of accepting no rector from elsewhere by force or by the power of any person. In that election, however, let the integrity and humble recommendation of the wiser elders of the community prevail, with our consent and counsel.

Moreover, we wish and decree that the properties, estates, cells, and possessions—wherever they may be situated in the provinces and however much they ought to serve the aforesaid place—shall always remain, under the protection and *mundiburdium* of our defense, exempt and untouched by every exaction and investigation.

No count, judicial authority, or any of those who administer public affairs shall have the right in them to hold an audience or court, to exact fines, *parafreda*, contributions, transport services, or any kind of ban or military ban, either from the servants and tenants who live scattered throughout those territories or from free men and those holding benefices there, because this is what Charles, the son of Pippin, the greatest emperor, decreed concerning them, as did all the kings and Augusti after him down to the present time.

The abbot shall also have permission to appoint his advocates, without the presence of the king, in whatever count’s court he wishes.

Whatever right of the fiscus could be exacted from the aforesaid properties for royal purposes and for the use of the king’s officials shall be assigned to the lighting of the same church and to the relief of the needy, as has been granted by them and as we grant it forever.

Concerning all tolls and exactions as well, in the manner evidently established by the aforesaid kings, we decree by command that no one may presume to exact anything from their servants and envoys who travel through different places for various causes and necessities. Nor shall any freight charge or toll be demanded from anyone belonging to the entire household of Saint Saviour in any market of our kingdom or at any seaport. Let them always and everywhere be exempt and secure from such exactors and exactions, wherever they may be able to reach within the territories under our authority.

We have also decided to insert this provision: if anything is found to be lacking among the imperial edicts, royal charters, or written documents by which properties or estates were lawfully granted to the aforesaid place and to the sons of noblemen, and if it is proved that these documents were lost through burning in a fire caused by the incursion of pagans, through some negligence, or through excessive age, let no one thereafter presume to bring any claim or pretext against that place and its privileges on account of such a matter.

Whatever was lawfully granted to that place by anyone and which it has until now possessed without a claim shall continue to be possessed forever without anyone’s opposition. If any of it has been removed or taken away through the wickedness of wicked men, the place shall have free power to reclaim it.

Among these liberal grants made by our predecessors, the kings, to that place, this too is found to have been conceded: if its rectors should judge it useful, they may establish a market in whatever place under their authority they wish, and, by royal authority, they may have permission to strike their own coin, that is, to establish a mint there.

We also gladly assent to this, if the abbot should deem it necessary, and strengthen it by our authority. Let that most illustrious place remain under the protection and immunity of our defense, just as it is proved to have been under the protection of all the kings who preceded us.

And because the heavenly King does not disdain to be the special possessor of that place—since the whole world and its fullness belong to him—the earthly king, insofar as he is able, should strive to be his tireless defender in his stead, so that the soldiers of Christ dwelling there may strive eagerly, day and night, to offer continual prayers and due praises to God for us, for everything belonging to us, for the condition of our kingdom, and for the whole Church spread throughout the world.

And so that this institution of our generosity may possess firmer stability in every future age, in the name of God, we have confirmed it below with our own hand and ordered it to be marked with the impression of our seal.

The sign of Lord Henry IV, king.

Winiter, chancellor, acting in place of Liutbold, archbishop and archchancellor, has verified this.

Given on the Nones of December, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1056, in the ninth indiction; in the year of Lord Henry IV, king, the third of his accession and the first of his reign.

Issued at Cologne, happily, in the name of God. Amen.

## Henry IV, emperor, fourth of this name among kings and third among Augusti (years 1056–1106)

[Col. 1125]

## Constitutions of Emperor Henry IV

(PERTZ, *Monumenta Germaniae Historica*, Laws, vol. II, p. 49.)

### I. The Assembly of Oppenheim [Note: [Col. 1125D] The king’s promise to render obedience to the pope and the edict revoking the sentence against Gregory VII seem to belong to the Assembly of Oppenheim. They are preserved: (1) in the epistolary codex of Ulrich of Babenberg, nos. 145 and 155; and (2) in the royal codex of Hanover, fols. 53 and 54. The edict is also inserted in the Collection of Tegnagel, p. 342.] (October 1076)

[Col. 1125C]

#### Promise of King Henry, made to Pope Hildebrand, who is also Gregory

Admonished by the counsel of our faithful, I promise to preserve in all things the obedience owed to the apostolic see and to you, Pope Gregory [Note: [Col. 1125] *p. s. o.* 2.], and I shall strive, with devoted satisfaction, to correct whatever appears to have arisen through us to the diminution of the honor of that see or of your own.

But since certain more serious charges are being spread about concerning us—things which I am said to have decreed against that same see and against your reverence—I shall, at the proper time, clear myself of them either by the support of innocence or, with God’s help, by appropriate means; or, finally, I shall willingly embrace suitable penance for them. It is fitting also that your holiness should not conceal those things circulated about you which produce scandal in the Church, but, once this matter and this scruple have been removed from the public conscience, establish through your wisdom universal tranquility both for the Church and for the kingdom.

#### General Edict

Henry, by the grace of God king, offers to archbishops, bishops, margraves, [Col. 1126B] counts, and persons of every rank and dignity the glorious favor of his good will. Since we have recognized, at the suggestion of certain of our faithful, that something had been secretly imposed upon our mildness against the apostolic see and its venerable prelate, Lord Gregory the pope, it has pleased us, on the advice of a salutary counsel, to change our former sentence and, following the custom of our ancestors and forebears, to preserve in all things the obedience owed to that most holy see and to its acknowledged head, Lord Gregory the pope, and, if anything harsher has been presumed against him, to make suitable satisfaction for it.

We wish you also, admonished by the example of our serenity, not to hesitate to offer solemn satisfaction to blessed Peter and his vicar [Note: [Col. 1125] *recusetis* (“you refuse”) in witness 2.], and to strive to be solemnly absolved by Lord Pope Gregory himself, whoever understands himself to be bound by his ban.

### II. The Assembly of Tricina [Note: [Col. 1125D] These acts, discovered by Irenaeus Affò on a membrane of the eleventh century in the archive of the cathedral church of Parma, were published by Canciani, vol. V, pp. 45–46. We present them here with a better arrangement. Since their date is uncertain, we have judged that they should chiefly be assigned to Henry’s Italian expedition of 1081, when, intending to march against Rome, he discussed their affairs with the bishops and the other leading men of Lombardy (Norbert, *Life of Benno*, ch. 22).]

In the council of Emperor Henry III.

Since we recognize that the holy Church of God, with God’s help, has escaped the persecutions of the pagans, it is exceedingly lamentable that she is weakened by the attacks of those who are counted as Christians. We plainly see that the resources of the churches, amassed most richly through the work of our predecessors and preserved with the greatest care by their diligence, have now been diminished and entirely dissipated through the fraud and cunning of our wicked men.

For the devastation of the churches they use leases written contrary to law, precarious grants, and exchanges made to the detriment of ecclesiastical property. To put an end to their insolent assault, the holy synod at which King Henry III was present decreed [Note: [Col. 1127] I have punctuated thus; Canciani reads: “Henry, concerning … to be made. It was ordered … we forbid concerning heresy,” etc.]: 

Concerning the property of churches, leases are to be made not at all; this was ordered in ancient times, and we forbid the same under anathema.

Concerning the Simoniac heresy—which, since it has increased, is absurd [Note: [Col. 1127] I have supplied this thus; Canciani has “dec [lacuna].”]—the holy synod decreed that no one may sell a bishopric, the consecration of churches, any clerical office or order, a diaconate, or [Note: [Col. 1127] *d. a.*: I have thus filled out the lacuna in Canciani.] a presbyterate, recommendations for altars, transfers of churches, abbacies, or provostships. Whoever has purchased or sold any of these things shall be anathema. Let it be done.

Concerning the command and firm loyalty of King Henry against the plunderers and raiders of his kingdom.

From this hour onward I shall aid King Heinricus, who now reigns in Italy, and his messengers, and the counts whom he shall himself appoint to administer justice and law, rendering service according to a rightful judgment, and also concerning other matters which the law forbids one to do; but concerning benefices, according to the rightful judgment of one’s peers. [Col. 1127C] I shall not knowingly or willingly commit theft, *schacum* [meaning uncertain], robbery, or plunder exceeding six solidi in a year. I shall not set fire to anything, nor make a sudden assault upon castles or houses. If it should happen that I do so, I shall, if I can, make restitution for it within one month; but if I cannot make that restitution, I shall restore according to its value, if the person who suffered the damage is willing to accept it. If through my fault it remains uncorrected for one month, I shall make amends according to what the law prescribes, if I am legally summoned.

I shall aid King Heinricus, or his appointed messenger, or the bishop or count who has summoned me for this purpose, in good faith, to devastate those people who refuse to make this oath or violate what has been sworn [Note: [Col. 1127] The Canc. reading has *violaverit*.], according to the king’s command [Col. 1127D] or that of his appointed messenger. Concerning myself, I shall render justice to everyone according to a rightful judgment in matters belonging to the law; but concerning benefices, according to the rightful judgment of my peers, if I have been admonished by law. [Col. 1128A] I shall observe all these provisions for ten years, except if, by the king’s command, I go on campaign or to war, whether against his enemy or against one who refuses to swear this oath or violates what has been sworn, while preserving loyalty to and the command of King Heinricus.

## III. THE COUNCIL OF MAINZ

*(Year 1084, November 29.)*

### The emperor’s letter inviting the princes to the council

Heinricus, by the grace of God august emperor of the Romans, sends grace and every good thing to R. [Note: [Col. 1127] That is, Robert.] bishop of the church of Babenberg.

You know how greatly the whole Church is shaken by danger, how great an error is arising throughout Saxony, and by what great desolation that noble church of Metz is being utterly destroyed; and not only there, but in various regions the Church of our empire is being divided. Therefore, with the counsel of our faithful men, we have decided that a conference should be held at Mainz on the Sunday before the coming feast of Saint Andrew. Let all the princes of our kingdom, our faithful men, attend this conference, [Note: [Col. 1127] *intersunt* in the Codex Vindobonensis and in Goldastus.] and, in addition, all those whose loyalty or prudent counsel is shown to be useful to us.

We earnestly ask you to come to it, since matters of such gravity concerning the kingdom, and the division of the Church, cannot possibly be brought together without your greatest wisdom, excellent counsel, and loyalty—which until now has often been available to us in necessities and in controversies of this kind concerning the kingdom, as we desired and circumstances required. All our faithful Saxons will come to this conference, earnestly asking us to go to Saxony and settle these new errors. The men of Metz, on the other hand, loudly call for us to cross over to Metz, so that at last peace and security may be restored there to the Church.

We too, at the invitation of the archbishop, shall celebrate the Nativity of the Lord at Cologne. For this reason we have decided that this conference should be held beforehand, so that we may first settle such dissensions in the kingdom before moving into more distant regions. We have therefore postponed the aforementioned expedition so that, with the common counsel of all our men, what we ought to do may be considered.

Therefore we ask you, by that love through which you have become our spiritual co-father, not to allow bodily illness or [Col. 1128D] any other matter to prevent you from coming to the aforesaid conference at the appointed time, and there, in accordance with your great wisdom and customary loyalty, to determine with us what is necessary for our welfare and that of the kingdom.

## IV. THE SYNOD OF MAINZ

[Note: [Col. 1129C] Emperor Heinricus III, according to the Annals of Saint Gall and of Babenberg, Hermannus Contractus, and Lambert of Aschaffenburg, at the council held at Constance in the year 1043 confirmed by an edict of royal authority a peace hitherto unheard of, both throughout all Swabia and in the other provinces of his kingdom. Since its wording is now largely unknown, we should be all the more grateful for the constitution of Heinricus IV concerning the same matter, promulgated, according to the Babenberg annalist, at the Synod of Mainz in the first months of the year 1085. In 1833 we found it in a Babenberg royal-library codex containing Saint Ambrose’s books *On the Duties of Ministers*, written in the twelfth century; alongside it we placed anew the constitution according to whose model it was exacted, namely that of the Synod of Cologne held under Archbishop Sigewin, copied again from a twelfth-century codex formerly belonging to Abdinghof and now belonging to the most distinguished D. Meyer, canon of Paderborn. During the preceding summer at Leiden we transcribed from a codex formerly belonging to Werden, of the eleventh century, the formula of the oath, which is missing from the Babenberg codex and which is also found copied again there in the thirteenth century.]

*(Year 1085, spring.)*

[Col. 1129]

### Constitution of the Peace of God promulgated at the Synod of Cologne, April 20, 1083

[Note: [Col. 1129A] The following divisions are printed in parallel in Migne.]

SIGEWINUS, bishop in name only of the holy church of Cologne, offers to FRITHERicus, his brother and fellow bishop, [Note: [Col. 1130C] Bishop of Münster, who died in 1084. Schaten I, 612.] the voluntary presentation of his most devoted prayer and service.

Since in our times the holy Church was afflicted in its members beyond measure by tribulations and various distresses, so that tranquility and peace were altogether despaired of, we resolved, moved by compassion for so many pressures and dangers, with God’s favor, to come to its aid. At last we provided this remedy for it, on the advice of our faithful men: that, since because of our sins we had been unable to maintain peace continuously, we should at least recover it to some extent on the days that fell within our jurisdiction.

We did this, and we made progress. Therefore, having summoned our parishioners to a legitimately appointed council, which was held at Cologne in the mother church of Saint Peter in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1083, in the sixth indiction, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of May, we had the measures we intended to take concerning these matters publicly read out. After everyone had discussed and reconsidered them for some time in different ways, through God’s mediation they were finally brought into one agreement; and, with clergy and people consenting by equal vote, we explained how and during what intervals of the year they should be observed.

Namely, this decree of peace shall be upheld from the first day of Advent until the end of Epiphany; from the beginning of Septuagesima until the octave of Pentecost, including that entire day; throughout the year on every Sunday and Friday, and on Saturday with the addition of the Ember Day; on the vigil of every apostle together with the following day; and, without distinction, on every day appointed or to be appointed canonically for fasting or abstinence.

Thus the safest security and tranquility may be provided both for travelers and for those remaining at home: no one shall commit killings, arson, plunder, or assaults; no one shall injure anyone with a staff, sword, or any kind of weapon; and no one guilty of any offense (*faicosus*) shall dare, from Advent until the octave of Epiphany and from Septuagesima until the octave of Pentecost, to take up weapons, a shield, a sword, a lance, or any burden of armor whatsoever. [Col. 1131A]

On the remaining days—namely Sundays and Fridays, the vigil of every apostle together with the following day, and every day appointed or to be appointed for fasting or abstinence—they may carry weapons, but on the condition that they inflict injury on no one in any way.

If it should be necessary for anyone, during the period covered by the peace—that is, from Advent until the octave of Epiphany and from Septuagesima until the octave of Pentecost—to leave our bishopric for another in which this peace is not observed, he may carry weapons, but only in such a way that he harms no one, unless he is attacked and must defend himself. Once he has returned to our bishopric, he shall immediately lay down his weapons.

If it happens that a castle must be besieged, during the days included within the peace they shall refrain from attacking it, unless they are attacked by the besieged [Col. 1131B] and compelled to resist.

And lest this established peace be rashly and with impunity violated by anyone, a common sentence has been prescribed by all for violators of this kind. If a free man or noble violates it—that is, commits homicide, wounds someone, or commits any other offense—he shall be expelled from the borders of his lands without any intervention of expense or friends; his heirs shall take possession of his entire estate, and, if he held a benefice, its lord shall receive it.

But if his heirs are found and convicted of having provided him, after his expulsion, with any support or assistance, their estate shall be taken from them and subjected to royal authority. If he wishes to purge himself of the charges brought against him, he shall swear with twelve men who are equally noble or equally free. [Col. 1131C]

If a slave kills a man, he shall be beheaded. If he wounds him, he shall be punished by the loss of his hand. If he commits an offense in another way, by striking with a fist, staff, or stone, he shall be tonsured and flayed. But if the person accused wishes to prove himself innocent, he shall clear himself by the judgment of cold water, with the condition that he himself, and no other on his behalf, be put into the water.

If, fearing the vengeance prescribed against him, he flees, he shall be subject to perpetual excommunication. Wherever he is heard of, letters shall be sent there announcing to everyone that he is excommunicated and that no one is permitted to communicate with him.

Hands must not be amputated from boys who have not yet completed twelve years of age, but from those who have reached the age—that is, from twelve years onward. [Col. 1131D] Nevertheless, if boys fight, they shall be punished with blows and deterred from fighting.

Peace is not violated if someone orders his delinquent slave, pupil, or anyone in any way subject to him to be beaten with scourges or staffs.

The following is also excepted from this constitution of peace: if the lord king publicly orders an expedition to be undertaken against the enemies of the kingdom, or wishes to hold a council in order to judge adversaries of justice.

Peace is not violated if meanwhile a duke, other counts, advocates, or those acting in their place hold judicial assemblies and exercise judgment against thieves, plunderers, and other offenders according to what the law provides. [Col. 1133A]

For the sake of security, this established peace is provided especially for all offenders (*faicosi*), but not so that, once the period of peace is over, they may dare to rob and plunder through villages and houses. The law and sentence pronounced against them before this peace was established shall be rigorously maintained, so that they may be restrained from wrongdoing; for plunderers and brigands are excluded from this divine peace and from every peace altogether.

If anyone attempts to oppose this pious institution, so that he neither wishes to promise peace to God with others nor to observe it, no priest in our bishopric shall dare to celebrate Mass for him or provide him with any care for salvation. If he falls ill, no Christian shall dare to visit him, and, unless he repents, he shall lack even the viaticum at the end.

The substance of the peace promised to God and praised by all in common shall be this: it shall be observed not only in our times but perpetually among our descendants. For whoever dares to invalidate, destroy, or violate it, whether now or one who shall be born many years hence near the end of the world, is irrevocably excommunicated by us. [Col. 1133B]

It shall not depend more upon the power and judgment of counts, tribunes, or powerful men than upon that of the whole people in common to inflict upon violators the punishments prescribed above. They must take the greatest care not to exercise friendship, hatred, or anything else contrary to justice in punishing people; nor, if they can be concealed, should they conceal the crimes of some, but rather bring them into public view.

Let no one accept money for redeeming those found guilty, nor attempt to help the guilty through any favor, because anyone who does so incurs an intolerable judgment upon his soul. All the faithful must remember that this peace was promised not to man but to God alone, and that it must therefore be observed with all the greater tenacity and firmness.

For this reason we beseech everyone in Christ that this necessary regulation of peace be inviolably guarded, so that if anyone henceforth dares to violate it, he may be entirely separated from the sons of the holy Church and condemned by the ban of irrevocable excommunication and by an anathema of enduring perdition.

In churches and in the cemeteries of churches, honor and reverence shall be shown to God. If a robber or thief takes refuge there, he shall not be killed or captured, but shall be besieged there until, compelled by hunger, he is forced to surrender.

If anyone dares to contrive for the accused weapons, food, or escape, he shall suffer the same penalty as the accused. Clerics and all who live under this order are forbidden by our ban to be punished by lay vengeance; if they are caught in an evident crime, they shall be presented to their bishop.

Where laymen are beheaded, clerics shall be degraded; where laymen are mutilated, clerics shall be suspended from their offices; and, with the consent of the laymen, they shall be afflicted by frequent fasts and beatings until satisfaction has been made.

### Constitution of the Peace of God of Emperor Heinricus IV, promulgated at the Synod of Mainz in 1085

[Col. 1130A]

Since in our times the holy Church was afflicted beyond measure by tribulations, moved by compassion for so many pressures and dangers, with God’s favor we resolved to come to its aid, so that the peace which, because of our sins, we had been unable to maintain continuously, might at least be strengthened for certain intervals.

In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1085, in the eighth indiction, through God’s mediation, with clergy and people consenting by equal vote, it was decreed that this peace should be upheld from the first day of Advent until the end of Epiphany; from the beginning of Septuagesima until the octave of Pentecost, including that entire day; and every Thursday, Friday, Saturday, and Sunday until sunrise on Monday, with the addition of the Ember Wednesday [Note: [Col. 1129] “Wednesday”; the codex has *quatuor* (“four”).]; on the vigil of every apostle together with the following day; and, in addition, on every day canonically appointed or to be appointed for fasting or abstinence.

Thus the safest security may be provided for travelers and those remaining at home: no one shall commit killings, arson, plunder, or assaults; no one shall injure anyone with a staff, sword, or any kind of weapon; and no offender, whatever his offense, shall dare from Advent until the octave of Epiphany, and from Septuagesima until the octave of Pentecost, to take up weapons, a shield, sword, lance, or any burden of armor whatsoever.

Similarly, on the remaining days—that is, Sundays, Thursdays, Fridays, Saturdays, the vigil of every apostle with the following day, and every day canonically appointed or to be appointed for fasting or abstinence—it is not permitted to carry weapons except to those traveling a long distance, and even then on the condition that they injure no one in any way.

If it should be necessary for anyone, during the period of the established peace, to go to another place where this peace is not observed, he may carry weapons, but only in such a way that he harms no one, unless he is attacked and must defend himself. Once he has returned, he shall again lay down his weapons.

If it happens that a castle is besieged, during the days included within the peace they shall refrain from attacking it, unless they are attacked by the besieged [Note: [Col. 1129] *impugnetur* in the codex.] and compelled to resist.

And lest this established peace be violated with impunity by anyone, a sentence has been pronounced by all. If [Col. 1132A] a free man or noble violates it—that is, if he commits homicide, wounds someone, or commits any other offense—he shall be expelled from the borders of his lands without [Note: [Col. 1131] *abseque* in c.] any intervention of expense or friends; his heirs shall take possession of his entire estate, and, if he held a benefice, its lord shall receive it.

But if his heirs are found and convicted of having provided him, after his expulsion, with any support or sustenance, their estate shall be taken from them and subjected to royal authority. If he wishes to purge himself of the charges brought against him, he shall swear with twelve men who are equally noble and free [Note: [Col. 1131] *jurent* in c.]

If a slave kills a man, he shall be beheaded; if he wounds him, his right hand shall be cut off; if he commits an offense in another way, by striking with a fist, stone, staff, or anything else, [Col. 1132B] he shall be beaten and have his hair cut off.

But if the person accused wishes to prove himself innocent, he shall clear himself by the judgment of cold water, with the condition that he himself, and no other on his behalf, be put into the water.

If, fearing the judgment prescribed against him, he flees, he shall be subject to perpetual excommunication. Wherever he is heard of, letters shall be sent there announcing that he is excommunicated and that no one is permitted to communicate with him.

Hands must not be amputated from boys who have not yet completed twelve years of age; if some have transgressed this rule, boys shall be punished only with blows.

Peace is not violated if someone orders his delinquent slave, pupil, or anyone in any way subject to him to be beaten with scourges or staffs.

The following is also excepted from this constitution of peace: if the lord emperor publicly orders an expedition to be undertaken against the enemies of the kingdom, or wishes to hold a council in order to judge adversaries of justice.

Peace is not violated if meanwhile a duke, other counts, advocates, or those acting in their place hold judicial assemblies and exercise judgment against thieves, plunderers, and other offenders according to what the law provides.

For the sake of security, this established peace is provided especially for all offenders (*faicosi*), but not so that, once the period of peace is over, they may dare to rob and plunder through villages and houses. The law and sentence pronounced against them before this peace was established shall be most diligently maintained, so that they may be restrained from wrongdoing, since plunderers and brigands are excluded from this divine peace [Col. 1132D] and from every peace altogether.

If anyone attempts to oppose this pious constitution, so that he neither wishes to promise peace to God nor to observe it, no priest shall dare to celebrate Mass for him or provide any care for his salvation. If he falls ill, no Christian shall dare to visit him, and, unless he repents, he shall lack even the viaticum at the end.

But if anyone should presume to violate it, whether in the present time or perpetually among our descendants, he is irrevocably excommunicated by us.

We have decreed that it shall depend no more upon the power of counts, tribunes, or powerful men than upon that of the whole people in common [Col. 1134A] to inflict the punishments mentioned above upon violators of the holy peace. They must take the greatest care not to exercise friendship, hatred, or anything else contrary to justice in punishing people; they must not conceal anyone’s crimes, but rather bring them into public view.

Let no one accept money for redeeming those who have been found guilty.

Merchants on the roads where they conduct their business, and peasants while engaged in agricultural work—plowing, digging, reaping, and similar tasks—shall have peace every day.

Women and all those enrolled in sacred orders shall enjoy perpetual peace. In churches and in the cemeteries of churches, honor and reverence shall be shown to God. If a robber or thief takes refuge there, he shall not be captured, but shall be besieged there until, compelled by hunger, he is forced to surrender.

If anyone dares to contrive for the accused defense, weapons, food, or escape, he shall be subject to the same penalty as the accused.

We also forbid by our ban that anyone convicted as a transgressor of this holy peace from the sacred order be punished by lay vengeance; he shall be presented to his bishop.

Where laymen are beheaded, clerics shall be degraded; where laymen are mutilated, clerics shall be suspended from their offices; and, with the consent of the laymen, they shall be afflicted by frequent fasts and beatings until satisfaction has been made. Amen.

## Oath of the Peace of God

[Col. 1133B]

[Col. 1133C] From Advent until the Monday following Epiphany, and likewise from Septuagesima until the octave of Pentecost, and likewise on all vigils and ferial feasts, and for three days in every week—that is, from Vespers on Thursday until dawn on Monday—let there be peace everywhere, so that no one injures his enemy.

Whoever kills shall suffer a capital sentence. Whoever wounds shall lose his hand. Whoever strikes with his fist, if he is noble, shall pay one pound as composition; if free or ministerial, ten solidi; if a slave, his skin and hair.

Every house and every courtyard shall have firm peace within its enclosures. No one shall invade, break into, or dare rashly to search out or violently oppress anyone within them. Whoever dares to do so, whatever his condition, shall be punished by death. [Col. 1135A]

If someone fleeing an enemy, whether his own or anyone else’s, enters an enclosure, he shall be safe there. Whoever throws a spear or any kind of weapon over the hedge after him shall lose his hand.

If violation of this peace is charged against anyone and he denies it, then, if he is freeborn or free, he shall clear himself with twelve reputable men. If he is a slave—whether a *litus* or a ministerial—he shall clear himself by the judgment of cold water, specifically by being put into the water himself.

If theft or robbery occurs, or war threatens the homeland and a customary public alarm is raised, all armed men shall pursue the culprit, and each person shall have peace both while going and while returning.

Whoever withdraws without unavoidable necessity shall pay, if he is one of the princes of the land, ten pounds; if noble, five; if free or [Col. 1135B] ministerial, two; if a *litus* or slave, five solidi—or he shall lose his skin and hair.

Whoever knowingly receives an excommunicated person or one condemned for any crimes, and defends him against either divine or human laws, shall incur the sentence of the condemned person.

No one shall deny hospitality to a traveler. If he has necessary supplies, let him sell them at a fair price; if he does not have them, let him acquire them from neighbors who have them, by the same agreement.

If someone denies hospitality and neglects either to sell or acquire necessary supplies, the traveler shall appeal to the master of the village. After summoning his fellow citizens, the master shall immediately have the person who denied the request tonsured and flayed.
