If the traveler proves troublesome and uses violence in the lodging, the host shall summon his neighbors and report the injury; with their advice he shall demand and receive satisfaction. If the traveler does not submit to them, let him be condemned as a robber.

If a traveler is in need, he may take two sheaves from a field, or, if necessary, three, and feed his horses with them in that field or in the nearest village. No one shall forbid the pasture of meadows or the gathering of fruit.

No one shall protect a fugitive slave. Whoever protects him shall suffer the penalty of the fugitive.

Whoever directs insults against another shall be punished with staffs if he is a soldier, and flayed with scourges if he is a peasant.

This is the end of the oath. The provisions that follow were praised by everyone’s mouth, promised into the hands of the bishops, and strengthened by the ban. Throughout the entire period of peace specified above, no one shall carry weapons except those which the necessity described above requires.

## + Oath of the Peace of God

[Col. 1134B]

[Col. 1134C] From Advent until the Monday following Epiphany, likewise from Septuagesima until the octave of Pentecost, and likewise on all vigils and ferial feasts and for three days in every week—that is, from Vespers on Thursday until dawn on Monday—let there be peace everywhere, so that no one injures his enemy.

Whoever kills shall suffer a capital sentence. Whoever wounds shall lose his hand. Whoever strikes with his fist, if he is noble, shall pay one pound as composition; if free or ministerial, ten solidi; if a slave, his skin and hair.

Every house and every courtyard shall have firm peace within its enclosures. No one shall invade, break into, or dare rashly to search out or violently oppress anyone within them. Whoever dares to do so, whatever his condition, shall be punished by death.

If someone fleeing an enemy, whether his own or anyone else’s, enters an enclosure, he shall be safe there. Whoever throws a spear or any kind of weapon over the hedge after him shall lose his hand.

If violation of this peace is charged against anyone and he denies it, then, if he is freeborn or free, he shall clear himself with twelve reputable men; if he is a slave, whether a *litus* or a ministerial, he shall clear himself by the judgment of cold water, specifically by being put into the water himself at once.

If theft or robbery occurs, or war threatens the homeland and a customary public alarm is raised, all armed men shall pursue the culprit, and each person shall have peace both while going and while returning.

Whoever withdraws without unavoidable necessity shall pay, if he is one of the princes of the land, ten pounds; if noble, five; if free or [Col. 1136B] ministerial, two; if a slave or *litus*, five solidi—or he shall lose his skin and hair.

Whoever knowingly receives an excommunicated person or one condemned for any crimes, and defends him against either divine or human laws [Note: [Col. 1135] The correction *deffenderet* to *deffenderit*; *deffenderit* is in the codex.], shall incur the sentence of the condemned person.

No one shall deny hospitality to a traveler. If he has necessary supplies, let him sell them at a fair price; if he does not have them, let him acquire them from neighbors who have them, by the same agreement.

If someone denies hospitality and neglects either to sell or acquire necessary supplies, the traveler shall appeal to the master of the village. After summoning his fellow citizens [Note: [Col. 1135] The codex has *vicibus*; the thirteenth-century copy has *civibus*.], the master shall immediately have the person who denied the request tonsured and flayed.

If the traveler proves troublesome and uses violence in the lodging, the host shall summon his neighbors and report the injury; with their advice he shall demand and receive satisfaction. If the traveler does not submit to them, let him be condemned as a robber.

No one shall protect a fugitive slave. Whoever protects him shall suffer the penalty of the fugitive.

If a traveler is in need, he may take two sheaves from a field, or, if necessary, three [Note: [Col. 1135] The word is obscure.], and feed his horses with them in that field or in the nearest village. No one shall forbid the pasture of meadows. Whoever directs insults against another shall be punished with staffs if he is a soldier, and beaten with scourges if he is a peasant.

This is the end of the oath. The provisions that follow were praised by everyone’s mouth [Note: [Col. 1135] Missing in c.], promised through the hands of the bishops [Note: [Col. 1135] Here the thirteenth-century copy ends.], and strengthened by the ban [Note: [Col. 1135] The codex has *robrata*.]. Throughout the entire period of peace specified above [Note: [Col. 1135] The word is more obscure.], no one shall carry weapons except those which the present necessity of circumstances [Note: [Col. 1135] This appears to be the correct reading; but it should be read as in the oath of the year 1081.] requires.

## V. THE COURT OF MAINZ

[Note: [Col. 1135D] B. Pez published the letters inviting attendance at it in *Codex Diplomaticus* II, p. 47, from a Tegernsee codex, but wrongly attributed them to Heinricus VI and the year 1191, since they seem to be assignable only to Heinricus IV and the year 1100, toward the end of which Pope Clement III died. We learn from Dodechinus that in that year the emperor celebrated the Nativity of the Lord at Mainz.]

*(Year 1100, December 25.)*

[Col. 1135C]

HEINRICUS, by the grace of God august emperor, sends grace and every good thing to the abbot of Tegernsee.

Having recently learned among us of the death of the apostolic lord C., the princes who were with us advised that we should summon a general court of all the princes at Mainz on the Nativity of the Lord, so that, by their common counsel, the Roman See might be ordered and a course of action might be found for restoring the unity of the Church, which has now for a long time been miserably divided.

Concerning this matter, by admonishing, asking, and commanding, we most earnestly call upon the loyalty owed to us by you: since you care for God and peace, and also for Christian love and our favor, do not fail to come to the aforesaid court for any reason, and do not let any occupation prevent you. You may be certain that we shall excuse no prince from this labor and shall tolerate no one’s negligence in this matter with equanimity.

## VI. THE COURT OF MAINZ

[Note: [Col. 1137D] The *Annals of Augsburg*, in a codex of the royal library at Munich, report that Heinricus, residing at Mainz in 1103, decided on Epiphany to establish the kingdom in peace for four years with an oath, and remitted the offenses of all who had forfeited his favor. Since the text of his constitution has now perished, we attempt to supplement it with the documents that follow. We found them written in the margins of a codex of the royal library at Munich, formerly belonging to Augsburg, containing Isidore’s *On the Birth and Death of the Fathers of the Old and New Testament*, written in the ninth century, with notes added by a hand from the beginning of the twelfth century. They provide information both about the peace established throughout the whole kingdom and about the peace concluded among certain princes of Swabia and Franconia. As an appendix we add the peace established in the bishopric of Constance by Bishop Gebehard.]

*(Year 1103, January 6.)*

### Constitution of the General Peace

In the year 1103 from the Lord’s Incarnation, Emperor Heinricus confirmed and established the peace at Mainz with his own hand, and the archbishops and bishops confirmed it with their own hands. The king’s son swore it, as did the chief men of the whole kingdom, dukes, margraves, counts, and many others. Duke Welf, Duke Berthold, and Duke Frederick swore the same peace until Pentecost and thereafter for four years. They swore, I say, peace for churches, clerics, monks, laymen, merchants, women, so that they might not be carried off by force, and Jews.

The oath is as follows:

No one shall invade anyone’s house in a hostile manner or ravage it by fire; no one shall seize anyone for money, nor wound, strike, or kill anyone. If anyone does this, he shall lose his eyes or hand. If anyone defends him, he shall suffer the same penalty.

If he flees into a castle, the castle, after being besieged for three days by the oath-bound men, shall be destroyed. If anyone escapes this judgment, if he has a benefice, his lord shall take it from him; his relatives shall take his patrimony from him.

If anyone commits theft worth five solidi or more, he shall lose his eyes or hand. If he commits theft worth less than five solidi, he shall lose his hair, be beaten with rods, and return the stolen property. If he commits such theft three times, or robbery for the third time, he shall lose his eyes or hand.

If your enemy meets you on the road, and you can harm him, harm him. If he flees into someone’s house or courtyard, he shall remain unharmed.

The king’s friends use this oath as a shield, but it is of no benefit whatsoever to his enemies.

### Constitution of the Provincial Peace

Such a peace was sworn by Duke Frederick and by many counts, with the bishop of Augsburg, the bishop of Eichstätt, and the priors of both consenting.

Clerics, churches, cemeteries, and the endowments of churches shall have peace. Likewise, all people shall have peace in their houses, in every building, and also in courtyards within the lawful areas of houses, which are commonly called *hovestete*, whether they are enclosed or surrounded by no hedge.

Women shall suffer violence from no one. Merchants and farmers shall have peace. No one at all shall be seized solely for the sake of money.

If anyone violates the aforesaid peace, he must lose his hand.

If anyone is accused of theft or of any offense connected with this violated peace, the person whose peace has been violated shall go to the parish of the accused and say to the people: “That man, N., has violated the peace in this matter [lacuna] me.” [Note: [Col. 1137] “in”?] He shall then grant him a delay of fourteen days.

If he has not obtained justice within fourteen days, a second delay of fourteen days shall be granted to him, and a third delay of fourteen days after that. If the accused does not come to make satisfaction, he shall be guilty of violating the peace.

This peace shall remain in force from now until Easter, and from the coming Easter until the following Easter, [source text breaks off here].

[Col. 1138B] If anyone steals property worth less than sixty denarii, he shall be plucked and scourged with rods, and burned with iron on both cheeks as far as the teeth. If anyone steals property worth sixty denarii or more, his hand shall be cut off. Everyone must swear this peace before the next feast of Saint Mary, or purge himself by the oath of seven truthful men of his own condition, declaring that he himself has not heard from anyone that this peace had been sworn; whoever does not do this shall lose his hand.

If anyone violates this peace, flees, and wishes to remain hidden until the peace has passed, then, if he should later return, he shall suffer the same penalty that he ought to have suffered at the time. If anyone refuses to swear, saying, “I harm no one, nor does anyone harm me,” and if anyone knowingly shelters, receives, protects, or, for money or in any other way, permits a violator of the [Col. 1138C] peace to escape, he shall undergo the same penalty as the violator of the peace.

If a violator of the peace flees, the duke, count, advocate, or any official under whose jurisdiction he had previously been shall seize and possess the violator’s estates for as long as the violator of the peace lives; after the violator’s death, his heirs shall obtain the inheritance. The lord from whom the violator of the peace had received benefices shall take those benefices away.

If a violator of the peace hides in some fortified place, the person whose peace was violated shall make a proclamation before the people, pursue the accused for one day and one night, and besiege the fortification with the people for three days and three nights. [Col. 1138D] If the fortification cannot be taken within three days, the duke or count shall be summoned, together with the leading men, to destroy the castle.

If anyone catches wild animals with snares or with the trap which we commonly call *druch*, namely stags, young deer, does, roe deer, [Col. 1139A] hares, and others, his lord shall take away everything he possesses; but the possessor of the land on which the wild animal was caught shall take from him his hand, or half a pound of denarii in place of his hand. Advocacy is excepted. [lacuna] [Note: [Col. 1139] The manuscript reads *reolos*.]

## Constitution of the Peace in the Diocese of Constance

The Lord Bishop of Constance, at a great assembly of abbots, clergy, and laypeople, in the presence of the apostolic legate—who, as is believed, had also arrived there at that time by God’s providence—established the following provisions, with everyone assenting and praising them.

For it was agreed that he would establish the peace until Pentecost, and that whoever agreed to this peace and faithfully kept it would receive the following benefit: In every monastery of his bishopric, seven Masses would be sung in the assembly of clergy and monks; twelve poor people would be fed three times; moreover, each priest would sing one Mass, each of the other literate men fifty psalms, and each lay brother fifty *Paternosters*. For the dead, whatever was done for those who had received their fellowship of communion would be done.

In addition, all the priests of the entire bishopric would each sing three Masses. For those who died in the meantime, each would sing one Mass and feed one poor person. Moreover, of the seven years imposed on penitents, the bishop would remit two years.

These provisions concerning the public peace were enacted on the twelfth day before the Kalends of November. Whoever keeps this peace shall receive this benefit. From that day onward, however, whoever commits an offense in their churches or their appendages, against priests or any ordained persons, against monks and lay brothers, or against anyone subject to the bishop’s jurisdiction, it was decreed by common consent that, unless he repents, he shall be deprived of communion both while living and after death.

A priest who knowingly gives communion to such persons shall know that he is forbidden to exercise his office [Col. 1140A] and shall have no communion among the other brothers until he makes worthy satisfaction.

## VII. Council of Regensburg

[Note: [Col. 1139C] I found in 1833 a statute concerning the advocates of churches, issued at the Council of Regensburg in the first months of 1104, written in a twelfth-century hand in a codex of the Royal Library of Munich, formerly Augsburgian and now preserved among the Latin codices as no. 2, folio 891. It is preceded there by these words: “From the African Council. It seemed to everyone that a request should be made to the emperors, on account of the affliction of the poor, by whose troubles the Church is ceaselessly wearied, that defenders should be appointed for them against the power of the rich, with the provision of the bishops.” The opening lines of the first constitution are preserved in the Altach codex of 1260, written by Abbot Hermann, and were published in *Monumenta Boica*, vol. XI, p. 26, no. 10; Meichelbeck gave a second edition from the Freising book in *Historia Frisingensis*, vol. I, part II, no. 1272.]

(Anno 1104, January, February, March)

From the Council of Regensburg, which the Emperor Henry III attended with many leading men.

It was decreed that all those belonging to the court of any advocate [Note: [Col. 1139] “of the great churches,” in the Altach copy], whenever they were summoned, should assemble once a year at specified places; and there, [Note: [Col. 1139] “that is, the advocates,” in the Altach copy] for their service, they should demand no more than two measures of wheat, two pigs, three casks of wine and [Note: [Col. 1139] “or,” in the Altach copy] mead, ten casks of beer, and five measures of oats [Note: [Col. 1139] “for fodder for thirty horses”; the remainder is missing in the Altach copy].

But so that the things belonging to the use of the brothers might be less diverted elsewhere, the following were assigned for the use of the advocates: namely, one-third of the fines and compensation for offenses, provided that, if the brothers’ property suffered any losses, their property should first be restored to them. The brothers’ wergelds are theirs [Note: [Col. 1139] “as in Meichelbeck”], and a serf in place of a serf.

Furthermore, if the prelates of the church, compelled by some necessity, were unable to recover a loss suffered by themselves or their property in a manner preserving their proper order, they should summon the advocates to a suitable place. There they were to examine the causes of complaint carefully, and were not to exact anything from them or from their tenants there under the pretext of justice; rather, they were to accept with charity whatever had been expended on them.

These acts were carried out in the city of Regensburg in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1104, indiction 12, while Pope Paschal II was presiding and [Note: [Col. 1139] “reigning,” in M.] Emperor Henry III was present; many princes both of the Church and of the realm praised and confirmed them. Their names [Note: [Col. 1139] “are contained in the Book of Traditions,” in M.] are written in the greater privilege.

[Col. 1139]

# Diplomas of Emperor Henry IV

## I. Privilege for the Church of Hamburg  
*(Year 1057, April 25)*

[Lappenberg, *Hamburg Documents*, p. 79.]

[Col. 1139C]

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity. Henry, by the gracious favor of divine clemency, king.

[Col. 1140C] If, following the custom of our predecessors, kings and emperors, we strive to enrich and exalt places devoted to divine worship, we clearly believe that an eternal reward will come to us from this. Therefore let the diligence of all Christ’s faithful and ours, both future and present, know how, for the remedy of the soul of our blessed father, King Henry III, Augustus, the second Roman emperor, and at the intervention of our beloved mother, Agnes, Augusta empress, and also at the request and through the devoted and faithful service of Adalbert, venerable archbishop of the Church of Hamburg, which was built in honor of Saint Saviour and of his most holy mother, the virgin Mary, we have given and donated, for the use of that Church, as its own property, a county belonging to our jurisdiction, namely in the districts of Hunesga and Fivilga, together with the same jurisdiction and every benefit which our predecessors possessed there or which might in any way arise from it in the future.

Moreover, we have granted to the same archbishop the license and authority to establish two [Col. 1141B] markets in that county, one at Wincheim and the other at Gerleviswert, with mints and tolls, both on water and on land, and with every jurisdiction belonging to the market and to royal authority, so that no judge, collector, or any other person, except at the pleasure of the aforesaid archbishop, should presume to invade or invalidate our royal grant.

We have confirmed this grant on the following condition: that the aforesaid archbishop and his successors shall henceforth have free power to hold the aforesaid properties or to do with them whatever they deem appropriate for the use of the aforementioned Church. And so that this royal grant of ours may remain stable and unshaken for all time, we ordered this charter, written for that purpose and strengthened by our own hand as appears below, to be marked with the impression of our seal.

Given on the seventh day before the Kalends of May, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1057, indiction 10; in the third year of the ordination of Lord Henry IV as king, and the first year of his reign.

Done at Werede. In God’s name, successfully. Amen.

## II. Privilege for the Church of Saint Peter of Minden  
*(Year 1059)*

[Erhard, *Westphalian Diplomatic Codex*, p. 117.]

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity. Henry, by the gracious favor of divine clemency, king.

We wish it to be known to all Christ’s faithful and ours, future and present, how Bishop Egilbert of the holy Church of Minden, built in honor of Saint Peter, prince of the apostles, brought before our presence documents of our most pious father, Emperor Henry Augustus, and of our other predecessors, kings and emperors. These documents stated that they had received the property of that aforementioned Church, together with everything belonging to those properties, under their protection and defense. He begged our Serenity not to refuse to have this same protection established with the consent of our imperial authority.

We, therefore, for the love of God and the remedy of our soul, and also for the stability of our kingdoms, following the customs of our predecessors and of our father and consenting to his request, have decreed that this should be done. We command that no public judge or anyone exercising judicial authority should ever dare to enter the churches, places, fields, or remaining possessions of the aforesaid Church—which it now legally possesses within the jurisdiction of our kingdom, or which divine mercy may thereafter wish to add to its rights—in order to hear cases, exact fines, make lodgings or provisions, take sureties, or unjustly constrain the men of that Church, whether free Franks, ecclesiastical *litones*, *maalmam* [reading uncertain], slaves of any condition, or tenants; nor should anyone presume to demand any payments or illicit pretexts from them, or to impose upon them any ban, military ban, or any of the matters mentioned above.

We also establish the aforesaid protection for the men serving that Church, so that they may be examined before no judicial authority except the bishop and his advocates, whom the bishop of that Church shall choose.

Furthermore, we granted that our ban, a mint, a toll, and a public market may be established there, together with whatever appeared to belong to our authority. Whatever the royal treasury might hope to receive from these, we granted to the aforesaid Church for eternal recompense, for the support of the poor and the provision of lamps. The bishop himself, with all his possessions, shall faithfully obey our imperial authority and remain under our protection, as do the other churches and bishops of our kingdoms, so that he and the brothers of that place may gladly pray for us to the Lord more effectively and continually.

We have also granted those brothers permission to choose among themselves a worthy and suitable shepherd, subject nevertheless to the consent of the king or emperor. And so that this royal confirmation of ours may remain stable and unshaken for all time, we ordered this charter to be written and, strengthening it with our own hand, to be marked with the impression of our seal.

Sign of Lord Henry IV, king. (L. M.)

I, Gebehard, chancellor, have examined this document in the place of Liutpald, archchancellor.

Given on the sixth day before the Kalends of August, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1059, indiction 12; in the sixth year of the ordination of Lord Henry IV as king, and the third year of his reign.

Done at Polide. In God’s name, successfully. Amen.

## III. Privilege for the Church of Paderborn  
*(Year 1064)*

[Erhard, *Westphalian Diplomatic Codex*, p. 118.]

[Col. 1142D]

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity. Henry, by the gracious favor of divine clemency, king.

Just as it belongs to royal liberality to donate properties or inheritances for the use of the Church, so it belongs to royal dignity and benevolence to confirm what has been donated with perpetual peace and stable law, so that those who rejoice in possessions well acquired may never grieve at having lost them through wrongdoing.

Therefore we wish it to be known to all Christ’s faithful and ours, future and present, how we have perpetually confirmed to the holy congregation of God serving in Paderborn in the Church of Saint Mary and Saint Liborius the Confessor ten hides situated in the village called Ersten, in the district of Engeren and in the county of Count Osolt. Our most beloved mother, Agnes, Augusta empress, had transferred these hides as their own property to the brothers, for the remedy of her soul and of the soul of our father, the piously remembered Emperor Henry Augustus, and also for our long life and peaceful times, together with all their appendages: that is, slaves of both sexes, fields, meadows, pastures, woods, hunting rights, millstones, mills, cultivated and uncultivated lands, roads and trackless places, exits and entrances, things acquired and things to be acquired.

We have granted them all these possessions in perpetuity, without contradiction, on the condition that the aforesaid brothers have free power over them to hold them, exchange them for something better, or do whatever they wish for their common benefit. And so that this royal confirmation or grant of ours may remain stable and unshaken for all time, we ordered this charter to be written and, strengthening it with our own hand, to be marked with the impression of our seal.

Sign of Lord Henry IV, king. (L. M.)

I, Sigehard, chancellor, have examined this document in the place of Sigefrid, archchancellor.

Given on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of August. [Text breaks off.]

## IV. Diploma of King Henry IV of the Romans for the Monastery of Stavelot

It confirms the privileges of the ancient kings, forbids the abuses of advocates, and orders that the two monasteries, Stavelot and Malmedy, have one abbot. *(Year 1065.)*

[Martène, *Amplissima Collectio*, II, 70.]

[Col. 1143C]

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity. Henry, by the gracious favor of divine clemency, king.

The height of royal prudence must in every way look after the peace and quiet of those who serve God. Therefore let the diligence of all our faithful, future and present, know that, watching over the welfare of the monastery of Stavelot, situated under our jurisdiction, and with the reverence of its abbot, Theoderic, prevailing before our exalted majesty, the same abbot petitioned us in accordance with the ancient sanctions concerning properties attached or transferred to that church, issued by the kings Sigibert, Childeric, Clovis, and Dagobert, who were the founders of the aforesaid place, as well as by the emperors Charles, Louis, the three Ottos, Henry, and also our grandfather, Emperor Conrad, of most serene memory, and our father, Emperor Henry Augustus, of pious memory.

From the time of Saint Remaclus through succeeding generations, we have confirmed these provisions with our royal authority. It is therefore sanctioned by our dignity that whatever was transferred or donated to that place in the time of his predecessors, or whatever Emperor Henry returned to his predecessor, Abbot Poppo, as a benefice from Hasbany for the benefit of his soul, or whatever was restored to him by our grandfather of blessed memory after it had been unjustly held for some time by Count Herimann from the estate of a dead heir—namely Scaletin and Palisiol, with all their appendages—and whatever he purchased for that place, namely the sixth part of Amblava and Tumbis from Count Gotfrid of Eingeis, or whatever he exchanged from the property of the church with Wendegias and Corvuoroimon, abbot of Saint Maximinus, giving the village of Astebronna in exchange, shall remain unbroken and unshaken.

Since our predecessors, kings and emperors, by the firmness of their authority, sanctioned for that place that its advocate should not presume, in the estates belonging to the place, to make lodgings or provisions, exact payments or fines, hold a court, or take *parefreds* for himself without the permission or will of the abbot, we likewise confirm and strengthen the same provision for that abbot. By imposing our ban [Col. 1144B] we reinforce it, so that no one henceforth may dare to violate these provisions. Whatever he has acquired or found acquired in any property of the church is also strengthened by the ratified provision of our authority and enjoys immunity from every harassment by advocates.

And because the sanctions of the ancient kings and emperors did not suffice for the monks of the other monastery, namely Malmedy, and they attempted to divide the two monasteries under two abbots—although they had remained united from the time of Saint Remaclus—we have determined, so that no dispute may henceforth arise between them, as is known to have happened in the time of Lord Emperor Otto II, that, according to our decree, both monasteries shall be subject to one abbot’s rule, as they have remained continually.

And so that this grant and confirmation of ours concerning all these matters may possess fuller authority, we have confirmed this charter below with our own hand and ordered it to be marked with the impression of our seal.

Sign of Lord Henry IV, king.

I, Sigehard, chancellor, have examined this document in the place of Sigefrid, archchancellor.

Given in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1115, indiction 3; in the twelfth year of Henry IV’s ordination, and the ninth year of his reign.

Done at Trier. In God’s name, successfully. Amen.

## V. Privilege for the Church of Osnabrück  
*(Year 1078)*

[Erhard, *Westphalian Diplomatic Codex*, from the manuscripts of Henseler.]

[Col. 1144D]

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity. Henry, by the gracious favor of divine clemency, king.

Justice is that by which we give each person his own right. If we proceed along this path, we enter the royal road into the land of promise under the great leader Jesus. But if, through human frailty, we should at some time stray from straight steps, ecclesiastical laws salutarily admonish us to return to the way of justice and to amend for the better what we have sinned through negligence or malice.

For this reason we wish it to be known for all time how our faithful servant Benno II, venerable bishop of the holy Church of Osnabrück, came to the clemency of our majesty, accompanied by a large number of his fellow bishops, and tearfully poured into our ears an old complaint concerning the tithes of his Church.

Although he had deserved extremely well from us throughout his life, he was all the more worthy of being heard because, in all our necessities, he had faithfully and steadfastly remained at our side as our companion. His complaint was as follows: our predecessor, Charles, a man of divine and imperial memory, had founded the church entrusted to him from its earliest foundations and had granted it, as its endowment, the tithes defined throughout the bishopric. At that time, because there were no gifts in those regions from estates or royal revenues with which to support them at the beginning of the faith and at the time of the new planting, he had given these tithes to the church.

He said that these donations, justly given to the aforesaid church by that prince and customarily confirmed in a royal document under the impression of a ring, had remained with the church for a long time, until, during the disturbances of war under Louis II, part of those tithes was severed from it through the agency of Coppo.

For this reason, after proceedings and investigations had repeatedly been conducted by the bishops of that city in the hearing of princes and of our predecessors, kings and emperors, the bishops’ claim was judged the more just, and that of their opponents the less just.

Indeed, the aforesaid Coppo, the first usurper of those tithes, when he seized the whole of them for his own use through unjust domination on the pretext of the wars, granted one part to his own full brother Warin, abbot of Corvey, and another part to his sister, the abbess Adela of Herford.

Thus the bishops, bringing this case before the court, proved by manifest evidence that the tithes ought to return to them by legitimate donation. The matter was debated in four councils: first at Rome under Pope Stephen, second at Tribur under Emperor Arnulf, third at Bonn, and fourth at Ingelheim. In all of them, possession of the tithes was adjudged to the bishops by common sentence. Finally, in the presence of nearly all the bishops of the German regions and through the mediation of Roman legates, under Pope John, the tithes were restored upon payment of a settlement of thirty pounds of gold.

Yet, as iniquity always rules among the unjust, the matter, previously corrected and repaired, was corrupted again. When our aforesaid faithful servant, the bishop of the Church of Osnabrück, repeatedly brought this case to our ears and requested that it be amended and corrected, we neglected to act for a long time, restrained by the weakness of age and moved by the pleas of his opponents.

At last, overcome by his continual admonitions and those of his fellow bishops, who recognized his right, we fixed a place and day at which the bishop and his opponents were to come with the written documents of both sides. Twenty or more bishops were present, together with princes of the kingdom and a great multitude of our other faithful. The charters of both parties were read aloud in everyone’s hearing; everything was examined and discussed with care.

All acclaimed that the bishop’s claim was just and the opponents’ claim unjust, and everyone pressed us most earnestly to render justice to the bishop and his Church. Therefore, considering it unjust to neglect equity and to resist justice any longer, we assented to the petition and counsels of our faithful.

Accordingly, by the authority of this decree of ours, we establish and decree that these same tithes shall return to the ownership and disposition of the bishop, as Charles established. No advocate or any other person, great or small, shall dare to trouble the bishops of that city any further in this matter. Rather, the bishops shall hold, possess, and administer these tithes in quiet order and perpetual peace, trusting in the hope and mercy of God that this just restoration of the tithes may become the remission of sins for the souls of our parents—our grandfather, grandmother, and our mother, the empress Agnes—and of our dear father, Emperor Henry Augustus; that the negligence which he himself committed in this matter may be forgotten by God; and that, on each day and on the anniversary of those who fell in the war against the Saxons, their memory may be commemorated there.

A special prayer for the soul of Sigefrid, who was killed in that war, shall also be established and performed, so that a special Mass may be celebrated for him every day, and every Tuesday one Mass may be sung in common by the brothers in the choir for all our slain and for all the faithful. At the canonical hours, one psalm shall be recited. A prebend shall also be given to the cleric who diligently observes these obligations owed to Sigefrid.

We have also agreed with the bishop, with the approval of his clergy, that every week thirty Masses for the living and the dead shall be sung there for the salvation of our body and soul. After our death, Masses and an equal number of psalters shall be sung there, now and for all future time, especially for the remedy of our soul and those of our parents.

For, desiring such things, we believe that through the merciful God our negligence will be erased and the offenses of our predecessors redeemed—those who acted negligently and maliciously in this matter.

And so that the authority of this decree of ours may remain stable and unshaken for all time, we ordered this charter to be written, confirmed it with our own hand, as is the custom of kings and emperors, and ordered it to be marked with our seal.

Sign of the most unconquered Lord Henry IV, king. (L. M.)

I, Gebehard, chancellor, have examined this document in the place of Sigefrid, archbishop.

Given on the sixth day before the Kalends of February, indiction 2, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1078; in the twenty-third year of the reign of Lord Henry IV, [Col. 1146D] king.

Done at Mainz. Successfully. Amen.

## VI. Privilege for the Church of Osnabrück  
*(Year 1079)*

[Erhard, *Westphalian Diplomatic Codex*, from the manuscripts of Henseler.]

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity. Henry, by the gracious favor of divine clemency, king.

If we pay careful attention to the complaints of priests which they have brought before us concerning the necessities of the Churches entrusted to them, and mercifully provide them justice and bring the matter to an end, we clearly trust that we shall thereby earn rewards of both present and eternal happiness.

Therefore we wish it to be known to all the faithful of the holy Church of God and to our own faithful, present and future, how our faithful servant Benno II, bishop of Osnabrück, who had long been most devoted in our service, came to the clemency of our Serenity. Following the Apostle’s precept, he accused, rebuked, entreated, and reproached our youth, complaining that he and his predecessors had suffered for a long time, during the reigns of our predecessors—namely our grandfather Conrad and our dear father, Emperor Henry, of blessed memory—who perhaps sinned unknowingly in this matter, many injuries and various oppressions from the powerful men of that region, especially from the abbot of Corvey and the abbess of Herford and their supporters, through the seizure of the tithes rightfully belonging to his Church.

Although his complaint had often been repeated, we refused for a long time to assent to it, more to our misfortune than to our benefit. We excused ourselves from deciding the matter on various pretexts, citing our youth and the dissuasion of certain counselors who at that time were advising our youth.

At last, however, overcome by frequent and even innumerable complaints concerning the lamentable decline of Christianity, and by the requests and counsel of many clergy and laypeople who recognized his right, we ordered the same bishop and his opponents to come to Worms, where we had decided that our princes should assemble for other affairs of the kingdom.

There, in the presence of ten bishops, ten abbots, and very many other clergy and laypeople, the bishop and his opponents brought forward the written documents of both parties. After the documents had been read and understood, we learned without any ambiguity that the Church of Osnabrück had originally been founded in the Westphalian province by the great and illustrious man Charles, with the counsel and consent of Pope Hadrian; that it had been consecrated by the venerable Egilfrid, bishop of Liège; and that, because at that time the bishop and the clergy serving God there had no estates or other gifts in that region from which they could be supported, it had been endowed on the day of its consecration with the tithes of all those dwelling within the boundaries of that bishopric and of those newly converted to Christianity.

We also learned that it had later been confirmed by the privileges of four apostolic men, namely Leo, Paschal, Eugenius, and Gregory, and that every person who, after these privileges had been reread before us, violated their provisions in any way stood condemned by anathema.

From the written document of the abbot, which he brought and which had been confirmed by royal authority, we understood that the younger Louis had granted to the Church of Corvey a certain cell called Meppen, and to the Church of Herford a church called Bunede, together with the tithes belonging to them, in the bishopric of Osnabrück.

To refute and annul these claims, the bishop publicly produced a charter of that same younger Louis, strengthened by his own hand and marked with his seal. In it Louis confirmed the provisions of his grandfather and father concerning those same tithes for the aforesaid Church of Osnabrück, and, as the abbot’s documents report, denied that he had diminished anything in the transfer of those tithes.

Since the abbot and abbess had nothing to rely on except what appeared to be some fabricated document, the bishop presented for reading charters of many of our predecessors, kings and emperors—namely Arnulf and his son Louis, Henry I, and the three Ottos—strengthened by their own hands and marked with their seals, confirming those same tithes to his Church.

After the opinions of both sides had been heard and carefully judged, the archbishops and bishops, together with all the clergy, and the dukes and counts—even those who had previously favored the opponents—unanimously declared that justice required them to consent to the bishop’s petitions.

The aforesaid bishop also promised us, with the dean and the other clergy of that Church assenting, that, as long as the place remained whole and undestroyed, during our life they would devoutly sing there each week, for the life and stability of our kingdom, thirty Masses and an equal number of psalters; after our death, they would do so for the remedy of the souls of ourselves, our dear father Emperor Henry Augustus, our mother Empress Agnes, our grandfather, and our grandmother. At every canonical hour they would recite one psalm.

In addition, it was decreed that forever, every Tuesday, the brothers in the choir would sing a special Mass in common for the soul of Sigefrid, our dear servant, and for the souls of the others who fell in public battle while defending our honor.

Therefore, for the sake of our Lord Jesus Christ, blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, and the most precious martyrs Crispin and Crispinian; also out of reverence for the great and peaceful Emperor Charles Augustus, the most devoted founder of that Church; for the other predecessors who strengthened that Church by their documents and decrees; and for the remedy and liberation of the souls of our grandfather, our father, ourselves, and the other kings who sinned by denying justice to that Church; and in response to the bishop’s diligent and long-standing complaint, we have decreed that a privilege of immunity and liberty concerning those tithes be made for the bishop and his Church, establishing them securely.

We therefore command that, just as the other holy Churches of God in our kingdom stand established by the decrees and documents of our predecessors, kings and emperors, so this Church of Osnabrück also, through this decree of ours and with the Lord’s assistance, shall remain established.

We also grant and permit the same bishop—or rather, we command him—in accordance with Charles’s institution, to receive into his episcopal authority the tithes of all those dwelling within the boundaries of his bishopric, which he has unjustly lacked for a long time, with no one contradicting him.

Let the aforesaid bishop also be permitted to possess peacefully those tithes and the other properties of his Church which he now possesses or may acquire in the future, and to correct his churches, as is the right of other bishops, and to settle their affairs without any contradiction.

It is therefore firmly established that all his successors shall receive from us these same provisions in the same manner. And so that this authority of ours may have firmer stability in God’s name, we have strengthened this charter with our own hand, as appears below, and ordered it to be marked with our seal.

Sign of the most unconquered Lord Henry IV, king. (L. M.)

I, Gebehard, chancellor, have examined this document in the place of Sigefrid, archchancellor.

Given on the third day before the Kalends of April, indiction 2, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1079; in the twenty-third year of the reign of Lord Henry IV, king.

Done at Regensburg. In God’s name, successfully. Amen.

## VII. Confirmation of the Privileges and Rights Granted to the Bishop of Passau and His Church by King Henry IV  
*(Year 1079)*

[Muratori, *Italian Antiquities*, II, 73.]

[Col. 1149B]

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity. Henry, by the gracious favor of divine clemency, king.

Since it is established that it is the duty of royal or imperial dignity that churches dedicated to God and the saints, for the advancement of divine worship, should always be fortified by new privileges against all attacks of those who threaten them, therefore we wish it to be known to all our faithful, present and future, how the venerable D., bishop of the Church of Padua, approaching the clemency of our serenity, requested that we should decree a grant of immunity and liberty for the church entrusted to him, constructed in honor of Saint Mary, Mother of God. Through this grant, he would be able to hold more firmly and fully the possessions and properties which appear to be subject to his bishopric, or which ought by right to be subject to it.

[Col. 1149C] Granting his petition out of love for our Lord Jesus Christ, we decreed that this should be done and ordered this grant to be written accordingly, firmly commanding that the holy see of the aforesaid bishop should henceforth, by this grant of ours and with God’s help, remain permanently and securely established.

We also confirm and firmly ratify, by this page of our grant, all the grants and protections of the emperors or kings which that same church appears to possess. We further establish by this grant whatever that church appears to possess, or whatever it is legally entitled to possess.

In particular, the river called the Retrone, from the ford of Silicis to the place where it enters the river called the Brenta; thence as far as the ditch called Baiba; and the ditch together with the river [Col. 1149D] which runs from the chapel of Saint Michael to the port of Ponte de Fossumba. No one shall be permitted to construct a mill in the aforesaid waters or places, or to make a weir, fishery, building, or obstruction there, without the permission of the same bishop or of his successors on behalf of the aforesaid bishopric.

Likewise, specifically, Ladrum with its meadows and all its appurtenances; and the bridge called Vicentinus, with all its arches and mills which the aforesaid bishopric appears to possess or to which it is legally entitled.

Likewise, specifically, all the ripaticum, tolls, ports, and markets mentioned above, throughout all that is contained within the boundaries of Padua.

Moreover, specifically, seven pounds of Venetian money which, upon our arrival in the kingdom of Italy, the people of Sacco say that they owe us on one account: because the bishop of Padua is count of Sacco, and because they say they owe it to us by the command of our father.

[Col. 1150A] We confirm and ratify all these things by this page of our grant, firmly commanding that henceforth no prince, no public judge, no duke, no other judicial authority or count, no royal envoy, and no person, great or small, should presume to violate this grant of ours.

If any person, great or small, should in any respect violate the provisions or concessions of this grant, or inflict any violence upon the persons or goods of the aforesaid bishopric, or upon the aforesaid bishop or his successors, that person shall pay one hundred pounds of gold, half to our treasury and half to [Col. 1150B] the aforesaid bishop, etc.

The sign of the lord King Henry IV, the most invincible.

Burchard, chancellor, acting in place of S. . . ., archchancellor, has verified this.

Given on the tenth day before the Kalends of August, in the second indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1079, and in the twenty-third year of the reign of the lord King Henry IV.

Enacted at Regensburg, happily, in the name of God. Amen.

## VIII. Privilege granted by Henry IV, king of Germany and Italy, to Abbot Peter for the monastery of Saint Eugenius in the county of Siena. (Year 1081.)

[MURATORI, *Antiquitates Italicae*, VI, 197.]

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, Henry, by the favor of divine clemency, fourth king.

Whatever we grant to holy places and to religious men serving God and his saints therein, in accordance with the custom and tradition of our predecessors, we hope will lead to the blessedness of eternal recompense. Therefore, let the understanding of all the holy Church of God and of our faithful, present and future, learn how Abbot Peter, together with the monks in the monastery of Saint Eugenius, situated in the county of Siena at a place called Pilosianus, [lacuna] informed us that, because of want, hunger, and nakedness, they could not serve God there, since wicked men had taken away the estates and lands which our predecessors had granted for their support.

[Col. 1150D] We [lacuna], that the possessions and estates granted there by our predecessors and confirmed and ratified [lacuna] should come under our lordship and ownership, have determined to confirm and ratify them—namely, so that they may hold them in complete peace and tranquility and possess them most firmly, without opposition from anyone. These are: the church of Saint Peter called Campus, with all its appurtenances; the estate of Untione; the church of Saint Savinus, with the small estates at Andrina, Citinella, Vagina, and Poagia; the church of Saint Peter at Arganello, with its appurtenances at Tudina and Grigi; the church of Saint Michael at Veronulla, with their appurtenances; and at Sicali, the church of Saint Cecilia at Meudina; the church of Saint Angelus at Lucinula, at Certina, and [Col. 1151A] at Calcina; the estate of Vescona, at Taverna and at Arbiola; the church of Saint Agnes; the church of Saint Peter at Monte Sinderi; the estate of Stine, with the castle itself; the church of Saint Anastasius at Haniaria; and the estate situated in the parish of Saint Peter in Valle; the church of Saint Angelus at Vajano; the church of Saint Angelus at Certano; the church of Saint Peter at Baruntulo, with the hill itself at Cerialta; the church of Saint Paul in the suburb of Siena; the church of Saint Miniatus; the church of Saint Angelus; and half of the church of Saint Romulus, with all their appurtenances and usages; the site of Saint Augustine, on which a castle has been built; the land of Cursiniano; two manses at Campriano; and the church of Saint Paul in the castle of Origia, with its [Col. 1151B] appurtenances; the church of Saint Eugenius with its appurtenances at Poliano; land at Saturniano; the estate of Serdille; part of the castle of Barcula; part of the castle of Leciniano; likewise portions of churches and lands; one-third of the church of Saint Peter at Malenino; and two-thirds of the church of Saint Mary at Malenina, with its appurtenances.

Moreover, we grant and entirely concede to them that the inhabitants of the aforesaid monastery may henceforth receive and peacefully possess the tithes from manses, lands, vineyards, and all things belonging to the aforesaid monastery, just as their predecessors [lacuna] had customarily possessed them under our imperial predecessors, by this grant of our authority.

We also firmly command that this confirmation of ours remain stable and unshaken in the future. No bishop, duke, margrave, count, viscount, or any person, great or small, shall presume to disturb or harass those aforesaid monks, or unjustly inflict any injury upon them on account of the aforementioned possessions.

If anyone should attempt to violate this grant of our authority, let that person know that he must pay one hundred pounds of the finest gold, half to our treasury and half to the abbot and his brothers. And so that it may be believed more certainly and observed more diligently by all, we have ordered it to be marked with our seal, strengthening it with our own hand.

The sign of the lord King Henry IV, the most invincible.

Burchard, bishop and chancellor, has verified this.

[Col. 1151D] In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1081, in the fourth indiction, on the second day before the Nones of June, in the twenty-seventh year of the lord Henry, and the twenty-fifth of his reign.

Enacted at Rome, happily, in the name of Christ. Amen.

## IX. Agreement between King Henry IV and the people of Pisa, in which the pacts made between them are set forth. (Year 1081.)

[MURATORI, *Antiquitates Italicae*, V, 19.]

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, Henry, by the favor of divine clemency, king.

Let it be known to all the faithful of Christ, future and present, how, with the counsel of our princes, we granted to our faithful citizens of the city of Pisa what they requested.

We have agreed and firmly established that no person, except with their common consent, shall seize, disperse, or seal [uncertain legal terms] within the city of Pisa, or in the suburbs, if they possess extensions outside the city; nor shall we order the walls of the aforesaid city to be destroyed, undermined, or damaged, nor shall we order the aforesaid city to be burned with fire or dug up.

If we bring any charge against any person, whether concerning land or any offense, we shall permit him to answer with twelve compurgators, without trial by combat—except in matters concerning our life, morals, or honor—if he wishes to establish his case by those with whom he has found counsel.

We shall not impose a ban except according to law. No man from the aforesaid city or suburbs shall be seized by us unless the law prohibits him from fulfilling his obligation and he possesses no allod within or outside the city.

Nor shall we obstruct men who have made preparations to sail, unless they have done so deliberately because of a complaint brought against them. If we accuse one of them who has made such preparations in order to evade justice, we shall allow him to defend himself by his oath.

If any of them is on a journey, we shall not place his wife under distraint.

Regarding any holding that a person possesses from us as a benefice, we shall not dispossess him except according to law.

We shall observe the customs which they have concerning the sea exactly as is their custom.

If a claim concerning land is brought against anyone, and he can produce a warrantor or wishes to establish his possession by oath, we shall not subject him to the ordeal of combat.

We shall not impose legal proceedings concerning Pisan men upon men from another city, another castle, another village, or another lordship, unless the men from those places, or their lords who caused the offense, first submit to legal proceedings before the Pisans.

We shall not take fodrum from the castles of the Pisan county except according to the custom that existed in the time of Marquis Hugh.

We shall not take fodrum from men living in the villages of their county. Nor shall we impose any new custom, except to the extent that the three best men of each village and castle, [Col. 1152C] chosen on behalf of their lords, swear that such was their custom in the time of the aforesaid Hugh. If they refuse to swear, we shall compel them to swear.

We shall not allow a castald or any envoy of ours from another county to remain in the aforesaid city or county in order to hold a court there.

We shall not forbid girls or widows to take husbands in the Pisan county. Nor shall we take their marriage payments against their will, nor marry any woman to someone against her will.

We shall not allow a market [lacuna] at Calci to be held in the villages of their county except according to the custom of Hugh’s time, established by oaths as stated above.

We shall not establish lodging in anyone’s property without the consent of the person whose property it is.

Within the aforesaid city, or near it as far as half a mile, we shall not take away or cause to be cultivated lands that were pasture or marsh, situated before their estates or those of churches, or common pastures not occupied on account of pasture. Nor shall we seek to have them cultivated through them or through anyone acting for us, [Col. 1153A] up to the boundaries determined by men whom they elect for this purpose. These men shall swear that they will assess and demarcate in good faith those lands which were pasture or marsh, and identify those which were pasture and ought to remain under cultivation.

We shall compel those men to swear, if they refuse, without allowing affection or hatred to influence them. Whatever they determine the land to be, we shall prohibit anyone, in good faith, from changing it to another condition.

If they disagree in choosing the aforesaid men, we shall choose no one, but shall compel them to swear.

In Rome, and from Rome itself to Pavia, they shall pay no ripaticum at those markets and places where they have customarily traveled on their own account, or where they can prove that they have already gone to trade.

Those merchants who wish to go to Pisa shall not be obstructed.

Nor shall we send any margrave into Tuscany without the approval of twelve men chosen at an assembly held with the bells sounding.

From the mouth of the Arno to Ripalta, we shall not permit anyone to plunder or assault them while traveling or returning by way of the Arno, unless perhaps because of desert [uncertain].

We shall not allow the aldium situated on both banks of the Arno, from the sea to Orticaria, to be obstructed.

Beyond the ancient walls of the city—that is, from the ancient walls to the Arno—we shall free the land for common use.

Nor shall we allow the construction of a house within the aforesaid boundaries to be prohibited up to a height of thirty-six cubits.

And so that this may remain firm and unshaken, we ordered this charter to be written, and, as appears below, strengthened it with our own hand and caused it to be marked with the impression of our seal.

We have also added that if any ship is detained from Gaeta to Luni, no one shall dare to plunder or attack the goods of those Pisans.

If anyone should violate this grant of ours, let him know that he must pay two hundred pounds of the finest gold, half to our treasury and half to the person against whom the wrong was committed.

The sign of the lord Henry, the most invincible king of the Romans.

Burchard, chancellor, acting in place of . . . ., archchancellor, has verified this.

Given in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1081, in the fourth indiction, in the twenty-fourth year of the ordination of the lord King Henry IV and the thirtieth of his reign.

Enacted happily in the name of Christ.

## X. Diploma of Henry IV among kings and third among emperors, by which he confirms and enlarges all the rights and privileges of the monastery of Farfa. (Year 1084.)

[MURATORI, *Rerum Italicarum Scriptores*, II, II, 605.]

[Col. 1153D]

Henry, by the favor of divine clemency, Roman emperor Augustus.

When we favor the reasonable petitions of the servants of God out of love for divine worship and bestow suitable benefits upon them, we do not doubt that the reward of eternal recompense will be repaid to us. Therefore, let the understanding of all the holy Church of God and of our faithful, present and future, learn how Berard, venerable abbot of the monastery of Saint Mary, the holy and ever-virgin Mother of God, situated in the duchy of Spoleto [Col. 1154A] and constructed in the county of Sabina at a place called Acutianus, came into our presence and showed us the grants of our predecessors, kings and emperors, made to that monastery and sealed with golden bulls—namely, those of the emperors Charles, Louis, and Lothar, as well as of another Louis.

These grants stated how they themselves, and their predecessors Liutprand, Rathgis, Haistulf, and Desiderius, kings of the Lombards, as well as the imperial ancestors of our family—namely, our grandfather Conrad and our father Henry of blessed memory—had always held the aforesaid monastery under their protection, for the love of God and in reverence for Saint Mary, the holy and ever-virgin Mother of God and our Lady.

For the greater security of the matter, [Col. 1154B] the aforesaid abbot requested that we confirm the grants of those same emperors by our authority and order a grant of immunity to be issued for his monastery.

We, therefore, consenting to his just requests, confirm to the same monastery whatever it may in future succeed in vindicating by written charters, insofar as we can do so justly and legally—namely, whatever it appears to possess in the territory of Sabina: the church of Saint Benedict with all its appurtenances; the castle of Arci in its entirety; the castle called Tribucum in its entirety; the whole bed of the Farfa in its entirety; the church of Saint Angelus at Tancia with the woodland and all its appurtenances, just as Duke Hildebrand confirmed it by his grants; the castle of Bucciniano [Col. 1154C] in its entirety; the castle of Farfa with all the dependencies belonging to it; the castle called Caput Farfae and that called Saint Angelus; the castles of Cerreto malo and Scandrilia; Petra Daemonum; Rocca Salici; the entire half of the five *sistora* [*sistorum*; uncertain]; together with half of Podium Majani and all its woodland; the castle of Vulpinianum; the castle of Marciliano; the castle of Terraniano; the hill of Catino; the castle of Cufi; the castle of Furano; the estate of Lori; and the church of Saint Helena.

In the city of Orte, the church of Saint Theodore; in Viterbo, the church of Saint Mary; the church of Saint Valentine in the suburb; in the territory of Tuscania, the cell of Saint Mary at Minione with its woodland, Mount Garberti, the bank of the Albella, and the maritime port; the church of Saint Lawrence [lacuna]; the church of Saint Severa by the river; half of the city of Vetula; and the port which Count Rainerius, son of Count Saxo, gave to the aforesaid monastery of Saint Mary for the sake of his soul, and which his son Saxo, before our presence, renounced and confirmed to that monastery by charter, under an irrevocable penalty of one hundred pounds of Pavia denarii for himself and his heirs; the church of Saint Peter outside the walls of the city of Corneto, and whatever it appears to possess within or outside that city; the church of Saint Peregrine; the church of Saint Angelus beneath the bank in the county of Siena; the estate of Leonina in the county of Narni; the monastery of Saint Angelus; and the hills of Saint Antimus, Saint Mary, and Saint John within [Col. 1155A] the city of Terni; the church of Saint Saviour and Saint Syrus; the church of Saint Mary at Mediano with half of that castle in the county of Perugia; the cell of Saint Mary at Diruta in the county of Assisi; the churches of Saint Bartholomew, Saint John at Satriano, and Saint Benedict.

In the county of Spoleto, the churches of Saint Mark, Saint Saviour, Saint Paul, and Saint Martin; in the county of Osimo, the estate of Monte Polisco; in the county of Senigallia, the estate of Luzano; in the county of Camerino, the estates of Sala Bona, Trevenano, Saint Abundius, and Saint Vitus; and in the castle of Petroso, the estate of Saint Antia; and of the castle of Albocavallo, two parts, just as Octavian gave them to that monastery by charters.

In the county of Fermo, the monasteries of Saint Mary and Saint Victoria, situated on Mount Mantenano, with their castles, cells, villages, and estates; the estate of Plotersano with its castle; the estate of Curestano with its castle; Saint Mary in Casule with the castle of Area Antiqua; the castle of Tariano; a portion of Morta; the castle of Aganello with its mills; Saint Mary in Strata; Saint Mary in Pontana; Saint Mary in Clenti, with its castles, churches, and mills, and the right to draw water wherever necessary.

Likewise, across from the river Clenti, the estate of Saint Silvester within the city of Fermo; elsewhere, the estate of Saint Sabinus; the estate called Praeterium with all its appurtenances; the estate of Saint Martin with half of the hill of Bonellus [Col. 1155C] and half of Morra, and one-quarter of another estate; the castle of Cubeta; a portion of Rose; the estate of Moliano, in which is the church of Saint Victoria; and a portion of the island of Verano.

At Troliano, lands and vineyards with the seashore and port; half of the castle of Monte Alberti; the estate of the sons of Rodsimundus with its castle and churches; the estate of Talasano; half of the castle of Lurotu; the monastery of Saint Saviour at Cantalupo; and Saint Benedict of Ripa.

In the county of Ascoli, beside the river Aso, the monastery of Saint Saviour with the castle of Furcia, Calliano, and Cimbriano; the fortress of Offida; Iscela; Beneventulum; Saint Valentine; Mount Aguscanus; the island of Saint Eliseus; [Col. 1155D] half of Porche; one-fifth of Ripa; Contenanum; Asinanum; Mount Cosi; Spinetulum; Avilanum; Dullianum; half of the hill of Saint Emidius; the castle of Curru; the monastery of Saint Lawrence at Polesio with the castle of Rotello; one-eighth of Postmont; the hill of Marius; the hill; Mount Prandonius; Mount Cretaceus; Scurcula; half of the mouth of the Tronto; and the estate of Mozano Sessu Pesile.

In the county of Abruzzo, the estate of Motiano; the estate of Surnaria; and the church of Saint Peter at Pedoniano.

In the county of Penne, the estate called Monte Peditto, with the castle built there; another estate near it; the estate of Saint Mary at Catilini; the estate of Saint Lucy at Ciciliano; and the churches of Saint Clement and Saint Elias.

In the county of Chieti, the monastery of Saint Stephen, situated at Lucania; Phara of the sons of Guarnesius; the hill of Hortonella; and Saint Clement, which Count Attus gave by exchange for his portion of Attissa.

In the county of Balva, the estate of Saint Mary at Griano; and those of Saint Angelus, Saint Lawrence, Saint John, and Sorzano; the church of Saint Peregrine; Saint Mary at Forfone; and Saint Mary at Sarzana in the territory of Samnium above the river Volturno; the monastery of Saint Vincent [Note: [Col. 1155D] See below, the same matter repeated in the year 1118, in the diploma of Henry V Augustus. The monks of Farfa had never previously obtained this, and perhaps had not even sought it, namely, to assert for themselves a right over the distinguished monastery of San Vincenzo al Volturno.] with its castles and all its appurtenances, which Saint Thomas acquired for the monastery of Farfa from Duke Gisulf by a grant [Col. 1156B].

In the county of Marsica, the estate of Saint Leucius; the estate of Transaquas; that of Saint Mary at Apinianici; and the estate of Saint Adrian.

In the county of Amiterno, the castle called Praetorium; the church of Saint Mary at Loriano with its male and female servants; the estate of the castle of Colle Monte with the church of Saint Mary at Casale; the estate of Vallantis; the churches of Saint Saviour and Saint Sebastian; the estate of Saint Martin; the convent of the women of Saint George; the church of Saint Michael the Archangel; the churches of Saint James and Saint George; the water of Manicone; the church of Saint Saviour with the land of Acupieta; and the churches of Saint Leopardus, Saint Gregory, Saint Agatha, Saint Elias, and Saint John; the church [Col. 1156C] at Asera; another church of Saint John at Tazano; the church of Saint Justinus; the castle called Lunianum; Asprum; and the hill of Saint Maximus.

Likewise, the church of Saint Peter at Pinsile; in the territory of Interocrea, the estate of Canate; in the territory of Carzolano, the churches of Saint Vincent and Saint Thomas the Apostle; the old fortress of Ophianum; the castle of Monte Liano; the monastery of Saint John; the church of Saint Agnes; the estate of Territa and Narnate at Tore; the estate of Saint Mary at Corneto; in the city of Tivoli, the church of Saint Mary, surnamed Saint Adrian; in the city of Rome, the cell of Saint Mary; the church of Saint Benedict at the place called Scorticlarii; the church of Saint [Col. 1156D] Mary at Formello, which Pope Leo IX mercifully granted; in the territory of Colli, the church of Saint Andrew; the churches of Saint Blaise and Saint Sebastian; Saint Mary near the castle outside the gate; the church of Saint Justina; and the church of Saint Christina; in the city of Pisa, the church of Saint Peter; and elsewhere, the church of Saint Thomas.

Moreover, by this grant of ours we confirm the land of Saint Mary near Pisa, one parcel at the place called La Revoluta; another parcel beside the river Arno at the place called Plaja de Plutiniano; and at Gompho, twenty-four modii of land.

In the territory of Rieti, the castle of Repastum; in the county of Fermo, the estate of Saint Saviour beneath the walls of the city of Fermo; the estates of Saint Gervasius and Saint Sigismund; the land of Paratini; the estate of Saint Angelus at Villa Magna; the estate of Saint Desiderius; the estate of Cupresseto; the estate of Saint Angelus at Niviano; the estate of Saint Venantius; the estate of Columelli; the estate of Saint Felicity; the land of Raviliano; the estate of Saint Venantius and that of Solarium; the estate of Saint Mary at Motiano; the estate of Caminatis at the place called Murrum; the estate of Brezzano at the place called Serranianus; the castle of the sons of Guinizzo; the estate of Saint Mary, Mother of the Lord; the estate of Saint Marotus; the estate of Valle; the estate of Saint Mary at Ortatiano; the estate of Saint [Col. 1157B] Saviour at Memoria; the estate of Blotenano; the estate of Saint Antimus; the estate of Monte Falcone; the estate of Saint Mary at Murra; the estate of Saint Angelus between two lands; another estate of Saint Angelus at Murgiano; the estate of Saint Angelus at Antiano; and the estate of the monastery of Lumerto with two churches, namely Saint Mary and Saint Benedict, with all their appurtenances.

All the aforesaid possessions which appear to belong to the aforesaid monastery, as well as whatever may in future justly and legally accrue to it from other people, and likewise whatever is unjustly possessed by anyone, whether in the city of Rome or in the other parts of our entire Italian kingdom, wherever it is known to possess property, we confirm to that holy place by this grant of ours.

By our ban and command, and by the authority of our predecessors, kings and emperors, we confirm these possessions together with lands, vineyards, monasteries subject to it, churches, castles, estates, houses, villages, chapels, waters, watercourses, fisheries, mills, markets, cultivated and uncultivated lands, tenant farmers, male and female aldii, resident tenants, and all persons residing above the land of that monastery, whether male or female servants, together with the entire household of either sex and all animals.

For the love of God and the salvation of our soul, we grant to the monastery and to those serving it that henceforth no one, whether now or in the future, shall dare to demand from any of them, or from their people, fines or tributes of any kind; lodging or provisions; or the taking of sureties; nor shall anyone dare to distrain or compel to public watches the men of the same monastery, whether free or servile, libellarii, clerics, chartularii, or oblate persons, or all those residing under the authority of this monastery; nor shall anyone dare to demand any render or any other pretext.

Nor shall anyone dare to enter their property, or demand portorium, ripaticum, glandaticum, herbaticum, or pontaticum at any place, whether from monks, nuns, clerics, or any persons residing upon their lands.

We confirm to the same monastery the privileges of the Roman pontiffs Adrian and Paul and their successors, together with all the possessions granted to it by various people, whether by exchanges, donations, or any other instruments of charter, as we have said, and whatever has been or shall be granted to the monastery, with all its appurtenances.

Regarding the tolls of merchants and bridges, we order that one-tenth be paid at the monastery gate.

Therefore we command and order that no archbishop, bishop, duke, margrave, count, viscount, or any envoy of ours who travels about, no sculdasio or castald, and no person of our empire, great or small, presume to disturb or harass the abbot of the aforesaid monastery, its monks, or any faithful person, or to dispossess them without legal judgment of any of the things written above, or attempt to diminish their rights.

Therefore we admonish your fidelity that, whenever the aforesaid abbot, the monks, or the advocate of that monastery comes into your jurisdictions to seek justice, the dukes or counts who are then in office, in whose duchy or county the aforesaid monastery is known to possess anything, should be its defenders and helpers in every matter—both for the aforesaid abbot and for his successors—so that they do not permit any person in authority to inflict violence or any other invasion upon what belongs to the aforesaid church.

No one shall dare to receive under his command or protection fugitives from that monastery or persons who have departed from it with evil intent.

We declare invalid and free from any penalty obligations the precariae and exchanges made or acquired unjustly. We do not wish the oblate persons of the aforesaid monastery to wander in the secular world; wherever they are found, the abbot in office, or even the monks, shall be permitted to recall them to the monastery, and, if necessary, the duke or count of that time shall compel them to return to the monastery.

If a dispute should arise concerning any matter on the side of that monastery, the truth of the case shall be investigated and settled not through low-ranking persons but through more noble and trustworthy men, as if it were brought before our presence.

No judicial fine shall be demanded at all by the advocate of that monastery, nor shall our ban ever be exacted on account of any matter concerning the aforesaid monastery. Rather, the abbot and his successors shall be permitted to possess the possessions and property of the aforesaid monastery under the protection and order of immunity.

If our treasury might expect fodrum or anything else from the possessions of the same monastery, we grant the whole of it to that monastery [Col. 1158D] as a reward for eternal recompense, for the nourishment of the poor and the support of the monks serving God there, so that it may increase in prosperity in our time and in the future. Thus may those servants of God more freely delight in praying to the Lord for us and for the stability of our empire.

Whenever the abbot of the same monastery departs from this life, the monks themselves, unanimously agreeing among themselves according to the rule of Saint Benedict, as their order teaches and as is right, shall have permission to elect as abbot the man whom they find more worthy.

If anyone should at any time violate this grant of our confirmation, or attempt to do against the aforesaid monastery anything that we have prohibited, let him know that, according to the constitution of the Lord, of our father Henry, emperor Augustus, and of the other emperors who strengthened the grants of this monastery, and by this grant of ours, he must pay one thousand pounds of the purest gold, half to our treasury and half to the aforesaid monastery and those governing it.

Given in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1084; in the thirtieth year of the ordination of the lord Henry IV, king and third Roman emperor Augustus; in the twenty-eighth year of his reign; and in the first year of his empire.

## XI. Confirmation by Henry IV, third emperor, of all the possessions and rights of the monastery of Saint Zeno of Verona. (Year 1084.)

[MURATORI, *Antiquitates Italicae*, I, 739.]

[Col. 1159B]

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, Henry, by the favor of divine clemency, Roman emperor Augustus.

It is fitting for imperial majesty that, the more exalted it is honored above other dignities, the more kindly and merciful it should be found toward the just petitions of those who serve God.

Therefore we wish it to be known to all the holy Church of God and to our faithful, both future and present, how Lord Sigebod, bishop of the Church of Verona, together with Werinher, abbot of the monastery of Saint Zeno the Confessor, came humbly to seek our clemency. He earnestly entreated us, for the love of almighty God and in reverence for blessed Zeno, to confirm to the aforesaid monastery all its properties and possessions, etc.

We, consenting to their just petitions, confirm and grant the following to the aforesaid monastery for the salvation of our soul: in the judicial district of Garda, the castle called Pasturingo, which Count Arduin of blessed memory and his son Eriprand granted to the monastery of Saint Zeno for the salvation of their souls by a charter of offering, etc.

Likewise, the castle called Nonense Island, which came to that monastery by offering, donation, and purchase, with all the revenue and jurisdiction, or fodrum, which it now appears to possess.

Moreover, we give and grant to the same monastery of Saint Zeno the free men commonly called Arimanni who dwell in the castle of Saint Vitus and in its territory; likewise the Herimanni dwelling in the village of Saint Zeno, from the church of Saint Martin at the watercourse as far as the slope, with every due, jurisdiction, action, and court.

Likewise, whatever was granted by Otbert and Adalbert, bishops of Verona, of blessed memory—namely, jurisdiction over theft, adultery, and the ripaticum from the aforesaid church as far as the slope—together with all things belonging to the aforesaid monastery: churches, castles, villages, tenant farmers, slaves, commendati, factitii, etc.

[Col. 1160A] Therefore we order and decree that, whatever the aforesaid church of Saint Zeno is known to possess justly and legally, etc., it shall hold securely, etc.

It shall not be compelled to pay any census, toll, or woodland tax. No one shall dare to enter their villages or castles, hold court there, distrain or pledge their free men or servants, lodge there, or demand any service or exaction.

If anyone should do so, etc.

The sign of the lord Henry III, Roman emperor Augustus.

Burchard, chancellor, acting in place of Sigewin, archchancellor, has verified this.

On the fifteenth day before the Kalends of July, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation [Col. 1160B] 1084, indiction VI; in the twenty-ninth year of the reign of Lord Henry III, Roman emperor, and the first of his empire.

Done at Verona, in the name of Christ. Amen.

Place of the surviving wax seal, bearing the emperor seated, holding a globe in his right hand and a spear in his left, with the inscription: “HEINRICUS, BY THE GRACE OF GOD THIRD … EMPEROR AUGUSTUS.”

### XII. Diploma granted by Emperor Henry III to Rudolph, abbot of Stavelot

It confirms all the monastery’s possessions, immunities, and exchanges; limits the rights of the advocates; and restrains the audacity of the monks of Malmedy. (Year 1089.)

[MARTENE, *Amplissima Collectio*, II, 75.]

[Col. 1160C]

In the name of the holy and indivisible Trinity. The third Henry, chosen by divine mercy, by the grace of God august emperor and patrician of the Romans.

Since we have learned from the authority of Holy Scripture that every person ought to take an example from good things, we acknowledge that it is especially fitting and just that imperial majesty should preserve this matter with the greatest care.
