For an authority of such eminence ought from time to time to review how the possessions of the churches of God are situated, and what has been handed over to them by preceding kings or emperors in their service, and ought to renew and strengthen by letters of its authority what has been handed over or granted by them.

Therefore let all our faithful, present and future, know that the distinguished man Rudolph, abbot [Col. 1160D] of the monasteries called Stavelot and Malmedy—both of which the holy Remaclus, while still living in the body, built and consecrated with the expense and assistance of King Sigebert within our forest, in the woodland of the Ardennes, and in the principal one of which, namely Stavelot, he chose to lie at rest bodily—has come to us with his monks. He brought and presented written accounts of the life of that holy confessor of Christ, Remaclus, as well as the charters of Kings Sigebert, Childeric, and Theuderic, who, at his request and urging, were the founders of those places, and the enactments of Emperors Charles, Louis, the three Ottos, and also of the most serene memory of our father, Emperor Henry. He petitioned our majesty [Col. 1161A] that we should confirm by the authority of our imperial decree all possessions attached or handed over to those churches from the time of Saint Remaclus through the succeeding ages.

Accordingly, by our favor, we have decreed that whatever was handed over or granted in those places during the times of his predecessors, and whatever Emperor Henry restored to Abbot Poppo in Hasbain for the benefit of his soul, or whatever was restored to him by our grandfather of divine memory from Count Hermann—having been unjustly withheld for some time after the death of the heir—namely Scalentin and Palisiol with all their appurtenances, together with the tithes of the churches which our imperial predecessors gave and confirmed to his predecessors, and whatever he purchased for those places—namely a sixth part of Amblava [Col. 1161B] and Tumbis from Count Godfrey of Enghien, or whatever he exchanged from the property of the church, namely Wendengias and Corworo, from the monk who was abbot of Saint Maximinus, giving the villa of Asteleburna in exchange, or whatever he exchanged with Bishop Hathelinus of Bamberg and his provost Liupold—namely the small estate of Lukesenges in exchange for Wendengus and two manses at Andernach, and for the new estate of Buobarde—shall remain unshaken and undisturbed.

[Note: [Col. 1161D] Hathelinus is missing from Bucelinus’s list of the bishops of Bamberg; he should be placed between Hermann, deposed by Gregory VII in 1075, and Rupert, who is found to have held office in 1089.]

Since our royal and imperial predecessors, by the firmness of their authority, decreed for those places that the advocate of those monasteries, in the courts belonging to those places, should not presume to make lodgings or preparations, demand payments or fines, hold a court, or take relay horses for himself without the abbot’s permission or consent, we too confirm and strengthen the same provisions for that abbot and his successors. By the imposition of our ban we reinforce them, so that henceforth no one may dare to violate them. Whatever, moreover, he is found to have acquired in any property of the Church is strengthened by the authority of our decree, and possesses immunity from every harassment by advocates.

And since the enactments of the ancient kings and emperors were not sufficient for the monks established at Malmedy, but under two abbots they attempted to divide those monasteries, which had remained unshaken from the time of Saint Remaclus, for this reason, I say, lest any dispute arise among them thereafter—as is known to have happened in the time of Lord Emperor Otto II, and as also happened for five years and more during the years of our childhood, when we were corrupted by the unsound counsel of certain men—but since at our court held at Liège at Easter in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1071, when Saint Remaclus himself was presented before us [Col. 1161D] to seek justice, it was made abundantly clear—through the miracles which almighty God deigned to display through him before us and our faithful—that what had been unjustly divided by us [Col. 1162A], we acknowledge that we justly restored to him forever.

Therefore we decree most firmly, according to our imperial edict, that henceforth both monasteries shall be subject to a single abbot’s rule, as they have continually remained. And so that our grant, renewal, and confirmation concerning all these matters may possess fuller authority, we have undersigned this decree with our own hand and ordered it to be marked with the impression of our seal.

The sign of Lord Henry III, Roman emperor Augustus.

I, Humbert, chancellor, have authenticated this in place of Ruothard, archchancellor.

Issued on the tenth day before the Kalends of December, in the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1089, indiction XII; in the thirty-sixth year of the reign of Lord Henry III, Roman emperor Augustus, and the sixth of his empire.

Done at Mainz, successfully, in the name of Christ. Amen.

### XIII. Diploma of King Henry IV, the third emperor of that name, by which he confirms certain castles to the Veronese monastery of Saint Zeno

(Year 1090.)

[MURATORI, *Antiquitates Italicae*, V, 623.]

In the name of the holy and indivisible Trinity, Henry, by the gracious favor of God, august emperor of the Romans.

It is fitting for imperial majesty, etc. Therefore, with this just and equitable consideration, out of fear of the Lord and for the salvation of our soul and of our parents, we perpetually confirm and in every way strengthen by this present authority of our munificence the monastery of blessed Zeno: namely, in the judicial district of Garda, the castle called Pastoringo, which Count Arduin of good memory and his son Eriprand, for the salvation of their souls, transferred to the monastery of Saint Zeno by a charter of offering, with all its appurtenances, etc.; and likewise the castle called Isola Nonense, which came to that monastery by offering, donation, and purchase, with every revenue, jurisdiction, and fodrum, etc.

It also pleased our serenity to establish, for eternal reward, [a provision …] that the castle called [Col. 1162D] Capavum, which is known to have been adjudicated and handed over to the monastery of Saint Zeno by Ubertus as a boy, for the salvation of his soul and those of his parents, together with everything belonging to the said castle, including servants and dependants, with all due jurisdiction. This too we confirm and make proprietary to the said monastery of Saint Zeno as an alms for the support of its monks, with all its appurtenances, jurisdictions, etc. Therefore, if any duke, margrave, etc.

[Col. 1163A]

The sign of Lord Henry III, most invincible emperor Augustus. Place of the lost wax seal.

I, Ogerius, by the grace of God bishop of Ivrea and chancellor, have authenticated this in place of Hermann, chancellor.

[…] of the Lord’s Incarnation 1090, indiction VI, while Emperor Henry III was reigning, in the twenty-fourth year of his reign and the eighth of his empire. This was done at Verona on the fourth day before the Ides of April. In God’s name, successfully. Amen.

### XIV. Donation of the castles of Castrum Novum, Campitello, and Scorciarolo, made to Cono, bishop of Mantua, and to his church by King Henry IV, the third emperor of that name

(Year 1093.)

[MURATORI, *Antiquitates Italicae*, V, 645.]

[Col. 1163B]

In the name of the holy and indivisible Trinity. Henry, ever august emperor.

Since we clearly recognize, from the sound counsels of our faithful, that it is opportune and very useful to the welfare and dignity of our kingdom and empire to incline carefully toward those matters which concern the care and honor of our rule, we ought in no way to disregard their salutary counsels if something should arise which does not diminish our honor but exalts the holy Church. For Wisdom says: “Do everything with counsel, and afterward you will not regret it” (Ecclesiasticus 32:24). Moreover, according to the Psalmist, it is the king’s honor to love judgment and justice, and in truth to be able to say with the Psalmist: “Lord, we have loved the beauty of your house” (Psalm 25:8).

Therefore, that through the honoring and enlargement of the gifts of God—whose service we ought unceasingly to pursue out of love, if we desire to be saved and attain eternal glory—we may hear the counsels of our faithful with pious ears, and kindly regard the worthy, humble, and praiseworthy petition of Cono, bishop of Mantua, we have granted by this charter of our decree to the Church of Mantua, to be held and possessed perpetually without disturbance by proprietary right, Castrum Novum, Campitello, and Scorciarolo, with all their appurtenances within and without, while preserving our royal justice.

Therefore, if any duke, margrave, count, viscount, or any other person, of whatever condition, [Col. 1163D] should presume to violate this charter of our decree, he shall be subject to our ban and shall pay a fine of one thousand pounds of pure gold, half to our treasury and half to the aforesaid Church. And so that it may be observed inviolably by all, we carefully ordered it to be marked with the image of our seal.

The sign of Lord Henry, emperor Augustus.

Issued in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1093, while Lord Henry, Roman emperor Augustus, was reigning in the thirty-ninth year, and ruling as emperor in the ninth, indiction V.

Enacted at Mantua successfully.

### XV. Confirmatory diploma of King Henry IV, the third emperor of that name, concerning all the rights of the Church of Pavia

(Year 1093.)

[MURATORI, *Antiquitates Italicae*, VI, 327.]

[Col. 1164A]

[…] also through the intervention of Margrave William, Arduin […] of the greater and lesser citizens of Pavia, to the Pavia Church of the most blessed Syrus, glorious confessor, through whose pious intervention our empire flourishes. […] By this charter of our decree we give and grant in perpetual right, namely the abbey of Bremet, with everything belonging to it: castles, courts, villages, chapels, woods, cultivated and uncultivated lands, pastures, marshes, waters and the courses of waters, fisheries, mills, jurisdictions, tolls, hospices, courts, investitures, […] conditions, and households; also the cells specifically listed here: Saint Peter at Novalesa, Merlet’s field, Saint Andrew at Turin, Babiano, the Serra of Saint Peter, the cell of Cavalaria, Saint Peter at Pagno, Pollentia, Saint Peter at Wascum, Saint Mary at Polexi, the cell of Supunigo, the cell of Laumello, Saint Agatha at Balsula, Rometta; also the castles of Castagneto, Gunzove, Saint Salvator, Cano, […] Taneto, Palaciolo, Cisalum, and the remaining cells […] courts and all possessions belonging to the aforesaid abbey and cells, […] in their entirety.

Therefore, if any duke, margrave, count, viscount, or [Col. 1164C] any other person should presume to violate this charter of our decree, he shall be subject to our ban and shall pay a fine of one thousand pounds of the finest gold, half to our treasury and half to the aforesaid Church of Pavia. And so that it may be believed more firmly and observed inviolably by all, we ordered it to be marked with the impression of our seal.

The sign of Lord Henry, most invincible and most pious Roman emperor, by the power of God.

I, Oglerius, by the grace of God bishop of Ivrea and chancellor, have authenticated this in place of Hermann, archbishop of Cologne and archchancellor.

In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1093, indiction I, while Henry was reigning in the thirty-ninth year and ruling as emperor in the ninth, in the month of May.

[Col. 1164D] Done at Pavia successfully.

### XVI. Decree of Emperor Henry III promulgated at a court held at Padua for the protection of certain properties belonging to the monks of Saint Justina of Padua

(Year 1095.)

[MURATORI, *Antiquitates Italicae*, II, 943.]

While Lord Henry, by the grace of God the third Roman emperor Augustus, was sitting in judgment in the city of Padua, in the Broilo beside the episcopal residence, there were present with him Walbrun, bishop of Verona and chancellor; Bruchard and Walner, margraves; Count Boniface; Count Manfred; Hisnard, Aldecher, Aichard, [Col. 1165A] Hugo, and Gumbert, judges; Peregrinus of Verona; Ubertus of Fontanaviva; Cono; Gumbert of Talsano; Odelric of Salvazano; Ucho of Casale; Baronzello; Cono of Patuaro; Bernard Almenardo; Odo of Justinus, judge; and many others.

There John, priest and monk, prior of the monastery of Saint Justina, came into their presence with the other monks of the same monastery, together with Ingelero, advocate of the aforesaid monastery. They reported, began to say, and requested a favor:

“We ask you, lord emperor, that for God’s sake and for your reward you place your ban upon us and upon those properties which Litulf of Cararia restored to us here in your presence, namely the court called Montesilice, with all the possessions belonging to that court; and upon those properties which the brothers Milo and Henry likewise restored to us here in your presence, namely the villa called Lignaria and the villa called Ronchi, with all their appurtenances; and the villa called Tribano and Caput Silvae.”

Then, when the aforesaid lord emperor had heard this petition, by the counsel of the judges who were present, and by means of the staff which he held in his hand, he placed his ban upon the aforesaid monks, upon their advocate, upon the aforesaid monastery, and upon all the aforesaid properties, as they are written above [Col. 1165C] in their entirety, so that no person whatsoever might dare to disturb, molest, or dispossess the aforesaid monastery of those properties [Col. 1166A].

Whoever should do so shall know that he must pay one hundred pounds of the finest gold: half to the treasury of the lord emperor and half to the aforesaid monastery of Saint Justina. Moreover, he imposed a ban so that no bishop or abbot might dare to give the aforesaid properties to anyone as a benefice, pledge them to anyone under the title of security, or remove them by any device whatsoever from the hands of the brothers. Whoever should do so shall know that he must pay one hundred pounds of the finest gold to the public authority.

When both the case and the record had been concluded, they instructed that the foregoing should be written for the security of the aforesaid monastery of Saint Justina.

And I, John the notary, at the command of the lord emperor and at the urging of the judges, wrote this in the year from the Incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ 1095, on the second day before the Kalends of June, indiction III.

I, Henry, by the grace of God third Roman emperor Augustus, have subscribed.

I, Wilbrun, chancellor, at the command of the lord emperor, have subscribed with my own hand.

I, Isnard, judge, have subscribed.

I, Aldegerius, judge, was present.

I, Hugo, judge, was present.

I, Gumbert, judge, was present.

I, Agichard, judge, was present.

[Col. 1166C] I, Peregrinus, judge, was present.

# Ecclesiastical Laws and Diplomas of the Kings of the English Who Flourished in the Eleventh Century

## Aethelred II

(Year 979–1016.)

### Ecclesiastical Laws of Aethelred

(MANSI, *Councils*, vol. XIX, col. 319.)

There are four parts in the Jornall manuscript. The first three contribute nothing to the matter of the Church; the fourth contains the following chapters.

### Titles of the Chapters

[Col. 1165D]

I. On giving the penny of the holy Church and on the tithing of the thegns.

II. On fasting and observing the three days before the feast of Saint Michael.

III. What is to be sung every day for the king and all the people.

IV. On restoring the customary dues of the holy Church of God.

[Col. 1166D]

V. That no one be sold outside the country.

VI. On robbery.

VII. On alms and the rights of the Church.

### These Chapters Were Established by King Aethelred and His Wise Men at Habam

#### I

First, that one God be loved and honored above all things, and that everyone obey his king as his predecessors did more faithfully, and together with him defend his kingdom. And first they established that God’s mercy and help should be invoked through fasts, alms, confession, and abstinence, and that they should abstain from evil deeds and injustice.

And that a penny, or something worth a penny, be given from every ploughland; and everyone who has a household shall ensure that each of his *hirmanni* gives one penny. If he does not have one, his lord shall give it for him. And every thegn shall tithe everything that he possesses.

#### II

And we decree that every Christian who has reached the proper age shall fast for three days before the feast of Saint Michael, fasting on bread and water and raw herbs [the printed text reads *bis*, apparently for *herbis*]. Every person shall go to confession and to church barefoot, and shall renounce all sins by making amends and ceasing from them.

Every priest shall go with his people in procession for three days barefoot. In addition, every priest shall sing thirty Masses; every deacon and cleric shall recite thirty psalms. For three days, a ration for each person shall be prepared without meat in food or drink, as he ought to eat it, and all of it shall be distributed to the poor.

Every servant shall be free from work during those three days, so that he may fast as well as possible; he may work for himself whatever he wishes. These are the three days: Monday, Tuesday, and Wednesday immediately before the feast of Saint Michael.

If anyone breaks his fast, a slave shall make compensation with his hide; a free poor man shall pay thirty pence; and a royal thegn one hundred and twenty shillings. This money shall be distributed to the poor. And every priest, *tungravius*, and tithing-man shall know that this alms and fast must take effect, as they will be able to swear by the holy things.

#### III

And we command that in every assembly one Mass be sung daily in common for the king and all his people, at the morning Mass, which is entitled “Against the Pagans.” At each hour the entire congregation shall sing, with their bodies extended on the ground, the psalm “Lord, how they have multiplied” (Psalm 3), and the collect against the pagans. Let this be done for as long as this necessity lies upon us.

And in every monastery or gathering of monks, every priest shall celebrate separately thirty Masses for the king and all the people, and every monk shall recite thirty [Col. 1167D] psalters.

#### IV

And we command that every person, out of love for God and all the saints, give *cyrisceat* and his proper tithe, as he did in the days of our predecessors, when he acted better. This means that as the plough travels through the land, a tenth acre shall be given.

Every customary due shall be rendered, out of friendship with God, to the mother church to which it is adjacent. Let no one take from God what belongs to God and what our predecessors granted.

#### V

And we prohibit anyone from being sold outside the country. If anyone presumes to do this, let him be outside the blessing of God and all the saints, and outside the whole Christian community, unless he repents and makes amends as his bishop shall instruct him.

[Col. 1168A]

#### VI

And we prohibit robbery for everyone. Every person, poor and rich, shall be worthy under the public law, and every robbery shall be compensated. If anyone commits one, let him make amends as was formerly established and afterward observed. If a reeve commits one, he shall make double the compensation that would be adjudged to another.

#### VII

And the money for alms shall be paid here by the feast of Saint Michael if it has fallen into arrears anywhere for a full year; and thereafter, every year, God’s dues shall be paid in all the matters mentioned above, for the love of God and all the saints, so that almighty God may show us mercy and grant us triumph over our enemies and peace. Let this be diligently entreated, so that we may obtain his mercy here and rest without end in the future. Amen.

### On the Office of a Judge

Every just judge shall dispense mercy and judgment in all things, so that first, through correct knowledge, he may prescribe compensation according to the fault and then measure it according to indulgence. Some faults are judged by us judges to require proper compensation; some are to be forgiven through God’s mercy.

Judgments must be free from every *Haderunga* [harassment or vexation], so that no one—poor, friend, or enemy—is excused from the public law owed to the ruler. Nothing is more unjust than accepting gifts in order to overturn a judgment, because gifts stir the hearts of the wise and subvert the words of the just (Deuteronomy 16).

The Lord Jesus said: “With what judgment you judge, you shall be judged” (Matthew 7). Let every judge fear and love his own judge, lest on the day of judgment he become speechless and be humbled before the eyes of the Judge who sees all.

Whoever oppresses the innocent and releases the guilty for money, friendship, hatred, or any faction will be oppressed by the almighty Judge. Let no lord appoint foolish or wicked judges, because the fool avoids the truth he has learned through ignorance, and the wicked through greed.

The poor are torn apart more grievously by corrupt judges than by bloodthirsty enemies. No enemy is more bitter, no plague more effective, than a familiar enemy. A person can sometimes avoid corrupt judges by flight or self-defense. Judges cannot do so when they are inflamed against their subjects by evil desires.

Often good judges also have wicked deputies and abominable ministers, whose conduct binds the judges themselves if they do not restrain them and hold them back from plunder, because the Lord and minister of the ages says: “Not only those who do evil, but all who consent to them, are worthy of eternal death” (Romans 1).

Often wicked judges pervert or delay judgment and do not conclude a case until their will has been fulfilled. And when they judge, wicked judges consider not deeds but gifts, according to the word of the Wise: “Like ravening wolves in the evening, they leave nothing until morning” (Wisdom 3)—that is, they think only of the present life and consider nothing of the future.

It is the custom of wicked reeves to take away whatever they can and scarcely leave a little of what is necessary for sustenance. An angry judge cannot approach a proper satisfaction of judgment, for, blinded by rage, he does not perceive the clarity of righteousness.

Judgment is just when a person’s status is not considered. It is written: “Do not regard the person of a man in judgment, nor act for anyone so as to turn away from the truth and judge unjustly.” Accepting a gift is the abandonment of truth.

## Privilege of King Aethelred for the Church of Canterbury

By which he rejoices in and confirms the expulsion of the clerics from Christ Church, Canterbury, and the introduction of monks, and grants that church many villages and very extensive privileges.

(MANSI, *Councils*, vol. XIX, col. 321, from the Cottonian manuscript Claudius A. 3.)

[Col. 1169B]

In the name of the Lord God almighty. I, Aethelred, by the grace of God king of the English people and also monarch of the other surrounding islands.

I make known to the Christian English that the venerable Archbishop Aelfric, through his episcopal wisdom, has often caused me to devote myself to the commandments of God; and I too, moved by God, wish diligently to learn whatever from his divine teaching and preaching is necessary for me. I understand that this discipline has been excessively destroyed and abolished through human wickedness and injustice.

In my understanding I also see and clearly perceive that this discipline has been negligently corrupted far and wide through the carelessness of priests, and I deeply grieve that the service of God has been abandoned and grown cold. I also told my counselors, who give me counsel about divine and worldly affairs, that God had given them understanding for the uplifting of my mind.

Then they said that, with God’s help, it would be better if I expelled the priests from Christ’s churches because of their manifest wickedness and crimes, and installed in Christ’s churches men of the monastic order who would properly offer prayers and thanks to God there for me and my people.

I did this. I installed monks in Christ’s churches, following the example of those whom Saint Augustine brought here—namely, those holy monks whom, at the command of Saint Gregory and with the counsel and assistance of the great King Aethelberht, he had placed in Christ’s churches, bringing them with him into this land. When those monks later became bishops because of their holy way of life, their ecclesiastical lands flourished.

I also confirm by this privilege that the monks living and assembled there shall remain there forever, and I specifically set down their estates, which in ancient times, and afterward from me, King of the English, and from other faithful men, have hitherto been granted to their holy see.

The first is Eastridge, which district I grant perpetually to Christ Church for the sake of my soul, both in its lands and on the seashore. Then Joccham, Bosingtun, Edesham and Apeldra, little Berwick, and Swordlings; Praostatum, Gravenea, Wylan, Ciart, Fernleah.

In Sussex, Peccingas.

In western Kent, Meapham and Culingas.

In Surrey, near London, Wealawyroth, likewise beyond the Thames.

Hrisebyrgan, at the edge of the Chilterns, adjoining the city of Christ Church.

In Essex, Laelling.

In eastern Anglia, Haedleh and the neighboring Illaleh.

In the region of Thanet, certain lands.

Henceforth let this aforesaid monastery be free from every earthly service, together with all the villages belonging to it: in fields, pastures, meadows, woods, salt marshes, fisheries, hunting, and fowling, except these three duties: military service, the repair of bridges, and the repair of fortifications.

If any well-mannered person increases this privilege of mine with benefits, may almighty God fill his dwelling in the heavenly mansions [Col. 1170C] with all the saints. But if any wicked person, inflamed by the devil, diminishes or despises this privilege of mine, may he be the companion of Judas, the betrayer of Christ, and may he be torn by the teeth of infernal dogs amid the dreadful punishments of Gehenna, with all the devils, without end—unless before his death he properly corrects what he has wickedly done against his lord.

Indeed, it is better for a person to guard against sins than laboriously to correct them. I beseech and adjure all my lawful successors—kings, bishops, senators, and rulers of the people—not to be plunderers of Christ’s Church, but diligent guardians of Christ’s patrimony and of those monks who serve God there, so that forever you may enjoy rest, eternal life, and joy with all his saints, always and forever. Amen.

I, Aethelred of England, confirm this privilege of Christ Church by the authority of Christ.

I, Aelfric, archbishop of Christ Church, strengthen the munificence of the good king forever with the sign of the cross.

I, Wulfstan, bishop of London, always consent to the noble gift of my lord.

I, Aelfheah, bishop of Winchester, confirm this writing of the aforesaid king with all my strength.

I, Ordbyrht, bishop, have done the same with God’s blessing.

I, Aethelric, bishop, have done the same.

I, Athulf, bishop, have done the same.

I, Godwin, bishop, have done all the same.

I, Lyfing, bishop, confirm forever the will and goodness of my lord.

[Col. 1172A]

I, Wulfric, abbot, am a true witness.

I, Aelsward, abbot, likewise.

I, Wulfosar, abbot.

I, Aelflige, abbot.

# King Canute

Second of this name among the Danish kings and first among the English.

(Year 1014–1036.)

[Col. 1171]

## Ecclesiastical Laws of King Canute

(MANSI, *Councils*, vol. XIX, col. 555, from the Cottonian manuscript Nero A. 1, compared with our Anglo-Saxon laws.)

This is the counsel which Cnut, king of all England, the Danes, and the Norwegians, established with the counsel of his wise men, for the praise of God, for his own royal honor, and for the benefit of the people. This was at the holy Nativity of our Lord at Winchester.

### I. On Properly Honoring God, Religion, and the King

[Col. 1171B]

This, therefore, is the first requirement: that they should always love one God above all other things, preserve one Christianity unanimously, and honor King Cnut with just fidelity.

### II. On the Peace of God, the King, and the Churches

Let them greet and protect the churches of God, and frequently attend them for the salvation of their souls and for our own benefit. Every church is by right in Christ’s own peace, and every Christian ought to labor greatly to hold that peace in high reverence.

For divine peace, and the king’s peace, which is closest to it, must be obtained and diligently preserved above every other peace. Therefore it is entirely just that the ecclesiastical peace of God within the walls, and the peace granted by the hand of the Christian king, should always remain inviolable.

If anyone violates either of them, let him lose country and life, unless the king wishes to pardon him. If anyone thereafter violates God’s ecclesiastical peace so severely that he becomes a murderer within the church walls, this is then inexpiable, and all who are friends of God shall pursue him—unless he manages to escape from there and flee to so great an asylum that the king, after full compensation both before God and before men, pardons him his life on that account.

First, he must pay Christ and the king the assessed value of his life, and in this way restore himself from outlawry by compensation. If the matter then comes to compensation and the king permits it, the ecclesiastical peace shall be paid to that church by full compensation for breach of the king’s peace, and he shall obtain reconciliation with the church as is fitting. Thereafter he shall fully pay compensation both to the relatives and to the men of the slain, and at least intercede before God.

### III. On the Fine to Be Paid According to the Dignity of the Church

If the peace of any church is violated without killing, it shall be diligently compensated according to the nature of what was done—whether the breach occurred through fighting, robbery, or anything else—and according to the dignity of the church.

Not all churches are equally worthy of earthly honor, although they possess the same ecclesiastical consecration. The breach of the primary peace of a church is equivalent to compensation for property under the king’s peace: namely, five pounds according to English law.

In Kent, for violation of the peace, five pounds shall be paid to the king and three to the archbishop. For an ordinary church, the amount is 120 shillings, and the same applies to the king’s fine. For an even smaller church, where the ministry is small but there is nevertheless a cemetery, it is 60 shillings; for a rural temple without a cemetery, 30 [Col. 1172C] shillings.

### IV. On the Reverence to Be Shown to Priests

It is especially fitting that all Christians should always attend and protect the sanctuary, the orders, and the consecrated house of God with the greatest diligence, and should honor each order according to its dignity.

Let everyone who wishes or is able understand how great and glorious is the task which a priest undertakes for the salvation of the people, if he properly pleases his Lord. Great is exorcism, and glorious is consecration, which drives away the devil and makes him flee whenever baptism is performed or the holy Eucharist is consecrated.

The holy angels are also present there in abundance, guarding those things and assisting the priest through God’s power whenever he properly serves Christ. They do this whenever he diligently invokes Christ from the depths of his heart and carefully intercedes for the needs of the people. For the fear of God, priests must be acknowledged with due regard to the dignity of their order.

### V. On the Purification of the Ordained
And if it should happen that someone burdens a priest who lives according to the rule with accusations and calumnies, while the priest himself is conscious of his innocence, let him celebrate Mass, if he dares, and clear himself alone by the Eucharist from a single accusation; and let him purge a threefold accusation, if he dares, even in the Holy Eucharist with two others of the same order as himself. If someone accuses a deacon who lives according to the rule on a single charge, let him take two others of the same order and clear himself with them. And if he is accused on a threefold charge, let him take six of the same order (and let himself be the seventh) and clear himself with them. If a parish priest is burdened with accusations that he does not lead a regular life, let him clear himself as a deacon who leads a regular life does. And if someone burdens an altar-servant, deprived of friends and without compurgators, with accusations, let him go to the accursed morsel, and let it be done there as God wills, unless he can clear himself by the Holy Eucharist. And if someone accuses a man ordained to sacred office out of enmity, saying that he is the perpetrator or adviser of a homicide, let him clear himself through his kinsmen, who ought either to endure or to make compensation for the enmity. And if he is without kinsmen, let him clear himself through associates, or undertake a fast, if he dares, and proceed to the accursed morsel; and let it be done there as God shall judge. And no temple-monk shall ever be obliged by law to demand compensation for an enmity, or to pay compensation for an enmity; let him lay aside the laws of kinship when he passes over to the regular laws. And if a priest should ever have been a false witness, or perjured, or conscious of theft, or have been an adviser to it, then let him be excluded from the consecrated church, and everywhere lose both fellowship and friendship, as well as everyone’s respect, unless he makes compensation in a greater manner before God and men, according to the instruction of the bishop, and finds a surety for himself that henceforth he will always abstain from a similar crime. And if he wishes to clear himself, let him purge himself according to the nature of the deed, whether by a threefold or a simple purgation, in accordance with the deed.

### VI. Exhortation to ecclesiastics, that they may live holily

And we wish men of every order diligently to submit themselves individually to the law that pertains to them; and especially God’s ministers—bishops and abbots, monks and nuns, canons and consecrated women—to incline toward what is right, to live according to the rule, and by day and night, often and repeatedly, to invoke Christ and diligently intercede for all the Christian people.

And we beseech and instruct all God’s ministers, especially priests, to obey God, to love chastity, and to guard themselves from God’s anger and from the seething fire that rages in hell. Let them know most diligently that they absolutely must not have intercourse with a woman. And if anyone wishes to abstain from this and preserve chastity, let him have God’s mercy and, as regards earthly honor, be worthy by law of a thane’s status. And let every Christian, out of fear of his Lord, diligently avoid unlawful intercourse and justly observe the ecclesiastical laws.

### VII. Concerning prohibited marriages

We also teach, beseech, and command in God’s name that no Christian shall ever take a wife within the sixth degree of kinship in his own affinity; nor his kinsman’s widow, to whom that kinsman was related in the same degree; nor his wife’s kinswoman whom he himself had previously had; nor his sponsor; nor a consecrated woman; nor a woman who has been repudiated. No Christian shall ever take as a wife, or pursue, any prostitute; nor shall he have more than one wife at a time, and she must be a lawfully married wife, but he shall live with her alone for as long as she lives. Thus must always act anyone who wishes to observe God’s laws rightly and guard his soul from the fire of hell.

### VIII. Concerning the payment of tithes

And God’s dues shall be justly and diligently paid every year: namely, the alms of the plough on the fifteenth day after Easter; the tithes of offspring at Pentecost; and the first-fruits of the earth at the feast of All Saints. And if anyone is then unwilling to pay the tithes, as we have said—that is, the tithes of the field, in the same manner as the plough has advanced—then the king’s and the bishop’s reeves, the owner of the estate, and the priest of the church shall meet, take by force from him a tenth part for the church to which it belongs, and assign to him a ninth part. The eighth part shall be divided in two, and the landowner shall receive one half and the bishop the other, whether the land belongs to the king or to a thane’s minister.

### IX. Concerning Peter’s penny

And Peter’s penny shall be paid at the feast of Peter. If anyone retains it until after that day, let him give the penny to the bishop, add thirty [pennies], and pay the king one hundred and twenty shillings.

### X. Concerning the first-fruits of seed

And the first-fruits of seed shall be paid at the feast of Martin. If anyone retains them after that day [casusque: uncertain reading], let him give them to the bishop, make compensation elevenfold, and pay the king one hundred and twenty shillings.

### XI. Concerning tithes belonging to a thane’s church

If there is a thane who has a church in his possession in which there is a cemetery, let him then give a third part of his own tithes to his church. And if anyone has a church in which there is no cemetery, let him give his priest whatever he wishes from the nine parts; and every church-tax shall be delivered first to the church from all the hearths of free men.

### XII. Concerning money for lamps

And the candle-money shall be paid three times a year: first, at the vigil of Easter, wax worth half an obol for each hide; then at the feast of All Saints the same amount; and afterward, similarly, at the Purification of Blessed Mary.

### XIII. Concerning the money called the soul-penny, and burial

And it is most equitable that the burial payment always be paid at the open grave. If anyone buries elsewhere a body from his own parish, the burial payment shall nevertheless be paid to the church to which it belongs.

### XIV. Concerning the preservation of God’s dues, feasts, and fasts

And all God’s dues shall be carefully preserved as necessity requires; feasts and fasts shall be observed in the proper manner. The celebration of every Sunday feast shall begin on Saturday afternoon and continue until dawn on Monday; and so shall every other feast, according to the manner in which it has been appointed.

### XV. Concerning Sunday

And on Sunday we most strictly forbid trading, every assembly of the people unless there is the greatest necessity, and hunting; and everyone must diligently abstain from all worldly work on this holy day.

### XVI. Concerning fasts

And every fast that has been imposed shall be observed with complete diligence, whether it is the fast of the Four Ember Seasons, the Lenten fast, or any other fast. There shall also be fasting on every feast of Blessed Mary and on the feast of every apostle, except the feast of Philip and James, because we do not impose any fast before the feast of Easter. There shall also be fasting on every Friday unless it is a feast. It is not necessary to fast from Easter until Pentecost unless a fast has been imposed or one wishes absolutely to fast; nor from the Nativity of the Lord until the octave of Epiphany—that is, seven days after the twelfth-day feast.

### XVII. Concerning the times for justice

And we forbid ordeals and oaths on feast days, on the days of the Four Ember Seasons, on the days of Lent, and on the appointed days of fasting; from the Advent of the Lord until the eighth day after the twelfth day has passed; and from Septuagesima until the fifteenth day after Easter.

And the wise chose the feast of Saint Edward to be celebrated throughout all England—namely, 14 March, the fifteenth day before the Kalends of April—and the feast of Saint Dunstan, the fourteenth day before the Kalends of June, that is, 30 May. During these holy seasons, as is just, let there be peace and concord among all Christians, and let every fraud be dispersed. And if anyone owes another a surety-payment or compensation for earthly goods, let him diligently repay it before or after.

### XVIII. Pious exhortation to confession and penance

We also beseech, for the love of God, that every Christian diligently understand his own true advantage. Above all, we ought to await a time when, having obeyed God’s will as diligently as we have been able for as long as possible, it will be more pleasing to us than everything that exists in the whole world. But then we must receive the single reward of what we previously did in life. Woe then to those who have earned hell’s punishment.

Therefore we must act, turning back from our sins with the utmost diligence, and each of us must diligently confess our offenses to our confessor, so that we may always abstain from them and diligently make compensation. And let each of us impose on others what we wish to be imposed upon ourselves. This is a just law and highly pleasing to God, and the person who keeps this law will be most blessed. For almighty God created us all and afterward redeemed us at a great price—that is, by his own life, which he gave for us all.

### XIX. Concerning the Eucharist and uprightness

And every Christian shall do what is required of him: let him diligently attend to his Christian duty and prepare himself for communion in the Holy Eucharist at least three times a year. Anyone who wishes to understand his own need must do this. Let him order his words and deeds toward every friend with justice, and carefully keep his oath and covenant. Let every injustice be diligently driven from this land, as far as possible, and from now on let God’s justice be diligently loved in word and deed. Then God’s mercy will be nearer to us all.

### XX. Concerning fidelity toward lords

Let us also diligently do as we teach: let us always be obedient and faithful to our lord, perpetually uphold his interests with all our strength, and carry out his will. For everything we have ever done faithfully for the true Lord, we do for our own greater benefit. God is surely gracious to the person who is truly obedient to his lord. It is also of great benefit to every lord that he govern his servants justly.

### XXI. Concerning worshiping God from the heart and faith

And we teach all Christians with the greatest diligence always to love God with their inner heart, willingly to preserve the true Christian faith, carefully to listen to ecclesiastical teachers, and often and repeatedly to contemplate and examine God’s teaching and laws for their own benefit.

### XXII. That they should know the Lord’s Prayer and the Creed by heart

We also teach that every Christian should learn enough to be able rightly to understand the true faith, and should learn the *Pater Noster* and the *Credo*, since every Christian ought to implore God by the one and to show the true faith by the other. Christ himself first prayed the *Pater Noster* and taught this prayer to his disciples (Matthew 6).

In this ecclesiastical prayer there are seven petitions. Whoever prays it from the heart always sends a message to God himself for whatever benefit is necessary to him, whether in this life or in the future one. But how can anyone ever pray to God from the heart unless he possesses inward charity and true faith in God? For the person who refuses to learn these things does not afterward die in the communion of Christians, nor rest in a consecrated cemetery, nor receive the Holy Eucharist during his life, nor is he a good Christian. Nor can he properly receive another person for baptism or confirmation unless he learns these things, so that he may know them well.

### XXIII. That they should avoid deadly sins

We also teach that deadly sins and devilish deeds be avoided by everyone with the greatest diligence; and if anyone, through the devil’s instigation, has fallen into sins, let him gladly make compensation according to the confessor’s counsel.

### XXIV. And among these, fornication

We also teach that people must always be admonished to abstain from disgraceful fornication, unlawful intercourse, and every form of adultery.

### XXV. That they should beware of the dreadful judgment

We also teach that every person should diligently keep the fear of God in his heart, beware of sins day and night, fear the day of judgment, abhor hell, and always consider that the end of his days stands before him.

### XXVI. That bishops and priests should faithfully perform their duties

Let bishops be heralds and teachers of God’s laws, and let them gladly explain ecclesiastical duties and teach them by their example. Let anyone who wishes attend to these matters. For a pastor who refuses to defend by his cry the flock that he ought to protect, whenever some harm begins to injure the flock, will be found useless, if he is otherwise able to do so.

No harm is so evil as the devil himself, who is always plotting only how he may injure human souls most greatly. Therefore pastors must be very watchful and cry out diligently; they must protect the people from this public robber. These are the bishops and presbyters, who ought to defend and protect the ecclesiastical flock through wise teachings, lest the mad werewolf tear it apart too severely or bite many from the ecclesiastical flock.

And if anyone takes the greatest care to obey God’s messengers, it is the same as obeying God himself. May the name of God always be blessed, and may praise, honor, and glory be his throughout all ages of the world. Amen.

[Col. 1177C] This is the secular counsel which, after consultation with my wise men, I wish to be observed throughout all England.

### I. Concerning justice and its enforcement (Laws of the Saxons 1)

This, then, is the first thing I desire: that just laws be enacted, that every injustice be diligently condemned, and that everything unjust be weeded out and eradicated from this land as diligently as possible; that God’s justice be advanced; and that thereafter all people, both poor and rich, enjoy the protection of public law and receive a just judgment.

### II. Concerning mercy to be shown in judgment (Laws of the Saxons 2)

We also teach that, even if someone commits an offense and afterward deeply repents, moderation should then be applied in imposing the punishment, as is fitting before God and tolerable before the world. Let the person presiding over the judgment remember most diligently what he himself has done when he says: “And forgive us our debts, as we also forgive” (Matthew 6).

And we forbid that a Christian be handed over to death, above all, for even a minor matter. Rather, let a mild punishment be established for the benefit of the people. Let the work of God’s hands not be destroyed for a small matter, nor his own possession, which the flesh redeemed.

### III. Concerning not selling a Christian outside the kingdom (Laws of the Saxons 3)

We also forbid that any Christian be sold far from the country or even led into heathenism. Instead, let him be carefully cherished, lest the soul perish which Christ redeemed with his own life.

### IV. Concerning the expulsion of sorceresses, diviners, and others (Laws of the Saxons 4)

We also forbid this, and command that they begin diligently to cleanse the land everywhere and abstain everywhere from wicked practices. If sorceresses, diviners, assassins, or prostitutes are found anywhere in the country, let them be carefully led out of that land, or let them perish there altogether, unless they cease from their evil deeds and make compensation in a greater manner.

We also command that fugitives and outlaws from God and men be expelled from their homeland unless they submit and amend their ways with the greatest diligence. Let public thieves and robbers quickly perish unless they cease from their crimes.

### V. Concerning the abolition of heathen superstitions (Laws of the Saxons 5)

We also seriously forbid paganism. Paganism is when someone worships idols or heathen gods, the sun or moon, fire or rivers, torrents or stones, or the wood of trees of any kind; or when someone loves sorcery, commits apostasy in any way, or accomplishes something by divination, a torch, or any kind of apparition.

### VI. Concerning homicidal, perjured, and adulterous persons (Laws of the Saxons 6)

Homicides, perjurers, violators of orders, and adulterers must submit and amend their ways, or knowingly die in their sins.

### VII. That sin is more shameful on holy days and in holy places, and that the great should be punished more severely (Laws of the Saxons 35)

Injustice is permitted at no time. Nevertheless, it must be avoided with the greatest diligence on feast days, during fasts, and in holy places. And always, the more powerful or higher in rank a person is, the more he must amend injustice before God and the world. Ecclesiastical compensation must always be diligently sought from written law, and secular compensation from secular law.

### VIII. Concerning killing an altar-servant (Laws of the Saxons 36)

If anyone kills an altar-servant, let him be an outlaw before God and men, unless he makes greater compensation through exile and also before the kinsmen, or clears himself by a capital purgation. Within thirty days he must begin paying compensation everywhere, both before God and before men, giving all that he possesses.

### IX. That the king should be the protector of the ordained and of foreigners (Laws of the Saxons 37)

If anyone in any way deceives a person ordained to sacred office or a foreigner in matters concerning money or life, then let the king stand to him in place of a kinsman and in place of a protector, unless he has another lord. Let compensation be made to the king as is fitting, or let that deed be avenged as severely as possible. It is most fitting for a Christian king to avenge God’s injury with the utmost severity on account of what has been done.

### X. Concerning an altar-servant who commits homicide, and so forth (Laws of the Saxons 38)

If an altar-servant becomes a homicide or commits some other great offense, let him thereafter lose both his order and his honor, and go into exile as far away as the pope prescribes. Let him willingly make amends; and if he wishes to clear himself, let him purge himself threefold. If within thirty days he has not begun compensation before God and men, let him be an outlaw.

### XI. Concerning binding, beating, or abusing an ordained person (Laws of the Saxons 39)

If anyone binds, beats, or grievously insults a person ordained to sacred office, let him compensate him as is just, pay the bishop a fine for the purification of the altar according to the dignity of the order, and pay the lord or king for the full violation of the peace; or let him clear himself by a complete defense.

### XII. Concerning an ordained person accused of a capital crime (Laws of the Saxons 40)

If anyone ordained to sacred office commits a capital crime, let him be apprehended and brought before the episcopal court for what he has done.

### XIII. Concerning an accused person requesting a confessor (Laws of the Saxons 41)

If anyone accused of a capital crime wishes diligently to confess, this must never be denied him. If anyone denies it to him, let him make compensation to the king of one hundred and twenty shillings, or clear himself by taking five men, with himself as the sixth.

### XIV. Concerning the observance of Sunday and feast days (Laws of the Saxons 42)

If it is possible to apprehend him, no person who is to be killed shall ever be killed on the feast of Sunday, unless he flees or fights. Rather, let him be apprehended and held until the feast day has passed.

If a free man works on a feast day, let him compensate for it with a neck-bound fine, and at least diligently make compensation before God, according to the teaching. If a slave works, let him be flogged, or pay the price of the flogging according to what he has done. If a lord forces his slaves to work on a feast day, let him lose the slave, and let the slave thereafter be free. The lord shall pay the penalty for violating the law among the Danes and a fine among the English, according to what he has done, or clear himself.

### XV. Concerning one who violates a fast (Laws of the Saxons 43)

If a free man breaks a true fast, let him pay the penalty for violating the law among the Danes and a fine among the English, according to what he has done. It is bad to eat before the meal during a true fast, and worse still to defile oneself with meat. If a slave does this, let him be flogged, or pay the price of the flogging according to what he has done.

### XVI. That Lent and the feasts should not be violated (Laws of the Saxons 44)

If anyone publicly breaks Lent through fighting, inheritance, robbery, or any wicked deed, let him make compensation twice over, as on a great feast, according to what he has done. If anyone denies this, let him clear himself by a threefold purgation.

### XVII. Concerning one who forcibly resists the church’s jurisdiction (Laws of the Saxons 45)

If anyone forcibly opposes ecclesiastical judgments, let him pay the penalty for violating the law among the Danes and a fine among the English, or clear himself by taking eleven men, with himself as the twelfth.

If he wounds anyone, let him make compensation for it, pay the lord the full fine, and redeem his hand from the bishop, or lose it. If he kills anyone, let him be an outlaw, and let all who wish justice pursue him with a public outcry. If he himself was the cause of the person’s death because that person opposed justice, and this is confirmed, let him lie unavenged.

### XVIII. Concerning one who violates a sacred order (Laws of the Saxons 46)

If anyone violates a sacred order, let him make amends according to the dignity of the order, whether by the assessed value of the person’s life, by a fine, by the penalty for violating the law, or by surrendering all his property.

### XIX. Concerning adultery (Laws of the Saxons 47)

If anyone commits adultery, let him make amends for what has been done. It is a bad adultery when a married man has intercourse with an unmarried woman, and much worse when he has intercourse with another man’s wife or with a woman who has taken sacred vows.

### XX. Concerning incestuous persons (Laws of the Saxons 48)

If anyone commits incest, let him make compensation according to the dignity of the kinship, whether by the assessed value of the person’s life, by a fine, or by surrendering all his property. It is not the same matter to have intercourse with one’s sister as with a more distant kinswoman.

### XXI. Concerning one who violates a widow (Laws of the Saxons 49)

If anyone violates a widow by force, let him make compensation according to the assessed value of the person’s life. If anyone violates a girl by force, let him make compensation according to the assessed value of the person’s life.

### XXII. Concerning the severe punishment of an adulterous wife (Laws of the Saxons 50)

If, while her husband is alive, a wife has intercourse with another man, and this becomes manifest, let her thereafter be infamous in the world. Let her true husband have everything that she possessed, and let her lose both her nose and her ears. If there is an accusation and the purgation fails, then let the bishop have authority over her and judge her with the utmost severity.

### XXIII. Concerning a married man who commits fornication or keeps a concubine (Laws of the Saxons 51)

If a married man has intercourse with his own female slave, let him lose her and make compensation for her before God and men. If anyone has a lawful wife and also a concubine, let no priest perform for him any of the rites that ought to be performed for Christians, unless he ceases, makes the greatest possible amends according to the bishop’s instruction, and afterward abstains from the same practices.

### XXIV. That foreign men who are sexually immoral should be expelled (Laws of the Saxons 52)

If foreign men refuse to reform their sexual conduct, let them be expelled from the country together with their possessions and sins.

### XXV. That a homicide who fails in his purgation should be handed over to the bishop (Laws of the Saxons 53)

If it becomes evident that someone has been killed, let the homicide be handed over to the kinsmen. If there is an accusation and the purgation goes badly, let the bishop judge.

### XXVI. Concerning one who keeps an excommunicated person or outlaw in custody (Laws of the Saxons 64)

If anyone unjustly retains a fugitive from God, let him hand him over to justice, make compensation to the person to whom he belongs, and make compensation to the king according to the assessed value of the person’s life. If anyone has an excommunicated person or an outlaw and keeps him in custody, let him pay with his life and all his property.

### XXVII. Concerning mercy to be shown (Laws of the Saxons 65)

And if anyone wishes diligently to turn back from injustice to justice, let him obtain mercy out of fear of God, in the best and most diligent manner possible.

### The pious conclusion of the pious king (Laws of the Saxons, Epilogue)

Now I diligently beseech and, in God’s name, pray every person to turn to his Lord from his inmost heart, and often and repeatedly to consider with the greatest diligence what he ought to do and what he ought to omit.

It is most fitting for us all to love God, obey God’s laws, and diligently obey ecclesiastical teachers, since they will lead us to judgment when God judges everyone according to his deeds. Blessed is the shepherd who, because of his deeds, can lead his flock to God’s kingdom and to joyful heavenly gladness. It is also well with that flock which follows the shepherd who rescued it from devils and acquired it for God.

Come, then, let us all, with one accord, diligently please our Lord by doing what is just, and henceforth carefully beware of the burning fire that prevails in hell. Let teachers and ecclesiastical heralds now explain ecclesiastical necessities often, as is just and necessary for each person; and let everyone who is prudent listen to them diligently and retain ecclesiastical teachings most firmly in his mind for his own benefit. Let every person always offer his God, in honor of his Lord, whatever he can, in word and deed, always gladly. Then God’s mercy will be more ready for us all.

May the name of God be blessed forever, and may glory, praise, and worship always be his forever and ever. May almighty God have mercy on us all, as it pleases him, and preserve us forever. May it be so. Amen.

[Col. 1181]

## LETTER OF KING CANUTE SENT TO THE NOBLES OF THE ENGLISH FROM ROME IN THE FIFTEENTH YEAR OF HIS REIGN, A.D. 1031

He reports how graciously he was received by Pope John, Emperor Conrad, and King Rudolf. He says that he obtained privileges for those travelling to Rome, and vows to reform the conduct of his life. He warns them to avoid injustice and to exact nothing improperly for the treasury. He commands that everything belonging to the Church be diligently paid.

[Col. 1181C] Canute, king of all England, Denmark, Norway, and part of Sweden, to Ailnoth [also Egelnoth], metropolitan, and Alfric of York, and to all bishops and primates, and to the entire English people, both noble and common, greeting.

[Note: [Col. 1181D] Malmesbury, *Deeds of the Kings*, Book II, chapter 11.]

I inform you that I have recently gone to Rome to pray for the redemption of my sins and for the welfare of the kingdoms and peoples subject to my rule. I had indeed vowed this journey to God long ago, but because of the affairs of the kingdom and impediments that intervened I could not complete it until now.

Now, however, I give very humble thanks to my almighty God himself, because in my lifetime he has granted me to visit the blessed apostles Peter and Paul and every holy place that I could learn of within or outside the city of Rome, and, according to my desire, to venerate and adore them in person. I did this especially because I learned from wise men that the holy apostle Peter received great power from the Lord to bind and loose, that he is the key-bearer of the heavenly kingdom, and that for this reason I considered it very useful especially to seek his patronage before God.

Let it be known to you that a great assembly of nobles was there, at the very solemnity of Easter, with Pope John and Emperor Conrad: namely, all the princes of the peoples from Mount Gargano to this neighboring sea. They all received me honorably and honored me with magnificent gifts. Above all, I was honored by the emperor with various gifts and precious presents, both golden and silver vessels and very costly cloaks and garments.

I therefore spoke with the emperor himself, with the lord pope, and with the princes who were there concerning the needs of all my people, both English and Danes: that a more equitable law and safer peace on the road to Rome be granted to them, that they not be shut out by so many barriers along the way, and that they not be harassed by unjust tolls.

The emperor granted the requests, as did King Rudolf, who was the chief lord of those barriers; and all the princes confirmed by edicts that my men, both merchants and other travelers journeying for prayer, should go to Rome and return in firm peace, free from every exaction by barriers and toll-collectors.

I complained again before the lord pope and said that I was greatly displeased that my archbishops were burdened by the immense sums demanded of them when, according to apostolic custom, they sought the pallium. It was decreed that this should not happen henceforth.

For everything that I requested from the lord pope, the emperor, King Rudolf, and the other princes through whose lands we must pass on the way to Rome, for the benefit of my people, they willingly granted, and they also confirmed the concessions by oath, in the presence of four archbishops and twenty bishops, and of the innumerable multitude of dukes and nobles who were present.

Therefore I render magnificent thanks to almighty God, because I successfully accomplished everything I had desired, as I had determined in my mind, and fulfilled my vows according to my will.

[Col. 1183A] Now, therefore, let it be known that I have humbly vowed to God himself to justify my life henceforth in all things, to govern justly and piously the kingdoms and peoples subject to me, and to observe equitable judgment in everything. If anything has hitherto been done through the intemperance or negligence of my youth beyond what was just, I intend, with God’s help, to amend it all.

For this reason I adjure and command my counselors, to whom I have entrusted the counsels of the kingdom, that in no way, whether out of fear of me or out of favor toward any powerful person, should they henceforth allow or cause any injustice to grow up anywhere in my kingdom.

I also command all the sheriffs and reeves of my entire kingdom, if they wish to have my friendship and their own salvation, not to inflict unjust force upon any person, rich or poor, but to ensure that all, noble and humble alike, may enjoy the benefits of just law. Let them in no way deviate from it, whether because of royal favor, because of any powerful person, or in order to heap up money for me, since I have no need for money to be amassed for me by unjust exaction.

I therefore wish you to know that, returning by the same route by which I came, I am going to Denmark to arrange, with the counsel of all the Danes, peace and a firm treaty with those peoples who wished, if it had been possible for them, to deprive us both of life and of our kingdom. But they could not, because God destroyed their strength. May he preserve us in kingdom and honor by his kindness, and annihilate the power of all our enemies.

When peace has been arranged with the peoples around us, and our entire kingdom here in the East has been ordered and pacified so that we need fear war or the hostility of anyone from any quarter, I intend to come to England as soon as I can have a fleet prepared this summer.

I have sent this letter ahead so that all the people of my kingdom may rejoice in my prosperity. For, as you yourselves know, I have never spared myself or my labor, nor shall I yet spare it, when it is necessary for the benefit of all my people.

Now, therefore, I adjure all my bishops and the reeves of my kingdom, by the faith that you owe to me and to God, to see that before I come to England all the dues that we owe according to the ancient law have been paid: namely, the alms for the ploughs; the tithes of the animals born in that year; the pennies that you owe to Rome, to Saint Peter, whether from cities or villages; the tithes of grain at the middle of August; and the first-fruits of seed at the feast of Saint Martin, to the church under whose parish each person lives, which is called *Curescet* in English [also *Chireseth*].

If these and the other dues have not been paid when I arrive, the person on whom the fault falls shall, by royal exaction according to the laws, strictly render them without pardon.

[Col. 1183]

## CHARTERS OF KING CANUTE

### I. He confirms the Church of the Savior at Canterbury as the mother and mistress of all the churches of the English kingdom. (A.D. 1018)

[Labbe, *Councils*, vol. IX, col. 817, from an old Canterbury manuscript.]

[Col. 1183C]

I, Emperor Canute, having obtained rule of the English realm on the island from Christ, the King of kings, after hearing of the benefits of my royal predecessors—namely, their royal privileges—and likewise seeing the freedom of the monasteries situated in Kent, and the admonition of the most devout archbishop Living, have resolved in my heart, with the agreement of both parties, to strengthen this present charter.

Namely, let the Church of the Savior situated at Canterbury, the mother and mistress of all the churches of the English kingdom, with everything belonging to it, be free. Let no one obtain or exact from it or its possessions any right or customary due except the archbishop and the monks serving God there.

For the hope of eternal salvation, let this decree of ours remain inviolable and firm forever, in my time and that of my successors, with the witnesses whose signs are written below.

I, Canute, governor of the English world, confirm this with my own hand.

I, Living, metropolitan archbishop, willingly agree.

I, Queen Emma, confirm it with the sign of the cross.

I, Wulstan of York, have strengthened it.

Bishop Ealdelm, approving it.

I, Bishop Algarius, grant it.

I, Bishop Leofric, confirm it.

I, Haldane, the king’s prince, give my assent to the best of my ability.

And I, Turkill, duke, grant it.

This concession was made in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1018.

### II. Charter of King Canute for the monastery of Saint Benedict at Hulme in Suffolk ( *Monasticon Anglicanum*, I)

[Col. 1184D]

To Christ almighty, who is the King of all kings, thanks must be rendered in every way for all the undeserved benefits by which, through his sole intervention in mercy, he assists human beings, although none of our merits have earned them.

Therefore, lest we prove ungrateful for such great benefits of his, we must strive with great effort to offer something to him to whom everything belongs, who granted us possession of things we did not possess, and to whom we can give nothing except what is his own. From his own property he grants us the means to purchase and use for our own purposes what we could by no means possess for our own use unless his grace granted it—namely, fellowship with the inhabitants of the heavenly kingdom.

By his abundant goodness, having been enthroned in royal dignity, I, Knut, king of the English nation, in order to obtain the gift of his immeasurable mercy, grant to him from his own property what he freely granted to me: the estate known by the name of Borninga, with its pastures, woods, and boundaries duly lying beneath it, namely Ludham with its appurtenances, and Retheshirth with its appurtenances.

Our gift, then, is one bestowed on us by Christ; in giving to him, we ask as a loan at interest that he may deign once more to receive from us the gift of his generosity, offered with every disposition of our will, so that through what he has given to him we may obtain what cannot be possessed by us unless it has been bestowed by him. If anyone—God forbid!—inflated by the devil’s prompting should attempt to withdraw by force or any fraud whatsoever from God, the possessor of all things, what he granted to us to give to him, may what we have granted remain to us for his grace, and may it be to that person’s destruction through eternal damnation—he who, with a perverse mind, attempts to transfer it elsewhere, unless the fullness of his satisfaction should come to his aid.

I, Knut, king, have bestowed this donation on Christ in order to obtain the rewards of the heavenly inheritance. I, Elgifu, queen, have confirmed this royal donation by enlarging it.  
[Col. 1185C] I, Wlstan, archbishop, have strengthened it. I, Aetheluth, archbishop, have confirmed it. I, Godwin, bishop, have strengthened it. I, Aelwin, bishop, have given my assent. I, Alfwin, bishop, have subscribed it. I, Etheric, bishop, have concluded it. I, Aelswius, bishop, have strengthened it. I, Huc, duke. I, Godwin, duke. I, Ulf, duke. I, Eglaf, duke. I, Hacun, duke. I, Leofwinc, duke. I, Godric, duke. I, Brithwald, bishop, have consented.  
[Col. 1185D] I, Brihtwiz, abbot. I, Leofric. I, Aelfward. I, Aethelstan.

### III. Charter of King Knut concerning the translation of the body of Saint Mildred, together with all her land, to the abbey of Saint Augustine at Canterbury

*(Monasticon Anglicanum, I.)*

I, Cnud, by the mercy of God basileus [emperor], to Aegelnoth, archbishop, and to all bishops, abbots, earls, sheriffs, and all the faithful of the whole of England, greeting and friendship.

Let it be known to all of you that I have given to Saint Augustine, my patron, the body of the holy and glorious virgin Mildred, together with all her land within the Isle of Thanet and outside it, with all the customs belonging to her church. I return all these things to God, and to Abbot Aelstan and the brothers of the place, so free and undisturbed as I have ever held them at their best, both on land and at sea and on the shore, so that they may have and possess them forever. And whoever attempts to violate or annul this donation of mine, let him be excommunicated by almighty God and by the whole holy Church. Amen.

### IV. Privilege of Saint King Knut for the church of Saint Edmund

*[Monasticon Anglicanum, I, 287.]*

[Col. 1186B] In the name of Jesus Christ, ruler of the heavenly city, Savior of the world, and Creator of the whole creation, whose divine lordship all dominions dutifully and submissively serve, and whose omnipotence all powers hasten with exact obedience to obey; for his goodness is incomprehensible in its goodness, his mercy boundless, the generosity of his goodness ineffable, and his long-suffering, in its extent, longer than any measure over the wickednesses of the perverse. He admonishes by daily exhortations those who lead a religious life, urging them, with fatherly affection, to pursue the worship of righteous piety and not abandon it by forsaking it, but rather to remain steadfast in its worship through persevering diligence. In the same affection he likewise commands sinners to repent of their iniquities and turn back, because he abhors their death.

[Col. 1186C] Supported by the stimulus of the love and faith of him by whose abundant mercy I, Cnut, king of the whole island of Albion and of many other nations, have been raised to the royal throne, I have chosen to decree, with the counsel and decision of the archbishops, bishops, abbots, earls, and all my other faithful men, and to have it confirmed by all with perpetual stability, that the monastery called Badricelmorde be assigned for all time to communities of monks for habitation, and be entirely free from the authority of all the bishops of that county, so that the monks serving the Lord there may, without any disturbance, be able to pray earnestly to the Lord for the welfare of the kingdom.

[Col. 1186D] I also resolved to strengthen this choice of my will by this privilege, in which I ordered the gift of liberty to be set forth that King Edmund of the West Saxons formerly granted to his namesake in order to obtain his grace and eternal reward—namely, to King Edmund and martyr. We desire to increase this gift by a good-will vow, so that through his prayers I may deserve to share in his blessedness after the course of this life.

With such liberty I grant the estate in which that saint rests the right to enjoy this freedom: whenever the whole people pay tribute to the Danes, whether for ships or for arms, the inhabitants of that estate shall pay the same for the uses chosen by the brothers of that place. May this be a remedy for us—for me, indeed, and for my queen Alfgifu, and for all our sons, and for all those who formerly bestowed this estate upon him.

To this liberty I grant an addition: namely, the sea-fish that ought annually to fall to me through the profit of the toll, and the fishery that Ulfkitel held in the estate, and all rights of every kind in the estates adjoining the monastery and those which are to be added by the grace of God. I have also given my assent to my queen, granting her, as her alms, four thousand eels with the dues belonging to them, as an annual tribute in the estate called Lacinga-hythe.

[Col. 1187A] If anyone—God forbid!—strives by any effort to subject this liberty to the yoke of servitude, or with perverse intent to alter it so as to place clerics there again, let him be delivered over to eternal captivity, deprived of perpetual liberty, enslaved to the service of the devil, and bound with unbreakable chains to his company, unless satisfaction for his error should come to his aid—which we most earnestly desire.

I, Cnut, king of the English people and likewise of other nations, ordered this privilege to be composed and, after it was composed, impressed it by confirming it with the sign of the Lord’s cross. I, Alfgifu, queen, have confirmed this with every eagerness of mind. I, Wlstan, archbishop, have consented. I, Adelnod, archbishop, have confirmed it. I, Godwin, bishop, have strengthened it. I, Alfwin, bishop, have given my assent. I, Alffinus, bishop, have subscribed it.  
[Col. 1187C] I, Atheric, bishop, have concluded it. I, Alfwius, bishop, have strengthened it. I, Brihtwald, bishop. I, Iric, duke. I, Godwin, duke. I, Ulf, duke. I, Eglaf, duke. I, Hacun, duke. I, Leofwin, duke. I, Godric, duke. I, Oslac, warrior. I, Thored, warrior. I, Thurkil, warrior. I, Thrym, warrior. I, Brosor, warrior.  
[Col. 1187D] I, Alfric, warrior. I, Alfwyn, warrior. I, Leofric, abbot. I, Alfward, abbot. I, Athelstan, abbot. I, Alffius, abbot. I, Leofwin, abbot. I, Wulfred, abbot. I, Ofkytel, abbot.  
[Col. 1188A] I, Alfwin. I, Alfric. I, Alfric. I, Leoffius. I, Leofric.

### V. Charter of King Knut by which he subjects all the affairs of the Isle of Glastonbury, ecclesiastical as well as secular, to the judgment of the abbot, excluding all other authorities

[Note: [Col. 1187D] Malmesbury, *Deeds of the Kings*, book II, chapter 11.]

[Col. 1188A] Reigning forever is the Lord, who by his ineffable power arranges and governs all things, wonderfully distinguishing the courses of times and of human beings, imposing their uncertain limit with equanimity as he wills, and mercifully teaching us from the hidden mysteries of nature, so that from things fleeting and undoubtedly transitory we may attain, by God’s aid, the kingdoms that endure.

[Col. 1188B] Therefore I, Cnuto, king of the English and governor and ruler of the other nations dwelling round about, with the counsel and decision of our archbishop Edelnoth, together with all the priests of God, and with the consent of my nobles, for the love of the heavenly kingdom, for the forgiveness of my crimes, and for the release from sin of my brother King Edmund, grant to the church of Saint Mary, holy Mother of God, at Glastonbury, its rights and customs throughout my whole kingdom, and all the forfeitures of all its lands. Let its lands be free and released from every accusation and disturbance, just as my lands are held for me.

[Col. 1188C] But especially, by the authority of almighty Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, and by the prohibition of the perpetual Virgin, I forbid and command all the officers and chief men of my kingdom, under penalty of their salvation, that absolutely no one, of whatever order or dignity, dare enter that island. Rather, in all matters, ecclesiastical as well as secular, let them await solely the judgment of the abbot and the convent, just as my predecessors decreed and confirmed by privileges: Cenwine, Ine, Cuthred, Ailred, Alfred, Edward, Aethelred, Alstan, and the most glorious Edmund, and the incomparable Edgar.

[Col. 1188D] But if anyone at any time hereafter should attempt, on any pretext, to violate and annul the testament of this privilege, let him be separated from the company of the righteous by the winnowing of the final judgment. But if anyone strives with benevolent intention to carry out, approve, and defend these provisions, may God, through the intercession of the most blessed Mother of God Mary and of all the saints, enlarge his portion in the land of the living. The grant of this privilege was written and promulgated in the Wooden Basilica in the presence of King Cnut, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1032, indiction . . . .

# MACCABAEUS, KING OF THE SCOTS

[Col. 1189]

## The Ecclesiastical Laws of Maccabaeus, Extracted from His Secular Laws

*(Mansi, Councils, vol. XIX, from Hector Boethius, History, book XII, who assigns them to the year 1050.)*

[Col. 1189A] Do not summon a person initiated into Christ before a secular judge; if summoned or appearing, do not judge him, but return him to the holy bishops.

Freely grant to the shepherds of the churches a tenth part of the produce of the land, and always worship God with the customary vows and offerings.

Whoever has contemptuously disregarded the authority of the bishop for a whole year, and has not meanwhile been reconciled, is to be regarded as an enemy of the state; but whoever has persisted in that contumacy for two years is to be deprived of all his property.

If anyone, as an attendant, has accompanied to a church, a public assembly, a forum, or market fairs someone whom he does not support at his own expense or with daily food, let him be guilty of a capital offense.

# SAINT EDWARD III, KING OF THE ENGLISH, CONFESSOR  
*(1041–1066)*

## The Ecclesiastical Laws of Saint Edward, Extracted from His Secular Laws
