[Note: [Col. 1189C] Hickes, *Dissertation on the Epistles*, folio 55, maintains that these laws are pseudonymous, and everyone agrees that no laws were enacted by King Edward. Therefore, when the English are said, after the Conquest, to have labored with all their strength through the reigns of several princes to renew the laws of Edward the Confessor, this should be understood as referring to the laws of the Anglo-Saxon and Danish kings as altered and corrected by Edward. Certain additions were made to this collection of laws after the time of William I; for when Tanegeld is discussed in chapter 12, mention is made of William Rufus. — Wilkins.]

*(In Mansi, Councils, vol. XIX, column 713, from Wilkins’s Collection.)*

### Titles of the Ecclesiastical Laws

[Col. 1189B]

I. Concerning clerics and their possessions.  
II. Concerning the times and days of the king’s peace.  
III. Concerning the justice of holy Church.  
IV. Concerning all tenants of the Church.  
V. Concerning accused persons fleeing to a church.  
VI. Concerning violation of the peace of the Church.  
VII. Concerning the tithes to be rendered to the Church, of sheep and of piglets.  
VIII. Concerning bees and many other small tithes.  
IX. Concerning those who have been adjudged by the justice of the king to undergo trial by iron or water.  
X. Concerning Saint Peter’s penny, which in English is called Rome-scot.  
[Col. 1189C] XI. What Danegeld is and on what occasion it was established.  
[Col. 1190B] XII. Concerning the king’s various kinds of peace, etc.; also concerning the *manbota* of the archbishop, bishop, etc.  
XIII. Concerning treasures hidden and found in the earth.  
XIV. What the king’s office is, and an example from Charles and Pippin his brother [read: son].  
XV. Concerning barons who have their own courts and customs.  
XVI. Concerning *sacha*.  
XVII. Concerning *soca*.  
XVIII. Concerning *thol*.  
XIX. Concerning *theam*.  
XX. Concerning *infangthefe*.  
XXI. Concerning Jews.  
XXII. The king’s decree concerning usurers.

Here begin the laws of Saint King Edward, which he maintained in England, and which William, his heir and kinsman, afterwards confirmed.

[Col. 1191A]

## Preface

After the acquisition of England, King William, in the fourth year of his reign, on the advice of his barons, caused notice to be given throughout all the counties of England to the noble Englishmen, wise men, and those learned in their law, so that he might hear from them their laws, rights, and customs. Accordingly, twelve men were chosen from each county of the whole country. First, in the presence of the king, they confirmed by oath that, as far as they could, proceeding along the straight path and turning neither to the right nor to the left, they would disclose the enactments of their laws and customs, omitting nothing, adding nothing, and changing nothing through perversion. Beginning, therefore, with the laws of holy Mother Church—for through her the king and kingdom possess a firm foundation on which to stand—they proclaimed her laws, liberties, and peace, saying:

## Ecclesiastical Laws

### I

Every cleric, and also every scholar, and all their property and possessions, wherever they may be, shall have the peace of God and of holy Church.

### II

From Advent of the Lord until the octave of Epiphany, the peace of God and of holy Church shall extend throughout the whole kingdom. Likewise from Septuagesima until the octave of Easter. Also from the Ascension of the Lord until the octave of Pentecost. Also on all the days of the Ember Seasons.

[Col. 1191C] Also on every Saturday from the ninth hour, and throughout the following day, until Monday. Also on the vigils of Saint Mary, Saint Michael, Saint John the Baptist, all the apostles, and the saints whose solemnities are announced by priests on Sundays, and on All Saints’ Day, on the Kalends of November, always from the ninth hour of the vigils and throughout the following solemnity. Also in parishes where the day of dedication is observed. Also in the parishes of churches where the proper feast of a saint is celebrated.

And if anyone comes devoutly to celebrate a saint, let him have peace while going, staying, and returning. Likewise, all Christians going to church for the sake of prayer shall have peace while going and returning. Similarly, those coming to dedications, synods, and chapters, whether they have been summoned or have business of their own to conduct, shall have complete peace.

[Col. 1191D] Even if an excommunicated person should flee to a bishop for the purpose of being absolved, once absolved, let him have the peace of God and of holy Church while going and returning. If anyone should wrong him, let the bishop administer justice in the matter. Nevertheless, if some arrogant person refuses to make amends according to the bishop’s justice, let the bishop inform the king. The king shall compel the wrongdoer to make amends to the person he has wronged—first to the bishop, then to the king. Thus there will be two swords, and one sword will help the other.

### III

Wherever the king’s court, or anyone else’s court, is being held, if the bishop’s officer appears there, the case of holy Church shall first be settled.

[Col. 1192A] For it is just that God be honored everywhere above all others.

### IV

Whoever holds anything from a church, or has a dwelling on church land, shall not be compelled to plead outside the church court, even if he has committed an offense, unless—God forbid!—justice should fail in the church court.

### V

Wherever an accused or guilty person flees to a church for refuge, once he has entered the churchyard, he shall in no way be seized by any pursuer, except by the bishop or his ministers. If, while fleeing, he enters the priest’s house or court, let him have the same security and peace there as at the church, provided that the priest’s house and court stand on church land.

[Col. 1192B] If he is a thief or robber, let him return what he wrongfully seized, if it is at hand; and if he has completely destroyed it but possesses from his own property the means to repay it, let him restore the full amount to the person whom he harmed. But if, as thieves commonly do, he has acted in this way and has repeatedly escaped by chance to a church or to priests’ houses, then, after restoring what he took, let him swear to leave the province and not return. If he should return, no one may dare to give him lodging unless permission has been granted by the king.

### VI

If anyone violently violates the peace of the holy Church, the matter belongs to the justice of the bishops. If the guilty person evades or arrogantly despises their sentence, a complaint shall be carried to the king after forty days. The king’s justice shall send for him by surety and pledges, if he can provide them, until he makes satisfaction first to God, and afterwards to the king and the Church.

[Col. 1192C] If he cannot be found within thirty-one days, either through friends or acquaintances or through the king’s justice, the king shall outlaw him by word of mouth. If he is afterwards found and can be detained, he shall be returned alive—or his head, if he resists. For from the day of his outlawry he bears a wolf’s head, which in English is called *Wulfesheofod*. This is the common and general law concerning all outlaws.

### VII

Of every crop, a tenth sheaf is owed to God and must therefore be rendered. If anyone has a flock of mares, let him render every tenth foal; whoever has only one or two mares shall give one penny for each foal. Similarly, whoever has several cows shall render the tenth calf; whoever has one or two shall give one obol for each calf.

[Col. 1192D] Whoever makes cheese shall give a tenth to God; if he does not make cheese, he shall give milk on the tenth day. Likewise, a tenth lamb, a tenth fleece, a tenth cheese, a tenth butter, and a tenth piglet.

### VIII

Likewise, a tenth of the produce of bees is owed; moreover, from woodland, meadow, waters, mills, parks, fishponds, fisheries, thickets, gardens, trade, and all things that the Lord gives, a tenth part must be rendered to him who gives the nine parts together with the tenth. Whoever withholds it shall, through the justice of the bishop and, if necessary, of the king, be compelled to render it.

[Col. 1193A] For Saint Augustine preached and taught this, and it was granted by the king, the barons, and the people. But afterwards, at the devil’s instigation, many withheld it, and wealthy priests, who were negligent, did not care to undertake the labor of pursuing it, because they possessed enough for the necessities of their own life. For in many places there are now three or four churches where at that time there was only one, and thus it began to diminish.

### IX

Regarding the person on whom judgment is to be carried out, the bishop’s officer shall come there with his clerks, and likewise the king’s justice with the lawful men of that province. Let them see and hear, so that everything may be done fairly; and let those whom the Lord, in his mercy and not through their merits, wills to save be at peace and depart freely. But upon those whom the wickedness of their offense, not the Lord, has condemned, let the king’s justice administer justice.

[Col. 1193B] Let the barons who have their own courts over their men see that they deal with them in such a way that they incur no guilt before God and do not offend the king. If a dispute concerning the men of other barons arises in their courts, let the king’s justice be present at the hearing, since without it the hearing may not be concluded. If any barons do not have judicial rights in the hundred where the hearing is held, the matter is to be determined at the nearest church where the king’s judgment will be given, without prejudice to the rights of those barons.

### X

Everyone who has thirty pence of movable property in his house, from his own possession, shall, according to English law, give Saint Peter’s penny; according to Danish law, half a mark. This penny is to be announced at the solemnity of the apostles Peter and Paul and collected by the feast called *Ad Vincula*, so that it is not withheld beyond that day.

[Col. 1193C] If anyone withholds it, a complaint shall be brought to the king’s justice, because this penny is the king’s alms. The justice shall compel the penny to be rendered, together with the forfeiture owed to the bishop and king. If anyone has several houses, he shall render the penny from the one in which he resides on the feast of the apostles Peter and Paul.

### XI

[Note: [Col. 1193D] This chapter appears to have been added in the time of Henry II.]

The payment of Danegeld was first established because of pirates; for, as they harassed the country, they devoted themselves to devastating it as far as they could. To restrain their insolence, it was decreed that Danegeld should be paid annually—namely, twelve pence from every hide throughout the country—to hire those who would oppose and resist the pirates’ invasion.

[Col. 1193D] The whole Church was free and exempt from this Danegeld; likewise every piece of land that belonged to the church’s own domain, wherever it lay, paid absolutely nothing in this contribution, because they trusted more in the Church’s prayers than in the defenses of arms.

The Church of the English therefore retained this liberty until the time of King William the Younger, who was called Rufus. When he sought aid from the barons of England to retain Normandy from his brother Robert, surnamed Curthose, who had departed for Jerusalem, it was granted to him—not by a law established or confirmed, but for this emergency—that four shillings should be given to him from every hide, with the Church not excepted.

[Col. 1194A] When the tribute was being collected, holy Church proclaimed her claim, demanding the restoration of her liberty; but she achieved nothing.

### XII

The king’s peace is of many kinds. One is that given by his own hand, which the English call *cynninger honde scalde grith*; another is on the day when he is first crowned, and that peace lasts eight days; at Christmas, eight days; at Easter, eight days; at Pentecost, eight days, and so forth. See below.

*Manbota*—that is, compensation to be paid to the lord for his man who has been killed—is, according to the law of the English, three marks to the king and archbishop for their own men; but to the bishop of the same county, to the ealdorman, and to the king’s steward, twenty shillings; and to other barons, ten shillings, and so forth.

### XIII

Treasures found in the earth belong to the king, unless they are found in a church or cemetery. Even if they are found there, the gold belongs to the king, and half the silver to the king and half to the church where it was found, whatever that church may be, rich or poor.

### XIV

The king, who is the vicar of the highest King, is established for this purpose: to rule the earthly kingdom and the people of the Lord, and above all to revere his holy Church, to govern it, to defend it from wrongdoers, and to remove, destroy, and utterly eliminate evildoers from it. If he does not do this, the name of king will not remain in him; indeed, as Pope John testifies, he loses the name of king.

[Col. 1194C] Pippin and his son Charles, not yet kings but princes under a foolish king of the Franks, wrote, asking whether the kings of the Franks ought to remain in that condition, content with the royal name alone. The answer given to them was: “Those deserve to be called kings who, watchful, defend the Church of God and his people,” imitating the Psalmist King, who says: “He who acts proudly shall not dwell in the midst of my house” (Psalm 100).

[Note: [Col. 1193D] What follows further in this chapter in Lambard, concerning the office of the king and the law and appurtenances of the crown of the kingdom of Britain, together with Pope Eleutherius’ letter to King Lucius, is found neither in our manuscript nor in Hoveden.]

### XV

Archbishops, bishops, earls, barons, and all who possess *sacha*, *soca*, *thol*, *theam*, and *infangthefe* shall keep their knights and personal servants—namely, stewards, cupbearers, chamberlains, cooks, and bakers—under their own *friborg*. Likewise, these men shall keep their own armed retainers or other servants under their own *friborg*.

[Col. 1194D] If any of them should commit an offense and a complaint from their neighbors should arise against them, they themselves shall hold them to justice in their own court—those, I mean, who possess *sacha*, *soca*, *thol*, *theam*, and *infangthefe*.

### XVI

*Sacha* means that if anyone accuses another by name of something, and the accused denies it, the forfeiture arising from proof or denial, if it occurs, shall belong to him.

### XVII

*Soca* means that if anyone seeks anything on his own land, even a theft, the justice belongs to him, whether it is found or not.

### XVIII

*Thol*, which we call toll, is the liberty to sell and buy on one’s own land.

### XIX

*Theam* means that if anyone claims something against another, and the person against whom it is claimed cannot produce his warrantor, the forfeiture shall be his; and likewise justice shall be done against the accuser if he fails.

### XX

Everyone who possesses *sacha*, *soca*, *thol*, *theam*, and *infangthefe*—that is, the aforesaid customs—has jurisdiction to try a thief who is his own man, if he is captured on his land. Those who do not possess these customs shall do right before the king’s justice in the hundreds, wapentakes, or shires.

### XXI

It must also be known that all Jews, wherever they are in the kingdom, must be under the king’s protection and defense, and none of them may submit himself to any rich man without the king’s permission. For the Jews and all their property belong to the king. If anyone should detain them or their money, the king may recover it, if he wishes, as his own property.

### XXII

King Edward also prohibited usurers, so that none might remain throughout his kingdom. If anyone were convicted of demanding interest, he would lose all his own substance and afterwards be regarded as an outlaw. That king asserted that he had heard this in the court of the king of the Franks, while he was staying there: that usury is the chief root of all vices.

[Col. 1195]

## Other Laws of King Edward, Written in the Norman Language

*(See under William the Conqueror, for the year 1087, in Patrologia, vol. CXLVII.)*

[Col. 1195]

# Diplomas of Saint King Edward

## Date

At the Westminster assembly held at Christmas in the year of grace 1066, indiction III, in the twenty-fifth and last year of the reign of that king, in the presence of King Edward, Queen Edgitha, Stigand, archbishop of Canterbury, Eldred, archbishop of York, and the other bishops of England, abbots, the king’s chaplains, earls, officials or royal *thegns*, and knights whose subscriptions are named in the following charters.

At this assembly discussion took place concerning the endowment, privileges, celebrated sanctuary, and other matters of the church of Saint Peter at Westminster, which had by then been completely rebuilt and dedicated and furnished with many extensive diplomas, as is evident from the three charters of the aforesaid King Edward and the letters of Popes Leo IX and Nicholas II that follow.

*(Mansi, Councils, vol. XIX, column 1049.)*

### I. Charter of King Edward the Confessor, drawn up for the church of Saint Peter at Westminster, in which Pope Leo IX’s letter to the same king is recited; but, apart from much intervening material—which undoubtedly contained the endowment—the beginning of the charter, called the *karangia*, and its conclusion are missing

[Col. 1195B]

Edward, by the grace of God king of the English, etc.

I wish you to know that in the time of my grandfathers and my father, many grievous dangers of war afflicted the English people and themselves, stirred up both by their own men and by outsiders, to such an extent that the hereditary succession of kings almost perished. A great interval also arose between my brother Edmund, who succeeded my father after his death, and me, when Swegn and his son Cnut, kings of the Danes, invaded the kingdom, together with Cnut’s sons Harold and Harthacnut.

[Col. 1195C] By these men my other brother Alfred was cruelly killed, and I alone escaped their cruelty, just as Joash escaped Athaliah’s slaughter. At last, after many years, through God’s merciful regard, I, Edward, returned to my father’s throne and obtained it without any labor of war. Like Solomon, beloved of God, I abounded in such peace and prosperity that none of the preceding kings had been like me in glory and wealth.

[Col. 1196B] But by God’s grace I was not, as commonly happens, seized by contempt arising from wealth and pride. Rather, I began to consider by whose gift and aid I had risen to the summit of the kingdom, since the kingdom belongs to God and he gives it to whomever he wills; and since the world passes away, together with its desire (1 John 2). Whoever submits himself wholly to God reigns happily and is perpetually rich.

Therefore I resolved to go to the thresholds of the exalted apostles Peter and Paul, and there to give thanks for the benefits bestowed upon me, and to pray that God would establish that peace permanently for me and my descendants. I accordingly prepared and counted out the expenses necessary for the journey, together with honorable gifts that I would bring to the holy apostles.

[Col. 1196C] But my nobles were weighed down by even greater sorrow over the matter, remembering the evils they had suffered under other kings. They feared that, while such a lord and the king of the country were absent, the kingdom, newly settled, might be disturbed by some hostile attack. They also feared what Saint Hezekiah feared: that if I should happen to fail on the journey through illness or some other misfortune, they would be left without hereditary kings, especially since I had no son.

[Col. 1197A] Therefore, after a common council had been held, they asked me to abandon my intention, promising that they would fulfill my vow to God both by offering Masses and prayers and by distributing abundant alms. But when I firmly resisted, at last both sides agreed that two envoys should be sent from each party: the bishops Eldred—first of Worcester and afterwards of York—and Herman of Sherborne, together with the abbots Wulfric and Elfwyn. They were to report to the apostle my will and vow and their petition; and, according to the answer he would send me, I promised to do everything.

[Col. 1197B] What we desired was therefore done. When our envoys arrived in Rome, by God’s will they found a synod assembled in that city. After they had explained my will and their petition before two hundred and fifty bishops and a great multitude of other holy Fathers, the apostolic bishop, on the advice of the holy synod, wrote this letter:

Leo, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son Edward, king of the English, greeting and apostolic blessing.

“Since your will …” and so forth. See Leo IX, *Patrologia*, vol. CXLIII.

[Col. 1197C] When the envoys had brought these and other apostolic instructions back to us, Saint Peter meanwhile revealed to a monk of proven life, shut up in seclusion, named Wulfino, that it was his will that I rebuild the place called Westminster. It had been founded in the time of Saint Augustine, the first bishop of the English, and honored by the generosity of many ancient kings, but because of its age and the frequent turmoil of wars it appeared almost destroyed.

When he had reported this vision to me and to my men, and the apostolic letters had conveyed commands of equal force, I brought my will into accord with God’s will and with the choice of the whole kingdom, and devoted myself to rebuilding that place.

[Col. 1197D] Accordingly, I ordered a tenth of all my substance to be set aside, both in gold and silver and in livestock and every kind of possession. After demolishing the old basilica, I built a new one from its foundations and caused it to be dedicated on the fifth day before the Kalends of January.

On that same day I placed there the relics that Pope Martin and Leo, who consecrated him, had given to King Alfred, and which Alfred had obtained to be given to him by Carloman, king of the Franks. Carloman’s daughter had been married by Alfred’s father, King Ethelwulf, after the death of his first wife; and these relics passed from Alfred to his successor Athelstan, then to Edgar, and finally to us.

[Col. 1198A] They were, namely, two parts of the Lord’s Cross, part of one of his nails, part of his seamless tunic, portions of the clothing of Saint Mary, and relics of the apostles Peter and Paul, Andrew, Bartholomew, Barnabas, and many other saints, together with five caskets full of the relics of other saints.

I decreed that whoever, accused of treason against the royal majesty or of any other offense, should flee to the place where these relics rest would obtain immunity for that offense, and for his limbs and life.

### II. For the same church of Saint Peter at Westminster
The beginning is missing.

Let all future generations know that, to fulfill my vow and for the remission of all my sins, for the souls of the kings—both my successors and my predecessors—and of all my parents, and for the peace and stability of my kingdom and the prosperity of the entire English people, I have granted that place, namely Westminster, complete freedom insofar as earthly authority is concerned; and I decree that it shall have this royal liberty in ecclesiastical matters.

Therefore, spurred by love of Him and supported by the fullest and most devout faith—by whose abundant mercy I have been raised to the royal throne—with the counsel and decree of the archbishops, bishops, earls, and my other nobles, foreseeing that this would be useful to that church and to those dwelling in it or belonging to it, not only in the present but also in the future, I have chosen to enact and to have confirmed by all with perpetual stability that, for the honor and love of Christ, and out of reverence for the chief of the apostles, Saint Peter, to whose protection I have entrusted myself, and out of devotion and veneration for the holy relics that I have given to that place—namely, those of the blessed apostles, martyrs, confessors, and virgins—the almighty God may, through the intercession of those saints, having driven away every adversity, guard, govern, and protect that place with the stability of His peace and honor and with the exaltation of perpetual tranquility. And, because of the magnificent dignity or royal excellence of that church and for the peace of the monks serving God there, such honor shall forever be held and observed toward that church that neither we nor our successors, nor any bishop, nor anyone exercising judicial authority, shall ever have any power over the holy basilica itself, or over those dwelling in it, or over persons who may wish to give or devote themselves to it together with their lands or any possessions, except by the will of the abbot and his monks.

And let this holy mother Church, belonging especially to our patron, the lord and great apostle, thrice-blessed Peter, be free and absolved from every invasion or disturbance by all persons, whatever their apparent authority. Moreover, I establish and confirm forever that any fugitive who, from whatever place, for whatever cause, and of whatever condition, fleeing to that holy place or its precinct, shall enter it, shall be entirely immune and shall obtain full freedom.

But if anyone should wish to enlarge and increase this our donation, may God increase his prosperous days here and hereafter. But if it should happen that any king among our successors, or any dependent of any person, which God forbid, should be lifted up or led astray by diabolical presumption so as to wish to violate, diminish, or alter this our statute, let him know that he is condemned by perpetual anathema, unless he corrects the matter by making satisfaction. But if he is unworthy of correction, he himself shall be burned with the traitor Judas in the fires of Gehenna; nevertheless, this charter shall remain in its freedom for as long as fear and love of the Christian name endure among our people.

Finally, I ordered this charter to be written and sealed, and I impressed it with my own hand with the sign of the holy cross, and ordered suitable witnesses to be recorded for its confirmation. Accordingly, I, Edward, by the gift of God king of the English, have impressed the sign of the venerable cross upon the charter of the freedom of my donation.

I, Queen Edith, consenting to this royal donation, have subscribed.

I, Stigand, archbishop, have consented and subscribed.

## III. For the same church of Saint Peter at Westminster

This charter contains a letter of King Edward the Confessor to Pope Nicholas II requesting confirmation of the privileges of the church of Westminster, and a letter of Pope Nicholas II to King Edward the Confessor, by which he granted the request and, in addition, several further privileges.

[Col. 1199D]

[Col. 1200A]

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity. Because of those who despise God’s justice and wish to establish their own, since they are not subject to God’s justice (Romans 10), those who establish privileges for the churches of God must take care to gather together many charters, a multitude of witnesses, and curses. By these means, even if not always, nevertheless at times the impious insolence and destructive presumption of the worst men may be worn down, blunted, and beaten back, and may also be utterly uprooted by the strongest force of defense.

Therefore I, Edward, by the grace of God king of the English, make known to all future generations of the world after me that, at the command of Pope Leo, as penance and for the remission of my sins, I renewed and improved that basilica of Peter which is situated near the walls of London, the chief city of the English, and which is called Westminster from its western side. It had indeed been built long ago under Mellitus, the first bishop of London, companion and contemporary of Saint Augustine, the first archbishop of Canterbury, and had been dedicated by that blessed Peter, through angelic service, with the impress of the holy cross and the mingling of sacred chrism. But because of the frequent incursions of barbarians, and especially of the Danes, who, while my father Æthelred was still alive, had invaded England and, after his death, had held half the kingdom with my brother Edmund under a treaty of friendship and peace, and had miserably killed another brother, Alfred, it appeared entirely neglected and destroyed.

When I had therefore renewed it and, through the blessed Pope Leo, established in it many privileges of royal power and apostolic authority, after Leo himself had died and Nicholas had been confirmed in his place, I decided to renew, improve, and confirm the customary payments and monetary donations that my royal predecessors had instituted for Saint Peter, because of the supreme devotion that the English people had always shown toward him and his vicars.

Accordingly, for this matter and several others, I sent envoys to Rome: one bishop, Aldredus, and two men chosen to be ordained bishops, namely Gliso and Walterus, so that they might be consecrated by the lord pope. When they came to Rome, they were received by the apostolic Nicholas with the honor that was fitting. There they found a great multitude of bishops, abbots, monks, clerics, and other faithful gathered for a synod. When, before the synod, they pleaded the cause of their embassy, they presented the substance of this letter to the lord pope.

To Nicholas, supreme father of the universal Church: Edward, by the grace of God king of the English, offers due submission and complete service.

We glorify God, who cares for His chosen Church, because He has appointed you as an excellent successor in the place of a good predecessor. Therefore we judge it right to hasten to you as to a solid rock [or: “to sharpen ourselves” (*acuere*)], to demonstrate all our good intentions and to have your knowledge and fellowship in what is good, so that you may renew and increase for us those donations and privileges that we obtained from your predecessor.

That is, we ask that you confirm what he imposed upon us under the name of obedience and penance: because of the vow I had made to go to Rome, and for the remission of all my sins, to build a monastery of monks in honor of the apostle Peter. We ask that you confirm, renew, and increase the privileges of the possessions and dignities of that place, and decree that they remain unchangeable forever.

I, for my part, according to my ability, increase and confirm the monetary donations and customary payments that Saint Peter possesses in England. I send those collected monies to you together with royal gifts, so that you may pray for me and for the peace of my kingdom, and establish that a continual and solemn commemoration of the entire English people be made before the bodies of the holy apostles. Farewell.

When the envoys had received these letters from the supreme pontiff and, after completing everything successfully according to their wish, were returning from Rome, they brought me, on the advice of the holy synod, the letter sent to me by the lord pope.

> Nicholas, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to our most glorious and devout son, worthy of every honor, our spiritual son Edward, king of the English: complete visitation, gracious greeting, and apostolic blessing.
>
> [Col. 1201C]
>
> “We render thanks to almighty God,” and so forth. See Nicholas II under the year 1061 in volume 143 of the *Patrologia*.

It therefore pleased me to insert this letter of apostolic privilege into our present confirmation, so that, in accordance with what had previously pleased and been commanded by Saint Leo, and since his successor Nicholas had given me the same or greater commands, all future generations might know that, for the fulfillment of the aforesaid vow, for the remission of all my sins, and for the reward of eternal life, for the souls of the kings—both my successors and predecessors—and of all my parents, and for the peace and stability of my kingdom and the prosperity of the entire English people, I granted that place complete freedom insofar as earthly authority is concerned, and decreed that it should have this royal liberty in ecclesiastical matters.

Therefore, spurred by love of Him and supported by the fullest and most devout faith—by whose abundant mercy I have been raised to the royal throne—with the counsel and decree of the archbishops, bishops, earls, and all my other nobles, foreseeing that this would be useful to that church and to those dwelling in it or belonging to it, not only in the present but also in the future, I have chosen to enact and to have confirmed by all with perpetual stability that, for the honor and love of Christ, and out of reverence for the chief of the apostles, Saint Peter, to whose protection I have entrusted myself, and out of devotion and veneration for the holy relics that I have given to that place—namely, those of the blessed apostles, martyrs, confessors, and virgins—the almighty God may, through the intercession of those saints, having driven away every adversity, guard, govern, and protect that place with the stability of His peace and honor and with the exaltation of perpetual tranquility.

And, because of the magnificent dignity or royal excellence of that church and for the peace of the monks serving God there, such honor shall forever be held and observed toward that church that neither we nor our successors, nor any bishop, nor anyone exercising judicial authority, shall ever have any power over the sacred basilica itself, or over those dwelling in it, or over persons who may wish to give or devote themselves to it together with their lands or any possessions, except by the will of the abbot and his monks. Rather, let this holy mother church, belonging especially to our patron, the lord and great apostle, thrice-blessed Peter, be free and absolved from every invasion or disturbance by all persons, whatever their rank or authority may appear to be.

Moreover, I establish and confirm forever that any fugitive who, from whatever place, for whatever cause, and of whatever condition, fleeing to that holy place or its precinct, shall enter it, shall be entirely immune and shall obtain this complete freedom.

And below:

I ordered this charter of my donation and freedom to be read on the day of the dedication of the aforesaid church before the bishops, abbots, earls, and all the nobles of England, with the entire people hearing and seeing it. In accordance with the decree of the apostolic Leo and his successor Nicholas, I caused those who might violate or permit the violation of our decree, insofar as it lay within their power, to be excommunicated.

But whoever among my successors shall firmly and inviolably preserve this freedom of my donation, may he be crowned with eternal glory and fully enjoy the happiness of the heavenly kingdom.

But if anyone, which God forbid, should wish to destroy it, or should become a contradictor, violator, and transgressor of this decree of ours, let him be subject, together with the traitor Judas, to eternal anathema, unless he makes satisfaction to God and His blessed apostle Peter through worthy repentance.

Therefore, so that this authority may remain perpetually firm and inviolate around that holy place in our times and in times to come, and may be preserved and maintained unharmed for all time, and so that it may be believed more securely and certainly by all our nobles and by public and private judges, we have decreed that it be strengthened by the subscription of our hand beneath it, that suitable witnesses be recorded, and that it be sealed with our seal.

I, Edward, by the grace of God king of the English, ordered this privilege to be composed, and I impressed the completed document with the sign of the Lord’s cross as confirmation.

I, Queen Edgida, have confirmed this with complete readiness of mind.

# In the Year 1038: Saint Stephen, First King of the Hungarians

[Col. 1203]

## Life of Saint Stephen, by Carthuitus or Carthuitius, Bishop

(From Bollandist, *Acta sanctorum*, September, volume I, day 2, p. 563, from the Kraków edition, collated with the Corsendonk manuscript and the edition of Surius.)

## Preliminary Notice

[Col. 1203D]

1. Various judgments have been given by different scholars concerning this Life of Saint Stephen. The author immediately declares his name and dignity in the preface with these words: “To his lord, the most excellent King Calamannus, Carthuitus, bishop,” and so forth. Yet he does not add of which city he was bishop, nor is this certainly established from any other source; we will not be surprised at this if we consider that we know few of the bishops of Hungary in that period.

The date when the Life was written is inferred from King Calamannus, or Colomannus, as he is called elsewhere. Formerly everyone thought that it had been written for Colomannus, the successor of Saint Ladislaus, and I consider this sufficiently certain, even though recently Godefredus Schwartzius, a heterodox writer, wished to oppose it. In 1740 he published a booklet entitled *The Beginnings of the Christian Religion among the Hungarians Asserted for the Eastern Church*.

[Col. 1204D]

Since this writer wished to wrest from the Latins the glory of Hungary’s conversion, he moved every stone to make it appear probable that the Hungarians had first been brought to the faith by the Greeks. Since the Life of King Saint Stephen could not be reconciled with that assertion, he wished to deprive the aforesaid Life of all authority. For this reason he argues that the Life was written at a later time, and he attempts to demonstrate this with certain little arguments. I shall examine each of his assertions carefully.

2. Concerning the date when the Life was written and the king for whom it was composed, Schwartzius speaks as follows on page 57:

“Third, just as our parchment-writer Chartuitius does not declare himself bishop of any place, so, in addressing his legend to King Colomannus, he once again displays a remarkable hallucination. The author did not reveal which king he meant, or at least the editor Surius has fostered the monstrosity on both sides.

[Col. 1205A]

For Colomannus, king of the Hungarians, who died in 1115, cannot be meant. In the letter the writer calls himself decrepit; hence he would have been a contemporary of Ladislaus, under whose auspices, in 1084 or the preceding year, the body of King Stephen was raised and publicly exposed for veneration. If he was a contemporary, it was absurd for him to write about Ladislaus to Colomannus, his immediate successor: ‘King Ladislaus, who was then seated at the helm of the state’; and much more absurdly would he have spoken of events carried out in his own time: ‘They made heaps of stones, which afterward remained there for a long time’; and, a little later: ‘A wonderful event, and astonishing in our times.’

“Finally, what we call Transylvania today was called Erdely by the ancient Hungarians, even in Latin writings; in the time of Andrew II, it was called Ultrasilvania; and only under Bela IV did it become Transylvania. Yet our legendary writer already calls it Transylvania. Fourth, if our writer is from a later period, as Timon acknowledges and admits that several statements indicate, and if the Colomannus to whom our legend is dedicated is to be understood not as the earlier king of Hungary but as the king of Galicia, brother of Bela VI, then he was separated from the time of Saint Stephen by more than two centuries.”

Thus far Schwartzius concerning the date when the Life was composed.

3. Schwartzius, however, set forth his arguments in a style much more bitter than sound, and in attacking Carthuitius he commits more errors against sound reasoning than Carthuitius appears to have committed in writing the Life. He saw hallucinations, monstrosities, and absurdities where there was no hallucination, no monstrosity, and no absurdity.

Carthuitius calls himself a bishop but does not add of what city; he calls the king Colomannus but does not add of what kingdom. If, in Schwartzius’s judgment, this is to hallucinate or produce monstrosities, then, so that he may learn to judge more correctly, let him read the finest ancient and modern writers. When he finds that many of them have done precisely the same thing, let him correct his error more modestly.

For the moment, let us consider whether better arguments exist. Colomannus, the successor of Saint Ladislaus, cannot be meant, if we believe our critic, because in that case decrepit Carthuitius would have had to be a contemporary of Ladislaus. We hold that Carthuitius was indeed a contemporary of Ladislaus. Let us also suppose that he was present at the raising of the body carried out under Ladislaus, although this is uncertain. What harm would follow from that?

Could the author write only absurdly, “King Ladislaus, who was then seated at the helm of the state,” simply because he had lived at the same time as Ladislaus? That certainly does not appear so to me. Rather, I demand the judgment of the man who considers the phrase badly added. Carthuitius was not writing only for Colomannus, but also for posterity, who would read the Life and would not all know that Ladislaus was reigning at that time.

There is no more serious fault in the words that Schwartzius considers even more absurdly written: “They made heaps of stones, which afterward remained there for a long time.” Why, I ask, could Carthuitius not properly write this twenty years after the event? Did the stones not remain there for a long time if they remained even for only a decade?

[Col. 1205D]

4. Nor is there anything absurd in Carthuitius’s words that follow: “A wonderful event, and astonishing in our times.” Carthuitius could appropriately have written this even if he had composed the Life on the very day on which the miracle occurred.

Indeed, I do not think it inappropriate to answer Schwartzius in almost the same words: “A wonderful event, and astonishing in our times”—that a man who desires to appear learned could have hoped, by arguments of this sort, to persuade the learned world that the Life of Saint Stephen was written later than has hitherto generally been believed.

Moreover, the later words of Carthuitius imply that the miracle of the raising of a dead person occurred in his own time. Take the words from chapter 37 of the Life:

> “A wonderful event and astonishing in our times: the woman did not cease praying until she received alive the son whom she had placed dead [at the tomb of the saint].”

The author does not contrast the time when he was writing with the time when the miracle occurred. Rather, he contrasts his own time with the time of the primitive Church, when the raising of the dead was less rare. He says that the event was both wonderful in itself and plainly astonishing because it had occurred in his own time, when the raising of the dead was extremely rare.

Carthuitius therefore implies that this miracle, which occurred after the body had been raised under Ladislaus, took place in his own time. Consequently, it may rightly be inferred from these words that the Life was written for Colomannus, the successor of Ladislaus.

5. As for Schwartzius’s final objection concerning Transylvania, which was called Erdely by the ancients, even among Latin writers, and which is sometimes found named Ultrasilvania, that point alone should have been brought forward, since it has at least the appearance of a difficulty, although in reality the difficulty is not great.

In the Life, chapter 22, we read:

> “He ordered a certain courier to hasten to Alba Transilvana within a day and a night.”

But Surius, changing the expression everywhere, published “to Alba of Transylvania,” and by that alteration provided an opportunity for the objection. For the writer did not actually call the province Transylvania; rather, he called Alba “Transilvana” in order to distinguish it from another Alba, namely Alba Regalis.

Thus, if the name Transylvania was not yet customary in the time of Colomannus, Carthuitius could have called Alba Julia Transilvana because it lay beyond the forests that eventually gave their name to the province.

Moreover, if the writer had really named Transylvania, as Surius incorrectly printed it, the use of that word could not prove that he belonged to a later period. For that province, still called Erdely in the vernacular, began to be called Transilvania by some Latin writers and Ultrasilvania by others. The name was derived from the dense forests by which it is surrounded.

Who could now, except rashly, determine which writer first used the name Transylvania? Someone certainly used it first. Why, then, could Carthuitius not have been the first to use that word, just as anyone else, if he used it at all?

6. Furthermore, just as the arguments cited do not prove that Carthuitius was later, other arguments decisively persuade us that he wrote for Colomannus, king of Hungary.

I have already given the first argument in section 4. I take the second from words of Surius also cited by Schwartzius: “King Ladislaus, who was then seated at the helm of the state.” In the manuscript one reads instead: “King Ladislaus, who was then administering the state,” and so forth.

He would undoubtedly have added “of the Hungarians,” or something similar, if he had been writing to a king other than the king of the Hungarians. But because he was a bishop of Hungary and was writing to the king of Hungary, he simply calls it “the state,” meaning the Hungarian state. Yet he could not have spoken so appropriately to Colomannus, king of Galicia, who did not administer the Hungarian state.

Furthermore, that Colomannus—whether duke or king—of Galicia in Black Russia reigned peacefully for only a few years, so that it is not probable that the Life was written for him, especially since it contains much that suggests it was written in Hungary, but nothing from which it could be inferred that it was composed after Colomannus, king of Hungary. It mentions no person who lived after Colomannus and recounts no event that occurred after him.

Rather, it reports the raising of the body under Ladislaus and the miracles performed at that time with various accompanying details, so that it may be inferred that the writer was either present at the event or at least living at that time.

Now I show by another argument that this Life was written before the time of Colomannus, king of Galicia. Colomannus, son of Andrew II, king of Hungary, and later king of Galicia, was not yet born at the beginning of the thirteenth century. Carthuitius therefore could not have written to him except many years after the canonization of Saint Ladislaus, which took place in 1192 according to the author of the ancient Life, or in 1198 if Bonfinius’s calculation is exact. These matters may be seen in volume V of June, page 319.

Nevertheless, in chapter II.33 Carthuitius adorns Ladislaus with a splendid eulogy but does not call him a saint, nor does he attribute anything to him that suggests that Ladislaus had by then been canonized or was being venerated as a saint.

Moreover, the Emperor Saint Henry had been enrolled among the saints by solemn canonization before the middle of the twelfth century, as has been shown in volume III of July, pages 715–716. Yet Carthuitius does not praise Henry with the title of holiness in chapter 13, but only for his piety.

Nor would the author have named either Ladislaus or Henry without mentioning their holiness if he had written after their canonization, since he does not omit the sanctity of any of the others who had received that title before Colomannus, king of Hungary, whenever he mentions them. He either calls them saints or blessed, or indicates their holiness by some circumlocution.

This is therefore a clear indication that Carthuitius wrote long before the time of Colomannus, king of Galicia, and that no other Colomannus should be sought for the dedication of the Life than Colomannus, king of Hungary and successor of Saint Ladislaus.

7. From what has been said, the date of the composition of the Life must be placed at the beginning of the twelfth century, since Colomannus obtained the kingdom in 1095 and died in 1114, if we accept the chronology of John of Thurocz, which it is unnecessary to examine here.

In his letter to the king, the author calls himself decrepit, so that he may already have been born in 1038, the year in which Saint Stephen died. He was therefore about the same age as the saint and, if he undertook to write this Life as a young man, could have said much about Stephen’s deeds from the testimony of those who had been present.

John Thurocz, mentioned above, probably praises this Life in chapter 27 of his *Chronicle of the Hungarians* in these words:

> “Geycha, warned beforehand by a divine oracle, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 969, as it is written in the Legend of Saint Stephen the king, begot Saint Stephen the king.”

Ranzanus also mentions it and reports much from it in epitome 8 of his *Compendium of Hungarian History*.

But Schwartzius, on page 59, says that Thurocz referred to another Life, because “the Chartuitian Legend does not specify any year of birth.”

I reply that Thurocz cites the Life not for the year of birth—which he himself added, and indeed added incorrectly—but only for the name of the father and for the divine oracle, which he says was reported beforehand in Carthuitius’s Life.

In the same place that writer warns that he will not write everything reported about Stephen and his son Emeric in their Lives. “Rather,” he says, “we intend to write briefly and summarily those things that have been omitted by other writers.”

8. Furthermore, although there seems to be no reason to doubt the age of Carthuitius, the Life of Saint Stephen written by him is nevertheless not free of errors or certain blemishes, and these were increased by Surius, its editor, when Gisela, the saint’s wife, is called by him the daughter of the Emperor Henry, although she was not his daughter but his sister, as she is correctly called in the manuscript and in the older edition.

There is also an error in the year of Stephen’s death, which both in the manuscript and in Surius is given as 1034. But this error too could easily have entered through the fault of copyists, who frequently corrupt numbers.

There also appears to be an error in the name of the duke of Poland, whom the author says requested a royal crown from the pontiff.

These two later errors—for the first is certainly not his error—are nevertheless of such a kind that they do not greatly diminish the authority of the *Acts*, especially since many things reported in them are confirmed by contemporary writers, and many others are made probable by those same writers.

For this reason, I do not dislike Baillet’s judgment concerning these *Acts*. In his critical table for 2 September, he writes in French, which I render into Latin:

> “His Life, written by a Hungarian bishop named Carthuitius and dedicated to King Colomannus, is not free from errors. Nevertheless, it possesses sufficient authority in other respects, although its author lived far from the time of the saint.”

The rest is correct. But his statement that the author lived far from the saint’s time suggests too great a distance, since he wrote only sixty or seventy years after the saint’s death.

This was more or less the judgment of other writers concerning the authority of this Life, and rightly so.

# The Life Begins

[Col. 1207]

## Preface

[Col. 1207C]

1. To his lord CALAMANNUS [Note: Calamannus, in Surius Colomannus, as his name is commonly rendered at this time. It is highly probable that the Hungarian name Kálmán was originally rendered as Calamannus. Later the name Colomannus or Colomanus was used, which had long been customary among the Latins. Colomannus was king of Hungary and successor to Saint Ladislaus. The fact that the king’s name is written Calamannus is itself a sign of antiquity, since later writers used Colomannus.], most excellent king, CARTHUITUS, a bishop who, by God’s mercy, has attained the spiritual office, wishes, after the end of this life, that blessed and everlasting “well done.”

As I was about to begin, my lord, illustrious king, the work which by your royal command you powerfully entrusted to me concerning the good life of King Stephen, I long endured the ignorance of my little mind, especially because Priscian [Note: The learned everywhere know that Priscian is counted among the foremost grammarians. By that allegory Carthuitus signifies that the grammatical rules once well known to him had gradually been consigned to oblivion with advancing age. Nevertheless, considering the time in which this author flourished, he wrote Latin moderately well; but certain errors crept here and there into the manuscript, especially toward the end.]—formerly known to me to the very marrow as the author of grammar—having gone far away, now presents his face to me, already decrepit, as though surrounded by some kind of darkness, and makes it exceedingly obscure. Yet, on the other hand, while consideration of your dignity weighed upon me with hesitant reflection, obedience, the light and jewel of every virtue, at last overcame the doubt of my anxious mind. Seeing that my strength failed me without its strong support, I received confidence to begin the work [Note: Since the phrasing is not entirely satisfactory, I suspect that the author wrote *recepio* or *recipi fiduciam* (“I receive” or “to receive confidence”).].

But since an undertaking performed confidently often generates fuel for envy, I beg, on bended knees, the sublimity of your triumphant excellence to receive this little work into the hands of royal protection, lest the badly sounding arrangement of words or the enormity of confused order offend your eye when you read it. If some unworthy stumbling-block should appear, I would rather that fire consume the book than that envy reach the eye in full. Therefore, since whatever is good flows from the mercy of the Creator, the discourse begun by his gift now sounds forth such things [Note: This preface, or dedication, is omitted in the Corsendonc manuscript. Surius reproduced it after altering its style, with the same freedom with which he altered the wording of the entire Life. Receive, diligent reader, Surius’s preface as a specimen of the whole work in its altered form:

“To his lord Colomannus, most excellent king, Chartuitius, a bishop who by God’s goodness has obtained the spiritual ministry, prays, after the end of this life, for that everlasting ‘well done.’ I now undertake, most serene king, the work entrusted to me by your command, from which the ignorance of my little mind has hitherto recoiled, especially because Priscian the grammarian, once sufficiently understood and known to me, has gone far from me and now, as though enclosed in a kind of darkness, displays an exceedingly obscure face to me in my decrepitude. But when, on the other hand, I considered the authority of your dignity, obedience, the light and jewel of every virtue, at last overcame all the doubt of my anxious mind. Trusting in its strong protection, although I saw that I had no strength at all, I conceived the confidence to begin the work. Since, moreover, things undertaken in confidence are generally exposed to envy, I humbly beg your royal sublimity not to disdain to receive this little work under your patronage, and not to be offended by its unsuitable diction or by the confusion of its order and narrative. If anything should appear that bears a shameful offence, I would rather the book be consumed by fire than that it be offered to anyone as material for envy. And since all good things proceed to us from divine mercy, by his gift I gladly begin this present little work.”

Here you see, reader, that the wording has been altered while the meaning remains everywhere the same. The same has often been done in the Life; there is no need henceforth to note those verbal alterations unless the meaning has also been changed. I shall therefore indicate below only changes of meaning; from the manuscript, however, I shall carefully record the actual changes of words, unless they are obvious errors, of which several occur toward the end of the Life.]

## CHAPTER I. The saint’s father; his birth illuminated by preceding visions; his baptism; the beginnings of his reign and his care for the advancement of religion; his victory over the rebels; and the monastery of Saint Martin founded in fulfillment of a vow

### 2.

“Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, descending from the Father of lights” (James 1:17). This good gift and perfect gift of the Father, abundantly bestowed upon all because he rejects no one but wills all people to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth (1 Timothy 2:4), extended even to the Hungarians, who are known formerly to have been the scourge of Christians [Note: Just as Attila was called the scourge of God, so the Hungarians truly were the scourge of Christians, as may sufficiently be gathered from what is said in the Commentary, no. 52.]. We have judged it fitting to commend to memory by the service of writing how and when this occurred.

At that time, when the aforesaid people was laying waste to the Church of God, there was among them a certain prince, fourth in succession from him who was originally the leader of the Hungarians’ entry into Pannonia—his name was Geysa [Note: The manuscript has the name Geysa. Concerning the entry of the Hungarians into Pannonia, or into present-day Hungary, and their earliest leaders, I have written in the Commentary, §5. Concerning Geysa, see more in §7 and those following.]—severe and cruel, acting with power toward his own people, but merciful and generous toward others, especially Christians, although he was still wrapped in pagan custom. Nevertheless, as the radiance of spiritual grace drew near, he began earnestly to discuss peace with all the neighboring peoples of the surrounding provinces, so that it might already be recognized in him whose son he desired to become, according to the saying of our Savior in the Gospel: “Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called sons of God” (Matthew 5:9).

He also established an ordinance that hospitality and security should be offered to all Christians wishing to enter his duchy [Note: The word “offered” is not in the manuscript and is not strictly necessary. This ordinance of Geysa was probably issued at the time of Otto I, after peace had been made with him, around the year 972, as I said in the same place, no. 80.]. He granted clerics and monks permission to approach his presence, and, gladly offering them free access, he took delight in seeing the seed of orthodox faith, sown in the garden of his heart, put forth a shoot.

### 3.

Why say more? The time ordained from heaven arrived. He himself believed with his household, was baptized, and promised that he would subject all under his authority to the Christian name. Since he was deeply concerned to subdue rebels, destroy sacrilegious rites, and establish bishoprics according to his judgment for the advancement of the holy Church, the Lord consoled him at night with a marvelous vision [Note: I have shown in the Commentary, §10, that there is no reason why this vision, properly understood, should necessarily be regarded as fictitious.].

He caused a pleasing young man to stand before him, who said to him:

“Peace be with you, elect of Christ. I command you to be free from your anxiety. What you are contemplating has not been granted to you, because you carry hands stained with human blood. A son will be born from you, to whom the Lord will entrust the arrangement of all these things according to the counsel of divine providence. He will be one of the kings chosen by the Lord, exchanging an earthly crown for an eternal one. Nevertheless, receive with honor the man who is to be sent to you on a spiritual embassy; having received him, hold him in reverence; give his exhortations the sincere assent of a faithful heart.”

The prince awoke stunned by the vision. After first considering it with himself, and then discussing it with Christ’s faithful and with his own people, he gave thanks to God, clinging to the pavement with outstretched hands. With tears he humbly commended himself, his principality, and the son yet to be born to the keeping of him who neither sleeps nor slumbers (Psalm 120:4).

### 4.

While he was therefore wondering about the man foretold by God, it was announced to him that blessed Adalbert, bishop of the Church of Bohemia, was coming to him for his conversion and the advancement of his sincere faith, in order to offer to the Lord God a sacrifice of praise. An indescribable joy arose among the new soldiers of Christ. The duke went out with all his faithful to meet the recruit of Christ [Note: The manuscript has “[.....]roni Christi”; Adalbert is called a recruit of Christ somewhat improperly, since he was a bishop.], received him honorably, and, as he had been warned in the vision, showed in every way that he would be a son of obedience.

At the prince’s command, a gathering of the untamed people took place everywhere [the word “people” was lacking in the edition and has therefore been added in brackets from the manuscript]. Through the holy bishop sermons were preached [Note: The phrase is faulty in the edition as well as in the manuscript. Surius has: “Through the holy bishop sermons are preached,” and I think that is how it should be read.], and through his continual exhortations the offspring of the nation were converted and baptized; churches were established in many places. For the light that enlightens every person, the darkness having been driven away, began to shine in Hungary, and in it were fulfilled the words of the prophecy that says: “The people of the nations who walk in darkness have seen a great light” (Isaiah 9:2) [Note: Surius has *ambulabat* (“was walking”), as Isaiah 9 in fact reads.].

The light of invisible light is Christ, whom the nations then deserved to see when, recalled from darkness, they came to believe perfectly that he was both the true God and true man [Note: The author has already indicated in no. 3 that the conversion of the Hungarians began before Adalbert’s arrival, and we have demonstrated this in the Commentary, §7. Nevertheless, that first conversion was incomplete, and even through Adalbert the Hungarians were not converted sufficiently perfectly, as stated in §10.].

Nor should this be passed over in silence: so that every ambiguity might be removed, lest the vision granted to the man alone seem to possess too little credibility, divine grace wished to console his wife, who was already approaching childbirth, with a similar vision. Blessed Stephen, the levite and protomartyr, appeared to her, adorned with the insignia of levitical dress, and began to address her:

“Trust in the Lord, woman, and be certain that you will bear a son, to whom the crown and kingdom are first owed in this nation. Give him my name.”

When the astonished woman replied, “Who are you, lord, or by what name are you called?” he said, “I am Stephen the protomartyr, who first suffered martyrdom for the name of Christ.” After saying this, he disappeared.

[Note: I have shown in the Commentary, §10, against the accusations of Schwartz, that this vision too is not incredible but is rather supported by other evidence.]

### 5.

Meanwhile the son foretold by the Lord was born to the prince—a son whom the Lord knew before he was conceived in the womb, according to the prophet, and to whom, before he was born, he gave a name through his protomartyr. The bishop Adalbert, beloved of God, immersed him in baptism with chrism, according to the truth of his faith. The name given to him was Stephen, which we do not believe to have been contrary to God’s plan. For *Stephanus* means “crown” in Greek. God wished to crown him in this world too with royal power, and decreed that in the future he should be crowned with the blessing of everlasting happiness, so that he might receive the unfailing glory of perpetual life.

He had the beginning of his birth in the town of Strigonium [Note: Strigonium, commonly Gran, is a city adorned by Saint Stephen thereafter with archiepiscopal dignity, which it still possesses. It is situated on the Danube and is well known.], and while still a boy he was fully instructed in the knowledge of grammatical art [Note: It certainly seems remarkable that the prince of the Hungarians should at that time have taken such care with Latin; nevertheless, there is no doubt that Stephen was imbued with the Latin language as a boy, since he issued many instructions and many charters to his son in Latin.].

The child grew, carefully brought up. When he had passed through childhood and taken the first step into adolescence, his father summoned the leading men of Hungary and, with the following order [Note: Surius has: “His father summoned the nobles of Hungary and the other orders.” The biographer says that one order was summoned together with the leading men; Surius improperly added several orders to the nobles.], by common counsel appointed his son Stephen over the people as the one who would reign after him, and to confirm this he exacted an oath from each person.

### 6.

Then, full of days, in the year 997 of the Lord’s Incarnation [Note: Writers agree on this death-year of Geysa, as also on that of Saint Adalbert. More concerning Geysa’s death and final deeds is said in §12. Stephen was then about thirteen or fourteen years old, as stated in no. 122.], he exchanged the troubles of this wicked age for heavenly joy. In that same year blessed Bishop Adalbert entered Prussia to preach the word of God and there was crowned with the palm of martyrdom.

After his father’s death, Stephen, still an adolescent, honorably ascended to his father’s throne with the favor of the nobles and people [the manuscript reads *actus*, “made”]. With more ardent spirit he began to become a propagator of the truth, because, although he flourished in the years of adolescence, he had not his heart on his lips but his lips in his heart. Mindful of the divine Scriptures, with which he burned intensely, he set judgment and justice before his eyes, in accordance with Solomon’s saying: “He who hears wisdom will become wiser, and he who understands will possess the helm” (Proverbs 1:5).

Thus, being a faithful steward of all God’s commandments, he began to consider within himself how he might devote the people subject to him to the worship of the one God. But because he perceived that this could by no means be done without consideration of the neighboring nations [Note: Surius has “alliance,” by which sense the author is to be understood.], he maintained peace with the peoples of foreign provinces [Note: Surius has “made peace,” in my opinion departing from Carthuitus’s meaning; I think Stephen merely strengthened the peace his father had made with the neighbors.] and faithfully reinforced the faith already established, so that he might more securely accomplish what he had conceived in his mind and be able to expel it from the new planting of Christianity.

But the devil, the enemy of all goodness, full of envy and malice, disturbed the purpose of Christ’s soldier by stirring up civil wars against him. At his instigation the pagan people, refusing to submit their necks to the yoke of the Christian faith, attempted, together with their princes, to withdraw themselves from his dominion [Note: The edition I otherwise follow reads “divine.” Since this is clearly an error, I have substituted “dominion” from the manuscript.].

### 7.

They began to lay waste his cities, ravage his estates, plunder his possessions, beat his servants, and—to say nothing of the rest—insult him. Since they refused to turn away from their perverse path and their fury was not satisfied, the duke himself, trusting in eternal strength, set out with the multitude of his army under the banner of God’s beloved pontiff Martin and of Saint George the martyr, to overcome the rage of the enemy.

In those days, perhaps, they besieged the city commonly called Vesprini, stirring up this opposition against him because the duke’s residence was perhaps located there [the text reads *forte ubi*, “perhaps where”], and because they wished to observe where they might find an easier entry for occupying his other strongholds. But he, preceded by divine mercy, rose against them, and they fought on both sides: he trusting in faith, they only in arms.

At last the enemies were defeated, some killed and others captured and bound. The victorious duke and his men carried home the rewards of victory. Accordingly, he wisely judged concerning their possessions, both in the fields and in the villages—not like Saul of old, who, after conquering Amalek, chose the best of its spoils, although the Lord had forbidden it. But because Pannonia glories in the birth of blessed Bishop Martin, and because the man faithful to Christ, as has already been said, had carried away victory over his enemies through the patronage of Martin’s merits, he reserved nothing of their goods for his own use. Instead, rightly, having taken counsel with the *theophili* [Note: Surius has “with the counsel of those who love God.” The author may have written *inito cum theophilis ... consilio*, “having taken counsel with the *theophili*, that is, those who love God.”], near the estate of the holy prelate, in the place called Sacer Modus [Note: The manuscript also has Sacer Modus, but Sacer Mons in Surius is more correct. The monastery of Saint Martin founded there was so called; I have discussed it at length in the Commentary, §15, where the reader will see that this monastery had already begun to be built before this victory.], where Saint Martin, while still living in Pannonia, had appointed a place of prayer for himself, he began to build a monastery in his honor. He endowed it sufficiently with possessions and revenues, and made it like the bishoprics, establishing such strict tithes from all their resources that, if anyone happened to have ten children, he would give the tenth child to the monastery of Saint Martin.

## CHAPTER II. Care for the advancement of religion; the arrival of many people in Hungary; the monastery built; bishoprics established; the legate sent to Rome, who obtains a royal crown and many privileges from the pope; his marriage to Gisela and the pious works of both

### 8.

After the enemies had been defeated, the soldier of Christ, filled with spiritual joy [the manuscript has “special joy”], resolved, with all the counsel of his mind, to become a receptacle for the evangelical seed. He devoted himself to almsgiving and prayers, frequently clinging to the pavement of the holy house, and, pouring out tears, entrusted the perfection of his purpose to God, who willed that he, since he could accomplish nothing without God, should be able, through the assistance of God’s providential fulfillment, to bring the good he had conceived to completion together with the beginning of his virtues.

To begin and complete this undertaking, since he considered the counsel of Christ’s faithful necessary, he spread his desire in every direction by messengers and letters. As a result, many priests and clerics, touched by a visitation of the Paraclete Spirit, left their own homes and chose to live as pilgrims for the Lord. Abbots and monks, desiring to possess nothing as their own, determined to live according to the rule under the governance of so religious a prince.

Among them Father Astricus of the regular life arrived with his disciples. One of them, named Boniface [Note: I find no more concerning the deeds of this martyr Boniface in other writers than what is read here, for Bonfinius mentions him briefly on page 174. Inchofer assigns his death to the year 1007 and says that three years earlier he had been sent by the king into Lower Hungary; in my opinion he fixes both dates by conjecture alone. He adds: “No mention of this Boniface appears in the martyrologies or other ecclesiastical histories, so that Hungary alone can claim him as its own.” He then asks whether perhaps he is the same as Saint Boniface the martyr, Saint Romuald’s disciple, who appears in the Roman Martyrology on 19 June, and says that he is certainly different: the other was a bishop and was crowned in Russia, whereas this man was an abbot and was killed in Hungary. Nevertheless, he is identified with that man in a booklet published at Tyrnau in 1692 entitled *Signs of Hungarian Sanctity*. There, on page 127, a brief eulogy is woven for Boniface, abbot of Saint Martin, who in the accompanying image is said to have been “killed by the Prussians around the year 1007,” but without plausibility.], later appointed abbot in the place of Father, was sent by the blessed king to preach in the lower regions of Hungary. He was struck on the head with a sword; although he survived afterward, he was not deprived of martyrdom.

Two others also came from the land of Poland [Note: The manuscript has “of Poland.” Bonfinius, on page 174, writes the following about them: “Also from that part of Dalmatia which they call Poliana came two hermits; one was named Andrew, the other Benedict. Andrew performed miracles through the merit of the holiness of his life. Benedict, when he shed his blood for Christ, was numbered among the blessed martyrs.” So runs Bonfinius’s History, unless an error has crept in. Since it is certain that these saints were Polish, not Dalmatian, I suspect that Bonfinius wrote “from that part of Sarmatia which they call Poland.” More concerning Saints Andrew—also called Zoerard, and in the Polish Office Andreas Suirardus—and Benedict may be seen in our volume IV for July, beginning on page 326, where their deeds have been carefully examined and their Life published.]. They chose an eremitical life for the sake of contemplation. One of them, named Andrew, was associated with the angelic choirs through the merit of his confession, as miracles performed by the Lord through him testify; the other, Benedict, was mercifully crowned after shedding his blood for Christ.

### 9.

Abbot Astricus and his companions were honorably received. At the foot of Iron Mountain he built a monastery under the title of the holy Father Benedict. There, even to this day, a monastic community, flourishing in regular discipline and abounding in temporal resources from the gifts of the holy duke, has no concern except to wash, according to the Gospel, the feet of its own members and of others with daily prayers and tears.

With these men the most Christian prince, the servant of God, sometimes conversing courteously with all together and sometimes individually with each one, showed himself so acceptable in divine eyes that he converted all the companions of his army to the worship of the true God. Those whom he found following another sect he subdued with threats and terrors, and, instructing them according to ecclesiastical teaching, placed the yoke and law of discipline upon their bowed necks [Note: The manuscript incorrectly has *suprapositis*, “placed above.” It is understood from the deeds in the Transylvanian war and from the laws given below that the king acted with great force against those opposing Christian law.]. He utterly destroyed all the uncleanness of evil.

### 10.

After this he divided the provinces into ten bishoprics and established the Church of Strigonium as the metropolis and mistress of the others. The prudent duke, recognizing the religion of the aforesaid Astricus, adorned him with the insignia of pontifical dignity, raised him by canonical election, and bestowed upon him the dignity of the bishopric of Colocium [Note: The manuscript here reads, probably incorrectly, although the phrase can to some extent be understood: “And he conferred Colocium upon him according to the dignity of a bishopric.” Colocia, later adorned with archiepiscopal dignity and now commonly called Kalocsa, lies on the Danube in Bács County.].

In the fourth year after his father’s death [Note: That is, in the year 1000.], by divine mercy’s prompting, he sent the same prelate Astricus, also called Anastasius, to the threshold of the holy apostles. He was to ask the successor of Saint Peter, prince of the apostles [Note: The manuscript reads *qui* (“who”) for *quod* (“that”).], to extend a generous blessing to the new Christianity that had arisen in the regions of Pannonia; to confirm the Church of Strigonium as a metropolis by the authority of his ratification; to strengthen the remaining bishoprics with his blessing; and also to deign to invest him with a royal diadem, so that, supported by this honor, he might establish more firmly what had begun through God’s grace.

### 11.

At approximately the same time, Myscha, duke of the Poles, embraced the Christian faith with his people. Through messengers sent to the prelate of the Roman See, he had requested to be supported by apostolic blessing and crowned with a royal diadem. The pope granted his petition and had already ordered a crown to be prepared, which he intended to send him with blessing and royal glory.

But because the Lord knows those who are his (2 Timothy 2:19), and because he preferred Matthias, chosen by lot through the apostles for the apostolate, and made him fill the apostolic number (Acts 1:26), that crown adorned Stephen, whom he would later adorn more happily with an eternal crown. When the appointed day arrived on which the crown already prepared was to be sent to the aforesaid duke of the Poles, on the preceding night a messenger of the Lord appeared in a vision to the pope and said:

“Know that tomorrow, at the first hour of the day, messengers from an unknown nation will come to you. They will ask you for a royal crown for their duke, together with the gift of apostolic blessing. Therefore take care to bestow upon their duke, without contradiction, the crown which you had ordered to be prepared, as they request [Note: The edition I otherwise follow reads *contractione*, “with contraction.” The manuscript has *contradictione*, which I have adopted here as certainly better.]; for know that it is owed to him, together with the glory of the kingdom, on account of the merits of his life.”

### 12.

Accordingly, at the hour prescribed for the following day according to the form of this vision, Bishop Astricus came to the pope. Wisely carrying out the duty entrusted to him and reporting in due order the deeds of the holy duke [Note: The *que* here is superfluous.
