The manuscript reads *qui*, which can refer to “the deeds of the holy duke,” yielding the sense: “reporting the deeds of the holy duke ... which ... requested.” The sense is also clear if *que* or *qui* is omitted, as Surius understood the passage.], he readily requested from the Apostolic See the insignia, indicating that he was worthy of such honor and dignity [the manuscript has *dignitati*, incorrectly], since through God’s help he had subjected many nations [Note: This passage deserves consideration, since nowhere do we read that before the year 1000 Stephen fought any war other than against the duke Koppány of Somogy and the other rebel subjects who adhered to Koppány. Nevertheless, in the king’s own charter for the abbey of Saint Martin, given in the Commentary, no. 150, the king himself suggests that he had also had another war to wage, for he says: “When the time of wars arose, because a great conflict had grown between the Germans and Hungarians, and especially because the ruin of civil war pressed upon us,” and so forth. He says again there: “If I should become victorious over his internal and external enemies through his [Saint Martin’s] merits,” and so forth. Both passages suggest that external wars occurred at the beginning of the reign. Ditmarus, as he is published by Leibniz and as he appears in our manuscript, also suggests near the beginning of Book VIII that Saint Stephen had some conflict with Boleslaus II, duke of Bohemia. After mentioning Boleslaus, he adds these words: “Something remains to be told concerning the misfortune of the aforesaid duke. He possessed a certain city situated on the border of his kingdom and the Hungarians, whose guardian was Prochnius [in Leibniz, Prochui], an elder and maternal uncle of the Pannonian king, expelled by him from his own seat, as before. Since he could not ransom his wife from captivity, he recovered her through the free gift of his nephew, although an enemy. I have never heard of anyone showing such mercy to the defeated; and therefore in the aforesaid city, as also in many others, God diligently granted him victory.” It is clear that these words concern Stephen, for he immediately continues concerning Geysa: “His father,” and so forth. Yet the matter itself is less clear, both because other writers are silent and because the words themselves are obscure, besides being related out of chronological order. We may nevertheless suspect that this war took place at the beginning of Saint Stephen’s rule and that it is the very war suggested by the words just quoted. Whatever the case, Ditmarus testifies that Stephen obtained victory both in this war and in many others.].

He had also converted many unbelievers to the Lord by his power. When the Roman pontiff heard this, he rejoiced greatly and graciously granted everything that had been requested. In addition, he sent a cross to be carried before the king as a sign of his apostolate [Note: The manuscript reads “as a sign of apostolate”; Surius has “as the insignia of apostolate.” The edition I am reprinting had *apostolitatus*, which I corrected from the manuscript.], saying:

“I am the apostolic one; he, deservedly, is an apostle of Christ, through whom Christ has converted so great a people for himself. Therefore we leave to him the task of arranging the Churches of God, together with their peoples and their way of life, according to the manner in which divine grace instructs him” [Note: The edition is corrupt here; the manuscript has the reading as I have rendered it, while its *vitiaque* (“and vices”) is no better. Surius correctly gives the passage as follows: “We leave to him, in our place, the task of arranging the Churches of God together with their peoples.”].

Having obtained everything as he had requested, Bishop Astricus returned joyfully to his own country, carrying with him the reason for which he had successfully undertaken his journey.

### 13.

When the letters of apostolic blessing were brought together with the crown and cross, and the prelates with the clergy and the nobles with the people proclaimed fitting praises, Stephen, beloved of God, was anointed with chrism and happily crowned with the diadem of royal dignity.

After receiving the sign of royal excellence, he made known, together with the bishops and nobles, the decree he had established for Hungary concerning the kind of man he was in life and judgment [Note: He is speaking of the laws enacted by Stephen.]. In it he prescribed an antidote opposed to each particular fault. To show himself a son of the peace through which Christ united the world, he established and left by a binding covenant to his descendants that no one should attack another with hostility, that no one should harm a neighbor without judicial examination, and that no one should oppress widows or orphans [Note: The manuscript perhaps has *forte*, “perhaps,” less correctly, and shortly afterward *qui* instead of *quod*.].

For the purpose especially of producing offspring, he took into marital companionship Gysla [Note: The edition again has Gysla, together with the manuscript; Surius printed Gisela, as modern writers commonly call her.], the sister [Note: This edition, as well as the manuscript, has “sister.” Surius incorrectly printed “daughter.” That error belongs to Surius, not to Carthuitus, although some attributed it to Carthuitus because they had seen only Surius’s edition.] of the Roman emperor, namely Henry, who because of the gentleness of his character was called the Pious, in marriage [Note: The manuscript has *matrimonio* (“marriage”) without *in*.]. He had her anointed with chrism and established her as his partner in bearing the crown of the kingdom.

How devoted she was to the worship and adornment of God [Note: Surius is more correct here with *ornandum*, “adornment,” which I think the author wrote.], and how frequently and blessedly she appeared among the congregations of those serving God [Note: The manuscript has *quasi* (“as if”) for *quam* (“how”); then *benedica* for *benedicta* (“blessed”), and *Deo* for *Dei* (“of God”), thus: “Quasi frequens et benedica circa Deo servientium congregationes,” etc. Again, a little later the manuscript has the less correct *usque die* for *usque hodie* (“to this day”).], is testified to this day by the crosses, vessels, and vestments of many churches, made or woven with marvelous workmanship. Above all, however, the house of the bishopric of Vesprimum, which she began from its foundations, she nobly adorned with every necessary provision for the service of God, in gold and silver and with many garments.

### 14.

The king himself arranged in royal fashion the bishoprics recently begun, both the archiepiscopal church and all the episcopal churches, assigning to each an extremely ample diocese and always placing over each a suitable prelate. He likewise provided the abbeys with estates, farms, dependents, and revenues, and sufficiently adorned each church with crosses, vessels, and other furnishings belonging to divine service, according to each one’s need. Every year, for as long as he lived [Note: These two words have been taken from the manuscript; the edition incorrectly reads *quo advitrix*.], he continually increased the gifts and offerings, so that those who presided over the sanctuary would not seek anything from outside.

He carefully examined the life and conduct of the monks, sometimes through others and sometimes in person, rebuking those who were sluggish and, with affection, setting the vigilant in positions of responsibility. He entrusted the ministry of the canons to the care of the bishops under the testimony of Christ and the Church, becoming, according to the Apostle, all things to all people in order to win them all (1 Corinthians 9:22).

15. At that same time there was in the monastery of Saint Martin a certain monk named Sebastian, whose life was considered exemplary and whose devotion in God’s service was esteemed. The venerable king began to love him with extraordinary affection, because the more religious a person was, the more acceptable he was to him. Judging him therefore worthy of episcopal honor on account of his merits of life, he appointed him to govern the archbishopric of Esztergom. And because God chastises every son whom he receives, he deprived the aforesaid Sebastian for a time of the light of his bodily eyes [Note: After this word, the printed edition adds *eum* (“him”), which is redundant and is absent from the manuscript.] in order to test his patience. But lest the young flock in the faith, deprived of a shepherd’s guidance, should stray from the purpose of the right path, with the consent of the Roman pontiff he substituted in his place the often-mentioned Astricus, bishop of Kalocsa. Then, when a cycle of three years had elapsed, Sebastian, having by God’s mercy received back his sight, was restored to his own see by apostolic counsel, while Astricus returned to his own church, namely Kalocsa, with the pallium.

## CHAPTER III. His devotion to the blessed Virgin: the church at Alba Regalis built, adorned, and endowed with gifts and privileges; pious foundations at Jerusalem, Rome, and Constantinople; the king’s mercy and generosity, and his miracles.

16. Meanwhile the same king was faithful in all his actions, perfectly devoted to God through vow and offering, continually commending himself and his kingdom, by assiduous prayers, to the perpetual protection of the Virgin Mary, Mother of God [Col. 1218D–1219A]. Her glory and honor are so celebrated among the Hungarians that even the feast of the Assumption of that Virgin, without the addition of her proper name, is called in their language “the Lady’s day.”

And so that he might obtain the greater mercy of her protection, in the very city of the royal seat called Alba, in praise and under the title of that perpetual Virgin, he began to build a famous and great basilica of marvelous workmanship. Its choir wall was decorated with carved panels, its floor was laid with marble slabs, and whoever sees it bears witness to the truth of our words: there were innumerable kinds of pallia and vestments; many panels around the altars were fashioned of the purest gold and contained rows of very precious stones; a ciborium of astonishing workmanship had been erected above Christ’s table; and a chamber was completely filled with every kind of vessel—crystal [variant: glass], onyx, gold, and silver.

17. Retaining the church described above, so splendidly adorned, as his own chapel, the king endowed it with such freedom that none of the bishops had any jurisdiction whatsoever in it. Even on the day of absolution and consecration of the chrism, whichever bishop the king, whether present there or absent and sending him, should appoint, was to absolve penitents there and consecrate the chrism. Likewise, if it happened that the king was present there, only that bishop was to celebrate the solemn divine Mass whom the king, with the consent of the provost and the brethren, ordered to celebrate [variant: nevertheless]. In the king’s absence, no bishop was to usurp for himself permission either to celebrate Masses or to exercise any episcopal office without the permission of the provost and the brethren.

Moreover, he established that the people of the same church should be so free that they were not required to give any tithes to any bishop, but should render service solely to the provost and the brethren, according to the arrangement he had established [Note: Bonfinius related all these matters concerning the church at Alba in almost the same way.]

18. Thereafter the servant of God strove to offer to Christ everything that he was then able to acquire, everything that had flowed from Christ’s gift, so that the one who had made him worthy of glory and honor in the present world might mercifully deign to associate him with the citizens of the heavenly homeland.

We read written in the prophecies concerning the apostles: “Their sound has gone out into all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world” (Psalm 18:5). This is shown to have been said not only of the Twelve, but of all those sent by God to evangelize, through whose faith, words, and conduct the Church grows. Among these, this most Christian king is proved to have been by no means the least. The reputation for good will and good works that he had acquired, in building churches throughout the extensive territory under his own jurisdiction [Note: That is, in his own dominion, and a very extensive one. Surius: “throughout the extent of his own dominion”], he had spread to lands and very famous cities far away.

For in Jerusalem itself, the city of Christ’s human sojourn, he built a coenobium of monks and enriched it with estates and vineyards, supplying an abundance for their daily sustenance. In Rome, the head of the world, he established, under the title of the protomartyr Stephen, a community of twelve canons [the manuscript reads “a community of twelve”], supplied with all its dependencies [variant: abounding in them], and built a stone wall around the property, together with houses [Note: The manuscript less correctly reads: “And a wall around it, built of stone, with houses,” and so forth. Immediately afterward, the manuscript also corruptly reads *quaerendum* (“to be sought”) instead of *quaerentium* (“of those seeking”).] and lodgings for Hungarians who, for the sake of prayer, were seeking the threshold of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles.

Nor did he deprive the royal city of Constantinople of gifts of benefaction; he endowed it with a church of marvelous workmanship [variant: marvelously made], together with all the things necessary for it. Therefore he deservedly acquired the name of “Apostle” within the boundaries of his dominion. Although he did not undertake the office of preachers by assuming the evangelization of those beyond his own realm, nevertheless he established himself as their leader and teacher, a support for their protection and sustenance.

19. Among all the benefits of heavenly compassion divinely granted to the blessed king, those most worthy of wonder and record are, above all, the qualities that hold first place in attaining the joys of eternal life—namely, mercy and truth. In all his fortunate deeds he aimed especially at this, which he had contemplated with a faithful heart through the testimony of the truth itself [Note: This passage is corruptly printed and is also different in the manuscript, though the manuscript is not more correct. Surius conveyed the complete sense but changed the wording. It can be emended by a slight correction if *testimonii* (“of the testimony”) is read as *testimonio* (“through the testimony”). The same word in the manuscript must likewise be corrected, and *testimonium* should be read there; for it has: “he contemplated with a faithful heart by sight,” and then “through the testimony of the truth itself”—read *testimonium*.], which says: “Blessed are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy” (Matthew 5:7), and elsewhere: “Give, and it will be given to you” (Luke 6:38).

Thus he embraced Christ’s poor—or rather Christ himself—with such great acts of compassion and arms of devotion that no guest or stranger ever departed from him in sadness, without some consolation of kindness. He established that daily expenses should unfailingly be provided for the relief of the needy. He was accustomed to spend the night watches briskly and cheerfully washing the feet of Christ’s faithful and secretly placing alms in the bosoms of the poor, resolving to console Christ in the needy members of his body for a time, so that he himself might deserve eternal joy when he found the chamber of heavenly life filled with every delight.

20. One night, touched by a spiritual prompting, and with no one knowing, the man of God went alone, carrying a full purse, as was his custom, to visit Christ’s little flock (Luke 12:32). Immediately the poor, as they jostled to receive the money of the heavenly treasure that was to be distributed, bore witness to the merit of the man of God by pulling out his beard.

Filled with the greatest joy because of this, the soldier of Christ went to the most blessed Mother of the Creator of all [the manuscript corruptly reads “the Creator”], prostrated himself on the ground, gave thanks, and exclaimed:

“Queen of heaven and my queen, the soldiers of the King whom you established have honored me in this way. If some enemy had inflicted this upon me, I would avenge my injury through your assistance. Knowing, therefore, Lady, that this eternal happiness has been granted to me, I rejoice exceedingly, giving thanks in the consoling words of the Savior with which he consoled his disciples, saying: ‘Not a hair of your head shall perish’ (Luke 21:18).”

After saying this, the man of God, perceiving that he had been visited by heavenly grace and drenched with spiritual chrism, resolved never to close the doors of his heart to those who believed [perhaps: those who sought help], but thereafter, both personally and through others—especially through Christ’s servants and household, namely clerics and monks—he caused the resources given to him from heaven to be deposited in eternal treasures through the hands of the poor.

21. Many people offer testimony to this, but among them one who shares eternal heavenly life with him is the blessed Gunther, a monk converted from secular nobility and an hermit. Attracted by the generosity of this charitable ruler, he often used to visit him from the land of the Bohemians [the words *cum Surio solebat*—“as Surius has it, ‘he used to’”—are to be added].

Whenever he entered the king’s court, illuminating it with the splendor of his arrival, the care of the kingdom placed in his hands was soon exhausted, after the resources it contained had been distributed among foreigners and natives, widows and orphans, monasteries and churches [the manuscript reads *consentiebat*, “agreed,” instead of *continebat*, “contained”] [Note: Surius reads *exinanita* (“emptied out”), for he expressed the sense as follows: “Then, after distributing among pilgrims, the needy, widows, orphans, monasteries, and churches the resources he had found in the court, he soon emptied it.” As for the statement that the care of the kingdom was entrusted to Gunther, I think it should be understood as the care of distributing alms throughout the kingdom; the following words supplied from Surius suggest this.]

At the bidding of that same servant of God, the king, devoted to God, began the monastery called Beel and endowed it with men. There the monk Gerard, coming from Venice, began to lead a contemplative life. Chosen by divine decree as a bishop, after the death of the holy king, when the Christian community was in turmoil, he was stoned and, through the gift of spiritual grace, was made worthy to share in the company of the martyrs [Note: The word *disturbatione* (“turmoil”) has been substituted from the manuscript; the printed edition corruptly reads *distributione* (“distribution”).]

22. Nor do I think this should be passed over: divine power wished to demonstrate during the man of God’s lifetime how great his merit would be after death. Whenever the illness of some person had been reported to his ears, he would send that person, as medicine that he could then provide, a piece of bread, an apple [Note: *Pomi* (“of an apple”) is omitted in the manuscript but is also found in Surius. Miracles of this kind are not unworthy of belief, for Stephen acquired a reputation for holiness through them in his Life, although he deserved it no less through holy works.], or a fragrant herb, commanding that the person rise healed. When God’s favor accompanied his word, the person immediately recovered health.

After our Savior’s glorious Ascension into heaven and his wondrous confession at the right hand of the Father [read *consessionem*, “session,” rather than *confessionem*, “confession”], he is said to have appeared bodily to a few, while through visions he consoled many and taught them to have foreknowledge of future events. The same thing happened to this holy king.

One night, suddenly awakened by a certain revelation [the manuscript corruptly reads *quidam*, “a certain man”], he ordered a courier to hasten to Alba Transilvana within a day and a night [Note: It is also called Alba Julia; among the Hungarians, Gyulafehérvár; among the Germans, Weissenburg. At that time it was the civil capital of all Transylvania and is still one of the principal cities of that principality], and to gather as quickly as he could all those living in the countryside into the fortifications of the cities.

For he foretold that enemies of the Christians were about to arrive—namely the Bessi, with whom the Hungarians were then at enmity—and to plunder their possessions. The messenger had scarcely fulfilled the king’s orders when, behold, the unexpected calamity of the Bessi devastated everything with fires and robberies. This occurred through a revelation granted by God on account of the blessed man’s merits, while the lives of all were saved by taking refuge in the fortifications.

## CHAPTER IV. The war brought by the emperor Conrad, quickly ended through God’s wondrous providence; the saint’s frequent prayer and rapture; a notable example of severity; the king’s illness and the deaths of his sons; various virtues.

23. After this, when the friend of the blessed king, the Augustus Henry the Pious of Roman dignity, had died, Conrad assumed the imperial crown through the election of the Germans [Note: The holy Emperor Henry died and Conrad, surnamed “the Salian,” was elected in 1024. War between Conrad and Stephen did not arise immediately; first there were certain disputes caused by the Bavarians, and then, in 1030, Conrad attacked Stephen in open war. Peace was restored the following year]. Having destroyed the peace of all Theotonia [Note: The manuscript reads *Teutonia*. The author means Germany, or the whole Empire] and united his forces, he attempted to invade the borders of Pannonia as an enemy.

Against him the king, having taken counsel with the bishops and nobles, brought out the armed forces of all Hungary to defend his country. First, however, recalling that he could accomplish nothing without Christ’s aid, he lifted his hands and heart toward heaven and commended his wrongs to his perpetual Lady, the Virgin Mother of God, his mother, breaking into these words:

“If it pleases you, Lady of the world, that a portion of your inheritance be devastated by enemies and that the young plantation of Christianity be destroyed, let this, I beg, not be charged to my negligence, but rather to the disposition of your will. If the shepherd’s fault deserves punishment, let him bear it himself; spare, I beg, all the innocent.”

After saying this, as though consoled by her, he confidently set out against the enemy. On the following day a messenger came to each of the German commanders and to the German camp from the emperor [Note: That is, as though sent by the emperor; unless Conrad really did send him and later refused to admit it], bringing them an order to return.

When the adversaries had withdrawn [Note: The manuscript reads “when they were setting out,” evidently referring to the enemies of the Hungarian kingdom], the holy man understood that he had been visited by God’s compassionate regard. He prostrated himself on the ground before Christ and his Mother [the manuscript more correctly reads “before Christ and his Mother”], and gave thanks. He commended himself and the administration of his kingdom to her protection through continual prayers.

The emperor, terrified by the sudden defection of his men, inquired how the matter had occurred. Knowing for certain that the messenger announcing their return had not been his own, he nevertheless did not doubt that it had happened through divine counsel, to strengthen the hope of the most faithful king. Thereafter, restrained by fear of the eternal Judge from invading his kingdom, he refrained from doing so.

24. The same king, occupied by the blessed concern of arranging royal affairs, spent the daytime in conversations and deliberations, while during the silence of night he devoted himself to vigils and prayers, contemplation, and the shedding of tears. He spoke to God in prayers and earnestly begged that the moderation of the just Judge might mercifully descend upon the daily examination of judgments.

When he diligently practiced this duty of spiritual desire, one night, far from any temple of God—for he had gone down with his great and noble retinue and pitched his tents in an open expanse of countryside—while the others were overcome by sleep, he rose from his bed, entered the chamber of his heart, and, bending his knees, knocked at the door of eternal mercy with groans and tears, using only the movement of his lips.

As he persisted for a long time in prayer, the ministers of his Lord, the eternal King, came together to receive his prayers. The tent stretched over him was lifted from the ground and began to hang suspended in the air until the man of God, returning to himself from contemplation, released his spirit from prayer.

Although this had been known invisibly to him alone who knows events before they occur, and to the angels who were aware of his secret, it was nevertheless revealed to a man of great simplicity and innocence [the manuscript reads *innocenti*, “to an innocent man”], who was perhaps at that moment engaged in a similar work. The holy king, taught by the Holy Spirit that this man was also aware of his secret, summoned him and first questioned him in gentle words about what he had seen. Then he strictly forbade him to reveal it to anyone as long as he himself lived.

25. The fame of his name had spread among the ears of many secular peoples, and the celebrated praise of his judgment was becoming known everywhere. Sixty men of the Bessi, whom we mentioned above, having departed from the regions of Hungary with all their equipment—namely, an abundance of gold and silver and a great variety of ornaments, loaded onto wagons—and wishing to come to the king, approached the borders of Pannonia [Note: More correctly, “of the Bulgarians”].

But many servants, whose wax-like character is easily bent toward vice, inflamed by the torch of their wickedness, went out to meet them. They struck some with the sword, took away everything that belonged to them, and left them empty-handed and half alive.

The Bessi, however, concealing from the king what had been done and what they had suffered, completed the journey they had begun. Hurrying to him, they threw themselves at his knees. When he saw them, he said: “What is the cause of these misfortunes?”

“Good lord,” they replied, “we, your servants, were coming with no evil plot, to hear the discipline of your judgments [these words are absent from the manuscript], but by the hands of certain men all the money we were carrying with us was taken away, though we had committed no offense. Moreover, they seized and beat some of us, and we have come scarcely alive to report it to you.”

The king, being a man of prudent mind, threatened them neither by his face nor by his words [the words “threatened them” are absent from the manuscript]. Rather, as it is written, “the prudent man holds back his spirit for later” [Note: The manuscript incorrectly reads *spiritu*, “with his spirit.” The author apparently has in mind the words of Proverbs 29:11: “The fool gives full vent to his spirit; the wise man quietly holds it back for later.”]. He immediately sent for the tribune under whom they served and, on the appointed day, ordered all those men of destruction to be brought before him.

It was done as he had commanded, and they were placed in his presence for examination. Addressing them, he said:

“Why, transgressing the law of God’s commandments, did you fail to understand mercy and condemn innocent men? As you have done, so the Lord will do to you before me today; for transgressors of the law must be struck.”

After receiving the sentence, they were led away, and throughout the kingdom’s territory two by two they perished by hanging [Note: The Milese manuscript has the same reading, and adds only these words concerning the deed: “By this, finally, he wished it to be understood that whoever would not submit to the judgment of justice which he had proposed on behalf of the Lord should be treated in this way. The inhabitants of the land heard the judgment that the king had judged and were afraid.”]

It should be believed that he did this out of zeal for justice in order to strike terror into the rest. Since he wanted the kingdom to be a powerful refuge for all guests, entry should be so free to everyone that no one entering would injure or presume to molest anyone else. And so it happened: for as long as he lived, no one presumed to inflict any trouble upon any guest.

26. In the blessed king it is also clear that the apostolic saying was fulfilled: “Through many tribulations we must enter the kingdom of heaven” (Acts 14:21); and the statement in the Book of Wisdom: “Those whom God loves, he chastises, and the Father scourges every son whom he receives” (Proverbs 3:11; Hebrews 12:6).

For he submitted to divine correction in many ways, laboring continuously under illness for three years [Note: The passage appears corrupt; it should read *continua laborans*, “laboring continually,” as was written in the copyist’s marginal note, and Surius conveyed this sense]. After he recovered from it through God’s healing mercy, nevertheless, by the judgment of the eternal and inscrutable counsel, he felt a certain testing imposed upon him through the death of his sons, whom, while still infants in the earliest stages of childhood, the one who had given them also took away [the manuscript reads *mittere*, “to send,” instead of *immittere*, “to impose”] [Note: Surius expressed this obscure and perhaps corrupt phrase more clearly as follows: “When at last he had been freed from that illness by the medicine of divine mercy, he felt the scourges of the eternal Judge in the death of his sons, whom death carried off while they were still infants.”]

The father restrained the grief that arose from their death because of his love for his surviving son, the boy Emeric, of excellent character. He loved him almost as his only remaining consolation and commended him daily in prayer to Christ and to his perpetual Mother, the Virgin.

He desired with all his prayers that this son should survive him and become heir to the kingdom. In order that he might become capable of holding the reins of so great a government through the instruction of orthodox men and the practice of daily reading, he had him give attentive ear to both kinds of hearing [Note: That is, the hearing of the body and the hearing of the mind].

The father himself, moved by the ardor of paternal affection, composed a little book for him on the formation of character. In it he addresses him faithfully and diligently with words of spiritual admonition [the manuscript reads “special admonition”], instructing him how, above all, he must observe the Catholic faith; strengthen the ecclesiastical order; show honor to the dignity of bishops; love princes and soldiers; uphold judgment; maintain patience in all actions; receive guests kindly and nourish them even more kindly [variant: kindly]; do nothing without counsel; always set his elders before his eyes as examples; frequently perform the duty of prayer; and possess piety and mercy together with the other virtues [Note: This little book, or the *Admonitions of Saint Stephen*, is found below. By comparing it with the brief summary that follows, the diligent reader will be able to judge how exactly Carthuitius followed the sources he used in composing this Life.]

27. Instructed in such and similar disciplines, the illustrious young man, obedient to the disposition of the eternal will to which all things are subject, exchanged this mortal life in the year 1031 of the Lord’s Incarnation and was joined to the eternal fellowship of the citizens above [variant: corruptly, *sempiternam* for *sempiterno*]. At the very hour of his passing, his soul was revealed to a certain Greek bishop [Note: This is related more fully in the Life of Saint Emeric, where that bishop is called Eusebius, metropolitan of Caesarea in Palestine. It is added there that the matter became known to the Hungarians through the report of a certain canon of Caesarea, who recounted it at Constantinople, where he was serving as legate. At that time there were bishops of Caesarea and of other places in Palestine, and they were in communion with the Roman Church, though they are less well known. Since the matter concerns Emeric more than Stephen, it can be discussed more fully on 4 November, the date on which Emeric’s memory is entered in the Roman Martyrology], a man of holy conduct, who was told that the soul was being carried by angels to the palaces of heaven.

But because he was loved by everyone with the greatest affection for the merits of his holiness, immense mourning arose among all, especially among the nobles. Among them his desolate father breathed a heavy sigh [the manuscript reads “contracted a heavy sigh”]. For he saw himself left alone, without hope of posterity, and grieved from an affection of piety [perhaps: with a pious affection]—yet, knowing that it is written, “There is no wisdom, there is no prudence, there is no counsel against the Lord” (Proverbs 21:30), and that “no one ought to grieve excessively over the death of loved ones,” he laid aside his sorrow [Note: I have elsewhere demonstrated that his mourning was not excessively prolonged, still less that he contracted an illness from it, as some have maintained].

He devoted himself entirely to seeking the generosity of divine mercy. He consoled the ministers of the coenobia and the Church, monks and clerics, with various gifts of alms, and distributed among pilgrims, widows, and orphans the whole amount of resources that he could then command. He also often visited monasteries in foreign provinces through his messengers, with countless gifts of royal generosity.

28. He retained until the end of his life the gravity of character [Note: The intended meaning is *gravitatem morum*, “gravity of character,” rather than *gravedinem morum*] that he had acquired in his youth. He scarcely ever moved his lips to laughter [Col. 1226A–B], recalling what is written: “Laughter is mingled with sorrow, and mourning occupies the end of joy” (Proverbs 14:13). He always appeared as though he were standing before Christ’s tribunal, contemplating Christ’s presence with a serene face through the eyes of his inner self [Note: “Of the inner self,” that is, of the mind]. He demonstrated that he carried Christ in his mouth, Christ in his heart, and Christ in all his actions [the words “he carried” are absent from the manuscript].

Always setting the final day before the eyes of his heart, he desired with the whole longing of his mind to dwell among the citizens of the heavenly homeland, as though already possessing a certain angelic way of life [variant: formerly]. Adorned with every kind of virtue pleasing to God, in holiness and righteousness he resolved to live before him all the days of his life, so that in him a certain image of future glorification might already seem to shine.

## CHAPTER V. His illness and the conspiracy revealed during it; his blessed death, burial, the decree for the raising of his body, and the miracles that occurred at the opening of his tomb.

29. Not long afterward he fell ill, and later died from that illness. As the long distress of his sickness grew worse, he was unable to stand on his feet.

Four of the most noble palatines saw him suffering gravely for a long time. For they were still wandering in the faithlessness of their hearts, had devised an evil plot, and attempted to bring about his downfall and death. As the day was already drawing toward evening, before a lamp had been lit in the house, one of them boldly entered in the darkness and concealed beneath his cloak a naked sword with which to cut the king’s throat.

As he restrained his step at the place where the king was resting, the sword truly fell through a heavenly impulse, and, striking the ground [Note: It would more correctly be said “and the ground, when struck, gave a ringing sound,” but the author has other less classical usages as well, which I have not thought necessary to note so long as the sense is understood], it produced a clang.

The king immediately heard it and asked the reason, for he already knew what had happened. The man, however, fell anxiously to the ground, recognized his murderous plot, grieved, approached, prostrated himself, embraced the king’s feet, confessed his offense, and begged to be forgiven. When he sought pardon, the king did not turn his face away and readily forgave him.

Finally, at the king’s command, the other murderers were found, and he spoke judgment against them [perhaps: judgments against them], imposing upon them a punishment they deserved.

30. At last, worthy through God’s mercy to receive the reward of a hundredfold, he was struck by fever. When he had no doubt that the day of his passing was near, he summoned the bishops and the chief men of the palace who gloried in the name of Christ. First he deliberated with them about appointing a king in his place. Then, as a father, he admonished them to observe the Catholic faith they had received, love justice, cherish the bonds of heavenly charity, devote themselves to charity, and diligently pursue humility. Above all, he urged them to guard the young plantation of Christianity [variant: “the plantation”].

After saying this, he raised his hands and eyes toward the stars and exclaimed:

“Queen of heaven, illustrious restorer of the world, under your protection I entrust the holy Church, with its bishops and clergy, and the kingdom, with its nobles and people, to your prayers. Bidding them a final farewell, I commend my soul into your hands.”

31. The principal solemnity was then approaching, celebrated by angels and human beings: the day of Mary’s Assumption. He hoped that, through the prayers of the Virgin, he would receive a greater hope of mercy when his body was dissolved [the manuscript reads “a greater hope,” rather than “the hope of greater mercy”]. He sought this with spiritual sighs and tears, and obtained it.

That blessed day was therefore present, soon to become more blessed through his death. The fatherly company of the bishops stood around him with the clergy, and with a company of ministers the chief choir of nobles. When the beloved king lay in their midst, having received the anointing of the spiritual sacrament, he surrendered his holy soul, refreshed by the viaticum of the body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ, into the hands of the perpetual Virgin and the holy angels, to be brought into the blessedness of eternal rest, in the year 1034 of the Lord’s Incarnation [Note: It is certain that the saint died in 1038. The ancient sources nowhere say in which city he died. Nevertheless, since the text soon says that his body was transferred to Alba Regalis, it seems to imply that he did not die there].

There was immense mourning among his people and joy among the angels. But this mourning was afterward changed into everlasting joy [Note: I think this was because of the miracles that followed and the saint’s glory], both for peoples yet to be born and for those already living.

32. People came together for his funeral from every region of Pannonia, and the body was brought to the royal seat, namely the city of Alba. Since the church of the Most Blessed Virgin, which he himself had built, had not yet been dedicated, the bishops rightly decided first to sanctify the basilica and then to entrust the body to the earth [Note: Perhaps the reading should be *statuere*, “to decide.” Various matters concerning Alba Regalis have been treated in several places; much concerning the construction of this church may also be seen in §25].

When the solemnity of the dedication had been completed, the holy body was placed in the middle of the house in a sarcophagus of white marble. There, for many years, the Lord, through his merits, bestowed countless benefits upon many who suffered afflictions, were tormented by fevers, proclaimed their distress and misery, and bore judgment [Note: Something is omitted here in the manuscript; for there one reads only: “There, for many years, the Lord through his merits bestowed countless benefits upon many who suffered afflictions.”]

Often during the night a melody was heard by many, with angels singing; frequently the sweetness of a most pleasant fragrance was spread throughout the sides of the church.

[Note: The phrase here is extremely corrupt both in the edition and in the manuscript, although they occasionally differ in wording. It was undoubtedly written, down to the end of this section, approximately as follows; this is the sense rendered by Surius: “The sacred body lay in that place for forty-five years, by a hidden ordinance of almighty God, who is wonderful in his saints [Col. 1228C] (Psalm 67:36), pressed by the weight of marble and reduced to dust, so that at the appointed time he might be declared worthy and be renewed more gloriously on the day of resurrection. What this signifies, since we by no means think it occurred without divine ordination and purpose, it is pleasing to contemplate with the inner eyes. Perhaps some small residue of earthly dust remained in him, to be purified by the fire of divine testing; without such a residue kings, supported by great power, can scarcely—or scarcely even—live out the present life.” I consider that Surius has given the sense correctly, but I by no means assent to the author’s speculation. The fact that the body, except for the right hand, as we shall see, was reduced to dust, and that it lacked public veneration for forty-five years, supplies no adequate basis for judging that after the saint’s death something remained in his soul to be expiated by purgatorial fires. Most saints’ bodies are reduced to dust according to the ordinary laws of nature, and many of them lacked public veneration for a longer time; yet it cannot therefore be inferred that after their blessed death any earthly residue remained in them. The author ought all the more to have refrained from this suspicion because the signs of holiness he had already set forth—the miracles, heavenly melody, and sweet fragrance—are so much clearer.]

When the blessed body had thus lain in the same place for forty-five years, pressed by the weight of a wondrous hidden ordinance, of him who is proclaimed wonderful in his saints [Col. 1228C], and reduced to dust, it merits at this foreordained time to be declared worthy and to be renewed gloriously on the day of resurrection. It delights the author to direct the eyes of the spirit toward what this signifies, since we do not think it occurred without divine purpose on the day of predestination.

Perhaps some residue of earthly dust remained in him, requiring purification by the fire of divine testing [the manuscript reads “excommunication”], without which rulers, as though by a certain right of power, can scarcely, or not at all, live out the present life.

### 33.

Accordingly, after forty-five years had passed, when God wished to reveal His saint’s merits in order to bestow through him the benefits of His mercy upon mortals, it was decreed by the institution of the Roman See and sanctioned by apostolic letters that the bodies of those who, lying in Pannonia, had sown the seeds of the Christian faith and converted it to the Lord by their preaching or instruction should be raised.

[Note: The reading was *interjectiones* (“interjections”), but I corrected it as plainly erroneous to *interjectis* (“after an interval”). Many further errors follow in the manuscript, and some also in the edition. I shall disregard the earlier ones; others I shall correct where they are obvious, but with notice to the reader.]

[Note: I supplied *cum* (“when”) from Surius.]

When the appointed time for his declaration arrived, and for the praises of his grace—which the Hungarian people had earned through him—to be spread throughout the world, King Ladislaus, who at that time governed the state, was esteemed outstanding in every moral excellence and conspicuous for the brilliance of his virtues. Perfectly devoted to the praise and service of God, and touched by the illumination of the Paraclete, he took counsel with the bishops, nobles, and wise men of all Pannonia. He proclaimed a three-day fast for everyone, so that whatever, for the common benefit of Catholics, appeared likely to be profitable through the gifts of the Holy Spirit, which bring salvation to souls and bodies, might be sought through the manifestation of signs and through the common supplication of all, grounded in fasting and almsgiving.

### 34.

But in order to show how great had been the mercy of the Lord’s holy king while he was still living in mortal flesh, and to demonstrate that he was already reigning with Christ, the Lord chose to confirm this above all his other works. For while they strove with all their strength for three days to raise his body, it could not be moved from its place by any device.

[Note: The manuscript has *approbatur* (“is approved”), but even so the sense is incomplete. Surius seems to have expressed the sentence correctly: “But in order to show with how great mercy the king, while still remaining in the body, had been endowed, and to declare that he had already shown this, while reigning with Christ, above his other works,” and so forth.]

At that time, because their sins demanded it, a serious quarrel had arisen between the aforementioned King Ladislaus and his brother Salomon, on account of which Salomon was being held captive in prison.

[Note: Salomon was not Ladislaus’s brother but his cousin. Perhaps he is called “brother” in a broader sense, unless an error entered through the copyists, or Carthuitius himself was mistaken. Salomon’s imprisonment and the cause of it are discussed in the Commentary, no. 439, where his release is also confirmed.]

When, therefore, they tried in vain to raise the body, a certain woman enclosed near the church of Saint Saviour, named Charitas, whose reputation for holiness was then widespread, sent word to the king through a heavenly revelation that they were striving in vain and could not transfer the relics of the holy king until Salomon had been released from prison and granted freedom by a merciful pardon.

[Note: I entirely do not know what the word *sumlui* means, unless perhaps it is a place-name. Bonfinius, recounting the same event, omitted the word, as did Surius.]

Accordingly, after Salomon had been brought out of prison and a three-day fast had been repeated, when the third day arrived for transferring the sacred relics, the enormous stone placed upon the tomb was lifted with such ease as though it had previously possessed no weight at all.

### Chapter VI. The raising of the body and miracles; the wondrous discovery and preservation of the right hand.

### 35.

When the evening office of the third day had been completed, and everyone was awaiting the benefits of divine mercy through the merit of the blessed man, suddenly, as Christ visited His people, the signs of miracles were poured forth from heaven throughout the spacious holy building. Since their number had exceeded the total during that very night, it is appropriate to introduce here the Gospel passage in which the Saviour had sent this answer to John, who was asking through messengers whether He was the one who was to come:

“ The blind see, the lame walk, the deaf hear, lepers are cleansed, the wicked are corrected, and paralytics are healed.”

[Note: The author indicates Christ’s words in Matthew 11:5: “The blind see, the lame walk, lepers are cleansed, the deaf hear, the dead rise, the poor are evangelized.” In my judgment, he did not give the words exactly because not all of them were applicable.]

Of these signs, however, we shall strive to make some known, since we cannot relate them all. A certain young man, with all his limbs slackened and having suffered paralysis for twelve years, lacked the use of his hands and feet. Carried there with the assistance of his parents, he recovered the health of his entire body and made the beginning of the signs. Then he ran energetically to the altar and increased the joy of all who were shouting praises to Christ.

### 36.

Another boy, seven years old, whose sinews had been contracted from birth at the knees and hands, was being carried.

[Note: *Reportabatur* means “was carried.” Surius altered the sense when he printed, “he crawled on his knees and hands.”]

His parents, full of faith, commending him to the intercession of the blessed man, laid him beside the tomb, prostrate with him, intending to seek grace. They soon obtained it and marvelled to see the contraction of the sinews in their son relaxed. When his knees and soles had been restored, everyone saw him walking and glorified the name of Christ in the merits of the blessed man with laudatory acclamation.

[Note: Another reading has the erroneous *incedentes* (“walking”), which I corrected from Surius to *incedentem* (“walking”).]

The king, devoted to God and weeping from excessive joy, lifted him from the ground in his hands and carried him to the altar. There, after a hymn of praise had been offered, he gave thanks to God for the benefits bestowed in the boy’s restoration to health, together with all who were present.

[Note: I think the reading should be “after a hymn of praise had been offered.”]

Thus God wonderfully illumined the entire night, in honour of His servant, with the radiance of many signs. The people, intent upon vigils and prayers, did not cease to make each miracle known through cries of praise.

[Note: The manuscript reads “through the veneration of His servant.”]

### 37.

It seems appropriate to insert here also the fact that not only those present there, but also people situated far away, obtained a celebrated result of salvation through the assistance of his merits.

When the fame of his elevation began to spread everywhere, people afflicted with various illnesses began to hasten from every part of Hungary to the holy tomb, each by whatever means he could. But since some arrived before the others, while others were prevented by more serious weakness from reaching the place at the same time, countless people were nevertheless healed along the road by a similar mercy.

Therefore, so that the memory of the holy king’s benefits might endure, many who had been healed through him gathered great heaps of stones at the place along the road where they had been cured; these remained there for a long time afterward.

[Note: The edition had *per mensuram* (“by measure”), but I corrected the error from Surius, who expressed the sense correctly.]

A certain woman, meanwhile, lost her son, who had been her only child, during these events. After he had breathed out his spirit, she laid his lifeless body beside the king’s tomb, intending to implore from God and His saint consolation for him.

A wondrous event, astonishing in our own times: the woman did not cease praying until she received alive the son whom she had placed there dead.

### 38.

At daybreak, on the fifth day after the Assumption of the most holy Virgin Mary, the princes assembled in the church with the king, and the bishops with the clergy. First a Mass for the dead was celebrated. Then the marble slab, which rose above the pavement, was lifted.

When they reached the tomb, such a fragrance of sweet-smelling odor surrounded everyone present when it was opened that they thought themselves transported into the midst of the delights of paradise.

The tomb itself was also full of a slightly reddish water, as though mixed with oil, in which the precious bones had rested as though in melted balsam.

After they had been gathered in the purest linen, they searched for a long time in the liquid for the ring that had been placed on the blessed man’s right hand.

[Note: The edition had *dextera* (“right hand”), but Surius has *dexterae* (“of the right hand”). The ring had been placed on the right hand at the time of burial. It was sought without the hand because the hand was believed to have decayed along with the rest of the body.]

When it was not found, certain men, by order of the king, began pouring the water into silver cauldrons and vats, so that, once the sarcophagus had been emptied, the discovery of the ring might be made more certain.

[Note: I supplied *ut* (“so that”) from Surius to complete the sense.]

But, remarkably, the more liquid was poured out, the more the tomb was filled as the liquid increased. When they saw this miracle, they returned the water they had drawn to its place. Yet even after it had been poured back, the tomb was no fuller on that account.

### 39.

Then, after the tomb had been covered, they proclaimed praises and thanks to divine mercy and restored the altar of the most blessed Mother of God, the Begetter and perpetual Virgin, with the treasure they had found.

Meanwhile God, who is wondrous in His saints (Psalm 67:36), made known through the abundant benefits of His generosity that He was present by the signs of His miracles granted to those who asked. So great was this manifestation that the time of the Lord’s sojourn among human beings seemed to have returned. Of that time it is written:

“All who had the sick suffering from various diseases brought them to Jesus, and they were healed.”

[Note: The author indicates Luke 4:40, with the wording altered slightly.]

Divine power deigned to perform all these things not only on that day but for a long time afterward as well.

[Note: The edition had *temporis* (“of time”), but I removed the error on the basis of Surius.]

When the fame of God’s benefits had been heard even in other regions, people suffering from illnesses of various kinds came with great eagerness to seek the assistance of the blessed man in order to recover their health.

[Note: The manuscript has *invaletudinum*, but the meaning is the same as *valetudinum*: “illnesses.”]

A certain countess of outstanding nobility, a matron named Mathide, had been burdened for three continuous years with pain in her internal organs and was already close to death.

[Note: Surius has *Mathildis*, as does Bonfinius in the Commentary cited at no. 446.]

Her attendants carried her on a litter. On the very day when she reached the tomb of the holy man, she felt herself gradually improving. In a short time she recovered her former health and proclaimed that God’s great works had been bestowed upon her through the merits of His servant.

### 40.

I have not left unwritten the other wonders of God’s miracles shown from heaven out of love for His servant because I disdain them. Rather, since the Lord is not pleased with me alone—He makes His sun shine upon the good and the wicked (Matthew 5:45)—and since I wish to promote the benefit of all through the abundance of His gifts, I have entrusted the innumerable wise men whom Hungary nourishes and embraces with the task of declaring them in writing.

[Note: It may perhaps be necessary to read *proficuo* (“for utility, advantage”) rather than *proficio*. The entire sentence is somewhat disordered. Surius expressed it as follows: “I have not omitted other miracles performed from heaven because I disdain them; but since the Lord, who makes His sun rise upon the good and the wicked, does not rain upon me alone, and since I desire that such an abundance of His benefits should serve everyone’s advantage, I leave it to the innumerable wise men whom Hungary nourishes and contains to set them forth in writing.”]

I have decided to attach only this account at the end of the book: the ring, long sought but not found by the wondrous gift of God’s mercy, was finally revealed together with the blessed man’s right hand after the completion of his translation.

A certain monk named Mercurius, who had been the guardian of the treasure of the perpetual Virgin in the clerical order, and who had already renounced the world out of love for the heavenly homeland, was removed far from there by royal rebuke at the very hour when the tomb had been opened, lest he seize any of the sacred relics.

[Note: The manuscript reads *ecclesiae* (“of the church”), but this is erroneous. The edition also has a single word, which I divided into two, as Surius does; the sense is thereby improved.]

As he sat in the choir with a sorrowful expression, a certain young man dressed in white handed him a wrapped cloth and said: “I entrust this to you for safekeeping; when the time comes, it is to be revealed.”

After the completion of the sacred office, the monk examined the cloth in a corner of the building. When he saw the entire hand of the man of God together with the wonderfully fashioned ring, he was terrified. Without anyone knowing, he carried it to the monastery entrusted to his administration, intending to await from Christ the time foretold to him by the young man. There he resolved to guard and watch over the treasure, hidden alone in a field, for a long time.

After he had made the founders of the monastery aware of it, and when the time for revealing the matter was at last approaching, he brought it to the king’s knowledge.

[Note: The manuscript has *consocios* (“associates”). Both this word and the following one require *fundatores* (“founders”) earlier, where the edition had *fundatoribus* (“to the founders”). A similar error is corrected shortly afterward from Surius; and *tempore* (“at the time”) is supplied in place of the incorrectly printed *temporis* (“of time”).]

The king immediately summoned the bishops and the leading men of Hungary and, while Christ was meanwhile displaying many benefits of miracles, appointed a solemn day for the raising of the man of God’s right hand.

[Note: Here again almost everything is corrupt. I suspect that *interim beneficiis* (“while meanwhile displaying benefits”) should replace *in beneficiorum*, and that *elevandae* (“for being raised”) should replace *elevare*. Surius reads: “He immediately summoned the bishops and the leading men of Hungary, and, while Christ meanwhile displayed many benefits of miracles, appointed a solemn day for the raising of the blessed king’s right hand.”]

### 41.

What does it mean, brothers, that while the other limbs had dissolved and the flesh had been reduced to dust, completely dead, God preserved the right hand alone in its integrity, with the bones, skin, and sinews adhering?

[Note: This phrase is disordered in the edition as well as in the manuscript, as I have observed in several places near the end of this Life. Surius presents it in complete form, either because he found it that way in his manuscript or because he corrected the errors. His words are: “But what does it mean, my brothers, that when the other limbs had dissolved and the flesh had been reduced to dust, God preserved the right hand alone intact, with its skin, bones, and sinews?”]

I think it signifies nothing other than that, through the depth of the divine plan, God wished to declare in this excellence of the saint that the work of almsgiving ascends through every degree of virtue.

[Note: This word also appears to be disordered, unless “the dissolution of captives” is intended, or unless *dissolutio* is understood as “release.” Otherwise one should read *distributio* (“distribution”), “piety,” “mercy,” or something similar, as the context suggests.]

Thus Truth says in the Gospel: “Blessed are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy” (Matthew 5:7). And again: “Give, and it shall be given to you” (Luke 6:38). In another place: “As water extinguishes fire, so almsgiving extinguishes sin” (Sirach 3:33).

Therefore the blessed man’s right hand rightly remained untouched by corruption. Always reviving with the flower of compassion, it was never empty of gifts for feeding the poor; it assisted those placed in need; it freed the oppressed from the yoke of captivity; it provided clothing and hospitality to strangers; it counted the sufferings and necessities of widows and orphans as its own; and in washing the feet of the needy it daily renewed the Lord’s Supper and commandment.

[Note: In the manuscript, *coenam* (“the supper”) is joined to what follows, as I have presented it. By the Lord’s commandment the author soon understands Christ’s words in John 13:14: “If I, then, the Lord and Master, have washed your feet, you also ought to wash one another’s feet,” and so forth. Since the Lord gave this commandment to His disciples at the Last Supper, and the saint regularly carried it out, the author says that he renewed the Supper and the Lord’s commandment.]

He caused alms to flow not from robbery or harm done to others, but from his own resources. In order to enrich the houses of God, he deprived himself of the desire to possess.

[Note: The manuscript reads *facultatem* (“the ability”), but *voluntatem* (“the desire”) gives the better sense.]

Thus, advancing all people according to the command of his dignity, he crucified his flesh with its vices and desires (Galatians 5:24).

From this came the delightful and wondrous veneration of his body and right hand; from this the sweet and blessed reward of eternal life; from this the desirable companionship of the citizens above, where there always shines the radiance—ever-luminous and unfailing—of the one supreme Godhead, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, through endless ages of ages. Amen.

---

## Admonitions with which Stephen instructed his son Emeric so that he might administer the kingdom rightly and piously

### Note

Although it is uncertain whether Saint Stephen wished to abdicate the kingdom in favour of his son Emeric, it is nevertheless certain that he intended the kingdom for his son and omitted nothing by which he might educate him for its proper and pious administration.

The documents given to his son, which Carthuitius briefly mentioned in no. 26, provide a clear testimony to that pious care; at the same time they show what Stephen himself was like, since it is unlikely that he neglected the matters he diligently impressed upon his son.

These Admonitions have been published by various writers. Werboczi included them in the second volume of his *Tripartite Work*, beginning on page 1, under the title: “The first book of the decrees of Saint Stephen, first king of Hungary, addressed to Saint Emeric, duke.”

They are counted among the decrees, or laws, of the kingdom of Hungary, although strictly speaking they are not laws but admonitions given to kings for the excellent administration of the kingdom.

I shall transfer them here from the edition just mentioned, as they are divided into a preface and ten chapters. I shall give the variant readings in the margin from the edition of John Sambucus, who published the same work after the works of Bonfinius and others. If anything appears obscure, I shall try to explain it briefly in the notes.

## Preface in which the king urges the duke to undertake his father’s admonitions and instructions

[Note: This title of the preface is omitted by Sambucus and certainly is not Saint Stephen’s. The invocation of the most holy Trinity, likewise omitted there, is probably the king’s, whose words follow.]

### In the name of the holy Trinity and undivided Unity

Since I understand through reason and intelligence that all things created by God’s will and ordered by His most evident foreordination are vigorous and enduring, both in the vast expanse of heaven and in these broad regions of the earth;

and since I see that all the things granted by God’s grace for the usefulness and dignity of this life—namely kingdoms, consulships, dukedoms, counties, bishoprics, and other dignities—are governed, defended, divided, and united partly by divine commands and institutions, partly by laws, partly by judicial principles, partly by civil regulations, and partly by the counsels, recommendations, and advice of noblemen and elders;

and since I know for certain that all orders everywhere on earth, whatever their dignity, not only command, advise, and persuade their attendants, friends, and servants, but also their sons;

therefore, dearest son, while I remain your companion in this life, I am not reluctant to prepare for you instructions, precepts, counsels, and exhortations by which you may adorn the conduct both of your own life and of those subject to you, when, by the concession of the supreme Power, you shall reign after me.

You, for your part, shall diligently listen and observe your father’s instructions, in accordance with the counsel of divine wisdom, which speaks through the mouth of Solomon: “Hear, my son, your father’s discipline, and do not forsake your mother’s law” (Proverbs 1:8), “so that grace may be added to your head and the years of your life may be multiplied.”

From this saying, therefore, you may understand that if you despise what I command you with fatherly affection—which God forbid!—you will no longer be a friend of God and human beings.

But hear the fall and ruin of those who disobeyed and transgressed a commandment.

Adam, whom the Lord, Creator and Former of all creation, fashioned in His own likeness (Genesis 1:26), and whom He made universal heir of dignity, broke the bond of the commandments and immediately lost the sublimity of his dignity and his dwelling in paradise (Genesis 3).

The ancient people, chosen and beloved by God, because they cast aside the bonds of the commandments engraved by God’s fingers, perished in various ways: the earth swallowed up some of them (Numbers 16:35), the destroyer put others to death, and some killed one another.

The son of Solomon, too, rejecting his father’s peaceful words and lifted up by pride, threatened the people with blows from a sword in place of his father’s whips. Therefore he suffered many evils in his kingdom and was finally overthrown (1 Kings 11:11).

Let this not happen to you. Obey me, my son. You are a boy, a child of luxury, an inhabitant of a cushioned chamber, reared and educated in every comfort, inexperienced in campaigns, labour, and the incursions of various peoples—matters in which I have already worn away almost my entire life.

The time has now arrived when you must not always be provided with the softness of cushions, which would make you dull and delicate, for that is the dissipation of virtues, the nourishment of vices, and contempt for commandments. At times, rather, hardship must be applied, so that it may make your understanding attentive to what I command.

With these matters prefaced, let us return to our subject.

## Chapter I. On preserving the Catholic faith

Since only the faithful and those imbued with the Catholic faith ought to approach the rank of royal dignity, we therefore give first place in our instructions to the holy faith.

Above all, I command, advise, and urge you, dearest son, if you wish to honour the royal crown, to preserve the Catholic and apostolic faith with such diligence and vigilance that you may provide an example to all those whom God has subjected to you. Then all ecclesiastical men will rightly call you a true man of Christian profession. Without this, know for certain, you cannot be called a Christian or a son of the Church.

Those who believe falsely, or do not fulfil and adorn their faith with good works—for faith without works is dead—neither reign honourably here nor share in the eternal kingdom or crown.

But if you retain the shield of faith, you also possess the helmet of salvation. With these weapons you will be able lawfully to fight against invisible and visible enemies. For the Apostle says: “He shall not be crowned unless he has competed lawfully” (2 Timothy 2:5).

The faith of which I speak is this: firmly and without any ambiguity you must believe and hold that God the Father Almighty, Maker of all creation, and His only-begotten Son, our Lord Jesus, born of the Virgin Mary when the angel announced it, who suffered on the cross for the salvation of the whole world, and the Holy Spirit, who spoke through the prophets, apostles, and evangelists, constitute one perfect, indivisible, undefiled Godhead.

This is the Catholic faith, which, as Athanasius says, unless someone believes faithfully and firmly, he cannot be saved.

[Note: Learned men now debate whether the Creed praised above under the name of Saint Athanasius was composed by that holy Father. That debate, however, was not yet known in Saint Stephen’s time.]

If anyone should ever be found under your authority—God forbid!—who attempts to divide, diminish, or increase this confession of the Holy Trinity, know that such people are servants of the heresiarchs and not sons of the holy Church.

You must neither nourish nor defend them, lest you too appear to be their friend and supporter.

Such men make the children of the holy faith altogether diseased, and they miserably destroy—and will also scatter—the young people of the holy Church.

Take particular care that this does not happen.

## Chapter II. On the Church and maintaining the ecclesiastical order

In the royal palace, after faith, the Church holds the second place. It was first planted by our Head, Christ; then transplanted and firmly built up through His members, namely the apostles and holy Fathers; and it was spread throughout the whole world.

Although it always brings forth a new offspring, in certain places it is nevertheless regarded as ancient.

In our kingdom, however, dearest son, it is still proclaimed to be young and newly established. For that reason it requires more watchful and more evident guardians, lest the good which divine clemency has granted to us undeserving people through its immense mercy be destroyed and annihilated by your laziness, idleness, and negligence.

For whoever diminishes or disfigures the dignity of the holy Church attempts to mutilate the body of Christ.

The Lord Himself said to Peter, whom He appointed guardian and teacher of the holy Church: “You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church” (Matthew 16:18).

[Note: A few matters should be observed here. Saint Stephen’s words, “He was indeed naming himself the rock,” may probably refer to Saint Peter; but it makes little difference whether he understood the passage in this way or another. Saint Augustine, in Book I of the *Retractations*, chapter 21, writes that he sometimes understood “rock” to mean Christ and sometimes Peter, adding: “Let the reader choose which of these two interpretations is the more probable.” These words of the great teacher show the uncertainty in which he stood concerning the true interpretation of the passage.

They also prove that Saint Augustine acknowledged that not Christ alone was the rock of the Church, but that Peter too was the rock of that Church, subordinated, of course, to Christ. For if he had not acknowledged this, he would not have left it open to everyone to understand the passage either of Christ or of Peter.

This is also clear from the verse of Saint Ambrose that he quotes in the same place: “By this Rock itself, when the cock crowed, he wiped away his guilt.” The holy doctor had first embraced the natural interpretation concerning Peter, whom he called the rock, as he says. Later, however, he slipped into the other interpretation, in my opinion solely through ignorance of the Hebrew and Syriac languages.

The doctor’s own words reveal this ignorance. For as his reason for interpreting the passage of Christ, he gives only the following: “For it was not said to him, ‘You are the Rock,’ but, ‘You are Peter.’” But Christ spoke in Syriac and used the same word twice, *Cepha* or *Kepha*. The same word is repeated in the Hebrew Gospel of Matthew published by Münster, as though Latin had said: “You are the Rock, and upon this rock.” Many Catholic interpreters have already shown this, and various heretics have admitted it.

Saint Augustine’s entire argument therefore collapses. Without doubt he would have followed only the common interpretation of the passage, abandoning the other entirely, if he had known that the same word was repeated twice in Syriac.

I have made these brief observations because Schwartzius abused this passage.]

Christ did not say that He was building upon Himself a wooden or stone Church, but He called and designated as the Church built upon Him the people of acquisition, the chosen nation (1 Peter 2:9), divine, a flock instructed in the faith, washed in baptism, and anointed with chrism.

If anyone, unhappy man, scandalizes the members or little ones of this holy Church, then, according to the Gospel commandment, he is worthy to have a millstone hung around his neck and to be cast into the depths of the sea (Matthew 18:6); that is, he should be thrown down from the dignity of power and remain outside the Church of the just, in that worldly misery, like a pagan and a publican.

Therefore, my son, you must watch over the holy Church from day to day with fervent zeal, so that it may receive increase rather than suffer loss.

For this reason kings were first called Augusti, because they increased the Church.

You too must do this, so that your crown may be considered more praiseworthy and your life happier and longer.

[Note: The argument made here by the heterodox writer is even more frivolous—indeed, completely ridiculous. From Saint Stephen’s words he tried to infer that by the Church built upon the rock he understood “a chosen and divine nation, not a hierarchy flourishing, powerful, splendid, and dominant under one visible head with its visible members.”

Saint Stephen, however, teaches here only that by “Church” one does not understand some house or building constructed of wood and stones, which is also called a church in a very different sense. Rather, by “Church” Christ designates the assembly of all the faithful, which truly is “a people of acquisition, a chosen and divine nation” (1 Peter 2:9), a flock taught in the faith, washed in baptism, and anointed with chrism.

Christ appointed Saint Peter guardian and teacher of this assembly, as Saint Stephen testifies. Thus the holy king not only does not oppose the hierarchical order of the Church in his words, but clearly asserts it, since he says that Peter was appointed by Christ as guardian and teacher of the Church—and of that very Church which, as he previously states, “was first planted by our Head, namely Christ, then transplanted through His members, namely the apostles and holy Fathers, firmly built up, and spread throughout the whole world.”

Saint Stephen says that Peter was appointed guardian and teacher of the Church spread throughout the whole world. He therefore clearly acknowledges the hierarchy of the Church under a visible head.

These brief observations have been made so that it may be clear by what frivolous arguments heterodox writers attempt to drag Saint Stephen’s words toward their false doctrines, although from all his deeds they could abundantly learn that they have departed far from the faith of the first Hungarians.

As for what is said at the end about the etymology of “Augustus,” it is merely an accommodation. Emperors were called Augusti after the emperor Augustus, just as Caesars are named after Julius Caesar.]

## Chapter III. The rank of bishops and the honour to be shown to prelates

The order of prelates adorns the royal throne; accordingly, in royal dignity the prelates hold the third place.

Dearest son, guard those elders as the pupils of your eyes. If you possess their goodwill, you will fear none of your adversaries. If they watch over you, you will be secure in all things, and their prayer will commend you to almighty God.

For God appointed them guardians of the human race and made them watchers over souls and over the entire ecclesiastical dignity, as well as dispensers and givers of the divine Sacrament.

[Note: Another reading has “of the divine race” rather than “of the human race.”]

Without them kings are not established, nor are principalities constituted.

Through their intercession the sins of human beings are blotted out. If you love them perfectly, you undoubtedly heal yourself and govern your kingdom honourably.

For into their hands has been placed the power of binding us in sins and releasing us from sins.

God established for them an everlasting covenant, separated them from other human beings, made them participants in His name and holiness, and forbade them to be reproached by human beings through David, the deified king: “Do not touch my anointed ones” (Psalm 104:15), and so forth.

[Note: Another reading has “For he touches God’s anointed,” rather than “But he touches God’s anointed.”]

He touches God’s anointed who, contrary to divine and canonical institution, disgraces men of the sacred order with false accusations and brings them into public view.

This I altogether forbid you to do, my son, if you wish to live happily and honour your kingdom, because in such matters God is especially offended.

If by some chance a fault deserving correction should be found in one of those of whom we are speaking—which God forbid!—rebuke him three or four times privately, between yourself and him alone, according to the Gospel commandment (Matthew 18:15).

If he then secretly refuses to listen to your admonitions, you must bring public measures against him, in accordance with the words: “If he will not hear you, tell it to the Church” (Matthew 18:17).

For if you observe this order, you will thoroughly exalt your glorious crown.

[Apparatus omitted from the main translation: §33, *jacentes* is also printed, erroneously, as *jacentes*. §34, *regnasse* may be *regnans*, “reigning.” §35, *subito* has the erroneous alternative *subdito*; the corrected reading replaces the erroneous *masserat*. §37, *post multum* may be *postmodum*, “afterward.” §39, *notificavit* has the erroneous alternative *notificabit*, “will make known”; *post tempore* corrects *temporis*, “of time.” §40, read *multiplicitatem*, “abundance,” for *multiplicitate*. §41: the manuscript has *nil*, “nothing,” for *non*, “not”; *Verum*, “but,” for *Unde*, “whence”; *vero*, “indeed,” for *ergo*, “therefore”; and *radiat*, “shines,” for *irradiat*, “radiates.”

Preface: *amplissimis*, “very broad,” may be *aptissimis*, “most suitable”; *juridicis*, “juridical,” may be *juridicialibus* or *jurisdictionibus*, “jurisdictional matters”; *consulere*, “to advise,” may be *consiliari*, “to take counsel”; *non piget*, “I am not reluctant,” may be *ne pigeat*, “let me not be reluctant”; *parare*, “to prepare,” may be *proponere*, “to set forth”; *quod amplius*, “that any longer,” may be *quod iam amplius*, “that now any longer”; *inobedientium*, “of the disobedient,” has the erroneous alternative *inobedientiam*, “disobedience”; *legamina*, “bonds,” may be *ligamina*, “bindings”; *patris*, “of his father,” is omitted in one reading; *deliciarum*, “of luxury,” may be *divitiarum*, “of riches”; *pulvinarium mollities*, “softness of cushions,” may be *pulvinar mollitiei*, “a cushion of softness”; and *expeditionum laboris*, “the labour of campaigns,” may be *totius expeditionum laboris*, “the labour of all campaigns.”
