Chapter I: *coronam*, “crown,” may be *curiam*, “court”; *viri*, “men,” may be *filii*, “sons”; *scutum*, “shield,” may be *statum*, “state”; *participant*, “share,” may be *participantur*, “are made participants”; *creaturae*, “creation,” may be *facturae*, “the thing made”; *sicut*, “as,” may be *sic*, “thus”; *conabuntur*, “will attempt,” may be *conantur*, “attempt”; and *amicus et fautor*, “friend and supporter,” may be *inimicus et ultor*, “enemy and avenger.”

Chapter II: *pariat*, “brings forth,” may be *habeat*, “has”; the second *clementiam*, “clemency,” may be *misericordiam*, “mercy”; *verum*, “but,” is omitted in one reading; *doctum*, agreeing with *gregem*, “a flock instructed,” has the erroneous variant *doctam*; and *Inde etiam*, “for this reason also,” may be *inde quidem*, “indeed for this reason.”

Chapter III: *habebis*, “you will have,” may be *habes*, “you have”; *humani generis*, “of the human race,” may be *divini generis*, “of the divine race”; *dispensatores*, “dispensers,” may be *dispositores*, “administrators”; *principatus*, “principalities,” may be *principantur*, “they rule”; *Testamentum enim*, “for [He established] a covenant,” may be *Testamentum vero*, “but [He established] a covenant”; *ab hominibus*, “by human beings,” has the corrupt alternative *ab humano die*, “from the human day”; and *Ille autem*, “but he,” may be *ille enim*, “for he.”]

## CHAPTER IV

### On the worthy honor of princes and barons

The fourth ornament of government is the loyalty, courage, agility, courtesy, and confidence of princes [alternative: “the princes” is absent, and immediately afterward “of nobles”], barons, counts, knights, and nobles. For they are the defenders of the kingdom [alternative: “the kingdom’s stronghold”], the protectors of the weak, the conquerors of adversaries, and the enlargers of monarchies.

Let them be fathers and brothers to you, my son. Do not reduce any of them to servitude or call them slaves; let them render military service to you, not be your slaves. Rule over all of them peacefully, humbly, and gently, without anger, pride, or envy, always remembering that all human beings are of one condition, and that nothing exalts except humility, while nothing casts down except pride and envy.

If you are peaceful, then you will be called a king and a king’s son, and you will be loved by all the soldiers. But if, being angry, proud, envious, and hostile, you raise your neck above counts and princes, then without doubt the courage of the soldiers will become weakness, the royal dignities will be blunted, and they will hand your kingdom over to strangers.

Fearing this, direct the life of your counts according to the rule of the virtues, so that, bound to you by affection, they may always remain attached to royal dignity without offense, and so that your kingdom may be peaceful in every respect.

[Col. 1240A]

## CHAPTER V

### On preserving the virtue of patience and administering judgment

The observance of patience and judgment is the fifth adornment of the royal crown. King and prophet David said: “Give your judgment to the king” (Psalm 121:2). And elsewhere: “The king loves judgment” (Psalm 98:4). The apostle Paul speaks of patience: “Be patient toward all” (1 Thessalonians 5:4). And the Lord says in the Gospel: “By your patience you will possess your souls” (Luke 21:19).

Strive toward this, my son. If you wish to possess the honor of the kingdom, love judgment; if you wish to possess your soul, be patient.

Whenever, my dearest son, either a case deserving judgment comes before you or someone guilty of a capital sentence is brought before you, do not bear it impatiently or bind yourself with an oath to punish him—for such a resolve should be unstable and fragile, since foolish vows must be broken—or judge the matter yourself, lest your royal dignity be stained by the usurpation of inferior affairs. Rather, send such a case to the judges to whom it has been entrusted, so that they may discern it according to their own law.

Fear being a judge, but rejoice to be and to be called a king. Patient kings reign; impatient ones tyrannize. Whenever something appropriate to your royal dignity for judgment comes before you, judge it with patience and mercy—or compassion—so that your crown may be praiseworthy and splendid.

[Note: In this passage Sambucus’s edition contains various errors beginning with the words “Fear being a judge,” as the diligent reader will easily notice. I therefore did not think it necessary to list each one individually.]

## CHAPTER VI

### On receiving foreigners and providing for guests

There is such great usefulness in guests and visiting men that this can rightly be regarded as the sixth element of royal dignity. From this, above all, the Roman Empire grew, and the Roman kings were exalted and made glorious: namely, because many noble and wise men gathered there from different regions. Rome would still be a slave to this day if the descendant of Aeneas had not made it free.

For just as guests come from different parts of the provinces, so they bring with them different languages and customs, as well as different instruction and weapons. All these things adorn and magnify the royal court and terrify the arrogance of foreigners. For a kingdom of one language and one custom [alternative: “one mortality”] is weak and fragile.

Therefore I command you, my son, to nourish them with goodwill and to keep them honorably, so that they may prefer to live with you rather than dwell anywhere else. For if you strive to destroy what I have built or scatter what I have gathered, your kingdom will undoubtedly suffer the greatest loss.

To prevent this, increase your kingdom daily, so that your crown may be regarded by all as august [the word “august” is absent in the alternative].

[Note: What is said here about the arrival of many guests in the city of Rome may be found in Livy, Book I, where it is related by what methods Romulus—called above the descendant of Aeneas—filled Rome with a multitude of people.]

## CHAPTER VII

### On the greatness of counsel

In the tribunals of kings, counsel claims the seventh place for itself. For by counsel kings are established, kingdoms governed, the homeland defended, battles arranged, victory won, enemies driven back, friends summoned, cities built, and the camps of adversaries destroyed.

Counsel is useful when it is present. For such men are not formed, as it seems to me, by fools, arrogant men, and mediocrities, but must be drawn out and refined by greater, better, wiser, and most honorable elders.

Therefore, my son, do not deliberate with young men or with those who are less wise, nor seek counsel from them; seek it instead from elders, for whom such business is suitable because of their age and wisdom. For the counsels of kings ought to be enclosed in the hearts of the wise, not spread abroad through the empty talk of fools.

If you walk with the wise, you will become wise; if you associate with fools, you will join them, as the Holy Spirit declares through Solomon: “Whoever walks with the wise will be a friend of the wise and will not be like fools” (Proverbs 13:20). And David sings: “With the holy you will be holy, with an innocent man you will be innocent, with the chosen you will be chosen, and with the perverse you will become perverse” (Psalm 17:26–27).

Let each person exercise himself in whatever business is appropriate to his age: young men in arms, senators in counsel. Nevertheless, young men must not altogether be excluded from counsel. Whenever you take counsel with them, even if it is useful, always refer it to your elders, so that you may measure all your actions by the rule of wisdom.

## CHAPTER VIII

### That elders should be imitated and sons obey their parents

The imitation [alternative: “execution”] of elders occupies the eighth place in royal dignity. Know that the greatest royal ornament is to follow preceding kings and to imitate honorable parents.

Whoever despises the decrees of his forefathers and does not uphold the divine laws will perish. Fathers are fathers for this reason: that they may nourish their sons. Sons are sons for this reason: that they may obey their fathers. Whoever resists his father is an enemy of God [alternative: “stands against God”]. For all the disobedient resist God. The spirit of disobedience scatters the flowers of the crown. Disobedience is the plague of the whole kingdom.

Therefore, my dearest son, may the commands of your father always be ready for you, so that your prosperity may everywhere be guided by royal reins. Follow without the bondage of any doubt the customs that you see to be fitting for royal dignity.

It is difficult for you to hold the kingdom of this region unless you become an imitator of the customs of the kings who ruled before. What Greek could rule Latins by Greek customs? Or what Latin could rule Greeks by Latin customs? No one.

Therefore follow my customs, so that you may be regarded as eminent among your own people and praiseworthy among foreigners.

## CHAPTER IX

### That one must pray, and how

The observance of prayer is the greatest acquisition of royal salvation, and therefore it occupies the ninth place [an addition in one witness: “it obtains its place”]; the ninth rule of royal dignity proclaims this. Continual prayer is the washing away [alternative: “abolition”] and remission of sins.

Whenever you run to the temple of God, my son, in order to worship God, always say, together with Solomon, the son of the king—and himself a king:

“Send forth, Lord, wisdom from the seat of your greatness, so that it may be with me and labor with me, that I may know what is acceptable before you at all times” (Wisdom 9:10).

And again:

“Lord, Father and God of my life, do not abandon me to a wicked thought; do not give me the lifting up of my eyes; and turn away wicked desire from me, Lord. Take lust away from me, and do not hand me over to a disrespectful and unrestrained mind [alternative: “unbridled mind”]” (Ecclesiasticus 23:4–6).

The ancient kings used this prayer. Use it also, so that God may deign to remove all these things from your life, and so that you may be called by all an unconquered king.

Pray also that he may drive idleness and dullness away from you and grant you an abundance of every virtue, by which you may conquer visible and invisible enemies, so that, safe and free from every attack of adversaries, you may finish the course of your life peacefully together with all who are subject to you.

## CHAPTER X

### On piety, mercy, and the other virtues

The pattern of the virtues adorns the crown of kings, and is placed tenth among the precepts, for the Lord of virtues himself is the King of kings. Therefore, just as the fullness of the heavenly army consists in ten choirs [see the note below], so let the conduct of your life persist in ten commandments.

[Note: What was said above—that the fullness of the heavenly host consists in ten “hours”—seems strange, since only nine choirs of angels are enumerated. But I suspect that by the tenth choir the saint means all human beings raised to heavenly glory. Here, reader, you have the Admonitions of the holy king, which clearly show how great he was, not only in Christian virtues but also in the art of ruling. They are indeed worthy to remain deeply engraved upon the minds of princes. Now I shall likewise give the laws that the same king prescribed for his subjects, so that from them all it may be clear what manner of man and how great he was, and how much Christian Hungary owes to its apostle and lawgiver.]

A king ought to be pious, merciful, and imbued and adorned with the other virtues. For a king stained by impiety and cruelty claims the name of king in vain, since he must be called a tyrant.

Therefore, my most beloved son, sweetness of my heart and hope of future offspring, I beg and command you to be supported by piety in everything and toward everyone. Be favorable not only to your family and relations, or to princes, dukes, and rich men, or to neighbors and inhabitants, but also to foreigners and to all who come to you. For the work of piety leads you to supreme blessedness.

Be merciful to all who suffer violence, always keeping in the depths of your heart that example of the Lord: “I desire mercy and not sacrifice” (Matthew 9:13).

Be patient toward all, not only the powerful but also those without power. Finally, be brave, so that prosperity may not lift you up too much or adversity cast you down. Also be humble, so that God may make you exalted, both here and in the future. Be moderate, and punish or condemn no one beyond measure. Be gentle, so that you may never oppose justice. Be honorable, so that you may never voluntarily inflict disgrace upon anyone. Be chaste, so that you may avoid all the foulness of lust as the sting of death.

All these things, touched upon above, compose the royal crown. Without them no one can reign here or attain the eternal kingdom.

[Col. 1243]

# THE LAWS OF SAINT STEPHEN

## Note

Carthuitius, no. 13, briefly discusses the laws established by “Saint Stephen with the bishops and leading men of Hungary,” and says that in them “he prescribed an antidote opposed to each individual fault.”

These laws are plainly such as suited an uncivilized people, who had partly embraced Christian discipline and partly rejected it. It is also probable that these laws received considerable reinforcement from the preaching of bishops and other clergy who instructed the people. For it is natural that a desire should arise to know what one does not dare to neglect.

I have not discovered in what year these laws were first issued or whether they were all decreed at once. Nevertheless, they were all promulgated together at some council of the bishops and nobles of Hungary. Concerning this promulgation, the edition in the *Tripartite Work* states: “Here ends the decree of Saint Stephen the king, promulgated at Esztergom [alternative: Tolna] in the year 1035.”

Peterfius, preparing to publish some of these laws, speaks of their promulgation as follows: “These ordinances and admonitions, which afterward acquired the force of statutes, were promulgated in the year of the Lord 1016 at Tolna or Esztergom.”

Inchofer, under the year 1016, writes of the laws established by Stephen:

“King Stephen, for the ordering of his kingdom, established salutary laws this year with the intervention of his leading men of both estates. These laws are contained in fifty-five chapters, arranged by some in such a way that they are placed in a second book of the *Decrees* attributed to King Stephen. In this matter, however, neither order nor chronological sequence has been preserved. For what appears in the first book consists not properly of decrees, but of admonitions composed separately for the instruction of his son Emeric and published later. The decrees themselves are falsely said by some to have been established in the thirty-fifth year of his reign. It is clear that many of them had been in force long before, although some relating to civil government were added later. It is better in this matter to follow the authority of the manuscript, which assigns the laws sanctioned by Stephen to this year. For it is not probable that Stephen, who had reigned piously and successfully for so many years, would, at the end of his life, when burdened with cares and illnesses, have wished to organize his kingdom by law, while previously, for so long a period, he had neglected it without law.”

These arguments very plausibly persuade us that most of the laws were established and promulgated much earlier than some have maintained, while others were added in the course of time. Whether the promulgation of all of them took place in 1035 or earlier cannot be determined with certainty.

Inchofer adds:

“Moreover, with regard to these decrees, some were corrected by later kings, some abolished, and most confirmed.”

What sort of decrees Stephen’s were, and why some of them were later corrected or abrogated, is explained in the preface to the *Decrees of King Coloman*, written to Seraphin, archbishop of Esztergom, in the cited Werboczius, volume II, page 28, in these words:

“For who would doubt that our holy father Stephen, a truly apostolic man, gave a law to our people that was harsher in some matters, more lenient in others, exacting punishment more severely in certain cases and showing indulgence more mildly in others, yet never dismissing anyone without the blow of discipline, since the time of predestination had not yet brought forth a true sponsor of the faith? Nor is it wrong to believe that this too occurred in accordance with divine dispensation. For in the time of the aforesaid king, when his whole kingdom was still devoted to barbarous rites, and the raw and constrained Christian still struggled against the goad of the admonisher of the holy faith, still gnawed back against the blows of the avenging rod imposed as penance, it was worthwhile that the compulsion of holy discipline should serve unbelievers for conversion to the faith, but those converted for the justice of penance.

“But our most Christian king Coloman, endowed with the simplicity of dove-like grace and with every discernment of the virtues, after seeing that the mature faith had received the strength of perfect religion, prudently considered loosening the bond of the legal chain, and so forth.”

Furthermore, there can be no doubt that the most prudent king adapted himself in establishing laws to the ancient customs of the Hungarians as far as could be done without injury to the Catholic religion and Christian virtues. He himself sufficiently indicates this in the preface with these words: “Since every nation is governed by its own laws.” And above, in the admonition to his son, chapter 8: “It is difficult for you to hold the kingdom of this region unless you become an imitator of the customs of the kings who ruled before. What Greek could rule Latins by Greek customs? Or what Latin could rule Greeks by Latin customs? No one.”

This prudent caution was necessary so that the laws might be received more easily and agreeably in practice. I think that this explains why, for certain more serious crimes, the penalties decreed by Stephen were not as severe as those later established by subsequent kings: namely, because the Hungarians had formerly imposed no penalties for them, or only lighter ones, and because the crimes themselves had not appeared equally serious to them before they accepted the faith.

I believe that Stephen followed the counsel of the Apostle, who adapted himself to the capacity of each person, writing in the First Epistle to the Corinthians, chapter 3: “And so, brothers, I could not speak to you as spiritual people, but as carnal people, as infants in Christ. I gave you milk to drink, not food, for you were not yet able.”

With these preliminary observations, I append the laws themselves from the cited *Tripartite Work*, noting variant readings from Sambucus wherever it seems worthwhile. This title is placed before them:

**The Second Book of the Decrees of Saint Stephen the King**

# PREFACE

[Col. 1243B]

### The purpose of the laws is explained

By the reign of divine clemency, the work of royal dignity, which more solidly expands the nourishment of the Catholic faith [alternative: “more extensively and more solidly”], is accustomed to support the works of another dignity. And since every nation is governed [alternative: “conducted”] by its own laws, therefore we too, by God’s will, governing our monarchy, imitate the ancient and modern Augusti and, after deliberation concerning decrees, have established for our people how they should lead an honorable and blameless life, so that, just as they have been enriched by divine laws, they may likewise be devoted to secular laws, in order that, as they increase in what is good under the divine laws, so they may diminish in what is evil and blameworthy under these laws.

What we have decreed, we have set down below.

[Note: The meaning of the beginning of this preface is somewhat obscure because it can be punctuated in various ways. It seems to me that it should be read and punctuated as I have rendered it, although others have punctuated it differently. The meaning is that the king’s work, by which the Catholic faith is more solidly advanced through its nourishment, is accustomed to support or assist the works of others laboring toward the same end.]

## CHAPTER I

### On the ecclesiastical order and reverence for the house of God

Whoever, lifted up by the arrogance of pride, makes the house of God contemptible, or dishonorably treats possessions consecrated to God and placed under the protection of royal immunity for the honor of God, or presumes to violate them, shall be excommunicated as an invader and violator of the house of God.

For it is fitting that he should feel the indignation of that same Lord the king, whose favor he has despised and whose ordinance he has violated. Nevertheless, let the king command that the immunity granted by him be preserved unharmed among those subject to his authority. Nor should he heed the reckless claim that the things of the Lord ought not to exist—that is, things handed over to the Lord of lords.

Therefore let them be under the king’s protection, and let him regard them as his own inheritance, or rather as something greater. For just as God is more excellent than man, so the divine cause is more excellent than mortal possession.

Accordingly, whoever takes more pride in his own possessions than in the Lord’s possessions is deceived. The person appointed as their defender and divinely established guardian ought, with diligent care, not only to preserve them but also to increase them; and he ought to defend and enlarge those things we have called more excellent rather than his own.

If, therefore, some madman, driven by his insolence and importunity, attempts to turn the king away from a right purpose and appears unable to be softened by any remedies, then—even if he is useful for certain services and temporary purposes—he must be cast away and expelled from him, according to the Gospel: “If your foot, hand, or eye causes you to stumble, tear it out and cast it away from you” (Matthew 18:8).

[Note: This entire chapter, as well as the following one, is taken from the Council of Mainz of 847 under Rabanus. This is its sixth canon, and the following chapter its seventh, as may be seen in Labbe, volume VIII, column 44. From this the error above is corrected, where *divinitatis* is read throughout instead of *divinitus*, as it appears in Labbe.]

## CHAPTER II

### On the authority of bishops over ecclesiastical property

We wish bishops to have authority to provide for, direct, govern, and distribute ecclesiastical property according to the authority of the canons. Laymen are therefore to obey their ministry in governing churches, defending widows and orphans, and preserving their Christianity; they are also to be obedient to them, and counts and judges are to cooperate with their bishops in administering justice according to the precepts of divine law. In no way is just law to be perverted by anyone’s lies, false testimony, perjury, or bribery.

[Note: More correctly, the preceding words in the Mainz text read as follows: “And let laymen obey the bishops in their ministry.”]

## CHAPTER III

### What sort of accusers and witnesses there should be, etc.

Witnesses and accusers must be free from every disgrace, have wives and children, and openly proclaim Christ. No one is to accept the testimony of a layman against a cleric. No one is to presume to examine—or, according to the alternative reading, excommunicate—any cleric in public, except in a church.

## CHAPTER IV

### On the constant and severe labor of priests

Know, all you brothers, that priests labor above everyone else. Each of you bears his own particular labor, but they bear both their own and that of each individual person [alternative: “he,” as also below]. Therefore, just as they labor on behalf of all of you, so all of you must labor for them with the greatest effort, even to the point that, if necessity requires it, you lay down your lives for them.

## CHAPTER V

[Note: The title placed in the margin can be expressed more clearly as: “On permission to distribute one’s own property.”]

### On the royal permission to dispose of personal property

By our royal power we have decreed that everyone shall have the right to divide and distribute his property to his wife, sons, daughters, and parents, or to the Church, and that after his death no one may dare to overturn this.

## CHAPTER VI

### Royal and treasury property is to remain untouched

Just as we have granted everyone else the freedom to dispose of his property, so we wish our property, soldiers, servants, and everything belonging to our royal dignity to remain undisturbed, and no one may seize or remove anything from it. Nor may anyone dare to obtain personal favor for himself through the matters mentioned above.

## CHAPTER VII

### On observing the Lord’s day, etc.

If any priest, count, or other faithful person finds anyone working on the Lord’s day, he is to be driven away. If he is working with oxen, an ox is to be taken from him and given to the townspeople for food. If he is working with horses, the horse is to be taken; its owner may redeem it with an ox if he wishes, and the ox is to be eaten, as stated above. If he is working with other tools, the tools and clothing are to be taken; if he wishes, he may redeem them with a hide.

## CHAPTER VIII

### That the same Lord’s day, etc.

The priests and counts are to commend this to all stewards, so that at their command everyone may assemble at church on the Lord’s day, great and small, men and women, except those who guard the fires [alternative: “who are guarding”].

If anyone remains obstinate, he shall be beaten and shaved.

[Note: In another edition the penalty is expressed as follows: “Because of their negligence, let them be beaten and shaved.”]

## CHAPTER IX

### Meat is not to be eaten on the Ember Days

If anyone violates the fasts of the Four Times, which are known to all, by eating meat, he shall fast confined for the space of one week.

## CHAPTER X

### Meat is not to be eaten on Friday

If anyone eats meat on Friday, which is observed by all Christians, he shall fast confined for one week [in another reading: “he shall fast confined in darkness—or in a cell”].

## CHAPTER XI

### Concerning those who die without confession

If anyone is so obstinate—which God forbid of every Christian—that he refuses to confess his crimes despite the advice of the priest, let him lie without any divine office or alms, like the unbelievers.

But if his parents and relatives neglect to call the priests, and he therefore dies without confession, let him be enriched with prayers and consoled with alms; but let his relatives pay for their negligence by fasting, according to the judgment of the priests.

Those who are endangered by sudden death are to be buried with every ecclesiastical honor. For hidden and divine judgments are unknown to us.

## CHAPTER XII

### On observing Christianity

If anyone, neglecting the observance of Christianity and lifted up by the stupidity of negligence, commits some offense against it, let him be judged by the bishop according to the seriousness of the offense and according to the disciplines [alternative: “discipline”] of the canons.

If, prompted by rebellion, he refuses to endure the penalty imposed upon him [alternative: “an equal penalty imposed”], let him again be restrained by the same judgment, even up to seven times. Finally, if he is found resisting and refusing in every respect, let him be handed over to royal judgment, that is, to the defender of Christianity.

## CHAPTER XIII

### On homicides, beginning with accidental homicide

If anyone kills someone by accident, let him pay twelve *pensa* of gold and fast as the canons command.

If a free man kills someone’s slave, let him return another slave or settle the matter by payment, and let him fast according to the canons.

[Note: A *pensa* of gold is a coin, but I have found no sufficiently certain evidence concerning its value.]

## CHAPTER XIV

### Concerning those who kill their wives

If any count, hardened in heart and neglecting his soul—which is far from the hearts of those who observe fidelity—stains himself with the murder of his wife, let him be reconciled with the woman’s relatives by means of fifty heifers, according to the decree of the royal council, and let him fast according to the commands of the canons.

If a soldier of some rank [alternative: “a man of abundance”] falls into the same offense, let him pay ten heifers to the relatives according to the same council, and let him fast as stated above.

If a commoner is found guilty of the same crime, let him be reconciled with the relatives by means of five heifers and be subjected to the fasts mentioned above.

[Note: This is a light penalty for so enormous a crime; but see what was said in the preceding admonition. I wish the same observation to apply to various laws that follow.]

## CHAPTER XV

### On perjuries

If anyone of the powerful [alternative, and preferable: “of the false speakers”] is found defiled in faith, polluted in heart, having broken his oath and devoted to perjury, let him pay for his perjury by losing his hand, or redeem his hand with fifty heifers.

If a commoner proves to be a perjurer, he shall be punished by having his hand cut off, or shall redeem it with twelve heifers, and shall fast as the canons command.

## CHAPTER XVI

### On voluntary homicides

If anyone, inflamed by anger and lifted up by pride, commits deliberate homicide, let him know that, according to the decree of our council, he must pay one hundred and ten *pensa* of gold. Of these, fifty are to be brought to the king’s treasury, another fifty given to the relatives, and ten remitted to the arbiters and mediators.

The homicide himself is to fast according to the institution of the canons.

[Note: The editor observes that this law is obsolete.]

## CHAPTER XVII

### On the freedom of slaves

If anyone, moved by mercy, grants freedom to his male or female slaves with testimony, we decree that after his death no one, moved by envy, may dare to return them to slavery.

But if he has promised freedom and, prevented by death, has not testified to it, his widowed wife and children shall have the power to testify to the same freedom and to perform an act of charity for the redemption of her husband’s soul, in whatever way they wish.

[Note: This law is published with considerable textual corruption in Sambucus. Here “to perform an *agape*” seems to mean “to perform an act of charity.”]

## CHAPTER XVIII

### On assembling at church and on those who murmur during Mass, etc.

If people who come to church to hear the divine office murmur among themselves there during the solemn hour of the Mass, disturb the others, tell idle stories, and fail to attend to the divine readings with their ecclesiastical nourishment, then, if they are great persons, they are to be rebuked and expelled from the church in disgrace.

If they are lesser people and commoners, they are to be bound in the church courtyard before everyone, because of such presumption, and corrected with scourges.

## CHAPTER XIX

### On not accepting slaves as witnesses against their masters, etc.

So that the people of this monarchy may remain free and undisturbed from every attack and accusation by slaves and female slaves, it is absolutely forbidden by royal decree that, in any case whatsoever, a servile person be accepted as an accuser or witness against masters or mistresses.

## CHAPTER XX

### No one is to reduce a free person to slavery

Since it is worthy of God and best for human beings that each person should lead the course of his life in the freedom produced by his own industry, it has been established by royal decree that henceforth no count or soldier may dare to subject any free person to slavery.

If, driven by the audacity of pride [alternative: “elevation”], anyone should presume to do so, let him know that he must pay the same amount from his own property. This payment is to be divided between the king and the count [alternative: “counts”], and so forth.

But if someone has until now been held in slavery and, seeking to defend [alternative: “purchase”] his freedom, has brought the matter before the royal court and been successful, let him simply enjoy his freedom, and let the person by whom he was held in slavery pay nothing.

## CHAPTER XXI

[Col. 1249A]

### Concerning those who entice away another’s soldiers or servants

We wish every senior—that is, lord—to have his own soldier, or servant. No one else is to persuade him to abandon his old lord and come to him. For litigation begins from this.

## CHAPTER XXII

### On receiving guests

If anyone receives a guest with goodwill and honorably provides him with sustenance, then, for as long as he is nourished according to the agreement, the guest shall not abandon his provider or transfer his hospitality to anyone else.

## CHAPTER XXIII

### Concerning those who are beaten while seeking what belongs to them

If someone’s soldier or slave flees to another person, and the person whose soldier or slave has escaped sends his representative to bring him back, and that representative is struck and beaten there by anyone, we decree, by the assembly of our leading men, that the person who struck him shall pay ten heifers.

## CHAPTER XXIV

### On widows and orphans

We wish widows and orphans to share in our law, on the following condition: if a widow remains with sons and daughters and promises to nourish them and remain with them as long as she lives, she shall have the authority granted to her by us to do so, and no one shall again compel her to marry.

If, however, changing her intention, she wishes to marry again and abandon the orphans, she shall claim nothing at all from the property of the orphans, except that she may take clothing suitable for herself.

But if a widow remains without children and promises to remain unmarried in her widowhood, we wish her to have authority over all her property and to do with it whatever she wishes. After her death, that property shall return to the parents of her husband, if he has parents [alternative: “if they are present”]. If not, the king shall be the heir.

## CHAPTER XXV

### On the abduction of girls

If any soldier, stained by immodesty, abducts a girl as his wife without her parents’ consent, we decree that the girl be returned to her parents, even if he has used some force against her, and that the abductor pay ten heifers for the abduction, even if he is later reconciled with the girl’s parents.

If a poor man or commoner attempts this deed, let him settle the abduction with five cattle [the editor thinks the text should read: “let him pay five cattle for the abduction”].

## CHAPTER XXVI

### On free men fornicating with another master’s female slaves

To preserve the freedom of free men undefiled, we wish to impose a warning and safeguard upon them, so that they do not fornicate with the female slaves of others.

If anyone, acting without foresight and transgressing this safeguard, fornicates with another person’s female slave, let him know that he is guilty of the crime, and for that crime he shall first be shaved and depilated [alternative: “flayed”].

If he fornicates with the same woman a second time, he shall again be shaved and depilated [alternative: “flayed”].

If he does so a third time, he shall become a slave together with the female slave, or redeem himself.

If the female slave conceives by him but cannot give birth and dies in childbirth, he shall replace her with another female slave.

If someone’s male slave fornicates with another person’s female slave, he shall be shaved and depilated [alternative: “flayed”]. If the female slave conceives by him and dies in childbirth, the male slave shall be sold, half of the price being given to the female slave’s master, while the other half shall always remain with the male slave’s master.

## CHAPTER XXVII

### On those who seek another’s female slaves as wives

So that none of those counted among the free may dare to wrong anyone, we have imposed fear and a safeguard. For it has been decreed in this royal council that if a free man chooses marriage with another’s female slave, with the knowledge of the slave’s master, he shall lose the freedom of his condition and become a perpetual slave.

## CHAPTER XXVIII
Those Who Flee from Their Wives Outside the Kingdom. So that people of both sexes may remain and flourish under a definite law and without injustice, it has been established in this royal decree that, if anyone, driven by insolence, flees his homeland because of hatred for his wife, his wife shall possess all the property that had been under her husband’s control, for as long as she wishes to await her husband; and no one shall presume to compel her into another marriage. But if she wishes to marry of her own accord, she may do so, taking suitable clothing [alternative: “having taken suitable clothing”] and leaving behind her other possessions. And if the husband, upon hearing this, returns, he may not take another wife because of his own fault [alternative: “apart from his own fault”], unless with the permission of the bishop.

[Note: This law must be understood cautiously as concerning a marriage between pagans, whose bond can be dissolved if the wife converts and the husband therefore departs, according to the Apostle, 1 Corinthians 7:15; it does not concern a validly contracted and consummated marriage between Christians, which cannot be dissolved in such a way that one may validly proceed to another marriage before the death of one’s spouse. These few observations ought to have been made here; theologians and canonists will provide a fuller treatment of the matter. It is also possible that some corruptions have entered the wording of the law.]

## CHAPTER XXIX

### On the Theft Committed by Married Women

Since it is dreadful to all and abominable to everyone that the male sex should have been found to commit theft, and even more so the female sex, it has been decreed according to the royal council that, if any married woman commits theft, she shall be redeemed by her husband; and if she falls into the same fault a second time, she shall likewise be redeemed; but if a third time, she shall be sold.

## CHAPTER XXX

### On the Burning of Houses

If anyone, out of enmity, burns another person’s buildings with fire, we have decreed that he restore the buildings, repay whatever household property has been burned, and in addition pay sixteen young oxen, worth sixty solidi.

## CHAPTER XXXI

### On Witches

If any witch [Note: The word *striga*, elsewhere *strix*, here designates a poisoner or sorceress. Greater punishments were subsequently established for such persons, as also for other crimes.] is found, let her be taken according to the judicial law to the church and entrusted to the priest for fasting and for learning the faith; after the fast, however, let her return home. If she is found a second time in the same crime, let her undergo a similar fast; after the fast, let an ecclesiastical nail be branded upon her breast, forehead, and between her shoulders in the form of a cross, and let her return home. But if a third time, let her be handed over to the judges.

## CHAPTER XXXII

### On Sorcerers and Diviners

So that God’s creature may remain removed from every injury inflicted by the wicked, and suffer harm from no one except God, by whom it is increased [alternative: “and by whom it is increased”], we establish, according to the decree of the council, as a great deterrent, concerning poisoners and sorcerers [alternative: “poisons and sorceries,”] that no person shall dare by sorcery or poison to overthrow any human being from his right mind or to kill him. But if anyone, male or female, thereafter presumes to do this, let that person be handed over for judgment to the hands of the one injured by the sorcery, or to the hands of that person’s relatives, according to their will. But if those who use divination are found—such as those who perform it in ashes and by similar means—let them be corrected by the bishops with lashes.

## CHAPTER XXXIII

### On the Invasion of Houses and the Battle That Follows There

We wish firm peace and unanimity to exist between the greater and the lesser, according to the Apostle: “Be all of one mind” (1 Peter 3:8), and no one shall dare invade another. For if any count, after the promulgation of this common council, should prove so rebellious as to seek out another at home in order to destroy him and scatter his property—and if the master of the house is present and fights with him or kills him—let him pay according to the law enacted concerning the drawing of the sword. But if that same count falls there, let him lie without composition.

If any knight invades the court, tower, or house of another knight, let him pay ten young oxen as compensation for the invasion. But if he himself does not come, but sends his knights, let him pay one hundred young oxen as compensation for the invasion. If an ordinary man invades the small dwelling of another man of his own standing, let him pay five young oxen for the invasion.

## CHAPTER XXXIV

### On the Construction and Endowment of a Church by Villages

Let ten villages build a church, and endow it with two manses [Note: For *mansionibus*, Peter of Peterf reads *mansis*, while Sambucus mistakenly has *mensis*. Villages or rural estates are intended], an equal number of slaves, a horse and a pack animal, six oxen, two cows, and thirty-four small animals. Let the king provide the vestments, altar cloths, and coverings, and the bishop the priest and books.

## CHAPTER XXXV

### On Royal Donations and Possession of One’s Own Property

We have therefore consented to the petition of the entire council that everyone should exercise dominion over his own property, and likewise over the king’s gifts, during his lifetime, except for what pertains to a bishopric or a county; and after his death, his sons shall succeed to the same dominion. No one shall suffer the loss of his property on account of any offense, unless he has plotted the king’s death, betrayed the kingdom, or fled to another province. Then, however, his property shall come into the royal power, while he himself shall undergo sentence, his innocent sons remaining unharmed.

## CHAPTER XXXVI

### On a Slave Killed by Another Slave

If someone’s slave kills another person’s slave, the master of the homicide shall, if able, pay half a slave to the master of the slain man. If not, after one quadragesima has been completed, let the slave be sold and let the price be divided.

[Note: It is not sufficiently clear what the words “after one quadragesima has been completed” mean. I nevertheless suspect that they designate a punishment imposed upon the slave for forty consecutive days, whether a fast or some other penalty at the master’s discretion.]

## CHAPTER XXXVII

### On the Redemption of a Homicidal Slave

Let a free man redeem his homicidal slave, if it pleases the master, with one hundred and ten young oxen, or surrender him.

[Note: No punishment is added; I think this is because one could be imposed by the master at his discretion.]

## CHAPTER XXXVIII

### On the Punishment of Those Striving to Acquire Freedom for Other People’s Slaves

If anyone strives to acquire freedom for other people’s slaves, let him pay as many slaves as there are slaves involved. Of these, two parts shall be given to the king and the third to the slaves’ master. The king, however, shall give a third of his share to the count.

## CHAPTER XXXIX

### On a Slave’s First Theft

If any slave commits theft once, let him return what was stolen and, if able, redeem his nose with five young oxen; but if not, let his nose be cut off.

[Note: St. Ladislaus subsequently established more severe punishments for the thefts of slaves and free persons, in Book II, chapter 12 and the following chapters, as well as elsewhere.]

## CHAPTER XL

### On the Punishment of One Who Commits Theft a Second and Third Time

If a person whose nose has been cut off commits theft, let him, if able, redeem his ears with five young oxen; but if not, let them be cut off. If he commits theft a third time, let him lose his life.

## CHAPTER XLI

### On the Theft of Free Persons, etc.

If any free person commits theft, we have decreed that this law be imposed [alternative: “that he appear before the law”]: he shall redeem himself once, if he can; but if not, let him be sold. If the same person, after being sold, commits theft, let him be subject to the laws governing slaves. If he commits it a second time, let him be subject to the same law. But if a third time, let him be sentenced to death.

## CHAPTER XLII

### Counts Shall Not Keep Back What Belongs to the King

If any count defrauds the king of his share, let him restore what he defrauded and pay double as compensation.

[Note: This law, whose penalty is certainly lighter than that commonly imposed for a similar crime, is not precisely explained by the title supplied in the margin.]

## CHAPTER XLIII

### On Contempt of the Count’s Just Judgment

If any knight, despising a judgment rightly rendered by his count, appeals to the king, wishing to make his count appear unjust, let him owe ten pounds of gold to his count.

## CHAPTER XLIV

### On Restoring Property to Knights, etc.

If any count, having found some pretext, unjustly takes anything from a knight, let him restore it and, in addition, pay an equal amount from his own property.

## CHAPTER XLV

### A Promise Becomes a Debt

But if any knight, claiming that a voluntary gift of his was taken from him by force, proves to be a liar, let him lose the gift and, in addition, pay an equal amount.

[Note: The title placed in the margin does not sufficiently explain the end of this law; rather, it concerns the punishment of liars or slanderers.]

## CHAPTER XLVI

### On Those Who Kill a Person with a Sword

If anyone kills a person with a sword, let him be slain with that same sword.

[Note: Chapter 33 is referred to in connection with this and the following laws; from it we understand that these laws were probably composed earlier.]

## CHAPTER XLVII

### On the Disabling of Limbs by the Sword

But if anyone, with a drawn sword, disables another person, whether in the eye, foot, or hand, let him suffer comparable damage to his own body.

## CHAPTER XLVIII

### On One Who Is Struck by a Sword and Receives a Wound

But if anyone wounds another with a sword, and the wounded person recovers from that wound safe and unharmed, let the one who inflicted the wound pay the composition for homicide.

## CHAPTER XLIX

### On Drawing the Sword Without Wounding

If anyone, filled with fury, draws his sword but nevertheless injures no one, let him pay half the composition for homicide merely for drawing the sword.

[Note: In Sambucus’s edition the penalty reads: “Let him pay the composition for homicide,” with the word “half” omitted.]

## CHAPTER L

### On the Testimony of Slaves Appointed over the Royal or Comital Household

If any slave is placed in charge of the royal or comital household, his testimony shall be accepted among counts, if a slave kills his master or a servant kills his count.

[Note: The editor adds: “From this arose the practice by which the officials of lords and nobles are made equal to nobles in giving testimony.”]

## CHAPTER LI

### On Conspiracy against the King and Queen

If anyone conspires against the king or the kingdom, let him have no refuge in a church. If anyone in any way conspires against the king’s safety or dignity, or attempts to conspire, or knowingly consents to one who attempts it, let him be anathematized and deprived of the communion of all the faithful. Or if anyone knows of such a person and, being able to prove it, does not report him, let him be subject to the aforesaid condemnation.

[Note: In the title placed in the margin, “and the queen” ought more correctly to read “and the kingdom,” as is clear from the law itself and agrees with Sambucus’s edition.]

## CHAPTER LII

### On Tithing

If God gives anyone ten things in a year, let him give a tenth to God. If anyone conceals his tithe, let him pay nine. If anyone steals a tithe set apart for the bishop, let him be judged as a thief, and let the entire composition for this offense belong to the bishop.

## CHAPTER LIII

### On Slanderers at Court

If any cunning person says to one of the counts or to another faithful person, “I heard the king speaking of your destruction,” and is found to have done so, let him perish.

## CHAPTER LIV

### On Those Who Assert Lies between Two Members of the Court

If anyone utters lies between two counts and urges them to be silent, so that by the devil’s cunning he may separate them from one another, let him pay two compositions for a deceitful tongue on account of his falsehood. If he has flattered only one of them, let his tongue be deprived.

## CHAPTER LV

### On the Theft of the Uduornici, That Is, Freedmen

If any person of those commonly called *Uduornic* commits theft, let him be judged according to the law of free persons. His testimony, however, shall not be accepted among them [alternative: “let them not accept his testimony among themselves”].

[Note: The word *Uduornic* is written *Udwornyck* by Sambucus. The marginal interpretation reads “a noble landed freedman.” The following is finally added: “Here ends the Decree of Saint Stephen, king, promulgated at Esztergom [alternative: Tolna] in the year 1035.” I have already noted, however, that the year of promulgation is not known with certainty.]

[Col. 1253]

# The Privilege Granted by Saint Stephen to the Proto-Abbey of Saint Martin in Pannonia

*(Year 1001.)*

*(Bollandists, Acts of the Saints, September, vol. I, p. 494.)*

In the name of the Lord, the supreme God. Stephen, by the clemency of divine [alternative: heavenly] providence, king of the Hungarians.

We believe, and truly know, that if we increase the powers and honors of places devoted to divine worship, this should not only be proclaimed with human praise but also rewarded with divine recompense. Therefore, let the careful attention of all the faithful of God’s holy Church, both present and future, and of our own people, learn that we, through the intervention, counsel, and consent of Lord Anastasius, abbot of the monastery of Saint Martin situated on the mountain above Pannonia, a monastery begun by our father and brought by us, with God’s help, to completion for the salvation of our soul and the stability of our kingdom, have granted it the same liberty enjoyed by the monastery of Saint Benedict on Mount Cassino. For, strengthened and crowned with victory through the holy prayers of the brothers of that monastery, with the aforesaid Lord Abbot Anastasius bringing this about and constantly assisting us, I have taken care to hand down to posterity the singular aid that I experienced in my youth through the merits of blessed Martin.

When a time of wars arose—for a very great sedition had grown up between the Germans and the Hungarians [alternative: “during which a very great sedition had grown up”]—and especially when the ruin of civil war was pressing upon us, a certain county of Somogy [alternative: “bearing the name Somogy”] wishing to drive me from my paternal seat, I was uncertain what counsel to take in my troubled mind and where to turn, being overcome by such shame, while the dukes stood by—namely Pagzanus [alternative: Poznanus], Contio [alternative: Cincio], and Orzio [alternative: Orthio]—together with my lord archbishop. I vowed a vow to Saint Martin that, if through his merits I should emerge victorious over my internal and external enemies, I would, under the testimony of the aforementioned dukes and many counts, without delay subject to him the tithe of that county from all its commerce, estates, lands, vineyards, crops, tolls, and the wine of guests produced on their estates, so that it might not appear to belong to the diocesan bishop but rather to the abbot of that monastery. When, after my resolve, I obtained victory, I strove to fulfill in deed what I had turned over in my mind.

For at that time there were not yet any bishoprics or abbeys in the Hungarian kingdom apart from that place [alternative: “apart from that place, there were no bishoprics or abbeys situated in the Hungarian kingdom”]. If, faithful ones, I was permitted to establish bishoprics and abbeys wherever I wished, was I not permitted to do what I wished for any place?

And so that the church of Saint Michael might not still appear vacant, or the diocesan bishop suffer injuries and complaints in the collection of the tithe, I gave him the estate called Cortou [alternative: Corten], with all that belonged to it [alternative: “with the people belonging to it”]. If he should wish to act or acquire anything contrary to my statutes, let him know that on the day of judgment he will have to contend with me before God, the judge of the living and the dead.

Furthermore, I add this: let that monastery itself be removed from every disturbance, and let the monks have the authority to elect another abbot securely after the death of each abbot, to have him consecrated by whatever bishop they wish; and let it be lawful for them to receive orders in any place and from anyone, etc.

The sign of the renowned lord Stephen, king. Dominicus, archbishop and vice-chancellor, issued this in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1001, in the fifteenth indiction, in the second year of Stephen, the first king.

[Note: A few observations should be made concerning this document. First, the diocesan bishop mentioned here is the bishop of Veszprém, and the cathedral church of Veszprém is dedicated to Saint Michael. Therefore certain writers are mistaken who have believed that the church of Saint Michael mentioned here should be replaced by the church of Saint Martin. Saint Stephen is reporting what he granted to the church of Veszprém as compensation for the loss it would otherwise suffer from the privilege granted to the abbey of Saint Martin.

Second, Archbishop Dominicus, who is mentioned by Raynaldus in this document, is not named in other editions. Indeed, I know of no archbishop in Hungary at that time who was called Dominicus, unless perhaps the first archbishop of Esztergom bore that name; I shall examine this more fully in §24. It is therefore obscure who he was, and it is not entirely certain that this reading is correct.

With these brief observations made, the site of the monastery must be investigated. It is said to have been situated “on the mountain above Pannonia.” Carthuitius, no. 7, says that it was built “near the estate of the holy prelate, in a place called the Sacred Mode [read: the holy mountain], where Saint Martin, while he still lived in Pannonia, had designated a place of prayer for himself.” These words sufficiently indicate that the place was not far from the city of Sabaria, later destroyed in Pannonia, where Saint Martin was born. I am therefore all the more astonished at Mabillon’s hallucination: in volume IV of the Benedictine Annals, p. 115, he confuses this monastery of Saint Martin with the monastery of Breunov in Bohemia, and repeats the error on p. 143, calling Astrictus the abbot of Saint Martin of Breunov. On p. 470 he even says that the monastery of Breunov is “twenty stadia from the city of Prague,” thereby wishing the monastery of Saint Martin, which Saint Stephen completed, to have been in central Bohemia. We believe that errors of this kind, into which learned men occasionally fall, should be noted, lest others adopt them, as we very often observe happening.

Gotardus Arthus, in his *Chronology of Pannonia*, p. 9, merely says: “In addition, he placed the monastery of Saint Martin on a very high mountain.” Inchofer, under the year 999, recounts the construction of this monastery but does not explain its location more precisely, as many others have likewise done.

Nevertheless, a very strongly fortified town grew up around this monastery of Saint Martin. It resisted the countless multitude of the Tartars while they had overrun almost all Hungary. For Bonfinius, decade 2, book VIII, after recounting the devastation of all Hungary and the most miserable destruction of the city of Esztergom, adds the following on p. 300:

“An attempt upon the fortress of Esztergom, which at that time was commanded by Simeon with a strong garrison, deterred the enemy. Abandoning it, the barbarian hastened to Alba Regia, … but this expectation frustrated him; for, situated among marshes, it could be captured by neither force nor art. Soon they hastened to the monastery of Saint Martin, from which they departed with their undertaking unfinished. Thus, he testifies, only these three places experienced the Tartar destruction.”

Yet the same town was easily taken by the Turks in the year 1574, as Isthuanfus relates in Book XXVIII of his *History*, p. 636, in words relevant to our purpose:

“After Tata had been reduced to his power, the fortress dedicated to Saint Martin lay before the enemy. It was distinguished by a wealthy college of Benedictine monks, which Saint Stephen, once the first king of Pannonia, had founded nearly six hundred years earlier on a high, pleasant, and long-extended hill, from the spoils and booty of Cuppanus, his defeated rebel, brought to that place … and had named it the Sacred Mountain of Pannonia. That fortress was subject to Abbot Paulus Baronianus; in command of the military garrison … was John Zadorius,” etc.

He then adds the surrender of the fortress, which is less relevant here. Martin Zeiller likewise reports it in his *Topography of Hungary*, written in German, p. 174, adding that the Christians recovered the fortress after three years and thereafter retained it. Furthermore, the fortress of Saint Martin is situated in the county of Győr, not far from Győr toward Alba Regia, from which it is much farther away. Tata is only a few miles distant; this is how I certainly find it commonly marked on maps of Hungary, and Zeiller’s and Isthuanfus’s statements agree correctly with these facts.]

[Col. 1257]

# Ecclesiastical Constitutions of Andrew, King of Hungary, in the Year 1048

*(Mansi, Councils, vol. XIX, col. 631.)*

I. Whoever, whether Hungarian or foreigner in Hungary, after abandoning the Scythian, pagan, and heathen rite, did not immediately return to the true faith of Jesus Christ and did not accept the sacred law handed down by Saint King Stephen, was to be punished with death and confiscation of property. Cities, towns, villages, and temples that had been demolished and destroyed were to be rebuilt.

II. Bishops and colleges of priests were to be maintained according to the ancient custom, and obeyed.

III. All Christian rites were to be restored.

IV. They were to abolish profane and Scythian ceremonies and false gods, and demolish their images.

V. If anyone cursed God, his saints, or priests, or did anything evil against them, let him know that he would incur first God’s vengeance and then their own.

VI. Whoever killed a person devoted to sacred service, or even a profane person, was to expiate the sin according to the ancient custom. Finally, let everyone abstain from killings, robberies, and all other injuries and acts of violence.

VII. Whoever despised this constitution and resisted it in mind was declared guilty of death and of all his possessions.

[Col. 1257]

# Laws of Bracila, Duke of Bohemia, in the Year 1039

### Issued for the Reform of Morals at the Tomb of Saint Adalbert

[Note: Bracila, duke of Bohemia, after taking Gniezno, the metropolis of the Poles, by force of arms, had nothing more at heart than to bring back from it a precious spoil—namely, the relics of Saint Adalbert the martyr. But when the Bohemians attempted to open the sacred tomb, they were suddenly overcome by stupor. Severus, bishop of Prague, learning of this, was warned by Saint Adalbert during the night in a dream; on the following morning he admonished the prince and people in a public sermon that, if they wished to have Adalbert as their fellow citizen, they should promise a reform of morals. Therefore, in his own name and that of the people, Bracila enacted these decrees, and proclaimed them publicly.]

*(Mansi, Councils, vol. XIX, col. 589.)*

“Extend, brothers, your right hands together toward God, and attend to my words, which I wish you to confirm by the sacrament of your faith. Let this be my greatest and first decree: that your marriages, which until now you have treated as brothels, shall henceforth, according to the prescriptions of the canons, be legitimate, private, and indissoluble, so that one man may live content with one wife and one wife with one man. But if a wife rejects her husband, or a husband his wife, and quarrelling between them boils over into a breach, I do not wish the one who refuses to return to the former union to be reduced to slavery according to the custom of our land; rather, by the compulsion of this decree, let that person, whatever his or her status, be driven into Hungary. Nor shall it be lawful for that person to ransom himself or herself with money or return to this land, lest the contagion of one little sheep spread through the entire fold.”

Bishop Severus said: “Whoever acts otherwise, let him be anathema. Let virgins, widows, and adulteresses who are known to have lost their good name and conceived through prostitution be punished by the same sentence.”

Then the duke added: “But if a woman should complain that she is likewise unloved but cruelly afflicted by her husband, let the judgment of God be given between them, and let the one found guilty pay the penalties.

“Likewise, concerning those who are notorious for homicides, let the archpriest record their names for the count of that city, and let the count summon them. If they are rebellious, let him place them in prison until they either perform suitable penance or, if they deny the charge, are examined by red-hot iron or by consecrated water.

“But let the archpriest assign fratricides and parricides, killers of priests, and those guilty of crimes of this kind that carry the death penalty to the count or duke, who shall expel them from the kingdom by means of an iron hand and iron belly, so that, like Cain, they may wander throughout the land as perpetual exiles and fugitives.

“We also prohibit a tavern, which is the root of all evils, from being established or, once established, acquired. If a tavern-keeper violates this decree, let him be hung at a stake in the marketplace, beaten until the herald is weary, and depilated. His property, however, shall not be confiscated; only the drink shall be poured out upon the ground, lest anyone be polluted by it. Drunkards who are caught shall not leave prison until each pays three hundred coins into the duke’s treasury.

“We prohibit markets from being held on Sundays, although they are held especially on those days in these regions, so that people may devote the other days to their work. If anyone is found publicly engaged in servile labor on Sundays or on feast days proclaimed as days of rest for the church, let the archpriest seize the work itself and whatever is found in connection with the work, and let the offender pay three hundred coins into the duke’s treasury.

“And from anyone who buries the dead in fields or woods, let the archpriest take an ox, and let them pay three hundred coins into the duke’s treasury. Let him nevertheless bury the dead again in the cemetery of the faithful.

“These are the things that God hates; these are the things that Saint Adalbert abhorred, yet he did not abandon his sheep and preferred to go to teach foreign peoples.”

Bishop Severus said: “Let this decision of the duke be just and confirmed by an anathema.”

# APPENDIX TO THE NINTH CENTURY

## In the Year of Our Lord 860: Angilbertus Pusterla, Archbishop of Milan

[Col. 1259]

### Historical Notice Concerning Angilbertus

*(Ughelli, *Sacred Italy*, IV, 79.)*

Angilbertus Pusterla succeeded Angilbertus, the first of that name, in the year 827. This is the Angilbertus whom prosperity corrupted when he attained such dignity, although he had previously administered the Church of Milan prudently and with moderation. Supported, as some relate, by the privileges and favors of Charles the Great, and beloved by the emperor Louis the Pious and his son Lothair, he so defected from the Roman Church that, with unheard-of arrogance, he did not hesitate to contend with the Roman pontiff over power and dignity.

This very bad example passed to his successors, so that for two hundred years that same defiance led them astray and infected them. Nevertheless, this Angilbertus obtained from Louis the Pious confirmation of all the privileges once granted by Charles the Great to his Church. There also survives his letter to that same emperor concerning the condition of ecclesiastical affairs, which, at the emperor’s command and with Andrew, patriarch of Aquileia, as his colleague, he had investigated.

He transferred the relics of Saint Calocerus. He bestowed many gifts upon the Ambrosian basilica and its monks, over whom he had placed Abbot Gaudentius, and he strengthened them with many other immunities and favors, as may be seen in his diploma, to which the authority of the emperor Lothair added weight. We extracted it from an authentic copy submitted to the Sacred Roman Rota, when a serious dispute over jurisdiction had arisen between the Ambrosian clergy and the monks.

[Col. 1259]

# Rescript of the Bishops’ Consultation or Exhortation to the Lord Emperor Louis

*(Baluze, Capitularies, II, 351.)*

[Col. 1259B] May peace, life, and victory be bestowed by God the Father and our Lord Jesus Christ upon the most glorious lord King Louis.

We, in the name of God, Angilbertus, archbishop, and Andrew, patriarch, together with Joseph, archchaplain, when we had come to this synod assembled in the royal city of Ticinum, repeated to them your pious exhortation, which you delivered to us orally, burning with the gift of the Holy Spirit. We conveyed it as being composed with every moderation, gravity, and savor of wisdom, beyond what the tenderness of this age might seem capable of grasping; and in their presence we also had the memorandum read that your magnificence had entrusted to us. After hearing these things, all unanimously gave worthy thanks to almighty God for your character, because he had given his people so pious and holy a prince, who desires to arrange everything in an orderly manner.

## CHAPTER I

Since your religious solicitude first sought to inquire about the conduct of bishops, priests, and the other clergy, we likewise preserve the same order, as far as could be done in a regular manner. We declare that a bishop ought to conduct himself so that his life may be a model of right living. Priests and clerics, however, ought to live in such a way that their conduct may benefit the people committed to them by its example.

Some of our fellow bishops, conscious of good conduct, refused to admit it openly lest they appear to praise themselves. Those who recognized their own negligence were afraid, as is human nature, to accuse themselves. Nevertheless, examining the matter more carefully according to your warning, we found some who are such as you desire and as pastors and rulers of God’s people ought to be. In others we found negligence either in guarding their clergy or in caring for their congregations. We humbly ask that you grant them some time for amendment. If they do not quickly correct their offenses, they will be subject to a more severe sentence.

## CHAPTER II

Moreover, if any layperson or cleric has a complaint against a bishop or against a cleric of any order, let them know that we are prepared to provide a lawful hearing, and that, if they are proved to have acted improperly, they will be punished with the discipline they deserve.

## CHAPTER III

Instruction and preaching to the people, partly through the fault of bishops and the other priests and partly through the negligence of the people, are not carried out as necessary. The carelessness of priests can in no way be excused.

Some laymen, especially the powerful and noble, whom it would have been more appropriate to see attending preaching diligently, have basilicas beside their houses. Because they hear the divine office there, they have become accustomed to come less often to the greater churches.

[Note: See the notes on Salvian, p. 419 at the end (*Patrology*, vol. LIII).]

And when only the afflicted and poor come, what else is there to preach to them than that they should bear their misfortunes patiently? But if the rich, who are accustomed to wrong the poor, did not refuse to come, they could certainly be admonished to redeem their sins by almsgiving and to restrain themselves from the flow of temporal possessions.

The powerful must therefore be admonished to assemble at the greater churches, where they can hear preaching, and, to the extent that they surpass others in wealth and honors through the gift of almighty God, to hasten all the more eagerly to hear the commandments of their Creator.

## CHAPTER IV

Certain counts and royal vassals receive our priests and other clerics without our permission, although even bishops are not permitted to do so. Moreover, wherever they have been ordained, and some concerning whom it is doubtful whether they have been consecrated, they compel them to celebrate Masses in our parishes without our examination. This must be prohibited in every way so that it does not happen again.

Therefore, in appointing those responsible for the congregations of the citizens, let the established rules [alternative reading: “the prescriptions of the canons for priests”] be observed, and let the vice of destructive ambition be rooted out. No unworthy person is to be ordained either because of someone’s kinship, for the sake of anyone’s friendship, or—what is most detestable—because of the receipt of money.

First, let the priest or other clerics of the place choose for themselves a suitable rector. Then let the assent of the people who belong to that same congregation follow. But if no one can be found within that congregation who is able to perform that office competently, then let the bishop appoint there one of his own whom he judges suitable.

## CHAPTER V

The insolence of certain laymen must certainly be removed. Merely because they are admitted to participate in elections, they presume to dominate their archpriests and despise as subordinates those whom they ought to venerate as fathers. Such men must therefore be reduced within the limits of their own jurisdiction. If they presume to exercise extraordinary domination in churches, they are to be restrained by royal discipline.

But those who have been lawfully advanced to govern congregations must not in any way be removed by their bishops unless they have incurred guilt in some crime or have treated those congregations badly.

## CHAPTER VI

The entirely wicked custom that has begun to arise in certain places must be abolished. Some archpriests or guardians of other titles carry away grain or other church revenues to their own homes. Others lease the possessions of other people so that they may store in them what they have improperly taken from their churches.

Some laymen even make themselves accomplices to such wickedness to such an extent that they conceal in their own houses what these transgressors have stolen from the Church.

Such men must first be rebuked by their bishops. If they do not quickly correct themselves, let them be struck by synodal judgment as persons who have handled ecclesiastical property with sacrilegious recklessness. As for laymen who, after this warning, offer themselves as partners in this plundering, judicial authority shall constrain them as guilty of theft.

## CHAPTER VII

Regarding the restoration of churches, the chapter established by your father in his capitulary is sufficient. But its observance requires your admonition.

## CHAPTER VIII

The same must be observed concerning hospices, as is contained in that same capitulary.

## CHAPTER IX

Concerning monasteries of men or women, which ought to be organized according to the Rule of Saint Benedict or according to canonical authority, we give thanks to you because, as we believe, the inspiration of almighty God has stirred the heart of your governance. For it is evident to everyone that they have already lost their proper order to a very great extent. Their restoration to their former condition depends upon the glorious disposition of your lord and father, and of yourself.

## Chapter X

Those monasteries that still retain their proper condition must be inspected by each bishop in whose diocese they are situated, to determine whether they are maintaining their rule. If he finds otherwise, he must correct the matter together with the monastery’s abbot. If the fault principally lies with the abbot, and he neglects to correct himself and his subjects when admonished by his bishop, he must be punished by synodal authority.

## Chapter XI

Certain bishops and abbots of monasteries complain that the possessions of their churches have been taken away and granted to other persons, and therefore say that they are entirely unable to fulfill their ecclesiastical obligations. [Col. 1263B] We implore your royal majesty that these possessions be restored. For if those who donated them to churches for the remedy of their souls deserve a reward, there is no doubt that those who attempt to take them away deserve condemnation.

## Chapter XII

The sacred canons prescribe that tithes be distributed according to the bishop’s disposition. Certain laymen, however, who possess basilicas either in their own property or as benefices, disregarding the bishop’s disposition, do not give their tithes to the churches where they receive baptism, preaching, the laying on of hands, and the other sacraments of Christ. Instead, they distribute them at their own pleasure either to their own basilicas or to their own clergy. This is plainly contrary in every respect to divine law and the sacred canons. Therefore we request your authority [Col. 1263C] to correct them.

## Chapter XIII

Sacred authority teaches that those who sin publicly are to be subjected to public penance. Some are found who have contracted incestuous marriages and have been joined either to their close relatives or to women consecrated to God. Some persons may also be subjected to public penance. We ask that they be supported by the assistance of your counts.

[Col. 1264A]

## Chapter XIV

We have learned that certain officials of the counts, because of their frequent judicial sessions, oppress the poorer people excessively. Therefore we beseech your majesty to order that the capitulary of your grandfather concerning this matter be observed.

## Chapter XV

Concerning the counts, about whose life and conduct your Sublimity wished to inquire of us: we know that some are such as God’s ministers and administrators of your commonwealth ought to be. Others, however, need your admonition in order to correct themselves and their officials. We ask that you nevertheless grant them some time for amendment. If they are unwilling to correct themselves promptly, they must be restrained by royal authority.

## Chapter XVI

We also decree that when bishops travel through the parishes to confirm the people, they should not burden their archpriests, but should be satisfied with the following provision: one hundred loaves, four *friskingae* [a provision of uncertain meaning], fifty sextarii of wine, seven chickens, fifty eggs, one lamb, one piglet, six *modii* of grain for the horses, three bundles of hay [perhaps “three baskets of hay”], and sufficient honey, oil, and wax. [Col. 1264B]

## Chapter XVII

We also ask that you order the immunities of your forebears to be preserved in the manner established by your glorious father in his capitulary.

## Chapter XVIII

In each parish, the people should endeavor to observe those festivals that their own bishop has proclaimed worthy of veneration, so that they neither neglect those which the priests have enjoined nor presume, through empty superstition, to celebrate those that are by no means to be observed. [Col. 1264C]

## Chapter XIX

If any are found who refuse to obey the priests, they are to be compelled by the officials of the commonwealth and forced to undergo the penance of satisfaction imposed by the priests.

[Col. 1263]

# ANGILBERT’S PRIVILEGE FOR THE AMBROSIAN BASILICA

*(Ughelli, Italia sacra, vol. IV, p. 79.)*

[Col. 1263D]

In the name of the Lord, I, Angelbertus, humble archbishop of the blessed Church of Milan,

when, with the Lord’s help, I was exercising care over the monasteries of my parish and had brought them, insofar as I was able, to the path of holy conduct by correcting and rebuilding them, turned my attention to the monastery of the most blessed Ambrose, where his body rests, since necessity required me to appoint an abbot there. For a long time I had been considering whom I ought to establish as its abbot—for no suitable person was found there, since through negligence the regular order had become severely corrupted—and I was entreating divine mercy together with my priests. Then, with the Lord’s favor and with the advice of our priests, I removed Abbot Gaudentius from the monastery of Saint Vincent—for I myself had appointed him abbot there some time earlier—and established him as abbot in the aforesaid monastery of Saint Ambrose. [Col. 1264D]

Now, so that those monks may be able to serve God and continually render Him the praises of thanksgiving, and so that they may be free from want, both for the stability of our kings, the unconquered emperors Louis and Lothar, and for the peace of the spotless mother Church, by this decree I confirm the church and altar that I have recently and magnificently built there, out of my great love for Ambrose, the confessor of Christ. They shall remain perpetually under the protection and entire guardianship of the aforementioned Abbot Gaudentius and in his authority, and in that of his successors without end.

Likewise, all the possessions and property of that monastery, situated in various places and bearing the following names—Oleoductus, Campelione, Ceresiolae Gratem, Lucum, Sinterani, Casteniade, and Catenadam—as well as all the property that they now appear to possess, or that from this time onward, by God’s gift, may be added to that venerable Church of those who fear God through the generosity of anyone and in any manner, shall belong to it, except for the estate of Dubbini, which we intend to exchange according to the terms of our agreement.

It has pleased us, for the love of God and of blessed Ambrose, with the consent of our priests, to establish by this our act of institution that neither we nor any of our successors shall inflict upon the aforesaid Abbot Gaudentius or his successors any unjust trouble concerning the aforesaid property, nor diminish it in any way.
