Rather, under our authority and that of our successors, according to the disposition of the Fathers, and while also obeying us as is proper, may they be permitted to enjoy these possessions and lead a peaceful life under the holy rule. [Col. 1265A]

We further establish by this protection of our authority that any person of whatever order, moved by heavenly love, who wishes there to submit his neck, together with his possessions, to the sacred rule shall, by our most ample generosity, have the freedom to do so without any impediment.

We also grant that whenever the abbot of that monastery departs from this world, the monks may choose a pastor for themselves from among their own number, if a person is found there who is able to govern them according to the rule and who is supported by a properly regular life. By our most tranquil concession they shall have this right.

And so that this decree of my concession may remain forever firm and inviolate, I ordered Ambrose, notary of our holy Church of Milan, to write it, and I confirmed it below with my own hand, in the eighteenth year of our lords Louis and Lothar, the emperors who confirmed this act, on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of March, in the thirteenth indiction. [Col. 1266B]

**Editorial note:** Here the characters indicating the date have been disastrously distorted by the copyists who transcribed the old parchment, especially the number of the indiction. If the original reading was VIII rather than XIII, so that the year of Christ would be 829, there would nevertheless have been an error—though a less serious one—in the imperial years, which would have been XVII and XIV. — Papebrochius. [Col. 1265B]

I, Angelbertus, unworthy archbishop, have subscribed to this decree.

Adoaldus Penio.

Deusdedit.

Ermaldus.

And many other priests, deacons, subdeacons, and notaries subscribed.

# IN THE YEAR OF OUR LORD 877: ANDREAS BERGOMAS, PRIEST

[Col. 1265]

# ANDREAS’S CHRONICLE

*(Edited by Pertz, Monumenta Germaniae historica, Scriptores, vol. III, p. 231.)*

## PREFACE

[Col. 1265C]

A book from a ninth-century manuscript, edited by a certain learned man who wished to be called Hermannus Philomuson, in Menkenius’s *Scriptores*, vol. I, pp. 89 ff., and subsequently reprinted by Muratori in the first volume of his *Antiquitates*, has now been brought forth for the first time complete and sound through the aid of the Vadian manuscript preserved in the library of the city of St. Gall, marked AC 23.

The same codex as that used by Philomusos will be recognized by anyone acquainted with the character of the editors of the earlier age; the lacunae in the first edition prove that the editor judged that material appearing contrary to the truth ought to be omitted. According to the account of the distinguished Greith, the codex contains the following:

1. “The *Admonitions of Saint Basil, bishop, concerning the virtues of the soul*, written in Carolingian minuscule of the tenth century. At the end are appended several old hymns for Epiphany, Saint Lawrence the martyr, and Saint Gall the confessor, together with musical neumes. It is followed by:

2. “The *Life of Saint Findan the Confessor*, published by H. Canisius. It contains several passages of interest to investigators of the ancient Irish language, taken from Book II of *The Miracles of Saint Fintan*, for example chapter 1:

> ‘When Findan wished to be confined and, while persisting in prayer, sought to learn the Lord’s will concerning this, a voice of this kind descended upon him: “It is permitted to you …” (*licet tibi a isket clui o Deo tre*; the Irish portion is uncertain); and concerning the abbacy in chapter 4: *Dia anathes et in dabdane* [Irish, meaning uncertain].’

“He perceived such an oracle with his ears, uttered in his own language:

> “Entreat Christ and Patrick, patron of the city. Entreat Christ and Patrick of Armagh” (*obsecra xpm et patricium nom. civitatis. Ataich crist ocus patriç artmache*). The remaining Irish words are materially uncertain: *Farna feiltâm nakîsel teilcbruchir tart doit teilco il farkysel*.

“And from this he perceived no fault of gluttony.

3. “A fragment of the Acts of the Apostles, containing 321 complete leaves, from the tenth century.

4. “The *Admonition of Saint Paul*, showing how the Lord had demonstrated to him the vision of good and evil. It is nothing other than a vision of the joys of the blessed and the punishments of hell, written in Carolingian majuscule of the tenth century and extending over thirteen leaves.

5. “A book by the great Aurelius Cassiodorus Senator, *Concerning the Soul*, defective from chapters 5 through 18.

6. “A fragment of the chronicle of the Lombards composed by Andreas the priest. It contains eight leaves, or sixteen pages, each page comprising twenty-eight lines. The thick parchment bears Lombardic writing of the ninth century, as can be seen from the facsimile of the letters appended to it and as is sufficiently clear from the conjunctions of the letters *e* and *r*, *e* and *s*, *r* and *i*, as well as from the abbreviations of syllables, the form of the initials, and so forth.” [Col. 1266C]

This parchment quarto manuscript of the ninth century was carefully collated for our use by the distinguished and reverend Carolus Greith. It now appears complete, in the condition in which the author could have published it, written—indeed almost excessively so—in the Lombard speech proper to the whole of Italy. It is complete insofar as one may infer from a single manuscript, since the writer’s style comes to an end in the middle of a page. [Col. 1267A]

The work consists of three parts, differing in the form of their letters and in their ink, and therefore written at different times, as Greith has observed. The first part ends with the death of King Bernard; the second extends to the year 876; the third consists of only a few lines. The author himself reveals not only his name and rank but also his period, when he writes that he was present at the funeral of the Emperor Louis II and accompanied his body, placed upon a bier, from the river Oglio to the Adda—that is, through the territory of the diocese of Bergamo. Hence he may properly be called the Bergamese, and is distinct from Andreas or Agnellus of Ravenna. [Col. 1268A]

The first chapter of the work derives almost word for word from Paul’s history of the Lombards. In what follows, the author added whatever he was able to learn truthfully from the sequence of written records or from ancient men; this material must be weighed against the genuine sources of the eighth and ninth centuries. The final portions, which he himself experienced and committed to writing, properly command great confidence. [Col. 1268D]

# CHRONICLE OF ANDREAS OF BERGAMO

[Col. 1267]

*Editorial note:* The division into chapters, for which no traces appear in the manuscript, has been supplied by the editor. In chapter 1 the manuscript reads *sustituit*, *tam*, *q*, *su*, and *hominbus* at the respective places where the printed text has normalized forms; it reads “Justinus” for Justinian, as noted above. “Held Ticinum for three years” means “besieged it”; Paul’s text has “to the besiegers,” whereas Andreas seems to have read *obsidibus* (“hostages”) for *obsidentibus*. Some manuscripts of Paul read “other and some” in connection with Grimoald’s nine chapters. In chapter 2 the manuscript reads *relega*; before *ego* the word *de* has been deleted. The preceding statements are excerpted verbatim from Paul the Deacon’s *History of the Lombards*; compare chapter 2. The author’s identification as Bergamese may be compared with chapter 14. For chapter 4 compare Paul’s *History of the Bishops of Metz*, *Monumenta Germaniae Historica* II, 268; the Monk of Angoulême I, 170–171; and the Monk of St Gall II, 733. For the battle in chapter 12 compare Paul the Deacon VI.23. In chapter 13, *vitae* means “vines”; *possidens* means “besieging”; and *juge* means “wife.”

## 1

Narses the patrician sustained the wars of the Romans and always defended them. Because of Roman jealousy, they brought accusations against him before the Emperor Justinian [the manuscript has “Justinus”]. The emperor himself, together with his wife Sophia, sent orders to Narses—because he was a eunuch—that he should come to him and divide wool in the women’s quarters for a wage.

Narses the patrician sent him this reply: that he would not merely divide wool, but would also weave such a web that she herself would be unable to put it down while she lived.

Narses sent envoys to the Lombards, along with fruits of various kinds and other gifts of honor, so that they might make their minds well disposed and induce them to come to Italy, where they would receive the land in full without a battle. As soon as the Lombards heard this, they rejoiced greatly.

They entrusted Pannonia, which they had possessed for forty-two years, to their friends the Avars. They departed from Pannonia with their wives, children, and everything they possessed in the month of April, in the first indiction, on the day after the Lord’s Easter—which fell on the Kalends of April—when 568 years had already passed since the Lord’s Incarnation.

Thus the Lombards entered Italy through the territory of the people of Friuli. Alboin granted Friuli to his nephew Gisulf and to the other noble Lombards. In those days the Lombards invaded Italy: they captured Vicenza, Verona, and the other cities of Venetia, and held Ticinum for three years [that is, “besieged it”].

Meanwhile Alboin invaded everything as far as Tuscany, except Rome and Ravenna. The people of Ticinum, having endured the siege for three years and seeing the valor of their own people overcome around them, surrendered to the Lombards because of the hostages whom they had given [Paul’s text has “to the besiegers”; Andreas seems mistakenly to have read *obsidibus* for *obsidentibus*].

I shall say little about much. After King Alboin had reigned in Italy for three years and six months, he was killed by a plot of his wife. By common consent the Lombards established Cleph, a most noble man, as their king in the city of Ticinum. He reigned for one year and six months and was killed with a sword by a boy from his own household.

After his death the Lombards had no king for ten years, but were under the authority of dukes. After ten years they chose Authari, the son of Cleph. Authari took as his wife a woman named Theudelinda, daughter of Garibald, king of the Bavarians, a holy and most noble woman. She built the church of Saint John at Modicia.

King Authari died at Ticinum, as they say after receiving poison, having reigned for six years. By common consent the Lombards gave their queen Theudelinda permission to marry whichever man she wished; they would establish him as king. What more need be said? She accepted Agilulf, duke of Turin. He reigned for twenty-five years and died.

His son Adalwald reigned in his place for ten years and was expelled from the kingdom. His kingdom passed to Arioald, who reigned for twelve years and died. Rothari reigned in his place. He composed the edict of the Lombards; his other achievements, his valor, and the wars that he waged—are they not written in the Chronicle of the Lombards above? Rothari reigned for sixteen years and died, leaving the kingdom to his son Rodoald.

Rodoald violated the wife of a certain man and was killed by that same man, after reigning for five years and seven days. Aripert succeeded him in the kingdom; he reigned for nine years and died.

He left the kingdom to his two sons, Perctarit and Godepert. Discord arose between the brothers through evil men, to such an extent that one invaded the other’s kingdom. Grimoald, duke of the Beneventans, came treacherously at their summons and killed Godepert with a sword, one year and six months after the death of their father.

Perctarit fled, and Grimoald took the kingdom. Much is contained in the history of Grimoald, but I shall write only a little of it in this abridgment. He composed nine chapters in the edict of the Lombards; he reigned for nine years and died, leaving the kingdom to his son Garibald.

Perctarit, of whom we have already spoken, having fled, departed from Gaul and boarded a ship to cross the sea to the island of Britain and the kingdom of the Saxons. While he was sailing over the sea, a divine messenger called out to him from the shore and said: “Return, Perctarit, to your land, because today is the third day since Grimoald died.”

What more need be said? He returned and was gladly received by the Lombards, who appointed him to govern the kingdom in the third month after Grimoald’s death. Perctarit reigned for seventeen years and died, leaving the kingdom to his son Cunipert.

We have found much written about his history. He endured the struggles against the tyrant Alahis, but Cunipert, with the joy of God, achieved a victorious triumph and ruled Italy for twelve years after his father’s death. On the field of Coronate, where he fought his battle against Alahis, he built a monastery in honor of blessed George the martyr.

He left the kingdom to his son Liutpert. Aripert rose against him, seized him alive, and after a few days deprived him of life in a bath. Aripert reigned for twelve years and was drowned by the waters of the river Ticino. Ansprand seized his kingdom; he reigned for three months and left the kingdom to his son Liutprand.

Liutprand was a man of great wisdom, merciful, chaste, eloquent, watchful, and generous in almsgiving. He enlarged the law of the Lombards and ordered additional provisions to be written into the body of the edict [the words “and” and the following abbreviations are not found in Paul]. He reigned for thirty-one years and seven months and died.

## 2

Whoever finds the foregoing summary incredible should reread the entire history of the Lombards [that is, Paul the Deacon’s history, from which these passages have been excerpted word for word]. Everything written here is found there truthfully, insofar as it is recorded here; and there one finds much more concerning their nobility and victories and the wars that they waged.

I, Andreas, although an unworthy priest, extracted the foregoing abridgment from the history of the Lombards, insofar as I was able. The matters whose history is contained above did not come to our knowledge; rather, insofar as I could learn truthfully from the sequence of written records or from ancient men, I have been pleased to write them here.

## 3

After Liutprand died, Ratchis was chosen and raised up as king by the Lombards. He reigned for five years and added eight chapters to the edict. When he too died, he left the kingdom to his brother Aistulf.

We cannot preserve a record of their deeds, but insofar as we have heard, both were bold, and in their time the Lombards feared no nation. Aistulf reigned for eight years, added thirteen chapters to the edict, and died. He left the kingdom to Desiderius.

After Desiderius had reigned for three years, he established his son, named Adelchis, as king under himself with the consent of the Lombards. During their time there was some peace. He also joined his daughter, Bertrada, in marriage to Charles, son of Pippin, king of the Franks; another daughter, named Liutperga, he joined to Tassilo, king of the Bavarians. They established very firm peace between the two parties, but did not preserve it.

The cause of the discord was this. Charles had an older brother named Carloman, a violent and most wicked man. He rose up angrily against Charles and forced him to swear that he would no longer have Bertrada as his wife. What more need be said? Charles sent her back to Ticinum, from where he had formerly taken her.

When their mother heard of this separation, she brought forward the blasphemy of her son Carloman; he was struck with blindness of the eyes and ended his life in peril.

## 4

At this time, in the year 753, Leo, pope of the Roman Church [that is, Stephen III], governed the Church and suffered many oppressions from the Lombards. He left his own see and went to Francia, bringing with him many men highly skilled in the arts of letters, especially singers.

When the Frankish people heard this, they rejoiced greatly. Charles [the manuscript has “Pippin”] and his men came on foot to meet him and provided him with an excellent place to stay in the city called Metz.

After he had remained there for three years, the singers achieved such distinction that throughout nearly all the cities of Francia and Italy the ornament of the Church still resounds to this day. The pope, having discovered that the Frankish people were shrewd and noble, gave them the advice that they should come against the Lombards and possess Italy. He himself returned to the seat of the Roman Church.

## 5

Charles, however, urged on by his own men, forgot the great kindnesses that King Desiderius had shown him. He assembled a large Frankish army. At the command of the apostolic authority, their oaths were annulled. Coming into Italy against the Lombards, terror fell upon the Lombards by divine judgment, and Charles invaded Italy without a serious battle, in the eighteenth year of Desiderius and the fifteenth of Adelchis, in the twelfth indiction, when 205 years had elapsed since the Lombards entered Italy.

At that same time Desiderius died. His son Adelchis prepared ships and crossed overseas, in the year 774. Such tribulation afflicted Italy that some were killed by the sword, others were struck down by hunger, and others were killed by wild beasts, so that scarcely a few remained in the villages or cities.

## 6

At that time, in the year 774, Rotcausus was duke over the people of Friuli, and Gaidus over Vicenza. When they heard of the devastation caused by the Franks and of Charles’s approach toward Friuli, they gathered whatever forces they could and went out to meet the Franks at the bridge called the Liquentia. There they inflicted a great slaughter upon the Franks.

When Charles heard this, he sent word that he would receive and honor them if they pledged their faithfulness. Rotcausus and Gaidus, the dukes, after consulting with the nobles of Friuli, decided that they should defend themselves courageously.

Among them, however, was a man whose heart had already been blinded by Charles’s gifts. He offered this advice: “What shall we do? How can we resist them? We have no head. The king who was the source of our strength has already been defeated. Let us submit to their allegiance; it will go well for us.”

What more need be said? They did as he wished. Nevertheless Charles preserved their honor.

## 7

After Italy had been subjected and organized, Charles went to Rome in the year 781 and built a palace there. Then, after the land had been pacified and oaths had been given, he entrusted Italy to his son Pippin to govern. After some time Charles himself returned to Francia, taking hostages with him—whatever sons of the leading and noblest men of Italy there were.

Not long afterward, they received Charles’s favor and were honored by him, and they returned to their own country. Pippin died while his father was still alive, in the year 810. He left a son named Bernard, to whom Charles granted Italy.

When Italy had been overcome by famine and poverty, as soon as Bernard received the kingdom, dignity and abundance came to it, and it remained so for as long as he reigned.

Charles, who had reigned for six years in Francia and, after entering Italy, for forty-one years, died peacefully in old age, full of days, in the year 814. Through him the name of the Franks spread far and wide, as it has continued to do down to the present day. He left his seat in Francia to his son Louis. This man began to be called emperor from the race of the Franks.

## 8

The wife of that same Louis, named Ermengard, conceived hostility against Bernard, king of the Lombards. She sent him word to come to her, supposedly for the sake of peace. He accepted an oath of good faith from the noble envoys sent by her and set out for Francia.

As soon as she was able, however, as we have heard, she had Bernard’s eyes torn out without the emperor’s knowledge. He died from the resulting pain, in the year 818, after having reigned for five years: two under Charles and three under Louis.

## 9

Louis the emperor was a man of great wisdom, prudent in counsel, merciful, and a lover of peace. There was great tranquility and peace everywhere. He loved readers, singers, and all who served God and ministered in the Church.

He had three sons: Lothar and Louis by Ermengard, and Charles by Judith, whom he took in marriage after Ermengard’s death. The aforesaid Emperor Louis established his son Lothar as holding the imperial seat under him while he was still alive.

*[A different hand begins here, in a script somewhat thicker and larger than the preceding one, though still Lombardic. — Greith.]*

## 10

Lothar had a son named Louis, to whom his grandfather Louis granted Italy; Bavaria was granted to Louis, the emperor’s son, and Aquitaine to Charles. The greater dignity, namely the imperial dignity, daily increased for Lothar.

His enemies gave him the advice that they should remove Judith, his stepmother, from his father and take her away to Italy. This they did. They placed her in custody in the city of Darton.

Who could describe the fury and how violently her father must have been angered? But Lothar retained all the military forces for himself.

[Col. 1272B]

## 11

Not many days later, Lothar came to recognize what an evil course of action he had taken. He sent his stepmother back to his father and, inflamed with anger against those who had given him such wicked advice, killed some and sent others into exile.

At that time Angelbert was governing the Church of Milan as archbishop. The emperor wished to say that Angelbert had been involved in this counsel, but the nobles who came sent him into favor. When they led him before the emperor, Angelbert merely bowed his head and spoke words of greeting; he refused to come to the emperor’s feet, out of reverence for the honor of the churches.

Then the emperor said: “You carry yourself as though you were Saint Ambrose!”

The archbishop replied: “I am not Saint Ambrose, and you are not the Lord God.”

The emperor then said to him: “Go to my father, whose hatred you have made me incur, and restore me to his former favor!”

Hearing this, Angelbert went to Francia. Emperor Louis received him honorably. While the two were dining, the emperor rose and said: “Good archbishop, what ought a man to do concerning his enemy?”

He replied: “The Lord said in the Gospel: ‘Love your enemies, and do good to those who hate you’” (Matthew 5:44).

The emperor said: “And if I do not do this?”

The archbishop replied: “If you do not, you will not have eternal life if you die in that hatred.”

The angry emperor said: “If I take vengeance on my adversary, shall I not have eternal life?” Immediately he added: “See, Angelbert, how you will defend these words!”

He set the matter for consideration until morning. When morning came, the emperor gathered learned men, as quickly as he could, to dispute these words against the archbishop.

In their presence the archbishop said: “Do you know that we are all brothers in Christ?”

They replied: “We know that we call one Father in heaven.”

He said: “Then if you know that we are brothers—whether free man and slave, or father and son—the apostle John said: ‘Whoever hates his brother is a murderer, and every murderer does not have eternal life abiding in him’” (1 John 3:15). “If, therefore, the hateful man is judged a murderer, how will he possess eternal life?”

They were convinced and agreed to these words.

The emperor placed his hand upon the ground, asked forgiveness, and restored his son to favor.

He ruled, both alone and together with his son, for twenty-seven years; Lothar ruled under the same father for twenty-one years.

In the third indiction, in the year 840, the sun was so darkened in this world and the stars appeared in the sky on the third day before the Nones of May, at the ninth hour, during the Lord’s litanies, for almost half an hour [the manuscript reads *latanias*]. Great tribulation occurred.

When the people observed this, many thought that the world would no longer continue. But while they were contemplating this distress, the sun shone again, and, as though trembling, began to flee before the advancing shadow.

On the following night, near the time of dawn, there was light as though it were day. When the learned men had observed these signs in the sky, they said in their admonitions to the people:

“Brothers, be ready, because what the Lord said in the Gospel has been fulfilled: ‘When you see these signs, know that the great and manifest day of the Lord is near!’” (Luke 21:31.)

In the following month, June, Emperor Louis died and ended his days in peace.

## 12

After his death, discord arose between the three brothers: Louis and Charles on one side, and Lothar on the other. Since neither side yielded ground, they joined battle at a place called Fontenay. Battle lines were drawn up on both sides, and a great slaughter took place, especially among the nobles of Aquitaine, in the year 841.

So many brave men were defeated there through evil quarrels and lack of foresight—men who by good concord and sound counsel could have laid low many thousands of opposing pagans. Thus the nobility of Aquitaine was scattered, and the Northmen also took possession of their lands; there was no one who could resist their strength.

Lothar ruled, both alone and together with his son Louis, for fifteen years after the death of his father, and died in the year 855. He left three sons: the aforementioned Louis, who ruled in Italy under him for six years; Lothar, in Francia; and Charles, in Provence.

Charles died not many days afterward, in the year 863. Lothar left his own territory and came to Italy to visit his brother for the sake of peace. He spoke with him in the territory of Benevento, in the district of Venosa.

But as he went and returned, he laid waste many poor men’s houses and incurred much blasphemy. On the return journey he began to fall ill along the road and suddenly died in the city of Piacenza, in the year 869. His body was buried there. The same thing happened in similar fashion to many of his men.

## 13

While I briefly set down in writing the deeds of the sons of kings, my mind runs over the remaining events. The Lombards endured much hardship and oppression from the people of the Slavs, until the emperor appointed Eberhard as prince of Friuli.

After Eberhard’s death, his son Unruoch assumed the principality. From Burgundy there arose a certain man named Hupert, who for some time claimed to be utterly faithful to our lord Emperor Louis. Later, having joined himself to the Burgundians, he planned to rebel against his own territory. He forgot the great benefits that the emperor had bestowed upon him and made void the oaths that he had given.

When Lord Louis heard this, he sent Chunrad with his other faithful men. They seized and killed Hupert in the field, and many of his party were killed with him, in the year 864.

Before this rebellion took place, so much snow fell in Italy that it remained for one hundred days in level places. There was an extremely severe frost; many seeds died, and almost all the vines in the level places dried up. Wine froze inside the vessels, so that nothing came out even through the opening of the spout until the ice itself had been broken with a stick in front of the spout.

This occurred in the tenth year of our lord Emperor Louis, in the eighth indiction, in the year 859.

Having briefly passed over the truth of these events, let us proceed, as we began, through the arrival of the first order.

Lord Louis Augustus endured much oppression from the people of the Saracens in the territory of Benevento and always resisted them, in the year 860. He killed Amelmasser, their leader, together with many Saracens who were staying there, in the year 867. The rest fortified themselves courageously in the fortress called Bari, where Lord Emperor Louis besieged them for five years with the Franks, Lombards, and the other nations of his faithful subjects [that is, “besieging them”].

His wife, named Angelberga, was likewise with him, together with many of their people.

Around this time divine inspiration was kindled among the people of the Bulgarians, so that they might become Christians and worship Christ the Lord. Such a great love of charity came upon their king that he himself came to the church of blessed Peter at Rome, offered gifts there, and, strengthened in the Catholic faith and instructed in the knowledge of divinity by Lord Pope Nicholas, was baptized and confirmed in the holy faith. He received teachers from that same apostolic lord and returned to his own country.

### 14

Therefore, while Lord Louis was guarding Bari with his men [Col. 1274D], messengers came from the territory of Calabria saying:

“Lord emperor, we wish to be yours, and we trust that through your protection we shall be saved. The Saracens have come, devastated our land, laid our cities waste, and overwhelmed our churches. We ask only this of you: give us a source of strength that may help and encourage us. We give you oaths of allegiance and pay tribute.”

Then the lord emperor, moved by compassion—not rejoicing in the promises of their avarice, but grieving over their wickedness—chose brave and most noble men: Otto from the territory of Bergamo, and the bishops Oschis and Gariardus. The lord emperor encouraged them and said:

“Go in peace, faithful ones of Christ. May the good angel of the Lord accompany you, so that I may see you again and may deserve to have undertaken the labors which I impose upon you!”

Then they went forward together with these envoys. From those on whose behalf they had acted, they received firm oaths, and they gathered ever more of the faithful people to themselves. When they came to a certain valley where the Saracens, confident and without any fear, were reaping grain together with the captives whom they held, the Christians rushed upon them, killed all the Saracens whom they found there, and liberated the captives.

When their leader, named Cincimus, heard this, he came out from the city of Amantea [Col. 1275D: In Calabria.] to meet them, prepared to fight bravely. From that point the Franks were discovered, and when these joined battle on one side and the others on the other, a great slaughter of the Saracens took place. They sought flight, but the Christians pursued them, killing them all the way to the city gate.

Otto, the aforesaid bishops, and their victorious followers returned to the lord emperor. The emperor rejoiced with great joy and bestowed upon them the honor due to their rank.

### 15

Cincimus gathered a multitude of Saracens from his own people and from his homeland as auxiliaries. They set out on the march and went with them to Bari, inflicting much damage with the aid of the sultan.

It had been announced to them that the Christians were celebrating a great feast, namely the nativity of our Lord Jesus Christ. They said:

“On that day they worship their God; they will neither fight nor take up arms. Let us go against them and seize them all in their simplicity!”

This plan was reported to the lord emperor. Then orders were given that at cockcrow [Note: [Col. 1275] That is, at *gallicinium*.], in the early dawn, the bishops and priests should celebrate the solemn rites of the Mass, and that the people should receive Communion and the blessing. Thus they did.

The Saracens went out seeking them, and the Franks, who were likewise seeking them, joined them at a place [lacuna]. A great sound arose: the blast of the trumpet, the neighing [Note: [Col. 1275] That is, *hinnitus*.] of horses, and the tumult of the people.

When they were about to join battle, the faithful of Christ prayed, saying:

“Lord Jesus Christ, you said: ‘Whoever eats my flesh and drinks my blood remains in me, and I in him’ (John 6:17). Therefore, if you are with us, what can be against us?”

Immediately the battle began. As they fought with determined courage, heavenly armor strengthened the Christians; but the pagans turned their backs and began to flee. The Christians pursued them, striking them without ceasing, until they had killed a multitude of the pagans and had taken whatever pay or property of the sultan was being carried away.

When the sultan heard this, he began to grieve in great fear. In the following month, February (871), after the lord emperor had completed the fifth year during which he had held Bari, he seized the sultan and killed the remaining Saracens who were staying there, in the twenty-first year of his reign and the fourth indiction.

When the Saracens in their own land heard this, they chose very brave men—as we have heard, twenty thousand in number—saying:

“A great disgrace arising from the killing of our people is being spoken of. Let us go there!”

When they had prepared their ships, they boarded them, sailed, and landed in the territory of Benevento. Then, in the arrogance of their boldness, they said:

“What confidence should we have in our ships? Let us destroy them, because the Franks can do nothing against us; and if the Franks should prevail against us, they can proceed into our kingdom without any fear!”

Having said this and done it, they began to seek the Franks. This was reported to the lord emperor, who immediately sent his commanders Hunroch, Agefrid, and Boso with a chosen force of Franks, Lombards, and men of the other nations.

They joined battle at the place called Saint Martin, on the road near Capua, at the Volturno. The two armies drew up on either side, and both fought with fierce determination. With the help of God’s mercy, the Saracens were defeated and overcome in numbers beyond counting. Those whom the sword did not kill were drowned in the river Volturno; the rest escaped only with difficulty by flight [Note: [Col. 1275] That is, *vix*, “scarcely” or “only with difficulty.”].

Thus it pleased God’s judgment: those who had come in exaltation were brought low.

### 16

After this victory had been accomplished, the lord emperor sat in the palace at Benevento. At that time Adelchis ruled the principality of Benevento. The emperor entrusted himself and everything to him, and they loved one another with affectionate devotion [Note: [Col. 1275] That is, *diligebat*, “loved.” An ancient form.].

But the ancient enemy, who always seeks hostility against affection, arose through wicked men. They secretly said among themselves:

“Why are we burdened under the power of the Franks?”

Thus the Beneventans, through treachery and by common agreement, plotted to repay good with evil, so that wherever they found the emperor’s most faithful men, they would guard them there and would not allow them to return to the emperor.

The Franks were scattered among castles and cities, trusting without any fear and relying upon the good faith of the Beneventans. This hostile separation lasted thirty-five days: from the Ides of August (August 13) until the fifteenth day before the Kalends of October, in the fifth indiction.

But God, who had appointed the lord emperor to the imperial governance of the kingdom, was with him, as it is written: “The heart of the king is in the hand of God” (Proverbs 21:1). In this way he caused his faithful men to come to him.

A heavenly fear, however, fell upon the Beneventans. They were scarcely able to release the Franks peacefully. The Franks returned from the lord emperor rejoicing.

When that year had passed, many signs appeared. Wine, once harvested and placed in vessels [Note: [Col. 1275] *uescula* in the manuscript.], immediately became turbid; this is called “turning.” At the very Easter of the Lord, it appeared on the trees, leaves, and other places as though the earth had rained. In the following year (872), on the fourth day before the Nones of May, frost fell. Many vines in level places and valleys dried up, their shoots together with their grapes; likewise the tender leaves of the woods [Note: [Col. 1277] That is, *silvae*, “woods” or “forests.”] became dry.

In the following month of August, a great number of locusts came from the territory of Vicenza into the territory of Brescia [Note: [Col. 1277] That is, “the Brescian territory.”], then into the territory of Cremona. From there they proceeded into the territory of Lodi and also into that of Milan. They moved in ranks, as Solomon said:

“Locusts have no king, yet they advance in companies” (Proverbs 30:27).

They destroyed many small grains, that is, millet and panic grass.

When the hundredth year since the Frankish people entered Italy had been completed (873), in the twenty-third year and fourth month of the lord emperor Louis, the sixth indiction ended. As the seventh indiction began—that is, when 873 years from the incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ had elapsed [Note: [Col. 1277] The reading may be *ann. c.*, “the year …”; uncertain.]— The emperor, having come from the territory of Benevento after many victories won over the Saracens—

### 17

Then, after a year—that is, in the eighth indiction (875)—a comet appeared in the sky, resembling a shining, distant tail, throughout the whole month of June, morning and evening.

Then, in the month of July, the Saracens came (June 13) and burned the city of Comacchio [Note: [Col. 1277D] Comacchio.].

In the following month of August, the emperor Louis died, on the day before the Ides of August (August 12), in the territory of Brescia. Antonius, bishop of Brescia, took his body and placed it in a tomb in the church of Saint Mary, where the body of Saint Filastrius rests.

Anspert, archbishop of Milan, sent to him through his archdeacon ordering him to return the body. He refused. Then Anspert sent orders to Garibald, bishop of Bergamo, and Benedict, bishop of Cremona, to come with their priests and all the clergy, just as the archbishop himself did.

The bishops did so and proceeded there. They drew the body from the ground, magnificently prepared it, and on the fifth day after the emperor’s death placed it in a coffin. With every honor, while hymns were sung to God, they carried it to Milan.

I speak the truth in Christ: I was there, carried part of the body, and walked with those who bore it from the river called the Oglio to the river Adda [Note: [Col. 1277] Evidently through the territory of the bishopric of Bergamo, from which it follows that the author was Andrew, a priest of Bergamo.].

When it had been brought into the city with great honor and mournful weeping, they buried it in the church of Saint Ambrose the Confessor [Col. 1277D] on the day of its week (875).

He had ruled for thirty-two years: twelve while his father was alive [Note: [Col. 1277] The text has been corrected in this way; the manuscript may have read “six” or “eleven.”], and twenty after his father’s death [Note: [Col. 1277] The manuscript reads “after his mother’s death.”].

### 18

After his death, great tribulation came upon Italy. The chief men gathered in the city of Pavia together with Angelberga, their queen, in the month of September, in the ninth indiction. They formed a wicked plan, namely to send for two kings: Charles in Francia and Louis in Bavaria. Thus they did.

Then Charles came, unaware of Louis. Louis did not know that Charles had come, and he sent his son, named Charles; because of the distance, people began to call him Charles the Younger (*Caroleto*).

King Charles came to Pavia; Charles the Younger was in the territory of Milan. When Charles the Younger learned that his uncle was in Pavia, the men who had joined him began to commit many evil acts. Beringherus and a great multitude immediately came into the territory of Bergamo, remaining for one week at the monastery of Fara, devastating houses and committing adultery and arson.

Then many men of Bergamo abandoned their houses, leaving them full of wine and grain, and went either to the city or to the mountains with only their wives and clothing.

When King Charles heard this, he immediately went with a multitude of people against the wrongdoers themselves, from the territory of Bergamo into that of Brescia, from there to Verona, and from there to Mantua. Charles the Younger went to Bavaria.

Then Carloman, his brother, came to meet King Charles, his uncle [Note: [Col. 1277] Corrected in this way; the text originally read *barbani*.] [Note: [Col. 1277D] That is, “uncle.”], at the river called the Brenta. They greeted one another with peaceful words and confirmed their agreement until the month of May.

Carloman went to Bavaria. King Charles proceeded to Rome, offered gifts at the church of Saint Peter, was anointed by the apostolic John, and was crowned with the imperial dignity on December 25. He returned to Pavia in the month of January, in the aforesaid ninth indiction [Note: [Col. 1277] From this point the work is by a third hand.].

### 19

When the same Charles, now emperor, had returned from Rome and was staying in Pavia (876), he heard that Carloman, the son of Louis, was coming against him. When he wished to gather his army and wage war against him (877), certain of his own men—men in whose loyalty he had placed the greatest confidence—deserted him and joined Carloman.

When Charles saw this, he took flight and returned to Gaul. He died immediately on the journey itself, on October 6.

Carloman, having taken control of the kingdom of Italy, returned to his father in Bavaria after not much time had passed (December) [Note: [Col. 1277] “To his father” is absent in the manuscript.].

Meanwhile, King Louis . . . [lacuna]

## In the Year of the Lord 892: Peter the Librarian

[Col. 1279]

# Abridged History of the Franks

*(Pertz, Monumenta Germaniae historica, Scriptores I, p. 416.)*

## Notice

Chesnius, who first published this history in volume III of the *Scriptores Francici*, p. 540, reports that Gabriel Naudé copied it at Rome from a certain manuscript. No one knows the author of the work. Following almost word for word the third manuscript of the *Annals of Fulda*, namely Vienna no. 600, it contains nothing of its own except this entry under 749: “Pippin remained in the kingdom with his brother Grifo, and they administered the affairs of the kingdom very well”; and another statement under 878: “The Slavs, Dalmatians, Suebi (Sorbs), and Bohemians are the same people.” Moreover, since its chronological computation is confused, it can now be accorded no authority. I judge that Bouquet’s opinion—that the author lived about the end of the ninth century—arose because he was compelled to stop his work where the *Annals of Fulda* stop, and that consequently nothing should be attributed to him.

[Col. 1279A]

Arnulf, bishop of the city of Metz, begot Ansegisel; Ansegisel, King Pippin, who after the death of Duke Wolfald ruled a part of Austrasia and obtained the kingdom of the Franks together with Kings Louis, Hildebert, and Dagobert. He died in the second year of Emperor Anastasius, 715 years from the Incarnation of the Lord.

Charles, Pippin’s son by his wife Alberda, held the kingdom of the Franks for twenty-seven years.

Plectrude, Charles’s stepmother, ordered him to be kept under public guard. Freed by divine help, he first waged war against Ratbod, king of the Frisians, his army not emerging unscathed, in 716.

Charles pursued Ragenfrid and King Chilperic, as they turned their backs in flight, as far as Paris on Palm Sunday. At this time Bishop Wilfrid was ordained and received the name Boniface; Pope Gregory sent him into Francia to preach the word of God.

In 717 Ragenfrid and King Chilperic ravaged the territory of Cologne and the regions adjoining the Rhine; having seized gifts from Plectrude, they returned.

In 718 Ragenfrid and Chilperic, together with Eudo duke of the Aquitanians, were again defeated by Charles. Charles took the treasure of his stepmother Plectrude and set up King Chlothar. Charles defeated and drove out the Saracens devastating Gaul in several battles.

Charles kept the Pannonian peoples and the Alamanni at peace.

Charles died in the twenty-seventh year of his reign at Paris, was buried at Saint-Denis, and was damned; Hincmar is witness in the prologue to the *Life of Saint Remigius*.

Saint Eucherius, bishop of Orléans, rests in the monastery of Saint Trudo; during prayer he saw Charles in hell.

Saint Eucherius, after prayer, summoned Saint Boniface and Fulrad, abbot of Saint-Denis and chaplain of King Pippin [Col. 1280A], and recounted all that he had seen concerning Charles. He gave them a sign: they were to go to the tomb, for Charles’s body would by no means be found there. They opened the tomb; a dragon came forth from it, and everything was found blackened.

Pippin and Carloman, sons of Charles, divided the kingdom in 741.

After illustrious deeds Carloman came to Rome in 747 and became a monk on Monte Cassino.

Pippin remained in the kingdom with his brother Grifo, and they administered the affairs of the kingdom very well.

In 751 Pippin sent envoys to Rome to Pope Zacharias, asking whether one descended from the ancient stock of the Merovingians should reign in Gaul. The pope granted the request and ordered the Gauls to have Pippin as their king.

In 753 Pope Stephen sought Pippin’s help against Aistulf, king of the Lombards; Pippin received him with veneration. At Paris he anointed Pippin’s two sons, Carloman and Charles, as kings. Carloman, the one who had been a monk, died at Lyons in 754. Pippin defeated Aistulf in Italy, compelled him to restore the property of the Church to Pope Stephen, and shut him up in Pavia. Stephen returned to Rome.

In 755 Aistulf broke his oaths, besieged Rome, and ravaged everything around the city.

In 756 Pippin again defeated Aistulf.

In 757 Aistulf died while hunting. Among other gifts Emperor Constantine also sent an organ.

Tassilo was Pippin’s nephew.

In 770 Queen Bertha brought from Italy the daughter of Desiderius, king of the Lombards, to be joined in marriage to her son Charles [Col. 1281A].

In 771 Carloman died on 2 December; his wife and sons went to Italy.

Charles came to Rome to Pope Hadrian for the defence of Saint Peter, having defeated Desiderius.

In 778 Charles destroyed Pamplona in Spain.

In 781 Pippin, Charles’s son, was baptized at Rome by Pope Hadrian. In this year the sign of the cross was seen on people’s garments, and blood flowed from heaven to earth.

In 786 Charles captured Benevento after defeating Grimoald, son of Arichis, duke of the Beneventans. Ermenrud, the king’s daughter, was betrothed to Emperor Constantine.

[Col. 1281B]

In 787 an army of Greeks was defeated by Franks, Lombards, and Beneventans.

In 796 Hadrian died, and Pope Leo succeeded him.

In 797 the emperor at Constantinople was blinded.

In 801, on the Nativity of the Lord, before the confession of Saint Peter, Leo placed a crown on Charles. Then the Roman people cried: “To Charles Augustus, crowned by God, the great and peace-giving emperor of the Romans, life and victory!” Thereupon he was adored in the manner of ancient rulers. In this year, on 30 April, there was an earthquake throughout Italy, such that cities fell and the roof of the basilica of Saint Paul at Rome fell with its beams.

[Col. 1281C]

In 806 Empress Irene sent from Constantinople an envoy named Leo to make peace between Greeks and Franks.

The Bohemians were Slavs called by another name.

Charles the Younger, son of the emperor, had a sister Henrodrud, who died in 811, on 6 June.

At this time Nicephorus was emperor of the Greeks. After many victories and successful undertakings he was killed by the Bulgars in 814. Michael immediately succeeded him; he received kindly at Constantinople Charles’s envoys who had been sent to Nicephorus, and sent his own envoys to Charles. In this year there was an eclipse.

In 815 Charles died on 28 January, in the seventy-first year of his age, the forty-seventh of his Frankish reign, the forty-fourth since Italy’s subjugation, and the fourteenth since he had been called Augustus [Col. 1281D]. His son Louis succeeded him. He received embassies sent to his father and then sent to himself; and at Rome certain men conspiring to kill Pope Leo were put to death in 816.

In 817, on 25 May, Pope Leo died; the deacon Stephen succeeded him.

In 818, on 5 February, an eclipse occurred, and at night a comet appeared. Pope Stephen died on 6 February; Paschal the priest succeeded him. The emperor crowned his son Lothair and assigned him a place in the empire. Bernard, king of the Lombards, surrendered to the emperor. Leo, emperor of the Romans in Greece, sent to Louis concerning peace.

[Col. 1282A]

In 819 there was a very great eclipse.

In 820 Pippin, Louis’s son, defeated the Basques.

In 823 Emperor Louis performed penance for his sins. Lothair came to Italy; his brother Pippin was sent with his wife into Aquitaine.

In 824 Lothair was crowned by Paschal and was called Augustus by the Roman people. Liudewit was killed through the treachery of Alvidemil, uncle of Borna, duke of the Dalmatians, and many portents occurred.

In 825 Pope Paschal died; Eugenius succeeded him.

In 827 the abbot of Saint-Denis sent to Rome, and, with Eugenius’s consent, the bones of the martyr Sebastian were transferred [Col. 1282B] and placed at the city of Soissons in the church of Saint Medard.

In 828 the bodies of the holy martyrs Marcellinus and Peter were transferred to Gaul. Pope Eugenius died; the deacon Valentine succeeded him, and then Gregory, priest of Saint Mark, succeeded Valentine.

In 833 the emperor came with an army against his son Lothair and deprived Pippin of his kingdom. There was an eclipse of the sun on 6 May and of the moon on 19 April.

In the following year the emperor was deserted by his own men and captured by his sons; Pope Gregory was with them.

In the following year, by the counsel of bishops, penance was imposed upon the emperor.

[Col. 1282C]

In 838 Pavia in Italy was said to have trembled on 30 December; a comet appeared in the sign Libra on 11 April for three nights. Leading men died in Italy, especially Lambert and Hugh among their own people.

In the following year, on 18 January, there was an earthquake at Saint Nazarius. Pippin the son, king of the Aquitanians, died in November.

In 840 the emperor divided the kingdom of the Franks among his sons Louis, Lothair, and the youngest, Charles; he left Lothair his own dignity. A comet appeared in the sign Aries; at night the cloudless sky reddened, and little fires like stars ran through the heavens.

The emperor died on 20 June on a certain island in the Rhine and was buried in the church of Saint Arnulf [Col. 1282D]. The Franks accepted his son Lothair; he defeated his brothers, Louis and Charles, who came against him, and then directed an army against Charles. Louis, however, secured the Franks, Alamanni, Saxons, and Thuringians to himself by peace with a strong hand.

In 843 there was a fierce war between the emperor and his brothers; there was an eclipse of the moon on 30 March.

In the following year the kingdoms were divided among the brothers and the emperor. Pope Gregory died and Sergius succeeded him. The Moors occupied Benevento.

In 845 Hrabanus the monk composed praises of the Cross in verse and sent them to Sergius.

In 847, since the Moors could not capture the city of Rome, they ravaged the church of Saint Peter.

In 856, on 17 October, little fires like darts wandered through the air toward the west [Col. 1283A], wherefore Emperor Lothair, abandoning everything, became a monk in the monastery of Prüm, and died on 29 September. The leading men of the realm, with the consent of Louis, king of the East, made Lothair, son of Lothair, their lord.

Emperor Lothair left three sons, Louis, Lothair, and Charles, who made peace with their uncles Charles and Louis in 867. In that year the winter weather was harsh, and blood-red snow fell from heaven.

Charles, brother of Emperor Lothair, had a son Carloman; at this time Nicholas was pope. [Note: [Col. 1283C] Chesnius reads “Carlus frator.” That the report in this year of the peace made by Lothair’s sons with their uncles derives from the *Annals of Fulda* under 868 is sufficiently shown by the blood-red snow which fell in that year [Col. 1284C].]

Rudolf, monk, poet, and historian, flourished in Germany and died on 8 March 866.

In 870 King Louis became ill, so that the physicians despaired of him. Perceiving this, he distributed almost all his goods to the poor and preferred to be healed by God.

Charles the brother invaded Lothair’s kingdom, ordered the bishop of Metz to adorn his head with a diadem, and made himself Augustus because of his brother’s illness.

In the following year King Louis recovered from illness.

In 876 Louis died and was buried at Milan in Saint Ambrose. When Charles learned this, he sought Italy and carried off the emperor’s treasures.

In January 878 Lambert, son of Guy, and Adalbert, son of Boniface, came to Rome with a strong force [Col. 1283C], put Pope John in chains, and compelled the leading men of the Roman people to recognize Carloman as Caesar. Having done this, Pope John removed and transferred the treasures of Peter and the Lateran; then he closed the church of Peter, whose altar had formerly been adorned by a sacred covering, so that those who came could not enter the church. The pope made for the Tyrrhenian Sea, seeking to deprive Carloman, who was afflicted by paralysis and could not speak a word.

On 29 October, at the ninth hour of the office, there was so great an eclipse of the sun that the stars appeared; and there was an eclipse of the moon in the last hour of the night on the Ides of October. A cattle plague occurred in Germany, followed by a mortality among human beings. The Slavs, Dalmatians, Suebi [Note: [Col. 1284C] Read “Sorbs.”], and Bohemians are the same people. Carloman died on 22 March 881.

In the following year, on 29 December, before cockcrow, there was a great earthquake at Mainz; and on 18 August Louis died, whose body was buried in the monastery of Saint Nazarius beside his father’s body.

Arnulf, Carloman’s son, was made king in Alamannia [Col. 1284B], against the wishes of his young uncle [Note: [Col. 1284C] That is, his uncle.] Charles. Charles died in 888, on 3 January.

In 892 there was a fierce war between Arnulf, the Christian king, and Siegfried and Godfrey, the pagan kings of the Northmen and Danes, so great that the kings were slain and nearly the whole army was destroyed, while only one Christian was found killed.

In the following year the Italians went to the king, asking him to free Italy from the hands of tyrants; the king promised this.

In 894 King Arnulf came into Italy with an army, soon captured Bergamo, bound the petty kings to loyalty, and returned.

In this same year Pope Formosus died at Rome and Stephen succeeded him. The Greeks made peace with the Huns. Leo, emperor of the Greeks, sent Lazarus as envoy to the Italian emperor.

In 898 Arnulf died; his young son Louis succeeded him.

# Appendix to the Tenth Century

[Col. 1283]

## In the Year of the Lord 916: Panegyric of Emperor Berengar, by an Anonymous Author

*(Edited by Pertz, Monumenta Germaniae historica, Scriptores IV, p. 189.)*

## Preliminary Notice

Berengar I, king and emperor, Frankish by descent and Lombard by nation, perhaps descended from Count Unruoch, whom we see administering Charlemagne’s affairs in 802, 806, and 811 [Note: [Col. 1283C] *Monumenta Germaniae*, *Leges* I, pp. 90, 137; Einhard, *Life of Charles*, ch. 33; *Annals* under 811.]. His father was Count Eberhard, duke of Friuli [Note: [Col. 1284C] Regino, under 888.]. By Gisla, daughter of Louis the Pious and Judith [Note: [Col. 1284C] Agnellus, *Lives of the Bishops of Ravenna*; in the *Life of George* [Col. 1285B] in Muratori, *Scriptores* II, p. 185, where nevertheless, as Eccard observes, “Evrardo” must be corrected; and the charters of Gisla, who calls Charles II, her king, if she may dare to say it, her brother.], he had sons Unruoch, Berengar, Adalhard, and Rudolf, and daughters Ingeltrude, Judith, and Heilwig. In the testament which he made [Note: [Col. 1285B] D’Achery, *Spicilegium* XII, p. 490. It is dated in the twenty-fourth year of the reign of Emperor Louis, but “nineteenth” must be read; that year runs from 6 April 868. For his widow Gisla, already on 15 April 869, in Gaul mentions her lord of sweet memory, her widowhood, and her change of habit.], Eberhard left his eldest son his possessions situated in Lombardy and Alamannia, and left the patrimony in Ripuarian and Belgian Gaul to be divided among Berengar and his other children. Their mother Gisla founded the monastery of Cisoing in the diocese of Tournai. When Eberhard died in 868, Unruoch [Note: [Col. 1285B] Andrew, priest of Bergamo, *Chronicle*, *Monumenta Germaniae*, *Scriptores* III, pp. 235, 237.] succeeded him in the duchy of Friuli. He survived into 887, when he is praised as a kinsman of Emperor Charles III [Note: [Col. 1286B] *Annals of Fulda*.], and died shortly afterward. Berengar succeeded to the duchy; in the following year he received the kingdom of the Lombards and, after various vicissitudes, in 916 the crown of the Roman Empire as well.

The author of the poem composed in his praise between 916 and 924 [Note: [Col. 1286B] After Berengar had been crowned and while he was still alive; IV, 208.] was a Lombard. Though advanced in years [Note: [Col. 1286B] Nor wealthy—which would certainly have been remarkable in a poet; Prologue to Book V, v. 17.], he was stirred by love for Berengar and by the example of Homer, Statius, and Virgil—whose *Eclogues* no less than whose *Aeneid* he had read—and proposed to celebrate in verse the king’s illustrious deeds down to his Roman coronation. In this task, a man equally learned in Greek and Latin literature generally followed chronological order; but he judged that his devotion to the king would be satisfied if he sang only Berengar’s principal expeditions, omitting everything that seemed less suited to his praise. Even in matters at which the author was evidently present, however, one misses careful writing: sharing Liudprand’s error, he treats as one and the same Arnulf’s two Italian expeditions, separated by more than a year, and writes that Guy survived both. Yet this does not prevent delight in the poem: amid the great dearth of writers at the beginning of the tenth century, it offers matters eminently worth knowing, vivid diction, forceful imagery drawn largely from Virgil, Statius, and Juvenal, and verses imitating the classical Roman authors.

The book appears to have lain hidden in the repositories of Italian libraries during the Middle Ages. The sole surviving manuscript, written on parchment in an eleventh-century hand, was found at Padua in the seventeenth century, in the library of Saint John in Viridario, by Nicolaus Heinsius, who cited it in his edition of Claudian of 1650. In 1654 it was copied through the efforts of Lucas Langermann of Hamburg and made public by Adrian Valesius. Valesius’s edition, accompanied by the poem of Adalbero, bishop of Laon, addressed to King Robert, appeared at Paris in octavo in 1663, furnished with a preface and extensive commentary [Note: [Col. 1286B] I used the copy of the Royal University Library of Göttingen, in which P. Burmann wrote in his own hand certain glosses and readings noted by Heinsius in Claudian.]. Leibniz inserted Valesius’s text in volume I of the *Scriptores Brunsvicenses* and adorned it with a few notes. Muratori, following Valesius’s text, preserved the notes of both Valesius and Leibniz in volume II of the *Scriptores Italici*, p. 371 ff. Finally Bouquet included the poem in volume VIII, p. 106 ff., of his collection, illustrating it partly with Valesius’s notes and partly with his own. Since several errors of the first edition had thus crept into the later editions, Jacob Morelli, librarian of Saint Mark’s Library at Venice, to which the Paduan manuscript had been brought [Note: [Col. 1286B] I examined it there in 1821, but refrained from collating it again with the printed editions.], had the book collated with the editions by his nephew, the distinguished Bettio, already Morelli’s successor, and recorded the corrections in his *Bibliotheca Manuscripta*. He also added certain glosses, both interlinear and marginal, some of which must be attributed to the poet himself [Note: [Col. 1286B] For example, I, 261.]. Consequently we are now permitted to offer an edition more corrected than the earlier ones.

## The First Book Begins

[Col. 1285]

“The Prologue Begins.”

[Col. 1285A]

Which ancient times bestowed upon their men.

The labyrinthine tale bestowed these things upon great Homer,  
and upon you, learned poet Maro, the *Aeneid*.

[5] Then the halls of the gods resounded with the song of bards;  
now every prayer rejects your Muse [Note: [Col. 1286B] That is, *precatio*, “prayer.”].

Their blood burned with the Pierian gift;  
no Thalia follows your step.

Therefore I fear that swift flames may blacken you,  
[10] because you offer worthless words to refined ears.

“Why do you so often pursue these times with empty words,” [Note: [Col. 1286B] The book replies.]  
“if you fear that the poems you produce must be devoured by fire?

[Col. 1285B] “Desist; for now no one cares for your poems;  
where these things are done, men do these things in the countryside as well.

[15] “What profit, moreover, was it to endure harsh labours  
and hasten along long roads?

[Col. 1286A] “The care of your *endromis* [Note: [Col. 1286B] That is, a garment.] and of food wearies you more;  
flee, then, the trifles you are preparing to recount.”

You heap vain murmurs upon me often, O book,  
[20] but they cannot add barriers to my wishes.

Let all grave matters fall away, I pray, and let every labour be absent,  
while I offer a small gift to the supreme head.

Do you not see what triumphs silent ages possess,  
which the man to be revered throughout the whole world achieves?

[25] Though you, burned, may dissolve into the empty air,  
the better part, through love of the great man, will write.

But let us joyfully ask Christ in humble prayer  
to favour my undertaking from the citadel of the Father.

I am not moved by the applause of the people or by the circus’s reward;  
[30] it is enough for me to set forth a few deeds of the pious man.

Christ, who turnest heaven’s vault by thy gracious power,  
grant that thy servant may be able to utter fitting things!

You cannot hope for ivy or laurel, little book,

## “The Panegyric of Berengar the Unconquered Caesar Begins”

[Col. 1287A]

If Greece sang, in studied speech, of kingdoms,  
so that it might raise to the stars as some deservedly blessed  
men uncouth in character and religion—tyrants—  
whom Lachesis had better condemned to black Avernus;

[5] if Rome afterward bore its own Augusti, in varied invention,  
to the radiant dwellings of heaven, while the Stygian abyss at the same time swallowed them amid unceasing agitation:  
shall one be ashamed to praise a shining ruler  
of Christians? For what opens heaven’s waters [Note: [Col. 1287D] Namely, the waters of baptism; editions read *odis*.],

[10] and what fills the whole world with the breath of the Lord?

[Col. 1287B] Therefore I shall duly sing Berengar, worthy to be read for his lineage and deeds,  
to whom lofty power gave the task of curbing  
Italy’s peoples, proud in war and in the cultivation of the soil.

It is worth knowing, once his lineage has been recounted,  
[15] by what stock he is powerful; for my Thalia cannot bear everything.

I acknowledge Charles, surnamed the Great, as a Frank by birth,  
before whom the earth, subject to the frozen pole, trembled,  
and the land which the golden Sun, seeking and leaving, washes with his waves [Note: [Col. 1287D] The manuscript has *ruit*, “rushes”; editions read *undis*, “with waves.”],  
and the land he scorches, so often borne there by panting horses.

[20] From his blood, from his ancestors and forefathers, comes the ruler  
of Ausonia; yet he was duly reared under the rule  
[Col. 1287C] of Charles’s descendant, who, last among the Franks to rule,  
compelled Rome beneath reins bearing a similar name [Note: [Col. 1287D] Charles III.].

Seeing the man glad in the image of war,  
[25] devout in judgment, and worthy of the royal diadem,  
that ruler chose him as the faithful companion of his distinguished side,
If wars perhaps break out, [he was] a minister suited to the imperial fasces and power. The Italian prince, hardened by arms, had learned thus to endure the harsh labors of Mars.

[30] Behold, the day had come [Note: [Col. 1287D] The year 888, January 13.] when the dark plague of fate claimed the king, their father, and fever coursed through all his limbs. As he was dying, he addressed his foremost friends. They report that he said these final words to his near kinsman Brengarius:

“The East should rightly bow its neck to you,

[35] and even those whom the Sun, sunk into the western waters, sees, and those whom either pole of the world looks down upon; nevertheless the nobles of the West burn, according to their strength, to submit properly to you, since all that you undertake is worthy of so great an effort. With you lies the glory of our empire, and by your destinies Roman power shall endure!

[40] Having spoken thus, the leader departed into the heavenly airs, and, groaning, left the reins of the kingdoms. He indeed thus ascended to the stars; but a pitiable ambition, acting upon the peoples, persuaded those who had been accustomed to assemble under the broad frontier of one empire to marvel thereafter at several tyrants across different lands, and for each people to choose its own ruler, while the same affection endured for all.

[45] [Col. 1288A] “Lest the Rhine or the Saône, long held in esteem, seize our joys, the nobles of Italy gather together and order such a message to be brought to the king: ‘This land, its farmers, and the rivers flowing beneath its ancient walls are well known to you. Let neither savage Gaul nor fierce Germany deter you from possessing the land worthy of you, since your scepter-bearing kinsmen have long cultivated it, and your father loved it more dearly than all other lands.’

Moved by these appeals, he hastened his steps toward the city watered by the swiftly flowing Ticino.

[Col. 1288B] After he had there taken up the royal insignia and crown, he was eager to overrun no other lands in haste, an undertaking that had plunged many young men into untimely death. Joy resounded and all the public squares echoed with applause; sacred temples trembled with the dances of men and mothers; unmarried girls raised bright ritual songs,

[65] and performed gentle dances. The right hand struck the drums, and the thumb ran across the slender strings of the lyre, modulating seven modes upon the pipes.

Others cultivated the fields; oxen plowed the heavy soil; flocks sheared the meadows, and little goats hung upon the cliff.

[70] [Col. 1288C] There was one rest for all, and one peace for all.

[Note: [Col. 1288D] Verses 71–75 are from Statius, *Thebaid* III, lines 253 ff.] It was as when the sea, released after a long peace from the winds, lies still, and the shores rest in untroubled sleep; when inactive summer soothes the leafy trees and the clouds after the wind has departed: then the resonant pools and lakes subside, and the rivers, exhausted by the sun, fall silent.

Inflamed by envy and unable to tolerate such things, Wido raged violently and poured excessive complaints from his breast:

[80] “I am continually ashamed to admit that there are peaceful conditions which nourish Latium! For I see men flourishing and reclining amid fertile possessions, and their chosen leader seated upon a lofty throne,

[Col. 1288D] whom they have selected for themselves. If only I had the strength to cross the deep mountains! Perhaps I could break the treaty and overturn the pliable minds of the young men who cultivate the Tyrrhenian fields! I believe they would willingly bow their necks to me. Am I less suited to arms?

[85] “What of it? Paris was able to disturb glorious Mycenae and summon the savage sons of Atreus to impious battles. What does it matter [Note: [Col. 1288D] The editions read *referam* (‘shall I mention’).] how great a man Rodulfus [Note: [Col. 1288D] King of Transjurane Burgundy.] sits in his court, or what sort of man Oddo, my former and familiar companion, rules over the Frankish fields?

[Col. 1289A] “Shall I alone be deprived of prosperous gifts and alone roll down to the boundary of a silent old age? No—not while my spirit feeds upon the pure air, or, if swift Mars should strike me with his weapons,

[95] “rolling fathers of young men in their blood!”

With such words of anger he loosened the reins, seething with bile in his mind. [Note: [Col. 1289D] *Jacto*—verses 100 onward—are from Statius, *Thebaid* II, lines 412 ff.] Like a harsh serpent that rises close at hand when it has been hurled upon a stone, beneath which its long thirst has lain hidden, and which, stirred throughout all its limbs,

[100] summons its venom into its jaws and scaly neck, he now selected companions suitable for his frenzied enterprise.

When flying rumor struck the king’s bright ears, reporting Wido’s unjust attempts to stir rebellion, while Fortune preserved due measure, he shook his dreadful head in royal fashion, looked upon the vault of heaven, and thus released his voice in sacred prophecy:

[105] “You, creator of heaven and earth, who whirl the thunderbolts, who measure the revolutions of the years and the appointed periods of night, the four quarters of the world—how far the north lies from the south, and how far the setting sun stands from the rosy rising sun—you measure, so that Phosphorus may undergo two risings,

[110] now preceding the horses of the Sun and driving away the darkness, now at times leading before him the cold steeds of Night. Be a merciful witness and remit the guilt, if this hand should inflict the losses of death upon Gauls who wickedly seek to seize fields due to me.

[Col. 1289C] “What unspeakable power has been granted to this man, that he should deprive me of my kingdoms? If you, creator of the world, sit ready to destroy men for their crimes, let no prayers delay you,

[120] but let arrogance rush through every danger, since iron Clotho now severs the threads of those about to die, and Alecto, cruel abomination, separates the serpents of the dreadful head from the wretched, deep beneath Acheron.”

Meanwhile night entered, marked by various shapes, when the excellent father withdrew into his high dwelling after the meal and relaxed his limbs upon his honorable couch.

The stars had scarcely shone throughout the whole sky beneath this annual peace. Behold, the brigand begins his attempts at fraud, by which once the Punic king [Note: [Col. 1289D] Hannibal.] cut through the Alpine crags with vinegar, eager for empire.

[130] When he reached the shores of Italy, now with threats, now with entreaty, he solicited the unstable bands of young men with these words:

“Whoever desires to extend his life through firm ages and to change the leader’s fasces, let him not hesitate to enjoy properly the gifts we offer freely and to gather our companies.

[135] “If anyone should perhaps regard what we are carrying as futile, because Brengarius places his strength in arms, and because once, moved by unjust provocations, he sought out the absent Gauls in the Etruscan borders, let him consider how great I am when I rush to arms, and how great when I come from my native shores into Ausonia. Let him be permitted to bring down the tyrant,

[Col. 1290A] “and let him come to be poured out together with him upon the beloved fields!

[145] “Those whose changes pleased them, and who found it sweet to move the powerful, placed their necks beneath a cruel yoke; but the Tyrrhenian force, disastrously unreliable, withdrew completely, and, exulting, carried its violent enemies into the kingdom. Ah, the savage counsels of the guilty!

“The prince was absent and was preparing peace for the empire where the health-giving Adige waters the cultivated land of Verona. Behold, a minister, drenched in sweat, quickly seeks the high dwelling of the leader.

[150] “‘Most valiant ruler,’ he says, ‘come to the aid of your people! A troop, exulting, has thrown itself over the steep mountain in a leap, proud enough of its numbers for war. Unless you persist in bringing very hard-hitting companies against them with swords, what need is there to tell of the losses they will inflict upon Latium once it is conquered?’

[Col. 1290B] “Angered by this, the king replied to him: ‘Young man, I command you—only stop agitating! While this head is governed by life spread through its limbs, this land will not yield after being conquered, and I am ashamed to admit that the affairs of Latium have been defeated!’”

He spoke and ordered his companions to be summoned. Companies, aroused throughout the broad fields, rushed out—men whose love was peace, whose concern was glory, children, and a sweet home, and who were weary of life—came, gathered together, before the peaceful king. Sudden reports sharpened their righteous anger.

[165] Once the companies had assembled from every side, they declared war before the leader’s tribunal with a great united roar.

At last the terrifying leader emerged into the clear air, when every side was being rubbed by iron seams beneath armor, a fiery disk broadly covered his shoulders and chest, and a bronze helmet trembled upon his head,

[170] while two spear shafts gleamed in his right hand with twin iron points. A splendid sword also flashed at his mouth—a beautiful adornment and the glory of kings.

“Most valiant young men,” he began amid the ranks, “the dealings of raging Mars are at hand. Let the hand be ready upon the hilt, and the spirit ready for toil, as befits the excellent!

[175] “Since Wido wishes to overthrow the kingdom, he is resolved to share out the land among his allies and those summoned, and to wrest from the young men’s embraces what has been promised. If he had the courage to fight with me alone and to defer the crime of sending peoples, wavering in arms, to destruction!” [Note: [Col. 1290D] The manuscript reads *partis*, that is, *paratis* (‘the troops being ready’), hence ‘his own’; Valesius conjectures *pactis*.]

He spoke, filled the foaming horse’s reins, and rushed toward the frontier of the war, where the hostile force was bringing Latium to ruin with arms.

[185] When dawn had driven the cold darkness from the sky, shaking out her dewy hair and reddening greatly after the following Sun, and when the threatening helmet had enclosed the man’s face, the trumpets sounded and the echo of the voice resounded; the peoples, divided into their respective turns, were raised upon the plain.

[Note: [Col. 1289D] Verses 189–194, “the leader in battle,” are from Statius, *Thebaid* II, lines 128 ff.] As when, hearing the murmur of hunters, a tiger bristles with spots and shakes off inert sleep,

[190] desires battle, opens its jaws, and readies its claws, then soon rushes upon the ranks and carries in its mouth a man breathing nourishment for its bloody young—so the leader, aroused by anger, fiercely hurled weapons against the opposing companies.

[Col. 1291A] Ranks rose everywhere, the sky was hidden by dust, and the air resounded with dreadful cries.

One man, thrown down in a swift rush across the plain, was trampled beneath the horses’ feet; another, pierced through the temples by a flying missile, fell headlong from the back of his hoofed horse; another’s severed head ran far from his neck [Note: [Col. 1291D] The edition reads *desectum* (‘cut off’).]; another lay lifeless, his brains spilled upon his armor.

[205] One man lacked a hand, another the power to walk; a third, no longer whole in his sight, was overwhelmed. The fields grew wet with sweat, and the earth ran with blood. Mars, growing harsher throughout the field, raged in close-packed combat, while Wido slipped into the ranks like a thunderbolt [Note: [Col. 1291D] One manuscript reads *fluminis*, ‘of a river,’ in Heinsius.],

[210] just as a Libyan lion, when from a distant mound it happens to see joyful herds of cattle in the fields, raises its mane upon its neck and thirsts for blood, then presses toward the middle of the crowd with its chest held high.

Here the leader of Ausonia roared; there Wido, the minister of death, raged, excessively proud of his own strength. Who, in truth, could withstand the weight of the unconquered tyrant’s power? At last his companions were forced to turn their backs and flee.

[215] He pursued the fugitives with shouts:

“What madness has seized you [Note: [Col. 1291D] Compare Virgil, *Aeneid* IX, 601.], that, enclosed by mountains, you wish to avoid the swords, comrades? Once you did not make such promises in your ancestral homes, when you pledged yourselves to every delight of the children of Hesperia.

[Col. 1291C] “Recall your step! Today you shall see what this right hand can do—come on! Do not trust your speed, chosen band!”

But he addressed the driven men in vain, because of the lightning-like strength of their leader.

[225] Abandoned by his friends, bereft of judgment, he stood uncertain whether to withdraw ingloriously from the battle while preserving his life in a renewed combat [Note: [Col. 1291D] An interlinear gloss noted by Heinsius: ‘rising again after a fall’; Burmannus conjectures *recidivo*, ‘recurring.’], or hasten to a beautiful death through wounds, for his enemies.

While he suddenly turned these thoughts over in his mind, one of his companions came up, pressing the flanks of his already sluggish horse with rapid spurs:

[230] “‘Illustrious guest,’ he said, ‘depart from the Gauls. Our companies have withdrawn completely.

[Col. 1292A] “Do not suppose it strange that a human being rages through the ranks; rather, they are monsters amid the dusty fields of Libya [Note: [Col. 1291D] The sense is: ‘Do not suppose that it is a remarkable human being who rages through the ranks, but rather monsters amid the dusty fields of Libya.’ Valesius emends *miserum* (‘wretched’) for *mirum* (‘strange’) and *agmen* (‘troop’) for *hominem* (‘human being’), and reads ‘rather than monsters.’].

“I myself saw him lay two men low with a single blow. Alas, I am ashamed to say what deaths he has inflicted upon the defeated! Withdraw, I beg you, so that you may be preserved for better undertakings!”

At last, overcome by love for his companion, he departed and joined his grieving men [Note: [Col. 1292D] Compare Liudprand, *Antapodosis* I, 18.].

Meanwhile night rushed in and composed the cares and labors of humankind, wrapping the heavens in a black covering.

[240] It was indeed gentle to all, but troubled for the man driven away.

He revolved the furies of his anger and the labor he had undertaken, yet not without purpose or the vigor of a profound mind.

[Col. 1292B] For when night had already turned beneath its setting reins and the stars had departed, once mighty Tethys first drove the hesitating Hyperion from the eastern sea, he led learned-speaking men to the threshold of the victorious man, lest he prevent those deprived of daylight from committing their dead to the earth.
