[250] After they had completed the road and, having entered, had been granted an opportunity to speak face to face, they began:

“Supreme power has granted you victory, leader; submit your spirit to our request amid these savage wars. For we ask that we may be permitted to commit our companions, deprived of the sky, to tombs, lest their limbs, made subject to evil wild beasts, perish as God’s work and decay when left upon the field.

[Col. 1292C] “The brave Wido and this people have compassion for their friends in this matter. Their strength and courage have not been so broken that they cannot survive battles and that the right of falling should belong only to our hope.”

“Young men,” replied the victor, “you all waste away in the vice of your nation, because you always possess an abundance of speech, and there is more strength in your mouths than in your breasts. Yet to have said more than one has done is accounted less honorable [Note: [Col. 1292D] ‘To have said more than to have done’: the word *quam* (‘than’) is written above *egisse* (‘to have done’).] [Note: [Col. 1292D] A marginal gloss says: ‘This verse belongs to a certain Frankish wise man.’]

[Col. 1292D] “Nevertheless, take up the bodies, since I spare rather those who are deprived of light and remain. I pity the many thousands lying there because of one man’s crime—men to whom the Creator granted, by a hidden ordinance, the breath of life in a body of earthly clay.

[265] “Let God himself see to that. But I call heaven to witness: either depart swiftly, Gauls, from the lands of Italy, or gather again your broken companies for war [Note: [Col. 1292D] Thus one manuscript. Compare Virgil, *Aeneid* XII, 264].”

When they had spoken these words, the men in large numbers turned their steps toward their companions, and swiftly lifted their dead from the field into biers, so that when the messenger who precedes the Thunderer from his heavenly citadel should stir everything with trumpets, they might return.

[Col. 1291] THE FIRST BOOK ENDS

THE SECOND BOOK BEGINS.

[Col. 1293]

[Col. 1293A] Meanwhile Wido wavered and repeatedly considered with what soldiers he should wage war and what hearts he should skillfully extend toward the sword. At last this plan pleased him: to trouble the peoples who were at rest in their native land, so that they might bring united strength to war and renew their exhausted forces, and might possess the land under equal reins.

“Supreme God, who cherish all things, who created all things, who rule heaven, sea, stars, and lands by your command, who make the stars shine and the shining constellations run,

[10] I beg you, attend and help me in my prayer; infuse my senses, so that I may commit to this humble page the dealings of war and the leaders whom I have enticed.”

[Col. 1293B] The Gallic hero is already the first to seize arms [Note: [Col. 1293D] Wido.], strengthened as the leaders cross the mountain heights, together with his brother Anscherius, who, with presumptuous right, sharpens five hundred ministers from his own people, equipped in spirit and swords and not inferior in strength.

Gauslinus orders three hundred horsemen, eager for savage wars, to hasten forward; Ubertus likewise brings two hundred men for glory. All have the same weapons, similar equipment, and the strength of their homeland in their breasts.

[Col. 1293C] The Tyrrhenian youth, once again taking up hostile weapons, a renowned people formerly, sufficiently suited to battle by land and sea but now treacherous and degenerate, eagerly desire war; and the Camerinian cohort likewise boasts of the gift of its sons and subjects a thousand companions to war.

[25] Albricus, still poor, relying more upon his offspring than upon his own valor—after his loyalty had been displayed—departs joyfully with a hundred soldiers. Now Camerina resounds with hope [Note: [Col. 1293D] Gloss: ‘For afterward he held the march of Camerina. It is certain that Albericus killed his fellow godfather Wido on a bridge, eager for honor; therefore this man wishes that he had reached the height of honor without the death of his friend.’]. Would that his companion might become wealthy without death!

“Why do you rush to crime, mad Raginerus, after choosing companions? He is overcome neither by counsel nor by any strength who weighs causes from heavenly Olympus

[Col. 1293D] and who granted ancestral Latium to Brengarius.”

[35] [Col. 1294A] Wilelmus also leads three hundred gathered companions, effective in breastplates and menacing in helmets, not sluggish with the javelin. Ubaldus drives forward just as many with similar ardor [Note: [Col. 1293D] Compare Liudprand, *Antapodosis* I, 21.].

Nor is the common people absent, stirred by unstable zeal and by petty leaders. I have no time to speak of them, since perhaps these labors will remain for learned men in the future; let it be enough for me to have touched upon the main point of the battle [Note: [Col. 1293D] Gloss: ‘*Duellium* and *duellum* differ: *duellium* is the period during which war is prepared, while *duellum* is the actual conflict. Others say that *duellum* properly means a conflict between two.’].

[40] They also come—three thousand in number—who recently endured the dangers of the field, drawn together under their leaders and standing stupidly upon the accursed plain. It would have been better for them to have fallen in battle than to have seen miserable days. For they perished under an unequal fate.

At last Lamberticus orders [Note: [Col. 1293D] A gloss says: ‘*Vacat tandem* is unnecessary and is a line about those who are called ‘tibicines,’ to whom something is added merely to sustain the meter. A *tibicen* is properly a fork placed to support collapsing walls; hence Juvenal, speaking of the city’s inconveniences: “We inhabit a city propped by a slender buttress” (*Satire* 3, line 193).] the chief man to be beheaded [Note: [Col. 1294D] That is, Lambertus, Wido’s son.]. Another dies of thirst in the fields; a third wishes to delay the unlucky arrows of the Hungarians;

[50] a third, sorrowful, climbs to the heights of heaven and the depths of the sea, so that perhaps he may raise himself to life-giving scepters. O the human mind ignorant of the future!

Now the battle lines gather, threaten war by their numbers, and rejoice; even courage has been briefly added to the fearful.

[55] Wido, moving through the middle of them, congratulates his friends, exults in their spirits, and already, in hope, anticipates the enemy’s defeat:

[Note: [Col. 1294D] Verses 56–62 are from Virgil, *Aeneid* XI, lines 491–497.] As when at last a free horse, its bonds broken, flees its stall and gains the open field,

[Col. 1294C] either heads toward the pastures and herds of mares,

[60] or, accustomed to being washed in familiar water, leaps forth and neighs with its neck held high in exuberance, while its mane plays over its neck and shoulders.

At last the armed glory of Latium and its renowned hope of war had perceived the terrible furies raging. He summons arms and orders the foremost men and ministers of the kingdom to gather the hastily summoned companies more quickly into battle, and orders the broad cities to be emptied of their inhabitants.

[Col. 1294D] The grim command now rages across Italian soil: let them assemble again to decide the matter with baneful steel; those to whom pious laws are pleasing burn—an impious thing—to renew them joyfully thereafter throughout the familiar cities [Note: [Col. 1294D] *Excide* (‘has fallen out’) in one manuscript.]. Thus, with swift movement, the young men accompany their horses and wear down their limbs with breastplates [Note: [Col. 1294D] Compare I. 169.].

[Col. 1295A] Without delay Walfredus [Note: [Col. 1295D] In the year 896, margrave of Friuli. *Annals of Fulda*.] gathers three thousand companions.

With their hands upon their hilts and fervor for the first clash, they disturb the hostile mass; there is no other stronger man whom the enemy youth would fear as he advances into battle, and whom Ausonia would favor.

[75] Likewise the three thunderbolts of war, the Supponids [Note: [Col. 1295D] Gloss: ‘*Supponidae* is a patronymic derived from the father and, by the metaplasm called systole, its second syllable is shortened, or this occurs by the license permitted in proper names. Three sons of Suppo were in the battle: Adalgisus, Wifredus, and Boso. Their sister had married Brengarius; their father is called Picenian count in the chronicle of Casauria. Compare Valesius, p. 120.’], come together; the wife, at that time sufficiently faithful, joined them to the beloved king—she who was later to perish by poisons,

[80] after she had drunk the hostile counsels of Circe.

They are accompanied by one thousand five hundred horsemen, their chests covered, according to the custom of the people, with Chalybian metal, and their heads shaded by shining crests. In Teutonic fashion, Leuto presses forward six hundred exultant men;

[85] [Col. 1295B] his brother Bernardus also resounds with a similar column. All spur the flanks of their swift-footed horses with long spurs and enclose their lofty sides with shields.

Thus the German wages war. Nor did Albricus, who had stained your waters with blood by treachery, O Tiber, depart sluggishly: he leads out five hundred warriors bristling with the strength of their homeland and once trained in harsh Frankish exercises.

Now impatient of delay, Bonifacus gathers his companions; from the opposite side Berardus advances, surrounded by an equal number of arms, three hundred men.

[95] The greatest part of the common people brandish, in Italian fashion, sarissas [Note: [Col. 1295D] Compare Statius, *Thebaid* VII, line 269.] and cover their left sides with shields in a circle and as a defense against Mars.

[Col. 1295C] Fierce Azo hastens forward [Note: [Col. 1295D] Valesius has already conjectured that he belonged to the Este family; compare verses 99–100.], driving his companions into battle. Olricus [Note: [Col. 1295D] Liudprand, *Antapodosis* II, 57 ff.], gathering his companies from the neighboring frontier, comes where Latium is enclosed by the Adriatic waters,

[100] and it is a labor to hold swords before the savage Iberians [Note: [Col. 1295D] Gloss: ‘Iberians are called Spaniards from the river Iberus, from which one part of Spain is called Iberia. For the Spaniards, secretly sailing through the Adriatic Sea to Liguria, which is part of Italy, inflict the greatest devastation; therefore he said: “Where it is a labor to hold swords before the savage Iberians.” But the Iberians here seem to be Hungarians, having come from Iberia—that is, Asia. Valesius preferred to read *Abaris*.].

I fear to speak of the priests, enticed on both sides by zeal for the wars of Mars. I pass over great matters in compressed words, nor is it permitted to express briefly the treaties of the Rhine [Note: [Col. 1296D] The treaty with Arnulf was concluded in November of the year 888; compare the *Annals of Fulda*.]; hence it is pleasing to turn my course elsewhere.

When the good leader at last sees that the companies have assembled, he leaps into their midst, conspicuous in shining armor, and brings these words:

[110] “O nobles, you who have already experienced funerals in the field, you understand whether it is pious to ward off the unjust threats of Wido, the defenses of our kingdom. Since he now wishes to extend his arrogance still further rather than bring an end to our exhausted circumstances, quickly take up your arms and defend your dear land,

[Col. 1296A] “under my leadership—I whom you formerly urged by your prayers to raise the fasces.”

He spoke. The crowd, roaring, complained that the battle had long been delayed, suddenly shaken by the tumult, scarcely waiting for the signal. A savage love of death and slaughter raged in every breast. Nothing hindered their burning ardor. They rushed forward and made up for lost time.

[120] So shores roar when the wind begins, when the harbor is abandoned; sails stream everywhere, loose ropes are tossed everywhere, now the oars float and the whole anchor floats upon the sea’s surface; now the land is seen from the middle of the sweet sea, and companions are left behind at the stern.

[Col. 1296B] The field had long been marked out by an unjust purpose; both battle lines moved toward it in their grim armor.

[Note: [Col. 1296D] Verses 127, 129–145 are copied almost word for word from Statius, *Thebaid* VIII, lines 334, 336–339, 346–352, 356–358, 363–364, 367–369.] But now they call for battle. You who weigh the world with silent reason, Creator, furnish other strength.

[130] A dark day brings near the fatal hour, which the peoples themselves demand; Death, sent forth from the Stygian darkness, enjoys the sky, flies over the battlefield, covers it, and invites the warriors with its black opening, stirring weapons, destroying homes, marriages, and children.

The love of fatherland and of life, which departs last from the mind, is driven away; the spirit, panting beyond the breastplates, strains forward,

[135] and the helmets tremble with the terror of their crests. Is it surprising that the men grew hot? The hoofed horses blaze against the enemy and drench the rich ground with a snow-white cloud.

[Col. 1296C] Now they rush forward, and the first dust of men beginning to clash rises; driven from both sides at equal intervals, they approach and see the middle of the field grow smaller.

[140] The appearance of the battle is still beautiful: cones stand upon their heads, the squadrons are full of men, and no rider is without his protector. But after fury and a courage prodigal of life released their spirits, they alternately strike down and fall beneath countless blows.

The north wind does not beat the airy Rhodope with such solid snow when the she-goats fall.

Meanwhile Walfredus approaches Wido, exulting in slaughter—not the king, but the man who had recently been drawn from the fields of the Sequani.

[150] [Col. 1296D] He catches him from a distance with a spear hurled by the man’s exceedingly powerful arm, at the extreme edge of the helmet and the foremost rim of the shield, where a path of light shines; with his breath stopped by the closed passage, he immediately died.

[Col. 1297A] As he died, the unfortunate man remembered his native land and beloved home, and that he had come to acquire losses in the Italian fields.

Then the battle follows its slain leader. The Atesine hero [Note: [Col. 1297D] Either Walfredus, or, as Valesius thinks, Berengarius.] rages, striking down Anscherius and Otho [Note: [Col. 1297D] That is, Ottonem.]; he cuts down the one standing close at hand, and the other, whose hamstring has been severed, with a thrusting point.

[160] He would have sent countless companions to the shades, had not the Rhodanian leader [Note: [Col. 1297D] Wido.] been warned and suddenly come to the aid of his exhausted friends as an avenger.

[Col. 1297B] As a wolf in the open fields sees flocks, when the shepherd himself is not present and the savage crowd of dogs does not frighten him, he rushes forward and rages throughout the whole field, so Wido, terrible, rises into the plain.

When he saw Erardus, indignant that he was throwing his companions into confusion upon his lofty horse, with one sword he pierced two bodies, horse and rider. The horse fell upon its falling master; while his hand sought the reins that had slipped away, it trampled helmet upon his face and shield upon his body. Wounded, at last, together with its final blood, it rejected the bit and fell with its neck joined to its master.

[Col. 1297C] His sword struck the face of Otgarius [Note: [Col. 1297D] Langermann read *Osharii* in the manuscript.], who was calling his companions with a savage cry; the efforts of his voice perished, intercepted by blood.

While Milo was taking the weapons from the fallen man, he was caught by an Italian spear; unhappy, he died and left behind both his own shield and that of the enemy.

At last the Ausonian youth, gathered for aid, came up.

[180] A great battle arose. Much blood was poured out here and there, and bodies were strewn throughout the fields. For courage is a changing thing [Note: [Col. 1297D] Verses 180–186, with a few changes, are from Statius, *Thebaid* VIII, lines 382–388.]: now the crowd withdraws, now presses forward, alternately losing and recovering the ground.

[Col. 1297D] As when the air [Note: [Col. 1298D] Leibniz also added *Juppiter*, from Statius.], threatening with winds and rainstorms, releases its reins and beats the world with alternating whirlwinds, the opposing battle line of the sky stands: now the southern wind is stronger, now the northern winter, until, as the storm fights, one side conquers with excessive waters or the other with calm.

[190] Here Anscherius sees his brother Albricus collapse from a wound, groans, and, twisting a missile with swift effort, says in a deep cry:

[Col. 1298A] “May the father of heaven distinguish your entire race in your own fields, as you grimly distinguish brothers in the Italian land!”

Having spoken these words, the spear flies with an immense whistling through the air toward the enemy; but, struck by the hard shield, it goes into the proud swift horse, bringing death.

[195] Albricus would have received death there, had not the nearby valor of the young men lifted him up and restored him to the ranks.

Moving amid thousands, Ubertus says: “Why do you expose hearts inert in war beneath hard arms, Italians? You prefer sacred cups, and more often to loosen your stomachs with splendid feasts, and to stuff your lofty houses with gleaming metal!

[205] [Col. 1298B] The Gauls are not troubled by the same concern: their aim is to conquer neighboring lands and support their humbled hearth with spoils collected from every side!”

While he was raising these ineffectual words, a spear, balanced by Wifredus’s hand, entered the hiding place of his proud spirit and searched it beneath the grim speaker.

“Unfortunate Gaul, it is not permitted for you, if I am not mistaken, to call the Ausonians sluggish; my spear, driven into your fingers, will remind you of that!”

While he looked upon the enemy with a savage gaze, he slipped and, dying, tore the grass with his teeth.

[215] In another part these reversals brought down both men.

But the ruler of Hesperia pressed more fiercely upon the wretched Etruscans and sought fearful Wido through the ranks, choosing nothing ordinary but the deaths most worthy of life, and with his bloodstained sword cutting down those foremost in years and spirit:

[Col. 1298C] just as a lion, having perhaps gained possession of countless slaughter,

[220] passes over unarmed calves and tender heifers; it is madness for him to be plunged in any blood except that of the ruling bull, and to recline only upon its neck.

But Wifredus’s unreliable warhorse, breaking its reins and dragging him free through the opposing ranks, carried him off, as his hand was already weary.

[225] The spear entered the shoulders of the prince and pierced the young man’s left groin, pinning him to the horse as he fell. The horse fled, carrying its slain master, now holding neither weapons nor reins.

Arduinus was already supporting his brother’s limbs upon the horse, sustaining his drooping neck with his left hand and his side with his right. Pain emptied the tight breastplate with sobs, and the helmet, overflowing with tears, could not restrain them;

[Col. 1299A] when a very heavy lance broke through his curved ribs with a groan,

[235] emerged, and joined kindred breasts to his brother with the weapon. The latter still fixed his eyes, swimming in the light, and, seeing his brother’s death, released them.

The two, equal in fate—pitiable wish of death—fell forward and closed their eyes with alternating right hands.

[Note: [Col. 1299D] Verses 238–241, ‘the battle lines rush,’ are from Virgil, *Aeneid* XII, lines 365–369.] And as when the breath of the north wind roars upon the deep Aegean and the wave follows toward the shores where the winds have fallen upon them, while the clouds give way to the sky,

[245] so before the king, wherever he cuts a path, the ranks give way; the battle lines turn and rush, and the youth before him falls.

When Ildeprandus saw the companions turning their backs before the pursuing king, he departed, shouting:

“Stand fast, comrades! Why do you flee? See whether I may perhaps drive this man away with steel!

[Col. 1299B] Nature the creator gave him limbs like ours, and similar blood sustains his entrails.

[250] “Has he been hardened in the sacred Styx? Does a hide impenetrable even to the soles of feet now cover him? We are pressed by a mortal enemy [Note: [Col. 1299D] Compare Virgil, *Aeneid* X, 375.], not by a legion that serves the Lord for a pious purpose.”

Thus he spoke, and, straining with his whole body, hurled his weapon and struck the thigh of the Latin leader with a mighty blow from afar.

[255] This was enough; and he was preparing to lift his step and depart quickly, compelled by fear of what he had done. But the leader, immediately twisting his javelin into the enemy’s face, pierced it and, rebuking him through four lawless lips [Note: [Col. 1299D] That is, four jaws—four lips already divided by the spear point, as Valesius explains.], said:

“No one will henceforth dare entrust secrets to you, Tyrrhenian, since you will flow abundantly here and there through this opening. Let these wounds be a memorial that you foolishly wished to mock my weapons!”

[260] He indeed escaped, surrounded by the arms of his companions. But the victor, kindled throughout his spirit by anger, sacrificed the innumerable multitude to the sword like a deadly plague [Note: [Col. 1299D] Verses 264–265 are from Statius, *Thebaid* VII, lines 709–710.] or the fierce ray of an opposing star:

“Go,” he shouted, “and tell your leader whether my spear is rightly dividing the Latin fields for you!”

The Tyrrhenian nobles, gathered again here and there out of shame,

[270] [Col. 1300B] resolved to advance and strengthened one another everywhere with arms. A most wretched slaughter arose on both sides, and iron rang against iron; blades intermingled and hissed against one another.

A dense line pressed on from both sides, and the fields, again sprinkled with fresh blood, grew wet, while Phoebus rushed into the western waters.

[275] What further limit, or what separation of the battle, would there have been, unless the creator of the world had granted an end from his heavenly court?

With night approaching, at last they withdrew sorrowfully from the field and were separated from their savage arms by the thick darkness [Note: [Col. 1299D] Compare Liudprand, *Antapodosis* I, 19.].

THE SECOND BOOK ENDS.

THE THIRD BOOK BEGINS.

[Col. 1299]

[Col. 1299C] Such battles had boiled throughout the Ausonian fields that the report of them was sung not only by neighboring peoples but also by those far away, while Arnulf’s Germanic power [Note: [Col. 1299D] In the year 891.], joined to Brengarius through royal lineages, pressed upon the countryside [Note: [Col. 1300D] Thus the manuscript; the edition reads *rura*, ‘fields.’], advancing toward empire with plumage more bristling than usual and embracing both the people and the savage tyrant [Note: [Col. 1300D] Wido.] with its gaping throat. It was brooding over its cares in its breast, and soon, calling its son, said:

“Go, Sinbaldus [Note: [Col. 1300D] Liudprand calls him Zwentebaldus; he gives Centebaldus. Compare *Antapodosis* I, 20–21.], and swiftly seek the Italian fields with your hard companies,

[10] where King Brengarius pursues the audacious Gauls in war. Yet tell them that they come through wounds—or, wonderfully, that they grow suddenly from the birth of a mountain—so many are they. Is it possible for you to endure so much pain, that our offspring should be harassed in its own court?

[15] “Nor do I fear that wars will be denied you, if you go joined to your friend. But if they should perhaps say that they prefer to preserve their lives behind proud walls and do not wish to serve under your arms, very well: from now on I shall change the roles and shatter the walls of Ausonia, until I reach the shining court

[20] of the Key-Bearer [Note: [Col. 1300D] The supreme pontiff, Wido, had received the imperial blessing on February 21, 891.], and empty the whole fury of the Saône.”

Sinbaldus obeyed his father joyfully, inflamed by a similar love. Soon, accompanied by the minister he had chosen, he entered Latium and sent some men ahead to report to their friend that they were advancing peacefully.

[25] Father Berengarius, with similar ardor, soon advanced to meet him, where the land raises lofty heights [Note: [Col. 1300D] The Alps.]

[Editorial corrections to the preceding translation: at I.93–95, *provolvens juvenum fusos in sanguine patres* means “laying fathers of young men prostrate in blood.” At I.114–123, do not add “wickedly” to *raptum ire volentibus*; the difficult Alecto/Acheron line is retained as corrupt rather than supplied with an unsupported syntax. At I.133–142, *solidis protendere legimus aevum*, *quae tendimus ultro*, and *Atque una caris veniat fundendus in agris* remain difficult readings and are not to be resolved by supplying a subject or argument absent from the text. At I.218–220, the fugitives had not formerly made these promises in their ancestral homes while promising every sweet thing of Hesperia to their children. At I.242–248, Wido acts at dawn and the deputation seeks burial for those “deprived of light.” At II.10–12, the speaker asks divine aid to set down the dealings of war and its incited leaders; II.68–72 is corrupt and preserved cautiously; II.102–105 does not unambiguously say that priests were “enticed.” At II.148 read *Widonem* [Note: [Col. 1296D] “*Widonem* ed. c.?”]. At II.207–213 the spear penetrates the proud man’s inner recess, and *digitis impacta ... hasta meis* is a spear driven or handled by Wifredus’s fingers. At II.238–239, *alterna ... dextra* denotes the brothers’ mutually joined/exchanged right hands as they die. At III.11–14 retain the corrupt comparison cautiously; at III.20, *totōs Araris vacuabo furores* means “I shall empty the whole furies of the Saône.”]

He separates the kingdom and the Rhine by precipitous [Note: I.e., precipitous?] banks.

When here they joined right hands in honorable encounter,

[Col. 1300D] the king first said: “O bravest of young men,

[30] why do you wish to enter our territories? There is no need for hesitation [Note: I.e., inquiry.].

Tell me the truth plainly. There is only one thing I must ask:

[Col. 1301A] since you present yourself unharmed before our eyes,

if your excellent father enjoys the prosperity he desires.”

But he replied: “My father is well, a solace shared by all,

[35] and he wishes you well, with a treaty of peace

to endure between the fields of Latium. For this reason he compelled us

to hasten to the Ausonian lands with a gathered army.

Meanwhile the Gallic leader seeks secure positions, yet sees

that by his own strength he cannot withstand the two tyrants.

[40] They provoke the men shut up within the walls—pitiable sight! [Note: Within the walls of Ticinum.]

by roaming the Latin soil on every side.

But when they see that everything has fallen silent before their hostile attacks,

Sinbaldus, at the king’s instruction, goes to his native shores,

so that he alone might overcome the enemy’s fury.

[45] Scarcely had the moon’s third horns filled themselves with light [Note: Cf. Virgil, *Aeneid* III.645],

when, rejoicing, he had reached his native court;

[Col. 1301B] behold, Wido, leading his army, hastens

to renew the conflict; against him the pious commander prepares weapons

to drive away the plague and cut down such arrogance.

[50] It does not escape Arnulfus that war is again growing

in Hesperia. He hears that Wido, still relying on his troops,

will be present and lift his neck in insolent pride.

He leaps up from the ivory throne on which he happened to sit

and fills the palace with a mighty shout:

[55] “Quickly write strong commands on papyrus,

commands that will compel the peoples to stand before their lord—

as diverse in language as they are fierce in heart and arms.

For it pleases me to see my renowned friend in Latium,

whom the Rhône so often troubles with the army

[60] of the swift-flowing Leman. Where, then, will they flee?

Will they climb beneath the sky, or seek the hiding places

of the earth or of the liquid deep?

[Col. 1301C] I shall see to it that the wicked leader of Hesperia

hates the name he loves, even if he is placed at the ends of the earth!”

Inflamed by such words and by the fearsome mass of his forces,

[65] he marshals his hosts and releases the heavy reins of his anger:

just as the Eridanus, when the snows have been melted by the heat,

bursts forth in a torrent into the steep fields,

sweeps herds away together with their stalls across all the plains,

and, as the floodwater flows away, swallows up the alders

[70] rooted along the bank.

And now that dread leader occupies Ausonian soil [Note: Cf. Virgil, *Aeneid* V.42],

when news of the affair, freed from Wido’s proud resentment,

reaches the camp. Immediately summoning his companions,

he says: “O nobles, what need is there to bring forth words

[Col. 1301D] about the burden of war under which the imperial realm is bending?

[75] When the Hister is here, flowing in from every side,

for our destruction, I advise you: preserve yourselves in prosperity

and spare yourselves such wars until Arnulfus withdraws

to his own fields.”

Meanwhile, while each king traverses the rich soil,

[80] they come to the city of Pergami, which Ambrosius holds,

having fortified it against attack with an abundance

of arrows and sharpened stakes;

[Col. 1302A] nature itself had provided the place with ample suitability for strongholds.

Alas, he was devoted to the unjust plague!

When the unhappy man’s situation is reported to the kings,

[85] they order the walls to be surrounded by a dense siege,

so that he may receive no ally from outside or send anyone out,

until the scattered peoples, on the following day,

come together in such numbers and strive by force

to drive the captured man from his fortified position,

[90] so that no one may again dare such things.

Afterward, as soon as dawn had driven away the stars [Note: In the year 894],

the German youth hastens toward the city’s destruction,

the sound of trumpets beating mournfully from every side.

Some fill the ditches and approach the wall;

others stretch ladders upward to climb the towers.

[95] For the presence of both kings presses them exceedingly,

[Col. 1302B] while the citizens pour out every kind of missile

against them, which the walls retain as a precious gift,

and prepare to drive the enemies back with very hard spears.

Yet they cannot withstand them; driven on by so many thousands,

[100] they give way. One man falls here with a fragment of the wall;

another collapses, pierced by a javelin; a third,

without strength, stands helpless and bewildered.

With the gates opened everywhere, the city lies exposed,

already confused by the enemy’s tumult.

Behold, the halls once held in highest reverence and honor

[105] are now violated; the virgin’s veils perish,

torn into strips, and the sacred minister himself flees,

while bonds constrain the two palms of certain men—

hands that had been accustomed to receive kisses

[Col. 1302C] when sacred offerings were made.

Ambrosius, the author and kindling of the crime,

[110] when at last he sees the merciless enemies ruling

the strongholds, hastens up a lofty tower by a rapid ascent,

trusting that nothing remains for him amid such danger.

The buildings, once noble, were already [Note: A word has fallen out here; the manuscript reads: *Ingenuis quondam morto Marte*; Valesius: *ingeniis quorumdam* [Col. 1302D] *Marte resertis*; I have inserted *jam* as the mildest remedy.]

filled with battle.

Yet he is driven from there, surrounded by defeated arms,

and dragged before Arnulfus with his hands bound behind his back.

[115] Burning with anger, Arnulfus calls the creator of all things to witness that he is to be suddenly lowered from the branches of a tall tree.

Oh, hateful kind of death—to hang limbs owed to the earth

in the winds! A second portion of things is granted to mortals,

[120] while the fallen limbs are denied the soil.

[Col. 1302D] At this the minds of the young men are chilled;

they leave the cities and tear apart the bars of the loosened gates,

leaving the savage enemies within the walls [Note: Arnulfus’s return to Germany and the second expedition are omitted here.].

But since the robber had not secured shelter in those lands,

[125] he suddenly turns his march toward the Etruscan shores,

intent, by the command of the kings, on seeking the Roman courts;

lest perhaps the Gaul should be able to say that, since he had remained

in the highest court, he had not been concealed,

after Arnulfus had returned to the wave-filled Rhine.

[130] This crafty man had fled the Roman heights,

lest the polluted waters [Note: I.e., he says, “if indeed”; Valesius.] capture the charming tyrants.

Nevertheless, having summoned their standard-bearers,

they disclose the enemy’s crimes and order them to lead the standards

out of the camp [Note: In the year 896],

and with all their forces press upon the closed gates,

[135] so that, at least by forcing them open, they may approach the threshold

of the church of the heavenly Prince;

let no empty fabrications drive back such men

or delay their vows promised at the present place

and in the dedicated temples.

[140] At these commands and with such exhortation from the kings,

all seize the weapons of Mars, panting for war,

eager to cut through the gates entrusted to the sword.

[Col. 1303B] Now, because the Romans perceive that their dark fate has overtaken them,

they open the city from every side by unsewing its inner fastenings

and admit the gentle commanders to the venerable shrines.

[145] When here the altars shone with vows completed,

the barbarian leader burns to unleash his unappeased fury.

Anger so exhausts his unbridled spirit.

He does not know what to do, where to turn, or which walls to look upon,

helpless and deprived of reason. For the chief hope

[150] of the pestilential Gauls still remained in the city.

But when the Latin commander sees the tyrant ally

advancing without restraint, he begins in a calm spirit:

“Cease, venerable king; enough has been achieved by valor,

and it is not fitting to lead the Rhine-men farther.

[155] For if Wido likewise places his hope in arms against the defeated,

let him come swollen with pride; allow me, I ask,

to subdue him with this right hand,

[Col. 1303C] while you rule over men joined by the ancient treaty.”

Softened by these words, he permits the barbarian nobles,

chosen from different regions, to return,

[160] the feared prince and arbiter of the German court.

The venerable king had scarcely reached his own borders

when Wido, amid the law-breaking trumpets [Note: Wido had already died before Arnulfus’s first return to Germany, in 894.],

takes up his renewed forces,

again desiring to invade the forbidden fields.

The father of the kingdom himself, even more savage toward his enemies,

[165] prepares weapons, eager to finish such great labors [Note: *Avidos* corrected to *avidus*].

Meanwhile the chosen lot of God [Note: I.e., the clergy.], clothed in sackcloth,

makes vows; their faces bathed in tears around the altars,

they uttered these words from the depths of their hearts:

“O creator of all things, power to be feared by all,

[170] [Col. 1303D] who rules wars and peace by everlasting authority,

grant that such deceits may cease; grant that the author of the crime

may perish by a swift death; grant long years to our leader,

who bears a double crown of glory—

for the merit of his valor and for the nobility of his lineage.”

[175] The father heard these prayers, he who bends the whole of Olympus.

He compels the day of death to approach the one stirring up savage wars,

yet in such a way that he may close his eyes on his own bed.

The final light is at hand, and now no hope of another day remains,

[Col. 1304A] when he calls his son, grieving for so great a death,

[180] and brings forth these memorable counsels in broken speech:

“My son, you see what harsh losses press upon life,

which that Father of mankind inflicted for the crime of the forbidden fruit

and with the broken covenant stained the human race.

You will no longer be able to protect yourself with your father’s arms,

[185] for nature is taking away the day and bringing back sleep.

Yet hear the words of a father placed at the end of life,

and, insofar as you possess reason and strength,

take the brave Brengarius as your ally.

For Hesperia will follow him under a better destiny,

[190] and he will also rule over our fields.”

He said no more; death interrupted him in the middle of his speech,

[Col. 1304B] and, dying, he left both life and speech.

The peoples rejoice that the minister of death has fallen,

and release their minds from cares and their arms from war—

[195] as when, under an evil sun, the rose gardens grow pale

and are scorched by the south wind; but if bright day

and the breeze of the west restore the sky,

all their beauty returns, the shoots shine forth,

and their glory adorns the shapeless branches [Note: Verses 194–197 are from Statius, *Thebaid* VII.223–226.].

A great part of the men also hasten, once Wido has been buried,

[200] to the court of the Latin commander, asking pardon,

while Wido’s son, accompanied by a feeble minister [Note: Namely, Ageltruda, Lambert’s mother and his guardian; Valesius.],

is overcome by a double grief—

by the death of his father and by the departure of his familiar arms.

[Col. 1304C] But remembering his father’s instructions, he orders his companion

to go and seek peace and humbly worship the king:

[205] he should not wish to remember his father as a man waging war,

but should choose as his ally in the kingdom one bound by a social treaty,

and, whenever Mars summons his servant to war,

he should also serve in battle.

Meanwhile the commander, venerable with age,

[210] readily offers the aid of piety to the approaching troops;

he does not reject the Gauls, nor does he charge the Etruscans with crimes,

but displays to all the merciful heart customary to him.

When at last the Lambertian messenger stands before him

and explains the man’s circumstances and desire for peace,

the gentle father answers from his heart:

[215] “The sacred laws refuse to return evils with excessive evil.

For we have drawn down from the heavenly citadel the mind [Note: *Sensum*—verse 220 is from Juvenal, *Satires* XV.146–150.],

which those creatures lack who are bent forward and look toward the earth.

At the beginning of the world the common creator granted them

only a soul, but granted us a mind as well,

[220] so that mutual affection might command us to seek help

and to offer it.

A child does not bear guilt for the crime of his parent,

as the prophet once sang with truthful voice [Ezekiel 18:20].

[Col. 1305A] Therefore let him come, to be called our friend on this condition:

let him not insolently violate the laws of loyalty,

adding deceit to the light-minded heart of his father.

But if he holds fast to the gift he has recovered in youthful spirit,

[225] let him quickly gather his arms and, resembling his father,

eagerly devote himself to action and prove himself in war.”

After the young fosterling had heard these words joyfully,

he fell down and, suppliant, revered the king’s love—

the love by which earth, sea, and stars preserve their order,

[230] lest the sea overturn the fields with its fluid reins

or the burning stars of heaven be drowned in the waters.

Returning from there, he conveyed to the youth the king’s message,

reporting everything in order.

At last the excellent king and Lambertus hasten

[235] to where the fertile river of Ticinum

washes the distinguished city named after the river,

in which the Latins were accustomed to behold their king.

They exchange words, after each promises

that the treaty will endure as long as, borne on rosy chariots [Note: Cf. Virgil, *Aeneid* VI.535.],

[240] the track of Phoebus is bathed by the waves of Ocean,

or the unmoving earth remains and does not yield beneath its weight,

looking everywhere upon the beautiful revolving heavens—

if a man’s life could last through so many years.

[245] O youthful glory, if only his mind had not been perverse!

[Col. 1305C] Often he turns over in his mind how to break the right hands

that had been given in peace, by devising treacheries.

But you, kindly father [Note: Berengarius.], detect the plots

with shrewd judgment and despise the murmurs.

Yet the third summer had brought him forth into Latium [Note: In the year 898],

[250] possessing the earth’s abundance in a withdrawn peace.

Behold, the day approaches, rivaling the deeds of his youth,

bringing bitter death. Already he goes eagerly

into the deep woods to hunt, desiring that a boar

or a shapeless bear should be sent rushing toward him.

[255] But when his impetuous companions wearied the remote places

with their excessive shouting, he, with only one attendant,

while he was digging his spurs into the shoulders of his stubborn horse,

entangled his neck beneath his own chest,

[260] breaking his tender life when his throat was crushed.

[Col. 1306A] The horn, sounding mournfully, summons his companions,

scattered far and wide, and announces their lord’s cruel death.

At this sound the whole grove trembles;

the birds flee, escaping on their wings,

and every animal abandons the lairs it had occupied.

At such a sound the chosen band of companions gathers from both sides,

[265] and calls out with mournful cries to the youth, mute with his throat broken.

The unfortunate man struggles

to bring forth broken words;

but, weakened, he collapses amid his efforts,

and thereafter his tongue can no longer move,

nor do words follow [Note: Cf. Virgil, *Aeneid* XII.912–913.].

[270] His companions are not slow [Note: Verses 270–277 are from Virgil, *Aeneid* XI.64–71.]

to weave a litter of wicker and soft branches

[Col. 1306B] from arbute rods and oak withes,

and shade the built-up couch beneath a covering of leaves.

Here they place the youth, raised upon rustic straw,

like a flower plucked by a maiden’s finger—

[275] whether the tender violet or the languishing hyacinth—

whose brilliance and beauty have not yet departed.

The nourishing earth no longer sustains him or supplies his strength.

With such devotion they carry him back to the temples,

to commit his youthful limbs to a worthy tomb.

[280] When the commander Brengarius hears the messenger’s report

that Wido’s son had been forced to fall

from the back of a swift-hoofed horse,

he draws these words from his breast:

[Col. 1306C] “Alas, the dreadful plague of death,

which is inserted into sweet years

and refuses to let the sorrowful suns complete their course!

[285] This man would have been worthier than his father, although the latter lived for many years and troubled Latium.”

From every side the whole company of the kingdom gathers together,

crying out as one: “Pious king, have pity on our labor!

[290] Do not force us henceforth to stand before two tyrants,

when you alone are pleasing as the survivor

of Latin affairs.

As Phoebus opens the fields with his rosy chariots

in the new spring, the animals rejoice and grow heavy with offspring;

moisture is present in the grasses and seeds in the broad furrows;

[295] the air is welcome to the wings and the sea passable to sailors.

Everything shines, for creative nature returns

and gives each thing its proper form at the appointed season.

So, too, the land of Italy rejoices under its ruler,

when the savage Guido has withdrawn from the heights

[Col. 1306D] with his offspring, unappeased,

and by dying has dissolved the arrogance of hatred.”

THE THIRD BOOK ENDS.

THE FOURTH BOOK BEGINS.

[Col. 1305]

[Col. 1305D] Thus scarcely had the fourth summer cooled in Latium [Note: From the year 896, when, according to our author, Lambertus was reconciled with Berengarius.]

[Note: In the year 900, October.], when the beast,

once again roused by its customary poison,

pouring savage hisses from the Tyrrhenian shores,

[Col. 1306D] troubles the people of the Rhône;

their ruler was the contemptible Ludovicus in character,

but worthy of respect by birth,

since he was joined to Berengarius through proud lineage.

[5] For a long time he had eagerly desired to rule over the Ausonian fields,

but fortune had forbidden it. Now, because he receives news favorable to his wishes,

he immediately summons his companions to the royal dwelling:

“What you have so often turned over in your minds, friends,

behold, the day itself has brought of its own accord,

[10] a day that must be turned over in your minds!

Be ready, and let us seek the very sweet fields!

For we are summoned to the neighboring countryside of Italy.

As soon as I have brought my proud forces there,

the commander will withdraw from his own shores.”

“O wretched man, wretched from day to day,

[15] would you challenge the unconquered one?

Has the fame of the commander, spread throughout the whole world,

passed you by? O Father of all things, restrain his furies!

For I do not know what evil his mind is foreboding

as he sets out.”

[Col. 1307B] Now Provence, having scarcely recovered its strength,

chooses its weakened sons for the Ausonian fields

under an enemy’s name.

Nor could the victor and glory of Latium, the kingdom’s only hope,

[20] then preserve the soil merely called Venetian,

since he was suffering from quartan fever,

nor could he extend the war against the enemy;

instead, he digested excessive anger in his heart:

just as, when a lion happens to be held in cages and chains,

[25] it cannot move its limbs or advance its strength,

but is merely oppressed under the harsh rule of its keeper;

yet if by chance it should be able to break the bonds

that had been forged for it,

and its mouth, long unused, should become wet with blood,

[30] it will first stain the torn keeper with its anger,

and then the opposing crowd of men will satisfy

its bitter bites.

Meanwhile Ludovicus rejoices and troubles the kingdom

with his boasts, flattering himself with such great honors,

as though, once the enemy had been killed [Note: I.e., *necato*; for the sake of the meter, as with *Brengarius*, *partus*, *postus*, etc.],

he would gain possession of rich spoils.

[35] Unhappily he also advances against the stronghold of Verona [Note: In the year 905.].

Yet, in the manner of a pious king, when he has settled

within its open walls, he assigns the ancient fields to his companions,

fearing nothing, since an excessively alarming report

had reached him that Berengarius had suffered

[40] the losses of death.

Ah, Latium, who would defend you with such great arms?

Therefore, pious Father of all things, preserve the master,

lest Latin joys perish in a single death!

But when the ruler recovered his strength,

chosen nobles gathered joyfully from every side,

[45] seized the standards from the camp,

and hastened toward the walls of the Adige,

opening their speech to the king in these courteous words:

“We seek you, honor of piety, and we do not think

that this request is insignificant.

[50] If you take the city by your own arms,

allow the limbs of those men who so often overthrow the treaties of the kingdom

to be cut short,

lest we suffer the damage of unjust mercy!”

To this the commander replied:

“Pay attention to my warning, O nobles,

[Col. 1308A] and do not attribute crimes to the captured man,

since he possesses the blood of a noble lineage

and perhaps, as his years mature,

will abandon his wrongdoing.

Let the sacred laws of heaven bear witness,

[55] and let him go once he has been released.”

That was enough. But they, with murmuring,

press forward in haste, sharpening the savage anger of their hearts.

Moved not at all by his words, they instead gnaw at fierce mutterings:

they say that they cannot afterward leave the evil unpunished.

[60] With such words they come to the city and approach the wall [Note: In the month of July.].

At once they enter the pitiable church,

where Ludovicus was, and suddenly seize and bind him,

and take away his beautiful eyes.

He had been sitting securely in the palace,

[65] and therefore lost the pious gift of light,

besieged by darkness even at the rising of the sun.

You too, Johannes, wearing a short sword upon your thigh,

hold the height of the tower, in case you are able to recover your life;

but from there you are dragged into the dangers of death,

and, miserable man, are beheaded naked

[70] in the arena of your homeland.

But when news of their companion reaches the ears

of the men deprived of common light,

they flee, helpless for counsel, and withdraw in every direction:

just as, when the west wind blows in the new spring,

the bronze-colored clouds melt into the air

[75] and the fields release the moisture compressed

by winter’s cold and the frequent frosts of the north wind.

Nor does the brave Adalbertus cease to remove

the proud men from their position [Note: Marquis of Eporegia, Berengarius’s son-in-law. Liudprand, *Antapodosis* II.33.],

[Col. 1308C] the Apennine troops, covered with youthful years,

whom he draws out under his auspicious name [Note: The name is composed from the words *Adal* and *bert*, indicating power and splendor.],

eager to serve an excellent master.

[80] Suddenly a blessed light shone amid the darkness,

and welcome peace returned to the pious,

once the mournful army had been removed far away

and the native commander and father had been recovered.

Although he had spread triumphs throughout the whole world,

[85] he had not yet enclosed his face with the diadem of empire,

nor had he stood, radiant in the Roman court,

in the robes customary to emperors of his ancestors’ line.

Why? Unless because, having conquered deceit by valor,

he ought to advance to the highest rank only after being repeatedly summoned?

[90] At that time John was the supreme pastor in the City,

[Col. 1308D] very renowned in office and filled with wisdom,

and for a long time had rightly been preserved for such a purpose.

Since the neighboring Charybdis was preventing this man

from possessing the wealth which purple, bestowed freely by his ancestors,

had given to the blessed one who opens the shining thresholds

[95] of chaste Peter,

he sends gifts to the leader, conveyed by sacred ministers,

so that, mindful of the final day,

he may grant his rights to the Romans,

under whose authority he cherishes the Ausonian lands,

[100] and may receive in return the imperial crown,

being alone called Caesar in the western world.

Overcome by such prayers, he orders the troops of the kingdom—

those with whom he waged war and those with whom he shared

the sacred gifts of peace—to be present

and accompany the approach of such an honor.

After he had traveled the road and reached the boundary

[105] of Rome [Note: In the year 916, in the month of March.],

he orders his companions to hasten to the temples

and announce that he is approaching.

Behold, the Sabura resounds with the raised voices of the people:

“Hasten in welcome! The king is coming,

long awaited from the Ausonian shores,

[110] who will lessen our customary labors

with his customary mercy!”

Then you might see Rome seething

and people proceeding through the gates—

as many nations as Rome surrounds

within her ancestral embrace.

[Col. 1309B] Meanwhile, the prince passes the hill [Note: Mount Malum; cf. *Leges* II, pp. 68, 193, 218, 533.]

that rises above the City,

where the road enters a pleasant meadow [Note: Nero’s meadow.].

The troops set each part of the sky ablaze

with marvelous displays. First the senate sings

[115] in its ancestral voice,

placing on stakes the open jaws of fleshless beasts [Note: A gloss in Valesius: “dragon heads carved in wood.”],

as a sign that henceforth defeated attempts would fall,

if enemies should wish to stir up anything with savage spirit.

A Greek follows, praising him in Daedalian speech;

[120] this Stoic of ours is renowned in learned Athens [Note: Gloss: *cluo* is Greek and means the same as “I listen.” But the word is polysemous: *cluis* can mean noble, warlike, attentive, and defender.],

and is skilled in the course through the Samian arena.

The remaining crowd follows the pious tyrant

in its native voice and proclaims its master

throughout the whole land.

Here, too, young men clothed in bright white—

[Col. 1309C] one the brother of the apostolic Peter [Note: Peter; cf. Liudprand, *Antapodosis* III.43; Benedict’s *Chronicle*, chapter 29.], the other

the son of the consul [Note: The one called Theophylactus in the gloss.]—

fasten kisses upon the king’s feet.

From there, where the prelate was, they accompany

the lord’s procession to the entrance of the vestibule,

[125] through which the accessible staircase [Note: St. Peter’s.] leads the eager

to enter the adorned court.

He was seated there, shining in his sacred vestment,

and, rejoicing, the minister approached the altar on either side.

What should I say of the peoples gathered here and there,

[130] and of the overflowing steps, when the king entered the temples,

borne upon the pastor’s horse [Note: Gloss: “It is the Roman custom that the man who is to be advanced to imperial dignity is carried into Rome on the prelate’s horse.”]?

Soon the priest himself was to become such a one;

the event was worthy of an everlasting title.

When at last he arrived, accompanied by a chosen attendant,

[Col. 1310A] and slowly attempted to ascend on foot from the lowest steps,

the crowd pressed in on every side,

and the attendant could scarcely hold it back,

threatening by voice and gesture.

Everyone burned to see the present king,

whom the ages desired.

[140] Three times the pious man also set his sacred feet upon the steps,

compelling the surging crowd to halt its tumult

by the majesty of his hands.

After he had climbed the entire ascent,

the prelate rose from his golden chair [Note: Gloss: *Cliophedrum* is Greek for a woven chair, commonly called a *valdestolum*.],

joyfully planted kisses upon him,

and received his friendly right hand.

[145] From there they approach the court dedicated equally to you, Peter,

you who open the thresholds of the heavenly temple.

Both stand before the doors of the house,

while the king offers his vows;

for he vows of his own accord to give everything in that place

[150] that had previously been granted to the sacred tyrants,

the nourishing ones.

At once, after these words, the doors roll upon their hinges,

and the sacred minister raises praises throughout the temples.

As though he were seeing Pope Silvester hastening forward,

and Constantine, cleansed by symbolic baptism.

[155] No less are the glory of the world and power over affairs present here—were it not that the times had grown worse, and that already the sacred purple of the king lies prostrate

upon the tomb of the fisherman [Note: Blessed Peter.],

while Christ is implored with rising tears.

After this the commander enters the temples,

where the dishes arranged as gifts by the pastor shine.

They serve Setina [Note: The Germans still call enormous wooden vessels of this sort *Setten* or *Satten*; such vessels are used for storing milk and also water. Leibniz.],

[160] and the ministers offer various rich dishes,

as is fitting for a king [Note: The gloss interprets the word as “royal banquets.” Valesius notes that Persius uses *tuceta* for fatty meat, while in Isidore’s glosses *tucetum* is seasoned beef among the Alpine Gauls; thus the meaning passed from a common dish to a royal one. LBN.].

[Col. 1310C] Soon the lamp of Phoebus, in its saffron chariots,

shines through the world,

the light by which God, made man, came forth

from the tomb-like cave.

The people rush together from the City

to see Augustus dressed in the military cloak

and the imperial crown [Note: March 24.].

[165] Repeated spectacles burn throughout the entire palace;

the altars shine with gilded hangings,

while the radiant prince advances in Tyrian purple,

his coverings of the legs clothed in gleaming metal [Note: The gloss explains: “greaves sprinkled with gold.”],

such as the rulers of the earth are accustomed to wear.

The pastor of the Lord also arrives,

[170] assigned to the sheepfold,

joyful in his office, although on every side the cry resounds:

“Come, prelate! Why do you so often delay

the joys desired in countless ways?

By the bonds of the master we ask you:

put aside your delays and satisfy our prayers!”

[175] [Col. 1311A] With such ceremonies they approach the altar

and the consecrated apse,

the lights of the world.

A little later, behold, Caesar has the diadem

raised upon his head with gems and gold,

and at the same time he is sprinkled with the oil

of nectar-like olive;

[180] such was the ancient custom among the Hebrews,

who, according to sacred law,

were accustomed to anoint kings and prophets,

because Christ was to come as ruler and priest,

for whose sake all things in heaven and on earth

would be restored.

Now the sacred halls resound and echo

[185] with the uproar of the shouting people:

“May your golden Rome prosper for a long time, O prince,

and may you raise up the empire, pressed down beneath its heavy burden,

and by your superior valor overthrow the rebels!”

The noise was excessive; but at last silence was made.

[Col. 1311B] A reader standing on the high steps reads aloud

the estates granted by the emperor’s gift

for the service of the prelate,

so that all may know what gifts have been given by Caesar,

and so that the robber may henceforth fear

[190] to seize the sacred lands for himself.

[Col. 1312A] At last the pious man brought splendid gifts to the temple:

broad belts of commanders, precious ornaments of ancestors,

exceedingly costly with gems and gleaming metal,

as well as garments stiff with figures and gold,

[195] and a diadem decorated with varied designs.

What should I say of the quantity of gifts with which he filled the walls?

Do I not seem to touch only a few drops of the sea,

and to enclose in my hand the sands taken from the Syrtes,

when in a brief speech I contain such great triumphs?

I believe this labor would burden eloquent Homer,

[200] and Mantua produced one worthy of such a task.

Nor shall I try to impose further weariness

with my words, O young men,

in whose breasts blood burns

and whom Clio moves with a better plectrum.

[Col. 1312B] It is enough for me to have touched upon a thousand labors in verse.

Though I may seem a Maevius, you be Marons,

and, after taking up again the imperial diadem,

resume the praises!

IN THE YEAR OF OUR LORD 968, SAINT MATHILDA, QUEEN

[Col. 1311]

THE OLDER LIFE OF SAINT MATHILDA

(Edited by D. Rud. Koepke, Ph.D., in Pertz, *Monumenta Germaniae Historica*, Scriptores, vol. X, p. 573.)

EDITOR’S PREFACE

What those who devote themselves to illuminating the ancient history of their homeland ardently desire, but which very rarely happens even to those who desire it—that, while searching libraries and turning over manuscripts, they should open up a new source and come upon some book buried in oblivion that either casts new light upon obscure matters or confirms and establishes known facts—has happened unexpectedly to me in the case of a little tenth-century book, from which scarcely anyone would have expected anything new to be brought forth.

For, while I was examining the manuscript of the Polidensis chronicle, which, at Pertz’s request, had been sent from Göttingen to this place for use in the sources of the *Monumenta Germaniae*, I found, as it were, a godsend (ἕρμαιον) by the wayside: an older Life of Saint Mathilda, now being published for the first time.

This Life is the foundation of the longer *Life of Mathilda* which readers possess in the *Monumenta Germaniae*, composed in the time of Henry II [Note: IV, 282 ff. (in *Patrologia*, vol. CXXXV.)]. But it is certainly remarkable that neither the author of that later Life indicated his source even in a single word, nor, so far as I know, has any memory of the older Life been preserved in other manuscripts, in the extensive chronicles compiled from six hundred books, or in catalogues of books, so that even the slightest traces of the little work seem to have perished.

All the greater thanks must be given to favorable fortune, which rescued this copy from so great a shipwreck.

No one who has even glanced at this Life can doubt its reliability. For every scruple will be removed from the mind by the preface written to the Emperor Otto, at whose command the author undertook the work and whom he made judge of what he had written [Note: *Prologue*: “But at the command of the most glorious Emperor Otto we have written it out completely … We make you, Emperor Otto, judge of this work.”].

Without doubt that Otto was Otto III [Note: The words written in the prologue to Otto—“Leader of all eloquence, whom not only the sublimity of a great empire exalts, but whom the authority of philosophy also favors, once the judgment of a certain speaker had been fulfilled, namely, that government would be blessed if rulers happened to be students of wisdom”—could be written to one pupil of the most distinguished philosopher Gerbert. The words of chapter 4 also support this: “O Germany … love the king by serving him happily, and do not cease to strive to help him as much as you can; and do not cease to hope for a prince from that line, lest, stripped of every degree of honor, you return to your former condition of servitude.” These words show that the author feared that another house might be raised to the summit of imperial power. That fear could have arisen from the serious disturbances over the succession to the empire after the death of Otto II, together with the further anxiety that the young Otto III was without children. Finally, whenever the author mentions Otto II in his narrative, he gives no indication whatever that this was the same Otto to whom he sent the book.].

Accordingly, the Life was written after Otto became emperor—that is, between the years 996 and 1002—approximately ten years before the later Life, which we know was composed before the year 1012.

Who the author was, or where he lived, you will search for in vain; yet the little book makes it clearer that he should not be counted among the learned. For, as he himself admits [Note: *Prologue*.], he wrote so crudely, in such an unpolished and barbarous style, that the construction of his sentences is only rarely carried through to a proper conclusion.

Since the whole little book is therefore obscure, the later author took it upon himself to make it somewhat smoother and more polished, as everyone agrees was done by others in the case of other Lives. Only the first lines of the older Life have been preserved, although several words from it recur elsewhere [Note: Compare the later Life, chapters 1, 2, 3, 4, 15, and 18, with the older Life, chapters 1, 2, 3, 4, and 9, 12.].

One matter, however, of no small importance has been cut away: the final chapter, in which the last fate of Otto I is related. These events are certainly not taken from Widukind, although they agree very well with him.

The author’s judgment in this chapter is remarkable. Writing approximately twenty-five years after the death of Otto I, he passes such severe judgment upon him that he says Otto obtained the imperial crown not legitimately but through the disorderly action of the army.

The sources to which he owed this and other material he passed over in silence. Nor did he narrate everything that was available to him, because he believed that it was enough to record only the outstanding matters [Note: *Prologue*.].

For the rest, he confirms only that he has written what he himself approved.

What the older author indicated in two or three words, the later author expanded at length, adorning the narrative with reflections and introducing people as speakers. Finally, he added everything concerning Duke Henry, the son of Henry I and grandfather of Henry II, including what he wrote about the great love of his mother for him and about his conflict with his brother Otto I.

In the older Life, Henry is mentioned only once, and then briefly [Note: Chapter 6.].

I would certainly not say that all these things were invented by the later author; they were added because they had been taken from another source, so that Henry II, the most religious king, might shine with a brighter glory because of such a holy grandmother.

Now, a few words must be said about the manuscript from which this has been taken. It is the Göttingen manuscript 5a, a paper apograph in quarto, from the fourteenth century, which contains a chronicle for the use of the Polide monastery, from [the uncertain reading “o. c.”] to 1182. [Note: [Col. 1314B] Archiv VI, 200.] This is a copy of a certain Cambridge manuscript, which today, by some unfortunate fate, is missing, so that the entire authority rests upon this one Göttingen copy.

Langbain examined the manuscript; this learned Englishman died in 1657. The scribe preserved his judgment on the first leaves of the copy in the following manner:

“Langbain, in his *Adversaria*, no. 1.12, p. 469, lists the Cambridge manuscript G. 85, which is an old parchment folio manuscript, in these words. The title of this manuscript, written on the verso in a recent hand, reads as follows: ‘An ancient chronology composed 300 years ago’; I would rather say composed 400 years ago and written 300 years ago, or even ‘Polide Chronicle’; for there are many indications that it was formerly a book of the monastery or church of Polide, which is in the Brunswick region: [lacuna]

“This entire manuscript consists of 110 folios, written in a sound and quite old hand; its orthography sometimes differs from common usage. In the chronicle itself, eclipses of the luminaries are usually marked by an illuminated asterisk. This manuscript is said to have been written around A.D. 1300 and to have belonged to the books of the Polide church. I infer both points from the chronological table on folio 25. It contains here and there strips of parchment inserted into the rest of the work, written in the same hand or in one not much less ancient.

“The chronological table mentioned is a catalogue of popes and emperors, in which some very brief notes are also entered concerning our Polide church for the years 1223, 1240, 1298, and 1390. The final entries are written under the year 1421. Although these entries do not all seem to have been written in the same hand, their orthography confirms that the manuscript was written in the fourteenth century.

“When Queen Mathildis is first mentioned in this chronicle, on folio 64 verso, the following words are read: ‘Turn the leaf and you will find her Life written out.’ What follows is the Life which we are now going to publish, on folios 65–69. Although the copy seems to have been prepared quite well, it nevertheless contains not a few errors, whether already present in the manuscript itself or arising from words that were not read accurately; consequently, conjecture had to be used in correcting these passages. We have supplied the chapter divisions, but the individual sections preserved in the copy often agree with the chapters of the later Life, so that one may readily believe that the ancient chapters have been preserved in them.

“This is what we have had to say about the older Life of Mathildis. The remaining material concerning the Polide Chronicle will be presented in its proper place.”

Written at Berlin in December 1849

**R. KÖPKE**

# HERE BEGINS THE PROLOGUE TO THE LIFE OF QUEEN MATHILDIS

[Col. 1313]

[Col. 1313A] While most mortals, vainly devoted to secular ambition, seek from it either everlasting remembrance of their name or the reward of human favor, and, by spreading the lives of famous men among the people, embellish them for philosophical ears in a fabulous style, we, at the command of the most glorious Emperor Otto, have written down—not philosophizing but speaking the truth—the praiseworthy life of his most worthy parents, a life soon to become an example to him and to later generations, although in an unpolished manner.

And although we acknowledge that we are wholly unfamiliar with this undertaking, and that in writing we are bringing forth something of doubtful quality, nevertheless, obeying imperial dignity, and driving great waves into a dry channel [Note: [Col. 1313] The manuscript falsely has *inpellenti*, “driving.”], we have rashly occupied material properly reserved for eloquent writers, not through bold confidence in our strength but through willing devotion. For we considered it a crime that the virtues of such great persons should remain hidden through the rashness of silence.

Therefore, O leader of all eloquence—whom not only the majesty of a great empire exalts [Col. 1314A], but whom the authority of philosophy also favors, in fulfillment of the judgment of one who said that government would be blessed if it happened that rulers were devoted to wisdom, so that honor comes not to virtues from rank but to ranks from virtue—we make you, Emperor Otto, the judge of this work. Whatever may have been omitted or badly expressed by us, commend it to the diligence of the wise to add or amend; and since it is impossible for us to bring so vast a sequence of material to its final completion, may the work shine more brightly through you, as though by the radiance of the sun. [Note: [Col. 1313] The manuscript inserts *in*.]

We have omitted much of what has come to our knowledge because we believed it sufficient for only the outstanding matters to be recorded; at the same time, we did so lest we burden readers with superfluous material. [Col. 1314B] We ask those who will read this to grant credence to what is said and not suppose that I have written anything except what has been established.

# HERE BEGINS THE TEXT OF THE SAME LIFE

[Col. 1315]

[Col. 1315A] **1.** Once, in the time of Conrad, king of the Franks, there was in all Germany a leading duke named Otto, most noble according to the dignity of the world, powerful in wealth, and surpassing everyone in honor because he was endowed with virtues. His wife was the venerable matron Haduwich, not unlike him in character.

They had daughters and three sons, whom their parents raised in accordance with their own nobility. But divine providence, directing all that it ordains toward the good, raised one of them, named Heinricus, to greater distinction. Although the youngest in age, he nevertheless shone forth first among the others in uprightness of character.

For from the earliest flowering of his youth, once he had been given a freer power to direct his life, he wisely ordered his conduct in every way by which character can be made sound. He was obedient and loving toward all with whom he associated, hostile toward no one, placing himself above nobody; by comforting the sorrowful and helping the miserable, he found praise without envy and friends who were his equals.

Although he was honored with the respect due to him, he was especially dear to everyone and honored more diligently because of the compelling grace of his gentleness and humility.

When his childhood had passed and he entered into manly strength, and his parents were considering which woman he should approach in marriage, one equal to him in birth and virtue, word reached their ears that there was in the monastery of Herford a very beautiful girl named Machtildis. She was being educated in the study of literary discipline, from which the active and contemplative life is sought, and her nobility proved no less illustrious than that of her future bridegroom.

For she descended from the stock of Widukind, duke of Saxony, who had once been seized by the error of demons and, because of the scarcity of preachers, worshiped idols and persistently persecuted Christians.

At that time Charles the Great held the imperial citadel. He was a most Christian man, vigorous in arms, instructed in law, wholly Catholic in faith, and benevolent and devoted toward worshipers of God. He entered into war with an army against that same Widukind for the defense of the faith, as he was always accustomed to do against pagans.

When they had come together, both princes agreed that each should rise to fight the other in single combat, and that whichever of them fortune granted victory should without question command the entire army. When they had engaged and struggled long and hard, at last the Lord, moved by the tears of Christians, granted his faithful warrior triumph over the enemy [Col. 1315D], as the faith deserved.

**2. (Year 785.)** Then such a change of mind seized Widukind’s obstinacy that he voluntarily submitted, together with his family and the entire pagan army, both to the king’s power and to the Catholic faith. The emperor received him kindly and had him baptized by Saint Boniface the bishop [Note: [Col. 1315D] Everyone can see that the author is seriously mistaken.], himself lifting him from the sacred font.

Having abandoned his error, he came willingly through repentance to knowledge of the truth. Just as he had previously been a persistent persecutor and destroyer of the Church, so afterward he became a most Christian worshiper of the churches and of God. He himself devoted all his strength to building individual cells [Note: [Col. 1315] The manuscript has *ipsas*, “the very ones.”] and left them completed with many relics of the saints and with other useful provisions [Note: [Col. 1315] The manuscript has *totas*, “whole.”]. One of these, called Aggerinensis, remains known to many even today [Note: [Col. 1315] Enger near Herford.], and some of the things just mentioned still survive there.

From his descendants, after they had submitted themselves to the Christian religion, came the father of the aforesaid girl, named Tiedericus [Col. 1316B]. He had as his wife the most noble Reinhalda, descended from the peoples of the Frisians and Danes.

As we have said, this same girl was in the monastery at Herford—not to be counted among the nuns, but to be educated, together with her father’s mother, in every useful branch of learning and work. This grandmother, who in widowhood had advanced so far in good deeds that she was appointed leader and abbess of the nuns, revealed both the girl’s nobility and the favor of her virtue.

For in her shone the image of her ancestral and paternal beauty: she had a lovely face, was lovable in childhood, industrious in her works [Note: [Col. 1315] The manuscript has *industrie*, “industriously.”], modest in conduct, humble and generous. And, as was fitting for a girl of that age, through the favor of divine mercy she was destined to be adorned with such praises that nothing could stand above her.

[Col. 1316C] **3.** When Duke Otto learned this, he sent Count Thitmar, the tutor of the boy Heinricus, to see whether the girl was as beautiful and praiseworthy as was reported. Seeing that she was suitable for her lord’s marriage and that she would become a future hope for the people, he returned and reported everything he had learned.

**(Year 909.)** When the father heard this, he again sent the same man, together with his son Heinricus and the rest of his attendants, to that place. Having received the duke’s command, they approached the aforesaid monastery.

At first, pretending to be strangers, a few of them went to the chapel and observed the girl in the church itself, modest and lovely in appearance. After leaving the city, they put on royal garments once more and entered accompanied by a great crowd. Approaching the abbess, they asked and urged that the virgin for whose sake they had come be presented to them.

She came forward, giving her cheeks colors in which whiteness was mingled with the redness of fire, like lilies mixed with red roses [Note: [Col. 1315] The manuscript has *permixta*, “mixed,” agreeing differently]. Heinricus, when he saw her and understood the matter completely, fixed his gaze upon the virgin and was so inflamed with love for her [Col. 1317A] [Note: [Col. 1317] The manuscript repeats *in*] that there was no delay in arranging the betrothal. But early the next day, while the rest of the parents knew nothing, and only his grandmother, who was abbess there, was aware of it, she was led away in silence—without the accompaniment of cymbals or organs, but amid the secretly summoned retinues of the princes—with all the honor of the Saxons into their homeland, until a wedding feast was prepared at Walehusen, as was fitting for nobles and future kings.

There they at last enjoyed lawful love, and he gave her that city and everything belonging to it as her dowry.

**4.** The aforesaid Duke Otto, Heinricus’s father, lived three years after this and then died (Year 912). The princes of the kingdom assembled in council and deliberated which of their nobles should hold the leadership. But, mindful of his earlier favor, they chose that same son as duke. He was also the strongest in arms among the Saxons, and by an affection greater than usual he won the people to himself through gentleness, so that they wished him to be king.

Not long afterward it happened that Conrad, king of the Franks, put off his mortal condition (Year 918); whether by war or peace, we do not know. The scepter and the entire power of the kingdom passed to Heinricus.

Once these matters had been arranged, as we have said, the Saxons, enriched by such a king, enjoyed an honor to which no such causes of primacy had ever before subjected them. O Germany! Formerly pressed down beneath the yoke of other peoples, but now raised up by imperial splendor: love your king faithfully in serving him, and strive to help him as much as you can. Do not cease to desire that a prince of his line should not be lacking, lest, stripped of all the steps of honor [Col. 1317C], you return to your former condition of servitude.

The aforementioned Heinricus, who had assumed the kingdom, now rising higher and higher in rank, had subjected to his rule by war the kingdoms surrounding him, namely the Slavs, Danes, Bavarians, Bohemians, and other peoples who had never seemed subject to Saxon rule.

Why should it be surprising that he won such a triumph of victory by overcoming enemies so often, when he continually gave thanks to the supreme triumphant King of heaven, and had churches restored at great expense? He was generous to the poor, protected widows and the oppressed, gave his soldiers gifts worthy of them [Note: [Col. 1317] The manuscript has *condigne*, “worthily”], and governed the others with piety and measured peace.

**5.** When Machtildis had been married to an earthly prince and secular power had come to her, her will was inclined more toward the service of God [Note: [Col. 1317] The manuscript adds *eam*, “her”] than toward the exaltation offered by worldly glory.
