Always subject to God and following the admonitions of priests, she shared more deeply in Christ than she was joined to her husband.

At night she would somehow withdraw secretly from the king and, devoting herself to prayers in the church, love it more than her husband’s bed. If the king was ever absent, who could believe how she poured herself out in prayers, how she bound herself to the feet of Christ as though he were present, from the first crowing of the cock until the next dawn showed its first light? She loved Christ not only in voice but also through perfect works.

If someone, as commonly happens, was brought before the tribunal for a capital offense and the king ordered him to be killed, the most holy queen, grieving with the condemned man, softened the prince’s spirit with such persuasions that, in the very anger of the king from which the sentence of death had proceeded, a word of salvation would proceed [Note: [Col. 1317] The manuscript has *sabatis*, an uncertain reading].

**6.** The distinction of their children must not be passed over either; all of both sexes were raised to high station and adorned with the highest honor.

Otto, the eldest, taking his name from his grandfather, was gentler in character and more modest in conduct than the others, beloved by the people from their hearts. After his father’s death he assumed the crown and kingdom. From the English Saxons a royal wife named Edith was brought to him, beautiful in body but most outstanding in virtue.

Heinricus, second in birth, was appointed illustrious duke over the Bavarians. They made Bruno, the youngest, a wise and worthy man of priestly rank, archbishop of Cologne. Their sister Gerburch had been given in marriage to Gilbert, prince of the Belgians.

Thus the aforesaid king and his most worthy wife, growing ever more ardent in the love of God and caring for Christ’s worshipers, distributed limitless gifts every year of their lives to all the monasteries around them; and wherever they themselves could not travel, they were present with a generous hand through remitted funds.

Diligently carrying out these works, they also devoted themselves, at the divine prompting, to building monasteries themselves. When they disclosed the inclination of their minds in conversation to the military princes, those men immediately suggested to the king, saying that the nuns enclosed within the fence of the monastery at Winedhusen could be transferred to Quedlingaburg. For the daughters of princes spent their lives in that same monastery, and their parents were displeased that they remain there because of the lack of resources.

**7.** When these matters had thus been arranged, the king went, as was customary, to Botfelden to hunt, and there was seized by a severe attack of illness. But when, as the disease worsened, he sensed that the dissolution of his body was approaching, he set out from there for Erpesford. Ordering all those subject to his authority to be present, he began to take counsel concerning the condition of the kingdom.

The abbess had also come at the king’s command [Note: [Col. 1317D] Diemot], the woman who presided over the aforementioned monastery. The king and his wife, mindful of their earlier desire, asked that the aforesaid women of God be transferred to Quedlingaburg [Col. 1318D]. She gratefully accepted their request, and, with several of the princes urging it, agreed that it should be carried out as the king had ordered.

When the council had ended and the people were returning home, the king, accompanied by a few men, went to Jemelevum [Note: [Col. 1318D] Memleben] and, by God’s command, ended his present life there (Year 936, July 2).

An immeasurable crowd of people flocked together for his funeral. Following the body with lamentation, they transported it all the way to Quedlingaburg and buried it honorably, as was proper.

Then the queen, determined to have her will fulfilled, urged that the company of girls be transferred there; but the abbess at first firmly refused and prevented it. But why say more? With the assistance of her son, King Otto, and of other princes, the queen achieved her desire. From that time forward she arranged that same community with great devotion, supplying everything it needed.

**8.** After the venerable King Heinricus had died and his elder son Otto occupied the throne of the kingdom, the aforesaid queen remained in widowhood in such uprightness that scarcely anyone of either sex could imitate her.

She was prudent in counsel, exceedingly gentle toward the good [Col. 1319B] and harsh toward the proud, generous in almsgiving, devoted to prayer, compassionate toward all in need, gracious in speech, and steadfast in love of God and neighbor and in purity.

But the envious enemy, the instigator of every evil, was present, stirring up certain princes. They told the king and his other sons that she had kept a very large amount of money which she ought to have handed over.

But those men, driven by the insatiable love of possession that spares not even one’s own relatives, compelled her to bring forth the hidden heaps of treasure that she distributed to churches and the needy in Christ’s name. They ordered spies to run about the mountain slopes, the bottoms of the hills, and the forest glades, carefully searching the places through which they thought the queen was sending money to the monasteries.

If they found anyone carrying anything valuable—for the beloved woman of God was striving secretly to offer whatever remained to Christ’s hand—they abused the servants, forcibly seized what they carried, and sent them away empty-handed.

They even compelled her, through this and many other injuries, to abandon the portion of the kingdom that had come to her as dowry, seek a monastery, and receive the sacred veil.

When she was afflicted by so many things, mindful of Holy Scripture, which says, “Through many tribulations we must enter the kingdom of God” (Acts 14:21), she abandoned the dotal cities, sought her patrimony, and went to the Aggerinensis monastery in the western region.

There she continued no less steadfastly than before in good works.

But many scourges came upon King Otto, as though to avenge the mother: the triumphs of his victories were reversed, together with other favorable circumstances [Note: [Col. 1319] *Prosperis*, “favorable things,” is a gloss added in the manuscript]. For the grace of the Holy Spirit rested in Machtildis, the king’s mother, and she possessed an exceedingly great love in Christ.

**9.** When the king saw that nothing was prospering for him as before [Col. 1320A], he became so distressed that he feared for his life. Then Edith, the queen of blessed memory, entered and said:

“Let not my lord the king be distressed, for you have been chastised by divine scourges because you drove your excellent mother from the kingdom as though she were unknown. Let the most holy woman be recalled, and let her possess the kingdom first, as is fitting.”

When the prince heard this, he was first filled with astonishment and then with the greatest joy. He sent bishops, governors, and other honorable attendants to recall his most worthy mother. He offered all that he possessed and declared himself ready to agree gladly to whatever terms she wished for his atonement, asking only that he be allowed to make use of her favor.

The joyful mother received her son’s message. As though forgetting the earlier events, she completed the journey with all speed and arrived at Grona [Col. 1320B]. The king and his wife went out to meet her. Falling at her feet, he promised that he would change whatever he had done contrary to her wishes.

But she, pouring noble tears down her cheeks, embraced and kissed her son, declaring that what had happened had been caused by her own sins.

Without delay, after receiving satisfaction sufficient for reconciliation and peace, she restored to him the portion of the kingdom that had been her dower.

While these bonds of affection endured for a long time, it happened that the pious Queen Edith departed from this present life, destined to live forever [Note: [Col. 1319D] On the date of Edith’s death, see *Jahrbücher des Deutschen Reichs* I, 2, p. 103] (Year 946, January 26).

**10.** The king, now advanced in age, had churches and cells built together with his mother, establishing peace, judging rightly, and imitating his father’s piety in all things. (Year 950, November 22.)

Meanwhile word reached King Otto that Lodewigus [Note: [Col. 1319D] Rather Lotharius. Widukind III, 7, fell into the same error; the author of the later Life correctly names the king Lotharius.] the famous king of the Latins had died, and that his most noble wife Adelheid was being oppressed by a certain Berengarius, who was taking away the kingdom so that he might usurp Italy as his own dominion.

Therefore King Otto, persuaded by the counsel of the princes and having properly prepared his affairs, went with his companions into Latium. Having rescued the queen through a triumphal victory, he honorably transported her back to his homeland (Year 951).

When they had been lawfully joined in marriage [Note: [Col. 1320D] The wedding did not take place in the homeland but in Italy; see Widukind III, 10], and most beautiful children of both sexes had been born to the rulers, as they governed wisely, the king gave a girl named after her grandmother Machtildis to the community of nuns in the monastery at Quedlingaburg, fulfilling the will of his excellent mother.

As for the boy Otto, named after his father, while he was still in the first flower of youth and while his father lived for many years afterward, they appointed him beforehand as king (Year 961, May 26). Blessed Machtildis had previously foretold this through the spirit of prophecy.

For whenever royal offspring were born and the news reached her ears, she would say, “Thanks be to God” (Year 955). When she heard the messenger announce the birth of this boy, she bent her knee to the ground and summoned the company of those serving God there. She ordered God to be praised by hymn-singers and the church bells to ring together, commending the little one, newly born, to the heavenly King and wishing prosperity for his life. She said:

“This child will be more illustrious in fame than the others and will provide something remarkable for us, his parents.”

**11.** Now let us return to the good works of the same Machtildis. If we were to pass through them one by one, we would produce an immense volume for readers; for it is impossible to include everything, nor can we allow everything to remain hidden.

Her mind was increasingly intent upon God, and she advanced from virtue to virtue. By enlarging monasteries, she established a company of clerics at Palithi. Later, in the valley at Quedlingaburg, another congregation of brothers arose through her arrangements, and on the mountain a monastery of nuns [Col. 1321B].

She also built another monastery in a nearby place called Gerendod [Note: [Col. 1321D] The Quedlinburg Annals under 1014 and Thietmar II, 13, state that the founder of the monastery was Margrave Gero; nor, so far as I know, is Mathildis otherwise mentioned in connection with this foundation], as well as several other monasteries.

She was pious not only toward those serving God in monasteries, as we have said, but toward all who were in need. Besides the daily feeding of the poor, she had a crowd gathered twice each day and refreshed them with royal food. Every Saturday, after preparing a bath, she had the poor and pilgrims restored there; sometimes she entered herself, while at other times, avoiding the crowd, she sent in her attendants. She washed each of the women’s limbs.

When they came out, she supplied them not only with their customary food but also with clothing. Thus the exercise of mercy was no less constant than the gathering of the needy from the common people: there was never a lack of those who asked, nor a shortage of what she could give.

Whenever she was about to dine, although delicacies of every kind were brought to the table three times each day, if she was at a monastery she tasted no food before distributing everything to the worshipers of Christ. If she was away from a monastery, she likewise offered these things fasting to sick guests and to those serving her.

This too must not be passed over: wherever she was, fire did not fail during the night, not only under roofs but also in the open air, for the benefit of all who remained there.

It was also the custom of this holy woman, whenever she undertook a long or short journey, to take candles with her for distribution among the individual oratories, and to carry provisions beside the carriage, so that she could refresh the needy along the road or care for the sick.

If sleep sometimes overtook her while she was sitting in the carriage—for perhaps she often passed the night watches awake in prayer—and a needy person happened to come along, the nun named Ricburg, who sat before her and had been chosen for her service, might carelessly neglect the poor person, whether she herself was drowsing or was looking into and reading a book [Note: [Col. 1321] *Et* seems to have dropped out; the construction of the sentence is confused]. If she did not wake the queen, the queen would immediately awaken and rebuke her dear attendant with saving words. She ordered the carriage to stop and, calling back the person who had passed, provided for the poor man.

What more should I say? Through those benefactions she had nearly won the palm of virginity, except that she flourished so greatly in the adornment of secular clothing.

No day, scarcely an hour, found her idle from good works. Even on feast days she occupied herself with reading, either reading herself or listening to others. On ordinary days, when work is permitted, she devoted herself to prayer or psalmody, as she always did, while nevertheless applying herself to manual labor.

If at times she was surrounded throughout the entire day by the various conversations of the people—as happens to those who preside over an earthly kingdom—at least at the hour of refreshment, standing before the table, she would do some work before tasting food, remembering and saying:

“Whoever is unwilling to work shall not eat” (2 Thessalonians 3:10).

**12.** While she was occupied with these blessed actions, divine mercy raised her so far that, by the Lord’s gift, she also became renowned through the light of miracles.

One day in the city of Quedlingaburg, while standing on the summit of the mountain, she saw a crowd of poor people eating in the valley. She asked her servant whether bread had been given to the poor along with the other food. He replied, “Not at all.”

Then, as though angry with the steward, she suddenly seized a loaf of bread, marked it with the sign of the cross, invoked the Lord’s name—as she always did in every matter—and threw it from the high summit. It rolled over rocks and a fence and reached the lap of a poor man unharmed. Those who were present, seeing this, marveled and testified that it had happened through divine power.

She also shone through another miracle in the same city. While she was most devoutly offering a holocaust to God in the church [Note: [Col. 1321] The manuscript has *devotissima*, “most devout”], a certain tame doe, domesticated within the enclosure, secretly stole and devoured a small flask and also a vessel of wine, as often happens in monasteries.

Those present were unable to find the animal, although they beat it, threatened it, and clapped their hands. At last the queen, worthy of God, extended her hand to the animal’s mouth and said in gentle words:

“Give it back; what you took is ours.”

At once the doe vomited up the flask which it had swallowed.

Who could doubt that the supreme Ruler had transformed the wild animal into human understanding through her merits?

The Lord worked many other things through her which, if they could be recorded one by one, would seem marvelous [Note: [Col. 1321] The manuscript has *super*, “above”]; but inwardly she shone more brightly through virtues than outwardly through signs of miracles.

**13.** Meanwhile, when the pope [Note: [Col. 1322D] John XII] summoned King Otto to Rome to receive, as we believe, the imperial crown by God’s command, he went to Italy to acquire it (Year 960), which Queen Adelheid had previously possessed as her dower.

After entrusting his kingdom to his son Otto, he departed, taking with him strong-hearted men and going together with his wife. With Christ as his leader, he conquered Latium in a most illustrious victory. He overwhelmed Berengarius, who had usurped the kingdom of the Latins, and ordered him to be led captive, together with his entire family, into the region of Bavaria.

Then, crowned as emperor with his wife at the chair of Saint Peter (Year 964), he held the Roman empire and ruled the Ausonian cities with supreme power.

During those days when the king had first gone to Italy (Year 962, February 2), his mother, seized by hope and fear, continually entreated God in prayers for her son, so that in the meantime, through a singular sacrifice, she might appease the most powerful Warrior on behalf of her son’s victory.

**14.** As she pondered this thought in her heart, she resolved upon the following.

She also built a monastery at Northusen, gathering a company of sisters for the salvation of the souls and bodies of herself and her own people [Col. 1323B], with the consent of her grandson, the younger Otto. Building it from its foundations, she always showed the greatest maternal care for it, supplying everything necessary for it as long as she lived in the present life.

When the emperor, after conquering Latium, had returned to his homeland, he went to the city of Cologne [Note: [Col. 1323D] See the tables of the Life of Otto I, pp. 293 ff., in Böhmer], where his brother Bruno was archbishop. He ordered his mother to be summoned there to meet him, together with her son the king and the beautiful girl [Note: [Col. 1324D] His daughter Mathilda].

Queen Gerburch, his sister, also came, along with the entire royal offspring of both sexes, gathered together by their love of seeing one another, as we trust by the arrangement of divine mercy. For after this they did not see one another together, nor were they destined to see one another again in temporal life.

That illustrious mother, Queen Machtildis, happy in having borne such great princes, was first received honorably by the emperor and then by all her descendants. She embraced her own grandchildren and rejoiced to see them, and above all she rejoiced and gave thanks to God that her son had come safely, august in such glory.

She explained to him in order everything she had meanwhile done concerning the monastery, and how she was troubled by the fear that she would be unable to complete the work she had begun, leaving the community deprived of her after her death. She also told him that she was now advanced in age and that she had therefore not undertaken the care of others, because her earlier undertakings were not yet complete [Note: [Col. 1323] The initials *i. n.* are missing in the copy but must be supplied].

The king, inflamed with love of God and neighbor, congratulated her on her merits and said that he knew he had been victorious because of them. To prevent her from imagining such fears, he soothed his mother’s mind with his words and swore that, as long as he lived and his descendants survived him, the monastery would never lack assistance of any kind.

With such words he comforted his mother. They crossed into the Saxon region and arrived at that same city of Northusen. Adding whatever his mother or the king her son had given, he himself firmly and perpetually granted further possessions, confirming them with his own chaste hand.

From there he traveled through other cities governing the people, and remained for some time in those regions (Year 966). He went to Rome again [Note: [Col. 1323] The copy has *decus*, “ornament,” an error], taking his son with him.

15. Now the hour was approaching when the Lord had appointed to repay his chosen handmaid Machtildis for her temporal labors. Having therefore been ill for a full year, she traveled through cottages and castles, concealing her infirmity as best she could. She went to Northusen and, with her faithful Ricburga brought before her—the woman whom she had appointed abbess over the aforesaid convent, in the hope of faithfully caring for the poor community—said to her:

“I feel that, as my illness increases, I shall soon depart, and I would wish to be buried here, so that my sons’ care for you might be greater. But I know [Note: c reads *sciens*, “knowing.”] that this cannot in any way be granted, for our lord Heinrich rests at Quidilingaburg. Where, then, must your hope be directed, and where must your heart be turned? To God, of course.”

[Col. 1323–1324B]

After giving them many salutary admonitions, she then came to Quidilingaburg, where at last she was seized by an excessive affliction and remained ill until her death. Seeing that her final day was approaching, and remembering the divine saying, “Sell everything that you have and give to the poor, and come, follow me” (Matthew IX, 21), she immediately ordered all the abundance of wealth that remained to be distributed among bishops, priests, and the needy, and divided among the monasteries. She kept only the garment with which she was covered, together with two other cloaks, one scarlet and the other linen, which she ordered to be preserved for her burial.

As crowds of rich and poor gathered, and no one departed without receiving a gift, Willehelmus, archbishop of Mainz and son of Emperor Otto, also arrived. Entering the doorway of the house with troubled mind, where the sick woman lay, he wept profusely and mourned her impending departure. Yet, if grief permitted any reasoning, he ought rather to rejoice, since she would, as we hope, be joined in peace to the company of the righteous and rest there.

[Col. 1324C]

When she saw him grieving, she groaned and said:

“To you I commend my soul; I also commend the abandoned community of Northusen, not only so that you may care for it yourself, but also so that you may admonish the emperor on its behalf, because, since the work has not yet been brought to completion, I have not given that convent the greatest care above the others.”

[Note: There is an omission in the manuscript (*excidit in cod.*).]

He promised that he would fulfill everything she had requested.

Besides these matters, she gave many instructions to be carried to her son Otto. But this was in vain, because he did not see the king again; for, after living only a short while longer, he died (968, March 2).

[Col. 1324D]

That holy servant of Christ, as though fully aware of it, foretold his death when she was departing, saying:

“Is there anything of ours that can be given to Bishop Wilhelm?”

When she was told that there was nothing, she said:

“Where are the cloaks that we ordered to be kept for our burial? Let them be given to him, for he will have greater need of them on his journey. But in our case the saying of the people will be fulfilled: ‘Parents find a wedding garment and a mourning garment.’”

Those standing around did not understand why she had said this; they thought that he was going to Mainz. Yet none of those things which the holy woman had prophesied remained unfulfilled—not the bishop’s death, nor the offering of the garments. For when the dead woman was being placed in her coffin, messengers of her daughter, Queen Gerburgis, arrived carrying a cloak woven with gold, which was suitable for covering her own tomb and that of her lord, King Heinrich.

[Col. 1325A]

On a certain Saturday, a day which she had always loved because of its good works, when her final hour had come, she summoned her granddaughter, the emperor’s daughter and abbess of the convent, to her. Insisting upon salutary admonitions, she instructed her carefully to provide for the flock entrusted to her: to be devout and humble, prudent and cautious; to leave the monastery rarely; to devote her mind to the sacred Scriptures; to teach others what she read [Note: The text has *alias*, “other women”; c reads *alios*, “other men”]; and whatever she urged others to do by her admonitions, first to fulfill herself through good works, leaving an example for all.

[Col. 1325B]

Moreover, handing her the book in which the names of deceased nobles were written, she commended to her the soul of Heinrich and also her own, as well as those of all the faithful whose memory she herself recalled.

Finally, Ricburg, abbess of Northusen, came forth sorrowfully and, embracing the queen’s feet, wept:

“To whom,” she said, “do you leave us, desolate, when you are the hope and consolation of us all?”

But she, raising her eyes and extending her hands, said:

“I commend you to the supreme Shepherd. For I believe that my son, mindful of his former promise—that neither during his lifetime nor under his descendants would consolation ever be lacking for that convent—will not forget you. But if that should fail, and you are abandoned by human beings, then, since God does not forsake those who hope in him, seek first the kingdom of God, and all these things will be added to you” (Luke XII, 31).

[Col. 1325C]

Then, turning to those standing around, she said:

“Act well, and place sackcloth beneath me, with me turned upward, so that the spirit may return to God and the flesh be reduced to dust.”

When all these things had thus been arranged according to divine order, full of days and complete in age, leaving to posterity an example of good works, and having seen her descendants and, through them, grandchildren down to the fourth generation [Note: Otto, duke of Swabia and son of Liudolf, was born in 954. Compare the Continuation of the Royal Annals], Queen Mactildis gave up her spirit to God and the angels and departed to the Lord on March 14, in the city of Quidilingaburg (968, March 14).

[Col. 1325D]

There she was honorably committed to burial in the basilica of Saint Servatius, bishop and confessor, and rests beside the tomb of her lord Heinrich.

[Col. 1326A]

16. After her death, envoys bearing letters entered Italy, where her son Otto, the emperor, governed the state in Latium—a man who deservedly ought to be praised for every piety, if only he had been able either to reject the diadem unlawfully imposed upon him by a rebellious soldiery or to abstain from arms. [Note: This is known to be false: the author has wrongly assigned to this event the wars which followed the coronation.] But a great empire could not be held without arms. Nevertheless, neither the wealth of the kingdom, nor the dignity of the empire, nor the diadem, nor the purple could tear him away from the service of Christ.

The envoys, as we have said, entered the palace where the king sat upon a lofty throne. When permission to speak had been granted and they had opened the letters, they announced that his mother had died. At these words he was utterly shaken; his face grew pale, tears welled up, and he wept copiously, stirred by his love for his mother. Then he affirmed that he would fulfill everything his mother had requested.

[Col. 1326B]

He immediately carried this out, and also assigned a portion of his mother’s marriage-property in the western region to the convent of Northusen. He sent there as well the privilege granted by the Roman pope, as the lady herself had previously requested.

But he remained for some time in Ausonia [Note: “Italy,” a gloss in the manuscript], until a splendid wife, called by the name Theophanu, had been brought from the regions of Greece and from the imperial palace for his son, the younger Otto, together with innumerable treasures (972, April 14). [Note: Compare the Annals of Hildesheim for the year 972.]

After he had caused both of them to be honored with the imperial name [Note: It is established that Otto II was crowned emperor in 967; only the Annals of Lobbes, for 972, in M.G. II, state that Theophanu received the imperial crown from Pope John XIII], he finally returned to the Saxon homeland, accompanied by his wife, with his son likewise traveling together with his wife. [Note: He had returned to Germany in 972 and came to Saxony in 973.]

[Col. 1326C]

At Easter he came to the city of Quidilingaburg (973, March 23), where the tomb of his father and mother stood. Received there with honor, while the entire people gathered to meet him [Note: “to him,” in the manuscript], he remained there for the most sacred days.

Having departed from there, he reached Mimilevum while ill (May 6). [Note: Compare Widukind III, 75.] There, one day, he was brought into the oratory and, while listening to the evening praises—as he had always loved churches and the service of God—he gave up his spirit, with the angels receiving him (May 7).

[Col. 1326D]

After his departure, therefore, his most excellent son, the younger Otto, possessed the kingdom of the Latins and of the Saxons. We believe that, through the favor of our Lord Jesus Christ, who lives and reigns forever and ever, he was not inferior in virtue to his father and grandfather. Amen.

[Col. 1327]

# An Unpublished Letter of Mathildis the Swabian, Sister of the Empress Gisla and Grandmother of Mathildis of Tuscany, Addressed in the Year 1027 or 1028 to Misego II, King of Poland

*(Serving as a preface to the Carolingian-Alcuinian Liturgical Codex)*

# A Critical-Historical-Exegetical Commentary on This Letter

—or, The Vindication of the First Four Kings of Latin-Christian Poland—

By Phil. Ant. Dethier, Doctor of Philosophy and Fellow of the Thuringian-Saxon Society of Antiquities, corresponding member.

*(With an engraved copperplate and a Mathildine genealogical table.)*

[Printed in 250 copies.]

(Berlin, at Behrius, 1842.—Printed by Haenel.)

# Preface

The codex which I now make public appears once to have been of no small importance, when among the Slavs on one side and the Germans on the other; between the Greek-Slavonic Christians of the East and the Latin Christians of the West, a most stubborn and bitter struggle for dominion over the world was waged with uncertain arms—sometimes successfully, sometimes unsuccessfully, but always amid grief and destruction.

That most bloody division between peoples and religions, rarely sleeping or at rest throughout so many centuries, is growing daily in our own time. Discord, already on the point of erupting and destined to become the mother of wars, is seizing almost everyone’s mind with its conflagration.

In publishing this monument of the study of the Latin rite among the Poles in the eleventh century, what could be easier than to accommodate oneself to or flatter one side or the other? What, by contrast, could be more difficult than preserving that tranquility of soul without which nothing upright can stand?

Yet this is something that not only the writer must guard against, but the reader no less. The author of this little book sought pure truth—would that without error!—and nothing but historical truth. Such truth can rarely please everyone, but it very often pleases every good person. If the reader is displeased by the small number of pages, the writer may not “touch the stars with his lofty head,” but both appear worthy of praise.

I wrote this in Berlin in January 1842.

# Chapter I.—The Method of Treating History

[Col. 1327]

Among all who study history, it is now sufficiently agreed how rare contemporary monuments are in the earlier part of the Middle Ages. No one fails to see that the history of the peoples living at that time is more obscure the farther they were removed from the light of the Christian faith, which, like a torch, illuminates not only hearts but also the liberal arts and drives away the deceptive darkness of ignorance.

The Christian dawn itself, alas, covered with blood-red clouds and flashing only with rare rays, does not illuminate lands, men, and deeds. Rather, it presents everything—shining in one place, horrifying in another—scarcely distinguishable even by the keenest eyes. Very often one must rely on the conjecture of a diviner.

[Col. 1328]

Add another major obstacle, in my judgment, to discovering the truth in history: nearly all those who have written histories, whether they wished it or not, have thought that they had to fight for their altars and hearths. Consequently, the same deed, according as it is reported by one side or the other, differs from itself more than black differs from white.

[Col. 1329A]

Ἄλλο γλαῦξ, ἄλλο κορώνη φθέγγεται.

“An owl utters one sound, a crow another.”

Take your profane hands away, contentious speaker, from the sanctuary of history, which God himself, that wisest governor of all things, willed to be as it is. No one has ever injured it with impunity by thinking himself wiser than God. I say “not with impunity” because history has always been a grave, severe, indeed bloody avenger—not only in books but in life itself; and all the bloodier the slower its vengeance.

[Col. 1329B]

Let no one object to me that in our own times those who direct public affairs promote this profanation of history, this plague, and that no one is permitted to remember Tacitus’ words, “Without anger and partiality”: “We, we consuls, are failing!” All the more does History resent writers who distort or defile the things within their own power through false zeal or often fabricated anger, and who abuse the time and judgment of their readers.

Although examples are by no means rare, I shall offer you one in Miceslaus II, or Misego, king of the Poles, whom you will find described so differently by native and German writers that scarcely anything can be said about him for which one does not possess an authority.

[Col. 1329C]

The best historians, in investigating history, now return to the monuments themselves. They bring contemporary documents from public and private archives to light, more industriously than ants. Others examine these heaps of monuments collected from every direction, compare them with chronicles and traditions, and reject as suspect, corrupt, or fabricated whatever in the latter does not agree with the documents. We have an excellent example of this in the celebrated book by Ranke, *Yearbooks of the Saxon Emperors*.

[Col. 1329D]

Let them nevertheless beware lest they pass from Scylla into Charybdis. For often there is something slightly impure in a tradition, and this can readily be proved; but is the whole tradition therefore to be rejected? For example, if a certain law is said to be Romulean, and the celebrated Niebuhr removes King Romulus into the realm of myth, has it thereby immediately been demonstrated that the law never existed?

In this dissertation we shall often attempt, while rejecting what is suspect, nevertheless to preserve that part of the tradition which appears true. Why we have undertaken this especially with regard to the first Christian kings of Poland, the following chapter will explain.

# Chapter II.—Description of the Manuscript Liturgical Book of Charlemagne and Alcuin

Some years ago, while, at the command of the venerable provost Fischer, I was examining the library of the Catholic Church of Saint Hedwig in Berlin—which consists for the most part of books from the Monastery of Saint Mary of Nova-Cella (Neuenzelle near Frankfurt on the Oder), secularized by the late King Frederick William III—I found a parchment manuscript of eighty-three leaves, square in format.

The negligently compiled catalogue of those books contains the following words concerning this volume:

> “A Latin manuscript on parchment, apparently very old, without a title, in Gothic script; in the opinion of Abbot Optatus Paul, a choir prayer-book.”

[Col. 1330A]

When I examined it more carefully, I immediately saw that the codex was of greater value.

On the first folio, as the book now stands, the following is written on the front in a very recent hand:

> “From the library of the lord abbot of the Monastery of the Blessed Virgin Mary of Nova-Cella.”

[Col. 1330B]

On the verso of the first folio and the front of the second is a hymn to the archangels Saint Michael, Gabriel, and Raphael. In the margin of the hymn appears *Alleluia*, with the notes to be sung. This hymn seems to have been written by a more recent hand than those found in the rest of the book. The letters are somewhat slanted, although the lines are absent from the musical notation and what appear to be Gregorian neumes are present. An example of these may be seen above, in Figure 2, at the verse:

> “Through whom the entire rejoicing structure of the world is adorned.”

The verso of the second folio and the front of the third contain a dedicatory letter, which begins with the words “To Lord M.” and which we shall discuss more fully in this dissertation.

[Col. 1330C]

The verso of the third folio is filled (see Fig. 1) with a painted image of a certain crowned and purple-clad prince seated upon a throne, holding a scepter in his left hand and receiving with his right a book offered by a woman with veiled hands. Above it we read, painted in red and in capital letters, the following pair of Leonine verses—that is, hexameters whose first half-line has at its end the same sound as the second, or, as vernacular languages call it, a rhyme:

> “This book Mathildis gives to King Misego,  
> whom the renowned Duke Hermann of the Swabians begot.”

[Col. 1330D]

Finally, on the front of the fourth folio is the true title of the book, painted in red and in capital letters:

> “In the name of Christ begins the book of offices which they call the Roman Order.”

In the margin a rubric is added in lowercase letters:

> “On the Nativity of the Lord.”

This follows in capital letters, with a very large and ornate initial (see Fig. 3):

> “The most sacred Nativity of this day is therefore called so, because on it Christ was born.”

And so forth. On the verso of the fifth folio the feast day “of the Circumcision of the Lord” is explained, and in the following leaves all the solemn days of the Christian year, from the Nativity of the Lord to the feast of All Saints (folio 42), are listed and their rites explained.

On the verso of folio 42 begins the order for visiting the sick; on the verso of folio 43, the order for the dead; folio 46 concerns the ecclesiastical orders; folio 48, how a bishop is ordained in the Roman Church; from folio 53 to folio 74 begins a brief exposition of the Mass; folio 74 concerns the Creed; and from the verso of folio 76 to folio 83 there is a transcription from another book concerning the sacred orders and priestly vestments.

[Col. 1331A]

This liturgical book is for the most part not unknown. It is commonly called Pseudo-Alcuinian. It has already been printed, though inaccurately, in the Hittorp collection and elsewhere. Yet many things absent from the printed editions are offered intact by our manuscript.

As for the author of the greater part of this extensive liturgical book, I believe I can demonstrate that Charlemagne and Alcuin composed it as one of their secondary undertakings. But we shall discuss this matter elsewhere.

[Col. 1332A]

It is therefore established thus far that our manuscript is a copy of the liturgical order of the Roman Church, presented by a certain Mathildis, daughter of a certain Hermann, Duke of the Swabians, to a king named Misego.

Let us return to the dedicatory letter of our copy, which can perhaps now be understood better. Here it is printed verbatim, with its orthographical errors and punctuation left untouched:

# Chapter III.—The Dedicatory Letter of Mathildis the Swabian to Misego, King

[Col. 1331]

## To Lord M.

[Note: “M.” stands for “Misego,” as is already apparent from the verses in the illustration.]

To the truest worshiper of true virtue and most invincible king, M. [Note: “M.” stands for “Misego,” as is already apparent from the verses in the illustration], supreme joy in Christ and a happy triumph over the enemy.

Since divine grace has granted you alike the royal name and honor, and has most honorably endowed you with the art of ruling necessary for it, as I have heard, with a fortunate beginning you consecrated the first fruits of your reign to divinity itself with devoted heart.

For which of your predecessors raised so many churches? Who gathered together so many tongues in praise of God? Although you could worthily worship God in your own language and in Latin, you were not satisfied with this; you preferred to add Greek as well.

These and similar pursuits proclaim you blessed if you persevere to the end, and most truly testify that you were chosen not so much by human as by divine judgment to govern God’s holy people. You are regarded as prudent in judgment, distinguished in goodness, and excellent in every moral integrity. You are approved by all as a husband to widows, as a father to orphans, and as an incorruptible defender of the needy and poor. You do not consider the person of the poor or revere the face of the powerful, but examine everything proposed upon the scales of justice.

Without doubt, like blessed Sebastian, you lead the life of a soldier of Christ hidden beneath the adornment of royal dress, so that you may restore to God alone the souls deceived by the devil’s fraud. You eagerly strive to return the talent entrusted to you a hundredfold, ready to hear the blessed voice that says, “Well done, good and faithful servant,” and so forth.

Indeed, instructed by the examples of your fathers, you dwell almost entirely among heavenly things. In that part of the world which you rule, your father was, as it were, a fountain and source of the holy Catholic and apostolic faith. For those whom holy preachers could not correct by word, he pursued with the sword, compelling barbarous and savage nations to enter the Lord’s banquet.

For this reason I have sent you this book, so that nothing in the divine offices might be unknown to your royal dignity. Knowing that you are endowed with spiritual privilege, I have no doubt that you will receive it favorably. In it the inquisitive reader will easily discover what the variations signify which are recalled in the same offices at different times.

May almighty God, by whose ordinance you have been crowned with the royal diadem, make you stronger than all your enemies by granting you length of life and the palm of victory.

Farewell, according to your wish.

# Chapter IV.—Concerning the Form of the Letters and the Punctuation of the Manuscript

[Col. 1331B]

The form of the letters is exceedingly elegant. In the capitals, square and rectilinear Latin letters are mixed with more rounded Gothic letters—examples of such letters are given in Figure 4 of the plate. This applies to the letters D, M, N, Q, A, C, U, L, R, E, H, I, T, and P. Only B, F, K, X, Y, and Z have the more rounded form.

[Col. 1332B]

The book presents the forms of the lowercase letters which I had engraved in Figure 5.

Very many sigla occur; several of their forms can be seen in Figure 6, which I shall discuss in Chapter XXXII.

This mixture of letters—square forms of capitals together with rounded forms—was especially used in the eleventh century after the birth of Christ, although examples from the preceding and following centuries also occur, though more rarely. Nor is this surprising: forms change gradually, and something of the old custom always remains and is preserved.

[Col. 1333A]

Concerning punctuation, it should be noted that a point placed in the lower position signifies our comma; a straight comma, though slightly inclined to the right and placed above such a point (!), is our semicolon. A point placed alone in the upper position is our colon. If below this point a curved comma is added (’), it indicates the strongest punctuation, comparable to our full stop. The question mark is nearly the ordinary form.

# Chapter V.—An Example of Singular Syntax

The statements made here about Misego now seem to need to be collected in order to define his person. His praise is so great that something of flattery flows through it. Yet even so, not everything can be retained as applying to Misego, if the passage of the letter from verse 21 to verse 26 is examined more carefully.

[Col. 1333B]

The syntax of the words is strange but not unheard of: at one moment the second person of the verb occurs—“you, the king”—and at another the third—“he was”—in one continuous construction. Yet at first sight no person other than Misego appears to be present.

As I considered the matter and realized that it fitted in no way, I finally seemed to see the cause of this singular feature in the extremely bold construction which grammarians call *synesis*. Through this *synesis*, in verse 22 the relative pronoun *qui* has as its antecedent *father*, supplied from the adjective *paternis*. Only by this explanation does everything become perfectly intelligible and coherent.

[Col. 1333C]

Perhaps *paternis* was substituted for *patris* by a corrector who failed to notice that the relative pronoun *qui* follows eight words later. Thus in Cicero, *Brutus* 29: “toward the senatorial opinion, of which he was the leader”; in Livy II.53: “a Veientine war arose, against which”; and in Caesar, *Gallic War* I.40: “with a servile tumult, whom”; compare Herzog there.

We therefore have a certain King Misego whose father was, in Misego’s kingdom, as it were a fountain of the Christian faith, and who compelled barbarous peoples by the sword to enter the Lord’s banquet.

# Chapter VI.—Concerning Misego III, Duke of the Poles

Kings named Misego occur only among the Lechitic people. The spelling varies: Mieszko, Meszko, Miseco, Misego, Mesico, Misacho, Miczceslaus, and even Miska and Miscio are found.

[Col. 1334A]

There were altogether three princes of this name in Poland. The third, surnamed the Elder, cannot possibly be meant here. It is evident from the following facts: he was never called king, for which the most certain testimony exists in all the writers; his father cannot be called a fountain of the Christian faith in Poland; and finally Misego III was worthy of no praise.

For his father, before he died, divided the kingdom among five sons, and Miesco, the second-born, became duke in 1139 of the western region—Gnesen, Posen, Kalisch, and Pomerania. He received the government of all Poland in 1173, but only under the true title of duke. Finally expelled in 1178, restored in 1199, expelled again in 1200, and restored for the last time in 1202, he died at last in 1205, giving a singular example of weakness.

[Col. 1334B]

# Chapter VII.—Misego I According to the Polish Sources

The first Misego, although born in 931, is said by the writers of that people not to have seen the light of day, for he was blind, and this was therefore the cause of his previously unheard-of name.

The nobles, thinking that a prince deprived of the light of his eyes could not govern the state and that he would thereby become the cause of disturbances—which in Polish is *Mieszko*, in German *Mischung*, and in Latin *mixtio*—gave him this name [Note: Kadlubek, edition appended to Dlugosz, Leipzig, vol. II, col. 640; the commentator on the same, ibid., col. 641; Dlugosz, and others].

At the age of seven, however, he is said to have miraculously received the light of his eyes [Note: Ibid.]. Misego succeeded his father Zemomislaus, who died in 964 [Note: Dlugosz, Leipzig edition, vol. I, col. 89. A. Roepell gives pages instead of columns in his citation, incorrectly].

[Col. 1334C]

Already at that time, some among the Poles, and those not born in an obscure station, were said to have worshiped the true God of the Christians [Note: Roepell, *History of Poland*, Hamburg, 1840, I, p. 622, thinks that this opinion arose from a misunderstanding of a passage in Constantine Porphyrogenitus, *On the Administration of the Empire*, edition of Meursius, p. 127. Dobner—and Dobrowski—had already demonstrated that Hagecius, *Chronicle of Bohemia*, p. 37b, edition of 1541, folio, and Stredowski, *Moravia Sacra*, passim, are not at all trustworthy in this matter. The same Roepell rightly observes that some Christian slaves, or captives, already existed in Poland. Nevertheless, many more recent writers think that the Christian faith was already known and propagated in Poland before the arrival of Dambrowka; among them are the celebrated Stransky, Piasczki, Dobrowsky, Naruscewicz, Lelewel, Bandtkie, and Friese.

Roepell overlooks the custom of that age—and indeed one still found today—by which Latin Christians commonly called Greeks or Slavs, and Greeks or Slavs called Latins, not Christians but pagans. At that time the Latin and Greek churches were engaged in fierce conflict from the Adriatic Sea all the way to the Baltic. There flourished not only purely Greek and purely Latin churches, but also, so to speak, mixed churches: that is, a Slavonic church subject to the Patriarch of Constantinople and a Slavonic church subject to the pope. All these Christians—the pure Latins and the pure Greeks—gave one another the name of pagans as circumstances dictated, and considered those whom they intended to convert to the faith of Christ through a new baptism to be pagans. Wenceslaus Alexander Maciejowski treated this matter very well in his book, *Historical Essay on the Christian Church of the Two Rites among the Slavs*, translated from Polish by Sauvé, Leipzig, Hinrichs, 1810.]

[Col. 1334D]

Nevertheless, it is said that it was not long before almost all the Slavic peoples renounced the worship of idols. The occasion for this—among the Poles as elsewhere—is said to have been provided by a certain Christian woman.

For Duke Misego, whom they often call king, had, as the custom of the people then allowed, several wives—seven are named, equal to the number of days in the week—and spent the nights with them by turns. Yet he remained without offspring.

A certain Christian therefore advised the prince that, after repudiating his concubines, he should take one wife, and that a Christian woman would be best; God, he said, would then not render his wishes fruitless. The counsel pleased the prince.

[Col. 1335A]

He sent marriage-brokers to Boleslaus the Fratricide, duke of Bohemia, asking in the duke’s name for his daughter Dambrowka in marriage—a most beautiful woman and deeply devoted to the Christian faith. Dombrowka, however, was unwilling to enter the marriage before the Poles, together with their duke, had accepted the Christian faith.

Misego therefore, with the agreement of the barons—who were scarcely moved except by a miracle—was baptized beforehand “with the entire Lechitic people,” and thereafter, in the year 966, married Dambrowka [Note: Gallus, p. 31; Kadlubek II, col. 740; and fourteenth-century authors: *Chronicle of the Poles* (Stenzel, *Writers of Silesian Affairs* I, p. 9), *Brief Chronicle of Silesia* (ibid., p. 33), *Chronicle of the Princes of Poland*, p. 47. [Lacuna.] Dlugosz embellished the same account in a remarkable manner, Leipzig edition, I, col. 89 and following, as did those who followed him: Michow, p. 22; Kromer; and others; finally Stredowski, *Moravia Sacra*, p. 136, and Balbinus, *Epitome*, book I, chapter 7].

Finally, all the idols in his entire dominion were broken at the duke’s command and the temples burned, on the Sunday called *Laetare* before the Nones of March in the following year. Thus, in a wondrous manner, at the first blow—or, so to speak, at the first glance and nod of the prince—the idolatry vanished without leaving even the smallest trace.

[Col. 1335B]

It is also said that, immediately after his sacred baptism, Misego—or Dambrowka—organized all the churches and bishoprics of Poland; established two metropolitan sees at Gnesen and Cracow; and appointed under them, by metropolitan right, seven bishops: the bishop of Posen, of Smogorzow, later Breslau, of Kruszwica, later Wladislaw or Leslau, of Plock, of Culm, of Lebus, and of Caminiec. I say nothing of the churches and monasteries.

They name among the bishops Cardinal Aegidius, bishop of Tusculum and apostolic legate of John XIII [Note: Roepell incorrectly has John III instead of John XIII, following the Leipzig copy of Dlugosz], who, sent by the supreme pontiff, confirmed the bishoprics and set their boundaries—the privileges concerning which were destroyed by fire. They also say that Misego assigned to the churches a tenth of all crops, and that the “baronage” of Poland emulated the practices of princes in constructing and founding churches [Note: *Chronicle of Poland* (as cited), p. 9; the commentator on Kadlubek (as cited), col. 641, although at col. 644 he relates the same things of Boleslaus; Dlugosz himself, col. 95 and following; Matthias of Miechów, *Chronicle*, pp. 22–23; Cromer, Bielski, and others].

[Col. 1335C–D]

# Chapter VIII.—The Same Misego I According to the German Sources

These or similar things are remembered by Polish authors concerning Misego I. But since none of them lived in those times, and all are at least several centuries later, I have judged that they were supported by vague tradition or led by a blind love of their homeland and the Roman rite; that each, in his own way, concealed part of the truth and distorted it, or even added a patch to it.

The German writers of this period, or at least those living not much later, portray the first Misego differently. They seem all the more worthy of belief because one or another of the most ancient Polish annalists agrees with them.

[Col. 1336A]

They therefore relate that King Mieszko was twice defeated in battle by a certain Wichmann (a kinsman of Otto the Great, but, because of quarrels with him, an exile from Germany), who at that time was leading barbarian forces—Pomeranian or otherwise [Note: [Col. 1335D] Widukind III, chapters 66 and 69, in Meibom I, p. 660]. Thietmar records that by Gero himself, Margrave of the eastern Lusici and Selpuli, Mieszko, together with those subject to him, was brought under imperial rule in the year 963 [Note: [Col. 1335D] Thietmar, edited by Wagner, p. 27]. The exceptionally astute Roepell rightly observes that at that time the Slavic peoples were being subdued by the Germans, not merely to advance the boundaries of the Empire, but also to propagate the Christian religion [Note: [Col. 1335D] Roepell, *History of Poland*, 1840, vol. I, p. 95].

Thus, in the second year after Mieszko’s defeat, they relate that Dubrawka, daughter of Boleslaus, brother of Saint Wenceslaus (or, as Boguphalus has it, the sister of that martyr) [Note: [Col. 1336D] *Chronicle of Batzko*; Paprocki, *Catalogue of the Archbishops of Gniezno*; Wostokow, *Life of Saint Wenceslaus*. Cf. Thietmar, p. 97, and Maciejowski, pp. 135 and 237], married him in the year 965; and that Mieszko, together with part of the Poles, was not washed in the waters of baptism until the following year. They further relate that Jordan, the first Christian prelate in this region, labored greatly among the Poles while diligently inviting them, by word and deed, to the worship of the heavenly vineyard [Note: [Col. 1336D] Thietmar, ibid., p. 97, with whom the Polish writers agree: Boguphalus, in Sommersberg, *Writers on Silesian Affairs*, p. 27; *Brief Chronicle of Kraków*, ibid., p. 79; *Annals of Poznań*, ibid., p. 81; other annals, ibid., p. 94; and the *Greater Annals of Kraków*, in the Danzig edition of Kadlubek, p. 34; all cited by Roepell, loc. cit.].

The same Jordan, they say, was ordained in 968 as bishop of Poznań—or bishop of all the Poles—and as suffragan of the archiepiscopal see of Magdeburg, which Otto the Great had established and founded at that very time [Note: [Col. 1336D] Boguphalus, in Sommersberg, p. 27; *Annals of Hildesheim*; *Annals of Weissenburg*; Lambert of Hersfeld; *Annals of Altaich*]. Through this ecclesiastical and political alliance with the Ottos, Mieszko acquired as enemies the aforementioned enemy of Otto, Wichmann, and the barbarian pagans under his command; a fierce battle was fought, the barbarians were put to flight, and Wichmann fell [Note: [Col. 1336D] Widukind, p. 660].

While Otto the Great was residing in Italy, war arose between the Margrave Udo and Mieszko. For the victor Udo’s pride could not be overcome even by Mieszko’s most humble arts [Note: [Col. 1336D] Thietmar, p. 116]. In the bloodiest battle, therefore, the Germans were defeated and paid the penalty of their pride; and the Margrave, together with the father of Dietmar, barely escaped by flight—a just vengeance [Note: [Col. 1336D] *Life of Saint Adalbert*, in Canisius, *Ancient Readings*, edited by Basnage]. In the following year Otto was present at the assembly at Quedlinburg, and by the emperor’s command the Polish duke Mieszko and the Bohemian duke Boleslaus II came together there [Note: [Col. 1336D] Thietmar, p. 37]. The dispute was settled, and, enriched with gifts, they returned joyfully to their own territories.

Soon after Otto the Great’s death, however, the same two dukes [Col. 1337A] took the side of Henry the Quarrelsome, Duke of Bavaria [Note: [Col. 1337D] Lambert of Hersfeld, under the year 974; *Annals of Altaich*, under the year 974 (Staindel, in Aventinus, p. 477)]. As the new King Otto II’s cousin, Henry followed the example of his father, who is known to have frequently fought with his brother Otto the Great; he raised a civil war in his ambition for the kingdom and proved worthy of the surname “Quarrelsome” [Note: [Col. 1337D] I do not know by what error Johann David Köhler, in his *Augustan Saxon Genealogy*, attached the surname “Quarrelsome” to the father rather than the son. Certainly, that otherwise very diligent writer, so rich in citations of authorities, names no author for this claim, although both father and son seem fully deserving of this surname.].

Some infer that there was a certain relationship among these three dukes, maintaining that Boleslaus II (the brother of Dambrowka) had married Emma of Burgundy, sister of Gisela, the wife of Henry the Quarrelsome [Note: [Col. 1337D] Palacký, *History of Bohemia* I, p. 230; Roepell I, p. 99].

Henry was defeated by Otto II and entrusted to the custody of the bishop of Utrecht. After Otto II’s death, however, he took up arms for a second time, intending to wrest the Empire from the young child Otto III, his cousin’s son. While Otto was staying at Quedlinburg, Mieszko, Mistui, and Boleslaus, together with the other dukes, came to him, affirming by oaths that they would henceforth give him aid as their king and lord [Note: [Col. 1337D] Thietmar, p. 65]. Henry nevertheless soon abandoned the armed struggle and returned to peace with Otto; the dukes followed him, and Mieszko submitted himself to King Otto [Note: [Col. 1337D] The same, p. 69].

By then Dubrawka had died (in 977) [Note: [Col. 1337D] *Saxon Annals*, under 977; Cosmas, *Chronicle*; Dobrowsky and Pelzel, *Writers on Bohemian Affairs* I, p. 53]. Mieszko took another wife, Oda, daughter of Margrave Dietrich, a nun, and therefore not without the gravest scandal to the clergy [Note: [Col. 1337D] Thietmar, p. 98; *Saxon Annals*, under 987. Dobner, in his notes on Hájek III, p. 297, places the event in 983], though God nevertheless willed this union.

For when, in the meantime, the pagans dwelling along the Elbe and Oder had expelled the Christians from their region, Mieszko repeatedly acted as ally of the Emperor or of the Margraves and fought against the pagans [Note: [Col. 1337D] *Annals of Hildesheim*, under 985, in Leibniz, *Writers on Brunswick Affairs*, I, col. 720: “Mieszko came with a large army as reinforcements.” The same, under 986: “King Otto, still a very young boy, came with a large army of Saxons into Slavonia; and Mieszko came to him there with a very great multitude, offered him a camel and many other gifts, and submitted himself also to his power.” The same, under 991: “Otto … with Mieszko’s reinforcements besieged and defeated Brandenburg.”]

Finally, the old man died in the year 992, on the eighth day before the Kalends of June—that is, 25 May [Note: [Col. 1338D] *Annals of Hildesheim*, under 992; Thietmar, p. 99].

## CHAPTER IX.—Whether Mieszko the First Could Be Called a King, and Whether He Is Our Mieszko

Neither the Poles nor the Germans seem to have spoken the unvarnished truth: the former maintain that Poland was in no way and at no time bound to the authority of the German Roman Empire; the latter everywhere represent it as subject to a feudal bond [Note: [Col. 1338D] In the very words of the *Polish Chronicle of Silesia*, in Stenzel, loc. cit., p. 9: “This Mieszko of Poznań himself acknowledged that he was a feudal vassal of the Empire.”].

It is certain that Mieszko established only one bishop for the Poles, at Poznań; that most of the Poles accepted the Christian faith with the Duke unwillingly, and not all of them; and that the neighboring barbarians and pagans were ready to fight for their idols and to wage war against the Christians. Mieszko therefore needed the Emperor’s assistance no less than the Emperor needed his. What more is there to say? A certain association was formed between the greater and the lesser—a loose but intimate one—which the Ottos were less eager to disturb through the arrogance of imperial dignity than Udo or the other Margraves [Note: [Col. 1338D] Thietmar, p. 116].

For this reason Widukind simply calls him “the Emperor’s friend” (III, ch. 69). Much, however, is said about Mieszko’s rank: whether he was a king or a duke. German sources usually call him a duke, though some also call him a king [Note: [Col. 1338D] Widukind, in Meibom I, p. 660; III, ch. 66, in Pertz’s edition of the *Monumenta*, p. 463]. In the Middle Ages barbarian rulers were often designated very carelessly as dukes, petty kings, or kings, though very often with a certain arrogance intended either to abase them or to exalt them. In the best Latin usage, *dux* would also sound inappropriate; for the feudal sense in which a duke presides over a hereditary fief at his lord’s command is wholly foreign to the Latins, and in the eleventh century of our era had not yet taken full effect.

To me this dispute seems to concern a mere trifle. It is enough to have touched upon it here, since we shall treat it more fully below (Chapter XXXIV). Whatever the case may be, no one will deny that this Mieszko was the first Christian prince in Poland, in the sense of the Latin Church; and therefore his father cannot be called the source of the Christian faith by a woman who favored the Latin Church.

It follows that what is said in our manuscript about Mieszko’s father cannot in any way be understood of Zemomysł; and therefore his son Mieszko I cannot be the Mieszko of our manuscript.

There remains the second Mieszko, whose father Boleslaus was truly a certain source of the Christian faith in this region, as we shall demonstrate in due order.

## CHAPTER X.—Of Boleslaus I, Father of Mieszko II. He Obtains Rule over All Poland and Supplies Auxiliaries to the Emperor

[Col. 1338C]

What Polish and German writers relate about Boleslaus I is more mutually consistent, and the Ruthenian writers do not wholly disagree. We shall therefore recount the points that are established, chiefly under the guidance of Roepell [Note: [Col. 1338D] Roepell, *History of Poland* I, pp. 105 ff.], in summary fashion, without omitting matters on which the authors disagree.

Dambrowka the Bohemian bore Mieszko a son in the year 967. He was given the name of his maternal uncle (and perhaps grandfather), Boleslaus, which means “very famous” [Note: [Col. 1338D] Długosz, loc. cit., col. 97]. While his father was still alive, and when he was only seventeen years old, he abandoned his first wife, the daughter of Rigdag, Margrave of Meissen [Note: [Col. 1339D] Thietmar, p. 99; of her Długosz and the others say nothing], and married his cousin Judith, daughter of Géza, king of Hungary, and of his own maternal aunt Adelheid [Note: [Col. 1339D] Długosz, loc. cit., col. 107].

It is known that Adelheid had been baptized together with her brother Mieszko I, and that, through her marriage to Géza, prince of the Hungarians, in 968 she brought the first seeds of the Christian—or Latin?—faith, if not into that region, at least into the Magyar dynasty [Note: [Col. 1339D] Ibid., col. 98. Clovis was not the first Christian in Gaul. Cf. Schwartz, Gabriel, *Beginnings of Religion among the Hungarians at Juxta Hornada*, Frankfurt and Leipzig, 1748, and Maciejowski, loc. cit., p. 194]. From Judith Boleslaus had a son in 990, who was given the name Bezprim or Otto [Note: [Col. 1339D] Thietmar, ibid., p. 99]. Others relate that he was Mieszko II, his grandfather rejoicing that he had seen his grandson before departing this life [Note: [Col. 1339D] Długosz, col. 110].

Boleslaus I succeeded his father, who died in 992; his reign of thirty-four years was among the most glorious in the annals of the Poles [Note: [Col. 1339D] Thietmar and the *Annals of Hildesheim*, as we have seen above. In opposition to them, Długosz and those who followed him—Miechow, Cremer, and others—give 999 as the year of Mieszko’s death].

Boleslaus enlarged the tender beginnings both of faith and of power that he had received from his father, extending the boundaries of the kingdom from the River Sala to the Borysthenes, and from the Danube to the Baltic Sea; founding monasteries, churches, and bishoprics; and attacking with the sword those who despised the Gospel (and the Latin rite?). His name became as great among the Poles as that of Charlemagne in the West, so that they represented every great undertaking as begun, accomplished, or completed by him [Note: [Col. 1339D] Gallus, loc. cit.; Długosz]. In virtues and vices alike he closely resembled him.

Mieszko, his father, is said to have ordered on his deathbed that the kingdom be divided among his sons: Boleslaus, the eldest, and those whom Oda had borne—Mieszko, Świętopełk, and another Boleslaus. His father’s wish, however, proved vain. Certainly, Boleslaus’s full brothers enjoyed the kingdom for no more than three years, since Boleslaus expelled them, together with their stepmother, whether at that time or earlier [Note: [Col. 1339D] Thietmar, p. 99; an old manuscript book cited by Dobner in his notes on Hájek IV, p. 409].

At that time he sent Emperor Otto III only auxiliary soldiers to fight against the pagan Slavs, the Havellians, who had not yet returned either to the Empire or to Christ [Note: [Col. 1339D] *Annals of Hildesheim*, in Pertz V, p. 69]; either because war was threatening him from Vladimir, prince of the Russians [Note: [Col. 1340D] *Annals of Hildesheim*, under 992], or because he had not yet obtained control of all Poland. In the year 995, however, fearing no further civil war at home, he himself was present with a large army; and there can be no doubt that a large part of the victory was owed to Boleslaus [Note: [Col. 1340D] *Annals of Hildesheim*, under 995, in Pertz V, p. 91].

## CHAPTER XI.—Boleslaus I Defeats the Pomeranians and Perhaps the Prussians

In that revolt of the pagan Slavs, the Havellians, although the sources and monuments are silent, I have no doubt that they made use of the neighboring Pomeranians and other barbarians, if not as allies or confederates, at least as auxiliaries. For at that time the Normans too (in 994) not only ravaged the coasts of Saxony and Frisia, but also ascended the rivers Elbe and Weser in ships and fought, though under adverse fortune in war [Note: [Col. 1340D] Mascov, *On Otto III*, p. 158].

It is therefore not surprising that, immediately after the Havellians had been subdued, Boleslaus attacked the enemies both of the Empire and of the faith with the sword in their own territories. He certainly reduced the Pomeranians to his authority at once and appointed a certain Reinbern bishop of Kolberg [Note: [Col. 1340D]

Helmold I, ch. 15: “At the same time Boleslaus, the most Christian king of the Poles, allied with Otto III, subjected all Slavonia beyond the Oder to tribute; and also Russia and the Prussians.”

Roepell I, p. 106, note 3, cites the author of the *Life of Saint Adalbert* (Canisius, *Ancient Readings*, edited by Basnage III, p. 56), where the following is read: “He himself [Saint Adalbert] visited the city of Gdańsk, whose shores touch the boundaries of the sea dividing the exceedingly extensive kingdom of the duke.”

Kannegiesser, *History of Pomerania* I, pp. 295–308.]

As for the neighboring Prussians—Gdańsk is named—the matter is not sufficiently clear. That the Prussians living beyond the Vistula were also defeated at that time is even less certain, so that judgment on the point should be suspended for the present. If Helmold, [Col. 1340B] whose testimony here is of the greatest value, had spoken only of the Prussians, I would believe that the Prussians—all of them—were then subdued. But since he adds the Russians, whom it is known the Poles attacked only when the great Vladimir was growing old—that is, approximately twenty years after these events—I would not grant this.

Add that in the *Life of Saint Adalbert* the city of Gdańsk is said to divide Boleslaus’s kingdoms. How, I ask, can this be understood if that city had been under Polish rule? The martyrdom of Saint Adalbert itself shows that Boleslaus possessed at most very limited authority among them. For if the Prussians had already been defeated or reduced under Polish power, Boleslaus would have appointed a bishop for the Prussians, just as he did for the Pomeranians.

## CHAPTER XII.—The Life and Death of Saint Adalbert

[Col. 1340C]

The matter itself seems to advise that we discuss Saint Adalbert more fully. According to Długosz’s account, Boleslaus the Bohemian had already founded a Latin episcopal see in Prague Castle in 973 or 974, at the urging of his sister Dambrowka. Its first bishop, Ditmar, a religious man who lived a monastic life, a Saxon by nation but somewhat versed in the Slavonic language, had been promoted to the office under the direction of that same Duchess of Poland [Note: [Col. 1340D] Długosz I, col. 102].

In 981, however, Ditmar, afflicted by a severe illness, declared before all who were present as he lay dying that he would be condemned, because he himself had lived too loosely and because the Bohemian people had willingly plunged themselves into their own desires and pleasures. [Col. 1340D] Adalbert was also present, Bohemian by nation and language, born of noble parents, and shortly afterward elected bishop of Prague by acclamation of the clergy and people [Note: [Col. 1341D] Ibid., col. 105 ff.].

Struck by the words of his predecessor, he abandoned all sumptuous foods and clothing, clothed his flesh at night in a hair shirt, sprinkled his head with ashes, and, transformed from a “delicate” soldier into another man, distributed everything he possessed among the poor, orphans, and widows [Note: [Col. 1341D] Ibid., col. 106].

But among so barbarous a people, passionately attached to the Slavonic-Greek rite, Adalbert, imbued with the principles of the West, achieved nothing either by words or by example. For, as they say, the Christian Bohemians abused several wives; practiced pagan and sacrilegious rites; sold their own subjects, sons and daughters marked with the sign of Christ, into slavery to the Jews; frequented the marketplaces on Sundays; chose [Col. 1341B] profane places for burial; and held in contempt every correction administered by the bishop.

For this reason the holy man abandoned his see in 989 and, intending to visit Jerusalem, went to Rome. In that city, however, he remained with his brother—“in Christ,” as some would have it [Note: [Col. 1341D] Vogt, *History of Prussia*]—Gaudentius, practicing the monastic life [Note: [Col. 1341D] Długosz, col. 110].

The Bohemians, driven into a frenzy by Adalbert’s departure, turned against his five brothers, who favored both the German and the Latin cause, and against their lineage and homeland, the town of Libice; they slaughtered the inhabitants and burned the town [Note: [Col. 1341D] Ibid., col. 113 ff.].

At the insistence of the archbishop of Mainz, whose suffragan the bishop of Prague then was, and at the urging of the Supreme Pontiff, he returned to Prague with Gaudentius and other pious men in 994. But he again abandoned his see and went to Hungary to promote the word of God—that is, the Latin rite—there.

In the following year he prepared to travel to Poland to Boleslaus I, with whom the one surviving brother already lived; he was received with great honor [Note: [Col. 1341D] Ibid., col. 113 ff.]. After staying for some time at Kraków, he taught and celebrated the office in the Bohemian language, which the inhabitants—of the same origin and at that time subject to the Bohemians—understood well enough.

From there, proceeding to Gniezno, he left his brother Gaudentius there, as some maintain [Note: [Col. 1341D] *Life of Saint Adalbert*, in the *Acts of the Saints*, 23 April, p. 185; Długosz, col. 118; Długosz already makes Adalbert and Gaudentius archbishops of Gniezno]. Others, however, relate that Gaudentius was Saint Adalbert’s faithful companion in all things [Note: [Col. 1341D] Vogt, loc. cit.].

To preach the true faith to the Prussians, Adalbert, provided with a ship by Boleslaus and accompanied by thirty soldiers, first went to the city of Gdańsk, where a large number [Col. 1341D] of barbarians were washed by him in the sacred waters of baptism. Then, in the same ship but leaving the escort behind, he went to eastern Prussia. After suffering many repulses, he profaned a sacred Germanic grove and was finally struck by seven wounds by a priest of the idols; thus he died near Tenkitten, situated between the towns of Fischhausen and Pillau, on the tenth day before the Kalends of May in the year 997. His companions were captured but released [Note: [Col. 1341D] Roepell, loc. cit., p. 108; Długosz, col. 119 ff.].

Boleslaus I is said to have bought the body of the holy martyr from the Prussians. They add that the barbarians demanded only as much silver [Note: [Col. 1341D] Długosz, col. 125 ff. Roepell has “gold”; I do not know from what source he dug it up. *Saxon Chronicle*, under 996: “with the duke as purchaser”] as the saint’s body weighed, and that by a miracle it was found to be very light [Note: [Col. 1341D] Długosz, col. 128 ff.].

The body was carried back to Poland accompanied by a great multitude of clergy and laymen, and was deposited in the city of Gniezno with the greatest pomp and buried with the highest honors. There, soon afterward, the martyr’s relics became celebrated among all Christians through the working of miracles [Note: [Col. 1341D] Ibid., col. 127].

## CHAPTER XIII.—Chrobatia Subdued by Boleslaus I

After Boleslaus the Pious, Duke of the Bohemians, died in 999, his son Boleslaus, surnamed the Red, succeeds him; he was the cousin [Note: [Col. 1341D] Adelbold, p. 440. He has “grandson,” apparently in the sense in which our “nephew” and “niece” were designated in medieval Latin by *nepos* and *neptis*. For Boleslaus the Cruel—the fratricide—was the grandfather of both Boleslauses: the Poles through their mother Dambrowka, the Bohemians through their father Boleslaus the Chaste] of our Polish Boleslaus.

Our Boleslaus, perhaps in order to vindicate a maternal inheritance in the Bohemian kingdom and to reap the fruit of the seed scattered there by Saint Adalbert, invaded Chrobatia and captured Kraków, the chief city of the region. He reduced most of Silesia, Moravia, and finally Slovakia to his power, intending to make Kraków the new seat of his kingdom, situated in the midst of his territories [Note: [Col. 1342D] Kadlubek I, p. 99; *Polish Chronicle*, loc. cit. I, p. 10; Cosmas, p. 66; Dobner, notes on Hájek IV, p. 456].

The fame of the Polish prince soon spread throughout the entire land. The greatest kings of the age sought a marital connection with him [Col. 1342C]. He gave his sister Sigrid in marriage to Sweyn, king of the Danes, who conquered Britain and by whom she bore a son, Canute the Great, king of the Danes, Normans, and Anglo-Saxons [Note: [Col. 1342D] *Old Scholarly Notes of Adam of Bremen*, 22; Thietmar, book VIII; Dahlmann, *History of Denmark* I, pp. 89 and 100; Roepell I, p. 110].

A daughter of Boleslaus, whose name is not recorded, married Sviatopolk, stepson of Vladimir the Great, king of the Russians, who had very recently been the first of the Normans in Russia to be converted to the Christian faith according to the Greek rite [Note: [Col. 1342D] Gallus, etc.; Thietmar, pp. 239, 244, and 265].

## CHAPTER XIV.—Otto III Comes to Gniezno. Archbishops and Bishops Are Ordained

The Emperor Otto III, then residing in Italy, astonished by the immense fame and glory both of Saint Adalbert and of Boleslaus, burned with a desire to visit either Adalbert [Note: [Col. 1342D] Boguchwal, in Sommersberg, *Writers on Silesian Affairs* II, p. 25, and the German sources], or Boleslaus [Note: [Col. 1342D] Certain Polish writers], or both [Note: [Col. 1342D] Gallus, p. 38; Kadlubek I, p. 93; Długosz, etc.].

Setting out from Rome toward the end of the year 999 [Note: [Col. 1342D] Roepell I, p. 110], he arrived in Poland in midwinter. Boleslaus received him with the highest honors, and honored him with the most precious gifts [Note: [Col. 1343C] Thietmar, p. 90 ff.; *Chronicle of Quedlinburg*, in Pertz V, p. 77, under 1000; Gallus, pp. 41–43; Długosz I, cols. 129, 130, and 134].

Whether Otto acted together with Boleslaus, or Boleslaus with Otto, or finally whether the Supreme Pontiff acted through both, the ecclesiastical affairs of Poland were arranged in such a way that, despite the opposition of the bishops of Magdeburg and Poznań [Note: [Col. 1343C] *Saxon Annals*, under the relevant year; *Saxon Chronicle*, under 996; Mascov, *On Otto III*, pp. 175 ff., and notes 12 and 40; Thietmar IV, p. 357], a new archiepiscopal see was established at Gniezno [Note: [Col. 1343C] Thietmar, p. 92; *Saxon Chronicle*, in Leibniz, *Additions to History*, p. 205; *Chronicle of the Princes of Poland*, in Stenzel, *Writers on Silesian Affairs* I; *Life of Saint Stanislaus*, in Bandtkie, *Great Chronicle of Gallus*, p. 322], with the new suffragan sees of Kraków [Note: [Col. 1343D] Thietmar, p. 92; *Saxon Chronicle*; *Saxon Annals*; *Life of Saint Stanislaus*, ibid.; *Chronicle of the Princes of Poland*, ibid.], Wrocław [Note: [Col. 1343D] Thietmar, p. 92; *Life of Saint Stanislaus*, ibid.; *Chronicle of the Princes of Poland*, ibid.], and the recently established see of Kolberg [Note: [Col. 1343D] Ibid.].

It is not sufficiently certain whether the bishops of Mazovia (Płock) and Lubusz were established by Boleslaus or after his death [Note: [Col. 1343D] Boguphalus, loc. cit. II, p. 25; a letter of Pope Gregory the Great from 1075; Friese, *History of the Polish Church* I, pp. 130–132; *Saxon Chronicle*, under 996; Thietmar IV, p. 357; *Annals of Altaich*, under 1000: “The Emperor Otto entered Slavonia for the sake of prayer to Adalbert, bishop and martyr; and, a synod having been assembled there, he arranged seven bishoprics and ordered Gaudentius, the monk and brother of Adalbert, to be ordained archbishop.” *Annals of Hildesheim* and Lambert of Hersfeld, under 1000].
