Nor would I dismiss, as Roepell and others have done [Note: [Col. 1343D] Roepell I, p. 113], those who relate that Boleslaus was then honored by the Emperor with the royal title [Note: [Col. 1344C] Długosz I, col. 131; Dubravius; Krantz; Neugebauer, *History of Poland* III, ch. 53; Ludewig, *On Royal Auspices*, ch. II, p. 77], with royal insignia—that is, a crown, lance, and sword [Note: [Col. 1343B] Commentary on Kadlubek and Długosz I, cols. 131 ff. and 134; Neugebauer, loc. cit. Cf. Ademar of Chabannes, in Labbe II, p. 169]. They also infer that the same Emperor arranged for Rixa, daughter of his sister Mathilda and Henry, Count Palatine of the Rhine, although still a child and therefore not married but betrothed, to be promised to Mieszko, the son of Boleslaus [Note: [Col. 1344C] Długosz I, col. 133].

## CHAPTER XV.—Boleslaus I Occupies Bohemia and the March of Meissen

After these events, unable to enjoy a long peace, Boleslaus I prepared new and less honorable wars. In January of the year 1002 the Emperor Otto III died, leaving no offspring. During his reign he had seemed a great friend to Boleslaus and the Poles. Henry the Saint, Duke of Bavaria, the last male descendant of Henry the Quarrelsome and Gisela of Burgundy, was elected king of Germany by a large part of the ecclesiastical and secular princes; his most powerful rivals were Hermann, Duke of Swabia, whom we shall discuss below, and Eckard, Margrave of Meissen, who was murdered while traveling at Poleda on the second day before the Kalends of May [Note: [Col. 1344D] Mascov, *On the Affairs of Henry II*, p. 192 ff.].

Without delay Boleslaus entered Germany, disturbed by civil unrest, with a huge army. He captured the city of Bautzen, invaded the March of Meissen, now deprived of its margrave, crossed the Elbe, captured the town of Strehla and Meissen itself, and finally the entire region as far as the Elster [Note: [Col. 1344D] Thietmar, p. 113 ff.; Roepell, p. 144].

Nevertheless, on the ninth day before the Kalends of August he came to Merseburg [Note: [Col. 1344D] *Annals of Quedlinburg*, in Pertz V, p. 78; the life of Henry by Bishop Adelbold, in Leibniz, *Writers on Brunswick Affairs* I, p. 433]. There he concluded peace with Henry II at the imperial assembly on these terms: Guncelinus, the brother of the murdered Eckard and connected with Boleslaus by loyalty and by some relationship of which I know nothing [Note: [Col. 1344D] Thietmar, p. 120; Kreysig, *Contributions to Saxon History*], would become Margrave of Meissen; while all the lands beyond the Elbe, the regions of the Liutizi and Milseni, whose principal center was in some sense Bautzen, would be ceded to Boleslaus [Note: [Col. 1344D] Thietmar, p. 120].

Yet this treaty did not close the gates of war with sufficiently tight fastenings. For when Boleslaus was attacked by an ambush while returning home, he immediately entered into an alliance with Henry, Margrave of Schweinfurt. The latter had supported Henry’s election as king by every means, driven by the hope of acquiring the duchy of Bavaria through the new king. But when the King granted Bavaria to Henry of Luxembourg, his wife’s brother, the Schweinfurt Henry, disappointed in his hope, took up arms, intending by raising a civil war to seize by force what had been denied him.

His ally, Boleslaus, who supported the rebellion—not so much to defeat the king as to seize for himself a province of Germany—prepared to reduce all Bohemia to his power. In this he used no less cunning than force and cruelty. The duke of that region, Boleslaus III, surnamed the Red, had, through the arrogance of his tyranny, made the Bohemians so hostile to him during the three years of his rule that he was expelled from the duchy in 1002. His brother Wladivoy [Note: [Col. 1344D] Thietmar, pp. 122–123. Roepell, loc. cit. I, p. 116, makes him a certain Pole, supported, I do not know by what testimony. Adelbold, ch. XIV, p. 434, calls him a certain Slav, Blademar. Hübner, certainly, in his genealogical tables I, no. 105, lists Wladivoy among the five sons of Boleslaus the Chaste; Palacký seems to agree with him, *History of Bohemia*, p. 252. I have not examined the work itself; but there seems to be an error in Roepell’s wording when he cites the claim that Wladivoy was the brother of Boleslaus Chobry] [Col. 1344C], being more acceptable to the Bohemians, was made duke at Regensburg by King Henry [Note: [Col. 1344D] Adelbold, loc. cit.].

When this duke died at the beginning of the following year, Udalric and Jaromir, who had escaped the anger of their brother Boleslaus the Red by fleeing to Germany, were summoned by the Bohemians, but without success. Boleslaus I Chobry himself was already present at Prague in January with a huge Polish army. There he restored his cousin Boleslaus the Red, utterly disregarding the Bohemians and the king of Germany. The Pole returned to his homeland under the pretense that this alone had been his intention.

Meanwhile, having recovered his position, Boleslaus the Red abused his authority and raged more fiercely than was just against the authors of his misfortune. The Bohemians, enduring this with difficulty, summoned the same Pole; after blinding his cousin, he seized the duchy for himself toward the end of February and sought to make Prague the second seat of his rule [Note: [Col. 1345C] Thietmar, p. 125; Adelbold, loc. cit., pp. 435 and 440; Gallus, p. 36; Kadlubek I, p. 99; *Brief Chronicle of Kraków*, under 1001; *Polish Chronicle*, in Stenzel, p. 10; *Chronicle of the Princes of Poland*, ibid., p. 48; Długosz; Dobner, notes on Hájek IV, pp. 482 ff. and 499 ff.; Palacký, *History of Bohemia* I, p. 256]. But God decreed otherwise.

## CHAPTER XVI.—Boleslaus I Is Expelled from Bohemia; Lusatia Lost and Recovered; Peace Made

The greatest disaster from the Poles threatened Germany. Inflated with pride, Boleslaus Chobry despised the provinces that King Henry was to cede to him, having already seized them, and desired greater things. He sent assistance to Henry of Schweinfurt and, believing that Guncelinus favored him, himself invaded the March of Meissen in May. Disappointed in his expectation, however, he devastated those regions and carried an immense number of inhabitants into captivity [Note: [Col. 1345D] Thietmar, pp. 125, 128 ff.; Adelbold, p. 436; Dobner, notes on Hájek IV, p. 507].

At length King Henry, having meanwhile defeated the Margrave of Schweinfurt and captured his castle of Crusna (Creussen, below the city of Bayreuth), led the Thuringians and Saxons against the Poles toward the end of winter, in February of the year 1004. But the army, hindered by cold and snow, after ravaging the lands of Mizlavia here and there, returned in that same month of February, and the King entrusted the Margraves of the Elbe with guarding the frontier. [Col. 1345D]  
[Note: Thietmar, p. 130, 136ff.; Adelbold, p. 437.]

Hardly had Henry returned from Italy when, in the summer of that same year, he renewed the war. [Col. 1345C] As soon as the German army had reached the Bohemian frontier, the Bohemians defected from the Poles and, having received back their duke Jaromir, drove Bolizlav into flight in August. King Henry, leaving Prague, occupied Budissin in September. [Col. 1345D]  
[Note: Thietmar, pp. 142–145; Annals of Quedlinburg (Pertz V), p. 79, under the year 1004; Dobner on Hájek, V, p. 8.]

Winter indeed interrupted the war; nevertheless, in the following year, “King Henry, his anger against Bolizlav continuing, having restored his battle-line and hastening against Poland itself, pursued the fugitive, as though he were about to defend his own wrong.” [Col. 1345D]  
[Note: Chronicon Saxonicum, under the year 1005.]

He crossed the Oder near the town of Crossen; [Col. 1346A] and, when he was no more than ten thousand paces from the city of Posen, a certain peace is said to have been concluded, whose terms were not good: “Although grieving, the King returned in tears after accepting a bad peace.” [Note: Chronicle of Quedlinburg (Pertz V), p. 79.] This may also be inferred from the fact that Thietmar, Henry’s secretary, left no account of them for posterity. [Col. 1345D]  
[Note: Thietmar, pp. 148–153, gives a fuller description of the expedition but reports no conditions of the peace. From this Roepellius (p. 122) infers that the terms were favorable. Wrongly. For if Bolizlav himself had sought peace and had come into the King’s presence in order to surrender, I would believe that. But the contrary happened. For Henry sent Tagino, archbishop of Magdeburg, to Bolizlav to propose peace. Bolizlav had deliberately undertaken no battle up to that point, as elsewhere; [Col. 1346C] and, as a new Fabius Cunctator, he may perhaps then have been preparing to attack the German army, which, according to Thietmar, had already been reduced by hunger and the harshness of the terrain to half its original strength. Thietmar’s actual words are these: “Henry, no more than two miles [Col. 1346D] from the city of Posen, sat down at the request of his leading men. The army, however, divided among the gathering of crops and other necessities, suffered heavy losses from enemies lying in ambush. Meanwhile Bolizlav sought the King’s favor through trustworthy intercessors and soon deserved to be heard. Archbishop Tagino, with other familiar companions of the King, came at Bolizlav’s request to the aforesaid city, and, with oaths and suitable compensations, concluded firm treaties of peace with him. Then our men returned joyfully, for they were enduring great hardship from the length of the journey and excessive hunger, combined with the rigors of war.” Book VI, chapter 20; Pertz V, p. 813, lines 19–27.]

Perhaps only a truce was made. Certainly King Henry returned to Germany with his army; and for several years Bolizlav tried to form an alliance with the Slavs bordering on his territory against the Germans. When Henry had been informed of these matters by the Lutici and by Jaromir, duke of the Bohemians, he is said to have sent Count Hermann to Bolizlav to break the peace or truce—and this was done less prudently than promptly. For at the same time Baldwin with the Beard, count of Flanders, had to be defeated across the Rhine. Thus it happened that the King’s affairs went badly in both places. [Col. 1346B]

For in the year 1007 Bolizlav, accompanied by a multitude of armed men, approached the Elbe, brought the whole region of Lusatia, Zara (Sorau), and Selpuli (Fürstenwalde) under his power, and recovered the city of Budissin after besieging it for some time. [Col. 1346D]  
[Note: Chronicon of Quedlinburg, under the year 1007; Thietmar, p. 157; Roepell, I, p. 123.]

At the same time civil war was raging in Germany, not only between the King and the nobles but also among the individual margraves. For Guncelin, margrave of Meissen and Bolizlav’s ally, attacked Hermann, margrave of Lusatia, with arms. [Col. 1346D]  
[Note: Roepell, p. 124.]

Finally, in the year 1010, at a solemn assembly of the princes of Germany held at Merseburg, King Henry deprived Guncelin of the margraviate and, having united the margraviates of Meissen and Lusatia, placed Hermann, Guncelin’s opponent, over them. [Col. 1346D]  
[Note: Thietmar, pp. 170–171; Roepell, p. 125.]

But behold a remarkable thing! The crafty Bolizlav appears to have negotiated at that time, or shortly afterward, concerning the marriage of his daughter to Hermann. [Col. 1346C]

In the two following years the war was indeed renewed; but in the first of them the King was afflicted by illness, and his army, after uselessly besieging the town of Glogau and ravaging the districts of Diedesi (Crossen and Glogau) and Cilenzi (in the Silesian region near Mount Zobten), returned. [Col. 1346D]  
[Note: Thietmar, p. 179; Chronicon of Quedlinburg, under the year 1010.]

In the second year it accomplished even less, for the German army barely crossed the Elbe. Bolizlav, on the other hand, occupied the borders of Dalmantia (Meissen and [Col. 1347A] Strehlen), stormed the town of Libusuam, and returned home with a great number of captives. [Col. 1347D]  
[Note: Thietmar, p. 184; Chronicon Saxonicum (Leibniz, Accessiones historicae); Chronicon of Quedlinburg, under the year 1012.]

At length Bolizlav himself sought peace from King Henry. He was preparing for war against Vladimir, prince of the Russians; Bolizlav was always sufficiently cautious never to fight several enemies at once. He therefore sent his son Misego to Magdeburg, to the King, for the purpose of arranging peace. [Col. 1347D]  
[Note: Thietmar, p. 190; Chronicon of Quedlinburg, under the year 1013.]

If Długosz had no other source for this matter, this embassy of Misego undoubtedly moved him to report that Misego’s marriage to Rixa of the Palatinate had been celebrated in that year. [Col. 1347D]  
[Note: Długosz, column 161.]

After hostages had been given to Bolizlav by King Henry, Bolizlav himself came to him at Merseburg; and, according to Thietmar, after the King had granted him the lands he had conquered, “he gave himself to him.” [Col. 1347B]  
[Note: Thietmar, p. 191: “with hands joined, he became a soldier.” Chronicon of Quedlinburg, under the year 1013.]

Was this on account of those lands, just as the kings of England in a certain sense gave themselves to the kings of France for the duchy of Normandy?

After this submission had been secured, King Henry set out for Italy for the second time; and although Bolizlav had been ordered by the King to do so, he nevertheless gave him no auxiliaries and sent him none. [Col. 1347D]  
[Note: Thietmar, p. 192; the same, ibid.]

## CHAPTER XVII — The War against Vladimir, Great Prince of the Russians

For Bolizlav himself, as we have said, was preparing for war against Vladimir, eager to liberate his daughter, his son-in-law Suatopluk, and Bishop Reinber, a Latin. [Col. 1347C]  
[Note: Luc. David’s conjecture (I, pp. 96–98) that Bolizlav made war on the Prussians in this year, 1013, is a very poor one.]

Vladimir, Suatopluk’s stepfather, paternal uncle, and father, had indeed adopted him; but since Suatopluk strove, by right of paternal inheritance, to be not merely one of the sons of the Grand Prince but himself the sole prince, and perhaps was also favorable to the Latin Church, he was defeated by Vladimir and thrown into chains.

Bolizlav therefore invaded Russia with an army of Germans, Poles, and Pechenegs, ravaged the land; but when a quarrel arose between his own men and the Pechenegs, he withdrew home with his followers after the latter had been slaughtered. [Col. 1347D]  
[Note: Roepell, p. 146, following Thietmar, pp. 192 and 245.]

Naruszewicz thinks that the expedition against the Prussians took place in the year 1014. [Col. 1347D]  
[Note: Naruszewicz, IV.]

I myself judge that this is wholly inconsistent with the events in which Bolizlav was engaged during that year. For it is reported that he prepared a great confederation of all the nations of the Slavic race against the Empire. For this reason Misego was sent by his father to Udalric, duke of Bohemia, who had received his brother Jaromir into the duchy. But the Bohemian, loyal to the Empire, captured Misego by treachery and handed him over to Henry, who at that time was being crowned emperor in Italy. [Col. 1347D]  
[Note: Annals of Quedlinburg, under the year 1014; Thietmar, p. 206.]

Thus, if Bolizlav had simultaneously made war on the Prussians, he would have prepared for himself a third enemy at one and the same time; [Col. 1348A] and in the following year, when both Germans and Russians, joined in alliance, invaded Poland, the Prussians would certainly have used the opportunity to assert their freedom by defeating the Poles. Nor can I affirm, for the same reason, that this could have happened in the year 1015, when Długosz thinks that the Prussians were attacked by Bolizlav. [Col. 1348D]  
[Note: Długosz, column 161ff.]

## CHAPTER XVIII — Bolizlav’s War against the Emperor and the Russians, Joined in Alliance; Peace Made with the Emperor

During the four following years Bolizlav successfully turned the greatest impending dangers to his own advantage by accomplishing great deeds.

For after Ardoin had died in Italy, the Emperor could approach Bolizlav with all his forces; and, to say nothing of Vladimir’s death, a war threatened in Russia against Suatopluk, Bolizlav’s son-in-law, from his younger full brother Jaroslav. [Col. 1348B]

Although summoned by the Emperor to Merseburg at Easter, Bolizlav preferred to celebrate his daughter’s wedding safely at home with Hermann, margrave of Meissen and Lusatia, having purchased the votes of the German princes summoned to Merseburg. In fact, Misego, Bolizlav’s captive son, was returned to his father after he had promised many things—we do not know what. [Col. 1348D]  
[Note: Thietmar, p. 207; Annals of Quedlinburg, under the year 1014 [the source appears to read 1014, though the context may suggest 1015]; Annals of Hildesheim (Leibniz, Scriptores rerum Brunsvicensium I), p. 723.]

But the Emperor, realizing that he had been outwitted too late and seeing that everything he had hoped for had come to nothing, immediately raised an army. [Col. 1348D] Saxons, Bohemians, and Bavarians were led against the Poles, each people separately. On the eighth day before the Ides of July the Oder was indeed crossed; but [Col. 1348C] the Emperor, separated from the other troops with his own force and fearing for the safety of his men, turned his back and was grievously harassed by the Poles on the march. [Col. 1348D]  
[Note: Thietmar, pp. 210–216; Annals of Quedlinburg, under the year 1015.]

In the following year, therefore, 1016, the Emperor devoted himself to affairs in Burgundy and elsewhere, so that everything might be settled before he undertook a new and great expedition against Bolizlav, an enemy extremely powerful in courage, skill, and the nature of the terrain. Meanwhile Suatopluk, Bolizlav’s son-in-law, defeated by his brother Jaroslav in the year 1016 near Liubitsch on the bank of the Dnieper, fled to Bolizlav. [Col. 1348D]  
[Note: Nestor, German translation by Scherer, p. 120.]

At the beginning of the year 1017, although the Emperor on one side and Jaroslav on the other, united by treaty, were threatening Poland, Bolizlav nevertheless rejected every proposal of peace and refused to withdraw from the place where he was then staying, Scicciani (Schitzch, near Glogau), for the sake of making peace. [Col. 1348D]  
[Note: Thietmar, p. 231.]

The Emperor therefore led his army through Luticia and, having summoned the Bohemians, approached the town of Glogau [Col. 1349A] on the day before the Nones of August. This made it possible for Misego, at his father’s command, to ravage Bohemia, which had been stripped of its garrisons, and to carry a multitude of its inhabitants into slavery.

The Germans unsuccessfully besieged the town of Nemzi (Nimptsch, beside the river Lohe between Reichenbach and Ohlau); during the siege its garrison was increased by the Poles. At length the Emperor led his greatly diminished army home, admitting that Bolizlav could be conquered neither by skill nor by courage. The Poles, elated by victory, crossed the Elbe and ravaged everything as far as the Mulde. [Col. 1349C]  
[Note: Thietmar, pp. 235–239; Annals of Quedlinburg, under the year 1017; Annals of Hildesheim, under the year 1017.]

## CHAPTER XIX — Kiev Captured by Bolizlav and the Cherven Cities Occupied

Nor did Jaroslav, prince of the Russians, accomplish anything else by his incursion into Poland except that, in the following year, after peace had been arranged between the Emperor and Bolizlav at Budissin—in Poland itself—and after Oda, daughter of Eckard I, margrave of Meissen, had been taken in marriage, he was pursued by the victor with a vast army. [Col. 1349B]

The Russians, having suffered defeat at the Bug River, turned their backs. The victorious Poles brought Suatopluk back to Kiev and placed him on the throne. [Col. 1349C]  
[Note: Nestor, cited above.]

They report that Bolizlav himself struck the Golden Gate with the sword he had received from Otto III; and that, by this act, he boasted that he would violate Peredslava, the sister of “King” Jaroslav, who had been forbidden to be given to him that same night. [Col. 1349C]  
[Note: Gallus, p. 46; Kadlubek, p. 99; Boguphal II, p. 25; Chronicon Polonorum, p. 10; Chronicon principum Poloniae, p. 50.]

This was permitted to the “old fornicator.” [Col. 1349D]  
[Note: Thietmar, p. 265.]

For he captured ten women of royal descent: Jaroslav’s stepmother—perhaps Anna of Constantinople?—his wife, and eight sisters. [Col. 1349D]  
[Note: Thietmar, p. 265.]

The sword is said to have received the name Sczczerbca from that blow, and was reverently preserved by the Poles at Kraków for the coronation of their kings. [Col. 1349C]  
[Note: Naruszewicz, History of the Polish Nation, IV, p. 138.]

But when the Poles showed no mercy whatsoever to the defeated inhabitants of Kiev, [Col. 1349D] Suatopluk and the Russians, angered by this, slaughtered them one by one. Bolizlav therefore, looking after himself and his men, turned his journey homeward in order to escape the assassins, laden with spoils and dragging with him two of Jaroslav’s sisters and many captives. On the way he captured the cities they call the Cherven cities—Chelm, Przemyśl, and others—and annexed them to Poland. [Col. 1350C]  
[Note: Thietmar, p. 265; Pertz V, p. 871, line 7; Adam of Bremen, chapter 66. Although Kiev, the capital of Russia, was in a certain sense wealthy, Roepellius nevertheless seems to be mistaken, following Thietmar, when he says that there were then four hundred churches there (I, p. 148). For in the year 980 Vladimir professed the Christian faith and was the first—certainly among the Normans—to establish a church there, or even to transform some temples into Christian churches. But how, pray, could four hundred churches have been built there in the space of twenty-eight years? The number could in no way have been reached, even if one granted that some Christian churches had previously been built there privately.]

## CHAPTER XX — The Coronation of Bolizlav I According to Some, and His Death; Whether Bolizlav I May Be Called a Certain Source, etc.

[Col. 1350A]

This was the last but most glorious war fought by Polish arms under Bolizlav I. Seven years later, in 1025, he died on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of July. [Col. 1350C]  
[Note: The oldest Polish Annals (Sommersberg II), p. 81; Brief Silesian Chronicle (Stenzel, cited above, p. 34); Greater Annals of Kraków, under the year; Boguphal (book I), p. 25; Cosmas, in Dombrowsky, Scriptores rerum Bohemicarum, p. 85. Only Długosz gives the third day before the Nones of April.]

This was after, as some maintain, he had been crowned and anointed king. [Col. 1350D]  
[Note: Annals of Corvey (Pertz, Monumenta V, p. 5), under the year 1025; Annals of Quedlinburg (ibid., p. 90); Wippo, Life of Conrad (Struve, Scriptores rerum Germanicarum III, p. 470); Brief Chronicle, cited above; Roepell, I, p. 162. Otto of Freising, in Gottfried of Viterbo, wishes this to have happened in the year 1020; and Lambert of Hersfeld, under the year 1077, wishes Boleslav II the Bold to have been established as the first king of Poland.]

A messenger sent beforehand to the Supreme Pontiff concerning this matter is said to have been captured by the guards or spies of Emperor Henry, but freed by a miracle. [Col. 1350D]  
[Note: Life of Saint Romuald (Acta Sanctorum, 7 February), p. 114.]

I will add only that Bolizlav founded abbeys at Międzyrzecz, Tyniec, and elsewhere, as well as a monastery at Ostrów. [Col. 1350D]  
[Note: Annals of Altaich, under the year 1010.]

We have dealt at greater length with Bolizlav not only so that it might be clearer than daylight that he was the father of the Misego of our manuscript and could truly be called a certain source of the Christian faith in Poland, since he founded so many Latin bishoprics, [Col. 1350B] but also so that it might be easier to investigate what benefit the more obscure part of his life could derive from our letter of Mathilda. [Col. 1350D]  
[Note: Thietmar, p. 152.]

## CHAPTER XXI — Misego II from Polish Sources

Concerning Bolizlav’s son, Misego II, writers transmit accounts diametrically opposed to one another.

The Poles themselves disagree among themselves. All report that he was Bolizlav’s only son. Gallus says that “he was a good soldier and accomplished many military deeds, which it would take too long to recount; that he also, because of his father’s unpopularity, became hateful to all his neighbors, and was not, like his father, rich in life, character, or wealth; that he is said to have been captured by the Bohemians during a conference through treachery, and to have been bound with thongs around his genitals so that he could not beget children, because King Boleslav his father had inflicted a similar injury upon them when he blinded their duke and his own maternal uncle. He did escape from captivity, but afterward had no further relations with his wife.” [Col. 1350C]  
[Note: Gallus, p. 84; followed by the Chronicon principum Poloniae (Stenzel, book I).]

Others say that he loved peace but was nevertheless not cowardly. [Col. 1350D]  
[Note: Kadlubek, column 651; used by the author of the Chronicon Polonorum (Stenzel, book I) and by Długosz, column 187.]

Others say that, excessively credulous of his wife’s words, he lost through indolence the provinces occupied by his father. [Col. 1351A]  
[Note: Boguphal (Sommersberg II), p. 25; copied word for word by Kadlubek’s commentator, column 653. Compare the Life of Saint Stanislaus (Bandtkie, M. Gallus’s Chronicle, p. 323).]

Others finally give a fuller account, saying that he was elected at an assembly of the magnates and immediately anointed and crowned with his wife. [Col. 1351C]  
[Note: Długosz, column 180; Miechow; Stanislaus Sarnicius, Polish Annals (Długosz edition, Leipzig II), column 1050.]

He “sent his son, then in his seventh year, to the study of letters and provided serious and learned teachers for the boy. He was the first among the princes of Polish blood to be found to have ennobled learning more than the sword. For it is established that the other princes of Poland were never exercised in the study of letters.” [Col. 1351D]  
[Note: Thus Długosz, column 181ff.; similar statements in Miechow II, chapter 13, p. 37. Cromer has the same account, but Sarnicius denies it (column 1054), although they seem to have understood it more of Casimir than of Misego.]

Długosz alone, using a worse source—or one that he misunderstood—adds: “At the very beginning of his reign he appeared slow in intellect, dull in spirit, uncultivated in character, incompetent in judgment, frivolous in action, and little suited to serious affairs; having dismissed wise counselors advanced in age and venerable by nature, he entrusted himself to the counsels of young and frivolous men.” [Col. 1351B]  
[Note: Długosz, column 182; Miechow II, p. 35.]

The reader will therefore be all the more surprised to find the same Długosz reporting, along with others: “In the first year of his reign Misego attacked the Russians, who were pressing the Polish garrisons in the fortresses under siege, and suppressed their insolence; he even captured the leading Russians and sent them as hostages to Kraków.”  
[Note: Długosz, column 181; Sarnicius, column 1051.]

Meanwhile Bretislaus, son of the Bohemian duke Udalric by a peasant woman named Bozena, was a fierce and energetic young man. [Col. 1351D]  
[Note: Sarnicius, cited above; Długosz, column 182. Długosz adds that Bretislaus persecuted those who favored the Poles in Bohemia and refused tribute, while Misego passed over the matter in silence; thus, he says, the Bohemian dared greater things (column 183). But what is easier than to pass over in silence things that never happened?]

In the year 1028 he invaded Moravia, surrounded and captured the fortresses occupied by Polish garrisons. [Col. 1352D]  
[Note: Długosz, column 183; Sarnicius, column 1051.]

At length Misego did indeed lead an army into Moravia; but, unable to subdue the Moravians, who had become alienated, he merely avenged the defection by burning the towns around them, ravaging everything, and carrying home a great deal of livestock and other booty. [Col. 1351C]  
[Note: Długosz, column 184, under the year 1029.]

The governors of the provinces situated along the Elbe, from the borders of Bohemia to the sea, imitated this bad example of defection. [Col. 1352D]  
[Note: The same, ibid., columns 184–185, under the years 1030 and 1031; Sarnicius, column 1051.]

The Pomeranians, however, attempting the same thing, were attacked and defeated by Misego’s great army, aided by the combined forces of the three sons of King Saint Stephen of Hungary—Andrew, Bela, and Levente. Misego also gave his daughter in marriage to Bela and assigned the whole Pomeranian tribute to him to maintain his ducal position. [Col. 1352A]  
[Note: Długosz, column 186, under the year 1032; Sarnicius, column 1051.]

According to others, the cause of this was a single combat between Bela and the Pomeranian tyrant. [Col. 1352D]  
[Note: Długosz, column 186ff., who adds: “some prefer this account.”]

In the following year, 1033, Misego, having grown weak through leisure and tranquility, preferred to languish in idleness and quiet rather than to be occupied with arms and, according to the assertion of some, having meanwhile dissolved into luxury and carnal pleasures, stained the rights of marriage and the royal name by the contagion of mistresses. [Col. 1352D]  
[Note: Długosz, column 187.]

He “made his reputation dark and mutilated among his own people and foreigners through the obscurity of his innate stinginess, which had been nurtured by his wife, Queen Rikscha.” [Col. 1352D]  
[Note: The same, ibid.; Miechow II, p. 35.]

“It therefore seemed a heavy burden to the nobles that Misego should shine in royal dignity but lack the ‘lamp’ of royal character and virtues, and should depend upon a woman’s will.” [Col. 1352B]  
[Note: Długosz, ibid.]

At length he fell into madness. [Col. 1352D]  
[Note: Greater Annals of Kraków, cited above, under the year 1025, followed by Długosz, column 188, and Miechow II, p. 36.]

He died after three months and was buried at Posen in the year 1034. [Col. 1352D]  
[Note: Długosz, ibid.]

## CHAPTER XXII — What Roepellius Thinks of Misego from the Polish Sources

Roepellius rejects everything that the Poles report about Misego II and considers that they knew nothing true about this king. [Col. 1352D]  
[Note: Roepell, History of Poland I, p. 122.]

In this judgment he is too severe. If he had said that Misego was pleasing to very few Poles, neither while he lived nor after his death, and that for this reason the Polish writers suppressed some things, added others, and distorted many more, I would grant that Roepellius had come close to the truth. But he is not satisfied with denying all credibility to the Poles concerning this king; he also adds that the German sources, especially Thietmar, never err, either through mistake or fault, and indeed never omit anything. [Col. 1352C]  
[Note: The same, p. 122, note 35.]

No one will deny that Thietmar easily holds the first place among the historians of his age; yet below we shall see that he did not narrate “without anger and partiality.” The same thing happened to the Germans as to the Poles; but, as commonly happens, we are more verbose in prosperous matters than in adverse ones.

Roepellius therefore, relying chiefly on German sources, records the following concerning Misego II. [Col. 1352D]  
[Note: The same, pp. 164–173.]

## CHAPTER XXIII — Misego II from German Sources

Bolizlav Chrobry had three sons: Bezprim, who was also called Otto, Misego, and Dobremir. [Col. 1353A]  
[Note: Thietmar, pp. 99, 247; Annals of Hildesheim, under the year 1031.]

Misego deprived his brothers of part of the kingdom and perhaps assumed the royal name in the year 1025. [Col. 1353B]  
[Note: Annals of Saxony, under the year 1030; Monumenta of Queen Richza in Tölner, *Codex diplomaticus Palatinus*, pp. 25–32.]

Otto went into exile with his uncle Saint Stephen, king of Hungary. [Col. 1353C]  
[Note: Wippo and others say that he fled to Russia, or Rukhia; Palacky, *History of Bohemia*, p. 269, brings this into Hungary because in the Annals of Hildesheim, under the year 1031 (Pertz, *Monumenta* V), p. 98, Emmeric, son of Saint Stephen, is called duke of the Ruzzians, while the island of Rügen could not be intended by this name. Compare chapter XXXIX.]

Stephen occupied Slovakia and part of Moravia for himself, rather than for Otto, his sister’s son; Otto scorned the “tyrant” of Poland and instead ravaged the marches with a great army of his own men. [Col. 1353C]  
[Note: Annals of Hildesheim, under the year 1028; Life of Meinwerk, chapter 100 (Leibniz, *Scriptores rerum Brunsvicensium* I), p. 558.]

The new German emperor Conrad perhaps challenged him “with words and threats” on account of the royal dignity he had usurped.  
[Note: Wippo, p. 470.]

In the following year, 1029, the Emperor invaded the Polish frontier with a vast German army in order to avenge the devastation of the Poles; but, after unsuccessfully besieging Budissin, he led his troops home. [Col. 1353C]  
[Note: Annals of Hildesheim, under the year 1029; Annals of Saxony (Eccard, *Corpus historiae medii aevi* I), p. 460; Chronicon Saxonicum, under the year 1029 (Leibniz, *Accessiones historicae* I), p. 241.]

Meanwhile Bretislaus, son of the Bohemian duke, wrested all Moravia from both the Poles and the Hungarians. [Col. 1353B]  
[Note: Dobner on Hájek, V, p. 156ff.; Palacky, p. 271. Palacky thinks it should be inferred from a certain document that Moravia was captured in 1028, which Roepellius denies. In the year 1029 a certain duke of Poland was present at Olomouc as a witness to a document of Bretislaus; see Roček, *Codex diplomaticus Moraviae* I, p. III. Was he Otto or Dobremir? See Roepell.]

From the year 1029 onward he entrusted its defense to a certain Bohemian castellan at the castle of Gradez, near Troppau. [Col. 1353D]  
[Note: Roepellius, note 8, p. 107, cites several documents.]

Nor did Misego consider the loss of this province insignificant. In the year 1030, after Ditmar, margrave of Lusatia, had died, while the Emperor was making war upon the Hungarians, the King of Poland crossed the Elbe with a huge army under Udo, son of the deceased margrave, ravaged the entire region with fire and sword, and led ten thousand captives into Poland. [Col. 1353D]  
[Note: Annals of Saxony and Chronicon Saxonicum, under the year 1030.]

[Col. 1354A] These events moved the Emperor, after making peace with the Hungarians, to prepare for war both to avenge the marches and to restore Poland to Otto the Pole. Otto with his troops approached Poland from one side, while the Emperor with the Saxons approached from the other; nor were the Russians absent from the plundering of Poland.

Misego, unable to withstand both civil war and the Germans and Russians, preferred to purchase peace from the Emperor by returning Lusatia and all the booty. [Col. 1353D]  
[Note: Annals of Altaich, under the year 1031; Annals of Hildesheim; Wippo, p. 438.]

But he gained nothing from this arrangement. For Jaroslav, king of the Russians, crossed the Bug River, captured the Cherven cities and the town of Belz, and Misego himself, defeated by his brother, fled to the Bohemian Udalric. [Col. 1353D]  
[Note: Annals of Nestor, German translation by Scherer, p. 125, under the year 1031; Karamzin, *History of Russia* II, p. 19; Annals of Altaich, under the year 1031.]

Otto, however, purchased the Emperor’s favor by returning the royal crown and insignia. [Col. 1354B]  
[Note: Annals of Hildesheim, under the year 1031; Life of Meinwerk, chapter 108, p. 568; Wippo, cited above, p. 477; Annals of Saxony and Chronicon Saxonicum, under the year 1031.]

In the following year, 1032, Otto was killed by the Poles because of his tyranny, and Misego was recalled. On the Nones of July he submitted himself at Merseburg to the Emperor. [Col. 1353D]  
[Note: Annals of Hildesheim, under the year 1032; Wippo, cited above, p. 477; Annals of Altaich, under the year 1032.]

What was then restored or not restored to him is reported rather obscurely by the writers. [Col. 1353D]  
[Note: Wippo reports that Poland was divided into three parts. The Annals of Hildesheim say that the Emperor divided Misego’s possessions between him and his cousin Theodoric of Wettin; nevertheless, Misego afterward recovered everything for himself alone. [Col. 1354B] The Annals of Saxony have exactly the same account, as does the Chronicon Saxonicum, which is silent about the recovery. Hahn, *German Imperial and Royal History* II, p. 242, thinks this division should be understood of the Slavic-German marches situated between the Oder and the Elbe; he calls Theodoric a cousin because his father may perhaps have been the brother of Oda, the wife of Boleslav I. [Col. 1354C] Dobner on Hájek, V, p. 190ff., wishes Moravia and Silesia also to be understood there. Johann Schulz (*Poland Never Tributary*), followed by Naruszewicz IV, pp. 156, 164–169, and Bandtkie I, p. 174, thinks that the German annalists confused the Polish Misego with his contemporary Misego of the Obodrites, and the Polish Otto with Udo, son of Mistivoi and father of Gottschalk. Roepellius denies this because no chronicler of that period mentions any Misego of the northern Slavs, and because the deeds of Udo reported by Adam of Bremen and Helmold in no way agree with what is said about Otto the Pole.]

From the Polish sources Roepellius adds that the rebelling Pomeranians were defeated and that Misego granted tribute in Pomerania to his son-in-law Bela. [Col. 1354C]  
[Note: Naruszewicz IV, p. 173. In note 13, p. 171, Roepellius observes that Długosz first mentions the Pomeranians at column 186, under the year 1032. Thurocz, *Hungarian Chronicle* II, chapter 38 (Schwandtner, *Scriptores rerum Hungaricarum* I, p. 126ff.), tells nearly the same story from an ancient chronicle written no later than the year 1358, but says that the tyrant of Pomerania challenged Misego and his sons to single combat; Bela accepted the challenge and won the victory. Cromer changed this into the usufruct of Pomerania being assigned for administration, and Bandtkie, *History* I, p. 186, follows the same interpretation.]

But Roepellius warns that all this is suspect. [Col. 1354D]

For, first, Thurocz says that the sons took part in the expedition; yet it is known that Casimir was either born after his father’s death or was still a child. Second, he reports that the sons’ flight was caused by their conspiracy against the king, which occurred shortly before the king’s death. Roepellius, however, says that “Stephen” died on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of September in the year 1033. [Col. 1355B]  
[Note: Engel, *History of Hungary* I, p. 133ff.]

Misego, on the other hand, had already departed this life in the year 1034; therefore those Hungarians cannot appear to have assisted Misego.

We consulted Długosz, book I, column 198, where he says that they were already in exile before Saint Stephen died. See below.

Finally, Misego died in the year 1034.

## CHAPTER XXIV — Rixa and Casimir, and What Is Reported about the Other Sons of Misego II

[Col. 1355A]

The matter itself seems to warn us that we should briefly touch upon what these same writers transmit concerning the wife of Misego II and his offspring, so that nothing may be lacking in a true judgment of this chameleon among writers.

There is an old tradition concerning a concubine or another wife of Misego, not to be confused with Rixa. [Col. 1355B]  
[Note: In Kadlubek himself, at the place cited, column 651, the account is remarkably strange; and, if there is truth beneath it, as I suspect, the person who transmitted it did not understand it sufficiently. For there several things are read about a concubine, the mother—wrongly, according to Kadlubek, of Casimir—who died in childbirth; about the stepmother of that same son; and about the counsels of this stepmother to kill the child, “so that her own offspring might not eventually obtain the succession to the kingdom.” [Col. 1355C] In my judgment these statements can in no way be understood unless one assumes that the son in question was someone other than Casimir, the son of Rixa—perhaps Boleslav, whom others call Misego’s firstborn. Certainly the tradition as Kadlubek reports it supports this interpretation; for he adds, “the stepmother is proscribed,” which everyone sees must be understood of Rixa.]

The monk of Brauweiler gives a somewhat different account (Leibniz, *Scriptores rerum Brunsvicensium* I, p. 313ff.): because of such a concubine, while Misego was still alive, Rixa fled from Poland with her son Casimir.

This tradition seems to be confirmed by a charter of Richza in Miraeus I, p. 1131: “Richeza, queen of Poland, expelled from the kingdom, gives herself as a servant to the church of Saint Ursula, around the year 1030.”

Roepellius also cites this document, or rather rejects it, because in the text of the charter the sole word is *Richeza*, without the title “once queen of Poland,” which is found elsewhere in all her charters. But Roepellius did not see [Col. 1355D] that this very fact demonstrates the charter’s authenticity. “Once queen of Poland” had to be said after her husband’s death, not while he was still alive, even if she was in exile; for she could recover the throne, as indeed happened. Conversely, such a queen is rightly called expelled from the kingdom.

Gelenius gives the same account in *De Col . . . magnitudine* [title incomplete in the source], p. 334. He says that “at the counsel and through the pious admonitions of Bishop Pilgrim, Richeza gave and bound herself to the holy eleven thousand Virgins, so that she was obliged to redeem herself from their annual dues by a payment of twenty pounds of wax.”

Two names are also preserved, one Judith [Note: [Col. 1355D] Life of Saint Stanislaus, p. 323; Annals of Cracow, under 1025; Polish Chronicle (Stenzel), I, p. 9; Chronicle of the Princes of Poland, ibid., p. 36.], the other Rixa [Note: [Col. 1355D] Gallus, p. 84; Kadłubek, I, p. 106; Boguphalus (Sommersberg), II, p. 25.]; to pass over what some report through error, or because of the usage of those times, namely that she was the sister of Otto III [Note: [Col. 1355D] Gallus, p. 84; Kadłubek, I, p. 106; Boguphalus, ibid.; Life of Saint Stanislaus, p. 323; Annals of Cracow, under 1025; Polish Chronicle (Stenzel), I, p. 9; Chronicle [Col. 1356B] of the Princes of Poland, p. 36; Annals of Altaich, under 1035 (Staindel).], instead of the daughter of his sister or brother [Note: [Col. 1356B] Of the full siblings this is merely asserted; but concerning Rixa it is entirely certain. Thietmar, p. 100; Saxon Chronographer, under 1034; Account of the Brunweiler Monk (Leibniz, I), p. 313ff.; charters in Tölner, *Codex diplomaticus Palatinus*, pp. 27–29.], that one or the other had already been betrothed by Otto III when he was at Gniezno in the year 1000 [Note: [Col. 1356B] Boguphalus, p. 25; Life of Saint Stanislaus, p. 323 (saying that she had already married then); Długosz, col. 161; Cromer, book 3; Wippo; and Crantz, *Vandalia*, II.36.], but was married in 1013, and [Col. 1355B] gave birth to Casimir in 1015 [Note: [Col. 1356B] Chronicle of the Princes of Poland, p. 36; Długosz, ibid.; Tölner, *Historia Palatina*, p. 260. A.].

We have already noted that Misego’s firstborn son, whether by Rixa or by another woman, was given the name of his grandfather Bolizlav [Note: [Col. 1356C] Długosz, col. 187 C. He nevertheless relates that the boy, born of Rixa herself, died after several months while his father was still alive.], while the second was Casimir; and that a daughter of Misego married Béla.

[Col. 1356A] Scarcely had the father died when a dispute over the kingdom arose among the brothers [Note: [Col. 1356C] Commentator on Kadłubek, col. 653.]; that their mother Rixa ruled on behalf of Casimir, whom many regard as a child [Note: [Col. 1356C] Kadłubek, col. 651.], or, as others nevertheless hold, as not yet mature [Note: [Col. 1356C] The same, ibid.], although he was already twenty years old [Note: [Col. 1356C] Chronicle of the Princes of Poland, p. 57.]; but that she was excessively favorable to the Germans [Note: [Col. 1356C] Długosz, col. 189 C; Miechow, II.13, p. 36.], whom she had brought with her, and certainly displeased the Poles [Note: [Col. 1356C] Kadłubek, col. 650; Długosz, cols. 189 D, 190 A, and 191 A; Miechow, II.13, p. 37.], whereupon she was expelled [Note: [Col. 1356C] Gallus, p. 80; Kadłubek, col. 651; Saxon Chronographer, under 1034.], and soon afterward her son as well [Note: [Col. 1356C] Gallus, pp. 87–88; Kadłubek, col. 650.]; that he first sought Hungary [Note: [Col. 1356C] Gallus, ibid.; Długosz, col. 192: “as some people believe.”], while others maintain that the son went into exile with his mother in 1036 [Note: [Col. 1356C] Life of Saint Stanislaus, p. 323; Boguphalus, p. 25; Account, etc.; Saxon Chronographer, under 1034; Commentator on Kadłubek, col. 653; Długosz, col. 191 B–D, [Col. 1356D] 192 A; Miechow, II.13, p. 37; Sarnicius, col. 1052 C; Annals of Altaich, under 1035: “He is expelled by the nobles.”], and that both fled to Germany [Note: [Col. 1356D] Commentator on Kadłubek, col. 653; Miechow, II.13, p. 37.]; that the mother carried away the two crowns of Poland and exhausted the royal treasury [Note: [Col. 1356D] Długosz, 192 A; Miechow, ibid.; Sarnicius, ibid. D; Brunweiler Manuscript in Tölner, *Historia Palatina*, p. 261 A; ibid. B; Miechow, ibid.]; that she purchased estates in Germany [Note: [Col. 1356D] Długosz.], while the son, already instructed in letters in the monasteries of his homeland—and the first among the princes of Poland to receive such instruction [Note: [Col. 1356D] Miechow, book I.], though this may perhaps be understood of Boleslav [Note: [Col. 1356D] Kadłubek, col. 652; but this may perhaps be understood of Boleslav (cf. note 1).]—there practiced the same monastic life [Col. 1356B] [Note: [Col. 1356D] Commentator on Kadłubek, col. 653.], and, as some prefer to believe, went to Gaul, first to Paris, in the years 1038–1049, and thereafter to Saint Romuald in Italy, in order to profess monastic vows in the monastery of Cluny [Note: [Col. 1356D] Boguphalus, p. 25; Life of Saint Stanislaus, p. 334ff.; Gallus, loc. cit.; Polish Chronicle, loc. cit.; Chronicle of the Princes of Poland, commentator on Kadłubek, loc. cit.; Długosz, 192 C; Miechow, loc. cit.; Sarnicius, col. 1053 B. Roepell notes that the Gniezno manuscript of Gallus from the fourteenth or fifteenth century, which Bandtkie used, does not contain the Cluny passage; [Col. 1357B] nevertheless, he says that Lengnich printed it in the first edition from the Heilberg manuscript, which is from the year 1426. Nor does he think that this interpolation was absent from the older manuscripts: for the *Chronicle of the Princes of Poland*, which in these matters copied Gallus for the most part and was already written in 1384, contains this account, as does the *Polish Chronicle*, written at the beginning of the [Col. 1357C] fourteenth century, though it drew from a source different from Gallus, the *Life of Saint Stanislaus*, or Boguphalus. Moreover, not only is a different pope named in these works, but different conditions of the dispensation are also given. The story may perhaps have arisen from Gallus’s words, p. 98: “he [Casimir], while still a little boy, was offered by his parents to a monastery, where he was liberally educated in sacred letters,” of which Kadłubek also makes mention. Finally, Mabillon had already seen that the whole matter was fabricated, *Annales Benedictini*, vol. IV, under 1034 and 1039, and Naruszewicz demonstrated it at greater length, loc. cit., IV, pp. 193–310. Roepell, I, p. 180, note 7.]; meanwhile, that his brother Boleslav ruled, but [Col. 1357A] ended his life badly because of his cruelty and therefore was not counted among the princes of Poland [Note: [Col. 1357C] Boguphalus, ibid.; Commentator on Kadłubek, col. 653.].

Thus not only did civil wars arise in 1037 [Note: [Col. 1357C] Gallus, pp. 89–91; Life of Saint Stanislaus, loc. cit., pp. 323–324; Annals of Hildesheim, under 1034; Saxon Chronographer, under 1034; Kadłubek, col. 652; Miechow, II.13, p. 37.], in which Christians became pagans [Note: [Col. 1357C] Długosz, col. 194 A; Sarnicius, col. 1052 D.], peasants fought magnates, slaves fought free men [Note: [Col. 1357C] Długosz, col. 193 D; Sarnicius, ibid.], tribe turned against tribe [Note: [Col. 1357D] Długosz, cols. 193 C and 194 A.], all things divine and human were thrown into confusion, and, according to the proverb commonly repeated, gamma pursued beta; but Poland was also miserably devastated by foreign enemies [Note: [Col. 1357D] Commentator on Kadłubek, loc. cit.; Długosz, col. 195 A.]. Bretislaus, who had succeeded his father in the duchy of Bohemia in 1037, captured Wrocław and Poznań in 1038–1039, laying everything waste; indeed, he even plundered the church at Gniezno and carried away, among many other things, an enormous golden cross weighing three hundred pounds, and transported to Prague the bodies of Saints Adalbert, Gaudentius, and five companions [Col. 1357B], together with a multitude of captives [Note: [Col. 1357D] Saxon Chronographer, under 1034; Gallus, p. 90; *Brief Chronicle of Cracow* (Sommersberg, II), p. 79, under 1038; Cosmas, loc. cit., p. 106ff.; Długosz, cols. 195 A, B, D, and 196 C, D (though he wishes Gaudentius to have been carried away in place of Adalbert, as do those who followed him); Miechow, II.13, pp. 37–38, and others.]; Jaroslav did similar things from the east in 1038 [Note: [Col. 1357D] Długosz, col. 200 B; Miechow, ibid., p. 38.]; and finally, in 1037, a certain Maslaus, Misego’s cupbearer [Note: [Col. 1357D] Długosz, col. 194 C; Miechow, ibid., p. 37.], supported by the Prussians, Jatvingians (Lithuanians), and Pomeranians [Note: [Col. 1357D] Gallus, pp. 92–96; Boguphalus, p. 26; Chronicle of the Princes of Poland, p. 58; Polish Chronicle, p. 11; Kadłubek: “Maritimi, Getae Daci (Danes?), Rutheni (Lithuanians).”], and by the pagan and servile faction in Poland [Note: [Col. 1357D] Długosz, col. 220 B; Miechow, p. 40.], became king or prince of Mazovia [Note: [Col. 1357D] Długosz, cols. 194 D and 264 C.].

[Col. 1358A] Thus, in 1040, misfortune is said to have taught the Poles better judgment, and they obtained from the supreme pontiff Benedict IX, through ambassadors [Note: [Col. 1357D] Commentator on Kadłubek, col. 653; Długosz, pp. 205ff. and 213; Sarnicius, 1053 B.], permission to bring Casimir back from the monastery of Cluny to the throne of Poland [Note: [Col. 1358B] Commentator on Kadłubek, ibid.; Długosz, 211; Miechow, p. 38ff.], and in gratitude for this a denarius for each person was promised annually to Saint Peter [Note: [Col. 1358B] Commentator on Kadłubek, ibid.; Długosz, 211 C; Miechow, p. 39.]; or, as a unique tradition preserved by Kadłubek has it, Casimir was summoned from a Polish monastery [Note: [Col. 1358B] Kadłubek, col. 652 B.]. Most writers nevertheless relate that he was brought back to his homeland accompanied by German auxiliaries and at the emperor’s command—the emperor having also restored the crowns [Note: [Col. 1358B]

Długosz, 214 D–215 A; Miechow, p. 39; Sarnicius, 1053 B.

[Col. 1358C] The *Polish Chronicle*, p. 10, and the *Chronicle of the Princes of Poland*, p. 58, maintain that he was crowned by the emperor himself; cf. Wippo, p. 27; Gallus, p. 91ff.; Life of Saint Stanislaus, p. 336; Tölner, *Historia Palatina*, p. 261 G.]

[Col. 1358C] and that he was crowned there in the year 1041 [Note: [Col. 1358C] Długosz, 216 D; Miechow, p. 40.]. Then, after peace had been made with Jaroslav, Casimir married his sister Maria, or Dobrogneiva, in the same year [Note: [Col. 1358C]

Nestor and other Russian sources in Karamsin, II, p. 25; Długosz, 218 A; Miechow, p. 40; Sarnicius, 1053 D; all the *Saxon Annals* under 1039: “the daughter of the prince of Russia.”

Gallus, p. 92: “a noblewoman from Russia.”

Life of Saint Stanislaus, p. 336: “the nobler among the princes of Russia.”

Boguphalus, p. 26: “the daughter of Roman, prince of Russia.”

[Col. 1358D] *Greater Annals of Cracow*, under 1025: “a wife from Russia.”

The *Polish Chronicle*, p. 11, simply has “Dobrogneiva,” but adds: “from Russia.” *Chronicle of the Princes of Poland*, p. 58.]

after she had renounced the Greek rite [Col. 1358B] [Note: [Col. 1358D] Długosz, 218 B; Miechow, p. 40 (Sarnicius does not have this).]. Casimir, moreover, defeated Maslaus in two very bloody battles in 1042 and 1043 [Note: [Col. 1358D] *Polish Chronicle*, p. 11 (cf. *Chronicle of the Princes of Poland*, p. 59); Długosz, 221 B, 223 C–225; Miechow, pp. 40–41.], with the Russians assisting [Note: [Col. 1358D] Nestor, under 1047; others.]; and that the defeated man was, not without mockery, fastened to a gallows by the Getae (Prussians) [Note: [Col. 1358D] Boguphalus, loc. cit.; *Polish Chronicle*, ibid.; *Chronicle of the Princes of Poland*, ibid.; Commentator on Kadłubek, loc. cit.; Długosz, 226 D; Miechow, p. 41; Sarnicius, 1054 A.], and that the Getae submitted themselves to the Poles.

Nor were the provinces which Bretislaus had occupied recovered except through the favor and three repeated expeditions of the Emperor Henry III [Note: [Col. 1358D] *Saxon Annals*, under 1040; Cosmas, loc. cit., under 1054; Długosz, 221ff.; Miechow, pp. 39ff.; Stenzel, *History of the Franconian Emperors*, I, p. 78ff.], [Col. 1359A] though they remained tributary to the Bohemians [Note: [Col. 1359C] Böhmer, *Regesta*, under 1158; Cosmas, under 1054, note 5 (cf. under 1093, p. 198; under 1099; under 1100).].

Rixa founded the monastery of Saint Kilian at Saalfeld [Note: [Col. 1359D] Długosz, 214 B; Miechow, p. 37.], newly built from its foundations the monastery of Saint Peter and Saint Nicholas at Brunweiler, and also erected a chapel at Klotten [Note: [Col. 1359D] The same authors, ibid.; Tölner, *Historia Palatina*, p. 262 D and p. 161 A.]. She finally died at Saalfeld in the year 1063 [Note: [Col. 1359D] 12 Kalends of April; *Account*, p. 323; Gelenius, *De admiranda sacra Colonia*, 1645, p. 677 and p. 313; Miechow, p. 37.] and was buried at Cologne [Note: [Col. 1359D]

The same authors.

Her testament in Martène and Durand, *Veterum monumentorum*, I, pp. 424–430.

Gelenius, *Life and Vindication of Richeza*, and *De admiranda Colonia*, p. 313.]

Casimir’s reign ended happily; he founded or restored the monasteries of Tyniec [Note: [Col. 1359D] Gallus, p. 98; *Polish Chronicle*, 11; *Chronicle of the Princes of Poland*, 58; Długosz, 228ff.; Sarnicius, 1054 C.] and Lubiąż (Leubus) on the Oder in Silesia [Note: [Col. 1359D]

*Chronicle of the Princes of Poland*, p. 99 (Roepell, p. 186, note, suspects that the date 1154 is an error of the century).

Długosz, 228ff.]

He recalled the two brothers Andrew and Levente, when the Hungarians rebelled in 1048 [Note: [Col. 1359D] Długosz, 233 D; Engel, *History of the Hungarian Kingdom*, I, pp. 146ff.; Stenzel, *History of the Franconian Emperors*, I.], and they promised that they would tolerate paganism (the Slavonic-Greek rite?) [Note: [Col. 1360C] Długosz, 234 B; Engel, loc. cit.; Stenzel, loc. cit.]. Andrew indeed proved to be Catholic, while Levente was an idolater (Greek?) [Note: [Col. 1360C] Długosz, 235 A; Engel, loc. cit.; Stenzel, loc. cit.]. Béla was summoned by his brother in the same year, 1050 [Note: [Col. 1360C] Długosz, 236 B; Engel, loc. cit.; Stenzel, loc. cit.].

Because Casimir had promoted the cause of Andrew, the new king of Hungary, with particular zeal, he would have incurred the emperor’s hostility had he not appeased his indignation by sending ambassadors to plead his case [Note: [Col. 1360D] Hermannus Contractus, under 1050; cf. under 1052; Długosz, 237 C.]. Finally, after the bishopric of Byczyna, or Smogorzów, had been transferred or restored [Note: [Col. 1360D] Stenzel, *Scriptores rerum Silesiacarum*, I, p. 157.] to Wrocław in 1052 [Note: [Col. 1360D] Długosz, 239 D.], Casimir died in 1058 and was buried in the cathedral church at Poznań [Note: [Col. 1360D]

Boguphalus, p. 26; Gallus, loc. cit.; *Polish Chronicle*, 11; *Chronicle of the Princes of Poland*, 58; Długosz, 247 A.

In the *Greater Annals of Cracow*, loc. cit., the year of his death is given as 1038, doubtless through a copyist’s error.

.

## CHAPTER XXV — That our book was in fact written concerning Misego II, apparently in the year 1027

Although what I have reported concerning Misego II is extremely diverse and mutually contradictory, I take pride in having aroused in the reader the suspicion that most of these matters can be reconciled with one another. It is certainly worthwhile to attempt this; but it will be done better below, after we have established through investigation both that our letter belongs to that subject and by whom it was written. It is nevertheless sufficiently clear that this Misego may be called the second, as our letter has it in its fourth line, and that at the beginning of his reign he was prosperous.

For even if the large number of churches founded seems there to be the precise subject, it would be absurd for Mathilda to praise him as prosperous after he had suffered defeat, or after a province had been seized by enemies, or finally after the German marches had been devastated and the Germans carried off into slavery. A greater obstacle seems to lie in that large number of churches if we assume that the letter was written at the beginning of his reign. Yet one should hardly believe that this is so significant. While his father was alive and occupied with military affairs, Misego and his pious wife, the blessed Rixa—whose brother Hermann, surnamed the Pious, was archbishop of Cologne, and whose six sisters had embraced the monastic life—could already have founded very many churches [Note: [Col. 1360D] Tölner, *Historia Palatina*, chapter IX, p. 249. They were: 1. Theophania, abbess of Essen; 2. Adelaide, abbess of Nivelles; 3. Heilewigis, abbess at Nuss; 4. Mathilda, abbess at Dietkirchen and Vilich; 5. Blessed Ida, abbess of Cologne; 6. Sophia, abbess of Mainz and Gandersheim.]. Moreover, that very zeal for Christian faith and piety in Misego and Rixa seems to have been the principal cause of their misfortunes. But more on this below.

Nothing, therefore, prevents us from concluding that this book was written at the beginning of the reign of Misego II, around the year 1027 after the birth of Christ.

## CHAPTER XXVI — Concerning Mathilda’s father Hermann: was he the first, third, or fourth?

It remains for us to examine Mathilda, daughter of Hermann, duke of the Swabians [Col. 1360B].

That such a woman appears nowhere in the monuments is sufficiently and explicitly demonstrated by the genealogical book. Although this question has already been treated by the two most celebrated scholars, Koeler and Pesler, I nevertheless think it should be revisited here, since many things are explained obscurely there or even left unmentioned.

Just as there are three Misegos among the Poles, so four Hermanns, dukes of the Swabians, are celebrated. Our manuscript book adds nothing except that he was illustrious. Let us therefore see of whom this can most properly be said.

Some investigators of genealogies conjecture that the first Hermann was of Frankish stock—though without any sufficiently certain testimony—and assert that he was the cousin of King Conrad I. Accordingly, after Burchard I, duke of Swabia, died in 925, Hermann married Thietberga, his widow, and governed the duchy of Swabia from 926 to 949. By Thietberga he had three daughters, one of whom, named Ida, by marrying Liudolf, the firstborn son of Otto the Great and the Englishwoman Edith, caused the duchy to pass to her husband. The monuments are silent about his other two daughters. No sane person, moreover, will make it possible for daughters born around the year 930 to have still been alive a century later and to have been the authors of our book [Note: [Col. 1360D] Jo. Dav. Koeler, *Fata Ducatus Alemanniae et Sueviae*, Leipzig, 1557, quarto.].

[Col. 1361A] Hermann II, however, was the father of Hermann III [Note: [Col. 1361C] Hermannus Contractus, under 997 (Pistorius, I, p. 269ff.)], and through his daughter Gisela, the empress, the grandfather of Hermann IV. We shall discuss these later—“the latter before the former,” in Homeric fashion.

Hermann IV, descended from Ernest I of the Austrian-Babenberg house [Note: [Col. 1361C] Austrian Chronicle in Freher, I.], was duke of Swabia from 1030 [Note: [Col. 1361C] Old Chronicle of the Dukes of Brunswick; Wippo, p. 436; Otto of Freising, *Chronicle*, VI.28; Hepidanus, under 1030.] and died of plague in Italy in 1038 [Note: [Col. 1361C] Wippo, p. 442; Hermannus Contractus, under 1038; Austrian Chronicle in Freher, I; Otto of Freising, *Chronicle*, VI.31, p. 134; Annals of Hildesheim, under 1038; Annals of Altaich, under 1038.], scarcely twenty-four years old [Note: [Col. 1361C] For Gisela’s marriage with Ernest took place around 1012, and Hermann II was born from this marriage.], and his marriage to the daughter of Maginfred, margrave of Italy, had begun only a few years earlier, in 1036 [Note: [Col. 1361D] Hermannus Contractus, under 1036.]. He can neither be called illustrious nor have had a daughter who could have written our book as early as 1027. Moreover, none of his children are mentioned, and after his death the honor of duke of Swabia passed to the Frankish line, and Henry III, son of Emperor Conrad II and the same Gisela, was created duke of Swabia in 1038.

Hermann III could still less have been the father of our Mathilda. He ruled, as the son of Hermann II, from 1004 [Note: [Col. 1361D] In that year his father died (cf. chapter XXVII, note 2).] to 1012 [Note: [Col. 1361D] Hermannus Contractus, under 1012.], when he died, having entered into no marriage and being ἄπαις, “childless.”

Although the duchy of Swabia, as it then existed, easily surpassed the present kingdom of Bavaria in size—for it surrounded Lake Bregenz on every side with equal breadth, and the duchy of Alsace was joined to it—its capital [Col. 1362C] and the chief city of all Hermann’s lands was Strasbourg [Note: [Col. 1362D] Thietmar, pp. 369 and 359; Spruner, *Historical-Geographical Atlas*.]; nevertheless, Hermann aspired to greater things. He grievously disturbed Germany for eight months and, although Henry was his maternal uncle, refused to concede the kingdom to Henry of Bavaria [Note: [Col. 1363C] Mascov, *On the Affairs of Henry II*, p. 192ff.]. At last he laid down his sword and died in the second year after peace had been concluded [Note: [Col. 1363C] 1 October 1002; Mascov, ibid.].

## CHAPTER XXIX — Mathilda, daughter of Gerberga (and of Hermann II)

[Col. 1364A]

The name and fate of our Mathilda, the third daughter, finally remained hidden, and came to light only through the conjecture—although an entirely certain one—of Koeler and Pesler [Note: [Col. 1364C]

Koeler, *De familia Augusta Franconica*.

Pesler, *Series of the Dukes of Carinthia*, pp. 16–22.].

But, astonishingly enough, this is that Mathilda through whom the allodial estates of Mathilda, the marchioness of Tuscany, were said to belong by hereditary right to the German emperors [Note: [Col. 1364C] *Guelphic Origins*, I, p. 443ff.].

Even today, names in families are customarily preserved in such a way that the name of a paternal or maternal grandfather or grandmother is repeated in a grandson or granddaughter. In the Middle Ages this practice was so regular that, when it did not occur while the grandfather or grandmother was still alive, there was some particular reason for it. Thus Mathilda, wife of Henry the Fowler, bore a daughter Gerberga; she, a Burgundian Mathilda; this Mathilda, a Swabian Gerberga; and it would be astonishing if one of Gerberga’s three daughters had not borne the name Mathilda. This is also confirmed by the testimony of the author of the life of Adalbero II, bishop of Metz [Note: [Col. 1364C] Labbe, *Bibliotheca manuscripta*, I, section V, p. 674. [Col. 1364D] “Lord Otto, duke, father of that venerable Conrad, duke of Carinthia, who sits with us, was born from a daughter of the great Otto (Luitgarda); her sister Gerbirga (wife of Louis IV) gave her daughter (Mathilda) to Conrad, king of the Burgundians. From Conrad’s daughter (Gerberga of Swabia) was born the lady Mathilda, wife of this Conrad, who sits beside us.” Add Thietmar, V, p. 367, and Adelbold, p. 432, who call that Conrad “the son-in-law of Hermann II.”]. Our Mathilda did not preserve her mother’s name in her daughter Beatrice, because the Swabian Gerberga had doubtless already died when Beatrice was born; but Mathilda’s own name was indeed received by her granddaughter, Mathilda of Tuscany, though it vanished because she left no offspring.

## CHAPTER XXX — Mathilda’s first husband, Conrad, duke of Carinthia; his sons

Mathilda married twice. First she married Conrad, who was related to her in the second degree [Note: [Col. 1364D] Author of the life of Adalbero II (see note 3 to the preceding chapter).], and who, after his father’s death, was duke of Carinthia for several years and margrave of Verona; he died in 1012 [Note: [Col. 1364D] Hermannus Contractus, under 1012; *Quedlinburg Annals*, under 1012; Guillimannus, *On the True Origin and Lineage of Conrad II*, p. 21; a charter of 1034 in the same author and in Shannat, *History of the Bishops of Worms*, authenticated document no. 56.]. This Conrad, buried at Worms [Note: [Col. 1364D] Charter of 1034 (ibid.)], belonged to the ducal Frankish family of Worms [Note: [Col. 1364D] Charter of 1034; Koeler, *On the Frankish Family*.].

His elder brother Henry, duke of Franconia from 982 to 989, was the father of Conrad the Salian [Note: [Col. 1364D] Charter of 1031; Wippo, p. 425.]. Second [Col. 1365A] he had as a brother Pope Bruno [Note: [Col. 1365C] Hermannus Contractus, under 1012; Wippo, ibid.], adorned with the apostolic tiara from 996 to 999. Finally, his third and younger brother was William, who occupied the episcopal see of Strasbourg from 1028 to 1057 [Note: [Col. 1365C] Wippo, ibid.].

His father was Otto, duke of Carinthia and margrave of Verona in 995 [Note: [Col. 1365C]

To this Conrad of Carinthia, therefore, our Mathilda bore two sons, Conrad [Note: [Col. 1365D] Hermannus Contractus, under 1012; Wippo, p. 425.] and Bruno, both [Col. 1365B] still young when their father died. Consequently, their maternal uncle Adalbero [Note: [Col. 1365D] Hermannus Contractus, under 1012; Wippo, p. 463.] was made duke of Carinthia.

The younger Bruno occupied the episcopal see of Würzburg for twelve years, from 1033 to 1045 [Note: [Col. 1365D] Hermannus Contractus, under 1034; *Annals of Hildesheim*, under 1034; Pesler, loc. cit., p. 19.]. Conrad, however, striving to obtain his father’s dignity by force, repeatedly waged war against Adalbero [Note: [Col. 1365D] Hermannus Contractus, under 1019.]. This younger Conrad had sought the kingship in Germany after the death of Emperor Henry II, striving in a manner similar to that of his grandfather Hermann [Col. 1365C] II [Note: [Col. 1366C] Wippo, p. 425; Hermannus Contractus, under 1024.].

She therefore seems to have been a widow when she wrote this book, or ordered it to be written; her dress in our painted picture is, in a way, evidence of this. Her head is veiled in the manner of religious women; perhaps she was then living in a monastery. I say “in a way,” because in the earliest periods that dress is also found among women while their husbands were still alive; compare the pictures (from the year 1230?) in *Saxon Land and Feudal Law* in *German Monuments* by Batt, Babo, Eitenbenz, Mone, and Weber, fascicle I, Heidelberg, 1820, plate I, figure 3, and the color plate, figure 19. Later custom easily misleads us, since a particular status came to be indicated by it; thus we mistakenly suppose that the same held in earlier times, when there was no such distinction among women [Col. 1366C].
