After I had completed all this, while leafing through volume V of Pertz’s *Monumenta*, I encountered there an ancient genealogical table, the second Steynvelten table (p. 215), which assigns to Gepae of Burgundy (the wife of Hermann II of Swabia) the daughters Matilda and Gisela, so that Matilda is named first. From this I infer that Matilda was the elder. For certainly, it would not have placed Gisela second if it named her as queen, indeed empress, and already called her the mother of King Henry [Col. 1367B] (cf. chapter XXIX).

## CHAPTER XXXII.—Our book appears not to have been written by Matilda’s own hand, but to be the work of several Franco-Gallic scribes.

It did not seem irrelevant to me to investigate whether Matilda herself wrote our exemplar, or whether the book and the painted image were produced by others at her command. Examples of great literary learning among women of that age are not lacking. You will find many examples of this below, in chapter XXXVIII. Who is unaware of Hroswitha’s achievements in every kind of writing? Who does not know that famous work of Matilda of Flanders, queen of England, preserved at Bayeux in the cathedral church—the tapestry in which she left to posterity, embroidered and inscribed with the needle, the outstanding deeds of her husband William the Norman when he gained possession of England [Col. 1367C] [Note: [Col. 1368D]

Montfaucon, *Monuments de la monarchie française*.

Thierry, *History of the Conquest of England by the Normans*.

Dibdin, *Bibliographical Tour*.]

?

On examining the matter more carefully, however, I seemed to see some diversity in the formation of the letters, such that the book appears to have been copied not by one person but by several. Moreover, on folio XI verso, in the middle of the page, a proposition ends abruptly and is continued on the following folio. From the second folio through the eleventh, the letters are more polished and more rounded in form, and also thicker in the middle, than on folio twelve and those that follow, where we encounter letters that are longer and thicker in their upper parts. Then, after folio XI verso, very many signs or abbreviations occur, some of which occur rarely, others differently, and others never before [Col. 1367D]. I shall provide examples in table, figure 6, so that the reader may judge the matter more easily. Those I have placed under letter A are from before folio XI verso; those under B are from afterward.

If I did not fear being accused by the reader of excessive ingenuity, I would assert that scribes of Franco-Gallic nationality copied this Carolingian liturgical exemplar. For there are many orthographical errors which, although each occurs elsewhere, nevertheless very readily arise from the Franco-Gallic manner of pronouncing Latin. Here are several examples.

The letter *h* is omitted or added: *ebdemada*, *actenus*, *scola*, or, conversely, it is added in *habundat*, *Israhelitici*, *hostiarii*, and six hundred other instances. On folio XVIII one reads *hebraice*—“in Hebrew”—where, if I am not mistaken, through the corrector’s hand, the ancient form of the rough breathing seems to have been restored by chance. On folio 67 one reads: “he is carried into heaven” (*in coelom rapitur*); in this no one who is not ignorant of the subject will fail to recognize the distinctive Franco-Gallic pronunciation, in which *um* sounds like *om*. The letter *u* has been written above it by the corrector. There are many solecisms and barbarisms of this kind, such as: “Let us make a comparison from it” (*Demus inde comparationem*; French, “Let us give a comparison of it”), which occurs in the as-yet unpublished *Symbolum*, folio 75, or: “He addressed the shepherds” (*pastoribus affatus est*). But such solecisms may belong to the authors—Alcuin or Charlemagne—for in the published portion one finds: “it is worthy from this” (*inde dignum est*; French, “it is worthy of it”).

For these reasons I judge it highly probable that the German Matilda did not write this book with her own hand, at least not the whole of it.

## CHAPTER XXXIII.—Bolizlav I: did he subjugate the Prussians before or after the martyrdom of Saint Adalbert? Only a very small part was subjugated; the date remains uncertain [Note: [Col. 1368D] Compare chapters XI and following, and chapter XXIV.]

After bringing to a clear conclusion everything concerning the person, what, and to whom the letter was written, I shall now attempt to determine what benefit the history of that period may derive from it.

[Col. 1368C] Above we saw all the writers affirming that an expedition was undertaken by Bolizlav I, king of the Poles, against the Prussians. Yet they do not agree among themselves about the time at which they were subjugated, the manner of their subjugation, or whether only part of them, or all of them, were subdued.

Our letter, therefore, from verse 24 to verse 26, may be considered to have some importance for deciding this question. “For,” it says, “those whom the holy preachers could not correct by the word, he [Bolizlav] pursued with the sword, compelling barbarous and fiercest nations to the Lord’s Supper.” Everyone will immediately suppose that Adalbert was one of those holy preachers. But, I ask, why are “barbarous and fiercest nations” expressed in the plural? You will reply: the Pomeranians [Col. 1368D] are meant; or other peoples may be indicated. But why does he add “correct”? Why does he expressly say “to the Lord’s Supper”? I know that these words can be drawn, in a rather bolder sense, to mean that sacred Baptism was administered to unwilling pagans; the well-known phrase “compel them to enter” seems to contribute something to that interpretation. It seems so, I say, for the Church generally applies, or applied, that phrase to heretics, and only very rarely to pagans [Col. 1369A].

No one will deny that our letter ought to have said: “compelling them to sacred baptism,” or something similar. As matters now stand, it is much simpler to refer these words to the Poles themselves and to the other peoples subjected to their scepter, who had been baptized according to the Roman rite at the command of the Polish rulers Mieszko I and Bolizlav I, yet nevertheless favored to a great extent either the Slavonic-Greek rite or secretly pagan beliefs and pagan customs. Their number cannot have been small, as became evident later under Mieszko II and Casimir I.

We know that the Bohemians, although Christians, lived scarcely differently from the ancient pagans or Greeks; and that this depravity drove their holy bishop Adalbert [Col. 1369B] to leave the episcopal see of Prague and seek a land where the sword of the prince—recently converted to the purely Latin rite, as in Hungary and Poland—might assist the bishop. In the same way, the Poles, newly converted, did not wish to attend the churches of the Christians or follow their ecclesiastical rites and strict penitential laws; they did not wish to abandon their ancient customs, mingled with and subject to the Greek religion, indeed even to paganism. They were not corrected by the words of the preachers. Hence Bolizlav compelled them by the sword to the Lord’s Supper—that is, to the Latin Mass.

According to Thietmar [Note: [Col. 1369D] Thietmar, pp. 247–248 (book VIII, chapter 2; Pertz V, p. 864, p. 18).], the teeth of anyone who ate meat after Septuagesima were cut out. Who does not know what pious fraud the Church had to employ, applying the Saturnalia and other festivals to Christian observances, so that little by little it might turn the souls and customs of pagans away from idolatry and the worship of false gods toward the true God? Who does not know how long the veneration—if not worship—of trees lasted among the peoples inhabiting the lands of the present-day Prussians, for several centuries after they had been converted to the faith of Christ? The memory of the worship of the trees themselves gradually faded through the often miraculous images of the saints which truly holy men had enclosed within those trees by a pious deception.

Who does not know that the chalice was granted by the Roman Church to the Hussites in Bohemia, contrary to the general practice? Yet so far were the words “the Lord’s Supper” in those times from being used in any other sense than the simplest one [Col. 1370A], that the words of the Lord’s Prayer, “Give us this day our daily bread,” are still drawn out and explained in our book in that manner. For we read on folio 70 verso:

> “That which is called ‘today’ cannot generally be referred to the body and blood of the Lord, because there are people who cannot communicate every day, either because they have been stained by some disagreement with their neighbor or because they have been defiled by nocturnal pollution. They are human beings; they cannot always be prepared.”

If, nevertheless, someone wishes the Prussians to be indicated by these words, the same words would have to bear another sense. Let him now produce an example in which “to compel to the Lord’s Supper” is used in such a sense. Then it would be easier to convince readers that war was waged against this nation by Bolizlav after Adalbert’s martyrdom among the Prussians [Col. 1370B]. At present I despair entirely of proving that point.

Many authors indeed report that the Prussians were subjugated by Bolizlav, but they do so in precisely the same words. There is even another tradition according to which the body of Saint Adalbert, immediately after his martyrdom, was purchased from the Prussians by Bolizlav for an equal weight of silver. That king would have been excessively lavish if, as an avenger, he had paid so much silver to subjugated peoples for the body of the victim. We must therefore conclude that perhaps a part, even a very small part, of the Prussians to the west—for the matter of Gdańsk itself is not established—was subjugated by Bolizlav around the years 996 or 998; that is, either before Adalbert’s death, as Roepell believes, or immediately afterward.

[Col. 1370C] Whatever the truth may be, if part of the Prussians was then converted to the Christian faith, certainly not much later, under Mieszko I, nearly all of them abandoned the word of God.

## CHAPTER XXXIV.—Bolizlav I could already have been called king before he was visited by Otto III. The use and abuse of royal dignity among all peoples.

The origins of all peoples show us the head of the household as priest, lawgiver, and judge, or, to put it in one word, as king of the family: by natural right over children, and by abuse—human abuse alone—over adults. The despot himself possesses every right and all liberty for himself alone, while the others—women and children (slaves)—possess no rights; for they are deprived of every freedom. The head of the household absorbs the *political animal* (*τὸ πολιτικὸν ζῷον*) [Note: [Col. 1369D]

Aristotle, *Politics* I, Bekker edition, p. 1252, column 2, line 20: “For every household is ruled by the eldest” (*πᾶσα γὰρ οἰκία βασιλεύεται ὑπὸ τοῦ πρεσβυτάτου*).

Almost the same words occur in an ancient Slavonic poem:

> *wsak ot suéi celedi voievodi*

“Everyone rules in his own family,” in *The Kraledvor Manuscript*, published by Václav Hanka, Prague, 1835, p. 51.

The Greek word *βασιλεύς* seems to have arisen from *βας*, “good” or “lord,” and *ἴλευς*, that is, *ἵλεως*, “propitious,” so that *βασιλεύς* is almost the same as the German *gnädiger Herr*, “gracious lord.” For *βας* seems to survive in the German comparative *besser* (“better,” superlative *best”); then in the adverbial word *fubass*, and finally in the Rhenish and Dutch provincial word *Bass* [Col. 1370D], that is, a master skilled in some art, a member of a guild of craftsmen, or a patron of craftsmen. Hence Emperor Peter I, or Peter the Great, after learning naval architecture in Holland, gave himself the name Peter Bas—that is, “Master Peter.”

It also seems to survive in the German word *Base*, which here is believed to mean “aunt,” and there, as in Luther, “paternal or maternal cousin”; properly, however, it means nothing other than “good” or “beloved.” Hence the Latin *amita*: Ramshorn, *Latin Synonymics*, 1833, vol. II, p. 612, additions no. 104: “*Amita*, Manchu: *Amou*, aunt; *Vash*, *Ama*, mother; hence also nurse”—“the good one” should be added. It follows that in German *Muhme* and *Base* are rightly confused in a certain sense.

My highly learned friend Bethmann points out to me that the word *βασιλεύς* may have been derived from *Baal* through *basal*: certainly, in the Phrygian language, the king is heard as *βάλλην*, and so forth. I would not object to adding weight to this opinion if *basal* were actually found in some dialect or language as a word for royal dignity. For now I remain uncertain between the two opinions.

The German word *König*, deriving from the ancient *Kön*, just as the Rhinelanders today say *Kön* for *Kühn*, signifies “bold,” not “powerful,” deriving it from *können* (“to be able”), and thus seems to express the warlike character of the office. It is nearly equivalent to *Dux*, a leader, a leader in war, or *voivode*, which the Slavonic poet cited above uses. That word is derived from *voia*, *boia*, meaning “war,” and *vod*, meaning “to lead.” The highly distinguished Thierry correctly observes in his book *Ten Years of Historical Studies* (II, no. 111, p. 178) that *konning* means nothing other than “leader” in the ancient expressions *Oberkoning*, *Unterkoning*, *Halfkoning*, *Seekoning*, *Heereskoning*, *Folkeskoning*, and so forth. From *chunne* (“lineage”).]

His will is the supreme law; nor is it limited by favor or compassion except at his discretion [Col. 1371A] [Note: [Col. 1371C]

Aristotle, *Nicomachean Ethics* VIII, chapter 12, Bekker edition, p. 1160, column 2, line 27: “Among the Persians the father’s rule is tyrannical; they treat their sons as slaves” (*Ἐν Πέρσαις δ᾽ ἡ τοῦ πατρὸς τυραννική· χρῶνται παρ᾽ ὡς δούλοις τοῖς υἱέσιν*).

Concerning the Jews, Flavius Josephus, *Antiquities of the Jews* XVI, chapter 8: “For, with authority available to him as king, and with authority available to him as father, he was permitted to proceed against those who did wrong—that is, against his sons” (*Καὶ γὰρ ἐξῆν, παρούσης μὲν ἐξουσίας ὡς βασιλεῖ, παρούσης δὲ ὡς πατρὶ τοὺς ἀδικοῦντας ἐπεξιέναι [υἱοὺς]*).

The Athenians and Spartans had a similar custom; see Plutarch, *Solon*, chapter 13: “Many were even compelled to sell their own children, for no law forbade it” (*Πολλοὶ δὲ καὶ παῖδας ἰδίους ἠναγκάζοντο πωλεῖν· οὐδεὶς γὰρ νόμος ἐκώλυε*).

Dionysius of Halicarnassus recalls the ancient Roman law, *Roman Antiquities* II, chapter XXVI, §20: “The lawgiver of the Romans gave, so to speak, complete authority to the father over his son, and for the whole duration of life, whether he should choose to flog him or kill him . . . granting the father greater authority over a child than a master over a slave.” At Rome, fathers were exceedingly tenacious in preserving this tyranny—not, let us say, as law or custom, but as abuse (human abuse alone!); hence they boasted that “there were no other men who possessed such power over their children as they did,” Justinian, *Institutes* I, title IX, law 1, §2.

Nevertheless, this tyrannical custom prevailed only among peoples eager to dominate. Others established paternal authority more equitably from the beginning. Thus the Bohemians and many Slavonic peoples possess paternal authority in the person of the one they call the *Staressina*, but all matters relating to the household are decided in council with the adults. In old age, the father chooses among his sons, brothers, or the sons of his brothers the best person to succeed him in paternal authority; and if a *Staressina* mismanages the household, the family deposes him in an assembly and elects a new *Staressina*. Palacký, *History of Bohemia* I, pp. 169 ff.; Wuk Stefanowicz, *Serbian Dictionary*.

Today, among the Kashmiris, as soon as the eldest son is born and marries, he not only succeeds his father in paternal authority but also becomes heir of everything his father possessed, on the condition, however, that he provide everything his father needs.]

Under Trajan, a law was finally enacted to ensure that paternal authority would not lack compassion [Note: [Col. 1372C] Cujacius, commentary on Papinian’s *Questions* XI, final law. Cassagnac, *History of the Working Classes*, p. 56, year 1.]: from this royal power within families arose the title of “father,” given especially to senators, and the surname “King” was preserved in certain Sabine families at Rome. Plutarch reports that this name existed among the Pomponii, Pinarii, Calpurnii, and Mamercii [Note: [Col. 1372C]

Plutarch, *Numa*, chapter XI: “For *Rex* became a surname, which means *king*” (*Ρῆγας γένεσθαι παρωνύμιον, ὅπερ ἐστὶ βασιλέας*).

Nor can it be unusual for someone to be “born from ancestors who were kings.”]

As the family grew and divided into several branches, it often came to possess several individual heads of households, whose definite blood relationship they generally forgot, since no genealogical records were preserved. Living or wandering in the neighborhood, though usually scattered (*σποράδην*), they formed a neighborhood, a clan, a kinship group—Greek *κώμη*, German *Gau* (“district”), Bohemian *Okolina*, Hungarian *Gespanschaften* (that is, *Gesippenschaften*?) [Note: [Col. 1372C] As Buttmann proposed; nevertheless the root *pan* and *supan* seems more appropriate.], Russian *Berb*, Polish *Opole* [Note: [Col. 1372C]

Aristotle, *Politics* I, Bekker edition, p. 1252, column 2, line 15: “The community formed from several households, for the sake of something more than daily needs, is a village (*κώμη*); and the village seems most naturally to be a colony of a household. Some call its members ‘children and children’s children of the same milk’; thus, too, colonies are ruled by the eldest on account of their kinship” (*Ἡ δ᾽ ἐκ πλειόνων οἰκίων κοινωνία πρώτη, χρησεως ἕνεκεν μὴ ἐφημέρου, κώμη· μάλιστα δὲ κατὰ φύσιν ἔοικεν ἡ κώμη ἀποικία οἰκίας εἶναι, οὓς καλοῦσί τινες ὁμογάλακτας παῖδας τε καὶ παίδων παῖδας· ὥστε καὶ αἱ ἀποικίαι διὰ τὴν συγγένειαν βασιλεύονται ὑπὸ τοῦ πρεσβυτάτου*).

Palacký, *History of Bohemia* II, p. 40.

*Russian Pravda*, §§3–4; *II. The History of Russia* by Esneaux and Chénéchaud, vol. I, p. 174. Strahl, *History of the Russian State* I, p. 415.

Roepell, *History of Poland* I, p. 87, and his excursus on the *Opole*, p. 614–617.

*Serbian Law Code of Tsar Stefan Dušan*, §§19 and 72; and Kucharski, *The Most Ancient Monuments of Slavonic Legislation*, Warsaw, 1838.]

And thus among all peoples we find the same neighborhoods or clans. They have among the heads of households—that is, among the petty rulers—a greater king, patriarch, or elder (*Seigneur*), whose power differs in no respect from that of the other heads of households (thus the *φυλοβασιλεῖς* among the Greeks) [Col. 1372A]. His only authority is to summon the assembly at the common hearth (*ἑστία κοινή*) of the clan [Note: [Col. 1372D] K. H. Lachmann, *The Spartan Constitution*, Breslau, 1836, pp. 136 ff., who cites Wachsmuth, *Greek Antiquities*, part I, vol. 1, pp. 245 ff.; see also Hüllmann, *Origins of the Roman Constitution*, in which highly ingenious book the distinguished author seems to me to err only in wishing to derive everything from external force.], to preside over the heads of households when common or public matters are discussed, to lead them in wartime, and to perform the common or public rites [Note: [Col. 1372D] Hence, after the kings had been expelled at Rome, a certain priest was created under the name *rex sacrorum*, “king of sacred rites,” Cicero, *Speech for His House*, 14, 38; and at Athens, the *archon basileus*, “king-archon.”]. Finally, he moderates the tribunal composed of the heads of households, which judges disputes. Thus the individual heads of households lose nothing, or only a small amount, of their freedom; nor can any change in customs—that is, in laws—be made except in their assembly. Among the tragedians, *ἄναξ* (“lord”) is applied not only to a king but also to heads of households, as in *Oedipus the King*, and elsewhere.

When these groups are gathered into *curiae* or *phratries* (*φρατρίαι*) and into a larger body politic, cities arise, either temporarily or permanently, with a more powerful king. Thus formerly the individual cities of the Greeks and other peoples obtained individual kings, such as those presented by Homer [Note: [Col. 1372D] Aristotle, in the same place, line 19: “Therefore cities too were originally ruled by kings, and even now peoples are so ruled” (*διὸ καὶ τὸ πρῶτον ἐβασιλεύοντο αἱ πόλεις καὶ νῦν ἔτι τὰ ἔθνη*).]. The first kings of the Romans were of this kind.

Cities or neighborhoods merged, through the vain ambition of tyrants, peoples, or both to dominate, or through the barbarous desire to seize booty, especially in war—as happens through human abuse—into a larger commonwealth. These, gradually and without setting themselves any limit except God’s slowly arriving avenging hand, were fused into a commonwealth [Col. 1373A] larger than was just, and through that plague of military glory, contrary to right and justice, into immense kingdoms, astonishing and horrifying monstrosities, such as the Persian and Macedonian kingdoms and the Roman Empire.

The larger a kingdom became, the greater the blind honor and power—not to say authority—which the king, or whoever was in charge, necessarily enjoyed; and the more the heads of households gradually lost. In the end, the only freedom left to individuals, if any remained, was to flatter and to deliver acclamations in the senate [Note: [Col. 1373C] “Or with offense to the ruler,” as Tacitus says.]. Occasionally they enacted certain laws through their agency, but in these only the number of voices acclaiming the emperor’s safety was recorded [Note: [Col. 1373C] As happened in the Roman senatorial decree when a copy of the Theodosian Code was sent from the East to the West.]. The praetor himself becomes the emperor’s “bailiff,” and the senate deliberates whether “a turbot should be cut up, or a tall dish prepared” [Note: [Col. 1373C] Juvenal IV, 77 and 130.]. The greater the commonwealth [Col. 1373B], the smaller the public sphere. Nevertheless, the condition of slaves and others within the family generally becomes more lenient, against the master’s will.

The titles Duke, King, Emperor, and so forth, used by those who rule over great or small commonwealths, mean almost the same thing in themselves, but must be distinguished according to usage or abuse. Often, too, the ruler of a larger commonwealth, puffed up with pride, arrogates to himself the title of higher king, or great king, or great duke, or great khagan, and so forth. Nor does the royal name always disappear in tributary provinces and conquered kingdoms. Hence in the East the kings of the Egyptians [Note: [Col. 1373C] “I am Osymandias, king of kings” (*Βασιλεὺς βασιλέων Ὀσιμανδίας εἰμί*), Diodorus Siculus, book I, chapter 47.], Babylonians [Note: [Col. 1373C] Daniel II, verse 37, concerning Nebuchadnezzar, who ruled over nearly all the kings of Asia; compare Ezekiel XXVI, 7.], Persians [Note: [Col. 1373D] Thus Artaxerxes Mnemon calls himself “king of kings” in his letter to Ezra, chapter VII, verse 17. At that time the kings of Armenia, Cyprus, Caria, and other regions were subject to the Persians.], the Arsacids and Parthians [Note: [Col. 1373D] Ezechiel Spanheim, *On the Excellence . . . of Coins*, dissertation VIII, chapter 2. Ammianus Marcellinus XXVII, chapter 5, where Sapor is “king of kings.” Visconti, *Greek Iconography*, passim. Suetonius, *Caligula* V, 4.], proudly called themselves “rulers of rulers,” *kings of kings* (*βασιλεῖς βασιλέων*); indeed Sesostris was “king of kings and lord of lords” (*βασιλεὺς βασιλέων καὶ δεσπότης δεσποτῶν*) [Note: [Col. 1373D] Diodorus Siculus, the cited place, chapter 55.]. The Macedonians and Romans themselves by no means rejected either allied or tributary kings [Note: [Col. 1373D] An example may be found in the king of the Sidonians, Quintus Curtius IV, book 18, and elsewhere.]. To use Tacitus’s words, this was “the ancient and long-established custom of the Roman people, that they should have instruments of servitude—and kings” [Note: [Col. 1373D] Tacitus, *Agricola*, 14.]. The same often occurred among the emperors of the East or West [Note: [Col. 1373D] The kings of Thrace, the Bosporus, Armenia, Judaea, and so forth; the kings of the Goths and others.]. Nor was the custom entirely foreign to the ancient Germans; for Attila was such a king of kings.

Thus among the Merovingian kings of the Franks there arose the practice of transforming the kings of conquered German peoples into dukes. In this way the kings of the Alemanni, Thuringians, and others became tributary dukes of the Frankish kings. Yet the title “king of kings” was afterward often bestowed upon Frankish princes as well [Note: [Col. 1373D]

“Lord, king of the Franks, earthly King of Kings,” Matthew Paris, year 754.

Hugh, brother of the king of the Franks, is called *βασιλεὺς βασιλέων*, “king of kings,” by Anna Comnena, p. 288.]

Charlemagne himself was an anointed king together with his brother, under his father, the king or emperor of the Franks, not of the Romans [Note: [Col. 1373D] Baronius, *Annals*, year 752, no. 6. Pagi, critical notes on the year 762, no. 2. Edmund Martène, *On Ancient Ecclesiastical Rites* III, chapter 10. Anastasius, *Life of Stephen II*. The *Caroline Letters*, letter 6. Seals.]. Later, whether imitating his father’s title or having become emperor through a new rite, he held subordinate kings—his sons and others—under him [Note: [Col. 1374C] The king of the Lombards; and his sons Charles, Pepin, Louis, and Lothair, and finally his grandson Bernard, son of Pepin, the unfortunate king of Italy.].

Wittekind, likewise, king of the Saxons—that is, the supreme king over twelve petty rulers in the individual districts, or supreme leader of leaders [Col. 1374B], supreme commander in war [Note: [Col. 1374C]

He is called “great duke” by Wittekind of Corvey I, p. 638.

Simply “duke” by Bede, *Ecclesiastical History of the English People*: “chosen leader of the war”; by Sigebert of Gembloux, year 785; by Matthew Paris, *Life of Offa*, p. 978; and in the *Capitularies* of Baluze I, p. 194.

Finally, he is called “one of the leading men of the Westphalians” in the *Lorsch Annals*, year 777.

was eventually made a duke by Charlemagne, after innumerable defeats, although one cannot tell whether this increased or diminished his dignity.

The emperor Louis the Pious left posterity a miserable example: his sons possessed not merely the royal name but also power subject to no definite limits. Under his successors, the kings of the Franks, Lotharingia, Burgundy, Bavaria, and Germany were often more powerful than the emperors. In Germany the Ottos revived the practice of the Merovingians and increased the arrogance of the monstrous imperial dignity. They insisted that royal honor belonged to them alone and had to be denied to everyone else. According to their new doctrine, all kings, once defeated, lost their royal dignity by that very fact [Col. 1374C].

From so extraordinary a doctrine arose the paradox that a ruler was called “duke,” while his land was called a “kingdom,” by one and the same writer and in nearly the same line [Note: [Col. 1374D] Thietmar IV, p. 360: “Duke Mieszko I, now aged and feverish, passes from exile into his homeland, leaving his kingdom to be divided among many.”]; indeed, in the Saxon *Chronicle*, Mieszko is simultaneously called “Duke” and “King” [Note: [Col. 1374D] *Saxon Chronicler*, year 1030: “Mieszko II, Duke . . . such, therefore, is the King,” see below, chapter XLVII.]. They did not see that this doctrine necessarily implied that the duke who had once been victorious could justly claim royal dignity. If, therefore, Mieszko I, defeated by Gero, became Otto’s soldier, so that he necessarily exchanged the royal name for the title of duke, Bolizlav, victorious on several occasions and free from every bond, could justly assume the royal name, despite the German writers. Did Henry IV, Roman emperor, therefore lack imperial honor because Anna Comnena called him merely *Ῥήξ Ἀλαμανίας*, “king of Germany” [Note: [Col. 1375C] Anna Comnena, Bonn edition V, p. 232, and frequently elsewhere.]?

He who rules his own people while subject to no foreign power may assume whatever title his people recognize. Thus many princes whose dominion was confined within narrower limits than Poland were not content even with the name of king, but arrogated to themselves the honors of emperor [Col. 1375B]. Among the Visigothic kings in Spain—although they ruled not even a quarter of present-day Spain—there were men called emperors of Spain: Sancho the Great [Note: [Col. 1375C] Alberic, *Chronicle*, year 1031; compare the Visigothic law-book XII, title II, §13, which gives Sisebut, 612–620, the title of emperor.], Alfonso VI [Note: [Col. 1375C] In a synod.], Alfonso VII [Note: [Col. 1375C] Roderic of Toledo, archpriest, book VII, chapter 7; compare Chifflet, *Vindication of Spain*.], Alfonso VIII [Note: [Col. 1375C] Du Cange, *Glossary of Medieval Latin*, s.v. “Imperator.”], Ferdinand III [Note: [Col. 1375C] Du Cange, *Glossary of Medieval Latin*, s.v. “Imperator.”], Alfonso IX [Note: [Col. 1375C] Mabillon, *On Diplomatics* V.], and Alfonso X [Note: [Col. 1375C] Mabillon, *On Diplomatics* V.].

Edgar of England assumed the title: “Basileus of the English and Emperor of the Kings of the Nations” [Note: [Col. 1375C] Du Cange, s.v. “Basileus”; and Selden, *On Titles of Honor* I, 2, §5.]. In Gaul, Pepin also seems to have used the title of emperor, and Charlemagne followed him before he was crowned at Rome [Note: [Col. 1375D] His diploma and seal in Zylles, *Defense of the Abbey of Saint Maximinus*. Compare Maciejowski, *Historical Essay on the Church among the Slavs*, Leipzig, 1840, p. 18, and Charlemagne’s letters to Alcuin, in which he bears the title “King of the Franks and Emperor of the Lombards.” For this reason, scholars up to the present have judged both the letters and the liturgy to be spurious, assuming that they were written by some “ignorant” monk who did not know that Alcuin had already died when Charlemagne was crowned emperor of the Romans at Rome. But the learned men did not notice that no one could have been so ignorant as to write the familiar phrase “emperor of the Romans” as “emperor of the Lombards.”]. In Germany Louis the Bavarian was called emperor by Rabanus Maurus [Note: [Col. 1375D] Rabanus Maurus, letter to Noting, bishop of Verona.]. In Denmark Harald called himself Caesar [Note: [Col. 1375D] Stephanus, in a note on Saxo, p. 204.], leaving aside the emperors of Brazil, Morocco, and others [Note: [Col. 1375D] Otto, *On the Title of Emperor among the Russians*, Halle and Magdeburg, 1724–1757.].

## CHAPTER XXXV.—The names of rulers among the Slavonic peoples.

The subject seems to require that we investigate more precisely the Slavonic peoples’ usage in the titles of their rulers. In much the same way as the ancient Saxons and nearly all other peoples, they were governed in neighborhoods—uncertain whether closer to democracy or aristocracy—by some elected or designated prince whose rights were very limited [Note: [Col. 1376C] The Peutinger Table, in Buat, *Ancient History of the Peoples of Europe* XI, p. 145.]. In times of war, however, the entire people followed a supreme leader. He, as their ruler, was subject to no other prince; he therefore enjoyed the highest princely honor, and the honor which universal usage established as royal [Note: [Col. 1376C] Roepell, in the cited work, chapter 2.].

(Frankish?) Samo was made king of the Bohemians in the year 623 [Note: [Col. 1376C]

Fredegar’s *Chronicle* (in Ruinart, *Works of Gregory of Tours*, Paris edition, 1699, pp. 626–627).

Palacký, *Yearbooks of the Bohemian Museum*, 1830, pp. 387 ff.

Roepell, in the cited work, p. 32. de Buat, *Ancient History of the Peoples of Europe*, vol. XII, pp. 114 ff.]

Swatopluk possessed imperial dignity in the great Moravian kingdom in the year 873 [Note: [Col. 1376C] Palacký, *History of Bohemia* I, p. 140. Roepell, [Col. 1376D] p. 40.].

The Greeks call the Slavonic princes *βασιλεῖς*, “kings” [Note: [Col. 1376D] Procopius, Dindorf edition II, p. 205: “Thus all the Slavonic peoples in succession changed their rulers, many of whom were of royal blood” (*Οὕτω γοῦν πολλῶν ἐκ τοῦ βασιλείου αἵματος ἡγουμένων σφίσιν ἤμειψαν μὲν τὰ Σκλαβηνῶν ἔθνη ἐφεξῆς ἅπαντα*).].

The Roman emperors did not deny them the Latin title of king [Col. 1376B]. Among the many testimonies, there is one especially significant inscription, of exceptionally fine marble, dedicated under Vespasian to Plautius Silvanus [Note: [Col. 1376D] Gruter, *Corpus Inscriptionum*, p. 353: “He led unknown kings, or kings hostile to the Roman people, who were about to worship the Roman standards, down to the bank which he guarded. He restored to the kings of the Bastarnae and Roxolani their captured sons, the brothers of the Dacians, or those rescued from the enemy. From some of them he received hostages, through whom he both confirmed and extended peace in the province. He also removed the siege laid by the king of the Scythians at Acheron, which lies beyond the Borysthenes.”]. Hadrian not only recognized royal honor but also paid an annual stipend to the king of the Roxolani [Note: [Col. 1376D] Spartianus, *Hadrian*, chapter 6]. The princes of the Russians are called kings by Adam of Bremen, Liutprand, Thietmar, in the *Life of Saint Marianus*, and by Sigebert of Gembloux [Note: [Col. 1376D] Adam of Bremen, [work cited]; Liutprand, V, chapter 6; Thietmar, VII, end; Bollandists, under 9 February, p. 569; Sigebert of Gembloux, under the year 1073]. Boleslav of Bohemia is called king by Widukind (III.69, under the year 967), under whom there were many sub-kings (II, chapter 3). The same author records other Slavic kings and sub-kings (III.66; III.68, and elsewhere).

The titles of Slavic princes—whether lesser or greater—were also changed among the Slavic peoples, sometimes by fortune and sometimes deliberately. Toward the end of the Middle Ages [Col. 1376C], the Russian prince was called *Czar*, the Polish prince *Krol*, the Bohemian prince *Kral*, and the Slavonic prince *Krail*. Consequently, in the Lord’s Prayer “kingdom” is rendered by the Russians as *Zrathie*, by the Poles as *Krolestwo*, by the Bohemians as *Kralowstwii*, and by the Slavs as *Krailestwu* [Note: [Col. 1376D] Herberstein, *Commentaries on Muscovite Affairs*, p. IX; Everard Otto, *On the Title of Emperor of the Russians*, Halle, Magdeburg, 1721, p. 26 ff. To the Turks all Christian kings are called *Kral* [Col. 1377D]. The Roma in modern Spain call a queen *Krali*]. Although these forms in the Lord’s Prayer may seem to breathe great antiquity, it will nevertheless be very easy to demonstrate that the same peoples did not always use the same titles.

The Russians certainly used the name *Czar*. Yet some say, falsely, that it derives from Caesar and that Vladimir Monomakh received this honor from the emperor of Constantinople [Note: [Col. 1377D] Genealogy compiled from the Russian Annals, in Cholin, Cologne]. Nor, as some maintain, did Vladimir the Great receive from the same people the name *Czar* [Note: [Col. 1377D] Anonymous Florentine, *On Muscovite Affairs*, chapter 8], but rather [the title] *Βασιλεύς* (*Basileus*, “king” or “emperor”). John III Vasilievich, who vindicated liberty for himself and the Russians, called himself “grand duke” [Note: [Col. 1377D] Otto, [work cited], p. 21]. His son Basil, however, almost always gave himself the name *Czar*, so that it is uncertain whether something of this kind had already been done earlier or whether the name was assumed from the Tatars, who had been defeated and reduced under his authority and among whom the name *Czar* was in use [Col. 1377B].

Because of the conflicts between himself and the Poles, and in order to have the Russians as friends or allies, the emperor Maximilian did not hesitate to honor Basil with the Latin title *Caesar*. This seems to have resulted from an error concerning those Slavic peoples who had either abandoned or did not know the name *Czar*, and who at that time certainly called their kings *Krol*, *Kral*, or *Krail* [Note: [Col. 1377D] The same, ibid.]. Under his successor, John IV, surnamed “the Terrible,” a certain boastfulness appears in the assumption of titles, together with an affectation of the name and insignia of Caesar or emperor. He called himself “the fourfold Czar”—of Russia, Kazan, Astrakhan, and Siberia—and “lord of the Czars of Kartli and Georgia,” and so forth [Note: [Col. 1377D] Adam Olearius, *Muscovite Journey*, p. 25]. He also ordered the following verses to be inscribed on a painted image of himself published in 1551:

[Col. 1377C]

> I am King and Lord of the Russians, by right of my father’s  
> blood; the titles of empire I have purchased from no one  
> by entreaty or by price; nor am I subject to any laws  
> of another, but obedient to Christ alone.  
> I scorn honors begged from others [Note: [Col. 1377D] Sigismundus, *Commentaries on Muscovite Affairs*, p. 13].

In the following century the envoys of the Netherlands made Michael, the founder of the present imperial dynasty, a “fourfold Keyser” (Emperor) [Note: [Col. 1377D] Aizéma I.10, p. 1045: “Another Russian Emperor . . . Emperor of Kazan, Astrakhan, and Siberia”].

It can easily be demonstrated that this name was not merely a name of the Russians or Tatars, nor merely a name of the Middle Ages, but a most ancient royal title in the East. For it appears in the names Nebuchadnezzar, Nabopolassar, Tiglath-pileser, Baltassar, and so forth [Note: [Col. 1377D] This is the opinion of the celebrated Strahl, author of a history of Russia [Col. 1378D], which he communicated to me when I visited him at Bonn]. It also occurs in the Slavonic translation of the Bible, attributed by many to Jerome and, more probably, by others to Saint Methodius, the apostle of the Slavs in Moravia and Bohemia. In this version one reads “Czar David” and “Czar Solomon”; and the passage “We have no king but Caesar” is expressed by *Czar* and *Kessar* [Note: [Col. 1378D] Otto, [work cited], p. 25].

There exists a Slavonic monument at Kalbensteinberg near Weissenburg in the Nordgau, made public by M. Johann Alexander Doederlein: a painted panel of Saint Pheodor the Duke, with Slavonic inscriptions in Cyrillic letters. Doederlein himself conjectures that its origin is Russian; an anonymous author in a Latin letter conjectures that it is contemporary with the Greek *Menologion*—that is, approximately the year 984, not, as Baronius had proposed, 885 [Note: [Col. 1378D] M. Johann Alexander Doederlein, *A Slavonic-Russian Sanctuary in the Middle of Germany*, Nuremberg, 1724, quarto]. To me, however, as to Baronius, the *Menologion* seems a century older. For it contains no figure younger than Leo the Philosopher and his wife. I hold the same view concerning this panel. The soldiers accompanying the prince are indeed extremely similar to the Normans whom Matilda of Flanders represented on the Norman tapestry at Bayeux. Its architecture is likewise Byzantine—for the arches of the doors are not pointed—and the roofs of the towers have an Oriental appearance, since beneath them an arch slightly pointed at the top extends on either side with a pronounced outward curve. Thus everything so far agrees with the Russians, or with a Slavic people not far removed from Constantinople.

The radiate form of the imperial crown, however, absolutely forbids this conclusion. It is well known that no images of the emperors of the East survive in which the crown is radiate—certainly none after the fourth century of the Christian era, except those of women [Note: [Col. 1378D] The last radiate crown among men is that of Constantine II; see Banduri, in Malliot [and Martin], *Researches on the Costumes of the Ancient Peoples*, Paris, 1804, quarto, vol. I, plate LV, no. 4]. For the image of Constantine VI made by Pope Leo at Rome is irrelevant to the matter.

In Germany, however, such a crown occurs in the ninth, tenth, and eleventh centuries, and it is in fact very similar to the ancient crown of the emperors. A crown preserved at Nuremberg is said to be that of Charlemagne, although it bears the name of Conrad, added in the upper semicircle [Note: [Col. 1378D] This crown is reproduced in *Wahl- und Krönungs-Diarium Kaiser Franz I.*, Frankfurt, 1746, folio]. There is also, apart from the upper semicircle, an exactly similar representation of a crown reproduced by Doederlein on p. 80. It is worn by the emperor Licinius as he orders Theodore to be beaten with rods and clubs; in all the other figures of the same work the customary radiate crown of the kings or emperors of Germany is represented.

It therefore appears that the panel was made by a Slavic people bordering on Germany. If we recall that the Slavic peoples—the Sorbs, who were not different from the Serbs, and others—formerly occupied those very regions where the panel is now found [Note: [Col. 1378D] Spruner, *Atlas*, no. 12], or at least that the great kingdom of Moravia was not far distant, where Saint Methodius, seated as archbishop at Weligrad (Hradish), had seven subject Slavic bishops in a mixed church, we shall not rashly conclude that the panel is a monument of the ancient Slavonic Church in those regions [Note: [Col. 1379C] My friend Hloudow, who is especially versed in the ecclesiastical antiquities of Russia, holds a different opinion. He says that most examples of radiate crowns occur not in secular but in ecclesiastical objects; he also considers the text to have the flavor of a more recent Russian language]. A similar image of the “ancient” Mother of God was found in the town of Oblau, near Breslau, with Cyrillic letters [Note: [Col. 1379D] Maciejowski, *Historical Essay on the Christian Church of the Two Rites*, p. 131].

In that panel, however, Caesar Augustus Licinius is always called *Czar Likin*. Moreover, the Slavic peoples of the Eastern Empire have always called the city of Constantinople *Czaragrad* [Note: [Col. 1379D] Herberstein, *Commentaries on Muscovite Affairs*, p. XI]—that is, “royal city” or “imperial city.” In the Byzantine authors Theophanes and Nicephorus, the Bulgarian princes are called *Xeres*, which Buat correctly observed to be the same as *Czars* [Note: [Col. 1379D] De Buat, *Ancient History of the Peoples of Europe*, vol. XII, p. 247 ff. He cites Theophanes, p. 289 (Bonn edition, p. 667.15), where one reads *τοὺς ἀπὸ σειρᾶς καταγομένους* (“those descended from the line”), and Nicephorus, p. 77, line 14: *τοὺς μὲν ἐκ Ξηρᾶς τὴν ἐπ’ αὐτοὺς κεκτημένους κτείνουσιν* (“they kill those who held power over them from Xeras”), where Goar wrongly thinks that *τοὺς μὲν ἐκ σειρᾶς* should be restored]. The kings of Serbia in the fourteenth century enjoyed the name *Tzaris*; thus in the laws of Serbia Dušan is always called *Tzar* [Note: [Col. 1379D] Maciejowski, [work cited], p. 266].

By contrast, the Russians generally used another title in the Middle Ages, and they were not alone in doing so. In their own language the princes of Russia were called *Knies* (“dukes”); their superiors were called *Weliki Knies*, that is, “great princes” or “great dukes”—with no greater, and certainly no lesser, right than the dukes of Austria, who are archdukes, or the Florentines, who are grand dukes.

For *Knies* is the same as *Chan*, *Kanis*, or *Chagan*, and denotes a king, just as the “Great Khan” in Crimea is the same as the *Veliki Knies* in Russia. Among the Tatars, *Khan*, *Chagan*, *Canis*, or *Cacanus* means “lord, king, emperor” [Note: [Col. 1379D] Vincent of Beauvais, XXXII.32; Pachymeres III.25, V.4, X.25; Du Cange, *Glossarium mediae et infimae Graecitatis*, s.v. *κάνης*, *κνέζης*, and in the Latin work s.v. *Caganus*; the Annals of Saint Bertin, under the year 839]. It is reported that both the Russians and the Hungarians used the very word *Chagan* or *Cacan* [Note: [Col. 1379D] Gregory of Tours, Paul the Deacon: “Caganus, king of the Hungarians”; and the Frankish Annals of Saint Bertin, under the year 839: “He also sent with them certain men who said that they—that is, their people—were called Rhos, whom their king, called Chaganus, had sent to him, as they claimed, for the sake of friendship.” Compare Roger, *On the Destruction of the Hungarians*, 33].

What shall I say about the Poles?

Should I say that the ancient Poles used the title *Czar*, *Chagan*, or some other title? No certain monument of this matter remains. Some say that *Krol*—pronounced *Kral* by the Bohemians—is derived from Charlemagne. But, unless I am mistaken, this is merely an etymological conjecture. In its place I seem to detect another, more plausible derivation from the root *Kri*, expressing the nature of a judge. This seems all the more probable because among the Slavs the expression *τῷ Kriwa* indicated the highest dignity, both priestly and judicial.

The Poles also use another word, namely *τῷ Ksiaze*, pronounced *Kjonje*, which seems to have some resemblance to the German *König*. Finally, among them *Wudz* means “duke.” We have already mentioned that the compound word *Woiewoda* means the same as “duke of war.” As matters now stand, no certain conclusion can be established. But whatever the outcome, this at least is beyond all doubt: none of these words in any way signifies a feudal duke, if the dignity we have demonstrated was what they expressed concerning the princes of Poland. In Roman times that dignity was undoubtedly expressed by the Latin word *Rex*, “king.”

Led by the desire to increase royal power, Boleslav perhaps judged the Latin title *Rex* especially suitable, since it was unknown to the Poles, and could make the monarchy, less dependent on the people, hereditary within his family [Col. 1380B] [Note: [Col. 1380D] Boleslav’s epitaph in Christoph Hartknoch, *On the Polish Republic*, II, section 8, seems to convey this meaning:

> You possessed, as Christ’s athlete,  
> the kingdom of the Slavs, Goths, or Poles,  
> outstanding Caesar, driving away from yourself  
> the ducal titles, and so forth.]

The following chapters will show that Boleslav did many other things for this purpose.

## CHAPTER XXXVI.—Boleslav, endowed by Otto III with a royal crown, a lance or scepter, and a sword, is called “a friend of the Roman people”

Boleslav I could therefore already rightly enjoy royal honor. The emperor Otto III seems to have done nothing more than recognize what he could not prevent, thereby preserving or creating for himself, in some fashion, the right to approve or disapprove—or even to grant or deny. At that time the emperors could do not the slightest thing more.

Otto therefore, invited by no one, came from Italy under the pretext, as some Polish writers maintain, of visiting the body of Saint Adalbert, to distant and uncultivated Poland—at that time a Hyperborean land—in the middle of winter. He was received with the greatest honor by Boleslav. As though to demonstrate his gratitude to the Pole, he presented his own royal crown, royal lance or scepter, and royal sword to his host. At the same time he proclaimed Boleslav “a friend and ally of the Roman people” [Note: [Col. 1380D] Gallus, pp. 41–42; Długosz, column 131; Miechow, I.II.4, section 27; Cromer, *History of Poland*, II.4; Guagnin I, p. 71; Ludewig, *On Royal Auspices*, II, p. 77; his epitaph, chapter XXXV, no. 24. Compare chapter XIV, notes 12 and 13].

Roepell himself correctly observed that this ancient Latin formula—hardly known to the Polish historians of the Middle Ages from Roman history—betrays the learning of Otto III, who, because of his previously unheard-of studies in humane letters and antiquity, was celebrated by the surname “Wonder of the World” [Col. 1381A] [Note: [Col. 1381D] Roepell, [work cited], p. 111].

Nevertheless, this should be understood only of the complete formula, “friend and ally of the Roman people.” For the expression “friend and ally” was also used in the time of the Ottos in a political sense, so to speak, of peoples who were subject to no yoke of servitude, however slight, under the empire—or under the Frankish kingdom. Thus Widukind first calls the Saxons “friends and allies of the Franks” against the Thuringians [Note: [Col. 1381D] Widukind, *Deeds of the Saxons*, I.9–11 (Pertz V, p. 418)].

It follows from this as well that Boleslav’s royal dignity was approved by the emperor Otto III. Thietmar himself, although he scarcely conceals his anger in his breast, seems, if read more attentively, to reveal unwillingly the truth of this matter. He mentions Boleslav I nearly ninety times. Sixty-six times he simply names him Boleslav, without any epithet. Ten times, and indeed twice under the year 1018 (Pertz V, p. 861, lines 2 and 9), he calls him merely the son of Mieszko; once a Pole; three times “the Elder” (*Seigneur*). But observe the remarkable fact: once, under the year 1004, he calls him “an adulterine duke” (Pertz, p. 808, line 13); twice, under the year 1004, “a roaring lion”; once “arrogant” (p. 807, line 35); once “puffed up with the magnanimity of pride” (p. 808, line 4); once, under the year 1012, “a proud victor” (p. 529, line 32); and once, under the year 1003, “ruler of the Poles” (p. 799, line 4).

Under the year 1002 he says that Boleslav was far inferior to his father Mieszko. This indicates nothing other than that Boleslav was less subject to the emperors. Under the year 1016 Thietmar reproaches the emperor because, although he could have had Boleslav ready and faithful to his service if only peace had been granted, he neglected to do so (p. 845, line 37). Under the year 1018 Thietmar says that Boleslav regarded the German emperor as equal to the emperor of Constantinople (p. 871, line 11).

The passage of Thietmar that seems most relevant to our subject occurs in book V, chapter 6 [Note: [Col. 1381D] Thietmar, book V, chapter 6, Pertz V, p. 193, lines 27–34], where he says that the roles had been reversed under Boleslav. He laments that, whereas formerly the prince of Poland had been subject to the empire or to the dukes and margraves of Saxony, the latter had now become subject to Boleslav:

> “Observing this, our men believed his embellished words and, having gone to the same man disgracefully, as though to a lord, exchanged their innate honor for supplication and unjust servitude. How unjustly our predecessors are to be compared with our contemporaries! While the excellent Hodo was alive, this man’s father, Mieszko, never dared enter the house wearing the *crusinatus*—the *crusina* being a Slavic fur garment—in which he knew Hodo to be, nor did he ever presume to sit when Hodo rose. May God forgive the emperor, who, making a tributary into a lord, ever raised him to such a height that, forgetting his Creator’s rule, he dared gradually to draw into subjection those always placed above him, and to catch, with the very cheap hook of transitory money, men baited to the detriment of servitude and freedom.”

The sword given by Otto, which the Poles called *Szcrzerbec*, was always preserved as a sacred object. They say that an inscription upon it recorded its Ottonian origin and suggested the eleventh century [Note: [Col. 1381D] Naruszewicz, *History of the Polish Nation*, IV, p. 138]. The emperor was always accompanied by a sword-bearer, as an ancient picture in the manuscript of Domnizo’s book shows: it depicts Otto the Great presenting certain relics of the saints to Atto, margrave of Tuscany [Note: [Col. 1381D] *Guelphic Origins*, vol. I, plate III, facing p. 407].

## CHAPTER XXXVII.—The crown in our picture is a model of the crown of the Ottos. A new form of the Lombard crown appears on the seals of the Ottos

When I carefully examined the form of the clothing in the picture of our book (see fig. 1), the crown with which King Mieszko is adorned seemed to me to bear a particular resemblance to the forms of crowns appearing on the seals of the Ottos.

Those who investigate sphragistic matters must take care not to place excessive confidence in certain figures as they are shown in published diplomatic editions. For not only did the artist of those times give the image an extremely crude form on the die or seal, but the seals impressed in wax have generally been very poorly preserved and cannot be recognized with sufficient accuracy except by men especially experienced in these matters. Moreover, in our own times those who engrave such seals [Col. 1382C] on copper add, as is customary, certain features according to their own judgment, which they call ornaments, or omit others.

The seals attributed to Conrad I, either display a simple or double radiate crown adorned with three crosses [Note: [Col. 1381D] Seal of the year 916, in *Monumenta Boica*, vol. XI], or present a diadem—that is, a circlet—with three trefoils, which they call lilies [Note: [Col. 1381D] Seal in Shannat]. A painted figure in a Saxon manuscript Psalter, written in the eleventh century and marked Tiberius C. VI, provides an excellently preserved example of this lily-adorned diadem: it depicts a certain king of the English [Note: [Col. 1382D] Strutt, *Horda Angel-Cynnan*, I, fig. XIX].

King Henry wears on his seals a crown either lily-shaped in a similar manner [Note: [Col. 1382D] Erath, *Quedlinburg Diplomatic Code*, seal of the year 953], or radiate [Note: [Col. 1382D] Götz, *Imperial Seals*], or, finally, a simple diadem with a cross raised at the middle of the head, although it is impossible to determine how the cross is attached [Note: [Col. 1382D] Seal in Shannat].

In the seals of Otto the Great, one must distinguish the seals of Otto, king of Germany before the year 962, from those of Otto the emperor. The former either have a diadem [Note: [Col. 1382D] Erath, [work cited], seal of 961] or a lily-shaped crown [Note: [Col. 1382D] Zylles, *Defense of the Abbey of Saint Maximin*, pp. 15 and 18, seal of 953]; in both, a royal banner is carried in the right hand. The seals of the emperor Otto, however, display a new form [Note: [Col. 1382D] *Guelphic Origins* (seal of 970), vol. V, p. 7].

See fig. 9 of our plate. The emperor leans his right hand upon a certain scepter, if not an ancient one [Note: [Col. 1382D] Lightly armed soldiers toward the end of the Roman Empire, from Boissard and Montfaucon, in Malliot, *Researches on the Costumes*, vol. I, plate LXXIX, nos. 7 and 8], at least a Carolingian one, which they call a spear or lance [Note: [Col. 1383D] Figure of Charles II, “the Bald,” king, on a painted panel in a royal Bible manuscript, in Montfaucon, *Monuments of the French Monarchy*, and Malliot, *Researches on the Costumes*, etc., vol. III, plate XIV; the same for the emperor Lothair I, ibid.], whose upper part is a simple little sphere and which, gradually narrowing, ends below in a point. In his left hand he holds a large globe adorned with a cross, representing the Christian world. The crown seems almost hemispherical, like a helmet, and is adorned with three slightly raised globules.

The meaning of those globules on the crown is demonstrated particularly well by a painted figure in the manuscript of Domnizo (see fig. 7 of our plate), in which Otto the Great wears a crown adorned with three long projections, the heads of which are those globules [Note: [Col. 1383D] Vatican manuscript of Domnizo, in *Guelphic Origins*, plate III, facing p. 405]. The golden crown of the Lombards, which they call the iron crown and which is preserved at Monza (see fig. 8 of our plate), is iron on the inside and is said to have been made from a plate resembling the nail of the Passion, in the same manner as the Burgundian lance [Note: [Col. 1383D] Muratori, *Writers of Italian Affairs*, I, p. 460].

Since our Redeemer was fastened to the cross with three nails, the Ottos, as I am persuaded, judged that all these things ought to be signified externally, and therefore seem to have ordered a new form of crown to be made.

There is some diversity in the seals of Otto II, although it is not sufficiently clear how much should be attributed to the ignorance of those who engraved the figures on copper. A certain seal in Zylles offers a distinctive cap [Note: [Col. 1383D] Zylles, [work cited], p. 25; Heineccius, *On Seals*, V.6, seal of 974]. The one published by Shannat also presents a cap, but of a somewhat different form; the three globules, however, are more clearly distinguishable here [Note: [Col. 1383D] Shannat, [work cited]; Struve, *Corpus of German History*, no. 14]. In Erath the same year and the same type are represented more accurately and faithfully [Note: [Col. 1383D] Erath, [work cited], seal of 974] (see fig. 10 of our plate). There the form of those globules is finally clearer, as it is in another type in *Guelphic Origins* and in Erath [Note: [Col. 1383D] *Guelphic Origins* V, p. 6, seal of 963] (see fig. 11). For this reason we judge the figure of Zylles and Heineccius to have been badly represented [Note: [Col. 1383D] Zylles, p. 21, seal of 963; Heineccius V.3].

The crown that Götz represents as radiate may perhaps be the ancient crown of the kings of Germany. Finally, so that nothing may be omitted, a seal of Otto II occurs in Muratori in which the head is adorned with no diadem [Note: [Col. 1383D] Muratori, V, p. 235].

There survive, in the choir of Magdeburg Cathedral, two celebrated but still unpublished sculpted stone statues of the two Ottos (see figs. 12 and 13). The father’s imperial insignia and the son’s royal insignia not only demonstrate the antiquity of the statues but also show that they were made while the father was still alive. A distinctive crown surrounds a pointed helmet. I shall discuss them more fully elsewhere. Such an appearance is military and Germanic [Col. 1384A]. Concerning it Widukind says (II.36): “The ancestral appearance, and one that never used anything foreign.” Here it is enough to have shown that there was then great diversity in head coverings or crowns, almost as there is today in the annual changes of clothing styles.

On the seals of Otto III we see a new crown adorned with three lilies [Note: [Col. 1384D] Erath, seal of 985; Shannat, ibid.; in Erath there is another type impressed in lead, of the year 999], or even a hemispherical cap adorned with three lilies; a fourth can be seen at the top [Note: [Col. 1384D] Seal of 990, in Zylles, p. 28, and Heineccius V.8]. In a single example, from the year 996 (see fig. 14), that crown occurs with three globules [Note: [Col. 1384D] Heineccius V.7].

Finally, there are several seals of Henry II [Note: [Col. 1384D] Erath, seal of 1005, “King”; the same, seal of 1021, “Emperor”], Conrad II [Note: [Col. 1384D] Zylles, seal of 1026; Erath, seal of 1036], and Henry III [Note: [Col. 1384D] Shannat, [work cited]; Struve, *Corpus of German History*, no. 18; Mader IV, no. 13, on a coin of Archbishop Pilgrim of Cologne] in which those globules appear attached to the crowns. After this I have found no example of globules on the crowns of the emperors of Germany. Nor have I encountered among the seals of other peoples any example of a crown adorned with those three globules.

I therefore seem able to affirm that the crown worn by Mieszko II in our painted figure is precisely the crown with which Otto III honored Boleslav, Mieszko’s father. I would add that the figure in our manuscript is preserved extremely well, so that it offers those interested in the matter a very accurate form of such crowns. For we see not only three golden globules projecting from the upper part of the crown, but also three other globules, blue in color, set into the lateral front of the crown; they seem to indicate the color of iron. This feature, badly represented on seals or easily worn away over a long period, could disappear from the surviving copies [Col. 1384C].

A passage of Martin the Gaul seems relevant to our subject, in which an ancient tradition concerning a holy nail given by Otto III to Boleslav has been preserved, although misunderstood [Note: [Col. 1384D] Martin the Gaul, p. 61]. The Polish kings therefore borrowed the form of their crowns from the kings—or emperors—of Germany in approximately the same way as the Russian kings borrowed the form of their crowns from the emperors of the East.

The Byzantines used a hemispherical crown filled with pearls and adorned at its peak with a cross; from it, on either side, hung ribbons adorned likewise with pearls or gems [Note: [Col. 1384D] Gold coin in the treasury of the king of France, of Nicephorus II and Basil, in Khell, supplement, p. 305; gold coins of Constantine VI and Romanus Lecapenus in Banduri, *Eastern Empire*, II, p. 783; hundreds of others occur on coins and in manuscripts]. The grand dukes of Russia wore the same crown from the time of Vladimir the Great onward (see fig. 15), although the ribbons were later removed [Note: [Col. 1384D]

Silver coin of Vladimir, published in *Annals of the Moscow Society*, III.2, no. 2.

The banner of the same Vladimir, preserved at Gruzino near Novgorod, on which his image is painted, published ibid. II, p. 107, according to Strahl, *History of Russia*, I, p. 363. It is absent from the copy in the Royal Library at Berlin [Col. 1385D]. Strahl likewise notes, on the authority of the *Voskresensk Chronicle* I, p. 205, that the grand dukes did not even remove these crowns or caps (*κολσονη*) in church.]

## CHAPTER XXXVIII.—A new anointing as king seems to have been performed by the archbishop of Gnesen, with the approval of the pope; the sons were anointed at the same time; and tribute was given to Saint Peter

[Col. 1385A]

Nevertheless, Boleslav I was crowned before he died in the year 1025; and we have already seen that not even Roepell denied this [Note: [Col. 1385D] Chapter XX, no. 2]. But, you may object, if he already possessed royal dignity; if Otto had voluntarily invested him with the royal crown, sword, and scepter, he had no need of a second or third coronation.

You seem now to be saying something. Nevertheless, we must take care not to be deceived by appearances. Examples of repeated coronations are not rare; they occur all the more often when there is greater fear that the dignity in question might be called into question from one side or the other. Thus Pippin, the father of Charlemagne, was elected by the Franks in the Field of Mars and raised upon a shield [Note: [Col. 1385D] Annals of Saint Bertin, under the year 750: “Pippin was elected king according to the custom of the Franks”]. He was certainly already king of the Franks; nevertheless, he was not content with that election. Nor was the approval of Pope Zachary, given by letter, sufficient for him [Note: [Col. 1385D] The Annals of Fulda, the Annals of Loisel, and the Annals of Lorsch]. He was crowned and anointed king by Saint Boniface at Soissons according to a new rite.

Nor did this seem sufficient to him. For when Stephen II, the pope, visited Pippin in the Frankish kingdom, Pippin himself—apparently in the capacity of emperor—together with his wife Bertrada, and their sons, were crowned and anointed a third time [Note: [Col. 1385D] Chapter XXXIV, no. 19].

His son Charlemagne was moreover crowned as many as four times [Note: [Col. 1385D]

1. First, while his father was still alive, in the year 755, by Pope Stephen.

2. After his father’s death, he was elected and crowned according to Frankish custom. The anonymous author of the chronicle in Du Chesne I, p. 350: “King Pippin died, and his sons Charles and Carloman were elected to the kingdom.”

The Annals of Lorsch, under the year 768: “Charles and Carloman were made kings by the consent of all the Franks.”

Einhard, *Life of Charlemagne*, chapter 3: “The Franks, having solemnly held a general assembly, appointed both as their kings, on the following condition, and so forth.”

3. When his brother Carloman renounced the kingdom or died, he was also elected king of that kingdom, crowned and anointed, although apparently in a disorderly manner.

The Annals of Metz, under the year 771: “And the leading men who had belonged to Carloman anointed Lord Charles as king over them.”

4. He was made king—or emperor?—of the Lombards.

5. He was made emperor of the Romans by the supreme pontiff and the Roman people.]

Boleslav therefore seems to have repeated this coronation chiefly for two reasons. The first was to prevent defections before his death; the second was to strengthen his sons against the emperors and against the group they call the *Szlachta*—that is, the soldiers, citizens, or nobles—who were passionately attached to liberty, by increasing through a new rite the power and honor inherent in royal dignity [Col. 1385C].

Boleslav had twice seen with his own eyes how the emperor and the Germans attached an abusive meaning to his presence at the assemblies of the German princes. He almost never did what the emperor ordered him to do as though he were a soldier, and the king was ashamed to attend such an assembly [Note: [Col. 1386D] See chapter XV, sections 3 and 5; chapter XVI, notes 14 and 16; and chapter XVIII, no. 1].

In the same way, while his father was alive, Mieszko had twice or three times attended the German assemblies, usually unwillingly, and had been compelled to repeat a certain act of homage [Note: [Col. 1386D] See chapter XVI, no. 12; chapter XVIII, no. 1]. For this very reason the anointing by the archbishop of the Poles was to be carried out with the approval of the supreme pontiff and with all the magnates of all the peoples recently subjected assisting at it.

Our dedicatory letter seems to indicate that Mieszko had already been made king while his father was still alive, in name but not in auspicious ceremony. For in its third line we read: “Since divine grace has granted you equally the royal name and honor.”

It is well known that Stephen, prince of Hungary, received a crown from the supreme pontiff. I therefore find no reason to say that such a crown was denied to the king of Poland by the Apostolic See, whether by Benedict VIII or John XX, provided that he requested it. The supreme pontiff would not have rejected an opportunity to bind the kingdom of Poland directly to the chair of Saint Peter.

There is an old tradition among the Poles that precisely this took place [Note: [Col. 1386D] Peter Damian, *Life of Saint Romuald*, section 48; Struve, *Corpus of German History*, I, p. 267, note 42]. Add to this that it would have provided the simplest opportunity for establishing the tribute of Saint Peter in Poland. This could have happened neither earlier nor later: not earlier, because of the isolation of the Christians and the recent conversion to the Latin rite—or to Christ; and not later, because the story that Casimir was sent back from the monastery of Cluny and imposed the tribute for that reason is considered by many to be entirely false [Note: [Col. 1386D] Roepell, Mabillon, Naruszewicz; see above].

Nor can it be doubted that the tribute imposed on the Poles by the father before his death increased their hatred of the religion among a people who were for the most part Christians in name but pagans, or Greek-Slavonic Christians, in heart [Note: [Col. 1386D] “Richeza, greedy and seeking new methods of collecting money.” Cromer III, p. 37; Miechow II.13]. Since this tradition therefore agrees in a remarkable way with the testimony of the German chroniclers, it does not seem to me remote from the truth.

Moreover, all the uncertainties in later writers could easily have arisen when they saw that so many coronations were reported, although they thought that only one of them could be genuine. The Poles preserved the sword as a monument of the coronation performed by the emperor, and for that reason considered this particular coronation the true one. The crown, however, could have perished in one way or another.

## CHAPTER XXXIX.—Mieszko II possessed royal dignity among the Poles, against the wishes of the German writers. He was versed even in Greek letters, as was the entire lineage of the empress Theophano, and so forth.

Whether that coronation was repeated immediately after the father’s death, as the Polish writers maintain, is uncertain. It could have happened. Certainly he was crowned either once, before or after his father’s death, or twice, by the pontiff, the archbishop of Gniezno, and was acknowledged or elected by the voice of the magnates. For our preface says not only, in its tenth line, “And you, elected not so much by human as by divine judgment,” but also, in its thirtieth line: “Almighty God, by whose ordinance you have been crowned with the royal diadem” [Note: [Col. 1387C] Tolner, *History of the Palatinate*, *Codex diplomaticus*, cited above.]. Hence the widowed Rixa is called in all the charters “once Queen of Poland.” Consider, then, how much confidence the historians deserve in these matters, when nevertheless they call Misego II merely a duke.

Our preface also teaches us another fact, hitherto unknown. It is sufficiently well known that a certain degree of learning then began in all schools. Charlemagne indeed imposed the study of the Greek language upon monasteries; but after his death this discipline was neglected, except at Monte Cassino in Italy, where, according to the biographer of Saint Adalbert, Greek priests lived. Examples of the study of languages were not uncommon. Thus Pope Bruno used three or four languages—German, Latin, French, and, apparently, Italian [Col. 1387C] [Note: [Col. 1387C]

His funeral eulogy in the Basilica of Saint Peter [Col. 1387D] (Leibniz, vol. I of *Writers on the History of Brunswick*, p. 576):

> “German in tongue, taught in the city of Wangia,  
> > Using the Frankish, the vernacular, and the Latin speech,  
> > He instructed peoples through a threefold eloquence.”]

. Mathildis, however, teaches us that not only was the Latin language propagated in Germany and Poland, but that several men already existed who were by no means unlearned in Greek; indeed, that the king of Poland, the king of the Slavic peoples, knew it. Yet this should not seem surprising. For the cause, as it appears to me, was a certain woman, and for that very reason she had greater influence in promoting morals and learning—though her influence did not extend beyond her own family and the circle in which she possessed some authority.

Theophano, of Greek origin, on marrying Otto II, must necessarily, through the arrogance of the Greeks at that time, have taught both her husband and her children this language [Col. 1388A]. Hence the learning of Otto III and of his teacher Gerbert (Sylvester II). Through her daughters Adelheid, abbess of Quedlinburg, and Sophia, abbess of Gandersheim, one or another of the nuns in those monasteries must have been instructed in these languages. A third daughter, named Mathildis, married Henry, Count Palatine of the Rhine, and became the mother not only of six daughters who were abbesses of the most celebrated monasteries of western Germany—among them one received the name Theophano, after her grandmother [Note: [Col. 1387D]

Tolner, cited above, p. 257.

Theophania, a nun in 989 and abbess of the monastery of Essen, after it had fallen into decay, arranged for another monastery to be erected there from its foundations in a new and elegant style in 1051. The year of her death is uncertain, but she was buried there.],

but also of Rixa, the wife of our Misego. Rixa therefore seems to have been the reason why Misego was educated in the Greek language.

For I would not believe that this language, preserved in Poland through the ancient connection of the Slavic peoples with the Greek Church, survived there, although in Bohemia there were certain monasteries [Col. 1388B] where Greek was taught.

Moreover, Mathildis’s letter itself prevents us from understanding the matter in this way. For she says: “You preferred to add Greek.”

What I have said about the monasteries of Quedlinburg and Gandersheim, and about the great learning of the nuns who worshiped God there, is confirmed by the fact that they instructed the children of kings and princes. Thus Beatrix, daughter of Emperor Conrad II, was entrusted to these nuns for upbringing and education, and already at the age of seven or eight became a prodigy of learning [Note: [Col. 1387D] A contemporary author, *Chronicle of Quedlinburg* (Leibniz, *Writers on Brunswick*, vol. II, p. 296), under the year 1025:

> “As they were going to Italy, Conrad and Gisela sent their only daughter to be raised by the abbess Adelheid. Soon afterward, when the aforesaid imperial abbess learned of Lady Beatrix’s arrival, she came joyfully with her attendants from Trobiki (Drübke) and brought her with her to the metropolis of Quedlinburg. But with what honor, as befitted royal offspring, with what affection, [Col. 1388C] and with what care she was received and afterward brought up by the abbess herself, by the nuns residing in the aforesaid place, and by all subject to her; or by what disposition of character, speech, and conduct she advanced with each increase of age—no ability or eloquence in speech is sufficient to tell. For with what praise shall I proclaim that among the first . . .” (the remainder has fallen out of the manuscript); see also Pertz V, p. 90.].

## CHAPTER XL.—That the Russians were afflicted by a defeat in the year 1026 is demonstrated.

[Col. 1388C] I do not see why we should reject what the Polish writers relate: that, after the death of the exceptionally vigorous Bolizlavus, the Russians besieged the fortresses in which Bolizlavus had stationed Polish garrisons. Otto (or Bezprim), who, as is well known, stirred heaven and earth against his brother Misego, was already then making war, either because he had been deprived of the portion which his father, according to the most ancient custom—by which the superior king became such only in wartime—had assigned to him, or because he aspired to the kingdom against his father’s final wishes. To this may be connected what some relate about Otto’s flight into Russia [Note: [Col. 1388D]

Roepell thinks that this Russia was some part of Hungary, although he himself does not know which part. For he does not dare reject the testimony of Wippo and others (see chapter XXIII, no. 3).

The ancient German writers commonly say *Rucia* or *Ruzzia* for Russia.

Helmold, *Chronicle of the Slavs* I: “The southern shore of the Slavs is inhabited by nations, of which the first from the east are the Russians, then the Poles.”

Adam of Bremen, *On the Situation of Denmark*, no. 221, mentions the kingdom of Russia as connected with Poland.

Thietmar likewise (p. 192) uses *Rucia* for Russia.];

and this gave Jaroslav [Col. 1389A] and the Russians an opportunity to attempt to drive the Poles from the lands which Vladimir (his father) had once possessed.

In this expedition Misego could easily have attained and preserved his father’s ancient glory. For the other enemies were not yet sufficiently prepared to defeat the Poles. Emperor Henry had died at almost the same time as Bolizlavus, and Conrad, who succeeded him, had not yet suppressed the civil disturbances that followed the new election. Nor could the Russians themselves repel the Poles with great force, since a major war was raging between the princely brothers. The words of Mathildis’s letter in the fourth and fifth lines seem to provide some testimony to this war, so distant from the conflict between the Poles and Russians, where she says that he ruled with a fortunate beginning. I insist that this cannot refer to raids into the border marches. For Mathildis was not only German and Christian, but also the sister of the wife of the new German king, Conrad II, with whom she was closely connected. She could not have called devastations in the marches fortunate events. Mathildis also aptly adds, “as I have heard,” thereby indicating events remote by a great distance.

For this reason I think the whole passage should be understood as the Polish writers transmit it, because it truly happened. Moreover, Roepell himself concedes elsewhere that ancient records among the Poles, now lost, once existed and were used by Długosz and others [Note: [Col. 1389D] Roepell I, p. 171, note 13, and elsewhere.].

## CHAPTER XLI.—That under Misego II the pagans and others who resisted the Latin Church and the king defected.

Bolizlavus I had enjoyed success in almost everything [Col. 1389C]. He had increased royal power through continual wars, enlarging the provinces and accumulating honors. The nobles and citizens, however, as usually happens, had lost as much as the king had gained. Something similar had happened to the peasants. But the pagans and Slavs, or Greek Christians, felt themselves most wretched—not only those who had gone into exile or lived in the forests, but also those who had been converted unwillingly or superficially to the Christian, or Catholic Latin, faith; all the more because a tribute had to be paid to the Church, and finally because they were oppressed by an iron penitential discipline.

It is clear that the propagation of the Christian religion occurred in one manner before Constantine the Great and in another afterward. In the earliest times this propagation was slow [Col. 1389D] and peaceful. So far were Christians from compelling pagans by force that they themselves instead became the martyrs of Christ. After Constantine, the situation was reversed: pagan temples were forcibly closed; pagans were subjected to persecution; and gentiles—through the abuse of ambition, lamenting the loss of their kingdom—were made worshipers of Christ by the sword no less than by the word. From the time of Charlemagne onward, the introduction of the Christian religion into pagan lands was almost always sudden and tumultuous, though in such a way that one cannot tell whether the Christians taught the Muslims this new custom, or the Muslims taught it to them.

In the earliest period, resistance was greatest, often bloody, and repeated a hundred times. Later the pagans resisted more rarely; nevertheless, in lands recently converted to Christ there were never lacking pagans who opposed the new faith. Thus in that part of Slavonia which is now Brandenburg, Christians were massacred or expelled and churches burned on more than four occasions. Thus in Hungary, as we saw above, Béla was summoned to become king chiefly by a pagan or Greek faction [Note: [Col. 1389D] See chapter XXIV, no. 58 and following.]. Thus in Bohemia, not only factions of nobles but also pagan customs—some stricter, others looser than those of the Christians—compelled Saint Adalbert to abandon his episcopal see, because the dukes of Bohemia, unlike the Polish Bolizlavus, did not establish themselves as defenders of the ecclesiastical canons. Thus in Carinthia the peasants professed the true religion, although the magnates opposed it with hand and foot for a long time, ridiculing and despising Christianity as the religion of the poor and peasants—just the opposite of what happened in the Roman Empire, where the noblest people were the first to convert to Christ and, scorning the ancient worship of gods and idols to which the peasants in the villages clung most tenaciously, called it paganism.
