Therefore the pagan Slavs, or those recently converted, detested the study of letters and all the liberal arts. Russian parents thought that knowledge of letters was a diabolical art; the schools remained deserted unless [Col. 1390C] the king’s command forcibly carried children into the schools [Note: [Col. 1389D]

Karamsin, *History of Russia*, vol. I.

Esneaux and Chénéchaud, *History of Russia* I, p. 121: “This novelty seemed so frightening that the children of distinguished ladies had to be dragged there by force, their parents believing that their children were lost, since writing was then regarded as the most dangerous invention of sorcery.”]

. It must also be added that the schoolmasters, being ecclesiastical men, generally lived in churches or monasteries.

If these things happened in Russia, there is nothing to prevent us from supposing that similar events occurred in Poland, where, as our Mathildis testifies, “Christians were compelled by the sword to attend the Lord’s Supper”; where Jordan, the first bishop of the Poles, is said by Thietmar to have “labored greatly, while diligently inviting them by word and deed to the worship of the vineyard on high” [Note: [Col. 1390D] Thietmar, p. 97.]. Add Thietmar’s own account of the barbarous way in which those who sinned against the laws of the Church were punished. For he says:

> “In the kingdom of this bridegroom”—Bolizlavus I—“there are many varied customs, and although dreadful, they are at times praiseworthy. His people must be pastured like oxen and chastised in the manner of a sluggish ass; and without severe punishment they cannot be treated with the salvation of the prince” (that is, the prince is condemned and loses the salvation of his soul unless he punishes ecclesiastical sinners with such severe punishment). “If anyone,” he continues, “dares to abuse the wives of others or to fornicate in this way, he immediately experiences the punishment of the ensuing vengeance. He is led to the market bridge, fastened by a nail through the scrotum, and, with a razor placed nearby, is given the hard choice either of dying there” (according to the ancient custom?) “or of being released from these things” (by a priest, according to Christian custom?). “And whoever is found to have eaten meat after Septuagesima is severely punished by having his teeth cut out. For divine law, newly arisen in these regions, is strengthened more effectively by such authority than by the fast imposed by the bishops. There are also other customs, far inferior to these, which please neither God nor the inhabitants and serve only to inspire terror; some part of them I have included above” [Note: [Col. 1391D] The same work, p. 247 and following.].

Thietmar therefore says nothing of certain penitential laws more terrible than those which, although dreadful, he considers praiseworthy. Our Mathildis also praises Bolizlavus for similar measures and, in praising the father, urges his son Misego [Col. 1391B] to become his father’s rival in these matters, so that he may “restore to God the souls deceived by diabolical fraud” [Note: [Col. 1391D] Chapter III, line 18.].

It will not be irrelevant to warn the reader not to confuse the severe ecclesiastical discipline of that age with the lax discipline of our own time. I shall add here a few passages from our book, from the penitential chapter, to recall that discipline to the reader’s memory.

The sinner confesses each sin to the priest, and among the things the priest is to do, the following is found on folio 17:

> “Whenever you give counsel to the sinner, also impose penance upon him, immediately stating how much he must fast and redeem his sins, lest you perhaps forget how long he ought to abstain. For it is necessary for you to ask him his sins again, because he may perhaps be ashamed to confess his sins again.”

Folio 18. Among the kinds of penance the following are listed:

> “They”—the priests—“determine what is just, prescribe punishments, bonds, tortures, scourges, exiles, mutilations of limbs, loss of possessions, deaths of various kinds . . . . . . There is also ecclesiastical severity, correction, excommunication, exclusion from the church, penitential laws, anathematization. Judges are appointed, officials attend to their duties, avengers are sent to correct this; and they cannot be removed from the Church.”

Folio 19. The sinner, humbly imploring the priest’s forgiveness, “shall prostrate himself completely upon the ground.”

Do not suppose that these are the dreadful laws not mentioned by Thietmar; rather, they were in force in every church. [Col. 1391D] It appears that the still more cruel and utterly inhuman measures which Thietmar preferred to leave unmentioned were such as pleased neither God nor the inhabitants.

Misego II, therefore, undoubtedly a supporter of the Church, imitating his father and continually encouraged by his wife Rixa, became a severe avenger of the laws of the Latin Church. He himself, a great lover of letters, seems to have taken the greatest care that children should be educated in monasteries against the wishes of their parents. The hatred of the native population grew stronger; those prepared to defect from Christ, from the Latin Church, and from the king were ready to seize the first opportunity to repay Christians, or Catholic Latins, in kind. That opportunity was provided both by the enemies of the kingdom and by the domestic dissension stirred up by Otto, Misego’s brother, as we have mentioned above [Note: [Col. 1391D] See chapter XXIV.].

## CHAPTER XLII.—A certain wife, Juditha, seems to have borne Misego II a son, his firstborn, Bolizlavus the Younger, a supporter of the pagans or of the Slavic-Greek Church.

The several traditions that relate to Misego II’s concubine, to a certain Juditha, and to his firstborn son Bolizlavus [Col. 1392B] are either unknown to many writers, rejected by them, or confused with other traditions [Note: [Col. 1391D] See chapter XXIV.]. We, however, by bringing them together, find them to be highly credible.

We have seen that his father, the great Bolizlavus, indulged himself in love more than was proper, following the ancient custom of the Slavic peoples and others. Why, then, should his son Misego not imitate “the ancient fornicator” in this matter as in others? Some have reported that he had relations with many concubines. Nothing therefore seems to prevent us from supposing that he had one, perhaps named Juditha—for that name is found in some sources as belonging to a wife—and that by her he fathered a firstborn son, to whom the famous grandfather gave the name Bolizlavus. Hence the son of Rixa seems to have received not the name of his grandfather Bolizlavus [Col. 1392C], but the new name Casimir. No other reason for departing from the custom of the time is apparent. We, instructed by the laws of civil right and the canons of the Church, distinguish the son of a lawful wife from the son of a servant woman or concubine. This custom, unknown to the Slavs of old just as it is today in the East, was a new canon of the Christian religion, and it prevailed all the more slowly because the priests themselves indulged even more immoderately in sexual matters. For clerical discipline was looser and had not yet been reformed by Gregory the Great. Indeed, according to the Roman order, as our liturgical book also states, a man could become a bishop if he had neither had a wife who was a widow, nor had relations with a woman consecrated to God, nor with animals [Col. 1392D], nor finally with a male [Note: [Col. 1391D]

Folio 48 of our manuscript: “Then the pontiff questions him”—the man who is to be ordained bishop—“about the four canonical matters, namely, *arsenokoitia* (ἀρσενοκοίτη, pederasty), a woman consecrated to God, animals, or whether he had a wife who had previously belonged to another man, which in Greek is called *deuterogamy* (δευτερογαμία).”

Council of Toledo IV, chapter 18 (A.D. 633), in Gregory IX’s *Decretals*, distinction 41, chapter 5, *Qui in aliquo*: “Those who have entered into a second marriage, or contracted numerous marriages; those who have married a widow or a woman abandoned by her husband; those who have corrupted married women; those who have had concubines or prostitutes, and so forth” (vol. I, p. 480.)].

.

That concubinage was not prohibited even in the ancient Church itself, to say nothing of the customs of the Slavs, but was entirely lawful outside marriage, is attested by canon 17 of the First Council of Toledo, whose wording is as follows:

> “He who has no wife but has a concubine in place of a wife is not to be excluded from Communion, provided only that he be content with the union of one wife or one concubine, whichever he prefers” [Note: [Col. 1393D] Laurentius Surius, *Universal Collection of Councils*, vol. I, p. 522.].

Misego II could therefore have fathered the younger Bolizlavus by a concubine before entering into marriage with Rixa. The ancient tradition preserved by Kadłubek, but poorly understood, that stepmotherly schemes were plotted against the firstborn by the second woman [Note: [Col. 1393D] See chapter XXIV, note 1.] contains nothing contrary to human nature. Indeed, such things happened in those times just as they happened elsewhere. We have seen that Ludolph, Otto the Great’s firstborn son by Edith, was subjected to every kind of mistreatment by his stepmother Adelheid, who intended her own son Otto II for the kingdom.

This younger Bolizlavus, therefore, is said to have been rescued from his stepmother—that is, Rixa—and entrusted to a monastery for education and upbringing. Nevertheless, his spirit seems to have inclined toward paganism or the Greek-Slavonic Church. An example of this is found in Godescalc, king of the Wends, who, although brought up as a boy in a monastery, nevertheless became the leader of his pagan people against the Christians, until a better cause gained the victory in him. Bolizlavus may likewise have supported this faction of the pagans and others, relying upon which he might obtain the royal dignity.

This younger Bolizlavus therefore seems, while his father was still alive, to have taken part in the Pomeranian war with his brother, who was still a child. At that time the children of princes, even when very young, often took part in wars fully armored, or were trained in military matters. Not only did Charles, son of Charlemagne, armed like a soldier, give an example of courage as a very young boy in the war against the Saxons [Col. 1393C]; Charlemagne himself, at the age of thirteen, when he went to meet Pope Stephen II, rode a horse while encased in iron from head to foot—a living and vivid example of his warlike people. The rebellious duke of the Pomeranians could therefore have challenged Bolizlavus and his brother Casimir to single combat; yet it would not have been wise to accept the challenge. Thus it happened that Béla the Hungarian, taking up their cause, emerged victorious. As for what Roepell remarks concerning the anachronism involving the death of Saint Stephen, I would say that it is of very little importance. They could have gone into exile before Saint Stephen’s death. Nor do the writers deny this [Note: [Col. 1393D] Długosz, cited above.].

## CHAPTER XLIII.—Misego II was unfortunate, not because he was unwarlike, but because he had many enemies all around him. Expelled from the kingdom, he was miserably made a eunuch at Prague. Sudden illness and death [Note: [Col. 1393D] See chapters XXI–XXV.]

[Col. 1393D]

Misego the king is said by most Polish writers to have been unwarlike. The best of them, however, deny this. The evidence for their view is all the wars which he sustained at once [Col. 1394A]. For this very reason he was less fortunate than his father, who had defeated his enemies one by one. Add to this the hatred of the pagans, already on the point of breaking out into rebellion; add the tireless ambition of his brother Otto. Is it surprising that success failed the Poles?

Otto, his brother, apparently stirred up the Hungarians as a second force; but they seized the province of Slovakia for themselves, not for Otto. The Bohemians, doing the same with the margraves, attempted each to recover his own part of Poland. While the nearest territories in the marches had to be defended and the distant ones in Moravia neglected, Conrad the king and Otto, invading the remaining lands of the Poles together—Conrad advancing through the marches, Otto through Bohemia—prepared the downfall of Misego II and Poland. After Misego’s cession of Lusatia [Col. 1394B], Conrad laid down his arms; nevertheless, brotherly hatred continued to blaze. Otto, apparently supported by the pagan or Greek-Slavonic faction, gained possession of the kingdom. His brother Misego, expelled, went to Prague to seek the hospitality of Bretislaus. But the duke is said to have subjected him to every insult. To avenge what had been done by Bolizlavus the Great, Misego’s father, against Bolizlavus the Red, duke of Bohemia, Bretislaus “captured him by treachery and tied his genitals with straps so that he could not beget children” [Note: [Col. 1393D] Gallus, p. 84; see also the beginning of chapter XXI above.].

This seems to me to have been the cause of his premature death. After his brother Otto had been killed, perhaps by the faction of the Latin Christians, which at that time already seems to have been the more powerful in that part of Poland, Misego indeed recovered the kingdom; but not long afterward, afflicted by a serious illness and for several months mostly deranged, he died.

That method of binding or amputating the genitals, ancient among the Indians [Note: [Col. 1393D]

Manu 8.372.

See also von Bohlen, *Ancient India*, Königsberg, 1830, vol. II, p. 7.],

the Egyptians [Note: [Col. 1393D] Diodorus Siculus I.78.], the Romans [Note: [Col. 1394D]

Horace, *Satires* I.2.45.

Leo’s *Novella* 32.],

and the Germans [Note: [Col. 1394D] *Lex Salica*, Emended text, title XXXI, chapters 18 and 19; *Lex Ripuaria*, title VI; *Law of the Angles and Werinians*, title V, chapters 3–7; *Law of the Frisians*, title XX and Supplement II; *Law of the Saxons* I.15; *Law of the Alemanni*, book LXV, chapter 28; and, as a punishment for theft in a temple among the pagan Frisians living between the Laubach and the Weser, *Law of the Frisians*, Supplement XII.]—was still customary among the Christian Slavs at that time, as Thietmar has already reported [Note: [Col. 1394D] Thietmar I, chapter, p. 247; see the preceding chapter.].

## CHAPTER XLIV.—Rixa may have been exiled from Poland twice: the first time with her son Casimir, and the second time before her son.

No one who has hitherto investigated Rixa’s fate has raised the question of what became of this queen and her son Casimir when Misego II was expelled from the kingdom of Poland. To me, Rixa does not at all seem to have remained in Poland. If you wish to suppose that this supporter of the Christians found refuge in monasteries [Col. 1394D], I warn you not to overlook that the monasteries themselves, the churches, and the priests were in the greatest danger. It is most probable that, uncertain of her husband’s return, she traveled with her son to Germany. “Wearied by the barbarous customs of the Slavs, [Col. 1395A] she came to Emperor Conrad,” as the monk of Brunweiler says [Note: [Col. 1395D] In Tölner, *History of the Palatinate*, p. 261A.]. Rixa could therefore have gone with her son to Cologne, where her brother was not yet archbishop—although the monk already expresses the dignity he later attained—but perhaps at that time a canon of the cathedral church; and where her sister Beata Ida was abbess of the monastery of Saint Mary in the Capitol. This was her homeland, the seat of her parents; for the castle of Tomberg, where she first saw the light, was not far away [Note: [Col. 1395D]

Tomberg, near Rheinbach in the ancient Duchy of Jülich.

See Spruner, *Historical Atlas*, no. 13, and my father, worthy of lasting remembrance, Johann Peter Dethier, *Contributions to the History of the District of Bergheim*, Cologne, 1833, p. 21.].

Not far from Cologne she had five other sisters who were abbesses. There, therefore, in the monastery of Saint Ursula, founded for another queen, she found an excellent refuge—and that she did so is attested by a charter [Note: [Col. 1396D] See above, chapter XXIV, no. 1 (in Miraeus).].

After her husband had returned to Poland and recovered the royal throne, nothing prevented Rixa from bringing her son back there as well [Col. 1395B].

After her husband’s death, Rixa, an ardent supporter of the Latin—that is, German—Church, acted as her son Casimir’s regent for a short time. The longstanding hatred of the native population, whom she herself also hated, was first directed against her alone. She therefore went into exile for the second time, alone, to her brother, now archbishop of Cologne. On this occasion her son seems soon to have followed her.

Thus all the traditions fit together perfectly, and no difficulty seems to remain in this matter.

## CHAPTER XLV.—Bolizlavus the Younger, relying on the pagans or the Greek-Slavonic faction, becomes king of the Poles after expelling his brother Casimir; but is soon killed by the Latin Christians. Poland is divided; the Latin Christians recall Casimir, while the Greeks or pagans briefly use Masla as king.

[Col. 1395C]

After Misego’s death, the pagan faction raises its head for the second time. Having driven Queen Rixa from the kingdom, it obtains as its leader the younger Bolizlavus, the firstborn, but born of another wife or concubine, and openly demonstrates what it wants. King Casimir is expelled; monasteries and churches are burned; priests are massacred; and Christians are attacked with the sword. Bolizlavus enjoys royal authority over the Poles, perhaps restoring to the people or nobles their ancient liberty, and seems, together with other Latin institutions, to have discarded the Latin word “king.” Certainly most writers do not count him among the kings of Poland, either because he did not assume the royal title or because he defected from the Latin Christian faith. Whatever dignity Bolizlavus possessed, however, did not benefit him; for the Latin Christians [Col. 1395D] soon emerged from that civil tumult as victors over most of Poland. Bolizlavus was killed, and Poland was divided into a southern—or Christian—and a northern—or pagan—part, so that the hostility between the Latin and Greek Churches benefited only the true pagans. The latter proclaimed a certain Masla, formerly cupbearer to Misego II, as prince or king. The former—that is, the Latin region—after being devastated for some time by civil war and by the Bohemians, finally recalled Casimir. Returning to Poland [Col. 1396A] and allied by treaty with Emperor Conrad and with the Russian king Jaroslav, he emerged victorious over Masla after a bloody and repeated war; and he subjected Poland to himself, if not in its entirety as his grandfather Bolizlavus I had organized it, at least as it had been before.

## CHAPTER XLVI.—The cruelty of the Poles at that time was the same as that of other peoples: Russians, Bohemians, Hungarians, Danes, Normans, Germans.—The origin of the word *Sklave*.

Many German writers accuse the Poles at that time, and their kings, in harsh terms—or rather heap accusations upon them—calling them barbarous plunderers. “Miseco,” says the Saxon Chronicler, “Duke of the Poles,” a false Christian, a murderer, a tyrant. . . . . . . . “Such, then, is King Mesecho; such is the detestable simplicity of his ways, such the condemnable purity of his innocence, such his justice, such the utterly false faith of his Christianity. If he is a king, why a plunderer? If simple, why an *apostrophus* (a turncoat, perhaps)? If faithful, why an apostate and tyrant? What business have you, bloody beast, with royal adornment, with a crown and a gilded spear? What agreement is there between Christ and Belial? What madness drives you arrogantly to carry arms rashly into the kingdom of Roman valor? How dangerous this will be for you, you will perceive only too late, when your unwarlike people, armed in great numbers, are crushed as they deserve by our men, who know and practice war” [Note: [Col. 1396D]

*Saxon Chronicler*, under the year 1030.

See also the *Saxon Annals*, under the year 1030.].

When we compare these insults with Mathildis’s highest praise, we cannot restrain our laughter, and we lament human nature, which, rarely content with truth, everywhere seeks superlatives. Besides, one might say that the Saxon Chronicler is responding to Mathildis’s preface. If ever in a man, certainly in this Misego, the golden mean is the best quality.

As for those Polish plunderings and raids, alas, the Chronicler spoke the absolute truth: he says, what are we to do with an ass that rubs another ass? All peoples at that time drank from the same cup. A war is prepared by a people greedy for glory and wealth; the borders of neighboring peoples are invaded; gold, silver, livestock, and valuable goods are seized; houses are burned; armed men, or those fit to bear arms, are slaughtered; women are violated and carried into slavery together with males not yet able to bear arms; finally, that part of the land which remains untouched promises tribute. The plunderers depart, the spoils—or, not to call them merely robberies, the booty—are divided; and the soldiers, laden with these things, return home, lift their heads to the stars, and, enriched in family and possessions, become the founders of a noble lineage, until they themselves suffer similar treatment at the hands of stronger or more fortunate neighbors. Τοιαῦθ᾽ ὁ τλήμων πόλεμος ἐνεργάζεται. “Such things does wretched war accomplish.”

Thus the Russians often plundered all the neighboring peoples and the Greek Empire, selling the inhabitants into slavery at auction.

Thus we saw the Bohemians, under Bretislaus, laying waste to Poland with fire and sword, indeed plundering the churches of Christians by Christians [Col. 1397A].

Thus the Hungarians often devastated Germany and treated the Slavic peoples most harshly [Note: [Col. 1397D]

Nestor II, pp. 116–117 (Schlözer edition).

Roepell, p. 31.].

Thus the Danes, almost every year, plundered everything in Britain.

Who does not know how the Normans ravaged every land of Europe?

Nor is this custom foreign to our own times.

It would take too long to enumerate the injuries, insults, and treacheries that the Germans of that period and of the Middle Ages inflicted upon the Slavic peoples.

Thus, according to Widukind, the name of the Saxons derives from the knives with which they slaughtered the Thuringian nobles who had been summoned to a council [Note: [Col. 1397D] Widukind I.7, Pertz V, p. 418: “There are also those who report that this name was given to them”—the Saxons—“because of that deed. For knives are called *Sahs* in our language, and therefore those who had slaughtered such a multitude with knives were called Saxons.”]. Thus Henry the Fowler, gathering robbers, settled them in the suburb of Merseburg on lands and in houses granted to them, on the condition that they practice robbery only against the Slavs [Note: [Col. 1397D] Widukind II.3 (Pertz V, p. 438).]. The Saxon law of the Middle Ages, the *Sachsenspiegel*, imposes upon the soldiers of the marches the duty of attacking the Slavs by every means for six weeks each year; and the illustration attached to this law, so that its meaning may not escape the reader, depicts three peaceful, seated Slavs—a Bohemian, a Pole, and a Wend—whom a Saxon soldier, fully armored from head to foot, wounds and slaughters [Note: [Col. 1397D] *German Monuments*, edited by Batt, von Babo, Eitenbenz, Mone, and Weber, part I, illustrations to Saxon land and feudal law, plate I, fig. 13.]. Thus Gero summoned thirty of the more distinguished Slavs to himself under the pretext of hospitality and slaughtered them when drunk [Note: [Col. 1397D] Widukind II.647.].

The history of the Teutonic and Livonian military orders offers innumerable examples of plundering [Col. 1397C]. Consequently, Germans are still badly regarded among all the Slavic nations. Their word *Niemez*, that is, “German,” has the same original meaning as the Greek word βάρβαρος, “barbarian.” A Slav is one who speaks; a *Niemez* is a dull person who does not know how to speak. Thus, among the insults with which nations burden one another, among Italians *il tedesco barbaro*—“the barbarous German”—is almost the same as a sleepy person without any intellectual gift; among the French, a clumsy, greedy person devoted to gluttony, or, if fortune favors him, one lost in the dreams of illness; and among the English, a babbler. The Slavic peoples scarcely conceal their deep-seated hatred [Note: [Col. 1397D]

In Merkel’s own words, in his book *The Letts*, Leipzig edition, 1800, p. 36:

“No nation is judged so unfavorably by another as the German. It is well known that not long ago—and perhaps it still happens—the Italian imagined a sleepy, talentless person in the German; the Frenchman, a clumsy, uncouth person; the Englishman, a pedantic person. The Russian calls every babbling, affected fool a *Niemez*, and the Lett and Estonian use the word for everything arrogant, miserly, malicious—in a word, for everything hateful.”]
; for whom German and the Devil are altogether the same thing [Note: [Col. 1398D] Maciejowski, cited above.].

[Col. 1397D] Yet so far were the Slavic peoples from being treated by the Germans in a more humane manner [Col. 1398A] that, rather, because a great number of Slavs were carried into slavery and cruelly tormented by labor and misery, the word for “slave”—that is, bondsman—came in almost all modern languages to be called *Sklave*, *esclave*, and so forth. An involuntary testimony to this misfortune of the Slavic peoples is found in Thietmar, who certainly showed the Poles no favor, saying that they ought to be chastised in the sluggish manner of an ass. Lamenting that his church had been divided by Otto, he says:

> “Now everything that previously belonged to our church has been miserably divided, in the manner of a Slavic household, which, once accused, is scattered by being sold.” [Note: [Col. 1398D] Thietmar, p. 345.]

For the rest, it would be the height of ignorance to deny that the ancient Germans described by Caesar, Tacitus, and others—and especially those who appear in the laws called the laws of the barbarians, that is, of the Saxons, Thuringians, Frisians, Alemanni, Bavarians, Ripuarian and Salian Franks, Burgundians, Lombards, Ostrogoths, Visigoths, and Anglo-Saxons—were barbarians.

## CHAPTER XLVII.—Why Mathildis sent this book to Misegon

It was very much in the interest of the kings of Germany to spread and consolidate the Latin Church everywhere. Through it they strove to bring the whole world under their imperial dominion, or at least to wrest as many provinces as possible from the Greek emperor [Note: [Col. 1398D] *Chronicon Mindense* (Meibom, *Rerum Germanicarum Scriptores*, vol. I, p. 555): “And thus, in the person of Charles [the Great], dominion over the world came to the Teutons, for they possess authority by reason of the Church. Hence the empire is not among the Greeks, although there he is called Emperor in the broad sense of the word, because outside the Church there is no Empire.”]. Hence their repeated attempts to establish Latin bishops in Kiev and Russia. Bolizlav himself, relying on the new rite, had also been the emperor’s rival in this matter, although unsuccessfully [Col. 1398C].

Since, then, our Mathildis was the sister of Empress Gisela, perhaps advised by King Conrad, she ordered the Carolingian liturgical book of the Roman Order to be produced in a splendid copy and adorned with painted illustrations as well as with a flattering letter.

For the same reason she also added the Latin Apostles’ Creed with its exposition, from folio 75 recto to folio 76 verso. There, immediately at the beginning, she indicates the purpose mentioned above in these words:

> “*Symbolum* in Greek means *collatio* in Latin, that is, a sign or indication. An indication, because in it the faith of the holy Trinity is indicated: how the Father, unbegotten, ought to be believed, and the Son, begotten; ‘the Holy Spirit proceeding from both.’”

[Col. 1399A] You have seen, benevolent reader, that many traditions can be preserved, while some falsehood is always attached to them; and that it is the duty of those who write history carefully to compare different traditions, rejecting only those that are faulty not merely in some part but throughout their entire substance. Indeed, even in this matter it seems that a certain moderation must be observed. For it may happen that monuments hitherto unknown should by some chance come to light and demonstrate that things previously thought false are true.

[Col. 1400A] For the rest, dear reader, I congratulate you if you have read this entire commentary with an even temper and have not imitated those who, being rather uncultivated, imagine that all love of one’s country consists in nothing other than loading other nations with insults.

Yet do not despise my arduous labor if in some respect it should be less than complete; do not go looking for the arts of a conjurer.

It remains for me to say with Mathildis: “Farewell to willing!” [*Ad velle vale!*]

## EPIMETRUM

[Col. 1399]

[Col. 1399B] When I was already about to make this little book, completed after so many struggles, public property, my bookseller brought me Volume I of a work entitled *Wspomniena Wielkopolski*, published by the most illustrious Count Edward of Raczynsky, a man most learned in Polish antiquities, at Poznań in 1842. That volume contains a copy of our letter in *Probationes*, no. 1, p. 1 ff., and a colored illustration on p. 8, with a brief note on p. 7, in which he maintains that this Misegon was the Polish king Mieszko II; for the codex appears to belong to the eleventh century, and no king of this name existed then except the Polish Mieszko, son of Bolizlav Chrobry [Note: [Col. 1399D]].

Here are the very words:

### p. 7. Note

“We saw in the treasury of the Catholic Church in Berlin a manuscript dating, as it seems, from the time of Mieszko II. It is a prayer book once given to Mieszko by Mathildis, Duchess of the Suevians. On the first page of this manuscript there is an image of Mieszko seated on a throne, with the following inscription:

> ‘This book, etc.’

“That is:

> ‘This book was given to King Mieszko by Mathildis, whom the noble Duke Hermann of the Suevians fathered.’

“Although neither in these verses nor in the dedication itself is the title ‘King of Poland’ expressed, nevertheless, considering that the script of this manuscript is evidently of the eleventh century, that at that time there was no other King Mieszko in Europe than the son of Chrobry, and that the author speaks of victories won by Mieszko’s father over distant nations, one must conclude that this manuscript was written for our Mieszko. We place the dedication of this manuscript at the end of this work, in the collection of documents, under number I. Here, however, we now place the illustration just mentioned.”

In *Probationes*, no. 1, the letter itself is read with the following prefatory words:

> “Dedication of the prayer book to Mieszko II, King of Poland, by Mathildis, daughter of Hermann, Duke of the Suevians. This book, or manuscript, is located in Berlin, in the Catholic Church there.”

At the end the following is appended:

> “The testimony of the manuscript deserves attention: it shows that Mieszko II possessed the Latin language. This is evidence of an exceptionally careful education for that age.”

I had commended the codex to his brother, now the King of Prussia’s envoy in Portugal, whom I name here out of respect. I regret that neither Count Raczynsky knew anything of my edition nor I anything of his. For I would most willingly have granted the count, most illustrious among men, everything that I am now publishing, so that under his leadership and direction the literary contest might more easily be undertaken [Col. 1399C].

It is even more regrettable that, although the remainder of his book deserves the praise of all learned men, that smallest part of the learned work is not complete in every respect.

The authority of the book might cause the errors with which our letter teems in that work to pass unnoticed by the reader and to be transmitted into other books. To prevent this, I wish to set down those errors here.

In the colored drawing reproduced lithographically on p. 8, it should be noted that the person who made what is called the lithograph altered the forms of the letters according to his own judgment, so that nothing can be determined from those forms concerning the time when the codex was written. Add that at the end of the first line not only the letter *o* is missing, but also the syllable “ni,” which is written above it.

The form of the image, particularly in the clothing, has been rendered fairly faithfully; but in the faces of Mathildis and the King, in the crown, and finally in many other details, it departs entirely from the image in the codex. I myself have now engraved that image on copper with the greatest care and have arranged for it to be imitated with colors as faithful as possible.

In the letter itself the following variation of reading is found [Col. 1400B]:

As for the system of punctuation, the editor did not preserve the practice of that period as he should have done. The point placed below does indeed indicate a comma in the same manner as in the codex, and this is found in very many places; nevertheless, eight times a comma of a later age has been inserted. But the true point is never placed above, as it is in the codex. The result is that the reader cannot know whether the new or the ancient punctuation is intended [Col. 1400D].

[Col. 1401] [Col. 1403]

# In the Year of Our Lord 990. John Smera Polovecius

[Col. 1405]

## HISTORICAL NOTICE

Cave, *Literary History of Ecclesiastical Writers*, p. 509.

[Col. 1405A] John Smera Polovecius, a Russian by nationality and physician and rhetorician to King Wladimir, flourished in the year 990. He has a place among ecclesiastical writers not because he left several minor works—for only one letter survives—but because of the singular novelty of its subject.

Wladimir, supreme prince of the Russians, was still a pagan. He married Helena, or, as others call her, Anna, sister of the Eastern emperors Basil and Constantine. On this occasion he embraced the Christian religion, and the Russians were transferred to the Greek rite.

Before this happened, however, Wladimir, still devoted to the worship of idols, began to investigate the various religions then in existence, sending out envoys everywhere for this purpose. When the Muslims pressed their case, he held their worship in contempt as foul and shameful. He inclined toward the Greek religion. To proceed with greater security, he sent our John to travel through various regions and report everything to him.

After traveling through Pannonia, Serbia, Bulgaria, Moesia, and the great Greek Empire, he went to Antioch, Jerusalem, and finally Egypt, where he remained for a long time in Alexandria and there received initiation through the sacred bath. From that city he sent a letter to Wladimir in which he informed him about the various [Col. 1406A] worshipers of different religions.

He attacks the customs and institutions of the Greeks with particular severity and predicts their ruin and destruction on account of their idolatry, hypocrisy, arrogance, cruelty, and other vices; and he predicts the conversion of the last Jewish nation to the teaching of Christ. He closes the letter with these words addressed to Wladimir:

> “Therefore, O king, you may not adopt Greek customs and religion. But if you do adopt them, I shall never travel to you; instead, I shall fall asleep here and await the judgment of the Son of God.”

He wrote this letter in the Bulgarian language, on bronze tablets, in letters made with iron. The tablets lay hidden in the Monastery of the Savior at Przemyśl, not far from old Sambor, until the year 1567, when Andrew Kolodynsky, a Russian deacon, translated them into the Russian and Polish languages. From the Polish, in the year 1677, Benedict Wissowatius translated them into Latin. Sandius published his version in the *Appendix to Ecclesiastical History*, p. 61. After him, Andrew Wengerscius included it in the *Appendix to the Ecclesiastical History of the Province of Slavonia*, p. 499. Considerable light will also be shed on this letter by Miechowita, *History of Poland*, book II, chapter 3, fol. 990; Cromer, *On the Origin and Deeds of the Poles*, book III, p. 31, to mention no others.

[Col. 1405]

# Letter of Smera Polovecius to Wladimir, King of the Russians

*(Sandius, Appendix to Ecclesiastical History, p. 61.)*

## Copy of the Letter

Written by Wladimir’s explorer or envoy, the supreme prince of the Russians, from Egyptian Alexandria, around the year 990, at a time when Russia had not yet received baptism; translated from the writings of the ancient teaching of the Russians by Andrew Kolodynsky of Vitebsk into the current script, from the Bulgarian language and from bronze tablets discovered in the Monastery of the Savior in the land of Przemyśl, not far from old Sambor, where the famous Duke Leo is buried, in the year 1567.

Afterward that same Andrew translated it from the Bulgarian writing into the Polish language. Benedict Wissowatius, son of Andrew Wissowatius, sent me the said letter from the Polish manuscript of I. Ryniowicz Trembecki, translated by him word for word into Latin, as follows:

[Col. 1405C] Most powerful King Wladimir, illustrious hero, my dear lord, hereditary ruler of the Slavonic regions, after the building of the tower of peoples descended from the generation of Japheth: may the living, omnipotent, and only wise God govern you, as he himself knows, in power and authority, for many years [Col. 1406C].

Today, O king, know from me that tears continually rise in me with a sigh because you sent me away into the Greek regions, away from the communion of your affection and from the Russian lands, to investigate religion and customs. For these reasons I have often been close to perishing here, and now no entry from here into your land lies open to me. Let your magnificence therefore understand matters as follows.

I crossed the wilderness over the mountain peaks with difficulty; I likewise crossed Pannonia and traversed the Danube amid great hardship. Afterward I was in Serbia, Bulgaria, Moesia, and the great and renowned Greek Empire with its five kingdoms; then I was in Antioch and afterward in Jerusalem. From Jerusalem I came here, to Alexandria.

Here I saw synagogues everywhere, built at great expense, in which there were men with the morals of asps and basilisks. I also saw quite a few Christian communities, among whom there are now no idols, but only a table and benches [Col. 1407B]. These men are theologians (in Polish *Bogomowey*, that is, “those who speak about God”), upright and devoted above all to peace, plainly like angels of God.

They gather daily for instruction at God’s command and for prayers before dawn, and again after sunset, sometimes also at the third and ninth hours of the day. Here people everywhere call them the holy new Israelite people of God, or Israel. Some kings, together with their teachers, follow this teaching here, and I myself continually go to them for the sake of instruction.

I have now been reborn among them through water and the Spirit, in the name of God the almighty Father, and of his Son Christ, and of the Holy Spirit proceeding from the same God. For this reason I am sending you, O king, their book called the Gospels, together with the teachings of the apostles, so that you may understand it [Col. 1407C].

But let your authority also know this: I saw in the dominion of Caesar that great injury is done to those upright and pious men. For the Greeks, being clever and arrogant in speech, can make a just matter out of falsehood, imitating in this certain Roman teachings and institutions, and drawing simple people by their cunning to their synagogues and churches . . . . [Here a word is missing, which cannot be read in the Polish copy.] They themselves say that there is one God, almighty; but that Jesus the Nazarene, the only-begotten Son of God, was conceived and born after some time, by the Holy Spirit of that same God, from the lineage of David, according to his ancient promises, in the chaste Virgin Mary [Col. 1407D]. His throne will endure forever, since he is rightly called the Son of God, the Savior, the mighty God, and the Father of the age to come. Moreover, he has been manifested to the whole world as king and judge by the God of Israel, as I learned long ago with certainty from a teacher.

But behold: the Greeks, abandoning the commandment of almighty God and their own proper explanation, order that the Caesar and the patriarchs, together with the rest of their council, also be called the new Israel. They also command that their poor brothers, while they themselves are alive, unwillingly serve them and pay tribute.

Moreover, they forbid them to take wives and to enjoy food according to their own will with thanksgiving. They likewise forbid liberal arts and weapons, although it has been established that these could be honorably maintained among Christians, even without urgent necessity, provided that they guard themselves against envy and inward bitterness [Col. 1408A]. They retain these matters in their own power so that through this prohibition they may keep a great people in their servitude.

Finally, after their death they order their images to be worshiped and impose their own names upon houses, together with the sign of their households, so that they may be memorable and celebrated forever. They command the people to go to those houses mentioned above for prayers with incense and candles and with sacrifices of every kind of food, calling or naming this “good reverence.” By establishing it for themselves on appointed days, they have secured it forever by privilege.

Nevertheless, I know that the final generation will be liberated to a great extent from all this when they realize that, in those forced churches, they are being polluted by extreme greed, contrary to the will of almighty God [Col. 1408B]. For after the worship of idols they stamp their feet, clap their hands, and raise their voices in song like various kinds of music, conducting themselves shamelessly in a way that may neither be spoken nor written. On those days they grant some people favor, as is proper, but afterward punish others as transgressors of the law.

Therefore certain Christians, gathering in places of retreat, in tombs, among the mountains, in forests, and in clefts of the earth because of the servitude of iniquity, prophesy, saying: “The arrogant Greeks themselves will perish in everlasting fire.”

Finally, those who take from them a model of conduct are themselves also dishonorable, infamous, liars, and detestable. It was told me, O king, my lord, that you and your generation would be like this; and it is said of such people living today that their eyes and hearts are blinded [Col. 1408C].

Therefore their final generation will judge them, calling them dogs, fabricators of tales, people who have departed from God and strayed from the truth. Yet those who judge them will themselves by no means escape great destruction, because of their shameful discord and the iniquity of their arrogance.

Some who are humble of heart will, through the omnipotent God and because of his Son, investigate all the writings of the Law by the work of the Holy Spirit for their salvation. But their path will be narrow. Having examined this matter by traversing the teaching and looking back to the beginning of the world, I considered whether it would go well for such powerful men, the wealthy Greeks, people of wise speech, together with the other generations of mankind [Col. 1408D]. I understood that within a short time they would see every kind of disgrace and their own destruction.

Their idols will become a proverb among foreign peoples, since they will not withstand the anger of the living God, being deaf and mute.

Moreover, certain Christians and members of the Jewish nation said—and I myself also understood this with them from certain writings—that the final Slavonic generation will unite with great zeal and devote itself to praising and professing the one God of Israel, Creator of visible and invisible things, who delivered his believing people from their sins through obedience to his Son and through the work of his Holy Spirit.

Together with them, the final Jewish nation too, recognizing together with other tongues the teaching of their Christ, his only-begotten one, will attain salvation by praising and blessing him, because they will obey the will of their God [Col. 1409A]. At that time it will be possible for such people to receive every honor and every power, according to the teaching and manner set out in the more ancient Scripture.

Therefore, O king, you may not adopt Greek customs and religion. But if you do adopt them, I shall never travel to you; instead, I shall fall asleep here and await the judgment of the Son of God [Col. 1410A].

I wrote this in letters made with iron, engraving it on twelve bronze tablets, in Egyptian Alexandria, in the year 5587; in the year 1179 of Pharaoh; in the fifth year of the celebrated reign of Alexander; in the first indiction, on the seventh lunar day, the fourteenth day before the Ides. This I faithfully report to you, your physician and rhetorician.

**Iwaniec Smera Polovlanin** [Note: [Col. 1409] Others have *John Smera Polovec*, which is the same thing.]

[Col. 1409]

# Unpublished Formulae Published from a Manuscript of the Strasbourg Library by M. Eugène de Rozière, Head of the Office of the Minister of Public Instruction and Religious Affairs, 1851

## Preface

It is impossible to understand properly the spirit of legislation or to judge its effects with certainty unless one joins the study of the laws, which establish the principles, to the study of the instruments that develop those principles and put them into action. The manner in which a legislative provision is applied in legal instruments frequently reveals its meaning, which until then had remained obscure. Instruments are for the law a living and active commentary; one may say that they are the law taken in the act.

Thus the necessity of joining practice to theory and completing one by means of the other is acknowledged by everyone who seriously studies the science of law. This necessity appears even in the study of our modern laws, which are generally so formal and explicit; all the more must it arise in the study of ancient laws, drafted in an age of barbarism, when law was established less by legal texts than by a series of customs and traditional usages.

Only legal instruments can help us establish these usages; and in this respect formulae must be treated like instruments proper. Formulae were models, generally drawn up from genuine instruments and intended to serve as guides for practitioners. Most of the time, it would be sufficient to add the date and the names of the parties in order to reconstruct the instruments themselves.

Their usefulness for explaining our ancient law has been proclaimed by all the scholars who have written on this subject, and I believe it unnecessary to reproduce here considerations that Bignon, Lindenbrog, Baluze, and their successors seem to me to have exhausted.

It is not surprising that the scientific movement of our century, which restored the historical study of law to honor, should have given the formula books of Merovingian and Carolingian times the same importance as the other monuments of barbarian legislation. Manuscripts of formulae had to be sought with the same eagerness as manuscripts of the Germanic laws and capitularies.

A twofold interest attached to this search. First, it was necessary to recover the sources of the publications made up to the present, in order to restore, from the originals, texts distorted by negligent or tendentious editors. This first part of the task has been fulfilled, and M. Pardessus has recorded the results of his research on this subject in an article published in the *Bibliothèque de l’École des Chartes* and full of useful information [Note: [Col. 1409] First series, vol. IV, pp. 1 ff.].

Next, it was necessary to examine manuscripts that had not yet been consulted, in the hope of discovering unpublished formulae and thereby obtaining either new knowledge or confirmation of what was already known. I have endeavored to carry out this second part, and more than once success has answered my expectations.

Thanks to the courtesy of several learned French and foreign librarians, who allowed me to visit the repositories entrusted to their care or honored me by entering into correspondence with me, I have been able to collect a fairly large number of unpublished formulae. My intention is to unite them in a single body with those previously published, whose texts I have collated with the originals.

But while awaiting the completion of this work, which requires lengthy preparation, I thought I could be useful to persons interested in our legal antiquities by publishing in advance some of the texts I have collected.

Today I offer several extracts from a manuscript belonging to the municipal library of Strasbourg. The manuscript is in quarto, on parchment, written in a ninth-century hand; the rubrics are traced in red ink and are generally quite carefully executed.

In the sixteenth century it belonged to Beatus Rhenanus, who bequeathed his library to the town of Schlettstadt. The local authorities took no care of this precious collection; the manuscripts were stored in a damp place, where they remained abandoned for more than two hundred years.

In 1813 the manuscript of which I speak passed into the hands of M. Bodman of Mainz, in a manner that cannot be condemned too severely. At the bottom of one of the leaves one indeed reads the following note, written in pencil:

> “This codex once belonged to Beatus Rhenanus, from whose library D. Armbruster, mayor, gave it to me as a gift while I was at Schlettstadt, 1813, . . . . Bodman.”

If this declaration is false, M. Bodman stole the manuscript from a repository to which he had been admitted on trust; if it is true, the mayor seriously failed in his duties by alienating public property entrusted to his safekeeping.

From M. Bodman’s hands the manuscript passed into those of Councillor Buchler. At the latter’s death it was purchased by M. Jung for the city of Strasbourg [Note: [Col. 1411A] I drew these details from letters addressed in 1839 and 1843 to M. Pardessus by M. Jung, librarian of the city of Strasbourg, and M. Dorlan, librarian of the town of Schlettstadt. The latter rescued what still remained of Beatus Rhenanus’s bequest and restored order to these treasures, which had been neglected for so long.].

The manuscript has suffered greatly from time and damp. The first and last leaves are destroyed, and the binding itself has completely disappeared. In its present condition it consists of sixty-seven leaves, four or five of which are so badly eaten away that no more than half the lines can be read.

The first twenty contain the second half of the *Lex Ripuariorum*, whose first part doubtless occupied the beginning of the manuscript. Folio 21 is filled by a fragment of a religious office bearing the title: “Here begins a verse for Sundays.”

On folio 22 the rubrics of the *Lex Alamannorum* begin, and on folio 25 the text of that law, which extends through the recto of folio 53 inclusive. The final leaves are occupied by twenty formulae, three of which correspond to nos. 32, 33, and 34 of Book II of Marculf; the other seventeen are unpublished.

I do not believe that this manuscript was used by the scholars who edited the law of the Ripuarians and that of the Alemanni; but the number of unpublished pieces it contains proves sufficiently that it remained unknown to those who published collections of formulae.

I collated the text of the Strasbourg manuscript with a manuscript in the library of Saint Gall. Although these two manuscripts are not identical, they nevertheless display such an analogy in certain parts that they appear to derive from a common source. I reserve the right to describe the Saint Gall manuscript in detail at a later time; here I have limited myself to recording the variants it presents in the passages common to both manuscripts.

## I.

[Col. 1411A]

The first formula offers a model for a donation between living persons, without any restriction or reservation, made jointly by two spouses in favor of a monastery.

### Charter of Transfer Made by a Husband and His Wife Concerning All Their Property [Note: [Col. 1411A] S. G. adds: “generally, all of it.”] Without Any Rent

Since the offspring of the human race, from the beginning of its creation until the present, has increased through successive generations, it has received this condition only from the [first] state of its creation [Note: [Col. 1411A] S. G. reads: “from the original state.”]. Once this has been determined by the Lord [Note: [Col. 1411A] S. G. adds: “until the end.”], it is diminished by no change.

And therefore Moses, the first legislator of divine authority [Note: [Col. 1412A] S. G. adds: “the first.”], described this matter in accordance with that indissoluble determination [Note: [Col. 1412A] S. G. adds: “saying.”]:

> “For this reason a man leaves his father and mother and clings to his wife, and the two become one flesh.”

Therefore we, in the name of the Holy Trinity, that husband, and I, his wife, that woman: it is established that we have been joined by this lawful and indissoluble bond, by divine will, as we believe, and that certain possessions have come to us both by hereditary right from our fathers and mothers, and also from a certain rightful acquisition [Note: [Col. 1412A] Here, as in many other formulae, a distinction is made between inherited property and acquisitions.].

We believe that these possessions will benefit us both in eternal blessedness if we endeavor to transfer them, for the salvation of our souls, to the holy places; and so we have resolved to do.

Therefore, by our power of disposal [Note: [Col. 1412A] S. G. adds: “with our own hand.” The expression *potestativa manu tradere*, which occurs in other formulae, meant to give something of which one is the full and free owner and whose full and free ownership one may consequently transfer to the recipient.], we hand over and transfer all our possessions [Note: [Col. 1413C] S. G. reads: “all my possessions.”] that we are presently seen to possess to the monastery called that, where that abbot and shepherd appears to preside over the holy flock [Note: [Col. 1413C] S. G. reads: “abbot.”], and which has been built in honor of that saint.

This is what we transfer: in the place called that, in the district whose name is that. All the possessions [Note: [Col. 1413C] S. G. adds: “my possessions.”] that we are seen to possess there, namely lands, houses, buildings [Note: [Col. 1413D] S. G. reads: “buildings.”], bondservants, meadows, pastures, vineyards, woods, waters and watercourses, rights of exit and entry, cultivated and uncultivated lands, movable and immovable goods, livestock of both sexes, animals together with their herdsmen, and whatever may be said or named and appears to be our present possession—we transfer all of it, in its entirety, to the holy places mentioned above.

Thus, from this day forward [Note: [Col. 1413D] S. G. adds: “from this day.”], the rector or administrators of the aforesaid monastery [Note: [Col. 1413D] By *rector* one should understand the abbot of the monastery, and by *administrators* those charged with managing its property or defending its rights, later called *advocati*, advocates.] shall have, hold, and possess these same possessions [Note: [Col. 1413D] S. G. adds: “for themselves.”], or whatever they decide to do with them for the benefit of the monastery itself; and in every respect they shall enjoy free power to do so [Note: [Col. 1413D] This final word is lacking in S. G.].

But if anyone—which we do not believe will happen—whether we ourselves, or any of our heirs or heirs of heirs, or any other person whatsoever, should wish to destroy this transfer, which we have resolved to make by mutual consent, let him in no way be able to complete what he has begun. For his rashness, let him pay to the monastery itself another amount equal to what he claims; and in addition let him be liable to the king’s treasury for so much gold and so much silver. Nevertheless, this transfer shall remain firm and unshaken for all time, secured by formal stipulation [Note: [Col. 1413D] These penal clauses, customary in instruments of donation, are validated by an explicit provision of the Law of the Alemanni (title I, § 2): “If any person, whether the donor himself or one of his heirs, should afterward wish to withdraw those possessions from the church, or any man or any person whatsoever should presume to do so, and should not achieve the result he has begun to pursue, let him incur the judgment of God and excommunication from the holy Church, and let him pay the fine contained in the charter, restore those possessions in their entirety, and pay the public composition, as the law provides.” It can be seen that the amount of the fine was left to the discretion of the parties; if they had neglected to fix it, the judge was probably charged with doing so. As for the words *secured by formal stipulation*, see M. Pardessus’s work on the Salic Law, p. 644, for their explanation.].

[Col. 1413C] Done publicly in that place [Note: [Col. 1414D] S. G. reads: “publicly.”], in the presence of those whose signatures are contained here. The signature of that man, the signature of that man, who by mutual consent confirmed this transfer. The signatures of seven or more witnesses [Note: [Col. 1414D] The requirement that a written instrument be drawn up and that at least six or seven witnesses be called for the execution of instruments of this kind was imposed by the Law of the Alemanni (title I, § 1): “If any free man wishes to transfer his possessions to a church . . . let him establish their security by a charter . . . AND LET HIM CALL SIX OR SEVEN WITNESSES, and let their names be contained in the charter itself.”].

I, that man, in that year of that king of the Franks [Note: [Col. 1414D] This word is lacking in S. G.], in that month, on that day, which makes that month [Note: [Col. 1414D] This phrase is lacking in S. G.], under that count [Note: [Col. 1414D] This mention is lacking in S. G. Most of the diplomas published in Neugart’s *Codex diplomaticus Alemanniae* show that in the land of the Alemanni it was customary to indicate at the end of instruments, besides the name of the reigning sovereign, that of the count charged with local administration.], wrote and subscribed this happily. Amen.

## II.

[Col. 1414A]

The following formula is divided into two paragraphs, for it actually contains two entirely distinct instruments. The first is a donation between living persons, made jointly by two spouses in favor of a monastery. This donation, drafted in approximately the same terms as the preceding one, differs from it through the donors’ reservation of the usufruct and the establishment of a payment to be made by them throughout the duration of that enjoyment.

The second is in reality nothing more than the acceptance of the donation and its clauses by the abbot of the receiving monastery. But the form of a precarious grant in which these two instruments are clothed requires some explanation.

It is known that precarious grants were concessions of land made by churches for a period of time and under conditions that canon law had carefully regulated. When the practice of pious donations became widespread, many donors, [Col. 1414B] wishing to retain the usufruct of the property whose ownership they transferred to the churches, employed the form customary for precarious grants. In a first instrument they made the community they wished to enrich a pure and simple donation; by a later instrument that community transferred back to them the enjoyment of the property it had received from them. This practice became so dominant that an instrument of retransfer was drawn up—as can be seen here—even in cases where the donor had expressly reserved the usufruct in the donation instrument.

§ I.—CHARTER OF TRANSFER, WHICH A HUSBAND AND HIS WIFE MAKE OF ALL [Note: [Col. 1414D] S. G.: “their.”] THEIR PROPERTY, WITH A RENT TO BE PAID DURING THEIR LIFETIME.

We have heard in the Gospel the words of our Author and Redeemer concerning the union of husband and wife, saying: “Therefore what God has joined together, let no man [Col. 1414C] separate.” Therefore I, N., and my wife N.: although it is not unknown but fully proclaimed how an inheritance has come to us by hereditary right, both on the paternal and maternal sides, as well as by any lawful acquisition—which inheritance, as we believe, we have been moved by divine inspiration [Note: [Col. 1414D] S. G.: “by divine inspiration.”] to transfer to holy places for the redemption of our souls—this, then, is what we transfer: in the places named [Col. 1415A] or in the place named N. [Note: [Col. 1415C] This phrase is absent from S. G.], in the district called N., all our property that we are presently seen to possess, namely, an enclosed house and estate [Note: [Col. 1415C] S. G.: “with an estate.”], with lands and buildings, structures, slaves, meadows, pastures, woods, vineyards, waters and watercourses, and whatever else can be said or named. All of it in its entirety we transfer and convey to the monastery called N., which is built in honor of Saints N., where N. is seen regularly to preside as abbot; on this condition, namely, that as long as we live together, or whichever of us survives the other, we shall hold the aforesaid property in usufruct and shall pay each year a rent [Note: [Col. 1415C] S. G. adds: “from it.”], namely, so many and so many [solidi]. Meanwhile, we shall have no power to diminish or alienate any of the aforesaid property, [Col. 1415B] except insofar as this concerns cultivating and using it; and after our death the aforesaid property shall immediately, without anyone’s opposition or any diminution, return to the aforesaid holy places, to be possessed forever. If anyone, however—as I do not believe will happen—whether we ourselves or any other [Note: [Col. 1415C] S. G.: “any other woman.”] person, should wish to destroy this transfer, may he be unable on any pretext to complete what he has begun; and for the violence he attempted to inflict upon the holy places, let him restore there twice as much as he sought wrongfully to take away, and let him pay to the public treasury so much gold and so much silver. Moreover, may this transfer remain firm for all time, with the witnesses listed below.

Executed publicly at N., in the presence of those whose seals are subscribed here. Seal of those who confirmed this transfer by common consent.

§ II.—PRECARIOUS GRANT [Note: [Col. 1415C] For precarious instruments to be complete, they must contain two parts: the first, properly called a precarious grant, is the request or prayer [Col. 1415D] addressed by the future grantee; the second, called a prestary, is the grantor’s reply. In the present case, the donation instrument above evidently takes the place of the precarious request; the concession or retransfer resulting from it should have been entitled a prestary. But the ignorance of legal practitioners often confused the designations, giving the name “precarious grant” indiscriminately to both the response and the request. Here we find an example of this confusion, which recurs in most of the following formulas.].

To the venerable lord and father in Christ, N., abbot [Note: [Col. 1415D] S. G.: “father abbot.”] of the monastery called N. [Note: [Col. 1415D] The copyist’s ignorance or negligence here produces a contradiction. From the grammatical form of this opening phrase one might indeed think that the instrument is addressed to the abbot of the monastery, whereas in reality it issues from him.]. Since it is established [Note: [Col. 1415D] S. G.: “since it was established.”] that you, N. and N., were first joined in lawful marriage [Note: [Col. 1415D] This word is absent from S. G.], and since it is not unknown to many of you both that certain property came to you by hereditary right, from both the paternal and maternal sides, or by some lawful acquisition [Note: [Col. 1416C] S. G. adds: “or other.”], situated in the district called N., in the village named N.—property that you, with one accord, together with lands and buildings, structures, slaves, meadows, pastures, woods, and all cultivated and uncultivated land, with all appurtenances, which it would be too long to enumerate, transferred and confirmed by charter [Note: [Col. 1416C] S. G.: “by charter”] to the holy places where, by God’s authority, we exercise stewardship—you subsequently requested that we should grant back to you in usufruct for the days of your life [Note: [Col. 1416C] This word is absent from S. G.] the property named above, or that more fully listed in your charter of transfer. We did so, therefore, as you requested, namely, on the condition that as long as you live [Col. 1416B] you shall possess the same property and pay each year a rent, namely, so much and so much [Note: [Col. 1416C] The word *census* clearly denotes here a private payment. Since the establishment of such payments depended solely upon the will of the parties, their nature and amount must have varied infinitely. Sometimes they really constituted a farm rent or an emphyteutic canon; sometimes they represented the interest on a sum of money lent. At other times they were purely honorary and recorded the debtor’s vassalage toward the creditor; often, too, their purpose was to prevent an inversion of titles and to give the bare owner security against usurpations by the usufructuary. The payment established in this formula belongs to the last class. Clauses of this nature, in cases of a donation followed by the retransfer of the usufruct, must have been frequent, for the Law of the Alemanni (title II) devoted a special provision to them: “If anyone gives his property to the church of God … and afterward receives it as a benefice from the church’s pastor, to obtain sustenance for the days of his life … let him pay to the church the rent from that land which he promised.”], [and meanwhile] [Note: [Col. 1416D] Supplied from S. G.] you shall have no power to diminish or alienate anything; but after your death the property itself, improved in every respect, shall return to the aforesaid monastery, to be possessed forever. No one—not we ourselves nor any of our successors—shall in any way be able to destroy this precarious grant that we have issued; rather, may it remain stable and firm for all time, as long as the period prescribed and the agreement written in it have been fulfilled. And so that it may be preserved more securely through the ages, we have inserted below the attestation of our hand and those of our brothers.

Seal of the abbot who ordered this precarious grant to be made. Seals of seven or more brothers.

## III.

The following formula is almost a literal reproduction of the preceding one; only the particular case differs. Here too we see a donation between living persons made to a monastery with reservation of the usufruct, followed by an instrument of retransfer. The donation, in fact, proceeds only from the husband and not from both spouses; but the usufruct is likewise stipulated for the benefit of the wife if she survives her husband. The observations I made concerning the preceding formula are therefore generally applicable to this one.

### § I.—CHARTER OF TRANSFER, WHICH A HUSBAND MAKES OF HIS PROPERTY, AND WISHES HIS WIFE TO HAVE AFTER HIM; OR WHICH A WIFE MAKES OF HER PROPERTY, AND WISHES HER HUSBAND TO HAVE AFTER HER.

[Note: [Col. 1417D] This heading shows that the formula could serve as a model for a donation made by the wife as well as for one made by the husband.]

In God’s name, each person must fulfill [Note: [Col. 1417D] This word is absent from S. G.] what God’s wisdom said through Solomon: “The redemption of a man’s soul is his own wealth.” Likewise the words of the Redeemer, who says: “Give alms, and behold, all things are clean for you.” Therefore I, N., moved and at the same time strengthened by these admonitions, give as a gift, for the redemption of my soul [Note: [Col. 1417D] These last four words are absent from S. G.], what I wish to exist in perpetuity; and this is what I give: in the district called N., [in the village] [Note: [Col. 1417D] Supplied from S. G.] whose name is N., [Col. 1417B] my entire share situated there [Note: [Col. 1417D] S. G.: “which falls to me there.”], namely, lands as well as houses, buildings, slaves, meadows, pastures, woods, waters and watercourses, with all their appurtenances, to the basilica built in honor of Saint N., where N., a servant of God, is seen to be rector; on this condition, namely, that as long as I live I shall possess the same property and pay a rent each year; and if my wife [Note: [Col. 1417D] S. G. adds: “my husband.”] survives me, since the procreation of children appears to have been very limited [Note: [Col. 1417D] This statement, which is also found in other formulas, shows that the donors’ complete freedom depended upon the absence of children, and thereby proves that the principle of reservation was known and practiced. Title 4 of the Ripuarian Law seems explicit on this point: “If anyone has had NO children, male or female, he shall have power over ALL his property … whether a man to a woman, or a woman to a man, or to anyone whatsoever …”], let her possess the same property for the days of her life and pay the aforesaid rent; and after her death let it return without any hindrance to the aforesaid property-transfer, to be possessed forever. No one—not I, nor any heir or sub-heir, nor any circumstance or person of any kind—shall be able by any artifice to invalidate this present transfer; rather, it shall remain firm with perpetual force. And so that it may be held more securely and not be destroyed at any future time [Note: [Col. 1418D] S. G.: “at any time to come.”], if anyone wishes to destroy it [Note: [Col. 1418D] This word is absent from S. G.], let him pay the penalty recorded in the public treasury [Note: [Col. 1418D] S. G.: “public.”], namely, so much gold and so much silver; and nevertheless let this present charter, with everything contained in it, remain unshaken forever, supported by a stipulation [Note: [Col. 1418D] S. G.: “stipulation.”].

Executed publicly at N. [Note: [Col. 1418D] This word is absent from S. G.], in the presence of those who are subscribed below, or of the remaining people. Seal of N., who requested that this transfer be made and confirmed.

### § II.—PRECARIOUS GRANT

Whenever anyone decides, for the redemption of his soul, to give away his own property acquired by lawful labor, he should know without doubt that this came to him through divine [Col. 1418A] inspiration. Therefore, you, N. [Note: [Col. 1418D] S. G. adds: “most faithful wife N.”], have determined that your property, which you were seen presently to possess in the village called N., in the district called N., should be transferred to the holy places of Saints N., to the monastery called N., where, by God’s authority, we preside. But afterward, when you requested that we grant those properties back to you in usufruct, we did not reject your request; rather, we acted as you had requested, namely, that as long as you live you should possess those properties in usufruct and pay a rent from them each year; and if your wife survives you, she should possess the aforesaid property for the duration of her life and likewise pay an annual rent from the same property. Immediately after this determination [Col. 1418B] has been established, with complete integrity, as your charter of transfer, which we retain, contains concerning those same properties, they shall return to us and our successors, improved in every respect and without anyone’s opposition, to be retained forever [Note: [Col. 1418D] S. G.: “perpetually.”]. No one—[not I] [Note: [Col. 1418D] Supplied from S. G.] nor any of our successors—shall at any time dare rashly to destroy this precarious grant [Note: [Col. 1418D] S. G.: “to construct.”]; rather, whatever has been determined by our statutes [Note: [Col. 1418D] S. G.: “by our determination.”] shall remain unshaken, so that the remaining faithful may be encouraged, without any contentious pretext or occasion [Note: [Col. 1418D] S. G.: “as if in.”], to transfer their own property to the church of God in order to relieve the poverty of Christ’s poor.

Executed in the monastery itself, in the presence of the abbot himself [Note: [Col. 1418D] S. G.: “present.”], or of the brothers and the other [Note: [Col. 1418D] S. G. adds: “secular.”] faithful. Seal of the abbot himself [Col. 1418C] who ordered this precarious grant to be made [Note: [Col. 1418D] S. G.: “who will have ordered it to be made.”].

## IV.

This formula differs from the two preceding ones only in extending to the donor’s children the reservations that he stipulated for himself.

### § I.—CHARTER OF TRANSFER, WHICH A MAN MAKES AND WISHES HIS CHILDREN TO HAVE AFTER HIM, WITH A RENT

I, N., in God’s name. It pleased me in my mind that I ought to donate something of my property for the redemption of my soul, and so I did; and this is what I transfer: in the small district called N., [in the place] [Note: [Col. 1418D] Supplied from S. G.] whose name is N., all those properties of mine that my father, dying, left to me there [Note: [Col. 1418D] Absent from S. G.], [which I obtained there against my brothers] [Note: [Col. 1418D] Supplied from S. G.] [Col. 1419A] or which there, against my co-heir [Note: [Col. 1419D] S. G.: “co-heir.”] N. [Note: [Col. 1419D] Absent from S. G.], a lawful share allotted to me by partition, or which I was afterward able to increase there by any lawful labor, in their entirety: namely, an enclosed estate with buildings, slaves [Note: [Col. 1419D] S. G. adds: “meadows, pastures.”], farmsteads, cultivated and uncultivated lands, meadows, woods [Note: [Col. 1419D] These last two words are absent from S. G.], waters, and mills. These, as I have said, with all appurtenances and accessories, I transfer to the church built in honor of Saint N., to the monastery called N., where N. is known regularly to preside over God’s flock as abbot; on this condition, namely, that as long as life accompanies me in the body, I shall receive the properties named above from you and your successors as a benefice in usufruct, and shall pay you and your successors the due rent [each year] [Note: [Col. 1419D] Supplied from S. G.], namely, so much [Col. 1419B]; and my son N. [Note: [Col. 1419D] S. G.: “the same property.”] shall possess the property for the days of his life only and pay the aforesaid rent; and if my children survive me [Note: [Col. 1419D] Absent from S. G.], they shall possess the same property only for the days of their lives and pay the same rent [Note: [Col. 1419D] Absent from S. G.]; and if God grants me a son by a lawful wife, he shall possess the same property only for the days of his life [Note: [Col. 1419D] S. G.: “the days.”]. After their death, the property itself, improved in every respect, shall return to your portion, to be retained forever [Note: [Col. 1419D] S. G. adds: “by you and your successors.”]. And if children are born to me from a lawful marriage, they shall retain the same property after my death and pay the aforesaid rent for the duration of their lives; but if not, after my death the property itself shall return forever, without anyone’s evasion, to be retained by authority of your right [Note: [Col. 1419D] This clause proves both that the principle of reservation existed and that it was still poorly defined and considerably restricted. In S. G., the copyist’s negligence, through the omission of many words, has rendered these two clauses unintelligible.]. But if anyone—as I do not believe will happen—whether I myself or any other person, wishes to violate the firmness of this transfer, let the order of truth oppose him, so that he may in no way complete his deceit [Note: [Col. 1419D] Absent from S. G.]; and for his rash attempt let him pay to the aforesaid monastery twice as much as, driven by wrongful greed, he sought to take away, and, in addition, let him be liable to royal authority for so much gold. Nevertheless, let this present charter, with everything contained in it, remain inviolate, with the witnesses listed below.

Executed publicly at N., in the presence of those subscribed below [present] or of the countless remaining multitude of the people.

### § II.—PRECARIOUS GRANT [Note: [Col. 1419D] This heading is absent from S. G.]

[Col. 1420A]

I, N., abbot, together with our assembled brothers. Since it is not unknown how you, N., prompted by divine exhortation, transferred all your property—which you appeared to possess in the district called N., in the village named N. [Note: [Col. 1420D] S. G.: “in the districts named, in the villages named.”]—property that your father left to you there when he died, or that you were able to earn there by your own labor, or that a just share allotted to you there against your brother [Note: [Col. 1420D] S. G.: “your brothers.”] or against your co-heir N. [Note: [Col. 1420D] S. G.: “your heirs.”] [Note: [Col. 1420D] Absent from S. G.] gave you, with an enclosed estate and buildings and fruit-bearing gardens, individual [Note: [Col. 1420D] S. G.: “individual.”] slaves, namely these [Note: [Col. 1420D] S. G.: “named.”], farmsteads, lands, meadows, woods, cultivated and uncultivated land, and all appurtenances and accessories belonging to it, which it would be too long to enumerate—all in their entirety [Col. 1420B] to the monastery N. [Note: [Col. 1420D] S. G.: “or.”], to the basilica known to have been built in honor of Saint N., where, by God’s authority, we exercise pastoral care. But afterward, at your request, it seemed appropriate to us [Note: [Col. 1420D] Absent from S. G.] to grant the properties themselves back to you to be held in usufruct [Note: [Col. 1420D] S. G.: “that you may hold them.”], provided that you do not neglect to pay the rent from them at the appointed times [Note: [Col. 1420D] Restored from S. G.], namely, so much. And if God grants you a son by a lawful wife, let him possess the same property only for the days of his life and not presume to neglect the aforesaid rent. Likewise, your sons [Note: [Col. 1420D] S. G.: “your son.”], whom [Note: [Col. 1420D] S. G.: “whom.”] you are presently seen to possess [Note: [Col. 1420D] S. G.: “you are.”], shall possess [Note: [Col. 1420D] S.
