G.: “let him possess.”] them for the days of their lives; after their death [Note: [Col. 1420D] S. G.: “after whose death.”] all the aforesaid property shall return to us and our successors forever. But if no procreation of children [Note: [Col. 1420D] Supplied from S. G.] should arise for you, immediately [Col. 1420C] after your death, without anyone’s prejudicial dispute, let it return forever to the administrators or defenders of the aforesaid church. Nor shall anyone—whether we ourselves or our successors—be able rashly and disorderly to destroy these provisions [Note: [Col. 1420D] S. G.: “to destroy.”]; rather, as the present precarious grant requires, may it remain unshaken. We have resolved to strengthen it with the consent of our brothers.

Executed at N., in the presence of those persons and of the others whom it is not necessary to enumerate. Seal of the abbot himself, who ordered this precarious grant to be made.

## V, VI, VII, VIII, IX

Nothing is better suited than the following five formulas [Col. 1421A] to make clear the infinite variety of situations that the freedom of contracts must have produced; nothing shows more clearly at the same time how a great number of agreements of diverse kinds were clothed in the form customary for precarious grants. In fact, these five formulas do not differ outwardly from those preceding them. The copyist even refrained from reproducing most of the donation instruments, as well as the instruments of retransfer or prestary; he confined himself to transcribing the various conditions imposed by the donors upon their gifts.

In the fifth, the donor reserves the enjoyment of the property whose bare ownership he alienates not only for himself and his children but also for all his descendants. The only advantages obtained by the recipient are therefore the receipt of an annual rent and the hope of joining the usufruct to the ownership if the donor’s descendants [Col. 1421B] should die out. It is permissible to believe that in contracts of this kind, under the appearance and form of an alienation, the parties were chiefly aiming at the creation of bonds of vassalage.

### WHAT ALL THE DESCENDANTS OUGHT TO HAVE

… On this condition, that as long as life remains with me, I may possess the properties named above and pay the rent each year [Note: [Col. 1421D] S. G.: “pay in full.”], and that my children do likewise after my death, as well as all the descendants who shall be born from them [Note: [Col. 1421D] S. G.: “who will be born.”], forever. But if it should happen that the property itself remains without an heir, without the lawful procreation of my descendants—which often happens—let none of the heirs or [sub-]heirs [Note: [Col. 1421D] Restored from S. G.] or others presume [Note: [Col. 1421D] S. G.: “presumed.”] to attach himself to it; but wherever [Col. 1421C] the rent was paid [Note: [Col. 1421D] S. G.: “wherever the rent may be paid,”] let it now return forever. But if anyone …

The sixth and seventh seem to us to offer models of pledge contracts; the donor and recipient were probably nothing other than a borrower and a lender, the stipulated redemption price presumably corresponding to the sum previously lent, and the annual rent representing its interest.

### WHEN A MAN WISHES TO REDEEM IT HIMSELF

… Under this agreement, namely, I establish the present transfer: if I myself should wish to redeem the aforesaid properties within so many years, I shall redeem them for so many and so many solidi and restore them to my ownership, as they formerly were, without anyone’s prejudice; and meanwhile I shall possess the same property with the aforesaid rent. But if anyone … [Note: [Col. 1421D] S. G. adds: “whatever you wish.”]

### WHICH HIS CHILDREN OUGHT TO REDEEM AFTER HIS DEATH

[Note: [Col. 1421D] Only this heading is found in S. G.; the copyist omitted to transcribe the text of the formula itself.]

… Namely, on this condition, that I possess the same property for the days of my life and pay the rent; and if my children should wish to redeem the same property after my death, they shall have permission to redeem it for so much and so much and restore it to their own ownership. But if anyone, and so forth.

The eighth is a genuine alienation in exchange for a maintenance pension. In this case, as in the preceding ones, the prestary instrument should not have contained a retransfer of the immovable property from the recipient to the donor, but only a promise to provide the stipulated maintenance. It would moreover be necessary to know the relative value of the property and of the maintenance pension in order to determine whether this agreement was in reality a donation or a sale.

### WHEN A MAN TRANSFERS PROPERTY IN EXCHANGE FOR FOOD AND CLOTHING

[Note: [Col. 1422D] This heading is absent from S. G.]

… Namely, on this condition, that from this day forward you, the administrators and defenders of the aforesaid monastery, possess the same property under your ownership forever, and that insofar as food and clothing are concerned [Note: [Col. 1422D] S. G.: “clothing.”], you provide for my needs with food and coverings for the days [Note: [Col. 1422D] S. G.: “during the days.”] of my life. But if anyone, and so forth.

The ninth contains a donation of the bare ownership with reservation of the usufruct, and counts among the causes terminating that usufruct the case in which the donor should go to live in the recipient monastery.

### WHEN HE GIVES HIS PROPERTY ON CONDITION THAT HE MAY ENTER RELIGIOUS LIFE IN THE MONASTERY

[Note: [Col. 1422D] This heading is absent from S. G.]

… On this condition, that as long as I wish, I may freely use the same property [Note: [Col. 1422D] Absent from S. G.] with the rent [Note: [Col. 1422D] S. G.: “with consent.”], namely, so much; and if at some time I wish to leave the world, then I may have among you a place of religious life and monastic conversion, as the discipline of the rule teaches, and the aforesaid property shall return forever to your ownership. But if anyone [Note: [Col. 1422D] S. G. adds: “whatever.”] …

## X [Note: [Col. 1422D] This formula is absent from S. G.]

Sales are frequent in the formularies of the first two dynasties. The one about to be read differs in no essential respect from those contained in the collections of Marculf, Sirmond, or Lindenbrog.

### SALE

I, N., son of the late N. Since it is not unknown how an agreement was reached between me and N., abbot of the monastery called N., which is built in honor of Saint N., that I should transfer to him or to the administrators [Col. 1422D] of that monastery a certain part of my inheritance—and so I sold it—and this is what I sold: in the district called N., one *wanc* [Note: [Col. 1422D] *Wanc* means *campus*, “field,” or “acre.” See Graff’s *Thesaurus of the German Language*, vol. I, col. 894, and Grimm’s *German Grammar*, vol. III, p. 395.], which appears to lie on the western side of the stream itself, which flows into the lake called N., together with all the wood attached to it, as far as the public road, as far as the lake, and upward to the *eccha* [Note: [Col. 1423D] *Eccha* appears to be the same as *evva*, which properly means “corner,” and by derivation a projecting point, the summit of a mountain, and so forth. See Graff, vol. I, col. 112.], in its entirety. I received from the aforesaid abbot and from the advocates or administrators of that monastery as the price one pound of silver, one horse, and one pallium worth one hundred solidi [Note: [Col. 1423D] It will be observed that the price consists both of money and of goods; but the latter are, in a sense, merely accessory and do not deprive the instrument of the character of a contract of sale.]. For this reason, in order to secure its firmness, we have resolved to have this present charter of sale made [Note: [Col. 1423D] The Law of the Alemanni contains no provision concerning the form of contracts of sale. The Ripuarian Law (titles 59 and 60) and the Bavarian Law (title XV, chapter 12) leave the parties free either to draw up a written instrument or to call witnesses; but it seems to us that these laws intended to indicate the best means of proof rather than to impose a condition of validity. We think that consent, payment of the price, and delivery were, as appears in formula XIX of Book II of Marculf, the only conditions required for the validity of a sale, and that in the absence of written or testimonial proof the existence of the contract could be established by acknowledgment or oath. It must nevertheless be added that the practice of drawing up an instrument spread in proportion to the growing influence of written proof.], so that neither we nor any of our heirs or successors may be able to overturn or destroy this sale; rather, may it remain firm for all time, supported by a stipulation.

## XI [Note: [Col. 1424D] This formula is absent from S. G.]

[Col. 1423B]

This formula has the greatest analogy with the one we published under number IV. It too is a donation made to a monastery, with reservation of enjoyment both for the donor and for her descendants and subject to an annual rent; like most of the preceding formulas, this agreement is drawn up in the form customary for precarious grants.

We shall merely point out: (1) that the donation is made by a widowed woman; (2) that the property she gives came to her from her deceased son; (3) that the donor’s grandchildren, who are to retain enjoyment of this property after her death, are subject to payment of a more substantial rent than the one she herself pays; (4) that a certain number of slaves, probably belonging to the donated property, are excepted from the donation; and (5) that instead of a single instrument of retransfer or prestary, there are two, one guaranteeing the donor and the other guaranteeing each of her grandchildren.

### § I.—CHARTER OF DONATION, WHICH A WOMAN MAKES FOR HER DECEASED [Note: [Col. 1424D] The word *absentibus* is evidently used here for *defunctis*, “deceased,” as the continuation of the formula proves.] HUSBAND AND SONS, TO A MONASTERY

In God’s name, everyone must fulfill what the evangelical voice admonishes, saying: “Give alms, and behold, all things are clean for you.” Therefore I, N., having considered the future life and eternal reward, transfer and convey everything that I possess in these two villages, whose names are N. and N., to the monastery built in honor of Saint Mary, ever-virgin, where N. appears to preside as abbot. My son N. transferred these properties to me by his own authority: everything that he appeared to possess in the aforesaid villages, namely, lands as well as houses, buildings, slaves, meadows, pastures, waters and watercourses, cultivated [Col. 1423D] and uncultivated land, with all appurtenances and accessories and in complete entirety. All this I transfer and convey to the monastery named above for the souls of my sons, N. and N., and for the soul of my husband N. and for the salvation of my soul, except for the slaves N. and N. I have transferred all the rest in its entirety, on this condition, namely, that as long as I live I shall possess the aforesaid property and pay each year a rent from it, namely, four solidi; and if those sons of my son survive me—one of whom is called N. and the other N.—then N. shall hold as a benefice, only for the days of his life, what I transferred in that village, and shall pay five solidi each year to the aforesaid monastery; the other N. shall hold what I transferred in that village under the same terms in every respect as his brother. [Col. 1424B] After my death and theirs, let the property return in its entirety, without anyone’s opposition, to the aforesaid monastery, to be possessed forever.

### § II.—PRECARIOUS GRANT

I, N., in God’s name, abbot of the monastery called N. Since it is known to many how you, N., gave and transferred to the monastery called N. everything that, in the village N. and in N., you were able to possess through the transfer of your son N.—all of it without any diminution and in its entirety, except for the slaves N. and N.—and, as we have said, everything that can be said or named, for the soul of your husband N., for the souls of your sons [Col. 1424C] N. and N., and for the salvation of your soul: afterward, however, you requested that we grant the same properties back to you as a benefice for the duration of your life. Our will did not reject your request; rather, we did so on this condition: that as long as you live, you shall possess the aforesaid property and pay each year a rent from it, namely, four solidi. After your death, if your grandchildren—that is, the sons [sons] of your sons N. and N.—survive you, they shall possess the same property only for the days of their lives and pay a rent from it: namely, N. shall possess that village and pay five solidi each year to the aforesaid monastery as rent, [and N. shall possess] that village under the same terms and shall likewise act as his brother. After their death, immediately and in its entirety, let the properties named above return to the aforesaid [Col. 1424D] monastery, to be possessed forever. No one, and so forth.

### § III.—PRECARIOUS GRANT OF THE SONS

[Col. 1425A]

I, in the name of God, that abbot of the monastery called that, which was built in honor of holy Mary ever-virgin. Since it is not unknown to many—and you too, that man, are not unaware—how your grandmother, that woman, transferred everything she appeared to possess in those places, except these slaves, those and those, to the aforesaid monastery for the salvation of the soul of her husband, that man, and of the souls of her sons, that man and that other man, and for the salvation of her own soul; but afterward her request was made, and our will likewise did not refuse, that after her departure we should grant the property to you as a benefice. We did not reject this petition, but did as she requested, namely on the condition that after her departure you should hold the aforesaid property only for the days of your life, and should pay a census annually, namely five solidi; but after your death the aforementioned property shall return, to be possessed perpetually.

XII [Note: This formula is not found in S. G.]

This concerns the renewal, or rather the extension, of an earlier agreement: a father had given his property to a monastery, reserving enjoyment of it both for himself and for his son; the son in turn requests and obtains that this enjoyment be continued to his children. Renewals of this kind must have been readily granted, either when the annual census was sufficiently high to constitute a rent or emphyteutic payment, or when the original agreement was in reality a contract of pledge, or finally when the monastery found an advantage in it, as in our case, through the increase of the census.

PRECARIA [Note: Of the two parts that ought to have composed this formula, the copyist transcribed only the second, to which he gave the title *Precaria* instead of the title *Prestaria*, which it ought to bear.]

[Col. 1425C]

To the venerable lord and father in Christ, the abbot of the monastery called that [Note: The grammatical form of this opening sentence attests the copyist’s ignorance and is unsuitable for the beginning of an act of *prestaria*; indeed, it would suggest that the grant is made to the abbot of the monastery, whereas it proceeds from him.]. Since it is established that that man, formerly, transferred everything that he had in that place to the monastery called that, to the church of that saint, and requested that his sons, until their death, should possess those same properties after him and should pay the census, namely so much and so much; now that man’s son, that man, requested that the aforesaid property should be granted to his children after that man’s death, for the days of their lives. We have granted this accordingly, on the condition that that man should annually increase this agreement by the same census, namely so much and so much, and should provide so many *friskingas* (pigs), whether the acorn harvest (*escas*) occurs in a given year or not [Note: The payment of a certain number of pigs (*friskingas*) was ordinarily stipulated only for years in which the acorn harvest (*escas*) took place, as may be seen in the sixty-second of the charters or formulas published by Goldast. Here the condition is harsher, and the payment is demandable every year, whether or not the acorn harvest takes place.], and so many solidi, and so many loaves; and he shall bring these to our court at Christmas. His children, after his death, shall likewise perform all these obligations for the days of their lives only, if they wish to possess those properties. After their death, without anyone’s opposition, the aforesaid properties, improved in every respect, shall return to us and our successors, to be possessed perpetually. Let no one be able to violate this, but, as time shall dictate, may it endure unshaken, supported by a stipulation.

Done in that monastery, in the presence of the brothers. Sign of that abbot, who ordered this *precaria* to be made. Signs of seven or more brothers.

XIII [Note: This formula is not found in S. G.—From this point onward, the Strasbourg manuscript’s leaves have been seriously damaged; a considerable number of syllables and even words have disappeared. I have attempted to restore them, taking care to place my conjectures in brackets.]

The charters and formulas of manumission [Col. 1426B] are likewise common, and this subject presents, so to speak, no obscurity. The following formula therefore adds nothing to our acquired knowledge; it merely offers a new model of manumission by private instrument.

FREEDOM.

I, in the name of God. It pleased me in my heart that I should release as free, for the remedy of my soul or for eternal reward, the slave under my authority, named that man, at the church of that saint [Note: These words indicate that the manumission took place in a church.], which is built in the estate called that, in the district whose name is that. This I have done [Note: It should be observed that the first part of this formula is drafted in the form of a charter, whereas the continuation is drafted in the form of a letter addressed directly to the person freed.]; namely on the condition that, for as long as you live, you and likewise your children born or begotten from you shall pay annually to the aforesaid church, in wax worth a tremissis, or in silver, or in any other money, and that they shall remain in the same freedom which I have granted to you for all time. You shall have the *mundeburdium*, or protection, of that church [Note: It is known that freed persons always had to be placed under someone’s *mundeburdium*, and that the designation of that protector belonged to the master. But in manumissions like the one whose model this formula provides, it was customary for the *mundeburdium* to devolve upon the church before which the manumission took place.].

But if anyone—which I do not believe will happen—whether I myself or any of my heirs, should attempt to trouble you, to act against this manumission made by me, or to violate it, let him pay a fine to the king’s treasury, namely three ounces of gold and five pounds of silver, compelled to make payment; and let him be unable by anyone’s device to vindicate what he claims. Rather, let this present letter of manumission remain firm and stable.

[Col. 1427A] Done in that estate, publicly, in the presence of those whose seals are contained below. Sign of that man, who requested that this manumission be made and confirmed. Signs of four or more witnesses.

In the year of the reign of that king, in that month, on that day.

Name of the chancellor.

XIV [Note: This formula is not found in S. G.—But Pithou, in his *Glossarium ad libros Capitularium*, under “Reclamare,” transcribed a fragment of a formula almost entirely similar, which he says he took *ex codice quodam pervetusto*, “from some very ancient codex,” without further identification.]

This formula offers a model of a judgment rendered by a count and revised by imperial envoys.

NOTICE.

[Let it be k]nown to all, present and future, how that count, after holding a court, dispossessed that man of his hereditary property because of the crime of incest [Col. 1427B] [Note: The crime of incest was indeed punished by confiscation under title 39 of the Law of the Alamanni, title 69 of the Law of the Ripuarian Franks, and title 1 of the Capitulary of the year 756.]. But after [that man and] that count, imperial envoys, had come into those regions to fulfill the command of the lord emperor and to administer just judgments, the aforesaid man complained that he had been deprived of his property by an unjust judgment and that the aforesaid count had wrongfully dispossessed him of his property.

Then the aforesaid imperial envoys ordered three men to testify what they knew to be true concerning the matter in question [Note: The persons summoned here as witnesses are evidently ordinary witnesses, not compurgators.]. Then, after taking an oath and giving their pledge, they said that this had been done according to the laws [Note: These words certainly allude to the passages of the Law of the Alamanni and the Law of the Ripuarian Franks cited above.]. Then the aforesaid imperial envoys, by command of the emperor, judged that he ought not to lose his property for such incest [Note: The circumstances of the trial would have to be known in order to assess the decision of the imperial envoys; they had probably determined that the alleged act did not possess the characteristics of incest.], and they restored the aforesaid property to him as his own.

These are the men who testify to this.

XV [Note: This formula is not found in S. G.]

[Col. 1427C]

This formula does not concern, as one might initially believe, a manumission, but only a settlement: an illustrious man, the son of a count, claimed a certain number of persons as slaves. A third party appeared before the court of the royal commissioner, before whom the claim had been brought, and obtained the claimant’s withdrawal in exchange for giving him a piece of land and the buildings covering it. Following this settlement, two instruments had to be drawn up: one issued by the claimant and guaranteeing the defendants against any later claim on his part; the other issued by the third party who had obtained the settlement and guaranteeing the claimant ownership of the piece of land in exchange for which he had withdrawn his claim. The following formula provides a model of this second instrument.

[Without rubric.]

But we, in the name of God, that man. Since it is not unknown to many how that illustrious man, that man, formerly the son of that count, sought from the father of that man a certain man, named that man, together with his sisters, whose names are these, for his service, we considered the matter with the advice of our relatives and of those who were present in the public court before the imperial commissioner, namely that abbot and that judge. We made a firm agreement and gave one *huba* in the place called that, which that man himself had possessed, together with all the equipment and the building situated there, so that the aforesaid named offspring might remain free and secure from the side of that illustrious man [Note: The settlement could not in fact guarantee the defendants in a general way; it merely protected them from any later claim by the claimant.]. And I have received a deed of security [Note: The instrument designated by the words “deed of security” was the one that the claimant must have drawn up to protect the defendants. The expression *securitas* is generic: it applies to releases, settlements, and simple declarations intended to protect one person from claims that another might bring against him.], and I have a firm pact of full security; moreover, I have received thirty solidi [Note: It appears that the piece of land abandoned to the claimant was more than sufficient to compensate him, since, upon withdrawing his claim, he also added a sum of thirty solidi.]. We therefore transfer and give that aforementioned *huba* to that man, so that from this present day he may have, hold, and possess it, and so that he may have complete freedom in every respect to do with it whatever he wishes. But if anyone [lacuna].

[Col. 1428C] The Strasbourg manuscript still presents two unpublished formulas, both entitled *Libellum dotis*; but the leaves containing them have been so badly damaged that scarcely half of their text remains legible. Moreover, these two formulas are also found in the Saint-Gall manuscript. I have therefore preferred to reserve their publication until the time when I present this second manuscript in detail.

[Col. 1429]

UNPUBLISHED FORMULAS PUBLISHED FROM A MANUSCRIPT OF THE LIBRARY OF SAINT-GALL, BY EUGÈNE DE ROZIÈRE, ASSISTANT PROFESSOR AT THE ÉCOLE DES CHARTES. 1853.

[PREFACE.]

Two years ago I published a series of unpublished formulas taken from a manuscript in the library of Strasbourg [Note: Paris, 1853, in octavo, published by Durand.]. I added variants supplied by a manuscript in the library of Saint-Gall, and promised to make this second manuscript known at a later date. Today I am fulfilling my promise, in carrying out which I was, in any event, more interested than the public.

The manuscript in question belongs to the chapter library of Saint-Gall and bears the number 550. It is in duodecimo format and contains 121 leaves, or 242 parchment pages. The handwriting appears to me to date from the end of the ninth century; the rubrics, formed from a mixture of capital and uncial letters, are written in red ink. Although much must certainly be forgiven the ignorance of the authors and the crudity of the copyists of that period, I must acknowledge that there are few texts in which language and spelling are so corrupt. Words distorted, endings misunderstood, and clauses truncated occur in such abundance that the meaning often becomes difficult, and sometimes even impossible, to understand.

The rather diverse materials contained in this manuscript are arranged in the following order:

1. Fragment of a grammatical art (pp. 1–2).

2. Passion of the holy and most blessed martyr George, beginning with the words: “At that time there was a king of the pagans named Decianus,” etc. (pp. 3–29).

3. Passion of Saints Felix and Regula (pp. 29–37).

4. History of the discovery of the church of Saint Michael the Archangel, beginning with the words: “The memory of the blessed archangel Michael, to be venerated throughout the whole world,” etc. (pp. 37–56).

5. FORMULAS OF CHARTERS, TRANSFERS, AND LETTERS (pp. 56–161).

6. The penitential book of Cummean the Scot.

Only the formulary contained between pages 56 and 161 is the subject of my work. It comprises eighty-five formulas, of which the first two correspond to nos. 7 and 8 of Book II of Marculf; two others were published in Mabillon’s *Analecta* (p. 418, folio edition); I myself printed twelve from the Strasbourg manuscript; and the final sixty-nine appear to me to be unpublished.

Nothing identifies the author of this collection. A note written in the last century in the margin of the manuscript attributes it to Ison, a monk of Saint-Gall, and M. Pertz, doubtless misled by this note, reproduced the same assertion in his *Archives* [Note: *Archiv der Gesellschaft für ältere deutsche Geschichts-Kunde*, vol. VII, p. 800.]. It is indeed known that Ison, who successively directed the schools of Saint-Gall and Grandfel, had composed formulas for the use of his pupils [Note: *Histoire littéraire de la France*, V, 401.]. But there is such a distance between the correct Latinity of the *Life of Saint Otmar* [Note: *De Miraculis S. Otmari libri duo* (in Pertz, *Monumenta*, II, 47).] and the barbarous style of our formulary that it seems impossible to me to attribute both works to the same author. Ison’s formulas, which appear to be lost to us, were moreover known to our predecessors: Goldast had them in his hands and published five of them [Note: *Rerum Alamannicarum Scriptores*, II, 4 (1661 edition).], which Baluze reproduced from him [Note: *Capitularia*, II, 586 ff.]. Now the collection in question contains none of these five formulas, and this reason is sufficient to reject M. Pertz’s opinion.

Although the author must remain unknown, it is nevertheless possible to form conjectures about the time and place in which he lived. Several formulas provide positive information on this point. Thus, among the numerous and crude spelling errors that I have already indicated, there are some whose frequent and almost systematic recurrence seems to attest the German origin of the work—for example, the substitution [Col. 1431] of *p* for *b*, *t* for *d*, and *f* for *v*. Thus one finds *puplice* for *publice*, *supscripcio* for *subscriptio*, *inpuendum* for *imbuendum*, *subtitus* for *subditus*, *tricto* for *dricto*, *fasallo* for *vasallo*, and so forth [lacuna].

[Col. 1431] The presumption arising from this spelling system is further confirmed by numerous and decisive passages. Formulas 27 and 29 contain, respectively, a model judgment and a model constitution of a dower, both drafted *according to the Law of the Alamanni*. Formulas 3, 5, 21, 24, 27, and 30 mention the signatures of seven witnesses, the number required by title 1 of the Law of the Alamanni; formula 24 even adds to the mention of the signatures the further phrase, “the signs of other Alamanni.” Formula 63 refers to damage caused to a monastery by dissensions stirred up *among the Alamanni and the Alsatians*. Finally, in formula 41, an abbot asks one of his fellow abbots to send him a seed that he has been unable to find *in all Francia*, an expression generally used to designate the kingdom of East Francia, of which the land of the Alamanni formed part [Note: See, in the *Annuaire de la Société de l’histoire de France* for 1849, a learned dissertation by M. Guérard on the name France and the various countries to which it was applied.].

I must observe here that the formulas contained in the Saint-Gall manuscript do not form a homogeneous whole and appear to belong to two separate collections. There is, in fact, a break between pages 121 and 122 of the manuscript that cannot be explained merely by the loss of a few leaves. Pages 122 and following differ from those preceding them in the nature of the parchment and in the character of the handwriting. This difference seems to indicate that fragments of two distinct works were bound together in one volume; and suspicion becomes certainty when one considers the names of persons and places preserved by the copyists.

In five formulas belonging to the first fragment, the abbey, monks, and abbots of Reichenau are mentioned. The abbey is designated by the names of its patrons, the Blessed Virgin, Saint Peter, and Saint Paul; the monks receive the epithet *insulanenses*, recalling the geographical situation of their convent; and the abbots mentioned are Peter and the celebrated Walafrid Strabo. In five other formulas belonging to the second fragment, the monastery of Morbach and its abbots Amico and Sindbert are mentioned. Should we not conclude that the Saint-Gall manuscript contains two distinct formularies, one of which was composed at Reichenau and the other at Morbach? These two abbeys were moreover situated in the land of the Alamanni, and this circumstance supports the conjectures previously set out.

It remains to establish, at least approximately, the period in which these two collections were composed. Several of the proper names already cited can provide information on this point. It is known that Peter was elected abbot of Reichenau in 781 and Walafrid Strabo in 842; that Amico was elected abbot of Morbach in 774; and that Sindbert governed the same monastery from 779 to 809. This is not all: two formulas offer models of petitions addressed to Charlemagne; a third is dated to the reign of Louis the German. Finally, the first fragment contains a letter addressed by the religious of Reichenau to Pope Gregory III, who reigned from 731 to 741, and the second fragment contains a letter from Saint Prudentius, who occupied the episcopal see of Troyes from 847 to 861. These observations suffice to show that the two collections are contemporary and that they were composed during the period of Carolingian rule.

I do not intend to publish the unpublished formulas of the Saint-Gall manuscript in the order in which that manuscript presents them. I believed I could be more useful to the reader by arranging them according to a certain method. I have therefore divided them into two classes: the first comprises all those that offer models of legal instruments; the second contains chiefly letters exchanged between bishops and abbots, or even between private persons.

FIRST PART.

I.

[Col. 1431]

I place this formula first because it is the only one relating to public law. It offers a model of orders issued by the sovereign for the lodging of his envoys. It is known that among the Romans the obligation to receive the emperor’s delegates and provide them with everything necessary for their food and travel was one form of taxation. This institution was maintained by the Germanic conquerors, and we find numerous proofs of its application in the Capitularies and in the collections of formulas. (See Du Cange, s.v. *Mansio*, *Tractoria*.)

TO THE PRINCE [Note: The word *princeps* is used here in its broadest sense and means the count or duke of the province.].

Know, that man, that when this man, that man, comes to you, you are to arrange that lodging be provided for him, for that woman, for his household, and for his men. Take care not to appear negligent in this matter. Farewell.

II AND III.

[Col. 1433A]

The following two formulas offer models of manumission, the first before the Church, the second by private instrument.

The introduction of manumission before the Church is generally traced back to Constantine. It is true that Sozomen (Book I, chapter 9) mentions three constitutions of that emperor on this subject, and that two of them were inserted into the codes of Theodosius and Justinian. Nevertheless, it seems probable to me that Christians manumitted their slaves before the ministers of their religion long before Constantine’s conversion; but this form of manumission was doubtless then regarded as private and did not confer upon the freed persons the status of Roman citizens. Constantine’s constitutions aimed to transform it into a public or solemn procedure by assimilating the priest to the magistrate. In any event, the tradition of the barbarian centuries attributed the origin of this institution to Constantine, as is seen in the fifty-sixth formula of the *Appendix ad Marculfum*. The Church carefully preserved the practice after the fall of the Empire, and we find in the laws of the Ripuarian Franks (title 58), the Alamanni (titles 17 and 18), and the Lombards (II, 35, and III, 9) evidence that it was accepted and practiced among the various Germanic peoples.

As for manumissions *by charter* or *by letter*, that is, by private instrument, under Roman law they conferred only a restricted freedom. But this distinction had disappeared in the Germanic states; a person freed by charter could enjoy complete freedom and receive, just as those freed before churches did, the title of *Roman citizen*. The condition of the freed person depended less on the form of manumission than on the restrictions imposed by the master.

MANUMISSION BEFORE THE CHURCH.

[Col. 1433C]

I, in the name of God, that man, considering, for God’s sake and for the remedy of my soul, that I should grant freedom to the slave under my authority, named that man—which I have done—and I ordered that man to be led before the sacred and holy altars, so that from this day forward he may remain free, as though he had been born of free parents; let him live for himself, work for himself, and possess his labor and its fruits at all times. Let the *mundeburdium*, or protection, belong to that church, and let him pay there annually wax worth a tremissis, or whatever he may be able to pay [Note: It was to the church in which the manumission took place that the *mundeburdium* of the freed person and all the advantages arising from it belonged by right. See *Lex Ripuaria*, title 58, and *Lex Alamannorum*, title 17.].

But if anyone—which I do not believe will happen—whether I myself or any of my heirs or heirs-at-law, should attempt to act against this manumission made by me [Col. 1433D] or wish to violate it, let him pay a fine together with the fisc, namely two ounces of gold and five pounds of silver, compelled to make payment; and let him be unable by anyone’s device to vindicate what he claims. Rather, let this present letter of manumission remain firm and stable for all time.

Done in that estate, publicly, in the presence of those whose seals are contained here.

Sign of that man, who requested that this charter be made.

[Col. 1434A] Signs of seven or more witnesses [Note: The number seven, which recurs in several of the following formulas, was required by the Law of the Alamanni (title 1).].

The date of the king or his name, the name of the chancellor with his subscription, and the month and day on which it was made [Note: Title 43 of the Law of the Alamanni declared invalid instruments that did not bear the date of the day and year.].

CHARTER FOR RELEASING A FREE PERSON OUTSIDE THE CHURCH.

In the name of God, I, that man, so-and-so. I have taken counsel with myself, for the love of God and the remedy of my soul, that I ought to release as free and absolve from the yoke of servitude the slave under my authority, named that man, because he has always faithfully served me in every respect, and because of the divine saying: “Whether slave or free, we are all one in Christ” [Note: First Epistle of Blessed Paul to the Corinthians, chapter XII, verse 1.]. Therefore I grant you complete freedom, so that you may be free, like the other free persons who are released under such a title; live for yourself, work for yourself, and possess your labor and its fruits; have open doors and the roads of Roman citizens; go wherever you wish in whatever direction you wish to learn; belong to the *mundeburdium* or protection of whomever you yourself choose; owe no obligatory service, but live in complete freedom.

But if anyone—which I do not believe will happen—whether I myself or any of my heirs or heirs-at-law, should wish to act against or violate this manumission, may he first incur the anger of God and his saints and fear experiencing the punishment of hell; and, moreover, together with the fisc, let him be compelled to pay three pounds of gold and five pounds of silver. Let this freedom granted by me remain firm and inviolate for all time, supported by a stipulation.

Done in that estate, which is called that.

[Col. 1434C] Sign of the person who requested that this manumission be made and confirmed, and signs of seven others.

IV, V, VI.

A free woman who united herself to a slave lost her freedom and, together with her children, belonged to her husband’s master. The Salic Law (title 14, § 7), the Law of the Alamanni (title 18), and the Third Capitulary of 819 (§ 3) leave no doubt about the custom followed in this matter by the Germanic peoples. But it lay within the master’s power to renounce the exercise of this right by allowing the woman to retain her freedom and transmit it to her children. Concessions of this nature, of which the following three formulas offer models, must even have been fairly common, judging from the number of examples encountered. (See *Form. Marc.* II, 29; *Bignon.*, 10; [Col. 1434D] *Andegav.*, 58.)

CHARTER CONCERNING A FREE WOMAN MARRIED TO A SLAVE.

I, in the name of God, that man and that other man. Since it is known that my slave, named that man, has taken as wife your daughter, relative, niece, or cousin, named that woman, I therefore send her this letter and guarantee concerning this union, so that on this account neither she nor her children who may be born from her ought to descend into the yoke of servitude, but may have the freedom’s license. Let them render the due owed to you, for the place where they [uncertain: *manum* may perhaps be read as *manent*, “remain”], according to agreement or law [Note: The sense of this clause is obscure. Perhaps, instead of *MANUM*, one should read *MANENT*, and understand by *pro id ubi manent* the payment made by those who lived on another person’s land. As for the expressions *secundum placitum vel legem*, they show that this payment was in some cases agreed upon by the parties and in others fixed by custom.]. And if they wish to leave, so that the above-mentioned woman or her children may take with them whatever lawful product of their labor they possess, let them depart with it without any opposition [Note: Since slaves were attached to their master’s land and were not permitted to leave it, the condition of a free person was characterized by saying that he or she had the power to leave. Thus the Law of the Alamanni (title 18, § 3) says of children born from a free woman and a slave: “Let them remain slaves and female slaves; let them have no power to leave.” The right to retain and carry away the product of one’s labor is likewise one of the signs of freedom, because a slave acquires exclusively for his master.].

But if any of our dependents, heirs or heirs-at-law, or any other person interposed, should attempt to act against this guarantee or wish to reduce them to servitude, let him pay a fine to the fisc, namely so much gold and so much silver, compelled to make payment; and let him be unable to vindicate what he claims. Rather, let this present letter be preserved for all time, supported by a stipulation.

[Col. 1435B] Done in that estate, publicly, in the presence of those whose seals are contained here.

Sign of that man, whose slave he was, who requested that this letter be made.

LETTER OF *CONCULCATIO* [Note: The expressions *epistola conculcatoria* or *conculcaturia*, and *epistola* or *carta conculcationis*, are almost always used in collections of formulas to designate instruments of the kind represented here. Bignon, in his notes on *Formulae Bignonianae*, no. 10, admits that he cannot explain the proper meaning of the word and proposes reading *conciliatoria*; but the word *conculcatoria* occurs in too many manuscripts of different ages and regions [Col. 1436C] for Bignon’s correction to be accepted. Du Cange, in his *Glossary*, derives *conculcatoria* from the verb *conculcare*, because, “the woman having been trampled upon and the marriage annulled because of the relationship between them, she is restored to her freedom.” But this explanation contradicts the meaning of the instrument itself, and the authors of the *Nouveau Traité de diplomatique* (I, 262) rightly pointed this out. Instruments entitled *conculcaturia* do not aim to dissolve the marriage, but only to modify its [Col. 1436D] severe consequences.]

In Christ, sister that woman, I, that man. Since it is not unknown to people how you took as husband my slave, named that man, which you indeed did, I now send you this letter of *conculcatoria*, so that you may incur no danger from it concerning your freedom, but may remain in complete freedom. But if anyone—which I do not believe will happen—whether I myself or any of my heirs or anyone [lacuna].

ALSO ANOTHER.

[Col. 1435C]

I, in the name of God, that man. Since it is not unknown how my slave, named that man, joined in marriage with a free woman whose name is that woman; but their request was made and my will determined that I ought to make for them a charter of *conculcatio* in return for payment, which I did. Therefore, by this charter, we make and confirm by hand this guarantee: if, God willing, offspring should be born from them, let that offspring remain in complete freedom for the whole of their lives [Note: It appears to follow from this sentence that in this case freedom was not granted to the woman, but only to the children who would be born from the marriage.]. Neither I myself nor my heirs shall ever recall them to servitude; rather, in return for our payment, as we have said, let them live for themselves and work for themselves, or let them choose under whose *mundeburdium* they wish to be placed for their protection.

This letter of *conculcatio* was made in the thirteenth year of the reign [lacuna].

VII AND VIII.

These two formulas concern the dower, in the Germanic sense—that is, the gift made by the husband to the woman before the marriage. The text is likewise found in the Strasbourg manuscript, but with many mutilations.

BOOKLET OF THE DOWER.

To the lord and father, that one [Note: Strasbourg: “To the lord and father”], I, that one. Since it is known that I took your sister or your niece as wife, with the consent of our relatives on both sides [Note: Strasbourg: “by the consent of”], therefore I have sent you this letter of dowry [Note: Strasbourg omits this] and order it to be written in these little letters according to the law of the Alamanni [Note: The law of the Alamanni contains no express provision obliging a husband to endow his wife before marriage; but Title 56 of that law fixes the amount of the dowry when it has not been stipulated, and thereby itself shows its necessity], from our property [reading uncertain], namely, an enclosed courtyard with a *spurima* [Note: This word is not found in Du Cange’s Glossary. Perhaps it means the place on a farm where manure was deposited] and whatever other buildings there are [Note: Strasbourg: “offices”], so many dependants, so many oxen or cows, as many pigs [Note: Strasbourg: “swine”] and sheep [Note: Strasbourg: “sheep”] as there are, cauldrons or iron tools, if there are any, so many arable fields, so many mowing meadows, and so many cartloads. Whatever we have said above, or whatever we give, while you live, you shall have, hold, and possess under usufruct, with the stipulation duly attached; but after your death, let these things return to me, if I am alive, or to my children, if the Lord wills that I have any; and if they do not exist, let the dowry itself, which I gave you, return to my nearest heirs according to law. But if anyone—which we do not believe will happen—whether I myself or any of my heirs or successors, should wish to bring an action or proceed against this little book of dowry, let him pay a fine to the treasury, that is, let him be compelled to pay so much gold and so many weights of silver, and let him be unable, by anyone’s ingenuity or contrivance [Note: Strasbourg: “by any ingenuity”], to vindicate the claim that he makes; but let this letter of dowry remain firm and stable for all time.

Sign of that one, who gave this dowry and requested that it be confirmed.

## BOOKLET OF DOWRY (*Libellum dotis*)

Since, by the disposition of our Lord Jesus Christ and with the consent of our friends, I, that one, took you, the daughter of that one, into lawful marriage, therefore I give you the lawful dowry decreed by my authoritative hand, in the district called that one, in the estate called that one: an enclosed courtyard with the other buildings, together with salic land [Note: See, concerning salic land, M. Pardessus’s work on the Salic Law, p. 705 and following], namely, so many *journals*, meadows amounting to so many cartloads [Note: Strasbourg adds: “so many named dependants”], and so many *hubae*, together with fields, meadows, woods, pastures, waters and watercourses, so that from the present day you may have, hold, and possess them; specifically on this condition: as long as you live, you shall have these same things in usufruct; but after your death, these things shall return to my authority, or to my lawful heirs, if you outlive me. But if anyone—which I do not believe will happen—whether I myself or any of my heirs or nearest relatives, should wish to violate this donation of dowry lawfully made by me, let him pay a fine to the treasury, namely, so many pounds of gold and so many pounds of silver, and, in addition, let him be compelled to pay you an equal amount to what you claim [Note: Strasbourg: “restore”]; but let this donation remain firm and stable, with the stipulation duly attached.

Done in the estate called that one, in the year of the unconquered King Louis, in the month called that one, on Thursday, in the third indiction, before Count that one and the assembled people and the witnesses subscribed below [Note: The sovereign designated in this date seems to me to be Louis the German; the document on which the formula was based therefore belonged to the years 840, 855, or 870, the only three years during that prince’s reign corresponding to the third indiction].

Sign of that one, who requested that this donation of dowry be made. Sign of the other witnesses.

I therefore, that one, recorded the day and year, wrote and subscribed this happily. Amen.

## IX

This formula and the eight others that immediately follow concern deeds of donation. The first are simple preambles; the last two provide complete models.

## PREAMBLE

Since each person, according to the measure of his wealth [Col. 1438A], determines a gift from his own generosity, he gives well who, although little, has nevertheless left nothing outside the gift. Therefore, in God’s … [lacuna].

## PREAMBLE

He possesses well who prepares for himself eternal rewards throughout the ages. Therefore I … [lacuna].

## XI

### PREAMBLE

To the lord of the sacred and holy basilica of Saint Mary, ever-virgin, or of Saint Peter the Apostle and the other saints [Note: The monastery designated here seems to me to be Reichenau, which was founded under the invocation of the holy Virgin, Saint Peter, and Saint Paul], which has been built in the place called that one. Since it is not unknown … [lacuna].

## XII

### PREAMBLE

[Col. 1438B] In the name of God, carrying out for each person what the Gospel voice urges when it says: “Give alms, and behold, all things are clean” [Note: Gospel according to Luke, chapter 11, verse 41]. Therefore, pierced by the admonition of this saving commandment, I give what has been given … [lacuna].

## XIII

### PREAMBLE

I, in the name of God, such a one. A decision arose in my mind that I ought to transfer some portion of the property to the church of that saint, and so I transferred it … [lacuna].

## XIV

### PREAMBLE

I nevertheless chose to give an example of this matter to the oratory whose name is that one, where, by Christ’s favor, a not inconsiderable company of monks appears to be present, all my possessions that seem to come to me by lawful right, so that from them it may have an increase of food and clothing … [lacuna].

## XV

### ROYAL MEMORANDUM (*Indiculum regale*; reading uncertain)

To that one, king of the Franks, the illustrious men, that duke, that count. We believe that this belongs, in the name of God, to eternal reward or the stability of our kingdom, if we effectively carry out the petitions of priests or the opportunity of holy places or churches that have been brought to our ears. Since some days ago a little document … [lacuna] … ours [Note: These final words, although truncated, seem to indicate that this is not a present donation but the confirmation of an earlier donation] … in the place called … [lacuna].

## XVI

### CHARTER OF DONATION TO A CHURCH, OF LAND, DEPENDANTS, OR ANYTHING WHATEVER

[Col. 1438D]

[Note: The word *denominatio*, which here simply means a donation, later expressed the official acknowledgment made by a vassal of the property he held from his lord; this was called an inventory or enumeration. See Du Cange, s.v. *Denominatio*, *Denominare*.]

In the name of God, I, that one. Remembering my countless sins [Col. 1439A], I give to the church of that saint; I give what I wish to be given in perpetuity, for the remedy of my soul and for eternal reward. This is what we have said: from the present day I transfer from my right to the church of that saint or to its rector, into their ownership, so that they may have, hold, and possess it, with completely free and most secure power to do whatever they wish with it, with the stipulation duly attached. But if anyone—which I do not believe will happen—whether I myself or any of my heirs or successors, should presume to act against this donation made by me, let him pay, together with the treasury, a restitution fine, namely, let him be compelled to pay two pounds of gold and five weights of silver, and let him restore double to that church; and let him be unable to establish by any means the claim that he makes.

## XVII

### CHARTER OF TRANSFER (*Carta traditionis*)

In the name of God, I, that one, such a one. A decision arose in my mind that I should transfer something from my property to that man, and so I transferred it. From the present day I transfer it from my right into your ownership, with free and most secure power to have, lend, sell, or do whatever else you wish with it for your benefit. And if any one of our agents, or of my heirs or successors, or any opposing person whatsoever, should wish to act or proceed against this transfer made by me, or to raise any claim, let him pay a fine to the treasury, namely, let him be compelled to pay two pounds of gold and five weights of silver; and let him be unable by any means to establish the claim that he makes. But let this present letter remain firm and stable for all time, with the stipulation duly attached.

Done publicly in the estate, in the presence of those whose signs are contained here.

Sign of the person who requested that this charter be made.

## XVIII

This formula, similar in substance to all the formulas of sale that are known, is drafted with greater intelligence than most documents of this kind. The author did not limit himself to slavishly copying the charter that served him as a model; he wished to give his work a general character and adapt it to the various applications of the contract of sale.

### CHARTER OF SALE (*Carta vinditionis*)

[Col. 1439D]

In the name of God, I, that one, the seller, and that one, the buyer. It is established that I have sold to you—and so I have sold—land or a dependent belonging to my right. If it is a dependent, [it is] in the name of that one; if it is land, [it is] in the place called that one, in that district, or in that estate or site, so much land; if it is a holding, with its appurtenances. And we have received from you the price assessed, in gold and silver, horses and oxen, and another price of so much and so much. This property, which I, that man, from the present day transfer into your ownership, you shall have free and most secure power to have, sell, lend, or donate for the salvation of your soul [Col. 1440A], or to do whatever else you wish with it in every respect.

## XIX

The observation I made concerning the drafting of the preceding formula is equally applicable to this one.

### CHARTER OF EXCHANGE (*Carta cumcambio*)

To the lord brothers in the association, that one and that one. Thus it was agreed and arranged between us that we ought to confirm something from our possessions in exchange, and so we have done; whatever we received, whether dependants or land, this is what it was. From you, this dependent, named that one, and I gave another dependent in this exchange, named that one, *vexatum* [reading uncertain]. And if it was land, we gave you this land in exchange, so much and so much, in the place called that one, in that site or district; and we received from you another piece of land, in the place called that one, in that site or district, so much and so much. Whatever I gave you, hold, have, and possess without any opposition, with permission to exchange it or donate it for the salvation of your soul, so that neither I myself nor any of my heirs may be able to oppose or diminish this for you. Whatever you wish to do with it, have free and most secure power to do so. But if anyone—which I do not believe will happen—whether I myself or any of my heirs or successors, should presume to act against or violate this little exchange document made by me, let him pay a fine together with the treasury, namely, let him be compelled to pay so much gold and so much silver.

## XX

The words *carta post cartam*, which serve as the heading of this formula, are synonymous with *precaria*. In contracts of precarious tenure, two originals were in fact to be drawn up: one contained the grantor’s stipulations, and the other the grantee’s obligations. It is therefore unsurprising that the second of these documents was called *carta post cartam*, since it was to be preceded by the first. I would only point out that this expression has been recorded neither in Du Cange’s Glossary nor in the *Nouveau Traité de diplomatique*.

### CHARTER AFTER A CHARTER (*Carta post cartam*)

In the name of the Most High God. Since it is known that, from my possessions and by my spontaneous will, I have transferred property to the church of that one for the salvation of my soul, I ask and entreat you, abbot that one, and his brothers, that you order these same things to be granted to me as a precarious holding while I live, and after my departure to my children, if they wish, under usufruct. Each year, on the feast of Saint Remedius the Confessor, which falls on the kalends of October, I shall pay a rent for it, namely, so much or so much. And if I should appear negligent regarding the rent we have mentioned on the feast of Saint Remedius in the first year, and in the second year should again be negligent, I shall pay double. And if in the third year, on that saint’s feast, I should appear negligent regarding this rent, the same things that I gave to that church by a charter of legal force [Col. 1441A] shall return there in every respect, improved in every respect, with my rights wholly safeguarded. But if anyone—which I do not believe will happen—whether I myself, the abbot, or another who comes after him, should wish to violate this precarious grant made by me, let him pay publicly three ounces of gold and be compelled to pay five weights of silver; and let him be unable to establish the just claim that he makes. But let this present precarious grant be preserved for all time.

Sign of the abbot who requested that this precarious grant be made and confirmed.

Sign of the provost, dean, chancellor, chamberlain, porter, and all the senior brothers.

Sign of seven consenting laymen from the church’s household.

[Col. 1441B] Sign of the other Alamanni, among whom this transfer appears to have taken place.

I, the chancellor, wrote and subscribed this in the year and on the day of the month indicated.

## XXI

The following formula offers a model of a judgment and deserves attention in several respects. A count, *rachimburgs*, and judges appear in it; the latter, distinct from the other members of the court, seem to me to be viscounts or vicars, who probably enjoyed the right to sit with the count when they happened to be present at the chief place of the district. Actual witnesses also appear, chosen from among the inhabitants of the neighborhood, as well as *fidejussors*, or sureties, doubtless intended to guarantee execution of the judgment by the condemned party. Finally, the copy of the judgment is subscribed by seven witnesses, in accordance with the [Col. 1441C] principle of the law of the Alamanni, which applied to all written acts.

### JUDGMENT OF VINDICATION BY AN ILLUSTRIOUS MAN (*Evindicate judicio viro inlustro*)

The illustrious man, Count that one. When I was seated in judgment in that district, in that estate, with the judges, *rachimburgs*, and many other people, to hear judgment, this man, named that one, came before us and claimed against that one, saying that he had taken away his property by wrongful action. We carefully investigated this case through their neighbors, through the sureties appointed and the sworn oath. They themselves told us that the matter had become known to them. And the other party, brought before the judgment, could not deny it and could give no account; and through his pledge he restored him before our presence. And when he had acknowledged that he had been stripped of everything [Col. 1441D], after the judgment had been determined, this other man, who had the claim against him, returned home according to the law of the Alamanni, restored by the hand in our palace. And if anyone should disturb that case—which was adjudicated before us, our judges and *rachimburgs*, the appointed judges, and the many other people of the district standing there, namely those one and that one—let them pay publicly sixty solidi and double restitution to the person who had the claim, and let them be unable to establish the claim they make again.

Sign of the seven witnesses standing there where this judgment was determined.

Sign of that count and of the judges by whom this matter was determined.

## XXII

This formula and the following three, although they do not offer models of judgments like the preceding one, nevertheless concern the administration of justice. They are petitions addressed to the king in cases that probably belonged to the jurisdiction of the palace court.

### MEMORANDUM TO THE KING (*Indiculum ad regem*)

To the most glorious man, adorned by God, that one, by the grace of God king of the Franks, Lombards, and Romans, I, the sinner called abbot, together with the congregation of Saint Peter and Saint Leodegarius, your petitioners, offer you perpetual salvation in the Lord [Note: The petition for which this formula provides the model is addressed by an abbot of Murbach to Charlemagne. He is in fact the only Carolingian sovereign who bore together the titles king of the Franks and Lombards. See Heumann, *Commentarii de re diplomatica*, vol. I. As for Murbach Abbey, it was first founded under the invocation of the Holy Virgin, Saint Peter, Saint Paul, and Saint Michael. The name of Saint Leodegarius was soon added to those of these patron saints because Count Eberhard, the monastery’s first benefactor, was a close relative of the illustrious bishop].

We humbly beseech your clemency not to disdain hearing our need. We make known to your Highness that, since you have the intention of having us serve God and of securing your reward, we have not dared to conceal from you the fact that within the district we are scarcely able to obtain our rights. For some years ago, when there was a disturbance between the Alamanni and the Alsatians, many of the dependants belonging to that saint’s legal rights escaped from that region and from their proper service; now some claim to be free persons, while others contend with us before that count [Col. 1442C], and other men in other counties say that they hold them in your benefice. Therefore we beseech you to order them, or whomever you please, to be entrusted to us, so that we may obtain our justice. For that bishop also donated to our monastery, in the valley of the Rhaetians, a little estate from his own property as an alms; but now that bishop has violently taken away from us a basilica, a small mountain fortress, and other appurtenances. Therefore we beseech your command concerning this.

## XXIII

### TO THE KING (*Ad regem*)

To the most glorious, excellent, and noble lord Charles, king, Amico, the abbot called sinner, together with the brothers dwelling in the monastery of Murbach, offers greetings in Christ Jesus [Note: Amico was elected abbot of Murbach in 774. See Mabillon, *Annales O. S. B.*, vol. II, p. 200].

Furthermore, we bring to your Highness’s attention that your count, named that one, has stripped us and dispossessed us of certain property—namely, property of which, under the protection of the Lord, through your grandfather, your father, and through your piety, we appeared to have remained possessed up to the present time. For this reason we humbly beseech your Sublimity to order your piety to act concerning it in such a way [Col. 1443A] that your excellent power, with the Lord inspiring it, may customarily act according to justice in an ineffable manner.

## XXIV

### [Without heading]

To that glorious king, most glorious, exceedingly dear to us, and worthy of the highest honor, your faithful servant, that one, offers faithful and most devoted service. Trusting in your most noble prudence, we have sent this letter to your clemency, begging you to act toward that son, for love of us, as we trust you will act toward us—namely, to allow him to retain his fiancée’s property without any deduction until he can come into your presence, released by us from this expedition. For you know what great necessity we are undertaking; therefore we do not think it useful to release either him or any of our other faithful men. As soon as he returns from there, we shall send him to you. Therefore we humbly beseech you to let him hold the property peacefully in the meantime; afterward he will endeavor to do in your presence whatever the law dictates. We wish you always to prosper in the Lord.

## XXV

### [Without heading]

To that most clement and serene king, adorned with the many emblems of august dignity, that one, the humble bishop of that holy church and servant of all God’s servants, offers, bowed down, the salvation of present and future blessedness in Christ Jesus. Let your most noble and exceptionally clear Sublimity know that the son of a certain client or dependant of mine, namely, that one, called by the name that one, lawfully took a certain girl, namely that one, as his fiancée. Certain people are therefore unjustly attempting to take away some of her property situated within the jurisdiction of your kingdom. For this reason I humbly implore the clemency of your most august Serenity that, for love of the blessed saint of Christ, that one, whose intercession I continually implore for your safety, you may deign to offer your assistance to the aforesaid man in recovering the property. May the Lord of all, in whose name all kings reign, continually exalt your kingdom by his aid and, by your prayers, graciously subject all your enemies to you.

## XXVI

This formula is not properly a petition, but only a recommendation addressed to a bishop or abbot who probably enjoyed the right to administer justice on the lands of his church.

### ANOTHER VERSION (*Item alium*)

To our venerable brother in Christ and sweetest friend, that one and that one, Donatus, bishop by the grace of God, as God knows, your true friend. Know, dearest one, that you should arrange a hearing with our vassal, that one, according to right reason concerning that matter of Saint that one, as he may state it, so that we too may receive our *trictum* [term uncertain]. Act concerning it in such a way that we may have such confidence in your good charity.

# SECOND PART

## XXVII

The formula with which I begin this second part is a letter from the monks of Reichenau to Pope Gregory III. Since the Abbey of Reichenau was founded in 724 and Gregory III reigned from 731 to 741, this letter must have been written only a few years after the monastery’s erection. Indeed, since Reichenau’s founder, Saint Pirminius, did not wish to begin his work without obtaining the special authorization of the Holy See, it was natural that the monks should hasten to inform the sovereign pontiff of the success of their new establishment [Note: Concerning the foundation of Reichenau Abbey, see Mabillon, *Annales O. S. B.*, book XX, chapter 65].

### [Without heading]

To that supreme pontiff of the Roman Church and most holy and excellent guardian of the see, the distinguished pope, that one, the most humble and devoted congregation of the faithful petitioners from the island which the inhabitants call the Alamannic Augia, wishes prosperity in the Lord and perpetual life. If the undying fire of true charity did not often inflame us, and if the exhortation of all orthodox believers did not kindle us, never, father, would we have dared, either in writing or through words by anyone, however illustrious, to make such a matter known to so great and eminent a person. Therefore, after so great, indeed so well-attested, a report of your fame, we have dared to send a messenger and a written letter to your Blessedness.

This place also, venerable father, which we have mentioned by name, holds primacy in these parts of the earth. Consecrated to Saint Mary ever-virgin and to Peter, chief of the Apostles [Note: Reichenau Abbey was in fact consecrated to the holy Virgin and Saint Peter. See Mabillon, *Annales O. S. B.*, book XX, chapter 65], it gathers together no small company of those who follow the rule of the religious life, whose abundant spiritual teaching nourishes our entire surrounding neighborhood with extensive instruction.

Therefore, the Rhine [Note: This word is certainly corrupt: the passage concerns the Rhine, whose waters surround the island on which Reichenau was built, and it should be corrected to *e Rheno*], rushing with tremendous roar from the Eastern Alps toward the West and flowing around the same place in a single surrounding course like a sea, makes the island, adorned with every ornament of new buildings, lie in its midst; while the aforesaid river, running along the channel opened before it, washes the sea called Orcarium [Note: This description has several features resembling that given by Walahfrid Strabo of the same places:

> The Rhine, which is borne from the Ausonian Alps,  
> mingles with the sea, spreading through the western regions;  
> in the midst of its vast current hangs  
> an island called Augia …  
> It is accustomed to produce distinguished companies of monks.]

From there, as the holiness of the most holy and blessed Virgin Mary, Mother of the Lord, shone forth, and as the radiance of Peter, the key-bearer of the heavenly house and shepherd of the Church, illumined us, such boldness grew within us that we, so weak and so insignificant, resolved to send writing and a messenger to so benign and eminent a person. Indeed … [lacuna] … the sacred examples of the heavenly teachings of your most holy namesake, Gregory [Note: These words prove that the pontiff to whom the monks of Reichenau’s letter is addressed can only be Gregory III, successor to Gregory II, who reigned from 731 to 741. He is in fact the only pope named Gregory to have succeeded his namesake], whose office you rightly repeat, and following, over the length of days, the most proven blessedness of the virtues of the disciples of Christ, we therefore entrust you to divine piety with the most devoted prayer, so that your days may yet be prolonged in the future for the edification and unity of the people entrusted to you by God [Note: The manuscript has here a lacuna of several leaves], and life everlasting … [lacuna].

## XXVIII

This formula and the following three concern the practice, constantly observed by the Church, of praying for the dead. It is known that in the eighth century spiritual associations began to form among episcopal churches, chapters of canons, and monasteries of men or women, whose purpose was to relieve the dead of each house through common prayers. The associates informed one another, by letters called briefs or encyclicals, of the members they had lost and whose names were to be entered in the obituary book [Note: See Mabillon, *Analecta*, p. 169, folio edition. See also an excellent study by M. Delisle entitled “Palaeographical Monuments Concerning the Practice of Praying for the Dead,” published in the *Bibliothèque de l’École des chartes*, vol. III, second series]. We see from an ancient document collected by Goldast that an association of this kind existed among the monasteries of Saint Gall, Murbach, and Reichenau [Note: *Rerum Alamannicarum scriptores*, vol. II, p. 140, 1661 edition].

### INDICULUM AD EPISCOPUM

To the most reverend lord, Bishop that one, Sindbert, called bishop and abbot by the grace of God, from the monastery of Murbach [Note: Sindbert was simultaneously bishop of Augsburg and abbot of Murbach. Bucelin and Father Lecointe claimed that he was only a bishop, but the very address of this formula shows that he held both dignities; and Mabillon provides evidence that he governed the monastery of Murbach for thirty years, from 779 to 809], together with the brothers, offers eternal salvation in Christ Jesus our Lord. Furthermore, let your Blessedness know that your brother, named that one, departed from this light on those kalends, as we believe, to Christ. For this reason we humbly beseech your holiness to act for his soul with psalms, Masses, and vigils, in the manner prescribed by your excellent custom. And we ask that you cause a letter to be sent back to us afterward.

## XXIX

### [Without heading]

To our venerable brothers in Christ dwelling in monasteries, I, an unworthy and insignificant abbot of the servants of God, send greetings in the Lord. Furthermore, know that our brother, named that one, departed from this light on the kalends. For this reason we humbly beseech your kindness to act concerning him according to your good custom, and to send this letter back afterward.

## XXX

### FOR A DECEASED BROTHER

To the most reverend lord abbot, that one, that one, abbot, offers greetings in the Lord. Furthermore, we make known to your Blessedness that your brother, named that one, departed from this light on those kalends. For this reason we beseech your holiness to act for his soul with psalms, Masses, and vigils, in the manner prescribed by your excellent custom.

## XXXI

### [Without heading]

To the truly venerable and blessed abbot, that one, and to all the brothers dwelling with him under the rule of Saint Benedict, that one, insignificant and a sinner, offers greetings in the Savior of the world. Let your willing benevolence know that I, insofar as the strength of my weakness permits, ask divine clemency for you in the celebration of Masses, in psalmody, and in the other prayers, so that this same clemency may preserve you here for many years, for my consolation and that of many others, and finally lead you to the joys of paradise.

I ask that I may be worthy to have the names of your brothers, which I have hitherto possessed separately, together with the brothers, since you have had the names of our brothers for a long time. I beseech you, all fathers and the abbot, to commend me to your holy congregation and arrange that it hold me as a familiar member, especially in its sacred prayers. And when the day of my death becomes known to you, deign most mercifully to act concerning me, as the Apostle James admonishes: “Pray for one another, that you may be saved” [Note: Catholic Epistle of Blessed James, chapter 5, §16]. For, as you know very well, I am deprived of every human counsel except yours, and such people, for the love of God, offer me some refreshment and help.

Whatever you have enjoined upon me, unworthy though I am, I am ready to carry out, insofar as divine grace grants me strength—and would that I might do so as usefully as willingly! Receive willingly the names of the deceased brothers, perform the customary prayers, and send them to the neighboring monasteries. May the Holy Trinity guard you forever.

## XXXII

In the Middle Ages, churches and monasteries were places of asylum, where all who had incurred the displeasure of their superiors and feared their justice or vengeance took refuge. The bishops and abbots then interceded on behalf of the fugitives and most often obtained the remission, or at least the moderation, of the punishment. The four formulas that follow provide examples of this intercession.

### INDICULUM AD EPISCOPUM

To the lord and venerable bishop, that one, the abbot called by the grace of almighty God, together with the brothers in Christ Jesus, offers greetings. Furthermore, we make known to your kindness that your man, named that one, came to us saying that he had acted very carelessly against you and, through that carelessness, had incurred your displeasure. For this reason we implore your holiness, so that, excused on account of our smallness and our intercession, he may be able to appear before you freed from the aforesaid offense. Deign to act concerning it in such a way that we may have ineffable confidence in your excellent benevolence. We wish you prosperity in Christ.

## XXXIII

### [Without heading]

To the illustrious man, that one, *centenarius*, Bishop Sindbert offers greetings in the Lord. Furthermore, know that your man came to us, saying that he had incurred your displeasure because of certain faults. For this reason we ask you to do him no harm because of it, but to let him remain with you excused. Act concerning it in such a way as I have very great confidence you will. Farewell in the Lord.

## XXXIV

### INDICULUM TO EXCUSE A MAN

To the venerable abbot, that one, in Christ, I, that one, wholly your friend and companion. First of all, we greet you, and, insofar as we are able, we pray for you—for your charity and congregation—and we have such confidence in you. Know that this man of yours, named that one, came to your holy patron, that one, and told us that he had committed faults. We, together with the counsel of our brothers, have considered what penance may be appropriate [the text is corrupt]. By these letters, know that you should show mercy concerning the aforesaid very poor man [reading uncertain]. We greet you.

## XXXV

### INDICULUM, FOR USE WHEREVER YOU WISH

To the most desired father, Abbot that one, with the entire congregation of that saint, that one, your well-wisher, offers greetings. That one came to us with letters of recommendation, and we gladly received him for his salvation, placing him in the place where he could save his soul without detriment. But it was told me that you wish to receive him again in peace and concord. For this reason I have sent another letter to you, so that, if your will and his are ready, you may know that I am well disposed toward your charity and eagerly desire your concord in the Lord. Fare well … [lacuna].

## XXXVI
The following two formulas, like the preceding ones [Col. 1448A], provide models of intercession, but of a particular kind; they concern monks expelled from their monastery. The case was provided for in most spiritual associations formed between monasteries. Religious who had incurred the displeasure of their abbots were to be mutually received and kept until the day of reconciliation [Note: [Col. 1447D] This condition is inserted verbatim in the association formed between the abbeys of Reichenau and Saint Gall. See Goldast, *Rerum Alamannicarum Scriptores*, volume II, page 143 (1661 edition).].

[Without rubric.]

To that venerable father in Christ, and to all the brothers subject to your governance, we brothers of that place of Saint so-and-so wish salvation. Since, in fact, in all the cases that arise and are accustomed to occur through various circumstances, it is necessary for us on both sides to console one another with mutual affection, we can therefore obtain more from you, just as you can from us. Hence it commonly happens that those who have offended our people in some respect turn to you, just as this present brother has turned to us—he who, as he himself admits, has been ordered to be deprived for so long of the convenience of his own place because of his sins.
