For this reason the father of that brother has tearfully sought from you the mercy of Saint so-and-so and our intercession, so that he might be suitably reconciled with you. Concerning this matter we humbly ask that you deign to receive him and not hesitate to restore the sheep that has long gone astray to your splendid flock; yet we do not believe that he should be rejected by your dignity, but rather received with kindly charity for love of us. Do for him as we place the greatest confidence in you. Farewell, sweetest father and brother in the Lord. Amen.

### XXXVII

#### Another example

[Col. 1448C] To that lord, a man and most sweet brother in Christ, whom we—and with the highest affection—venerably embrace, from that man and that abbot, if not by our deeds, then by those of our servants, the least of God’s servants, God knows, and your true friend in all things, in the name of Christ, that bishop.

Our present brothers and your friends, namely that man and that man, who are there, were pleading for you concerning the offenses that you have committed against him, asking that you cause no disturbance on this account if you wish to have his favor and friendship, to the extent that you should return to him. And if your heart is so hardened that you do not wish to live in his monastery, let him afterward release you from the obedience by which you are bound to him, and let him give you his counsel and letters so that you may go to another abbot or to any other man, in order that you may remain where you are without sin. Finally, do not cause another [to come], but arrange that you come to him through that messenger of his. We salute those brothers, or monks, if they approve the words written here.

### XXXVIII

The formulas that follow evidently reproduce simple correspondence and do not offer the kind of interest usually sought in formularies; nevertheless, they contain curious details concerning foodstuffs, fabrics, means of communication, the condition of trade and agriculture, and, generally, the habits of domestic life in monasteries [Col. 1449A].

#### Letter to an abbot

To that venerable man, abbot by the grace of God and worthy of all love, from that man, abbot by the gift and mercy of God: perpetual salvation in God the Father.

Let your fraternity know in Christ that our assiduous prayer is offered unceasingly for you by day and night, asking that you may so happily complete the course of this life in the Lord that you may be able to attain the reward of eternal happiness. We further admonish you to deign to remember us in Christ, and we earnestly ask your affection to lend us the book *The City of God*. Let your command cause it to reach us through the messenger and bearer of this letter [Col. 1449B]. Receive and understand this popular proverb according to the language of our rustic speech:

> May health and honor, through fatherly devotion, be with you;  
> May peaceful times and every good thing be yours.

### XXXIX

#### To an abbot

That insignificant man to that abbot, the dearest of my friends: abundant salvation in Christ.

I received the little letter of your sweetness, which the present bearer had brought, and I understood what it contained. But I shall send you, as soon as I can, that mutual and trustworthy man, through whom I shall send back word concerning the terms of the purchase of the furs and concerning whatever else I wish.

For now I rejoice, assured of your well-being, which until now I had not known, and, as I would for a friend united with me in affection, I have been greatly troubled. Yet I ask your sweetness and charity that we may visit one another more frequently through letters and messengers, and that long distances of land not separate those whom Christ’s love unites.

I also ask you to have the history entitled *The War of the Greeks and Trojans*, which we know to be in your possession, copied out and, through the aforementioned mutual and trustworthy man, sent back to us when I send him to you, because we cannot find it anywhere among our people.

Farewell in the Lord, sweetest brother. Always remember me kindly through yourself and your people, and love one who loves you. May the God of peace guard you everywhere.

### XL

[Without rubric.]

To that venerable lord abbot and to the brothers of Insula [Col. 1449D] [Note: [Col. 1449D] The monks of Reichenau were so called because of the location of their monastery. See Mabillon, *Annales O. S. B.*, volume II, pages 375 and 485.], from that abbot by God’s gift: greetings.

Let your immense fatherly affection know that everywhere I place my confidence in your assistance, as though it were diligently applied in both divine and worldly matters. I have sent your books to be brought to their proper place, for which I offer immense thanks to your charity, and to you.

For every kindness you have shown me, I ask that, if it can in any way be done, you order that physician to come to me after the feast of Saint so-and-so, because I need his help. Also give thanks to that lord for my little brother, that man, because, as I have heard from those who report it, he is kindly taking good care of him by teaching him in the school [Col. 1450A].

Farewell in good health, remembering me.

### XLI

[Without rubric.]

To that sweetest father in Christ, that archbishop, from that abbot, unworthy though he is: the highest salvation in the Lord.

The letter that you sent through that itinerant messenger laid certain foundations in us for the joy we conceived on hearing of your health; but through that faithful messenger of yours, who is also our friend, a living likeness of the same structure of joys, conveyed by word of mouth, raised that edifice of gladness considerably higher: for we rejoice in your prosperity no less than in our own.

As you ordered, we shall send through our messenger the shield-maker, the brewer, and whatever else we can obtain for your service [Col. 1450B]. We were unable to find immediately what you commanded, because the difficulties of the bad season, which also impede you somewhat, hinder us in many things.

Therefore let him be greeted by your wiser voice,

That precious part of our soul, our bishop.

Happy are those peoples to whom this grace is given,

That they should have such leaders of light in the heavenly citadel!

Stand firm together and fight manfully, so that, while you reign,

You may always rule the flocks whom you nourish.

Remember me; I am yours. I owe you

And vow to you all that love . . .

Farewell.

### XLII

[Without rubric.]

[Col. 1450C] To our familiar friend, that lord, from that man, your servant forever in Christ.

Having recently received your letter, sent to us, we rejoiced at its open statements, while in its topical passages we praised the sharpness of your intellect, hoping that these matters might one day be explained in common conversation. Meanwhile, with God’s help, know that we are well, and at last let us know how you are; for the day is desirable on which we deserve to hear of the health of you and your people.

We earnestly request your abundant kindness that, if it can in any way be done, you send us Matthew the glazier with the bearer of this little note, so that he may show our boys a model for a great window at the basilica of Saint Vitus the martyr [Note: [Col. 1449D] Several monasteries were placed under the invocation of Saint Vitus; perhaps this refers to the monastery of Corvey (*Corbeia nova*), which possessed the relics of the holy martyr.]. Immediately after the course of one week he will be able to return.

Concerning our little brother, that man, we earnestly ask that he be permitted to be sent to that blessed man with another young boy, who may care for him among his own people; and write back when and how he ought to be sent.

As for the abundance of honey, by which you asked to be assisted, know that we wish to extend our thanks to you more rarely than you have extended your gifts to us. Send your messenger, who will bring you ten measures of honey.

Farewell in good health, always remembering us.

### XLIII

[Without rubric.]

To that truly venerable and dearest father, that abbot [Col. 1451A], from that insignificant and sinful man: eternal salvation in the Lord.

Long and greatly shaken by the well-known disturbances of this world, I delayed rendering the due return for your benefits through appropriate acts of thanksgiving. The difficulties in which I was then held, when I was greatly relieved by your consolations, continued to oppress me; and the necessity of poverty compelled me rather to appease enemies than to calm friends.

Now, however, since the Lord has at last granted some relief from our labors, I did not wish to omit any longer, lest I should seem ungrateful, the duty of greeting owed to you. Thus the prudence of your affection might understand that the ardor in the little altar of my heart had been lulled to sleep rather than extinguished.

Therefore deign to regard me as faithful to you, as your holiness has deserved. Do not doubt that I wish to devote everything living within me to your service [Col. 1451B].

I sent to your dearest fatherhood small tokens, namely a towel and a comb—not because I judged them worthy of your sight, but because I wished to show that it is better to demonstrate mutual affection by a small pledge than by none at all.

I always wish you good health in the Lord, and ask you to remember us in your sacred prayers. Regard me as the debtor you have made me, for I am toward you what the closest friend ought to be toward his closest friend.

### XLIV

[Without rubric.]

That humble overseer of that holy church, to that excellent and outstanding man, his most worthy brother, that abbot, and to all the brothers laboring with you for the Lord: greetings of present and future happiness.

When rereading the letter of your holiness, we were exceedingly glad, because its wording revealed to us your health and benevolence. But what you indicated concerning the hides ought to have been communicated beforehand, since they are bought at a much higher price in winter than in summer.

Nevertheless, we have now sent to your most generous charity twenty-five hides, and we shall give more if God grants us life and opportunity. Finally, we ask you not to delay sending that brother to us, as soon as circumstances permit and as you promised.

Farewell, all brothers. Greet one another on our behalf, and I humbly ask that you remember us among the petitions of your prayers [Col. 1451D].

### XLV

#### Letter to an abbot

> You carry honey with you, enclosed by firmly sealed glue;  
> You give sweets to whomever you wish, but not to me.

To that most distinguished abbot, that man, most approved and especially adorned with the skill and dignity of divine worship, from that bishop, unworthy though he is: greetings that the tongue cannot sufficiently express.

Since I am heaped with your constant kindnesses, I cannot repay with fitting thanks the abundance of such great affection. But because I fail to discharge what I owe, I now wish, with every eagerness, to repay what you already possess, searching out the feelings you have found in the altar of your heart [Col. 1452A].

Concerning the gifts you recently sent, I now offer immense and abundant thanks. They have so stirred me to your service that, apart from my superior, I take pleasure in serving no one more than you; and if your discernment should decide to impose anything upon my smallness, you will find me devoted in all things, with the Lord’s favor.

The horse that you sent some time ago, although good for work, is not as useful as we had hoped. Therefore we ask your dignity to make every effort henceforth to find an excellent one, better suited to the work I have chosen and capable of being useful to us at times for riding.

Through the bearer of this note, therefore, take care to send back word concerning whatever your will discovers about this matter [Note: [Col. 1451D] The reading *qerulum* must evidently be corrected to *gerulum*.].

Finally, most sacred father, I commend myself to your prayers. Although my sins make them ineffectual, know that I pour them out without difficulty before the ruler of the world on your behalf.

May your most holy religious community flourish for countless years.

### XLVI

[Without rubric.]

To that most reverend and truly blessed father, whom I embrace with the constant grace of charity, that distinguished abbot of abbots, from that bishop, unworthy though he is: perpetual joys, present and future.

Because you took pains to signify by letter that you burned with all your heart to have our bond of charity joined to your affection, I was inwardly and outwardly filled with the greatest joy; and I desire with all my sighs that the creator of all things permit this to happen.

The tokens that your holiness decided to send were great and exceedingly welcome; even if they had been small, we would certainly have received them as great because they were sent by you. But when your letter announced how much you wished to prepare for us hereafter, if we might enjoy your familiarity, it stirred me so deeply that I asked myself: who am I to deny familiarity to such great fathers on account of my own insignificance, when I rather need the consolation of your charity, and do not doubt that your prayers will finally raise me up?

Concerning the benefit that you say we promised through the messenger recently sent: we certainly gave no such instruction. Rather, a boy, still immature in judgment, made such promises without being ordered to do so and did not receive them from our authority.

Trusting in your charity, I presume to commend myself, languishing beneath the enormity of my sins, to your most holy prayers [Col. 1452D]. As for my own prayers for you, although they are worthless, I shall unquestionably continue from now on to pour them out before the Lord on bended knee.

We are sending small gifts to your dignity, which your lofty station should not refuse to receive as significant. If the grace of circumstance restores the journey to the regions assigned to you, greater gifts would certainly have been sent.

We are sending four barrels of oil, six goat hides for making footwear, and three pounds of silver.

May the creator of all things grant you to pass your present life with upright steps and to enjoy the future eternally with the saints.

Farewell in Christ.

### XLVII

[Col. 1453A]

[Without rubric.]

That insignificant man to his man, Strabo [Note: [Col. 1453D] The person designated here seems to me to be the famous Walahfrid Strabo, abbot of Reichenau. He is mentioned again in the following formula.]: greetings.

That brother who was returning from you has reached us safely, by God’s will, and brought us the gifts you sent, which were very welcome to us. But after obtaining in part the business for which he had come, I could not keep him any longer, because he was hurrying to enter his own country before winter and to show you what he was carrying.

Since I could not send you what I wished, and what was worthy to be presented to your sight, I shall remember you through him as soon as the Lord places such things in our hands.

Moreover, not wishing the aforementioned brother to return to you empty-handed, I sent you through him one woolen carpet, so that, by sitting on it, you might more pleasantly await better things [Col. 1453B].

Greet all our brothers, namely the monks of your monastery, and admonish them, with whatever prayers you can, to deign to remember me in their sacred prayers and in the offerings of their sacrifices. Although some of my relatives have lived among them and have proved most devoted to them, nevertheless, if they wish, we promise beyond doubt, with God as our author and life as our companion, to advance vigorously in their interests.

Although we do not commit the rest to this letter, we have entrusted what must be said to you to our brother in the customary manner.

Farewell, sweetest of my friends, and farewell in the Lord to all who are with you. As soon as you find the opportunity, send us a crystal larger than the one you sent now, and twin horns, so that if you wish we too may continually send you what our region abounds in [Col. 1453C].

### XLVIII

[Without rubric.]

That man to his man: eternal salvation.

I ask your fraternal heart to make a more earnest remembrance of us and our people in your prayers during the present Lent, just as we wish to do so for you and for all your people together with all ours.

Since you have delayed coming to us until now, write back when the lodging already prepared for you twice must be prepared for a third time. You seek an even-tempered man, though you order one thing on one day and forbid it on the next. For if I had been as troublesome a bee as you are [Note: [Col. 1454D] The manuscript gives *tuis* as one word; but I think it should be read *tu is*, “you are.”], I would have sensed the sting somewhere, even while flying away [Col. 1453D].

Moreover, we earnestly ask you, if you have any means, to help us with leek seed (*porri*), because throughout all France we have neither found nor been able to purchase anything of this kind.

Finally . . . I give thanks to Strabo . . . for his little gift, with which fools usually wander about in the house.

Farewell most excellently in the grace of God.

### XLIX

[Without rubric.]

To my dearest teacher, that lord abbot, from that abbot with his brothers: eternal salvation in Christ.

I offer your fatherhood thanks, since you constantly raise us up not only with divine but also with bodily consolation, and continue without failing to provide assistance, as you did most recently when you sent us that physician. He sympathized with our illnesses with such care and affection that we felt very strongly how well he had been sent to us by your benevolence.

Therefore, so that you may know what favor he obtained among us, we ask you to give immense thanks on our behalf, first to the brothers and then to the physician himself, for their common labor and for our health.

Furthermore, my lord and father, if you are intending to travel anywhere nearby to visit our senior lord, do not pass us by, because both I and all our brothers greatly desire to enjoy your conversation, even if only for a single moment.

And let not Phoebus’ coming hinder your arrival: Bacchus has perished among us this year together with Ceres; only the easily won palm remains. Or come for this very purpose, so that you may learn how to tame it thoroughly.

May holy and unshaken charity preserve you, always remembering us. Amen.

### L

[Without rubric.]

To that most reverend abbot, a sacred man devoted to the most sacred studies, from that lowest of Christ’s servants: I wish you boundless blessedness in the Lord.

I offer your holiness manifold praises of thanksgiving for the gift you sent. Your kindly charity wished to regard something great as belonging to the lowliness of my person, and ordered a gift to be brought to me in another kingdom [Col. 1454C].

The letter of your wisdom reached me on that calend, at about the ninth hour, while my superior was setting out on a journey in these regions on that same calend.

Concerning the vessels you requested, I immediately took care to find out what kind they ought to be—iron, earthenware, or stone. I asked one of our craftsmen what they were and where they might be found. He said that they were made from black stone mixed with veins of a reddish color, which among us are commonly called “stone vessels,” and that they are found at Saint Maurice. But that place was a three-day journey from where we then were, and for this reason I was completely unable to obtain them.

If you indicate what kind or what objects they should be, when I have the opportunity I shall most willingly fulfill your command, as far as my strength permits, in this and in other matters.

I wish you, most holy father, long and happy health in the Lord.

### LI

[Without rubric.]

That humble bishop by the gift of heavenly generosity, to that dearest brother, an abbot richly adorned with wisdom and the beauty of holiness: present and future abundance of happiness in the Lord.

For the many benefits of your conspicuous devotion, we ought frequently to offer you the greatest thanks in many forms. Nevertheless, we thought it right to inform your most abundant benevolence that we were unable to keep your brother with us, since he was burning with desire to enjoy your presence.

Therefore we humbly ask your most gracious fraternity, with the greatest favor toward God and his confessor Ambrose, to deign to send him back to us as soon as possible, so that he himself may complete what is lacking in the work so well begun.

We are always and everywhere wholly devoted to your most loving charity, ready to repay it suitably if it should graciously please your goodness to assign anything to us.

Farewell, most worthy brother, always remembering us in prayer.

### LII

[Without rubric.]

To that outstanding and prudent man, most reverend: from that man, greetings in the Lord.

I ask your charity to urge more vigorously toward the pursuit of learning that boy, the nephew of that bishop. He could have sent him elsewhere for instruction, wherever he wished, but at my strongest urging he entrusted him to you to be formed by your teaching.

Therefore I ask that, from now on, by applying diligence, he may also perceive that our request is useful to him with you. Wherever you go, permit him to go with you. As for the payment for your labor, whatever can be provided at present, I shall repay.

Know also that I have excused that man, the boy’s servant, with that bishop. Therefore I ask that you cause the man who has been troublesome to him to come into your presence [Col. 1455C], and restore them to harmony; nevertheless, let him perform penance for his fault according to what seems right to you.

### LIII

[Without rubric.]

Peter [Note: [Col. 1455D] Peter was elected abbot of Reichenau in 781. See Mabillon, *Annales O. S. B.*, volume II, page 260.], relying on divine assistance, that humble man, wishes manifold salvation in the Lord to that beloved brother.

When, at last, through the health of you, dearest brother, we are informed both by the presence of your messenger and by your sweetest letter, we are filled with immense joy in every respect. We also sincerely perceive your diligence and pious affection toward the young boy whom you have received in the Lord.

Therefore, dearest brother, your skill must investigate what should first be put into that boy’s philosophical instruction and what should follow, so that his natural abilities may be formed with clear indications [Col. 1455D]. Indeed, there is no doubt that in all things, like a wise architect, you first lay the foundations and then raise the structure upward from different stones. We believe that the one who gives growth works upon the building according to its proper measure.

Everything, therefore, must be ordered according to your judgment: what he should first learn from the divine books and what afterward from the fables of the pagans. We ask you, as a pious, honey-voiced father and teacher, to devote no small care to this, so that the boy himself, the sole object of our affection, may grow through good instruction [Col. 1456A], learning how to recognize and fear God and desiring to attain his commandments; and so that all your praiseworthy teaching may flourish in him forever and become known everywhere through him. May you also receive a reward from the one who gave you the doubled talent, and may you receive from us service worthy in every respect.

We have therefore sent small gifts to your kindness, dearest brother. We ask that you receive what has been sent with affection. We had indeed decided to send more, but we feared that the journey might be interrupted.

As we now hasten, as ordered, to render service to the pious Augustus, we do not fail to seek your presence, and we shall endeavor in every respect to supply what is lacking, as is fitting.

Concerning that brother about whom you instructed us that he should be made a stranger to this place [Col. 1456B] until we arrive here, we ask that he remain with you. When, with God’s help, we have come, we shall remove him and take the collector with us.

In all things you act as we trust you do. Farewell, man of God, and remember me.

### LIV

[Without rubric.]

To that dearest abbot and all his people, from that man, a *syncellus*: abiding salvation in the Savior.

I suspect that you are not unaware that, while that lord emperor was recently staying at that estate located not far from you, I was prompted by the fame of your religious community to visit your monastery and arrived there. After seeing your most kindly holiness, I was pleased to commend myself, though filthy with crimes, to the prayers of you and your people [Col. 1456C]; and you and yours, being full of charity, received me with the greatest kindness.

Since I cannot repay you with a return worthy of the favor, I shall nevertheless not delay offering the greatest and most devoted thanks, as far as I can. Now I leave you thirty solidi of silver, and I earnestly and humbly beg and submissively ask that, in your most diligent prayer, you retain that remembrance of me; and I, as far as I can, shall preserve an unblemished friendship with you.

If our pack animals and horses had not become exhausted from the excessive journey that we made this year in going to Rome and returning from Rome, I would by no means have omitted conversing with you and sharing peace with my fathers who live under your fatherhood.

Concerning their health and sound prosperity, and concerning your own, I ask you to write back, if it is not burdensome to dip a pen in ink and draw it across the parchment [Col. 1456D]. . . .

> You who are to receive the greatest rewards of the everlasting kingdom,  
> Worship the Lord, who is life to his own.  
> I beg you: [remember] me in your prayers; tell the Thunderer  
> That with you I may receive a share in the kingdom of heaven.

*Kere kyri agapite* [“Hail, beloved lord”].

### LV

#### Letter to an abbot

[Note: [Col. 1455D] This document is extremely curious for the information it provides about the political situation. Although it may not be possible to determine the events to which it alludes, one can nevertheless recognize that it concerns one of the phases of the struggle waged against Louis the Pious by his sons.]

That insignificant deacon to that man: greetings.

When we visit friends with affection, we fulfill the due reward of lasting friendship; when we inquire about their health, we take care of them through the effects of our messengers; when we desire to see and hear of their good fortune, we become above all participants in their charity without hesitation. But if, God forbid, a report of an unfavorable opinion concerning the fellowship of our friends should spread, then, according to the Apostle, “Who is weak, and I am not weak? Who is made to stumble, and I am not inflamed?”

For this reason we thought it useful to write all this, so that, insofar as it concerns the cause of your lords or friends, you may exercise the greatest caution in the future, lest perhaps, God forbid, the choice of the lord emperor be frustrated in your affair.

We have also sent that friendly vassal of ours [Col. 1457B], and we ask your charity to receive him kindly and to assist him wherever he may need it. Show him the place where our horses are to remain under your authority, or whatever they ought to have, so that he may be able to inform us reliably about these matters on the road and arrange with the household officials of the lord emperor who are in the estate called Domo that, on account of the duty entrusted to us, they provide suitable lodging there for our man. Thus, when he comes to us, he will not make us anxious about this matter.

When your charity has fulfilled all this, please send our messenger back to us, informing us of everything your goodness has done.

At present we can give no news concerning new matters, except that Ella is outside the palace and that service concerning him has been imposed upon me in every respect; and that your former count has recovered his allodial property. It seems to me that he is still intent on its recovery, yet he has been commended to Count Atto.

Since the king sent his messengers to his father on the Kalends of March, asking three things, the first was that he be permitted to keep with him the men whom he had brought from here, and to allow them to retain their properties within our kingdom until he came with his brother and presented them before the lord emperor; the second, that neither the emperor himself nor his army should treacherously invade the boundaries granted to him by the lord emperor until the aforementioned brother and he had come to their father; the third, that he release him, so that during the approaching Lent the matter might be contested for the common welfare.

To this a reply was given.

We, however, when we learned their report, took care to communicate it to your charity, so that you too, for the sake of our common charity and the faith owed to the Lord, might cause God’s mercy to be entreated without ceasing, so that the Lord of all things, if it can in any way be done, may mercifully grant concord and unity to his Church.

May God always guard you, most loving brother and father. Be mindful of us in all things.

### LVI

#### To an abbot

To that dearest father and lord, that abbot, from that humble man, not yet a monk: a greeting imploring eternal happiness [Col. 1458A].

The fact that until now I have written very little to your fatherhood and have not made clear what was happening around me was caused by difficulties, not by unwillingness. If opportunity allowed, I would wish very frequently to converse with you, even though this would require enduring the difficulty of the long journey.

I deeply regret that, when your monk whom you sent to that bishop was here, I was unable either to speak with him or to ask him for the desirable news of your health and prosperity. You know that after the death of our venerable lord and father, that abbot of blessed and good memory, I was entirely unable to send anything to you as I wished, so that you might deign rightly and piously to remember him in your sacred prayers.

Therefore, although late, I now send three pounds of silver to your benevolence, so that, after receiving them, you may prepare a meal for the brothers as you are able, and I humbly ask you to make up from your own resources whatever is lacking from ours.

Just as he himself trusted, and as we place the greatest confidence, deign to exhort and ask the brothers on his behalf and ours to remember him frequently.

That noble vassal of his, who was dearer to him than the others, also sends you many greetings and, together with me, asks you—although you do not know him, you will nevertheless come to know him, and he has always been devoted to you—to deign likewise to remember him.

As for me, that man, I am ready to serve you obediently, respectfully, and amicably in those things that are found more abundantly among us, provided that the powerful abbot does not forget the poor [Col. 1458C]. You possess among yourselves and in your region those things suited to divine worship, from which you can provide us consolation, so that, clothed in sacred linens, when—although unworthy—we approach the holy altar, we may remember you, just as you remember us, and devote ourselves more earnestly to prayer, imploring the Lord’s mercy for your health.

There is also another matter of great importance: if you take pains to grant our smallness what you were gracious enough to promise, you will thereby acquire for yourselves a great and eternal reward from God—namely, that you send us copies of the books of that lord, which he composed on the Heptateuch and on the deeds of the Maccabees. And if there are any books among us that you need, we shall likewise send you copies of them most devotedly, if you wish.

May almighty God preserve you safely, praying for us, and happily preserve you for yourselves.

### LVII

#### Letter to an abbot.

Most Reverend lord and distinguished father, that unworthy last of all God’s servants and your former fosterling, I wish you greetings in the rosy blood of Christ. May it please your kindness to remember my request of long ago, which I showed you most fully not only with my mouth but from my heart, indeed with my very body prostrate before you. For what I then did in your presence, I now repeat once more—absent in body but present in spirit—through that intermediary of mine, humbly and in every way, so that you may deign to agree to me, if this wish of mine can be fulfilled through you or not.

But know that in many places I have been urged even by the archimandrites themselves [Note: [Col. 1459D] This should probably be corrected to *suasus sum*, “I have been urged.”], so that, abandoning the world, I might at least live among them naked in the monastic way. But I have so far given my consent to none of them, nor shall I do so, if the Lord grants me health, until I am refreshed by your reply—or, which God forbid, cast down.

For I greatly thirst to hear something coming from you, since, as it is written, I am wounded by your love and therefore languish from love [Note: [Col. 1459D] Song of Songs, chapter II, § 5; chapter IV, § 9]. Mary, formerly a sinner, humbly approached the feet of Jesus, bathed them with her tears, wiped them with her hair, and kissed his feet; for this she deserved to hear the Lord say: “Her many sins are forgiven, because she loved much” [Note: [Col. 1459D] Gospel according to Luke, chapter VII, verse 47].

Therefore, in this matter I must follow her example rather than that of the Pharisee who arrogantly reproved the very fountain of mercy, the Lord, saying: “If this man were a prophet, he would certainly know what sort of woman this is who touches him, for she is a sinner” [Note: [Col. 1459D] Ibid., chapter VII, verse 39].

For you, who have cast off this world and have been made worthy to anoint the Lord’s head with fragrant nard, must fittingly consider that the Lord’s saying should be preserved by you: “Be merciful, therefore, just as your Father also is merciful” [Note: [Col. 1459D] Ibid., chapter VI, verse 36], who makes his sun rise upon the good and the evil and rains upon the just and the unjust [Note: [Col. 1459D] Gospel according to Matthew, chapter V, verse 45].

But you, who shine like God’s stars, illuminating the earth, as the Lord says, “You are the light of the world” [Note: [Col. 1459D] Ibid., chapter V, verse 14], consider that lights shine not only on mountains and fields, in woods and pleasant meadows, but also in marshes and sewers.

The Apostle too, stooping down to and sharing compassionately in the lower members of Christ, says: “In a rich man’s house there are vessels not only of gold and silver, but also of wood and earthenware; one vessel indeed for honor, another for dishonor” [Note: [Col. 1459D] Second Epistle of Blessed Paul to Timothy, chapter II, verse 20].

He also urges us elsewhere to be grafted into a good olive tree [Note: [Col. 1460D] Epistle of Blessed Paul to the Romans, chapter XI, verses 17 and 20]; and since I am a useless wild olive, I therefore desire to be grafted into a good olive tree.

Leaving aside all the other fruit-bearing trees, I shall speak to you of the elm and the willow, because although they themselves bear no fruit, they nevertheless bear fruit together with the vine.

But since you say that a multitude cannot be sustained by poverty [Col. 1459D], I trust in God that, if I am received by you at his prompting, I shall not be unbearable to you or too great a burden. For I do not recoil from the poverty or calamity of the world [Col. 1460A], but I shall strive to flee from it and truly seek God, as the Lord Christ says: “Ask and you shall receive, seek and you shall find, knock and it shall be opened to you; for everyone who asks receives, and whoever seeks finds, and to the one who knocks it shall be opened” [Note: [Col. 1460D] Gospel according to Matthew, chapter VII, verses 7 and 8]. And he will not give it to him merely because he is his friend; yet because of his persistence he will rise and give him whatever he needs [Note: [Col. 1460D] Gospel according to Luke, chapter XI, verse 8].

I greatly desire in this matter to imitate the prophet who says: “From the ends of the earth I cried out to you, Lord, when my heart was in distress” [Note: [Col. 1460D] Psalm LX, verse 3].

May he deign to guard your kindness, which comes to the aid of the world and of me, the least of all, to the very hem of divine mercy.

## LVIII

### A Short Letter to a Faithful Friend

[Col. 1460B]

To that most reverend and dearest lord—or, rather, one to be embraced by all orthodox people—distinguished by manifold knowledge and by the grace of various virtues, who in all things discerningly and most vigilantly distinguishes what is necessary and useful for souls: I, that insignificant newcomer, send the sincerest greeting in the Lord God eternal to my own prelate.

Come now, my dearest brother. I desire to fill you with the banquets of wisdom, so that the heavenly cultivator may prune you, a branch of the chosen vine, once you have been watered by the rains of the divine fountain; and may we be received together into one and the same delight of paradise, so that in the freedom of the heavenly kingdom we may rejoice with the saints in eternal blessedness [Col. 1460C], where no corruption that might threaten true blessedness exists, and so that through the love alone of Christ Jesus we may be able to arrive there.

Above all, we must strive toward this love, so that after this world we may reign with Christ without end in eternal blessedness. Therefore I beg you firmly and without doubt to hold to the words of this letter, for the person who is fickle and unbelieving is like the waves of the sea and like a reed shaken by every wind [Note: [Col. 1460D] Epistle of Saint James, I, verse 6; Gospel according to Matthew, chapter XI, verse 7].

For this reason I advise you: even if we are divided and separated by the distance of the earth and parted by a barrier [Note: [Col. 1460D] Perhaps this passage should be corrected by reading *intervallo*, “by an interval”], and even if we are divided by the unequal climate of the sky, we are nevertheless oppressed by the same torch of tribulations.

Therefore I earnestly beg you that we may continually fortify one another by an exchange of prayers, remembering the Lord’s saying, which he spoke according to its meaning: “And I say to you: even three upon earth, concerning whatever matter they may ask, let it be done for them by the Father” [Note: [Col. 1460D] Gospel according to John, chapter XVI, verse 23], and so forth.

May your desires prosper in Christ, whose heavenly wisdom I embrace sufficiently. I, the undersigned, have taken care to convey to you material from the *agia crafa* (“holy writings”) and from distinguished Catholic men and religious matters. We warmly greet you and have sent you some little examples through the bearer.

## LIX

### A Short Letter from an Abbess to an Abbot

To that lord, a servant of God, the abbot whom we love greatly and with the utmost reverence: I, the least of all Christ’s women servants, together with all the sisters in Christ who are your servants, and wishing you well in everything, venture to send your kindness a most loving and gentle greeting in the Lord, unto everlasting joy.

Know, dearest ones, that during these holy days the whole congregation sings the Psalter every day for your life and stability, asking that the Lord may deign to preserve it for many years, and for your consolation.

And we have directed this to your people in great confidence. We humbly beg you to order that we be consoled with some amount from this, so that I may have something from you for that holy person, because from this we shall have great need.

May we, most loving and sweetest lord and father, deserve for many years to rejoice in your prosperity and happiness.

## LX

### A Short Letter to an Abbot or Bishop

To that lord abbot or bishop, conspicuously adorned with the title of the summit of religion, I, your servant in every respect, your own servant, together with all your servants in Christ, venture to send your kindness a most devout greeting in the Lord, unto everlasting joy.

Know, most pious father, what need we have. For this reason we humbly beg you to order that we be consoled in this need, because it is necessary for us.

Most benevolent lord, act in such a way that an everlasting reward and prayer may remain for you.

## LXI

### Another Short Letter

To that abbot conspicuously adorned with the title of the summit of religion, I, your last native woman-servant [Note: [Col. 1461D] Correct to *vernacula*, “native woman-servant”], venture to send you a most loving and gentle greeting in the Lord, unto everlasting joy.

I humbly beg you to order that you remember me, infirm as I am, in your holy prayers, because I, although indebted and fragile, attend upon you in prayer.

Know, most pious lords, in how great poverty and want I have remained after the death of my elders, who caused me to come to this monastery.

Therefore I venture to send the little petition of my insignificance to your clemency. I humbly beg you to deign to console me, so that I may provide lamps for the souls of those who received me into this monastery, or whatever the Lord may inspire and command, because I lack everything necessary.

From you, sweetest lord and father, I hope for all help and consolation before God and that holy person.

## LXII

[Col. 1462A]

[Without a rubric.]

To that memorable and excellent man, most gentle, filled with peaceful goodness, as well as with honesty and dignity of conduct, and with every meekness, and with an insatiable service of Christ: I, who by no comparison with your goodness, though flourishing in youthful age, nevertheless remain your faithful and well-devoted servant forever, send a desirable and enduring greeting in the Lord.

The letter expressing your reverence and dignity reached me, lowly as I am. I read it through with all my effort, wishing to lock it away in the depths of my heart; by repeating it again and again, I stored it in a small chamber of my memory, because it carried the sweetness of honey into my throat. Supported by masterly composition [Col. 1462B], it strengthened the mind of my insignificance with the most pious admonition and built up my youth by the example of old age.

Therefore let your most sagacious prudence know that I am beset by no small anxiety, because I cannot find with what words I might respond to that sweetness, nor how I might fulfill my pledge in fitting language, except that I may embrace your shadowy kindness with the humblest praise and most honorably and suitably place an end upon my little work, so that through the favor of your fatherhood it may be granted useful and irreproachable.

For the rest, your kindness knows that at present I am clothed in the basest garments and use no parchment, unless your excellence comes to my aid with its customary support and, from its most generous hand, supplies at a fitting time and allows me to enjoy those things in which I appear needy and poor [Col. 1462C].

And, so to speak, our Lord despises my youth and refuses to chastise it; moreover, he abhors my ways and rejects me as some kind of filth, and delays extending himself as a helper to me as I fall. Yet he now wishes to see in me the highest steps of dignity; thus he casts away my foolish thoughts for a long while, asks of me what I do not have, and what he desires has not yet come to pass.

Before God grants me this, and before, instructed by the examples of others, I become a perfect and peaceable man, I therefore earnestly beg you to come here as quickly as possible and let your most serene face appear. It had already seemed terrible and hateful to me; but now, with the old law destroyed and all things forgotten, it judges as dear and serene [Col. 1462D].

And know this for certain: placing my greatest confidence in you, I have chosen you as judge of all these matters, and I strive to be confirmed before the Lord by your most learned judgment.

The High-Throned One, who reigns before the heavens’ heights,

May he give you rest and grant you everlasting life.

And may he cause you to climb the great threshold of Olympus,

Then drive far away the livid and deadly realms of Tartarus.

For a great reward shall remain in store for you,

Since you have deserved a great one in the olive fields.

For, always practicing what is right, you shall be called innocent.

Almighty God, grant to your unworthy servant

What I ask, you who indeed are the creator of the world:

Grant that saving health may be increased for the aforesaid man,

Nor may an unjust illness touch him, with Christ as guide;

[Col. 1463A]

And while this fleeting life remains, while breath is drawn,

Grant an eternal dwelling, you who reign everywhere.

## LXIII

The editor has gathered under this number and the following ones a certain number of incomplete formulas, in which one finds only models of opening or closing phrases.

### A Short Letter to a King

To that most excellent and supremely excellent illustrious lord, the king of the race of the Franks, to whom the Lord has extended the care of government, I, your servant and subject of all your faithful people, beg your clemency as though I were lying at your feet.

When this little letter reaches you, whatever matters of need it makes known to you [Col. 1463B], may you deign to hear it with a kindly disposition and report your answer to us according to your mercy.

May Almighty God, the King of all kings, make your kingdom unchanging and establish the stability of your kingdom for the salvation and prosperity of all your faithful, and may it be so.

## LXIV

### A Short Letter to a Queen

To that most glorious and most excellent lady, that daughter, queen, I, that servant of the servants of God.

Since the royal solicitude of your excellence must, in praiseworthy governance, devote itself vigilantly and display prudent foresight for the increase of its glory, so that it may not permit those whom it rules outwardly by counsel to perish inwardly, you may, after the heights of this temporal kingdom which you administer [Col. 1463C], with God as author, reach eternal and everlasting joys, O queen . . .

## LXV

### A Short Letter to an Abbot

To that venerable and honorable lord abbot, that one called a gift of God, I send eternal greetings in the Lord.

Our humility begs your holiness not to disdain sending us, through this present envoy of ours, that thing called [such-and-such], namely for the matter to be carried out; and when it has been completed, we shall immediately hasten back safely to you.

[Col. 1463D]

Fare well always in the Lord.

## LXVI

[Col. 1464A]

[Without a rubric.]

To that abbot beloved by us above all other spiritual fathers, I, the last of the servants of servants and your faithful one in every respect in the Lord.

Therefore, lord and most blessed father, I, although an unworthy sinful monk, your own faithful servant and mi[ni]ster, send greetings in the Lord.

For the rest, we ask . . . [lacuna]

## LXVII

### Another

To that lord of mine, venerable through Christ and through his merits, I, that one, as though an unworthy sinner and the least of all your servants, presume to send you a loving greeting in the Lord.

I beg the inseparable Trinity to preserve you everywhere.

For the rest, we ask [lacuna]

Fare well in the Lord, man of virtues, ornament of your friends, everywhere rejoicing, instructed in Jesus, the redeemer of all.

## LXVIII

[Without a rubric.]

To that beloved brother of ours, most dear to me, the provost of that holy congregation and monastery, I, your last little dependent and servant, presume to send you a loving greeting in our Lord Jesus Christ.

And I beg that your love, friendship, or command may remain over me, as you began and have always acted, so that henceforth your good affection and love may endure.

And insofar as there is sense or understanding, with God’s help I shall always be united with you in heart and mind, sharing in your will.

Again and again we greet you unto joy.

## LXIX

### A Short Letter from Brother to Brother

To that beloved and very dear brother in Christ, I, the insignificant one, send eternal greetings in the Lord.

For the rest, we ask your diligence that, when this letter reaches the presence of your charity, you may not disdain to send us that matter.

Fare well, safe and unharmed, through many courses of years.

[Col. 1465]

To make the manuscript better known and to enable the reader to restore its arrangement, I present here a table in which one will find the order number and rubric of each formula, the place where those that were already known are printed, and the position occupied by the unpublished ones in my edition.
